# Introductio in Theologiam


## 1 On the Name and Distinctions of Theology

Theology, so called as if it were ὁ περὶ τῶν Θεῶν λόγος, by the force of the word, is reason or discourse about God; but by the usage of speech it is a certain knowledge of God and divine things, or certainly a habit analogous to knowledge.

I. Theology is an abstract noun, derived from the concrete θεολόγος. The word λόγος, however, which constitutes the other part of the concrete, is absolute outside of composition, signifying by the mode of standing by itself, as the Dialecticians say, and denotes both reason, the dictate of reason, a concept of the mind; and speech or dissertation; but when placed after in composition it is connotative, and signifies λόγον, that is, reason, or the concept and cognition of reason, or speech as adjacent to another, and by the force of the etymology θεολόγος is he in whom ὁ λόγος περὶ τῶν Θεῶν, that is, some reason about God or some cognition of God exists, or who has a discourse about God or discourses concerning Him. But by the usage of speech, λόγος, in composition, does not signify any λόγος whatsoever, but a habitual λόγος, as adjacent to another, and θεολόγος is he in whom λόγος περὶ τῶν θεῶν exists by way of a habit, or who is instructed with the habit of knowing God and of discoursing about Him. Indeed, not all those in whom some habit of knowing God and discoursing about Him exists are, by received usage, called θεολόγοι: for there are found among peoples not entirely barbarous, and especially among simpler Christians, males and females who possess some habitual knowledge of God, and can in some way speak or discourse about Him, whom nevertheless no one calls theologians; but he at last is and is called θεολόγος, to whom λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ is present by way of a scientific habit, and who is able, as is usually done in the sciences, to discourse about God and divine things, that is, to explain terms and the things signified by them, to deduce conclusions from their principles, to confirm them, and to vindicate and defend them from the objections of those who dissent. Just as in other cases abstract and concrete, absolute and connotative terms signify one form, and abstract and absolute terms signify it according to itself, without connoting the subject in which it resides; but concrete and connotative terms signify it as adjacent to another, and with the connoted subject: so Theology signifies that very habit of knowing God and discoursing about Him, from which the theologian is named, that is to say, a scientific habit concerning God and divine things, or at least one analogous to science.

II. I say: analogous to science; on account of Revealed Theology, which, because it relies on a mode of assent that is non-evident and obscure, namely the revelation of primary truth, does not seem to be science properly and in the strict sense: yet it is occupied with its object by way of science, namely by explaining terms, deducing conclusions from its principles, confirming premises, and responding to the objections of adversaries, and thus it performs the very same thing regarding its object that sciences properly so-called perform regarding their objects; which therefore, if not properly science, is nevertheless a habit analogous to science.

III. In the Scriptures the abstract form never occurs. The concrete form θεολόγος, however, is attributed to John the Apostle in the inscription of the Apocalypse. Among the Gentiles, however, both terms were received into frequent use, and priests, poets, and philosophers were called θεολόγοι, because they were instructed in the habit of discoursing about the gods, their origin and their worship, and were accustomed to discourse about them in bound or unbound speech; and θεολογία was the very habit of discoursing about them with which they were instructed, although, as will be said shortly, quite improperly and abusively. From them these terms were later transferred to Christians.

IV. The Latins, having retained the same meaning, bestowed both names upon their own language.

Latin:

THeologia, quasi ὁ περὶ τῶν Θεῶν λόγος dicta, vi vocis, est ratio vel oratio de Deo; ex usu loquendi autem est quædam de Deo divinisque rebus scientia, vel certè habitus, scientiæ analogus.

I. Theologia nomen abstractum est, à concreto θεολόγος deductum. Vox λόγος autem, quæ alteram concreti partem constituit, extra compositionem, absoluta est, significans per modum per se stantis, ut Dialectici loquuntur, denotatque & rationem, dictamen rationis, conceptum animi; & orationem vel dissertationem; sed in compositione postposita connotativa est, & significat λόγον, h. e. rationem, aut rationis conceptum & cognitionem, vel orationem ut alteri adjacentem, estque vi etymi θεολόγος is, cui ὁ λόγος περὶ τῶν Θεῶν h. e. aliqua ratio de Deo aut aliqua cognitio Dei inest, vel qui de Deo sermonem habet aut de eo disserit. Ex usu loquendi autem λόγος, in compositione, non significat quemcunque λόγον, sed λόγον habitualem, ut alteri adjacentem, estque θεολόγος, cui λόγος περὶ τῶν θεῶν per modum habitus inest, sive qui habitu cognoscendi Deum, deque eo disserendi instructus est. Quin nec omnes, quibus aliquis Deum cognoscendi deque eo disserendi habitus inest, ex usu recepto, θεολόγοι dicuntur: Inveniuntur enim inter populos non planè barbaros, maximè autem inter Christianos simpliciores, masculi ac fœmellæ, qui aliqua habituali Dei cognitione pollent, deque eo utcunque loqui aut disserere possunt, quos tamen Theologos nemo dicit; sed is demum est & dicitur θεολόγος, cui λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ inest per modum habitus scientifici, & qui ita, ut in scientiis fieri solet, de Deo rebusque divinis disserere, hoc est, terminos & res iis significatas explicare, conclusiones ex suis principiis deducere, confirmare, & ab objectionibus dissentientium vindicare ac defendere potest. Quemadmodum autem alias abstracta & concreta, absoluta & connotativa, unam formam significant, & abstracta quidem ac absoluta eam significant secundum se, subjecto, cui inest, non connotato; concreta autem & connotativa ut adjacentem alteri, & cum connotato subjecto: ita Theologia significat illum ipsum habitum cognoscendi Deum, deque eo disserendi, a quo ὁ θεολόγος denominatur, puta habitum scientificum de Deo rebusque divinis, vel saltem scientiæ analogum.

II. Dico: scientiæ analogum; propter Theologiam Revelatam, quæ quia nititur ratione assentiendi inevidente & obscurâ, revelatione scilicet veritatis primæ, scientia quidem propriè & in rigore non esse videtur: versatur tamen circa suum objectum per modum scientiæ, explicando scilicet terminos, conclusiones ex suis principiis deducendo, præmissas confirmando, ad objectiones adversariorum respondendo, atque adeò id ipsum præstat circa suum objectum, quod scientiæ propriè dictæ præstant circa sua objecta; quæ proinde, si non propriè scientia, habitus tamen scientiæ analogus est.

III. In Scripturis abstractum nusquam occurrit. Concretum verò θεολόγος tribuitur Johanni Apostolo in inscriptione Apocalypsis. Apud Gentiles autem vox utraque usu frequenti recepta fuit, & dicti sunt θεολόγοι Sacerdotes, Poëtæ & Philosophi, quod habitu de diis, illorumque ortu & cultu disserendi instructi essent, deque illis ligatâ aut solutâ oratione disserere solerent; θεολογία autem ipse, quo instructi erant, habitus de illis disserendi, quanquam, ut mox dicetur, admodum impropriè & abusivè. Ab his postea ad Christianos translatæ sunt.

IV. Nomen utrumque Latini, retento significatu eodem, suâ civitate donârunt.


### II. Just as the names of the sciences are otherwise transferred also to the…

II.

Just as the names of the sciences are otherwise transferred also to the doctrine by which they propose and explain their object to others, so too the name of Theology is often accepted for the doctrine in which the habit of Theology is occupied in delivering and explaining.

This meaning seems to be metonymical, by which the name of the cause is transferred to signify the caused. For the doctrine concerning God and divine things proceeds from the habit of Theology, and is its effect. For those who deliver the doctrine concerning God to others do so by the aid of Theological science, which concurs with the intellect toward it by way of an efficient cause.

III.

However, not every habit occupied in the knowledge of God and divine things is properly Theology, but only that which is conformable to its object, and by which we deliver true things concerning it.

I. Just as, according to Aristotle in Nicomachean Ethics VI, chapter III, it is common to all habits of the mind which are indeed numbered among the virtues to τὸ ἀληθεύειν, that is, to enunciate the truth about their object by affirming or denying, so too it is for Theology; which deserves a place all the more superior among the intellectual virtues the more noble its object is: which consequently, unless it delivers true things concerning God and divine things, does not even deserve the name of Theology, except improperly and abusively.

II. Therefore, the three kinds of Theology of the Gentiles, mythical or Fabulous, physical or Natural, and political or Civil, which Augustine commemorates from Scaevola and Varro in The City of God, book IV, chapter XXVII and book VI, chapter V, do not equally properly claim the name of Theology for themselves. For the first and third kinds claim it for themselves quite equivocally. For the former embraces the most mendacious fables of the poets concerning the gods and their origin and worship (whence it also obtained its name), and the latter embraces the impious and superstitious commentaries concerning the same introduced into cities. But the second kind, received in the schools of the philosophers, by which one supreme God, by the guidance of the light of nature, from created things is known, in itself indeed and in so far as it relies upon the principles of nature, is conformable to its object, and delivers true things concerning God and divine matters: but as it was accustomed to be delivered by Heathen Philosophers, it has not a few false things mixed with the true. For Heathen Philosophers, although otherwise learned men and studious of the truth, were often deceived in their διαλογισμοῖς, and wandered far from the true knowledge of God. Which, however, is to be ascribed to the fault of men, through the corruption of nature and the innate blindness of the mind not penetrating as far as they ought into the knowledge of God, not to Natural Theology itself. Which therefore, viewed in itself and by itself, is simply [Theology]; but as it is actually delivered by Heathen Philosophers, it is [Theology] in a qualified sense, and only in that part in which it enunciates true things concerning God, does it deserve the name of Theology.

Latin:

II.

QUemadmodum autem alias nomina scientiarum transferuntur etiam ad doctrinam, quâ aliis suum objectum proponunt & explicant, ita & Theologiæ nomen accipitur sæpè pro doctrina, in qua tradenda & explicanda Theologiæ habitus occupatur.

Significatio hæc videtur esse metonymica, quâ nomen causæ transfertur ad significandum causatum. Doctrina enim de Deo rebusque divinis provenit ab habitu Theologiæ, estque ejus effectus. Qui enim doctrinam de Deo aliis tradunt, faciunt id adminiculo scientiæ Theologicæ, quæ cum intellectu per modum causæ efficientis ad eam concurrit.

III.

NOn autem quilibet in Dei rerumq; divinarum cognitione occupatus habitus propriè Theologia est, sed is demum, qui objecto conformis est, & quo vera de eo tradimust.

I. Quemadmodum, teste Aristotele VI. Nic. c. III. omnibus mentis habitibus, qui quidem in virtutibus numerantur, commune est τὸ ἀληθεύειν, h. e. ut verum de objecto suo enuncient affirmando aut negando, ita & Theologiæ; quæ in virtutibus intellectus eò potiorem meretur locum, quò nobilius ejus objectum est: quæ proinde nisi vera tradat de Deo rebusque divinis, ne nomen quidem Theologiæ meretur, nisi impropriè & abusivè.

II. Gentilium igitur tria Theologiæ genera, μυθικὸν sive Fabulosum, Φυσικὸν seu Naturale, & πολιτικὸν sive Civile, quæ ex Scævola & Varrone Augustinus lib. IV. de C. D. c. XXVII. & lib. VI. c. V. commemorat, non æquè propriè Theologiæ nomen sibi vendicant. Primum enim & tertium genus vendicant id sibi planè æquivocè. Illud enim Poëtarum mendacissimas de Diis illorumque ortu & cultu fabulas, (unde & nomen fortitum est) hoc introducta in civitates impia & superstitiosa de iisdem commenta complectitur. Secundum verò, in Philosophorum scholis receptum, genus, quo unus summus Deus, ductu luminis naturæ, ex rebus creatis cognoscitur, per se quidem & in quantum naturæ principiis nititur, conforme est objecto, & vera de Deo rebusque divinis tradit: prout autem à Philosophis Ethnicis tradi consuevit, falsa non pauca veris admixta habet. Ethnici enim Philosophi, etsi alioqui Viri docti & veritatis studiosi, in suis διαλογισμοῖς sæpè decepti funt, & à vera Dei cognitione longè aberrârunt. Quod tamen, vitio hominum, per naturæ corruptionem & connatam mentis cæcitatem non eo usque, quò debebant, in cognitione Dei penetrantium, adscribendum est, non ipsi Theologiæ Naturali. Quæ proinde, in se & per se spectata, simpliciter; prout verò actu à Philosophis Ethnicis tradita est, secundum quid, & eâ tantùm parte, quâ vera de Deo enunciat, Theologiæ nomen meretur.


### IV. The Theology which enunciates true things concerning God and divine matters is…

IV.

The Theology which enunciates true things concerning God and divine matters is distinguished into Archetypal and Ectypal.

V.

That is called Archetypal, which resides in God primarily and independently, and is the exemplar of the Theology communicated to other intelligent creatures.

VI.

That is called Ectypal, which has been communicated to intelligent creatures by God for the imitation of His own Theology, as an exemplary cause.

I. Those who use this distinction do not look so much to the usage of speech as to the etymology and force of the word Theology. For by the usage of speech, only Ectypal Theology—and not even all of this, but only that which belongs to men who are Wayfarers—claims this name for itself. Archetypal, however, is accustomed to be called not so much Theology as the knowledge of God.

II. The very names of these, both Archetypal and Ectypal Theology, suggest these descriptions. An archetype is properly the original exemplar of an effect produced in imitation of itself, and by the force of the word it imports two things: One, an exemplar or form which some effect imitates by the intention of the agent. The other, the denial of dependence upon another exemplary cause; so that Archetypal Theology, by the force of the words, is a Theology which is so an exemplary cause of some other Theology, that it does not itself depend upon another, as if from an exemplary cause. Such a Theology, because besides the Theology of God none is given, Archetypal Theology is not inappropriately described as the Theology which resides in God primarily and independently; and is the exemplary cause of another Theology, communicated to intelligent creatures. Conversely, Ectypal can be described as the Theology communicated by God to intelligent creatures in imitation of His own Theology. For an Ectype is the correlate of an Archetype, and is properly a certain effect produced in imitation of another, as if from an exemplary cause: of which kind is all Theology that is found in intelligent creatures, angels and men; although it is not our purpose now to treat of the Theology of angels.

III. Archetypal Theology is commonly said to be that by which God knows Himself. Some add, by which He knows Himself and all things outside Himself through Himself, with no difference in meaning, except that in the latter is expressed what is implicitly contained in the former. For God, by knowing Himself, knows at the same time in Himself and through Himself all things that are outside Him, and thus in the knowledge of God, by which He knows Himself, is contained also the knowledge of all things that are outside Him. Both, however, are a description of Archetypal Theology, taken materially for the Theology which is the exemplar of another Theology, not formally, insofar as it is the exemplar of another. For the knowledge by which God knows Himself is speculative. Archetypal Theology, however, viewed formally and insofar as it is the exemplar of another Theology, besides that speculative knowledge, imports also a practical act of the intellect, by which God conceives the knowledge of Himself as the form of another Theology to be communicated to intelligent creatures, and therefore Archetypal Theology formally is not simply the knowledge which God has of Himself, but the knowledge which He has of Himself, conceived as the form of another Theology to be communicated to intelligent creatures.

IV. The aforementioned distinction, although most accepted in usage, is rejected by Reinerus Vogelsangius, in Exerc. Theol. I. page 3, as superfluous and of laborious subtlety: which John Owen, an English writer, preceded in his Tractate on Natural Theology, book 1, chapter 1, page 11, where he says that he strongly doubts whether they themselves, who use these terms, understand what they wish to be understood by Archetypal Theology. They object, however, against it,

(I) that if it should prevail, no reason can be given why it should not be applied in all other disciplines as well. Although it is by far most certain that God is equally the ocean, the fountain, and the inexhaustible source of all wisdom whatsoever; yet no one, even a splitter of cumin seeds, has hitherto been found who has foisted upon us Logic, Ontology, Arithmetic, Physics, Astrology, and Pneumatics, each as a twin science, Archetypal and Ectypal.

(II) that it would be necessary for Archetypal Theology to express itself in Ectypal; but Divine Theology, by which God infinitely knows his infinite self, cannot be expressed in any creature.

(III) that Archetypal Theology cannot be understood otherwise than with a certain predefinition, by which God, from the immense bosom of his wisdom, determined our Theology from all eternity within himself, and therefore if the distinction ought to be admitted, Archetypal Theology would have to be defined by an exemplar predefined from eternity in the divine mind of that Theology which it pleased God to communicate to rational creatures at a predetermined time. Vogelsang urges all three reasons; Owen, however, the latter two.

V. Concerning the concept and description of Archetypal Theology, we have already declared our mind in no. III above. Regarding the description provided by Vogelsang, however, we advise that it is stated ambiguously that Archetypal Theology is an exemplar predefined from eternity, etc. For it is understood either of Archetypal Theology, taken materially, that the very form, to the imitation of which the Theology communicated to us is made, is predefined in the divine mind from eternity, and is posterior to God's predefinition or decree in our mode of understanding; or it is understood of the same taken formally, that in so far as it is a certain form of another Theology to be communicated to men, it is an exemplar predefined in the mind of God from eternity. In the former sense, the assertion is not true, except concerning that part, if I may so speak, of Archetypal Theology which concerns things outside of God, decreed or made for our good, of which kind the ways are the blessedness to be imparted or restored to man, and the means of attaining it, and what is annexed to these and other things pertaining thereto, which as they depend upon the free will of God, so without doubt they have their ideas in the divine mind, predetermined by His free will, which in Archetypal Theology, if it be permitted to speak in our mode of understanding, come into a part, and make a certain part of it, constituted in an exemplar predetermined from eternity in the mind of God. But in the other part, by which God intuitively knows Himself and all His perfections, Archetypal Theology, viewed materially in itself, is not a certain exemplar in the divine mind, predetermined by the free will of God, but His very natural knowledge, by which He necessarily and before every act of will or predetermination knows Himself and all His perfections from eternity. But in the latter sense the assertion is indeed simply true: for just as every exemplar on the part of the efficient cause implies practical knowledge, by which it is conceived as the form of another effect to be produced, so also Archetypal Theology, besides that knowledge by which God knows Himself, implies also in the divine intellect a practical act, by which He knows the same as the form of Theology to be communicated with others, and this, in our mode of understanding, is subsequent to the divine decree concerning the Theology to be communicated with us: in view of which Archetypal Theology altogether has the nature of an exemplar, predetermined in the mind of God. But these things do not at all hinder the opinion of those who say that Archetypal Theology is that by which God knows Himself. For they, as was said above, consider it materially, not formally, that is, they consider and describe the Theology which is Archetypal and the exemplar of our Theology, not insofar as it is Archetypal and the exemplar of that.

VI. And hence it is clear what must be answered to the last objection of Vogelsang, to begin from this: namely, that God from the immense bosom of His wisdom determined our Theology in Himself from all eternity, is most true. From that, however, it does not follow that the Theology of God is not the exemplar of our Theology. For God could have [determined] our Theology from the immense bosom of His wisdom; much to the imitation of His Theology, to determine in Himself from all eternity. And what idea will be given in the divine mind, to the imitation of which God determined in Himself from all eternity, to be communicated with us in time, our Theology in that part in which it contains the knowledge of Himself and His perfections, besides that knowledge by which He knows Himself, conceived by a practical act as the form of the Theology to be communicated with us in time? What idea will be given, to the imitation of which He determined the same in Himself from all eternity for the other parts, which are concerning our blessedness and the causes and means of obtaining it, besides His knowledge which He had of them in His mind from eternity, conceived by a practical act as the form of the knowledge of the same to be communicated with us in time? But what else is this knowledge of God than the Theology of God, by which He knows Himself and other things outside Himself pertaining to our Theology from all eternity? The same, conceived by a practical act of the divine intellect as the form of another Theology to be communicated with us, what else is it than Archetypal Theology?

VII. Nor is there more strength in the remaining two objections. And the second indeed, that we may proceed in the order in which we began, namely that divine Theology, by which God infinitely knows Himself as infinite, cannot be expressed in any creature; assumes as certain that it is required for an exemplar that whatever of perfection is in it must be expressed in the exemplatum (if one may speak so), which is false. For what? Did not God in the creation of man, saying, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, Gen. 1:26, constitute Himself the exemplar of producing man? For the words, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, cannot have any other meaning than this: Let us make man to the imitation of us, as an exemplar cause, that he may bear an image of us as similar as possible. In whatever, however, the reason of the image may be constituted, to the imitation of God as an exemplar cause expressed in man, this is certain, that it does not in the least reach to the very perfection of the exemplar, namely God. For in God nothing is, which is not infinite; in man, however, there is nothing which is not finite. Which Vogelsang also acknowledges below in Exercit. XIX. th. XXII.: We properly call an image, he says, either the exemplar according to which something is expressed by some kind of imitation, or a likeness expressed according to the exemplar. — But those things which can be viewed in man as representations of divine perfections must be understood as entirely shadowy: and thus as distant, and even more so, from them, as the fluid image of a man, which is perhaps reflected to our eyes in a mirror, differs from the man. And a little later he says that Scripture explains the image and likeness of God as being dedicated primarily in the rectitude of the intellect and will, and consequently of all faculties. But was that rectitude of the intellect and will and of all faculties in man not a certain Ectypal wisdom and holiness, expressed in the soul of man in imitation of the Archetypal wisdom and holiness which is in God? Yet the Ectypal wisdom and holiness in the first man was not infinite, just as the Archetypal wisdom and holiness in God is.

IIX. But the first objection, that, while the distinction of Theology into Archetypal and Ectypal stands, no reason can be given why it should not likewise be applied in all other disciplines, is of no weight. For although it is most certain that God is equally the ocean, the fountain, and the inexhaustible source of all wisdom whatsoever: which the Author urges; yet it is wrongly inferred from this that, if God, the ocean and fountain of all wisdom whatsoever, is not the exemplar of all other disciplines, so that they can each be constituted as it were twofold, Archetypal and Ectypal, then God, the ocean and fountain of all wisdom whatsoever, is not the exemplar of our Theology either, and therefore Theology also cannot be constituted as it were twofold, Archetypal and Ectypal. For the reason for the diversity is manifest. For because all other disciplines are occupied with things which of themselves fall under our cognition, no reason appears why we should establish that their sciences are communicated to us by God in imitation of His wisdom as an exemplar cause: since the things themselves, about which they are occupied, are of themselves apt to terminate the true cognition of themselves in our intellect, and, with our labor, study, and meditation added, the sciences to generate in it those conformable to itself. But the matter stands otherwise with our Theology. For God and his infinite perfections, in the knowledge of which it is chiefly occupied, do not of themselves fall under our cognition. For God is a spiritual essence, and all his perfections are most simply one with him; our intellect, however, left to itself, depends on the senses in knowing, and cannot ascend to know God and his perfections, unless he himself manifests himself to it through proportionate means, and thus communicates to us a certain knowledge of himself. He has indeed communicated it from the time the world was created with men, not by chance or fortune, but, according to his immense wisdom and goodness, in imitation and likeness of his own knowledge, which he himself has of himself, either through notions implanted in their minds, and certain traces of his perfections impressed upon created things, or through supernatural revelation, or finally through the light of glory infused into the intellect, as will be shown later in the special declaration of Ectypal Theology.

But if anyone should object that God, in his immense wisdom, made created things also in imitation of his knowledge which he had of them, and consequently also communicated to us the knowledge of them in imitation of his knowledge which he had of them; and yet that a twofold science of created things is not therefore established, Archetypal in God, and Ectypal in us; we answer that this is indeed most true, that God made created things according to his immense Wisdom in imitation of his knowledge which he has of them. But on what foundation it is asserted that God also communicated the knowledge of created things to men in imitation of his knowledge of them, we do not see. For our knowledge of them is not occupied in knowing them as effects produced in imitation of the knowledge which God has of them, as an exemplary cause, but absolutely and in themselves, as they are things apt to terminate a true knowledge of themselves, and which, when known by the intellect, generate a science conformable to them viewed absolutely in themselves. But that this knowledge of ours of them is also conformable to the knowledge which God has of the same, that arises not so much from the free intention of God as from a certain necessity of nature. For created things, as through are at once essence and conformable to the cognition which God has of them, and are apt in our intellect to terminate a true cognition of themselves, or a cognition conformable to themselves, thus when known by us they cannot but generate in us a science at once conformable both to themselves and to the cognition which God has of them, although God did not make them to this end, that when known by the intellect they should generate in us a science, or a cognition conformable to that which He has of them, just as also the Scriptures nowhere mention that God made them to that end.

Latin:

IV.

Quæ vera de Deo rebusque divinis enunciat Theologia, distinguitur in Archetypam & Ectypam.

V.

Archetypa dicitur, quæ Deo inest primò & independenter, & alterius cum creaturis intelligentibus communicatæ Theologiæ exemplar est.

VI.

Ectypa dicitur, quæ cum creaturis intelligentibus à Deo ad imitationem Theologiæ suæ, velut causæ exemplaris, communicata est.

I. Qui hac utuntur distinctione, non tam respiciunt ad usum loquendi, quàm ad etymon & vim vocis Theologiæ. Nam ex usu loquendi tantùm Theologia Ectypa; neque hæc omnis, sed tantùm quæ hominum Viatorum est, id nominis sibi vendicat. Archetypa autem non tam Theologia, quàm scientia Dei dici solet.

II. Descriptiones hasce cùm Archetypæ, tum Ectypæ Theologiæ vel ipsa illarum nomina suggerunt. Archetypum propriè est exemplar effectus, ad sui imitationem producti, primigenium, & vi vocis importat duo: Unum, exemplar sive formam, quam effectus aliquis ex intentione agentis imitetur. Alterum, negationem dependentiæ ab alia exemplari causa; ut Theologia Archetypa vi vocum sit Theologia, quæ ita alterius cujusdem Theologiæ causa exemplaris est, ut ab alia, velut à causa exemplari, ipsa non dependeat. Cujusmodi Theologia, quia præter Theologiam Dei, nulla datur, non incommodè describitur Theologia Archetypa per Theologiam, quæ Deo inest primò & independenter; & alterius, cum creaturis intelligentibus communicatæ, Theologiæ exemplar est. Contra Ectypa describi potest per Theologiam, à Deo ad imitationem Theologiæ suæ cum creaturis intelligentibus communicatam. Ectypum enim Archetypi correlatum est, & propriè est effectus quidam, ad imitationem alterius, velut causæ exemplaris, productus: cujusmodi est Theologia omnis, quæ in creaturis intelligentibus, Angelis & hominibus, reperitur; quanquam de Angelorum Theologia agere, nunc nobis propositum non sit.

III. Vulgò dicitur Theologia Archetypa, quâ Deus se ipsum cognoscit. Nonnulli addunt, quâ se ipsum, & extra se universa per se ipsum cognoscit, sensu nihil diverso, nisi quod in posteriori ponitur expresse, quod in priori implicitè continetur. Deus enim cognoscendo seipsum cognoscit simul in seipso & per se ipsum universa, quæ extra eum sunt, & sic in cognitione Dei, quâ se ipsum cognoscit, continetur etiam cognitio omnium, quæ extra eum sunt. Utraque tamen est descriptio Theologiæ Archetypæ, materialiter acceptæ pro Theologia, quæ est exemplar Theologiæ alterius, non formaliter, quatenus est alterius exemplar. Nam cognitio, quâ Deus se ipsum cognoscit, speculativa est. Archetypa autem Theologia, formaliter & in quantum Theologiæ alterius exemplar est, spectata, præter illam cognitionem speculativam, importat etiam actum intellectus practicum, quo cognitionem sui Deus concipit ut formam alterius cum creaturis intelligentibus communicandæ Theologiæ, & proinde Theologia Archetypa formaliter non est simpliciter cognitio, quam de seipso Deus habet, sed cognitio, quam de seipso habet, concepta ut forma alterias cum creaturis intelligentibus communicandæ Theologiæ.

IV. Memoratam distinctionem, etsi usu receptissimam, rejicit Reinerus Vogelsangius, in Exerc. Theol. I. pag. 3. ut supervacuam & operosæ subtilitatis: cui præivit Johannes Ovvenus, Scriptor Anglicanus, Tract. de Nat. Theol. lib 1. c. 1. p. 11. ubi intelligantne ipsi, qui ea utuntur, quid per Theologiam Archetypam intelligi velint, se vehementer dubitare ait. Objiciunt autem contra eam,

(I) quòd si obtineat, ratio dici non possit, quare in aliis itidem disciplinis omnibus non adhibeatur. Quum longè certissimum sit, omnis omninò sapientiæ oceanum pariter & fontem esse Deum atque scaturiginem inexhaustam; Nemo tamen hactenus cuminisector usque adeò repertus sit, qui Logicam, Ontologiam, Arithmeticam, Physicam, Astrologiam, Pneumaticam, quasi geminam scientiam singulas, Archetypam & Ectypam, obtruserit.

(II) quòd oporteat Theologiam Archetypam in Ectypa se exprimere; Divina autem Theologia, quâ sese ipsum Deus infinitum infinitè cognoscit, exprimi non possit in ulla creatura.

(III) quòd Archetypa Theologia aliter intelligi non possit, nisi cum quadam præfinitione, quâ ex immenso sinu sapientiæ suæ Deus nostram Theologiam ab omni æternitate in seipso determinavit, & proinde si admitti deberet distinctio, Archetypa Theologia definienda esset per exemplar ab æterno præfinitum in mente divina ejus Theologiæ, quam Deo placitum est præstituto tempore creaturis rationalibus communicare. Omnes tres rationes urget Vogelsangius; Ovvenus autem duas postremas.

V. De conceptu & descriptione Theologiæ Archetypæ jam præced. n. III. mentem nostram declaravimus. De traditâ autem à Vogelsangio descriptione monemus, ambiguè dici, Theologiam Archetypam esse exemplar ab æterno præfinitum &c. Vel enim intelligitur de Theologia Archetypa, materialiter accepta, quòd ipsa forma, ad cujus imitationem Theologia nobiscum communicata est, in mente divina ab æterno præfinita, & Dei præfinitione sive decreto, nostro modo intelligendi, posterior sit; vel de eâdem formaliter sumta, quòd in quantum est forma quædam alterius cum hominibus communicandæ Theologiæ, exemplar sit, in mente Dei ab æterno præfinitum. Priori sensu assertio vera non est, nisi de ea, ut ita loquar, parte Theologiæ Archetypæ, quæ concernit res extra Deum, nostro bono decretas aut factas, cujusmôdi sunt beatitudo homini impertienda aut reparanda, ejusque consequendæ media, & quæ his annexa sunt & eò pertinent alia, quæ ut à Dei liberâ voluntate dependent, ita in mente divina citra dubium suas habent ideas, ejus liberâ voluntate præfinitas, quæ in Theologiæ Archetypæ, liceat nostro modo intelligendi sic loqui, partem veniunt, faciuntque quandam ejus partem, in exemplari ab æterno in mente Dei præfinito constitutam. Alterâ autem parte, quâ semetipsum Deus & omnes suas perfectiones intuitivè cognoscit, Theologia Archetypa, in se materialiter spectata, non est exemplar quoddam in mente divina, liberâ Dei voluntate præfinitum, sed ipsa ejus cognitio naturalis, quâ se & suas perfectiones omnes necessariò & ante omnem voluntatis actum sive præfinitionem ab æterno cognoscit. Posteriori autem sensu assertio simpliciter quidem vera est: nam quemadmodum exemplar omne ex parte causæ efficientis importat cognitionem practicam, quâ ut forma alterius effectus producendi concipitur, ita & Theologia Archetypa præter cognitionem illam, quâ semetipsum Deus cognoscit, importat etiam in intellectu divino actum practicum, quô eandem cognoscit ut formam communicandæ cum aliis Theologiæ, eumque nostro modo intelligendi posteriorem decreto divino de communicanda nobiscum Theologia: cujus intuitu Theologia Archetypa omninò habet rationem exemplaris, in mente Dei præfiniti. Sed hæc nihil obsunt sententiæ eorum, qui Theologiam Archetypam dicunt, quâ Deus se ipsum cognoscit. Illi enim, ut dictum suprà, considerant eam materialiter, non formaliter, h. e. considerant & describunt Theologiam, quæ est Archetypa & nostræ Theologiæ exemplar, non quatenus est Archetypa & exemplar illius.

VI. Atque hinc patet, quid respondendum sit ad ultimam, ut hinc ordiamur, Vogelsangii objectionem: nempe Deum ex immenso sinu sapientiæ suæ determinâsse in seipso Theologiam nostram ab omni æternitate, verissimum est. Inde autem non sequitur, Theologiam Dei non esse Theologiæ nostræ exemplar. Potuit enim Deus Theologiam nostram ex immenso sinu sapientiæ suæ; mul ad imitationem Theologiæ suæ, ab omni æternitate in seipso determinare. Et quæ dabitur in mente divina idea, ad cujus imitationem Deus Theologiam nostram eâ parte, quâ ipsius & ejus perfectionum cognitionem continet, in tempore nobiscum communicandam, ab omni æternitate in seipso determinaverit, præter eam cognitionem, quâ seipsum cognoscit, actu practico, ut formam Theologiæ, in tempore nobiscum communicandæ, conceptam? Quæ dabitur idea, ad cujus imitationem partibus cæteris, quæ sunt de nostra beatitudine ejusque consequendæ causis & mediis, eandem ab omni æternitate in se ipso determinaverit, præter suam cognitionem, quam de illis in mente sua habuit ab æterno, actu practico ut formam cognitionis eorundem, in tempore nobiscum communicandæ, conceptam? Hæc verò cognitio Dei quid aliud est, quàm Theologia Dei, quâ se ipsum & extra se alia, ad nostram Theologiam pertinentia, ab omni æternitate cognoscit? Eadem actu intellectus divini practico concepta ut forma alterius, nobiscum communicandæ, Theologiæ, quid aliud est, quàm Theologia Archetypa?

VII. Neque plus roboris inest reliquis duabus objectionibus. Et secunda quidem, ut eo, quo cœpimus, ordine pergamus, quòd scilicet divina Theologia, quâ se ipsum infinitum Deus infinitè cognoscit, exprimi non possit in ulla creatura; sumit tanquam certum, ad exemplar requiri, ut quicquid in eo est perfectionis, in exemplato, (liceat ita loqui) exprimatur, quod falsum est. Quid enim? Annon Deus in creatione hominis: Faciamus, inquiens, hominem ad imaginem nostram, ad similitudinem nostram, Gen. I. 26. semetipsum constituit exemplar producendi hominis? Neque enim verba: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, ad similitudinem nostram; alium habere sensum possunt, quàm hunc: Faciamus hominem ad imitationem nostri, velut causæ exemplaris, ut imaginem nostri quàm simillimam gerat. In quocunque autem constituatur ratio imaginis, ad imitationem Dei, velut causæ exemplaris, in homine expressæ, certum hoc est, ad ipsam perfectionem exemplaris, Dei scilicet, id minimè pertingere. In Deo enim nihil est, quod non infinitum; in homine autem nihil, quod non finitum sit. Quod & Vogelsangius infrà in Exercit. XIX. th. XXII. agnoscit: Imaginem, inquiens, propriè dicimus vel exemplar, juxta quod qualicunque imitatione aliquid exprimitur, vel similitudinem ad exemplar expressam. — Quæ verò in homine spectari possunt perfectionum divinarum veluti repræsentamina, prorsus umbratilia intelligi oportet : adeoque tantùm & magis etiam ab illis distantia, quàm ab homine differt fluida ejus imago, quæ fortè in speculo ad oculos nostros repercutitur. Et paulò pòst dicit, Scripturam exponere imaginem Dei atq; similitudinem in rectitudine intellectus potissimùm & voluntatis, omniumque adeò exinde facultatum, quasi dedicatam. Illa verò rectitudo intellectus & voluntatis omniumque facultatum in homine annon erat sapientia & sanctitas quædam Ectypa, ad imitationem sapientiæ & sanctitatis Archetypæ, quæ in Deo est, in hominis animo expressa? Neque tamen sapientia & sanctitas Ectypa in primo homine perinde, ut sapientia & sanctitas Archetypa in Deo, infinita erat.

IIX. Prima verò objectio, quòd, stante distinctione Theologiæ in Archetypam & Ectypam, non possit ratio dici, quare in aliis itidem disciplinis omnibus non adhibeatur, nullius ponderis est. Quamvis enim longè certissimum sit, omnis omninò sapientiæ oceanum pariter & fontem esse Deum atque scaturiginem inexhaustam: quod urget Auctor; malè tamen hinc infertur, si Deus, omnis omninò sapientiæ oceanus pariter & fons, non est exemplar aliarum disciplinarum omnium, ut geminæ quasi singulæ, Archetypa & Ectypa, constitui possint, etiam nostræ Theologiæ exemplar non esse Deum, omnis omninò sapientiæ oceanum & fontem, & proptereà Theologiam etiam non posse geminam quasi, Archetypam & Ectypam, constitui. Est enim ratio diversitatis manifesta. Quia enim aliæ disciplinæ omnes occupantur circa res, quæ per se sub nostram cognitionem cadunt, nihil apparet causæ, cur illarum scientias à Deo ad suæ sapientiæ velut causæ exemplaris imitationem nobiscum communicari statuamus: cùm res ipsæ, circa quas occupantur, per se aptæ sint veram sui cognitionem in intellectu nostro terminare, &, accedente nostro labore, studio & meditatione, scientias sibi conformes in eo generare. Secus autem res habet cum Theologia nostra. Nam Deus & ejus perfectiones infinitæ, in quarum cognitione potissimùm occupatur, per se sub nostram cognitionem non cadunt. Est enim Deus essentia spiritualis, & ejus perfectiones omnes sunt cum eo simplicissimè unum; noster autem intellectus, sibi relictus, in cognoscendo à sensibus dependet, nec ad Deum ejusque perfectiones cognoscendas adscendere potest, nisi ipse per media proportionata se ei manifestet, & sic quandam sui cognitionem nobiscum communicet. Eam verò communicavit inde à condito mundo cum hominibus, non casu aut fortunâ, sed, pro sua immensa sapientia & bonitate, ad imitationem & similitudinem suæ cognitionis, quam ipse de se habet, vel per notitias illorum mentibus insitas, & impressa rebus creatis quædam suarum perfectionum vestigia, vel per revelationem supernaturalem, vel denique per infusum intellectui lumen gloriæ, ut posteà in speciali Theologiæ Ectypæ declaratione ostendetur.

Quod si quis excipiat Deum pro sua immensâ sapientiâ fecisse res creatas etiam ad imitationem suæ cognitionis, quam de illis habebat, & consequenter communicâsse etiam nobis illarum scientiam ad imitationem scientiæ suæ, quam de illis habebat; neque tamen scientiarum rerum creatarum proptereà constitui geminam, Archetypam in Deo, & Ectypam in nobis; respondemus, verissimum quidem hoc esse, quòd res creatas Deus pro suâ immensâ Sapientiâ fecerit ad imitationem cognitionis suæ, quam de illis habet. Quo autem fundamento asseratur, Deum communicâsse etiam scientiam rerum creatarum cum hominibus ad imitationem suæ de illis scientiæ, non videmus. Nam nostra de illis scientia non occupatur in iis cognoscendis, ut effectibus ad imitationem cognitionis, quam Deus de illis habet, velut causæ exemplaris productis, sed absolutè & in se, ut sunt res, veram sui cognitionem terminare aptæ, & quæ intellectu cognitæ generant scientiam, sibi in se absolutè spectatis conformem. Quod verò hæc nostra de illis scientia etiam conformis est cognitioni, quam Deus de iisdem habet, id non tam ex Dei intentione libera, quàm ex quadam necessitate naturæ provenit. Res creatæ enim, ut per effentiam simul & conformes sunt cognitioni, quam Deus de illis habet, & aptæ in nostro intellectu veram sui cognitionem, sive cognitionem sibi conformem terminare, ita à nobis cognitæ non possunt non scientiam simul & sibi & cognitioni, quam Deus de illis habet, conformem in nobis generare, licet Deus hoc fine eas non fecerit, ut intellectu cognitæ generent in nobis scientiam, sive, quam de illis habet, cognitioni conformem, sicut etiam, Deum eo fine illas fecisse, Scripturæ nuspiam memorant.


### VII. Concerning the Theology of union, whether it is to be referred to Archetypal or…

VII.

Concerning the Theology of union, whether it is to be referred to Archetypal or to Ectypal Theology, is not entirely agreed upon among theologians, some assigning it to the former, others to the latter.

I. The Theology of union is so called from the personal union of the two natures in Christ, divine and human, and through that it pertains to the human nature of Christ. However, just as those things are not properly said to pertain to the human nature of Christ by the grace of union, the cause of which, why they pertain to it, resides precisely in the personal union alone; just as divine attributes, which do not inhere in it formally and subjectively, pertain to it for no other reason than because it is personally united to the divine nature; so properly and when the Theology of union was to be named, it was that very Theology which pertains to the divine nature of Christ primarily, formally, and independently; but to the human nature, only because it is personally united to the divine nature.

II. Yet by many theologians of no low name, that is called the Theology of union which, although in its own way it draws its origin from the personal union, nevertheless inheres in the human nature of Christ formally and subjectively, and denominates it not so much on account of the personal union, as because it inheres in it formally and subjectively. Which latter mode of speaking, as is evident, is indeed less proper than the former, yet is more received by usage.

III. Taken in the former sense, the Theology of union, as to the thing itself, is Archetypal Theology itself. For because it does not pertain to the human nature of Christ in itself formally and subjectively, but only through and on account of the upersonal union, not some created and finite knowledge, but the very knowledge of the divine nature itself, which is proper and infinite. For all created and finite knowledge in Christ resides in his human nature subjectively and formally; and on the contrary, that which does not reside in his human nature subjectively and formally, yet in the unity of the person because of the personal union truly and really belongs to him, that is the very divine and infinite knowledge, and it belongs to the divine nature itself primarily, independently, and formally; but to the human nature only through and because of the personal union. For from the personal union Christ the man has that he is full of wisdom and truth, Luke II. 40, John I. 14, and that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. II. 3, and the whole fullness of the Deity dwells in him bodily, v. 9. Which knowledge, proper to the divine nature, does not really differ from Archetypal Theology.

IV. In the latter sense, however, the Theology of union is the knowledge of God and divine things, most perfect indeed, yet habitual, efficiently depending on the divine nature of Christ, and derived and diffused from the same into the human nature, personally united to itself, in imitation of that knowledge which is proper and essential to it itself. Which, as is evident, is not Archetypal, but Ectypal Theology.

V. But the reason why most of our theologians call this, rather than that, the Theology of union, seems to be that the divine knowledge, which does not really differ from Archetypal Theology, being communicated to the human nature of Christ through the personal union, on the part of the human nature, partakes of the nature of neither Archetypal nor Ectypal Theology entirely and in all respects. Not Archetypal; because this, both by the force of the words and by the usage of speech, is the primary and independent exemplary Theology, which is also called prototypical. But the Theology of union, taken in the former sense for the divine knowledge itself communicated to the human nature of Christ, although in reality it is the same with his divine nature, and as to the thing itself is the primary and independent exemplary Theology, yet it does not belong to the human nature of Christ primarily and independently; indeed, it does not belong to it subjectively and formally at all, but only because of the personal union, and thus, in our mode of understanding, dependently upon the divine nature, personally united to it, to which alone it belongs formally, primarily, and independently. Nor does Ectypal Theology participate in the reason: because this is by essence a created and finite knowledge, expressed in imitation of that which belongs to God primarily and independently. The Theology of union, however, so called in the prior sense, although it does not belong to the human nature of Christ primarily and independently, but through and because of the personal union, is nevertheless not a created and finite knowledge, expressed in his soul in imitation of that which belongs to his own divine Nature primarily and independently, but is one and the same Theology with it, as regards the thing itself.

Latin:

VII.

De Theologia unionis, sitne ad Archetypam; an ad Ectypam Theologiam referenda, inter Theologos non planè convenit, quibusdam illi, aliis huic eam accensentibus.

I. Dicitur Theologia unionis ab unione personali duarum in Christo naturarum, divinæ & humanæ, & per illam humanæ Christi naturæ conveniat. Quemadmodum autem non propriè humanæ Christi naturæ per unionis gratiam convenire dicuntur, quorum causa, cur ei conveniant, præcisè in sola unione personali residet; sicut attributa divina, quæ formaliter & subjectivè ei non insunt, non alia de causa ipsi conveniunt, quam quia divinæ naturæ personaliter ipsa unita est; ita propriè & quando Theologia unionis dicenda erat illa ipsa Theologia, quæ divinæ Christi naturæ primò, formaliter & independenter; humanæ autem naturæ non, nisi quia naturæ divinæ personaliter unita est, convenit.

II Multis tamen non infimi nominis Theologis unionis Theologia dicitur, quæ quamvis suo modo ex unione personali originem trahat, humanæ Christi naturæ tamen formaliter & subjectivè inest, eamque denominat non tam propter unionem personalem, quàm quia ei formaliter & subjectivè inest. Qui posterior loquendi modus, ut patet, minus quidem proprius, quàm prior, usu tamen magis receptus est.

III. Priori sensu accepta Theologia unionis, quoad rem, est ipsa Theologia Archetypa. Quia enim Christi humanæ naturæ non in se formaliter & subjectivè convenit, sed tantùm per & propter unionem personalem, non creata quædam & finita, sed ipsa divinæ naturæ propria & infinita scientia est. Nam creata & finita in Christo scientia omnis inest ejus naturæ humanæ subjective & formaliter; & contra quæ eius naturæ humanæ non subjective & formaliter inest, in unitate personæ tamen propter unionem personalem ei verè & realiter convenit, ea est ipsa divina & infinita scientia, & convenit divinæ ipsius naturæ primò, independenter & formaliter; humanæ autem naturæ tantùm per & propter unionem personalem. Ex unione personali enim habet Christus homo, quod plenus est sapientia & veritate, Luc. II. 40. Joh. I. 14. quodque in eo reconditi sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ, Col. II. 3. & tota plenitudo Deitatis in ipso habitat corporaliter, v. 9. Quæ Naturæ divinæ propria scientia à Theologia Archetypa realiter non differt.

IV. Posteriori autem sensu Theologia unionis est scientia Dei & rerum divinarum, perfectissima quidem, habitualis tamen, à divina Christi natura efficienter dependens, & ab eadem in Naturam humanam, personaliter sibi unitam, derivata & diffusa ad imitationem ejus, quæ ipsi propria & essentialis est, scientiæ. Quæ, uti patet, non ipsa Archetypa, sed Ectypa Theologia est.

V. Quòd autem nostrates Theologi plerique potiùs hanc, quàm illam, unionis Theologiam dicunt, causa videtur esse, quòd scientia divina, quæ ab Archetypa Theologia realiter non differt, per unionem personalem humanæ Christi naturæ communicata, ex parte Naturæ humanæ, nec Archetypæ, nec Ectypæ Theologiæ rationem prorsus & per omnia participat. Non Archetypæ; quia hæc & vi vocum & ex usu loquendi est Theologia exemplaris prima & independens, quæ & prototypa dicitur. Sed Theologia unionis, sensu priori pro ipsâ humanæ Christi naturæ communicata scientiâ divinâ accepta, licet à parte rei cum ejus natura divina idem, & quoad rem ipsa prima & independens Theologia exemplaris sit, humanæ tamen naturæ Christi non convenit primò & independenter, imò subjectivè & formaliter ei planè non convenit, sed tantùm propter unionem personalem, & sic, nostro modo intelligendi, dependenter à natura divina, personaliter ei unitâ, cui soli formaliter, primò & independenter inest. Neque Ectypa Theologiæ rationem participat: quia hæc per essentiam est scientia creata & finita, ad imitationem ejus, quæ Deo primò & independenter inest, expressa. Theologia unionis autem, sensu priori sic dicta, licet humanæ Christi naturæ non primò & independenter conveniat, sed per & propter unionem personalem, non tamen scientia creata & finita, ad imitationem ejus, quæ divinæ ipsius Naturæ primò & independenter inest, in ejus anima expressa, sed cum ea, quoad rem, una & eadem Theologia est.


### VIII. Ectypal Theology is divided according to the diverse state of men into the…

VIII.

Ectypal Theology is divided according to the diverse state of men into the Theology of the Way or of Wayfarers, and of the Fatherland or of the Comprehenders.

I. I speak of Ectypal Theology in men. Angels also rejoice in their own Theology, which itself can also be divided into the Theology of the Way and of the Fatherland. But we are not dealing with this and its distinctions now.

II. It is called the Theology of the Way and of Wayfarers because through it men, while they are still established on the way in this mortality, are directed toward actually attaining the heavenly fatherland and blessedness. It is called the Theology of the Fatherland and of Comprehenders because, once the course of this life is finally finished, the pious attain it in the heavenly fatherland, and as it were comprehend the goal set before them.

III. The names of the Way and of Wayfarers, of the fatherland and of Comprehenders, have been taken and transferred here from the Pauline passages 1 Cor. 9:24 and 2 Cor. 5:6, 8, in the latter of which the Apostle compares the faithful before they have attained blessedness with Wayfarers and pilgrims, because ἐκδημῶντες ἀπὸ τῷ Κυρίω, being away from the Lord, they desire ἐκδημῆσαι ἐκ τῶ σώματος καὶ ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, to migrate from the body (in which they are as if in a foreign house) and to go to dwell with the Lord, just as Wayfarers, when they are away from home, have nothing more in their wishes than that it may happen to them to return to their fatherland and dwell at home among their own. In the former, however, he compares the same with

ςαδιοδρόμοις, and commands them so to run that they may lay hold, namely of blessedness, toward which, as toward a fixed goal, they tend in their course.

IX.

The Theology of the Fatherland consists in the intuitive knowledge of God, which they otherwise call the beatific Vision. I. It is also called the Theology of Vision, because by its power the blessed know God, as He is in Himself, as clearly and distinctly as corporeal things are known when they strike the eyes and are seen, the name, as it seems, being taken from the words of Christ: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall SEE GOD, Matt. V. 8. and of the Apostles, Paul: We see now through a glass, in a riddle, but then FACE TO FACE, 1 Cor. XIII. 12. and John: We know that if He shall appear, (what we shall be) we shall be like Him, because WE SHALL SEE Him as He is, 1 John III. 2. II. This is a description of the Ectypal Theology of the blessed, viewed materially, not formally, in so far as it is Ectypal. Viewed formally, it can be described as being a clear and intuitive knowledge of God, in imitation of that by which God intuitively knows Himself, communicated to man through the infused light of glory. On the other hand, Archetypal Theology, considered formally and in so far as it is the correlate of this, can be described as being the knowledge by which God intuitively knows Himself, by the practical act of the intellect, as conceived by Him as the form of another Theology to be communicated to man through the infused light of glory. The reason for these descriptions will be evident from Annot. II. to the following thesis XII.

Latin:

VIII.

THeologia Ectypa pro diverso hominum statu dividitur in Theologiam Viæ sive Viatorum, & Patriæ sive Comprehensorum.

I. Loquor de Theologia Ectypa in hominibus. Gaudent suâ quoque Theologiâ Angeli, quæ & ipsa in Theologiam Viæ & Patriæ dividi potest. Sed de hac ejusque distinctionibus nunc non agimus.

II. Viæ & Viatorum Theologia dicitur, quòd per eam homines, dum in hac mortalitate adhuc in via constituti sunt, ad cœlestem patriam beatitudinemque reapse consequendam, dirigantur. Patriæ & Comprehensorum Theologia dicitur, quòd demum finito hujus vitæ cursu pii in patria cœlesti illam consequantur, & velut metam præfixam quasi comprehendant.

III. Desumta autem Viæ & Viatorum, patriæ & Comprehensorum nomina, hucque translata sunt ex locis Paulinis 1. Cor. IX, 24. & II. Cor. V. 6, 8. in quorum posteriori Apostolus fideles ante adeptam beatitudinem comparat cum Viatoribus & peregrinantibus, quòd ἐκδημῶντες ἀπὸ τῷ Κυρίω peregrè absentes à Domino, ἐκδημῆσαι ἐκ τῶ σώματος καὶ ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, migrare è corpore (in quo velut in peregrina domo sunt) & ad Dominum habitatum ire desiderent, perinde ut Viatores, cum peregrè absunt, nihil magis in votis habent, quàm ut ad patriam reverti & domi apud suos habitare sibi contingat. In priori autem eosdem comparat cum

ςαδιοδρόμοις, & jubet illos sic currere ut comprehendant, scilicet beatitudinem, ad quam, velut ad metam præfixam, cursu suo tendunt.

IX.

PAtriæ Theologia consistit in Dei cognitione intuitiva, quàm aliàs Visionem beatificam appellant. I. Dicitur & Theologia Visionis, quòd ejus vi beati Deum, ut in se est, tam clarè & distinctè cognoscant, quàm clarè & distinctè cognoscuntur res corporeæ, cùm in oculos incurrunt & videntur, denominatione, ut videtur, desumtâ ex verbis Christi: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi DEUM VIDEBUNT, Matth. V. 8. & Apostolorum, Pauli: CERNIMUS nunc per speculum, in enigmate, tunc antem FACIE AD FACIEM, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. & Johannis: Scimus, quòd si apparuerit, (quod futuri sumus) similes ei erimus, quoniam VIDEBIMUS eum sicuti est, 1. Joh. II. 2. II. Est hæc descriptio Theologiæ Ectypæ beatorum, materialiter, non formaliter, in quantum Ectypa est, spectatæ. Formaliter spectata describi potest, quòd sit cognitio Dei clara & intuitiva, ad imitationem ejus, quâ semetipsum Deus intuitivè cognoscit, cum homine per infusum lumen gloriæ communicata. Contrà autem Theologia Archetypa, formaliter & in quantum hujus correlatum est, considerata, describi poterit, quòd sit scientia, quâ seipsum Deus intuitivè cognoscit, actu intellectus practico, ut forma alterius per infusum lumen gloriæ cum homine communicandæ Theologiæ ab ipso concepta. Quarum descriptionum ratio patebit ex Annot. II. ad seq. th. XII.


### X. The Theology of the Way and of Wayfarers is again distinguished into Natural…

X.

The Theology of the Way and of Wayfarers is again distinguished into Natural and Revealed.

XI.

Natural is the knowledge concerning God, as man's end and highest good, and concerning blessedness and the causes and means of attaining it in God, resting upon the light or principles of nature.

XII.

The science concerning God, as the end and highest good of man, and concerning blessedness and the causes and means of attaining it in Him, is revealed, resting upon divine revelation.

I. This distinction is sought from the diverse manner of knowing. For God and divine things are known by us either naturally, partly through notions implanted in us by nature, partly through the traces of the invisible things of God impressed upon created things; or supernaturally, through divine revelation. The former manner of knowing, since it contains nothing exceeding the order and powers of nature, but is merely natural, constitutes and denominates Natural Theology. The latter, since it consists in divine and supernatural revelation, constitutes and denominates Revealed Theology, distinguished from Natural.

II. These are also descriptions of Ectypal Theology, viewed in themselves materially, not formally, in so far as they are Ectypal. For in neither is there mention of the exemplary cause, to the imitation of which they are expressed in us. For since an Ectype formally is an effect produced to the imitation of some form from the intention of an agent determining an end for itself, in the definition of Ectypal Theology viewed formally and in so far as it is Ectypal, something must necessarily be added by which it is declared to have been produced in us to the imitation of some form from the intention of the agent, and therefore Natural Theology will be able to be defined as the science concerning God, as the end and highest good of man, and concerning blessedness and the causes and means of attaining it in Him, communicated to man by God TO THE IMITATION OF HIS OWN THEOLOGY partly through implanted notions, partly through the traces of His perfections impressed upon created things and shining forth in them; but Revealed [Theology] as the science concerning God, as the end and highest good of man, and concerning blessedness and the causes and means of attaining it, communicated to us by God to the IMITATION OF HIS OWN THEOLOGY through supernatural revelation. On the other hand, the Archetype by essence is a certain form which the effect imitates from the intention of the agent determining an end for itself; and it always imports on the part of the agent a practical knowledge, by which it [is] as the form of another conceives of the forms to be produced in imitation of it. Whence in the definition of Archetypal Theology also, viewed formally and as such, something must be added, by which the reason and relation of the exemplary cause, which it includes in order to our Theology, may be expressed, and Archetypal Theology, which is the correlate of Natural Ectypal [Theology], may be defined as the knowledge of God concerning himself, as the end and supreme good of man, and concerning beatitude and the causes and means of attaining it, conceived by him by a practical act of the intellect AS THE FORM OF ANOTHER, to be communicated to us partly through innate notions, partly through the traces of his perfections impressed upon created things; and that which is the correlate of Revealed Ectypal Theology may be described as the knowledge of God concerning himself as the end and supreme good of man, and concerning our beatitude and the causes and means of attaining it, conceived by him by a practical act of the intellect AS THE FORM of another Theology to be communicated to man through supernatural revelation.

III. That both have been communicated to man in imitation of the Theology which resides in God primarily and independently, and that this [latter] truly holds the status of an exemplary cause in relation to those [former], the Holy Scriptures signify not obscurely. For first, in the history of creation, they record that God, about to create man, as if in shared counsel, said: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, Gen. 1. 26. But whether you understand by the image of God God himself and his perfections, conceived in the mind of God by way of an idea or form, in imitation of which man was to be produced, in this sense: Let us make man in imitation of us as an exemplary cause; or whether you understand the image as expressed in man in imitation of God and his perfections, so that the sense is: Let us make man, who may be our image, or in whom our image may be expressed: it remains fixed and immovable, however, that immediately in the first creation there was expressed in man a certain form, which, according to God's intention, imitates God and his perfections as an exemplary cause. Under that, however, there is undoubtedly contained also a certain perfection and rectitude of the intellect for knowing God, expressed in him in imitation of the knowledge which God has of himself, which itself it embraces the innate notions, as they are wont to be called. Furthermore, all created things, arranged in a wonderful order, as they are notable effects, so they are illustrious signs of God and of His divine perfections, and when known by the intellect, they are a certain method of knowing God and His invisible things, and they generate in us, with our study and effort added, a habit of knowing those things, which excellently perfects the notions innate in the intellect in the primeval creation according to the image and likeness of God, and coalesces with them into one complete habit of Theology, imitating the Theology of God from the very intention of God, which is nothing else than Ectypal Natural Theology. To this pertains the fact that the heavens are said to declare the glory of God, Psalm 19, certainly not without the intention of God the Creator, who in His infinite wisdom founded them for that very purpose so wisely, and adorned them with stars, fixed and wandering, arranged in a most beautiful order, and ordained their various, yet equable and always constant motions, with such exact harmony, that among men, created in His own image, they might be as it were perpetual heralds and witnesses of His glory, and might exhibit His invisible perfections, when known in themselves, as clearly to be known as if they were declared in words, conformably indeed to that knowledge which He Himself has of them in Himself. To the same sense the Apostle of the Gentiles speaks in Romans 1:19 et seq. τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, i.e., that which can be known of God, is manifest in them (the Gentiles), for God has made it manifest to them: for His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and divinity, to this end, that they may be without excuse. For that it does not happen without the intention of God, that the invisible things of God, namely His eternal power and divinity, are as it were exhibited to be clearly seen in created things, but that God determined this end for Himself in the very production of them, that when known by the intellect they might be means for generating in us a knowledge of His invisible things, conformable to the knowledge which He Himself has of them in Himself, is understood even from this, that the Apostle premises that God has made manifest to them that which can be known of Him, and establishes the mode of manifestation in this, that His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

Thirdly, concerning supernatural revelation, which is the proper ratio cognoscendi of revealed Theology, there is no doubt that it is a communication made to men in imitation of the knowledge which God has in Himself concerning Himself and our beatitude, and the principles and means of attaining it. For this revelation was made divinely through concepts inspired in holy men, which conform to the concepts that God has in His own mind concerning the things revealed: which are in themselves certain effects, expressed in the intellect of holy men in imitation of those which are in the mind of the revealing God as an exemplary cause, and from them committed to writing. Moreover, the knowledge of God and divine things, which divine revelation generates in the intellect of men who are wayfarers, is called by the Apostle an acknowledgment according to the image of God, Col. III. 10, certainly for no other reason than that their revelation is a communication made to us in imitation of the knowledge which God has of them in Himself, as an exemplary cause, and is an expressed image of it.

IV. Nor is it less certain concerning the Theology of Vision or of the Fatherland, that it is expressed in the intellect of the blessed in imitation of the Theology by which God knows Himself. For besides the fact that God does nothing outside Himself of which He has not conceived an idea and a certain exemplary form in His intellect; and indeed no other idea of the intuitive knowledge of God to be communicated to men can even be imagined, besides the knowledge by which God intuitively knows Himself, conceived by a practical act as the form of that Theology to be expressed in the intellect of man; the intuitive knowledge of God in the intellect of the blessed also approaches most closely of all to the Theology of God, i.e., to His knowledge, by which He alone knows clearly and intuitively. To which pertains what the Apostle John says in 1 Ep. c. III. 2: It has not yet appeared what we shall be: but we know that if He shall appear, we shall be LIKE Him, BECAUSE WE SHALL SEE HIM, AS HE IS. If the reason why we shall be like God consists in this, that we are to see God as He is, the Vision of God, or His intuitive knowledge, by which we are to know Him immediately in Himself as He is, will certainly be similar to the knowledge which God has of Himself, and expressed in the intellect of the blessed in imitation of it.

Latin:

X.

THeologia Viæ & Viatorum rursum distinguitur in Naturalem & Revelatam.

XI.

NAturalis est scientia de Deo, ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine & ejus in Deo consequendæ causis & mediis, lumini sive principiis naturæ innixa.

XII.

Revelata est scientia de Deo, ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine & ejus in ipso consequendæ causis ac mediis, divinæ revelationi innixa.

I. Distinctio hæc petita est ex diversa ratione cognoscendi. Cognoscuntur enim Deus & divina à nobis vel naturaliter, partim per notitias nobis naturâ insitas, partim per vestigia invisibilium Dei, rebus creatis impressa; vel supernaturaliter, per divinam revelationem. Prior cognoscendi ratio, cùm nihil naturæ ordinem & vires excedens contineat, sed merè naturalis sit, constituit & denominat Theologiam Naturalem. Posterior, cùm in divinâ, eâque supernaturali revelatione consistat, constituit & denominat Theologiam Revelatam, Naturali contradistinctam.

II. Hæ etiam sunt descriptiones Theologiæ Ectypæ, in se materialiter spectatæ, non formaliter, in quantum Ectypæ sunt. In neutra enim causæ exemplaris, ad cujus imitationem in nobis expressæ sint, mentio fit. Cùm enim Ectypum formaliter sit effectus, ad imitationem alicujus formæ ex intentione agentis, determinantis sibi finem, productus, in definitione Theologiæ Ectypæ formaliter & in quantum Ectypa est, spectatæ, necessariò addendum aliquid erit, quo eam ad imitationem alicujus formæ, ex intentione agentis in nobis productam esse, declaretur, & proinde Theologia Naturalis definiri poterit per scientiam de Deo, ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine & ejus in ipso consequendæ causis & mediis, à Deo AD IMITATIONEM THEOLOGIÆ SUÆ partim per notitias insitas, partim per vestigia suarum perfectionum, rebus creatis impressa, & in illis relucentia, cum homine communicatam; Revelata verò per scientiam de Deo, ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine & ejus consequendæ causis & mediis, à Deo ad IMITATIONEM THEOLOGIÆ SUÆ per revelationem supernaturalem nobiscum communicatam. Contra autem Archetypum per essentiam est forma quædam, quam imitatur effectus ex intentione agentis, determinantis sibi finem; & importat ex parte agentis semper cognitionem practicam, quâ eam ut formam alterius ad ejus imitationem producende formæ concipit. Unde in definitione Theologiæ Archetypæ etiam, formaliter & ut fic spectatæ, aliquid erit addendum, quo ratio & habitudo causæ exemplaris, quam in ordine ad Theologiam nostram includit, exprimatur, poteritque Theologia Archetypa, quæ Ectypæ Naturalis correlatum est, definiri, quòd sit scientia Dei de se ipso, ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine & ejus consequende causis & mediis, actu intellectus practico ut FORMA ALTERIUS, partim per notitias infitas, partim per impressa rebus creatis vestigia suarum perfectionum nobiscum communicandæ scientiæ, ab ipso concepta; & quæ Revelatæ Theologiæ Ectypæ correlatum est, describi poterit, quòd sit scientia Dei de se ut hominis fine & bono summo, deque beatitudine nostra & ejus consequende causis & mediis, actu intellectus practico UT FORMA alterius per revelationem supernaturalem cum homine commucandæ Theologiæ, ab ipso concepta.

III. Quòd utraque ad imitationem Theologiæ, quæ Deo primò & independenter inest, cum homine communicata sit, & hæc ad illas verè causæ exemplaris rationem habeat, non obscurè fignificant sacræ Literæ. Primùm enim in creationis historia memorant, Deum, conditurum hominem, communicato quasi consilio, dixisse: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, ad similitudinem nostram, Gen. 1. 26. Sive autem per imaginem Dei intelligas Deum ipsum ejusque perfectiones, in mente Dei per modum ideæ sive formæ, ad cujus imitationem homo producendus esset, conceptas, hoc sensu: Faciamus hominem ad imitationem nostri velut causæ exemplaris; sive intelligas imaginem, ad imitationem Dei ejusque perfectionum in homine expressam, ut sensus sit: Faciamus hominem, qui sit imago nostra, aut in quo imago nostra sit expressa: fixum tamen immotumque manet, in prima statim creatione expressam esse in homine formam quandam, quæ Deum ejusque perfectiones, velut causam exemplarem, ex Dei intentione imitetur. Sub ea autem continetur indubiè etiam perfectio quædam & rectitudo intellectus ad cognoscendum Deum, ad imitationem cognitionis, quam de seipso Deus habet, in eo expressam, quæ ipsas insitas, ut dici solent, notitias complectitur. Deinde res creatæ universæ, miro ordine dispositæ, ut effectus insignes, ita signa illustria sunt Dei divinarumque perfectionum, & intellectu cognitæ, sunt ratio quædam cognoscendi Deum ejusque invisibilia, generantque in nobis, accedente nostro studio & labore, habitum ea cognoscendi, qui notitias in primæva creatione ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei intellectui insitas egregiè perficit, & cum iisdem in unum completum Theologiæ habitum, Theologiam Dei ex ipsa Dei intentione imitantem, coalescit, qui nihil est aliud, quàm Theologia Naturalis Ectypa. Quò pertinet, quòd Cœli dicuntur enarrare gloriam Dei, Psal. XIX. non sanè præter intentionem Dei Creatoris, qui pro suâ infinitâ sapientiâ illos eo ipso fine ita sapienter condidit, stellisque, fixis & erraticis, pulcerrimo ordine dispositis ornavit, & illorum motus varios, æquabiles tamen, sibique semper constantes tam exactâ harmoniâ ordinavit, ut apud homines, ad ipsius imaginem conditos, gloriæ suæ velut præcones & testes perpetui essent, & invisibiles ejus perfectiones in semetipsis cognitis ita clarè, ac si verbis enarrarentur, cognoscendas exhiberent, conformiter utique illi cognitioni, quam ipse de iisdem in semetipso habet. Eundem in sensum dicit Apostolus Gentium Rom. I. 19. seq. τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ h. e. quod de Deo cognosci potest, esse manifestum in illis (Gentibus) Deum enim illis id patefecisse: Ipsius enim invisibilia jam inde à condito mundo ex rebus factis intellecta pervidi, æternam scilicet ejus cùm potentiam, tùm divinitatem. ad hoc, ut sint inexcusabiles. Quod enim non citra intentionem Dei fiat, ut invisibilia Dei, æterna videlicet ejus potentia & divinitas in rebus creatis pervidenda quasi exhibeantur, sed hunc finem Deus in ipsa illarum productione sibi determinaverit, ut intellectu cognitæ media sint ad generandam in nobis cognitionem invisibilium ipsius, conformem cognitioni, quam de illis ipse in se ipso habet, vel inde intelligitur, quod præmittit Apostolus, Deum patefecisse illis id, quod de ipso cognosci potest, & patefactionis modum constituit in hoc, quòd invisibilia ejus inde à condito mundo ex rebus factis intellecta pervideantur.

Tertiò de revelatione supernaturali, quæ Theologiæ revelatæ ratio cognoscendi propria est, dubium non est, eam esse ad imitationem cognitionis, quam de seipso deque nostra beatitudine & ejus consequendæ principiis & mediis Deus in seipso habet, cum hominibus communicatam. Nam hæc revelatio facta est divinitùs per conceptus, Viris sanctis inspiratos, conformes conceptibus, quos in mente sua Deus de rebus revelatis habet: qui per se sunt effectus quidam, ad imitationem eorum, qui in mente Dei revelantis sunt, velut causæ exemplaris, in Virorum sanctorum intellectu expressi, & ab his in literas relati. Quin & cognitio Dei rerumque divinarum, quam in hominum Viatorum intellectu revelatio divina generat, dicitur ab Apostolo agnitio juxta imaginem Dei, Col. III. 10. certè non aliâ de causâ, quàm quòd illorum revelatio ad imitationem cognitionis, quam in semetipso Deus de illis habet, velut causæ exemplaris nobiscum communicata, & ejus quædam imago expressa sit.

IV. Neque minùs de Theologia Visio sive Patriæ certum est, quòd ad imitationem Theologiæ quâ seipsum Deus cognoscit, in beatorum intellectu expressa sit. Præterquam enim quòd Deus nihil agit extra se, cujus non ideam & formam quandam exemplarem intellectu conceperit; alia verò idea cognitionis intuitivæ Dei, cum hominibus communicandæ, ne fingi quidem possit, præter cognitionem, quâ seipsum Deus intuitivè cognoscit, actu practico ut formam illius in intellectu hominis exprimendæ Theologiæ conceptam; cognitio Dei intuitiva etiam in beatorum intellectu accedit omnium proximè ad Theologiam Dei, h. e. ad ejus cognitionem, quâ solum clarè & intuitivè cognoscit. Quò pertinet, quod Johannes Apostolus in 1. Ep. c. III. 2. Nondum, ait, apparuit, quod erimus: scimus autem, quòd si apparuerit, SIMILES ei erimus, QUONIAM VIDEBIMUS EUM, SICUT EST. Si ratio, cur futuri simus similes Deo, consistit in hoc, quòd Deum sumus visuri, sicut est, Visio Dei utique, sive cognitio ejus intuitiva, quâ eum in se immediatè, sicut est, cognituri sumus, erit similis cognitioni, quam de se ipso Deus habet, & ad ejus imitationem in beatorum intellectu expressa.


### XII. In the Theology of Vision is found the likeness of Archetypal Theology most…

XII.

In the Theology of Vision is found the likeness of Archetypal Theology most perfectly of all; but in Natural and Revealed [Theology] it is expressed much more imperfectly, yet in the latter more perfectly than in the former.

I. It is found most perfectly of all in the Theology of Vision: because Archetypal Theology is intuitive, by which God knows Himself and His perfections through Himself immediately without an impressed species, as they are in themselves. But there is given no intuitive Ectypal Theology, by which God and all His perfections are known through Himself immediately and without an impressed species, except for one and only the Theology of Vision. But just as there is a greater agreement between the intuitive knowledge of God, which resides in God primarily and independently, and the same [knowledge] which resides in blessed men dependently and is expressed in them in imitation of that, than between that and abstractive knowledge, by which men who are Wayfarers know God and His perfections through foreign species, whether from created things or from divine revelation: so the image or likeness of Archetypal Theology is found expressed so much more perfectly in the Theology of Vision than in Natural and Revealed [Theology], as its agreement with Archetypal Theology is greater than that of the latter.

II. But the same is found expressed more perfectly in Revealed than in Natural Theology: because the realities which, under the guidance of the light of nature, constitute the proper object of knowing for Natural Theology, do not signify or manifest God and His perfections formally, proximately, and immediately, but only virtually, remotely, and by means of discourse, concluding from the perfection of the effect to the perfection of its cause.
