For effects do indeed imitate their cause, and are certain signs of it, yet they do not signify it formally and through themselves immediately, but at least suggest to the intellect a reason for knowing it and its perfections through discourse, e.g., this universe, insofar as it has been brought from nothing and from non-being to being, offers to the intellect a reason for knowing God and His infinite power; and what is seen in it, namely the most exact ordering and harmony of all parts, and its wonderful beauty, suggests to the same a reason for knowing the infinite wisdom of God, but by means of discourse, whereby one concludes from the perfection of the effect to the perfection of the cause, from the production of the world out of nothing to the infinite power of the producer, and from the ordering, harmony, and beauty of the parts to the infinite wisdom of the creator, etc., so that created things, by means of discourse, may finally generate a knowledge of God and of his invisible things that is conformed to the knowledge which God has of himself and his own invisible things. Divine revelation, however, which is the proper way of knowing for Revealed Theology, represents not only God and his invisible things, but also the very knowledge and concepts which God has in his mind concerning himself, and concerning our blessedness and its principles and causes, formally, in themselves, and immediately. For divine revelation consisted in concepts, inspired by God in holy men, which were entirely conformed both to the things themselves and to the concepts which God has of them. But now, with the Holy Spirit inspiring it, divine revelation recorded in letters consists of words signifying by institution, as signs, but which, when known by the intellect, generate in us of themselves, immediately and without discourse, concepts that are conformed both to the things themselves and to the concepts which God once inspired in holy men, and which he himself has of the things within himself. There is a greater agreement with Archetypal Theology in that theology by which those things that fall under the Theology of Wayfarers are known through concepts inspired by God in conformity with his own concepts, or through the written Word of God, which, when known by the intellect, generates of itself immediately a knowledge conformed to the knowledge which God has of the same things, than in that [theology] by which the same things are known from created things, which, when known by the intellect, do not generate of themselves immediately, but only through discourse, a knowledge of them conformed to that which God has of the same things. I pass over for now the fact that in revealed theology many things are known and handed down from divine revelation, entirely conformed to the knowledge which God has in himself, to the knowledge of which Natural Theology, through known created things, does not reach at all.

Latin:

XII.

IN Theologia Visionis invenitur Theologiæ Archetypæ similitudo omnium perfectissimè; in Naturali verò & Revelata multò imperfectiùs, in hac tamen perfectiùs, quàm in illa, expressa.

I. Omnium perfectissimè invenitur ea in Theologia Visionis: quia Theologia Archetypa est intuitiva, quâ Deus se & perfectiones suas cognoscit per se immediatè absque specie impressa, uti in se sunt. Nulla autem datur Theologia Ectypa intuitiva, quâ Deus omnesque ejus perfectiones per se immediatè & absque specie impressa cognoscantur, præter unam & solam Visionis Theologiam. Quemadmodum autem inter cognitionem Dei intuitivam, quæ Deo primò & independenter inest, & inter eandem, quæ inest hominibus beatis dependenter, & ad illius imitationem in ipsis expressa, major convenientia est, quàm inter illam & cognitionem abstractivam, quâ homines Viatores Deum ejusque perfectiones per species alienas sive ex rebus creatis, sive ex divina revelatione cognoscunt: ita imago sive similitudo Theologiæ Archetypæ in Visionis Theologia tantò perfectius invenitur expressa, quàm in Naturali & Revelata, quanto major illius, quàm harum cum Archetypa Theologia convenientia est.

II. Perfectiùs verò reperitur eadem in Revelata, quàm in Naturali Theologia, expressa: quia r eatæ, quæ ductu luminis naturæ cognitæ Theologiæ Natura nem cognoscendi propriam constituunt, non significant aut manifestant Deum ejusque perfectiones formaliter, proximè & immediatè, sed virtualiter tantùm, remotè & mediante discursu, à perfectione effectus ad perfectionem suæ causæ concludente. Effectus enim imitantur quidem suam causam, & sunt quædam ejus signa, non tamen significant eam formaliter, & per se immediatè, sed suggerunt saltem intellectui rationem cognoscendi illam, ejusque perfectiones per discursum, v. g. hoc universum, in quantum ex nihilo & à non esse traductum est ad esse, præbet intellectui rationem cognoscendi Deum ejusque potentiam infinitam; & quæ in eo conspicitur partium omnium ordinatio & harmonia exactissima, ejusque mira pulchritudo, suggerit eidem rationem cognoscendi sapientiam Dei infinitam, sed mediante discursu, quò à perfectione effectus ad perfectionem causæ, à productione mundi ex nihilo ad producentis potentiam infinitam, & à partium ordinatione, harmonia & pulcritudine ad conditoris sapientiam infinitam concluditur &c. ut ita res creatæ mediante discursu demùm cognitionem Dei, ejusque invisibilium, cognitioni, quam de se suisque invisibilibus Deus habet, conformem generent. Divina revelatio autem, quæ Theologiæ Revelatæ ratio cognoscendi propria est, repræsentat non tantùm Deum ejusque invisibilia, sed & ipsam cognitionem & conceptus, quos Deus de seipso, deque nostra beatitudine & ejus principiis & causis in mente sua habet, formaliter, per se & immediatè. Consistebat enim revelatio divina in conceptibus, Viris sanctis à Deo inspiratis, qui & rebus ipsis & conceptibus, quos de illis Deus habet, prorsus conformes erant. Nunc verò, Spiritu S. inspirante in literas relata divina revelatio constat vocibus ex instituto significantibus, velut signis, sed quæ intellectu cognitæ per se immediatè & sine discursu generant in nobis conceptus, cùm rebus ipsis, tum conceptibus, quos olim Viris sanctis Deus inspiraverat, & quos ipse de rebus in se ipso habet, conformes. Major autem cum Theologia Archetypa convenientia est illius Theologiæ, quâ quæ sub Viatorum Theologiam cadunt, cognoscuntur per conceptus, à Deo conceptibus suis conformiter inspiratos, vel per Verbum Dei scriptum, quod intellectu cognitum per se immediatè generat cognitionem, conformem cognitioni, quam de iisdem Deus habet, quàm ejus, quâ eadem cognoscuntur ex rebus creatis, quæ intellectu cognitæ non per se immediatè, sed per discursum demum generant cognitionem illorum, ej quam de iisdem Deus habet, conformem. Taceo nunc, quòd in Theologia revelata ex divina revelatione cognoscuntur & traduntur multa, cognitioni quam in se ipso Deus habet, prorsus conformia, ad quorum notitiam Theologia Naturalis per res creatas cognitas planè non pertingit.


### XIII XIII. Moreover, the aforementioned distinctions of theology into archetypal and…

XIII.

XIII.

Moreover, the aforementioned distinctions of theology into archetypal and ectypal, and of ectypal into natural, revealed, and the theology of vision, are not divisions of a univocal genus into its species, but distinctions of an analogous name into its analogates.

I. They are not divisions of a univocal genus into its species. For archetypal theology differs from ectypal in its entire genus. For the latter is a habit, and is contained in the genus of quality. The former, however, is substance, and as to the thing itself, it is the infinite essence of God. Among the ectypal theologies, however, the theology of vision or of the fatherland is a habit immediately infused and in substance supernatural, by which the intellect of the blessed is elevated to know God, as He is in Himself, immediately and without an impressed species, and by one simple act without discursive reasoning: natural theology, however, which constitutes the other species of the theology of wayfarers, is an acquired habit and in substance natural; finally, revealed theology is a habit in some measure supernatural, granted to man by the intervention indeed of our industry, study, and labor, yet by the supernatural grace of God. Which, as is evident, do not agree in one univocal genus.

II. They are distinctions of an analogous name into its analogates: because ectypal theology depends upon the archetypal, and the name of theology relates to both after the manner of those things which are called by Aristotle κοινὰ ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἕν, common from one, or to one. For it agrees with archetypal theology primarily; with ectypal secondarily. Natural and revealed theology, however, agree with the theology of vision by proportion rather than univocally in one generic concept.

XIV.

Those who make theology thus manifold do not look so much to the usage of speaking as to the force of signifying, which the word theology imports by reason of its etymology.

I. For by the usage of speech, at least the theology of wayfarers is called theology, and among us Christians indeed, only revealed theology is called so absolutely and without qualification; natural theology, however, claims that name for itself only with an addition. But that which is appropriate to God, the knowledge of God, and the theology of the blessed, when viewed in first act, is accustomed to be called the light of glory; but in second act, the beatific vision.

II. By the force of the word, however, theology can be called any λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, such as is all knowledge of God, whether that which God has of himself, or that which human wayfarers have of God from the contemplation of this universe and from divine revelation, and which the blessed have from the light of glory.

Latin:

XIII.

XIII.

CAterùm memoratæ distinctiones Theologiæ in Archetypam & Ectypam; & Ectypæ in Naturalem , Revelatam & Visionis Theologiam, non sunt divisiones generis univoci in suas species, sed distinctiones nominis analogi in sua analogata.

I. Non sunt divisiones generis univoci in suas species. Nam Theologia Archetypa dissert ab Ectypa toto genere. Hæc enim habitus est, & in genere qualitatis continetur. Illa verò substantia, & quoad rem, ipsa infinita Dei essentia est. Inter Ectypas autem Theologia Visionis sive Patriæ est habitus immediatè infusus & in substantia supernaturalis, quo Beatorum intellectus elevatur ad Deum, ut in se est, immediatè & sine specie impressa, unoque simplici actu sine discursu cognoscendum : Theologia Naturalis verò, quæ alteram Theologiæ Viatorum speciem constituit, habitus acquisitus & in substantia naturalis est; Revelata denique habitus quadantenus supernaturalis est, interventu quidem nostræ industriæ, studii & laboris, Dei gratiâ supernaturali tamen, homini concessus. Quæ, uti patet, in uno genere univoco non conveniunt.

II. Sunt distinctiones nominis analogi in sua analogata : quia Theologia Ectypa dependet ab Archetypa, & habet se Theologiæ nomen ad utramque per modum eorum, quæ Aristoteli dicuntur κοινὰ ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἕν, communia ab uno, aut ad unum. Convenit enim Theologia Archetypæ per prius; Ectypæ per posterius. Naturalis autem & Revelata Theologia cum Theologia Visionis proportione potius, quàm univocè in uno generico conceptu conveniunt.

XIV.

QUi Theologiam ita multiplicem faciunt, illi non tam respiciunt ad usum loquendi, quàm ad vim significandi, quam ratione etymi Theologiæ vox importat.

I. Ex usu loquendi enim Theologia Viatorum saltem Theologia dicitur, & apud nos Christianos quidem sola Theologia Revelata absolutè & sine apposito; Naturalis autem non nisi cum additamento id nominis sibi vendicat. Quæ autem Deo convenit, scientia Dei, & Beatorum Theologia, in actu primo spectata, lumen gloriæ; in actu secundo autem visio beatifica vocari consvevit.

II. Ex vi vocis autem Theologia dici potest quilibet λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, qualis est cognitio Dei omnis, cùm quam Deus de seipso; tùm quam homines Viatores ex intuitu hujus universi & ex divina revelatione, & beati ex lumine gloriæ de Deo habent.


### XV. Nor, however, are the aforementioned distinctions therefore superfluous and of…

XV.

Nor, however, are the aforementioned distinctions therefore superfluous and of no use. For they lead us

I. To the first origin and source of all theology that is given to men. For archetypal theology, as it is the first of all, is likewise the exemplar, source, and origin of every other theology.

II. To the source of the truth and certainty which is given in ectypal theology. For since every other theology communicated to man is, as it were, an express form of the theology which exists in God independently, and is formed in its imitation, although the means of communication are diverse; it is repugnant to any ectypal theology in itself, and insofar as each relies upon its own means or principles of knowing, for falsehood to underlie it. And the theology of vision indeed, because it consists in the intuitive knowledge of God, which is the most perfect of all, is entirely conformable to the knowledge which God has of himself, to which it is simply repugnant for falsehood to underlie. The theology of wayfarers, however, because it is abstractive and relies upon certain principles or means of knowing, is certain and devoid of falsehood insofar as each relies upon its own principles or means of knowing—natural theology indeed upon the light of nature and created things, as signs of divine perfections; revealed theology, however, upon divine revelation. If any error occurs in either or both, it is not to be ascribed to theology, but to the fault of men, who in the use of the means deviate from the truth.

III. To the source of the harmony and consensus which exists between Revealed and Natural Theology, at least in those matters which fall under the cognition of both. For because both have been communicated to us in imitation of the one Theology which is in God as an exemplary cause, it is as impossible for them to fight against each other, and for that to be false in one which is true in the other, or vice versa, as it is impossible for the Theology of God to fight against itself. Otherwise, either one or the other would not have been communicated to us in imitation of that Theology which is in God, or the Theology of God would be going to fight against itself.

Latin:

XV.

NEque tamen supervacuæ proptereà & nullius usus sunt prædictæ distinctiones. Deducunt enim nos

I. ad primam Theologiæ omnis, quæ in hominibus datur, originem & fontem. Theologia Archetypa enim, ut omnium prima, ita alterius cujusque Theologiæ exemplar, fons & origo est.

II. Ad fontem veritatis & certitudinis, quæ in Theologia Ectypa datur. Cùm enim ad imitationem Theologiæ, quæ Deo independenter inest, alia omnis cum homine communicata, ejusque quædam quasi forma expressa sit, quamvis communicationis media sint diversa; repugnat alicui Theologiæ Ectypæ per se, & in quantum suis quæque mediis sive principiis cognoscendi nititur, subesse falsum. Et Theologia Visionis quidem, quia in cognitione Dei intuitiva, quæ omnium perfectissima est, consistit, prorsus conformis est cognitioni, quam de seipso Deus habet, cui falsum subesse simpliciter repugnat. Viatorum Theologia autem, quia abstractiva est, & certis cognoscendi principiis sive mediis nititur, in tantum certa falsique expers est, in quantum suis quæque principiis sive mediis cognoscendi, Naturalis quidem lumini naturæ, rebusque creatis, velut divinarum perfectionum signis; Revelata autem, divinæ Revelationi innititur. Si quid erroris in alterutra vel utraque occurrit, non id Theologiæ, sed vitio hominum, in mediorum usu à vero aberrantium, adscribendum est.

III. Ad fontem harmoniae & consensus, qui inter Revelatam & Naturalem Theologiam datur, in iis quidem, quae sub utriusque cognitionem cadunt. Quia enim utraque ad unius, quae in Deo est, Theologiae velut causae exemplaris, imitationem nobiscum communicata est, tam fieri non potest, ut inter se pugnent, & falsum sit in una, quod in altera verum est, vel contra; quam fieri non potest, ut Theologia Dei secum pugnet. Alias enim vel alterutra non esset ad imitationem ejus, quae in Deo est, Theologiae nobiscum communicata, vel Theologia Dei secum esset pugnatura.


## 2 On Natural Theology

I.

We accept Natural Theology here as a habit occupied with God as man's ultimate end and highest good; by which not only the essence and essential perfections of God are treated, but also the means of attaining blessedness in Him, in so far as they can be known by the guidance of the light of nature.

I. God can be considered from the light and principles of nature in two ways. One, absolutely and in Himself, as He is a being abstracted from matter in reality and in reason, or an immaterial being. The other, in relation to man, in so far as He is his ultimate end and highest good.

II. Philosophers hitherto, Gentiles and Christians alike, have passed over the latter consideration almost dry-shod: the former perhaps because, fearing the promiscuous multitude of idolatrous peoples, they dared not teach in the Schools by set purpose any other method of worshipping God and attaining blessedness in Him than that which, although utterly abhorrent to right reason, was publicly received;

these perhaps, because they did not find in the ancient philosophers, especially Aristotle, a leader whom they might follow. Content therefore with the former consideration, they treated only of God as a being, abstracted in reality and reason from matter, i.e., of his essence and essential perfections, some indeed after the example of Aristotle in Metaphysics, which in VI Met. c. 1 he calls Φιλοσοφίαν θεολογικὴν; others in a peculiar discipline, in which, having passed over the doctrine of being and its attributes, they only hand down what can be known of God's essence and his essential perfections from the light of nature: which they call Natural Theology, more conveniently indeed than those who call it Metaphysics, which in its whole common part treats of nothing concerning God in himself and in the abstract, but only of being in general and its most universal predicates, and thus does not contain even a shadow of Theology, in that part at least. III. But the other consideration, which is of God as the end of man and the highest good, why philosophers, especially Christians, to whom the light of divine revelation, conspiring amicably with the light of nature, holds up as it were a torch and opens a way much easier than that which was open to the philosophers of the Gentiles formerly deprived of it, leave it untouched; I for my part do not see the cause of it: since the light of nature and philosophy resting upon it suggest principles equally to both considerations. IV. Nor is there any reason why one might perhaps say that both considerations indeed fall under philosophy, yet not under one science of Natural Theology. For first, if it is not the business of Natural Theology to treat of God as the end of man and the highest good, to which philosophical science will this treatment finally belong? Then if it is fitting for Natural Theology to treat of God by reason of his essence and essential perfections, why should it not also be fitting for it to treat of the same as the end of man and the highest good? For neither can the essence and essential perfections of God be so absolutely explained and known, without at the same time the reason of the highest good, the appetite for which is implanted in man by nature, being explained and known in reality: since that which is contained in God as the highest good of man, consists in his essence and essential perfections. Just as it is the task of one and the same science to explain an end, whether to be obtained or to be effected, and the means of obtaining or effecting it, for example, it is the task of the same science of architecture to consider a house and the principles and means of effecting it; and it is the task of the same Moral science to consider the supreme civil good of man, and the principles and means of obtaining it; so it is the task of one and the same Theological science to explain the essence and essential perfections of God, in which the absolutely supreme good of man consists, and the means of obtaining that good. Thirdly, the essence and essential perfections of God contain in themselves radically, as the Schools love to speak, and virtually the rule of right operation concerning God, as the end of man to be obtained, so that practical conclusions, formally constituting it, can be deduced from there by an easy and ready consequence, as will be shown more fully below in its place. Moreover, it is the task of one and the same science to consider the objective end, and to elicit and hand down from the same known thing the rule of operation concerning the same, which it contains radically and virtually within itself, as can be shown by an induction of all disciplines which are occupied with such an object. Fourthly, speculative sciences, which are occupied with some thing considered in itself absolutely, as the thing is, fill and satisfy the appetite of man with the bare knowledge of the object, so that he may rest in it. Natural theology, however, does not satisfy the appetite of man with the bare knowledge of God, but the more fully and accurately one knows God and His perfections, the greater the desire of that appetite to enjoy Him is held, so that His known perfections are not only on the part of the intellect a reason for knowing the means by which one must arrive at the enjoyment of Him, but also on the part of the will they excite and direct the appetite toward operation concerning the same, as its supreme good, to be obtained by it through practical conclusions, which flow from there by a consequence so ready and easy that they seem to force themselves upon the mind, or to be innate to it. A proof of this matter can also be that there is hardly anyone so rude or simple who, once God is known, is not spontaneously carried toward His worship, by which he strives to deserve Him and to render Him propitious and favorable to himself, for the sake of attaining blessedness in Him. Therefore, Natural Theology is not such a knowledge of God as is concerned with God absolutely in Himself, as He is a being in reality and by reason abstracted from matter; but rather one that is concerned with the same as the end and supreme good of man.

V. In this sense, therefore, we also accept Natural Theology here, namely as a habit concerned with God as the end and supreme good of man, by which at the same time the nature and attributes of God are explained, and the means of attaining blessedness in Him, as far as can be done under the guidance of the light of nature, are deduced, confirmed, and defended from those declared things.

Latin:

I.

Theologiam Naturalem accipimus heic pro habitu, circa Deum, ut hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum occupato; quo non tantum de Dei essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus, sed & de mediis consequendae in eo beatitudinis, in quantum quidem ductu luminis naturae cognosci possunt, agitur.

I. Deus potest ex lumine & principiis naturae duobus modis considerari. Uno absolute & in se, ut est ens re & ratione a materia abstractum, sive ens immateriale. Altero in ordine ad hominem, in quantum est ejus finis ultimus & bonum summum.

II. Considerationem posteriorem Philosophi hactenus, Gentiles pariter & Christiani, fere sicco pede praeterierunt: illi forsan, quod promiscuan populorum idololatricorum multitudinem veriti non auderent aliam Dei colendi consequendaeque in ipso beatitudinis rationem, quam quae, licet a ratione recta prorsus abhorrens, publice recepta esset, in Scholis ex instituto tradere;

hi fortè, quòd in Philosophis priscis, Aristotele præsertim, ducem, quem sequerentur, non invenirent. Contenti ergo consideratione priori, de Deo tantùm, ut ente, re & ratione à materia abstracto, h. e. de ejus essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus egerunt, nonnulli quidem, ad exemplum Aristotelis, in Metaphysica, quam VI. Met. c. 1. is Φιλοσοφίαν θεολογικὴν appellat; alii in disciplina peculiari, quâ, prætermissâ doctrinâ de ente ejusque attributis, tantùm quæ de Dei essentia ejusque perfectionibus essentialibus ex lumine naturæ cognosci possunt, tradunt: quam Theologiam Naturalem appellant, convenientiùs sanè, quàm illi Metaphysicam, quæ totâ parte communi de Deo per se & in actu signato nihil, sed tantùm de ente in communi, ejusque prædicatis universalissimis agit, atque adeò ne umbram quidem Theologiæ, eâ quidem parte, continet. III. Alteram verò considerationem, quæ est Dei, ut hominis finis & boni summi, cur intactam relinquant Philosophi, Christiani præsertim, quibus lumen divinæ revelationis, cum lumine naturæ amicè conspirans, facem quasi præfert, & viam aperit multò faciliorem, quàm olim destitutis illo Philosophis Gentilium patebat; ejus causam equidem non video: cùm considerationi utrique sua æquè principia lumen naturæ & ei innixa Philosophia suggerat. IV. Neque est, quòd quis fortè dicat, utramque quidem considerationem cadere sub Philosophiam, non tamen sub unam Theologiæ Naturalis scientiam. Primùm enim si Theologiæ Naturalis non est agere de Deo, ut hominis fine & bono summo, cujus scientiæ Philosophicæ tandem hæc tractatio erit? Deinde si Theologiæ Naturali convenit agere de Deo ratione essentiæ & perfectionum essentialium, cur non etiam ei conveniat de eodem agere, ut hominis fine & bono summo? Neque enim Dei essentia & perfectiones essentiales ita absolutè explicari & cognosci possunt, quin simul in iis ratio summi boni, cujus appetitus naturâ homini implantatus est, quoad rem, explicetur & cognoscatur: cùm quod in Deo continetur hominis bonum summum, in ejus essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus consistat. Quemadmodum autem alias scientiæ unius & ejusdem est explicare finem, sive obtinendum sive efficiendum, & ejus consequendi vel efficiendi media, v. g. ejusdem scientiæ οἰκοδομικῆς est considerare domum & ejus efficiendæ principia & media; & ejusdem scientiæ Moralis est considerare hominis bonum summum civile, & ejusdem consequendi principia & media; ita unius & ejusdem scientiæ Theologicæ est explicare Dei essentiam & perfectiones essentiales, in quibus hominis bonum absolutè summum consistit, & media consequendi illius boni. Tertiò Dei essentia & perfectiones essentiales continent in se radicaliter, ut loqui Scholæ amant, & virtualiter regulam rectæ operationis circa Deum, ut hominis finem obtinendum, ita ut conclusiones practicæ, eam formaliter constituentes, facili & pronâ consequentiâ inde deduci possint, ut infra suo loco uberiùs ostendetur. Unius autem & ejusdem scientiæ est considerare finem objectivum, & regulam operationis circa eundem, quam radicaliter & virtualiter in se continet, ex eodem cognito eruere & tradere, ut inductione omnium disciplinarum, quæ circa tale occupantur objectum, ostendi potest. Quartò scientiæ speculativæ, quæ circa rem aliquam in se absolutè, ut res est, spectatam occupantur, explent & satiant hominis appetitum cognitione objecti nudâ, ut in eâ acquiescat. Theologia naturalis autem non satiat hominis appetitum cognitione Dei nudâ, sed quò quis Deum ejusque perfectiones cognoscit pleniùs & accuratiùs, eò majori ejus fruendi desiderio tenetur appetitus illius, ita ut ejus perfectiones cognitæ non solùm ex parte intellectus sint ratio cognoscendi media, quibus ad ejus fruitionem perveniendum sit, sed & ex parte voluntatis appetitum ad operationem circa eundem, velut suum bonum summum, eâ obtinendum, excitent & dirigant per conclusiones practicas, quæ consequentiâ ita pronâ & facili inde fluunt, ut se ultrò menti ingerere, vel ei connatæ esse videantur. Cui rei documento & illud esse potest, quòd vix quisquam ita rudis aut simplex est, quin cognito Deo, ultrò feratur in ejus cultum, quo illum demereri sibique propitium & faventem reddere studeat, consequendæ in eo beatitudinis causâ. Non ergo Theologia Naturalis talis de Deo scientia est, quæ circa Deum, in se absolutè, ut est ens re & ratione à materia abstractum; sed quæ circa eundem, ut hominis finem & bonum summum occupetur.

V. Hunc ergo in sensum & nos Theologiam Naturalem heic accipimus, nempe pro habitu, circa Deum ut hominis finem & bonum summum occupato, quo simul natura & attributa Dei explicantur, & media consequendæ in eo beatitudinis, quoad luminis naturæ ductu fieri potest, ex illis declaratis deducuntur, confirmantur, & defenduntur.


### II. However, just as it is one thing to rightly acknowledge and worship God, and…

II.

However, just as it is one thing to rightly acknowledge and worship God, and another to deduce, explain, and confirm from their own principles those things which pertain to the acknowledgment and worship of God: so also the habit by which we perform the former is different from that by which we perform the latter. You would more correctly call the latter the habit of Theology, and the former the habit of religion.

In theoretical disciplines, it is the same habit to contemplate one's object, or to know it scientifically, and to teach it and explain it to others. In practical matters, however, the situation is different. He who can teach what virtue is, by what principles and actions it is to be acquired, and what extremes are to be avoided and how, etc., is not immediately virtuous himself, nor can he necessarily act according to virtue; nor is he who is virtuous and can act according to virtue immediately able to teach and explain to others what is required for acquiring virtue. On this matter, let him who wishes see Aristotle discussing it at greater length in Eudemian Ethics, Book I, Chapter V. Similarly, in Theology, the habit by which we teach what pertains to the acknowledgment and worship of God is not the same as that by which we rightly acknowledge and worship God. For to acknowledge and worship God falls even to simple men and those unlearned in letters, whom no one calls theologians, and thus one would not easily call the habit by which they rightly acknowledge and worship God, Theology. Conversely, to teach what pertains to the acknowledgment and worship of God falls even to men imupright, who, having held the right worship of God in contempt, live impiously and flagitiously. There is, therefore, one habit by which we pursue God with fitting worship; another, by which we teach those things which pertain to the true worship of God. The former you would more rightly call the habit of religion; the latter, of theology.

III.

The habit by which we teach those things which pertain to the knowledge and worship of God, under the guidance of the light of nature, is science.

I. That Natural Theology is a science is evident from the requirements of science. For it is an evident habit, occupied with a necessary object, deducing its conclusions from necessary principles. For those things which Natural Theology hands down concerning God and His fitting worship, it fetches from its own genuine and evident principles, which are also of necessary truth.

II. Since, however, science is a demonstrative habit; and demonstration is of one kind τῶ ὅτι (that it is), and of another τῶ διότι (why it is), of which the latter infers its conclusions a priori from first, immediate, better-known, and prior principles, which contain the cause of the conclusion, and shows the cause why a thing is; the former proves that a thing is a posteriori and from the effect: Natural Theology is a science which uses both kinds of demonstration.

III. And it argues a posteriori and from the effect almost always in the first part, which is concerning the objective end, namely God, and His essence and essential perfections. For because God has no causes either of His being or of His perfections, nay, does not fall under our cognition as Wayfarers, except through effects and concepts derived from them, the thing itself speaks, that those things which intrinsically belong to Him cannot be demonstrated of Him a priori, through the cause on account of which the thing is, but only a posteriori, by concluding from those things which are in the effects, namely in created things, to those things which are in God, as their cause.

IV. But a priori and from first, immediate principles, which contain the cause of the conclusion, the same argues especially in that part which is concerning the means of attaining blessedness in God. For the essential perfections of God, demonstrated a posteriori

and known, are the cause of the worship owed to God (in which almost alone the method of obtaining blessedness in God is left to itself) and they infer practical conclusions, prescribing the same, by a demonstration διότι, and which contains the cause for which a thing is.

V. Sometimes, however, it uses the same demonstration à priori even in the first part, but more rarely, and only then when one divine perfection, demonstrated and known à posteriori, stands in relation to another in our mode of understanding as a cause or reason à priori, just as, for example, immateriality in God stands in relation to his immortality in our mode of understanding as its cause, or as its reason à priori. For then, from one perfection, demonstrated and known à posteriori, another divine perfection can be demonstrated by a demonstration διότι, for example, the immortality of God can be demonstrated from his immateriality, once demonstrated and known, not because the immateriality of God is the true cause of his immortality, but because in our mode of understanding it stands as its cause, as if the immortality of God were really caused, its immateriality would be its true cause. Which suffices for a demonstration διότι.

Latin:

II.

QUemadmodum autem aliud est Deum rectè agnoscere & colere; aliud quæ ad Dei agnitionem cultumque pertinent, ex suis principiis deducere, explicare, & confirmare: ita & alius est habitus, quo illa; alius quo hæc præstamus. Hunc Theologiæ; illum religionis habitum rectiùs dixeris.

In disciplinis theoreticis ejusdem habitus est objectum suum speculari, sive scientificè cognoscere, & id docere, aliisque explicare. In practicis autem res secus habet. Non statim qui docere potest, quid sit virtus, quibus principiis & actionibus acquirenda, quæ & quomodo vitanda sint extrema &c. virtuosus etiam est, & secundum virtutem operari potest; nec qui virtuosus est, & secundum virtutem operari potest, statim docere & aliis explicare potest, quæ ad virtutem comparandam requiruntur. Qua de re, qui vult, videat pluribus disserentem Aristotelem lib. I. Eudem. c. V. In Theologia similiter non idem habitus est, quo docemus, quæ ad Dei agnitionem & cultum pertinent; & quo Deum rectè agnoscimus & colimus. Nam Deum agnoscere & colere cadit etiam in homines simplices & literarum rudes, quos ut Theologos nemo dicit, ita nec habitum, quo Deum rectè agnoscunt & colunt, Theologiam facilè quis dixerit. Contrà docere, quæ ad Dei agnitionem & cultum pertinent, cadit etiam in homines improbos, qui, recto Dei cultu susque deque habito, impie & flagitiose vivunt. Alius ergo habitus est, quo Deum conveniente cultu prosequimur; alius, quo quæ ad verum Dei cultum pertinent, docemus. Illum religionis; hunc Theologiæ habitum rectiùs dixeris.

III.

Habitus, quo ad Dei agnitionem & cultum quæ pertinent, ductu luminis naturæ docemus, scientia est.

I. Scientiam esse Theologiam Naturalem patet ex requisitis scientiæ. Est enim habitus evidens, circa objectum necessarium occupatus, deducens conclusiones suas ex principiis necessariis. Quæ enim de Deo ejusque cultu conveniente Theologia Naturalis tradit, ea accersit ex suis genuinis, iisque evidentibus principiis, quæque necessariæ sunt veritatis.

II. Cùm verò scientia sit habitus demonstrativus; demonstratio autem alia sit τῶ ὅτι, alia τῶ διότι, quarum hæc à priori ex principiis primis, immediatis, notioribus, & prioribus, & quæ conclusionis causam continent, suas infert conclusiones, causamque cur res sit, ostendit; illa à posteriori & ex effectu probat rem esse: Theologia Naturalis scientia est, quæ utroque demonstrationum genere utitur.

III. Et à posteriori quidem atque ab effectu argumentatur ea ferè semper in parte prima, quæ est de fine objectivo, Deo scilicet, ejusque essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus. Quia enim Deus nullas sive sui esse sive suarum perfectionum causas habet, imò sub nostram, Viatorum, cognitionem non cadit, nisi per effectus & conceptus, ab illis desumtos, res ipsa loquitur, quòd quæ ei intrinsece conveniunt, demonstrari de ipso non possint à priori, per causam, propter quam res sit, sed tantùm à posteriori, ab iis, quæ sunt in effectibus, nempe in rebus creatis, concludendo ad ea, quæ in Deo, velut illarum causa, sunt.

IV. A priori autem & ex principiis primis, immediatis, & quæ conclusionis causam continent, argumentatur eadem in illa potissimùm parte, quæ est de mediis consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis. Nam perfectiones Dei essentiales, à posteriori demonstratæ

& cognitæ, sunt causa cultus, Deo debiti (in quo ferè solo media consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis ratio sibi relicta constituit) & inferunt conclusiones practicas, eundem præscribentes, demonstratione διότι, & quæ causam, propter quam res est, continet.

V. Quandoque tamen utitur eadem etiam in parte prima demonstratione à priori, sed rariùs, & tum demùm, cùm una perfectio divina, à posteriori demonstrata & cognita, ad aliam nostro modo intelligendi se habet ut causa sive ratio à priori, sicut v. g. immaterialitas in Deo habet se nostro modo intelligendi ad ejus immortalitatem ut causa illius, sive ut ejus ratio à priori. Tunc enim ex una perfectione, à posteriori demonstrata & cognita, alia perfectio divina demonstrari potest demonstratione διότι, v. g. immortalitas Dei ex ejus immaterialitate demonstrata & cognita, demonstrari potest, non quòd Dei immaterialitas vera causa sit immortalitatis ipsius, sed quòd nostro modo intelligendi se ut ejus causa habeat, ut si immortalitas Dei realiter causaretur, immaterialitas ipsius vera ejus causa esset. Quod ad demonstrationem διότι sufficit.


### IV Natural Theology is, moreover, a practical science

IV.

Natural Theology is, moreover, a practical science.

I. Aristotle, Metaphysics VI, ch. 1, distinguishes sciences into speculative and practical. He calls those speculative whose end is truth, or, which amounts to the same thing, which stop ultimately at the knowledge of truth and do not tend further toward any operation; but practical, those whose end is a certain practice, or which do not stop ultimately at the knowledge of truth, but tend further toward some operation.

II. In that part which concerns the means of obtaining blessedness in God, Natural Theology is without doubt practical. For it is occupied with conclusions that prescribe the right worship of God, to be deduced from known divine perfections, which, as they are formally practical or directive of some operation, so also Natural Theology, in this part at least, is a formally practical science. For by the very fact that its conclusions are formally practical, and direct the will toward practice or operation, it does not stop at the mere knowledge of truth, but tends toward practice through those very practical conclusions which it introduces. In the former part, however, by which it is occupied in the consideration of the divine essence and the essential perfections of God, it is not formally practical, but speculative. For the conclusions by which the perfections of God are inferred from created things are formally speculative, not practical. For they prescribe nothing to be done or omitted. In which part one might perhaps number Natural Theology among the speculative sciences, but taken as a whole, one might call it partly speculative and partly practical, in the manner in which Thomas in p. 1. q. 1. a. IV. called Revealed Theology partly speculative and partly practical, because it treats partly of God and partly of human acts.

III. We reckon it among the sciences that are simply practical. Our reason is: because even in that part where it treats of God and His essential perfections, it does not stop at the mere knowledge of truth, but whatever it delivers there, it transfers afterwards to inferring practical conclusions, prescribing the right worship of God, as will be shown below, and thus even that part which is about God is in some way practical, namely, virtually. For a science to be called simply practical, it suffices that it does not stop at the mere knowledge of truth, but tends further toward practice or operation, even if not all its conclusions are formally practical, provided that those which are not formally practical are used in the same science to infer other formally practical conclusions, and thus are transferred to practice at least mediately, namely, through the mediation of other conclusions which they infer. On this matter, see what Gregory of Rimini discusses accurately in Prol. in I. Sent. q. V. art. II. and what we, with God's help, are about to treat regarding this matter below in the following chapter III.

Latin:

IV.

Est autem Theologia Naturalis scientia practica.

I. Aristoteles VI. Met. c. 1. distinguit scientias in speculativas & practicas. Speculativas dicit, quarum finis est veritas, sive quod eodem redit, quæ ultimò sistunt in cognitione veritatis, nec longiùs ad aliquam operationem tendunt; Practicas verò, quarum finis est praxis quædam, sive quæ non sistunt ultimò in cognitione veritatis, sed longius ad aliquam operationem tendunt.

II. Eâ parte, quæ est de mediis consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis, Theologia Naturalis citra dubium practica est. Occupatur enim in conclusionibus, quæ rectum Dei cultum præscribunt, ex perfectionibus divinis cognitis deducendis, quæ ut formaliter practicæ sive operationis alicujus directivæ sunt, ita & Theologia Naturalis, hac quidem parte, scientia formaliter practica est. Eo ipso enim quòd ejus conclusiones formaliter practicæ sunt, & voluntatem ad praxin sive operationem dirigunt, non sistit ipsa in cognitione veritatis nuda, sed tendit ad praxin per illas ipsas, quas infert, conclusiones practicas. Priori autem parte, qua occupatur in consideratione divinae essentiae & perfectionum Dei essentialium, eadem formaliter practica non est, sed speculativa. Conclusiones enim, quibus Dei perfectiones ex rebus creatis inferuntur, formaliter speculativae sunt, non practicae. Nihil enim agendum omittendumve praescribunt. Qua parte Theologiam Naturalem quis forte in scientiis speculativis numeraverit, totaliter vero sumtam partim speculativam, partim practicam dixerit, eum in modum, quo Theologiam Revelatam Thomas in p. 1. q. 1. a. IV. partim speculativam, partim practicam dixit, quod partim de Deo, partim de actibus humanis agat.

III. Nos accensemus eam scientiis simpliciter practicis. Ratio nostra est: quia ea etiam parte, qua de Deo ejusque perfectionibus essentialibus agit, non sistit in nuda veritatis cognitione, sed quaecunque ibi tradit, transfert postea ad inferendas conclusiones practicas, rectum Dei cultum praescribentes, ut infra ostendetur, atque adeo ea etiam parte, quae de Deo est, aliquo modo practica est, virtualiter scilicet. Ad scientiam vero, ut simpliciter practica dicatur, sufficit, quod non in nuda veritatis cognitione sistat, sed ulterius ad praxin sive operationem tendat, licet non omnes ejus conclusiones formaliter practicae sint, modo quae formaliter practicae non sunt, in eadem scientia ad alias formaliter practicas conclusiones inferendas adhibeantur, & sic mediate saltem, mediantibus scilicet aliis, quas inferunt, conclusionibus, ad praxin transferantur. Qua de re videantur, quae accurate disserit Gregorius Ariminensis in Prol. in I. Sent. q. V. art. II. & quae nos infra in seq. cap. III. hac de re bono cum Deo acturi sumus.


### V. Since Natural Theology is a practical science, the consideration of its end…

V.

Since Natural Theology is a practical science, the consideration of its end will claim the first place in it.

In every action and every active science, the first thing that offers itself to be known is the end. For by it the will of the agent is moved for acting; and from the same knowledge practical science deduces its conclusions, by which the agent is directed in acting. The knowledge of the end, therefore, is prior to the action, which is for the sake of the end, and to the means leading to the end: indeed, the end known in practical sciences is the reason for knowing the means, and contains within itself virtually, as has been said, the rule of the entire remaining treatment.

VI.

But the end, for the sake of which Natural Theology exists, and to which it ultimately refers everything that it delivers, is man's beatitude and highest good.

I. That the ultimate end of Natural Theology is rightly established in man's beatitude is easily shown. For first, Natural Theology, as it is the noblest of all sciences, so it is also occupied with the noblest and most perfect end of all. But the noblest and most perfect end of all is the beatitude of man and his highest good. Then the same, as has been shown, is by its intrinsic nature a practical science concerning God as man's ultimate end and highest good. It is, however, common to all practical sciences which are occupied with some thing viewed by way of an end and a good, that they do not consider it for the sake of idle speculation, but for the sake of its being effected or obtained, so that they also explain the causes of its being effected or obtained, and prescribe the means. Therefore, neither does Natural Theology consider God, as man's end and highest good, for the sake of idle speculation, but as an end and good to be attained by man, so that it declares the principles and causes of attaining the same, and prescribes the means, as far as can be done by the guidance of the light of nature, and thus has as its ultimate end the attainment of God as man's end and highest good. But what else is the attainment of the ultimate end and highest good of man than his beatitude? Thirdly, man is undoubtedly subjected to Theology, and is its subject, as one to be made blessed. For he is subjected to it as a science concerning God, as the ultimate end and highest good to be attained by man. Therefore he is subjected to it for the sake of beatitude: since the attainment of the ultimate end and highest good of man, as has been said, is nothing other than his beatitude. Therefore, man's beatitude is his ultimate end. Nor, finally, can any other ultimate end of Natural Theology be given than the beatitude of man. For whatever other end you may assign to it, it will always be sought for the sake of something else, and it will not be the ultimate end. If you say its end is the knowledge of God, you have not stated the ultimate end, unless you constitute the very beatitude of man in the knowledge of God. For just as nothing, besides beatitude, can satisfy the appetite of man, so neither can the knowledge of God, which is not the beatitude of man and his ultimate end, satisfy him. But if you say the worship of God is its end, again you have not stated the ultimate end. For the worship of God is prescribed to man in Natural Theology, not for its own sake, but for the sake of obtaining beatitude by the grace and gift of God. But that which is not prescribed or taught in Natural Theology for its own sake, but for the sake of something else, is not its ultimate end. Since, therefore, all things which are taught in Natural Theology for their own sake are ultimately referred to the beatitude of man, it must be admitted that this is its ultimate end.

II. Someone might say: No one can attain beatitude by the help and support of Natural Theology. Therefore, the beatitude of man is not its ultimate end. For just as a power that is not brought into act is in vain, so also is a science whose end cannot be obtained through it in vain. But God and nature do nothing in vain.

III. I reply that the antecedent is not universally true concerning man, viewed in whatever state he may be. For in the primeval state, when sin and death did not yet exist, man could attain beatitude by the help and support of Natural Theology. For he could, under its guidance, reach such a knowledge of God and of divine worship as was necessary for attaining beatitude by His grace and gift: he also possessed integral and perfect powers to perform the worship and obedience owed to God, without defect or sin. But that now in the state of sin no one attains to beatitude by the help and support of Natural Theology is accidental, and happens by the fault of our first parents, by which they lost for themselves and for all their posterity the powers concreated with them both correctly to know God, and to love the same above all things and to worship him sincerely, and on the contrary they contracted, both for themselves and for their descendants, on the part of the intellect indeed, most dense darkness; but on the part of the will, a perverse propensity toward every evil. However, a power is not in vain which, accidentally and by the fault of men, is not brought into act.

IV. Nor is there any reason for anyone to object that there was one Natural Theology in the state of man when whole, and that there is another now in the same state when corrupt. That its ultimate end was the blessedness of man, and that this one's is not. I say, there is no reason for anyone to object thus. For although we do not deny that Natural Theology now in the state of corrupt man differs much from Natural Theology in the same state when primeval and whole, we nevertheless deny that one differs from the other in species, but whatever difference exists between the two, it all seems to concern the degrees of perfection and imperfection contained within the latitude of the same species. For the common notions about God and his worship, which are now by nature present in the minds of men, are not specifically different from the common notions about the same things which existed in the first man by the power of the concreated divine image. Nor does the knowledge of God and his essential perfections which is acquired today from created things through discourse differ in species from that which the protoplast could acquire for himself, and did acquire, from the same things in the state of integrity, although by reason of perfection the latter left the former far behind. But those things which are of the same species of knowledge, their end also is the same in species, even if one attains its end and the other fails of it. For this arises partly from their unequal perfection, in that one teaches what is necessary to be known for attaining the end more perfectly than the other, as has just been said, and partly from the diversity of the subjects, in that one is occupied with man, who enjoyed whole powers for knowing and doing as he ought whatever that theology prescribed to be known or done concerning God and his worship: but the other is occupied with man, corrupted by sin, and who [lacks] good powers for the same things which concerning It [the human mind] prescribes both what must be known and what must be done regarding God and His worship, as is fitting; yet it is utterly destitute of what must be known and done, and, under the guidance of the light of nature, it can neither rightly know God nor perform what pertains to His worship as it ought. Which, as is evident, is clearly accidental.

Latin:

V.

Cum practica scientia sit Theologia Naturalis, primam in ea considerationem ejus finis sibi vendicabit.

In omni actione omnique scientia activa primum, quod se cognoscendum offert, finis est. Ab eo enim movetur voluntas agentis ad agendum; & ex eodem cognito deducit scientia practica suas conclusiones, quibus agens in agendo dirigitur. Cognitio finis igitur prior est actione, quæ est propter finem, & mediis, ad finem ducentibus: imò finis cognitus in scientiis practicis est ratio cognoscendi media, continetque in se virtualiter, uti dictum, regulam totius reliquæ tractationis.

VI.

Finis verò, cujus gratiâ Theologia Naturalis est, & ad quem omnia, quæ tradit, ultimò refert, hominis beatitudo & bonum summum est.

I. Finem ultimum Theologiæ Naturalis rectè constitui in hominis beatitudine, facilè ostenditur. Primùm enim Theologia Naturalis, ut scientiarum omnium nobilissima est, ita & circa finem omnium nobilissimum & perfectissimum occupatur. Finis autem omnium nobilissimus & perfectissimus est beatitudo hominis, ejusque summum bonum. Deinde eadem, uti ostensum, suâ intrinsecâ naturâ est scientia practica de Deo, ut hominis fine ultimo & bono summo. Est autem scientiis practicis omnibus, quæ circa rem aliquam per modum finis & boni spectatam, occupantur, commune, ut eam non otiosæ speculationis causâ considerent, sed ut efficiendam vel obtinendam, ita ut ejusdem efficiendæ vel obtinendæ causas quoque explicent, & media præscribant. Ergo nec Theologia Naturalis Deum, ut hominis finem & bonum summum, otiosæ speculationis causâ considerat, sed ut finem & bonum homini adipiscendum, ita ut ejusdem adipiscendi principia & causas declaret, & media, quoad ductu luminis naturæ fieri potest, præscribat, atque adeò pro fine ultimo habet adeptionem Dei, ut hominis finis & boni summi. Adeptio autem finis ultimi & boni summi hominis, quid aliud est, quàm ejus beatitudo? Tertiò homo substernitur Theologiæ indubiè, estq; ejus subjectum, quâ beandus. Substernitur enim ei ut scientiæ de Deo, tanquam fine & b. no summo, homini adipiscendo. Ergo substernitur ei beatitudinis causâ: cùm adeptio finis ultimi & boni summi hominis, uti dictum, nihil aliud sit, quam ejus beatitudo. Ergo hominis beatitudo est ejus finis ultimus. Nec quarto denique alius Theologiæ Naturalis finis ultimus, quam hominis beatitudo, dari potest. Quemcunque enim alium ei assignaveris finem, semper is propter aliud expetetur, finisque ultimus non erit. Si finem ejus dixeris cognitionem Dei, ultimum finem non dixeris, nisi in cognitione Dei ipsam hominis beatitudinem constituas. Ut enim nihil, præter beatitudinem, appetitum hominis satiare potest, ita nec cognitio Dei, quæ beatitudo hominis & finis ejus ultimus non est, eum satiare potest. Sin Dei cultum ejus finem dixeris, rursum finem ultimum non dixeris. Cultus Dei enim præscribitur homini in Theologia Naturali, non propter se, sed propter adipiscendam Dei gratia & dono beatitudinem. Quod autem non propter se in Theologia Naturali præscribitur, aut traditur, sed propter aliud, id non est ejus finis ultimus. Cum ergo quæ per se in Theologia Naturali traduntur, ultimo ad hominis beatitudinem omnia referantur, hanc ejus finem ultimum esse fatendum est.

II. Dicat quis: Theologiæ Naturalis ope & adminiculo beatitudinem nemo consequi potest. Ergo beatitudo hominis non est ejus finis ultimus. Ut enim frustra est potentia, quæ non traducitur in actum, ita & scientia, cujus finis per eam obtineri non potest, frustra est. Deus autem & natura nihil faciunt frustra.

III. Resp. antecedens non esse universaliter verum de homine, in quocunque ejus statu spectato. In statu primævo enim, cum peccatum & mors nondum esset, poterat homo Theologiæ Naturalis ope & adminiculo beatitudinem consequi. Poterat enim, ejus ductu, ad tantam pertingere cognitionem Dei cultusque divini, quanta ad consequendam, ejus gratia & dono, beatitudinem necessaria erat: pollebat etiam viribus integris & perfectis ad cultum obsequiumque Deo debitum, absque defectu peccatoque præstandum. Quod autem nunc in statu peccati nemo Theologiæ Naturalis ope & adminiculo ad beatitudinem pertingit, per accidens est, & primorum parentum culpa fit, qua & sibi & suæ posteritati toti perdiderunt vires sibi concreatas cum ad Deum rectè cognoscendum, tum ad eundem super omnia diligendum fincerèque colendum, & contrà contraxerunt cùm sibi tum posteris suis ex parte intellectus quidem tenebras densissimas; ex parte voluntatis autem perversam in nullum non malum pronitatem. Non autem frustra est potentia, quæ per accidens & hominum culpâ in actum non traducitur.

IV. Neque est, quod quis excipiat, aliam fuisse Theologiam Naturalem in statu hominis integro, aliam esse nunc in ejusdem statu corrupto. Illius finem ultimum fuisse hominis beatitudinem, hujus non esse. Non, inquam, est, quod sic quis excipiat. Quamvis enim non inficiemur, Theologiam Naturalem nunc in statu hominis corrupto multùm differre à Theologia Naturali in statu ejusdem primævo & integro, negamus tamen specie alteram ab altera differre, sed quicquid discriminis inter utramque intercedit, id totum concernere videtur gradus perfectionis & imperfectionis, intra latitudinem ejusdem speciei contentæ. Notiones communes enim de Deo ejusque cultu, quæ nunc mentibus hominum naturâ insunt, non specie diversæ sunt à communibus de iisdem notionibus, quæ in homine primo vi concreatæ imaginis divinæ existebant. Neque quæ ex rebus creatis hodiè per discursum acqviritur scientia de Deo ejusque perfectionibus essentialibus, specie differt ab illa, quam in statu integritatis protoplasti ex iisdem sibi comparare poterant, & comparabant, quamvis ratione perfectionis hæc illam longo post se intervallo relinqueret. Quæ autem scientiæ ejusdem sunt speciei, illarum etiam idem specie finis est, ut ut altera finem suum consequatur; altera eodem excidat. Hoc enim provenit partim ex inæquali illarum perfectione, quòd quæ ad consequendum finem cognitu necessaria sunt, una doceat perfectiùs, quàm altera, ut modò dictum, partim ex diversitate subjectorum, quòd una occupetur circa hominem, qui integris gaudebat viribus ad cognoscendum, agendumque pro eo ac oportebat, quæcunque de Deo ejusque cultu illa sive cognoscenda sive agenda præscribebat: altera verò occupetur circa hominem, peccato corruptum, & qui viribus bonis ad eadem, quæ de Deo ejusque cultu ipsa cùm cognoscenda tùm agenda præscribit, pro eo ac oportet, cognoscenda & facienda prorsus destituitur, & Deum, luminis naturæ ductu, nec cognoscere rectè, nec quæ ad ejus cultum pertinent, sicut oportet, præstare potest. Quod, uti patet, planè per accidens est.


### VII. Happiness, therefore, or the supreme good of man, includes two things in its…

VII.

Happiness, therefore, or the supreme good of man, includes two things in its concept: one, that thing in which the perfect and supreme good of man consists; the other, its attainment and enjoyment. The former can be called the objective end of Natural Theology; the latter, its formal end.

I. In practical sciences, the end is sometimes a practice or a certain operation, just as the end of the science of Ethics is operation according to virtue; sometimes it is both an operation and some work to be produced, just as the end of οἰκοδομικῆς [architecture] is building and a house; sometimes it is an operation and at the same time some pre-existing good to be obtained through it, just as the end of χρηματιστικῆς [money-making] is wealth existing in the world, and the acquisition of it. When the end of a science, besides the operation, is some thing to be produced or obtained through the operation, then the end is rightly distinguished into formal and objective.

II. That thing for the sake of which the science exists, to be produced or obtained, is called the objective [end]. The formal [end] is the operation itself by which that thing is produced or obtained. The former is called objective because it is the object of that operation by which it is produced or obtained. The latter is called the formal end because it is the formal reason itself by which that thing is produced or obtained. Thomas in I. II. q. I. a. VIII. distinguishes between the end OF WHICH and the end BY WHICH, in clearly the same sense. He calls the end of which the thing itself in which the nature of the good is found. Which he also calls the end AS A THING. He constitutes the end BY WHICH in the use or attainment of that thing, which he also calls the end AS USE: e.g., the end of the miser is money as a thing, or the possession of money as use. Compare the same author ibid. in q. II. a. VII. in the body and in q. III. a. I. in the body. Where the end of which, and the end as a thing, is the same as the objective end; but the end by which, and as the use of a thing, is the same as the formal end.

III. Both taken together constitute one complete end.

VIII.

The objective end, or that thing in which the perfect and highest good of man consists, is one and only God. That the objective end of theology and the highest good of man consist in one God alone is evident from the preceding thesis VI, and Thomas shows this in I. II. q. II. a. VIII in this manner: Happiness is a perfect good, which totally quiets the appetite: otherwise it would not be the ultimate end if something still remained to be desired. Now the object of the will, which is the human appetite, is the universal good, just as the object of the intellect is the universal truth. From which it is evident that nothing can quiet the will of man except the universal good; which is not found in any created thing, but ONLY IN GOD: because every creature has participated goodness. Whence GOD ALONE can fulfill the will of man; according to what is said in Psalm 103: Who satisfies the desire with good things, etc. IN GOD ALONE, therefore, the happiness of man consists.

Latin:

VII.

Beatitudo igitur sive bonum hominis summum includit in suo conceptu duo: Unum, eam rem, in qua hominis bonum perfectum & summum consistit. Alterum ejus adeptionem & fruitionem. Illa Theologiæ Naturalis finis objectivus; hæc ejusdem formalis finis dici potest.

I. In scientiis practicis finis interdum est praxis sive operatio quædam, sicut scientiæ Ethicæ finis est operatio secundum virtutem; interdum operatio simul & opus aliquod efficiendum, sicut οἰκοδομικῆς finis est ædificatio & domus; interdum operatio & simul bonum aliquod præexistens, per eam obtinendum, sicut χρηματιστικῆς finis sunt divitiæ, in mundo existentes, & illarum acquisitio. Quando finis scientiæ, præter operationem, est res aliqua per operationem efficienda, aut obtinenda, tùm rectè finis distinguitur in formalem & objectivum.

II. Objectivus dicitur ea res, cujus efficiendæ aut adipiscendæ causâ scientia est. Formalis est ipsa operatio, quâ res illa efficitur aut obtinetur. Ille dicitur objectivus, quòd objectum sit illius operationis, quâ efficitur aut obtinetur. Hic formalis finis appellatur, quòd sit ipsa ratio formalis, quâ res illa efficitur aut obtinetur. Thomas in I. II. q. I. a. VIII. distinguit inter finem CUJUS & finem QUO, sensu planè eodem. Finem cujus dicit ipsam rem, in qua ratio boni invenitur. Quam etiam finem UT REM vocat. Finem QUO in usu vel adeptione illius rei constituit, quem & finem UT USUM appellat: v. g. finis avari est pecunia ut res, vel possessio pecuniæ, ut usus. Confer eundem ibid. in q. II. a. VII. in corp. & in q. III. a. I. in corp. Ubi finis cujus, & finis ut res, idem quod objectivus; finis quo autem, & ut usus rei, idem quod formalis finis est.

III. Uterque junctim sumtus constituit unum completum finem.

VIII.

Finis objectivus sive res illa, in qua hominis bonum perfectum & summum consistit, est unus & solus Deus. Quod in uno solo Deo Theologiæ finis objectivus & hominis bonum summum consistat, patet ex præced. thesi VI. idque Thomas in I. II. q. II. a. VIII. ostendit hunc in modum: Beatitudo est bonum perfectum, quod totaliter quietat appetitum: alioquin non esset ultimus finis, si adhuc restaret aliquid appetendum. Objectum autem voluntatis, quæ est appetitus humanus, est universale bonum, sicut objectum intellectus est universale verum. Ex quo patet, quòd nihil potest quietare voluntatem hominis, nisi bonum universale; quod non invenitur in aliquo creato, sed SOLUM IN DEO: quia omnis creatura habet bonitatem participatam. Unde SOLUS DEUS voluntatem hominis implere potest; secundum quod dicitur in Psal. 103. Qui replet in bonis desiderium &c. IN SOLO igitur DEO beatitudo hominis consistit.


### IX. The formal [end] consists in the attainment of the perfect and highest good,…

IX.

The formal [end] consists in the attainment of the perfect and highest good, which resides in God, which in reality will be a certain operation of the rational soul concerning God, and that a perfect one, by which we are made participants of His goodness in such a way that our appetite is satisfied by it. Which is otherwise simply called the happiness of man. I. Although happiness includes both partial ends of man, objective and formal, in its concept: For neither is one happy unless he is with God and enjoys His goodness; nor does any operation of the soul deserve the name of happiness unless it includes God as its object and makes man a participant of His goodness; yet by usage of speech, the attainment of the highest good, or that operation of the soul by which we possess and enjoy God as our highest good, is accustomed to be called simply the happiness of man. is accustomed. In which sense Thomas also in 1. II. q. I. a. VIII. says, Beatitude names the attainment of the ultimate end. And q. II. a. VII. The thing itself, which is sought as an end, is that in which beatitude consists, and which makes one blessed: but the attainment of this thing is called beatitude.

II. That the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good consists in a certain operation of the rational soul, the very notion and concept of beatitude indicates. For the common people and the wise alike accept beatitude and a blessed life, to be blessed and to live blessedly, indiscriminately and as the same things, as Aristotle teaches in Nic. book I, ch. IV. But since vital operations in man are threefold: vegetative, sensitive, and rational, the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good can be established in none other than the operation of the rational soul. For the highest good is the proper good of man, which belongs to him as he is man. Therefore it is also obtained through the proper operation of man, and that which belongs to him as man. However, the operations of the sensitive soul are common to man with the brutes; those of the vegetative soul are common even with plants. It remains, therefore, that the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good of man consists in the operation of the rational soul alone. For this alone is proper to man, and belongs to him as man. On which matter the praised Aristotle discourses elegantly in Nic. book I, ch. VII.

III. That the same consists in a certain operation of the rational soul concerning God is understood from the preceding theses VI. and VIII. and is further shown thus: The beatitude of man, by the consent of all, is a good absolutely perfect and highest, which is sought only for its own sake, not for the sake of another, and by the obtaining of which the appetite is satisfied and rests. Therefore it is an operation of the rational soul concerning a thing absolutely and perfectly good, whose goodness is sought only for its own sake, not for the sake of another: for otherwise it could not satisfy the appetite of man. But such a good, besides the one and only God, is not given. For all other goods are created and finite, and as they have their goodness from another more perfect and better being, namely from God, so they are ordered to God, nor can they satisfy the appetite of man, but always leave a desire for that more perfect and better Being, on whom they depend in their being, and have their goodness, namely God. God therefore alone is that ultimate and absolutely highest good, which is from itself, and from which all other things have their goodness: who is also commonly conceived and defined by this, that he is the most perfect and most excellent mind, than which nothing better and more perfect can be or be thought. Therefore, in the sole operation of the rational soul, which is occupied with that absolutely and perfectly highest good, God, consists the attainment of the highest good and man's happiness.

IV. The same consists in the most perfect operation concerning God. For otherwise, if it were imperfect, it could not satisfy man's appetite. For either it would not reach every reason of good that is in God, or it would not perfectly reach that which it did reach, and thus would always leave a desire for a certain more perfect operation, by which it would reach both every reason of good that is in God, and in a perfect manner.

V. But just as the faculties of the rational soul are two: intellect and will: so also its operation concerning God is given as twofold: one of the intellect; the other of the will. The former consists in the knowledge of God; the latter in his love, veneration, and worship. Through both, man reaches the reason of good which is in God, and is in a certain way made a participant of it. For by knowledge our intellect, as it is joined with every known thing, so also is it joined with the absolutely perfect and highest good, God, when known, so that in some way they become the same. By love, however, the will adheres to God as its absolutely perfect and highest good, and venerates and worships him with acts of trust, fear, hope, invocation, thanksgiving, and moral virtues, directed to his praise and glory. But for the state of the way, both operations are imperfect. The former indeed: because while we are on the way, we know God only abstractively and through foreign species, taken from created things. Which, as is evident, is an imperfect knowledge in many ways, and cannot fulfill and satisfy man's appetite. The latter, however; because the will also, for the state of the way, is not borne toward acts of love and worship in God otherwise than as he is at least abstractively and thus imperfectly known, and with a desire for a certain of a more perfect union with Him. And thus does each operation of the rational soul stand in relation to God in man as a Wayfarer, even before the fall. In the state of sin, however, they are imperfect for another reason as well, namely on account of the corruption of nature, by which it comes to pass that the intellect stands in relation to even those things which are the most manifest of all, as the eyes of bats to the light of day, as Aristotle acknowledges in Metaphysics II, ch. 1; the will, however, turned away from God, inclines toward every evil, so that although it cannot but embrace the universal and highest good in general with some act of simple complacency and love, it nevertheless turns away from God, as the good of man, to be worshipped with a pure mind free from carnal concupiscences and with perfect holiness of life, and is carried more quickly toward any earthly, fleeting, and perishable things than toward Him, being indeed destitute of all good powers. But if anyone has become accustomed to living by right instruction and good education according to the rules of honesty and in accordance with virtue, this life of his will nevertheless still be imperfect in many ways, both on account of the disordered motions of concupiscence, which greatly deform the actions of the virtues, and on account of manifold defects in the various circumstances of his actions.

VI. From which it follows that the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good does not consist in the operation of the rational soul concerning God in the state of the Way, whether you consider man the Wayfarer in the state of his primeval integrity, or the same in the state of sin and corruption. For it is, as has been shown, imperfect in both states, and in the latter far more imperfect than in the former.

VII. It remains, therefore, that it consists in the operation of the rational soul concerning God in the state of the other life or the Fatherland. But what the specific nature of that operation is, and how it differs from the operation, both of the intellect and of the will, concerning God in the state of the Way, natural reason, led by the light of nature, cannot investigate and distinctly explain.

VIII. In the state of integrity, where there was no death, man could have known, if he had persisted in his integrity, that he would be led as a gratuitous reward for his obedience, as to his soul, to the perfect fruition of God; as to his body, however, he would be exempted from the danger of dying, as one who then he was able not to die, thereafter he would not be able to die, about to live blessedly in soul and body forever: He was also able to know, the enjoyment of God being established both in the knowledge and in the love of God far more perfectly than those in which he rejoiced in the state of the Way. Indeed, his will also seems even then to have desired a more perfect knowledge of God, with the hope of the same being actually attained at some time: since Eve, by the promise of perfect knowledge, by which she would be like God in the future, although fraudulent and false, so easily allowed herself to be induced by the Serpent to transgress the divine law, Gen. III. 5, the example of which Adam followed with equal ease, moved, as it seems, by the same promise. Nor does it seem inconsistent with the truth that it was known to the first-formed before the fall that God would in his own time elevate their intellect to an intuitive and clear knowledge of himself, not, however, by the guidance of the light of nature, but from divine revelation. For besides the fact that it is doubtful and controversial among the Scholastics whether the possibility of an intuitive and clear knowledge of God being communicated to the human intellect can be certainly known and demonstrated from the light of nature, this is placed beyond controversy, that the beatific vision is a supernatural gift, to be conferred upon the human intellect by the gratuitous and free will of God, which, that it would at some time be actually conferred upon him, by the grace of God, as a reward of obedience, could no more be known from the light of nature than other supernatural gifts depending on the free will of God.

IX. In the state of sin, however, and after death entered into the world through sin, man can know by the guidance of the light of nature,

(1) that after this life there will be another: since it is evident from its operations that the soul of man is immortal and remains surviving after death.

(2) In it, it will be well for the good and ill for the evil, with God as the rewarder of the good and the avenger of crimes, rewarding the good deeds of the former with a blessed life, but punishing the evil deeds of the latter with penalties. For God does not always reward the good and punish the evil in this life, but, as experience testifies, the affairs of the evil sometimes prosper in this life are superior to those of the good. Which Asaph well observed in Psalm 73:6 et seq. Therefore, in the other life He will reward the former and punish the latter.

(3) That the blessedness of souls surviving after death is established in the knowledge of God can be shown in the same manner in which Aristotle, in Nicomachean Ethics Book X, chapter VIII, shows that the blessedness of God consists in the contemplative life; because, namely, neither poiesis nor praxis fall to them, as they are spirits. For it is not fitting for them to build, to prepare medicines for the sake of restoring health, etc. Nor are the actions of moral virtues, e.g., justice, fortitude, liberality, temperance, etc., fitting for them, inasmuch as these are actions occupied with affections and goods of fortune, which they lack, since they are devoid of bodies, and do not need these. But with praxis or action, and poiesis or production, taken away from an intelligent nature, what remains for it in which its happiness and blessedness can be established, besides the contemplation of God, as its absolutely perfect and highest good?

(4) Nevertheless, by the guidance of the light of nature, man cannot know that the souls of the good, surviving after death, will know God intuitively and clearly, as He is in Himself, for the reason brought forward a little before in no. VIII.

(5) Nor can he know with certainty that the bodies of the dead are at some time to be resurrected and reunited with their souls. For, to say nothing now of whether the possibility of those to be resurrected from the ashes into which they have been resolved, from the number of those same dead bodies, can be demonstrated from the light of nature, that they will in fact be recalled to life at some time is a mystery and a matter of the free divine will. For God could have, if He had willed, left the bodies of the dead in death, with only the souls, as immortal spirits, reserved for another immortal life. But those things which depend upon the free will of God can be known with certainty to the race of mortals as being about to happen at some time only when God reveals them and makes His will known.

X. But here it can be objected that in practical sciences the ultimate end must be distinctly known: for from it must be derived the rule of operation, by which one must arrive at that: which cannot be done, unless the ultimate end is distinctly known.

XI. Response: Here we are dealing with the formal end of Natural Theology. However, in practical sciences, of which a twofold end is given, formal and objective, it is not the formal, but the objective that contains radically and virtually the rule of right operation, by which one must arrive at it, and this must be known to the extent that it suffices for knowing the means and the rule of operation to be derived from it. The formal end, however, in practical sciences is sometimes the operation which the science itself prescribes and directs, and by which the objective is efficiently produced. And this must indeed be distinctly known, not indeed before the science is acquired, but in it and through it: just as, for example, the building or construction of a house is not distinctly known before the acquired science of ὀικοδομικὴν, nor before the acquired Medical science is the prescription and application of medicines for recovering the health of a sick person distinctly known, but only in it and through it. Sometimes, however, the ultimate formal end is a certain operation which the science itself does not prescribe or direct, but to which one must arrive by the promise, grace, and liberality of another; of which kind at present is the intuitive knowledge of God, which God, out of grace and liberality, will bestow after this life upon those who shall have departed from here with Him propitious. And the reason for this end is on a par with the objective end, to be obtained by the promise, gift, and grace of another, e.g., with a prize proposed to athletes by the liberality of another, by which athletes can be moved to wrestle bravely, even if they do not have it distinctly known whether it consists in gold or in silver. For it suffices in this kind of end if it is known confusedly under the aspect of a good and suitable thing, by which the will of the agent can be moved to act, and specifically for the science of Natural Theology it suffices if it is known confusedly that the soul of a man, departing from this life with God propitious, will live thereafter happily by the gift and grace of God, and that his felicity and blessedness is constituted in the vital operation of the intellect and will concerning God, as his absolutely perfect and highest good, and that much more perfect than such as in this life can fall into the intellect and will of man, although distinctly, that it was not known in what the vision or intuitive knowledge of God consists.
