For as to the means of obtaining it from God, to be prescribed through the science of Natural Theology, as far as can be done by the guidance of the light of nature, a knowledge of the objective end as great as can be had through innate notions and the consideration of this universe, together with this confused knowledge of the formal end, can suffice.

Latin:

IX.

Formalis consistit in adeptione perfecti & summi, quod in Deo residet, boni, quæ quoad rem, erit operatio quædam animæ rationalis circa Deum, eaque perfecta, quâ bonitatis ipsius ita reddimur participes, ut eâ appetitus noster satietur. Quæ aliàs simpliciter hominis beatitudo dicitur. I. Quamvis beatitudo finem hominis partialem utrumque, objectivum & formalem, in suo conceptu includat: Neque enim beatus est, nisi qui cum Deo est, & ejus bonitate fruitur; neque etiam animæ operatio ulla beatitudinis nomen meretur, nisi in quantum Deum, velut objectum suum, includit, & bonitatis ipsius hominem participem facit; ex usu loquendi tamen adeptio boni summi sive operatio illa animæ, quâ Deo velut nostro bono summo potimur & fruimur, simpliciter beatitudo hominis dici solet. solet. Quem in sensum & Thomas in 1. II. q. I. a. VIII. Beatitudo, inquit, nominat adeptionem ultimi finis. Et q. II. a. VII. Res ipsa, quæ appetitur ut finis, est id, in quo beatitudo consistit, & quod beatum facit : sed hujus rei adeptio vocatur beatitudo.

II. Adeptionem finis ultimi & boni summi consistere in operatione quadam animæ rationalis, vel ipsa beatitudinis notio & conceptus indicat. Beatitudinem enim & vitam beatam, beatum esse & beatè vivere vulgus pariter & Sapientes promifcuè & pro iisdem accipiunt, docente Aristotele l. Nic. c. IV. Cùm verò operationes vitales in homine triplices sint : vegetativa, sensitiva & rationalis, adeptio finis ultimi & boni summi in nulla, quàm in operatione animæ rationalis, constitui potest. Bonum summum enim est bonum hominis proprium, quod ei, quà homo est, convenit. Ergo & per operationem hominis propriam, & quæ ei ut homini convenit, obtinetur. Operationes autem animæ sensitivæ homini cum brutis ; vegetativæ autem etiam cum plantis communes sunt. Relinquitur ergò, quòd in sola operatione animæ rationalis adeptio finis ultimi & boni summi hominis consistat. Hæc enim sola hominis propria est, eique ut homini convenit. Qua de re eleganter disserit laudatus Aristoteles l. Nic. c. VII.

III. Eandem consistere in operatione quadam animæ rationalis circa Deum, intelligitur ex præcedentibus thesibus VI. & VIII. & porro ita ostenditur : Beatitudo hominis, omnium consensu, est bonum absolutè perfectum & summum, quod tantùm propter se, non propter aliud expetitur, & quo obtento appetitus satiatur & quiescit. Ergo est operatio animæ rationalis circa rem absolutè & perfectè bonam, cujus bonitas tantùm propter se, non propter aliud expetitur : aliàs enim appetitum hominis satiare non posset. Hujusmodi autem bonum, præter unum & solum Deum, nullum datur. Cætera enim bona omnia creata & finita sunt, & ut ab alio ente perfectiori & meliori, à Deo scilicet, suam bonitatem habent, ita ad Deum ordinantur, nec satiare possunt hominis appetitum, sed relinquunt semper desiderium illius Entis perfectioris & melioris, à quo in suo esse dependent, suamque bonitatem habent, Dei scilicet. Deus igitur solus est ultimum illud & absolute summum bonum, quod a se est, & a quo res aliae omnes suam bonitatem habent : qui etiam vulgo concipitur & definitur per hoc, quod sit mens omnium perfectissima & excellentissima, qua nihil melius & perfectius esse aut cogitari possit. Ergo in sola operatione animae rationalis, quae circa bonum illud absolute & perfecte summum, Deum, occupatur, consistit summi boni adeptio hominisque beatitudo.

IV. Eadem consistit in operatione circa Deum perfectissima. Alias enim si imperfecta esset, satiare hominis appetitum non posset. Vel enim non omnem, quae in Deo est, rationem boni attingeret, vel non perfecte attingeret, quam attingeret, & sic semper relinqueret desiderium cujusdam operationis perfectioris, qua & omnem, quae in Deo est, rationem boni, & modo perfecto attingeret.

V. Quemadmodum autem facultates animae rationalis duae sunt: intellectus & voluntas : ita & operatio ejus circa Deum duplex datur: Una intellectus; altera voluntatis. Illa in cognitione Dei; haec in ejusdem amore, veneratione & cultu consistit. Utraque attingit homo rationem boni, quae in Deo est, ejusque quodammodo redditur particeps. Cognitione enim intellectus noster, ut alias cum omni re cognita, ita & cum bono absolute perfecto & summo, Deo, cognito conjungitur, ut aliquo modo idem fiant. Amore autem voluntas inhaeret Deo velut suo absolute perfecto & summo bono, veneraturque & colit eum actibus fiduciae, timoris, spei, invocationis, gratiarum actionis, virtutumque moralium, ad ejus laudem & gloriam directis. Sed pro statu viae operatio utraque imperfecta est. Prior quidem: quia dum in via sumus, Deum cognoscimus abstractive tantum & per species alienas, a rebus creatis desumtas. Quae, uti patet, multis modis imperfecta cognitio est, hominisque appetitum explere & satiare non potest. Posterior vero; quia voluntas etiam, pro statu viae, actibus amoris cultusque in Deum aliter non fertur, quam ut abstractive saltem & sic imperfecte cognitus est, & cum desiderio cujusdam perfectioris cum ipso conjunctionis. Atque sic habet se utraque animæ rationalis operatio circa Deum in homine Viatore per se, etiam ante lapsum. In statu peccati autem etiam alia de causa imperfectæ sunt, nempe ob naturæ corruptionem, quâ fit, ut intellectus ad ea etiam, quæ manifestissima omnium sunt, ut vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei se habeat, agnoscente id Aristotele II. Met. c. I. voluntas verò, à Deo aversa, in nullum non malum propendeat, ut licet bonum universale & summum in communi non possit non aliquo simplicis complacentia & amoris actu amplecti, Deum tamen, ut bonum hominis, purâ & à carnalibus concupiscentiis liberâ mente, vitæque sanctimoniâ perfectâ, colendum aversetur potiùs, citiusque in terrena, fluxa & caduca quævis, quàm in ipsum sic feratur, omnibus quippe bonis viribus destituta. Quod si quis rectâ institutione & bonâ educatione juxta regulas honestatis & secundum virtutem vivere advetus sit, hæc tamen ejus vita adhuc multis modis imperfecta erit, cùm ob inordinatos concupiscentiæ motus, actiones virtutum valdè deformantes, tum ob defectus multiplices in variis actionum circumstantiis.

VI. Ex quo fluit, quod adeptio finis ultimi & boni summi non consistat in operatione animæ rationalis circa Deum in statu Viæ, sive hominem Viatorem in statu primævo & integritatis; sive eundem in statu peccati & corruptionis spectes. Est enim, uti ostensum, in statu utroque imperfecta, & in hoc longè imperfectior, quàm in illo.

VII. Relinquitur ergo, quod consistat in operatione animæ rationalis circa Deum in statu alterius vitæ sive Patriæ. Quæ autem operationis illius ratio specifica sit, & quid differat ab operatione, cùm intellectus tùm voluntatis, circa Deum in statu Viæ, ratio naturalis ductu luminis naturæ investigare & distinctè explicare non potest.

VIII. In statu integritatis, ubi mors non erat, nosse poterat homo, si in integritate suâ persisteret, se in gratuitum suæ obedientiæ præmium, quà animam ad fruitionem Dei perfectam perductum; quà corpus verò à periculo moriendi exemptum iri, ut qui tunc poterat non mori, posthac mori non posset, animâ & corpore in perpetuum beatè victurus: Cognoscere etiam poterat, fruitionem Dei constitutam cùm in cognitione, tùm in amore Dei longè perfectiori, quàm quibus in statu Viæ gaudebat. Quin & voluntas ejus videtur jam tùm cognitionem Dei perfectiorem desiderâsse, cùm spe ejusdem aliquando reapse consequendæ: cùm Eva pollicitatione scientiæ perfectæ, quâ Deo futura esset similis, quamvis fraudulentâ & falsâ, tam facilè passa sit à Serpente se induci ad transgrediendum legem divinam, Gen. III. 5. cujus exemplum & Adam pari facilitate secutus est, pollicitatione eâdem, ut videtur, permotus. Neque absonum à vero videtur, protoplastis ante lapsum cognitum fuisse, Deum suo tempore elevaturum esse ipsorum intellectum ad intuitivam & claram sui cognitionem, non tamen ductu luminis naturæ, sed ex divina revelatione. Præterquam enim quod dubium & inter Scholasticos controversum est, an possibilitas communicandæ hominis intellectui intuitivæ & claræ cognitionis Dei ex lumine naturæ certò cognosci & demonstrari possit, hoc extra controversiam positum est, visionem beatificam esse donum supernaturale, Dei gratuitâ & liberâ voluntate hominis intellectui conferendum, quam ei aliquando reapse, Dei gratiâ, in præmium obedientiæ collatum iri, non magis, quàm alia à Dei voluntate liberâ dependentia dona supernaturalia, ex lumine naturæ innotescere potuit.

IX. In statu peccati verò, & postquam mors per peccatum introiit in mundum, cognoscere potest homo ductu luminis naturæ,

(1) post hanc vitam futuram esse aliam: cùm hominis animam immortalem esse, & post mortem superstitem manere, ex ejus operationibus pateat.

(2) In ea bonis benè, malis malè futurum, Deo bonorum remuneratore & scelerum vindice illorum benefacta vitâ beatâ remunerante, horum malefacta autem pœnis vindicante. Neque enim Deus semper in hac vita bonos remuneratur & malos punit, sed, experientiâ teste, malorum res in hac vita interdum prosperiores sunt, quàm bonorum. Quod benè observavit Assaph Psal. LXXIII. 6. seq. Ergo in vita altera illos remunerabitur, hos puniet.

(3) Beatitudinem animarum, post mortem superstitum, in cognitione Dei constitutam, eundem in modum ostendi potest, quo Aristoteles lib. X. Nic. c. VIII. ostendit, beatitudinem Dei consistere in vita contemplativa; quia scilicet nec ποίησις nec praxis in eas, velut spiritus cadunt. Non enim eis convenit ædificare, valetudinis reparandæ causâ medicamenta parare &c. Neque actiones virtutum moralium, v. g. justitiæ, fortitudinis, liberalitatis, temperantiæ &c. eis conveniunt, utpote quæ actiones sunt circa affectus & bona fortunæ occupatæ, quorum illis, cùm corporum expertes sint, carent, his non egent. Ademptâ autem Naturæ intelligenti praxi sive actione, & ποίησει sive effectione, quid ei superest, in quo ejus felicitas & beatitudo constitui possit, præter contemplationem Dei, tanquam sui boni absolutè perfecti & summi?

(4) Non tamen ductu luminis naturæ homo cognoscere potest, quòd animæ bonorum, post mortem superstites, Deum intuitivè & clarè, ut in se est, cognituras sint, ob rationem, paulò ante n. VIII. adductam.

(5) Neque quòd corpora demortuorum aliquando resuscitanda & cum animabus redunienda sint, certò cognoscere potest. Ut enim de possibilitate resuscitandorum ex cineribus, in quos resoluta sunt, numero eorundem corporum demortuorum, an ex lumine naturæ demonstrari possit, nunc nihil dicamus, reapse ea aliquando in vitam revocatum iri, mysterium & liberæ voluntatis divinæ res est. Potuisset enim Deus, si voluisset, demortuorum corpora in morte relinquere, solis animabus, velut spiritibus immortalibus, alteri immortali vitæ reservatis. Quæ autem ex Dei liberâ voluntate dependent, ea aliquando futura esse, non nisi Deo revelante, suamque voluntatem patefaciente, mortalium generi certò innotescere potest.

X. Sed hîc objici potest, in scientiis practicis oportere finem ultimum esse distinctè cognitum: ex eo enim desumendam esse regulam operationis, quâ ad illum perveniendum est: quod fieri non possit, nisi finis ultimus distinctè cognitus sit.

XI. Resp. hîc agi de fine formali Theologiæ Naturalis. In scientiis practicis autem, quarum duplex datur finis, formalis & objectivus, non formalis, sed objectivus continet radicaliter & virtualiter regulam operationis rectæ, quâ ad eum perveniendum est, & hunc oportet in tantum esse cognitum, in quantum ad cognoscenda media & regulam operationis, inde desumendam, sufficit. Finis formalis autem in scientiis practicis interdum est operatio, quam scientia ipsa præscribit & dirigit, & quâ objectivus efficienter producitur. Et hanc oportet quidem esse distinctè cognitam, non quidem ante scientiam acquisitam, sed in illa & per illam: sicut v. g. ædificatio sive effectio domus non est distinctè cognita ante acquisitam scientiam ὀικοδομικὴν, nec ante acquisitam scientiam Medicam distinctè cognita est præscriptio & applicatio medicamentorum ad valetudinem, ægroto recuperandam, sed in ea demum & per eam. Interdum verò finis formalis ultimus est operatio quædam, quam scientia ipsa non præscribit aut dirigit, sed ad quam ex alterius promisso, gratiâ & liberalitate pervenienda; cujusmodi impræsentiarum est cognitio Dei intuitiva, quam Deus ex gratia & liberalitate post hanc vitam collaturus est his, qui se propitio hinc decesserint. Et hujus finis par ratio est cum fine objectivo, ex alterius promisso, dono & gratiâ obtinendo, v. g. cum præmio, palæstritis alterius liberalitate proposito, quo moveri possunt palæstritæ ad fortiter luctandum, licet distinctè, in auro? an in argento consistat, cognitum non habeant. Sufficit enim in hoc finium genere, si confusè sub ratione rei bonæ & convenientis, quâ agentis voluntas ad agendum moveri possit, cognitus sit, & speciatim ad scientiam Theologiæ Naturalis sufficit, si confusè cognitum sit, animam hominis, Deo propitio ex hac vita discedentis, victuram deinceps Dei dono & gratiâ beatè, ejusque felicitatem & beatitudinem constitutam in operatione vitali intellectus & voluntatis, circa Deum, velut suum absolutè perfectum & summum bonum, eaque multò perfectiori, quàm qualis in hac vita in hominis intellectum & voluntatem cadere potest, licet distinctè, quòd in visione sive intuitiva Cognitione Dei constitura sit, cognitum non fuerit. Ad media enim ejus à Deo impetrandæ, per scientiam Theologiæ Naturalis, quoad ductu luminis naturæ fieri potest, præscribenda, finis objectivi tanta, quanta per notitias infitas & hujus universi considerationem haberi potest, cognitio cum hac finis formalis cognitione confusa sufficere potest.


### X. Its subject is man the Wayfarer

X. Its subject is man the Wayfarer.

I. By subject we understand here the subject of operation, or that which is placed under the operation which Natural Theology prescribes for the sake of attaining blessedness. We shall treat of the subject of consideration or object later. The subject of operation, however, as in other practical sciences, so also here in Natural Theology, coheres closely with the end, and with it constitutes one adequate end. Wherefore it is commonly called the end FOR WHICH.

II. We establish the subject of operation here not, as in Revealed Theology, as man the sinner, but as man the Wayfarer. For Natural Theology was not granted to man, like Revealed Theology, only after the fall, as a remedy for sin and to reconcile sinful man with God; but its foundations were laid by God in creation itself, before man had become subject to sin and through sin to death. Whence it cannot provide for sinful man a suitable means for expiating sins and for his reconciliation with God. Man the Wayfarer, however, extends more broadly, and includes in its scope also man still established in his primal state.

III. That man the Wayfarer is rightly established as the subject of operation in Natural Theology is understood from the requirements of the subject of operation. For it is required for that in every practical science, both that it should lack that perfection which is its end, and that it should be able to become a participant of the same through the principles and means which are prescribed in it. Both of which for man the Wayfarer, by himself and in his primal state considered, it is agreed. For by this very fact, that he is a Wayfarer, that is, established on the way to attaining blessedness, he lacks that perfection which is the end for Natural Theology, namely, blessedness. He could, however, have become a partaker of it in his primordial state through the principles and means which are prescribed in it. But in the state of sin, man the Wayfarer cannot indeed become a partaker of blessedness through the principles and means which Natural Theology prescribes: but this is accidental. For it is accidental that man has sinned, and through sin has fallen from his end, for which he was created. By this, however, he does not now in the state of sin cease to be a subject of Natural Theology. For the practical acts which it itself prescribes bind him now also no less than in the state of integrity, although he cannot attain through them to the end for the sake of which they exist.

XI. The efficient cause of blessedness is God.

Aristotle investigates the efficient cause of blessedness in Nicomachean Ethics book I, chapter IX, and says among other things, if any other Θεῶν δώρημα (gift of the gods) is given to men, εὐδαιμονίαν θεόσδοτον εἶναι (that blessedness is God-given): since it is the best of human things; or if it is not θεόπεμπτος (sent by God), but is produced by virtue and some teaching or exercise, it is nevertheless to be numbered among the most divine things. The Philosopher, however, is dealing with the efficient cause of blessedness for the state of this life, and speaks therefore disjunctively, that it is either a gift given by God, or at least a most divine thing, and he adds that to inquire into this matter belongs to another place and institution. If it had been his purpose to deal with the blessedness of the soul surviving after death, he would undoubtedly have asserted without hesitation that it is θεόσδοτον or θεόπεμπτον, a gift given or sent by God. For the cause which he ascribes to the blessedness of this life in the same place, namely teaching, habit, and exercise, does not apply to it. For the soul surviving after death is not capable of teaching, habit, and exercise; nor is there a place in the other life for blessedness to be acquired through teaching and exercise: since for rewarding by blessedness a life here well spent, and for avenging by perpetual misery the crimes committed here, the other life is destined, not for blessedness to be finally acquired through teaching and exercise. To which is added, that the blessedness of the other life, even according to the dictate of reason, consists in the perfect knowledge of God, which may altogether satisfy and fulfill the desire of the soul, as has just been shown. But to it neither the soul itself surviving after death can raise itself, nor can it be raised by any other cause than God. Therefore, the blessedness of the other life cannot be ascribed to any other efficient cause than God, who rewards a life well spent here.

Latin:

X. Ejus subjectum est homo Viator.

I. Per subjectum intelligimus hîc subjectum operationis, sive id, quod operationi, quam Theologia Naturalis consequendæ beatitudinis causâ præscribit, substernitur. De subjecto considerationis sive objecto posteà acturi sumus. Subjectum operationis autem ut in scientiis practicis aliis, ita & hîc in Theologia Naturali cum fine cujus arctè cohæret, & cum eo unum adæquatum finem constituit. Quapropter communiter finis CUI vocatur.

II. Subjectum operationis constituimus hîc non perinde, ut in Theologia Revelata, hominem peccatorem, sed hominem Viatorem. Theologia Naturalis enim non concessa est homini, sicut Revelata, post lapsum demum, in remedium peccati, & ad reconciliandum hominem peccatorem cum Deo; sed in ipsa creatione, priusquàm peccato & per peccatum morti homo esset obnoxius factus, ejus fundamenta à Deo posita sunt. Unde etiam homini peccatori de medio ad expianda peccata idoneo, deque sui reconciliatione cum Deo prospicere non potest. Homo Viator autem patet latiùs, & comprehendit suo ambitu etiam hominem, adhuc in suo statu primævo constitutum.

III. In Theologia Naturali constitui subjectum operationis rectè hominem Viatorem, ex requisitis subjecti operationis intelligitur. Requiritur enim ad illud in unaquaque scientia practica, cùm ut careat eâ perfectione, quæ ei pro fine est, tùm ut ejusdem particeps fieri possit per principia & media, quæ in ea præscribuntur. Quod utrumque homini Viatori, per se & in suo primævo statu spectato, convenit. Hoc ipso enim, quod Viator, h. e. in via ad adipiscendam beatitudinem constitutus est, caret perfectione eâ, quæ Theologiæ Naturali pro fine est, beatitudine scilicet. Ejus verò particeps fieri poterat in suo statu primævo per principia & media, quæ in ea præscribuntur. In statu peccati autem homo Viator beatitudinis quidem per principia & media, quæ Theologia Naturalis præscribit, particeps fieri non potest: sed hoc per accidens est. Per accidens enim est, quòd homo peccavit, & per peccatum fine suo, ad quem conditus est, excidit. Per hoc tamen jam in statu peccati non desinit esse subjectum Theologiæ Naturalis. Actus practici enim, quos ipsa præscribit, stringunt eum jam quoque non minus, quàm in statu integritatis, licet ad finem, cujus gratiâ sunt, per eos pertingere non possit.

XI. Causa beatitudinis efficiens Deus est.

Causam beatitudinis efficientem investigat Aristoteles l. Nic. c. IX. & dicit inter alia, si quod aliud Θεῶν δώρημα munus à Diis datum est hominibus, εὐδαιμονίαν θεόσδοτον εἶναι, beatitudinem esse donum divinitus datum: cùm rerum humanarum optima sit; vel si non sit θεόπεμπτος, à Deo dono missa, sed virtute, ac doctrinâ aliquâ aut exercitatione pariatur, in rebus divinissimis tamen esse numerandam. Agit autem Philosophus de causa efficiente beatitudinis pro statu hujus vitæ, & loquitur propterea disjunctivè, eam vel esse donum divinitùs datum, vel saltem rem divinissimam, additque, hac de re disquirere alterius esse loci & instituti. Si de beatitudine animæ post mortem superstitis agere ipsi propositum fuisset, haud dubiè sine hæsitatione asseruisset, eam esse θεόσδοτον sive θεόπεμπτον, donum divinitus datum sive missum. Causa enim, quam beatitudini hujus vitæ ibidem adscribit, doctrina scilicet, adsvetu do & exercitatio in eam non cadit. Non enim superstes post mortem anima doctrinæ, adsuetudinis exercitationisque capax; vel comparandæ per doctrinam exercitationemque beatitudini in vita altera locus est: cùm remunerandæ per beatitudinem vitæ heic benè transactæ, vindicandisque perpetuâ miseriâ sceleribus, hîc patratis, destinata sit altera vita, non acquirendæ demum per doctrinam & exercitationem beatitudini. Quò accedit, quòd beatitudo vitæ alterius, etiam juxta rationis dictamen, consistit in cognitione Dei perfectâ, quæ desiderium animæ prorfus satiet & expleat, ut modò ostensum. Ad eam verò nec ipsa post mortem superstes anima sese elevare, nec à causa alia, quàm Deo elevari potest. Non ergo alii causæ efficienti, quàm Deo, vitam hîc benè transactam remuneranti, vitæ alterius beatitudo adscribi potest.


### XII. The προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause of the same is the goodness, grace,…

XII.

The προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause of the same is the goodness, grace, and mercy of God toward men who depart from this life with Him propitious. For moved by that, He rewards them with the happiness or perpetual blessedness of the other life.

I. That God is good and a rewarder of the good is known to all by the guidance of the light of nature.

II. Moreover, that it is to be ascribed to His goodness rather, as an impulsive cause, than to His justice itself, that He rewards the good with blessedness in the other life, is evident from the fact that man has no right before God. For man depends on God in being and acting, and if he does any good and virtuous thing, he does it all out of obligation, nor does he merit anything by it, properly and strictly speaking. Whence whatever good God repays to those living well and according to virtue in this or the other life, He repays it to them not out of justice and obligation, but out of mere goodness and grace.

XIII.

The means by which, according to the prescription of Natural Theology, one must arrive at the end, namely the blessedness of the other life, consist in acts of the mind and will concerning God, placed in His acknowledgment and worship.

I. Since blessedness is the end of man to be obtained from God, as has just been shown, out of His goodness and grace, the means of attaining it they must be moral, which, although they are not meritorious of it, strictly and properly speaking, yet stand in relation to the benevolent will of God as the reason or condition of the subject, in consideration of which He wills to impart and does impart it in the other life. Which cannot be constituted in anything other than in the acts of the mind and will occupied with God, as the ultimate end and highest good of man, by which, namely, we both rightly acknowledge and worship God. These also, and no others, Natural Theology prescribes for the sake of obtaining blessedness from God.

II. Hence, means are not to be taken here in that stricter signification in which those things are called means, for the choosing of which a known end so moves the will that they are, in turn, the properly called cause of attaining the end, whether efficient or meritorious, but more generally, as those things are called means which in any way exist and are chosen on account of an end, even if they are not the cause of attaining the end, but at least stand in relation to the subject as a condition or a cause without which it would not be: just as, for example, he who wishes to illuminate a room whose windows are obstructed on all sides by shutters, and for this end removes the shutters so that the light of the sun may enter through the windows, is indeed moved to remove the shutters by a known end, and the removal of the shutters can be called a means of illumination, but in a looser and less proper signification, in which whatever exists or is done on account of an end is called a means to an end; not in the strict and proper sense, in which that is called a means which is so on account of an end that it is the cause of its being effected or attained: since the removal of the shutters is not the cause of the illumination of the room, but only a condition or a cause by which that which was hindering the illumination of the room is removed. The matter stands likewise at present. Since man has his being and whatever he needs for his own preservation from God, he owes in turn to God worship and whatever he can perform to testify his thanks, by nature, and therefore he can neither properly merit blessedness nor anything else from God by his worship and obedience, but ought to obtain the same and all other benefits from Him as gratuitous rewards for worship and obedience. Worship, therefore, exhibited by man to God, is a condition required on the part of the subject for obtaining blessedness from God, or a cause without which it would not be, rather than its cause, properly and strictly so called. III. That the worship of God, instituted according to the prescription of right reason, is in a certain way ordered toward the attainment of blessedness by the goodness and grace of God, Paul indicates not obscurely when he teaches in Rom. 1:19 that the Gentiles are inexcusable because, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor were they thankful—that is, they have nothing by which to excuse themselves, or to claim that they fell short of salvation without their own fault: for they had God known, and natural reason itself dictated to them that those who wish to attain blessedness by His goodness and grace ought to glorify Him with fitting worship and testify their gratitude toward Him, which, however, they did not do. For to glorify God as God is to worship Him as God, and to attribute to Him the glory fitting for such worship.

IV. The divine worship which Natural Theology prescribed in the primordial state of man could then suffice for man to attain blessedness by the goodness and grace of God. For in the state of integrity, man had God from the beginning of his existence as propitious, favorable, and inclined toward the blessedness to be imparted to him in due time; he also possessed integral and sufficient powers to render the worship owed to God as was fitting, nor did anything remain for the actual attainment of blessedness, other than that he should subsequently also, as he was able, abstain from sin and persist in the worship and obedience of God until that time when it would have seemed good to Him to reward his perseverance in good with the gift of blessedness.

V. However, the divine worship which can now be prescribed, and is prescribed, through Natural Theology in the state of corruption and sin, is by no means able to suffice for obtaining blessedness from God. For first, all men propagated through carnal generation are by nature sinners, turned away from God, children of wrath, and subject to eternal damnation, who therefore cannot attain blessedness unless their sins are expiated and God is rendered propitious or reconciled to them. Yet in the entire divine worship which Natural Theology can or could prescribe, whether in the state still integral or in the corrupt state, no valid means is found of expiating sins and reconciling

man with God. Therefore, neither is a means of obtaining the goodness and grace of God for blessedness found in it. For now, in the state of corrupted nature, the reconciliation of the sinful man with God claims for itself the very first place of all in divine worship, without which preceding reconciliation, the remaining worship which Natural Theology prescribes cannot even be offered to God. For no one can love God, hope in Him, trust in Him, invoke Him in necessities, give Him thanks for benefits, etc., unless he has known Him as good, propitious, and favorable to himself. Furthermore, divine worship, which Natural Theology now prescribes in the corrupted state, is imperfect even as regards its other parts. For the intellect of man, through the fall of Adam and the corruption of human nature that followed therefrom, has been so obscured that, by the guidance of whatever light remains, it cannot sufficiently penetrate into the nature of the acts that constitute divine worship, nor explain it perfectly, whether you look at the acts of the first or the second table. This will easily be evident to one who compares Natural and Revealed Theology with each other, and who has considered more deeply what the former teaches from the light of nature, and likewise what the latter teaches from the light of revelation, concerning the human acts that constitute the worship of God. Thirdly, human nature has been so corrupted by sin and destitute of good powers that it cannot perform for God, as it ought, even that worship which Natural Theology can and does prescribe even in the state of corrupted nature: e.g., the light of nature and Natural Theology under its guidance teach that, just as God is the first and most perfect being of all and the cause of all other things, so He must be loved above all things. But no mortal can do this through the powers of nature. For there is no one who does not sin. Moreover, whoever sins postpones God either to his own desires and concupiscences or to other created things, and loves these more than God, as often as he sins. The matter stands in the same way with other human acts also, which Natural Theology prescribes for divine worship, of which, although unregenerate men may perform some outwardly, yet if one looks to the mind of the agents and the circumstances of the actions you examine them, they will all be imperfect and unclean, so that they cannot please God.

VI. Therefore, modern Naturalists wander very far from the truth, who contend that man, now in a state of corrupt nature, can attain to eternal blessedness under the guidance of Natural Theology. On which matter, those things may be seen which we have previously discussed at length in a special Disputation against Edward Herbert of Cherbury, an English Baron.

Latin:

XII.

Causa ejusdem προηγουμένη sivè impulsiva interna est Dei bonitas, gratia & misericordia erga homines, qui ipso propitio ex hac vitâ discedunt. Eâ enim motus remuneratur illos vitæ alterius felicitate sive beatitudine perpetuâ.

I. Deum bonum & bonorum remuneratorem esse, luminis naturæ ductu notum omnibus est.

II. Ejus autem bonitati potius, velut causæ impulsivæ, quàm justititæ ipsius adscribendum esse, quòd in vita altera bonos beatitudine remuneratur, vel inde patet, quod homini ad Deum jus nullum est. Homo enim dependet à Deo in esse & operari, & si quid boni ac secundum virtutem agit, totum ex debito agit, nec quicquam eo meretur, propriè quidem & strictè loquendo. Unde quicquid boni Deus benè & secundum virtutem viventibus in hac vel altera vita retribuit, id non ex justitia & debito, sed ex mera bonitate & gratia iis retribuit.

XIII.

Media, quibus ex præscripto Theologiæ Naturalis ad finem, beatitudinem scilicet vitæ alterius, perveniendum, consistunt in actibus mentis & voluntatis circa Deum, in ejus agnitione & cultu positis.

I. Cùm beatitudo sit finis hominis à Deo, ut modò ostensum, ex ejus bonitate & gratiâ impetrandus, ejus consequendæ media moralia sint oportet, quæ licet ejus non sint meritoria, propriè & strictè loquendo, ad Dei benevolam voluntatem tamen se habeant ut ratio vel conditio subjecti, cujus intuitu eam in vita altera impertire velit & impertiat. Quæ in alio constitui non possunt, quàm in actibus mentis & voluntatis circa Deum, velut hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum, occupatis, quibus scilicet Deum rectè & agnoscimus & colimus. Hos etiam, non alios, Theologia Naturalis impetrandæ à Deo beatitudinis causâ præscribit.

II. Hinc media hîc accipienda non sunt in eo strictiori significatu, quo media dicuntur, ad quæ eligenda finis cognitus ita voluntatem movet, ut vicissim causa consequendi finis propriè dicta, efficiens aut meritoria sint, sed generaliùs, prout media dicuntur, quæ quoquo modo sunt & eliguntur propter finem, licet consequendi finis causa non sint, sed ex parte subjecti saltem ut conditio aut causa sine qua non sese habeant: sicut v. g. qui illuminari vult conclave, cujus fenestræ undique valvis obstructæ sunt, & hoc fine valvas removet, ut per fenestras lumen solare intrare possit, is ad removendas valvas movetur utique ex fine cognito, potestque valvarum remotio dici medium illuminationis, sed in significatu laxiori & minus proprio, quo medium ad finem dicitur, quicquid est aut fit propter finem; non stricto & proprio, quo medium dicitur, quod ita est propter finem, ut ejus efficiendi aut consequendi causa sit: cùm remotio valvarum non sit causa illuminationis conclavis, sed tantùm conditio vel causa, quâ removetur id, quod illuminationem conclavis impediebat. Perinde impræsentiarum res habet. Homo, cùm suum esse & quibuscunque ad sui conservationem eget, à Deo habeat, debet vicissim Deo cultum & quicquid ad testandam suam gratitudinem præstare potest, per naturam, & proinde nec beatitudinem nec quicquam cultu & obsequio suo apud Deum mereri propriè potest, sed eandem & alia beneficia omnia impetrare ab ipso debet, tanquam gratuita cultus & obsequii præmia. Est ergo cultus, Deo ab homine exhibitus, conditio potius, ad impetrandam à Deo beatitudinem, ex parte subjecti requisita, vel causa sine qua non, quàm ejus causa, propriè & in rigore sic dicta. III. Cultum Dei, ad rectæ rationis præscriptum institutum, ordinari quodammodo ad beatitudinem, Dei bonitate & gratiâ consequendam, non obscurè innuit Paulus, quando Rom. I. 19. docet, Gentes esse inexcusabiles, quòd cùm Deum cognoverint, non ut Deum glorificaverint, neque grati fuerint, h. e. non habere, quo se excusent, aut quod citra suam culpam salute se excidisse obtendant: Eas enim habuisse Deum cognitum, & ipsam naturalem rationem dictitâsse ipsis, quòd qui ejus bonitate & gratiâ beatitudinem consequi velint, eum cultu conveniente glorificare, suamque gratitudinem erga ipsum testari debeant, quod tamen non fecerint. Glorificare enim Deum, ut Deum, est eum colere, ut Deum, cultuque gloriam ei convenientem tribuere.

IV. Cultus divinus, quem Theologia Naturalis in statu hominis primævo præscribebat, sufficere tum poterat homini ad beatitudinem, Dei bonitate & gratiâ consequendam. In statu integritatis enim homo habebat Deum inde ab initio sui esse sibi propitium, faventem, & ad beatitudinem, suo tempore sibi impertiendam, propensum; pollebat etiam viribus integris & sufficientibus ad cultum Deo debitum, pro eo ac oportebat, exhibendum, nec ad beatitudinem reapse consequendam quicquam supererat, quàm ut deinceps etiam, sicut poterat, à peccato abstineret, & in Dei cultu atque obsequio ad illud usque tempus, quo ejus in bono perseverantiam beatitudinis dono remunerari ipsi visum esset, persisteret.

V. Qui autem nunc in statu corruptionis & peccati per Theologiam Naturalem præscribi potest, præscribiturque cultus divinus, ad impetrandam à Deo beatitudinem sufficere minimè potest. Primùm enim homines per carnalem generationem propagati omnes naturâ sunt peccatores, à Deo aversi, filii iræ, damnationique æternæ obnoxii, qui proinde beatitudinem consequi non possunt, nisi expiatis ipsorum peccatis, Deoque iis propitiato sive reconciliato. In universo autem cultu divino, quem Theologia Naturalis sive in statu adhuc integro sive in corrupto præscribére potest aut potuit, validum expiandorum peccatorum hominis-

que cum Deo reconciliandi medium nullum reperitur. Ergo nec impetrandæ Dei bonitate & gratia beatitudinis medium in eo reperitur. Nunc enim pro statu naturæ corruptæ in cultu divino locum omnium primum sibi vendicat hominis peccatoris reconciliatio cum Deo, absque qua prævia cultus reliquus, quem Theologia Naturalis præscribit, Deo ne deferri quidem potest. Non enim Deum diligere, in eo sperare, ipsi confidere, in necessitatibus eum invocare, pro beneficiis ei gratias agere &c. potest, nisi qui eum, ut sibi bonum, propitium & faventem cognitum habuerit. Deinde etiam quà partes cæteras cultus divinus, quem nunc in statu corrupto Theologia Naturalis præscribit, imperfectus est. Intellectus hominis enim per lapsum Adæ & hinc secutam naturæ humanæ corruptionem ita obscuratus est, ut ductu qualiscunque, quod superest, luminis in naturam actuum, cultum divinum constituentium, satis penetrare, eamque perfectè explicare non possit, sive primæ sive secundæ tabulæ actus spectes. Quod facilè patebit comparanti inter se Naturalem & Revelatam Theologiam, & quæ illa ex lumine naturæ; quæ item hæc ex revelationis lumine de actibus humanis, qui cultum Dei constituunt, docet, penitius consideraverit. Tertiò natura humana per peccatum usque adeò corrupta bonisque viribus destituta est, ut ne eum quidem cultum, quem Theologia Naturalis jam in statu naturæ corruptæ præscribere potest, præscribitque, sicut oportet, Deo præstare possit: v. g. sicut Deus ens omnium primum & perfectissimum, cæterorumque omnium causa est, ita eum super omnia diligendum esse, lumen naturæ & ad ejus ductum Theologia Naturalis docet. Sed hoc mortalium nemo per naturæ vires facere potest. Nemo enim est, qui non peccet. Quisquis autem peccat, postponit Deum sive suis desideriis & concupiscentiis, sive rebus creatis aliis, & has diligit magis, quàm Deum, quotiescunque peccat. Eundem in modum res habet cum aliis etiam actibus humanis, quos in cultum divinum Theologia Naturalis præscribit, quorum licet aliquos exterius homines non renati facere possint, tamen si ad animum agentium actionumque circumstantias respexeris, imperfectæ & immundæ erunt omnes, ut Deo placere non possint.

VI. Aberrant igitur à vero longissimè Naturalistæ hodierni, qui hominem nunc in statu naturæ corruptæ Theologiæ Naturalis ductu ad beatitudinem æternam pertingere posse, contendunt. Qua de re videri possunt, quæ antehac in Disputatione peculiari contra Edoardum Herbert de Cherbury, Baronem Anglum, prolixè disseruimus.


### XIV. Having considered the end, the subject of operation, the causes, and the means…

XIV.

Having considered the end, the subject of operation, the causes, and the means of Natural Theology, we proceed to its object, which, as in other sciences, so also here is twofold, material and formal.

I. Practical sciences have two duties. One is to teach, that is, to deduce, confirm, and defend conclusions about the subject matter assigned to it from its own certain and necessary principles. The other is to direct the power of operating toward practice or operation through the conclusions which it infers from its principles. The former belongs to it insofar as it is a science; the latter, insofar as it is practical.

II. Having thus far, with respect to this latter duty of Natural Theology, weighed its end, the subject of operation, and the principles and means leading to the end, which are indeed required for πεπαιδείαν (education), we now consider these three, for they occur in every practical habit. However, with a view to the former duty, its object, both material and formal, must be considered. For every science is about some thing which it considers, and about which it infers its conclusions to explain its nature, and it proceeds from some antecedent knowledge, or from certain prior and better-known principles from which it infers its conclusions, as Aristotle well teaches in II Post. Anal. c. 1. The thing itself, about which the science is and about which it infers its conclusions, is called the material object of the science. But that from which, as previously known, the same science deduces its conclusions, or which amounts to the same thing, the prior and better-known principles upon which its conclusions depend, is its are called the formal object. Which itself finds a place in practical sciences as well.

XV.

The material object of Natural Theology embraces within its scope both the subject, as they call it, of the operation, and the causes and means of attaining the end. The formal object consists in the ultimate end itself, and that an objective one.

I. The first thing that is known in every practical science, and which, once known, is the reason for knowing the rest, is the end. But that which is first known in any science, and which, once known, is the reason for knowing the rest that are taught in it; that, by the consent of all, is its formal object. Therefore, the end of Natural Theology is its formal object, and indeed its ultimate end. For an intermediate end has the nature of a means rather than of an end.

II. But since the ultimate end of Natural Theology is twofold, objective and formal, the formal object of the latter is constituted not so much by the formal end as by the objective one. For the knowledge of the formal end, if not distinct, is at least confused and depends upon the objective end, and it behaves in Natural Theology rather as a thing to be known than as a reason for knowing.

III. The rest of the things which Natural Theology teaches, namely the subject, the causes, and the means of attaining the end, are contained within the scope of the material object. For they behave in it as things to be known, not as a reason for knowing.

IV. The subject of the operation, therefore, is also the subject of consideration, or the material object of Natural Theology, but in one respect and another. For it is the subject of the operation and is so called with respect to the operation, for the sake of attaining the blessedness prescribed by Natural Theology, to which it is subjected. But it is the subject of consideration and is so called in order to the act of knowing, which the intellect elicits concerning it by the aid of Natural Theology, and which it terminates objectively. It is, however, an inadequate material object or object of consideration of that [theology]: because besides that, also the causes and means of attaining the end, as has been said, come into the reckoning of things which Natural Theology considers, which when taken together and jointly with it finally constitute the subject of that consideration or its adequate material object.

Latin:

XIV.

COnsideratis Theologiæ Naturalis fine, subjecto operationis, causis & mediis, ad ejusdem objectum progredimur, quod, ut in scientiis aliis, ita & heic duplex est, materiale & formale.

I. Scientiæ practicæ duo sunt munia. Unum docere, hoc est, conclusiones de re sibi substrata ex suis certis & necessariis principiis deducere, confirmare & defendere. Alterum potentiam operandi per conclusiones, quas ex suis principiis infert, ad praxin sive operationem dirigere. Prius convenit ei, in quantum scientia; posterius, in quantum practica est.

II. Hactenus habito respectu ad hoc posterius munus Theologiæ Naturalis finem, subjectum operationis, & principia ac media, ad finem ducentia, quædam quidem ad πεπαιδείαν requiritur, expendimus. Hæc tria enim in omni habitu practico occurrunt. Prioris autem muneris intuitu considerandum venit ejus objectum cùm materiale tùm formale. Omnis enim scientia est de re aliqua, quam considerat, & de qua conclusiones suas ad explicandam ejus naturam infert, & procedit ex aliqua antecedente cognitione, aut ex principiis quibusdam prioribus & notioribus, ex quibus conclusiones suas infert, ut benè docet Aristoteles II. Post. Anal. c. 1. Res ipsa, de qua scientia est, & de qua conclusiones suas infert, dicitur scientiæ objectum materiale. Id verò, ex quo prius cognito eadem conclusiones suas deducit, sive quod eodem redit, principia priora & notiora, ex quibus conclusiones ejus dependent, ejusdem objectum formale appellantur. Quod ipsum in scientiis practicis quoque locum invenit.

XV.

Objectum materiale Theologiæ Naturalis complectitur suo ambitu cùm subjectum, ut vocant, operationis, tùm consequendi finis causas & media. Formale in ipso fine ultimo, eoque objectivo, consistit.

I. Primum quod in unaquaque scientia practica cognoscitur, quodque cognitum est ratio cognoscendi cætera, finis est. Quod autem in aliqua scientia primò cognoscitur, & quod cognitum est ratio cognoscendi cætera, quæ in ea traduntur; id omnium consensu ejus objectum formale est. Finis ergo Theologiæ Naturalis est ejus objectum formale, & quidem finis ejus ultimus. Intermedius enim medii potiùs, quám finis rationem habet.

II. Cùm verò finis ultimus Theologiæ Naturalis duplex sit, objectivus & formalis, objectum formale illius non tam constituit finis formalis, quám objectivus. Cognitio finis formalis enim, si non distincta, confusa tamen dependet à fine objectivo, habetque se in Theologia Naturali potiùs ut res cognoscenda, quam ut ratio cognoscendi.

III. Cætera, quæ tradit Theologia Naturalis, subjectum scilicet, causæ & media consequendi finis, objecti materialis ambitu continentur. Habent enim se in illa ut res cognoscendæ, non ut ratio cognoscendi.

IV. Subjectum operationis ergo est etiam subjectum considerationis, sive objectum materiale Theologiæ Naturalis, sed alio atque alio respectu. Operationis enim subjectum est & dicitur respectu operationis, consequendæ beatitudinis causâ per Theologiam Naturalem præscriptæ, cui substernitur. Considerationis verò subjectum est & dicitur in ordine ad actum cognoscendi, quos Theologiæ Naturalis adminiculo intellectus circa illud elicit, & quos objectivè terminat. Est tamen illius objectum materiale sive considerationis inæquatum: quia præter illud etiam causæ & media consequendi finis, uti dictum, veniunt in censum rerum, quas Theologia Naturalis considerat, quæ cum eo simul & junctim sumtæ demum illius subjectum considerationis sive objectum materiale adæquatum constituunt.


### XVI. The formal object, therefore, of Natural Theology is GOD

XVI.

The formal object, therefore, of Natural Theology is GOD.

The reason is: because GOD is its objective end. But the objective end in every practical science, as has been said, is the first thing known and the reason for knowing the rest, and thus it is the formal object.

XVII.

But since God can be known in two ways, especially among us Christians: one by the light of nature; the other by divine revelation; known in the former way, He finally performs the function of the formal object in Natural Theology.

I. The reason is: because God, insofar as He becomes known from divine revelation, is the objective end of Revealed Theology, nor is it the task of Natural Theology to fetch from divine revelation what it hands down about God, unless perhaps a Christian Philosopher, in the case where the light of nature seems not to suggest sufficiently firm and suitable principles for solidly declaring and confirming the truth, might wish to call upon divine revelation for the sake of a fuller declaration and greater certainty, and to append its testimonies to principles derived from the light of nature. But to wish to hand down in Natural Theology those things about God from divine revelation which exceed the light of nature would be to commit a μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, and to confuse Natural Theology with Revealed.

II. By the name of the light of nature, Aristotle in III De Anima, text 18, understands the agent intellect, and calls it a light, because when joined to the phantasms of things it performs what light performs when joined to colors, and just as this makes things potentially visible actually visible, so that one makes things potentially intelligible actually intelligible. Whence he says that the agent intellect is a habit, such as light is. It is called, however the agent intellect is the light of nature, in that it is a habit, analogous to light, owed to man for the purpose of knowing the law of nature. Others understand by the light of nature the very principles of nature and reason, which have the character of light, because just as light manifests both itself and other things to the visual power, so those principles, since they are known by themselves, both manifest themselves to the intellect and shine before it for the knowing of other things, and as it were carry a torch before it. These two opinions do not conflict with each other. For Aristotle understands by the light of nature the natural faculty of simple apprehension, and that the ultimate one, which determines the possible intellect to acts of knowing not by way of a known medium, but by way of a principle, virtually representing the object, and which efficiently concurs to elicit the same: into which even the first principles of nature and reason themselves are resolved. For they are known to be true through species, impressed upon the possible intellect by the agent intellect, which is joined to the phantasms of things, by which, as if by certain rays, the things represented in the phantasms are as it were illuminated, and are actually constituted in intelligible being, just as color, illuminated by solar rays, is actually constituted in visible being. On the other hand, those who constitute the light of nature in the first principles of nature and reason, by that name understand the natural faculty of knowing, not simply the ultimate one, but the ultimate one in the genus of complex faculty of knowing, and which moves the intellect into the knowledge of other things by way of a known medium. The former represents the object to the intellect virtually, in so far as it effectively concurs with the intellect to elicit the act of cognition by which it is represented in act: the latter represents it formally through its own formal and express cognition, by which the identity of the extremes of a conclusion with each other is exhibited to be seen from the identity of the same with a third term.

III. We accept the light of nature here in a broader sense, as it embraces both natural faculties of knowing within its scope, and not only those things which are known from the principles of nature known by themselves; but also those things which, by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms, are known immediately from apprehended terms concerning God, are said to be known from the light of nature. For the knowledge of God, [is] to the light resting upon nature, is here distinguished from the knowledge which relies upon supernatural revelation, and the former is the same as natural, the latter the same as supernatural knowledge of God. Natural knowledge of God, moreover, comprises both that which is acquired from the principles of nature through discourse, and that which, by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms, comes to us immediately of itself from apprehended terms. In which sense Scotus also, in Prologue to Book 1 of the Sentences, question 1, accepts natural and supernatural knowledge. He calls supernatural that which is from some agent that is not naturally born to move the possible intellect to such knowledge. For this state, he further says, according to the Philosopher, the possible intellect is born to be moved to knowledge by the agent intellect and the phantasm. Whence supernatural knowledge will be that which is not generated by the agent intellect and the phantasm, but by some supernatural agent, namely God, moving the possible intellect to it through supernatural revelation. Conversely, natural knowledge, according to Scotus, is said to be that which is generated by the agent intellect and the phantasm, for instance through impressed species, which determine the possible intellect to elicit an act of knowledge, by which the identity of the predicate with the subject is represented to it either of itself immediately, as it is in first principles, or by means of the knowledge of first principles, as it is in conclusions, the knowledge of which depends upon premises known by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms.

IV. We establish, however, the formal object of Natural Theology, not precisely in the light of nature, whether taken for the agent intellect or for principles known by nature: for this is a certain mode of knowing that is too general and remote; but in God, known from the light of nature. God is known, however, from the light of nature through propositions declaring His existence, essence, and essential perfections, some of which become known to us by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms of themselves immediately from apprehended terms; others through discourse from the first and immediate principles of nature and reason. Whence, while we establish the formal object of Natural Theology in God, known from the light of nature, our mind returns to this: that the formal object of Natural Theology is constituted by propositions declaring the existence, essence, and essential perfections of God, insofar as they are known either from the principles of nature and reason through discourse, or by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms from terms apprehended in themselves immediately and without discourse.

Latin:

XVI.

Objectum formale igitur Theologiæ Naturalis DEUS est.

Ratio est: quia DEUS est illius finis objectivus. Finis objectivus autem in unaquaque scientia practica, uti dictum, est primum cognitum & ratio cognoscendi cætera, atque adeò est objectum formale.

XVII.

Deus verò cùm duobus modis, maximè apud nos Christianos, cognosci possit: Uno per lumen naturæ; altero per divinam revelationem; priori modo cognitus demum in Theologia Naturali objecti formalis munus obit.

I. Ratio est: quia Deus, in quantum ex divina revelatione innotescit, Theologiæ Revelatæ finis objectivus est, nec Theologiæ Naturalis est, ex divina revelatione, quæ de Deo tradit, accersere, nisi forsan Philosophus Christianus eo casu, quo naturæ lumen ad veritatem solidè declarandam & confirmandam non satis firma & idonea principia suggerere videtur, uberioris declarationis & majoris certitudinis causâ divinam revelationem in subsidium vocare, & ejus testimonia principiis, ex lumine naturæ petitis, subjungere velit. Ea verò, quæ lumen naturæ excedunt, in Theologia Naturali de Deo ex divina revelatione tradere velle, esset μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος committere, & Theologiam Naturalem cum Revelata confundere.

II. Luminis naturæ appellatione Arist. III. de Anima t. XIIX. intelligit intellectum agentem, eumque lumen dicit, quòd rerum phantasmatibus junctus id præstet, quod lumen coloribus junctum præstat, & sicut hoc res potentiâ visibiles facit actu visibiles, ita ille res potentiâ intelligibiles actu intelligibiles faciat. Unde dicit, intellectum agentem esse habitum, quale lumen est. Dicitur autem intellectus agens naturæ lumen, quòd sit habitus, lumini analogus, homini ad cognoscendum de lege naturæ debitus. Alii per lumen naturæ intelligunt ipsa naturæ & rationis principia, quæ luminis rationem habeant, quòd sicut lumén potentiæ visivæ & se & alia manifestat, ita illa cùm per se nota sint, & se ipsa intellectui manifestent, & eidem ad alia cognoscenda præluceant, & facem quasi præferant. Quæ duæ sententiæ inter se non pugnant. Aristoteles enim per lumen naturæ intelligit naturalem rationem cognoscendi incomplexam, eamque ultimam, quæ intellectum possibilem ad actus cognoscendi determinat non per modum medii cogniti, sed per modum principii, objectum virtualiter repræsentantis, & quod ad eosdem eliciendos efficienter concurrit: in quam & ipsa prima naturæ & rationis principia resolvuntur. Cognoscuntur enim vera esse per species, intellectui possibili ab intellectu agente, rerum phantasmatibus juncto, impressas, quibus velut quibusdam radiis res, in phantasmatibus repræsentatæ, collustrantur quasi, & actu in esse intelligibili constituuntur, sicut color, radiis solaribus collustratus, actu in esse visibili constituitur. Contra autem qui lumen naturæ constituunt in primis naturæ & rationis principiis, illi ejus appellatione intelligunt rationem cognoscendi naturalem, non simpliciter ultimam, sed ultimam in genere rationis cognoscendi complexæ, & quæ per modum medii cogniti intellectum in cognitionem aliorum movet. Illa repræsentat intellectui objectum virtualiter, in quantum cum intellectu effectivè concurrit ad actum cognitionis, quo repræsentatur actu, eliciendum: hæc formaliter illud repræsentat per sui cognitionem formalem & expressam, quâ identitas extremorum conclusionis inter se ex indentitate eorundem cùm uno tertio conspicienda exhibetur.

III. Nos lumen naturæ accipimus hîc in significatu latiori, prout naturalem rationem cognoscendi utramque suo ambitu complectitur, & non solùm quæ ex naturæ principiis per se notis; sed etiam quæ virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatum per se immediatè ex apprehensis terminis de Deo cognoscuntur, ex lumine naturæ cognosci dicuntur. Cognitio Dei enim, lumini naturæ innixa, contradiftinguitur hîc cognitioni, quæ revelatione supernaturali nititur, estque illa idem, quod naturalis; hæc idem quod supernaturalis de Deo cognitio. Naturalis autem cognitio de Deo complectitur cùm eam, quæ ex principiis naturæ per difcursum acquiritur, tùm hanc, quæ virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatû ex apprehensis terminis per se immediatè nobis obtingit. Quem in sensum & Scotus in Pral. in l. Sent. q. I. naturalem & supernaturalem cognitionem accipit. Supernaturalem dicit, quæ est ab aliquo agente, quod non est natum movere intellectum possibilem ad talem cognitionem naturaliter. Pro statu autem isto, inquit porro, secundum Philosophum intellectus possibilis natus est moveri ad cognitionem ab intellectu agente & phantasmate. Unde cognitio supernaturalis erit, quæ non generatur ab intellectu agente & phantasmate, sed ab aliquo agente supernaturali, Deo scilicet, intellectum possibilem per revelationem supernaturalem ad eam movente. Contrà naturalis cognitio, juxta Scotum, dicitur, quæ generatur ab intellectu agente & phantasmate, puta per species impressas, quæ intellectum possibilem determinant ad eliciendum cognitionis actum, quo identitas prædicati cum subjecto ei repræsentatur vel per se immediatè, ut sit in principiis primis, vel mediante cognitione principiorum primorum, ut sit in conclusionibus, quarum cognitio ex præmissis, virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatum cognitis, dependet.

IV. Constituimus autem objectum formale Theologiæ Naturalis, non præcise in lumine naturæ, sive pro intellectu agente, sive pro principiis naturâ notis accepto: hæc enim est ratio quædam cognoscendi nimis generalis & remotior; sed in Deo, ex lumine naturæ cognito. Cognoscitur autem Deus ex lumine naturæ per propositiones, ejus existentiam, essentiam & perfectiones essentiales declarantes, quarum quædam virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatum per se immediatè ex apprehensis terminis; aliæ per discursum ex primis & immediatis naturæ & rationis principiis nobis innotefcant. Unde dum objectum formale Theologiæ Naturalis constituimus in Deo, ex lumine naturæ cognito, mens nostra redit hûc: objectum formale Theologiæ Naturalis constituere propositiones, Dei existentiam, essentiam & perfectiones essentiales declarantes, in quantum vel ex principiis naturæ & rationis per discursum; vel virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatum ex terminis apprehensis per se immediatè & citra discursum cognitæ sunt.


### XVIII. God, therefore, in Natural Theology is the first thing known

XVIII.

God, therefore, in Natural Theology is the first thing known.

Because He is its formal object. Now it is of the nature of a formal object in every science that it be the first thing that is known in it.

XIX.

God is known, however, by the guidance of the light of nature, in two ways. One by knowledge innate by nature, the other by acquired knowledge.

I. The distinction of our natural knowledge into innate and acquired is most accepted by usage. That is called innate which, once the terms are apprehended, is immediately present to the intellect without discourse, just as if it had been actually put into and implanted in it with nature itself. Such is the knowledge of first principles, both speculative, e.g., it is impossible for something to be and not to be at the same time, the whole is greater than its part; and practical, e.g., God is to be worshipped, to each his own is to be rendered. That is called acquired which is obtained through use, study, and effort by a certain method of knowing, brought in from elsewhere, by discourse, or by experience, or finally from the testimony of others.

II. Since, however, the statement that certain items of knowledge are by nature innate to the intellect can be taken in a triple sense: one concerning knowledge in second act; another concerning knowledge in first act; and a third concerning knowledge in proximate potency; the first sense finds no place here. For knowledge in second act always implies some act of knowing elicited by the intellect, and thus efficiently produced by it, which, by the very fact that it is produced by the intellect, is not by nature innate or inborn in us. But neither does it seem that knowledge innate by nature should be taken in the second sense. For knowledge in first act is properly called that which the intellect in the being of a complete principle and in the first act sufficient, it is constituted for eliciting the act of knowing. Just as, however, without impressed species the intellect is not a complete principle and in the first act sufficient for eliciting the act of knowing, so neither can any notions in the first act be said to be naturally implanted or innate to it, unless impressed species themselves are naturally implanted or innate to it. But impressed species, which a notion in the first act intrinsically includes, are not born with us, but are transmitted from objects through the senses and phantasms, with the concurrence of the agent intellect, to the intellect, as is taught elsewhere. It remains, therefore, that in the third sense certain notions are said to be naturally implanted, namely, that they are implanted in the intellect by a proximate power, such that as soon as the terms are apprehended, by its own intrinsic power of knowing—implanted in it from the womb—it sees the identity of the predicate with the subject, and determines itself to elicit the act of assenting.

III. I say pointedly: by a proximate power. For the acquired knowledge of conclusions also exists in the intellect by a power, but a remote one. For the intellect cannot immediately determine itself to the assent of those [conclusions] once the terms are apprehended, but only through the intervention of another cognition, by which other prior principles are known. For the intellect is determined to the assent of a conclusion from known premises, not of itself immediately.

IV. The addition: by a proximate power; imports two things: One, the negation of act, both first and second. For to exist by power is opposed here to existing in act, both first and second. The other, a certain innate perfection, by which the intellect is constituted as capable of eliciting the act of knowing, once the other things required for understanding are posited, of itself immediately, which they commonly call the light innate or naturally implanted in the intellect. Thomas in p. 1. q. XII. a. II. calls it an intellective virtue, which is a participative likeness of Him who is the first intellect; and a certain intelligible light, as if derived from the first light. Philippus Melanchthon, that common Doctor of Germany, calls the same thing a light in our minds, by which we count, recognize the principles of arts, and discern the honest and the base: and he adds: THAT THIS LIGHT is DIVINELY [GIVEN] NOTIONS SPARSAS in our minds, it is rightly said, in the book on the soul.

V. Nor do those philosophers or theologians seem to think differently, who call innate knowledge habitual knowledge, implanted or innate by nature. For by habitual knowledge they do not understand impressed species, well coordinated and arranged among themselves, as intellectual habits are usually understood otherwise: for they acknowledge freely that impressed species are not inborn in us; but a certain perfection, inborn in the intellect before any impressed species, analogous to a habit, which they wish to deserve the name of disposition rather than habit. What this could be or could be other than the perfection asserted by us, innate to the intellect, by which the intellect is constituted powerful, or in proximate potency to elicit acts of knowing by itself immediately and without any reason for knowing taken from elsewhere, we do not see. But if impressed species are added, the intellect will be constituted by the same and the impressed species together no longer in proximate potency, but in first act sufficient to elicit those by itself immediately, and that innate perfection and the impressed species taken together will be a certain properly called habitual knowledge, which nevertheless, not according to its whole self, but at least by that part by which it contains a certain perfection innate to the intellect, will have to be called innate.

Latin:

XVIII.

Deus ergo in Theologia Naturali est primum cognitum.

Quia est objectum formale illius. Est autem de ratione objecti formalis in unaquaque scientia, ut sit primum, quod in ea cognoscitur.

XIX.

Cognoscitur autem Deus, ductu luminis naturæ, modis duobus. Uno per notitiam naturâ insitam, altero per notitiam acquisitam.

I. Usu receptissima est distinctio nostræ naturalis cognitionis in insitam & acquisitam. Insita dicitur, quæ apprehensis terminis statim intellectui citra discursum inest, non secus, ac si cum ipsa natura ei actu indita & implantata esset. Qualis notitia est principiorum primorum cùm speculativorum, v. g. impossibile est aliquid simul esse & non esse, totum est majus suâ parte; tum practicorum, v. g. Deus colendus, suum cuique tribuendum est. Acquisita dicitur, quæ usu, studio & labore per rationem quandam cognoscendi, aliunde adscitam, discursu, vel experientiâ, vel denique ex aliorum testificatione comparatur.

II. Cùm verò triplici sensu accipi possit, quod notitiæ quædam naturâ intellectui infitæ sint: uno de notitiis in actu secundo; altero de notitiis in actu primo; & tertio de notitiis in potentia propinqua; primus sensus hîc locum non invenit. Nam notitiæ in actu secundo semper important aliquem actum cognoscendi ab intellectu elicitum, atque adeò ab eo efficienter productum, qui hoc ipso, quod ab intellectu producitur, naturâ nobis infitus sive innatus non est. Sed nec sensu altero accipiendæ videntur notitiæ naturâ infitæ. Nam notitia in actu primo dicitur propriè, quæ intellectum in esse principii completi & in actu primo sufficientis constituit ad actum cognoscendi eliciendum. Quemadmodum autem absque speciebus impressis intellectus principium completum & in actu primo sufficiens non est ad actum cognoscendi eliciendum, ita nec notitiae in actu primo ei naturâ insitae sive innatae ullae dici possunt, nisi & species impressae naturâ ipsi insitae sive innatae sint. Sed species impressae, quas notitia in actu primo intrinsece includit, non nascuntur nobiscum, sed transmittuntur ab objectis per sensus & phantasmata, cum concursu intellectus agentis, ad intellectum, ut alibi docetur. Relinquitur ergo, quòd in sensu tertio notitiae quaedam dicantur naturâ insitae, nempe quod intellectui insitae sint potentiâ propinquâ, ita ut simul ac termini apprehensi sunt, suâ solâ intrinsecâ sibique inde ab utero insitâ vi cognoscendi identitatem praedicati cum subjecto videat, & ad actum assentiendi eliciendum se determinet.

III. Notanter dico: potentiâ propinquâ. Nam conclusionum etiam notitia acquisita inest intellectui potentiâ, sed remotâ. Non enim apprehensis terminis statim intellectus ad illarum assensum se determinare potest, sed interventu demum alterius cognitionis, quâ alia priora principia cognoscuntur. Ex praemissis cognitis enim determinatur intellectus ad assensum conclusionis, non per se immediatè.

IV. Additamentum: potentiâ propinquâ; duo importat: Unum, negationem actus cum primi, tùm secundi. Potentiâ enim inesse opponitur hîc τῷ inesse actu cùm primo, tùm secundo. Alterum, innatam quandam perfectionem, quâ intellectus potens constituitur ad actum cognoscendi, positis caeteris ad intelligendum requisitis, per se immediatè eliciendum, quam communiter lucem intellectui ingenitam sive naturâ insitam appellant. Thomas in p. 1. q. XII. a. II. vocat eam virtutem intellectivam, quae sit participativa similitudo ipsius, qui est primus intellectus; & lumen quoddam intelligibile, quasi à prima luce derivatum. Philippus Melanchthon, communis ille Germaniae Doctor, eandem vocat lucem in mentibus, quâ numeramus, agnoscimus principia artium, discernimus honesta & turpia: & addit: HANC LUCEM esse NOTITIAS DIVINITUS SPARSAS in mentibus nostris, rectè dicitur, in lib. de anima.

V. Neque diversum sentire videntur illi sive Philosophi sive Theologi, qui notitiam insitam dicunt notitiam habitualem, naturâ insitam sive innatam. Per habitualem enim notitiam non intelligunt species impressas, inter se benè coordinatas & dispositas, ut habitus intellectuales aliàs accipi solent: agnoscunt enim ultro, species impressas non esse nobis ingenitas; sed perfectionem quandam, ante species impressas ullas intellectui ingenitam, habitui ἀνάλογον, quam potius dispositionis quàm habitus appellationem mereri volunt. Quæ quid aliud sit aut esse possit, quàm modò asserta à nobis perfectio, intellectui innata, quâ intellectus potens, vel in potentia propinqua constituitur ad actus cognoscendi per se immediatè & citra ullam aliunde affumtam rationem cognoscendi eliciendos, non videmus. Quod si species impressæ accesserint, constituetur intellectus per eandem & species impressas simul non amplius in potentia propinqua, sed in actu primo sufficiens ad illos per se immediatè eliciendos, eruntque innata illa perfectio & species impressæ simul junctim sumtæ quædam propriè dicta notitia habitualis, quæ tamen non secundum se totam, sed eâ saltem parte, quâ continet quandam intellectui innatam perfectionem, innata dicenda erit.


### XX. Since, however, God, insofar as He is the end and supreme good of man, can be…

XX.

Since, however, God, insofar as He is the end and supreme good of man, can be conceived by us in two ways: One confusedly, under the common notion of happiness and the supreme good: the other distinctly, under a proper notion, as the first and most perfect Being, which is from itself, and the cause of all other things, or than which nothing better and more perfect can be or be thought: a double question emerges from this: One, whether a confused; the other, whether a certain distinct knowledge of God is implanted in us by nature?

The distinction of our knowledge into confused and distinct is better known than to deserve explanation here. At least we advise with Thomas, p. 1, q. II, a. 1, ad 1, that to know God confusedly under by the common notion of beatitude and the highest good, is not simply to know God, although God is our beatitude and highest good, just as to know the one coming is not simply to know Peter, although Peter is the one coming, which example Thomas uses in the same place.

XXI.

The former question does not come into controversy here.

For that a certain confused knowledge of God under the common notion of beatitude and the highest good is implanted in us by nature, is proven by the appetite for Him, thus conceived, which is implanted by nature in the minds of all. For there is no one who does not wish to be happy. Hence, Augustine in book XIII of the De Trinitate, chapter III, corrects that mime who, about to say what everyone had in their mind and what everyone wanted, had said: 'You want to buy cheaply and sell dearly'; saying: If he had said, 'You all want to be happy, you do not want to be miserable,' he would have said something that no one would not recognize in his own will. For whatever else anyone may secretly want, he does not depart from this will, which is sufficiently known to all men. But whose appetite is implanted by nature in the will, of him a certain knowledge must also be implanted by nature in the intellect: since the will is not moved except toward what is known. In which sense also Augustine in the same place. Chapter V. Wherefore, he says, since it is true that all men wish to be happy, and desire this one thing with the most ardent love, and for the sake of this desire whatever else they desire, and no one can love what he is entirely ignorant of as to what it is or what kind of thing it is, nor can he be ignorant of what it is that he knows he wants, it follows THAT ALL KNOW A HAPPY LIFE, namely, to the extent that they want it. But they want it under the common notion of beatitude, or the highest good. Therefore, under the same notion, all also have knowledge of it by nature. In the same sense, Thomas in Part I, Question II, Article I, to the first point: To know, he says, that God exists in some common way under a certain confusion, IS NATURALLY IMPLANTED IN US, insofar as God is man's beatitude: for man naturally desires beatitude: and what is naturally desired by man is naturally known by the same. Compare the same in I-II, Question V, Article VIII.

Latin:

XX.

Cùm autem Deus, in quantum hominis finis & bonum summum est, duobus modis à nobis concipi possit: Uno confusè, sub ratione communi beatitudinis & boni summi: altero distinctè, sub ratione propria, ut Ens primum & perfectissimum, quod à se, & cæterorum omnium causa est, sive quo nihil melius & perfectius esse aut cogitari potest: emergit hinc quæstio duplex: Una, an confusa; altera an distincta quædam notitia Dei naturâ nobis insita sit?

Distinctio notitiæ nostræ in confusam & distinctam notior est, quàm quæ hic explicationem mereatur. Illud saltem cum Thoma p. 1. q. II. a. 1. ad 1. monemus, quod cognoscere Deum confusè sub communi ratione beatitudinis & boni summi, non sit simpliciter cognoscere Deum, quamvis Deus sit nostra beatitudo & bonum summum, sicut cognoscere venientem, non est simpliciter cognoscere Petrum, quamvis Petrus sit veniens, quo exemplo utitur Thomas d.l.

XXI.

Prior quaestio heic in controversiam non venit.

Quod enim confusa quaedam Dei notitia sub ratione communi beatitudinis & boni summi natura nobis insita sit, evincit ejus, sic concepti, appetitus, natura omnium mentibus insitus. Nemo enim est, qui non velit esse beatus. Hinc Mimum illum, qui dicturus, quid in animo omnes haberent, & quid vellent omnes; dixerat: Vili vultis emere, & care vendere; scite Augustinus lib. XIII. de Trinit. c. III. corrigit: Si, inquiens, dixisset, omnes beati esse vultis, miseri esse non vultis, dixisset aliquid, quod nullus in sua non agnosceret voluntate. Quicquid enim aliud quisquam latenter velit, ab hac voluntate, quae omnibus hominibus satis nota est, non recedit. Cujus autem appetitus voluntati natura insitus est, ejus notitiam quandam etiam intellectui natura insitam esse necesse est: cum voluntas non feratur, nisi in cognitum. Quem in sensum & Augustinus d.l. c. V. Quapropter, inquit, quoniam verum est, quod omnes homines esse beati velint, idque unum ardentissimo amore appetant, & propter hoc caetera quaecunque appetunt, nec quisquam potest amare, quod omnino quid vel quale sit, nescit, nec potest nescire, quid sit, quod velle se scit, sequitur, UT OMNES BEATAM VITAM SCIANT, puta in tantum, in quantum eam volunt. Volunt autem eam sub communi ratione beatitudinis, sive boni summi. Ergo sub eadem etiam ejus notitiam natura omnes habent. Eundem in sensum Thomas in p. I. q. II. a. I. ad primum: Cognoscere, inquit, Deum esse in aliquo communi sub quadam confusione, EST NOBIS NATURALITER INSERTUM, in quantum scilicet Deus est hominis beatitudo: homo enim naturaliter desiderat beatitudinem: & quod naturaliter desideratur ab homine, naturaliter cognoscitur ab eodem. Confer eundem in I. II. q. V. a. VIII.


### XXII. Regarding the latter question, however, whether a distinct knowledge of God is…

XXII.

Regarding the latter question, however, whether a distinct knowledge of God is implanted in us by nature, there is no slight disagreement.

I. The disagreement, however, does not so much concern propositions regarding the EST of the third adjacent, for example, that God is an intelligent mind, is good, just, and is to be worshipped: for no one would easily deny that propositions of this kind are implanted in us by nature, in the sense which we explained a little earlier in thesis XIX; rather, it concerns the proposition regarding the EST of the second adjacent, namely this: God exists; concerning which authors depart into different camps.

II. And the Scholastics indeed dispute about it laboriously, though under different terms. For they propose the question thus: Is the existence of God known per se? Thomas, in part I, question II, article I, calls those propositions known per se whose predicate is included in the definition of the subject. But if the proper and quidditative concept of the subject and predicate (or of either one) is hidden from us, so that the truth of the proposition does not immediately become known to us from the apprehended terms, then he says it is known per se, as far as it is in itself, or only in itself. If, on the contrary, the proper and quidditative concept of the extremes is known to everyone, so that upon their apprehension the truth of the proposition immediately appears to us without discursive reasoning, he says it is known per se in itself and in relation to us. The question, therefore, is: Is the existence of God known per se? is understood as concerning that which is known per se in itself and in relation to us, and it seems at first glance to coincide with the other question debated among modern theologians and philosophers: is the existence of God implanted in the minds of men by nature? For the Scholastics name propositions known per se from the knowledge of them, to which the intellect is determined by itself from the apprehended terms, without any reason for knowing assumed from elsewhere: which seems to be the same as the knowledge which they commonly call implanted. It is not, however, entirely and in all respects the same, as will be shown later.
