Therefore, Thomas, in the cited question II, article I, part I, holds this opinion on the proposed question: that the existence of God is not known per se to us, or in relation to us; since the proper and quidditative concept of God is hidden from us, or, as he speaks, since we do not know what God is; yet it is known per se in itself: since the predicate is the same as subject. For God is His own being. The old and most of the recent Scholastics embrace this opinion of Thomas, as far as the matter is concerned, although in establishing it they do not entirely agree either among themselves or with Thomas.

III. Those, however, who are accustomed to propose the same question under these terms: Whether the existence of God is innate in us by nature, commonly descend into the affirmative side, and prove it against those who dissent

(1) from the Scriptures. For first, what the Apostle says in Rom. 1:18: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; they do not explain this badly as referring to the truth of common notions, which contain both the distinction between honorable and base things, and τὸ γνωσὸν τῦ θεῦ: the truth of which, being innate by nature, the Gentiles, through the malice of their will and the works of injustice, hold as it were captive, and prevent it from exerting itself toward the honesty of morals and the true worship of God. For it follows immediately: Because that which can be known of God is manifest ἐν ἀυτοῖς in them, i.e., within their souls, as the more common explanation holds. Then in Rom. 2:14, the praised Apostle says that the Gentiles, who do not have the law (solemnly promulgated), when they do by nature the things that are of the law, not having the law, are a law unto themselves: for they show the work of the law written in their hearts. Where the reason why they are said to be a law unto themselves, not having the law, can be rendered in no other way than that by practical notions concerning the distinction of honorable and base things, innate by nature without any promulgated law, they are a law unto themselves, and know what they ought to do and what they ought to flee, with each one's own conscience teaching it. Wherefore those notions are also called in the same place, v. 15, the work of the law, written in their hearts. But the reason for common notions about God is equal, inasmuch as they are contained under the law inscribed on the hearts of men, and constitute its tablet or the former part.

(2) From the testimony of conscience. For the good rejoice in their right actions, even if no one rewards them: the wicked, on the contrary, sometimes tremble, terrified by the mere recollection of their crimes, although they neither think of God nor fear the avenging hand of any man. Which cannot originate from elsewhere than from a certain internal and naturally implanted sense of a Divinity, who rewards good deeds but punishes crimes. To which also the divine Paul looked, when he showed that the law is implanted in the Gentiles by nature, even from the internal testimony of conscience: saying, their conscience bearing witness together, and their thoughts mutually accusing or even excusing one another. For neither could conscience, bearing witness concerning things rightly done, and thoughts mutually accusing and excusing one another among the Gentiles, who do not have the promulgated law, have their origin from elsewhere than from the first practical principles, implanted by nature in the hearts of men, which attest within and in the mind what has been done well and laudably, and what otherwise, convict the wicked of their crimes, and denounce divine vengeance to them; but raise up the good by the rectitude of their good deeds, and excuse them from voluntary malice in those things, indeed, which they have done rightly.

(3) From the consensus of the ancients, both Gentiles and Christians alike. Among the Gentiles, Epicurus taught the implanted knowledge of God in the most explicit words, whose opinion Cicero reports and commends in book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods: He (Epicurus) alone, he says, saw that there are gods, because NATURE ITSELF HAD IMPRANTED THE NOTION OF THEM IN THE MINDS OF ALL. For what nation, or what kind of men, is there that does not have without instruction a certain anticipation of gods? which Epicurus calls πρόληψιν, that is, a certain information anticipated in the mind. Likewise Cicero says, we have IMPLANTED or rather INNATE cognitions of them. And in book II of On the Nature of the Gods: It is, he says, innate and engraved in all that there are gods. To which, however, the notion is wrongly transferred to GODS, which nature has imprinted upon the minds of men only concerning the one true God, with the expression accommodated to the opinion of the common people. Among Christians, however, and Ecclesiastical writers, Arnobius in book I against the Gentiles: Is there any man, he says, who has not entered the day of his first birth WITH THE NOTION OF THAT PRINCE (he speaks of God), to whom it is not innate, not affixed, nay, almost imprinted and implanted in the very womb of his mother, that He is King and Lord and moderator of all things, whatsoever they are? And Jerome in his Commentary on Job, chapter XXXVI: By the good of nature, he says, The knowledge of the Creator is inherent in the hearts of men: in the very gaze of the heart, man understands that which is above him, that divine name (Divinity) which he attempts to contemplate. And in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, ch. 1, v. 15, Vol. VI of his works, he says that the knowledge of God is naturally in everyone. And Damascenus, book I, On the Orthodox Faith, ch. 1: In all, the knowledge τῶ εἶναι θεὸν, that God exists, has been naturally implanted by Him (God). Furthermore, that the notion not of gods, as Epicurus would have it, but of one true God is naturally implanted in the minds of men, Tertullian elegantly shows in his booklet On the Testimony of the Soul: where he brings forward the soul of a Gentile man, not one that is formed by schools, exercised in libraries, and belches forth wisdom acquired in academies and Attic porches, but one that is simple, and rude, and unpolished, and unlearned, such as those have who have only that, that very one from the street corner, from the crossroads, from the weaving shop, speaking openly and with full freedom for Christians against the worshippers of gods, both at home and abroad, in this way: 'What God has given,' and 'If God wills.' By that voice, he says, you both signify that someone exists, and you confess all power to Him to whose will you look, and at the same time you deny that the others are gods, while you name them by their own names, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Minerva. For you confirm only God, whom you name as God, so that when you sometimes call those others gods, you seem to be using them as something foreign and as if on loan. After these things, he introduces the same soul speaking thus about the nature of God, about divine blessing, and about divine judgment: 'God is good,' 'God does good,' 'May God bless you,' 'God sees all things,' and 'I commend to God,' and 'God will repay,' and 'God will judge between us.' These testimonies, so conspicuous concerning the one God, when they are brought forth by a soul, both crowned with the ribbon of Ceres, and wrapped in the scarlet cloak of Saturn, and clothed in the linen of the goddess Isis (these are the words of Tertullian), cannot be attributed to acquired knowledge of God. For this soul is inclined to be carried toward fictitious gods and goddesses, and it ought not to name God in the singular or as one, but rather those very gods whom it is accustomed to worship, to implore, and to appoint as witnesses and judges. It must therefore be ascribed to knowledge naturally implanted, which exerts itself in the very worshippers of fictitious gods and goddesses even when, unmindful of the one true God, they serve false gods. He inculcates a twin argument in his Apology against the Gentiles, ch. XVII, where, exclaiming, he calls that testimony of the Gentile soul the testimony of a NATURALLY CHRISTIAN soul. Following closely in his footsteps are Minucius Felix in his Octavius, and Arnobius in book 1 against the Gentiles, the former of whom was his contemporary; the latter was not much later than him. Lactantius, formerly a student of Arnobius, pursues this matter more fully in book 1 of his Divine Institutes, chapter 1, where among other things he says: Since, he says, we often see the very worshippers of the gods both confess and proclaim the supreme God, what pardon can they hope for their impiety: who do not acknowledge the worship of Him, whom it is not right for man to be entirely ignorant of? For both when they swear, and when they wish, and when they give thanks, they do not name Jupiter or many gods, but GOD, so much does truth itself, NATURE COMPEL- LING, break forth even from unwilling hearts. He adds, however, that these things are accustomed to happen in adverse circumstances rather than in prosperous ones. For, he further says, God then most of all slips from memory, when, enjoying His benefits, they ought to give honor to divine indulgence. But indeed if any necessity presses more heavily, then they remember God: if the terror of war has roared, if the pestilential force of diseases has settled in, if a long drought has denied food to the crops, if a savage storm, if hail has encroached: they flee to God, help is sought from God, God is prayed to that He may assist, etc. More may be seen in the same place.

Latin:

XXII.

De quaestione posteriori autem, an notitia Dei distincta naturâ nobis insita sit, non levis est dissensus.

I. Dissensus tamen non tam concernit propositiones de EST tertii adjecti, v. gr. Deum esse mentem intelligentem, esse bonum, justum, esse colendum: hujusmodi propositiones enim esse nobis naturâ insitas, eo quidem sensu, quo paulò antè in th. XIX. declaravimus, nemo facilè negaverit; quàm propositionem de EST secundi adjecti, hanc scilicet: Deus est; de qua Auctores in partes diversas abeunt.

II. Et Scholastici quidem operosè de ea disputant, sub aliis tamen terminis. Proponunt enim quaestionem sic: An Deum esse sit per se notum? Propositiones autem per se notas vocat Thomas p. I. q. II. a. I. quarum praedicatum includitur in ratione subjecti. Quod si subjecti & praedicati (vel alterutrius) conceptus proprius & quidditativus nos latet, ut non statim ex apprehensis terminis propositionis veritas nobis innotescat, tum dicit eam per se notam, quantum in se est, sive secundum se tantùm. Sin contrà extremorum conceptus proprius & quidditativus omnibus notus sit, ut illis apprehensis propositionis veritas statim citra discursum nobis appareat, dicit eam per se notam secundum se & quoad nos. Quaestio igitur, an Deum esse sit per se notum? intelligitur de eo, quod est per se notum secundum se & quoad nos, & videtur primo intuitu coincidere cum altera, inter Theologos & Philosophos modernos disceptata quaestione: an Deum esse mentibus hominum naturâ insitum sit? Denominant enim Scholastici propositiones per se notas ab illarum notitia, ad quam intellectum per se ex apprehensis terminis, citra ullam aliunde assumtam rationem cognoscendi, determinant: quae eadem esse videtur cum notitia, quam vulgo dicunt insitam. Non tamen prorsus & per omnia eadem est, ut posteà ostendetur. Thomas igitur in citatâ q. II. a. I. part. I. sententia de quaestione proposita est: Deum esse, non esse nobis, sive quoad nos, per se notum; cùm Dei conceptus proprius & quidditativus nos lateat, sive, ut ille loquitur, cùm non sciamus de Deo, quid est; esse tamen per se notum secundum se: cum praedicatum sit idem cum subjecto. Deum enim esse suum esse. Hanc Thomæ sententiam amplectuntur, quoad rem, Scholastici veteres & recentiores plerique omnes, licet in ea adstruenda nec inter se, nec cum Thoma prorsus consentiant.

III. Qui autem sub hisce terminis: An Deum esse, naturâ nobis insitum sit? quæstionem eandem proponere solent, communiter in partem affirmativam descendunt, eamque adversus dissentientes probant

(1) ex Scripturis. Primùm enim quòd Apostolus Rom. I. 18. ait: Palam est ira Dei è cælo adversus omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum, qui veritatem in injustitia detinent; id non malè explicant de veritate notionum communium, cùm quæ discrimen honestorum & turpium, tùm quæ τὸ γνωσὸν τῦ θεῦ continent: quarum veritatem, naturâ insitam, Gentes per malitiam voluntatis suæ & injustitiæ opera captivam quasi detineant, & ne ad honestatem morum & verum Dei cultum se exerere possit, impediant. Sequitur enim statim: Quoniam id, quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est ἐν ἀυτοῖς in illis, h. e. intus in illorum animis, ut communior explicatio habet. Deinde Rom. II. 14. dicit laudatus Apostolus, Gentes, quæ legem (solenniter promulgatam) non habent, cùm naturâ quæ legis sunt, fecerint, legem non habentes sibi ipsis legem esse: ostendere enim opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Ubi ratio, cur legem non habentes sibi ipsis lex esse, dicantur, alia reddi non potest, quàm quòd per notitias practicas de discrimine honestorum & turpium, absque ulla lege promulgatâ naturâ insitas, sibi ipsis lex sint, & quæ agere, quæ fugere oporteat, sciant, suâ quemque conscientiâ id docente. Quamobrem etiam notitiæ illæ ibidem v. 15. dicuntur opus legis, scriptum in cordibus illorum. Par autem ratio est notionum communium de Deo, utpote quæ sub lege, hominum cordibus inscriptâ, continentur, ejusque tabulam sive partem priorem constituunt.

(2) Ex testimonio conscientiæ. Gaudent enim boni rectè factis, etiamsi nemo ea remuneretur: mali contrà expavescunt nonnunquam, suorum scelerum recordatione nudâ territi, licet nec de Deo cogitent, nec hominis ullius manum ultricem metuant. Quod aliunde provenire non potest, quàm ex interno quodam & naturâ infito sensu Numinis, benefacta remunerantis, scelera verò vindicantis. Quò & respexit d. l. Paulus, cùm legem Gentibus naturâ insitam esse etiam ex interno conscientiæ testimonio ostendit: Unà, inquiens, testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientiâ, & cogitationibus sese mutuò accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. Neque enim conscientia, testimonium perhibens de rectè factis, & cogitationes se invicem accusantes, & excusantes à Gentilibus, legem promulgatam non habentibus, aliunde originem suam habere poterant, quàm ex primis principiis practicis, naturâ hominum cordibus insitis, quæ quid benè & laudabiliter, quid secus factum sit, intus & apud animum attestantur, sceleratos suorum scelerum convincunt, iisque vindictam divinam denunciant; bonos autem rectitudine benefactorum erigunt, & à voluntaria malitia excusant in iis quidem, quæ rectè egerunt.

(3) Ex consensu veterum, Gentilium pariter & Christianorum. Inter Gentiles notitiam Dei insitam verbis apertissimis docuit Epicurus, cujus sententiam refert & commendat Cicero lib. 1. de Nat. Deorum: Solus (Epicurus) inquiens, vidit, primùm esse Deos, quòd IN OMNIUM ANIMIS EORUM NOTIONEM IMPRESSISSET IPSA NATURA. Quæ enim Gens, aut quod genus hominum, quod non habeat sine doctrina anticipationem quandam Deorum? quam appellat πρόληψιν Epicurus, id est, anteceptam animo quandam informationem. item dicit Cicero, nos habere INSITAS eorum vel potius INNATAS cognitiones. Et lib. II. de Nat. Deor. Omni bus, inquit innatum est & insculptum, esse Deos. Quibus tamen perperam ad DEOS transfertur notio, quam non nisi de uno vero Deo natura hominum mentibus impressit, locutione ad opinionem vulgi accommodata. Inter Christianos verò & Ecclesiasticos Scriptores Arnobius lib. I. adversus Gentes: Quisquamne, ait, est hominum, qui non CUM ISTIUS PRINCIPIS (loquitur de Deo) NOTIONE diem primæ nativitatis intraverit, cui non ingenium, non affixum, imò ipsis penè in genitalibus matris non impressum, non insitum, esse Regem ac Dominum cunctorum, quæcunque sunt, moderatorem? Et Hieronymus in Comm. in Job. c. XXXVI. Per naturæ bonum, inquit, notitia creatoris inest cordibus hominum: - in ipso obtutu cordis intelligendo videt homo, quod suprà ipsum est, illud divinum nomen (Numen) quod contemplari conatur. Et in Comm. in Epist. ad Gal. c. 1. v. 15. Tom. VI. operum dicit, naturâ omnibus Dei inesse notitiam. Et Damascenus lib. I. de Orth. fide c. 1. Omnibus notitia τῶ εἶναι θεὸν, quòd Deus sit, ab ipso (Deo) naturaliter inserta est. Porro non Deorum, ut Epicurus volebat, sed unius veri Dei notionem naturâ mentibus hominum insitam esse, eleganter ostendit Tertullianus in libello de testimonio animæ: ubi in medium affert animam hominis Gentilis, non quæ scholis formata, bibliothecis exercitata, academiis & porticibus Atticis partam sapientiam ructat, sed simplicem, & rudem & impolitam, & idioticam, qualem habent, qui eam solam habent, illam ipsam de compito, de trivio, de textrino, pro Christianis contra Deorum cultores palàm & tota libertate, domi ac foris ita pronunciantem: Quod Deus dederit, & si Deus voluerit. Eâ voce, inquit, & aliquem esse significas, & omnem illi confiteris potestatem, ad cujus spectas voluntatem, simul & cæteros negas Deos esse, dum suis vocabulis nuncupas, Saturnum, Jovem, Martem Minervam. Nam solum Deum confirmas, quem tantùm Deum nominas, ut cùm illos interdum Deos appellas, de alieno & quasi pro mutuo usa videaris. Post hæc introducit eandem de natura Dei, de benedictione divina, & de divino judicio sic loquentem: Deus bonus est, Deus benefacit, benedicat te Deus, Deus videt omnia, & Deo commendo, & Deus reddet, & Deus inter nos judicabit. Quæ tam conspicua de Deo uno testimonia cum proferuntur ab anima, & vittâ Cereris redimitâ, & pallio Saturni coccinatâ, & Deâ Isidis linteatâ (verba sunt Tertulliani) non possunt notitiæ Dei acquisitæ accepta referri. Hâc enim prona in Deos Deasque fictitias fertur, nec Deum in singulari sive unum, sed illos ipsos Deos, quos colere consuevit, nominare, implorare, testes & judices constituere deberet. Adscribenda igitur est notitiæ naturâ insitæ, quæ in ipsismet fictitiorum Deorum Dearumque cultoribus tùm etiam se exerit, cùm unius veri Dei immemores Diis falsis serviunt. Gemina inculcat in Apologetico adversus Gentes c. XVII. ubi testimonium illud animæ Gentilis exclamabundus vocat testimonium animæ NATURALITER CHRISTIANÆ. Quem κατὰ πόδα sequuntur Minutius Felix in Octavio, & Arnobius lib. 1. adversus Gentes, quorum ille ejus æqualis; hic illo non multò posterior fuit. Fusius autem rem hanc persequitur Lactantius, Arnobii quondam auditor, lib. Div. Instit. c. 1. ubi inter alia: Cùm, inquit, ipsos Deorum cultores sæpè videamus Deum summum & confiteri & prædicare, quam sibi veniam sperare possint impietatis suæ: qui non agnoscunt cultum ejus, quem prorsus ignorari ab homine fas non est? Nam & cum jurant, & cum optant, & cum gratias agunt, non Jovem aut Deos multos, sed DEUM nominant, adeò veritas ipsa, COGENTE NATURA, ettiam ab invitis pectoribus erumpit. Subjungit tamen, hæc fieri solere in rebus adversis potius, quàm in prosperis. Nam, ait porro, tùm maximè Deus ex memoria elabitur, cùm beneficiis ejus fruentes, honorem dare divinæ indulgentiæ debent. At verò si qua necessitas gravius presserit, tunc Deum recordantur: si belli terror infremuerit, si morborum pestifera vis incubuerit, si alimenta frugibus longa siccitas denegaverit, si sæva tempestas, si grando ingruerit: ad Deum confugiunt, à Deo petitur auxilium, Deus ut subveniat, oratur &c. Plura videantur ibidem.


### XXIII. By what reason, however, the knowledge of the existence of God is implanted by…

XXIII.

By what reason, however, the knowledge of the existence of God is implanted by nature in the minds of men, on that point the authors vary not a little.

I. RENÉ DESCARTES, the author of a new, but everywhere accepted philosophy, contends that God is, and that it is implanted in us by nature through the IDEA OF GOD, representing His existence to the intellect, implanted or innate in us by God Himself. Because we have in us the IDEA OF GOD or OF A SUPREME BEING, we can rightly examine from what cause we have it, and we shall find in it such immensity that we are clearly certain from it, THAT IT COULD NOT HAVE BEEN IMPLANTED IN US, except by a thing in which there is truly the complement of all perfections, that is, EXCEPT FROM GOD REALLY EXISTING, he says in part 1 of the Principles of Philosophy, no. XVIII. And in the following no. XXII. Looking, he says, to the IDEA OF HIM (God) BORN IN US, we see Him to be eternal, omniscient, omnipotent, the source of all goodness and truth, the creator of all things, and finally all those things containing in itself, in which we can clearly perceive some infinite perfection, or one terminated by no imperfection. Which opinion, because today it is not only praised and defended by all who come forth from his School, but is also propagated further day by day and instilled into studious youth; nay, is established as the principle and foundation from which the beginning of philosophizing is to be made and conclusions are to be deduced, it comes here to be examined a little more deeply and discussed more fully.

I. Descartes takes the word 'idea' not for an internal exemplary cause, or for a form conceived by the intellect which an effect imitates by the intention of the agent, as it is usually taken in accepted usage, but simply for the notion or concept of a thing. But since he could easily understand that notions or concepts of things are not born with us—for they are acts of knowing which are efficiently produced by the intellect, aided and determined by impressed species—he invented a twofold, really distinct, being in an idea. One of cognition or thought; the other objective, or of the thing represented. See p. 1 of the Principles of Philosophy, no. XVII, and Meditation III on First Philosophy, p. 18 of the edition. Johannes Clauberg among others inculcates the same distinction in his Treatise on the Cognition of God and ourselves, Exercise VII, laboriously, and he calls the being of cognition the formal or proper being of an idea; but he also calls the objective being the vicarious being: the former he constitutes in the operation of the mind; the latter in the image of the thing thought or known. He contends that both beings are something real in the human mind and have their own real cause; and that the cause of the proper and formal being is the human intellect, but the cause of the objective or vicarious being is the object itself, e.g., God in the idea of God, a stone in the idea of a stone.

II. Therefore, they hold that the idea of God is innate to the human mind, not as regards the being of cognition or thought—for they acknowledge, as has been said, that all acts of knowing are elicited by the intellect and are not born with us—but as regards the objective or vicarious being, insofar as it is the image of God, bearing his place in the intellect and representing him. For which reason Descartes also preferred to define an innate idea by the thing thought, insofar as it has a certain objective being in the intellect, rather than by the notion or concept of the thing, as in the Dissertation on Method, in the marginal note, p. m. 22. Note, he says, in this place and everywhere in the following, that the name of idea is taken generally for every thought-of thing, insofar as it has only objective being in the intellect: so that, namely, in its definition it might signify that which he judges to be innate to the intellect, namely the objective being of a thing or an image, by which the thing itself is represented, in the direct case; but the act of cognition, which is not innate, in the oblique case and by way of a connoted term. Florentius Schuyl, Physician and Senator of Bois-le-Duc, expresses his mind more clearly in his Orat. de verit. Scient. & art. Acad. pag. 11. when he compares the idea of God, innate to the minds of men, with the image of Phidias, inscribed upon the statue of Minerva, and wishes it to be called innate because our creator has impressed his morphosis, likeness, and image, certainly a spiritual one, upon our mind, just as once Phidias, that famous sculptor, is read to have inscribed his own image upon the statue of Minerva so skillfully that it could not be removed from there unless the whole statue were destroyed. Where he describes the Idea of God simply by the image of God, innate to the intellect, with the act of knowing, which they wish to be distinct from it, not being connoted. For he understands by morphosis, likeness, and image of God in the human mind a certain real entity, [existing] in the intellect before every act of knowing... representing essential perfections... the image of Phidias, impressed upon the statue of Minerva, Phidias... just as he could conceive Phidias in his intellect... he was looking at his image in the statue of Minerva. ... e essential perfections to conceive and know in the intellect... could, whoever was looking at his image, inborn in himself, within himself. To this also pertains what Descartes says in part I. Princip. Phil. n. XXII. Looking, he says, at the IDEA inborn in us (of God), we see that he is eternal, omniscient, omnipotent, the source of all goodness and truth, the creator of all things, and finally having in himself all those things in which we can clearly perceive some infinite perfection, or one not limited by any imperfection. Where he first posits the idea of God, inborn in us, prior to our act of knowing; then the turning of our intellect toward it, and thirdly, finally, the cognition itself of the divine perfections, represented by the impressed image.

III. But that objective, or vicarious, being, which, beyond the act of knowing, implies an idea in the human intellect, and which represents an object existing outside the intellect, is a pure and simple fiction, which up to this point neither Descartes nor his disciples have been able to explain, much less prove with any suitable foundation. In the first objections, page 47, it had been asked of Descartes, what is it to be objectively in the intellect? Formerly, his antagonist said, I learned: it is to terminate the very act of the intellect by way of an object: which is certainly an extrinsic denomination, and nothing of the thing. However, in the responses to those objections, page 53, intending to satisfy the proposed question: He says, one must note that he refers to the thing itself, as placed outside the intellect, by reason of which it is certainly an extrinsic denomination that it is objectively in the intellect; but I speak of an idea, which is never outside the intellect, and by reason of which to be objectively (in the intellect) signifies nothing other than to be in the intellect in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in it. Where, compelled by the force of truth, he concedes that to be objectively in the intellect belongs to the things themselves, which are the objects of the acts of knowing, through a mere extrinsic denomination. But the fact that he adds that he is speaking of an idea, which is never outside the intellect, does nothing to the point. For the question here is not about the idea, whether it is or can be outside the intellect, but about the objective being of things, which are said to be represented by ideas existing in the intellect, whether they are not in the intellect, distinct from the act of knowing? Or whether they are in fact nothing else within, except that they are its objects, and which they terminate, by reason of which they are said to be understood through a merely extrinsic denomination? Here is the knot! Here one must leap! If anything else is posited to exist than the act of knowing, by reason of which things are said to be objectively in the intellect, it had to be explained here, what that thing is? What is its entity? From where does it become known to us? None of which Descartes was able to explain, but he assumes as conceded that an idea includes in its concept a certain real entity, distinct both from the act of knowing and from the things themselves known, through which things are said to be objectively in the intellect by an intrinsic denomination. Which is an open begging of the question. Descartes adds, however, that by reason of the idea, which is never outside the intellect, to be objectively in the intellect signifies nothing other than to be in the intellect in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in it. But this too is a begging of the question. For he who asks what it is to be objectively in the intellect, he asks this very thing: in what way are objects in the intellect? Is it through the mere act of knowing, which they terminate, and thus through a merely extrinsic denomination? Or is it truly through some real entity intrinsic to the intellect and distinct from the act of knowing? Therefore he explains the same by the same, and the obscure by the equally obscure. He further attempts to illustrate the matter with an example, which he can neither explain nor prove. Thus, he says in the same place, for example, if someone should ask what happens to the Sun from the fact that it is objectively in my intellect, it is best answered that nothing happens to it, except an extrinsic denomination, namely that it terminates the operation of the intellect by way of an object. By which very thing he confirms with his own calculation the opinion received in the schools. But if, he continues, one asks about the idea of the sun, what it is, and it is answered that it is a thought-of thing, insofar as it is objectively in the intellect, no one will understand that it is the sun itself, insofar as that extrinsic denomination is in it: nor will being objectively in the intellect there signify terminating its operation by way of an object, but being in the intellect in that way in which its objects are accustomed to be, so that the idea of the sun is the sun itself existing in the intellect, not indeed formally, as in the sky, but objectively, that is, in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in the intellect, which mode of being is certainly far more imperfect than that by which things exist outside the intellect; but it is not for that reason entirely nothing. To those things which he says, if one asks about the idea of the sun, what it is, and it is answered that it is a thought-of thing, insofar as it is objectively in the intellect, that no one understands that it is the sun itself, insofar as that extrinsic denomination is in it, we admit. The idea of the sun is not properly the sun itself, but a certain image of the sun, expressed in the intellect through the act of knowing. Nor does the added restriction, 'insofar as that extrinsic denomination is in it,' hold correctly. For if being objectively in the intellect is said of the sun through an extrinsic denomination, how can it be in the sun? Since it is a contradiction that something be said of the sun through an extrinsic denomination, and yet that it be in the sun. Nor has anyone among the antagonists of Descartes spoken in such a way. But why should being objectively in the intellect not signify terminating the operation or cognition of the intellect by way of an object,

Latin:

XXIII.

QUâ ratione verò naturâ hominum mentibus insita sit notitia de exsistentia Dei, de eo Auctores non parum variant.

I. RENATUS DES-CARTES, novæ, sed passim locorum receptæ, Philosophiæ Auctor, contendit, Deum esse, naturâ nobis insitum esse per IDEAM DEI, ejus exsistentiam intellectui à repræsentantem, à Deo ipso nobis inditam, sive innatam. Quia DEI sive ENTIS SUMMI IDEAM habemus in nobis, jure possumus examinare, à quanam causa illam habeamus, tantamque in ea immensitatem inveniemus, ut planè ex eo sumus certi, NON POSSE ILLAM NOBIS FUISSE INDITAM, nisi à re, in qua sit revera omnium perfectionum complementum, h. e. NISI à DEO REALITER EXISTENTE, inquit in part. I. princip. Phil. n. XVIII. Et seq. n. XXII. Ad ejus (Dei) ait, IDEAM NOBIS INGENITAM respicientes, videmus illum esse æternum, omniscium, omnipotentem, omnis bonitatis veritatisque fontem, rerum omnium creatorem, ac denique illa omnia in se habentem, in quibus aliquam perfectionem infinitam, sive nulla imperfectione terminatam, clarè possumus advertere. Quæ opinio quia hodiè ab omnibus, qui ex ejus Schola prodeunt, non solùm laudatur & defenditur, sed etiam in dies longius propagatur, & juventuti studiosæ instillatur; imò principium & fundamentum, unde philosophandi initium faciendum, & conclusiones deducendæ sint, constituitur, paulò penitiùs hîc expendenda, & uberiùs excutienda venit.

I. Ideæ vocem Cartesius accipit, non pro causa exemplari interna, sive pro forma, intellectu concepta, quam imitatur effectus ex intentione agentis, ut aliàs usu recepto accipi solet, sed simpliciter pro rei notione sive conceptu. Cùm verò facilè intelligeret, notiones sive conceptus rerum non nasci nobiscum: sunt enim actus cognoscendi, qui ab intellectu, per species impressas adjuto & determinato, efficienter producuntur; commentus est in idea duplex, realiter distinctum, esse. Unum cognitionis sive cogitationis; alterum objectivum sive rei repræsentatæ. Videatur p. 1. Princip. Phil. n. XVII. & Med. III. de Phil. prima p. m. 18. Eandem distinctionem inculcat inter alios Johannes Claubergius in Tr. de Cognit. Dei & nostri Exerc. VII. operosè, & esse cognitionis vocat esse formale seu proprium ideæ; objectivum verò vocat etiam esse vicarium: illud constituit in operatione mentis; hoc in imagine rei cogitatæ sive cognitæ. Utrumque esse contendit esse reale quid in hominis mente, & habere suam causam realem; & esse proprii quidem ac formalis causam esse hominis intellectum, objectivi autem sive vicarii causam esse ipsum objectum v. g. Deum in idea Dei, lapidem in idea lapidis.

II. Innatam ergo volunt hominis menti ideam Dei, non quoad esse cognitionis sive cogitationis: agnoscunt enim, uti dictum, actus cognoscendi omnes elici ab intellectu, non autem nasci nobiscum; sed quoad esse objectivum sive vicarium, in quantum scilicet est imago Dei, vicem ejus in intellectu gerens, eumque repræsentans. Quamobrem etiam Cartesius ideam innatam maluit definire per rem cogitatam, quatenus habet esse quoddam objectivum in intellectu, quàm per notionem sive conceptum rei, sicut in Dissert. de Method in Not. Margin. p. m. 22. Nota, inquit, hoc in loco & ubique in sequentibus, nomen ideæ generaliter sumi pro omni re cogitata, quatenus habet tantùm esse objectivum in intellectu: ut scilicet in ejus definitione id, quod intellectui innatum esse censet, nempe rei esse objectivum sive imaginem, quâ res ipsa repræsentatur, in recto; cognitionis actum verò, qui innatus non est, in obliquo & per modum connotati significaret. Mentem ejus exprimit clarius Florentius Schuyl, Medicus & Senator Sylvæ Ducensis in Orat. de verit. Scient. & art. Acad. pag. 11. cùm ideam Dei, mentibus hominum innatam, comparat cum imagine Phidiæ, statuæ Minervæ insculptâ, vultque eam dici innatam, quòd creator noster sui morphosin, effigiem atque imaginem, utique spiritualem, menti nostræ impresserit, uti quondam Phidias, celebris ille statuarius, sui imaginem statuæ Minervæ tam affabrè insculpsisse legitur, ut non nisi totâ statuâ dirutâ exinde posset eximi. Ubi Ideam Dei simpliciter describit per imaginem Dei, intellectui innatam, actu cognoscendi, quem ab eâ distinctum esse volunt, non connotato. Intelligit enim per morphosin, effigiem, & imag... Dei in hominis mente entitatem quandam realem, intellectui ante omnem actum cognosc... ... perfectiones essentiales repræsentan... ... imago Phidiæ, statuæ Minervæ impressa, Phidiam ... quemadmodum Phidiam intellectu concipere poter... imaginem ejus in statua Minervæ intuebatur. ... e perfectiones essentiales intellectu concipere & cognosc... potuit, quisquis imaginem ejus, sibi ingenitam, in semetipso intuebatur. Eò & pertinet, quod Cartesius in part. I. Princip. Phil. n. XXII. Ad jus (Dei) inquit, IDEAM nobis ingenitam RESPICIENTES, videmus, illum esse æternum, omniscium, omnipotentem, omnis bonitatis veritatisque fontem, rerum omnium creatorem, ac denique illa omnia in se habentem, in quibus aliquam perfectionem infinitam, sive nulla imperfectione terminatam, clarè possumus advertere. Ubi primò ponit ideam Dei, nobis ingenitam, nostro actu cognoscendi priorem; deinde conversionem intellectus nostri ad illam, & tertiò denique cognitionem ipsam perfectionum divinarum, per imaginem impressam repræsentatarum.

III. Verùm esse illud objectivum, sive vicarium, quod præter actum cognoscendi idea in hominis intellectu importet, quodque objectum extra intellectum existens, repræsentet, purum putum commentum est, quod huc usque nec Cartesius nec discipuli ejus explicare, nedum aliquo fundamento idoneo probare potuerunt. In objectionibus primis, pag. 47. quæsitum fuerat ex Cartesio, quid sit esse objectivè in intellectu? Olim, inquiebat ejus Antagonista, didici: est ipsum actum intellectus per modum objecti terminare: quod sanè extrinseca denominatio est, & nihil rei. In responsionibus autem ad istas objectiones pag. m. 53. quæstioni propositæ satisfacturus: Advertendum, ait, illum respicere ad rem ipsam, tanquam extra intellectum positam, ratione cujus est sanè extrinseca denominatio, quòd sit objectivè in intellectu; me autem loqui de idea, quæ nunquam est extra intellectum, & ratione cujus esse objectivè (in intellectu) non aliud significat, quàm esse in intellectu eo modo, quo objecta in illo esse solent. Ubi veritatis vi coactus concedit, esse objectivè in intellectu convenire rebus ipsis, quæ actuum cognoscendi objecta sunt, per meram denominationem extrinsecam. Quòd autem addit, se loqui de idea, quæ nunquam est extra intellectum, nihil ad rem facit. Non enim de idea, an sit aut esse possit extra intellectum? hîc quæritur, sed de esse objectivo rerum, quæ per ideas, in intellectu existentes, repræsentari dicuntur, an non sint in intellectu, ab actu cognoscendi distincta? an verò sint intus nihil aliud, nisi ejus objecta sunt, & quem terminent, ratione cujus intellecti esse dicantur per denominationem merè extrinsecam? Hic nodus! hîc saltandum! Si quid aliud, quàm actum cognoscendi statuatur esse, ratione cujus res objectivè in intellectu esse dicantur, exponendum hîc erat, quidnam illud sit? quæ ejus entitas? unde nobis innotescat? Quorum nihil Cartesius explicare potuit, sed sumit tanquam concessum, ideam includere in suo conceptu entitatem quandam realem, cùm ab actu cognoscendi, tùm ab ipsis rebus cognitis distinctam, per quam res denominatione intrinsecâ objectivè in intellectu esse dicantur. Quæ est aperta petitio ejus, quod in principio est. Addit tamen Cartesius, ratione ideæ, quæ nunquam est extra intellectum, esse objectivè in intellectu non significare aliud, quam esse in intellectu eo modo, quo objecta in illo esse solent. Sed & hæc petitio est ejus, quod est in principio. Qui enim quærit, quid sit esse objectivè in intellectu, is hoc ipsum quærit, quo modo objecta in intellectu sint? An per solum actum cognoscendi, quem terminant, atque adeò per denominationem mercè extrinsecam? an verò per aliquam intellectui intrinsecam & ab actu cognoscendi distinctam entitatem realem? Idem ergo per idem, & obscurum per æquè obscurum explicat. Exemplo rem porro illustrare conatur, quam nec explicare, nec probare potest. Ita, inquit ibidem, exempli gratia, si quis quærat, quid Soli accidat ex eo, quod sit objectivè in meo intellectu, optimè respondetur, nihil ei accidere, nisi extrinsecam denominationem, quod nempe operationem intellectus per modum objecti terminet. Quo ipso receptam in scholis sententiam suo comprobat calculo. Si autem, pergit, de idea solis quæratur, quid sit, & respondeatur, illam esse rem cogitatam, quatenus est objectivè in intellectu, nemo intelliget, illam esse ipsum solem, quatenus in eo extrinseca ista denominatio est: neque ibi objectivè esse in intellectu significabit ejus operationem per modum objecti terminare, sed in intellectu eo modo esse, quo solent ejus objecta, adeò ut idea solis sit sol ipse in intellectu existens, non quidem formaliter, ut in cœlo, sed objectivè, hoc est, eo modo, quo objecta in intellectu esse solent, qui sanè essendi modus longè imperfectior est, quàm ille quo res extra intellectum existunt; sed non idcircò planè nihil est. Quibus quod dicit, si de idea solis quæratur, quid sit, & respondeatur, illam esse rem cogitatam, quatenus est objectivè in intellectu, neminem intelligere, illam esse ipsum solem, quatenus in eo extrinseca ista denominatio est, admittimus. Idea solis propriè non est ipse sol, sed solis quædam imago, per actum cognoscendi in intellectu expressa, Neque etiam restrictio addita: quatenus in eo extrinseca ista denominatio est; rectè habet. Si enim esse objectivè in intellectu de sole dicitur per denominationem extrinsecam, quomodo in sole esse potest? Cùm contradictio sit, dici aliquid de sole per extrinsecam denominationem, & tamen id esse in sole. Neque quisquam ex Cartesii Antagonistis ita locutus est. Cur autem esse objectivè in intellectu non significet, operationem sive cognitionem intellectus per modum objecti terminare,


### as Descartes contends, I do not yet see the cause of it

as Descartes contends, I do not yet see the cause of it. A thing thought or known, in itself and as it is distinguished from cognition, is not the idea itself, but its object, and that is an added restriction: insofar as it is objectively in the intellect, it indicates. For its force and reason for signifying is this: that the idea of the sun is not the sun according to its real being, but only according to its objective being, and the question now returns, what is that objective being of the sun in the intellect? We, with the usage accepted by philosophers, say that it is nothing other than that the sun is the object of cognition, or that it is known by the intellect, and terminates the act of knowing by way of an object, which belongs to the sun only by extrinsic denomination. Nor do those who are indeed familiar with the terms conceive anything else in the intellect when that phrase is heard. If this sense is not to Descartes's taste, it is necessary that he provide us with another more convenient one, and prove it solidly. What, therefore, does he provide? But, he says, (to be objectively in the intellect is) to be in the intellect in that way in which its objects are accustomed (to be in it), so that the idea of the sun is the sun itself existing in the intellect, not indeed formally, as in the sky, but objectively, i.e., in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in the intellect. But I ask you, candid reader, what is trifling if this is not? To be objectively in the intellect is not to be known by the intellect and to terminate the act of cognition by way of an object, as Descartes contends, but it is to be in the intellect in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in it. But to one asking in what way objects, e.g., the sun, are accustomed to be in the intellect, he answers that it is the same as to be in the intellect, not formally, as e.g., the sun is in the sky, but objectively, i.e., in that way in which objects are accustomed to be in the intellect. Is this not a piece of trifling unworthy of boys? And yet he says that to be objectively in the intellect is, on the part of things, a certain mode of being, indeed far more imperfect than that by which things exist outside the intellect; yet not for that reason to be nothing. Who, pray, could grasp these things? He has not been able to teach up to this point that to be objectively in the intellect imports something real on the part of the object, distinct both from the object itself as it is outside the intellect and from the act of knowing which it terminates, but when it has come to that point, besides the trifling that to be objectively in the intellect is nothing other than to be in the intellect in the way in which objects are accustomed to be in it, he could bring forward nothing: for the manner in which objects are or are accustomed to be in the intellect otherwise than through the bare act of knowing, he can no more teach than he can teach that to be objectively in the intellect implies, besides the act of knowing, something real that is on the part of the object and is distinct from the object itself as it exists outside the intellect. By what reason, therefore, or at least by what appearance of truth, can it be said that to exist objectively in the intellect is a true mode of being, which is not nothing, yet more imperfect than that by which they exist outside the intellect? And what, I ask, is the perfect or imperfect mode of being that supervenes upon a stone by the fact that it is known by me, and is represented to my intellect by the act of knowing? Since, therefore, beyond the act of knowing, nothing can be shown by which known things are said to exist objectively in the intellect, what remains but that we say the ideas of the Cartesians, which are said to be innate only according to objective or vicarious being, not according to formal and proper being, are a sweet dream? In reality, there is only one being of ideas, which consists in the act of knowing, representing the known thing, or in the species or image of the object expressed by the act of knowing. But as for the species or image of the thing expressed, which by its essence is the act of knowing itself, what else does he do who says that the act of knowing is innate to the intellect, but denies that the act of knowing is innate to the same, than affirm and deny the same thing at once, through an open and palpable contradiction?

IV. Descartes, however, and his disciples, as we have just seen, urge that the cause of an idea is one thing, insofar as it is called an act of knowing, or as he likes to speak, a mode of thinking, and the cause of the same is another, insofar as it is an image of this, not another thing: or, according to Clauberg, that the cause of an idea is one thing according to its formal and proper being, or insofar as it is an operation of the mind; and the cause of it is another according to its objective and vicarious being, or insofar as it is an image of such a thing: from which they seem to conclude that the entity of the act of knowing is one thing, and that of its objective or vicarious being is another; since from two really distinct causes there cannot but proceed a double effect, or at least a double being of an effect, of which one is not the other, and thus which are really distinct among themselves. Toward this all the arguments of Clauberg seem to aim, by which in Exercitation VII he attempted to prove that there is objective or vicarious [being] of an idea is real, and really distinct from the act of knowing. v. Although we do not deny that in an idea, according to our way of understanding, there is a duality: one of cognition, as such; the other of an image, or of such cognition which is representative of this and not another thing, can be conceived, and one cause can be assigned to the former and another to the latter: yet we deny and utterly deny that there is a duality on the part of the thing, or that two entities are given in an idea, of which one is a certain cognition, the other an image of the thing known. The idea of any thing, as the word idea is taken here, is nothing else than a concept, or act of knowing, by which a thing is represented to the intellect: which, however, is conceived by us through two inadequate concepts, one generic, the other specific, distinct only by reason. In order that you may rightly understand this, it must be known that the intellect, considered precisely in itself, without the concurrence of an object, is an incomplete principle of knowing, determined no more to one act of knowing than to any other, and cannot by itself alone elicit the cognition of any thing. Therefore, in order that it may be constituted as a complete principle of knowing, it is required that an object concur with it, and determine it by way of a partial principle to elicit the cognition of itself. But because objects cannot by themselves be joined with the intellect and determine it to elicit the cognition of themselves, they transmit their species through the intervention of the senses to the phantasy, and through phantasms, elevated by the agent intellect, further to the possible intellect, which in place of the objects determine it to elicit a cognition similar to the objects and representing them, so that the idea, as regards the thing, is nothing else than an act of cognition, similar to the object and representing it, which philosophers customarily call the expressed species of the object, and distinguish from the impressed species, as an effect from a cause. Although therefore there are two efficient causes of an idea: namely the intellect and the impressed species, the effect of both, however, as regards the thing, is one, namely the very simple being of the idea, constituted in the act of knowing, similar to the object and representing it. What is said in the objection, that from two really distinct causes there cannot but proceed two really distinct effects, is not true of incomplete causes. This For the very reason that they are incomplete causes, and when taken together jointly constitute one complete cause, it is necessary that not two, but one effect, as regards the thing itself, proceeds from them. This is evident from the example of the first and second cause, which are two really distinct but incomplete causes, and for this very reason, that when taken together jointly they constitute one complete cause, they produce nothing but one effect as regards the thing itself. Moreover, there is the same account, as regards the present matter, of the intellect and the impressed species. For the intellect, since it is of itself indeterminate and indifferent to any act, corresponds by analogy and proportion to a universal cause: but the impressed species of the object, since it determines the intellect to a certain species of the act of cognition, corresponds by analogy and proportion to a second and particular cause. VI. Nor is it an objection that the generic being of an idea, namely being a cognition, is referred to one cause; and the specific being, namely being such or such a cognition, which is to say the image of such or such a thing, is referred to another: the generic being indeed to the intellect; but the specific being to the species of the object impressed upon the intellect. For that is not to be understood in the sense as if the intellect separately and alone influenced the being of cognition, and the species of the object similarly separately and alone influenced the being of the image, as if into two really distinct effects, but the sense is that the intellect and the species of the object, as two incomplete causes coalescing into one complete cause, produce an idea which is essentially the cognition of a certain object, and indeed of that object whose species concurs with the intellect for its production, and the intellect determines the indeterminate power of acting to produce it. This also happens in the effects of secondary and primary causes. God, as the primary cause, concurs with an ox for the generation of an ox, with a horse for the generation of a horse, etc., and each cause jointly constitutes one complete cause of generation, upon which the whole effect simultaneously depends: but the concurrence of the primary cause is indeterminate and is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause, and that one is the generation of an ox, not of a horse; the other is the generation of a horse, not of an ox, that is from the second, not from the first cause, so that nevertheless, as regards the thing itself, there is one undivided effect of both causes. VII. Nor do the arguments of Clauberg prove otherwise, which we do not adduce for the sake of brevity, though they are in his cited Exercit.

VII. can be seen. All things, if anything, conclude this, that there is a specific [being] of an idea, or, as he speaks, that it is its objective and vicarious [being], that it is some real thing, not nothing: which we willingly grant. But that it is some real thing, really distinct from generic being, or, which is the same thing, from the being of cognition, in such a way indeed that the specific or objective and vicarious being is innate to the intellect before every act of cognition; but the generic being, or that of cognition, is elicited by the intellect or can be said to be, this is what comes into question, and what it was incumbent upon Clauberg to prove. Because he did not even attempt to prove this, what else did he do with all his arguments, produced in a long series but straying from the point, than [produce] great trifles with great effort?

Latin:

ut Cartesius contendit, ejus causam nondum video. Res cogitata sive cognita, in se & ut à cognitione distingvitur, non est ipsa idea, sed ejus objectum, idque restrictio addita: quatenus est objectivè in intellectu, indicat. Ejus enim vis & ratio significandi hæc est: ideam solis nor. esse solem, secundum ejus esse reale, sed tantùm secundum esse objectivum illius, & redit jam quæstio, quidnam sit illud esse objectivum solis in intellectu? Nos cum usu Philosophis recepto dicimus, nihil esse aliud, quàm solem esse objectum cognitionis, sive eum cognosci ab intellectu, & terminare actum cognoscendi per modum objecti, quod soli per denominationem extrinsecam convenit. Neque aliud quicquam, phrasi eâ auditâ, intellectu concipiunt, qui quidem terminorum gnari sunt. Qui sensus si Cartesio ad palatum non est, necesse est, ut alium commodiorem nobis tradat, & solidè probet. Quem ergo tradit? Sed, ait, (esse objectivè in intellectu est) in intellectu eo modo esse, quo solent ejus objecta (in eo esse) adeò ut idea solis sit sol ipse in intellectu existens, non quidem formaliter, ut in cælo, sed objectivè, h. e. eo modo, quo objecta in intellectu esse solent. Sed quæso te, lector candide, quid est nugari, si hoc non est? Esse objectivè in intellectu non est cognosci ab intellectu & cognitionis actum per modum objecti terminare, ut contendit Cartesius, sed est esse eo modo in intellectu, quo objecta in eo esse solent. Sed quærenti, quo modo objecta v. g. sol, in intellectu esse soleant, respondet, idem esse, atque esse in intellectu, non formaliter, ut v. g. sol in cœlo est, sed objectivè h. e. eo modo, quo objecta in intellectu esse solent. Quæ annon pueris indigna nugatio est? Et tamen dicit, esse objectivè in intellectu esse, ex parte rerum, modum quendam essendi, longè imperfectiorem quidem, quàm illum, quo res extra intellectum existunt; nec tamen proptereà nihil esse. Quæ quis tandem capiat? Esse objectivè in intellectu importare ex parte objecti aliquid reale, cum ab objecto ipso, ut extra intellectum est, tum ab actu cognoscendi, quem terminat, distinctum, huc usque docere non potuit, sed eò cùm deventum est, præter nigationem, quòd esse objectivè in intellectu nihil aliud sit, quàm eo modo esse in intellectu, quo objecta in eo esse solent, adferre nihil potuit: modum enim, quo objecta aliter quàm per nudum actum cognoscendi in intellectu sint vel esse soleant, tam docere non potest, quam docere non potest, esse objectivè in intellectu importare, præter actum cognoscendi, aliquid reale, quod ex parte objecti se habeat, & ab objecto ipso, ut extra intellectum existit, distinctum sit. Quâ ratione ergo, aut quâ saltem speciæ veri dicere potest, esse objectivè in intellectu esse modum essendi verum, qui non sit nihil, imperfectiorem tamen illo, quo extra intellectum existant? Et quinam, quæso, perfectus vel imperfectus modus essendi supervenit lapidi per hoc, quòd à me cognoscitur, & per actum cognoscendi meo intellectui repræsentatur? Cùm ergo, præter actum cognoscendi, nihil possit ostendi, per quod res cognitæ dicantur esse objectivè in intellectu, quid superest, quàm ut Cartesianorum ideas, quæ tantùm secundum esse objectivum sive vicarium innatæ esse dicuntur, non secundum esse formale & proprium, suave somnium esse dicamus? Ideæ secundum rem non nisi unum est esse, quod consistit in actu cognoscendi, rem cognitam repræsentante, sive in specie seu imagine Objecti, per actum cognoscendi expressâ. Speciem autem sive imaginem rei expressam, quæ per essentiam est ipse actus cognoscendi, qui intellectui innatam dicit, actum cognoscendi autem eidem innatum esse negat, quid aliud facit, quàm ut idem simul affirmet & neget, per apertam & palpabilem contradictionem?

IV. Cartesius tamen ejusque discipuli, ut modò vidimus, urgent, aliam esse causam ideæ, quatenus dicit actum cognoscendi, sive ut ille loqui amat, modum cogitandi, aliam esse ejusdem causam, quatenus est imago hujus, non alterius rei: vel, juxta Claubergium, aliam esse causam ideæ secundum ejus esse formale & proprium, sive quatenus est operatio mentis; aliam esse causam illius secundum ejus esse objectivum & vicarium, sive quatenus est imago talis rei: Ex quo colligere videntur, aliam esse entitatem actus cognoscendi; aliam ipsius esse objectivi sive vicarii: cùm â duabus realiter distinctis causis non possit non effectus duplex, vel saltem duplex esse effectus provenire, quorum unum non sit alterum, atque adeò quæ sint realiter inter se distincta. Quo collineare videntur omnia Claubergii argumenta, quibus in Exercit. VII. probatum ivit, esse objectivum sive vicarium ideæ esse reale, & ab actu cognoscendi realiter distinctum. v. Quamvis verò non inficiemur, in idea, nostro modo intelligendi, duplex esse: Unum cognitionis, ut sic; alterum imaginis, sive cognitionis talis, quæ hujus non alterius rei repræsentativa est, concipi, & aliam illi, aliam huic causam assignari posse: tamen ex parte rei duplex esse, sive duas entitates, quarum una sit cognitio quædam, altera imago rei cognitæ in idea dari, negamus & pernegamus. Idea cujusq; rei, prout quidem hîc vox ideæ accipitur, nihil est aliud, quàm conceptus, sive actus cognoscendi, quo res intellectui repræsentatur: qui tamen duobus inadæquatis conceptibus, uno generico, altero specifico, sola ratione distinctis, à nobis concipitur. Quod ut rectè intelligas, sciendum est, intellectum per se præcisè, citra concursum objecti, spectatum, esse principium cognoscendi incompletum, non magis ad unum, quàm ad alium quemvis actum cognoscendi eliciendum determinatum, nec posse per se solum ullius rei cognitionem elicere. Ut ergo in esse principii cognoscendi completi constituatur, requiritur, ut objectum cum eo concurrat, & per modum principii partialis ad cognitionem sui eliciendam illum determinet. Objecta verò quia per se ipsa cum intellectu conjungi, eumque ad cognitionem sui eliciendam determinare non possunt, transmittunt interventu sensuum species suas ad phantasiam, & per phantasmata, ab intellectu agente elevata, porro ad intellectum possibilem, quæ vice objectorum eum ad cognitionem, objectis similem, eaque repræsentantem, eliciendam determinant, ut ita idea, quoad rem, nihil aliud sit, quàm cognitionis actus, objecto similis, idque repræsentans, quam Philosophi usitatè speciem objecti expressam appellant, & à specie impressa, velut effectum à causa, distinguunt. Quamvis ergo causæ efficientes ideæ duæ sint: intellectus scilicet & species impressa, effectus utriusque tamen, quoad rem, unus est, ipsum scilicet simplex esse ideæ, in actu cognoscendi, objecto simili, idque repræsentante, constitutum. Quod dicitur in objectione, à duabus realiter distinctis causis non posse non duos realiter distinctos effectus provenire, de causis incompletis verum non est. Hoc ipso enim, quòd incompletæ causæ sunt, & simul junctim sumtæ unam completam constituunt causam, non duos, sed unum, quoad rem, effectum ab illis provenire necesse est. Quod patet exemplo causæ primæ & secundæ, quæ duæ realiter distinctæ, sed incompletæ causæ sunt, & hoc ipso quod simul junctim sumtæ unam completam causam constituunt, non nisi unum quoad rem effectum producant. Est autem intellectus & speciei impressæ, quoad præsens, parratio. Intellectus enim cùm ex se indeterminatus & ad quemvis actum indifferens sit, respondet analogiâ & proportione causæ universali: species objecti impressa autem, cùm intellectum ad certam speciem actus cognitionis determinet, respondet analogiâ & proportione causæ secundæ & particulari. VI. Neque obstat, quod in aliam causam esse genericum ideæ, puta esse cognitionis; in aliam esse specificum, puta esse talis vel talis cognitionis, quæ scilicet talis vel talis rei imago est, refertur: esse genericum quidem in intellectum; esse specificum verò in speciem objecti, intellectui impressam. Id enim non eo intelligendum est sensu, quasi intellectus seorsim & solus influat in esse cognitionis; & species objecti similiter seorsim & sola influat in esse imaginis, tanquam in duos realiter distinctos effectus, sed sensus est, intellectum & speciem objecti, tanquam duas incompletas causas, coalescentes in unam causam completam, producere ideam, quæ essentialiter sit cognitio certi cujusdam objecti, & quidem illius objecti, cujus species cum intellectu ad ejus productionem concurrit, & intellectus virtutem agendi indeterminatam ad eam producendam determinat. Quod etiam in effectibus causarum secundarum & primæ usu venit. Deus velut causa prima concurrit cum bove ad generationem bovis, cum equo ad generationem equi &c. & causa utraque junctim constituit unam causam generationis completam, à qua effectus simul totus dependet: sed concursus causæ primæ indeterminatus determinatur per concursum causæ secundæ, & quod una generatio bovis, non equi; altera equi, non bovis generatio est, id à secunda, non à prima causa est, ut tamen causæ utriusque, quoad rem, unus indivisus effectus sit. VII. Neque diversum evincunt argumenta Claubergii, quæ brevitatis studio non adferimus, apud eum tamen in citata Exercit.

VII. videri possunt. Omnia, si quidquam, hoc concludunt, esse specificum ideæ, sive, ut ille loquitur, ejus esse objectivum & vicarium, esse reale quid, non nihil: quod ultrò largimur. Quod autem sit aliquid reale, ab esse generico, sive, quod idem est, ab esse cognitionis realiter distinctum, ita quidem, ut esse specificum sive objectivum & vicarium intellectui ante omnem cognitionis actum innatum; esse genericum autem sive cognitionis, ab intellectu elicitum sit aut dici queat, hoc est, quod in quæstionem venit, quodque Claubergio probandum incumbebat. Quod quia ne quidem conatus est probare, quid aliud suis, longâ serie productis, sed à scopo abludentibus omnibus, argumentis egit, quàm magnas nugas, magno conatu?


### VIII. One difficulty remains to be examined concerning the idea of God

VIII. One difficulty remains to be examined concerning the idea of God: namely, that God does not transmit a species of himself through the intervention of the senses and phantasms to the possible intellect: for he is an immaterial being, which does not fall under the senses. Therefore, the specific or vicarious being of the idea of God is not from an impressed species. Therefore, it is implanted or innate to the intellect by God himself. Thus Descartes seems to conclude in Medit. III, p. m. 24, where, intending to investigate by what reason he received that idea (of God); For neither, he says, did I draw it from the senses, nor did it ever come to me when I was not expecting it, as the ideas of sensible things are wont to do, when those things occur, or seem to occur, to the external organs of the senses; nor was it fashioned by me, for I can clearly take nothing away from it, nor add anything to it, and therefore it remains that it is innate to me, just as the idea of myself is also innate to me.

IX. But this difficulty is not as great as it appears in the eyes of the Cartesians. For although God in himself falls under no sense, nor does he himself immediately imprint any proper species of himself upon the human intellect, yet his effects, which are signs of his essence and essential perfections, do fall under the senses, and transmit their species to the possible intellect through the intervention of the senses and phantasms. Just as, however, the sensible effects of God lead us into the knowledge of God: For the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament (expanse) showeth his handywork, Psalm XIX. 1, 2, and his invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood from the things that are made, namely his eternal power and divinity, Rom. I. 20. So also our intellect is determined to elicit acts of knowing, which represent God and his essential perfections, by means of the species of sensible effects produced by God, transmitted to it through the intervention of the senses and phantasms, yet by means of discourse and by consequence. For in every discourse, impressed species determine the intellect proximately to the knowledge of the premises; but remotely and by means of the knowledge of the premises, to the knowledge of the conclusion. Therefore, an idea or knowledge of God can be had, although his proper species is neither innate to the intellect nor impressed by the intervention of the senses; indeed, although no proper species of him is given in the intellect. For to conceive this in the mind, the species of created things can suffice, as has been said. For in the discourse by which we are led from created things into the knowledge of God and his essential perfections, the species of created things determine the intellect to elicit the knowledge of the premises, which contain the medium of concluding, sought from created things as if from the effects of God, and infer the existence of God or his essential perfections: but the knowledge of those [premises] further determines the same [intellect] to the knowledge of the conclusions, which assert the existence of God or his essential perfections; and thus the species of created things determine the intellect to the knowledge of God at least remotely and by means of discourse; but proximately and immediately they determine it to the same [knowledge] through the premises known, which are sought from created things, or rather through the knowledge of them.

X. But here Descartes objects again in the third Meditation, page 21 of the edition, that there is more reality in an infinite substance than in a finite one, and consequently that the perception of the infinite is in a way prior in me than that of the finite, that is, of God than of myself: for by what reason would I understand that I doubt, that I desire, that is, that something is lacking to me, and that I am not altogether perfect, if there were no idea of a more perfect being in me, by comparison with which I might recognize my defects? The sum returns to this: Whoever has in himself the idea of a finite and imperfect being, he has in himself prior, if not in time, yet in nature, the idea of an infinite and perfect being. But he who has in himself the idea of himself, he has in himself the idea of a finite and imperfect being. Therefore, he who has in himself the idea of himself, he has in himself prior, if not in time, yet in the order of nature, the idea of an infinite and perfect being, i.e., God. Therefore, the idea of God is not acquired finally through external species and impressed upon the intellect by created things, but is prior in the order of nature to every idea of a created thing, and therefore innate to the intellect. The reason for the major proposition is: because a finite and imperfect being, by the very fact that it is finite and imperfect, implies certain defects of perfection. Defects of perfection, however, cannot be known unless a comparison is instituted with a more perfect being, known beforehand through its own pre-existing idea in the intellect. For more on this matter, see Clauberg in Exerc. IX.

xi. This seems to be the principal foundation of the Cartesians, upon which they rely to establish that the idea of God is innate in the minds of men: to which, however, nothing solid or strong underlies. For the major proposition is false, to which the passage of Paul, Rom. 1:20, just cited, is diametrically opposed. For the invisible things of God, namely his eternal power and divinity, are undoubtedly contained objectively in the idea, i.e., the concept of God. But these, from the creation of the world, τοῖς ποιήμασι νούμενα καθορᾶται, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, as Paul says in the aforementioned place. Therefore, the idea of an Infinite being can be had from known finite and created things; since the καθόρασις τῶν ἀοράτων τοῦ θεοῦ, τοῖς ποιήμασι νουμένων, the clear view, if I may so speak, of the invisible things of God known from the things that are made, is, as to the thing itself, nothing other than the knowledge or idea of God, drawn from created things. It is not, therefore, simply necessary that the idea of an infinite being should precede the idea of a finite being in the human intellect, if not in time, then in the order of nature, and a progression can be made in the reverse order from the latter to the former. What is said in confirmation of the major proposition, that a finite and imperfect being implies certain defects of perfection, is true. Indeed, it is also true that the defects of perfection which are found in this or that finite being cannot be known unless a comparison is instituted with some more perfect being, in which those perfections, the lack of which this or that finite being implies, are in some way contained. But that that more perfect being, by comparison with which the imperfections of finite beings are known, must be God, and that its idea must therefore precede all ideas of finite beings, at least in the order of nature, this is what we deny. For there are given in created and finite beings there are degrees of perfections, and their defects can be known from a comparison of created beings among themselves: e.g., from a comparison of a stone with a plant I know that in the stone there is not the perfection of the vegetative faculty, and of the vital operations depending thereon, and that the stone is more imperfect than the plant; from a comparison of a plant with a brute I know that in the plant there is not the perfection of the sensitive and locomotive faculty, which is in the brute, and that the plant is more imperfect than the brute; and from a comparison of the brute with man I know that in the brute there is not the perfection of the faculty of reasoning, which is in man, and consequently that the brute is more imperfect than man. If furthermore man descends into himself, he can easily know his own imperfections, even if he does not recur in his intellect to the perfections of an infinite being, namely God. e.g. That the faculty of knowing in himself is not perfect in all ways, he can know from a comparison of the acts of knowing themselves among themselves and with their objects. For the intellect knows some things evidently and without fear of the opposite: others it knows obscurely and with fear of the opposite, some it clearly does not know. Moreover, evident knowledge is more perfect than non-evident and obscure knowledge, and both are more perfect than ignorance, and consequently the faculty of knowing, which does not know all things knowable, but is entirely ignorant of some, and knows others indeed, but non-evidently and imperfectly, is finite and imperfect. Thus also that the power of acting in himself is not perfect in all ways, man can know from the things produced, of which many are given, which he cannot produce by his own power. For he cannot produce the heaven and the elements, not stones and metals, not plants, not brute animals, etc. But he who by his own power of acting cannot produce all things which can be produced, and are produced by other causes, his power is finite and imperfect. And so the matter stands in other things.

XII. But, the Cartesians will say, be it so! the defects of things can be known from a comparison of them among themselves, yet the idea of God cannot be obtained from that comparison among them: since that, from which the idea of God depends as to its specific being, or as they say, as to its objective and vicarious being, must contain in itself really all the perfections which are represented by it. But those created and finite things do not contain [these] in themselves, whether viewed individually or collectively, but God alone. Therefore, the idea of God depends on God alone, as regards its objective or vicarious being, not on created and finite things, and thus it is immediately implanted in the intellect by God in its very production, or is innate to it. To which the words of Descartes, cited a little earlier in n. x., seem to point.

xii. But this exception again contradicts Paul, who in the said passage expressly teaches that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. For the invisible things of God, understood by the things that are made, cannot be clearly seen otherwise than through an idea or cognition drawn from the things that are made, by which they are represented to the intellect. Since, therefore, the things that are made do not contain in themselves all the perfections which are represented to the intellect by the idea of God, and yet the idea of the invisible things of God can be had from them, it cannot be universally true, as the Cartesians assume as certain, that that upon which an idea depends for its specific being, or, as they speak, for its objective and vicarious being, must contain in itself all the perfections which are represented by it. It proceeds, therefore, only concerning that upon which an idea depends proximately and immediately for its specific being; not concerning that upon which it depends at least remotely and by means of discourse. For just as in discourse the conclusion is not actually and formally or really contained in the premises, but only potentially and virtually, so also it is not necessary that the perfections of the thing about which the conclusion is inferred, and which its idea represents, be actually and formally or really contained in the things signified by the premises, but it suffices if they are contained in them at least potentially and virtually. And the thing itself speaks to this: for example, when the idea of a cause is conceived from a known equivocal effect, the essential perfections of the cause, which are represented by its idea, are never contained really in that upon which the idea depends remotely and through discourse for its specific, or objective and vicarious being, i.e., in the equivocal effect: otherwise it would not be an equivocal effect, but a univocal one: but only significatively, or as a thing signified is said to be contained in its sign. For effects and their perfections are only signs of causes and of the perfections that are in them, but they do not really contain their efficient causes in themselves: for they are distinguished from one another.

Latin:

VIII. Una excutienda superest difficultas de idea Dei: nempe Deus non transmittit sui speciem interventu sensuum & phantasmatum ad intellectum possibilem: est enim ens immateriale, quod sub sensus non cadit. Ergo esse specificum sive vicarium ideæ Dei non est à specie impressa. Ergo est à Deo ipso intellectui inditum sive innatum. Ita colligere videtur Cartesius in Medit. III. p. m. 24. ubi investigaturus, quâ ratione ideam istam (Dei) à Deo acceperit; Neque enim, inquit, illam sensibus hausi, nec unquam non expectanti mihi advenit, ut solent rerum sensibilium ideæ, cùm istæ res externis sensuum organis occurrunt, vel occurrere videntur; nec etiam à me efficta est, nam nihil ab ea detrahere, nihil illi superaddere planè possum, ac proinde superest, ut mihi sit innata, quemadmodum & mihi innata est idea mei ipsius.

IX. Sed difficultas hæc tanta non est, quanta in oculis Cartesianorum apparet. Quamvis enim Deus per se sub nullum sensum cadat, neque etiam aliquam sui speciem propriam per se immediatè hominis intellectui imprimat, ejus effectus tamen, qui ipsius essentiæ & perfectionum essentialium signa sunt, cadunt sub sensus, & transmittunt sui species ad intellectum possibilem interventu sensuum & phantasmatum. Quemadmodum autem effectus Dei sensibiles in notitiam Dei nos deducunt: Cæli enim enarrant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum ipsius indicat firmamentum (expansum) Psal. XIX. 1. 2. & Invisibilia ipsius inde à condito mundo ex rebus factis intellecta pervidentur, æterna scilicet ejus potentia & divinitas, Rom. I. 20. ita & intellectus noster per species effectuum sensibilium, à Deo productorum, interventu sensuum & phantasmatum ad se transmissas, determinatur ad actus cognoscendi eliciendos, qui Deum ejusque perfectiones essentiales repræsentant, mediante discursu tamen & per consequentiam. In omni enim difcursu species impressæ determinant intellectum proximè ad cognitionem præmissarum; remotè autem & mediante cognitione præmissarum ad cognitionem conclusionis. Potest ergo haberi idea sive cognitio Dei, licet ejus species propria intellectui nec innata, nec sensuum interventu impressa sit, imo licet ejus species propria in intellectu nulla detur. Ad hanc enim animo concipiendam sufficere possunt species rerum creatarum, uti dictum. In discursu enim, quo ex rebus creatis in cognitionem Dei ejusque perfectionum essentialium deducimur, determinant species rerum creatarum intellectum ad eliciendam cognitionem præmissarum, quæ medium concludendi, à rebus creatis velut effectibus Dei petitum continent, & Dei existentiam ejusve perfectiones essentiales inferunt: illarum verò cognitio determinat eundem porro ad cognitionem conclusionum, quæ Dei existentiam ejusve perfectiones essentiales asserunt;& sic species rerum creatarum determinant intellectum ad cognitionem Dei remotè saltem & mediante discursu; proximè autem & immediatè determinant illum ad eandem petitæ à rebus creatis præmissæ cognitæ, vel potiùs illarum cognitio.

X. Sed hîc objicit rursum Cartesius in Medit. tertia, pag. m. 21. plus realitatis esse in substantia infinita, quàm in finita, ac proinde priorem quodammodo in me esse perceptionem infiniti, quàm finiti, hoc est, Dei, quàm meipsius: quâ enim ratione intelligerem me dubitare, me cupere, hoc est, aliquid mihi deesse, & me non esse omninò perfectum, si nulla idea entis perfectioris in me esset, ex cujus comparatione defectus meos agnoscerem? Summa redit huc: Quicunque in se habet ideam entis finiti & imperfecti, is habet in se prius, si non tempore, tamen naturâ ideam entis infiniti & perfecti. Atqui qui habet in se ideam sui ipsius, is habet in se ideam entis finiti & imperfecti. Ergo qui habet in se ideam sui ipsius, is habet in se prius, si non tempore, ordine naturæ tamen ideam entis infiniti & perfecti, h. e. Dei. Ergo idea Dei non acquiritur demum per fpecies alienas, & à rebus creatis intellectui impresas, sed ordine naturæ omni ideâ rei creatæ prior, adeoque intellectui ingenita est. Ratio propositionis majoris est: quia ens finitum & imperfectum hoc ipso, quod finitum & imperfectum est, importat defectus quosdam perfectionis. Defectus autem perfectionis cognosci non possunt, nisi institutâ comparatione cum ente perfectiori, per suam in intellectu præexistentem ideam prius cognito. Plura hanc in rem videantur apud Claubergium in Exerc. IX.

xi. Hoc videtur esse præcipuum Cartesianorum fundamentum, quo nixi ideam Dei mentibus hominum ingenitam statuunt : cui tamen nihil solidi, roboris nihil subest. Major enim propositio falsa est, cui locus Pauli Rom. I. 20. modò allegatus, è diametro adversatur.
