Nam invisibilia Dei, æterna scilicet ejus potentia & divinitas, continentur haut dubiè objectivè in idea, h. e. conceptu Dei. Ea verò inde à condito mundo τοῖς ποιήμασι νούμενα καθορᾶται, ex rebus factis intellecta pervidentur, dicente Paulo d. l. Ergò idea entis Infiniti potest haberi ex rebus creatis & finitis cognitis : cùm καθέρασις τῶν ἀοράτων τῦ θεῦ, τοῖς ποιήμασι νουμένων, pervisio, ut ita loquar, invisibilium Dei ex rebus factis cognitorum, quoad rem, nihil aliud sit, quàm cognitio sive idea Dei, ex rebus creatis haufta. Non ergo simpliciter necessarium est, ut ideam entis finiti, si non tempore, ordine naturæ tamen, idea entis infiniti in hominis intellectu præcedat, potestque ordine inverso ab ista ad hanc fieri progressus. Quod ad confirmationem propositionis majoris dicitur, ens finitum & imperfectum importare defectus quosdam perfectionis, verum est. Quin verum & illud est, defectus perfectionis, qui in hoc, illo ente finito dantur, non posse cognosci, nisi institutâ comparatione cum aliquo ente perfectiori, in quo perfectiones illæ, quarû defectum hoc, illud ens finitum importat, aliquo modo contineantur. Quòd autem ens illud perfectius, cujus comparatione entium finitorum imperfectiones cognoscuntur, Deum esse, ejusq; ideam entium finitorum ideas omnes, minimùm ordine naturæ, proptereà præcedere oporteat, hoc est, quod negamus. Dantur enim in entibus creatis & finitis gradus perfectionum, & possunt illorum defectus ex comparatione entium creatorum inter se cognosci: v. g. ex comparatione lapidis cum planta cognosco, in lapide non esse perfectionem facultatis vegetativæ, & hinc dependentium operationum vitalium, & lapidem esse plantâ imperfectiorem; ex comparatione plantæ cum bruto cognosco, in planta non esse perfectionem facultatis sensitivæ & locomotivæ, quæ est in bruto, & plantam esse imperfectiorem bruto; & ex comparatione bruti cum homine cognosco, in bruto non esse perfectionem facultatis ratiocinandi, quæ in homine est, & proinde brutum esse imperfectius homine. Si porro in semetipsum homo descendat, potest facilè suas imperfectiones cognoscere, licet ad perfectiones entis infiniti, Dei scilicet, intellectu non recurrat. v. g. Facultatem cognoscendi in se non esse modis omnibus perfectam, cognoscere potest ex comparatione ipsorum actuum cognoscendi inter se & cum objectis. Quædam enim cognoscit intellectus evidenter & absque formidine oppositi: alia cognoscit obscurè & cum formidine oppositi, quædam planè non cognoscit. Cognitio autem evidens perfectior est inevidente & obscurâ, & utraque perfectior est ignorantiâ, & proinde facultas co gnoscendi, quæ non omnia cognoscibilia cognoscit, sed quædã penitùs ignorat, alia cognoscit quidem, sed inevidenter & imperfectè, finita & imperfecta est. Sic & potentiam operandi in se non esse modis omnibus perfectam, cognoscere potest homo ex rebus productis, quarum multæ dantur, quæ suâ potentiâ producere non potest. Non potest enim producere cœlum & elementa, non lapides & metalla, non plantas, non bruta animantia &c. Qui autem suâ potentiâ operandi non potest producere omnia, quæ produci possunt, & per causas alias producuntur, ejus potentia finita & imperfecta est. Et ita in aliis res habet.

XII. Sed, inquient Cartesiani, esto! possint defectus rerum cognosci ex comparatione illarum inter se, idea Dei tamen non potest obtineri ex ista inter eas comparatione: cùm id, ex quo idea Dei quoad suum esse specificum, vel ut illi loquuntur, quoad esse objectivum & vicarium dependet, oporteat omnes perfectiones, quæ per eam repræsentantur, in se realiter continere. Eas verò non continent in se res creatæ & finitæ realiter, sive sigillatim, sive junctim spectentur, sed solus Deus. Ergo à solo Deo dependet idea Dei, quoad esse objectivum sive vicarium, non à rebus creatis & finitis, adeoque à Deo immediatè intellectui in ipsa ejus productione indita, sive ei ingenita est. Quò collineare videntur verba Cartesii, paulò antè n. x. adducta.

xii. Verum exceptio hæc rursum contradicit Paulo, qui d. l. difertè docet, invisibilia Dei, ex rebus factis intellecta, pervideri. Non possunt enim invisibilia Dei, ex rebus factis intellecta, aliter pervideri, quàm per ideam sive cognitionem, ex rebus factis haustam, quâ intellectui repræsentantur. Cùm ergo res factæ non contineant in se realiter omnes perfectiones, quæ per ideam Dei intellectui repræsentantur, & tamen ex illis idea invisibilium Dei haberi possit, universaliter verum esse non potest, quod sumunt Cartesiani tanquam certum, illud, ex quo idea quoad suum esse specificum, sive, ut illi loquuntur, quoad suum esse objectivum & vicarium dependet, oportere in se realiter continere omnes perfectiones, quæ per eam repræsentantur. Procedit igitur tantum de eo, à quo idea in suo esse specifico dependet proximè & immediatè; non de illo, à quo dependet remotè saltem & mediante discursu. Quemadmodum enim in discursu conclusio non actu & formaliter sive realiter continetur in præmissis, sed potentiâ tantum & virtualiter, ita nec perfectiones rei, de qua conclusio infertur, & quas ejus idea repræsentat, in rebus per præmissas significatis actu & formaliter, sive realiter contineri necesse est, sed sufficit, si potentiâ saltem & virtualiter in illis contineantur. Quod & res ipsa loquitur: v. g. cùm ex cognito effectu æquivoco concipitur idea causæ, perfectiones essentiales causæ, quæ per ejus ideam repræsentantur, nunquam continentur realiter in eo, à quo idea in suo esse specifico, sive objectivo & vicario remotè & per discursum dependet, h. e. in effectu æquivoco: aliàs enim non effectus univocus, sed æquivocus esset: sed tantùm significativè, sive ut signatum in suo signo contineri dicitur. Effectus enim illorumque perfectiones sunt tantùm signa causarum &, quæ illis insunt, perfectionum, non autem realiter in se continent suas causas efficientes: distinguuntur enim ab invicem


### adequately; or even their essential perfections, unless they are univocal…

adequately; or even their essential perfections, unless they are univocal effects. Which also finds a place in the present question concerning the idea of God. When we turn our eyes to this universe, we are led directly into the knowledge of its cause, and we conceive of some first being, upon whom it depends in its existence. That cause is none of those things which are contained in this universe, and yet from this known universe we conceive some idea of God, but an idea of God as a cause, from this universe as an effect and sign. Furthermore, when we contemplate in it an innumerable multitude of parts, their wonderful variety, the vicissitude of causes and effects, the adornment of the heavenly bodies, and their motion, which is always constant and uniform, we immediately perceive that it was produced by a cause whose power, wisdom, and knowledge is infinite. For no reason can be given why He who produced all these things that exist could not produce all other possible things; or why anything could escape the knowledge and wisdom of Him who made all these things so congruously and beautifully, and who so wisely rules and governs them. Where the infinite power, knowledge, and wisdom of God is not contained really in created things, which this universe embraces, but only as the thing signified in its sign. For the dependence of this universe upon the first cause, by reason of all its parts, is a sign of His infinite power, and when known, it leads us into the knowledge of divine omnipotence; and the wonderful variety, arrangement, adornment, and most wise government of all the parts is a sign of the same infinite knowledge and wisdom; and when known, it leads us into the knowledge of divine omniscience and omnisapience; and both items of knowledge are obtained by us from created things through discursive reasoning, although the created things do not really contain those divine perfections. Let the same judgment apply to the other divine perfections, of which certain traces, as it were, exist in created things, and which can be elicited and known from them by consequence.

XIII. But if, furthermore, the disciples of Descartes should object that they, having followed the method of philosophizing of their teacher, suppose now that there is no heaven, no bodies, and that they themselves have no hands, nor feet, nor finally any body, and by this very act free themselves from preconceived opinions or prejudices and ideas, from the intuition of the heaven and other arising from the parts of this universe, and to devote themselves now entirely to the contemplation of ideas, with their thoughts turned away from sensible things, which the intellect has within itself, and which are not received from elsewhere and from sensible objects, but are innate; we respond that they can indeed imagine these things: but that they can by no means strip the intellect of the species of sensible things, impressed upon it over some years by the intervention of the senses, so that it might seriously judge and determine thus. For the intellect is a necessary power, nor is it subject to the command of the will in those things which it evidently knows (just as it certainly knows proper sensibles, when exposed to the senses at a due distance), nor can it be induced to judge, for example, that fire does not exist, or that it is not hot, but cold, which it perceives by touch to exist and to be hot, or to judge that a crow is white, which it sees to be black. Nor will the reasons for doubting, brought forward by Descartes, either persuade such a thing to a man who is of sound mind, or erase the species of sensible things, impressed upon the intellect from tender years, which things, never not obvious to the senses, do not cease to excite, foster, and preserve. Whence, however much they may imagine that there is no heaven, no bodies, and that they themselves have no hands, nor feet, nor finally any body, because they nevertheless imagine this while the senses and most evident reasons protest, and because to them no less than to others who imagine no such thing, the heaven, bodies, hands, feet, and each one's own body always strike their senses, their species remain in any case, like spiritual qualities, fixed and permanent, never not impressed upon their intellect, and constitute it in the first act sufficient for those sensible objects, and further for God and his invisible things, namely his infinite power, wisdom, goodness, etc., to be known through discourse from them, as has been said. But enough and more than enough concerning the Cartesian fictitious idea of God, as far as it is innate in the minds of men as an objective or vicarious being, by the contemplation of which they might know that God exists.

II. Some others among modern theologians hold the opinion that a certain species, both of the existence and of the divine attributes, is innate to the intellect, which determines its power, indifferent in itself, to elicit the knowledge of them: which [is] also the notion They think it can be called habitual, if with Thomas the habits of the intellect are constituted in impressed species, well coordinated and arranged among themselves. For thus the impressed species of God, naturally implanted in the intellect, and determining it to know the existence of God and His attributes, will be a certain habit of knowing the existence and attributes of God, innate to the intellect. But this opinion also is pressed by its own difficulties. For that impressed species of the divine existence and attributes is either proper to God; or it is foreign and a species derived from created things, or rather a certain complex of species derived from created things. But neither can be conveniently said. Not the former: because even if it were granted in the highest degree that by the absolute power of God a species proper to God could be produced in the human intellect; which the Thomists in p. 1. q. XII. art. 11. deny, but Vazquez ibid. Disp. XXXVIII. and some others affirm, yet if it were naturally in the human intellect, it would determine it equally in all men to elicit a proper and quidditative concept of God. For it is common to proper impressed species that they determine the intellect to elicit a proper and quidditative concept of a thing, and if a species proper to God were naturally in the intellect of all, it would be necessary that it determine it in all men to elicit a quidditative and proper concept of God. But the consequent is against experience. For all men who are wayfarers experience in themselves that they do not conceive or can conceive God otherwise than in relation to created things, as the first Being, which is from itself and the cause of all other beings, and preserves and governs all things, or as the most excellent being of all, than which nothing better can be or be thought. Nor do the Scriptures otherwise describe God to us and present Him to be known. I am the first, also the last: My hand also has founded the earth, and my right hand has extended the heavens with a span: when I call them, they stand together, says God, describing Himself to us, Isa. XLVIII. 12. Jehovah the most high, terrible, a great King over all the earth, says the Psalmist, Ps. XLVII. 3. God is the King of all the earth, v. 8. Compare Ps. XCIII. 1. Ps. XCV. 3. and elsewhere. Nor can the latter be conveniently said. For first, the species of created things are not born with us, but they are transmitted to the intellect from objects, through the intervention of the senses. Furthermore, if they were born with us, either all or some would be born with us. But no one, without absurdity, would say that all are born with us. But if some? Why the species of these things rather than others? Since all things are equally effects of divine power and wisdom, and testify of their author God and of his existence and essential perfections. But thirdly, let us suppose that some species of created things, and these rather than others, are born with us; yet those would not of themselves immediately determine the intellect to elicit the concept of God, but only mediately through discourse. For any species determines the intellect of itself immediately to elicit the concept of the thing of which it is the proper species, but to the concept of another thing only mediately through discourse. The knowledge of God, however, born from discourse, would have to be reckoned among acquired knowledge, not innate, even if the species of created things, by whose aid the discourse might be instituted, were innate.

III. The more common opinion, and the one more accepted by theologians, is that of those who maintain that the knowledge of the existence of God and of other common notions about God is implanted in us by a certain habit of knowing, innate to the intellect. Those who embrace this seem to suppose that there are habits of the intellect distinct from impressed species. For they distinguish habitual knowledge, implanted by nature, from impressed species. Or if they do not presuppose this, but on the contrary think with Thomas that the habits of the intellect consist in impressed species, or at least include them, then they will not count the habitual knowledge, which they call innate, among the properly so-called habits of the intellect: just as they frequently call it an imperfect habit and a disposition; likewise a τελείωσιν of the intellectual power, analogous to a habit. See what we have brought forward above in the Explanation of thesis XIX regarding this matter. This opinion, although it has no difficulty regarding common notions about God, which are of the 'est' of the third adjacent, such as: God is an intelligent, wise, good, just mind, that He is to be worshipped, etc.; yet regarding the proposition of the 'est' of the second adjacent, 'God is', it is rendered difficult and doubtful by the Scholastics, who deny that it is known of itself as far as we are concerned. That we should enter into this controversy here, the narrowness of the page does not permit. IV. There are, finally, those who refer the innate knowledge of the existence of God to a certain instinct, implanted by nature in the minds of men, by which the intellect is carried toward assent to it. For just as in other things, even those devoid of life and reason, there is implanted by nature a certain inclination toward their end and perfection, e.g., in a stone toward downward motion, in fire toward upward motion, which philosophers call innate appetite: so also in the faculties of the rational soul, the intellect and the will, there seems to be implanted by nature a certain inclination toward God, by which they of their own nature incline toward Him, as toward their end and highest good. For man was created by God for God, so that his appetite cannot be satisfied except in God. Although indeed an appetite, as they call it, innate, does not of itself imply or presuppose cognition: for it exists by nature even in things destitute of the faculty of knowing; yet in intelligent natures it seems to add weight to the intellect and will, so that they are carried by nature toward their end, namely God, and the intellect indeed embraces His existence, when it apprehends the terms, with undoubted assent, without discursive reasoning, even assuming that the terms are not so known to the intellect that, upon their being apprehended, it immediately sees the identity of the predicate with the subject. To which they refer what we produced above from Tertullian, Arnobius, Minucius Felix, and Lactantius concerning the testimony of the soul. For that the Gentiles, even when occupied with the vain superstitions and errors of the gods, often break out into these expressions: What God has given; If God wills: Likewise God is good, God does good, may God bless you; and God sees all things; I commend you to God; God will judge between us; they think this arises from an instinct implanted by nature toward God, by which it happens that, as if nature were compelling, as Lactantius says, they are carried by intellect and voice alike toward the one true God, and truth breaks forth even from unwilling hearts. Concerning the instinct or innate appetite of both the intellect and the will toward God as their end and perfection, see Scotus in IV. Sent. Dist. XLIX. q. IX. & X. Durandus in the same place q. VIII. & others. Vazquez indeed in I. II. q. V. a. VIII. Disp. XXII. c. II. attacks the opinion of Scotus and Durandus concerning innate appetite of the rational creature toward beatitude laboriously. But his arguments, if anything, at least prove this, that there is not in the rational creature an innate appetite for the beatific vision, which is not the subject here, but only an innate appetite for God, known abstractively, and his existence. Although in the same place Vazquez, ch. IV, finally admits that there is in the rational creature a certain appetite for beatitude in general and in particular, which can and ought deservedly to be called a natural appetite, which, however, he contends is elicited, not innate. Which is a disagreement about the word rather than the thing itself.

V. Perhaps one might not inconveniently join this fourth opinion with the preceding third, so that the common notions about God are said to be implanted in the minds of men by nature, both through a certain perfection innate to the intellect, analogous to a habit, and through an instinct or appetite innate to the intellect for God and his existence, so that just as by the power of that intellect it knows the truth of common notions about God, which are of the 'is' of the third adjacent, immediately from the apprehended terms, without discursive reasoning, so by the power of this, as if by a certain weight, it is inclined and carried toward the existence of God, and if it does not know immediately by itself from the apprehended terms that God exists, it nevertheless admits it, compelled by the instinct of nature. This knowledge born from the instinct of nature will rightly be called implanted by nature: since the intellect elicits it by itself immediately, without discursive reasoning. It does not, however, entirely coincide with the knowledge from which propositions known by themselves to us are denominated by the Scholastics, but it extends somewhat more broadly. For the latter is generated precisely from apprehended terms, in which the identity of the predicate with the subject is represented to the intellect so clearly and evidently that, by the power of innate light, it sees it in them by itself immediately, and determines itself to assent without discursive reasoning. But implanted knowledge is called by the ancient Fathers and modern Theologians any knowledge whatsoever which the intellect elicits by itself immediately and without discursive reasoning from apprehended terms, whether it determines itself to elicit it precisely by the evidence of the propositions and the light innate to it, or by an instinct implanted in it by nature and its inclination drawn toward the object: the former of which occurs in propositions known by themselves to us; the latter in on the proposition of the second-adjunct EST: God is; maintaining that, as the Scholastics contend, it is not so evident that, upon the apprehension of the terms, the identity of the predicate with the subject immediately appears to the intellect of itself. For in order for a notion to be called naturally implanted in us, it can suffice if, upon the apprehension of the terms, the intellect immediately determines itself to assent to it without discursive reasoning, if not by the force of the innate light alone, by which it might perceive the identity of the predicate with the subject in the apprehended terms, then by the force of an innate instinct or inclination, which adds weight to the faculty of understanding and, as it were, draws it immediately of itself into assent.

VI. To contract at last into a few words what the matter is, modern theologians do not assert that an actual knowledge of God, or some express species of Him, exists in man before the use of reason. Indeed, there are those who expressly deny it. Nor are there wanting those who deny that an impressed species of Him exists in the intellect by nature and before the use of reason. Whatever, therefore, it is that, according to their mind, can be said to exist in the intellect by nature or to be innate to it, it must necessarily return to a certain innate perfection or light of the intellect, by which, being aided, it may perceive the truth of common notions about God in the apprehended terms immediately, without discursive reasoning. And in this they almost all agree, although some call that innate perfection a habit, others something analogous to a habit, and some call it an imperfect habit and a disposition. And whoever adds to this the instinct inculcated by the ancient Fathers, implanted in man by nature, which adds weight to the intellect and, together with that innate perfection of whatever kind, determines it to grant assent immediately and without discursive reasoning both to other common notions about God and especially to that which is about His existence, will, in our judgment, have strayed in no way from the truth. And so much for the implanted or innate knowledge of God, indeed more prolixly than the nature of our plan required, yet demanded for the convenience of learners: since this matter is usually treated so intricately and obscurely, both by those who come from the school of Descartes and by others, that learners can scarcely grasp the mind of the authors everywhere, let alone determine in their own minds what they ought to embrace or what they ought to reject in such a great variety of opinions.

Latin:

adæquatè; vel etiam illarum perfectiones essentiales, nisi sint effectus univoci. Quod & in quæstione præsenti de idea Dei locum invenit. Cùm in hoc universum convertimus oculos, deducimur oppidò in cognitionem de ejus causa, & concipimus aliquod ens primum, à quo in suo esse dependeat. Causa illa nihil est eorum, quæ in hoc universo continentur, & tamen ex hoc universo cognito concipimus aliquam ideam Dei, sed ideam Dei ut causæ, ex hoc universo, ut effectu & signo. Cùm porro in eo innumeram partium multitudinem, miram illarum varietatem, causarum & effectuum vicissitudinem, corporum cœlestium ornatum, motumque sibi semper constantem & æquabilem intuemur, deprehendimus statim, id productum esse à causa, cujus potentia, sapientia & scientia infinita est. Non enim ratio reddi potest, cur non alia possibilia omnia producere possit, qui hæc, quæ extant, omnia produxit; vel cur scientiam & sapientiam illius, qui hæc omnia tam congruè & pulcrè fecit, & tam sapienter regit & gubernat, quicquam subterfugere possit. Ubi potentia, scientia & sapientia Dei infinita in rebus creatis, quas hoc universum complectitur, non continetur realiter, sed tantùm ut signatum in suo signo. Dependentia enim hujus universi à causa prima ratione omnium suarum partium signum est potentiæ ejus infinitæ, & cognita deducit nos in cognitionem omnipotentiæ divinæ; & mira partium omnium varietas, dispositio, ornatus, ac gubernatio sapientissima signum est ejusdem scientiæ & sapientiæ infinitæ; & cognita deducit nos in cognitionem omniscientiæ & omnisapientiæ divinæ; & utraque cognitio obtingit nobis ex rebus factis per discursum, licet res factæ illas perfectiones divinas realiter non contineant. Idem esto judicium de cæteris perfectionibus divinis, quarum quædam quasi vestigia in rebus creatis extant, & quæ ex iisdem per consequentiam erui & cognosci possunt.

xIII. Quod si porro excipiant discipuli Cartesii, se Præceptoris sui methodum philosophandi secutos supponere jam, nullum esse cœlum, nulla corpora, & seipsos non habere manus, nec pedes, nec denique ullum corpus, & hoc ipsoliberare se à præconceptis opinionibus sive præjudiciis & ideis, ex intuitu cœli cæterarumque hujus univerfi partium provenientibus, & cogitationibus à rebus fenfibilibus averfis incumbere jam totos in contemplationem idearum, quas intra se intellectus habet, easque non aliunde & ab objectis senfibilibus acceptas, sed innatas; respondemus, hæc eos fingere quidem posse: intellectui autem, ut feriò sic judicet & statuat, persuadere, aut speciebus rerum sensibilium, inde ab aliquot annis sensuum interventu ipsi impressis, eum exuere minimè posse. Intellectus enim est potentia necessaria, nec voluntatis imperio subest in iis, quæ evidenter cognoscit (quomodo sensibilia propria, in debita distantia sensibus exposita, utique cognoscit) nec induci potest, ut judicet, v. g. ignem non esse, vel non calidum, sed frigidum esse, quem existere, & calidum esse, tactu percipit, aut ut judicet, corvum esse album, quem nigrum esse videt. Neque rationes dubitandi, à Cartesio allatæ, vel tale quid persuadebunt homini, qui sanâ mente fuerit, vel delebunt species rerum sensibilium, intellectui inde à teneris impressas, quas res sensibus nunquam non obviæ excitare, fovere & conservare non cessant. Unde ut ut fingant, nullum esse cœlum, nulla corpora, & seipsos non habere manus, nec pedes, nec denique ullum corpus, quia tamen sensibus & rationibus evidentissimis reclamantibus id fingunt, & ipsis nihilo minus, quàm aliis, qui tale nihil fingunt, cœlum, corpora, manus, pedes, & suum cujusque corpus semper in ipsorum sensus incurrunt, manent utique illorum species, velut qualitates spiritales, fixæ & permanentes, nunquam non ipsorum intellectui impressæ, & constituunt eum in actu primo sufficientem ad ista objecta sensibilia, & porro ad Deum ejusque invisibilia, infinitam scilicet ejus potentiam, sapientiam, bonitatem &c. per discursum ex illis cognoscenda, uti dictum. Sed plus satis de Cartesianorum commentitia idea Dei, quoad esse objectivum sive vicarium mentibus hominum ingenita, cujus contemplatione Deum esse cognoscant.

II. Nonnulli alii ex Theologis modernis sentiunt, intellectui ingenitam esse speciem quandam impressam cùm existentiæ tum attributorum divinorum, quæ ejus potentiam, de se indifferentem, determinet ad illorum cognitionem eliciendam: quam & notitiam habitualem dici posse opinantur, si cum Thoma habitus intellectus constituantur in speciebus impressis, inter se bene coordinatis ac dispositis. Ita enim species Dei impressa, intellectui naturâ insita, eumque ad Dei existentiam ejusque attributa cognoscenda determinans, erit habitus quidam cognoscendi existentiam & attributa Dei, intellectui innatus. Sed hæc etiam sententia suis urgetur difficultatibus. Nam illa existentiæ & attributorum divinorum impressa species vel est Dei propria; vel est aliena & à rebus creatis desumta species, seu potius complexus quidam specierum, à rebus creatis desumtarum. Sed neutrum commodè dici potest. Non prius: quia si vel maximè concedatur, Dei potentiâ absolutâ posse in hominis intellectu produci speciem Dei propriam; quod Thomistæ in p. 1. q. XII. art. 11. negant, Vazquez autem ibid. Disp. XXXVIII. & nonnulli alii affirmant, tamen si naturâ hominis intellectui inesset, determinaret eum æquè in omnibus hominibus ad conceptum Dei proprium & quidditativum eliciendum. Est enim speciebus impressis propriis hoc commune, ut intellectum ad proprium & quidditativum conceptum rei eliciendum determinent, & si naturâ species Dei propria omnium intellectui inesset, necesse esset, ut eum in omnibus hominibus ad quidditativum & proprium Dei conceptum eliciendum determinaret. Sed consequens est contra experientiam. Experiuntur enim in se homines Viatores omnes, quòd Deum non aliter concipiant aut concipere possint, quàm in ordine ad res creatas, ut Ens primum, quod à se & cæterorum entium omnium causa est, & omnia conservat ac gubernat, vel ut ens omnium excellentissimum, quo nihil melius esse vel cogitari potest. Neque etiam Scripturæ Deum aliter nobis describunt & cognoscendum exhibent. Ego sum primus, etiam ultimus: Etiam manus mea fundavit terram, & dextera mea palmo extendit cælos: me vocante ea, consistunt pariter, inquit Deus, semetipsum nobis describens, Jes. XLIIX. 12. Jehova altissimus, terribilis, Rex magnus super omnem terram, ait Psaltes, Psal. XLVII. 3. Rex universæ terræ Deus, v. 8. Confer. Psal. XCIII. 1. Psal. XCV. 3. & alibi. Neque posterius commodè dici potest. Primùm enim species rerum creatarum non nascuntur nobiscum, sed transmittuntur ad intellectum ab objectis, interventu sensuum. Deinde si nobiscum nascerentur,vel omnes,vel aliquæ nobiscum nascerentur.Sed omnes nasci nobiscum, citra absurditatem, nemo dixerit. Sin aliquæ? cur harum potiùs, quàm aliarum rerum species? cùm res æquè omnes sint effectus potentiæ & sapientiæ divinæ, & de suo autore Deo ejusque existentia & perfectionibus essentialibus testentur. Sed tertiò faciamus, aliquas rerum creatarum species, & has potiùs, quàm alias nasci nobiscum, illæ tamen non per se immediatè determinarent intellectum ad conceptum Dei eliciendum, sed mediante discursu demum. Quælibet species enim determinat intellectum per se immediatè ad conceptum ejus rei,cujus propria, eliciendum, ad alterius autem rei conceptum demum mediante discursu. Notitia Dei autem, ex discursu nata, referenda esset in censum acquisitarum notitiarum, non innatarum, ut ut species rerum creatarum, quarum adminiculo discursus institueretur, innatæ essent.

III. Communior & Theologis magis recepta sententia est eorum,qui statuunt, notitiam de existentia Dei aliarumque de Deo notionum communium esse nobis insitam per habitum quendam cognoscendi, intellectui innatum. Quam qui amplectuntur, supponere videntur, dari habitus intellectus, à speciebus impressis distinctos. Distinguunt enim notitiam habitualem, naturâ insitam, à speciebus impressis. Vel si id non præsupponunt, sed contrà cum Thoma sentiunt, habitus intellectus consistere in speciebus impressis, vel saltem illas includere, tum habitualem, quam dicunt innatam, notitiam in propriè dictis habitibus intellectus non numerabunt: sicut etiam illam frequenter habitum imperfectum & dispositionem; item τελείωσιν potentiæ intellectualis, habitui analogam appellant. Videantur, quæ supra in Explicatione th. XIX. hanc in rem adduximus. Sententia hæc, etsi difficultatem non habet in notionibus communibus de Deo, quæ sunt de est tertii adjecti, cujusmodi sunt, Deum esse mentem intelligentem, sapientem, bonam, justam, esse colendum &c. quantum ad propositionem tamén de est secundi adjecti, Deus est; difficilis & dubia redditur à Scholasticis, qui eam quoad nos per se notam esse, inficiantur. Quam in controversiam ut hic descendamus, chartæ angustia non permittit. IV. Sunt denique, qui notitiam insitam de existentia Dei referunt in quemdam instinctum, naturâ hominum mentibus insitum, quo intellectus in ejus assensum feratur. Quemadmodum enim rebus aliis, etiam vitæ & rationis expertibus, naturâ insita est inclinatio quædam in finem & perfectionem suam, v. g. lapidi ad motum deorsum, igni ad motum sursum, quam Philosophi appetitum innatum appellant: ita & facultatibus animæ rationalis, intellectui & voluntati, naturâ insita esse videtur quædam in Deum inclinatio, quâ suâpte naturâ in eum, velut in suum finem & bonum summum propendeant. Conditus enim est homo à Deo ad Deum, ut, nisi in Deo, ejus appetitus satiari non possit. Licet verò appetitus, ut vocant, innatus, per se cognitionem non importet aut præsupponat: inest enim naturâ etiam rebus, facultate cognoscendi destitutis; in naturis intelligentibus tamen intellectui & voluntati pondus superaddere videtur, ut in finem suum, Deum scilicet, naturâ ferantur, & intellectus quidem existentiam ejus, ubi terminos apprehendit, indubitato assensu, absque discursu, amplectatur, posito etiam, terminos non esse intellectui ita notos, ut in iis apprehensis statim identitatem prædicati cum subjecto videat. Quò referunt, quæ superius ex Tertulliano, Arnobio, Minutio Felice, & Lactantio de testimonio animæ produximus. Quod enim Gentiles, etiam vanis Deorum superstitionibus ac erroribus occupati, sæpè in has erumpunt voces: Quod Deus dederit; Si Deus voluerit: Item Deus bonus est, Deus benefacit, benedicat te Deus; & Deus videt omnia; Deo te commendo; Deus inter nos judicabit; id provenire existimant ex naturâ insito instinctu erga Deum, quo fiat, ut naturâ quasi cogente, ut Lactantius ait, ferantur intellectu simul & voce in unum verum Deum, & veritas, etiam ab invitis pectoribus erumpat. De instinctu sive appetitu innato cùm intellectus tùm voluntatis, in Deum velut finem & perfectionem suam, videantur Scotus in IV. Sent. Dist. XLIX. q. IX. & X. Durandus ibidem q. VIII. & alii. Vazquez quidem in I. II. q. V. a. VIII. Disp. XXII. c. II. impugnat sententiam Scoti & Durandi de appetitu innato creaturae rationalis ad beatitudinem operose. Sed argumenta ejus, fi quicquam, hoc saltem evincunt, creaturae rationali non inesse appetitum innatum ad visionem beatificam, de quo hic non agitur, sed tantum de appetitu innato ad Deum, abstractive cognitum, ejusque existentiam. Quanquam ibidem Vazquez c. IV. tandem fatetur, creaturae rationali inesse appetitum quendam beatitudinis in universum & in singulari, qui merito dici possit & debeat naturalis appetitus, quem tamen elicitum, non innatum esse contendit. Quae de voce potius, quam de ipsa re dissensio est.

V. Forsan non incommode quis hanc quartam sententiam cum praecedente tertia conjunxerit, ut communes de Deo notiones hominum mentibus natura insitae dicantur cum per quandam intellectui connatam perfectionem, habitui ἀνάλογον, tum per innatum intellectui instinctum sive appetitum ad Deum ejusque existentiam, ut quemadmodum vi illius intellectus veritatem communium de Deo notionum, quae sunt de est tertii adjecti, ex apprehensis terminis statim, citra discursum cognoscit, ita vi hujus velut pondere quodam inclinatus in existentiam Dei feratur, Deumque esse, si non per se immediate ex apprehensis terminis statim evidenter cognoscat, naturae instinctu tamen cogente admittat. Quae ex instinctu naturae nata notitia recte dicetur natura insita: cum intellectus eam per se immediate, citra discursum eliciat. Non tamen prorsus coincidit cum notitia, a qua Scholasticis propositiones quoad nos per se notae denominantur, sed ea nonnihil latius patet. Haec enim generatur praecise ex terminis apprehensis, in quibus identitas praedicati cum subjecto intellectui ita clare & evidenter repraesentatur, ut vi lucis ingenitae eam per se immediate in illis videat, & citra discursum se ad assensum determinet. Insita vero notitia dicitur Patribus priscis & Theologis modernis notitia quaelibet, quam terminis apprehensis intellectus per se immediate & citra discursum elicit, sive praecise propositionum evidentia & ingenita sibi luce; sive natura sibi insito instinctu ejusque inclinatione in objectum tractus ad eam eliciendam se determinet: quorum illud fit in propositionibus per se notis quoad nos; hoc in propositione de EST secundi adjecti: Deus est; stante, quòd Scholastici contendunt, eam non esse ita evidentem, ut in apprehensis terminis statim identitas prædicati cum subjecto intellectui per se immediatè appareat. Ut enim notitia nobis naturâ insita dicatur, sufficere potest, si apprehensis terminis intellectus statim ad ejus assensum citra discursum se determinet, si non vi solius lucis ingenitæ, quâ identitatem prædicati cum subjecto in apprehensis terminis perspiciat, tamen vi ingeniti instinctus sive inclinationis, facultati intelligendi pondus superaddentis, eamque in assensum per se immediatè quasi trahentis.

VI. Ut in pauca tandem, quod res est, contraham, non asserunt Theologi moderni, ante rationis usum homini inesse cognitionem Dei actualem, sive aliquam ejus speciem expressam. Quin inveniuntur, qui id expressè negant. Neque desunt, qui ejus speciem impressam intellectui naturâ & ante rationis usum inesse inficiantur. Quicquid ergo est, quod, ex illorum mente, intellectui naturâ inesse, sive ei connatum dici possit, ad ingenitam quandam perfectionem sive lucens intellectus, quâ adjutus veritatem communium de Deo notionum in apprehensis terminis statim, citra discursum, perspiciat, redeat necesse est. Atque in hoc ferè conveniunt, licet perfectionem illam innatam alii habitum, alii quippiam habitui analogum, nonnulli habitum imperfectum & dispositionem appellent. Cui qui addiderit inculcatum à Patribus priscis instinctum, naturâ homini insitum, qui intellectui pondus superaddat, eumque unà cum illa ipsi innatâ perfectione qualicunque ad assensum cùm aliarum communium de Deo notionum, tum ejus inprimis, quæ est de existentia ipsius, immediatè & citra discursum præbendum determinat, à vero nihil, nostro quidem judicio, aberraverit. Et tantum de notitia Dei insita sive innata, prolixius quidem, quàm instituti ratio exigebat, discentium commodo tamen exigente: cùm res hæc ita intricatè & obscurè, cùm ab iis, qui ex Cartesii schola prodeunt, tùm ab aliis tradi soleat, ut discentes vix Auctorum mentem ubique assequi, ne dum quid in tanta sententiarum varietate amplecti, quidve rejicere debeant, apud animum suum statuere possint.


### XXIII. The acquired knowledge of God is either vulgar and common, or exquisite and…

XXIII.

The acquired knowledge of God is either vulgar and common, or exquisite and accurate.

I. I call vulgar and common a certain confused knowledge concerning the existence and attributes of God, such as is wont to be in all people generally, even the simpler ones, who are not capable of demonstrations. II. I call exquisite and accurate a more distinct knowledge concerning the existence and attributes of God, which relies upon its own certain demonstrations sought from nature.

XXIV.

Vulgar and common [knowledge] is acquired either from the testimony of others, or from the intuition of this universe, by consequence indeed, but an easy one and obvious to anyone, even one unlearned in letters.

I. We establish a twofold way of acquiring vulgar knowledge. One, the testimony of men. For parents instill the name and knowledge of God into children from their tender years and as it were with their milk: great and small invoke God daily: by him they swear, bless, and curse: they call upon the same as witness, judge, etc. And thus, by the more frequent mention of the divine name in daily life, which has been imbibed from childhood by the instruction of parents, the knowledge is confirmed and grows with us. The other, the intuition of this universe. For just as this machine of the world, constructed with a wonderful variety, order, and beauty of parts, strikes the senses of all, so at the very first glance it moves the learned and unlearned alike into the thought of a cause by which it may have been founded, preserved, and governed, by a discourse indeed, if not formal, yet virtual, but easy, prone, and without art, thrusting itself spontaneously into the mind of everyone. What can be so open and so clear, when we have looked up at the sky and contemplated the celestial things, as that there is some Divinity of most excellent mind by which these things are ruled, says Cicero, book II, On the Nature of the Gods. And after some things interposed: He who doubts that there is a God, I truly do not understand why he cannot also doubt whether there is a Sun, or whether there is none. II. Concerning vulgar and common knowledge, which from the contemplation of this universe is born, and of its own accord forces itself upon the minds of men; the passages of Scripture alleged above speak primarily of this, from Psalm 19:1 et seqq. and Romans 1:20 et seqq., in the former of which the heavens are said to declare the glory of God, and the firmament to announce the work of his hands, through an elegant prosopopoeia, by which the heavens are introduced as if they were public heralds declaring the glory of their Creator, because they provide mortals everywhere with proofs for knowing Him, and those no less perspicuous and clear than if someone were to declare it in open words. By this, the invisible things of God, namely His eternal power and divinity, are said to be clearly seen, being understood from the things that are made, that is, to be known as clearly and perspicuously as if they were seen with the eyes, so that the Apostle pronounces even the promiscuous multitude of the Gentiles, who had changed the glory of the immortal God for an image made not only to the likeness of mortal man, but also of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things, to be inexcusable, because when they knew God (from the things that are made), they did not glorify Him as God.

Latin:

XXIII.

Acquisita notitia Dei vel vulgaris & communis, vel exquisita & accurata est.

I. Vulgarem & communem dico confusam quandam de Dei existentia & attributis notitiam, qualis vulgo omnibus, etiam simplicioribus, qui demonstrationum capaces non sunt, inesse solet. II. Exquisitam & accuratam dico notitiam distinctiorem de existentia & attributis Dei, quæ suis certis, ex natura petitis, demonstrationibus nititur.

XXIV.

Vulgaris & communis comparatur vel ex aliorum testificatione, vel ex intuitu hujus universi, per consequentiam quidem, sed facilem & cuivis, etiam literarum rudi, obviam.

I. Consequendæ notitiæ vulgaris duplicem constituimus viam. Unam, hominum testificationem. Nam nomen & notitiam Dei instillant parentes liberis à teneris & cum lacte quasi: Deum quotidiè invocant magni & parvi: per eum jurant, benedicunt, maledicunt: eundem advocant testem, judicem &c. & sic crebriori nominis divini mentione in vita quotidiana, quæ à pueritia ex institutione parentum hausta est, notitia confirmatur, & nobiscum incrementa capit. Alteram, intuitum hujus universi. Quemadmodùm enim hæc mirabili partium varietate, ordine, pulcritudine constructa machina mundi in omnium sensus incurrit, ita primo statim intuitu doctos pariter & indoctos movet in cogitationem causæ, à qua condita sit, conservetur & gubernetur, discursu quidem, si non formali, virtuali tamen, sed facili, prono, & absque arte ultrò cujusque animo se ingerente. Quid potest esse tam apertum tamque perspicuum, cùm cælum suspeximus, cælestiaque contemplati sumus, quàm esse aliquod Numen præstantissimæ mentis, quo hæc regantur, ait Cicero lib. II. de Nat. Deorum. Et post quædam interjecta: Esse Deum qui dubitat, haud sanè intelligo, cur non idem, Sol sit, an nullus sit? dubitare possit. II. De notitia vulgari & communi, quæ ex intuitu hujus universi nascitur, hominumque mentibus ultrò se ingerit, loquuntur cumprimis loca Scripturæ superiùs allegata ex Psal. XIX. 1. seqq. Et Rom. I. 20. seqq. quorum illo cœli enarrare dicuntur gloriam Dei, & opus manuum ejus annunciare expansum illorum, per elegantem prosopopœian, quâ cœli velut publici præcones, gloriam Conditoris sui enarrantes, introducuntur, quòd ejus cognoscendæ documenta mortalibus ubique locorum præbeant, eaque non minùs perspicua & clara, quàm si quis eam verbis apertis enarraret. Hoc dicuntur invisibilia Dei, æterna scilicet ejus potentia & divinitas, ex rebus factis intellecta, pervideri, hoc est, ita clarè & perspicuè cognosci, ac si viderentur oculis, ut etiam promiscuam Gentilium multitudinem, quæ gloriam immortalis Dei mutaverat per imaginem non solùm ad mortalis hominis similitudinem effictam, verùm etiam volatilium, & quadrupedum & reptilium, Apostolus inexcusabilem pronunciet, quòd cùm Deum (ex rebus factis) cognitum, non ut Deum glorificaverint.


### XXV. An exquisite and accurate [knowledge] is also obtained from the consideration…

XXV.

An exquisite and accurate [knowledge] is also obtained from the consideration of this universe, but a more exact one.

c This knowledge is not of all men, but of the learned, who, being well imbued with philosophical disciplines and sciences, can more accurately demonstrate the existence and attributes of God a posteriori and from effects, and can solidly refute the objections and exceptions of Atheists.

XXVI.

And the existence of God is indeed demonstrated by various arguments drawn from a more exact consideration of this universe.

Thomas, Part I, Question II, Article III, shows five ways by which it can be demonstrated that God exists. The first, from movers subordinated to one another to one first mover; the second, from causes subordinated to one another to one first cause; the third, from the contingency of things to the necessary existence of one first Being; the fourth, from the various degrees of goodness and perfection to the existence of one best and most perfect being; and the fifth, finally, from the governance of this universe and of all things contained in it to one supreme governor is concluded. Now the first mover, by whom all things are moved, so that he himself is unmoved; likewise the first cause, which is from itself, and from which all other things are, is by the consensus of all God. Nor do we conceive in our mind by a necessary Being, which cannot not be, and therefore is always from itself; likewise by a Being that is the best and most perfect of all; and by the supreme governor of this universe, anything other than God. Let him who wishes see these reasons, more fully deduced, more deeply considered, confirmed, and vindicated from various objections; as also many others, which are wont to be urged by others against Atheists and employed to demonstrate the existence of God, in the interpreters of Thomas in the cited q. II. a. III. of part I. and in other Scholastics.

XXVII.

Moreover, the attributes and essential perfections of God are demonstrated, no less than his existence, a posteriori, by reasons sought from created things.

I. Johannes Baptista Gonet in Clypeo Theol. Thomisticæ part. I. Disp. I. Art. II. notes from Cajetan that by those five reasons brought forward by Thomas, not only the existence of God is demonstrated, but also his attributes. And indeed by the first, by which it is proven that there is given one unmoved Being, it is further proven that that unmoved Being is immutable, immense, and eternal: By the second, by which it is proven that there is given one first cause, from which all things are, it is also proven that it is omnipotent. By the third, by which it is concluded that there is given a certain Being, which is from itself and necessary, it is also proven that it contains in itself all perfections, e.g., goodness, immateriality, the nature of a most pure act, etc. By the fourth, by which it is proven that there is given a certain Being that is best and most perfect, it is also proven that it is simple, infinite, one, etc. Finally, by the fifth, by which it is proven that there is given one supreme Governor of this universe, it is also proven that his wisdom, providence, love, justice, mercy, and other perfections, which shine forth in the governor of this universe, are proven.

II. Others establish a threefold way by which both the existence of God and his attributes and essential perfections can be demonstrated a posteriori and from effects. One of causality, by which, through arguments concluding from effect to cause, the first cause of all things, and which exert themselves in their production, conservation, and governance, we demonstrate His attributes. The second is of eminence and perfection, by which we prove that the perfections of creatures exist in their first causes, if not formally, yet eminently, by the power of a principle most known by nature: Whatever is in the effect, pre-exists in the cause. The third is of negation, by which we remove the imperfections of creatures from their first cause, by an argument deduced from the repugnance which exists between them and the perfections of this [cause].

III. By that [way] it can be demonstrated that God exists: for that there is given some first cause, upon which all other things depend, is in reality the same thing as that God exists; and that He is a free, intelligent, wise, good, holy, and just agent; that He possesses the power of effecting all things, is present to all things, provides for all things, moves, rules, and governs all things. For just as the vicissitude of causes and effects obvious to the eyes [leads] directly to one first cause; so the most beautiful ordering and disposition of the same, the equable motion of celestial bodies, constant to itself in all things, and the altogether admirable conservation and governance of all things, lead to the knowledge of the rest of the attributes and operations which we have commemorated. By this [way] also these attributes which we have recounted become known in good part, namely all those which are also found in certain creatures, although in a more imperfect mode, and shine forth in them as in a mirror: of which kind are the power of understanding and willing, wisdom, goodness, justice, and others which imply perfection simply, i.e., perfection mixed with no imperfection, in their formal concept. That these exist in God, besides the most beautiful ordering and most wise governance of this universe, is also clearly proven by the fact that they exist in certain creatures, namely in humans. For they could not exist in them unless they also pre-existed in some way in God, as in their first cause. And because they include no imperfection in their formal and proper concept, through which they would be repugnant to existing formally in God, it is rightly concluded that they exist formally in God, as in the first cause.

By this, finally, the Negative Attributes become known, of which kind are, to be incorporeal, immortal, infinite, immense, independent,

& similar things. Which, because as to the thing they are nothing else than the perfections of God, signified with the negation of the imperfections occurring in creatures, are then finally fully known when they are known to be repugnant to those imperfections, and are conceived with the negation of them.

Latin:

XXV.

Exquisita & accurata comparatur etiam ex consideratione hujus universi, sed exactiori.

c Notitia hæc non est omnium hominum, sed eruditorum, qui disciplinis & scientiis Philosophicis benè imbuti existentiam & attributa Dei à posteriori & ex effectibus accuratiùs demonstrare, & Atheorum objectiones & exceptiones solidè refutare possunt.

XXVI.

Et Dei existentia quidem demonstratur diversis ex exactiori hujus universi consideratione petitis argumentis.

Thomas p. I. q. II. a III. ostendit quinque vias, quibus Deum esse, demonstrari possit. Primâ à moventibus inter se subordinatis ad unum primum motorem; alterâ à causis inter se subordinatis ad unam primam causam; tertiâ à rerum contingentia ad unius primi Entis existentiam necessariam; quartâ à variis gradibus bonitatis & perfectionis ad existentiam unius optimi & perfectissimi entis; & quintâ denique à gubernatione hujus universi omniumque in eo contentarum rerum ad unum supremum gubernatorem concluditur. Primus autem motor, à quo moventur omnia, ut ipse sit immobilis; causa item prima, quæ à se est, & à qua res aliæ omnes sunt, omnium consensu Deus est. Neque per Ens necessarium, quod non potest non esse, & proinde à se semper est; per Ens item omnium optimum & perfectissimum; & per gubernatorem hujus universi supremum aliud quid, quàm Deum animo concipimus. Quas rationes fusiùs deductas, consideratas altiùs, confirmatas, & à variis objectionibus vindicatas; ut & alias plures, quæ contra Atheos ab aliis urgeri & ad demonstrandam Dei existentiam adhiberi solent, videat, qui vult, apud interpretes Thomæ in citata q. II. a. III. partis I. & apud alios Scholasticos.

XXVII.

Dei attributa autem & perfectiones essentiales demonstrantur non minùs, quàm ejus existentia, à posteriori, rationibus, ex rebus creatis petitis.

I. Johannes Baptista Gonet in Clypeo Theol. Thomisticæ part. I. Disp. I. Art. II. notat ex Cajetano, quinque istis à Thoma adductis rationibus demonstrari non tantùm Dei existentiam, sed & attributa illius. Et primâ quidem, quâ evincitur, dari unum Ens immobile, evinci porro, Ens illud immobile esse immutabile, immensum & æternum: Secundâ, quâ evincitur, dari unam causam primam, à qua sunt omnia, evinci etiam, eam esse omnipotentem. Tertiâ, quâ concluditur, dari Ens quoddam, quod à se & necessarium est, evinci etiam, id continere in se omnes perfectiones, v. g. bonitatem, immaterialitatem, rationem actus purissimi &c. Quartâ, quâ evincitur, dari Ens quoddam optimum & perfectissimum, evinci etiam, id esse simplex, infinitum, unum &c. Quintâ denique, quâ probatur, dari unum supremum hujus universi Gubernatorem, evinci etiam illius sapientiam, providentiam, amorem, justitiam, misericordiam, aliasque perfectiones, quæ in gubernatore hujus universi relucent.

II. Alii triplicem constituunt viam, quâ cùm Dei existentia, tum ejus attributa & perfectiones essentiales à posteriori & ex effectibus demonstrari possint. Unam causalitatis, quâ argumentis, ab effectu ad causam concludentibus, rerum omnium causam primam, & quæ in illarum productione, conservatione & gubernatione sese exerunt, attributa illius demonstramus. Alteram eminentiæ & perfectionis, quâ creaturarum perfectiones primæ illarum causæ, si non formaliter, tamen eminenter inesse evincimus, vi principii naturâ notissimi: Quidquid est in effectu, præexistit in causa. Tertiam negationis, quâ creaturarum imperfectiones à prima illarum causa removemus, argumento à repugnantia, quæ inter illas & hujus perfectiones intercedit, deducto.

III. Illâ demonstrari potest, & quòd sit Deus: nam dari aliquam primam causam, à qua res aliæ omnes dependent, quoad rem idem est, atque Deum esse; & quòd sit agens liberum, intelligens, sapiens, bonum, Sanctum, justum; quòd polleat vi efficiendi omnia, adsit rebus omnibus, provideat omnibus, moveat, regat, gubernet omnia. Ut enim oculis obvia causarum & effectuum vicissitudo rectà in unius primæ causæ; ita earumdem ordinatio ac dispositio pulcherrima, corporum cœlestium motus æquabilis, sibique per omnia constans, conservatio & gubernatio omnium prorsus admiranda, in cæterorum, quæ commemoravimus, attributorum & operationum notitiam deducunt. Istâ etiam hæc, quæ recensuimus, attributa bonam partem innotescunt, nempe ea omnia, quæ etiam in quibusdam creaturis, quamvis modo imperfectiori, inveniuntur, & & in illis, velut in speculo, relucent: cujusmodi sunt potentia intelligendi & volendi, sapientia, bonitas, justitia & alia, quæ perfectionem simpliciter, h. e. perfectionem, nullâ imperfectione mixtam, in suo conceptu formali important. Quos Deo inesse, præter hujus universi ordinationem pulcherrimam & gubernationem sapientissimam, id quoque liquidò evincit, quod in quibusdam creaturis, hominibus scilicet, insunt. Non enim inesse illis possent, nisi etiam in Deo, tanquam in prima illarum causa, quodammodo præexisterent. Et quia nullam in suo formali & proprio conceptu imperfectionem, per quam Deo formaliter inesse repugnent, includunt, rectè colligitur, quòd Deo, tanquam causæ primæ, formaliter insint.

Hâc denique Attributa Negativa innotescunt, cujusmodi sunt, esse incorporeum, immortale, infinitum, immensum, independens,

& similia. Quæ, quia quoad rem nihil aliud sunt, quàm Dei perfectiones, cum negatione occurrentium in creaturis imperfectionum significatæ, tum demum plenè cognoscuntur, cùmimperfectionibus istis repugnare cognoscuntur, & cum illarum negatione concipiuntur.


### XXVIII. Natural Theology presupposes in its hearers both innate and acquired common or…

XXVIII.

Natural Theology presupposes in its hearers both innate and acquired common or vulgar knowledge of God; but it delivers and suggests the exquisite knowledge to them through the demonstrations just indicated. I. In any practical science, the end must be to some extent known beforehand: for otherwise, no one would easily allow himself to be induced either to undertake the practice or operation which is for its sake, or to learn the science which is directive of the operation. Which also happens in the natural science concerning God, which necessarily presupposes a certain knowledge of the existence of God, as its end. II. But because the acquired vulgar knowledge of the existence of God is confused and at least probable; and the innate is also very languid and greatly obscured by the corruption of nature, so that Atheists are found everywhere who deny that God exists: therefore the existence of God must be more accurately demonstrated and defended from the attacks of Atheists, so that it may be more certainly established. Natural Theology, however, does not presuppose it in its hearers in the same way as it does the other, confused one. For it is not for everyone to deduce from their genuine principles the demonstrations of this kind by which it is obtained, and to defend them from objections, but for this, much industry, study, and labor is needed. III. Someone might say: Therefore God is not the formal object of Natural Theology, but the material. For that, concerning which its existence and its essential perfections are demonstrated in Natural Theology, is the subject of the demonstrations, and a part of its material object. IV. Resp. That the proximate and proper formal object of Natural Theology is established by us as God, known from the light of nature: which, as is evident, is something concrete from God, and from the light or principles of nature. God is the proximate and proper formal object of Natural Theology: the light or principles of nature are the more remote and common formal object of the same. For they undertake the function of a formal object in Natural Theology, in so far as, when applied to created things as effects of God, they infer conclusions concerning God's existence and essential perfections. However, the conclusions inferred concerning God's existence and essential perfections contain at last virtually the rule of right operation concerning God, as the ultimate end of man, and constitute the proper and proximate formal object of Natural Theology. Whence God has in Natural Theology the status of an object both material and formal, but in one respect and another. In so far as His existence and attributes are to be demonstrated in Natural Theology from effects, to that extent He has the status of a material object. But in so far as His existence and attributes, once demonstrated, virtually contain the rule of right operation concerning Him, as man's end and highest good, and are a certain reason for knowing and eliciting it, to that extent they sustain the status of a formal object: just as elsewhere in demonstrations the premises of a principal syllogism have the status of a formal object in relation to the principal conclusion; and they have the status of a material object in relation to the premises of the prosyllogisms by which they are confirmed. And so much for the formal object of Natural Theology.

Latin:

XXVIII.

Notitiam Dei cùm insitam, tùm acquisitam vulgarem sive communem, præsupponit Theologia Naturalis in suis auditoribus; exquisitam verò tradit & suggerit ipsa iis per demonstrationes, modò indicatas. I. In quavis scientia practica finem oportet esse quadantenus præcognitum: aliàs enim nec ad praxin sive operationem, quæ ejus causâ est, suscipiendam, nec ad scientiam, operationis directivam addiscendam, quisquam se induci facilè pateretur. Quod & in naturali de Deo scientia usu venit, quæ cognitionem quandam de existentia Dei, velut sui finis, necessariò præsupponit. II. Quia autem acquisita vulgaris notitia de existentia Dei confusa & probabilis saltem; & insita quoque admodùm languida & per naturæ corruptionem valdè obscurata est, ut passim inveniantur Athei, qui Deum esse negent: idcircò existentia Dei accuratiùs demonstranda, & ab Atheorum impugnationibus vindicanda venit, ut de ea certiùs constet. Eam verò Theologia Naturalis non perinde, ut alteram confusam, in suis auditoribus præsupponit. Non enim cujusvis est id generis demonstrationes, quibus comparatur, ex suis genuinis principiis deducere, & ab objectionibus vindicare, sed ad hoc industriâ, studio & labore multo opus est. III. Inquiat quis: Ergo Deus non est objectum formale Theologiæ Naturalis, sed materiale. Id enim, de quo sua existentia & suæ perfectiones essentiales in Theologia Naturali demonstrantur, est subjectum demonstrationum, & pars objecti materialis illius. IV. Resp. Objectum formale proximum & proprium Theologiæ Naturalis constitui à nobis Deum, ex lumine naturæ cognitum: quod, uti patet, est concretum quid ex Deo, & ex lumine seu principiis naturæ. Deus est Theologiæ Naturalis objectum formale proximum & proprium: lumen sive principia naturæ sunt ejusdem objectum formale remotius & communius. Subeunt enim munus objecti formalis in Theologia Naturali, in quantum ad res creatas, velut effectus Dei, applicata, conclusiones de Dei exxistentia & perfectionibus essentialibus inferunt. Conclusiones autem de Dei existentia & perfectionibus essentialibus illatæ continent demum virtualiter regulam rectæ operationis circa Deum, velut finem hominis ultimum, & constituunt Theologiæ Naturalis objectum formale proprium & proximum. Unde Deus habet in Theologia Naturali rationem objecti cùm materialis, tùm formalis, sed alio atque alio respectu. In quantum ejus existentia & attributa in Theologia Naturali ex effectibus demonstranda sunt, in tantum habet rationem objecti materialis. In quantum verò ejus existentia & attributa demonstrata virtualiter continent regulam rectæ operationis circa ipsum, velut hominis finem & bonum summum, & sunt ratio quædam eam cognoscendi & eruendi, in tantum sustinent rationem objecti formalis: perinde ut aliàs in demonstrationibus præmissæ syllogismi principalis habent rationem objecti formalis in ordine ad conclusionem principalem; & habent rationem objecti materialis in ordine ad præmissas prosyllogismorum, quibus confirmantur. Et tantum de objecto formali Theologiæ Naturalis.


### XXIX. We established its material object above in thesis XV, in the subject of…

XXIX.

We established its material object above in thesis XV, in the subject of operation, and in the causes and means of attaining the end.

XXX.

We called the subject of operation man the Wayfarer, not indeed absolutely and simply, but in so far as he is subjected to the operation prescribed by Natural Theology for the sake of the blessedness to be attained in God.

The judgment concerning the subject of operation in practical sciences must be derived from the end. For the end is the measure of both the subject and the means, and the subject falls under the consideration of practical science insofar as it is placed under the operation prescribed by it, and its knowledge is necessary for attaining the end.

XXXI.

The operation, however, which Natural Theology prescribes for the sake of attaining blessedness in God, consists in acts of the intellect and will occupied with God as man's ultimate end and highest good. Whence, first of all, the faculties of the soul, the intellect and the will, must be considered in man, and their powers for pursuing God with fitting worship.

I. Since Natural Theology, viewed precisely in itself, has as its subject man the wayfarer in the state of nature, both integral and corrupt, the natural powers of the intellect and will must be considered here in themselves, and it must be shown that, since man is rational by nature, and the rule of moral goodness consists in rational nature as it is rational, powers must also be owed to his intellect and will, per se and connaturalistically, by which he can perform what is fitting and good for rational nature as rational, and avoid what is unfitting and evil for the same. Reason can indeed easily attain from its own natural light that these powers are now lacking to man. But that they were created in him at the beginning, and afterwards lost, it cannot attain under its own guidance. Wherefore, for the Christian philosopher, divine revelation must here be called to aid, and from it must be taught with what powers man was created in the beginning, and what powers he now possesses.

II. Since now in the state of corrupt nature all men by nature incline toward every kind of evil, and daily offend God with sins—which no one fails to notice in himself—next, sin must also be treated. And because also concerning the fall of the first man and hence arisen and through carnal generation into all With depraved concupiscence and a propensity toward evil having been propagated, reason, left to itself, knows nothing; in order to declare more fully the corruption and perversity of human nature, one must again have recourse to divine revelation, and from there, things which the light of nature cannot suggest must be supplied.

Latin:

XXIX.

Materiale ejus objectum constituebamus supra thes. XV. in subjecto operationis, & in potiundi finis causis ac mediis.

XXX.

Subjectum operationis dicebamus hominem Viatorem, non quidem absolutè & simpliciter, sed in quantum operationi, consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis causâ à Theologia Naturali præscriptæ, substernitur.

De subjecto operationis in scientiis practicis ex fine ferendum est judicium. Finis enim est mensura simul subjecti & mediorum, & subjectum cadit sub considerationem scientiæ practicæ, in quantum operationi, ab ipsa præscriptæ, substernitur, ejusque cognitio ad consequendum finem necessaria est.

XXXI.

Operatio autem, quam consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis causâ Theologia Naturalis præscribit, consistit in actibus intellectûs & voluntatis circa Deum, ut hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum, occupatis. Unde cumprimis in homine considerandæ sunt facultates animæ, intellectus & voluntas, illarumque vires ad Deum conveniente cultu prosequendum.

I. Cùm Theologia Naturalis, in se præcisè spectata, pro subjecto habeat hominem Viatorem in statu naturæ, cùm integræ tùm corruptæ, considerandæ hîc veniunt vires naturales intellectûs & voluntatis secundum se, ostendendumque, quòd cùm homo natura rationalis sit, & regula bonitatis moralis in natura rationali, ut rationalis est, consistat, ejus intellectui etiam & voluntati per se & connaturaliter debeantur vires, quibus quæ naturæ rationali, ut rationali, conveniunt & bona sunt, agere; quæ eidem disconveniunt & mala sunt, vitare possit. Quas vires deesse nunc homini, ratio ex suo naturali lumine quidem facilè assequi potest. Quod autem initio ei concreatæ, & postea amissæ fuerint, adsequi ejus ductu non potest. Quamobrem Philosopho Christiano hîc in subsidium vocanda est revelatio divina, & quibus viribus initio homo fuerit conditus; & quas nunc habeat, ex ea docendum.

II. Cùm jam in statu naturæ corruptæ homines naturâ omnes in nullum non malum propendeant, & quotidiè Deum peccatis offendant: quod nemo non in semetipso animadvertit; deinceps etiam de peccato agendum est. Et quia etiam de lapsu hominis primi & hinc ortâ atque per carnalem generationem in omnes propagatâ pravâ concupiscentiâ ac pronitate in malum ratio, sibi relicta, nihil novit, ad corruptionem & perversitatem naturæ humanæ pleniùs declarandam rursum recurrendum est ad divinam revelationem, & inde quæ naturæ lumen suggerere non potest, supplenda veniunt.


### XXXII. Concerning the causes of the blessedness to be conferred upon man, the…

XXXII.

Concerning the causes of the blessedness to be conferred upon man, the efficient and the internal impulsive, there is no difficulty: concerning which, therefore, one need not labor greatly. However, the means of obtaining the same in and from God, which occupy both sides of the material object of Natural Theology, must be considered and explained in order.

That the efficient cause of blessedness is God, and the impulsive cause is His goodness, grace, and mercy toward men who depart from this life with Him propitious, we taught above in thesis XI and XII. Which all easily acknowledge even by the guidance of the light of nature alone, so that there is no need to demonstrate it laboriously with arguments. Let those things be seen which we brought forward in that place regarding this matter.

XXXIII.

That the means consist in the acts of the mind and will concerning God, by which He is rightly acknowledged and worshipped, was shown in the previous thesis XIII.

The moral law, implanted by nature in the minds of men and once repeated and solemnly promulgated by God on Mount Sinai, exhibits these acts in summary; it is accustomed to be distinguished by the name of the Decalogue from the ten precepts into which it is contracted, and it is the rule and norm to which the learned and unlearned alike are bound to conform themselves in rightly instituting and performing the worship of God. Natural Theology also prescribes and delivers the same, yet more abundantly, and in such a way that it simultaneously explains more accurately the habits of the virtues, of which they are the effects, and their principles, causes, and affections.

XXXIV.

These acts can be divided into two classes, of which one contains those who pertain to the first; the second contains the rest, who pertain to the second table of the Decalogue.

XXXV.

Contained by the precepts of the first table are those which direct man straight to God, and they are either internal—and these are of either the mind or the will—or external acts. I. Internal acts, indeed of the mind, consist in the meditation and knowledge of the divine essence, attributes, providence, works, and benefits; those of the will, however, consist in acts of faith, love, trust, hope, fear, patience, submission toward God, etc. II. External acts consist in sensible actions by which they testify to their faith, love, hope, fear, submission, and reverence toward God; of this kind are prayers, the invocation of God in public assemblies, thanksgiving for benefits received, and the celebration of the divine name, goodness, and justice, etc.

XXXVI.

Contained by the precepts of the second table are acts which direct man straight to himself or to his neighbor, but consequently to God: these likewise are either internal or external. Internal are the elicited acts of moral virtues, occupied in moderating the affections so that they do not go astray: External are the commanded acts of the same. Both are occupied either with ourselves: of this kind are acts of temperance, chastity; or with our neighbor, as are acts of justice, liberality, etc.

Latin:

XXXII.

De causis conferendæ homini beatitudinis, efficiente & impulsiva interna, nihil est difficultatis: de quibus proptereà magnoperè laborandum non est. Media autem ejusdem in & à Deo consequendæ, quæ in objecto materiali Theologiæ Naturalis utramque paginam faciunt, ordine consideranda & explicanda veniunt.

Causam beatitudinis efficientem esse Deum; impulsivam ejus bonitatem, gratiam & misericordiam erga homines, qui ipso propitio ex hac vitâ discedunt, docuimus suprà thesi XI. & XII. Quod vel solius luminis naturæ ductu facilè omnes agnoscunt, ut argumentis id operosè demonstrare opus non sit. Videantur, quæ d. l. hanc in rem adduximus.

XXXIII.

Media consistere in actibus mentis & voluntatis circa Deum, quibus rectè agnoscitur & colitur, in superiori thesi XIII. ostensum est.

Actus hos compendio exhibet lex moralis, hominum mentibus naturâ implantata, & in monte Sinai olim à Deo repetita ac solenniter promulgata, quæ à decem, in quæ contracta est, præceptis Decalogi nomine insigniri solet, & regula ac norma est, ad quam docti pariter & indocti in cultu Dei rectè instituendo & peragendo se conformare tenentur. Eosdem præscribit & tradit etiam Theologia Naturalis, uberius tamen, & ita ut simul habitus virtutum, quorum effectus sunt, & illorum principia, causas, & affectiones accuratiùs explicet.

XXXIV.

Actus isti dispesci possunt in duas classes, quarum una continet eos, qui ad primam; altera cæteros, qui ad fesecundam Decalogi tabulam pertinent.

XXXV.

Primæ tabulæ præceptis continentur, qui hominem directè ad Deum ordinant, & sunt vel interni, iique vel mentis vel voluntatis; vel externi actus. I. Interni actus, mentis quidem, in meditatione & cognitione effentiæ, attributorum, providentiæ, operum & beneficiorum divinorum, voluntatis verò, in actibus fidei, dilectionis, fiduciæ, spei, timoris, patientiæ, submissionis erga Deum &c. consistunt. II. Externi consistunt in actibus sensibilibus, quibus suam fidem, dilectionem, spem, timorem, submissionem, & reverentiam erga Deum testantur; cujusmodi sunt preces, invocatio Dei in conventibus publicis, gratiarum actio pro acceptis beneficiis, celebratio nominis, bonitatis, & justitiæ divinæ &c.

XXXVI.

Secundæ tabulæ præceptis continentur actus, qui directè hominem ad seipsum vel ad proximum, consequenter autem ad Deum ordinant: qui itidem vel interni vel externi sunt. Interni sunt virtutum moralium actus eliciti, in moderandis affectibus, ne exorbitènt, occupati: Externi sunt earundem actus imperati. Utrique occupantur vel circa nosmetipsos: cujusmodi sunt actus temperantiæ, castitatis; vel circa proximum, ut sunt actus justitiæ, liberalitatis &c.


### XXXVII. Those who are contained by the precepts of the second table of the Decalogue,…

XXXVII.

Those who are contained by the precepts of the second table of the Decalogue, although they are not occupied directly and immediately with God, nevertheless have the character of divine worship, in so far as they are ultimately referred to God as to their end, and are done in his obedience, praise, and glory.

Just as God is the ultimate end of man, so all human actions, both those which are good and which befit rational nature, which we perform, and those which are evil and which do not befit the same, which we flee, must ultimately be referred to God, indeed in such a way that we do whatever we do out of the motive of charity towards God, and in his obedience, praise, and glory. To which the Apostle looks, when he commands in general that all things which we do, we should do for the glory of God, 1 Cor. 10:31, and when in particular he exhorts parents, children, husbands, and wives, masters and servants, that each should do what is his duty for the sake of God, and in his obedience and glory, Eph. 6:1 ff., Col. 3:20 ff.

XXXVIII.

Natural Theology prescribes acts of both orders either through first practical principles, implanted by nature, or through practical conclusions, deduced by discourse from the essence of God and his essential perfections known, of which one of the premises is a certain practical principle, known by nature; the other is a certain proposition, explaining the essence of God, or some essential perfection of his, known by nature, or certainly demonstrated and known from the principles of nature. I. The first principles, implanted by nature, are e.g. that God exists, that he is to be worshipped, that no one is to be harmed, that to each his own is to be rendered, that parents are to be honored, etc., which, however, it is not repugnant to demonstrate also a posteriori. II. Acts of the former order, which namely direct man immediately to God, and pertain to the first table of the Decalogue, Natural Theology prescribes through conclusions, deduced from the essence of God and his essential perfections immediately, by a very easy and ready consequence. From the essence of God indeed: e.g. where it is known that God is the first and supreme being of all, which is from itself, and the cause of all other beings, (for thus God is commonly conceived) it infers by an easy and ready consequence that he is to be worshipped above all, by the force of a practical principle, Solidly founded in the light of nature: The first and supreme being of all, which is from itself and the cause of all others, is to be worshipped above all things: when it is known that God is a spiritual being devoid of matter and passive potency, it is known again by a ready and easy consequence that he is to be pursued with spiritual worship, by the force of the practical principle: Everyone to whom worship is owed is to be pursued with worship congruent and proportionate to his nature. To which Christ seems to have looked, when in John IV. 24, he says, God is a Spirit, and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth; and Paul in Acts XVII. 25, God who made the world, and all things that are in it, does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he worshipped with hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. From the essential perfections of God, however, once known, it infers the same practical conclusions, which explain the individual parts of divine worship more distinctly: e.g., when it is known that God is supremely truthful, who in speaking can neither be deceived nor deceive, it is inferred immediately by a ready consequence that his words and promises are to be believed without hesitation, by the force of a principle most known by nature: He who is supremely truthful, and in speaking can neither be deceived nor deceive, his words and promises are to be believed without hesitation. When it is known that God is supremely good and the Author of all good, it is inferred immediately by an easy consequence that he is to be loved above all things, by the force of a practical principle most known by nature: He who is supremely good and the Author and giver of all good, he is to be loved supremely and above all things. When it is known that God is not only supremely good toward men, but also omnipotent, and therefore both wills and is able to help us, it is known at once that he is to be trusted above all things, and that he is to be invoked in necessities, by the force of the practical principle: He who is supremely good toward man and at the same time omnipotent, so that he both wills and can help him, in him is to be placed the confidence of obtaining aid; and he is to be invoked in necessities.
