When it is known that God is just and a severe avenger of crimes, it is known also that he is to be feared, and that care must be taken lest he be offended by sins, by the force of the practical principle: He who is just and a severe avenger of crimes, he is to be feared, and not to be offended by sins. When it is known that From the goodness of God we have both life and whatever is necessary for us for the sustenance of life, it is also known that thanks must be given to Him, by way of a practical principle: For benefits received, thanks must be given to Him from whom you have received them. The same judgment applies to other similar parts of divine worship.

III. Natural Theology prescribes, through practical conclusions likewise deduced from the known perfections of God, acts of the latter order which pertain to the second table of the Decalogue, insofar as they are referred to God as the objective end of man and the attainment of Him: e.g., when it is known that God is holy and delights in the holy life of men, but is averse to impiety; that He is just, a rewarder of the good, and an avenger of crimes; it is inferred by an easy and ready consequence that one must live justly and holily according to virtue, and that crimes must be fled, if we wish to have God propitious and favorable, and to enjoy Him as our highest good. To this pertains this divine exhortation to the holiness of life: Be holy, for I am holy, Levit. XI. 44, ch. XIX. 2, ch. XX. 7, resting especially on that principle, most known by nature, that the perfection and happiness of man consist in the imitation of God and in his life being conformed to the life of God. To which Aristotle also looks when he teaches in book X of the Nicomachean Ethics, ch. VIII, that the blessedness of man consists in the contemplative life, and he shows this among other things from the fact that the blessed life of God consists in the contemplative life; but to this, the contemplative life of man is most familiar and is a certain ὁμοίωμα or likeness of it, and that he is not only most rightly disposed in himself, but also most friendly to God, and furthermore most blessed, who conducts himself in accordance with the mind and cultivates and perfects it by the contemplation of things. Again, when it is known that God is supremely good and to be loved above all things, it is inferred by an easy and ready consequence that effort must be devoted to the holiness of life, and care must be taken lest He be offended by sins. When it is known that God loves the good and rewards their good deeds, if not here temporally, yet in the other life with perpetual happiness, and punishes the wicked here with temporal calamities, but in the other life with perpetual misery; it is inferred by a likewise easy and ready consequence that one must live well and that one must live according to virtue, but that sins must be avoided, if we wish, with God being propitious, to depart from this life at some time and attain eternal happiness by His gift, and indeed to avoid eternal misery, which is destined for the wicked. To this end, even among the Gentiles, not only the learned, but also the simpler and uneducated, as many as devote effort to pursuing virtue and fleeing crimes, look: namely, that by the honesty of their life and the flight from crimes they may merit God's favor, and, with Him being propitious, departing from this life, may at length arrive at true and perfect happiness. For it is most well-known by nature that the souls of men remain surviving after death, and will live happily or miserably, according as they have conducted themselves well or badly in this life, with God rewarding good deeds with a happy life; but punishing crimes with perpetual misery.

Latin:

XXXVII.

Qui præceptis secundæ tabulæ Decalogi continentur, quamvis non directè & immediatè circa Deum occupentur, habent tamen rationem cultus divini, in quantum ad Deum, tanquam ad finem, ultimò referuntur, & in ejus obsequium, laudem & gloriam fiunt.

Quemadmodum Deus hominis finis ultimus est, ita ad Deum humanæ actiones omnes, cùm quibus bona & quæ naturæ rationali conveniunt, facimus, tum quibus mala & quæ eidem disconveniunt, fugimus, ultimò referri debent, ita quidem ut ex motivo caritatis erga Deum, & in ejus obsequium, laudem & gloriam faciamus, quæcunque facimus. Quò respicit Apostolus, cùm quando in genere omnia, quæ facimus, in gloriam Dei facere jubet, 1. Cor. X. 31. tùm quando in specie parentes, liberos, maritos, & uxores, heros & servos, hortatur, ut quisque sui quod officii est, faciat propter Deum, inque ejus obsequium & gloriam, Eph. VI. 1. seqq. Col. III. 20. seqq.

XXXVIII.

Utriusque ordinis actus præscribit Theologia Naturalis vel per principia prima practica, naturâ sibi insita, vel per conclusiones practicas, ex Dei essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus cognitis deductas per discursum, cujus altera præmissarum est principium quoddam practicum, naturâ notum; altera propositio quædam, Dei essentiam, vel aliquam ejus perfectionem essentialem explicans, naturâ nota, vel certè ex naturæ principiis demonstrata & cognita. I. Principia prima, naturâ insita, sunt v. g. esse Deum, eum esse colendum, neminem lædendum, suum cuique tribuendum, parentes esse honorandos &c. quæ tamen à posteriori etiam demonstrari non repugnat. II. Prioris ordinis actus, qui scilicet hominem directè ad Deum ordinant, & ad primam tabulam Decalogi pertinent, præscribit Theologia Naturalis per conclusiones, ex Dei essentia & perfectionibus essentialibus proximè,consequentiâ admodùm facili & pronâ,deductas. Ex Dei essentia quidem: v. g. ubi cognitum est, Deum esse ens omnium primum & supremum, quod à se, & aliorum entium omniu causa est, (sic enim Deus vulgo concipitur) consequentiâ facili & pronâ infert, eum esse super omnia colendum,vi principii practici, in lumine naturæ solidè fundati: Ens omnium primum & supremum, quod à se & aliorum omnium causa est, colendum est super omnia: ubi cognitum est, Deum esse ens spirituale materiæ & potentiæ passivæ expers, cognoscitur rursum consequentiâ pronâ & facili, eum prosequendum esse cultu spirituali, vi principii practici: Unumquemque, cui debetur cultus, prosequendum esse cultu, suæ naturæ congruo & proportionato. Quò respexisse videtur Christus, cum Joh. IV. 24. Deus, inquit, Spiritus est, & qui eum adorare volunt, in spiritu & veritate adorare debent; & Paulus Act. XVII. 25. Deus qui fecit mundum, & omnia quæ in eo sunt, in manufactis templis non habitat, nec manibus colitur, alicujus rei indigens quum ipse det omnibus vitam & halitum & omnia. Ex Dei perfectionibus essentialibus autem cognitis infert eadem conclusiones practicas, quæ singulas cultus divini partes distinctius explicant: v. g. ubi cognitum est, Deum esse summè veracem, qui in dicendo nec falli nec fallere possit, infertur statim pronâ consequentiâ, ejus dictis & promissis esse fine hæsitatione habendam fidem, vi principii naturâ notissimi: Qui est summè verax, & in dicendo nec falli nec fallere potest, ejus dictis & promissis fine hæsitatione credendum est. Ubi cognitum est, Deum esse summè bonum & boni omnis Auctorem, infertur statim facili consequentiâ, eum esse super omnia diligendum, vi priucipii practici naturâ notissimi: Qui est summè bonus & boni omnis Auctor & dator, is summè & super omnia diligendus est. Ubi cognitum est, Deum non tantùm summè bonum esse erga homines, sed & omnipotentem, & proinde velle ac posse nos juvare, cognoscitur oppidò, in ipso esse super omnia confidendum, & eundem in necessitatibus esse invocandum, vi principii practici: Qui summè in hominem bonus & simul omnipotens est, ut juvare eum & velit & possit, in eo impetrandi auxilii fiducia collocanda; isque in necessitatibus invocandus est. ubi cognitum est, Deum esse justum & scelerum vindicem severum, cognoscitur etiam, quòd timendus sit, cavendumque, ne peccatis offendatur, vi principii practici: Qui justus & scelerum vindex severus est, is timendus est, nec peccatis offendendus. Ubi cognitum est, ex Dei bonitate habere nos & vitam, & quæcunque nobis ad vitæ sustentationem neceffaria sunt, cognoscitur etiam, ei agendas esse gratias, vi principii practici: Pro beneficiis acceptis gratiæ agendæ sunt ei, à quo acceperis Idem de aliis similibus cultus divini partibus judicium est.

III. Posterioris ordinis actus, qui ad secundam Decalogi tabulam pertinent, in quantum quidem ad Deum, velut ad finem hominis objectivum ejusque adeptionem referuntur, præscribit Theologia naturalis per conclusiones practicas, itidem ex Dei perfectionibus cognitis deductas: v. g. ubi cognitum est, Deum esse sanctum, & delectari hominum vitâ sanctâ, aversari autem impietatem; esse justum, remuneratorem bonorum, & scelerum vindicem; facili & pronâ consequentiâ infertur, secundum virtutem vivendum esse justè & sanctè, scelera autem fugienda, si Deum propitium & faventem habere, eoque, velut nostro bono summo frui velimus. Quò pertinet hæc divina ad sanctimoniam vitæ exhortatio: Sancti estote, nam ego sanctus sum, Levit. XI. 44. c. XIX. 2. c. XX. 7. eo potissimum principio, naturâ notissimo, nixa, quòd hominis perfectio & felicitas in imitatione Dei, & in ejus vita vitæ Dei conformi consistat. Quò & Aristoteles respicit, cùm lib. X. Nic. c. VIII. docet, beatitudinem hominis consistere in vita contemplativa, idque inter alia ex eo ostendit, quòd Dei vita beata consistat in vita contemplativa; huic verò hominis vita contemplativa familiarissima & quoddam ejus ὁμοίωμα sive simulacrum sit, & quod non tantùm in se rectissimè affectus, sed & Deo amicissimus, & porro beatissimus sit is, qui se consentaneè gerit menti, eamque contemplatione rerum excolit & perficit. Rursum ubi cognitum est, Deum esse summè bonum, & super omnia diligendum, facili & pronâ consequentiâ infertur, dandam esse operam sanctimoniæ vitæ, cavendumque, ne peccatis offendatur. Ubi cognitum est, Deum diligere bonos, & remunerare illorum benefacta, si non hîc temporaliter, in altera tamen vita felicitate perpetuâ, & punire sceleratos hîc calamitatibus temporalibus, in altera verò vita miseriâ perpetuâ; consequentiâ itidem facili & pronâ infertur, benè & secundum virtutem vivendum esse, peccata autem vitanda, si Deo propitio ex hac vita aliquando discedentes beatitudinem æternam, ejus dono, consequi, miseriam æternam verò, improbis destinatam, evitare velimus. Quò respiciunt etiã inter gentiles, non modò eruditi, sed & simpliciores ac rudes, quotquot virtutem datâ operâ sectantur, & scelera fugiunt: ut scilicet honestate vitæ & scelerum fugâ Deum demereantur, & ipso propitio ex hac vita emigrantes ad veram & perfectam beatitudinem tandem perveniant. Est enim naturâ notissimum, hominum animas manere post mortem superstites, & victuras beatè vel miserè, prout in hac vita benè vel malè se gesserint, Deo benefacta vitâ beatâ remunerante; scelera autem miseriâ perpetuâ vindicante.


### XXXIX. And hence it is clear that those who constitute man's happiness in operation…

XXXIX.

And hence it is clear that those who constitute man's happiness in operation according to virtue philosophize less appropriately.

I. Thus Aristotle constitutes the happiness of man in operation according to virtue, and just as virtue is twofold: διανοητικὴ or intellectual, and ἠθικὴ or moral, of which the former directs the intellect and the latter the will in operating: so also he constitutes the ultimate end and supreme good of man in ἐνεργείᾳ or operation according to both virtues, yet especially in ἐνεργείᾳ or operation according to intellectual virtue, and above all according to wisdom. On which matter see Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book I, chapter VII, and Nicomachean Ethics Book X, chapter VII and following.

II. But when the matter is more deeply considered, it will be clear that man's happiness and ultimate end are not rightly constituted in either operation instituted according to virtue. For first, each operation according to virtue is imperfect, whether they are viewed on their own part or on the part of the object. And indeed, the operation which is directed by moral virtue is imperfect on its own part: because it is always joined with the disordered motions of concupiscence, and from time to time deflects to one or the other extreme, and sins either in excess or in defect. Which Aristotle does not entirely deny, who in X. Nic. c. VIII. subordinates it even on this account to the contemplative life, because in many things it is joined with perturbations. But on the part of the object: because it is occupied about contingent things, namely contracts, human necessities, perturbations, etc., which are proper to human weakness, as the Philosopher says in the same place: in which, therefore, the appetite of man does not find the reason of a perfect good, by which it can be tranquilized and satisfied. But that which is directed by intellectual virtue is imperfect on its own part, as for other reasons, so especially also on account of the blindness of the mind. For just as the eyes of bats behave toward the light of day, so also does the intellect of our soul toward those things which are the most manifest of all, as Aristotle himself confesses in II. Metaph. c. 1. Which darkness of the human mind, although it may be diminished in some way through speculative sciences, acquired by study and labor, nevertheless cannot be entirely removed, and however far the speculations of our mind may finally progress, they will nevertheless everywhere find certain abstruse things, to the causes of which they cannot penetrate. But on the part of the object: For either our contemplation is occupied about the first and uncreated being, or about created beings. Created beings, even if they were known as perfectly as possible (which, however, cannot happen), nevertheless could not impart to our cognition or contemplation that perfection and reason of good by which the appetite of the will might be satisfied. For all things are finite, and whatever goodness they contain in themselves, it is entirely finite. But the appetite of man cannot be satisfied unless by a good that is absolutely perfect and supreme, which contains in itself every reason of good, and is therefore infinite. But the first and uncreated being, although it is infinite, and contains in itself every reason of good, nevertheless does not satisfy the appetite of man, except as the ultimate end of man, and as the supreme good known and apprehended. But the contemplation of the first and uncreated Being, commended by Aristotle, is only the contemplation of being, viewed in itself absolutely, as it is abstracted from matter in reality and in reason.

III. Furthermore, under operation according to moral virtue, Aristotle includes only the acts of the virtues commanded in the second table of the Decalogue, which, namely, [direct] man either toward himself, or toward direct the nearest: such as are the acts of temperance, fortitude, liberality, magnificence, magnanimity, modesty, justice, truth, urbanity, etc. But concerning the acts of the other virtues, which directly order man to God, and are prescribed in the first table of the Decalogue, it is silent. But that these acts of the latter order cannot be absent from man's beatitude, the very notion of beatitude, implanted in the minds of all, proves. For all conceive by its name the absolutely highest good of man, ἄυταρκες or self-sufficient, and which is desirable for its own sake, not for the sake of another, as Aristotle himself teaches at length in 1 Nic. c. VII. But such a good, outside of God, is given nowhere. Whence if man's beatitude is rightly constituted in any operation according to virtue, it must certainly be constituted in that which directly orders man to God, as to a good end absolutely perfect and highest, by which alone his appetite is satisfied. But the operation, directly ordering man to God, consists in the acts of the virtues, which have God for their nearest and immediate object, and are prescribed in the first table of the Decalogue: such as are the true acknowledgment of one God, faith towards God, love of God above all things, trust and hope in God, fear, invocation of God, thanksgiving for benefits received, etc. nor is he to be called blessed, unless he who acknowledges the one true God, applies undoubted faith to his words, loves him, fears him, invokes him in necessities, trusts in his help, etc.

IV. Thirdly, the ultimate end of man and the highest good is an everlasting good. For as the soul of man is an immortal spirit, created for immortal life, so also by nature there is implanted in it an appetite for life and everlasting beatitude. But an operation according to virtue is both a temporal good, and deserts man when life itself deserts him. Therefore, an operation according to virtue is not the ultimate end of man and the highest good. For neither can a temporal thing, which deserts man with this mortal life, fulfill and satisfy the appetite for everlasting beatitude, which is implanted in him by nature. On which matter Augustine discourses skillfully and elegantly in book XIII de Trin. c. VIII. His words, worthy to be read here, They have it thus: Whatever sort of happiness, which is rather called so than is, is sought in this life, or rather is imagined, while immortality is despaired of, without which true happiness cannot exist. For he indeed lives happily, as we have already said above and have sufficiently established by argument, who lives as he wishes, and wishes for nothing evil. Now no one wishes for evil regarding immortality, if human nature is capable of it, with God granting it, of which if it is not capable, it is not capable of happiness either. For in order for a man to live happily, it is necessary that he live. Furthermore, when he is dying, life itself deserts him; how can a happy life remain with him? Now when it deserts him, it deserts him either against his will, without a doubt, or willingly, or neither. If against his will, how is it a happy life, which is so much in the will that it is not in one's power? And since no one is happy by wishing for something, nor by having it, how much less is he happy who is deserted against his will, not by honor, not by possession, not by any other thing, but by the happy life itself, when there will be no life for him? Whence, even if no sense remains by which he might be miserable—for the happy life departs precisely because the whole life departs—he is nevertheless miserable as long as he feels, because he knows that he is being consumed against his will, on account of which he loves other things and what he loves above all others. Therefore, a life cannot be both happy and desert one against his will, because no one is happy against his will. — But if it deserts him willingly, even so, how was it a happy life, which he who possessed it wished to perish? It remains for them to say that neither is in the mind of the happy person, that is, when he is deserted by the happy life, when the whole life deserts him through death, he neither wishes nor is unwilling, because he stands ready and with an equal mind for both. But not even that is a happy life, because it is such that it is unworthy of the love of him whom it makes happy. For how is it a happy life, which the happy person does not love? Or how is that loved, which is received indifferently whether it flourishes or perishes? Unless perhaps the virtues, which we love in this way only for the sake of happiness, dare to persuade us that we should not love happiness itself. But if they do this, we certainly cease to love them as well, when we do not love that for the sake of which alone we loved them. Then how will that opinion be true, so perfect, so examined, so refined, so certain, that all men wish to be happy, if they themselves, who are already happy, neither wish nor are unwilling to be happy? Or if they do wish, as truth cries out, as nature compels, to which the supremely good and immutably happy creator bestowed this. If they wish, I say, to be happy, those who are happy, they certainly do not wish not to be happy. But if they do not wish not to be happy, without a doubt they do not wish to be consumed and to perish, because they are happy, nor can they be happy unless they are living. Therefore, they do not wish to perish, because they are living. Therefore, whoever truly either are happy or desire to be happy wish to be immortal. But he does not live happily to whom that which he wishes is not present. Therefore, in no way will a life be able to be truly happy unless it is eternal.

V. Fourthly, the operation of man according to virtue is ordered by itself and by its own nature to something else, as to an end, and to the attainment of eternal happiness in it. Therefore, the ultimate end and supreme good of man does not consist in it. The consequence is evident: because the ultimate end and supreme good of man is always sought for its own sake, never for the sake of something else, as Aristotle himself teaches in Nic. Ethics, book I, ch. VII, where among other things he says: That which is to be sought for its own sake, he says, is more absolute or perfect than that which is sought for the sake of something else, and that which is never sought for the sake of something else is more perfect than those things which are chosen both for their own sake and for the sake of something else. Therefore, the supreme good of man will also be that which is always chosen for its own sake, never for the sake of something else. Such, however, seems to be happiness above all. The antecedent is proved from the ordination of man to God. For just as man was created for the sake of God and to attain happiness in Him, so all his operation, which is according to virtue, must ultimately be referred to the same and to the attainment of happiness in Him. If it is done otherwise, and one stops ultimately at the bare operation according to virtue, man, however much he may be endowed with virtue, will not be happy, but miserable, both in his whole life and especially at the approaching hour of death. In his whole life indeed; because operation according to virtue, as has been said, is entirely imperfect. But nothing imperfect can satisfy the appetite of man. Indeed, even if it were most perfect, and constituted a man, as Aristotle says in Nic. Ethics, book I, ch. X, truly good and square without reproach (which, however, never happens in this corruption of nature), yet unless it ordered man to God, as to a good absolutely perfect and supreme, not even then would it contain in itself the reason of a good by which his appetite would be satisfied: it

Latin:

XXXIX.

Atque hinc patet, de hominis beatitudine minus convenienter philosophari eos, qui illam in operatione secundum virtutem constituunt.

I. Ita Aristoteles beatitudinem hominis constituit in operatione secundum virtutem, & quemadmodùm virtus duplex est: διανοητικὴ sive intellectualis, & ἠθικὴ sive moralis, quarum illa intellectum, hæc voluntatem in operando dirigit: ita & hominis finem ultimum ac bonum summum constituit in ἐνεργείᾳ sive operatione secundum utramque virtutem, potissimùm tamen in ἐνεργείᾳ sive operatione secundum virtutem intellectualem, & cumprimis secundum sapientiam. Qua de re videatur Aristoteles I. Nic. c. VII. & X. Nic. c. VII. seq.

II. Verùm re penitiùs perpensa patebit, in neutra secundum virtutem institutâ operatione hominis beatitudinem & finem ultimum rectè constitui. Primùm enim utraque secundum virtutem operatio imperfecta est, sive ex parte sui, sive ex parte objecti spectentur. Et quidem quæ virtute morali dirigitur operatio, imperfecta est ex parte sui: quia semper cum inordinatis concupiscentiæ motibus conjuncta est, & subinde ad alterutrum extremorum deflectit, atque vel in excessu vel in defectu peccat. Quod non planè diffitetur Aristoteles, qui X. Nic. c. VIII. eam hoc etiam nomine vitæ contemplativæ postponit, quòd multis in rebus conjuncta sit cum perturbationibus. Ex parte objecti verò: quia occupatur circa res contingentes, contractus scilicet, humanas necessitates, perturbationes &c. quæ humanæ imbecillitatis propria sunt, ut ibidem ait Philosophus: in quibus proinde hominis appetitus non invenit rationem boni perfecti,quo tranquillari & satiari possit. Quæ autem virtute intellectuali dirigitur, ex parte sui imperfecta est, cùm aliis de causis, tum inprimis etiam ob cæcitatem mentis. Quemadmodum enim vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei se habent, ita & intellectus animæ nostræ ad ea quæ manifestissima omnium sunt, fatente ipsomet Aristotele II. Metaph. c. 1. Quæ mentis humanæ caligo, licet per scientias speculativas, studio & labore acquisitas, quodammodò minui possit, penitùs tamen tolli non potest, & quocunque tandem mentis nostræ speculationes progrediantur, ubique tamen invenient abstrusa quædam, ad quorum causas penetrare non possunt. Ex parte objecti verò: Vel enim contemplatio nostra occupatur circa ens primum & increatum, vel circa entia creata. Entia creata, si vel maximè perfectè cognita essent (quod tamen fieri non potest) cognitioni tamen sive contemplationi sui eam perfectionem bonique rationem, quâ voluntatis appetitus satietur, impertire non possent. Sunt enim finita omnia, & quicquid bonitatis in se continent, finitum totum est. Appetitus hominis autem satiari non potest, nisi bono absolutè perfecto & summo,quod rationem boni omnem in se continet, atque adeò infinitum est. Ens primum verò & increatum, licet infinitum sit, & omnem rationem boni in se contineat, non tamen hominis appetitum satiat, nisi ut finis hominis ultimus, & bonum summum cognitum & apprehensum. Contemplatio autem Entis primi & increati, ab Aristotele commendata, est tantùm contemplatio entis, in se absolutè spectati, ut est re & ratione à materia abstractum.

III. Deinde sub operatione secundum virtutem moralem comprehendit Aristoteles tantum actus virtutum, in secunda tabula Decalogi præceptos, qui scilicet hominem vel ad se ipsum, vel ad proximum dirigunt : quales sunt actus temperantiæ , fortitudinis, liberalitatis , magnificentiæ, magnanimitatis, modestiæ, justitiæ, veritatis , urbanitatis &c. de cæterarum verò virtutum actibus, qui directè hominem ad Deum ordinant, & in prima Decalogi tabula præscribuntur , altum filet. At verò hos posterioris ordinis actus non posse abesse ab hominis beatitudine, vel ipsa beatitudinis notio, omnium mentibus insita, evincit. Omnes enim ejus nomine concipiunt bonum hominis absolutè summum, ἄυταρκες sive seipso contentum, & quod propter se expetibile est, non propter aliud, ut Aristoteles ipse 1. Nic. c. VII. pluribus docet. Tale autem bonum, extra Deum, nullum datur. Unde si quâ in operatione secundum virtutem beatitudo hominis rectè constituitur, in ea certè constituatur oportet, quæ directè hominem ordinat ad Deum, velut ad finum bonum absolutè perfectum & summum, quo solo ejus appetitus satiatur. Operatio autem, directè hominem ad Deum ordinans, consistit in actibus virtutum, quæ pro objecto proximo & immediato habent Deum, & in prima Decalogi tabula præscribuntur: ut sunt agnitio unius Dei vera, fides erga Deum, dilectio Dei super omnia, fiducia & spes ad Deum, timor, invocatio Dei, gratiarum actio pro acceptis beneficiis &c. neque beatus prædicandus est, nisi qui unum verum Deum agnoscit, ejus dictis indubitatam adhibet fidem, eum diligit, timet, in necessitatibus invocat, in ejus auxilio confidit &c.

IV. Tertiò finis hominis ultimus & bonum summum est bonum sempiternum. Ut enim anima hominis spiritus immortalis est, ad vitam immortalem conditus, ita & naturâ ei insitus est appetitus vitæ & beatitudinis sempiternæ. Operatio autem secundum virtutem utramque bonum temporale est, & deserit hominem, cùm ipsa vita eum deserit. Operatio secundum virtutem igitur non est finis hominis ultimus & bonum summum. Neque enim temporale, quid & quod cum hac mortali vita hominem deserit, appetitum beatitudinis sempiternæ, naturâ ei insitum, explere & satiare potest. Quam in rem scitè & eleganter disserit Augustinus lib. XIII. de Trin. c. VIII. Verba ejus, digna, quæ hîc legantur, habent ita: Qualiscunque beatitudo, quæ potiùs vocetur, quàm sit, in hac vita quæritur, immò verò fingitur, dum immortalitas desperatur, sine quâ vera beatitudo esse non potest. Ille quippe beatè vivit, quod jam superiùs diximus, & astruendo satis fiximus, qui vivit ut vult, nec malè aliquid vult. Nemo autem malè vult immortalitatem, si ejus humana capax est, DEO donante, natura, cujus si capax non est, nec beatitudinis capax est. Ut enim homo beatè vivat, oportet ut vivat. Quem porrò morientem vita ipsa deserit, beata vita cum illo manere quomodo potest? Cùm autem deserit, aut nolentem deserit procul dubio, aut volentem, aut neutrum. Si nolentem, quomodo beata vita est, quæ ita est in voluntate, ut non sit in potestate? Cùmque beatus nemo sit aliquid volendo, nec habendo, quantò minùs est beatus, qui non honore, non possessione, non qualibet alia re, sed ipsâ vitâ beatâ nolens deseritur, quando ei nulla vita erit? Unde etsi nullus sensus relinquitur, quo sit misera, proptereà enim vita beata discedit, quoniam tota vita discedit, miser est tamen, quamdiu sentit, quia scit se nolentem consumi, propter quod cætera & quod præ cæteris diligit. Non igitur potest vita & beata esse, & nolentem deserere, quia beatus nolens nemo sit. — Si autem volentem deserit, etiam sic quomodo beata erat, quam perire voluit, qui habebat? Restat ut dicant, neutrum esse in animo beati, id est, cùm deseri à beata vita, cum per mortem deserit tota vita, nec nolle nec velle, ad utrumque enim parato & æquo animo consistere. Sed nec ista beata est vita, quia talis est, ut quem beatum facit, amore ejus indigna sit. Quomodo enim est beata vita, quam non amat beatus? Aut quomodo amatur, quod utrum vigeat, an pereat, indifferenter accipitur? Nisi fortè virtutes, quas propter solam beatitudinem sic amamus, persuadere nobis audent, ut ipsam beatitudinem non amemus. Quod si faciunt, etiam ipsas utique amare desistimus, quando illam, propter quam solam istas amavimus, non amamus. Deinde quomodo erit vera illa tam perfecta, tam examinata, tam eliquata, tam certa sententia, beatos esse omnes homines velle, si ipsi, qui jam beati sunt, beati esse nec nolunt nec volunt? aut si volunt, ut veritas clamat, ut natura compellit, cui summè bonus & immutabiliter beatus creator indidit hoc. Si volunt, inquam, beati esse, qui beati sunt, beati utique non esse nolunt. Si autem beati non esse nolunt, procul dubio nolunt consumi & perire, quod beati sunt, nec nisi viventes beati esse possunt. Nolunt igitur perire, quod vivunt. Immortales ergo esse volunt, quicunque verè beati vel sunt vel esse cupiunt. Non autem vivit beatè, cui non adest, quod vult. Nullo modo igitur esse poterit vita veraciter beata, nisi fuerit sempiterna.

V. Quartò hominis operatio secundum virtutem per se & suâpte naturâ ordinatur ad aliud, velut ad finem, & ad consequendam in eo beatitudinem æternam. Ergo in ea non consistit hominis finis ultimus & bonum summum. Consequentia evidens est: quia finis ultimus & bonum summum hominis semper propter se, nunquam propter aliud expetitur, docente ipsomet Aristotele l. Nic. c. VII. ubi inter alia: Quod, inquit, propter se expetendum est, eo quod propter aliud expetitur, absolutius seu perfectius est, & quod nunquam propter aliud (expetitur) iis (perfectius est) quæ & propter se & propter aliud eliguntur. Ergo etiam summum hominis bonum id erit, quod propter se semper eligitur, nunquam propter aliud. Talis autem videtur esse inprimis beatitudo. Antecedens probatur ex hominis ordinatione ad Deum. Quemadmodum enim homo propter Deum & ad consequendam in ipso beatitudinem conditus est, ita ad eundem & consequendam in ipso beatitudinem operatio ejus omnis, quæ secundum virtutem est, ultimò referenda est. Secus si fiat, & sistatur ultimò in nuda operatione secundum virtutem, homo utcunque virtute pollens non beatus, sed miser erit, cùm in vita tota, tùm inprimis instante horâ mortis. In vita tota quidem; quia operatio secundum virtutem, uti dictum, tota imperfecta est. Nihil autem imperfectum hominis appetitum satiare potest. Quin si vel maximè perfecta esset, & constitueret virum, ut l. Nic. c. X. Aristoteles ait, verè bonum & sine vituperatione quadratum (quod tamen in hac naturæ corruptione nunquam contingit) tamen nisi hominem ad Deum, velut ad bonum absolutè perfectum & summum ordinaret, ne sic quidem in se contineret rationem boni, quo appetitus ejus satiaretur: esset e-


### for it is still finite, and consequently the notion of good also, which it…

for it is still finite, and consequently the notion of good also, which it might contain in itself, would be finite. The appetite of man, however, as it is for the universal good, so it cannot be satisfied except by the universal and infinite good, which is found only in God. But in that in which the notion of the universal good is not found, by which the appetite of man might be satisfied, by that man is not constituted happy, but the appetite is left restless, and the man miserable. Whence it is so far from the case that by an operation according to virtue alone, not related to its ultimate end, God, a man is constituted truly good and square without blame, so that he might bear all the accidents of fortune most beautifully, and in every respect, as is fitting, as Aristotle contends in the said book, that rather in adverse circumstances, especially in the case of an ignominious death, he is left restless, timid, fluctuating hither and thither, devoid of consolation, and truly miserable. Which David, a man beyond controversy good, nay, divinely instructed with signal grace and supernatural gifts of virtues, but tossed by various accidents of fortune, experienced abundantly in himself, who confesses that his soul never rested except in God, Ps. LXII. 2, and that he finally bore whatever accidents by which he was tossed, as was fitting, by leaning upon God as an immovable rock and his portion, Ps. LXXIII. 25, seq. But at the instant hour of death, the thing itself speaks that an operation according to virtue, viewed in itself as an ultimate end, leaves a man miserable. For if it then constituted him happy, or raised him up by itself—because it is the very thing that will accompany the soul after its departure from the body and will constitute it happy by itself—or if it raised him up by the hope of another future blessedness, by which God, for his immense goodness toward men who have lived according to virtue, is about to reward his life, spent here well and according to virtue. The former cannot be said. For operation according to virtue is proper to wayfaring men, and deserts them as soon as this temporal life deserts them. If the latter be said, it must be confessed that operation according to virtue is not the ultimate end and supreme good of man, but a means of attaining it in the other life, and that it is ordered by itself toward God and the attaining of blessedness of the other life in Him and from Him, as toward an ultimate end. Which is what we wish and contend.

VI. Nor is the reasoning of Aristotle of great weight, by which, relying on it, he establishes the ultimate end and supreme good of man in activity according to virtue. It comes down to this: The perfection and end of each thing consists in its proper function and work. Therefore, the perfection and end of man also consists in some proper function and work of his. He proves the antecedent in Book I of the Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter VII, by induction: For just as for the flute player and the sculptor and every craftsman, and in general for those who produce some work and perform some action, their good and their own end and perfection seem to consist in the work itself, so also for man, if there is some work and function of his, it will be probable that his good and living well are placed in that very thing. But since the proper function and work of man consists in activity according to virtue, he concludes from this that the ultimate end and supreme good of man also consists in the same. But who does not see that the nature of activity according to virtue, which is proper to man, and of the effective habits, which the Philosopher brings forward here as an example, is not equal? The art of playing the flute, the art of sculpture, and the like, are by themselves and by their own nature effective habits, which have as their end an operation, or some work to be produced by it. Man by himself and by his own nature is not created for the sake of an end, by which his desire is satisfied, to be produced by himself, but for the sake of an end, which is the absolutely perfect and supreme good, to be attained from God and in God. However, for those agents whose end is not some work to be produced by them, but a pre-existing good to be attained by the benevolent will and gift of another or by some operation of their own, their ultimate end never consists in their operation in itself, but always in the attainment of the pre-existing good, and thus in the pre-existing good itself, as being obtained: for example, the end of χρηματιστικῆς (money-making) is money, to be attained by the operation of man, not the operation itself, undertaken for the sake of attaining money. If someone were to act throughout his whole life with every zeal and effort in ways that are suitable for acquiring money, yet did not attain the money sought, then he who studies the pecuniary art will indeed have the operation proper to the art, yet he will not be thought to have attained the end, as long as he does not attain the money sought. The matter stands similarly with operation according to virtue, which is proper to man. If anyone has studied virtue throughout his whole life, yet departs without God and without the hope of attaining blessedness in Him in the other life, he shall not be said to have attained the ultimate end and the highest good, even though he may have attained operation according to virtue, which is the proper function of man.

VII. Let someone say: that Aristotle treats in his Ethics of the ultimate end of man, not absolutely and simply, but at least in the genus of the goods of this life. That the same man treats of the ultimate end of man, viewed in civil society. But in the genus of the goods of this life, the operation of the soul according to virtue is altogether the ultimate. And that acts commanded in the first table of the Decalogue do not pertain to the ultimate end and highest good of man viewed in civil society, but that acts of virtues pertaining to the second table are sufficient.

VIII. Resp. I. We do not deny that the Philosopher in his Ethics treats of the blessedness of man for the state of this life. But that it is rightly constituted in operation according to virtue, whether moral or intellectual, and that either one or both is the ultimate good of man for the state of this life, which is always desirable for its own sake, never for the sake of another (which Aristotle in book I of the Nicomachean Ethics attributes to it), this is what we deny. And indeed concerning operation according to moral virtue, it is evident from what has been said thus far that it is imperfect in itself; and the goods also which it attains outside of God are all fleeting and perishable, so that it has nothing, neither in itself nor in any objects outside of God, which can tranquilize the soul of man. But when related to worshipping and glorifying God with obedience, it indeed has, not however in itself, but in God alone, as in its own and man's perfect end, that which may tranquilize and satisfy the appetite of man, but thus it will not even have the nature of an ultimate end and blessedness in the genus of the ends and goods of this life, but of a means ordained to it, contrary to what Aristotle contends, that it is the ultimate end and highest good of man. But as regards operation according to intellectual virtue, it can be considered in two ways. In one way, as it is the contemplation both of God and of things made by God, in themselves absolutely, as they are beings, either in reality and reason; or by reason only abstracted from matter, or even as they are in sensible matter. In which manner Metaphysics [treats of] being and its affections in common; and the first Being or God specifically as abstracted from matter in reality and reason; Physical beings, as they are in sensible matter, have the principle of motion and rest within themselves; but Mathematics contemplates quantity, as a being abstracted from sensible matter only in reason. In the second way, as it is the contemplation of the first being, that is, God, viewed in relation to man by way of an end and the highest good, and of other beings as effects of God, which exhibit certain signs and traces of their cause and its perfections to be seen in themselves. Aristotle establishes the happiness of man in the contemplation of things in the former and absolute way, but by a reason no better than that by which he established it in operation according to moral virtue, viewed absolutely in itself. For besides the fact that this ἐνέργεια according to virtue is clearly imperfect, as shown above, it does not even imply the relation of a means to the enjoyment of God, whether inchoate or complete (in the former of which the happiness of this life, and in the latter that of the other life consists), for the very reason that it is not referred to God as to an end, much less does it deserve to be called happiness itself. But the contemplation of God and of things made by God, instituted in the latter way, can indeed sustain a certain relation of a means to the happiness of man: since the nature and perfections of God, known from created things, virtually, as said above, contain the rule of right operation concerning God, as the end of man, and through the practical conclusions which it infers, it prescribes the worship owed to God and necessarily required on the part of man, who wishes to enjoy God as his perfect and highest good here inchoately, but perfectly in the other life; yet it cannot be called the ultimate end and happiness of man, whether for the state of this life or the other. It remains fixed and immovable, therefore, that only God and the enjoyment of Him is the ultimate end of man, and his ἄυταρκες and highest good, even in the category of the goods of this life II. Furthermore, the Philosopher in his Moral writings does not treat precisely of the end and happiness of man, viewed in relation to civil society, as is falsely supposed in the second objection, but he treats chiefly of the end and happiness of man, which belongs to him as man. In the books of Politics, however, he finally treats of the happiness of man, as he is a member of civil society and the republic. But in whatever way man is finally considered, whether in himself, as man, or in relation to civil society, and as a part of it, his true happiness, even for the state of this life, is given in nothing outside of God. For a man, or a citizen of a republic, is not to be considered happy who finally stops at the mere operation according to virtue, and does not direct it to the worshipping and glorifying of God through obedience: nor is he to be esteemed happy who does not acknowledge the one true God, according to the precepts of the first table of the Decalogue, who does not love Him above all things, fear Him above all things, who does not hope in Him, does not trust in Him, who does not call upon Him in adverse circumstances, or in prosperous ones does not give thanks to Him for benefits received, but whoever is destitute of this operation directly occupied about God, is the most miserable of all, nor has he anything by which his appetite may be filled and satisfied, however much he may otherwise abound in goods of the soul, or of the body, or of fortune. Whence it is also false that for the happiness of man, viewed in civil society, the acts of virtues pertaining to the first table of the Decalogue, and prescribed in it, are not required. But it is sufficiently clear from what has been said so far that there has been more than enough about operation according to virtue, inculcated by Aristotle, which does not have the status of man's ultimate end and highest good, but only the status of a means, ordered to man's ultimate end and highest good. Returning from the digression to the path, we shall add a very few things concerning the parts and description of Natural Theology.

Latin:

nim adhuc finita, & proinde ratio boni etiam, quam in se contineret, finita esset. Appetitus hominis autem ut est boni universi, ita satiari non potest, nisi bono universo & infinito, quod non nisi in Deo invenitur. In quo autem non invenitur ratio boni universi, quo appetitus hominis satietur, eo homo non constituitur beatus, sed relinquitur appetitus inquietus, & homo miser. Unde tantum abest, ut operatione secundum virtutem nuda, non ad finem ejus ultimum, Deum, relata ita vir vere bonus & sine vituperatione quadratus constituatur, ut omnes fortunae casus pulcerrime, omnique ex parte, sicut oportet, ferat, sicut Aristoteles d. l. contendit, ut potius in rebus adversis, praesertim in casu ignominiosae mortis, irrequietus, timidus, huc illucque fluctuans, solatiique expers & vere miser relinquatur. Quod in semetipso abunde expertus est David, vir citra controversiam bonus, quin insigni gratia virtutumque donis supernaturalibus divinitus instructus, sed variis fortunae casibus jactatus, qui fatetur, nunquam, nisi in Deo, conquievisse animam suam, Psal. LXII. 2 & Deo velut rupi immota, & portioni sua innixum se tulisse demum casus quosvis, quibus jactabatur, sicut oportebat, Psal. LXXIII. 25. seq. Instante vero hora mortis operationem secundum virtutem, in se velut finem ultimum spectatam, relin urere hominem miserum, res ipsa loquitur. Si enim tum eum co stitueret beatum, aut per se illum erigeret, quod ipsa animam post discessum a corpore comitatura, eamque per se beatam constitutura sit, aut erigeret eum spe futurae alterius beatitudinis, qua ejus vitam, hic bene & secundum virtutem transactam, Deus pro sua immensa in homines, qui secundum virtutem vixerint, bonitate remuneraturus sit. Prius dici non potest. Nam operatio secundum virtutem hominum Viatorum propria est, & deserit eos, simulac haec temporalis vita illos deserit. Posterius si dicatur, fatendum erit, operationem secundum virtutem non esse hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum, sed medium ejus in vita altera consequendae, eamque ordinari per se ad Deum & consequendam in ipso atque ab ipso beatitudinem alterius vitae, velut ad finem ultimum. Quod nos volumus & contendimus.

VI. Neque magni ponderis est ratio Aristotelis, quâ nixus hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum in operatione secundum virtutem constituit. Ea redit huc: Uniuscujusque rei perfectio & finis consistit in ejus munere & opere proprio. Ergo & hominis perfectio ac Finis consistit in aliquo ejus munere & opere proprio. Antecedens probat l. Nic. c. VII. per inductionem: Ut enim tibicini & statuarum fictori omnique adeò artifici, & omninò iis, qui opus aliquod efficiunt, actionemque aliquam obeunt, in opere ipso bonum suum suus que finis & perfectio consistere videtur, sic & homini, si quod est ejus opus & munus, in eo ipso bonum ejus & benè vivere positum esse probabile erit. Cùm verò hominis munus & opus proprium consistat in operatione secundum virtutem, concludit hinc, in eâdem consistere etiam hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum. Sed quis non videt, non esse parem operationis secundum virtutem, quæ hominis propria est, & habituum effectivorum, quos hîć in exemplum Philosophus affert, rationem? Ars canendi tibiâ, ars statuaria & a s per se & naturâ suâ sunt habitus effectivi, qui pro fine ha operationem, vel opus aliquod, eâ efficiendum. Hom per se & naturâ suâ non est conditus propter finem, quô eju itus fatietur, â se efficiendũ, sed propter finem, qui est bonum absolutè perfectum & summum, à Deo & in Deo consequendum Illorum autem agentium, quorũ finis non est opus aliquod ab ips efficiendũ, sed bonũ præexistens alterius benevolâ volutate & dono vel aliquâ ipsorum operatione consequēdum, finis ultimus nunquam consistit in illorum operatione secundum se, sed semper in consecutione boni præexistentis, atque adeò in bono ipso præexistente, ut obtinendo: v. g. χρηματιστικῆς finis est pecunia, operatione hominis consequenda, non ipsa operatio, consequendæ pecuniæ causâ suscepta. Si quis per totam vitam omni studio & conatu agat, quæ comparandæ pecuniæ sint idonea, pecuniam tamen quæsitam non consequatur, tunc qui arti pecuniariæ studet, habebit quidem operationem, arti propriam, finem tamen conseqvutus esse non putabitur, quamdiu pecuniam quæsitam non consequitur. Perinde res habet cum operatione secundum virtutem, quæ hominis propria est. Si quis per vitam totam virtuti studuerit, decedat tamen absque Deo & absq; spe consequendæ in ipso beatitudinis in vita altera, is non dicetur consecutus finem ultimum & bonum summum, ut ut operationem secundum virtutem, quæ hominis munus proprium est, assecutus fuerit.

VII. Dicat quis : Aristotelem agere in Moralibus de fine hominis ultimo, non absolutè & simpliciter, sed l.saltem in genere bonorum hujus vitæ. ll. Eundem agere de fine ultimo hominis, in societate civili spectati. In genere bonorum hujus vitæ autem omninò ultimum esse operationem animæ secundum virtutem. Neque ad finem ultimum & bonum summum hominis, in societate civili spectati, pertinere actus, in prima tabula Decalogi præceptos, sed sufficere actus virtutum, ad secundam tabulam pertinentium.

VIII. Resp. I. Philosophum in Moralibus agere de beatitudine hominis pro statu hujus vitæ, non negamus. Quod autem illa in operatione secundum virtutem, sive moralem sive intellectualem, rectè constituatur, & alterutra vel utraque sit hominis, pro statu hujus vitæ, bonũ ultimum, quod semper propter se, nunquã propter aliud expetibile est (quod Aristoteles lib. I. Nicom. 7l. ei tribuit) hoc est, quod negamus. Et quidem de operatione secundum virtutem moralẽ constat ex hactenus dictis, quod in se imperfecta; & bona etiam, quæ extra Deum attingit, fluxa & caduca sint omnia, ut nec in se nec in ullis, extra Deum, objectis habeat, quod hominis animum tranquillare possit. Ad Deum verò obsequio colendum glorificandumque relata, habet quidem, non tamen in se, sed in Deo solo, velut in suo & hominis fine perfecto, quod tranquillet & satiet hominis appetitum, sed fic ne quidem in genere finium & bonorum hujus vitæ finis ultimi & beatitudinis, sed medii, ad eam ordinati, rationem habebit, contra quàm Aristoteles contendit, eam esse hominis finem ultimum & bonum summum. Quod verò attinet ad operationem secundum virtutem intellectualem, potest ea dupliciter considerari. Uno modo, ut est contemplatio cùm Dei tum rerum, à Deo factarum, in se absolutè, ut entia sunt, vel re & ratione; vel ratione tantùm à materia abstracta, vel etiam ut in materia sensibili sunt. Quem in modum Metaphysica ens ejusque affectiones in communi; & Ens primum sive Deum in specie ut abstracta a materia re & ratione; Physica entia, ut in materia, sensibili sunt, & principium motus & quietis in se habent; Mathematica verò quantitatem, velut ens tantùm ratione à materia sensibili abstractum, contemplatur. Altero, ut est contemplatio entis primi h. e. Dei, in ordine ad hominem per modum finis & boni summi spectati, & cæterorum entium velut effectuum Dei, qui suæ causæ ejusque perfectionum signa & vestigia quædam in se conspicienda exhibent. Aristoteles constituit hominis beatitudinem in contemplatione rerum priori & absolutâ, sed ratione non meliori, quàm quâ in operatione secundum virtutem moralem, in se absoluté spectatâ, eam constituebat. Præterquam enim quòd hæc etiam secundum virtutem ἐνέργεια planè imperfecta est, ut suprà ostensum, ad fruitionem Dei etiam, inchartam aut completam, (in quarum illa hujus, in hac alterius vitæ beatitudo consistit) eo ipso quod non ad Deum, velut ad finem, refertur, ne medii quidem habitudinem importat, multò minus beatitudo ipsa dici meretur. Posteriori autem modo instituta contemplatio Dei rerumque à Deo factarum ad beatitudinem hominis quandam medii habitudinem quidem sustinere potest: cùm Dei natura & perfectiones, ex rebus creatis cognitæ, virtualiter, ut supra dictum, contineant regulam rectæ circa Deum, velut hominis finem, operationis, & per conclusiones, quas infert, practicas cultum Deo debitum & ex parte hominis, qui Deo velut suo perfecto & summo bono hîc inchoatè, in vita altera verò perfectè frui vult, necessariò requisitum præscribat, finis autem ultimus & beatitudo hominis sive pro hujus sive pro alterius vitæ statu dici non potest. Fixum ergo immotumque manet, solum Deum ejusque fruitionem esse hominis finem ultimum, & ejus ἄυταρκες & summum bonum, etiam in genere bonorum hujus vitæ II. Deinde Philosophus in suis scriptis Moralibus non agit præcisè de fine & beatitudine hominis, in ordine ad societatē civilem spect ati, ut in objectione altera falsò supponitur, sed agit præcipuè de fine & beatitudine hominis, quæ ei ut homini convenit. In libris Politicorum autem agit demum de beatitudine hominis, ut societatis Civilis & reipublicæ membrum est. Quocunque autem modo homo tandem consideretur, sive in se, ut homo, sive in ordine ad societatem Civilem, & ut pars illius, vera tamen illius beatitudo, etiam pro statu hujus vitæ, extra Deum nulla datur. Non enim beatus censendus est homo, aut civis reipublicæ, qui in nuda secundum virtutem operatione ultimò fistit, nec ad Deum obsequio colendum glorificandumque eam dirigit: nec beatus æstimandus est, qui non unum verum Deum, juxta præcepta tabulæ primæ Decalogi, agnoscit, super omnia diligit, timet super omnia, qui non sperat in eo, non confidit ei, qui in rebus adversis eum non invocat, aut in secundis ei pro acceptis beneficiis non gratias agit, sed quisquis hac circa Deum directè occupatâ operatione destituitur, miserrimus omnium est, nec habet, quo ejus appetitus expleatur & satietur, quibuscunque etiam bonis, animi, aut corporis, aut fortunæ alioqui abundet. Unde falsum & illud est, quod ad beatitudinem hominis, in societate civili spectati, non requirantur actus virtutum, ad primam Decalogi tabulam pertinentes, & in ea præscripti. Sed plus satis de operatione secundum virtutem, ab Aristotele inculcatâ, quam non finem hominis ultimum & bonum summum esse, sed tantùm rationem medii, ad finem hominis ultimum & bonum summum ordinati habere, ex hactenus dictis liquidò constat. Ex diverticulo in viam redeuntes, de partibus & descriptione Theologiæ Naturalis paucissima subjungemus.


### XL. The parts of Natural Theology, just like those of other practical sciences, can…

XL.

The parts of Natural Theology, just like those of other practical sciences, can be established as three. The first is concerning the ultimate end of man, both objective and formal; the second is concerning the subject of operation, namely, concerning man as a wayfarer, in so far as he can become a participant in happiness, or it owes; the third treats of the causes and means of blessedness.

XLI.

Natural Theology can, however, be described as a practical science, prescribing to man the Wayfarer the worship suitable and due to God from the light and principles of nature, and explaining, confirming, and defending it, for the sake of attaining eternal happiness in God and from God.

I. That the proximate genus of Natural Theology is rightly established as a practical science, to which, as a science, it is appropriate to explain, confirm, and defend its object, but as a practical one, to prescribe the means of attaining the end, has been shown above in theses III, IV, and XIV, where what we have discussed regarding this matter may be seen.

II. The specific difference is sought partly from the subject of the operation, partly from the object and the end.

III. The description provided embraces the subject of the operation under the designation of man the Wayfarer, to whom Natural Theology prescribes the worship suitable to God. And in this, Natural Theology differs from the theology of the fatherland or of the blessed. For the latter does not have as its subject men who are Wayfarers, but those who have attained, who, having finished their pilgrimage in the mortal body, now dwell in the heavenly fatherland and have attained the goal, namely, blessedness.

IV. We established the end, the objective one indeed, as God; but the formal one as the attainment of Him, which we commonly designate by the name of blessedness or eternal happiness. Our description embraces both with the words: For the sake of attaining eternal happiness in GOD: where the little words (in God) denote the objective end; but blessedness or eternal happiness denote the formal end.

V. We said above that the material object is all things which confor the sake of eternal happiness to be followed in God, Natural Theology teaches, confirms, and defends those things which consist primarily in the causes and means of obtaining blessedness. We established God as its efficient cause; His goodness as the internal impulsive cause; but the means, the worship suitable and due to God, although now, for the state of corrupted nature, it is in no way sufficient for obtaining the end. For that this is accidental was shown above in thesis VI, Explanation no. III. Our description embraces both when it says: that Natural Theology prescribes to man the Wayfarer worship suitable and due to God, for the sake of eternal blessedness to be obtained from God. Where the little words, 'from God,' express the efficient and internal impulsive cause of blessedness; the remaining part expresses the means of obtaining the end.

VI. Moreover, we taught in the previous thesis XVII, Explanation no. IV, that the formal object coincides with the objective end, known from the light of nature, and consists in propositions declaring the existence, essence, and essential perfections of God, insofar as they become known to us from the light of nature, that is, either by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms, by themselves immediately and from apprehended terms, or through discourse, deduced from the first and immediate principles of nature and reason. Which we have encompassed in our description when we said, Natural Theology prescribes, explains, confirms, and defends worship suitable and due to God, from the light and principles of nature. And in this Natural Theology differs from Revealed. For the formal object of this is the primary truth, insofar as it manifests through supernatural revelation those things which are necessary to be known or done by those about to attain salvation, as we are to show below in its proper place. And so much for this time,

Latin:

XL.

Partes Theologiæ Naturalis, perinde ut aliarum scientiarum practicarum, tres constitui possunt. Prima de fine hominis ultimo, cùm objectivo, tùm formali; altera de subjecto operationis, nempe de homine Viatore, in quantum beatitudinis particeps fieri potest, aut debet; tertia de beatitudinis causis & mediis aget.

XLI.

Describi autem potest Theologia Naturalis, quòd sit scientia practica, homini Viatori cultum Deo convenientem & debitum ex lumine & principiis naturæ præscribens, eumque explicans, confirmans, & defendens, consequendæ in Deo & à Deo felicitatis æternæ causâ.

I. Theologiæ Naturalis genus proximum rectè constitui in scientia practica, cui, ut scientiæ, conveniat objectum suum explicare, confirmare & defendere, ut practicæ autem, præscribere media consequendi finis, ostensum est suprà th. III. IV. & XIV. ubi quæ hanc in rem disseruimus, videantur.

II. Differentia specifica petitur partim à subjecto operationis, partim ab objecto & fine.

III. Subjectum operationis descriptio tradita complectitur appellatione hominis Viatoris, cui Theologia Naturalis cultum Deo convenientem præscribit. Atque in hoc differt Theologia Naturalis à Theologia patriæ sive beatorum. Hæc enim pro subjecto non habet homines Viatores, sed comprehensores, qui peregrinatione suâ in corpore mortali defuncti, in cœlesti patria jam degunt, metamque, beatitudinem scilicet, comprehenderunt.

IV. Finem, objectivum quidem, constituebamus Deum; formalem verò ejus adeptionem, quam communiter beatitudinis sive felicitatis æternæ appellatione indigitamus. Utrumque complectitur descriptio nostra verbis: Consequendæ in DEO beatitudinis æternæ causâ: ubi voculæ (in Deo) finem objectivum; beatitudo autem sive felicitas æterna finem formalem denotant.

V. Objectum materiale diximus suprà esse omnia, quæ consequendæ in Deo felicitatis æternæ causâ Theologia Naturalis docet, confirmat & defendit, quæ potissimùm consistunt in consequendæ beatitudinis causis & mediis. Causam ejus efficientem constituebamus Deum; impulsivam internam, ejus bonitatem; media verò, cultum DEO convenientem & debitum, quamvis nunc pro statu naturæ corruptæ ad finem consequendum is nullatenus sufficiat. Hoc enim per accidens esse, ostensum est supra th. VI. Explic. n. III. Utraque complectitur descriptio nostra, cùm dicit: Theologiam Naturalem præscribere homini Viatori cultum, Deo convenientem & debitum, consequendæ à Deo beatitudinis æternæ causâ. Ubi voculæ, à Deo, causam beatitudinis efficientem & impulsivam internam; reliqua pars media consequendi finis exprimunt.

VI. Objectum formale autem coincidere cum fine objectivo, ex lumine naturæ cognito, & consistere in propositionibus, Dei existentiam, essentiam & perfectiones essentiales declarantibus, in quantum ex lumine naturæ h. e. vel virtute intellectus agentis & phantasmatum per se immediatè & ex apprehensis terminis, vel per discursum, ex primis & immediatis naturæ & rationis principiis deductum, nobis innotescunt, docuimus in superiori thes. XVII. Expl. n. IV. Quod complexi sumus in descriptione nostra, cùm diximus, Theologiam Naturalem præscribere, explicare, confirmare & defendere cultum, Deo convenientem & debitum, ex lumine & principiis naturæ. Atque in hoc differt Theologia Naturalis à Revelata. Hujus enim objectum formale est prima veritas, in quantum per revelationem supernaturalem, quæ salutem adepturis cognitu aut factu necessariæ sunt, manifestat, ut infra suo loco ostensuri sumus. Et tantum hac vice,


### Chap. III. …

CHAP. III.

Latin:

CAP. III.


## 3 On Revealed Theology

I.

That which for the sake of distinction we call revealed Theology, common usage simply and without addition calls Theology.

I. We call it revealed Theology in opposition to Natural [Theology], which was treated in the preceding chapter. It is called revealed, however, from revelation—not that general revelation by which τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ [that which is known of God] becomes known to the minds of men partly through innate notions, partly through things made by God, Rom. I. 19 (for from this, Natural Theology could also be called revealed, since its method of knowing is proper to it)—but from special revelation, by which those things that it concerns our salvation to know about God and His worship were manifested in a supernatural way through men who were θεοπνεύστους [God-breathed/inspired].

II. It claims for itself, by common usage, the name of Theology simply and without addition, either because the things that Natural Theology can teach about God and His worship are few and very imperfect, so that it scarcely seems to deserve the title of Theology, especially in the Christian world, which is instructed in a far more perfect knowledge of God; or rather because Natural Theology, as it is usually handed down by philosophers, has until now been confined within the boundaries of Metaphysics and considered a part of it. For philosophers have not hitherto been accustomed to treat of God otherwise than as of a being, in reality and reason abstracted from matter, and as it is contained under the object of Metaphysics, persisting within its idle speculation. But as for those things which could and should have been handed down concerning God as the ultimate end and highest good of man, and concerning divine worship and the method of attaining blessedness in God, and transferred to practice—to which the knowledge of God by itself and by its own nature leads—there was deep silence in their schools. However, the science which considers God only as an immaterial being, or as a being in reality and reason abstracted from matter, and keeps itself within the bare speculation of Him, concerning His right worship and the blessedness to be obtained in Him, is not so much a part of Theological science as it is of the speculative science of being as being, and therefore of Metaphysics.

II.

That divine revelation exists, and Theology based upon it, is as most certain to us, who are born and educated in the Church, as it is not entirely unknown to the Gentiles.

I. To us, who are born and educated in the Church, this is most certain: because with our mother's milk we are accustomed to imbibe immediately a certain knowledge of the divine revelation contained in the Scriptures; and the revealed Word of God, when it has been introduced into the heart, subsequently testifies of itself that it has proceeded from God and is truly divine, and produces a supernatural or divine faith in itself. However, once divine revelation is admitted, there can be no doubt about the Theology based upon it, whether it exists. For it is not immediately at hand for everyone who possesses the revealed Word of God to deduce from it, and to explain and confirm to others, those things which have been revealed concerning God and His worship, and the blessedness to be obtained in Him; but for this, a habit is needed, by which one is rendered prompt and ready for the duty of teaching those things, which can be no other than the habit of Theology, based upon divine revelation.

II. The same is not entirely unknown to the Gentiles either: because no nation is found which, in matters pertaining to religion and divine worship, subsists solely in the light of nature, nor which does not boast of some revelations received from God, however falsely. And not without cause. For the more prudent among the Gentiles were able, by the very guidance of the light of nature, to observe that there are some things necessary for salvation to be known, to the knowledge of which, however, one could not arrive except through supernatural revelation. For they had it naturally known that the soul of man is immaterial, and does not perish with the body, but remains surviving after death, and that it, according to whether it has behaved well or ill in this life, and has had God propitious or angry, will live happily or miserably in the other; yet they could not know from the light of nature what the future state of souls after death would be, and in what their blessedness or misery would consist. Known Furthermore, they held that no one could attain to the blessedness of the other life unless he departed from this life with God being propitious; but that all men are not only inclined by nature to every kind of evil, but also offend God daily by their sins, and provoke His wrath against themselves: yet they could not investigate by the light of nature the certain way and method of placating God, who is offended and angered by sins, and of arriving at the happiness and blessedness of the other life. This alone could be an argument to the Gentiles that a certain divine revelation is given in the world. For it is not credible that God, so benign and beneficent, would have begrudged the human race the knowledge of a certain thing, absolutely necessary for salvation to be known: since that is most alien to His immense goodness and provident care, by which He looks out for all things, and especially for the salvation of men.

Latin:

I.

Quam differentiæ causâ Theologiam revelatam dicimus, eam usus loquendi simpliciter & sine additamento Theologiam appellat.

I. Revelatam Theologiam dicimus in oppositione ad Naturalem, de qua in capite præcedente actum est. Dicitur autem revelata à revelatione, non illâ generali, quâ τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ partim per notitias insitas, partim per res à Deo factas mentibus hominum innotescit, Rom. I. 19. (ab hac enim Naturalis etiam Theologia revelata dici posset: cùm ejus ratio cognoscendi propria sit) sed à revelatione speciali, quâ modo supernaturali, quæ de Deo ejusque cultu nôsse nostræ interest salutis, per viros θεοπνεύστους manifestata sunt.

II. Ea vendicat sibi, ex usu loquendi, Theologiæ nomen simpliciter & sine additamento, vel quòd pauca & imperfecta admodùm sint, quæ de Deo ejusque cultu Theologia Naturalis docere potest, ut Theologiæ appellationem, præsertim in orbe Christiano, longè perfectiori de Deo cognitione instructo, vix mereri videatur, vel potiùs quòd Theologia Naturalis, ut à Philosophis tradi solet, huc usque intra cancellos Metaphysices conclusa, ejusque pars habita fuerit. Neque enim Philosophi hactenus de Deo aliter agere consueverunt, quàm ut de ente, re & ratione à materia abstracto, & prout sub objecto Metaphysices id continetur,intra otiosam ejus speculationem persistentes. Quæ autem de Deo, ut hominis fine ultimo & bono summo, deque cultu divino & ratione consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis tradi, & ad praxin, quò per se & suâpte naturâ Dei cognitio ducit, transferri poterant & debebant, de iis altum in illorum Scholis silentium fuit. Scientia autem, quæ Deum tantùm ut ens immateriale, sive ut ens re & ratione à materia abstractum confiderat, & intra nudam ejus speculationem se continet, de recto ejus cultu & consequenda in ipso beatitudine nihil quicquam solicita, non tam scientia Theologica, quam scientiæ, entis ut ens est, speculativæ, atque adeò Metaphysices pars est.

II.

Dari autem revelationem divinam eique innixam Theologiam, ut nobis, in Ecclesia natis & educatis, certissimum; ita nec Gentilibus prorfus ignotum est.

I. Nobis, qui in Ecclesia nati & educati sumus, certissimum id est: quia cum lacte materno statim notitiam quandam contentæ in Scripturis revelationis divinæ imbibere solemus; & Verbum Dei revelatum, ubi in cor intromissum est, testificatur deinceps de semetipso, quòd à Deo profectum & verè divinum sit, efficitque fui fidem supernaturalem sive divinam. Admissâ autem semel revelatione divina, de innixâ ei Theologiâ, an detur? dubitari non potest. Neque enim cuivis statim, cui Verbum Dei revelatum suppetit, in promtu est ex eo deducere, aliisque explicare & confirmare, quæ de Deo ejusque cultu, & de consequenda in ipso beatitudine revelata sunt, sed ad hoc habitu opus est, quo ad munus ea docendi reddatur promtus & expeditus, qui non alius, quàm Theologiæ, divinæ revelationi innixæ, habitus esse potest.

II. Idem Gentilibus quoque non planè ignotum est: quia nulla gens reperitur, quæ in rebus, ad religionem & cultum divinum pertinentibus, in solo naturæ lumine subsistat, nec aliquas revelationes, à Deo acceptas, quamvis falsò, jactet. Neque præter causam. Potuerunt enim prudentiores Gentilium ipso luminis naturæ ductu animadvertere, dari nonnulla cognitu ad salutem necessaria, ad quorum notitiam tamen non nisi per revelationem supernaturalem perveniri possit. Naturaliter enim cognitum habebant, animam hominis esse immaterialem, nec interire cum corpore, sed post mortem manere superstitem, eamque prout in hac vita benè maléve se gesserit, & Deum propitium vel iratum habuerit, in altera beatè aut miserè victuram; neque tamen qui animarum post mortem status futurus, & in quo illarum beatitudo aut miseria constitura esset, ex lumine naturæ cognoscere poterant. Cognitum prætereà habebant, ad vitæ alterius beatitudinem neminem posse pertingere, nisi Deo propitio ex hac vita discesserit; homines verò omnes non tantùm naturâ in nullum non malum propensos esse, sed & offendere Deum quotidiè peccatis, & provocare in se iram ipsius: neque tamen quæ Deum peccatis offensum iratumque placandi & ad alterius vitæ felicitatem & beatitudinem perveniendi via & ratio certa esset, ex naturæ lumine investigare poterant. Quod vel solum Gentilibus argumento esse poterat, dari quandam in mundo revelationem divinam. Neque enim credibile est, Deum tam benignum & beneficum rei cujusdam, cognitu ad salutem prorsus necessariæ, notitiam mortalium generi invidisse: cùm ab ejus immensa bonitate & provida cura, quâ ut rebus omnibus, ita maximè hominum saluti prospicit, id alienissimum sit.


### III. However, authors do not take theology, so called κατ’ ἐξοχήν or revealed, in…

III.

However, authors do not take theology, so called κατ’ ἐξοχήν or revealed, in one single meaning.

I. The ancient Fathers sometimes distinguish between θεολογίαν and οἰκονομίαν, and by θεολογίαν they understand precisely and strictly the doctrine or habit occupied in the consideration of God, and likewise of the divine perfections and persons, following the etymology of the word. For it is derived, as we saw above in chapter I, ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ λόγου, and is, by force of its origin, λόγος περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, a discourse about God, as most wish, or rather a habit of discoursing about God. But they refer οἰκονομίαν to the other part of theology, which is concerning the incarnation and those things which Christ did and suffered for the sake of our salvation in the flesh he assumed. For οἰκονομία, according to usage, is the administration and dispensation of domestic affairs, suitable to a house or family, and directed to its advantage and utility; but transferred here by metaphor, it is for the holy Fathers the administration and dispensation of the causes of salvation, and especially of the incarnation of the Son of God and of those things which He did and suffered for the sake of our salvation in the flesh He assumed, suitable and profitable to the Church, which is the house of God, and to its members; and it is sometimes taken simply for the incarnation, the source and fountain of all spiritual goods which are dispensed in the house of God or the Church. Thus Basil, Epist. CXLI, says that our understanding is fortified by the Holy Spirit, lest, being intent upon theology, we despise the economy. And Cyril of Alexandria, lib. I in John, on the words: He came unto his own; He says, He proceeds very aptly to the discourse on the incarnation, from pure theology to the explanation of the economy of the incarnation, which the Son of God performed for our sake. But this acceptance of the word, theology, is too narrow, and it comprises at least one part of theology, and indeed the first, which is concerning the objective end, namely God, and those things which intrinsically pertain to Him.

II. Theology is more commonly taken for the habit occupied in all parts of doctrine revealed for the sake of our salvation, and it comprises, besides theology strictly taken, the economy itself also.

III. The ancient Scholastics again make a threefold signification of theology, taken in this latter sense. One, by which it is taken for the habit by which we solely or principally assent to those things which are handed down in Scripture, and as they are handed down in it. Another, by which it is taken for the habit by which faith and those things which are handed down in Holy Scripture are defended and declared from certain better-known principles; and a third, by which it is used for the habit of those things which are deduced from the articles of faith, and from the sayings of Holy Scripture, just as conclusions from principles. Thus Durandus in Prol. in I. Sent. q. I. a. I., whom Marsilius followed ibid. q. II. a. II., Dionysius the Carthusian ibid. q. I., and others.

IV. But the first acceptance, according to which theology coincides with faith, is not received by usage. For faith is present indiscriminately in all the faithful, the learned and unlearned alike, males and females, whom, however, no one would call theologians; thus, neither would one call faith, precisely considered, theology.

Durandus in the said place ascribes the second to Augustine, who in lib. XIV de Trin. c. I, on the words of the Apostle: To another is given the word of knowledge; distinguishes between knowledge and faith, and judges that to knowledge should be attributed that by which the most wholesome faith, which leads to true blessedness, is begotten, nourished, defended, and strengthened; and he adds: With which knowledge very many of the faithful are not endowed, although they are endowed with faith itself in the highest degree. For it is one thing to know only what a man ought to believe for the sake of attaining the blessed life; which is nothing if not eternal; it is another thing to know how this very thing may assist the pious, and be defended against the impious: which it seems proper to call by the specific term science. That which is called science by the august Father, distinguished from faith, is called Theology by Durandus, in this intermediate meaning signifies be that of this passage. The Scholastics commonly accept Theology in the third meaning, so that it is a habit of conclusions, deduced from those things which have been divinely revealed. V. But when the matter is more deeply weighed, it does not appear how the two latter acceptations can be torn away from each other, or from the first, or certainly the usage of speaking does not permit them to be torn away. For to Theology, according to the usage of speaking, belongs everything which is contained under the aforementioned triple acceptation. For it is its task to hand down those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, by the authority and testimonies of Scripture, and to declare and defend the same by reasons and arguments sought from Scripture; and while it declares and defends those things by arguments sought from Scripture, it also draws out conclusions from those things which have been revealed, and confirms them for a fuller understanding of revealed things. VI. For the sake of greater clarity we think it must be repeated here, what we were saying in the preceding chapter, Th. II, just as it is one thing to rightly acknowledge and worship God; another, to deduce, explain, and confirm from their own principles those things which pertain to the acknowledgment and worship of God; so there is one habit by which we perform the former; another, by which we perform the latter. For that holds true also of our Theology, which for the sake of distinction we call revealed. Just as it is one thing to rightly and savingly acknowledge and worship God under the guidance of divine revelation; another, to hand down, confirm, and defend under the aspect of divine revelation those things which pertain to the saving acknowledgment and worship of God: so there is one habit by which we acknowledge and worship God as He has revealed Himself in His Word, another by which we teach those things which pertain to the saving acknowledgment and worship of God from His revealed Word, and defend them against dissenters. The former pertains to the habit of religion and faith; the latter to the habit of Theology. For those who rightly acknowledge and worship God, as He has revealed Himself in His Word, are called religious and faithful; Theologians are not so called, unless they are also able to deduce, explain, confirm, and defend from divine revelation those things which pertain to saving faith and worship. In this sense we accept Theology here as it is used: For all writers, ancient and modern, agree on this, that by received usage Theology is called the habit by which we explain, confirm, and defend those things which pertain to the saving knowledge and worship of God. And this acceptance of Theology seems to coincide with that which we were saying a little before encompasses all three acceptances handed down by Durandus.

Latin:

III.
