THeologiam autem, κατ’ ἐξοχήν sic dictam sive revelatam, Auctores non uno accipiunt significatu.

I. Patres prisci distinguunt nonnunquam inter θεολογίαν & οἰκονομίαν, & per θεολογίαν præcisè ac strictè inte ligunt doctrinam vel habitum, in consideratione Dei; perfectionum item & personarum divinarum occupatum, secuti vocis etymon. Deducitur enim, ut suprà in cap. I. vidimus, ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ λόγου, estque, vi originis, λόγος περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, Sermo de Deo, ut plerique volunt, vel potiùs habitus differendi de Deo. Οἰκονομίαν verò referunt ad alteram Theologiæ partem, quæ est de incarnatione & iis, quæ nostræ salutis causâ Christus in assumta carne egit & passus est. Nam οἰκονομία, ex usu loquendi, est rerum domesticarum administratio & dispensatio, domui sive familiæ conveniens, & ad ejus commodum atque utilitatem directa; per metaphoram verò huc translata Patribus sanctis est administratio & dispensatio causarum salutis, cumprimis verò incarnationis Filii Dei & eorum, quæ nostræ salutis causâ in assumta carne egit & passus est, Ecclesiæ, quæ domus Dei est, ejusque membris conveniens & proficua; & accipitur interdum simpliciter pro incarnatione, bonorum spiritualium, quæ in domo Dei sive Ecclesia dispensantur, omnium fonte & scaturigine. Ita Basilius Epist. CXLI. dicit, à Spiritu S. præmuniri nostram intelligentiam, ne τῇ θεολογίᾳ intenti, ὀικονομίαν contemnamus. Et Cyrillus Alexandrinus lib. I. in Joh. ad verba: In sua venit; Valdè, inquit, appositè ad sermonem de incarnatione progreditur, ἐξ ἀκράτυ θεολογίας εἰς ἐξήγησιν ὀικονομίας τῆς μετασαρκώσεως, à mera Theologia ad explicationem œconomiæ incarnationis, quam propter nos gessit Filius Dei. Sed hæc vocis, θεολογία, acceptio nimis angusta est, & complectitur saltem unam Theologiæ partem, & quidem primam, quæ est de fine objectivo, Deo scilicet, & iis, quæ intrinsecè ipsi conveniunt.

II. Usitatiùs accipitur Theologia pro habitu, in omnibus nostræ salutis causâ revelatis doctrinæ partibus occupato, & complectitur, præter θεολογίαν, strictè sumtam, etiam ipsam οἰκονομίαν.

III. Theologiæ, in hoc posteriori significatu acceptæ, Scholastici veteres rursum triplicem faciunt significationem. Unam, quâ sumitur pro habitu, quo solum vel principaliter assentimur his, quæ in Scriptura traduntur, & prout in ea traduntur. Alteram, quâ accipitur pro habitu, quo fides & ea quæ in Sacra Scriptura traduntur, ex quibusdam principiis notioribus defenduntur & declarantur; & tertiam, quâ pro habitu eorum, quæ deducuntur ex articulis fidei, & ex dictis Sacræ Scripturæ, sicut conclusiones ex principiis, usurpatur. Ita Durandus in Prol. in I. Sent. q. I. a. I. quem sequuti sunt Marsilius ib. q. II. a. II. Dionysius Carthusianus ib. q. I. & alii.

IV. Sed prima acceptio, juxta quam Theologia cum fide coincidit, usu recepta non est. Fides enim promiscuè omnibus inest fidelibus, doctis pariter & indoctis, masculis & fœminis, quos tamen ut Theologos nemo dixerit, ita nec fidem, præcisè spectatam, Theologiam quis dixerit.

Secundam adscribit Durandus d. l. Augustino, qui in lib. XIV. de Trin. c. I. ad verba Apostoli: Alii datur sermo scientiæ; inter scientiam & fidem distinguit, & scientiæ illud tribuendum censet, quo fides saluberrima, quæ ad veram beatitudinem ducit, gignitur, nutritur, defenditur, roboratur; & subjungit: Quâ scientiâ non pollent fideles plurimi, quamvis polleant ipsâ fide plurimum. Aliud enim est scire tantummodò, quid homo credere debeat propter adipiscendam vitam beatam; quæ non nisi æterna est; aliud scire, quemadmodùm hoc ipsum piis opsituletur, & contra impios defendatur: quam proprio appellare vocabulo scientiam videtur. Quæ augusto Patri dicitur scientia, fidei contradistincta, ea Durando dicitur Theologia, in hoc medio significatu accepta, quam significationem hujus loci esse existimat. In significatu tertio accipiunt Theologiam Scholastici communiter, ut sit habitus conclusionum, ex iis, quæ divinitus revelata sunt, deductarum. V. Sed re penitiùs perpensâ, non apparet, quomodo duæ postremæ acceptiones à se invicem, vel à prima divelli possint, vel certè ut divellantur, usus loquendi non permittit. Theologiæ enim, ex usu loquendi, convenit id omne, quod sub prædicta triplici acceptione continetur. Ejus enim est tradere ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, auctoritate & testimoniis Scripturæ, & eadem declarare ac defendere rationibus & argumentis, ex Scriptura petitis; & dum argumentis ex Scriptura petitis ea declarat & defendit, eruit etiam conclusiones ex iis, quæ revelata sunt, confirmatque illa ad uberiorem rerum revelatarum intelligentiam. VI. Majoris perspicuitatis causâ repetendum hîc ducimus,quod in capite præced. Th. II. dicebamus, quemadmodùm aliud est, Deum rectè agnoscere & colere; aliud, quæ ad Dei agnitionem cultumque pertinent, ex suis principiis deducere, explicare & confirmare; ita alium esse habitum, quo illa; alium, quo hæc præstamus. Id enim procedit etiam de nostra, quam differentiæ causâ revelatam dicimus, Theologia. Sicut aliud est, Deum ad ductum divinæ revelationis rectè & salutariter agnoscere & colere; aliud, quæ ad Dei salutarem agnitionem cultumque pertinent, sub ratione divinæ revelationis tradere, confirmare, & defendere: ita alius est habitus, quo Deum, ut sese in Verbo suo revelavit, agnoscimus & colimus, alius, quo quæ ad salutarem Dei agnitionem cultumque pertinent, ex ejus Verbo revelato docemus, & adversus dissentientes defendimus. Illud ad religionis & fidei; hoc ad Theologiæ habitum spectat. Qui enim Deum rectè, ut in Verbo suo se revelavit, agnoscunt & colunt, religiosi & fideles dicuntur; Theologi non item, nisi etiam quæ ad salutarem fidem cultumque pertinent, ex divina revelatione deducere, explicare, confirmare & defendere possint. Quo significatu Theologiam nos cum usu heic accipimus: Omnes enim, veteres & recentiores Scriptores, consentiunt in hoc, quòd ex usu recepto Theologia dicatur habitus, quo quæ ad salutarem Dei agnitionem cultumque pertinent, explicamus, confirmamus & defendimus. Et videtur hæc Theologiæ acceptio coincidere cum ea, quam paulò ante dicebamus omnes tres à Durando traditas acceptiones complecti.


### IV. But since to explain the underlying matters, to deduce conclusions from their…

IV.

But since to explain the underlying matters, to deduce conclusions from their principles, and those certain and indubitable, and to defend them against dissenters, is the task of the sciences, no more convenient genus could be given for declaring the nature of Theology, to which we have just said the same duty belongs, than science, taken however in a looser sense.

I. Aristotle, book VI of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, establishes five habits of the mind by which we enunciate the truth by affirming and denying: Art, science, prudence, wisdom, and mind or intelligence; of which three are speculative and two are practical. The speculative are mind or intelligence, which is the habit of principles; science, which is the habit of deducing conclusions from their principles; and wisdom, which is the habit of both principles and conclusions at once. The practical are prudence, which is the habit of acting with right reason; and art, which is the habit of making with right reason. And this distinction of the habits of the mind is founded on the diversity of objects. For the things about which the intellect enunciates the truth by affirming or denying are either necessary or contingent. Necessary things are either principles or conclusions. Concerning the former, the mind or intelligence; concerning the latter, science; concerning both together, the habit of wisdom enunciates the truth by affirming and denying. Contingent things fall either under ποίησιν or under πρᾶξιν. Concerning the former, art; concerning the latter, prudence enunciates the truth by affirming or denying, Which foundation of the distinction, as is evident, is general, and falls also into our Theology. For it is occupied either with necessary things, or with contingent ones. If with the former, then either with principles, or with conclusions, or with both, etc., to which therefore either some genus from the aforementioned five habits of the intellect must be assigned, which is suitable to its underlying subject matter, or some other habit of the intellect different from those five, by which its more proximate generic concept may be expressed, and whether it is occupied with necessary things or with contingent ones? with principles or with conclusions? must be declared and devised. For if you stop at a more remote genus, and define Theology simply as a habit of the intellect, you will not have sufficiently expressed its nature. For what kind of habit it is—speculative? or practical? of principles? or of conclusions? or of both? you will insinuate into the mind of the reader, which nevertheless is necessary for declaring the nature of Theology. But if in place of a generic difference you add that it is a practical habit, as is usually done by modern Theologians, not even thus will you declare the generic concept of Theology sufficiently conveniently. For by usage of speech, a habit is called practical when it is the proximate principle of practice or operation, and prescribes to the will, with prior deliberation, what is fitting or not fitting to do here and now in a particular case: such a habit in civil matters is prudence; in sacred matters it is the habit of religion; then [it is also called practical] when it is at least a remote principle of operation, and by means of universal conclusions, prescribes in general what is fitting to do or not to do: such a habit in civil matters is Ethical science; in sacred matters it is Theology. For neither prescribes to the will in a particular case what is fitting to do or omit here and now, but both do so in general; the former indeed hands down what things are to be done or not done in accordance with right reason; the latter what things are to be done or not done in accordance with divine revelation, so that from their own certain and necessary principles, to which it is repugnant for falsehood to underlie, they may deduce, confirm, and defend them. From which it happens that if a definition of Theology is forged by using 'practical habit' in place of a genus, which is more suitable to the habit of religion, common to the learned and unlearned, than to Theology, which is proper to the learned, or certainly equally to both.

II. However, we have not hitherto observed that any new genus, different from the five mentioned habits, has been devised by anyone, by which the generic concept of Theology might be conveniently expressed, and whether it is occupied with necessary things or contingent ones, with principles or with conclusions, might be sufficiently declared. But if indeed some genus of Theology must be assigned from the five habits handed down by Aristotle, no other can be assigned to it than science. For if you compare Theology with them, you will discover that it has no greater agreement with any than with the habit of science. For Theology teaches what is necessary to be believed and done by a man who is to attain salvation, from its own certain and immovable principles, and it also defends what it teaches against any dissenters: which, as has been said, suits no other than the habit of science. For understanding is a habit of principles, not of conclusions deduced from principles. Prudence, however, is an operative habit, whose function is not to teach, but to deliberate about means suitable for attaining an end, and to judge which things conduce more or less to it, and to prescribe to the will those things which have been found to be more suitable. Furthermore, art is an effective habit, with which Theology has no commerce. Finally, wisdom, according to Aristotle, is a habit of both principles and conclusions, with which, although Theology may agree in this respect, inasmuch as it itself not only deduces conclusions from its own principles, but also explains its own principles, demonstrates their genuine sense according to the rules of good interpretation, and defends them against dissenters: it does not, however, admit the other conditions of wisdom handed down by Aristotle, especially the first, which is to know all things, not indeed in particular, but in universal. For Theology is not a universal science, to which it is suitable to know all things in universal, but it has its own particular and determined object, namely, the salvation of men and the means which contribute to attaining it, the boundaries and sphere of which it does not exceed. Nor is it an objection that science is said to have necessary and everlasting things as its object; whereas Theology is occupied in delivering the means of attaining salvation, which are contingent. For the things that fall under science are called necessary and everlasting, not by reason of actual existence, but by reason of the connection of the extremes. For the object of science is properly constituted by conclusions, to be deduced or already deduced from their principles, to which, in order for them to be called necessary and everlasting, it suffices that the connection of the extremes be necessary and everlasting; and that the principles also, upon which they depend, be of perpetual and eternal truth. Which applies well to Theology. For the things that are taught in it can be reduced to three: namely, the end, the subject, the causes and the means. Which, in so far as they are delivered in it, always behave in the same way, and as regards the connection of the extremes are all necessary, and, according to the order of salvation divinely instituted, are of perpetual truth, so much so that anathema is pronounced by the Apostle upon whoever, whether Apostle or Angel, should dare to preach another Gospel besides that which had once been preached by the Apostles, Gal. I. 8.

III. And in this we have the Scholastics, ancient and modern, almost all of them, agreeing, who by unanimous consent have reckoned Theology among the sciences both in the past and still do so today. Whom the august Father Augustine preceded, when in book XIV de Trin. c. 1, he openly called the habit of mind, by the aid of which most saving faith, which leads to true blessedness, is begotten, nourished, defended, and strengthened (which is Theology itself), SCIENCE, and in order to distinguish it from faith, he added: It is one thing to know only what a man ought to believe for the sake of attaining the blessed life, which is nothing if not eternal: but it is another thing to know how this very thing may both help the pious and be defended against the impious, which the Apostle seems to call by the proper term SCIENCE. Augustine refers, however, to the passage of the Apostle I Cor. XII. 8, in which the word of knowledge is distinguished from the word of wisdom, thinking that by the term knowledge is denoted there the science by which those things which pertain to faith and the worship of God are taught and defended, although in the Greek text the word ἐπιστήμη, science, does not exist, but γνῶσις, which is more general and is used for any knowledge whatsoever.

IV. Whether, however, Theology is a science properly and strictly, or improperly and in a looser sense, is a matter of controversy: where the Scholastics diverge into different opinions. For some assume or suppose as certain that it is of the nature of science to deduce its conclusions from principles that are self-evident and clear, and because this does not suit our Theology—for this deduces its conclusions from divine revelation, which is not evident—having called into aid the distinction between Theology in itself and the same as it is in us, they judge it to be truly and properly a science in itself; for its principles in themselves are evident and self-evident, since they are evidently known both to God and to the blessed; but as it is in us, it is not a science properly and strictly, but improperly and in a looser sense: for its principles are not known to us of themselves and evidently, but are believed on account of divine revelation, which is to us non-evident and obscure. Others, on the contrary, deny that it is of the nature of every science that its principles be evident and known by themselves, but they say that this is only of the nature of subalternating sciences. For subalternated sciences deduce their conclusions from principles that are not evident, and which have been demonstrated elsewhere, namely in the subalternating science. And these thinkers hold that Theology, even as it exists in us wayfarers, is a science truly and properly, but an imperfect one: for it is a subalternated science, and is subalternated to the Theology which is in God and the blessed. Just as, therefore, other subalternated sciences are, by the consensus of all, truly, properly, and strictly called sciences, although imperfect due to a lack of evidence; so too Theology, even as it is in us, is truly, properly, and strictly a science, although imperfect due to a lack of evidence. For to this end, that it may be truly, properly, and strictly a science, it suffices that its principles in the Theology of God and the blessed, as subalternating sciences, be self-evident and clearly known. V. We, intending to declare our mind on this matter, will first of all inquire into the notion and concept of science.

(1) By the received usage of speaking, however, we are said to know each thing simply and properly, first indeed when we know the cause through which a thing is, in such a way that it is its cause, that the thing cannot be otherwise. For all who either truly know, or think they know, for that reason either know, or think they know, because they know the thing to be as we have said, either in reality or in their own opinion, as Aristotle says in I Post. c. II. From the usage of speaking, therefore, to know some thing is to know the cause through which the thing is, to be the cause of that thing, so that it cannot be otherwise. From which Aristotle infers that science is from principles that are true, primary, immediate, better known, and prior, and which contain the cause of the conclusion.

Then we are also said to know by the usage of speaking, when we know certainly and indubitably that a thing is, either a posteriori and from the effect, or through induction, or through a remote cause, although we may be ignorant of the proximate cause through which the thing is. Which Aristotle in the said book, c. X, calls the science of τꭣ ὅτι, or that the thing is.

(2) If, therefore, the concept and proper definition of science consists in the knowledge of the cause through which a thing is, that it is its cause in such a way that it cannot be otherwise; or in the knowledge that a thing is, through induction, or from an effect better known to us, or through a remote cause, Theology will certainly be truly and properly a science. For by its aid the theologian knows the causes of eternal salvation being obtained for sinful man (which is its principal object) to be its causes in such a way that salvation for mortals can neither be obtained, nor is obtained, otherwise or through causes other than those. The principles also, from which it derives this knowledge, are true, primary, immediate, better known, and prior, and they contain the cause of the conclusion, which is about obtaining eternal salvation: e.g., the principles and causes of our salvation are the grace of God, the merit or satisfaction of Christ for sins, and faith, apprehending the merit of Christ and appropriating it to us, which taken together constitute one adequate and proximate cause of obtaining salvation, which is the grace of God, in the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith and appropriated to us, from which, once it is known, such a scientific demonstration is constructed: Whoever apprehends by faith the merit or satisfaction of Christ for sins, and has God in heaven propitious to himself through Christ, he obtains by His grace the remission of sins and eternal salvation. But every believer in Christ apprehends the merit or satisfaction of Christ for sins, and has God in heaven propitious to himself through Christ. Therefore, every believer in Christ obtains by the grace of God the remission of sins and eternal salvation. Both premises are true, primary, immediate principles of Theology, better known and prior to the conclusion, and they contain the proximate cause of the conclusion, and that which clearly satisfies the question of the 'why'. Furthermore, just as other sciences do not always demonstrate why a thing is from first, immediate, prior, and better-known principles, which are the cause of the conclusion, but sometimes prove the τὸ ὅτι at least, or that the thing is, by induction, or from the effect, or through a remote cause, so too does Theology, where it is not granted to penetrate into the cause of a thing, prove that a thing is a posteriori and from the effect, or at least from divine revelation, with a certainty surely greater than that with which other sciences demonstrate that a thing is a posteriori. If, therefore, we are said to know each thing both simply and properly when we know the cause through which or because of which a thing is, that it is its cause, and that it cannot be otherwise, but [to know] in a qualified sense and that a thing is when we know that the thing is a posteriori, why should we not also be said to know simply and properly in Theology when we know the cause through which a thing is, that it is its cause, and that it cannot be otherwise; but [to know] in a qualified sense, and that a thing is, when we know that the thing is either from the effect, or through a remote cause, or from the bare testimony or revelation of God, which is more certain than any demonstration? (3) But if, indeed, you require for knowledge simply and properly that we know evidently and from principles known by themselves the cause through which a thing is, and that it is its cause, and that it cannot be otherwise, as authors commonly wish (although neither the usage of speaking nor the notion of knowledge derived from it seems to require this precisely), then It must be said that Theology is not a science simply, properly, and in the strict sense, but in a less proper and looser sense, insofar as any knowledge of a thing is called a science, which is born from certain, immovable principles to which no falsehood can underlie, whether the principles are evident and known by themselves, or whether they become known from elsewhere certainly and infallibly. For although Theology also deduces its conclusions from principles which are first, immediate, prior, and better known, and are the causes of the conclusion; as when, for example, it proves that Christ is omnipotent from the fact that He is God; yet for the most part it uses an inartificial mode of argumentation, taken from revelation or divine testimony, which is non-evident, yet certain and infallible. Moreover, when it uses an artificial kind of argumentation, and deduces conclusions from principles that are first, immediate, prior, better known, and the causes of the conclusions, the other principle of the argument is always non-evident, the proof of which finally returns to divine revelation or testimony, in which one must ultimately stop: for example, in this syllogism: Whoever is true God, he is omnipotent. But Christ is true God. Therefore Christ is omnipotent; the minor proposition is non-evident, the truth of which cannot become known to us from elsewhere than from divine revelation, in which one must ultimately stop. Which cannot stand with science, strictly and properly so called, given that evidence is of the reason and concept of science taken properly and in the strict sense.

VI. Nor do the Thomists remove the difficulty by the distinction of science, taken properly and in the strict sense, into subalternating and subalternated, adduced above. For let us grant that our Theology is subalternated to the Theology which is in God and the blessed; yet in us, who do not have its principles known evidently from the Theology of the blessed or of God, but believe them on account of divine revelation or testimony, it can no more have the nature of science, properly so called, than Optics or Music, of which the former is subalternated to Geometry and the latter to Arithmetic, has the nature of science in one who does not have the principles of those things known evidently, but only knows them obscurely on account of the authority and testimony of a Master who assents. For even for a subalternated science it is required that its principles be evidently known by the one knowing, although not from the terms themselves, nor through a demonstration instituted within the science itself, yet through a demonstration made in the subalternating science, and therefore to whom the subalternated science belongs, so that it has the nature of a science properly so called in him, it is necessary that the subalternating science also belong to him, from which its principles derive light and evidence.

VII. Since, therefore, it stands that the evidence of principles is of the nature of science, it remains fixed and immovable that our Theology is not a science, strictly and in rigor, but only in a looser meaning taken for a habit by which we infer from certain and immovable principles conclusions that are certain and which are of necessary truth. Which meaning, as it is not unusual, so it will not make the definition of Theology obscure or vicious, if something by which it is declared that it is accepted in this general meaning shall have been added. For since most words are equivocal and signify many things, necessity often compels us to use in place of a genus a word that is in itself equivocal, provided that by something added or premised the equivocation is removed and the meaning in which we accept it has been declared. We do not, however, wish to contend with anyone about this matter, but if anyone prefers to subsist in a more remote genus and to define Theology by a habit of the intellect, it will be permitted by us, provided that something is added in place of a generic difference by which it is declared to be a habit of knowing and to be occupied in teaching: otherwise the definition will be obscure and will fit the habit of religion rather than of Theology.

Latin:

IV.

Cùm verò explicare res substratas, conclusiones ex suis principiis, iisque certis & indubitatis deducere, atque contra dissentientes defendere, scientiarum sit, ad naturam Theologiæ, cui idem convenire munus modò diximus, declarandam vix convenientius genus dari poterit, quàm scientia, in laxiori tamen significatu accepta.

I. Aristoteles lib. VI. Nic. c. 3. quinque constituit habitus mentis, quibus affirmando & negando enunciamus verum: Artem, scientiam, prudentiam, sapientiam, & mentem sive intelligentiam; quorum tres speculativi, & duo practici sunt. Speculativi sunt mens sive intelligentia, quæ est habitus principiorum; scientia, quæ est habitus deducendi conclusiones ex suis principiis; & sapientia, quæ simul principiorum & conclusionum habitus est. Practici sunt prudentia, quæ est habitus cum recta ratione activus; & ars, quæ est habitus cum recta ratione effectivus. Et fundatur hæc habituum mentis distinctio in diversitate objectorum. Res enim, de quibus intellectus verum enunciat affirmando aut negando, vel sunt necessariæ, vel contingentes. Necessariæ vel principia sunt, vel conclusiones. Circa illa mens sive intelligentia; circa has scientia, circa utraque simul sapientiæ habitus verum enunciat affirmando & negando. Contingentes vel sub ποίησιν vel sub πρᾶξιν cadunt Circa illas ars; circa has prudentia enunciat verum affirmando vel negando, Quod distinctionis fundamentum, uti patet, generale est, & in nostram quoque Theologiam cadit. Ea enim vel occupatur circa res necessarias, vel circa contingentes. Si circa illas, vel circa principia, vel circa conclusiones, vel circa utraque &c. cui proinde vel assignandum erit genus aliquod ex prædictis quinque habitibus intellectus, quod ejus materiæ substratæ conveniens sit, vel alius quispiam à quinque illis diversus habitus intellectus, quo ejus conceptus genericus propinquior exprimatur, & sitne circa res necessarias, an circa contingentes? circa principia, an circa conclusiones occupatus? declaretur, excogitandus erit. Si enim in genere remotiori substiteris, & Theologiam simpliciter per habitum intellectus definieris, naturam ejus satis non expresseris. Non enim cujusmodi habitus ea sit, speculativus? an practicus? principiorum? an conclusionum? an utrorumque? legentis animo insinuabis, quod tamen ad Theologiæ naturam declarandam necessarium est. Quod si differentiæ genericæ loco addas, eam esse habitum practicum, ut à Theologis modernis fieri solet, ne sic quidem Theologiæ conceptum genericum satis convenienter declarabis. Ex usu loquendi enim habitus practicus dicitur, cùm qui praxeos sive operationis principium propinquum est, & voluntati, præviâ deliberatione, in particulari quæ hîc & nunc agere conveniat aut non conveniat, præscribit: cujusmodi habitus in civilibus prudentia; in sacris habitus religionis est; tùm qui principium operationis saltem remotum est, & mediantibus conclusionibus universalibus, in genere quæ agere aut non agere conveniat, præscribit: cujusmodi habitus in civilibus scientia Ethica; in sacris Theologia est. Neutra enim voluntati in particulari, quæ hîc & nunc agere aut omittere conveniat, præscribit, sed utraque in genere, illa quidem quæ rectæ rationi; hæc quæ divinæ revelationi convenienter agenda vel non agenda sint, tradit, ita ut ex suis certis & necessariis principiis, quibus falsum subesse repugnat, ea deducant, confirment & defendant. Ex quo fit, ut adhibito generis loco habitu practico Theologiæ definitio cudatur, quæ potiùs habitui religionis, doctis & indoctis communi, quàm Theologiæ, eruditorum propriæ, vel certè utrique æquè conveniat.

II. Non autem animadvertimus hactenus, novum quoddam à memoratis quinque habitibus diversum genus á quoquam excogitatum esse, quo Theologiæ conceptus genericus propinquior convenienter exprimi, & sitne ea circa res necessarias, an circa contingentes? circa principia, an circa conclusiones occupata? satis declarari possit. Quod si verò ex traditis ab Aristotele habitibus quinque aliquod Theologiæ genus assignandum sit, aliud ei assignari non poterit, quàm scientia. Si enim Theologiam cum illis conferas, deprehendes, eam cum nullo majorem habere convenientiam, quàm cum scientiæ habitu. Docet enim Theologia, quæ adepturo salutem homini creditu & factu necessaria sunt, ex suis certis & immotis principiis, & defendit etiam, quæ docet, adversus quosvis dissentientes: Quod, uti dictum, non alii, quàm scientiæ habitui convenit. Intelligentia enim principiorum habitus est, non conclusionum, ex principiis deductarum. Prudentia verò habitus operativus est, cujus munus non est docere, sed consultare de mediis, ad consequendum finem idoneis, & quæ magis minusve ad eum conducant, judicare, voluntatique quæ idonea magis deprehensa fuerint, præscribere. Ars porro, habitus effectivus est, cum qua Theologiæ nihil est commercii. Sapientia denique, juxta Aristotelem, est simul principiorum & conclusionum habitus, cum qua licet Theologia, quantum ad hoc, conveniat, utpote quæ & ipsa non tantùm conclusiones ex suis principiis deducit, sed & principia sua explicat, illorum sensum genuinum ad regularum bonæ interpretationis ductum, demonstrat, & adversus dissentientes defendit: non tamen cæteras ab Aristotele traditas sapientiæ conditiones admittit, præsertim primam, quæ est, scire omnia, non quidem in particulari, sed in universali. Theologia enim non est scientia universalis, cui conveniat omnia scire in universali, sed habet suum particulare & determinatum objectum, nempe hominum salutem &, quæ ad eam adipiscendam faciunt, media, quorum cancellos & sphæram non egreditur. Neque obstat, quod scientia dicitur pro objecto habere res necessarias & sempiternas; Theologia autem in tradendis adipiscendæ salutis mediis, quæ contingentia sunt, occupatur. Nam sub scientiam quæ cadunt res, necessariæ dicuntur & sempiternæ, non ratione actualis existentiæ, sed ratione connexionis extremorum. Propriè enim scientiæ objectum constituunt conclusiones, ex suis principiis deducendæ aut deductæ, ad quas ut dicantur esse necessariæ & sempiternæ, sufficit, quod extremorum connexio necessaria & sempiterna; & principia etiam, ex quibus pendent, perpetuæ & æternæ veritatis sint. Quod benè cadit in Theologiam. Quæ enim in ea docentur, ad tria revocari possunt: Finem scilicet, subjectum, causas & media. Quæ in quantum in ea traduntur, eodem semper modo sese habent, & quantum ad connexionem extremorum necessaria omnia, &, juxta ordinem salutis, divinitùs institutum, perpetuæ veritatis sunt, adeò ut ab Apostolo anathema dicatur, quisquis sive Apostolus sive Angelus aliud prædicare ausit Evangelium, præter id quod ab Apostolis prædicatum semel fuerat, Gal. II. 8.

III. Atque in hoc consentientes habemus Scholasticos, veteres & recentiores, plerosque omnes, qui consensu unanimi Theologiam scientiis & olim accensuêre, & adhuc hohieque accensent. Quibus præivit augustus Pater Augustinus, cùm lib. XIV. de Trin. c. 1. habitum mentis, cujus adminiculo fides saluberrima, quæ ad veram beatitudinem ducit, gignitur, nutritur, defenditur, roboratur, (qui ipsa Theologia est) apertè SCIENTIAM dixit, & ut à fide eam distingueret, subjunxit: Aliud est SCIRE tantummodo, quid homo credere debeat, propter adipiscendam vitam beatam, quæ non nisi æterna est: aliud autem scire, quemadmodùm hoc ipsum & piis opituletur, & contra impios defendatur, quam proprio appellare vocabulo SCIENTIAM videtur Apostolus. Respicit autem Augustinus ad locum Apostoli I. Cor. XII. 8. in quo sermo scientiæ à sermone sapientiæ distinguitur, ratus, scientiæ voce denotari ibi scientiam, quâ quæ ad fidem & Dei cultum pertinent, docentur & defenduntur, quamvis in textu Græco non extet vox ἐπιστήμη, scientia, sed γνῶσις, quæ generalior est, & de qualibet cognitione usurpatur.

IV. Utrum verò Theologia propriè & in rigore; an impropriè & in significatu laxiori scientia sit? controvertitur: ubi in divortia opinionum abeunt Scholastici. Quidam enim sumunt aut supponunt velut certum, de ratione scientiæ esse, ut conclusiones suas deducat ex principiis per se notis & evidentibus, & quia hoc nostræ non convenit Theologiæ: hæc enim deducit suas conclusiones ex divina revelatione, quæ inevidens est; vocatâ in subsidium distinctione inter Theologiam secundum se; & eandem, ut est in nobis, censent, eam secundum se esse verè & propriè scientiam; ejus enim principia secundum se esse evidentia & per se nota, cùm & Deo & hominibus beatis evidenter nota sint; ut autem in nobis est, non esse scientiam propriè & in rigore, sed impropriè & in significatu laxiori: ejus enim principia nobis non esse per se & evidenter nota, sed credi propter divinam revelationem, quæ nobis inevidens & obscura est. Alii contrà negant de ratione scientiæ omnis esse, ut ejus principia sint evidentia & per se nota, sed dicunt, id esse tantùm de ratione scientiarum subalternantium. Subalternatas enim deducere conclusiones suas ex principiis inevidentibus, & alibi, nempe in scientia subalternante demonstratis. Atque hi sentiunt, Theologiam, etiam ut in nobis viatoribus est, esse scientiam verè & propriè, sed imperfectam: esse enim scientiam subalternatam, & subalternari Theologiæ, quæ est in Deo & beatis. Quemadmodùm ergo aliæ scientiæ subalternatæ, omnium consensu, verè, propriè & in rigore dictæ scientiæ sunt, licet imperfectæ, ob defectum evidentiæ; ita & Theologiam, etiam ut in nobis est, esse verè, proprie & in rigore scientiam, licet imperfectam, ob defectum evidentiæ. Ad hoc enim, ut verè propriè & in rigore scientia sit, sufficere, quòd ejus principia in Theologia Dei & beatorum, tanquam scientiis subalternantibus, sint per se & evidenter nota. V. Nos nostram hac de re mentem declaraturi, primò omnium in scientiæ notionem & conceptum inquiremus.

(1) Usu loquendi autem recepto scire unamquamque rem dicimur simpliciter & propriè, primò quidem cùm causam, per quam res est, cognoscimus ita ejus causam esse, ut res omninò aliter habere non possit. Omnes enim, qui aut revera sciunt, aut scire se putant, ob id aut sciunt, aut scire se existimant, quod rem ita se habere, uti diximus, aut revera aut suâ opinione cognoscunt, dicente Aristotele I. Post. c. II. Ex usu loquendi ergo scire rem aliquam est cognoscere causam, per quam res est, esse ejus rei causam, ita ut aliter se habere non possit. Ex quo infert Aristoteles, scientiam esse ex principiis veris, primis, immediatis, notioribus & prioribus, & quæ continent causam conclusionis.

Deinde scire etiam ex usu loquendi dicimur, cùm rem esse certò & indubitatò cognoscimus vel à posteriori & ex effectu, vel per inductionem, vel per causam remotam, licet causam proximam, propter quam res est, ignoremus. Quam Aristoteles d. l. c. X. dicit scientiam τꭣ ὅτι sive quòd res sit.

(2) Quod si ergo scientiæ conceptus & ratio propria consistit in cognitione causæ, per quam res est, quòd ita ejus causa sit, ut aliter se habere non possit; vel in cognitione, quòd res sit, per inductionem, vel ex effectu nobis notiori, vel per causam remotam, Theologia utique verè & propriè erit scientia. Ejus enim adminiculo Theologus cognoscit causas obtinendæ homini peccatori salutis æternæ (quæ præcipuum illius objectum est) ita esse ejus causas, ut aliter aut per causas alias, quàm illas, salus mortalium nemini obtingere possit aut obtingat. Principia etiam, ex quibus cognitionem hanc arcessit, sunt vera, prima, immediata, notiora & priora, continentque causam conclusionis, quæ est de adipiscenda salute æterna: v. g. salutis nostræ principia & causæ sunt gratia Dei, Christi meritum sive satisfactio pro peccatis, & fides, Christi meritum apprehendens nobisque approprians, quæ junctim sumtæ constituunt unam adæquatam & proximam salutis consequendæcausam, quæ est gratia Dei, in Christi merito, fide apprehenso nobisque appropriato fundata, ex quâ prius cognitâ talis conficitur demonstratio scientifica : Quicunque Christi meritum sive satisfactionem pro peccatis fide apprehendit, & Deum in cœlis per Christum sibi propitium habet, is consequitur ejus gratiâ remissionem peccatorum & salutem æternam. Atqui omnis credens in Christum apprehendit Christi meritum sive satisfactionem pro peccatis, & Deum in cœlis per Christum sibi propitium habet. Ergo omnis credens in Christum consequitur Dei gratiâ remissionem peccatorum & salutem æternam Ambæ præmissæ sunt Theologiæ principia vera, prima, immediata, notiora & priora conclusione, continentque causam conclusionis proximam, & quæ quæstioni propter quid planè satisfacit. Deinde quemadmodùm scientiæ aliæ nō semper cur res sit,ex principiis primis,immediatis,prioribus,& notioribus,& quæ conclusionis causa sunt, demonstrant, sed nonnunquam per inductionem, vel ex effectu, vel per causam remotam τὸ ὅτι saltem, sive quòd res sit, probant, ita & Theologia, ubi in rei causam penetrare non datur, à posteriori & ex effectu, vel saltem ex divina revelatione rem esse probat, certitudine sanè majori, quàm scientiæ aliæ rem esse à posteriori demonstrant. Si ergo unamquamque rem tùm simpliciter & propriè scire dicimur, cùm causam, per, vel propter quam res est, quòd ejus causa sit, quodque aliter se habere nequeat, cognoscimus, secundum quid verò & quòd res sit, cùm rem esse à posteriori cognoscimus, cur non in Theologia etiam scire simpliciter & propriè dicamur, cùm causam, per quam res est, quòd ejus causa sit, quodque se aliter habere nequeat, cognoscimus; secundum quid verò, & quòd res sit, cùm rem esse vel ex effectu, vel per causam remotam, vel ex nuda Dei testificatione sive revelatione, quæ demonstratione omni certior est, cognoscimus? (3) Quod si verò ad scientiam simpliciter & propriè requiras, ut causam, per quam res est, quòdque ejus causa sit, ut aliter se habere nequeat, evidenter & ex principiis per se notis cognoscamus, sicut communiter Auctores volunt (quamvis id nec usus loquendi nec ex eo depromta notio scientiæ præcisè exigere videatur) tùm dicendum erit, Theologiam non esse scientiam simpliciter, propriè & in rigore, sed, in sensu minus proprio & laxiori, prout scientia dicitur quælibet cognitio rei certa, ex principiis certis, immotis & quibus falsum subesse non potest, nata, sive principia evidentia & per se nota sint, sive aliunde certò & infallibiliter innotescant. Quamvis enim Theologia etiam conclusiones suas deducat ex principiis, quæ prima, immediata, priora ac notiora, & causæ conclusionis sunt; ut cùm v. g. Christum esse omnipotentem probat ex eo, quod sit Deus; ut plurimum tamen utitur ratione argumentandi inartificiali, ex revelatione sive testificatione divina, quæ inevidens, certa tamẽ & infallibilis est, desumta. Quin & cùm artificiali utitur argumentandi genere, & deducit conclusiones ex principiis primis, immediatis, prioribus, notioribus & causis conclusionum, argumenti alterum principium semper inevidens est, cujus probatio tandem ad divinam revelationem sive testificationem redit, in qua sistendum ultimò: v. g. in hoc syllogismo: Quicunque est verus Deus, ille est omnipotens. Atqui Christus est verus Deus. Ergo Christus est omnipotens; minor propositio est inevidens, cujus veritas nobis aliunde innotescere non potest, quàm ex divina revelatione, in quâ ultimò sistendum. Quod cum scientia, strictè & in rigore dictâ, stare non potest, stante quidem, quòd evidentia sit de ratione & conceptu scientiæ propriè & in rigore acceptæ.

VI. Neque difficultatem tollunt Thomistæ distinctione scientiæ, propriè & in rigore acceptæ, in subalternantem & subalternatam, superiùs adductâ. Faciamus enim, nostram Theologiam subalternari Theologiæ, quæ in Deo & beatis est, in nobis tamen, qui ejus principia nec ex beatorum nec ex Dei Theologia evidenter cognita habemus, sed propter divinam revelationem sive testificationem credimus, non magis rationem scientiæ, propriè dictæ, habere potest, quàm Optica vel Musica, quarum illa Geometriæ, hæc Arithmeticæ subalternatur, scientiæ rationem habet in eo, qui illarum principia evidenter cognita non habet, sed iisdem, obscurè cognitis, tantùm ob auctoritatem & testificationem Magistri assentitur. Nam ad subalternatam etiam scientiam requiritur, ut ejus principia sint evidenter cognita à sciente, licet non ex ipsis terminis, neque per demonstrationem, in ipsa institutam, tamen per demonstrationem, in scientia subalternante factam, & proinde cui scientia subalternata inest, ita ut scientiæ propriè dictæ rationem in eo habeat, ei oportet etiam inesse scientiam subalternantem, ex qua ejus principia lucem & evidentiam sortiuntur.

VII. Stante igitur, quòd evidentia principiorum sit de ratione scientiæ, fixum immotumque manet, Theologiam nostram non esse scientiam, strictè & in rigore, sed tantùm in significatu laxiori acceptâ pro habitu, quo ex principiis certis & immotis inferimus conclusiones certas, & quæ sint necessariæ veritatis. Quæ significatio ut inusitata non est, ita nec obscuram aut vitiosam efficiet Theologiæ definitionem, si aliquid, quo hoc generali significatu eam accipi declaretur, additum fuerit. Cùm enim voces pleræque æquivocæ sint, & plura significent, necessitas sæpè cogit, ut generis loco utamur voce, in se æquivocâ, modò aliquo addito aut præmisso æquivocatio sublata, & quo significatu eam accipiamus, declaratum fuerit. Nolumus tamen cum quopiam hac de re contendere, sed si quis malit in genere remotiori subsistere, & Theologiam per habitum intellectus definire, per nos licebit, modò aliquid differentiæ genericæ loco addatur, quo eam habitum cognoscendi esse, & in docendo occupari declaretur: aliàs definitio erit obscura, & in habitum religionis potiùs, quàm Theologiæ, quadrabit.


### V But since some sciences are theoretical and others practical, we reckon Theology among the practical sciences

V.

But since some sciences are theoretical and others practical, we reckon Theology among the practical sciences.

I. We said in the preceding chapter, thesis IV, that sciences are distinguished by Aristotle into theoretical and practical. Whether this is a distinction of a univocal genus into its species, or of an analogical term into its analogates, we shall not now inquire. For that is not the business of the present place and undertaking. This at least we advise: that a practical science in its concept imports more than a practical habit. For it imports a habit of knowing

and of deducing necessary and certain conclusions from certain and necessary principles, which is something formally speculative, and is appropriate to the sciences; the word 'practical', however, when added, designates the end toward which the science aims, and signifies that practical science does not stop at the mere speculation of conclusions, and their confirmation and defense, but tends further even toward practice and operation, though remotely and mediately, namely by means of the conclusions which it speculates upon, confirms, and defends, applied to the singular circumstances of actions, so that in this way practical science is the speculative science of conclusions that are by their own nature practical, or, which amounts to the same thing, a habit of knowing and of deducing and demonstrating from its own principles conclusions that are by their own nature practical. A practical habit, however, is said by common usage to be any habit which has practice or operation as its end, whether it is occupied with singulars, and, relying on experience or even on universal principles applied to the singular circumstances of actions, prescribes what is to be done here and now, or whether it is occupied with universal practical conclusions, to be deduced, confirmed, and defended from its own principles. There is at least this difference, that he who is occupied with singulars, and is supported either by experience or by universal principles indeed, but applied to the singular circumstances of actions, prescribes what it is fitting to do or not to do here and now, is practical in such a way that he is a proximate principle of operation, but does not deserve the name of science: since he does not demonstrate and defend, but takes as certain conclusions that have been demonstrated elsewhere, and applies them to practice or operation, which are by their own nature practical, and by them directs the faculty of operating proximately to action or practice. He, however, who is occupied with conclusions that are indeed by their own nature practical, but universal, and is occupied not so much with applying them to operation as with demonstrating and defending them from their own certain and immovable principles, he is indeed a principle of operation, but a remote one, in so far as he speculates, or demonstrates and defends conclusions that are by their own nature practical, which only later, when they are applied to the singular circumstances of actions, and what it is fitting to do or not to do here and now, to the will prescribe, they constitute the proximate principle of operation, as was said above. And this is called science by Aristotle, on account of the speculation and demonstration of universal conclusions; but it is practical science, because the conclusions which it speculates upon and demonstrates are practical.

II. Speculative and practical science therefore agree with one another, in that both are occupied with universal conclusions, to be confirmed from their own certain and immovable principles.

III. They differ, however, (1) in object. By the object of any science are understood either the things themselves, about which they are occupied, or the conclusions about the same, to be inferred and demonstrated from their own certain and immovable principles. If the things themselves come under the name of object, they will differ in that speculative science has for its object things which do not fall under our operation; of which kind is physical science; but practical science has for its object those which do fall under our operation, of which kind is moral science. But if conclusions come under that name, they will differ again, in that speculative science is occupied in demonstrating conclusions which are about things not falling under our operation, and which therefore prescribe nothing to be done or omitted, but are known only for the sake of truth; but practical science is occupied in demonstrating conclusions which are about things falling under our operation, and which prescribe something to be done or omitted, or some manner or means of acting.

(2) In acts: The acts of speculative science are simply speculative; but those of practical science are simply practical.

IV. Now the act of science is speculative, which by itself and by its own nature stops at the bare cognition of truth. It is practical, which by itself and by its own nature does not stop at the bare cognition of truth, but prescribes something to be done or omitted.

Aristotle distinguishes speculative and practical sciences, as also the speculative and practical intellect, sometimes by the end, sometimes by the object. By the end indeed in III De Anima c. X, text 49, where he speaks of the practical intellect: This, he says, differs from the contemplative intellect by its end; and II.

Met. c. 1. The end of speculative science is truth; but of practical, work. From the object, however, VI. Nic. c. 1. where he speaks of the speculative intellect, which contemplates necessary things; the practical, by which we know things that can be otherwise. But the matter finally returns to the same thing. For when he draws the distinction from the end, by the term end he does not understand the end formally and under the aspect of an end, but materially, and viewed under the aspect of the thing which is the end: in which way the end coincides with the object. For truth, in the knowledge of which speculative science is occupied, is that thing for the sake of which the science exists, and is also its object: and the work, which is said to be the end of practical science, is that thing for the sake of which it also exists, and is also its object.

IV. Finally, praxis is a certain operation, directed and prescribed by prior acts of the intellect. And for the most part, indeed, praxis is an act of a power other than the intellect, exercised according to the prior judgment of the practical intellect, though not always. For it happens sometimes that the intellect also operates at the command of the will, directed by its own prior practical judgment, and turns its thoughts, for example, to the meditation of the divine Word, or to the speculation of some thing: which meditation or speculation of its, in so far as it is exercised at the command of the will directed by the prior practical judgment of the intellect itself, is truly a certain praxis, and yet it is not an act of a power other than the intellect. Wherefore the definition, by Scotus in Prol. lib. 1. Sent. q. IV. handed down, that praxis is an act of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, born to be elicited conformably to right reason, in order that it may be a right act; is too narrow.

V. Having thus premised these things concerning the distinction of sciences into speculative and practical; and the practical and speculative acts pertaining thereto, and praxis itself in general, we return to the principal question concerning Theology, whether it is a speculative science? or a practical? concerning which authors vary remarkably.

(1) Thomas in 1. part. q. 1. a. IV. establishes that it is a science partly speculative, partly practical. His reason is: because practical science is about things operable by man: but Theology it deals partly with God and divine things, which do not fall under our operation; but partly indeed with human acts, which, elicited according to a prior practical judgment of the intellect, are a certain praxis, and therefore in that part in which it deals with a non-operable thing, namely God and divine things, it is speculative; but in the other part, in which it deals with a thing operable by man, namely human acts, it is practical. Because, however, it deals more principally with divine things than with human acts: for it deals with these only insofar as they order man to the perfect knowledge of God, in which eternal beatitude consists; it further concludes that it is more speculative than practical.

(2) Scotus, on the contrary, in Prol. in I. Sent. q. IV., teaches that Theology is per se and formally practical, not speculative, led by the reason that it is not precisely for the sake of speculation, but for the sake of praxis, according to that saying: The end of the law is love, Rom. XIII. 10. And: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like to this, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the Prophets, Matt. XXII. 37. seqq. To which he also refers that saying of Augustine on the praise of charity: He holds whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest in divine discourses, who preserves charity in his morals.

(3) Some, as reported by Durandus q. VI. Prol. a. III., having devised a certain third kind of habit, which they called affective, maintained that Theology is neither a speculative nor a practical habit, but an affective one, because its principal end is to excite the affection of love toward God. Which opinion is ascribed to Giles and Thomas of Strasbourg.

(4) Others think that the distinction of habits into theoretical and practical concerns only natural habits, and therefore it is in vain to ask about Theology, whether it is a theoretical or a practical habit: since it is not contained within the scope of natural habits.

VI. The third of these opinions has long been exploded, and not without cause. For to be an affective habit, and to excite the affection of love toward God, is something common to both a speculative and a practical habit. For one is excited to the affection of love towards God, both when one considers God speculatively according to His being and essential perfections, and when one considers His precepts concerning the holiness of life practically. But that which is common to both habits cannot be the constitutive element of a third habit essentially distinct from both. Nor does the fourth opinion, which is that of certain moderns, have any more probability. For practical and speculative are essential differences of both natural and supernatural habits. For habits derive their specific being from acts, just as acts do from objects. Moreover, it is essential to the acts of the intellect, both natural and supernatural, that by themselves and by the force of the known object they either stop at the cognition of truth and prescribe nothing to be done or omitted; or they do not stop there, but tend toward some operation, prescribing it or some mode or circumstance of it. If the former, they are speculative; if the latter, they are practical. Just as it is no less essential to supernatural acts than to natural ones that they be either speculative or practical, so it is also for habits: since a speculative habit, whether of the natural or supernatural order, is defined by this, that its acts are not directive of any operation, but stop ultimately in the cognition of truth; and a practical habit, on the contrary, is defined by this, that its acts do not stop ultimately in the cognition of truth, but are directive of some operation. Therefore, either Theology stops ultimately in the cognition of truth, or it does not stop ultimately in it, but tends toward operation. If the former, it will be a speculative habit; if the latter, a practical one, notwithstanding that it is a supernatural habit.

And from this it is also clear what should be thought of the first opinion, which is that of Thomas. The Thomists indeed do not agree in explaining it. For some wish Theology, according to Thomas, to be simply speculative, but practically in a certain respect; others, that it is formally speculative, but eminently practical; others again, that it is eminently speculative and practical. But in whatever way the mind of Thomas is finally explained, that which I was just saying remains unshaken, that practical and speculative are essential differences of the acts and habits of the intellect, and that they are opposed to each other contradictorily, so that they cannot fall together into one science in number. Either, therefore, Theology rests ultimately in the cognition of truth, or it does not rest in it ultimately, but tends of itself toward operation. If the former, it will be formally entirely speculative; if the latter, it will be formally entirely practical.

VII. The Thomists, intending to avoid the difficulty, do indeed distinguish between practical and speculative, as they are taken as opposite differences, dividing finite habits and those of a lower order; and as they meet in one notion of a higher order when imperfections are removed; but in vain. For first, that twofold acceptance of practical and speculative is invented without foundation. For practical, that is, directive of some operation; and speculative, that is, directive of no operation, are always opposite differences, and divide habits into opposite species.

Then, in explaining the notion of a higher order, into which the practical and speculative are said to meet, Thomas and the Thomists do not agree. For Thomas, who establishes it in divine light, without doubt understands by that term divine revelation; but Bannes and Nazarius understand God himself, who, insofar as he is the highest truth, has the nature of the speculable; but insofar as he is the highest goodness, directs toward operation. Whichever of these opinions you embrace, it will nevertheless remain fixed and firm, what we have said, that the speculative and practical are opposite differences, dividing sciences of both the lower and the higher order. For if you embrace the former explanation, which is Thomas's, it is certain that divine revelation, even though it may fall upon acts of knowing both practical and speculative, nevertheless does not bestow upon the acts and habits themselves either being practical or being speculative, but that the acts have this entirely from the fact that by their intrinsic nature they direct some operation, by prescribing that, or some mode of it, or some means or instrument, or they direct no operation, but rest in bare cognition, and that the habits obtain such a being from the acts. But if you embrace the other opinion, then it will indeed be true that Theology [considers] God not only as the highest good of man but also by reason of essence, of essential attributes and persons, and in the latter consideration God may have the nature of a speculable object; yet you will wrongly infer from thence that Theology is a science partly speculative, partly practical. For in other sciences also, which are of an inferior and natural order, and without doubt are practical, there is found in this manner the nature of the speculative and the practical. For the end of all practical habits has some being, in which the nature of the true and the speculable [resides]; and some goodness, in which the nature of the practical can be founded; and in every practical habit the knowledge of the end according to its being is not formally practical: since it is not actually and formally directive of any operation: e.g., in Moral Philosophy the knowledge by which we know that the happiness of man does not consist in honors, not in riches, not in the pleasures of the body, not in the habit of virtue, but in operation according to virtue; likewise the knowledge of the affections of the highest good, namely that it is desirable for its own sake, self-contented, etc., is not formally practical: since it is not actually and formally directive of any operation. Who, however, would therefore say that the science of Ethics is not in its entirety practical, but partly practical, partly speculative? For a practical science, therefore, it is not required that all its acts of knowing be formally practical, but it suffices if of themselves they are all ultimately ordered and referred to practice.

That you may understand this more correctly, it must be observed that a science is said to order its acts to practice or operation in two ways. In one way directly and formally, in so far as it infers formally practical conclusions from premises, and through them actually prescribes practice or operation. In another way indirectly and virtually, in so far as it delivers what is necessary to be known for practice or operation, not for the sake of bare knowledge, but for the sake of operation, so that from these pre-cognitions it may then deduce practical conclusions in convenient places. For a science to be simply and wholly practical, it is not required that all its acts, and all the conclusions which it infers from its principles, be formally practical, and actually direct some operation: otherwise no knowledge will be given, which deserves to be called simply and entirely practical; but it suffices that whatever it delivers, it does not deliver for the sake of bare cognition, but for the sake of practice or operation, even if some of these things are formally speculative, provided they relate to practice, at least as certain necessary prerequisites for it, and it delivers them in order to it. Thus the science of Ethics, as has been said, delivers many things which are not formally practical, but speculative: e.g., what it teaches concerning the nature and affections of the highest good, concerning the nature of virtues and vices, concerning the soul of man and its faculties, are formally speculative, not practical: since their consideration is occupied in delivering the quiddities, natures, and affections of things, namely of the highest good, of virtues, of vices, etc. Nevertheless, this notwithstanding, Ethics is a science simply and entirely practical: because it considers even those things which are formally and in themselves speculative, not for the sake of bare knowledge of the truth, but for the sake of practice or operation, at least as certain things necessary as prerequisites for operation: e.g., it treats of the nature of the highest good, so that once known it may subsequently be the reason for investigating and finding the means of attaining it; of the nature of virtues and vices, and their principles and causes, so that from those things known it may prescribe the method of acquiring virtue and fleeing vice: it treats of the faculties of the human soul, so that from those things known it may prescribe to each its own duties in acquiring virtue and attaining the highest good. To which Aristotle refers in II Nicom. c. II, saying: We do not inquire what virtue is, that we may know, but that we may become good.

IIX. There remains therefore the second opinion, which is that of Scotus, that Theology is a merely practical science, not partly practical, partly speculative: which we consider to be preferred to all others and entirely agreeable to the truth. But since this question, whether Theology is a practical science or a speculative one, depends chiefly upon the end of Theology and its principles and causes of attainment, we shall treat of these before we proceed to a fuller declaration and confirmation of it.

Latin:

V.

Cùm verò scientiæ aliæ theoreticæ, aliæ practicæ sint, Theologiam accensemus scientiis practicis.

I. Scientias distingui ab Aristotele in theoreticas & practicas, diximus in cap. præced. thes. IV. quæ sitne distinctio generis univoci in suas species? an analogi in sua analogata? nunc non disquiremus. Non enim id præsentis loci & instituti est. Hoc saltem monemus: Scientiam practicam in suo conceptu plus importare, quàm habitum practicum. Importat enim habitum cognoscendi

& deducendi conclusiones necessarias & certas ex principiis certis & necessariis, quod formaliter speculativum quid est, & scientiis convenit; vox, practica, autem adjecta designat finem, ad quem scientia collineat, & significat, scientiam practicam non sistere in nuda conclusionum speculatione, illarumque confirmatione & defensione, sed tendere longiùs etiam ad praxin & operationem, remotè tamen & mediatè, mediantibus scilicet conclusionibus, quas speculatur, confirmat & defendit, ad actionum circumstantias singulares applicatis, ut ita scientia practica sit scientia speculativa conclusionum, suâpte naturâ practicarum, sive, quod eodem redit, habitus cognoscendi & ex suis principiis deducendi ac demonstrandi conclusiones, suâpte naturâ practicas. Habitus practicus autem ex usu loquendi dicitur quilibet habitus, qui pro fine habet praxin seu operationem, sive in singularibus is versetur, & experientiâ, vel etiam principiis universalibus, ad singulares actionum circumstantias applicatis, nixus quæ hic & nunc agenda sint, præscribat, sive in conclusionibus practicis universalibus, ex suis principiis deducendis, confirmandis, & defendendis occupetur. Hoc saltem inter est discriminis, quòd qui versatur in singularibus, & vel experientiâ vel principiis universalibus quidem, sed ad singulares actionum circumstantias applicatis, suffultus, quid hic & nunc agere aut non agere conveniat, præscribit, ita est practicus, ut sit principium operationis propinquum, scientiæ autem nomen non mereatur: cùm non demonstret & defendat, sed alibi demonstratas velut certas sumat & ad praxin sive operationem conferat conclusiones, suâpte naturâ practicas, iisque facultatem operandi proximè ad actionem sive praxin dirigat. Qui autem in conclusionibus, suâpte naturâ quidem practicis, sed universalibus, iisque non tam ad operationem conferendis, quàm ex suis principiis certis & immotis demonstrandis ac defendendis occupatur, is principium operationis quidē est, sed remotum, in quantū scilicet speculatur, sive demonstrat & defendit conclusiones, suâpte naturâ practicas, quæ posteà demū, cùm ad singulares actionū circumstantias applicantur, & quid hîc & nunc agere aut non agere conveniat, voluntati præscribunt, operationis principium propinquum constituunt, ut superius dictum. Atque hæc dicitur Aristoteli scientia, ob speculationem ac demonstrationem conclusionum universalium; sed scientia practica, quòd conclusiones, quas speculatur & demonstrat, practicæ sint.

II. Conveniunt ergo inter se scientia speculativa & practica, quòd utraque occupatur in conclusionibus universalibus, ex suis certis & immotis principiis confirmandis.

III. Differunt verò, (1) objecto. Per objectum autem cujusque scientiæ intelliguntur vel ipsæ res, circa quas occupantur, vel conclusiones de iisdem, ex suis principiis certis & immotis inferendæ ac demonstrandæ. Si ipsæ res objecti nomine veniant, different, quòd speculativa scientia pro objecto habet res, quæ sub nostram operationem non cadunt; cujusmodi est scientia Physica; practica verò pro objecto habet quæ cadunt sub nostram operationem, cujusmodi est scientia moralis. Sin conclusiones ejus nomine veniant, different rursú, quod speculativa scientia occupetur in demonstrandis conclusionibus, quæ sunt de rebus, sub nostram operationem non cadentibus, & quæ proinde nihil agendum aut omittendum præscribunt, sed tantum veritatis causâ cognoscuntur; practica verò occupetur in demonstrandis conclusionibus, quæ sunt de rebus, sub nostram operationem cadentibus, & quæ aliquid agendum vel omittendum, vel aliquem agendi modum aut medium præscribunt.

(2) Actibus: Scientiæ speculativæ actus simpliciter speculativi; practicæ autem actus simpliciter practici sunt.

IV. Est autem actus scientiæ speculativus, qui per se & naturâ suâ in nuda veritatis cognitione sistit. Practicus est, qui per se & naturâ suâ non sistit in cognitione veritatis nuda, sed præscribit aliquid agendum aut omittendum.

Aristoteles distinguit scientias speculativas & practicas, ut & intellectum speculativum & practicum modò ex fine, modò ex objecto. Ex fine quidem III. de Anima c. X. text. 49. ubi de intellectu practico: Hic, inquit, fine ab intellectu contemplativo differt; & II.

Met. c. 1. Scientia speculativa finis est veritas; practica autem opus. Ex objecto autem VI. Nic. c. 1. ubi speculativum intellectum dicit, qui contemplatur necessaria; practicum, quo cognoscimus, quæ aliter se habere possunt. Sed res redit tandem eodem. Quando enim ex fine accersit distinctionem, appellatione finis non intelligit finem formaliter & sub ratione finis, sed materialiter, & sub ratione rei, quæ finis est, spectatum: quomodo finis cum objecto coincidit. Veritas enim, in cujus cognitione scientia speculativa occupatur, est res illa, cujus gratiâ scientia est, & est etiam ejus objectum: & opus, quòd practicæ scientiæ finis dicitur, est res illa, cujus gratiâ & ipsa est, & est etiam objectum illius.

IV. Praxis denique est operatio quædam, præviis actibus intellectus directa & præscripta. Et utplurimùm quidem praxis est actus alterius potentiæ, quàm intellectus, ad prævium judicium intellectus practici exercitus, non tamen semper. Contingit enim quandoque, ut etiam intellectus ad imperium voluntatis, prævio suomet judicio practico directæ, operetur, & cogitationes v. g. ad meditationem Verbi divini, vel ad speculationem alicujus rei convertat: quæ ejus meditatio aut speculatio, in quantum ad imperium voluntatis prævio ipsiusmet intellectus judicio practico directæ exercetur, verè est praxis quædam, nec tamen alterius potentiæ actus est, quàm intellectus. Quamobrem definitio, à Scoto in Prol. lib. 1. Sent. q. IV. tradita, quòd praxis sit actus alterius potentiæ, quàm intellectus, naturaliter posterior intellectione, natus elici conformiter rationi rectæ, ad hoc, ut sit actus rectus; justo angustior est.

V. His de distinctione scientiarum in speculativas & practicas; & eò pertinentibus actibus practicis ac speculativis, ipsáque praxi ita ingenere præmissis, ad quæstionem principalem de Theologia, sitne scientia speculativa? an practica? redimus, de qua mirè variant Autores.

(1) Thomas in 1. part. q. 1. a. IV. statuit, eam esse scientiam speculativam partim, partim practicam. Ratio ejus est: quia scientia practica est de rebus operabilibus ab homine: Theologia autem agit partim de Deo rebusque divinis, quæ sub nostram operationem non cadunt; partim verò de actibus humanis, qui ad prævium judicium practicum intellectûs eliciti, sunt praxis quædam, & proinde eâ parte, quâ agit de re non operabili, Deo scilicet rebusque divinis, speculativa; alterâ autem parte, quâ agit de re operabili ab homine, nempe de actibus humanis, practica est. Quia tamen principalius agit de rebus divinis, quàm de actibus humanis: de his enim agit tantùm, quatenus hominem ad perfectam Dei cognitionem, in qua æterna beatitudo consistit, ordinant; statuit porro, illam esse magis speculativam, quàm practicam.

(2) Scotus contrà in Prol. in I. Sent. q. IV. docet, Theologiam esse per se & formaliter practicam, non speculativam, eâ ductus ratione, quòd non præcisè sit propter speculationem, sed propter praxin, juxta illud: Finis legis est dilectio, Rom. XIII. 10. Et: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota mente tua. Hoc est primum & magnum præceptum. Secundum autem est simile huic, Diliges proximum tuum, sicut te ipsum. In his duobus mandatis tota lex & Prophetæ pendent, Matth. XXII. 37. seqq. Quò refert & illud Augustini de laude charitatis: Ille tenet, quicquid latet, & quicquid patet in divinis sermonibus, qui charitatem servat in moribus.

(3) Quidam, referente Durando q. VI. Prol. a. III. excogitato tertio quodam habituum genere, quod affectivum dixêre, statuerunt, Theologiam neque speculativum, neque practicum habitum esse, sed affectivum, quòd ejus præcipuus finis sit excitare affectum amoris erga Deum. Quæ opinio adscribitur Ægidio & Thomæ Argentinensi.

(4) Alii existimant, distinctionem habituum in theoreticos & practicos concernere solos habitus naturales, & proptereà frustra de Theologia, sitne theoreticus, an practicus habitus? quæri: cùm habituum naturalium ambitu non contineatur.

VI. Harum opinionum tertia explosa est dudum, nec præter causam. Nam esse habitum affectivum, & excitare affectum amoris erga Deum est commune quid habitui speculativo & practico. Excitatur enim ad affectum amoris erga Deum, cùm qui Deum secundum suum esse & perfectiones essentiales speculative; tùm qui ejus præcepta de sanctimonia vitæ practicè considerat. Quod autem habitui utrique commune est, id non potest esse constitutivum tertii cujusdam & ab utroque essentialiter distincti habitus. Neque plus probabilitatis habet opinio quarta, quæ quorundam recentiorum est. Nam practicum & speculativum sunt differentiæ essentiales cùm naturalium tùm supernaturalium habituum. Habitus enim sortiuntur suum esse specificum ab actibus, sicut actus ab objectis. Est autem essentiale actibus intellectus cùm naturalibus tùm supernaturalibus, ut per se & vi objecti cogniti vel sistant in cognitione veritatis, nec quicquam agendum aut omittendum præscribant; vel non sistant in ea, sed ad aliquam operationem tendant, præscribendo illam, vel aliquem ejus modum aut circumstantiam. Si illud? speculativi; sin hoc? practici sunt. Quemadmodùm auté actibus supernaturalibus non minus, quám naturalibus essentiale est, ut vel speculativi vel practici sint, ita & habitibus: cùm habitus speculativus, sive naturalis sive supernaturalis ordinis is sit, per hoc definiatur, quòd ejus actus non sint alicujus operationis directivi, sed in veritatis cognitione ultimò sistant; & practicus contrà per hoc, quòd ejus actus non sistant ultimò in cognitione veritatis, sed operationis cujusdam directivi sint. Aut ergo Theologia sistit in cognitione veritatis ultimò, aut non sistit in ea ultimò, sed tendit ad operationem. Si prius? speculativus; Sin posterius? practicus habitus erit, non obstante, quod habitus supernaturalis sit.

Atque hinc patet etiam, quid de opinione prima, quæ Thomæ est, sentiendum sit. Thomistæ quidem in ea explicanda non conveniunt. Quidam enim volunt, Theologiam, juxta Thomam, esse simpliciter speculativam, secundum quid verò practicam: alii, eam esse formaliter speculativam, eminenter verò practicam: rursum alii esse eminenter speculativam & practicam. Verùm quocunque tandem modo mens Thomæ explicetur, inconcussum tamen manet, quod modò dicebamus, practicum & speculativum esse differentias actuum & habituum intellectus essentiales, & opponi inter se contradictoriè, ut in unam numero scientiam simul cadere non possint. Vel ergo Theologia sistit ultimò in cognitione veritatis, vel non sistit in ea ultimò, sed tendit per se ad operationem. Si illud? formaliter tota speculativa; Sin hoc? formaliter tota practica erit.

VII. Thomistæ, difficultatem declinaturi, distinguunt quidem inter practicum & speculativum, prout accipiuntur ut differentiæ oppositæ, dividentes habitus finitos & inferioris ordinis; & prout remotis imperfectionibus in unam altioris ordinis rationem conveniunt; sed frustra. Primù enim duplex illa practici & speculativi acceptio conficta est absq; fundamento. Practicū enim h. e. operationis cujusdam directivum; & speculativum, h. e. nullius operationis directivum, semper sunt differentiæ oppositæ, & dividunt habitus in species oppositas.

Deinde in explicanda ratione altioris ordinis, in quam practicum & speculativum convenire dicuntur, Thomas & Thomistæ non conveniunt. Thomas enim, qui eam in lumine divino constituit, dubio procul ejus appellatione intelligit divinam revelationem; Bannes autem & Nazarius intelligunt Deum ipsum, qui in quantum est summa veritas, rationem speculabilis habeat; in quantum verò est summa bonitas, ad operationem dirigat. Utram verò ex his opinionem amplectaris, manebit nihilominus fixum & firmum, quod diximus, speculativum & practicum esse differentias oppositas, dividentes scientias cùm inferioris tum superioris ordinis. Si enim priorem, quæ Thomæ est, explicationem amplectaris, certum est, divinam revelationem, ut ut cadat super actus cognoscendi cùm practicos, tùm speculativos, ipsis actibus tamen & habitibus nec esse practicum, nec esse speculativum largiri, sed hoc totum habere actus ex eo, quòd suâ intrinsecâ naturâ aliquam operationem dirigant, illam, ejusve aliquem modum, aut aliquod medium instrumentumve præscribendo, vel nullam dirigant operationem, sed in cognitione nuda sistant, habitus autem sortiri tale esse ex actibus. Sin amplectaris opinionem alteram, tùm verum quidem erit, quòd Deum Theologia non tantùm ut hominis bonum summum sed etiam ratione essentiæ, attributorum essentialium & personarum consideret, & in consideratione posteriori Deus rationem objecti speculabilis habeat; malè tamen inde colliges, Theologiam esse scientiam partim speculativam, partim practicam. Nam in aliis etiam scientiis, quæ inferioris & naturalis ordinis, & citra dubium practicæ sunt, invenitur hunc in modum ratio speculativi & practici. Finis enim omnium habituum practicorum habet aliquod esse, in quo ratio veri & speculabilis; & aliquam bonitatem, in qua ratio practici fundari potest; & in omni habitu practico cognitio finis secundum suum esse non est formaliter practica: cùm actu & formaliter non sit directiva alicujus operationis: v. g. in Philosophia Morali cognitio, quâ cognoscimus, hominis beatitudinem non consistere in honoribus, non in divitiis, non in voluptatibus corporis, non in habitu virtutis, sed in operatione secundum virtutem; item cognitio affectionum summi boni, quòd scilicet sit propter se expetibile, seipso contentum &c. formaliter practica non est: cùm actu & formaliter non sit alicujus operationis directiva. Quis autem proptereà dixerit, scientiam Ethicam non esse se totâ practicam, sed partim practicam, partim speculativam? Ad scientiã practicam ergo non requiritur, ut omnes ejus actus cognoscendi sint formaliter practici, sed sufficit, si per se omnes ultimò ad praxin ordinentur & referantur.

Quod ut rectius intelligas, observandum est, duobus modis dici scientiam aliquam actus suos adpraxin sive operationem ordinare. Uno modo directè & formaliter, in quantum conclusiones formaliter practicas ex præmissis infert, & per eas praxin sive operationem actu præscribit. Altero modo indirectè & virtualiter, in quantum, quæ ad praxin sive operationem cognitu necessaria sunt, tradit, non nudæ cognitionis causâ, sed propter operationem, ita ut ex iis præcognitis deinde conclusiones practicas locis convenientibus deducat. Ut scientia simpliciter & tota practica sit, non requiritur, ut omnes ejus actus, omnesque conclusiones, quas ex suis principiis infert, formaliter practicæ sint, & actu operationem aliquam dirigant: alias enim nulla dabitur scientia, quæ simpliciter & tota practica dici mereatur; sed sufficit, quòd quæcunq; tradit, non tradat nudæ cognitionis causâ, sed propter praxin sive operationé, licet eorum quædam formaliter speculativa sint, modò ad praxin, minimùm ut quædam ejus necessaria præcognita, se habeant, eaque in ordine ad illam tradat. Sic scientia Ethica, uti dictum, tradit multa, quæ formaliter practica non sunt, sed speculativa: v. g. quæ de natura & affectionibus summi boni, de natura virtutum & vitiorum, de anima hominis ejusque facultatibus docet, formaliter speculativa sunt, non practica: cùm eorum consideratio occupetur in tradendis rerum, summi boni scilicet, virtutum, vitiorum &c. quidditatibus, naturis, & affectionibus.
