Est tamen, hoc non obstante, Ethica scientia simpliciter & tota practica: quia illa etiam, quæ formaliter & secundum se speculativa sunt, non propter nudam veritatis cognitionem considerat, sed propter praxin sive operationem, saltem ut quædã necessaria ad operationem præcognita: v. g. De natura summi boni agit, ut cognita sibi deinceps sit ratio investigandi & inveniendi ejus consequendi media; de natura virtutum & vitiorum, illorumque principiis & causis, ut ex illis cognitis præscribat rationem comparandæ virtutis, & vitii fugiendi: de facultatibus animæ hominis agit, ut ex iis cognitis sua cuique munia in acquirenda virtute consequendoque summo bono præscribat. Quò respicit Aristoteles II. Nicom. c. II. Non, inquiens, quid sit virtus, quærimus, ut sciamus, sed ut boni efficiamur.

IIX. Superest ergo secunda, quæ Scoti est, sententia, quòd Theologia sit scientia merè practica, non partim practica, partim speculativa: quam cæteris omnibus præferendam veritatique prorsus consentaneam ducimus. Cum verò quæstio hæc, sitne Theologia scientia practica? an speculativa? potissimùm ex Theologiæ fine ejusque consequendi principiis & causis dependeat, de his agemus priùs, quàm ad uberiorem ejus declarationem & confirmationem progrediamur.


### V. The end of Theology is one internal, another external

V.

The end of Theology is one internal, another external.

VI.

The internal [end] is constituted by the acts of knowing, for the eliciting of which around its object it elevates and facilitates the intellect.

I. Since the end is that for the sake of which something is or exists, the acts of Theology are rightly constituted as its end. For just as every habit is for the sake of its acts, so also is Theology. The acts, however, for the sake of which Theology exists, and for the eliciting of which it elevates the intellect, are acts of knowing the object, not in any way whatsoever, but scientifically, or so fully and perfectly that we may also explain it to others, deduce and confirm conclusions from its certain and immovable principles, and defend them against those who dissent. For in this, as we saw above from Augustine, Theology differs from faith, that the latter is occupied with the simple knowledge and assent of things to be believed; the former with the scientific knowledge of the same, by which we may explain, confirm, and defend them to others.

II. We call these acts the internal end of Theology: because Theology attains them by itself, and the Theologian, by the power of the science existing within him, always has them in his own power.

III. Although, however, this end is common to all sciences: For it is the duty of all to explain, confirm, and defend those things which fall under their consideration; yet it is not equally common to all that they should stop ultimately in the acts of knowing by which each explains, confirms, and defends its own object, but this is proper to speculative sciences, of which, therefore, there is no other end besides the acts of knowing, or besides the knowledge, confirmation, and defense of truth. On the contrary, however, it is proper to practical sciences that they do not stop ultimately in the acts of knowing by which they explain, confirm, and defend the truth subject to them, but tend further toward practice or operation: of which, therefore, besides the knowledge of truth, there is another end, which is either a certain operation, or some thing to be effected or obtained through operation. And Theology is also of the census of these. For indeed, that besides the knowledge of truth, it has as its end practice or a certain operation, and is therefore practical, no one will easily deny. Whether, however, it is a merely practical science, as this is called into doubt, so it must be judged primarily from the end toward which, besides the knowledge of truth, it tends.

VII.

Since, however, the Theology which teaches refers everything to this, that sinful men may be reconciled to God through faith in Christ, and once reconciled may thereafter abstain from sins and live holily, so that persevering in faith and holiness of life they may enjoy God as their infinitely perfect and supreme good, both here for the state of the present life and in the other life fully and perfectly; the thing itself demands that we constitute these as its external end.

I. We are dealing here with the Theology of men who are Wayfarers after the fall. Before the fall, just as there was no sin, so there was no need for the reconciliation of man with God through faith in Christ. For the reconciliation of man with God presupposes that God is offended by the sins of men, and where there is no offense, there reconciliation finds no place. Before the fall, therefore, man always had God as propitious and favorable, and if he had persisted in his original state, that is, in his concreated righteousness and holiness, he would have finally attained blessedness, established in the full enjoyment of God, as a gratuitous reward for his obedience.

II. Of those things which are contained in the end, now outlined in a rough manner, nothing is placed in the hand and power of the Theologian, so that he might be able to attain it by himself and by the force of the theological habit whenever he wishes. Not faith in Christ, which is a gift of God: nor the reconciliation of sinful man with God, which is the effect of faith in Christ: nor the holiness of life, which depends on faith and charity and on the actual aids of grace: nor finally the full enjoyment of God, which is a good of the other life, where there will be no place for our Theology. Which

All of which, therefore, are rightly comprehended within the scope of an external end.

III. Moreover, as is evident, several partial ends are contained within it. And indeed, there are contained within it I. the end of which, and the end for which; II. The end of which, both objective and formal; and III. The formal end, both intermediate and ultimate: concerning which it is necessary to treat a little more distinctly.

Latin:

V.

Finis Theologiæ alius internus, alius externus est.

VI.

Internum constituunt actus cognoscendi, ad quos circà objectum suum eliciendos intellectum elevat & facilitat.

I. Cum finis sit id, cujus gratiâ aliquid est aut sit, Theologiæ finis rectè constituuntur ejus actus. Quemadmodùm enim omnis habitus est propter suos actus, ita & Theologia. Actus autem, quorum gratiâ Theologia est, & ad quos eliciendos intellectum elevat, sunt actus cognoscendi objectum, non utcunque, sed scientificè, sive ita plenè & perfectè, ut aliis etiam id explicare, conclusiones ex suis principiis certis & immotis deducere ac confirmare, & contra dissentientes defendere possimus. In hoc enim, ut supra ex Augustino vidimus, differt Theologia à fide, quòd hæc in simplici credendorum cognitione & assensu; illa in eorundem cognitione scientifica, quâ illa aliis explicare, confirmare & defendere possimus, occupetur.

II. Actus hosce dicimus Theologiæ finem internum: quia Theologia eos per se attingit, & Theologus, vi scientiæ sibi inexistentis illos semper in sua potestate habet.

III. Qamvis verò finis hic cōmunis sit scientiis omnibus: Omnium enim munus est explicare, confirmare & defendere, quæ sub illarum considerationem cadunt; non tamen æquè omnibus commune est, ut in actibus cognoscendi, quibus suum quæque objectum explicat, confirmat & defendit, ultimò sistant, sed hoc speculativarum scientiarum proprium est, quarum proinde præter actus cognoscendi, sive præter cognitionem, confirmationem & defensionem veritatis alius nullus finis est. Contrà autem practicarum proprium est, ut in actibus cognoscendi, quibus veritatem sibi subjectam explicant, confirmant & defendunt, non sistant ultimò, sed longiùs ad praxin sive operationem tendant: quarum proinde, præter cognitionem veritatis, alius finis est, qui vel operatio quædam est, vel res aliqua, per operationem efficienda aut obtinenda. Et harum ex censu etiam Theologia est. Quin enim, præter cognitionem veritatis, pro fine habeat praxin sive operationem quandam, & proinde practica sit, nemo facilè negaverit. Utrum autem merè practica scientia sit, id uti in dubium vocatur, ita potissimùm ex fine, ad quem, præter veritatis cognitionem, tendit, dignoscendum est.

VII.

Cùm verò Theologia, quæ docet, eò omnia referat, ut homines peccatores Deo per fidem in Christum reconcilientur, & reconciliati deinceps à peccatis abstineant & sanctè vivant, quò in fide & sanctimonia vitæ perseverantes Deo velut suo infinitè perfecto & summo bono, cùm hîc pro statu vitæ præsentis, tùm in vita altera plenè & perfectè fruantur; in his ut ejus finem externum constituamus, res ipsa exigit.

I. Agimus hîc de Theologia hominum Viatorum post lapsum. Ante lapsum ut peccatum non erat, ita nec reconciliatione hominis per fidem in Christum cum Deo opus erat. Reconciliatio enim hominis cum Deo præsupponit, Deum esse hominum peccatis offensum, & ubi offensio nulla est, ibi nec reconciliatio locum invenit. Ante lapsum igitur homo Deum semper habuit propitium & faventem, & si in primævo suo statu, h. e. in concreata justitia & sanctitate perstitisset, beatitudinem tandem, in plena Dei fruitione constitutam, in gratuitum suæ obedientiæ præmium consecutus esset.

II. Quæ in fine, jam rudi Minerva delineato, continentur, eorum nihil in Theologi manu & potestate positum est, ut per se & vi habitus Theologici id, quandocunque vult, consequi possit. Non fides in Christum, quæ Dei donum est: nec reconciliatio hominis peccatoris cum Deo, quæ fidei in Christum effectus est: neque sanctimonia vitæ, quæ à fide & charitate, & ab auxiliis gratiæ actualibus dependet: nec denique fruitio Dei plena, quæ alterius vitæ, ubi Theologiæ nostræ locus non erit, bonum est. Quæ

Quæ proinde omnia finis externi ambitu rectè comprehenduntur.

III. Continentur autem eo, uti patet, plures partiales fines. Et quidem continentur eo I. finis cujus, & finis cui; II. Finis cujus cùm objectivus, tùm formalis; & III. Finis formalis cùm intermedius, tùm ultimus: de quibus paulò distinctiùs agendum venit.


### IIX. The end of which of theology, and that the objective one, is God, infinitely…

IIX.

The end of which of theology, and that the objective one, is God, infinitely perfect and supremely good.

I. That there is one objective end for man and theology, and that it is God alone, the best and greatest, inasmuch as He alone perfectly contains in Himself every reason for the good by which the appetite of man is fulfilled and satisfied; that all the effort of theology also aims at this, that it may teach by what reason it is necessary to arrive at the enjoyment of Him, as the supreme good, was shown at greater length in the preceding chapter, in which we treated of Natural Theology, thesis XI and following. For, as far as the objective end is concerned, the account of Revealed and Natural Theology is the same. To which I refer the reader.

II. Augustine teaches the same thing when, in book 1 of De Doctrina Christiana, chapter III, he distinguishes between things, that some are to be enjoyed, others to be used; the former make us blessed, but by the latter we are helped and, as it were, supported while tending toward blessedness, so that we may be able to arrive at those things which make us blessed and to cling to them. For among the things to be enjoyed, ibid. chapter V, he counts only one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who therefore is the only thing that makes us blessed, and is the objective end of man and theology.

IX.

The formal end is again twofold: ultimate and intermediate.

X.

Each consists in a certain operation of the soul concerning God, as the objective end and supreme good, the former indeed in the operation by which we act for the state of another; the latter in the operation by which we obtain and enjoy him for the state of this life. I. We distinguish the formal end only into ultimate and intermediate. For the objective end is but one, namely God, toward whom the will of man in whom the happiness and blessedness of both lives resides. II. We also establish both in the operation of the soul concerning God, by which we both obtain and enjoy him. For God is the end of man and of Theology, to be obtained by an operation according to the prescription of Theology, which does not satisfy the appetite unless we have obtained and are enjoying him. Therefore, both formal ends of Theology embrace a double operation of the soul: one, by which we obtain God as the objective end and highest good; the other, by which we enjoy the same.

XI.

The ultimate consists both in the intuitive and clear knowledge of God, and in the love of God, known intuitively or clearly. By the former we obtain him; by the latter we enjoy the same. I. The intuitive or clear knowledge of God is commonly called the beatific vision: a vision indeed, by metaphorical expression, because by it we shall know God as distinctly and clearly as we know a thing which we see with our eyes; beatific, however, because it is the formal reason by which we are constituted blessed, according to that of Christ: BLESSED are the pure in heart, for they shall SEE GOD, Matt. V. 8. To which also pertain the passages 1 John III. 2. We know that if he shall appear (what we shall be) we shall be like him (God), for WE SHALL SEE HIM, AS HE IS, and 1 Cor. XIII. 12. We see now through a glass in a riddle, but then face to face: now I know in part; but then I shall know, even as I am known. II. Love, by which we cleave to God for his own sake, follows vision or the intuitive knowledge of God by itself, and is in order posterior to it. For it cannot happen that God, in whom the reason of all good perfectly and without defect is contained, the intellect intuitively and clearly knows, nor yet is the will enticed into love of it, by which it might adhere to it thus known for its own sake. III. By that we are said to possess God, as our highest good; because through it God is apprehended by the intellect, and is rendered present to us and is intimately united. By this we are said to enjoy the same: since to enjoy some thing, as Augustine teaches in book 1 of the City of God, chapter 111, is nothing other than to adhere to it by love for its own sake.

Latin:

IIX.

THeologiæ finis cujus, isque objectivus, est Deus infinitè perfectus & summè bonus.

I. Hominis & Theologiæ esse unum finem objectivum, eumque esse solum Deum optimum maximum, utpote qui solus in se perfectè continet omnem rationem boni, quâ hominis appetitus expletur & satiatur; Theologiæ operam etiam eò omnem collineare, ut quâ ratione ad ejus, velut boni summi, fruitionem pervenire oporteat, doceat, in capite præcedente, in quo de Theologia Naturali egimus, th. XI. & seqq. ostensum est pluribus. Est enim, quod ad finem objectivum attinet, Theologiæ Revelatæ & Naturalis par ratio. Quò lectorem remitto.

II. Idem docet Augustinus, quando lib. 1. de D. C. c. III. distinguit inter res, quòd aliis fruendum, aliis utendum sit, quarum ille beatos nos faciant, his verò tendentes ad beatitudinem adjuvemur quasi & adminiculemur, ut ad illas, quæ beatos faciunt, pervenire atque his inhærere possimus. In rebus fruendis enim ibid. c. V. numerat unum solum Deum, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, qui proinde solus res illa, quæ beatos nos facit, finisque hominis & Theologiæ objectivus est.

IX.

FOrmalis finis rursum duplex est: ultimus, & intermedius.

X.

UTerque consistit in quadam animæ operatione circa Deum, velut finem objectivum & bonum summum, ille quidem in operatione, quâ pro statu alterius; hic in operatione, quâ pro statu hujus vitæ eo potimur & fruimur. I. Finem formalem solum distinguimus in ultimum & intermemedium. Objectivum enim non nisi unus est, nempe Deus, in quem velut in suum bonum perfectum & summum voluntas hominis cùm in hac, tùm in altera vita fertur, & in quo vitæ utriusque felicitas & beatitudo residet. II. Utrumque etiam constituimus in operatione animæ circa Deum, quâ eo & potimur & fruimur. Est enim Deus hominis & Theologiæ finis, operatione, ex Theologiæ præscripto, obtinendus, qui appetitum non satiat, nisi cùm eo potiti sumus & fruimur. Complectitur ergo Theologiæ finis formalis uterque operationem animæ duplicem: Unam, quâ potimur Deo, velut fine objectivo & bono summo; alteram, quâ eodem fruimur.

XI.

Ultimus consistit cùm in cognitione Dei intuitiva & clara, tùm in amore Dei, intuitivè sive clarè cogniti. Illâ potimur eo; hâc eodem fruimur. I. Cognitio Dei intuitiva sive clara dicitur vulgo visio beatifica: Visio quidem, locutione metaphoricâ, quòd eâ tam distinctè & clarè Deum cognituri simus, quàm distinctè & clarè cognoscimus rem, quam oculis videmus; beatifica autem, quòd sit formalis ratio, quâ constituimur beati, juxta illud Christi: BEATI mundi corde, quoniam ipsi DEUM VIDEBUNT, Matth. V. 8. Quò pertinent & loca 1. Joh. III. 2. Scimus, quòd si aparuerit (quod futuri sumus) similes ei (Deo) erimus, quoniam VIDEBIMUS EUM, SICUTI EST, & 1. Cor. XIII. 12. Cernimus nunc per speculum in anigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte; tunc verò cognoscam, quemadmodum cognitus sum. II. Amor, quo Deo propter se inhæremus, sequitur visionem sive intuitivam Dei cognitionem per se, estque eâ ordine posterior. Fieri enim non potest, ut Deum, in quo ratio boni omnis perfectè & fine defectu continetur, intellectus intuitivè & clarè cognoscat, nec tamen voluntas in ejus amorem, quo ei sic cognito inhæreat propter se, alliciatur. III. Illâ dicimur potiri Deo, velut nostro summo bono; quia per illam Deus apprehenditur ab intellectu, nobisque præsens redditur uniturq; intimè. Hoc dicimur eodem frui: cùm frui aliquâ re, docente Augustino lib. 1. de D. C. c. 111. nihil aliud sit, quàm amore ei inhærere propter seipsam.


### XII. The intermediate end of theology consists also in the twofold operation of the…

XII.

The intermediate end of theology consists also in the twofold operation of the soul: one of faith, by which we are borne toward Christ the Mediator, and by trust fixed in him as the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God, we obtain the remission of sins before God, and are received into grace; the other of love, by which we adhere to the same, rendered propitious to us through faith, for his own sake: by the former we likewise possess God, for the state of this life, we who had been turned away and separated from him by sins; by the latter we enjoy the same.

I. That the operation by which we possess God, as our highest good, for the state of this life, consists in the already mentioned operation of faith, is easily evident. For by that operation sinful men are reconciled to God, and having obtained the remission of sins, they thereafter have God intimately present to them by his grace, propitious and favorable, by that they possess God, as their infinitely perfect and highest good, for the state indeed of this life. But by the operation of faith, by which they are borne toward Christ the Mediator, and by trust fixed in him, as the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God, sinful men are reconciled to God, and having obtained the remission of sins, they thereafter have God intimately present to them by his grace, propitious and favorable. The reason for the major proposition is: because for the state of this life, in which we know God only abstractively, we do not possess him otherwise than by our reconciliation with him, by which, his anger against sin being appeased, and the remission of sins having been obtained, we are received into favor by him, and we have him thereafter present, propitious, and favorable to us by his grace. For when, having obtained the remission of sins, we are reconciled to God, and we have him thereafter propitious and favorable, we have every good thing in him as in the fountain of all goodness, of which we are capable and which we need for the state of this life, and we have attained that happiness or blessedness which can indeed fall to our lot in this mortality, according to that: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered: Blessed is the man to whom God does not impute sin, Psal. XXXII. 2. Rom. IV. 7. 8. But the minor proposition is everywhere inculcated and confirmed by Holy Scripture. They say that Christ is set forth by God to us as ἱλαστήριον, a propitiation THROUGH FAITH in his blood, Rom. III. 25. that he is ἱλασμὸν, a propitiation for our sins, I. Joh. II. 2. and that he gave himself ἀντίλυτρον for all, I. Tim. II. 6. and that God out of his immense love gave him, that everyone WHO BELIEVES in him should not perish, but have eternal life, Joh. III. 16. that WHOEVER BELIEVES in him should not be condemned, v. 18. That all the Prophets bear witness to him, that everyone who believes in him shall receive remission of sins through his name, Act. X. 43.

II. Faith in Christ, by which we are reconciled to God, is followed by an inseparable bond of love for God, by which we cleave to him, propitiated to us through Christ, for his own sake; and if to cleave to any thing by love for its own sake is to enjoy it, as we have heard Augustine teaching, the enjoyment of God for the state of this life will certainly consist in the love of God, propitiated to us through faith in Christ, by which we cleave to him for his own sake, saying with the Psalmist: Whom have I in heaven but thee, O God! and there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee, Psal. LXXIII. 25. My soul rests only in God: from him is my salvation, Psal. LXII. 1.

III. Although Augustine sometimes, and specifically in book X de Trin. c. XI, uses the word 'enjoy' in a stricter sense, so that to enjoy is the same as to use with joy, not of a thing still hoped for, but already possessed (which will only befall man in the other life), yet in book I de D. C. c. IV, he uses it in the aforementioned broader sense, just as to enjoy is the same as to cleave to any thing by love for its own sake. In which sense, taking the word 'enjoy', even in this mortality they enjoy God who are reconciled to Him by faith in Christ: for they cleave to Him in love for His own sake. Which Augustine also expressly taught in Book I of The City of God, chapter XXX, when he said that in this life we enjoy God either through a mirror or in a riddle. For by saying, either through a mirror or in a riddle, he signifies that the enjoyment of God in this life is imperfect and inferior to the other, which is of the future life. For by enjoyment through a mirror and in a riddle he understands the enjoyment of God, abstractly through foreign species and those taken from created things, and thus imperfectly, and as it were through a mirror, or as known in a riddle, and which is with joy in the hope of the future perfection of knowledge and enjoyment. But in the other life we shall enjoy God, clearly, face to face, known, and with joy in the thing, that is, in God, actually obtained. To which the Master of the Sentences also adds his own calculation in Book I, Distinction I: We, he says, enjoy [God] both here and in the future: but there properly and perfectly and fully, where we see through the species, that which we shall enjoy; here, however, while we walk by faith, we do indeed enjoy, but not so fully. And Thomas in I. II. q. XI. a. IV. to the same sense: To enjoy, he says, imports a certain comparison of the will to the ultimate end, according to which the will has something as an ultimate end. Now the ultimate end is had in two ways: In one way perfectly, and in another way imperfectly. Perfectly indeed, when it is had not only in intention, but also in reality: imperfectly, however, when it is had in intention only. Therefore, perfect enjoyment is of the end already had in reality; but imperfect is also of the end, not had in reality, but in intention only.

IV. Under the love of God, propitiated to us through faith, we also embrace other acts of the will flowing from this concerning God, by which we are made participants of the divine goodness for the state of this life, and perceive a certain taste of it, as it were, such as are the acts of trust in God, propitiated to us through faith in Christ, and likewise of certain hope and joy in the same. For to enjoy some thing, if you look at the force of the word, is to take its fruit, as is in Thomas, loc. cit., a. I. & IV. But they take the fruits of divine goodness, not only those who cleave to God by love for His own sake, but also those who, with faith fixed on God in Christ reconciled to themselves, with filial confidence, and the Holy Spirit bearing witness to their spirit, that they are children of God, can cry out to God, Abba Father, Rom. VIII. 15. who, resting in the same as if upon an immovable rock in favorable and adverse circumstances, are of good courage, saying: God is our protection and fortress, though the earth be removed and the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea, Psalm XLVI. 2, 3. You are my rock and my fortress (O Lord): you are my hope: Lord God, my trust from my youth, Psalm LXXI. 3, et seqq. Moreover, they also reap the fruits of divine goodness, who, trusting in divine promises, expect from God both temporal and spiritual goods: the former indeed under the condition, if they are to be profitable to them; the latter absolutely, with a certain persuasion that they will obtain them; who likewise, persuaded in their own minds of divine grace, rejoice in their God, even in the midst of afflictions, etc.

Latin:

XII.

Intermedius Theologiæ finis consistit etiam in operatione animæ duplici: Una fidei, quâ ferimur in Christum Mediatorem, & fiduciâ in eo velut causâ impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum defixâ, remissionem peccatorum apud Deum consequimur, & in gratiam recipimur; alterâ amoris, quâ eidem, per fidem nobis propitiato, inhæremus propter seipsum: Illâ similiter Deo, pro statu hujus vitæ, potimur nos, qui peccatis ab eo fueramus aversi & separati; hâc eodem fruimur.

I. Operationem, quâ Deo, velut nostro summo bono, pro statu hujus vitæ potimur, consistere in jam dictâ operatione fidei, facilè patet. Quâ operatione enim homines peccatores Deo reconciliantur, & impetratâ remissione peccatorum Deum deinceps habent gratiâ suâ sibi intimè præsentem, propitium & faventem, illâ potiuntur Deo, velut suo infinitè perfecto & summo bono, pro statu quidem hujus vitæ. Sed operatione fidei, quâ feruntur in Christum Mediatorem, & defixâ in eo, velut causâ impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum, fiduciâ homines peccatores reconciliantur Deo, & impetratâ remissione peccatorum Deum deinceps habent gratiâ suâ sibi intimè præsentem, propitium & faventem. E. Propositionis majoris ratio est: quia pro statu hujus vitæ, in quo Deum tantùm abstractivè cognoscimus, non aliter eo potimur, quàm reconciliatione nostri cum ipso, quâ, placatâ ejus irâ adversus peccatum, & impetratâ remissione peccatorum ab ipso in gratiam recipimur, eumque deinceps habemus gratiâ suâ nobis praesentem, propitium & faventem. Ubi enim, impetratâ remissione peccatorum, Deo sumus reconciliati, eumque deinceps propitium & faventem habemus, oppidò in eo velut fonte omnis bonitatis, habemus omne bonum, cujus pro statu hujus vitae capaces sumus & indigemus, & consecuti sumus eam felicitatem sive beatitudinem, quae in hac mortalitate quidem in nos cadere potest, juxta illud: Beati, quorum remissa sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata: Beatus vir, cui Deus non imputat peccatum, Psal. XXXII. 2. Rom. IV. 7. 8. Minorem verò propositionem Scripturae Sacrae nullibi non inculcant & confirmant. Dicunt, Christum esse à Deo nobis propositum ἱλαστήριον, placamentum PER FIDEM in sanguine ipsius, Rom. III. 25. esse ἱλασμὸν propitiationem pro peccatis nostris, I. Joh. II. 2. eumque dedisse semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, I. Tim. I. 6. & Deum ex immensa charitate suâ dedisse eum, ut omnis, QUI CREDIT in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam, Joh. III. 16. ut QUI CREDIT in eum, non condemnetur, v. 18. Ei omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibere, quòd remissionem peccatorum accepturus sit per nomen ejus, quisquis crediderit in eum, Act. X. 43.

II. Fidem in Christum, quâ Deo reconciliamur, nexu individuo sequitur dilectio Dei, quâ ei, per Christum nobis propitiato, inhaeremus propter se; & si amore alicui rei inhaerere propter se est eâ frui, ut Augustinum docentem audivimus, fruitio Dei pro hujus vitae statu consistet utiq; in amore Dei, per fidem in Christû nobis propitiati, quo ei inhaeremus propter seipsum, dicentes cum Psalmista: Quis mihi in caelis praeter te, ô Deus! & praeter te nullo delector in terra, Psal. LXXII. 25. Tantummodò in Deo conquiescit anima mea: ab eo salus mea est, Psal. LXII. 2.

III. Quamvis verò Augustinus quandoque, & speciatim lib. X. de Trin. c. XI. fruendi verbo in significatu strictiori utatur, ut frui idem sit, quod uti cum gaudio, non ad huc spei, sed jam rei (quod in altera demum vita homini obtinget) in lib. I. tamen de D. C. c. IV. eodem in praedicto significatu latiori utitur, prout frui idem est, quod amore alicui rei inhaerere propter seipsam. Quo significatu accep o ruendi verbo etiam in hac mortalitate fruuntur Deo, qui ei fide n Christum reconciliati sunt: inhærent enim ipsi amore propter seipsum. Quod etiam Augustinus lib. I. de D. C. c. XXX. expresse docuit, quando in hac vita Deo nos frui dixit vel per speculum, vel in ænigmate. Quod enim dicit, vel per speculum, vel in ænigmate, eo significat, fruitionem Dei in hac vita esse imperfectam & nferiorem alterâ, quæ est futuræ vitæ. Per fruitionem enim per speculum & in ænigmate intelligit fruitionem Dei, abstractivè per species alienas & à rebus creatis desumtas, & sic imperfectè, ac velut per speculum, aut ut in ænigmate cogniti, & quæ sit cum gaudio in spe futuræ perfectionis cognitionis ac fruitionis. In altera verò vita fruemur Deo, clarè, facie ad faciem, cognito, & cum gaudio res, h. e. in Deo, reapse obtento. Cui & Magister Sententiarum lib. I. Dist. I. D. suum adjicit calculum: Nos, inquiens, & hic & in futuro fruimur: sed ibi propriè & perfectè & plenè, ubi per speciem videmus, quo fruemur; hic autem, du in specie ambulamus fruimu quidem, sed non adeò plenè. Et Thomas in I. II. q. XI. a. IV. in sensum eundem: Frui, inquit, importat comparationem quandam voluntatis ad ultimum finem, secundum quod voluntas habet aliquid pro ultimo fine. Habetur autem ultimus finis dupliciter: Uno modo perfectè, & alio modo imperfectè. Perfectè quidem, quando habetur non solum in intentione, sed etiam in re: imperfectè autem, quando habetur in intentione tantùm. Est ergo perfecta fruitio jam habiti finis realiter; sed imperfecta est etiam finis, non habiti realiter, sed in intentione tantum.

IV. Sub amore Dei, per fidem nobis propitiati, complectimur etiam alios hinc promanantes actus voluntatis circa Deum, quibus divinæ bonitatis pro statu hujus vitæ reddimur participes, ejusque quendam quasi gustum percipimus, cujusmodi sunt actus fiduciæ in Deo, per fidem in Christum nobis propitiato, spei item certæ & gaudii in eodem. Frui enim aliqua re, si vim vocis spectes, est ejus fructum capere, ut est apud Thomam d. l. a. I. & IV. Capiunt autem fructus divinæ bonitatis, non tantùm qui amore Deo inhærent propter se, sed etiam qui defixâ in Deum, fide in Christum sibi reconciliatum, fiducia filiali, & Spiritu S. ipsorum spiritui testimoninm perhibente, quòd sint filii Dei, clamare possunt ad Deum, Abba Pater, Rom. IIX. 15. qui in eodem velut rupe immotâ recumbentes in secundis & adversis rebus bono sunt animo, dicentes: Deus protectio nostra & munitio, auxilium in tribulationibus opportunum valdè: propterea non timebimus, simoveatur terra & commoveantur montes in medio mari, Psal. XLVI, 2. 3. Petra mea & munitio mea es tu (Domine): tu expectatio mea: Dominus Deus fiducia mea inde à pueritia, Psal. LXXI, 3. seqq. Quin & fructus capiunt bonitatis divinæ, qui in divinis confisi promissionibus expectant à Deo cùm temporalia tùm spiritualia bona: illa quidem sub conditione, si sibi profutura sint; hæc absolutè, cùm persuasione certâ, se ea impetraturos; qui item de gratia divina apud animum suum persuasi gaudent in Deo suo, etiam in mediis afflictionibus &c.


### XIII. To the intermediate end of Theology we also refer the holiness of life and…

XIII.

To the intermediate end of Theology we also refer the holiness of life and perseverance in faith and holiness.

I. Theology not only teaches by what method and by what causes a sinful man ought to be reconciled to God, namely by the merit of Christ and faith in Christ, but it also teaches that those who have been reconciled to God through faith in Christ ought thereafter to abstain from sins and live holily, lest by sins they shake off faith in Christ and fall from the grace of God. As both imply a certain habit toward the ultimate end, namely eternal blessedness, so also can they be contained within the scope of an intermediate end, though in a different way. For faith in Christ and the reconciliation of a sinful man with God through faith, since it implies a causal relationship to the ultimate end, is an intermediate end, strictly and rigorously so called. For it is an end in such a way that it is also a cause of attaining the ultimate end. Abstinence, however, from sins and holiness of life do not relate to the ultimate end as a cause of attaining it, but as that which, on the part of the subject, removes what hinders and takes care that we do not, through sins, lose faith in Christ, which is the sole cause of salvation, on our part, and fall from the grace of God and salvation. Therefore, an intermediate end can be spoken of in a looser sense, by which anything that is or is done for the sake of something else is called a means or an intermediate end, even if it is not the cause of attaining it, but relates to its attainment either as a bare condition, or as a cause without which it would not be, or as that which removes an impediment. Because holiness of life perpetually accompanies faith in Christ, which strictly speaking is its intermediate end, perhaps with the addition of 'concomitant' it will not be inappropriately called an intermediate end.

XIV.

The Apostles John and Paul have encompassed both formal ends of Theology, the ultimate and the intermediate, in a few words: the former indeed in the Gospel history, chapter XX. 31, saying: 'These are written, that you may BELIEVE that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that BELIEVING you may HAVE LIFE through his name.' The latter, however, in II Tim. III. 15, when he bears witness to his Timothy that from childhood he has known the sacred writings, and adds: 'Which are able to make you wise UNTO SALVATION THROUGH FAITH which is in Christ Jesus.' Both join life or eternal salvation and faith in Christ as two subordinate ends, and attribute to the latter the nature of an intermediate end, and to the former that of an ultimate end. Although both speak of Holy Scripture, and John indeed of that part of it which exhibits the recorded miracles of Christ, but Paul of the whole of it, yet what they taught there concerning Scripture is rightly transferred to Theology. For just as Scripture and Theology have the same material and formal object, so also the end of both is one and the same. For those things which Holy Scripture teaches under divine revelation, Theology likewise teaches, explains, and defends under divine revelation, and with no other end than that to which the things themselves, as God reveals them, were committed to writing, and to which they themselves tend, either by their own nature or by the benevolent will of the revealing God. Indeed, Holy Scripture, and Theology, taken metonymically for doctrine, and that which proceeds from the habit of Theology, and which proposes and delivers it to others, do not differ, except that the latter teaches and declares distinctly by the method used in the disciplines, what the former delivers historically to the grasp of the common people. And thus far concerning the end of Theology, both objective and formal, and this last and intermediate.

Latin:

XIII.

Ad finem Theologiæ intermedium referimus etiam Sanctimoniam vitæ & perseverantiam in fide ac sanctitate.

I. Theologia non tantùm docet, quâ ratione quibusque causis hominem peccatorem Deo reconciliari oporteat, nempe Christi merito & fide in Christum, sed docet etiam, eos qui Deo per fidem in Christum reconciliati sunt, oportere deinceps à peccatis abstinere & sanctè vivere, ne peccatis fidem in Christum excutiant, & gratiâ Dei excidant. Utrumque ut habitudinem quandam ad finem ultimum, beatitudinem æternam scilicet, importat, ita & finis intermedii ambitu contineri potest, modo tamen diverso. Fides in Christum enim & hominis peccatoris reconciliatio cum Deo per fidem cùm ad finem ultimum causæ habitudiné importet, est finis intermedius, strictè & in rigore sic dictus. Ita enim finis est, ut etiam causa sit consequendi finis ultimi. Abstinentia autem à peccatis & sanctitas vitæ non habent se ad finem ultimum ut ejus consequendi causa, sed ut id, quod exparte subjecti removet impediens, cavetque, ne fidem in Christum, quæ unica, ex nostræ quidem parte, salutis causa est, peccatis amittamus, & gratiâ Dei ac salute excidamus. Dici ergo potest finis intermedius in significatu laxiori, quo quodlibet, quod alicujus gratiâ est aut fit, medium aut finis intermedius dicitur, licet ejus consequendi causa non sit, sed ad illius consecutionem se vel ut conditio nuda, vel ut causa sine quâ non, vel ut id quod removet impediens, sese habeat. Quia fidem in Christum, quæ strictè loquendo ejus finis intermedius est, vitæ sanctitas perpetuò comitatur, forsan cum additamento finis intermedius concomitans non incommodè appellabitur.

XIV.

Finem Theologiæ formalem utrumque, ultimum & intermedium, paucis complexi sunt Johannes & Paulus Apostoli: ille quidem in historia Evangelica cap. XX. 31. Hæc, inquiens, scripta sunt, ut CREDATIS, Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei, & ut CREDENTES VITAM HABEATIS per nomen ipsius. Hic verò in II. Tim. II. 15. cùm Timotheo suo testimonium perhibet, quòd à puero noverit sacras literas, & subjungit: Quæ te possunt eruditum reddere AD SALUTEM PER FIDEM, quæ est in Christo Jesu. Ambo vitam sive salutem æternam & fidem in Christum, tanquam duos subordinatos fines conjungunt, & huic intermedii; illi ultimi finis rationem tribuunt. Quamvis verò uterque de Scriptura Sacra loquatur, & Johannes quidem de parte ejus, quæ Christi miracula consignata exhibet; Paulus verò de ea tota: rectè tamen ad Theologiam transferuntur, quæ de Scriptura ibi docuerunt. Quemadmodùm enim idem materiale & formale objectum habent Scriptura & Theologia, ita & finis utriusque unus & idem est. Nam quæ sub divina revelatione docet Scriptura Sacra, ea docet, explicat & defendit Theologia itidem sub revelatione divina, nec fine alio, quàm quo res ipsæ, Deo revelante, in literas relatæ sunt, & ad quem ipsamet sive suâpte naturâ, sive ex Dei revelantis benevola voluntate tendunt. Quin Scriptura Sacra, & Theologia, sumta metonymicè pro doctrina, ex Theologiæ habitu profecta, & quæ eum aliis proponit & tradit, non differunt, nisi quòd hæc methodo in disciplinis usitatâ distinctè docet & declarat, quæ illa ad vulgi captum historicè tradit. Atque hæc hactenus de Theologiæ fine cujus cùm objectivo tùm formali, & hoc ultimo ac intermedio.


### XV The end for whom is man, corrupted by sin

XV.

The end for whom is man, corrupted by sin.

I. The end for whom of Theology is nothing other than the subject, for whose good, or in whose favor Theology explains, confirms, and defends those things which make for attaining the end for whom, namely, eternal blessedness. That this is indeed the sinful man is easily evident. For whatever Theology delivers for the sake of attaining eternal blessedness in God, it delivers all those things in favor of the sinful man, so that, freed from sins, he may at length actually become a participant in eternal blessedness. II. It is otherwise called the subject of operation: since the most important acts of Theology are occupied about the sinful man, and aim most especially at this, that reconciled to God through faith in Christ, he may at length actually attain eternal blessedness. The end of Theology being thus declared, we must look into the principles and causes of attaining the same.

XVI.

Among the principles and causes of attaining eternal blessedness, the first place is deserved by the grace or mercy of God, with which He pursued men who had fallen into sin, and did not wish them to perish in the destruction which they had brought upon themselves by their sins, Ezek. 18:32, ch. 33:11, 1 Tim. 2:4, 2 Pet. 3:9. I. We are treating here of the principles and means of attaining the ultimate end, namely, eternal blessedness. But the intermediate end, strictly and in rigor so called, as causes and it implies the relation of a means, and thus it also finds a place among causes and means.

II. Eternal blessedness, however, is not an end to be obtained by the proper powers of man or by an operation proceeding from some one of them and directed by the practical acts of theology, but it befalls whomsoever it befalls by the gratuitous benevolence and gift of God. Wherefore it is also necessary that the principles, causes, and means leading thereto should reside in God, or be instituted or proceed from Him. Among these, however, the first place is undoubtedly owed to the grace of God, or His benevolent will and mercy, which is the προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause of our salvation, and as it were its fountain and source.

XVII.

We assign the place next to the grace of God to Christ the Mediator, who satisfied the divine justice injured by sins in our stead, and obtained that, with that justice preserved, salvation could be conferred upon us.

I. The grace of God is an inadequate principle of our salvation. For when it is posited, our salvation is not yet posited, although if it were removed, our salvation would be removed. The reason for this is that God is merciful and at the same time just, and just as He, moved by His mercy, wishes to have mercy on us and to rescue us from the destruction in which we are immersed through sin, so, induced by His immutable justice, He demands satisfaction for our sins. Wherefore, since the grace or mercy of God required another cause to concur for the restoration of our salvation, by which the divine justice injured by sins might be satisfied.

II. But no such cause is given, except Christ, the unique Mediator of God and men, who gave Himself as an ἀντίλυτρον or price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. 2:5-6, who is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:2. Who is therefore the meritorious cause of our salvation, and thus the external impulsive cause.

Latin:

XV.

Finis cui est homo, peccato corruptus.

I. Theologiæ finis cui nihil est aliud, quàm subjectum, cui bono, vel in cujus gratiam Theologia explicat, confirmat & defendit, quæ ad consequendum finem cujus, beatitudinem æternam scilicet, faciunt. Id verò esse hominem peccatorem facilè patet. Quæcunque enim consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis æternæ causâ Theologia tradit, ea omnia tradit in hominis peccatoris gratiam, ut à peccatis liberatus æternæ beatitudinis aliquando reapse particeps fiat. II. Dicitur aliàs subjectum operationis: cùm circa hominē peccatorem Theologiæ actus potissimi occupentur, & eò maximè collineent, ut Deo per fidem in Christum reconciliatus reapse tandem beatitudinem æternam consequatur. Fine Theologiæ sic declarato, dispiciendum est de ejusdem consequendi principiis & causis.

XVI.

Inter principia & causas consequendæ beatitudinis æternæ primum locum meretur gratia sive misericordia Dei, quâ prolapsos in peccatum homines proseqnutus est, eosque noluit in exitio, quod peccatis sibi attraxerant, perire, Ezech. XIIX. 32. c, XXXII. 11. I. Tim. II. 4. II. Petr. III. 9. I. Agimus hîc de principiis & mediis consequendi finis ultimi, beatitudinis aeternæ scilicet. Intermedius autem finis, strictè & in rigore sic dictus, ut ad consequendum finem ultimum causæ & medii habitudinem importat, ita & ipse inter causas & media locum invenit.

II. Beatitudo æterna autem non est finis, propriis hominis viribus vel aliquâ ex illis profectâ & Theologiæ actibus practicis directâ operatione obtinendus, sed obtingit Dei gratuitâ benevolentiâ & dono, cuicunque obtingit. Quamobrem etiam principia, causas ac media, eò ducentia, in Deo residere, vel ab eo instituta aut profecta esse oportet. Inter ea verò indubiè debetur locus 'primus gratiæ Dei, sive benevolæ ejus voluntati & misericordiæ, quæ salutis nostræ causa προηγουμένη sive impulsiva interna, ejusque quasi fons & scaturigo est.

XVII.

LOcum à gratia Dei proximum tribuimus Christo Mediatori, qui læsæ peccatis justitiæ divinæ nostro loco satisfecit, & ut eâ salvâ salus nobis conferri posset, obtinuit.

I. Gratia Dei est principium salutis nostræ inadæquatum. Eâ enim positâ nondum ponitur salus nostra, quamvis eâ sublatâ salus nostra tolleretur. Cujus rei causa est, quòd Deus misericors & simul justus est, & ut suâ motus misericordiâ nostrûm misereri, & ex exitio, cui per peccatum sumus immersi, nos eruere vult, ita suâ justitiâ immutabili inductus exigit satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris. Quamobrem cum gratia sive misericordia Dei causam aliam, quâ læsæ peccatis justitiæ divinæ satisfieret, ad reparandam nobis salutem concurrere oportuit.

II. Hujusmodi causa verò nulla datur, præter Christum, Dei & hominum Mediatorem unicum, qui semetipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον sive redemtionis pretium pro omnibus, I. Tim. II. 5. 6. qui est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non autem pro nostris tantùm, sed & pro totius mundi peccatis. I. Joh. II. 2. Qui proinde causa salutis nostræ meritoria, atque adeò causa impulsiva externa est.


### XIX. The third place in the principles and means of obtaining…

XIX.

The third place in the principles and means of obtaining salvation we attribute to faith in Christ, not indeed considered in itself absolutely, as it is a quality or act, nor even as it is effective through charity and a principle of good works, but as it is considered in relation to the merit of Christ, and in so far as it is borne toward that, and apprehends it and applies it to us.

I. Since faith in Christ can be considered in three ways: one in itself absolutely, as it is a quality or act; another, as it is effective through charity and a principle and cause of good works; and thirdly in relation to its object, namely Christ the Mediator, and his merit and satisfaction for our sins: it finds a place among the causes and means of our salvation when viewed in neither the first nor the second way. For it is both imperfect in itself, and an imperfect principle of holiness and good works, which therefore, and the good works proceeding from this, are of no value, dignity, or merit before God in themselves; indeed, on account of the blemishes and stains of multiple imperfections adhering to them, they are like a polluted garment, Isa. 64:6. It remains, therefore, that faith is to be numbered among the causes and means of salvation only when viewed in the third way.

II. The merit of Christ is indeed a ransom for our sins, in itself alone most valid and most sufficient, by which satisfaction has been abundantly made to the divine justice injured by sins, so that no dignity, perfection, or value can be added to it by our faith: rather, it is from that merit that faith entirely possesses the fact that it finds a place among the causes and means of our salvation. But just as Christ acted and suffered in our place and for us, which he did and suffered as our Mediator and the cause of our salvation being restored: so it is required on our part that we apprehend his merit and satisfaction, performed for us and in our place, as our own, and having apprehended it, apply it to ourselves: which, as it is accomplished by faith, so faith, in so far as it apprehends the merit of Christ and applies it to us, and thus not by reason of itself, but by reason of the apprehended merit of Christ, comes into the part of the causes of our salvation. It is commonly called the instrumental cause of our salvation, because it behaves like an organ, by which the merit of Christ, as the meritorious cause of our salvation, we apprehend and make our own. But because it is not as a physical efficient cause that it concurs to our salvation (which is otherwise the case of an instrumental cause) but by way of an impulsive cause, namely by reason of the apprehended merit of Christ, which is the principal impulsive cause of our salvation, faith may not inconveniently be called the less principal impulsive cause of our salvation. Of which matter in its own place.

Latin:

XIX.

TErtium locum in consequendæ salutis principiis & mediis tribuimus Fidei in Christum, non quidem in se absolute spectatae, ut qualitas vel actus est, neque etiam ut per charitatem efficax & bonorum operum principium est, sed ut in ordine ad meritum Christi consideratur, & in quantum in illud fertur, idque apprehendit & nobis applicat.

I. Fides in Christum cum considerari possit modis tribus: uno in se absolute, ut qualitas vel actus est; altero, ut per charitatem efficax & bonorum operum principium & causa est; & tertio in ordine ad objectum suum, Christum Mediatorem scilicet, ejusque meritum & satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris: nec primo, nec secundo modo spectata in salutis nostrae causis & mediis locum invenit. Est enim & in se imperfecta, & sanctitatis ac bonorum operum principium imperfectum, quae proinde, & hinc procedentia bona opera per se nullius coram Deo valoris, dignitatis, aut meriti; quin ob adhaerentes imperfectionum multiplicium naevos & maculas ut vestimentum inquinatum sunt, Esa. LXIV. 6. Relinquitur ergo, quod solo tertio modo spectata fides in causis & mediis salutis numeranda veniat.

II. Meritum Christi quidem ἀντίλυτρον est pro peccatis nostris, per se solum validissimum & sufficientissimum, quo laesae peccatis justitiae divinae abunde factum est satis, ut ei a fide nostra nihil dignitatis, perfectionis atque valoris accedere possit: quin ab eo potius habet fides in solidum, quod in salutis nostrae causis ac mediis locum invenit. Quemadmodum autem nostro loco & pro nobis Christus egit & passus est, quae ut Mediator noster & reparandae nostrae salutis causa egit & passus est: ita ex parte nostra requiritur, ut ejus meritum & satisfactionem, pro nobis & nostro loco praestitam, velut nostram, apprehendamus, apprehensamq; nobis applicemus: quod ut fide peragitur, ita fides, in quantum Christi meritum apprehendit, nobisque applicat, atq; adeo non ratione sui, sed ratione apprehensi meriti Christi, in partem causarum salutis nostrae venit. Vulgo dicitur ea salutis nostrae causa instrumentalis, quod se habeat instar organi, quo Christi meritum, velut causam salutis nostrae meritoriam apprehendimus, & nostrum facimus. Quia autem ad salutem nostram non causa efficiens physica concurrit (quod alias causæ instrumentalis est) sed per modum causæ impulsivæ, ratione apprehensi meriti Christi scilicet, quod est causa salutis nostræ impulsiva principalis, non incommodè dicetur fides causa salutis nostræ impulsiva minus principalis. Qua de re suo loco.


### XIX. Christ has embraced all three causes of our salvation in John 3:16

XIX.

Christ has embraced all three causes of our salvation in John 3:16. Thus, he says, God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

He designates the internal impulsive cause of our salvation, on the part of God, by the word of love, with which God loved the world, that is, the men existing in the world, which, as to the thing itself, is nothing other than the grace of God, or his gratuitous favor and benevolence toward men; but he designates the meritorious or external impulsive cause, and that the principal one, by the appellation of the only begotten Son of God, delivered to death for us; finally, he denotes the instrumental or less principal external impulsive cause by the phrase: to believe in him (namely, the only begotten Son). That each one sustains the nature of a cause in relation to our salvation, the Savior implies by the added determination: that whosoever believeth in him, may have eternal life.

XX.

Furthermore, faith, which is the sole cause of our salvation on our part, is not a work of human powers, but God kindles, increases, and confirms it in our hearts through the Word and Sacraments, which themselves are therefore causes of our salvation, but mediate and instrumental, in so far as they are organs and causes of kindling and confirming faith, which is its less principal impulsive cause.

XXI.

Finally, the holiness of life, although it too is in its own way for the sake of the ultimate end of Theology, namely eternal blessedness to be attained in God, is nevertheless not for the sake of it, as a cause and means of attaining it, but as that which, on the part of the subject, removes what hinders salvation, as was said in the previous thesis XIII.

I. That the holiness of life is in some way for the sake of the ultimate end of Theology, namely blessedness, is evident from the places of Scripture: Heb. X. 36. You have need of patience, that after you have done the will of God, you might receive the promise. c. XII. 14. Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.

II. But that it is not for the sake of it, as a cause and means of attaining it, strictly so called, is proven among other things by all those places of Scripture which deny the power of justifying to good works, and claim it for faith in Christ alone. For that which is not the cause of the justification or reconciliation of a sinful man with God, is not the cause of attaining salvation, as will be taught in its proper place.

III. Its treatment, therefore, is referred to that part of Theology which concerns the causes and means of salvation, not because it is a cause and means of attaining it, but because it accompanies the cause and means of attaining it, namely faith, with an inseparable bond, and stands in relation to blessedness as that which, on the part of the subject, removes the causes hindering its acquisition.

Latin:

XIX.

Omnes tres salutis nostræ causas complexus est Christus Joh. III. 16. Sic, inquiens, Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.

Causam salutis nostræ impulsivam internam, ex parte Dei, designat voce dilectionis, quâ mundum, h. e. homines in mundo existentes Deus dilexit, quæ, quoad rem, nihil aliud est, quàm gratia Dei, sive gratuitus ejus favor & benevolentia erga homines; meritoriam verò sive impulsivam causam externam, eamque principalem, designat appellatione Filii Dei unigeniti, pro nobis in mortem traditi; instrumentalem denique sive impulsivam externam minus principalem phrasi: credere in eum (Filium scilicet unigenitum) denotat. Singulas verò sustinere rationem causæ in ordine ad salutem nostram, innuit Servator adjecto προσδιορισμῷ: ut omnis, qui credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam.

XX.

Fides porro, quæ unica, ex parte nostra quidem, causa salutis nostræ est, non est humanarum virium opus, sed Deus accendit, auget & confirmat eam in cordibus nostris per Verbum & Sacramenta, quæ & ipsa propterea salutis nostræ causæ sunt, sed mediatæ & instrumentales, in quantum scilicet sunt organa & causæ accendendæ, & confirmandæ fidei, quæ ejus causa impulsiva minus principalis est.

XXI.

Sanctimonia vitæ denique, quamvis & ipsa suo modo sit propter finem Theologiæ ultimum, beatitudinem æternam scilicet, in Deo consequendam, non tamen est propter illum, ut ejus consequendi causa & medium, sed ut id, quod ex parte subjecti removet impediens salutis, ut superiori thesi XIII. dictum.

I. Sanctimoniam vitæ esse aliquo modo propter finem Theologiæ ultimum, beatitudinem scilicet, patet ex locis Scripturæ Ebr. X. 36. patientiâ vobis opus est, ut voluntatem Dei peragentes reportetis promissionem. c. XII. 14. Pacem sectamini cum omnibus & sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum.

II. Quòd verò non sit propter eum, velut ejus consequendi causa & medium, in rigore sic dictum, inter alia evincunt ea Scripturæ loca omnia, quæ vim justificandi bonis operibus denegant, eamque uni ac soli fidei in Christum vendicant. Quod enim justificationis sive reconciliationis hominis peccatoris cum Deo causa non est, id nec consequendæ salutis causa est, ut suo loco docebitur.

III. Ejus igitur tractatio ad eam Theologiæ partem refertur, quæ est de causis & mediis salutis, non quòd ejus consequendæ causa & medium sit, sed quòd ejus consequendæ causam & medium, fidem scilicet, nexu individuo comitetur, & ad beatitudine se habeat tanquam id quod ex parte subjecti removet causas impedientes illius adeptionem.


### XXII. With these things concerning the end of Theology, both objective and formal,…

XXII.

…With these things concerning the end of Theology, both objective and formal, and the one for whom it is, as well as the subject, and also the causes and means of attaining the end, to which all consideration of Theology can be reduced, having been thus premised, it must be further examined how Theolo may be engaged, so that it may become more manifest that it is entirely practical.

I. But first, on the part of the objective end, it is not necessarily required for a practical science that it be πρακτόν τι, that is, something to be brought about by our operation, but it suffices if it be something attainable by our operation and to be obtained through it. For not all practical habits, for which there is some other end besides practice or operation, have as their objective end something to be produced by our operation, but some are occupied with a pre-existing thing to be obtained, just as, for example, οἰκονομικὴ is a practical habit on account of practice, occupied in procuring or acquiring riches already existing beforehand in the world. This Nazarius, a celebrated writer of the Thomist sect, acknowledges and teaches in the place cited above, that in Theology, as it is practical, there is a twofold object; one is operable, and this contains all human acts by which we are said to operate well; another is ATTAINABLE through practical operation, and indeed is also that from which the rule of operating is taken, and this object is God under the aspect of the highest good and the ultimate end, to the attainment of which all operations directed by the science of our Theology are ordered.

II. Furthermore, on the part of the objective end, it is not necessarily required for a practical science that it be directed toward it in all its acts under the aspect of an end, whether to be effected or to be obtained, and thus that all its acts occupied about it be formally practical, but it suffices if it refers even those acts, by which it is directed toward it as a thing which is an end and toward the knowing of its quiddity, ultimately to practice; this is given to be understood from those things which we taught above in thesis V, Explanation, number VII. Whence, although Theology considers God not only under the aspect of an end and the highest good, but also in Himself under the aspect of His essence, essential attributes, and persons, as well as His works, namely corporeal and incorporeal creatures, and the divine providence occupied in them, the knowledge of which we readily grant is not formally practical: yet because it does not consider that for the sake of mere speculation so as to stop ultimately in it, but refers that entire consideration ultimately to practice, on the part of the objective end certainly nothing it, because it prohibits classifying it among the simply practical sciences: for example, that Theology teaches that God, by reason of his essence, is the supreme being, who surpasses all other things in perfection and is the cause of all things, and that he is a spiritual being, it refers all of that to practice through practical conclusions deduced from there, which dictate that God is to be worshipped above all things, and that he is to be pursued with worship convenient to his nature, namely spiritual. That it considers the same one by reason of essential perfections as omniscient, as supremely good, supremely truthful, as all-wise, omnipotent, just, etc., it similarly refers to practice through practical conclusions, which it infers from here by an easy consequence, which dictate that God is to be believed above all things, that he is to be trusted above all things; that he himself is to be loved above all things, feared, invoked in necessities, etc., which was shown at length above in Chapter II, thesis XIX. That by reason of the persons it considers God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with a certain work appropriate to each person externally, the former as the creator of us and of this universe, the latter as our redeemer, the third as our sanctifier, it refers that very thing also to practice through practical conclusions inferred from there, which dictate that the three persons of the same essence, power, wisdom, goodness, etc., are to be pursued with equal worship of honor, trust, fear, etc., and that each one is to be acknowledged and venerated with due reverence in the works by which they graciously exert themselves in us. Likewise, Theology considers the works of God externally, namely corporeal and incorporeal creatures, and divine providence, not for their own sake and for the sake of speculation, but in relation to God, as the end and supreme good of man, as notable effects by which he has communicated his goodness with man, so that from his immense goodness toward us, known also from this, it may direct us to religious worship, to be exercised around him by acts of trust, hope, fear, invocation, and glorification, by means of practical conclusions which follow from there of their own accord. What, therefore, on the part of the objective end prevents us from classifying Theology among the practical sciences?

III. Thirdly, the intermediate formal end, namely faith in Christ,

& the reconciliation of sinful man with God through it, is formally a certain practice, directed by the practical acts of Theology. And faith in Christ indeed includes two acts. One of assent, by which we believe that Christ is the sole Mediator of God and men, and that God wills to be propitious to us and to remit sins on account of the merit and satisfaction of Christ. The other of trust, fixed upon Christ the Mediator and the divine promises concerning the remission of sins on account of Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God. If not both of these, yet that the latter act is formally a certain practice, admits of no doubt. For it is an act of the will, elicited by a prior practical act of Theology (that trust in obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God must be fixed upon Christ, the Mediator of God and men, and the divine promises concerning the imparting of the remission of sins to us on account of Christ): although the former act also is commanded by the will, directed by the practical acts of Theology, and in this regard can be called a certain practice.

Moreover, the reconciliation of sinful man with God is performed on our part by the very acts of faith themselves, by which the merit of Christ is apprehended, and is exhibited to God as a λύτρον for our sins; which is undoubtedly a certain practice.

III. Nor is there any doubt that the holiness of life, which perpetually accompanies faith in Christ, is formally a certain practice. For it consists entirely in operation, instituted according to the prescription of Theology, in conformity with the divine law.

IV. Finally, the ultimate formal end, since it consists in the clear or intuitive knowledge of God, is indeed a certain theory or contemplation, yet not of our theological science, which is that of Wayfarers, through which it could be established in the category of speculative science; but it is the contemplation of the Theology of the blessed in the other life, in which there will no longer be a place for our Theology. Nor does the intuitive knowledge of God have the character of an end for our Theology otherwise than insofar as it is proposed to the will by its acts as the good of the other life, and that absolutely perfect and supreme, to be obtained from God through faith in Christ: that the faith fixed upon Christ is a certain practice and an intermediate end of Theology, we have just said. From this intermediate end, however, as a practice directing the practical acts of Theology, and from the practical acts themselves, by which it directs it, theological science finally obtains its denomination, and indeed a denomination not of a contemplative, but of a practical science.

V. Furthermore, we grant again that the things which Theology teaches concerning the subject, which is man the sinner, are not formally practical. Yet it does not teach them for the sake of mere speculation, but insofar as they are necessary to be known for practice and operation, and thus for the sake of practice. For just as a sick person does not desire a physician, nor prepares himself for the use of medicines, unless the disease and the danger to life in which he is involved are known: so neither does man the sinner require the Physician and the remedies of the soul, namely Christ and his merit, for restoring the salvation of the soul, nor does he prepare himself for the use of the means of grace, namely the divine Word and the Sacraments, or seek the assistance of God and the aids of grace for recovering the powers of the soul lost through sin, unless the disease of the soul is known, namely original and actual sin, and the eternal destruction into which he has fallen through sin. To what end, finally, does Theology refer whatever it teaches concerning man the sinner, concerning sins, original and actual, but that, despairing of his own powers by which he might struggle out of destruction, he may betake himself to the means of grace, the Word of God and the Sacraments; that, grieving over sins committed, he may flee to Christ the Mediator and his satisfaction, performed in our place and for our sins, and through it, apprehended by faith, may seek and find with God the remission of sins; that through the remaining life he may implore the assistance of God and the aids of grace with ardent prayers; that likewise, with recovered powers, he may restrain, crucify, and mortify the lusts of the flesh, as if by casting a bridle upon them, so that they cannot break forth into act. Which also, on the part of the subject, suffices for a practical science.

VI. Finally, among the principles and causes of obtaining eternal blessedness, the grace of God holds the first place; next to this, Christ the Mediator and his merit; the third, faith in Christ, as was said above. But Theology considers that again not for the sake of speculation or bare knowledge, but on account of practice. And it proposes the grace of God, or His gratuitous favor toward us, and Christ the Mediator as the impulsive causes of our reconciliation with God and salvation; the former as an internal impulsive cause in God, the latter as an external and meritorious impulsive cause, in such a way indeed that it directs the will of the sinful man by practical acts toward a confidence of obtaining from God the remission of sins and eternal salvation, to be fixed in His grace and the merit of Christ. Which is indeed the function of a practical science, not a speculative one. But Theology not only prescribes and directs faith in Christ, which is formally a certain practice, by its acts, but it also prescribes the right use of the means divinely instituted to kindle and confirm it, namely the Word and the Sacraments, and teaches how a sinful man is to be led by the Word of the law to the acknowledgment of sins, so that, with fears and terrors of conscience struck into him concerning committed sins, he may seriously grieve; and how hearts crushed by the hammer of the law are to be raised up by the Word of the Gospel through gratuitous promises concerning the remission of sins on account of Christ, and how saving faith is to be kindled in them. Similarly, it teaches concerning the Sacraments, what their nature, power, operation, and efficacy is, how, to what men, with what previous preparation they are to be administered, and how by their administration faith is either to be kindled, or confirmed and sealed. Which consideration itself is formally partly, and partly virtually practical, and tends toward practice, to be exercised not so much by the sinful man as by the Ministers of the Church, to whom the duty of teaching and administering the Sacraments has been entrusted, except that it also prescribes to the man being converted his own duties in his conversion regarding the use of the means by practical acts.

Latin:

XXII.

Quibus de Theologiæ fine cùm cujus, eoque tâm objectivo quàm formali, tùm cui sive de subjecto, nec non de consequendi finis causis & mediis, ad quæ Theologiæ consideratio omnis reduci potest, ita præmissis, dispiciendum porro est, quomodo circa unumquodque eorum Theologia versetur, ut eam totam practicam esse, manifestiùs evadat.

I. Primùm autem ex parte finis objectivi ad scientiam practicam non requiritur necessariò, ut sit πρακτόν τι h. e. aliquid nostrâ operatione efficiendum, sed sufficit, si sit aliquid nostrâ operatione attingibile & per eam obtinendum. Non enim omnes habitus practici, quorum præter praxin sive operationem datur alius quidam finis, pro fine objectivo habent aliquid nostrâ operatione producendum, sed nonnulli occupantur in re præexistente, obtinendâ, sicut v. g. οἰκονομικὴ est habitus practicus ob praxin, in comparandis sive acquirendis divitiis, jam antè in mundo existentibus, occupatam. Quod agnoscit Nazarius, Scriptor è Thomistarum Secta celebris, & docet loco suprà citato, in Theologia ut practica est, duplex esse objectum; alterum operabile, & hoc continere omnes actus humanos, quibus dicimur benè operari; aliud esse ATTINGIBILE per operationem practicam, imò esse etiam illud, unde sumitur regula operandi, & hoc objectum esse Deum sub ratione summi boni, & ultimi finis, ad cujus consecutionem ordinentur omnes operationes directæ per scientiam nostræ Theologiæ.

II. Deinde ex parte finis objectivi ad scientiam practicam non requiri necessariò, ut omnibus suis actibus in eum feratur sub ratione finis sive efficiendi, sive obtinendi, atque adeò ut omnes ejus circa illum occupati actus formaliter practici sint, sed sufficere, si illos etiam, quibus in eum ut in rem, quæ finis est, ejusque quidditatem cognoscendam fertur, ad praxin ultimò referat; intelligi datur ex iis, quæ suprà th. V. Expl. n. VII. docuimus. Unde quamvis Theologia Deum non tantùm sub ratione finis & boni summi, sed etiam in se ratione essentiæ, attributorum essentialium & personarum ut & ejus opera, creaturas scilicet corporeas & incorporeas, & occupatam in illis providentiam divinam consideret, quorum cognitionem formaliter practicam non esse ultrò largimur: quia tamen illa non considerat nudæ speculationis causâ ut in ea ultimò sistat, sed istam considerationem totam refert ultimò ad praxin, ex parte finis objectivi sanè nihil datur, quod eam scientiis simpliciter practicis annumerare prohibeat: v. g. quòd docet Theologia, Deum ratione essentiæ esse ens supremū, quod cætera omnia perfectione superat, omniumque causa est, eumq; esse ens spirituale, id totū refert ipsa ad praxin per deductas inde conclusiones practicas, quæ Deum super omnia colendum, quæ eum cultu, suæ naturæ conveniente, spirituali scilicet, prosequendum esse dictitant. Quòd eundem ratione perfectionum essentialium considerat ut omniscium, ut summè bonum, summè veracem, ut omnisapientem, omnipotentem, justum &c. id similiter refert ad praxin per conclusiones practicas, quas hinc pronâ infert conssequentiâ, quæ Deo super omnia credendum, ei super omnia confidendum; quæ ipsum super omnia diligendum, timendum, in necessitatibus invocandum &c. dictitant, quod supra in Cap. II. th. XIX. prolixè ostensum fuit. Quòd ratione personarum Deum considerat ut Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, cum appropriato personæ cuique opere quodam ad extra, illum ut conditorem nostri & hujus universi, istum ut nostrum redemptorem, hunc ut nostrum sanctificatorem, id ipsum etiam refert ipsa ad praxin per illatas inde conclusiones practicas, quæ tres ejusdem essentiæ, potentiæ, sapientiæ, bonitatis &c. personas pari honoris, fiduciæ, timoris &c. cultu prosequendas, & unamquamque in operibus, quibus se in nobis gratiosè exerunt, debitâ reverentiâ agnoscendam & venerandam dictitant. Perinde opera Dei ad extra, creaturas scilicet corporeas & incorporeas, divinamque providentiam considerat Theologia non propter se, & speculationis causâ, sed in ordine ad Deum, ut hominis finem & bonum summum, velut effectus insignes, quibus suam bonitatem cum homine communicavit, ut ex immensâ ejus in nos bonitate, hinc etiam cognitâ, ad cultum religiosum, actibus fiduciæ, spei, timoris, invocationis, glorificationis circa eum exercendum, mediantibus conclusionibus practicis, quæ inde ultrò sequuntur, nos dirigat. Quid ergo, ex parte finis objectivi impedit, quò minùs Theologiam scientiis practicis accenseamus?

III. Tertiò finis formalis intermedius, fides in Christum scilicet,

& reconciliatio hominis peccatoris cum Deo per illam, formaliter praxis quædam est, Theologiæ actibus practicis directa. Et fides in Christum quidem includit actus duos. Unum assensus, quo Christum Dei & hominum Mediatorem unicum esse, Deumque velle nobis propter Christi meritum & satisfactionem propitium esse & peccata remittere, credimus. Alterum fiduciæ, in Christum Mediatorem & divinas promissiones de remissione peccatorum propter Christum, ut causam impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum, defixæ. Horum si non utrumque, posteriorem tamen actum formaliter praxin quandam esse, dubium non habet. Est enim actus voluntatis, ad prævium Theologiæ actum practicum, (quòd fiducia impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum in Christum, Mediatorem Dei & hominum, & divinas promissiones de impertienda nobis remissione peccatorum propter Christum defigenda sit) elicitus: quamvis prior etiam actus à voluntate, Theologiæ actibus practicis directa, imperatus sit, & hoc intuitu praxis quædam dici queat.

Reconciliatio autem hominis peccatoris cum Deo ex parte nostra peragitur ipsismet actibus fidei, quibus Christi meritum apprehenditur, & Deo velut λύτρον pro peccatis nostris exhibetur; quæ indubiè praxis quædam est.

III. Neque dubium est, Sanctimoniam vitæ, quæ fidem in Christum perpetuò comitatur, formaliter praxin quandam esse. Confistit enim tota in operatione, ad Theologiæ præscriptum, legi divinæ conformiter institutâ.

IV. Finis denique formalis ultimus, cùm in clara sive intuitiva Dei cognitione consistat, theoria quidem sive contemplatio quædam est, non tamen nostræ, quæ Viatorum est, scientiæ Theologicæ, per quam in ratione scientiæ fpeculativæ constitui possit; sed est contemplatio Theologiæ beatorum in vita altera, in qua nostræ Theologiæ locus non amplius erit. Neque ad nostram Theologiam cognitio Dei intuitiva aliter rationẽ finis habet, quàm in quantũ voluntati ut bonum alterius vitæ, idque absolutè perfectũ & summũ, à Deo per fidem in Christum obtinendũ, ejus actibus proponitur: quam in Christum defixam fidem praxin quandam & Theologiæ finem intermedium esse, modò diximus. Ab hoc autem fine intermedio, velut praxi, Theologiæ actibus practicis directâ, & ab ipsis actibus practicis, quibus eam dirigit, scientia Theologica demum suam sortitur denominationem, & quidem deominationem, non contemplativæ, sed practicæ scientiæ.

V. Porrò quæ de subjecto, quod homo peccator est, Theologia tradit, formaliter practica non esse, rursum largimur. Neque tamen nudæ speculationis causâ illa tradit, sed in quantum ad praxin & operationem cognitu necessaria sunt, atque adeò propter praxin. Quemadmodum enim ægrotus medicum non desiderat, nec ad medicamentorum usum se comparat, nisi cognito morbo & vitæ periculo, in quo versatur: ita nec homo peccator Medicum & pharmaca animæ, Christum scil. ejusque meritum, ad reparandam animæ salutem requirit, nec ad usum mediorum gratiæ, Verbi divini scil. & Sacramentorum se comparat, aut Dei adsistentiam & auxilia gratiæ ad recuperandas animæ vires, per peccatum amissas, expetit, nisi cognito animæ morbo, peccato originali scilicet & actualibus, exitioque æterno, in quod per peccatum prolapsus est. Quò refert tandem Theologia, quæcunque de homine peccatore, de peccatis, originali & actualibus, tradit, ut scilicet de suis viribus, quibus ex exitio eluctetur, desperans, ad gratiæ media, Verbum Dei & Sacramenta se conferat, ut dolens de peccatis admissis ad Christum Mediatorem ejusque satisfactionem, nostro loco & pro peccatis nostris præstitam, confugiat, & per illam, fide apprehensam, apud Deum remissionem peccatorum quærat & inveniat, ut per vitam reliquam Dei adsistentiam & gratiæ auxilia ardentibus precibus imploret, ut item recuperatis viribus novis carnis concupiscentias, ne in actum erumpere possint, injecto quasi freno cöerceat, crucifigat, mortificet. Quod etiam ex parte subjecti ad scientiam practicam sufficit.

VI. Inter principia denique & causas consequendæ beatitudinis æternæ primum locum obtinere gratiam Dei, ab hac proximum Christum Mediatorem ejusque meritum; tertium fidem in Christum, dictum est supra. Ea vero rursum Theologia non speculationis sive nudaæ cognitionis causa considerat, sed propter praxin. Et gratiam Dei quidem sive gratuitum ejus favorem erga nos, Christumque Mediatorem proponit ipsa ut causas nostræ cum Deo reconciliationis & salutis impulsivas; illam ut impulsivam, Deo internam; hunc ut impulsivam externam & meritoriam, ita quidem, ut actibus practicis hominis peccatoris voluntatem dirigat ad fiduciam impetrandæ apud Deum remissionis peccatorum & salutis æternæ, in ejus gratia Christique merito defigendam. Quod sane practicæ scientiæ munus est, non speculativæ. Fidem in Christum vero, quæ formaliter praxis quædam est, Theologia non tantum præscribit & dirigit suis actibus, sed præscribit etiam mediorum ad eam accendendam & confirmandam divinitus institutorum, Verbi scilicet & Sacramentorum, rectum usum, docetque, quomodo Verbo legis homo peccator ad agnitionem peccatorum perducendus sit, ut incussis conscientiæ pavoribus ac terroribus de peccatis admissis serio doleat; & quomodo contrita malleo legis corda Verbo Evangelii per gratuitas promissiones de remissione peccatorum propter Christum erigenda, & fides salvifica in iis accendenda sit. Similiter de Sacramentis docet, quæ illorum natura, vis, operatio & efficacia sit, quomodo, quibus hominibus, qua præparatione prævia administranda, & illorum administratione fides vel accendenda, vel confirmanda & obsignanda sit. Quæ & ipsa consideratio formaliter partim, partim virtualiter practica est, tenditque ad praxin, non tam ab homine peccatore, quam ab Ecclesiæ Ministris, quibus munus docendi & Sacramenta administrandi demandatum est, exercendam, nisi quod etiam homini convertendo in sui conversione circa mediorum usum sua munia actibus practicis præscribit.


### VII. From which it is evident to everyone that in Theology as a whole nothing…

VII.
