From which it is evident to everyone that in Theology as a whole nothing is handed down for its own sake and in the abstract merely for the sake of speculation, but that even those things which are not formally practical are considered in it on account of practice and operation. What else, therefore, remains than that we should say that this science is simply practical?

VIII. Gregory of Rimini explains this matter skillfully in the Prologue to Book 1 of the Sentences, q. ult., a. II & IV. After he had warned in art. 11 that knowledge is called practical in three ways: first, strictly and properly, as that which is formally in itself immediately directive of practice is called practical; second, broadly and improperly, as that which is only virtually, yet closely, directive of practice is called practical; third, more broadly and more improperly, as that which is also only virtually directive of practice, but very remotely, is called practical; and furthermore, concerning the habit of the intellect, he had noted that it is taken either for one simple habit, which is of only one conclusion; or for a collection of several partial habits, having among themselves, on account of the unity of the genus of the subject, a certain agreement and unity; he immediately adds that a habit, taken in this latter way, is then finally called speculative when the partial habits which it includes are all speculative; but if of the partial habits some are speculative and others practical, yet in such a way that the speculative ones, by the agreement of the genus of the subject and analogy to the practical ones, and their conclusions, bear a relationship to the conclusions of these as principles, and thus are virtually and closely practical, then the habit, taken collectively in this way, is conveniently denominated simply practical, not partly speculative and partly practical. Which he proves

(1) by the induction of examples, e.g., Medicine, and similarly Moral Philosophy is called simply practical, although both include several partial habits, whose conclusions are not formally and in themselves immediately practical, but only virtually, yet closely, on account of the agreement of the genus of the subject and the analogy to the partial practical habits, and because they behave toward their conclusions as their principles. The matter is the same with other habits taken collectively, which are aggregated from several partial habits, partly speculative and partly practical.

(2) By reason, sought from demonstration and syllogism. Just as a demonstration is denominated universal, particular, affirmative, negative; and a syllogism is called practical or speculative from the conclusion, not from the premises: so also the total habit, aggregated from several partial habits, some speculative, others practical, derives its denomination from those partial habits whose conclusions are deduced from the conclusions or propositions of other partial habits, as from principles, not from those whose conclusions speculative partial habits always stand to the conclusions of the practical partial habits as their principles, not the reverse. Therefore, habits of this kind are denominated from the practical partial habits, not from the speculative, and thus they are denominated practical, not speculative, or partly practical, partly speculative. The minor is evident by induction. The major, however, is proven: because the reason for science and demonstration, as far as concerns the present, is the same, and from that from which demonstration derives its denomination, from that also science derives it. For science is a demonstrative habit. A demonstrative habit, however, is nothing other than a habitual demonstration, and conversely, demonstration in act is nothing other than actual science.

(3) By the authority of the Commentator in II Metaph., whose words Gregory produces: Operative science, although it uses reasoning and speculates about causes, is nevertheless not worthy to be called speculative science: because it does not investigate the causes of things and their definitions except so that those who know it may act, and not so that they may know, as is the case with speculative sciences; and he adds: It is clear, however, that the science which speculates about the causes of things, or the natures of causes and the definitions of things, is speculative: therefore such a science, of which he (the Commentator) speaks, comprehends also speculative habits; and yet he says it is not worthy to be called speculative, but practical. And he adds the reason: because such speculative notions are ordered to practical ones, as their principles to the conclusions principally intended, and therefore it is denominated practical from its final part.

(4) This he says in the said place, article II, concerning speculative and practical habits in general. Which, when transferred in the following article IV to Theology in particular, he says that Theology, taken as a total habit embracing all the partial habits concerning theological truths, is a practical science. He confirms this conclusion of his from what has been said thus far in this manner: Every total habit, including some partial practical habits, and some speculative ones as well, (in such a way that the acts of the speculative ones are virtually, though proximately, directive of practice; and the conclusions of the practical ones depend upon their conclusions or propositions as if from principles) is conveniently denominated practical. But Theology, taken in the aforementioned manner as a total habit, is such a habit, which is to say it includes some partial practical habits, and some speculative ones as well, in such a way that the acts of the speculative ones are virtually, though proximately, directive of practice, and the conclusions of the practical ones depend upon their conclusions or propositions as if from principles. Therefore Theology, taken in the aforementioned manner as a total habit, is conveniently denominated practical.

The major proposition is that conclusion which he gave as proven in the preceding article II. 1. by induction of examples, of Medicine and Moral Philosophy; 2. by reason, sought from demonstration and the syllogism, that they take their denomination from the condition of the conclusion, just as a demonstration is called universal, particular, affirmative or negative, if the conclusion is such, notwithstanding that one of the premises is of a different quantity or quality; and a syllogism is called practical, if the conclusion is practical, even if one of the premises is speculative.

He proves the minor: because all theological truths, signifying some divine perfection, or some divine operation ad extra, namely of creation, or providence, or some other benefit of His, such as our incarnation, redemption, glorification, or whatever others are contained in Scripture, which are not in themselves formally directive of the love of God, all, I say, proximately contain truths formally directing us to love God, and thus are virtually, though proximately, practical. This he confirms by the authority of Scripture and the Fathers. From Scripture he brings forward for this purpose the passages Matthew XXII. 40. On these two commandments (concerning the love of God and neighbor) the whole Law and the Prophets depend, Rom. XIII. 10. The fullness (consummation) of the Law is love, 1. Tim. I. 5. The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. From the Fathers he brings forward a passage of Augustine from his Enchiridion to Laurentius, the last chapter: All divine commandments are referred to charity, of which the Apostle says: But the end of the commandment is charity. For this charity of God and neighbor is: and certainly on these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Add the Gospel, add also the Apostles. For this law is from nowhere else: The end of the commandment is charity. To which he is about to add his own ἐπίκρισιν: Behold, he says, that the whole Law and all the Prophecies, the Gospel and Apostolic doctrines, and consequently the whole Theology are ordered toward charity, and virtually lead us. Of all things that have been said, since we are treating of things, this is the sum, that it may be understood that the fullness and end of the law and of all divine Scriptures is the love of the thing which is to be enjoyed, and of the thing which can enjoy that thing with us. And book II, ch. VII: In this every student of the divine Scriptures exercises himself, finding nothing else in it than that God is to be loved for God's sake, and neighbor for God's sake. And book X of the City of God, ch. V: Whatever is read in the ministry of the tabernacle or temple to have been divinely commanded in many ways concerning sacrifices, is referred to the signifying of the love of God and neighbor. For on these two commandments, as it is written, the whole law and the Prophets depend. And Gregory, homily X on Ezekiel: For this purpose alone God speaks to us through the whole of sacred Scripture, that He may draw us to the love of Himself and of our neighbor. Gregory concludes at last: Therefore whatever is contained in it (Scripture), either formally or virtually concerning our neighbor, directs us to charity.

And so much for the genus, end, subject of operation, principles, and means of Theology. It remains that we proceed to its subject of consideration or object.

Latin:

VII. Ex quibus nemini non patet, in Theologia universa tradi nihil per se & in actu signato tantum speculationis causa, sed ea etiam, quæ formaliter practica non sunt, considerari in ea propter praxin & operationem. Quid ergo aliud superest, quam ut eam scientiam simpliciter practicam esse dicamus?

VIII. Scitè rem hanc explicat Gregorius Ariminenfis in Prol. in 1. Sent. q. ult. a. II. & IV. Postquam art. 11. monuerat, notitiam dici practicam tribus modis: Uno strictè & propriè, prout practica dicitur, quæ formaliter secundum se immediatè directiva est praxeos; altero largè & impropriè, prout practica dicitur, quæ tantùm virtualiter, de propinquo tamen, directiva est praxeos; tertio largius & magis impropriè, prout practica dicitur, quæ etiam tantum virtualiter directiva est praxeos, sed valdè remotè; & porro de habitu intellectus notaverat, eum accipi vel pro uno habitu fimplici, qui est unius tantùm conclufionis; vel pro collectione plurium partialium habituum, propter unitatem generis subjecti convenientiam & unitatem quandam inter se habentium; subjicit statim, habitum, hoc posteriori modo acceptum, tùm demum dici speculativum, cùm habitus partiales, quos includit, omnes speculativi funt; sed fi habituum partialium alii speculativi, alii practici sint, ita tamen, ut speculativi convenientiâ generis subjecti & analogiam ad practicos; & illorum conclufiones ad horum conclufiones principiorum habitudinem importent, atque adeò virtualiter de propinquo practicæ sint, tùm habitum, sic collectivè sumtum, convenienter denominari simpliciter practicum, non partim speculativum, partim practicum. Quod probat

(1) inductione exemplorum, v. g. Medicina, & similiter Philosophia Moralis dicitur simpliciter practica, licet utraque plures includat habitus partiales, quorum conclufiones non sunt formaliter & secundum se immediatè practicæ, sed virtualiter tantùm, de propinquo tamen, propter convenientiam generis subjecti & analogiam ad habitus partiales practicos, & quòd ad illorum conclufiones se ut illarum principia habeant. Perinde res habet cum aliis, collectivè sumtis habitibus, qui ex pluribus partialibus, speculativis partim, partim practicis habitibus aggregantur.

(2) Ratione, à demonstratione & syllogismo petitâ. Quemadmodum demonstratio denominatur universalis, particularis, affirmativa, negativa; & syllogismus dicitur practicus vel speculativus ex conclufione, non ex præmissis: ita & habitus totalis, ex pluribus partialibus habitibus, speculativis aliis, aliis practicis aggregatus, suam sortitur denominationem ab illis partialibus habitibus, quorum conclusiones deductae sunt ex conclusionibus vel propositionibus aliorum habituum partialium, velut ex principiis, non ab illis, quorum conclusiones ad conclusiones caeterorum habituum partialium se habent, ut principia illarum. Sed in id generis habitibus totalibus habituum partialium speculativorum conclusiones habent se semper ad conclusiones habituum partialium practicorum, ut principia illarum, non contra. Ergo ab habitibus partialibus practicis denominantur id generis habitus totales, non a speculativis, atque adeo denominantur practici, non speculativi, vel partim practici, partim speculativi. Minor patet per inductionem. Major vero probatur: quia scientiae & demonstrationis, quod ad praesens attinet, par ratio est, & a quo demonstratio suam sortitur denominationem, ab eo & scientia eam sortitur. Scientia enim est habitus demonstrativus. Habitus demonstrativus autem nihil est aliud, quam habitualis demonstratio, & contra demonstratio in actu nihil est aliud, quam actualis scientia.

(3) Auctoritate Commentatoris in II. Metaph. cujus Gregorius haec producit verba: Scientia operativa, quamvis utatur ratiocinatione, & speculetur de causis, non tamen est digna vocari scientia speculativa: quia non perscrutatur de causis rerum, & de definitionibus earum, nisi ut scientes eam agant, & non ut sciant, sicut est de scientiis speculativis; & subjicit: Constat autem, quod scientia, quae speculatur causas rerum, vel naturas causarum & definitiones rerum, est speculativa: comprehendit ergo talis scientia, de qua loquitur (Commentator) & habitus speculativos; & tamen dicit, eam non esse dignam vocari speculativam, sed practicam. Et rationem subdit: quia tales notitiae speculativae ordinantur ad practicas, velut sua principia ad conclusiones principaliter intentas, & ideo a finali parte denominatur practica.

(4) Haec ille d. l. art. II. de habitibus speculativis & practicis in genere. Quibus in seq. art. IV. ad Theologiam in specie translatis, dicit, Theologiam, acceptam pro habitu totali, omnes habitus partiales de veritatibus Theologicis complectente, esse scientiam practicam. Quam suam conclusionem ex hactenus dictis confirmat hunc in modum: Omnis habitus totalis, includens aliquos partiales habitus practicos, & aliquos etiam speculativos, (ita ut speculativorum actus sint virtualiter, de proximo tamen, praxis directivi; & ex illorum conclusionibus vel propositionibus conclusiones practicorum tanquam ex principiis dependeant) convenienter denominatur practicus. Atqui Theologia, prædictum in modum pro habitu totali sumpta, talis habitus est, qui scilicet includit aliquos partiales habitus practicos, & aliquos etiam speculativos, ita ut speculativorum actus virtualiter, de proximo tamen, praxis directivi sint, & ex illorum conclusionibus vel propositionibus, conclusiones practicorum tanquam ex principiis dependeant. Ergo Theologia, prædictum in modum pro habitu totali sumta, convenienter denominatur practica.

Major propositio est conclusio illa, quam in præced. art. II. probatum dedit. 1. inductione exemplorum, Medicinæ & Philosophiæ Moralis; 2. ratione, à demonstratione & syllogismo petita, quòd ex conditione conclusionis sumant denominationem, ut demonstratio dicatur universalis, particularis, affirmativa vel negativa, si conclusio talis sit, non obstante, quòd altera præmissarum sit alterius quantitatis vel qualitatis; & syllogismus dicatur practicus, si conclusio sit practica, etiamsi altera præmissarum sit speculativa.

Minorem probat: quia omnes veritates Theologicæ, significantes aliquam perfectionem divinam, aut divinam quandam operationem ad extra, creationis scilicet, vel providentiæ, aut alterius ejus beneficii, ut incarnationis, redemtionis, glorificationis nostræ, aut quæcunque aliæ in Scriptura contentæ, quæ non secundum se formaliter directivæ sunt dilectionis Dei, omnes, inquam, de proximo continent veritates, nos formaliter dirigentes ad diligendum Deum, atque adeò virtualiter, de proximo tamen, practicæ sunt. Quod confirmat auctoritate Scripturæ & Patrum. Ex Scriptura hanc in rem adfert loca Matth. XXII. 40. In his duobus mandatis (de diligendo Deo & proximo) tota Lex & Prophete pendent, Rom. XIII. 10. Plenitudo (consummatio) Legis est dilectio, 1. Tim. I. 5. Finis præcepti est charitas ex puro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non simulata. Ex Patribus affert locum Augustini ex Enchir. ejus ad Laur. c. ult. Omnia præcepta divina referuntur ad charitatem, de qua dicit Apostolus : Finis autem præcepti est charitas. Charitas quippe ista Dei & proximi est: & utique in his duobus præceptis tota Lex pendet & Prophetæ. Adde Evangelium, adde & Apostolos. Non enim aliunde lex ista est: Finis præcepti est charitas. Quibus suam adjecturus ἐπίκρισιν: Ecce, inquit, quòd tota Lex & omnes Prophetiæ Evangelis & Apostolicæ doctrinæ, & per consequens tota Theologia ad charitatem ordinantur, & virtualiter nos inducunt. Deinde & sequentia subjungit loca ex ejusdem lib. I. de D. C. c. XXXV. Omnium, quæ dicta sunt, ex quo de rebus tractamus, hæc summa est, ut intelligatur legis & omnium divinarum Scripturarum plenitudo & finis esse dilectio rei, quâ fruendum est, & rei, quæ nobiscum ea re frui potest. Et lib. II. c. VII. In eo se exercet omnis divinarum Scripturarum studiosus, nihil aliud in eo inveniens, quàm diligendum esse Deum propter Deum, & proximum propter Deum. Et lib. X. de C. D. c. V. Quæcunque in ministerio tabernaculi sive templi multis modis de sacrificiis leguntur divinitus esse præcepta, ad dilectionem Dei & proximi significandam referuntur. In his enim duobus præceptis, ut scriptum est, tota lex pendet & Prophetæ. Et Greg. homil. X. super Ezech. Ad hoc solum Deus per totam nobis sacram Scripturam loquitur, ut nos ad suum & proximi amorem trahat. Concludit tandem Gregorius: Igitur quæcunque in ea (Scriptura) continentur, vel formaliter vel virtualiter de proximo nos dirigunt ad charitatem.

Et hæc hactenus de Theologiæ genere, fine, subjecto operationis, principiis ac mediis. Superest, ut ad ejus subjectum considerationis sive objectum progrediamur.


### XXIII. The subject of consideration or object, as in all other sciences, so also in…

XXIII.

The subject of consideration or object, as in all other sciences, so also in Theology is rightly distinguished into material and formal. I. All practical sciences claim for themselves a twofold subject: one of operation, the other of consideration. They claim a subject of operation insofar as they are practical. For operation, directed by the acts of practical science, by its own nature requires a subject in which it may be exercised, or about which it may be occupied in order to be brought to an end. But they claim a subject of consideration for themselves insofar as they are sciences. For science is the knowledge of a knowable thing, and just as to know is to recognize a thing through its cause, so every science requires some thing in the knowing, or the handing down and explaining of which it is occupied, which, in distinction from the subject in which the operation, directed by the practical acts of science, is performed, is called the subject of consideration or the object of cognition. Aristotle, Posterior Analytics, Book I, Chapter VII, calls τὸ γένος τὸ ὑποκείμενον, the genus, the subject, which is so placed under a science that it contains within itself all things that fall under its consideration, as a genus contains its species, or as an analogate contains its analogates, or at least that the rest of the things which fall under the consideration of the science are ordered toward it, and have with it a certain unity of order.

II. But because every science arises from certain prior and better-known principles, and therefore we are said to know a thing when we recognize its cause, through which it is, that it is its cause, and that it cannot be otherwise; it is necessary that Theological science also claim for itself its own certain principles, from the knowledge of which it may derive the knowledge of the things subject to it. The principles from which the knowledge of things itself is derived constitute its formal object; but the things, the knowledge of which is derived from them, constitute its material object.

XXIV.

The material object of Theology is all things whatsoever revealed by the first Truth for the sake of our salvation; the formal object is the first Truth itself revealing, as revealing.

I. In assigning the subject of consideration for Theology, the Scholastics vary, whose diverse opinions it is not the place here to recount and weigh. They commonly constitute it, however, in God, led by the reasoning that Theology treats of God principally; but of other things only insofar as they have an order toward God, regarding which matter see Thomas, p. I, q. 1, a. VII. By the very fact that they concede that Theology considers, besides God, also other things, although in relation to God, they must admit that God is not the adequate subject of consideration for Theology, but an inadequate one, and that you might call his more perfect part the subject of perfection, and the fact that the others are considered only in relation to that, the subject of attribution.

II. The adequate subject of consideration, therefore, or the adequate material object, is rightly constituted by all things revealed by the First Truth for the sake of our salvation, which, although they do not have a univocal unity among themselves, nevertheless have among themselves a unity of order: since all things that fall under the consideration of Theology are referred to God, as the end and supreme good of man, and are considered under one formal aspect. This suffices for them to constitute, in a certain way, ἕν τὸ γένος τὸ ὑποκείμενον, one genus as subject or one adequate subject of consideration, and to fall under the consideration of one Theological science.

III. The formal object of Theology, if we wish to follow the method customary in practical sciences, would have to be established in its end. For in every discipline, that is called the formal object which is primarily known as the reason for knowing the others that are taught in it. In practical sciences, however, that which is known first of all, and which, once known, is the reason for knowing the others, is the end. The other things, however, which are considered in practical disciplines besides the end, either pertain to the subject of operation, or are the principles, causes, and means of attaining the end, which, just as they are finally known from the known end, are accustomed to be constituted as the material object or subject of consideration. But in Theology, the matter seems to be otherwise. For it does not so presuppose its end as known, without first teaching, explaining, confirming, and defending it distinctly under another previously known reason for knowing, namely, under the First Truth revealing it. For first, God, as He is the objective end of Theology and of man, besides His essence and essential attributes, which are in a certain way known from the light of nature, also contains in Himself certain things not obvious to the light of nature, of what kind they are, that He is one in essence and three in persons, that the Son of God is begotten from the substance of the Father from eternity, that He is of the same essence, power, glory, and Majesty as the Father; that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, that He is one God with both, and whatever other things pertain to explaining the most profound mystery of the Holy Trinity. As these cannot become known to us from anywhere other than from supernatural divine revelation, so neither can they be assumed in Theology as known, but must be delivered from supernatural divine revelation. Furthermore, those things which can to some extent be known about God under the guidance of the light of nature, Theology does not consider as naturally known, but insofar as they have been supernaturally revealed. Thirdly, the formal end, and that the ultimate one, even if it be naturally known under a certain confused notion of blessedness, Theology nevertheless does not consider it so precisely under a confused notion, but according to its specific and proper notion, namely, insofar as it consists in the beatific vision of God: according to which notion it cannot be known from anywhere other than from divine revelation. Fourthly, in the subject of the operation, namely, man as a sinner, there are likewise contained certain things necessary to be known which are not accessible to the light of nature, such as that man was originally created in the image of God with justice and holiness, that by the transgression of the divine law he contracted sin, and that he propagated it through carnal generation to his entire posterity, that by nature he is dead to the good, a son of wrath, and guilty of eternal damnation, etc., the knowledge of which Theology again derives from divine revelation, just as it cannot be derived from anywhere else. Fifthly and finally, once the end and the subject of the operation are known from divine revelation, the principles and means by which the end is reached cannot yet be distinctly known, but these also must in good part be revealed in themselves, and be delivered and explained from divine revelation. For although from those things known, the worship due to God by reason of His essence and essential attributes, which the law of the Decalogue prescribes, can to some extent be known, nevertheless by what Mediator, by what ransom the divine justice, injured by sins, may be satisfied, the wrath of God against sins appeased, His lost grace recovered, and to Him the sinful man can and ought to be reconciled, can by no means be known or investigated from those things. For these do not depend, as the worship prescribed in the Decalogue does, upon the nature and divine attributes once known, but upon the free will of God, and can be known from nowhere else than from divine revelation. Wherefore Authors commonly constitute the formal object of Theology in the primary Truth and its revelation; but they call the revealed things themselves the material object, within the scope of which even the objective as well as the formal end itself, as also the subject of the operation, is contained. And not wrongly. For whatever Theology teaches and explains in signate act from another primarily known reason of knowing, and one proper to itself, it considers all those things as substrated things, and by way of a material object, not as the reason of knowing and the formal object. But it considers itself in this way, besides the principles and means, also the end and the subject.

Latin:

XXIII.

Subjectum considerationis sive objectum, ut in aliis scientiis omnibus, ita & in Theologia rectè distinguitur in materiale & formale. I. Scientiæ practicæ omnes duplex sibi vendicant subjectum: unum operationis; alterum considerationis. Operationis subjectum sibi vendicant, in quantum practicæ sunt. Operatio enim, scientiæ practicæ actibus directa, suâpte natura exigit subjectum, in quo exerceatur, aut circa quod ad finem perducendum occupetur. Considerationis subjectum verò vendicant sibi, in quantum scientiæ sunt. Scientia enim est rei scibilis scientia, & quemadmodum scire est rem cognoscere per suam causam, ita scientia omnis requirit aliquam rem, in qua cognoscenda, vel tradenda & explicanda occupetur, quæ ad differentiam subjecti, in quo operatio, actibus practicis scientiæ directa, peragitur, subjectum considerationis vel objectum cognitionis dicitur. Aristoteles I. Post. c. VII. vocat τὸ γένος τὸ ὑποκείμενον, genus subjectum, quod ita substernatur scientiæ, ut omnia, quæ sub ejus considerationem cadunt, sub se contineat, ut genus continet suas species, vel ut analogum sua analogata, vel saltem quòd ad illud cætera, quæ sub scientiæ considerationē cadunt, ordinentur, & cum eo quandam ordinis unitatem habeant.

II. Quia autem omnis scientia ex principiis quibusdam prioribus & notioribus oritur, & proptereà tùm scire dicimur rem, cùm ejus causam, per quam est, quòd ejus causa sit, quodque aliter se habere non possit, cognoscimus; scientia Theologica etiam sua certa principia, ex quibus cognitis rerum sibi subjectarum cognitionem accersat, sibi vendicet necesse est. Principia, ex quibus ipsa rerum cognitio accersitur, formale; res verò, quarum cognitio ex illis accersitur, materiale illius objectum constituunt.

XXIV.

Materiale objectum Theologiæ sunt res quæcunque, nostræ salutis causâ à Veritate prima revelatæ; formale est ipsa prima Veritas revelans, ut revelans.

I. In assignando Theologiæ subjecto considerationis Scholastici variant, quorum opiniones diversas recensere & expendere hujus loci non est. Constituunt tamen illud communiter in Deo, eâ ducti ratione, quod de Deo Theologia agat principaliter; de aliis autem rebus tantùm, in quantum ordinem ad Deum habent. Qua de re videatur Thomas p. I. q. 1. a. VII. Eo ipso autem, quo concedunt, Theologiam considerare, præter Deum, etiam alia, quamvis in ordine ad Deum, fateantur oportet, Deum non esse adæquatum Theologiæ subjectum considerationis, sed inadæquatum, ejusque partem perfectiorem, quam non incommodè subjectum perfectionis, & quòd cætera non nisi in ordine ad illud considerentur, subjectum attributionis dixeris.

II. Subjectum considerationis adæquatum igitur, sive objectum materiale adæquatum rectè constituuntur res omnes, nostræ salutis causâ à Veritate prima revelatæ, quæ licet non habeant inter se unitatem univocam, habent tamen inter se unitatem ordinis: quandoquidem ad Deum, velut hominis finem & bonum summum, omnia, quæ sub Theologiæ considerationem cadunt, referuntur, & sub una ratione formali considerantur. Quod sufficit ad hoc, ut quodammodo ἕν τὸ γένος τὸ ὑποκείμενον, unum genus subjectum sive subjectum considerationis adæquatum unum, constituant, & sub unius scientiæ Theologicæ considerationem cadant.

III. Objectum formale Theologiæ, si usitatam in scientiis practicis methodum sequi velimus, in ejus fine constituendum esset. Dicitur enim in unaquaque disciplina objectum formale, quod primò cognitum est ratio cognoscendi cætera, quæ in ea traduntur. In practicis autem scientiis quod omnium primò cognoscitur, & quod cognitum est ratio cognoscendi cætera, finis est. Cætera autem, quæ præter finem in disciplinis practicis considerantur, vel ad subjectum operationis pertinent, vel consequendi finis principia, causæ & media sunt, quæ ut ex fine cognito demum cognoscuntur, ita objectum materiale sive subjectum considerationis constitui solent. Sed in Theologia res secus habere videtur. Ea enim finem suum non ita ut notum supponit, quin sub alia prius cognita ratione cognoscendi, nempe sub Veritate prima revelante eum distinctè tradat, explicet, confirmet & defendat. Primùm enim Deus, ut Theologiæ & hominis finis objectivus est, præter essentiam & attributa essentialia, quæ ex lumine naturæ quodammodo nota sunt, continet etiam in se quædam lumini naturæ non obvia, cujusmodi sint, eum esse in essentia unum & in personis trinum, Filium Dei esse ex substantia Patris ab æterno genitum, esse ejusdem cum patre essentiæ, potentiæ, gloriæ & Majestatis; Spiritum S. procedere à Patre & Filio, esse unum cum utroque Deum, & quæ alia ad profundissimum S. S. Trinitatis mysterium explicandum pertinent. Quæ ut aliunde, quàm ex Dei revelatione supernaturali nobis innotescere non possunt, ita nec in Theologia, ut nota supponi possunt, sed ex Dei revelatione supernaturali tradenda veniunt. Deinde quæ ductu luminis naturæ de Deo cognosci quadantenus possunt, ea Theologia non considerat ut naturaliter nota, sed in quantum supernaturaliter revelata sunt. Tertiò finis formalis, isque ultimus, etsi sub ratione quadam confusa beatitudinis naturaliter notus sit, Theologia tamen non considerat eum ita præcisè sub ratione confusâ, sed secundum suam rationem specificam & propriam, prout scilicet in visione Dei beatifica consistit: secundum quam rationem aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione cognosci non potest. Quartò in subjecto operationis, homine peccatore scilicet, continentur similiter quædam cognitu necessaria, quæ lumini naturæ pervia non sunt, ut quòd primitùs homo conditus fuerit ad imaginem Dei cum justitia & sanctitate, quòd transgressione legis divinæ contraxerit peccatum, idque per carnalem generationem in posteritatem totam propagaverit, quòd naturâ emortuus sit ad bonum, filius iræ & damnationis æternæ reus &c. quorum cognitionem rursum Theologia ex divina revelatione accersit, sicut aliunde accersi non potest. Quintò denique cognitis ex divina revelatione fine & subjecto operationis, nondum distinctè cognosci possunt principia & media, quibus ad finem pervenitur, sed hæc etiam bonam partem secundum se revelari, & ex divina revelatione tradi & explicari oportet. Quamvis enim ex iis cognitis cultus, Deo ratione suæ essentiæ & attributorum essentialium debitus, quem lex Decalogi præscribit, quadantenus cognosci possit, tamen quo Mediatore, quo lytro justitiæ divinæ, peccatis læsæ, fieri satis, ira Dei adversus peccata placari, ejus gratia amissa recuperari, eique homo peccator reconciliari possit & debeat, ex illis cognosci aut investigari minimè potest. Haec enim non pendent perinde, ut cultus in Decalogo praescriptus, ex natura & attributis divinis cognitis, sed à Dei voluntate libera, nec aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione cognosci possunt. Quamobrem Auctores communiter objectum formale Theologiae constituunt in Veritate prima ejusque revelatione; materiale autem dicunt ipsas res revelatas, quarum ambitu etiam ipse cum objectivus tum formalis finis, ut & subjectum operationis, continetur. Neque malè. Quae enim Theologia ex alia primò cognitâ ratione cognoscendi, eâque sibi propriâ, in actu signato docet & explicat, ea omnia considerat ut res substratas, & per modum objecti materialis, non ut rationem cognoscendi & objectum formale. Ita autem considerat ipsa, praeter principia & media, etiam finem & subjectum.


### XXV. The formal object, since it consists in the primary Truth revealing, involves…

XXV.

The formal object, since it consists in the primary Truth revealing, involves two things: namely, the primary Truth, and the revelation of things proceeding from it, in the consideration of which Theology is occupied.

I. By primary Truth we understand with the Authors the truth of God, who as the being first and independent of all; so also His truth, which does not differ from His essence, is the first and independent Truth of all.

II. Primary Truth is spoken of among the Scholastics in three ways: one in being, another in knowing, and a third in speaking. Primary Truth in being, according to them, is the very independent essence of God, insofar as it is apt to terminate the true knowledge of itself. Primary Truth in knowing consists in the conformity of the divine intellect with the things which it knows, and is, as to the thing, the very independent essence of God, with the connoted knowledge, always conformable and true to things. Truth in speaking consists in the supreme veracity of God, by which through His infinite knowledge as well as goodness He can neither be deceived nor deceive in those things which He says or reveals. At present, when the formal object of Theology is established in the First Truth, the First Truth is taken in the third sense, namely for the First Truth in speaking.

III. Although the First Truth and God do not differ in reality, and are even accustomed to be taken promiscuously by authors, they differ, however, in the mode of signifying. For God signifies by way of a suppositum; the First Truth, however, by way of a form. The former stands to Theology as its formal object 'that which' (Quod). The latter as the formal reason, according to which God performs the function of the formal object in Theology, at least in our mode of conceiving it, is distinct from Him, and can be called the formal object or motive 'by which' (Quo) of Theology. For that by which God moves the intellect of man to the assent, to be elicited by the habit of Theology, is His own first and independent Truth or Veracity.

IV. That the revelation of the things which come into consideration is also included in the formal object of Theology, the thing itself speaks. For the First Truth performs the function of the formal object of Theology by testifying to the truth of the things about which it is occupied. But it does not testify about them except through revelation. Wherefore also, when asked why we offer assent to the doctrines handed down in Theology, we do not derive the cause from the First Truth alone, but from it and its revelation together, saying that we assent to it on account of the First Truth revealing, or because the First Truth revealed it, or on account of the revelation of the First Truth. For the First Truth revealing and the revelation of the First Truth do not differ except in the mode of signifying, while in the former expression the First Truth is enunciated in the nominative case; but revelation is connoted by way of a form adjacent to it; in the latter, however, revelation is enunciated in the nominative, with the First Truth connoted in the oblique case: by either phrase the reason of the formal object is constituted simultaneously in the First Truth and in the revelation: in the former indeed, as in a partial motive, so perfect by its intrinsic nature that it is entirely repugnant for falsehood to underlie it, on account of the infinite knowledge as well as goodness of God, through which He can neither be deceived nor deceive in speaking: in the latter, however, as in the other motive partial, to which it is no less repugnant, than to the primary Truth itself which is incapable of being deceived or deceiving, that a falsehood should be subject to it, on account of its dependence upon that. V. But we do not here take the word Revelation in that general sense, as we also warned at the beginning of this chapter, in which in Rom. I. 19, τὸ γνωσὸν τῶ θεῶ, that which can be known of God, is said to have been manifested by God to the Gentiles, namely for any manifestation of things made by God, even through nature, but in a stricter sense, for the supernatural manifestation of them. Which again is accustomed to be taken in a double sense: One narrower, yet most agreeable to the origin of the word, for the supernatural manifestation of hidden and occult things. For to reveal, in Greek ἀποκαλύπτειν, by the force of its origin, is to uncover and manifest things that are hidden and as it were lying under a certain veil. In which sense the Scriptures receive revelation in many places. See I. Cor. II. 10. Gal. I. 12. Matth. XI. 25. c. XIII. 11. c. XVI. 17. Rom. XVI. 25. Eph. III. 3. In the other, broader sense, for the manifestation of any things whatsoever, even those which can be known by the guidance of the light of nature, provided it is made supernaturally by God. In which way things are said to be supernaturally revealed, e.g., that God exists, that He is one, good, truthful, just, the avenger of crimes, and generally all things which are contained in the divinely inspired Scriptures. For since θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration is a certain species of supernatural revelation proceeding from God, and indeed the whole Holy Scripture is θεόπνευστος or divinely inspired, as Paul teaches in II. Tim. III. 16, it is not beside the point to say that whatever has been made manifest through the divinely inspired Scriptures is supernaturally revealed by God, whether it be otherwise known also from the light of nature, or less so. The former meaning, although it agrees most with the origin of the word, as has been said, is nevertheless not adequate to the present place and purpose. For Theology, simply so called, which we otherwise call Revealed in opposition to Natural Theology with the addition, is occupied not only in handing down those things which exceed the grasp of human reason, and are called mysteries hidden from the ages, but also in other things necessary to be known for salvation, which can also be known by the guidance of the light of nature, as will be taught later. Yet it does not hand them down, nor ought it to hand them down, otherwise than in so far as they are divinely revealed or manifested. In order, therefore, that the formal objective reason of Theology may be adequate, the thing itself demands that we accept divine revelation in the latter sense, just as it also includes under itself the supernatural manifestation of other things which fall under the light of nature. Whatever more could be taught here concerning divine revelation, we defer to the other part of our introduction, which will be concerning the first principle of knowing in Theology, where they may be seen.

Latin:

XXV.

Objectum formale, cùm in prima Veritate revelante consistat, involvit duo: Veritatem primam scilicet, & profectam ab ea revelationem rerum, in quarum consideratione Theologia occupatur.

I. Per Veritatem primam intelligimus cum Auctoribus veritatem Dei, qui ut ens omnium primum & independens; ita & ejus veritas, quae ab essentia ipsius non differt, omnium prima & independens Veritas est.

II. Dicitur autem apud Scholasticos Veritas prima tribus modis: uno in effendo, altero in cognoscendo, & tertio in dicendo. Veritas prima in effendo, juxta illos, est ipsa Dei independens essentia, quatenus veram sui cognitionem terminare apta est. Veritas prima in cognoscendo consistit in conformitate intellectus divini cum rebus, quas cognoscit, estque, quoad rem, ipsa Dei independens essentia, cum connotatâ cognitione, rebus semper conformi & verâ. Veritas in dicendo consistit in Dei veracitate summa, qua per suam infinitam cum scientiam tum bonitatem nec falli nec fallere potest in his, quae dicit sive revelat. Impraesentiarum cùm Theologiæ objectum formale constituitur in Veritate primâ, accipitur Veritas prima in significatu tertio, nempè pro Veritate prima in dicendo.

III. Quamvis verò Veritas prima & Deus, quoad rem, non differant, & ab Auctoribus etiam promiscuè accipi soleant; differunt tamen in modo significandi. Deus enim significat per modum suppositi; Veritas prima autem per modum formæ. Ille habet se ad Theologiam ut ejus objectum formale Quod. Hæc ut ratio formalis, secundum quam Deus objecti formalis munus in Theologia obit, saltem nostro modo concipiendi ab eo distincta, potestque Theologiæ objectum sive motivum formale Quo appellari. Id enim, quo Deus intellectum hominis ad asfensum, habitu Theologiæ eliciendum, movet, est ipsius prima & independens Veritas sive Veracitas.

IV. Quòd etiam revelatio rerum, quæ in considerationem veniunt, in Theologiæ objecto formali includatur, res ipsa loquitur. Veritas prima enim obit munus objecti formalis Theologiæ testificando de veritate rerum, circa quas occupatur. Non autem testificatur de issa, nisi per revelationem. Quamobrem etiam interrogati, cur traditæ in Theologia doctrinæ præbeamus asfensum, causam non accersimus à sola Veritate prima, sed ab illa & ejus revelatione simul, dicentes, nos asfentiri ei propter primam Veritatem revelantem, vel quia Veritas prima illam revelavit, sive propter revelationem Veritatis primæ. Non enim differunt Veritas prima revelans, & revelatio Veritatis primæ, nisi in modo significandi, dum in locutione priori Veritas prima in casu recto enunciatur; revelatio autem per modum formæ ei adjacentis connotatur; in posteriori autem revelatio in recto enunciatur, Veritate primâ in obliquo connotatâ: utrâque autem phrasi constituitur ratio objecti formalis simul in Veritate prima, & in revelatione: in issa quidem, ut in motivo partiali, suâ intrinsecâ naturâ ita perfecto, ut ei falsum subesse prorsus repugnet, ob infinitam Dei cùm scientiam tum bonitatem, per quam in dicendo nec falli nec fallere potest: in hac verò velut in altero motivo partiali, cui non minus, quàm ipsi primæ falli ac fallere nesciæ Veritati, repugnat subesse falsum, ob suam ab illa dependentiam. V. Revelationis vocem verò, ut etiam sub initium hujus capitis monuimus, heîc non eo generali accipimus significatu, quo Rom. I. 19. τὸ γνωσὸν τῶ θεῶ, quod de Deo cognosci potest, Deum Gentibus patefecisse dicitur, nempe pro qualibet rerum à Deo, etiam per naturam, facta manifestatione, sed strictiori, pro manifestatione illarum supernaturali. Quæ rursum accipi solet in significatu duplici: Uno angustiori, vocis origini tamen maximè congruo, pro rerum latentium & occultarum manifestatione supernaturali. Revelare enim, Græcè ἀποκαλύπτειν, vi originis, est occulta & quasi sub quodam velamine latentia retegere & manifestare. Quo significatu revelationem Scripturæ passim locorum accipiunt. Videatur I. Cor. II. 10. Gal. I. 12. Matth. XI. 25. c. XIII. 11. c. XVI. 17. Rõ. XVI. 25. Eph. III. 3. Altero latiori, pro rerum quarumvis, etiam quæ ductu luminis naturæ cognosci possunt, manifestatione, modo supernaturali à Deo factâ. Quomodo supernaturaliter revelata dicuntur, v. g. Deum esse, ipsum esse unum, bonum, veracem, justum, scelerum vindicem, & generatim omnia, quæ in Scripturis divinitùs inspiratis continentur. Cùm enim θεοπνευσία sive inspiratio divina sit species quædam profecta à Deo revelationis supernaturalis, & verò tota Scriptura Sacra θεόπνευστος sive divinitùs inspirata sit, docente Paulo II. Tim. III. 6. non præter rem dicitur supernaturaliter à Deo revelatum, quicquid per inspiratas divinitùs Scripturas patefactum est, sive aliàs etiam ex lumine natæ notum sit, sive minus. Prior significatio, licet origini vocis maximè, uti dictum, conveniat, loco tamen & instituto præsenti adæquata non est. Theologia enim, simpliciter sic dicta, quam aliàs in oppositione ad Theologiam Naturalem cum apposito Revelatam dicimus, non tantùm in iis tradendis occupatur, quæ humanæ rationis captum excedunt, & mysteria, inde à seculis abscondita dicuntur, sed etiam in aliis ad salutem cognitu necessariis, quæ etiam ductu luminis naturæ cognosci possunt, ut posteà docebitur. Non tamen ea aliter tradit aut tradere debet, quàm in quantum divinitùs revelata sive manifestata sunt. Ut ergo ratio objectiva formalis Theologiæ adæquata sit, res ipsa exigit, ut revelationem divinam in significatu posteriori accipiamus, prout etiam aliarum rerum, quæ sub lumen naturæ cadunt, manifestationem supernaturalem sub se comprehendit. Quæ plura de revelatione divinâ hîc tradi poterant, rejicimus ad alteram introductionis nostræ partem, quæ erit de Theologiæ principio cognoscendi primo, ubi videantur.


### XXVI The material object is customarily distinguished into things to be believed and things to be done

XXVI.

The material object is customarily distinguished into things to be believed and things to be done.

I. The distinction, however, is not adequate. For things to be done, by the very fact that they are supernaturally revealed, are also things to be believed; and conversely, those things which come into the category of things to be believed are not considered in Theology for the sake of mere speculation, but are also referred in their own way to practice, as shown above. The distinction is therefore inadequate, and they are called things to be believed because they are so subject to faith that they are not formally operations directed by prior practical acts. But they are called things to be done because, although they themselves are also divinely revealed and to be believed on account of divine revelation, they are formally actions prescribed and directed by the prior acts of Theology, or things to be transferred to operation or to be obtained through operation.

II. By things to be believed here we do not mean whatever deserves faith, but what is necessary to be believed by those about to attain salvation: nor do we call things to be done those which for any reason are incumbent upon man to do, but those which, if not for the sake of attaining salvation, yet so that we do not fall from salvation, have been instituted and commanded by God to be done. For in Scripture, divinely inspired, there are found scattered and mixed histories and various matters, to be believed indeed by the very fact that they are contained in it, but which carry no relation to our salvation. Many things to be done also occur in the Scriptures which likewise are not ordered toward the eternal salvation of man, and therefore do not come into the category of the material object of Theology, unless perhaps indirectly and by accident, in so far as in some indirect and accidental manner they can be referred to the salvation of man. For in practical sciences the breadth of the object is to be estimated from the end of Theology, but the end, and that the ultimate one, is the salvation of men, as shown above: to which therefore, in their own way, whatever is delivered in it in itself and in the designated act ought to be ordered and referred.

XXVII.

Things to be believed and things to be done are of a twofold difference. Some are so subject to divine revelation that they are also accessible to the light of nature; others cannot be known without divine revelation.

I. Things to be believed of the first order are that God exists, that He is one, good, truthful, just, merciful, etc. Things to be done of this kind are the love of God and neighbor, the fear of God, the invocation of Him, thanksgiving for benefits received, and other actions prescribed in the Decalogue, which are so revealed and commanded by God in the Scriptures that they are also known and commanded by the power of the light of nature.

II. Things to be believed of the latter order are that God is one in essence and triune in persons, that Christ is God and man in one undivided person, that He is the Son of God, begotten from the substance of the Father from eternity; and the Son of man, born of Mary, the undefiled Virgin, etc. Things to be done of this kind are, for example, the apprehension of the merit of Christ, trust in obtaining grace and the remission of sins from God, fixed upon Him, the love of Christ θεανθρώπꙋ above all things, the hope of obtaining eternal salvation through Him, the administration and use of the sacraments according to the prescription of divine institution, etc., which consist in actions instituted by the free will of God, and those supernatural: the knowledge of which therefore comes to us from divine revelation alone.

Latin:

XXVI.

OBjectum materiale distinguitur usitatè in credenda & agenda.

I. Distinctio tamen adæquata non est. Agenda enim eo ipso, quod supernaturaliter revelata sunt, credenda etiam sunt; & contrà quæ in credendorum partem veniunt, non nudæ speculationis causâ in Theologia considerantur, sed referuntur etiam suo modo ad praxin, ut suprà ostensum. Est ergo inadæquata distinctio, & dicuntur credenda, quòd ita subsint fidei, ut formaliter non sint operationes, præviis actibus practicis directæ. Agenda autem dicuntur, quòd licet & ipsa divinitùs revelata & propter divinam revelationem credenda sint, formaliter tamen sint actiones, præviis Theologiæ actibus præscriptæ & directæ, vel res ad operationem transferendæ aut per operationem obtinendæ.

II. Credenda hîc dicimus, non quæcunque merentur fidem, sed quæ salutem adepturis creditu necessaria sunt: nec agenda dicimus, quæ quacunque de causâ homini agenda incumbunt, sed quæ si non consequendæ salutis causâ, tamen ne salute excidamus, à Deo ut agantur, instituta & præcepta sunt. In Scriptura enim, divinitus inspirata, reperiuntur sparsim admixtæ historiæ & res variæ, eo ipso quidem quòd in ea continentur, credendæ, sed quæ ad nostram salutem nullam important habitudinem. Multa etiam agenda in Scripturis occurrunt, quæ itidem ad hominis salutem æternam non ordinantur, & proptereà in partem objecti materialis Theologiæ non veniunt, nisi forsan indirectè & per accidens, in quantum scilicet aliquâ ratione indirectâ & accidentali ad hominis salutem referri possunt. In scientiis practicis enim latitudo objecti æstimanda est ex fine Theologiæ, finis autem, isque ultimus, est hominum salus, ut supra ostensum: ad quam proinde suo modo ordinari & referri debent, quæcunque in ea per se & in actu signato traduntur.

XXVII.

Credenda & agenda in duplici sunt differentia. Quædam ita divinæ subsunt revelationi, ut etiam lumini naturæ pervia sint; alia citra divinam revelationem cognosci nequeunt.

I. Prioris ordinis credenda sunt, Deum esse, eum esse unum, bonum, veracem, justum, misericordem &c. Agenda hujus generis sunt dilectio Dei & proximi, timor Dei, invocatio ejus, gratiarum actio pro beneficiis acceptis, & cæteræ in Decalogo præscriptæ actiones, quæ ita à Deo in Scripturis revelatæ & præceptæ sunt, ut etiam vi luminis naturæ notæ & præceptæ sint.

II. Posterioris ordinis credenda sunt, Deum in essentia unum esse trinum in personis, Christum esse Deum & hominem in una indivisa persona, esse filium Dei, ex substantia Patris ab æterno genitum; & filium hominis, ex Maria, Virgine illibata, natum &c. Agenda hujus generis sunt v. g. apprehensio meriti Christi, fiducia impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum, in eo defixa, dilectio Christi θεανθρώπꙋ super omnia, spes obtinendæ per eum salutis æternæ, sacramentorum administratio & usurpatio ad præscriptum institutionis divinæ &c. quæ in actionibus, Dei liberâ voluntate institutis, iisque supernaturalibus, consistunt: quorum cognitio proinde ex sola revelatione divina nobis obtingit.


### XXIIX. Theology indeed claims for itself to be considered both things to be believed…

XXIIX.

Theology indeed claims for itself to be considered both things to be believed and things to be done of either order; but those which pertain to the latter class, absolutely and simply; those which pertain to the former, at least in a certain respect, namely in so far as they have been revealed by the primary Truth.

I. The reason is: because those things which pertain to the latter class fall under no other principle of knowing than divine Revelation, which is the formal object and proper principle of knowing of Theology so called κατʼ ἐξοχὴν. But those things which are of the former order fall under a double principle of knowing: one placed in the light of nature, the other in divine revelation, of which the former is the formal object and proper principle of knowing of natural theology, the latter of revealed. However, just as the consideration of any discipline extends no further than its formal object, so Theology, regarding those things which can be known naturally about God and His worship, cannot claim them for itself simply and according to every principle by which they can be known, but only according to the principle of knowing proper to it, namely divine revelation, and in so far as they become known through it. Otherwise Theology would be confused with Philosophy and with Natural Theology, which constitutes a part of it, and a μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος would be committed.

II. That Theology also claims for itself, essentially and in the abstract, the objects of the former order, namely those which can be known naturally about God and His worship, is evident from the fact that they have an essential relation to its end, namely the eternal salvation of men. For some of them are such that, unless they are known and believed, faith in the others necessary for salvation cannot be had: e.g., unless you believe that God exists, that He is a rewarder of the good and an avenger of crimes (which the light of nature teaches), you will not be able to believe that God, having pity on the human race fallen into sin, sent His only-begotten Son, that He might make satisfaction for our sins in assumed flesh; that on account of the merit of Christ He will freely forgive sins to those who believe, and will grant eternal salvation to those persevering in faith in Christ and in holiness of life; but will condemn those persisting in sins to eternal torments, etc. To which the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews refers, when in ch. XI. 6, he says: Without faith, it is impossible to please God. For he who approaches God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him. Similarly, those things which by moral or natural law are prescribed to be done have such an order toward the end of Theology, namely the salvation of men, that if one does not do them or does the contrary, he falls from salvation and incurs eternal damnation. It is, however, common to all practical disciplines that those things which are ordered in themselves toward the end intended through them, and are necessary to be known or done by one who is to attain that end, they deliver in themselves and in the designated act.

III. Nor is there any reason why anyone should object that these things, by the very fact that they are known from the light of nature, should be presupposed in Theology as revealed, as known, but not delivered by design. For why they ought to be delivered in this also under their own proper reason for being known, namely divine revelation, in the designated act, besides the reason already adduced, many other causes are available.

For first, those things which are necessary to be known or done by one who is to attain eternal salvation must be proposed and delivered in such a way that they can be apprehended and known by man as soon as he can use his reason. For man is at any age subject to death, and therefore also at any age at which he can indeed use his reason, he ought to have in readiness those things which are necessary to be known for attaining salvation, or to be done so that he does not fall from it, so that whenever he must die, he may die happily. But those things which are necessary to be known for attaining salvation, although they may be in part obvious to the light of nature, are not so at every age at which a man can use his reason. For science, to which it pertains to prove that God exists and other things of this kind about God, is proposed to be learned by men last, with many other things presupposed: so that if those things which are necessary to be known about God were to be approached from the light of nature alone and arguments sought from there, man would not arrive at the knowledge of God until after a long time of his life. The words are those of Thomas in II. II. q. II. a. II. Children can indeed in a still tender age be imbued by parents and teachers with some knowledge of God and divine things: but this knowledge, such as it is, as it relies only on human testimony, is not certain and indubitable, but is opinion or human faith, which does not exclude the fear of the opposite: but for salvation, a certain and indubitable knowledge of God is required.

Furthermore, just as salvation ought to be for all: for God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. II. 4, so it is the task of Theology to instruct men of every condition in it. However, not all are capable of demonstrations deduced from the light of nature. For many, whether through slowness of wit, or through age, or hindered by occupations and the necessities of temporal life, cannot penetrate to them. Thirdly, human reason is quite weak in investigating the knowledge of God, and often wanders from the right path in its διαλογισμοῖς. This is taught even by the examples of the most learned among the Gentile philosophers. For not one of them is found who has correctly and without error penetrated into the knowledge of all things which can in some way be known and demonstrated about God by the reason of nature. But the promiscuous multitude of the Gentiles wandered so far from the right path that, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, but were frustrated by their own διαλογισμοὺς and their foolish heart was darkened, and they changed the glory of the immortal God for an image made not only in the likeness of mortal man, but also of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things, Rom. I. 21, seqq. But those things which are necessary to be believed for salvation must be so obvious that they can be known by all certainly and without errors. It is necessary, therefore, that in Theology they be handed down and proposed to be believed from divine revelation in a plain style of speech and doctrine accommodated to the grasp of all, so that all indiscriminately may be led into a certain and undefiled knowledge of them. Thomas has embraced these causes of necessity in a few words in p. I. q. I. a. I. To those things, he says, which can be investigated about God by human reason, it was necessary for man to be instructed by divine revelation: because the truth about God investigated by reason would come to man by few, and over a long time, and with the admixture of many errors: yet upon the knowledge of this truth depends the whole salvation of man, which is in God. Therefore, in order that salvation might come to men more conveniently and more certainly, it was necessary that they be instructed about divine things through divine revelation. The same causes of necessity are repeated and more fully deduced in II. II. q. II. a. IV., where they may be seen.

IV. But when something can be said to be necessary both with regard to the end and the subject, and indeed with regard to the end either for its simple existence, or at least for its well-being; but with regard to the subject, either to individual men, or to the same taken universally, or to the whole community; Cajetan in I. Thomas q. I. a. I. judges that it was and is necessary that those things which can be known naturally about God should be revealed in a supernatural way, and be handed down in Theology under divine revelation, with regard to the end indeed only for its well-being; but with regard to the subject, not for individual men, but for all, or only for the Community, relying primarily on the words of Thomas cited, in which he thinks it is implied by the comparatives (more conveniently and more certainly) that salvation can indeed be obtained by men without supernatural revelation of those things which can be known naturally about God, but less certainly, and less conveniently, and that it is therefore necessary for the whole community or the Church, that in its assemblies they should be handed down also under divine revelation by the aid of Theology, so that salvation might be obtained more conveniently and more certainly by those who, through age or dullness of intellect, or through the kind of life to which they are devoted, are not capable of philosophical demonstrations. But the reasons of Thomas adduced, especially the first and third, prove entirely that this is necessary simply, and not only with regard to the community, but also to individuals. For it is in the interest of all and of each for their salvation that there should exist publicly a doctrine, and one that is certain and knows not how to deceive or be deceived, by which we may be able to use reason quickly and at the same time to arrive at a certain and indubitable knowledge of God, especially since the nature of all and of each has been so corrupted by sin that the intellect, even in those things which are most manifest, is blinded like the eyes of owls to the light of the sun; but the will, by nature turned away from God, leans entirely toward earthly things and those which are alien to the truth of God. Let those things be seen which Gabriel Vazquez discusses well on this matter, in p. 1. Thomas Disp. I. c. II. where he also, among other things, responds not badly to the words of Thomas, cited from 1. q. 1. a. 1. (which Cajetan urges for his own opinion), that although they are comparatives, they should nevertheless be taken in a positive sense, and he shows this from II.II. q. II. a. IV.: where he expresses the same thing of Thomas in words of the positive degree: Therefore, saying, so that there might be indubitable

and certain knowledge among men concerning God, it was necessary that divine things should be delivered to them by way of faith.

Latin:

XXIIX.

Theologia quidem consideranda sibi vendicat utriusque ordinis cùm credenda tùm agenda; sed quæ ad classem posteriorem pertinent, absolutè & simpliciter; quæ ad priorem, secundum quid saltem, in quantum scilicet à Veritate prima revelata sunt.

I. Ratio est: quia ad posteriorem classem quæ pertinent, sub nullam aliam cadunt rationem cognoscendi, quàm sub divinam Revelationem, quæ solius κατʼ ἐξοχὴν sic dictæ Theologiæ objectum formale & ratio cognoscendi propria est. Quæ verò priori ex ordine sunt, sub duplicem cadunt rationem cognoscendi: Unam in lumine naturæ; alteram in divina revelatione positam, quarum illa Theologiæ naturalis; hæc revelatæ objectum formale & ratio cognoscendi propria est. Quemadmodum autem cujusque disciplinæ consideratio non longiùs, quàm ejus objectum formale, se porrigit, ita Theologia quæ naturaliter de Deo ejusque cultu cognosci possunt, non potest sibi vendicare simpliciter & secundum omnem rationem, secundum quam cognosci possunt, sed tantùm secundum rationem cognoscendi sibi propriam, divinam revelationem scilicet, & in quantum per eam innotescunt. Aliàs Theologia cum Philosophia &, quæ ejus partem constituit, Theologia Naturali confunderetur, & μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος committeretur.

II. Quod etiam prioris ordinis objecta, quæ scilicet de Deo ejusque cultu naturaliter cognosci possunt, Theologia per se & in actu signato sibi consideranda vendicet, vel inde patet, quòd per se ordinem habent ad ejus finem, hominum salutem æternam scilicet. Quædam enim illorum ita se habent, ut nisi cognita & credita fuerint, cæterorum ad salutem creditu necessariorum fides haberi non possit: v. g. nisi credideris, Deum esse, eum esse remuneratorem bonorum, & vindicem scelerum (quæ lumen naturæ docet) nec credere poteris, Deum prolapsi in peccatum generis humani misertum, misisse filium suum unigenitum, ut in assumta carne pro peccatis nostris satisfaceret; eum propter Christi meritum credentibus peccata gratis remissurum, & perseverantibus in fide in Christum & sanctimonia vitæ salutem æternam impertiturum; persistentes autem in peccatis ad cruciatus æternos damnaturum &c. Quò respicit Auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos, quando c. XI. 6. Sine fide, inquit, impossibile est Deo placere. Accedentem enim ad Deum credere oportet, eum esse, & remuneratorem esse eorum, qui ipsum requirunt. Similiter quæ lege morali sive naturæ agenda præcipiuntur, ad Theologiæ finem, salutem hominum scilicet, eum habent ordinem, ut si ea non agat aut contraria agat, salute excidat, damnationemque æternam incurrat. Est autem disciplinis practicis omnibus commune, ut quæ ad finem, per eas intentum, per se ordinantur, & adepturo illum cognitu factuve necessaria sunt, per se & in actu signato tradant.

III. Neque est, quod quis excipiat, ea hoc ipso quod ex lumine naturæ nota sunt, in Theologia revelata supponenda esse, ut nota, non autem ex instituto tradenda. Cur enim in hac etiam sub sua ratione cognoscendi propria, divina revelatione scilicet, in actu signato tradi debeant, præter jam adductam, aliæ plures causæ suppetunt.

Primùm enim quæ salutem æternam adepturo cognitu factuve necessaria sunt, debent ita proponi & tradi, ut ab homine, simul ac ratione sua uti potest, apprehendi & cognosci possint. Est enim homo ætate quavis obnoxius morti, & propterea etiam ætate quâvis, quâ quidem ratione sua uti potest, in promtu habere debet, quæ ad salutem consequendam cognitu, vel ne illa excidat, factu necessaria sunt, quò quandocunque sibi moriendum fuerit, mori beatè possit. Sed quæ ad consequendam salutem cognitu necessaria sunt, licet naturæ lumini ex parte obvia sint, non tamen quâvis ætate, quâ sua ratione homo uti potest. Scientia enim, ad quam pertinet probare Deum esse, & alia hujusmodi de Deo, ultimo hominibus addiscenda proponitur, præsuppositis multis aliis: ut sic, si ex solo lumine naturæ & hinc petitis argumentis accessenda essent, quæ de Deo cognitu sunt necessaria, non nisi post multum tempus vitæ suæ homo ad Dei cognitionem perventurus esset. Verba sunt Thomæ in II. II. q. II. a. II. Possunt quidem in ætate adhuc tenera liberi à parentibus & præceptoribus aliqua Dei & divinorum cognitione imbui: sed hæc qualiscunque cognitio, ut humana tantùm testificatione nititur, ita certa & indubitata non est, sed opinio vel fides humana, quæ formidinem oppositi non excludit: ad salutem autem requiritur certa & indubitata Dei cognitio.

Deinde quemadmodum salus debet esse omnium: Deus enim vult omnes salvos fieri & ad veritatis agnitionem pervenire, 1. Tim. II. 4. ita Theologiae est cujuscunque conditionis homines ad eam erudire. Demonstrationum autem, ex lumine naturae deductarum, non omnes capaces sunt. Multi enim vel per tarditatem ingenii, vel per aetatem, vel per occupationes & vitae temporalis necessitates impediti ad eas penetrare non possunt. Tertio ratio humana in investiganda cognitione Dei admodum debilis est, & saepe in suis διαλογισμοῖς a recto tramite aberrat. Quod vel doctissimorum inter gentiles Philosophorum exempla docent. Neque enim quisquam illorum reperitur, qui recte &amp; absque errore penetraverit in notitiam omnium, quae ratione naturae de Deo quodammodo cognosci & demonstrari possunt. Promiscua autem Gentilium multitudo usque adeo aberravit a recto tramite, ut licet Deum cognoscerent, non tamen ut Deum glorificarent, sed frustrati per suos διαλογισμοὺς obtenebratique nesciente corde suo, mutarent gloriam immortalis Dei per imaginem non solum ad similitudinem mortalis hominis effictam, verum etiam volatilium, & quadrupedum & reptilium, Rom. I. 21. seqq. Quae autem ad salutem creditu necessaria sunt, debent ita esse obvia, ut certo & sine erroribus cognosci ab omnibus possint. Necesse igitur est, ut in Theologia ex divina revelatione plano & omnium captui accommodato sermonis & doctrinae genere tradantur, & credenda proponantur, quo promiscue omnes in certam & intemeratam illorum notitiam perduci possint. Quas necessitatis causas paucis complexus est Thomas in p. I. q. I. a. I. Ad ea, inquiens, quae de Deo ratione humana investigari possunt, necessarium fuit hominem instrui revelatione divina: quia veritas de Deo per rationem investigata, a paucis & per longum tempus, & cum admixtione multorum errorum homini proveniret: a cujus tamen veritatis cognitione dependet tota hominis salus, quae in Deo est. Ut igitur salus hominibus convenientius & certius proveniat, necessarium fuit, quod de divinis per divinam revelationem instruerentur. Eaedem necessitatis causae repetitae & uberius deductae sunt in II. II. q. II. a. IV. ubi videantur.

IV. Cùm verò necessarium quippiam dici possit cùm finis tùm subjecti intuitu, & quidem finis intuitu vel ad esse ejus simpliciter, vel saltem ad benè esse illius; subjecti intuitu autem, vel hominibus singulis, vel iisdem universè sumtis, sive toti communitati; Cajetanus in I. Thomæ q. I. a. I. censet, ut quæ de Deo naturaliter cognosci possunt, modo supernaturali revelarentur, & in Theologia sub divina revelatione tradantur, fuisse & esse necessarium, ex parte finis quidem tantùm ad benè esse illius; ex parte subjecti verò, non singulis hominibus, sed universis, sive Communitati tantùm, nixus cumprimis verbis Thomæ allegatis, in quibus per comparativos,(convenientius & certius) innui existimat, salutem posse quidem hominibus obtingere absq; supernaturali revelatione illorũ, quæ naturaliter de Deo cognosci possunt, sed minùs certè, minúsque convenienter, & esse proinde toti communitati sive Ecclesiæ necessarium, ut in ejus conventibus Theologiæ adminiculo etiam sub divina revelatione tradantur, quò convenientius & certius salus obtingeret his, qui per ætatem aut ingenii hebetudinem, vel per vitæ genus, cui vacant, demonstrationum Philosophicarum capaces non sunt. Verùm adductæ Thomæ rationes, præsertim prima & tertia, evincunt omninò, id esse simpliciter, nec solùm communitatis, sed etiam singulorum intuitu, necessarium. Interest enim omnium & singulorum salutis, ut publicè extet doctrina, eaque certa fallique & fallere nescia, quâ citò & simulac ratione uti poterimus, ad certam & indubitatam Dei cognitionem pertingamus, præsertim cùm omnium & singulorum natura per peccatum usque adeò sit corrupta, ut intellectus in iis etiam quæ manifestissima sunt, velut noctuarum oculi ad solis lumen, caliget; voluntas autem, à Deo aversa naturâ, in terrena & quæ à veritate Dei aliena sunt, tota propendeat. Videantur quæ hanc in rem benè disserit Gabriel Vazquez, in p. 1. Thomæ Disp. I. c. II. ubi etiam ad verba Thomæ, ex 1. q. 1. a. 1. citata, (quæ pro sua opinione Cajetanus urget) inter alia non malè respondet, quòd licet comparativa sint, accipienda tamen sint sensu positivo, idq; ex II.II. q. II. a. IV. ostendit: ubi Thomæ rem eandē verbis positivi gradus exprimit: Ut ergo, inquiens, esset indubitata

& certa cognitio apud homines de Deo, oportuit, quòd divina eis per modum fidei traderentur.


### XXX. Things to be believed, which can become known to us from no other source than…

XXX.

Things to be believed, which can become known to us from no other source than divine revelation, are called mysteries of faith; and the doctrines of the Christian religion which contain those things are called articles of faith.

I. Articles and mysteries of faith differ as assertions or enunciations constituting a part of Christian doctrine, and the things underlying them.

(1) Mysteries, according to the usage of speech, are called arcane, abstruse things, not at all accessible to human reason, and in the Scriptures of the New Testament this word is frequently used concerning the restoration of our salvation through the only-begotten Son of God, made man for its sake, crucified, dead, and resurrected from death: which is the most abstruse of all things, and so hidden from human reason that, when revealed and preached by the Apostles, it was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, 1 Cor. 1:23. But Paul in the same place, v. 24, calls it the wisdom of God, by a metonymy of the cause for the effect, because it was decreed and established by the most wise counsel of God from eternity that thus, and not otherwise, salvation lost through the fall of our first parents should be restored to us. Wherefore he immediately adds that it is the wisdom in a mystery (latent), that hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages for our glory. Compare Rom. 16:25. However, the word mystery is also read as applied to other abstruse things pertaining to religion and faith, as in Eph. 5:32 concerning the spiritual union of Christ with the Church, Rom. 11:25 concerning the blindness and conversion of the Jews, Eph. 3:4 ff. concerning the calling of the Gentiles, 1 Cor. 15:51 concerning the resurrection of the dead and the sudden transformation of those whom the final day will find alive, etc., 1 Cor. 4:1 concerning the whole doctrine of the Gospel and the sacraments annexed to it. The ancient Fathers sometimes used the same word specifically for the Sacraments. Today, however, by usage accepted in the Church, all things are called mysteries which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, in such a way that they cannot be known by us from any other source than divine revelation.

(2) The word articuli, however, whether derived from the Greek ἄρθρον, i.e., a member, or from arctando [to bind together], according to Thomas II. II. q. I. a. IV., signifies a certain fitting together of some distinct parts: and therefore the particles of the body fitted to one another are called the joints of the members, e.g., the parts of the fingers, clinging together in a tight bond, are called the joints of the fingers.

By metaphor, however, transferred to the doctrine of faith, it denotes parts of the doctrine of faith or assertions concerning matters divinely revealed for the sake of our salvation, so tightly connected among themselves that if one is removed, the others cannot remain safe and sound. They are called articles of faith, with the word faith taken for the doctrine of faith, so that articles of faith are the same as articles or parts of the doctrine of faith.

(3) Therefore, mysteries and articles of faith differ as things abstruse, revealed to us for the sake of our salvation, and the assertions or enunciations by which those things are enunciated and proposed to the intellect to be known.

II. For an article of faith, it is usually required: 1. That it be about a non-evident matter. For faith is of things not appearing, and thus non-evident, Heb. XI. 1. 2. That it be divinely revealed. For divine revelation is of the essence of the doctrine of faith, and the formal object of faith. 3. That it import a necessary relationship to the salvation of men, and consequently be a part of Christian doctrine, necessary to be believed for salvation.

By the first requirement, those parts of doctrine are excluded from the census of articles of faith which, although delivered in the Holy Scriptures and thereby divinely revealed, and even importing a necessary relationship to the salvation of men, are nevertheless in themselves evident and can be investigated and known by the guidance of the light of nature: such as, that God exists, that He is one, truthful, good, the avenger of crimes, etc., which the usage of speech does not reckon among the articles of faith in the same way as the other non-evident parts of Christian doctrine, without doubt because they do not fall under faith absolutely and simply, but only in a certain respect, insofar, namely, as they fall under divine revelation. Thomas in I. q. II. a. II. ad I. calls them preambles to the articles of faith, because the Christian faith presupposes their knowledge, just as grace presupposes nature. By the second requirement, all doctrines not divinely revealed are excluded from the class of articles of faith, which, by the very fact that they are not revealed, do not fall under faith. By the third, truths are excluded from the census of articles of faith which, although divinely revealed, do not carry a necessary relationship to the salvation of men: such are histories and various matters contained in the Scriptures, and questions that emerge concerning the doctrine of faith, which can be ignored or disputed on either side while salvation remains intact, provided malice is absent.

III. Others, however, take articles of faith in a broader sense, and just as every assent resting upon divine revelation, on the part of the formal object, is non-evident and an assent of faith, so under the name of articles of faith they include also those parts of Christian doctrine which can be known naturally about God, not indeed insofar as they are naturally known and evident, but insofar as they are subject to divine revelation and are to be believed on account of it. In this they have as a predecessor the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews c. XI. 6, saying: Without faith, it is impossible to please (God). For he who approaches God must believe that He is (God) and that He is a rewarder to those who seek Him. Nor do all understand in one way the necessity which articles of faith carry for the salvation of men. Some understand an absolute necessity, and require for an article of faith that it be so necessary to be believed for salvation that it cannot even be ignored while salvation remains intact. Others, on the contrary, think it sufficient for an article of faith if it is so necessary that it cannot be denied while salvation remains intact, although it may be ignored by the simpler sort without the loss of salvation.
