IV. Just as some extend or restrict the concept of articles of faith more than others, so they make more or fewer articles of faith, although the disagreement seems to concern the manner of speaking rather than the thing itself.

Latin:

XXX.

Credenda, quæ non aliunde, quàm ex divinâ revelatione nobis innotescere possunt, mysteria fidei; &, quæ illa continent, doctrinæ christianæ partes articuli fidei dicuntur.

I. Differunt articuli, & mysteria fidei, ut assertiones, vel enuntiationes, doctrinæ Christianæ partem constituentes, & res, eis substratæ.

(1) Mysteria, ex usu loquendi, dicuntur res arcanæ, abstrusæ, humanæ rationi haud perviæ, & in Scripturis N. T. usurpatur vox hæc frequenter de reparatione salutis nostræ per Filium Dei unigenitum, ejus causâ hominem factum, crucifixum, mortuum, & ex morte resuscitatum: quæ rerum omnium abstrusissima, & humanæ rationi usque adeò abscondita est, ut ab Apostolis patefacta & prædicata Judæis scandalo, Græcis stultitia esset, 1. Cor. I. 23. Paulus verò ibidem v. 23. vocat eam Dei sapientiam, per metonymiam causæ pro causato, quòd Dei sapientissimo consilio ab æterno decretum & constitutum fuerit, ut sic, non aliter, salus per lapsum protoplastorum amissa, nobis repararetur. Quamobrem subjungit statim, esse sapientiam in mysterio (latentem) occultam illam, quam præfinierat Deus ante secula ad gloriam nostram. Confer Rom. XVI. 25. Legitur tamen mysterii vox etiam de aliis rebus abstrusis, ad religione & fidem pertinentibus adhibita, ut Eph. V. 32. de spirituali conjunctione Christi cum Ecclesia, Rom. XI. 25. de excæcatione & conversione Judæorum, Eph. III. 4. seqq. de vocatione gentium, I. Cor. XV. 51. de resurrectione mortuorum, & eorum, quos dies extremus vivos deprehendet, subitanea mutatione &c. I. Cor. IV. 1. de tota doctrina Evangelii & annexis ei sacramentis. Patres veteres voce eâdem specialiter nonnunquam usi sunt de Sacramentis. Hodiè autem usu, in Ecclesia recepto, mysteria dicuntur omnia, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, ita, ut aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione, à nobis cognosci non possint.

(2) Articuli vox autem sive a Graeco ἄρθρον, i. e. membrum, sive ab arctando derivata, juxta Thomam II. II. q. I. a. IV. significat quandam coaptationem aliquarum partium distinctarum: & ideo particulae corporis sibi invicem coaptatae dicuntur membrorum articuli, v. g. digitorum partes, arcto nexu cohaerentes, dicuntur articuli digitorum.

Per metaphoram vero ad doctrinam fidei translata denotat partes doctrinae fidei sive assertiones de rebus, nostrae salutis causa divinitus patefactis, ita arcto inter se connexas, ut una demta caeterae falvae & incolumes esse non possint. Dicuntur articuli fidei, fidei voce pro doctrina fidei accepta, ut articuli fidei idem sint, atque articuli sive partes doctrinae fidei.

(3) Differunt ergo mysteria & articuli fidei, ut res abstrusae, nostrae salutis causa nobis patefactae; & assertiones sive enunciationes, quibus res illae enunciantur, & intellectui cognoscendae proponuntur.

II. Ad articulum fidei requi solet 1. Ut sit de re inevidente. Fides enim est rerum non apparentium, atque adeo inevidentium, Ebr. XI. 1. 2. Ut sit divinitus revelatus. Nam revelatio divina est de ratione doctrinae fidei, & fidei objectum formale. 3. Ut habitudinem necessariam importet ad hominum salutem, & proinde doctrinae Christianae pars sit, ad salutem creditu necessaria.

Per primum requisitum excluduntur ex censu articulorum fidei illae doctrinae partes, quae in Scripturis Sacris quidem traditae, & per hoc divinitus patefactae sunt, quin & ad salutem hominum necessariam habitudinem important, in se tamen evidentes sunt, & ductu luminis naturae investigari & cognosci possunt: cujusmodi sunt, Deum esse, eum esse unum, veracem, bonum, scelerum vindicem &c. quas usus loquendi non perinde, ut caeteras inevidentes doctrinae Christianae partes, articulis fidei accenset, dubio procul, quod non absolute & simpliciter sub fidem cadant, sed secundum quid tantum, in quantum scilicet sub divinam revelationem cadunt. Thomas in I. q. II. a. II. ad I. vocat eas preambula ad articulos fidei, quòd illarum cognitionem fides Christiana præsupponat, sicut gratia naturam. Per requisitum alterum excluduntur ex classe articulorum fidei omnes doctrinæ, divinitùs non revelatæ, quæ hoc ipso quod revelatæ non sunt, sub fidem non cadunt. Per tertium excluduntur ex censu articulorum fidei veritates, quæ quidem divinitùs revelatæ sunt, non tamen necessariam ad salutem hominum habitudinem important: cujusmodi sunt historiæ & res variæ, in Scripturis contentæ, & quæ circa doctrinam fidei emergunt quæstiones, quæ salute salvâ ignorari vel in utramque partem, modò malitia absit, disputari possunt.

III. Alii tamen articulos fidei in significatu latiori accipiunt, & quemadmodùm omnis divinæ revelationi innixus assensus, ex parte objecti formalis, inevidens & fidei assensus est, ita sub appellatione articulorum fidei comprehendunt etiam eas doctrinæ Christianæ partes, quæ naturaliter de Deo cognosci possunt, non quidem quatenus naturaliter notæ & evidentes sunt, sed quatenus divinæ revelationi subsunt, & propter illam credendæ. In quo præeuntem habent Auctorem Epistolæ ad Hebræos c. XI. 6. Sine fide, inquientem, impossibile est placere (Deo). Credere enim oportet accedentem ad Deum, quòd sit (Deus) & remunerator sit quærentibus se. Neque necessitatem, quam ad hominum salutem fidei articuli importent, omnes uno modo intelligunt. Quidam intelligunt necessitatem absolutam, requiruntq; ad articulum fidei, ut ita creditu necessarius sit ad salutem, ut ne ignorari quidem possit salute salvâ. Alii contrà ad articulum fidei sufficere existimant, si ita necessarius sit, ut salute salvâ negari non possit, licet ignorari à simplicioribus possit, citra salutis jacturam.

IV. Prout alii atque alii conceptum articulorum fidei extendunt aut restringunt, ita plures vel pauciores faciunt articulos fidei, quamvis dissensus modum loquendi potiùs, quàm ipsam rem concernere videatur.


### XXXI XXXI. Those who take the articles of faith in the later and looser sense distinguish…

XXXI.

XXXI.

Those who take the articles of faith in the later and looser sense distinguish them I. into pure and mixed; and II. into fundamental and non-fundamental.

XXXII.

They call those pure which become known from nowhere else than divine revelation, and therefore fall only under faith, which rests upon divine revelation, not under science or evident knowledge. They call those mixed which can be known from the light of nature and from divine revelation, and fall under faith insofar as they are divinely revealed; under science, insofar as they are known from the principles of nature and reason.

I. This distinction finds a place only in articles of faith taken in the later and looser sense. For according to the former and narrower sense, all articles of faith are pure and of mere faith: since they all become known from divine revelation alone. But those parts of doctrine which can be known from the light of nature, or which can be disputed on either side without prejudice to the foundation of faith and salvation, those who take articles of faith in the stricter sense do not even deem worthy of the name of articles of faith.

II. Articles of faith are called pure and mixed based on the reason for assenting: pure, indeed, are those whose proper reason for assenting is pure, namely divine revelation, not reason or its principles; mixed are those whose reason for knowing is twofold: one established in divine revelation, the other in the principles of nature and reason: which therefore are known and believed according to the different reason for assenting: they are known through the evident principles of nature and reason; but they are believed on account of divine revelation, which is non-evident and obscure.

XXXIII.

Fundamental articles are called those which carry such a necessary relation to the foundation of faith and salvation, so that, it being preserved, they cannot be ignored or at least denied; Non-fundamental, which, with the foundation of faith and salvation preserved, can be disputed on either side, or even denied. There is also this distinction of articles of faith, accepted in a looser sense. For according to the other, stricter meaning, all articles of faith have a necessary connection with the foundation of faith and salvation, so that, it being preserved, they cannot be ignored or at least denied, and thus all are fundamental.

XXXIV.

The foundation of faith and salvation is Jesus Christ, according to that 1 Cor. 3:11: 'For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.' I. Fundamental articles are so called from the foundation of faith and salvation, which they constitute, or with which they have a necessary connection. Moreover, 'foundation' is a word of broad meaning, and of the number of those things which are said in relation to another: for it implies a respect to that which it founds, and to which it is laid down to support; and in its more general concept it denotes that which is first in every thing, and which is the reason or cause why the other, namely that which it founds, is or can be. And it is indeed called the first foundation in every thing, because it is the beginning of the whole structure, and the very first part of it. It is also called the reason or cause why another thing is or can be: because it implies the relation of a cause to that of which it is the foundation, or at least the reason a priori, behaving in the manner of a cause, not indeed an adequate cause, by the positing of which the thing itself is immediately posited and actually comes to be, but an inadequate one, by the positing of which the thing either comes to be and is posited in act, if indeed the other parts also are built upon it and thus actually posited; or can be and be posited, if indeed the other parts are not yet built upon it, yet can be built upon it, just as, for example, when the foundation of a house is laid, the house is not immediately posited in act, unless the other parts necessary for its constitution are also built upon it and actually posited. According to this notion of a foundation, the foundation of faith and salvation will be that which is first in saving faith and the salvation of men, and what is the reason and cause why saving faith and the very salvation of man becomes or can be. Although indeed saving faith and man's salvation differ, and are two subordinate ends of Theology: for faith is for the sake of the salvation of men, and is the cause of it; yet the foundation of both is one and the same, and upon which the salvation of men [rests]; upon it also the faith of those [men] rests as upon a foundation, since faith, as will be shown below in its place, has from its foundation that it is saving, and from the same, through faith, the salvation of men also depends.

II. The foundation of faith and salvation is taken in the Scriptures in a double sense. The one for the thing itself, upon which saving faith and the salvation of men rests. The other for the doctrine by which that, upon which the faith and salvation of men rests, is explained and presented to the human intellect to be believed. In the former sense, the foundation is taken by Paul in I Cor. III. 11, and here by us. In the latter, however, it is taken in Eph. II. 20, when the faithful are said to be built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets. This is called by authors the dogmatic foundation; that [the former] the real, substantial, or essential. On which matter see, among others, Nicolaus Hunnius in Diascepsi de fund. dissensu, page 59, §. 90.

III. The foundation of faith and salvation, taken in the former sense, the Holy Scriptures customarily call the foundation of the faithful and of those to be saved, both of individuals and of all gathered into one mystical body of the Church, expressing with concrete terms the thing built or to be built upon the foundation, which we, following common usage of speech, express with abstract terms, in sense, as regards the thing, one and the same. For the faithful, both individually and collectively, are built upon the foundation as faithful and to be saved, or, which amounts to the same thing, by reason of faith and of the salvation which they now have in hope, to be actually obtained after departure from this life, so that they say the same thing as regards the matter, who speak of the foundation of the faithful as faithful and to be saved, and who speak of the foundation of faith and salvation.

…IV. In the passage cited from I Cor. III. 11: No one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, Jesus Christ; the Apostle speaks of the Church, which in the verses immediately preceding, [he describes] with a double metaphor, with a cultivated field and with a building; but himself with a husbandman so great, and with the architect, laying the foundation, he had compared, and just as in the preceding v. 9 he had spoken concerning the converted Corinthians and their Church: θεῦ γεώργιον, θεῦ ἐποδομή ἐςε, you are God's tillage (cultivated field), God's building (edifice); so in the following v. 10, persisting in the latter metaphor: According to the grace, he says, which was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation. But another builds upon it, etc. And then in the cited words he says that that foundation is nothing other than Jesus Christ. In which the Scriptures everywhere harmonize with him, and having regard to the Church, as a spiritual house, they call Christ the cornerstone, the stone of the founded foundation, placed by God the founder of Zion (mystical or the Church), Isa. XXIX. 16, the stone indeed rejected by the builders, but which was made by the Lord into the stone of the corner, Ps. CXVIII. 22. ἀκρογωνιαῖον, i. e., the lowest corner stone, 1 Pet. II. 6, Eph. II. 20, signifying the very thing which Paul had said in the cited passage: namely, that Jesus Christ is the foundation, upon which the faith and salvation of the entire mystical building, which is the Church, and of individual believers, as members of it, is partly built, and partly to be built.

V. Nor does the notion of the foundation of faith and salvation, both of the Church and of individual believers, belong to any other than our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. We saw above that the foundation in any thing is called that which is first, and which is the reason and cause why another thing is or can be. Where it is especially to be noted that what is called first here is not that which is absolutely and simply first, but that which is first in the genus of those things which enter into the constitution of a building, as its parts: for otherwise in any building the first of all is the will of the efficient cause, moved by the final cause to build, by which it determines to erect the building, to lay its foundation, and to build the other parts upon it. But besides the fact that the will of the builder does not enter into the intrinsic constitution of the building, even when it is posited, there is not immediately, nor can there be, a building; but in order for it to be or to be able to be, it is necessary that something else be placed, which so enters into the constitution of the building that it is prior to all its other parts, and they subsist by it. And this finally is and is called the foundation of the building. At present the case is just the same. In the spiritual building of the Church, the benevolent will of God, by which, moved by our misery and His own immense mercy toward us, He willed and wills all to be saved, is indeed prior to Jesus Christ, nay, the first cause of our faith and salvation, but the first in the category of the efficient cause, which does not enter into the very constitution of this spiritual building: nor is it so primary that, once it is posited, the spiritual building of the Church, or the faith of individual believers, by which they are joined together into one mystical body and are saved by hope, is or can be, but for this to be or to be able to be, it is necessary, besides the benevolent will of God toward us, that something else be posited, which so enters into its constitution that it is prior to all other parts, which is nothing other than Jesus Christ, that stone rejected by the builders (the Jews), but which has been made the head of the corner, i.e., the cornerstone, supporting the joint of the whole mystical building: nor is there salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved, Acts IV. 11. 12. He, namely, alone satisfied the divine justice injured by sins by suffering and dying, and merited that, with that justice preserved, God, according to His benevolent will toward us, might be able both to remit our sins and to impart eternal salvation.

VI. CHRIST is therefore the foundation both of the Church and of individual believers and those to be saved, and thus of their faith and salvation, insofar as He is the meritorious cause of the remission of sins and eternal salvation obtained from God, promised to those who believe in Him out of mere grace, and therefore GOD, and His benevolent WILL toward us, by which He both willed our salvation and accepted the merit and satisfaction of Christ as a λύτρον for our sins, and promised the remission of sins and eternal salvation to those who believe in Him, is also included in the foundation of faith and salvation, but indirectly and by way of connotation. And God is indeed connoted in it as the efficient cause of the remission of sins to be imparted to us; and His benevolent and gratuitous will as the προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause of the same: but the intrinsic and proper reason of the foundation resides in Christ, as the meritorious cause of our salvation, who alone is that first thing, upon which being posited, saving faith and the salvation of men is or can be, and in whom therefore the faith and salvation of men, and even the entire spiritual building of the Church is founded.

VII. But if God is joined with the merit of Christ, and is trusted as reconciled to us through Christ and his merit, God, viewed in this way, can also be constituted the foundation of faith and salvation, as can his gratuitous promises concerning the remission of sins and the salvation to be imparted to us on account of Christ. By which consideration the Scriptures also attribute to faith in God that it is salvific, namely faith in God as rendered propitious to us through Christ, or as having been moved by the merit and satisfaction of Christ for our sins, so that he might promise that he would remit sins to those who believe and would impart salvation, according to that: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, Gen. XV. 6. Rom. IV. 3. He who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed to him for righteousness, v. 5. But the foundation, thus accepted, is an aggregate of several things, which do not all equally share in the nature and essence of a foundation, but this, as has been said, returns at last to Christ alone, as the meritorious cause of our salvation. For that God can remit sins to sinners, while his justice remains intact, and has promised that he will remit the same to those who believe, all that is from the merit and satisfaction of Christ for our sins, in which both the grace of God, by which he remits sins to us, and the gratuitous promises concerning the remission of sins and the salvation to be imparted to us are founded. Wherefore we, having been reconciled to God and made heirs of eternal salvation, are indeed commanded to glory IN GOD, but through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have obtained reconciliation, Rom. V. 11. so that thus also the nature of the foundation, upon which our faith rests and in which we can glory, returns to our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose merit the wrath of God against sins has been appeased, and we have been reconciled to him.

Latin:

XXXI.

XXXI.

Qui in significatu posteriori & laxiori articulos fidei accipiunt, distinguunt eos I. in puros & mixtos; & II. In fundamentales & non fundamentales.

XXXII.

Puros dicunt, qui non aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione innotefcunt, & proinde tantùm cadunt sub fidem, divinæ revelationi innixam, non sub scientiam sive cognitionem evidentem. Mixtos dicunt, qui ex lumine naturæ, & ex divina revelatione cognosci possunt, & sub fidem cadunt, in quantum divinitùs revelati sunt; sub scientiam, in quantum ex principiis naturæ & rationis cognoscuntur.

I. Distinctio hæc locum demum invenit in articulis fidei, in significatu posteriori & laxiori acceptis. Juxta priorem enim & angustiorem significationem articuli fidei omnes puri ac meræ fidei sunt: cùm omnes ex sola divina revelatione innotefcant. Quæ autem doctrinæ partes ex lumine naturæ cognosci, vel salvo fidei & salutis fundamento in utramque partem disputari possunt, eas ne quidem appellatione articulorum fidei dignantur illi, qui in significatione strictiori articulos fidei accipiunt.

II. Puri & mixti dicuntur articuli fidei ex ratione assentiendi: puri quidem, quorum ratio assentiendi propria est pura puta revelatio divina, non ratio ejusve principia; Mixti, quorum ratio cognoscendi duplex est: una in divina revelatione; altera in principiis naturæ & rationis constituta: qui proinde pro ratione assentiendi diversa sciuntur & creduntur: sciuntur per principia naturæ & rationis evidentia; creduntur verò ob divinam revelationem inevidentem & obscuram.

XXXIII.

Fundamentales articuli dicuntur, qui ita necessariam habitudinem ad fundamentum fidei & salutis important, ut eo salvo ignorari vel saltem negari non possint; Nonfundamentales, qui salvo fidei & salutis fundamento in utramque partem disputari, vel etiam negari possunt Est & hæc distinctio articulorum fidei, in laxiori significatu acceptorum. Juxta alteram enim strictiorem significationem articuli fidei omnes necessariam habent connexionem cum fundamento fidei & salutis, ut eo salvo ignorari vel saltem negari non possint, atque adeò omnes fundamentales sunt.

XXXIV.

Fundamentum fidei & salutis est Jesus Christus, juxta illud 1. Cor. III. 11. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter hoc quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus. I. Fundamentales articuli dicuntur à fundamento fidei & salutis, quod constituunt, vel cum quo necessariam connexionem habent. Est autem fundamentum vox latæ significationis, & ex numero eorum, quæ dicuntur ad alterum: importat enim respectum ad id, quod fundat, & cui sustentando substernitur; & in suo generaliori conceptu denotat id, quod in unaquaque re primum, quodque ratio vel causa est, cur aliud, illud scilicet, quod fundat, sit aut esse possit. Et primum quidem dicitur fundamentum in unaquaque re, quia est principium totius structuræ, & pars ejus omnium prima. Dicitur etiam ratio vel causa, cur aliud sit aut esse possit: quia importat habitudinem causæ ad id, cujus fundamentum est, vel saltem rationis à priori, per modum causæ se habentis, non quidem causæ adæquatæ, quâ positâ statim res ipsa ponatur, & actu fit, sed inadæquatæ, quâ positâ res vel fit & ponatur actu, si scilicet cæteræ partes etiam ei superstructæ & sic actu positæ sint; vel esse & poni possit, si scilicet cæteræ partes ei nondum superstructæ sint, superstrui tamen possint, sicut v. g. posito fundamento domus, non statim actu ponitur domus, nisi & aliæ ad ejus constitutionem necessariæ partes superstructæ & in actu positæ sint. Juxta hanc fundamenti notionem fidei & salutis fundamentum erit id, quod in fide salutari hominumque salute primum est, quodque ratio ac causa est, cur fides salvifica & salus ipsa hominis fit aut esse possit. Quamvis verò fides salvifica & hominis salus differant, & duo Theologiæ fines subordinati sint: fides enim est propter hominum salutem, & causa illius; fundamentum tamen utriusque unum & idem est, & cui hominum salus; ei & illorum fides, ut fundamento innititur, cùm fides, ut infrà suo loco ostendeiur, à suo fundamento habeat, quod salvifica est, & ab eodem, mediante fide, etiam salus hominum dependeat.

II. Fundamentum fidei & salutis accipitur in Scripturis in duplici significatu. Uno pro ipsa re, cui fides salvifica & hominum salus innititur. Altero pro doctrina, quâ id, cui fides & salus hominum innititur, explicatur, & hominis intellectui credendum exhibetur. Priori significatu fundamentum apud Paulum in I. Cor. III. 11. & heic à nobis accipitur. Posteriori verò sumitur Eph. II. 20. cùm fideles dicuntur superstructi super fundamentum Apostolorum ac Prophetarum. Hoc ab Auctoribus dicitur fundamentum dogmaticum; illud reale, substantiale, vel essentiale. Qua de re videatur inter alios Nicolaus Hunnius in Diascepsi de fund. dissensu pag. 59. §. 90.

III. Fundamentum fidei & salutis, in significatu priori acceptum, Scripturæ Sacræ usitatè fidelium & salvandorum, cùm singulorum, tùm universorum, in unum Ecclesiæ corpus mysticum aggregatorum fundamentum appellant, terminis concretivis rem, fundamento superstructam aut superstruendam, exprimentes, quam nos, usum loquendi vulgarem secuti, terminis abstractivis exprimimus, sensu, quoad rem, uno & eodem. Fideles enim singuli & universi, superstructi sunt fundamento, quà fideles & salvandi, sive, quod eodem redit, ratione fidei, &, quam nunc spe habent, salutis, post exitum ex hac vita reapse consequendæ, ut quoad rem idem dicant, qui fidelium, quà fidelium & salvandorum; & qui fidei & salutis fundamentum dicunt.

IV. In loco ex I. Cor. III. 11. allegato: Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter id, quod positum est, Jesus Christus; loquitur Apostolus de Ecclesia, quam versiculis proximè præcedentibus, geminâ metaphorâ, cum agro culto & cum ædificio; se autem cum agricola plantante, & cum architecto, fundamentú ponente, comparaverat, & quemadmodum in præcedente v. 9. de conversis Corinthiis illorumque Ecclesia dixerat: θεῦ γεώργιον, θεῦ ἐποδομή ἐςε, Dei agricolatio (ager cultus) Dei ædificatio (ædificium) estis; ita in subsequente v. 10. in metaphora posteriori persistens: Juxta gratiam, inquit, quæ data est mihi, ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui. alius autem superædificat. &c. Et deinde in verbis citatis fundamentum illud ait non esse aliud, quàm Jesum Christum. In quo ei Scripturæ undique accinunt, & habito respectu ad Ecclesiam, velut domum spiritualem, Christum dicunt lapidem angularem, lapidem fundamenti fundati, à Deo fundatore Sionis (mysticæ sive Ecclesiæ) positi, Jes. XXIX. 16. lapidem ab ædificantibus quidem reprobatum, sed qui à Domino factus in lapidem anguli, Psal. CXIIX. 22. ἀκρογωνιαῖον, i. e. imum angularem lapidem I. Petr. II. 6. Eph. II. 20. id ipsum, quod loco allegato Paulus dixerat, significantes: nempe Jesum Christum esse fundamentum, cui fides & salus universi ædificii mystici, quod Ecclesia est, & singulorum fidelium, velut membrorum illius, superstructa partim, partim superstruenda est.

V. Neque etiam notio fundamenti fidei & salutis cùm Ecclesiæ, tùm fidelium singulorum, ulli alii, quàm Domino & Servatori nostro Jesu Christo, convenit. Vidimus suprà, fundamentum in unaquaque re dici id, quod primum, quodque ratio, & causa est, cur alterum sit vel esse possit. Ubi cumprimis notandum, quòd primum hîc non dicatur id, quod absolutè & simpliciter primum, sed quod primum est in genere eorum, quæ constitutionem ædificii, velut ejus partes, ingrediuntur: aliàs enim in quoliber ædificio primum omnium est voluntas causæ efficientis, per causam finalem ad ædificandum motæ, quâ ædificium extruere, ejusque fundamentum ponere & partes cæteras superstruere constituit. Sed præterquam quod voluntas ædificantis intrinsecam ædificii constitutionem non ingreditur, eâ etiam positâ non statim est aut esse potest ædificium, sed ut illud sit aut esse possit, necesse est aliud quid poni, quod constitutionem ædificii ita ingrediatur, ut cæteris ejus partibus omnibus prius sit, iisque subsistet. Et hoc demum est & dicitur ædificii fundamentum. Impræsentiarum perinde res habet. In spirituali Ecclesiæ ædificio Dei benevola voluntas, quâ nostrâ miseriâ, suâque immensâ in nos misericordiâ motus, voluit & vult omnes fieri salvos, prior quidem Jesu Christo, imò prima fidei & salutis nostræ causa est, sed prima in genere causæ efficientis, quæ ipsam hujus ædificii spiritualis constitutionem non ingreditur: nec ita prima est, ut eâ positâ Ecclesiæ ædificium spirituale, vel fidelium singulorum fides, quâ in unum corpus mysticum coagmentati & spe salvi sunt, sit aut esse possit, sed ad hoc, ut illud sit aut esse possit, necesse est, præter Dei benevolam in nos voluntatem, aliud quid poni, quod ejus constitutionem ita ingrediatur, ut cæteris partibus omnibus prius sit, quod non est aliud, quàm Jesus Christus, lapis ille ab ædificantibus (Judæis) rejectus, sed qui factus est caput anguli, h. e. lapis angularis, totius ædificii mystici juncturam sustinens: nec est in alio quoquam salus; nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo datum, in quo nos salvos fieri oporteat, Act. IV. 11. 12. Ille scilicet solus læsæ peccatis justitiæ divinæ patiendo & moriendo satisfecit, & ut, eâ salvâ, Deus pro suâ benevolâ in nos voluntate nobis & peccata remittere & salutem æternam impertire posset, promeruit.

VI. Est ergo CHRISTUS fundamentum cùm Ecclesiæ tùm fidelium & salvandorum singulorum, atque adeò fidei & salutis illorum, in quantum est causa meritoria consequendæ à Deo remissionis peccatorum & salutis æternæ, credentibus in ipsum ex merâ gratiâ promissæ, & includitur proinde in fundamento fides & salutis etiam DEUS, ejusque benevola in nos VOLUNTAS, quâ & nostram salutem voluit, & Christi meritum ac satisfactionem, velut λύτρον pro peccatis nostris acceptavit, & credentibus in ipsum remissionem peccatorum & salutem æternam promisit, sed in obliquo & per modum connotatorum. Et Deus quidem connotatur in eo ut causâ efficiens impertiendæ nobis remissionis peccatorum; & ejus benevola & gratuita voluntas ut ejusdem causa προηγουμένη sive impulsiva interna: ratio autem fundamenti intrinseca & propria residet in Christo, ut causa salutis nostræ meritoria, qui solus est illud primum, quo posito fides salvifica & salus hominum est aut esse potest, & in quo proinde hominum fides & salus, atque adeò Ecclesiæ ædificium spirituale totum fundatur.

VII. Quod si Deus cum Christi merito conjungatur, & confideretur ut nobis per Christum ejusque meritum reconciliatus, potest fundamentum fidei & salutis etiam constitui Deus, sic spectatus, ejusque gratuitæ promissiones de remissione peccatorum & salute nobis impertienda propter Christum. Quo intuitu Scripturæ etiam fidei in Deum tribuunt, quòd salvifica sit, puta fides in Deum, ut propitiatum nobis per Christum, aut ut motu Christi merito & satisfactione pro peccatis nostris, ut peccata credentibus se remissurum & salutem impertiturum promitteret, juxta illud: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam, Gen. XV. 6. Rom. IV. 3. Qui credit in eum, qui justificat impium, ei imputatur fides sua ad justitiam, v. 5. Sed fundamentum, sic acceptum, est aggregatum quid ex pluribus, quæ non æquè omnia fundamenti rationem & essentiam participant, sed hæc, uti dictum, in unum Christum, ut causam salutis nostræ meritoriam, tandem redit. Quod enim Deus peccatoribus, salvâ suâ justitiâ, peccata remittere potest, & eadem credentibus se remissurum promisit, id totum est ex Christi merito & satisfactione pro peccatis nostris, in quo & gratia Dei, quâ peccata nobis remittit, & promissiones gratuitæ de remissione peccatorum ac salute nobis impertienda fundantur. Quamobrem nos Deo reconciliati, salutisque æternæ hæredes facti jubemur quidem gloriari IN DEO, sed per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, per quem reconciliationem assecuti sumus, Rom. V. 11. ut sic etiam ratio fundamenti, cui fides nostra innititur, & in quo gloriari possumus, redeat in Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, cujus merito ira Dei adversus peccata placata est, nosque ei reconciliati sumus.


### XXXV. Fundamental articles of faith, moreover, are divinely revealed enunciations, or…

XXXV.

Fundamental articles of faith, moreover, are divinely revealed enunciations, or certain parts of Christian doctrine, which explain that real foundation of faith and salvation, and present to the minds of men for knowing and believing, and are therefore so necessary to be known and believed for salvation, that without them neither can the foundation of faith and salvation be entire, nor can faith and salvation be obtained by man.

I. They are called, as we saw above, fundamental, from the real foundation of faith and salvation, because they have that as their object, and because the things signified by them constitute it, or are so connected with it, that without them it cannot be whole and entire.

II. Although Jesus Christ, who is the real or substantial foundation of our faith and salvation, is something incomplex, yet he cannot be apprehended and known by us in one adequate concept, but must be known and explained by us through several inadequate concepts, and those complex, or several enunciations. Which enunciations, viewed individually, are called fundamental articles or parts of the doctrine of faith; but taken together and jointly they constitute the entire foundation of faith and salvation, but a foundation, as authors love to speak, dogmatic, established in the doctrine that explains the real foundation of faith and salvation, of which seems to be understood that foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, upon which the faithful are said to be built, Eph. II. 20, by which nothing else seems to be denoted than the doctrine of the Apostles and Prophets concerning Christ, who is the foundation of faith and salvation.

III. The dogmatic and the real or substantial foundation of faith and salvation therefore differ

1 As the thing, underlying diverse enunciations, and the enunciations, explaining it. For the real foundation is the thing itself, underlying the dogmatic foundation, and is its object: but the dogmatic are the divinely revealed enunciations, explaining that thing, upon which our faith and salvation rests as if upon a foundation.

2. The real foundation is something incomplex, which nevertheless as it contains in itself as it were several parts and perfections, so it must be apprehended by us through several inadequate concepts, and explained by several enunciations, and therefore the dogmatic foundation is not only something complex, but also an aggregate of several divinely revealed enunciations, which we call articles of faith. For all these enunciations are indeed articles or fundamental parts of the doctrine of faith: since each one enunciates something which either Jesus Christ, the foundation of faith and salvation, contains in himself, or at least has a necessary connection with him; yet none, viewed separately, is the whole foundation of faith and salvation itself. Wherefore also, not when some, but when all fundamental articles are posited, is the faith and salvation of man finally posited or can be posited. For the faith and salvation of man require for their existence an integral foundation, which is constituted not by one or another, but by all fundamental articles: however, if one or another article, simply necessary for salvation to be believed or fundamental, is lacking, then saving faith and the salvation of man itself utterly fails.

3. Just as every enunciation is founded upon its object, and has its being from it, so those divinely revealed enunciations concerning Christ, which are the fundamental articles or parts of the doctrine of faith, taken together, indeed constitute the dogmatic foundation of faith and salvation, yet so that they in turn lean upon Jesus Christ as their object and real foundation: from whom also they have entirely the fact that they found and sustain the faith and salvation of men. To which the Apostle looks, when in the place already cited he says that the faithful are built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίε λίθε ἀυτᾶ ἰησᾶ χρισῦ, indeed with Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone. For with the addition of the qualification: indeed with Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone; he signifies that the Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine is a foundation in such a way that it both leans upon Jesus Christ himself, as the cornerstone and ultimate foundation, and the reason for the foundation ultimately returns to him.

Latin:

XXXV.

Fundamentales autem articuli fidei sunt enunciationes, divinitùs revelatæ, sive partes quædam doctrinæ Christianæ, quæ illud fidei & salutis reale fundamentum explicant, & hominum mentibus ad cognoscendum & credendum exhibent, & sunt proinde cognitu & creditu ad salutem ita necessarii, ut absque iis nec fundamentum fidei & salutis integrum esse, nec fides & salus ab homine obtineri possit.

I. Dicuntur, ut supra vidimus, fundamentales, a fundamento fidei & salutis reali, quod illud habeant pro objecto, quodque res illis significatae illud constituant, aut cum eo ita connexae sint, ut absque illis sartum tectum id esse non possit.

II. Quamvis Jesus Christus, qui fidei & salutis nostrae fundamentum reale sive substantiale est, sit aliquid incomplexum, non tamen uno adaequato conceptu a nobis apprehendi & cognosci potest, sed pluribus inadaequatis conceptibus, iisque complexis, sive enunciationibus pluribus a nobis cognoscendum & explicandum est. Quae enunciationes singulatim spectatae, dicuntur articuli sive partes doctrinae fidei fundamentales; simul autem & junctim sumtae constituunt fundamentum fidei & salutis integrum, sed fundamentum, ut loqui auctores amant, dogmaticum, in doctrina, fundamentum fidei & salutis reale explicante, constitutum, de quo accipiendum videtur illud Apostolorum & Prophetarum fundamentum, cui fideles superstructi dicuntur, Eph. II. 20. quo nihil aliud denotari videtur, quam Apostolorum & Prophetarum doctrina de Christo, qui fidei & salutis fundamentum est.

III. Dogmaticum igitur & reale sive substantiale fidei ac salutis fundamentum differunt

1 Ut res, enunciationibus diversis substrata, & enunciationes, eam explicantes. Fundamentum reale enim est ipsa res, fundamento dogmatico substrata, & est objectum illius: dogmaticum vero sunt enunciationes divinitus revelatae, rem illam, cui fides & salus nostra velut fundamento innititur, explicantes.

2. Fundamentum reale est aliquid incomplexum, quod tamen ut plures quasi partes & perfectiones in se continet, ita pluribus conceptibus inadaequatis a nobis apprehendendum, pluribusque enunciationibus explicandum est, & proinde fundamentum dogmaticum non tantùm est complexum quid, sed etiam ex pluribus divinitùs revelatis enunciationibus, quas articulos fidei dicimus, aggregatum. Omnes enim istæ enunciationes articuli quidem sive partes doctrinæ fidei fundamentales sunt: cùm quælibet aliquid enunciet, quod vel Jesus Christus, fidei & salutis fundamentum, in se continet, vel saltem necessariam cum eo connexionem habet; nulla tamen, seorsim spectata, est ipsum totum fidei & salutis fundamentum. Quamobrem etiam non positis aliquibus, sed positis omnibus articulis fundamentalibus, ponitur demum aut poni potest fides & salus hominis. Fides enim & salus hominis exigunt ad sui existentiam fundamentum integrum, quod non uno alterove, sed omnibus articulis fundamentalibus constituitur: deficiente autem uno alterove articulo, creditu ad salutem simpliciter necessario sive fundamentali, deficit oppidò fides salvifica & salus hominis ipsa.

3. Quemadmodum omnis enunciatio fundatur in suo objecto, & ab eo suum esse habet, ita enunciationes illæ divinitùs revelatæ de Christo, quæ articuli sive partes doctrinæ fidei fundamentales sunt, junctim sumtæ, constituunt quidem fidei & salutis fundamentum dogmaticum, ut tamen ipsæ vicissim Jesu Christo, velut suo objecto & fundamento reali nitantur: à quo etiam, quod fidem ac salutem hominum fundant & sustinent, in solidum habent. Quò respicit Apostolus, quando loco jam citato fideles superstructos dicit super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίε λίθε ἀυτᾶ ἰησᾶ χρισῦ, imo angulari lapide exsistente ipso Jesu Christo. Addito enim προσδιορισμῷ: imo angulari lapide existente ipso Jesu Christo; significat, doctrinam Propheticam & Apostolicam ita esse fundamentum, ut & ipsa Jesu Christo, velut imo angulari lapide & fundamento ultimo nitatur, & ratio undamenti ultimò in eum redeat.


### XXXVI. Fundamental articles of faith are accustomed to be distinguished into primary…

XXXVI.

Fundamental articles of faith are accustomed to be distinguished into primary and secondary. Those can be called primary, which not even can be ignored, while the foundation of faith and salvation is kept intact; Secondary [articles], which indeed can be ignored, but not denied, with the foundation of faith and salvation kept sound and whole.

1. Certain fundamental articles imply a relationship to the foundation of faith and salvation, from which they are named fundamental, so necessary that, unless they are explicitly known, neither can the foundation be held intact, nor can saving faith be generated and sustained through it: of this kind are, for example, the articles concerning the person of Christ as θεανθρώπῳ [God-man], concerning his merit and satisfaction for our sins, the signified matter of which is of the intrinsic nature of the foundation; likewise the articles concerning eternal life, concerning God and his benevolent will toward men, by which he wills their salvation, etc., the signified matter of which, although it may not be of the intrinsic nature of the foundation, is yet so connected with it that, unless it is explicitly known, the other things entering into its constitution would not be suitable for generating and sustaining saving faith. The reason is: because Christ is the foundation of our faith and salvation by reason of his merit and satisfaction for our sins, and he stands toward saving faith indeed as an object and foundation upon which it rests; but toward salvation, as its meritorious cause, and thus as a means to an end, or as a cause to an effect, to be acquired or already acquired by meriting: but God, willing the salvation of men according to his benevolent will, and bestowing the same upon them in view of the meritorious cause, is the efficient cause of the same. Moreover, there is this perpetual nexus between the meritorious cause, the effect to be obtained by its merit, and the efficient cause which, moved by his merit, bestows the effect, so that every meritorious cause is meritorious of the effect to be obtained from the efficient cause moved by its merit, so that if either the effect, for the sake of which the merit exists; or the efficient cause, which moved by his merit confers it, is not given, the meritorious cause would be nothing, or certainly its effort, labor, action, or passion, undertaken for the sake of meriting the effect, would be vain and void.

Similarly, if anyone should ignore or deny that the effect is given, for example, the blessed life, which they who have departed from this life with God propitious shall eventually attain; or if he should ignore that there is a God, who is to bestow upon those who have departed from this life propitiously, he can neither acknowledge Christ as the meritorious cause of our salvation, nor have his trust for obtaining eternal life from God fixed in him. This the Apostle shows excellently in 1 Cor. 15:13-14. If, he says, there is no resurrection of the dead (and blessed life), then Christ has not been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is vain, and your faith is also vain. And v. 16 seqq. If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain: you are still in your sins: indeed, those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If we hope in Christ in this life only, we are of all men most miserable. And articles of this kind are rightly numbered among the primary fundamental articles: since their explicit or express knowledge is simply necessary for the foundation of faith and salvation to be kept safe and sound, so that they cannot even be ignored while that foundation is kept intact.

II. Other fundamental articles, however, are not simply necessary to be known for the foundation of faith and salvation—from which they are named fundamental—to be kept safe and sound, and therefore, while that foundation is kept safe, they can be ignored: just as, for example, the article concerning the personal union of the two natures in Christ, and concerning the communication of them and of their idioms, as it was handed down and declared in the Ecumenical Councils, Ephesian and Chalcedonian, against Nestorius and Eutyches according to the guidance of Scripture, and is still handed down in orthodox schools, is a fundamental article of faith. For the personal union and the communication of the natures and of the idioms is of the intrinsic nature of the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and upon it depends both the unity of his person θεανθρώπης, and the value and dignity of his merit, by which he is constituted in the nature of the foundation of faith and salvation, so that unless his natures, human and divine, were inseparably, yet unconfusedly, united, and had a communion of properties or idioms between them, his obedience, rendered to his Father even unto the death of the cross, could not be the meritorious cause of our salvation. To this end, however, that one may be considered to hold the foundation of faith and salvation intact, explicit or express knowledge of this doctrine is not simply necessary: since most of the simpler faithful, both men and women, are not capable of it, and nevertheless have saving faith firmly fixed in Jesus Christ and his merit, as the sole foundation of salvation, as experience abundantly testifies. But the explicit or express knowledge of that doctrine which is not simply necessary for keeping the foundation of faith and salvation safe and sound, can be ignored while the foundation of faith and salvation is kept intact.

Nor, however, while that is safe, can it be denied just as it can be ignored. For there is a different reason for ignorance and denial. The former implies a mere lack of explicit knowledge, and indeed a lack of knowledge not simply necessary for generating saving faith on the part of the foundation, and therefore it does not in itself detract anything from the foundation of faith and salvation: since it overturns nothing of those things which are contained in it, or are necessarily connected with it; nor is it in itself joined with an error, whether directly or indirectly opposing it: since simple ignorance signifies at least a lack or defect of knowledge, not an opposite error. But the denial of such a fundamental article necessarily and always implies an error, indirectly opposing the foundation of faith and salvation, and by which, as a consequence, that or something without which it cannot be safe, is destroyed: e.g., he who believes that Christ is God and man, who by suffering and dying satisfied for the sins of the human race, and restored eternal salvation to us by his merit and satisfaction, he is considered to hold the foundation of faith and salvation intact, even if he does not have a distinct and express knowledge of the doctrine concerning the personal union and the communication of idioms, as it is handed down by the orthodox against the Nestorians and Eutychians. For the personal union and the communication of idioms is contained in the person of Christ θεανθρώπω, and his merit necessarily presupposes both, so that he who acknowledges and believes in the person of Christ θεάνθρωπον, by that very fact, if not explicitly, yet implicitly, and as an antecedent in its consequent acknowledged and believed, also acknowledges and embraces the personal union and the communication of idioms, which he would also expressly acknowledge and embrace, if he could grasp an express knowledge of it through the slowness and weakness of his mind. But whoever, either with Nestorius, denies the personal union and the communication of idioms, or with Eutyches, confuses the natures and their properties, he overturns the foundation of faith and salvation, although indirectly and by consequence. For if, with Nestorius, the personal union and the communication of idioms is denied, it follows necessarily that a mere man, not God, suffered and died for us. But the suffering and death of a mere man cannot be the meritorious cause of our salvation, and thus the foundation of our faith and salvation. Again, if with Eutyches the unconfused union of natures is denied, and it is said that Christ's human nature was converted into the divine, or absorbed by the divine, it will follow necessarily that Christ is not true man, nor could he have suffered and died for us in the assumed human nature, which he no longer possessed. By which very thing the foundation of faith and salvation is again overturned. The matter stands likewise with other fundamental articles of the same order or kind, nor is it possible for anyone to deny any of them without, however, indirectly and by consequence striking at the foundation of faith and salvation, although it is possible for someone to be ignorant of any of them, with the foundation of faith and salvation remaining unharmed. Wherefore, secondary fundamental articles are not inconveniently so called: fundamental indeed, because they cannot be denied while the foundation of faith and salvation remains; but secondary, because their express knowledge is not absolutely and simply necessary for keeping the foundation of faith and salvation intact and for generating saving faith, and therefore they can be ignored while it remains.

III. Commonly, however, authors explain this distinction a little differently, and say that primary fundamental articles are those which cannot be ignored without prejudice to faith and salvation; secondary are those which can indeed be ignored without such prejudice, but cannot be denied. Which explanation, as far as primary articles are concerned, has no difficulty, and agrees well with that which we have delivered. For the express knowledge of those articles is simply necessary for keeping the foundation of faith and salvation intact, so that while it is preserved whole they cannot be unknown, their explicit knowledge is also simply necessary for generating faith through it and causing salvation, so that without prejudice to faith and salvation they cannot be unknown. For the foundation of faith and salvation does not generate faith or cause the salvation of a man unless it is known, and therefore whether you define the primary articles in this way or that, the matter will return to the same thing. But in that part where they are called secondary articles, which indeed can be unknown without prejudice to the faith and salvation, but cannot be denied, it seems to have some difficulty. For it can happen in two ways that an article of this kind is denied: One, that he who denies it neither admits the force of the consequence, by which the error, striking against the foundation of the faith, is inferred from the negative, nor the error deduced from it by consequence, but denies that the former holds correctly; he rejects and condemns it, and thus through ignorance, without malice, embraces the negative. The other, that he who denies it, even after noticing the evidence and validity of the consequence by which the error striking against the foundation of the faith is inferred, persists in the negative, or openly approves or defends the error itself, deduced from it by consequence, with his own judgment.

There is no doubt that in the latter way secondary fundamental articles of faith cannot be denied without prejudice to the faith and salvation. For he who denies one of them in this way not only destroys the foundation of faith and salvation implicitly, indirectly, and by consequence through the force of his negative, or at least something of those things without which it cannot be safe, but also, having recognized the force and validity of the consequence, he now directly destroys the foundation of faith and salvation itself through the error deduced from the negative, and renders it, as far as in him lies, ineffective for generating faith and causing salvation: which can be done by no one while faith and salvation are safe. But in the former way, the denial seems, on the part of the denier, to be able to stand with his faith and salvation. For although in this way also the denial is opposed to the foundation of the faith indirectly and by consequence: for an error, repugnant to the foundation of the faith, follows from the negative, whether he who embraces the negative knows that it follows from it or does not know it; yet because the error is neither approved by him who embraces the negative, nor does he acknowledge that it follows from it, he who embraces the negative retains the foundation of faith and salvation intact, not indeed absolutely and simply, but in so far as it is necessary to be known for causing faith and for obtaining salvation by faith. For he denies through mere ignorance, n in so far indeed as it is necessary to be known for generating faith and obtaining salvation by faith; but something, indeed contained in it, or connected with it, but whose express knowledge is not simply necessary for generating saving faith. Which denial, proceeding from ignorance, seems able to stand at the same time both with the foundation of faith and salvation, in so far as it is necessary to be known for causing faith and obtaining salvation; and likewise with the man's own faith and salvation. With the former indeed: because it is not opposed to the foundation, except by consequence, which he who embraces the negative does not grasp, does not acknowledge; and through error, brought in by consequence from thence, which he does not approve, but rejects and condemns. With the latter truly: because of that whose express knowledge is not simply necessary for generating faith and causing salvation, its denial, if it has proceeded from mere ignorance, and the rest of the foundation itself, in so far as it is necessary to be known for causing faith and salvation, is retained, can neither take away faith and salvation, nor prevent that through that which is acknowledged faith might be generated, and salvation obtained. Which, however, I would wish to be said without prejudice to the judgments of others.

Latin:

XXXVI.

Articuli fidei fundamentales distingui solent in primarios & secundarios. Primarii dici possunt, qui ne ignorari quidem possunt, retento fidei & salutis fundamento integro; Secundarii, qui ignorari quidem, non autem negari possunt, fundamento fidei & salutis sarto tecto servato.

1. Articulorum fundamentalium quidam ad fidei & salutis fundamentum, à quo fundamentales denominantur, habitudinem ita necessariam important, ut, nisi explicitè cogniti sint, nec fundamentum integrum teneri, nec fides salvifica per illud generari & sustentari possit: cujusmodi sunt v. g. articuli de Christi persona θεανθρώπῳ, de ejus merito & satisfactione pro peccatis nostris, quorum res significata est de intrinsecâ ratione fundamenti; item articuli de vita æterna, de Deo ejusque benevola in homines voluntate, quâ illorum salutem vult &c. quorum res significata licet de intrinseca ratione fundamenti non sit, ita tamen cum eo connexa est, ut nisi explicitè cognita sit, cætera illius constitutionem ingredientia ad generandam & sustentandam fidem salvificam idonea futura non sint. Ratio est: quia Christus est fundamentum nostræ fidei & salutis ratione meriti & satisfactionis suæ pro peccatis nostris, & habet se ad fidem salvificam quidem ut objectum & fundamentum, quo nititur; ad salutem verò, ut ejus causa meritoria, atque adeò ut medium ad finem, vel ut causa ad effectum, promerendo acquirendum vel acquisitum: Deus autem, pro sua benevola voluntate hominum salutem volens, & eandem causæ meritoriæ intuitu illis impertiens, est ejusdem causa efficiens. Est autem inter causam meritoriam, inter effectum, ejus merito obtinendum, & inter causam efficientem, quæ merito illius mota effectum impertit, hic perpetuus nexus, ut causa meritoria omnis sit meritoria effectus, à causa efficiente, ejus merito motâ, consequendi, ut si vel effectus, cujus causâ meritum est; vel causa efficiens, quæ merito illius mota eum conferat, non detur, causa meritoria nulla futura, vel certè ejus conatus, labor, actio aut passio, promerendi effectus causâ suscepta, vana & irrita futura sit.

Similiter si quis ignoret vel neget dari effectum, v. g. vitam beatam, quam tandem aliquando consecuturi sint, qui Deo propitio ex hac vita discesserint; vel si ignoret esse Deum, qui eam impertiturus sit his, qui se propitio ex hac vita discesserint, is nec Christum pro causa salutis nostræ meritoria agnoscere, nec in eo fiduciam impetrandæ à Deo vitæ æternæ defixam habere potest. Quod egregiè ostendit Apostolus in I. Cor. XV. 13. 14. Si, inquiens, resurrectio mortuorum (& vita beata) non est, Christus quoque non est excitatus. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est prædicatio nostra, inanis autem & fides vestra. Et v. 16. seqq. Si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoque non est excitatus. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra: adhuc estis in peccatis vestris: nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo, perierunt. Si in hac solùm vita speramus in Christum, miserrimi omnium hominum sumus. Atque hujus generis articuli rectè numerantur in articulis fundamentalibus primariis: cùm illorum cognitio explicita sive expressa ad fundamentum fidei & salutis sartum tectum servandum simpliciter necessaria sit, ut ne ignorari quidem possint, eodem retento integro.

II. Alii verò articuli fundamentales ad fundamentum fidei & salutis, à quo fundamentales denominantur, sartum tectum servandum, non simpliciter cognitu necessarii sunt, & proinde, eo salvo ignorari possunt: sicut v. g articulus de unione personali duarum naturarum in Christo, deque illarum & idiomatum communicatione, ut in Conciliis Oecumenicis, Ephesino & Chalcedonensi, contra Nestorium & Eutychen ad Scripturæ ductum traditus & declaratus est, & etiamnum in Scholis orthodoxis traditur, articulus fidei fundamentalis est. Unio personalis enim & communicatio Naturarum atque idiomatum est de intrinseca ratione fundamenti, quod est Jesus Christus, & ab ea pendet cùm unitas ejus personæ θεανθρώπης, tùm valor & dignitas meriti ipsius, quo in ratione fundamenti fidei & salutis constituitur, ut nisi ejus naturæ, humana & divina, inseparabiliter, inconfusè tamen, unitæ essent, & proprietatum sive idiomatum communionem inter se haberent, ejus obedientia, suo Patri ad mortem crucis usque præstita, causa salutis nostræ meritoria esse non posset. Ad hoc tamen, ut quis censeatur fidei & salutis fundamentum integrum tenere, explicita sive expressa doctrinæ hujus cognitio simplicite necessaria non est: cum fidelium simpliciores plerique, masculi ac fœmellæ, ejus capaces non sint, & nihilo minùs fidem salvificam in Jesum Christum ejusque meritum, velut salutis fundamentum unicum, firmiter defixam habent, ut abunde testatur experientia. Cujus autem doctrinæ cognitio explicita sive expressa ad fundamentum fidei & salutis sartum tectum servandum simpliciter necessaria non est, ea retento fundamento fidei & salutis integro ignorari potest.

Neque tamen, eo salvo, ut ignorari, ita & negari potest. Est enim ignorantiæ & negationis dispar ratio. Illa importat nudum defectum cognitionis explicitæ, & quidem defectum cognitionis, ad generandam fidem salvificam ex parte fundamenti non simpliciter necessariæ, & proinde fundamento fidei & salutis nec per se aliquid detrahit: cùm nihil eorum, quæ ei insunt, vel necessariò cum eo connexa sunt, evertat; nec cum errore, sive directè sive indirectè ipsi adversante per se conjuncta est: cùm ignorantia simplex dicat saltem carentiam sive defectum cognitionis, non errorem oppositum. Negatio autem hujusmodi articuli fundamentalis necessariò & semper importat errorem, fundamento fidei & salutis indirectè adversantem, & quo per consequentiam illud vel aliquid, absque quo id salvum esse non potest, destruitur: v. g. qui credit, Christum esse Deum & hominem, qui patiendo & moriendo pro peccatis generis humani satisfecit, & salutem æternam suo merito & satisfactione nobis reparavit, is fundamentum fidei & salutis tenere censetur integrum, ut ut doctrinæ de unione personali & communicatione idiomatum, ut ab orthodoxis ea contra Nestorianos & Eutychianos traditur, cognitionem distinctam & expressam non habet. Unio personalis enim & communicatio idiomatum continetur in Christi persona θεανθρώπω, & ejus meritum præsupponit necessariò utramque, ut qui Christi personam θεάνθρωπον agnoscit & credit, is eo ipso si non explicitè, implicitè tamen, & velut antecedens in suo consequente agnito & credito, etiam unionem personalem & communicationem idiomatum agnoscat & amplectatur, quam & expresse agniturus atque amplexurus esset, si per tarditatem & imbecillitatem mentis ejus cognitionem expressam capere posset. Qui autem vel cum Nestorio negat unionem personalem & communicationem idiomatum, vel cum Eutyche naturas & illarum proprietates confundit, is evertit fundamentum fidei & salutis, quamvis indirecte & per consequentiam. Si enim cum Nestorio unio personalis & communicatio idiomatum negetur, sequitur necessario, hominem nudum, non Deum, passum & mortuum esse pro nobis. Passio autem & mors nudi hominis non potest esse causa salutis nostrae meritoria, atque adeo fidei & salutis nostrae fundamentum. Rursum si cum Eutyche unio naturarum inconfusa negetur, & Christi naturam humanam in divinam conversam, vel a divina absorptam esse dicatur, sequetur necessario, Christum non esse verum hominem, nec potuisse in assumta natura humana, quam non amplius habuit, pro nobis pati & mori. Quo ipso rursum fundamentum fidei & salutis evertitur. Perinde res habet cum aliis ejusdem ordinis aut generis articulis fundamentalibus, neque fieri potest, ut quis aliquem illorum neget, nec tamen indirecte & per consequentiam in fundamentum fidei & salutis impingat, quamvis fieri possit, ut quis aliquem illorum ignoret, fundamento fidei & salutis illæso. Quamobrem non incommode articuli fundamentales secundarii dicuntur: fundamentales quidem, quod fundamento fidei & salutis salvo negari non possint: secundarii vero, quod illorum cognitio expressa ad fundamentum fidei & salutis sartum tectum servandum & generandam fidem salvificam non absolute & simpliciter necessaria sit, eoque salvo ignorari possint.

III. Vulgo tamen Auctores distinctionem hanc paulo aliter explicant, dicuntque articulos fundamentales primarios, qui salva fide & salute non possunt ignorari; secundarios, qui eadem salva ignorari quidem, non autem negari possunt. Quæ explicatio, quod ad articulos primarios quidem attinet, nihil habet difficultatis, & cum ea, quam nos tradidimus, bene concordat. Quorum enim articulorum cognitio expressa ad fundamentum fidei & salutis sartum tectum servandum simpliciter necessaria est, ut eo retento integro ignorari non possint, illorum cognitio expressa etiam ad generandam per illud fidem causandamque salutem simpliciter necessaria est, ut salvâ fide & salute ignorari non possint. Nam fundamentum fidei & salutis non generat fidem causatve salutem hominis, nisi cognitum, & proinde sive hoc, sive illo modo articulos primarios definias, eodem res redibit. Eâ verò parte, quâ articuli secundarii dicuntur, qui salvâ fide & salute quidem ignorari, non autem negari possunt, non nihil difficultatis habere videtur. Potest enim duobus modis fieri, ut aliquis hujus generis articulus negetur: Uno, ut qui eum negat, neque vim consequentiæ, quâ error, in fundamentum fidei impingens, ex negativâ infertur, neque errorem, per consequentiam inde deductum, admittat, sed illam rectè habere neget; hunc rejiciat & damnet, atque adeò per ignorantiam, citra malitiam, negativam amplectatur. Altero, ut qui eum negat, etiam animadversâ evidentiâ & bonitate consequentiæ, quâ error in fundamentum fidei impingens infertur, in negativa persistat, vel ipsum quoque errorem, per consequentiam inde deductum, apertè suo comprobet calculo, vel propugnet.

Posteriori modo articulos fidei fundamentales secundarios, salvâ fide & salute, negari non posse, dubium non habet. Qui enim sic aliquem illorum negat, is non solùm vi negativæ suæ implicitè, indirectè & per consequentiam destruit fundamentum fidei & salutis, vel saltem aliquid eorum, absque quo id salvum esse non potest, sed etiam, agnitâ consequentiæ vi & bonitate, jam per errorem, ex negativâ deductum, fundamentum fidei & salutis ipsum directè destruit, idque ad generandam fidem causandamque salutem, quantum in ipso est, inefficax reddit: quod à nemine, fide & salute salvâ, fieri potest. Priori autem modo videtur negatio, ex parte negantis, stare posse cum fide & salute illius. Quamvis enim sic etiam negatio fundamento fidei adversetur indirectè & per consequentiam: error enim, fundamento fidei repugnas, sequitur ex negativa, sive is, qui negativam amplectitur, sciat eum ex illa sequi, sive id nesciat; quia tamen errorem nec approbat is, qui negativam amplectitur, nec eum ex illa fequi agnoscit, retinet is utique fundamentum fidei & salutis integrum, non quidem absolutè & simpliciter, sed in quantum ad causandam fidem & ad salutem fide consequendam cognitu necessarium est. Negat enim per meram ignorantiam, non ipsum fundamentum: hoc enim, uti dictum, amplectitur, in quantum quidem ad generandam fidem & salutem fide consequendam cognitu necessarium est; sed aliquid, in eo quidem contentum, vel cum illo connexum, sed cujus cognitio expressa ad generandam fidem salvificam simpliciter necessaria non est. Quæ ex ignorantia pro fecta negatio videtur simul stare posse & cum fundamento fidei ac salutis, in quantum ad causandam fidem salutemque consequendam cognitu necessarium est; & pariter cum ipsa hominis fide ac salute. Cum illo quidem: quia fundamento non adversatur, nisi per consequentiam, quam non capit, non agnoscit is qui negativam amplectitur; & per errorem, per consequentiam inde illatum, quem non approbat, sed rejicit & damnat. Cum hac verò: quia cujus cognitio expressa ad generandam fidem causandamque salutem simpliciter necessaria non est, ejus negatio, si ex mera ignorantia profecta sit, & cætera fundamentum ipsum, in quantum ad causandam fidem & salutem cognitu necessarium est, retineatur, fidem & salutem nec tollere, neque ne per illud agnitum fides generetur, & salus obtineatur, impedire potest. Quod tamen salvis aliorum judiciis dictum velim.


### XXXVII. Near to the distinction of fundamental articles into primary and secondary is…

XXXVII.

Near to the distinction of fundamental articles into primary and secondary is another distinction, most accepted by the Scholastics, into articles necessary by necessity of precept and by necessity of means. The latter can be called those whose explicit or express knowledge is simply necessary, so that they cannot even be ignored, with faith and salvation intact. The former, those whose knowledge, although it is divinely commanded, is yet not so simply necessary, but that they can be ignored without the loss of faith and salvation.

I. The necessity of precept, viewed in relation to the articles of faith, can be understood in a double sense. In one more general sense, just as it also includes under itself the necessity of means. For those things which are necessary to be believed by necessity of means, faith in them is also commanded by God, and thus they are also necessary to be believed by necessity of precept. In another stricter sense, as it is distinguished from the necessity of means. In which sense those things are necessary to be believed by necessity of precept which do not oblige one to believe by their own nature, or from a certain relation of theirs to the attainment of the end, but only from the will of God commanding. But those things are necessary to be believed by necessity of means which oblige one to believe not from the sole will of God commanding, but also from their own necessary relation to the attainment of salvation, since without those things being believed, saving faith and salvation cannot consist for man. And in this sense the Scholastics commonly take the distinction.

II. If you look at the force of the words, only those articles whose signified matter has the nature of a means necessary for attaining salvation should be called necessary by necessity of means. But here in a looser sense, those articles are called necessary by necessity of means whose knowledge is so necessary for generating faith and attaining salvation that without it neither saving faith nor salvation itself can be obtained, and therefore they seem to be called necessary by necessity of means, not because their signified matter is always a means of attaining salvation, but because faith, whose object they are, and which without those things being believed can either not exist or not be saving, is a necessary means of attaining salvation. And thus articles necessary by necessity of means, and primary fundamental articles; likewise secondary fundamental articles, and articles necessary by necessity of precept coincide.

XXXIIX.

The Apostles' Creed presents a certain epitome of the articles of faith, and they are commonly numbered among the Scholastics as fourteen, or twelve.

I. It is called the Apostles' Creed either from the Apostles, because when they had departed into the orb of the lands to preach the Gospel, it was composed by unanimous consent, and handed down to the Church by living voice, as some ancients maintain; or, which is more agreeable to the truth, from Apostolic doctrine, because it was collected from it, although the author is uncertain, and it contains as it were its nucleus and summary we do not make our own at this time.

II. Some count fourteen articles of faith, comprised in the Apostolic Creed, which Thomas in II. II. q. I. a. VIII. divides into two classes. Into the former he refers the articles pertaining to the majesty of the divinity, of which there are four: one concerning the unity of God, and three concerning the mystery of the Trinity, according to the number of the three persons. 2. Articles concerning the works of the divinity, which pertain to the being of nature, or to the being of grace, or finally to the being of glory. The article concerning creation concerns the works of the divinity pertaining to the being of nature; the article concerning sanctification concerns the works of grace; the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life concerns the works pertaining to the being of glory, so that the first class contains these seven articles: the first concerning one God, the second concerning the Father, the first person of the Deity, the third concerning the Son, the second person of the divinity, the fourth concerning the Holy Spirit, the third person of the divinity, the fifth concerning creation, the sixth concerning sanctification, and the seventh concerning the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. In the latter class Thomas refers the articles pertaining to the humanity of Christ, of which the first is concerning the incarnation or conception of Christ, the second concerning his birth from the Virgin, the third concerning his passion, death, and burial, the fourth concerning his descent into hell, the fifth concerning his resurrection, the sixth concerning his ascension into heaven, and the seventh finally concerning his coming to judgment. But those who count at least twelve articles of the creed, they comprehend the three articles concerning the three divine persons under one, but they distinguish the article concerning glorification into two, one concerning the resurrection of the flesh, and the other concerning eternal life, and thus they make six articles of the first class, pertaining to the divinity and its works. Similarly, in the second class, they contract two articles, one concerning the conception and the other concerning the birth of Christ, into one, and thus they make six articles pertaining to the human nature of Christ, as Thomas refers in the aforementioned place.

III. Does the Apostles' Creed fully contain all articles necessary to be believed? This is a question, especially in this age of ours, that is highly controversial. It can, however, be understood in a double sense. One: Does it so fully contain the articles of faith which it does contain, that the genuine sense of each can be perceived from the very words? The other: Does it contain all articles necessary to be believed, with none missing? In both senses, the negative seems to us to be in accordance with the truth. In the former, indeed: because it contains most of them at least nominally, or in such few words, that unless one has the genuine sense known from elsewhere, from the Scriptures or from the public doctrine of the Church, or fetches and supplies it from there, heresies fighting with opposing fronts could easily be hidden under the covering of so few words: e.g. Sabellians, Arians, Samosatenes, and Photinians, both ancient and modern; likewise Nestorians and Eutychians could, by the words of the creed, while keeping their own heresies, even if contradictorily opposed, profess that they believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord; all of them, however, in a heretical sense. For the Sabellians believed in God, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, as in one divine person, who is called Father in view of the work of creation, but Son in view of the flesh assumed. Arians, on the contrary, believed in God the Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, as in two distinct persons, but of which only one, namely the Father alone, is the true and supreme God, while the other, namely the Son, is not God, but a creature, made indeed before the ages out of nothing, but not from eternity, and who is called God because, as a legate of God, he performed his duties on earth. Samosatenes and Photinians, however, believed and believe in God, the Father almighty, as in one and the only God; but in Jesus Christ as in a mere man, who nevertheless, in view of the office which he performed on earth, is God. Again, Nestorians believed in God, the Father almighty, and in his only Son, as in two persons of one and the same divinity, but of which one, namely the Son, was not born as man and God from the Virgin Mary, but came upon Christ the man, born of her, and dwelt in him, as the Holy Spirit dwells in other saints. The Eutychians, however, did indeed believe, just like them, in God the Father Almighty, and in Jesus Christ, our Lord, but [believed] that he who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary was only God, with the humanity absorbed by the divinity, or converted into the same, etc.

In the latter sense, however, the negative is also consistent; because in the Apostles' Creed several articles necessary to be believed are missing. The article concerning original sin is missing, upon which the doctrine of the necessity of grace depends; and Pelagians and semi-Pelagians can embrace the whole creed, while their heresies, although long since condemned by the Church, remain intact. The article concerning the merit and satisfaction of Christ for our sins, and concerning the universality of his grace and divine grace, is missing. For although mention is made in it of the passion and death of Christ, yet that it has the power of satisfying for our sins, and is meritorious for the remission of sins and for salvation, is not even hinted at by a word, and Socinians can subscribe to the creed, notwithstanding that they utterly deny the merit and satisfaction of Christ. The articles concerning regeneration, repentance, gratuitous justification by faith, and renewal are missing, unless perhaps you wish them to be either included under the communion of saints and the remission of sins, which are mentioned toward the end of the creed, or counted among things to be done rather than things to be believed, both of which, however, will have their own difficulty. For the communion of saints indeed connotes sanctification or renewal: since from it the saints have the fact that they are saints; and the same presupposes regeneration: yet they are not one and the same article, those which are about the Church or communion of saints, and about regeneration and renewal, but three different ones, never to be confused with one another: and Pelagians believe that the Church or communion of saints exists on earth, yet they do not believe the articles concerning regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit: similarly, the remission of sins indeed presupposes repentance, and imports the formal reason of justification, yet the articles concerning repentance and concerning justification are different: not to mention that to believe in the remission of sins does not sufficiently significantly express the article concerning gratuitous justification by faith: since they also believe in the remission of sins, who believe that sins are remitted to them by works. Nor can regeneration, repentance, justification, and renewal be so numbered among things to be done, without them also properly coming into the category of things to be believed. For if the remission of sins being given is an article of faith, which deserves a place in the creed of things to be believed, notwithstanding that actual justification can in its own way be referred to the class of things to be done, why should not also the fact that regeneration, repentance, and renewal are given be articles of faith, and find a place in the creed of things to be believed, notwithstanding that actual regeneration, repentance, and renewal can in their own way be referred to the class of things to be done.

It must be said, therefore; that not all articles of faith are contained in the Apostolic creed, but at least the more important ones, which concern the ultimate end of man, namely eternal blessedness, and its principles and principal means, and that they are touched upon in such few words that they rather presuppose their genuine sense as known from the Scriptures and the public doctrine of the Catholic Church, or leave it to be sought from there, than significantly express it. And so much for the material object.

Latin:

XXXVII.

Distinctioni articulorum fundamentalium in primarios & secundarios vicina est altera Scholasticis receptissima distinctio in articulos necessarios necessitate præcepti & necessitate medii. Hi dici possunt, quorum cognitio explicita sive expressa simpliciter necessaria est, ut ne ignorari quidem possint, fide & salute salvâ. Illi, quorum cognitio, licet divinitùs præcepta sit, non tamen ita simpliciter necessaria est, quin citra fidei & salutis jacturam ignorari possint.

I. Necessitas præcepti, in ordine ad articulos fidei spectata, accipi potest duplici fignificatu. Uno generaliori, prout etiam necessitatem medii sub se comprehendit. Quæ enim necessaria sunt creditu necessitate medii, illorum fides etiam à Deo præcepta est, & sic ea sunt etiam necessaria creditu necessitate præcepti. Altero strictiori, prout necessitati medii contradistinguitur. Quo sensu necessaria sunt creditu necessitate præcepti, quæ non suâpte naturâ, aut ex quâdam sui habitudine ad consequendum finem necessariâ, sed solùm ex voluntate Dei præcipientis ad credendum obligant.
