Necessitate medii verò necessaria sunt creditu, quæ non ex sola Dei præcipientis voluntate, sed etiam ex sua ad consequendam salutem habitudine necessariâ ad credendum obligant, cùm absque iis creditis fides salvifica & salus homini constare non possit. Atque hoc fignificatu Scholastici communiter distinctionem accipiunt.

II. Si vim vocum spectes, necessitate medii necessarii dicendi essent ii solùm articuli, quorum res fignificata habet rationem medii, ad consequendam salutem necessarii. Sed heîc in sensu laxiori dicuntur articuli necessarii necessitate medii, quorum cognitio ad generandam fidem consequendamque salutem ita necessaria est, ut absque ea nec fides salvifica nec salus ipsa obtineri possit, & videntur proinde necessarii dici necessitate medii, non quòd eorum res fignificata semper sit medium consequendæ salutis, sed quòd fides, cujus objectum sunt, & quæ absq; illis creditis vel non esse, vel non salvifica esse potest, sit medium consequendæ salutis necessarium. Atque sic articuli necessarii necessitate medii, & articuli fundamentales primarii; item articuli fundamentales secundarii, & articuli necessarii necessitate præcepti coincidunt.

XXXIIX.

Articulorum fidei Epitomen quandam exhibet Symbolum Apostolicum, & numerantur apud Scholasticos vulgo quatuordecim, vel duodecim.

I. Symbolum Apostolicum dicitur vel ab Apostolis, quòd ab illis, in terrarum orbem ad praedicandum Evangelium digressis, unanimi consensu concinnatum, & Ecclesiae voce viva traditum fit, ut nonnulli veteres volunt; vel, quod vero magis consentaneum, a doctrina Apostolica, quod ex illa collectum sit, licet incerto auctore, ejusque quasi nucleum & summam contineat, ut aliis placet. Quam controversiam nunc nostram non facimus.

II. Articulos fidei, in Symbolo Apostolico comprehensos, nonnulli numerant quatuordecim, quos Thomas in II. II. q. I. a. VIII. in duas dispescit classes. In priorem refert articulos, pertinentes ad majestatem divinitatis, quorum quatuor sunt: Unus de Dei unitate, & tres de mysterio Trinitatis, juxta numerum trium personarum. 2. Articulos concernentes opera divinatatis propria, quae ad esse naturae pertinent, vel ad esse gratiae, vel denique ad esse gloriae. Opera divinitatis, ad esse naturae pertinentia, qui concernit est articulus de creatione; opera gratiae vero concernit articulus de sanctificatione; opera, ad esse gloriae pertinentia, concernit articulus de resurrectione carnis & vita aeterna, ut ita classis prima hosce septem contineat articulos: primum de uno Deo, secundum de Patre, prima Deitatis persona, tertium de Filio, persona divinitatis secunda, quartum de Spiritu Sancto, persona divinitatis tertia, quintum de creatione, sextum de sanctificatione, & septimum de resurrectione carnis & vita aeterna. In classem posteriorem refert Thomas articulos, ad Christi humanitatem pertinentes, quorum primus est de incarnatione sive de conceptione Christi, secundus de ejus nativitate ex Virgine, tertius de ejus passione, morte & sepultura, quartus de descensu ad inferos, quintus de resurrectione ipsius, sextus de adscensione ad caelos, & septimus denique de ejus adventu ad judicium. Qui autem duodecim saltem articulos symboli numerant, illi tres articulos de tribus personis divinis comprehendunt sub uno, articulum vero de glorificatione distinguunt in duos, unum de resurrectione carnis, & alterum de vita aeterna, atque sic sex faciunt articulos primae classis, ad divinitatem ejusque opera pertinentes. Similiter in classe altera articulos duos, unum de conceptione, & alterum de nativitate Christi contrahunt in unum, & sic sex ad Christi humanam naturam pertinentes articulos faciunt, referente Thoma d. l. III.

III. Contineatne Symbolum Apostolicum plenè omnes creditu necessarios articulos? quæstio est, hâc nostrâ inprimis ætate valdè controversa. Potest autem duplici sensu intelligi. Uno, An quos continet articulos fidei, ita plenè contineat, ut cujusque sensus genuinus ex ipsis verbis percipi possit? Altero, an articulos creditu necessarios omnes, nullo deficiente, contineat? Utroque sensu negativa videtur nobis vero consentanea. Priori quidem: quia plerosque titulotenus saltem, vel verbis ita paucis continet, ut nisi aliunde ex Scripturis vel ex publica Ecclesiæ doctrina sensum genuinum quis cognitum habeat, vel inde accersat & suppleat, sub integumento Verborum tam paucorum pugnantes frontibus adversis hæreses occultari facilè possint: v. g. Sabelliani, Ariani, Samosateniani & Photiniani veteres & recentiores; Nestoriani item & Eutychiani poterant verbis symboli, salvis suis, etsi contradictoriè oppositis, hæresibus, profiteri, se credere in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, creatorem cæli & terræ, & in Jesum Christum, Filium ejus unicum, Dominum nostrum; omnes tamen sensu hæretico. Sabelliani enim credebant in Deum, & in Jesum Christum, Filium ejus unicum, velut in unam personam divinam, quæ intuitu operis creationis Pater, intuitu adsumtæ carnis autem Filius appelletur. Ariani contra credebant in Deum Patrem, & in Jesum Christum, Filium ejus unicum, velut in duas personas distinctas, sed quarum una tantùm, nempe Pater solus, verus & summus Deus, altera verò, Filius scilicet, non Deus, sed creatura sit, ante secula quidem facta ex nihilo, non autem ab æterno, & quæ Deus dicatur, quod velut legatus Dei vices ejus in terris gesserit. Samosateniani & Photiniani autem credebant & credunt in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, tanquam in unum & solum Deum; in Jesum Christum verò tanquam in hominem nudum, qui tamen intuitu officii, quo in terris functus est, Deus sit. Rursum Nestoriani credebant in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, & in Filium ejus unicum, tanquam in duas unius & ejusdem divinitatis personas, sed quarum altera, Filius scilicet, non sit ex Virgine Maria homo & Deus natá, sed in Christum hominem, ex illa natum, supervenerit, atque in eo habicaverit, ut in aliis sanctis habitat Spiritus Sanctus. Eutychiani verò credebant quidem, perinde ut illi, in Deum Patrem omnipotentem, & in Jesum Christum, Dominum nostrum, sed qui de Spiritu Sancto conceptus, & ex virgine Maria natus sit tantùm Deus, humanitate à divinitate absorptâ, vel in eandem conversâ &c.

Posteriori autem sensu etiam vero consentanea est negativa; quia in Symbolo Apostolico plures desunt articuli creditu necessarii. Deest articulus de peccato originis, ex quo doctrina de necessitate gratiæ dependet; & possunt Pelagiani ac semi-Pelagiani symbolum totum amplecti, hæresibus suis, licet ab Ecclesia dudum damnatis, salvis. Deest articulus de merito & satisfactione Christi pro peccatis nostris, deque ejus & gratiæ divinæ universalitate. Quamvis enim passionis & mortis Christi in eo fiat mentio, eam tamen vim habere satisfaciendi pro peccatis nostris, & meritoriam esse remissionis peccatorum ac salutis, ne verbo quidem innuitur, & possunt Sociniani subscribere symbolo, non obstante, quòd Christi meritum & satisfactionem prorsus negant. Desunt articuli de regeneratione, de pœnitentia, de gratuita justificatione per fidem, & de renovatione, nisi forsan vel sub communione sanctorum & remissione peccatorum, quorum sub finem symboli mentio fit, comprehensos, vel in agendis potiùs, quàm in credendis numerandos velis, quorum utrumque tamen suam habebit difficultatem. Nam communio sanctorum quidem connotat sanctificationem sive renovationem: cùm ab ea sancti habeant, quod sancti sunt; & eadem præsupponit regenerationem: non tamen articulus unus & idem sunt, qui de Ecclesia sive communione sanctorum, & de regeneratione ac renovatione sunt, sed tres diversi, inter se nunquam confundendi: & credunt Pelagiani Ecclesiam sive communionem sanctorum in terris dari, nec tamen credunt articulos de regeneratione & renovatione per Spiritum Sanctum: similiter remissio peccatorum præsupponit quidem pœnitentiam, & importat formalem rationem justificationis, articuli tamen de pœnitentia & de justificatione diversi sunt: ut taceam, quòd, credere remissionem peccatorum, articulum de gratuitâ justificatione per fidem non satis significanter exprimat: cùm & remissionem peccatorum credant, qui ex operibus peccata sibi remitti credunt. Neque ita agendis annumerari possunt regeneratio, pœnitentia, justificatio & renovatio, quin & credendorum in partem propriè veniant. Si enim remissionem peccatorum dari articulus fidei est, qui in credendorum symbolo locum meretur, non obstante, quòd justificatio actualis agendorum in classem suo modo referri possit, quidnî & regenerationem, pœnitentiam & renovationem dari, articuli fidei sint, & in credendorum symbolo locum inveniant, non obstante, quòd regeneratio, pœnitentia & renovatio actualis in classem agendorum suo modo referri possint.

Dicendum ergo; in symbolo Apostolico non contineri omnes planè articulos fidei, sed potiores saltem, qui finem hominis ultimum, beatitudinem æternam scilicet, & ejus principia ac media principalia concernunt, eaque verbis ita paucis attingi, ut genuinum illorum sensum velut notum ex Scripturis & publica Ecclesiæ Catholicæ doctrina præsupponant potiùs, vel inde accerfendum relinquant, quàm significanter exprimant. Et tantum de objecto materiali.


### XXXIX. The formal object, which we have said is the First Truth revealing, as…

XXXIX.

The formal object, which we have said is the First Truth revealing, as revealing, cannot perform its function in Theology, and move the intellect to assent to itself of itself immediately, unless it also affects the will, strikes it, and entices and draws it to command the intellect to assent to it.

I. The First Truth revealing, as revealing, is the formal object or reason for assenting to non-evident and obscure Theology, not indeed according to its whole self, but according to some part of itself. For it includes two complex principles in the objective formal reason. One is, that the First Truth, i.e., God, in revealing can neither be deceived nor deceive, or what amounts to the same thing, whatever the First Truth or God reveals, is certainly and infallibly true. The other, that God has revealed to the sacred writers what is contained in the sacred Scriptures. The former principle is indeed evident, and from the apprehended terms is immediately known to be true, which therefore can of itself immediately determine the intellect to its assent. The latter, however, is non-evident or obscure to our intellect. For when all the terms which it comprises are perceived, it still remains non-evident and obscure, whether it be true or false that those things which are contained in the sacred Scriptures were written by God revealing them? Whence if the intellect is to provide a certain and immovable assent to it of itself immediately, as it must altogether happen if it is to fulfill the function of the formal object and the ultimate reason for assenting in the habit of Theology, it is necessary that it also affect the will, strike it, and draw it to command the intellect to assent. For this is the connatural manner of non-evident objects, that since on account of their non-evidence they cannot represent the things themselves to the intellect so clearly that it perceives the identity of the predicate with the subject in the perceived terms, and thus the truth itself, they entice the will and draw it to command the intellect to assent; and it is similarly connatural to our intellect that, when it cannot have truth clearly known, it obeys the will drawn into consent and commanding assent to it, and at its command elicits the act of assenting.

II. And to this the Scholastics refer the passages of Scripture Rom. X. 10. With the heart one believes unto righteousness; which Thomas in this place, Lect. II., explains: with the heart, i.e., the will moving and applying (the intellect) to believe, one believes, etc. John XII. 39, 40. Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart, etc. By which the cause of the unbelief of the Jews is referred to the hardness of the heart, i.e., the obstinacy of the will; and by force of opposition the cause of faith will have to be referred to the pious affection of the will, opposed to its hardness or obstinacy; Acts XVI. 14. The Lord opened the heart of Lydia, a seller of purple, that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul: where to open the heart is to move the will, so that it may apply and determine the intellect to attend to the preached Word and to believe it: and Luke XXIV. 25. slowness of heart to believe, reproached by Christ to the disciples on the road to Emmaus, undoubtedly pertains to the will, and implies on its part a defect of pious affection toward divine revelation, through which it came about that they were slow and sluggish to believe. To which it is also accustomed to be referred, that in the Second Council of Orange, canon V, the beginning of faith is established in an affection of credulity, correcting our will from infidelity to faith: which, as regards the matter, can be nothing else than a pious affection or motion of the will toward believing. Which passages of Scripture and of the Council of Orange, although they treat of faith and of a pious affection on the part of the will required for the assent of faith, which is to be commanded to the intellect, are nevertheless rightly accommodated to Theology: since of both, faith and Theology, there is one formal object, namely, the First Truth revealing; to which if the intellect, elevated by the habit of either faith or Theology, ought to yield assent of itself immediately, and to other things on account of it, there will always be required on the part of the will a pious affection for this, that it may determine the intellect by its command to the assent to be yielded to it of itself immediately.

Latin:

XXXIX.

Formale objectum, quod diximus esse primam Veritatem revelantem, ut revelantem, munus suum in Theologia obire, & intellectum in sui assensum per se immediatè movere non potest, nisi etiam voluntatem afficiat, pulset, & ad sui assensum intellectui imperandum alliciat & trahat.

I. Veritas prima revelans, ut revelans, est objectum formale sive ratio assentiendi Theologiæ inevidens & obscura, non quidem secundum se totam, sed secundum aliquam sui partem. Includit enim in ratione objectiva formali duo principia complexa. Unum est, Veritatem primam, h. e. Deum in revelando nec falli nec fallere posse, sive quod eodem redit, quicquid Veritas prima sive Deus revelat, certò & infallibiliter verum esse. Alterum, Deum revelasse Scriptoribus sacris, quæ in Scripturis sacris continentur. Prius principium quidem evidens est, & ex apprehensis terminis statim verum esse cognoscitur, quod proindè intellectum per se immediatè ad sui assensum determinare potest. Posterius verò inevidens sive obscursum est nostro intellectui. Perceptis enim omnibus terminis, quos complectitur, adhuc inevidens & obscurum manet, sitne verum? an falsum, quòd quæ in Scripturis sacris continentur, Deo revelante conscripta sint? Unde si ei per se immediatè intellectus assensum certum & immotum præbere debeat, sicut omninò fieri oportet, si munus objecti formalis & rationis assentiendi ultimæ prima Veritas revelans in Theologiæ habitu obire debeat, necesse est, ut voluntatem etiam afficiat, pulset, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum trahat. Hæc enim est objectorum inevidentium connaturalis ratio, ut cum ob suam inevidentiam non possint res ipsas intellectui ita clarè repræsentare, ut in terminis perceptis statim identitatem prædicati cum subjecto, atque adeò veritatem ipsam perspiciat, voluntatem alliciant, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum trahant; & intellectui nostro similiter connaturale est, ut cùm veritatem clarè cognitam habere non potest, voluntati in consensum tractæ, & assensum sibi imperanti obtemperet, & ad ejus imperium actum assentiendi eliciat.

II. Atque huc referunt Scholastici loca Scripturæ Rom. X. 10. Corde creditur ad justitiam; quod Thomas in h. l. Lect. II. explicat, corde, i. e. voluntate (intellectum) movente & applicante ad credendum, creditur &c. Joh. XII. 39. 40. Proptereà non poterant credere, quia iterum dixit Jesaias: Excæcavit oculos eorum, & induravit cor eorum &c. Quibus causa incredulitatis Judæorum refertur in duritiem cordis, h. e. obstinationem voluntatis; & vi oppositionis causa fidei referenda erit in voluntatis piam affectionem, ejus duritei sive obstinationi oppositam; Act. XVI. 14. Dominus aperuit cor Lydiæ, purpurarum venditrici, ut intenderet his, quæ dicebantur à Paulo: ubi aperire cor est voluntatem movere, ut intellectum ad attendendum Verbo prædicato, eique credendum applicet & determinet: & Luc. XXIV. 25. tarditas cordis ad credendum, discipulis Emaunticis à Christo exprobrata, indubiè pertinet ad voluntatem, importatque ex parte illius defectum affectionis piæ erga divinam revelationem, per quem fiebat, ut tardi & segnes essent ad credendum. Quò & referri solet, quòd in Concil. Araus. II. can. V. initium fidei constituitur in credulitatis affectu, corrigente voluntatem nostram ab infidelitate ad fidem: qui, quoad rem, nihil aliud esse potest, quàm pia voluntatis affectio sive motio ad credendum. Quæ Scripturæ & Synodi Arausicanæ loca, etsi agunt de fide, deque pia affectione, ex parte voluntatis ad assensum fidei, intellectui imperandum, requisitâ, rectè tamen ad Theologiam accommodantur: cùm utriusque, fidei & Theologiæ, unum sit objectum formale, Veritas prima revelans scilicet; cui si intellectus, sive fidei sive Theologiæ habitu elevatus, per se immediatè præbere debeat assensum, & rebus aliis propter illam, ex parte voluntatis semper requiretur affectio pia ad hoc, ut intellectum ad assensum, ei per se immediatè præbendum, imperio suo determinet.


### XL. Hence it follows that Theology, although it is formally a habit of the…

XL.

Hence it follows that Theology, although it is formally a habit of the intellect occupied in delivering, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, nevertheless on the part of the will connotes a certain habit, which they call that of pious affection, by which, namely, the will is rendered piously affected and prompt toward the First Truth revealing and its revelation contained in the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, to captivate the intellect, if by chance it resists with its own διαλογισμοῖς, into its obedience, and to determine it by its command to assent.

I. Here the Scholastics do not agree. Scotus in III, Dist. XXV, q. II, judges that for assenting to the First Truth revealing on its own account, the habit of believing in the intellect is sufficient. His reason is: because the intellect alone is the efficient and per se cause of the act of assenting; the will, however, relates to it only as a moving cause, and as it were accidentally, which therefore requires no habitual perfection for this.

II. Thomas, on the contrary, in II. II. q. IV. a. II., establishes that for the act of assenting to the First Truth for its own sake to be perfect, there is required also on the part of the will a certain habit, by which it is determined to command the intellect to assent. The words of Thomas are these: Since faith is a certain virtue, it is necessary that its act be perfect. But for the perfection of an act which proceeds from two active principles, it is required that each of the active principles be perfect. For it cannot be well cut unless both the one cutting has the skill and the saw is well disposed for cutting. But the disposition for acting well in those powers of the soul which relate to opposites is a habit. And therefore it is necessary that an act proceeding from two such powers be perfected by some habit pre-existing in both of the powers. But it has been said above that to believe is an act of the intellect, according as it is moved by the will to assent: but an act of this kind proceeds from the will and from the intellect, both of which are naturally perfected by a habit according to the aforesaid: and therefore it is necessary that there be some habit in the will as well as in the intellect, if the act of faith is to be perfect.

III. Among the more recent authors, Suarez in De Trip. Virt. Theol. Disp. VII. Sect. II., Medina in lib. IV. de recta in Deum fide, c. II., Molina in Concord. q. XIV. Disp. VIII., Coninck Disp. XIII. n. LXXI., Arriaga Tract. de Fide Divina Disp. XVII. Sect. V., and many others follow the opinion of Thomas. Modern Thomists, however, although they do not deny that for the act of assenting to the First Truth revealing for its own sake, a pious motion is required on the part of the will, by which it is moved and determined to the assent of the intellect; they contend, however, that for eliciting that motion no habit pre-existing in the will is required, but that the actual help of God suffices. But they interpret the passage of Thomas cited as referring to an act of faith that is perfect, not only with the essential perfection which even that act has which is not informed by charity, but also with an accidental perfection, by which it is constituted in the state of virtue simply so-called, or meritorious, such as is only the act of faith, informed by divine charity, as Gonet proposes and declares the mind of the Thomists, Tom. IV of the Clypeus Theologiae Thomisticae, Disp. VI. on the internal act of faith, Art. II

IV. What the Scholastics dispute among themselves concerning the habit of the will required for the acts of faith, we have just said proceeds also concerning the acts of assenting to the First Truth revealing in Theology. We think, however, that the opinion of Thomas which has been adduced is most agreeable to the truth, and to be preferred to the others. For faith is a habit by which the intellect is rendered powerful, unencumbered, and prompt to assent to the First Truth for its own sake, and to revealed things on account of it; and Theology is similarly a habit by which the intellect is rendered powerful, unencumbered, and prompt to teach, confirm, and defend those things which have been divinely revealed for the sake of our salvation, from principles resting upon the First Truth revealing and its revelation, as the ultimate reason for assenting, and believed on account of the same. But just as the First Truth revealing, which is the ultimate reason for assenting for both faith and Theology, cannot move the intellect to its own assent unless the will is drawn into consent and determines the intellect to assent, and thus it is connatural to acts of assenting to the First Truth for its own sake that there be given from the part of the will an actual pious motion by which the intellect is determined to elicit it: so also to the habit of assenting to the First Truth for its own sake in the intellect, such as both faith and Theology are, it is connatural that there be given from the part of the will some habit of pious affection toward the First Truth revealing, and its revelation contained in the Scriptures, by which it [the will] itself is rendered powerful, unencumbered, and prompt to captivate the intellect under its obedience, and to command assent to it. For the promptness and habitual perfection of the intellect to assent to the First Truth revealing and its revelation for its own sake depends connaturally upon the habitual affection of the will toward the same, and upon its habitual promptness and perfection to command assent to it.

Latin:

XL.

Hinc sequitur, quòd Theologia, quamvis formaliter sit habitus intellectus, in iis, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, tradendis, confirmandis & defendendis occupatus, ex parte voluntatis tamen connotet habitum quemdam, quem piæ affectionis dicunt, quo scilicet voluntas erga primam Veritatem revelantem ejusque in Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis contentam revelationem piè affecta & promta reddatur ad captivandum intellectum, si fortè suis διαλογισμοῖς obsistat, in ejus obsequium, eumque ad assensum imperio tuô determinandum.

I. Hic non consentiunt Scholastici. Scotus in III. Dist. XXV. q. II. censet, ad assentiendum Veritati primæ revelanti propter se sufficere habitum credendi in intellectu. Ratio ejus est: quia intellectus solus est causa actus assentiendi efficiens & per se; voluntas autem habet se ad eum tantum ut causa movens, & quasi per accidens, quæ propterea nullà ad hoc perfectione habituali egeat.

II. Thomas contrà in II. II. q. IV. a. II. statuit, ad actum assentiendi Veritati primæ propter se, ut perfectus sit, requiri etiam ex parte voluntatis habitum quendam, quo ad imperandum intellectui assensum determinetur. Verba Thomæ sunt hæc: Cùm fides sit quædam virtus, oportet, quod ejus actus sit perfectus. Ad perfectionem autem actus, qui ex duobus activis principiis procedit, requiritur, quod utrumque activorum principiorum sit perfectum. Non enim benè potest secari, nisi & secans habeat artem, & serra sit benè disposita ad secandum. Dispositio autem ad benè agendum in illis potentiis animæ, quæ se habent ad opposita, est habitus. Et ideò oportet, quòd actus procedens ex duabus talibus potentiis sit perfectus habitu aliquo præexistente in utraque potentiarum. Dictum autem est suprà, quòd credere est actus intellectus, secundum quod movetur à voluntate ad assentiendum: procedit autem hujusmodi actus à voluntate & ab intellectu, quorum utrumque natum est per habitum perfici secundum prædicta: & ideò oportet, quòd tam in voluntate sit aliquis habitus, quàm in intellectu, si debeat actus fidei esse perfectus.

III. Thomæ sententiam ex recentioribus sequuntur Suarez de Trip’. Virt. Theol. Disp. VII. Sect. II. Medina in lib. IV. de recta in Deum fide, c. II. Molina in Concord. q. XIV. Disp. VIII. Coninck Disp. XIII. n. LXXI. Arriaga Tract. de Fide Divina Disp. XVII. Sect. V. & alii plures. Thomistæ moderni tamen, licet non negent, ad actum assentienti Veritati primæ revelanti propter se requiri ex parte voluntatis motionem piam, quâ ad assensum intellectus moveatur, & determinetur; contendunt tamen, ad motionem illam eliciendam non requiri aliquem habitum, in voluntate præexistentem, sed sufficere Dei auxilium actuale. Locum Thomæ allegatum verò interpretantur de actu fidei perfecto, non solùm perfectione essentiali, quam habet etiam ille, qui non informatur charitate, sed etiam perfectione accidentali, per quam constituitur in ratione virtutis simpliciter dictæ, sive meritoriæ, qualis est duntaxat actus fidei, charitate divina informatæ, uti Thomistarum mentem proponit & declarat Gonet Tom. IV Clypei Theol. Thomisticæ, Disp. VI. de Actu fidei interno Art. II

IV. Quæ de habitu voluntatis, ad actus fidei requisito, Scholastici inter se disputant, ea procedere etiam de actibus assentiendi Veritati primæ revelanti in Theologia, modò diximus. Existimamus autem, sententiam Thomæ adductam esse vero maximè consentaneam, & cæteris præferendam. Est enim fides habitus, quo intellectus potens, expeditus & promtus redditur ad assentiendum Veritati primæ propter se, & rebus revelatis propter illam; & Theologia similiter est habitus, quo intellectus potens, expeditus, & promtus redditur ad docendum, confirmandũ & defendendum ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ divinitùs revelata sunt, ex principiis, primæ Veritati revelanti ejusque revelationi, tanquam rationi assentiendi ultimæ innixis, & propter eandem creditis. Quemadmodum autem Veritas prima revelans, quæ & fidei & Theologiæ ratio assentiendi ultima est, intellectum insui assensum movere non potest, nisi voluntate in consensum tractâ, & intellectum ad assensum sui determinante, atque adeò actibus assentiendi Veritati primæ propter se connaturale est, ut ex parte voluntatis detur actualis motio pia, quâ ad eum eliciendum intellectus determinetur: ita & habitui assentiendi Veritati primæ propter se in intellectu, qualis & fides & Theologia est, connaturale est, ut ex parte voluntatis detur aliquis habitus piæ affectionis erga primam Veritatem revelantem, ejusque in Scripturis contentam revelationem, quo & ipsa potens, expedita & promta reddatur ad captivandum intellectum sub ejus obsequium, & ad imperandum ipsi assensum. Promtitudo enim & perfectio habitualis intellectus ad assentiendum primæ Veritati revelanti ejusque revelationi propter se, dependet connaturaliter ab habituali affectione voluntatis erga eandem, & ab ejus habituali promtitudine ac perfectione ad imperandum ipsi assensum.


### XLI. Since, however, the first Truth revealing, as revealing, is supernatural in its…

XLI.

Since, however, the first Truth revealing, as revealing, is supernatural in its objective formal reason and force, and through revelation, elevated by its own supernatural concurrence, illuminates the intellect and strikes, draws, and entices the will to command assent to the intellect, Theology also is a habit supernatural in substance.

I. Habits, both of the intellect and of the will, derive their specific reason from their formal object, and if this is natural in its objective formal force and reason, the habit is also natural in substance; but if it is supernatural, the habit must necessarily be supernatural in substance.

II. That the first Truth revealing, as revealing, is supernatural in its objective formal force and reason, the Holy Scriptures teach and suggest in many places. In 1 Thessalonians 2:13, Paul counts among the chief benefits of God that the Thessalonians had received the λόγον ἀκοῆς, the Word of hearing, that is, the Word preached and perceived by hearing, not as the word of men, but (as it truly is) as the word of God, and for that reason he gives thanks to God unceasingly. But to receive the Word, preached by the Apostles, not as the word of men, but as the word of God, what else is it than to believe that the first Truth revealing, or God, is the one who was speaking through the Apostles that word by which they were learning of God? By what reason, however, or in what manner it was given to them by God to receive the preaching of the Apostles as the word of God, they declare in what follows immediately: ὃς καὶ ἐνεργεῖται ἐν ὑμῖν τοῖς πισεύουσιν, i.e., who also works in you who believe: Where by the word ἐνεργεῖται he does not understand an ἐνέργειαν or operation separated from the preached word, but an ἐνέργειαν most closely joined to it, and that a supernatural one, which is elevated beyond and above the condition of any other Word to illuminate the intellect and draw the will, so that by testifying of itself that it has proceeded from God and is truly divine, it may move the minds of men of itself immediately into its own supernatural assent. Just as, however, the preached Word has from God's supernatural concurrence or operation that it moves the minds of men immediately by itself into its own supernatural assent, so also does the written Word of God: since they do not differ, except in extrinsic connotations, in that the former is introduced into the hearts of men by voice through hearing; the latter by writing through sight. To this also pertain the passages in which the Word of God is called the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. I. 16; the power of God to them that are saved, I Cor. I. 18; the power of God to the called themselves, both Jews and Greeks, v. 24. Compare I Cor. II. 4, 5. And these things are attributed to the Word of God, not because either the words of which it consists, or the things signified by them, considered precisely in themselves, are powerful or apt for moving the intellect to a certain and immovable assent to itself: for words, since they are taken from common usage of speech, cannot by themselves contribute more than to signify to the intellect the things of which they are signs; but the things signified, since they are non-evident, cannot by themselves move the intellect to assent to them; but because God, through it, elevated by His supernatural concurrence, is powerful to move the minds of men, so that they may by themselves immediately offer it indubitable assent.

Latin:

XLI.

Cùm verò prima Veritas revelans, ut revelans, in ratione & vi objectiva formali supernaturalis sit, & per revelationem, suo concursu supernaturali elevatam, intellectum illuminet, voluntatemque pulset, trahat & ad imperandum intellectui assensum sui alliciat, Theologia etiam habitus in substantia supernaturalis est.

I. Habitus, cùm intellectus, tum voluntatis, sortiuntur suam rationem specificam ab objecto formali, & si hoc in vi & ratione objectiva formali naturale sit, habitum etiam in substantia naturalem; sin supernaturale, habitum in substantia supernaturalem esse necesse est.

II. Quod autem prima Veritas revelans, ut revelans, in vi & ratione objectiva formali supernaturalis sit, docent & insinuant Scripturæ sacræ passim locorum. In I. Thess. II. 13. numerat Paulus in præcipuis Dei beneficiis, quòd Thessalonicenses λόγον ἀκοῆς Verbum auditus, h.e. Verbum prædicatum & auditu perceptum, acceperant non ut sermonem hominum, sed (sicut verè est) ut Dei sermonem, & eo nomine Deo gratias agit indefinenter. Accipere autem Verbum, ab Apostolis prædicatum, non ut hominum, sed ut Dei sermonem, quid aliud est, quàm credere, primam Veritatem revelantem, sive Deum esse, qui per Apostolos loqueretur sermonem illum, quo Deum discebant? Quâ ratione autem, quove modo ipsis à Deo datum fuerit, ut prædicationem Apostolorum acciperet ut Dei sermonem, declarant, quæ mox sequuntur: ὃς καὶ ἐνεργεῖται ἐν ὑμῖν τοῖς πισεύουσιν, i. e. qui etiam operatur in vobis, qui creditis: Ubi verbo ἐνεργεῖται non intelligit ἐνέργειαν sive operationem, à verbo prædicato sejunctam, sed ἐνέργειαν ipsi conjunctissimam, eamque supernaturalem, quæ ultra & supra conditionem alterius cujusque Verbi id elevatur ad illuminandum intellectum, & trahendum voluntatem, ut de semetipso, quòd à Deo profectum & verè divinum sit, testificando hominum animos per se immediatè in sui assensum supernaturalem moveat. Quemadmodum autem Verbum prædicatum à Dei supernaturali concursu sive operatione habet, quòd hominum animos in sui assensum supernaturalem per se immediatè movet, ita & Dei Verbum scriptum: cùm non differant, nisi connotatis extrinsecis, quòd illud voce per auditum; hoc scripturâ per visum hominum cordibus immitattur. Quò pertinent etiam loca, quibus Verbum Dei dicitur potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. potentia Dei iis, qui servantur, I. Cor. I. 18. potentia Dei ipsis vocatis, tùm Judæis, tùm Græcis v. 24. Confer I. Cor. II. 4. 5. Atque hæc tribuuntur Verbo Dei, non quòd vel voces, quibus constat, vel res iis significatæ, per se præcisè spectatæ, potentes vel aptæ sint ad movendum intellectum in assensum sui certum & immotum: voces enim, cùm ex usu loquendi vulgari desumtæ sint, per se plus conferre non possunt, quàm ut res, quarum signa sunt, intellectui significent; res significatæ autem, cùm inevidentes sint, per se intellectum in assensum sui movere nequeunt; sed quòd Deus per illud, suo concursu supernaturali elevatum, potens sit ad movendos hominum animos, ut per se immediatè ei assensum indubitatum præbeant.


### XLII. Theology is, however, a habit supernatural in substance, both by reason of…

XLII.

Theology is, however, a habit supernatural in substance, both by reason of itself, as it is a habit of the intellect, and by reason of the connoted habit of pious affection, on the part of the will.

I. That Theology is a supernatural habit on both sides, its formal object proves. For it is a habit of teaching, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, under the First Truth revealing, and its revelation, so that it may be ultimately resolved into it, as into a non-evident reason for assenting, and into its supernatural formal motive power, as has been shown. It is repugnant, however, for any habit of teaching to be resolved ultimately into the First Truth revealing, as into a non-evident reason for assenting, and into its supernatural formal power and objective reason, and yet for it not to be supernatural in substance, either on the part of itself; or on the part of the will is not conjoined with a habit of supernatural pious affection. For the reason for the will is the same as for the intellect, as far as non-evident habits are concerned, and because the formal motive by its own nature generates on the part of the intellect a supernatural habit of assenting, it also by its own nature affects the will, and generates on its part a supernatural habit, by which, being well-affected toward that [motive], it is elevated to command assent to its intellect: since a non-evident habit of assenting, and that a supernatural one, cannot, without a supernatural habit of pious affection, be generated or exist in a way connatural to itself, as is evident from what has been said. Which the thing itself also demands. For just as the intellect of the natural man does not grasp the things that are of the Spirit of God (and revelation itself, as having proceeded from the Holy Spirit as from the First Truth, is also of the census of these things), since they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, I Cor. II. 14, so his will is alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in the intellect, and through its own hardness of heart, Eph. IV. 18, nor is it better affected toward the First Truth revealing and its revelation than the intellect; and therefore both faculties are in need of a supernatural habit: the intellect indeed to assent to the First Truth revealing and its revelation for its own sake; the will, however, to command assent to the intellect.

H. We intend these things, however, to be understood of Theology, such as it is and ought to be by itself and by virtue of its genuine object or formal motive. For a twofold habit of Theology can be given. One, which rests ultimately in the First Truth revealing, as revealing, as in the proper reason for assenting, and from divine revelation, believed through and for itself, teaches, confirms, and defends those things which are necessary for those about to attain salvation, whether to be believed or to be done. The other, which does not rest ultimately in the First Truth revealing and its revelation, but in the testimony of parents, ancestors, the Church, or other signs of credibility. For he who is born and educated in the Church, and has imbibed with his mother's milk, as it were, the opinion that the book of the Scriptures contains the Word divinely revealed and committed to writing by divine inspiration, he certainly believes this on account of the testimony and authority of his parents. By which he can be confirmed in the faith by the authority of the Church, diffused far and wide throughout the world, and by signs or other motives of credibility, even though he may be a hypocrite, and through malice may place an obstacle to the grace of this matter, which works certain and divine faith through the Word itself. And if he offers assent to the Scriptures, although only of human faith or opinion, he can furthermore by human study acquire for himself the habit of interpreting the Scriptures, of deducing, confirming, and defending conclusions from them, and that again with assent, resting on human authority. Which experience also testifies. For there are found impious men, and even heretics, who in explaining the Scriptures, and in deducing, confirming, and defending conclusions from them, are often more expeditious than other orthodox and most pious Theologians. which is perhaps the reason why grave Authors have ascribed Theology simply to natural habits, and which fall even to unregenerate men.

But this, which we readily acknowledge to be a natural habit, is Theology spoken equivocally, and is as far removed from Theology properly so called as human faith or opinion, conceived in the mind from external motives concerning the truth of divine revelation, is removed from divine faith. For its ultimate reason for assenting is clearly different from the ultimate reason for assenting of Theology, properly so called. For the ultimate reason for assenting of the latter, as has been said, is the primary Truth revealing, as revealing, which through the revelation related in the Scriptures, elevated by its supernatural concurrence, moves the intellect and will of itself immediately, the latter indeed to command assent to the intellect; the former to elicit the same in itself, so that the assent ultimately rests in it. But the ultimate reason for assenting of the former, as has just been shown, is human authority, namely of parents and of the Church, which generates human faith; or miracles or other motives, which generate opinion: e.g., a hypocrite, or a secret heretic, who feigns to be a Theologian, will indeed assent to this conclusion deduced by him from the Scriptures: Christ is ὁμούσιος to God the Father, because of this: Christ is the only-begotten Son of God; but not through and because of it immediately believed, so that his assent ultimately rests in the authority of the first Truth revealing, but because he sees it contained in the Gospel of John; and those things which are contained in the Gospel of John, he believes to be true, because from his tender years he has been so taught by his parents or teachers, or has received from the Church that the things which are contained therein are revealed by God and infallibly true. And in this testimony of parents, teachers, or the Church, as in the ultimate reason for assenting, his assent finally stops. But just as that testimony is human, so it can beget nothing but human faith or opinion, and as the acts of assent of Theology, spoken of in this second sense, stopping ultimately in this testimony, are in substance natural and merely opinative, so Theology itself, thus accepted, is a habit in substance natural and merely opinative. But Theology properly so called, because it stops ultimately in the first Truth revealing, is a habit in substance supernatural, and simply certain. For the first Truth revealing, whenever it sustains the office of the ultimate reason for assenting, and moves the intellect of itself immediately into its own assent, begets an assent in substance supernatural, and one that is not opinative, but simply certain, to which it is altogether repugnant that falsehood should underlie it.

Latin:

XLII.

ESt autem Theologia habitus in substântia supernaturalis, cùm ratione sui, ut est habitus intellectus, tùm ratione connotati habitus piæ affectionis, ex parte voluntatis.

I. Quòd ex utraque parte Theologia habitus supernaturalis sit, evincit ejus objectum formale. Est enim habitus docendi, confirmandi & defendendi ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, sub prima Veritate revelante, ejusque revelatione, ut in eam, velut rationem assentiendi inevidentem, eamq; in vi motiva formali supernaturalem ejus assensus ultimò refolvatur, uti ostensum. Repugnat autem, habitum aliquem docendi resolvi ultimò in Veritatem primam revelantem, tanquam in rationem assentiendi inevidentem, eamque in vi & ratione objectiva formali supernaturalem, & tamen eum vel ex parte sui non in substântia supernaturalem; vel ex parte voluntatis cum habitu piæ affectionis supernaturali non conjunctum esse. Est enim voluntatis cum intellectu, quod ad habitus inevidentes attinet, par ratio, & quod motivum formale suâpte naturâ ex parte intellectus generat habitum assentiendi supernaturalem, id suâpte naturâ etiam afficit voluntatem, generatque ex parte illius habitum supernaturalem, quo erga illud benè affecta elevatur ad assensum ejus intellectui imperandum : cùm habitus assentiendi inevidens, isque supernaturalis, absque supernaturali habitu piæ affectionis, modo sibi connaturali, nec generari nec esse possit, uti ex dictis constat. Quod & res ipsa exigit. Quemadmodum enim hominis animalis intellectus non capit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei (horum autem ex censu est etiam ipsa à Spiritu S. velut à Veritate prima profecta revelatio) stultitia siquidem illi sunt, nec potest ea cognoscere, I. Cor. II. 14. ita ejusdem voluntas est ab alienata à vita Dei propter ignorantiam, quæ est in intellectu, & per obdurationem suam, Eph. IV. 18. nec meliùs affecta est erga primam Veritatem revelantem ejusque revelationem, quàm intellectus; & indiget proinde facultas utraque habitu supernaturali: intellectus quidem ad assentiendum Veritati primæ revelanti ejusque revelationi propter se; voluntas verò ad assensum intellectui imperandum.

H. Intellecta tamen hæc volumus de Theologia, qualis per se & vi sui genuini objecti sive motivi formalis est & esse debet. Nam habitus Theologiæ potest dari duplex. Unus, qui in prima Veritate revelante, ut revelante, tanquam in ratione assentiendi propria ultimò sistit, & ex divina revelatione, per & propter se creditâ, docet, confirmat & defendit, quæ salutem adepturis sive creditu sive factu necessaria sunt. Alter, qui non in prima Veritate revelante, ejusque revelatione sistit ultimò, sed in testificatione parentum, Majorum, Ecclesiæ aliisve credibilitatis signis. Qui enim in Ecclesia natus & educatus est, & à parentibus cum lacte quasi imbibit opinionem, quòd Scripturarum codex contineat Verbum divinitùs patefactum, & ex divina inspiratione in literas relatum, is credit utique hoc propter testimonium & auctoritatem parentum. Quâ in fide confirmari potest auctoritate Ecclesiæ, longè latéque per orbem diffusæ, & signis sive motivis credibilitatis aliis, quamvis hypocrita sit, & per malitiam gratiæ, hujus rei fidem certam divinamque per Verbum ipsum operatuiæ, obicem ponat. Et si assensum præbeat Scripturis, licet fidei humanæ tantùm vel opinionis, potest porro studio humano sibi acquirere habitum Scripturas interpretandi, conclusiones ex illis deducendi, confirmandi ac defendendi, idque rursum cum assensu, humana auctoritate nixo. Quod & experientia testatur. Reperiuntur enim homines impii, quin & hæretici, qui in explicandis Scripturis, & conclusionibus inde deducendis, confirmandis ac defendendis sæpè expeditiores sunt, quàm alii orthodoxi & pientissimi Theologi. quæ forsan causa est, cur Theologiam simpliciter habitibus naturalibus, & qui in homines non renatos etiam cadunt, Auctores graves adscripserint.

Verùm hæc, quam habitum naturalem esse ultrò agnoscimus, æquivocè dicta Theologia est, & à Theologia propriè dicta tanto distat intervallo, quanto fides humana vel opinio, ex motivis externis de veritate divinæ revelationis animo concepta, à fide divina distat. Ejus enim ratio assentiendi ultima planè diversa est à ratione assentiendi ultima Theologiæ, propriè dictæ. Hujus enim ratio assentiendi ultima, uti dictum, est prima Veritas revelans, ut revelans, quæ per relatam in Scripturas revelationem, suo supernaturali concursu elevatam, intellectum & voluntatem per se immediatè movet, hanc quidem ad assensum intellectui imperandum; illum ad eundem in se eliciendum, ita ut assensus ultimò in illa sistat. Illius verò ratio assentiendi ultima, ut modò ostensum, est auctoritas humana, parentum scilicet, & Ecclesiæ, quæ fidem humanam; vel miracula aut motiva alia, quæ opinionem generant: v. g. Hypocrita, vel hæreticus occultus, qui Theologum mentitur, assentietur quidem huic ex Scripturis à se deductæ conclusioni: Christus est Deo Patri ὁμούσιος, propter hanc: Christus est Filius Dei unigenitus; sed non per & propter se immediatè creditam, ut in auctoritate primæ Veritatis revelantis ultimò sistat assensus, sed quòd videt eam in Evangelio Johannis contineri; quæ autem in Evangelio Johannis continentur, credit esse vera, quòd à teneris ita à parentibus vel præceptoribus edoctus sit, vel ab Ecclesia acceperit, quæ in eo continentur, esse à Deo revelata & infallibiliter vera. Atque in hoc parentum, præceptorum vel Ecclesiæ testimonio, velut in ratione assentiendi ultima, sistit tandem assensus ipsius. Sicut autem testimonium illud humanum est, ita non nisi fidem humanam vel opinionem gignere potest, & ut Theologiæ, in hoc altero sensu dictæ, actus assentiendi in hoc testimonio ultimò sistentes, in substantia naturales & merè opinativi sunt, ita Theologia ipsa, sic accepta, habitus in substantia naturalis & merè opinativus est. Sed Theologia propriè dicta, quia in prima Veritate revelante ultimò sistit, habitus in substantia supernaturalis, & simpliciter certus est. Nam prima Veritas revelans, quandocunque sustinet munus rationis assentiendi ultimæ, ac per se immediatè intellectum in sui assensum movet, gignit assensum in substantia supernaturalem, eumque non opinativum, sed simpliciter certum, cui falsum subesse prorsùs repugnat.


### XLIII. Nor, however, is Theology a habit immediately infused by God, but it is a habit…

XLIII.

Nor, however, is Theology a habit immediately infused by God, but it is a habit acquired indeed by our acts, but elicited by the powers of grace, and by the first Truth illuminating the intellect through the revealed Word, and drawing the will into consent.

I. That it is not a habit immediately infused by God is evident from experience. For habits that are immediately infused are conferred all at once in an instant: but our Theology must be learned successively by study and labor. Formerly, indeed, the habit of Theology was infused into the Apostles immediately and without their study and labor. For on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit having been poured out upon them, they were suddenly and in a moment made Theologians, fit to teach all Nations, Matt. last v. 19. to preach the Gospel to every creature, Mark last v. 15. to speak in various tongues the mighty works of God, Acts II. 11. But this was something extraordinary and accidental, the state of those times so requiring, in which the Gospel concerning Christ was first to be promulgated throughout the world, and the Canon of the Scripture of the New Testament was to be compiled. To perform which duty it was necessary indeed for certain men to be instructed immediately by God, not only by a habit of infused Theology, but also by the actual inspiration of those things which were either to be delivered by voice or to be committed to letters, lest they should admit anything in teaching or writing that was foreign either to the truth or to propriety. Today, however, the habit of Theology is obtained by no one, unless by spending some years of time in learning it, and with much study and labor.

II. That it is a habit, however, compared to our acts, elicited by the powers of grace and the First Truth, illuminating the intellect through the revealed Word and drawing the will, is evident from its very nature. For it is in itself and by its own nature a habit, leaning upon the First Truth and its revelation as the ultimate reason for assenting, and it is not infused in an instant, but successively acquired through previous acts. But it cannot be acquired through other acts than those into which the First Truth revealing, as revealing, moves it by itself and by its own nature, as its ultimate reason for assenting, namely through acts that are supernatural in substance, which, with the First Truth illuminating the intellect through its revelation and drawing the will into consent, once elicited, leave behind them a disposition inclining toward other similar acts, from the repetition of which at length a habit of the same nature as them is generated, that is, supernatural in substance. For as previous acts depend proximately upon the formal object, so habits depend proximately upon acts; but remotely and through the intervention of acts, they depend upon the formal object. Nor do we delay here with the Scholastics, who think differently and contend that supernatural habits can neither be acquired nor increased through acts, even supernatural ones, but are all equally infused in an instant. To whom I have already, having written a special Disputation on faith, abundantly, as I think, satisfied.

Latin:

XLIII.

NEque tamen Theologia est habitus, immediatè à Deo infusus, sed est habitus comparatus nostris actibus quidem, sed viribus gratiæ, & Veritate primâ intellectum per Verbum revelatum illuminante, voluntatemque in consensum trahente, elicitis.

I. Quòd non sit habitus, à Deo immediatè infusus, patet per experientiam. Habitus enim immediatè infusi simul toti in instanti conferúntur: Theologia nostra verò successivè studio & labore addiscenda est. Olim quidem Apostolis infusus est Theologiæ habitus immediatè & absque illorum studio & labore. In die pentecostes enim, effuso in ipsos Spiritu Sancto, repentè & in momento effecti sunt Theologi, idonei ad docendum omnes Gentes, Matth. ult. v. 19. ad prædicandum Evangelium omni creaturæ, Marc. ult. v. 15. ad loquendum linguis variis magnalia Dei, Act. II. 11. Sed hoc extraordinarium quid & per accidens fuit, exigente sic illorum temporum statu, quo Evangelium de Christo primùm per orbem promulgandum, & Canon Scripturæ N. T. condendus erat. Ad quod obeundum munus oportebat utique à Deo immediatè instrui Viros quosdam, non modò per habitum Theologiæ infusum, sed etiam per actualem inspirationem eorum, quæ sive tradenda voce, sive consignanda literis essent, ne vel in docendo, vel scribendo quicquam, quod vel à vero vel à decoro alienum esset, admitterent. Hodiè autem Theologiæ habitus nemini obtingit, nisi insumto in eo addiscendo aliquot annorum tempore, studioque & labore multo.

II. Quod autem sit habitus, comparatus nostris actibus, viribus gratiæ tamen & Veritate primâ, intellectum per Verbum revelatum illuminante, voluntatemque trahente, elicitis, ex ipsa ejus natura patet. Est enim per se & suâ naturâ habitus, Veritati primæ ejusque revelationi, tanquam rationi assentiendi ultimæ, innixus, isque non infusus in instanti, sed successivè acquisitus per prævios actus. Non autem per actus alios acquiri potest, quàm eos, in quos per se & suâpte naturâ movet prima Veritas revelans, ut revelans, tanquam ejus ratio assentiendi ultima, nempe per actus in substantiâ supernaturales, qui, Veritate primâ intellectum per suam revelationem illuminante, voluntatémque in consensum trahente, eliciti relinquunt post se dispositionem, ad alios similes actus inclinantem, ex quibus iteratis tandem gignitur habitus ejusdem cum illis naturæ, h. e. in substantiâ supernaturalis. Ut enim actus prævii ab objecto formali proximè, ita habitus proximè ab actibus; remotè autem & interventu actuum ab objecto formali dependent. Neque moramur heîc Scholasticos, qui diversum sentiunt, contenduntque, habitus supernaturales nec acquiri nec augeri posse per actus, etiam supernaturales, sed infundi æquè omnes in instanti. Quibus antehac, conscriptâ de fide Disputatione peculiari, abunde, ut puto, satisfeci.


### XLIV. It is commonly said that Theology is a Θεόσδοτον habit, that is, divinely…

XLIV.

It is commonly said that Theology is a Θεόσδοτον habit, that is, divinely given, yet not in the exact same sense in which we have called it a supernatural habit.

I. Θεόσδοτον, by the force of the word, is that which is given by the gift of God, and it seems to be used in opposition to those things which are acquired by our own study and labor, just as Aristotle in Nicomachean Ethics I, ch. 9, calls happiness Θεόσδοτον in opposition to the blessedness which is acquired by teaching, or custom, or exercise. And thus a Θεόσδοτον habit will be a habit bestowed upon us by God, apart from our own study and labor. But that in this sense our Theology is not a Θεόσδοτον habit is clear. For it does not come to us except through teaching, meditation, and long-continued exercise. Nor do the authors who speak in this way take the term in that sense either, but, as Meisner reports in Philosophia Sobria, part I, p. 298, they only distinguish the Θεόσδοτον habit from habits invented by human ingenuity and study, and they call Theology Θεόσδοτον, not because it is immediately bestowed upon us by God, but because the principle of knowing from which it is learned (namely, Holy Scripture) is given by God, and the object also which it delivers is truly divine. In this sense we do not deny that Theology is a Θεόσδοτον habit. But whether the expression is sufficiently appropriate, we doubt. For the principle of knowing and the object of Theology are one thing, and the habit of Theology is another. The principle and object of Theology are not in themselves something within us: for the former consists in the Word of God, inspired long ago to the Prophets and Apostles, and recorded in writing by divine inspiration, which today is contained in the Biblical codex. This consists in things revealed through the Word of God, which are not really inherent in us nor in the Scriptures, but are in the Scriptures as things signified in their signs; but in us only when they are known, through cognition, and as things known they are in the knower, namely objectively and intentionally. Both can be called Θεόσδοτον, because, having been recorded in writing through the inspiration which long ago came divinely to the Sacred writers, and by God's benevolent will and a merely gratuitous gift have been propagated to us. But the habit of theology in itself and essentially is a certain quality in us, and directly it denotes a habit of knowing in the intellect; indirectly, however, it connotes a habit of pious affection on the part of the will: which, if it is properly and in itself a habit θεόσδοτος or given by God, it is necessary that one or the other or both habits by their own nature and by essence be such that it does not come to us except by God giving it, or by the gift of God: for otherwise it could not be defined by the habit θεόσδοτον. But this, as will be said presently, those very authors deny.

II. Furthermore, B. Meisner concedes that the habit of theology falls even upon unregenerate and wicked men, and thus can be learned from the Scriptures by human study without the supernatural concurrence of the illumination and operation of the Holy Spirit. It will therefore be, he says, a habit θεόσδοτος or divinely given, not because all who teach and know theology are in a state of grace and specially illuminated by the Holy Spirit. For the habit of theology falls even upon an unregenerate subject and a man of perverse life, which examples teach and reason proves. For otherwise it would follow that the habit of theology would perish if any theologian committed a mortal sin, and would return if he performed penance, such an alternating departure and return of habits is absurd, etc. Which again are not obscure arguments that theology itself, properly speaking, is not a habit θεόσδοτος. For neither can a habit be properly called θεόσδοτος which even the unregenerate, without the special illumination of the Holy Spirit, can acquire for themselves by their own study, labor, and exercise, and frequently do acquire for themselves.

III. Because, however, it is not without obscurity what B. Meisner says in the words just cited, that the habit of theology falls upon an unregenerate subject, and is neither lost through mortal sins nor returns through penance; for a fuller illustration of a matter otherwise intricate and difficult, we shall examine the whole thing a little more deeply. It must therefore be repeated from the previous th. XLII. n. II. Expl. that theology can be taken in a double sense. One, for the habit of declaring, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, precisely by the First Truth revealing, as revealing, as if upon the ultimate reason for assenting. In the other, [it is] a habit of explaining, confirming, and defending the same things indeed from the Scriptures, yet not leaning upon the First Truth revealing, but upon human authority or other motives of credibility generating opinion, as if upon the ultimate reason for assenting. We grant that Theology accepted in this latter sense falls even upon unregenerate men. But this, as we showed in the aforementioned place, is Theology spoken equivocally. However, we deny and utterly deny that Theology taken in the former way falls upon unregenerate men. For it is, as we taught in the same place, a habit supernatural in substance, which therefore finds a place only in the regenerate, nor can it be obtained without the supernatural grace of God and [His] concurrence with His Word, elevating it to testify of itself. Let those things be seen which we taught on this matter in the preceding th. XLII. Expl. n. I. But if anyone should wish to call this Theology, strictly and univocally spoken, a habit θεόσδοτον [God-given], because it comes to us by the supernatural grace and illumination of God through His Word, although not without our industry, reading, and meditation, we shall not object, although it remains doubtful whether it can be defined quite conveniently by the habit θεόσδοτον, with reasons for doubting also militating here, which we brought forward almost at the beginning of this chapter, th. III. n. I.

IV. What was said, that if Theology (univocally and strictly spoken) did not fall except upon the regenerate, it would follow that the habit of Theology perishes if any theologian sins mortally, and returns if he does penance and returns into grace with God, proceeds in a qualified sense, not simply. That this may be rightly understood, it must be known that the habit of Theology, strictly accepted, involves two things. One concerns the impressed species, well disposed and coordinated among themselves and with things, by which the intellect is constituted in the being of a complete principle for congruously apprehending and explaining the divine revelation which is contained in the Scriptures, and for deducing conclusions from it. The other concerns a certain habit of the intellect for easily and firmly assenting to the First Truth revealing and to its revelation for its own sake immediately. The former, as natural to the intellect of man and The habit of Theology, properly and univocally so-called, is common with another habit equivocally so-called, and thus it is not lost through mortal sins committed by a theologian. For mortal sins neither physically nor demeritoriously expel the species impressed upon the intellect by objects. Not physically: because they are not opposed to them. Nor demeritoriously: because in substance they are natural, and are acquired in a natural way, both by reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and by listening to the voice of those who teach Theology, whether by words through the eyes, when writings are read, or through the ears, when they are perceived by hearing as the voice is uttered, transmitting their species to the interior sense and the imagination, and these phantasms, elevated by the agent intellect, impressing their intelligible species upon the possible intellect. Moreover, sins do not demeritoriously expel those things which are natural to a man's intellect, but only those which depend upon the supernatural influx and operation of God. And hence it is that a reborn man, in whom the habit of Theology, properly and univocally so-called, resides, remains after any crimes committed just as prompt and ready to explain Scripture and to deduce conclusions from it as he was prompt and ready before in the state of grace. For this explanation of Scripture and the deduction of conclusions from it depends entirely upon the impressed species, duly coordinated and disposed among themselves, which, as has been said, are not shaken out by mortal sins. The latter, however—namely, the habit of assenting easily and firmly to the First Truth revealing and to its revelation per se immediately—is certainly lost through mortal sins, while there remains only a certain natural habit of assenting, based upon the authority of parents, elders, the Church, etc. based upon, and thence obtained from tender years by long use. The reason is: because that habit of assenting to the First Truth revealing and to its revelation per se immediately is in substance supernatural, depending upon the supernatural influx of the First Truth with the species impressed upon the intellect by the hearing or reading of the divine Word, by which they are elevated beyond their native power and nature to illuminate the intellect and draw the will into consent. As this habit of assenting depends upon the Holy Spirit in its becoming and in its being, so, when He is driven out by sins against conscience, it utterly expires. And from this it must be admitted entirely as a consequence, what was inferred in the doubt brought up above, namely that the habit of Theology perishes in that part by which it contains the habit of assenting to divine revelation in itself immediately, if one sins mortally; and returns, if one does penance. For just as, with the Holy Spirit cast out through sins, the influx of grace together with the impressed species for illuminating the intellect and drawing the will into consent expires: so with Him recovered through conversion and faith, the same influx returns by right of postliminy, and the impressed species which had remained of the habit of Theology, joined with a certain habit of assenting resting upon human motives, and which were as it were a certain corpse of it, begin to be elevated again by Him, to be animated as it were, and to revive. That this alternating departure and return of habits is not absurd, even the example of divine faith, as it is called, can teach. For it is the constant assertion of our Churches that it is cast out through sins against conscience. It is cast out, however, not only on the part of the will regarding trust, fixed upon Christ the mediator and the grace of God, which cannot stand together with sins against conscience; but also regarding the supernatural habit of assenting to divine revelation in itself immediately, as the remaining impressed species, with whatever facility of assenting resting upon human motives, are rather a shadow of the former divine faith than divine faith itself. For with the Holy Spirit cast out through sins, and the supernatural concurrence of the Holy Spirit with the impressed species ceasing, the supernatural habit of assenting, which depends on this for its being, cannot survive and endure. For this reason also Theologians call the faith which remains in sinners after crimes have been committed, for the sake of distinction, human faith; but the Apostle James calls it dead faith, ch. II of his Epistle, v. 17. Nor is the opinion of our Churches less constant, that faith, lost through sins, is restored in the conversion of the sinful man by the voice of the Gospel, not only regarding saving trust on the part of the will, but also regarding supernatural illumination and the habit of assenting to divine revelation in itself immediately on the part of the intellect: since the former cannot exist without the latter. But because the account of theology and faith, as far as the present is concerned, is the same: for the ultimate reason for assenting is one and the same for both, and through the same causes that supernatural habit of assenting to the Word of God is lost and recovered in the one, through them the same is also lost or recovered in the other; it does not appear why the aforementioned loss and return of habits should be considered more absurd in theology than in divine faith.

Latin:

XLIV.

VUlgò dicitur, Theologiam esse habitum Θεόσδοτον, h. e. divinitùs datum, non tamen eodem planè sensu, quo nos eam habitum supernaturalem diximus.

I. Θεόσδοτον, vi vocis, est, quod Dei dono datur, & videtur dici in oppositione ad ea, quæ nostro studio & labore comparantur, sicut Aristoteles I. Nic. c. IX. εὐδαιμονίαν θεόσδοτον dicit in oppositione ad beatitudinem, quæ doctrinâ, vel consuetudine, vel exercitatione comparatur. Atque sic habitus θεόσδοτος erit habitus, à Deo, citra nostrum studium & laborem, nobis collatus. Sed hoc significatu Theologiam nostram habitum θεόσδοτον non esse, in aprico est. Non enim obtingit nobis, nisi per doctrinam, meditationem & exercitationem diuturnam. Neque etiam eo significatu Auctores, qui sic loquuntur, terminum accipiunt, sed, referente Meisnero in Philosophia Sobria part. I. pag. m. 298. habitum θεόσδοτον contradistinguunt tantùm habitibus, humano ingenio ac studio inventis, & Theologiam dicunt θεόσδοτον, non quòd à Deo immediatè nobis conferatur, sed quòd principium cognoscendi, ex quo addiscitur (Scriptura Sacra scilicet) à Deo datum, & objectum quoq; , quod tradit, verè divinum sit. Quo sensu Theologiam habitum θεόσδοτον esse non inficiamur. Num verò locutio satis congrua sit, dubitamus. Aliud enim sunt principium cognoscendi & objectum Theologiæ, aliud Theologiæ habitus. Principium & objectum Theologiæ per se non sunt aliquid in nobis: illud enim consistit in Verbo Dei, Prophetis olim & Apostolis inspirato, & ex inspiratione divina in literas relato, quod hodiè in codice Biblico continetur. Hoc in rebus, per Verbum Dei revelatis, consistit, quæ nec nobis, nec Scripturis realiter insunt, sed in Scripturis sunt ut res significatæ in suis signis; in nobis autem tùm demum, cùm cognoscuntur, per cognitionem, & ut res cognitæ sunt in cognoscente, objectivè scilicet & intentionaliter. Utrumque θεόσδοτον dici potest, quòd per inspirationem, quæ Scriptoribus Sacris olim divinitùs obtigit, in literas relata, & Dei benevolâ voluntate & dono merè gratuito ad nos propagata sunt, Sed habitus Theologiæ per se & essentialiter est qualitas quædam in nobis, & in recto dicit habitum cognoscendi in intellectu; in obliquo autem connotat habitum piæ affectionis ex parte voluntatis: qui si propriè & per se habitus θεόσδοτος sive à Deo datus sit, necesse est, ut alteruter vel uterque habitus suâpte naturâ & per essentiam talis sit, qui non nisi Deo dante, sive Dei dono nobis obtingat: aliàs enim per habitum θεόσδοτον definiri non posset. Sed hoc, ut mox dicetur, illi ipsi Auctores negant.

II. Deinde B. Meisnerus concedit, Theologiæ habitum cadere etiam in non renatos & improbos homines, atque adeò addisci posse ex Scripturis studio humano absque supernaturali concursus illuminatione & operatione Spiritus Sancti. Erit ergo, inquit, habitus θεόσδοτος sive divinitus datus, non quòd omnes, qui Theologiam docent & sciunt, sint in statu gratiæ & à Spiritu S. specialiter illuminati. Etenim habitus Theologiæ cadit etiam in subjectum non renatum & hominem perversæ vitæ, quod exempla docent, & ratio evincit. Sequeretur enim aliàs Theologiæ habitum perire, si quisquam Theologus mortaliter peccaret, illum redire, si pœnitentiam ageret, qualis alternata habituum abitio & reditio est absurda &c. Quæ rursum argumento non obscuro sunt, Theologiam ipsam, propriè loquendo, non esse habitum θεόσδοτον. Neque enim propriè θεόσδοτος dici potest habitus, quem etiam non-renati citra specialem Spiritus S. illuminationem, suopte studio, labore & exercitatione sibi comparare possunt, & subinde sibi comparant.

III. Quia tamen obscuritatenon caret, quod verbis jam citatis dicit B. Meisnerus, habitum Theologiæ cadere in subjectum non renatum, neque amitú per peccata mortalia, aut redire per pœnitentiam; ad uberiorem rei aliàs intricatæ & difficilis illustrationem rem totam paulò altius expendemus. Repetendum ergo ex superiori th. XLII. n. II. Expl. Theologiam posse accipi in significatu duplici. Uno, pro habitu declarandi, confirmandi & defendendi ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, præcisè Veritate primâ revelante, ut revelante, velut ratione assentiendi ultimâ, nixo. Altero, pro habitu eadem quidé ex Scripturis explicandi, confirmandi & defendendi, non tamen Veritate primâ revelante, sed auctoritate humanâ aliisve opinionem generantibus motivis credibilitatis, velut ratione assentiendi ultimâ, nixo. Hoc posteriori significatu acceptam Theologiam cadere etiam in homines non renatos, largimur. Sed hæc, ut d. l. ostenfum, æquivocè dicta Theologia est. Priori autem modo sumtam Theologiam in homines non renatos cadere, negamus & pernegamus. Est enim, ut ibidem docuimus, habitus in substantiâ supernaturalis, qui proinde non nisi in renatis locum invenit, nec citra supernaturalem Dei gratiam & concursum cum Verbo suo, ad testificandum de semetipso id elevantem, obtineri potest. Videantur, quæ præced. th. XLII. Expl. n. I. hanc in rem docuimus. Quòd si hanc, propriè scilicet & univocè dictam, Theologiam habitum θεόσδοτον quis appellare velit, quòd Dei supernaturali gratiâ & illuminatione per Verbum ipsius, licet non citra nostram industriam, lectionem & meditationem, nobis obtingat, non repugnabimus, quamvis an per habitum θεόσδοτον fatis convenienter definiri possit, adhuc dubium maneat, militantibus heîc etiam rationibus dubitandi, quas ferè sub initium hujus capitis th. III. n. I. adduximus.

IV. Quod dicebatur, si Theologia (univocè & propriè dicta) non caderet, nisi in renatos, secuturum, quòd Theologiæ habitus pereat, siquis Theologus peccet mortaliter; & redeat, si pœnitentiam agat, & cum Deo in gratiam redeat, secundum quid procedit, non simpliciter. Quòd ut rectè intelligatur, sciendum est, habitum Theologiæ, propriè acceptæ, involvere duo. Unum concernit species impressas, inter se benè rebusque convenienter dispositas & coordinatas, quibus intellectus in esse principii completi constituitur ad divinam revelationem, quæ in Scripturis continetur, congruè apprehendendam, explicandam, & conclusiones inde deducendas. Alterum concernit habitudinem quandam intellectus ad facilè & firmiter assentiendum Veritati primæ revelanti ejusque revelationi propter se immediatè. Prius, ut hominis intellectui naturale & habitui Theologiæ, propriè & univocè dictæ, cum alterius æquivocè dictæ habitu commune est, ita per admissa á Theologo peccata mortalia non amittitur. Peccata mortalia enim nec physicè nec demeritoriè expellunt species, ab objectis intellectui impressas. Non physicè: quia eis non opponuntur. Nec demeritoriè: quia in substantiâ naturales sunt, & modo naturali acquiruntur, cùm legendo & meditando Scripturas, tum auscultando vocem eorum, qui Theologiam docent, verbis sive per oculos, cùm scripta leguntur, sive per aures, cum voce prolata auditu percipiuntur, ad sensum interiorem & phantasiam species suas transmittentibus, & horum phantasmatibus, ab intellectu agente elevatis, species sui intelligibiles intellectui possibili imprimentibus. Peccata autem non expellunt demeritoriè ea, quæ hominis intellectui naturalia sunt, sed tantùm quæ à supernaturali Dei influxu & operatione dependent. Atque hinc est, quòd homo renatus, cui Theologiæ, propriè & univocè dictæ, habitus inest, post patrata scelera quæque, tam promtus & expeditus manet ad explicandam Scripturam & conclusiones ex ea deducendas, quàm promtus & expeditus anteà in statu gratiæ fuit. Hæc enim Scripturæ explicatio conclusionumque ex ea deductio tota dependet à speciebus impressis, inter se ritè coordinatis & dispositis, quæ per peccata mortalia, uti dictum, non excutiuntur. Posterius verò, habituso scilicet affentiendi facilè & firmiter primæ Veritati revelanti ejusque revelationi per se immediatè, amittitur utique per peccata mortalia, remanente tantùm naturali quâdam habitudine assentiendi, auctoritati parentum, majorum, Ecclesiæ &c. innixâ, & inde á teneris usu longo obtentâ. Ratio est: quia habitudo illa Veritati primæ revelanti ejusque revelationi per se immediatè assentiendi in substantiâ supernaturalis est, dependens à supernaturali Veritatis primæ influxu cum speciebus, auditu vel lectione Verbi divini intellectui impressis, quo ultra suam nativam vim & indolem elevantur ad illuminandum intellectum voluntatemque in consensum trahendam. Quæ habitudo assentiendi ut in fieri & in esse à Spiritu Sancto dependet, ita, eo per peccata contra conscientiam excusso, oppidò exspirat. Atquede hac admittendum omninò est consequens, quod in dubitatione superiùs allatá inferebatur, nempe Theologiæ habitum perire eâ parte, quâ continet habitudinem assentiendi divinæ revelationi per se immediatè, si mortaliter peccet; & redire, si pœnitentiam agat. Quemadmodum enim, Spiritu S. per peccata excusso,influxus gratiæ cum speciebus impressis ad illuminandum intellectum, voluntatemque in consensum trahendam, exspirat: ita eo per conversionem fidemque recuperato, influxus idem redit postliminiò, & quæ de Theologiæ habitu supererant species impressæ, cum quadam motivis humanis innixa habitudine assentiendi conjunctæ, & ejus quasi cadaver quoddam erant, illo rursum elevari, animari quasi, & reviviscere incipiunt. Quam alternatam habituum abitionem & reditionem absurdam non esse, vel solum fidei, ut dicitur, divinæ exemplum docere potest. Eam enim per peccata contra conscientiam excuti, Ecclesiarum nostrarum constans assertio est. Excutitur autem non tantùm ex parte voluntatis quoad fiduciam, in Christo mediatore & gratia Dei defixam, quæ cum peccatis contra conscientiam simul stare non potest; sed etiam quoad supernaturalem habitudinem assentiendi divinæ revelationi per se immediatè, ut quæ remanent species impressæ cum qualicunque motivis humanis innixâ facilitate assentiendi, umbra potiùs sint pristinæ fidei divinæ, quàm fides divina ipsa. Neque enim excusso Spiritu Sancto per peccata, & Spiritus Sancti concursu supernaturali cum speciebus impressis cessante, quæ hinc in esse suo dependet habitudo assentiendi supernaturalis superesse & durare potest. Quamobrem etiam Theologi fidem, quæ post patrata scelera in peccatoribus reliqua est, differentiæ causâ humanam fidem appellant; Jacobus Apostolus autem vocat eam fidem mortuã c. II. Epist. v. 17. Neque minus constans est Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententia, fidem, per peccata amissam, restitui in conversione hominis peccatoris voce Evangelii, non tantùm quoad salutarem fiduciam ex parte voluntatis, sed etiam quoad supernaturalem illuminationem & habitudinem assentiendi divinæ revelationi per se immediatè ex parte intellectus: cùm illa absque hâc esse non possit. Quia autem Theologiæ & fidei, quod ad præsens attinet, par ratio est: utriusque enim una est ratio assentiendi ultima, & per quas causas supernaturalis illa habitudo assentiendi Verbo Dei per se immediatè amittitur & recuperatur in una, per eas amittitur vel recuperatur eadem etiam in altera; non apparet, cur prædicta habituum abitio & reditio in Theologia magis, quàm in fide divina pro absurda habeatur.


### XLV. And from this, it is easily understood how theology and faith differ

XLV.

And from this, it is easily understood how theology and faith differ: they differ, namely, inadequately, as the including and the included. For theology includes faith, and, besides that, it also includes the faculty of explaining, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, which faith does not include.

I. That one differs from the other is acknowledged by all. For faith falls even to those unlearned in letters, who are not capable of theology. And those who possess only faith are called believers, not theologians; but those who possess theology, properly so called, are denominated both theologians and believers. Therefore, faith can exist in a man without the habit of theology; yet, conversely, the habit of theology, properly so called, cannot exist in anyone without the habit of faith. But that those things of which one can exist without the other differ among themselves, no one doubts. In what, however, they differ, is a matter of controversy.

II. Aureolus, as reported by Ockham in the prologue to Book 1 of the Sentences, question 3, taught that faith is an adhesive habit; but that theology is merely a declarative habit. He understood by an adhesive habit, a habit inclining one to elicit an act of assenting, and of adhering to the object through assent. He called a declarative habit, however, one inclining to acts of declaring and explaining those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, not to acts of assenting to and adhering to the same.
