He thought, therefore, that in the theologian there concur at the same time the habit of faith and the habit of theology: and that from the latter he has the quality of being prompt and ready to declare and explain the doctrine Christian; from that which is apt for assenting to the same, and by assent adhering to it.

III. Other Scholastics commonly seek the reason for the difference in the formal object. For although they cannot deny that the formal object of faith and of Theology alike is the primary Truth revealing and its revelation, they nevertheless contend that it performs this function in one way in Theology, and in another in faith. Moreover, in declaring the manner of the diversity, they do not even agree among themselves. And (1) Cajetan indeed in I. Thom. q. I. a. III. establishes that divine revelation is the formal object of faith, as it is non-evident and obscure; but of Theology, as it abstracts from evidence and non-evidence. (2) Gregorius de Valentia Tom. I. Disp. I. q. I. punct. III. constitutes the formal object of faith in divine revelation, as it moves the intellect to assent immediately and without discourse; but of Theology, in divine revelation, as it moves the intellect to assent by means of discourse. Which is the more common opinion of the Scholastics: from which those do not depart, as regards the matter, who say that faith and Theology differ in this, that the formal object of the former is formal and immediate revelation; of the latter, virtual and mediate revelation. For they distinguish revelation into formal and virtual; immediate and mediate, not on the part of the revealer, but on the part of the thing revealed, and they call formal and immediate that which actually, formally, and immediately is borne toward the thing whose revelation it is said to be, and manifests it; virtual and mediate, that which is borne toward the thing whose revelation it is said to be only by means of another proposition, formally and immediately revealed, in which it is contained virtually and by consequence, and thus virtual and mediate revelation is revelation which moves to assent by means of discourse deduced from another formally and immediately revealed proposition; formal and immediate, that which moves to assent immediately and without discourse deduced from another revealed proposition: e.g., when Scripture says that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, this testimony is the formal and immediate revelation of that proposition. But when from this formally and immediately revealed proposition it is inferred by consequence that Christ is to God, the Father, ὁμοούσιον or of the same with of that essence, as well as that very testimony of Holy Scripture, by which it declares Christ to be the only-begotten Son of God, is a virtual and mediate revelation of another proposition inferred from it by consequence, namely this one: Christ is ὁμούσιος to his Father, or of the same essence with him; which consequently moves the intellect to assent to this through a discourse deduced from another formally and immediately revealed proposition; but to the assent of that [first proposition] it moves immediately and without discourse, [as it is] deduced from another formally revealed proposition. See on this matter Suarez in Tr. de Virt. Theolog. Disp. III. Sect. XI. Gonet in Clyp. Theol. Thom. p. I. Disp. proœm. a. III.

(3) Vazquez, however, in I. Thomæ Disp. V. c. III. acknowledges that divine revelation moves the intellect even to the assent of faith through discourse; and he thinks that the difference between faith and Theology is that the assent of the former relies upon a discourse deduced proximately from divine revelation, and is resolved immediately into these two principles: God says or reveals; and God is supremely truthful; but the assent of the latter relies proximately upon some revealed proposition, or one confirmed by tradition or the authority of councils, and is believed either by divine faith, or, which pleases him more, only by human faith, according to which Theology is also a habit of acquired faith or opinion, if it infers its conclusions from articles of faith believed by human and acquired faith; or a habit intermediate between infused or divine faith and acquired faith, if it infers its conclusions from articles of faith believed by divine faith. Hence, also regarding conclusions inferred from one or two revealed premises, he devises a twofold assent: One, to which the intellect is moved by the force of the premises, believed by human or divine faith, which he calls theological assent; the other, by which faith is borne of itself and immediately toward a conclusion deduced through discourse from one or both revealed premises, and known from the discourse to be revealed: which he calls the assent of faith. In this, Tanner, Suarez, and others add their support to him.

IV. But all these opinions suffer from their own difficulties. And the first indeed, which is attributed to Aureolus, has long been exploded. And not without cause. For it is of the nature of intellectual habits (of whose number theology also is) that each inclines the intellect toward its own object under the mode of assenting proper to itself, toward assent: which Aristotle therefore in Nicomachean Ethics VI, ch. 2 and 3, defines by this, that according to them the intellect expresses the truth by affirming or denying. But to enunciate the true by affirming or denying, what else is it than to compose in the intellect those things which are composed in the thing, and to divide those which are divided in the thing, and to determine that those things are composed or divided in the mind, that is, to assent. Nor does it appear how the habits of faith and Theology can be distinguished on the part of the formal object: since the formal object of both is one and the same, namely the First Truth revealing, or divine revelation. But what is said, that the First Truth revealing moves the intellect differently into the assent of faith, and differently into theological assent: into the former immediately and without discourse, into the latter by means of discourse; is a frivolous invention. For the assent of faith is resolved equally, as is the theological, ultimately into discourse, resting upon these two principles: Whatever God reveals is certainly and infallibly true; and: God reveals this or that. Nor is it any less the case for faith than for theology, from one revealed proposition and another that is evident, or from two revealed ones, to infer conclusions and to assent to them, so that the assent is resolved proximately into the premises, but ultimately and remotely into divine revelation. Both of which we have laboriously proven heretofore in our Tract on Conversion: the former indeed in Disputation VII, the latter in VIII: where we also brought forward, weighed, and refuted the principal objections and exceptions of the Scholastics. These things indeed standing, the invention of Vazquez brought forward above falls of its own accord, that the assent of faith relies only on discourse, proximately from divine revelation; but theological [assent relies] on discourse, proximately deduced from the articles of faith.

Nor is it without absurdity, what Vazquez contends in the same place, that theological assent relies on discourse deduced from articles of faith believed by human faith. For thus the formal object and the ultimate mode of assenting of theology and of theological assent will have to be established in human authority and testimony. For human faith, by which the articles of faith are believed, relies on human authority and testimony, as on its formal object and ultimate reason for assenting. But what is more absurd? What can be said or imagined more alien to the nature of the subject matter and the common sense of the Doctors than that Theology, that prince of sciences, by whose protection the most abstruse mysteries of faith and all the chapters of the doctrine of salvation are explained, confirmed, and defended, should rely upon human authority and testimony as its formal object and ultimate reason for assenting? When, however, it is clear to every one of the faithful, even the simpler ones, that the mysteries of faith and the doctrine of salvation far exceed the grasp of human reason. For this reason it is called wisdom, not of this world, nor of the princes of this world, but the wisdom of God in a mystery (hidden) that was kept secret, which God ordained before the world unto our glory, I Cor. II. 6. seq., wisdom occupied with those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, v. 9. which the holy Apostles did not receive from man, nor did they learn it; but by the revelation of Jesus Christ, Gal. I. 12. which God revealed through His Spirit, I Cor. II. 10. In short: No one of the faithful is ignorant that the doctrine of our salvation depends upon the divine revelation contained in the Scriptures, not upon human testimony and authority. Why, therefore, should its formal object and ultimate reason for assenting be established in human authority and testimony rather than in divine revelation and testimony? And why should Theology, which is occupied in delivering and defending it, be said to derive its conclusions from propositions that are indeed revealed or articles of faith, yet not because of the divine testimony or revelation upon which they depend in themselves and are believed by divine faith; but because of human testimony, upon which they do not depend, and are believed by human faith? Who does not see the trifles of a man otherwise most learned, unworthy of an erudite man?

The distinction of a double assent regarding conclusions inferred from one or both revealed premises contains an equally absurd fiction, of which one depends upon that very Theological discourse by which it is inferred and upon the assent to the premises; the other does not depend upon it, but is directed toward the conclusion because of divine revelation immediately in itself, after it has been known from the discourse by which it is inferred that it is divinely revealed. For first, as it is common to all habits of the intellect to incline the intellect toward the assent of its object under its own proper mode of assenting, so it must be that the same applies to Theology. And because the proper mode of assenting for Theology is divine revelation, it cannot incline the intellect toward the assent of its object in any other way than under divine revelation, and consequently its assent, just as the assent of faith, must rely upon divine revelation as its formal and proper motivating reason. But as for the fact that there exists between the acts of assent of Theology such a diversity, that in some cases divine revelation moves the intellect of itself and immediately, in others by means of another revealed proposition, and by consequence, deduced from it, according as the object is revealed either formally and immediately, or virtually and by means of another revealed proposition, the very same thing happens also to the acts of assent of faith. For divine revelation cannot move toward assent, whether of faith or of Theology, in any other way than as it stands on the part of the thing itself, and if the material object is revealed immediately, it will also move the intellect toward the assent of that object immediately; but if it is revealed by means of another proposition or doctrine, from which it is deduced by consequence, it is necessary that it first move the intellect toward the assent of the revealed doctrine, and by means of that assent also toward the assent of the conclusion, which follows from it by necessary consequence. Furthermore, if the intellect therefore assents to a conclusion, deduced from one or both revealed premises, on account of divine revelation of itself and immediately, because it has known through discourse that it is divinely revealed, then it is necessary that divine revelation also be directed toward that conclusion of itself and immediately, and that it be known through that discourse that it is revealed of itself and immediately. The reason for the consequence is: because divine revelation, as has been said, does not move toward the assent of an object in any other way than as it is directed toward it, nor does the intellect assent to it in any other way than as it has known it to be revealed, namely immediately, if divine revelation is directed toward it immediately; and the intellect has known it to be so directed toward it; but mediately and by means of another revealed proposition, if it is at least mediately and by the intervention of discourse, from another revealed proposition be deduced, that divine revelation is brought to bear upon it, and that it is known to be brought to bear upon it in this way. But the consequent is absurd. For by the very fact that a conclusion is deduced through discourse from one or both revealed premises, divine revelation is brought to bear upon it mediately, namely by means of the revealed premise and the discourse by which it is deduced from it: and by that very fact the discourse, because it deduces the conclusion from one or both revealed premises, declares that it is at least mediately and by virtue of the premises from which it is inferred by consequence, and thus only virtually revealed. The antecedent, therefore, which is that of Vazquez and others who think with him, is absurd, namely that the intellect assents to a conclusion inferred through discourse from one or both premises because of divine revelation per se immediately, for the reason that it has known from the discourse that it is divinely revealed. Therefore, the assent to a conclusion inferred from one or both revealed premises is one, not double, which is an assent born from the assent to the premises: but the other assent, which is brought to bear upon the same conclusion because of divine revelation per se immediately, is a rotten fiction. But I return to where I digressed.

V. Since, therefore, no difference can be shown on the part of the formal object that intervenes between faith and Theology, it must be admitted that both are by essence a habit of assenting to the doctrine of salvation revealed by God because of divine revelation. But because Theology extends more widely than faith: for the latter is properly a habit of things to be believed; the former is a habit of things to be believed and at the same time things to be done: the latter is a habit of assenting to the doctrine of salvation, apprehended by any knowledge whatsoever, whether from clear and perspicuous words of Scripture, or through an easy consequence obvious to anyone, even the illiterate; the former is a habit of explaining, confirming, and defending the same more accurately: it must further be said that the one differs from the other inadequately, as the including and the included. For Theology, which is indeed properly such, includes faith actually and formally: for it is, as has been shown, by essence a habit of assenting to the doctrine of salvation revealed by God because of divine revelation, in which the nature and quiddity of faith consists, and besides it, it also includes the faculty of explaining, of confirming and defending the doctrine both of faith and of morals more accurately than faith, as such, and of itself does not include. Theology therefore is more perfect than faith, not indeed intensively, as the Schools speak, because it inclines the intellect to assent more strongly and intensely than faith: for divine revelation, elevated by the supernatural concurrence of God, is equally effective in simpler believers as in the learned and subtle Theologian, and, as far as it is in itself, moves both equally to the assent of itself and of revealed things; but extensively, because it extends itself to more acts than faith. For Theology extends itself, as has been said, to the acts of explaining, confirming and defending the doctrine of faith and salvation, to which faith of itself, and as it is in any believers whatsoever, does not extend itself.

Latin:

XLV.

Atque hinc, quid differant Theologia & fides, facilè intelligitur: differunt nempe inadæquatè, ut includens & inclusum. Theologia enim includit fidem, &, præter illam, includit etiam facultatem explicandi, confirmandi & defendendi ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, quam fides non includit.

I. Differre alteram ab altera, in confesso est apud omnes. Fides enim cadit etiam in homines literarum rudes, qui Theologiæ capaces non sunt. Et qui fide tantùm pollent, fideles, non Theologi; qui autem Theologiâ, propriè dictâ, pollent, Theologi & fideles denominantur. Potest ergo fides inesse homini sine habitu Theologiæ; non tamen contrà Theologiæ propriè dictæ habitus inesse cuipiam potest absque fidei habitu. Quorum autem unum absque altero esse potest, ea differre inter se, nemo dubitat. In quo autem differant, controversum est.

II. Aureolus, referente Occam in prol. in. 1. Sent. q. III. docuit, fidem esse habitum adhæsivum; Theologiam verò esse habitum declarativum tantùm. Intellexit autem per habitum adhæsivum, habitum inclinantem ad eliciendum actum assentiendi, objectoque adhærendi per assensum. Declarativum verò dixit habitum, inclinantem ad actus declarandi & explicandi ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, non ad actus iisdem assentiendi & adhærendi. Sensit igitur, in Theologo concurrere simul habitum fidei, & habitum Theologiæ: & ab hoc habere eum, quòd promtus & expeditus est ad declarandam & explicandam doctrinam Christianam; ab illo, quod aptus est ad assentiendum eidem, & per assensum illi adhærendum.

III. Scholastici alii differentiæ rationem quærunt communiter in objecto formali. Quamvis enim inficiari non possint, fidei pariter & Theologiæ objectum formale esse Veritatem primam revelantem ejusque revelationem, contendunt tamen, eam obire id muneris modo alio in Theologia, alio in fide. In declarando autem diversitatis modo ne inter se quidem conveniunt. Et (1) Cajetanus quidem in I. Thom. q. I. a. III. statuit, revelationem divinam esse objectum formale fidei, ut inevidens & obscura est; Theologiæ autem, ut ab evidentia & inevidentia abstrahit. (2) Gregorius de Valentia Tom. I. Disp. I. q. I. punct. III. constituit objectum formale fidei in revelatione divina, ut movet intellectum ad assensum immediate & sine discursu; Theologiæ autem, in revelatione divina, ut movet intellectum ad assensum mediante discursu. Quæ communior Scholasticorum sententia est: à qua, quoad rem, non abeunt, qui fidem & Theologiam in hoc differre ajunt, quòd illius objectum formale sit revelatio formalis & immediata; hujus revelatio virtualis & mediata. Distingvunt enim revelationem in formalem & virtualem; immediatam & mediatam, non ex parte revelantis, sed ex parte rei revelatæ, & formalem ac immediatam dicunt, quæ actu, formaliter & immediatè fertur in rem, cujus revelatio dicitur, eamque manifestat; virtualem & mediatam, quæ fertur demum in rem, cujus revelatio dicitur, mediante alia, formaliter & immediatè revelatâ, propositione, in qua virtualiter & per consequentiam continetur, atq; adeò revelatio virtualis & mediata est revelatio, quæ mediante discursu, ex alia formaliter & immediatè revelata propositione deducto, movet in assensu; formalis & immediata, quæ immediatè & citra discursum, ex aliâ revelata propositione deductum, in assensum movet: v. g. cùm dicit Scriptura, Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum, hæc testificatio est propositionis illius revelatio formalis & immediata. Quando autem ex hac formaliter & immediatè revelata propositione per consequentiam infertur, Christum esse Deo, Patri ὁμοούσιον sive ejusdem cum eo essentiæ, tum ea ipsa Scripturæ sacræ testificatio, quâ Christum Filium Dei unigenitum esse declarat, est revelatio virtualis & mediata alterius, per consequentiam ex illa illatæ, propositionis, hujus scilicet, Christus est Patri suo ὁμούσιος, sive ejusdem cum illo essentiæ; quæ proinde in assensum hujus movet per discursum, ex alia formaliter & immediatè revelata propositione deductum; in assensum illius verò immediatè & citra discursum, ex alia formaliter revelata propositione deductum. Videatur hac de re Suarez in Tr. de Virt. Theolog. Disp. III. Sect. XI. Gonet in Clyp. Theol. Thom. p. I. Disp. proœm. a. III.

(3) Vazquez verò in I. Thomæ Disp. V. c. III. agnoscit, divinam revelationem movere intellectum etiam in assensum fidei per discursum; & inter fidem ac Theologiam id interesse existimat, quòd illius assensus nitatur discursu, proximè ex divinâ revelatione deducto, & resolvatur immediatè in hæc duo principia: Deus dicit sive revelat; & Deus est summè verax; hujus verò assensus proximè nitatur aliquâ propositione revelatâ, vel traditione aut conciliorum auctoritate firmatâ, eâque vel fide divinâ, vel, quod ipsi magis arridet, fide humanâ tantùm creditâ, juxta quem etiam Theologia est habitus fidei acquisitæ vel opinionis, si conclusiones suas inferat ex articulis fidei, humanâ & acquisitâ fide creditis; vel habitus, inter fidem infusam sive divinam & acquisitam medius, si conclusiones suas inferat ex articulis fidei, fide divinâ creditis. Hinc & circa conclusiones, ex una vel duabus præmissis revelatis illatas, duplicem comminiscitur assensum: Unum, in quem intellectus moveatur vi præmissarum, fide humanâ aut divinâ creditarum, quem vocat assensum Theologicum; alterum, quo fides in conclusionem, per discursum ex alterutra vel utraque præmissa revelata deductam, & ex discursu, quòd revelata sit, cognitam, feratur per se immediatè: quem assensum fidei appellat. In quo Tannerus, Suarez, aliique suum ei calculum adjiciunt.

IV. Verùm omnes hæ opiniones suas patiuntur difficultates. Et prima quidem, quæ Aureolo accepta refertur, dudum explosa est. Neque præter causam. Est enim de ratione habituum intellectualium (quorum e censu & Theologia est) ut intellectum circa suum quisque objectum sub ratione assentiendi sibi propria ad assensum inclinent: quos propterea Aristoteles VI. Nic. c. II. & III. per hoc definit, quod secundum eos intellectus verum enunciet affirmando aut negando. Enunciare autem verum affirmando aut negando, quid aliud est, quam intellectu componere, quæ in re composita sunt, & dividere, quæ in re divisa sunt, eaq; composita aut divisa esse apud animum statuere, h.e. assentiri. Neque etiam apparet, quomodo ex parte objecti formalis distingui possint fidei & Theologiæ habitus: cùm utriusque objectum formale unum & idem sit, nempe Veritas prima revelans, vel revelatio divina. Quod verò dicitur, Veritatem primam revelantem movere intellectum aliter in assensum fidei; & aliter in assensum Theologicum: in illum immediatè & sine discursu, in hunc mediante discursu; frivolum commentum est. Nam assensus fidei resolvitur æquè, ac Theologicus, ultimò in discursum, duobus hisce principiis: Quicquid Deus revelat, certò & infallibiliter verum est; &: hoc, vel illud Deus revelat; innixum. Neq; etiam minùs fidei, quàm Theologiæ est, ex una propositione revelata, & altera evidente, aut ex duabus revelatis inferre conclusiones, iisque assentiri, ita ut assensus in præmissas proximè; in divinam revelationem verò ultimò & remotè resolvatur. Quod utrumque antehac in Tract. de Conversione operosè probatum dedimus: illud quidem in VII, hoc in VIII Disputatione: ubi & Scholasticorum objectiones & exceptiones præcipuas adduximus, expendimus, & confutavimus. Iis verò stantibus, cadit ultrò adductum supra commentum Vazquezii, quòd assensus fidei nitatur tantùm discursu, proximè ex revelatione divina; Theologicus verò discursu, proximè ex articulis fidei deducto.

Neque absurditate caret, quod ibidem Vazquez contendit, assensum Theologicum niti discursu, ex articulis fidei, humana fide creditis, deducto. Ita enim objectum formale & ratio assentiendi ultima Theologiæ assensusque Theologici constituenda erit in auctoritate & testificatione humana. Fides humana enim, quâ credentur articuli fidei, nititur auctoritate & testificatione humana, velut objecto formali & ratione assentiendi ultima. Quid verò absurdius? quid à natura rei subjectæ, & communi Doctorum sensii alienius dici aut fingi potest, quàm scientiarum illam principem, Theologiam, cujus præsidio mysteria fidei abstrusissima & doctrinæ salutis capita universa explicantur, confirmantur & defenduntur, niti auctoritate & testificatione humana, velut objecto formali & ratione assentiendi ultima? cùm tamen nemini fidelium, etiam simpliciorum, non constet, mysteria fidei & doctrinam salutis excedere humanæ rationis captum longissimè. Quamobrem ea dicitur sapientia, non seculi hujus, neque principum seculi hujus, sed sapientia Dei in mysterio (latens) recondita illa, quam præfinierat Deus ante secula in gloriam nostram, I. Cor. II. 6. seq. sapientia, occupata in iis, quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audivit, & in cor hominis non adscenderunt, v. 9. quam non ab homine acceperunt, neq; didicerunt sancti Apostoli; sed per revelationem JEsu Christi, Gal. I. 12. quam Deus revelavit per Spiritum suum, I. Cor II. 10. Breviter: Nemo fidelium nescit, doctrinam salutis nostræ dependere ex contentâ in Scripturis revelatione divina, non ex testificatione & auctoritate humana. Cur ergo in auctoritate & testificatione humana potiùs, quàm in revelatione & testificatione divina ejus objectum formale & ratio assentiendi ultima constituatur? Et quæ in ea tradenda & defendenda occupatur Theologia, cur dicatur potiùs conclusiones suas deducere ex propositionibus revelatis sive articulis fidei quidem, non tamen propter testificationem sive revelationem divinam, ex qua per se dependent, & fide divina; sed propter testificationem humanam, ex qua non dependent, & fide humana creditis? Quis non videt Viri, alioqui doctissimi, nugas, Viro erudito indignas?

Commentum æquè absurdum continet distinctio assensus duplicis circa conclusiones, ex alterutra vel utraque præmissa revelata illatas, quorum unus dependeat ex illo ipso discursu Theologico, quo infertur, & assensu præmissarum; alter non dependeat ex illo, sed feratur in conclusionem propter divinam revelationem per se immediatè, postquam ex discursu, quo infertur, cognitum est, eam esse divinitùs revelatam. Primùm enim ut habitibus intellectus omnibus commune est, ut intellectum inclinent in assensum sui objecti sub sua ratione assentiendi propriâ, ita Theologiæ idem conveniat oportet. Et quia Theologiæ ratio assentiendi propria est divina revelatio, non potest ea aliter intellectum in assensum sui objecti inclinare, quàm sub divina revelatione, & consequenter ejus assensum æquè, ac assensum fidei, divinâ revelatione, tanquam ratione motivâ formali & propriâ, niti oportet. Quod autem inter actus assentiendi Theologiæ ea intercedit diversitas, quòd in alios divina revelatio intellectum movet per se immediatè, in alios mediante alia propositione revelatâ, & per consequentiam, ex ea deductam, prout objectum revelatum est vel formaliter & immediatè, vel virtualiter & mediante aliâ propositione revelatâ, id ipsum etiam actibus assentiendi fidei contingit. Revelatio divina enim non potest aliter in assensum sive fidei sive Theologiæ movere, quàm prout ex parte rei sese habet, & si objectum materiale revelatum sit immediatè, intellectum etiam in illius assensum immediatè movebit; sin revelatum sit mediante propositione vel doctrinâ aliâ, ex qua per consequentiam deducitur, necesse est, ut intellectum priùs moveat in assensum doctrinæ revelatæ, & mediante illius assensu etiam in assensum conclusionis, quæ per consequentiam necessariam ex illa sequitur. Deinde si intellectus ideò assentitur conclusioni, ex alterutra vel utraque præmissa revelata deductæ, propter revelationem divinam per se immediatè, quod per discursum cognovit, eam esse divinitùs revelatam, tunc necesse est, ut revelatio divina etiam feratur in conclusionem illam per se immediatè, eamque per se immediatè revelatam esse per discursum illum cognoscatur. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia revelatio divina, uti dictum, non aliter movet in assensum objecti, quàm prout in illud fertur, nec intellectus aliter ei assentitur, quàm prout revelatum esse cognovit, immediatè scilicet, fi revelatio divina in illud feratur immediatè; eamq; sic super illud ferri intellectus cognoverit; mediatè autem & mediante alia propositione revelata, si mediatè saltem & interventu discursus, ex alia propositione revelata deduci, revelatio divina super illud feratur, eamque sic super illud ferri cognitum sit. Sed consequens est absurdum. Eo ipso enim, quòd ex alterutra vel utraque præmissa revelata conclusio per discursum deducitur, fertur revelatio divina super eam mediatè, mediante scilicet præmissâ revelatâ, & discursu, quo ex illa deducitur: & eo ipso discursus, quòd conclusionem ex alterutrâ vel utrâque præmissâ revelatâ deducit, declarat, eam esse mediatè saltem & vi præmissarum, ex quibus per consequentiam infertur, atque adeò virtualiter tantùm revelatam. Absurdum ergo est antecedens, quod Vazquezii & aliorum, cum ipso sentientium, est, nempe intellectum assentiri conclusioni, ex alterutra vel utraque præmissa per discursum illatæ, propter divinam revelationem per se immediatè, proptereà quòd eam divinitùs revelatam esse ex discursu cognoverit. Unus ergo, non duplex est assensus conclusionis, ex alterutra vel utraque præmissâ revelatâ illatæ, qui est assensus, ex assensu præmissarum natus: alter verò assensus, qui feratur in eandem conclusionem propter revelationem divinam per se immediatè, putidum commentum est. Sed eò, unde digressus sum, redeo.

V. Cùm ergo ex parte objecti formalis nihil ostendi possit discriminis, quod inter fidem & Theologiam intercedat, fatendum est, utramque per essentiam esse habitum assentiendi patefactæ à Deo doctrinæ salutis propter divinam revelationem. Quia autem Theologia latiùs patet, quàm fides: hæc enim propriè est credendorum; illa credendorum & simul agendorum habitus: hæc est habitus assentiendi doctrinæ salutis, notitiâ quâlicunque sive ex claris & perspicuis Scripturæ verbis, sive per consequentiam facilem & cuivis, etiam illiterato, obviam, apprehensæ; illa est habitus eadem accuratiùs explicandi, confirmandi & defendendi: dicendum porro est, alteram differre ab altera inæquatè, ut includens & inclusum. Theologia enim, quæ quidem propriè talis est, includit fidem actu & formaliter: est enim, ut ostensum, per essentiam habitus assentiendi patefactæ à Deo doctrinæ salutis, propter divinam revelationem, in quo fidei ratio & quidditas consistit, & præter eam includit etiam facultatem explicandi, confirmandi & defendendi doctrinam cùm fidei tùm morum accuratiùs, quam fides, quà talis, & per se non includit. Theologia ergo perfectior est fide, non quidem intensivè, ut Scholæ loquuntur, quòd fortiùs & intensiùs intellectum ad assensum inclinet, quàm fides: divina revelatio enim, Dei supernaturali concursu elevata, æquè efficax est in fidelibus simplicioribus, quàm in Theologo erudito & subtili, &, quantum in ipsa est, in utrisque movet ad assensum sui rerumque revelatarum æqualiter; sed extensivè, quòd ad plures actus se extendat, quàm fides. Extendit enim se Theologia, uti dictum, ad actus explicandi, confirmandi & defendendi doctrinam fidei & salutis, ad quos fides per se, & qualis in quibusvis fidelibus est, se non extendit.


### XLVI. FROM these things, concerning the nature and constitution of Theology thus…

XLVI.

FROM these things, concerning the nature and constitution of Theology thus expedited and declared, Theology can be defined as being a practical science, teaching from divine revelation what things are necessary for man the sinner, both to be known for faith in Christ and to be done for the holiness of life, for the sake of attaining eternal blessedness in God.

I. We define it by practical science. Where the word science is the genus; the word practical holds the place of the generic difference. What each imports, and in what meaning they are taken here, has been declared above at greater length: namely, science is not taken in that rigor in which it is accustomed to be taken by the Aristotelians, insofar as it precisely denotes an evident habit, leaning upon principles known and evident of themselves, but in a looser meaning, for a habit leaning upon necessary principles, and to which it is repugnant that falsehood should underlie them, whether the principles be evident and immediately known of themselves from the terms apprehended, or whether they have from elsewhere and from their dependence upon the first Truth and its supernatural concurrence that they move the intellect of itself immediately to an assent of itself that is certain, and to which it is repugnant that falsehood should underlie it. See above th. III. n. V. But we call practical science any science whatsoever, which does not stop ultimately in bare cognition, but whose conclusions, which it deduces from its own principles, are partly formally, partly virtually, practical, and direct the will to practice or operation. That Theology is a science of this kind has been shown above. See Thesis V, no. VII, and Thesis XXII.

II. The remaining things which the provided definition contains concern the object and end of Theology, and constitute its specific difference.

III. The object, indeed the material one, embraces all things which are necessary to be known or done for faith in Christ and the holiness of life; the formal object, however, is the revelation of the First Truth, that is, of God, who is the primary truth: which formerly befell the Prophets and Apostles divinely, but today remains in the Scriptures composed by the same men from divine inspiration, and when read in the sacred codex, or proposed by the voice of teachers, and transmitted to the intellect of the learners, it is always joined with the supernatural concurrence of God, by which, once elevated, it illuminates the intellect (unless an obstacle is placed), and entices and draws the will to a supernatural assent to itself, which is to be commanded to the intellect. By this very fact it is so clearly evident that Theology is a science supernatural in substance, that to add this in its definition in express words would be superfluous.

IV. The definition includes the internal end of Theology in the word 'teaching'; the external end, and that an intermediate one, is faith in Christ and holiness of life; the ultimate end is the attainment of eternal blessedness in God: where eternal blessedness is the formal end; but God, by whose intuitive knowledge we are made blessed, has the character of the objective end.

V. 'To teach,' in which we said the internal end of Theology is contained, embraces three acts: namely, to explain, to confirm, and to defend. For he teaches both when he explains terms, unfolds the ambiguities of words, and declares more obscure things through clearer ones; and when he deduces conclusions from their principles, confirms them, and vindicates them from exceptions and objections brought to the contrary, and thus defends the truth against those who dissent. And Paul seems to embrace these acts in the one word 'teaching,' when he wishes a Bishop to be διδακτικὸν, apt to teach I Tim. III. 2. Elsewhere, however, he expresses the same things more distinctly with other words and phrases: as when he includes among the duties of a good Bishop τὸ ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, to rightly divide the word of truth, II Tim. II. 15, and requires of a Bishop that he be δυνατὸς παρακαλεῖν ἐν διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ, powerful to exhort in sound doctrine, καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, and to convince those who contradict, and to stop their mouths, Tit. I. 9, 11. Where by the phrases, ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, and παρακαλεῖν ἐν διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ, he points his finger to the first two acts, which are to explain and to confirm; but by the others, τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, to the third. For to rightly divide the word of truth is nothing else than to treat rightly the doctrine of truth, i.e. revealed by the primary Truth, and therefore most true, in such a way that you separate what should be separated, join what should be joined, confirm with the testimonies of Scripture what needs proof, and thus propose and inculcate each part, according to the capacity of the hearers and the convenient place and time, for the edification of faith and morals. Similarly, to exhort in sound doctrine is to propose, explain, and confirm the doctrine concerning our salvation so aptly and harmoniously that by it the hearers may be reminded of their duty and be excited to the pursuit of piety. Finally, ἐλέγχειν τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, is to convince those who contradict by arguments by which the truth of the doctrine is built up and the opposing falsehood is destroyed, so that, constrained by the force of the arguments, they are at length compelled to be silent, which is certainly to defend the truth of the doctrine.

VI. Although indeed to teach, or to explain, confirm, and defend, are external acts of Theology, ordered in themselves toward others, whether learners or those who contradict: for no one, properly speaking, is said to teach or refute himself; and Theology can exist in a man even if he teaches or refutes no one: yet Theology is defined by them rather than by the internal acts themselves, because they are better known to us, and therefore more suitable for declaring the nature of Theology than the internal acts: of which kind are the acts of the intellect by which, according to the prescription of Theology, we weigh within ourselves both what is necessary to be known for faith in Christ and what is necessary for the holiness of life, and ambiguities, if they occur anywhere, to the acwe develop a more careful understanding of things, we consider from which principles each one depends, and we examine the doubts that have arisen here and there, and whatever objections there may be. These internal acts contribute to the intellect of the Theologian that very thing which the external acts of teaching, depending on them, contribute to others for the purpose of acquiring an understanding of the same things and for learning the habit of Theology.

Latin:

XLVI.

EX his, de natura & constitutione Theologiæ sic expeditis & declaratis, definiri potest Theologia, quòd sit scientia practica, ex divina revelatione docens, quæ homini peccatori cùm ad fidem in Christum cognitu, tùm ad vitæ sanctimoniam factu necessaria sunt, consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis æternæ causâ.

I. Definimus eam per scientiam practicam. Ubi scientiæ vox generis; vox practica differentiæ genericæ locum sustinet. Quid importet utraque, & quo heic significatu accipiantur, suprà declaratum est pluribus: nempe scientia non accipitur in eo rigore, quo ab Aristotelicis accipi solet, prout scilicet præcisè denotat habitum evidentem, principiis per se notis & evidentibus innixum, sed in significatu laxiori, pro habitu, principiis necessariis, & quibus falsum subesse repugnat, nixo, sive principia evidentia & per se ex apprehensis terminis statim nota sint, sive aliunde & ex sua dependentia à Veritate prima ejusque concursu supernaturali habeant, quòd per se immediatè intellectum in assensum sui certum, & cui falsum subesse repugnat, moveant. Videatur suprà th. III. n. V. Practicam verò scientiam dicimus scientiam quamcunque, quæ non in cognitione nuda ultimò sistit, sed cujus conclufiones, quas ex suis principiis deducit, formaliter partim, partim virtualiter, practicæ sunt, & voluntatem ad praxin sive operationem dirigunt. Cujusmodi scientiam Theologiam esse, ostensum est suprà. Videantur Thef. V. n. VII. & Thef. XXII.

II. Cætera, quæ tradita definitio continet, Theologiæ objectum & finem concernunt, ejusque differentiam specificam constituunt.

III. Objectum, materiale quidem, complectitur omnia, quæ ad fidem in Christum vitæque sanctimoniam cognitu factuve necessaria sunt; formale autem est revelatio Veritatis primæ, h. e. Dei, qui prima veritas est: quæ Prophetis olim & Apostolis divinitùs obtigit, hodiè autem in Scripturis ab iisdem, ex divina inspiratione, concinnatis, superest, & lecta in codice sacro, vel docentium voce proposita, & ad discentium intellectum transmissa, semper cum concursu Dei supernaturali conjuncta est, quo elevata intellectum (nisi ponatur obex) illuminat, voluntatemque ad supernaturalem sui assensum, intellectui imperandum, allicit & trahit. Quo ipso Theologiam scientiam in substantia supernaturalem esse ita apertè constat, ut verbis expressis id in ejus definitione addere, superfluum fuerit.

IV. Finem Theologiæ, internum quidem, comprehendit definitio verbo docendi; externum verò, eumque intermedium, fides in Christum & sanctimonia vitæ; ultimum consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis æternæ appellatione: ubi beatitudo æterna formalis; Deus verò, cujus intuitivâ cognitione beati constituimur, objectivi finis rationem habet.

V. Docere, quo Theologiæ finem internum contineri diximus, tres complectitur actus: explicare scilicet, confirmare, & defendere. Docet enim cùm qui terminos explicat, ambiguitates vocum evolvit, & obscuriora per mamfestiora declarat; tum qui conclusiones ex suis principiis deducit, confirmat, & ab exceptionibus objectionibusq; in contrarium allatis vindicat, atque sic veritatem adversus dissentientes defendit. Quos actus & Paulus uno docendi verbo complecti videtur, cùm Episcopum vult esse διδακτικὸν, aptum ad docendum I. Tim. III. 2. Alibi autem eosdem verbis & phrasibus aliis distinctius exprimit: ut cùm inter munia boni Episcopi refert τὸ ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, rectè secare sermonem veritatis, II. Tim. II 15. & ad Episcopum requirit, ut sit δυνατὸς παρακαλεῖν ἐν διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ, potens exhortari doctrinâ sanâ, καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν. & contradicentes convincere, iisque os obturare Tit. I. 9. 11. Ubi phrasibus, ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, & παρακαλεῖν ἐν διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ, digitum intendit ad duos priores actus, qui sunt explicare & confirmare; cæteris autem, τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, ad tertium. Secare enim rectè sermonem veritatis, nihil est aliud, quàm doctrinam veritatis, h. e. à prima Veritate revelatam, adeòque verissimam, rectè tractare, ita, ut quæ sejungenda sunt, sejungas, quæ conjungenda, conjungas, quæ probatione egent, Scripturæ testimoniis confirmes, & sic partes quasq;, pro auditorum captu, loco & tempore conveniente, ad fidei & morum ædificationem proponas & inculces. Similiter, exhortari doctrinâ sanâ, est doctrinam de nostra salute ita aptè & concinnè proponere, explicare & confirmare, ut per illam auditores sui moneantur officii, & ad pietatis studium excitentur. Denique ἐλέγχειν τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, est contradicentes argumentis, quibus doctrinæ veritas adstruatur, & opposita falsitas destruatur, convincere, ut argumentorum vi constricti tandem obmutescere cogantur, quod utique est defendere doctrinæ veritatem.

VI. Quamvis verò docere, sive explicare, confirmare & defendere sint actus Theologiæ externi, ad alios, sive discentes, sive contradicentes, per se ordinati: nemo enim, propriè loquendo, semetipsum dicitur docere aut refutare; Theologia etiam homini inesse possit, licet neminem doceat aut refutet: per eos tamen Theologia potiùs definitur, quàm per ipsos actus internos, quòd nobis notiores, & proinde ad Theologiæ naturam declarandam accommodatiores sint, quàm actus interni: cujusmodi sunt actus intellectus, quibus, ad Theologiæ præscriptum, cùm quæ ad fidem in Christum, tùm quæ ad sanctimoniam vitæ cognitu necessaria sunt, apud nos expendimus, ambiguitates, sicubi occurrant, ad accuratiorem rerum intelligentiam evolvimus, ex quibus principiis unumquodque dependeat, consideramus, dubia hinc inde oborta, objectionesque quascunque excutimus. Qui actus interni conferunt intellectui Theologi illud ipsum, quod dependentes ex illis externi actus docendi aliis ad comparandam earundem rerum intelligentiam habitumque Theologiæ addiscendum conferunt.


### XLVII. Just as in other practical sciences the treatment is usually instituted in an…

XLVII.

Just as in other practical sciences the treatment is usually instituted in an analytical order, and first of all the end for which, then the subject of the operation, or the end to which, and thirdly and finally the principles and means leading to the end are discussed: so also for Theology, for the very reason that it is a practical science, the same order of doctrine must be appropriate.

I. It might have seemed that the order of doctrine which is otherwise observed in practical sciences, namely the analytical, does not suit Theology, on account of the notable diversity which exists between it and other practical sciences. For in other practical sciences the end is of the class of natural things, and it is the first thing that is known in them, and this, once known, is the reason for knowing the means: in which, therefore, the beginning of the treatment is deservedly taken from the end, as from the first thing known, and the progress is further instituted toward the subject and the means: for the knowledge of these depends on the knowledge of that. The end of Theology, however, is of the class of supernatural things, and those which exceed the grasp of reason, left to itself, and therefore it is not the first thing that is known in it, but divine revelation is that which is known first of all in it: nor does this, once known from divine revelation, seem to be the reason for knowing the means, but the knowledge of these, just as the knowledge of the end, must be sought from divine revelation: so that the reason which otherwise in practical sciences persuades one to progress from the end to the subject, and from this to the means, seems not to find a place in Theology.

II. Notwithstanding this, however, we consider this order of doctrine to be no less suited to Theology than to other practical sciences. For first, although the end of Theology, according to its specific nature, is of the class of supernatural things, and neither is known to us from elsewhere than from divine revelation known, and thus it is not simply the first thing that is known in Theology, yet its knowledge, although drawn from divine revelation, is here also by nature prior to the knowledge of the means, likewise drawn from divine revelation; nor can the means in the capacity of means, and their relation to the end, be known from divine revelation, unless the end is first known from the same. But just as the knowledge of the end is by nature prior to the knowledge of the means, although both finally come to us from divine revelation, so also the consideration of the former must be prior to the consideration of the latter, as the order of doctrine requires. Then, the distinct knowledge of the end of Theology, which is the intuitive knowledge or beatific vision of God, one in essence and triune in persons, is indeed posterior to the knowledge of divine revelation; but a certain confused knowledge of it is prior to the knowledge of divine revelation, and thus the end in Theology is also in some way the first thing known. For it is naturally known to the human intellect, before all divine revelation, that God exists, and that He is the rewarder of good deeds and the avenger of crimes; and that after this life there is another, in which souls at the very least will survive, and according to whether men have conducted themselves well or badly in this life, they will live happily or miserably, with God rewarding their good deeds with a blessed life, but avenging their evil deeds with eternal misery. Moreover, there is naturally implanted in the minds of men a certain sense of a supreme Deity and an appetite for beatitude, by which all are stimulated to wish to be happy, and no one wishes to be miserable, to use the words of Augustine from book XIII of De Trinitate, chapter III; without which, if it existed, no one would easily labor to learn Theology, or would think about divine revelation, upon which the distinct knowledge of our beatitude depends. Thirdly, the knowledge of principles and means, if not distinct, is nevertheless confused, and depends upon the end, at least as confusedly known by the guidance of the light of nature. And indeed, where it is known in part regarding the end, that beatitude, in whatever its specific nature may consist, is not an end to be effected or acquired by us, but to be obtained from God (which not only the revelation contained in the Scriptures, but even the light of nature itself teaches), it is thoroughly known that its efficient cause is God; the internal impulsive cause being the grace of God and his benevolent will toward men. When it is known that blessedness is obtained by man only through God being propitious and by his grace, it is immediately known, with the light of Scripture and nature as a guide, that for one to have God propitious and to obtain blessedness by his grace, it is necessary for him to abstain from sins and to pursue God with fitting worship: which things stand in the relation of means to an end, broadly speaking. Nor does the light of nature and Scripture allow man to be ignorant of this, that right and fitting worship of God is to be derived from his nature and attributes, as those of a known objective end, and thus that the knowledge of the means is in good part to be sought from the known objective end. See what we have discussed above regarding this matter in ch. II, th. XXXVIII. Furthermore, when it is known that blessedness is obtained by us only through God being propitious, and that we are sinners and offend God daily by our sins—both of which can be known under the guidance of the light of nature—it is further known, at least confusedly, that for the attainment of blessedness from God, there must intervene a certain mediator between God, offended by sins, and sinful men, or at least a certain satisfaction for sins, by which the injured divine justice may be satisfied, and God, his anger being appeased, may be reconciled to men: so that thus the knowledge of the meritorious causes of our blessedness also, though confused, may depend upon the knowledge of the end and the subject. Although, however, a distinct knowledge of Christ, who is the Mediator of God and men and the meritorious cause of our blessedness, as also of faith in Christ and the efficient causes of faith, cannot be had from the end, whether known confusedly or distinctly: for these causes of our salvation, as they depend upon the free will and ordination of God, so they do not become known to us from elsewhere than from divine revelation; yet in reality Christ the Mediator and faith in Christ are the causes and means of obtaining blessedness from God, and, the order of doctrine so requiring, they presuppose the knowledge of the end before the knowledge of themselves. These things suffice for Theology, just as other practical sciences, to be correctly treated in an analytical order. For the order of doctrine in practical sciences is founded upon the relation of the things to be considered, and according as one has the relation of end or means to the other, so also the consideration of them is to be instituted earlier or later, although they fall equally under one common reason of knowing.

Latin:

XLVII.

QUemadmodum in scientiis practicis aliis tractatio ordine analytico institui, & primò omnium de fine cujus, deinde de subjecto operationis, sive de fine cui, & tertiò denique de principiis & mediis, ad finem ducentibus, agi solet: ita & Theologiæ, eo ipso quòd scientia practica est, ordo doctrinæ idem conveniat oportet.

I. Videri poterat, Theologiæ non convenire eum doctrinæ ordinem, qui aliàs in scientiis practicis observatur, analyticum scilicet, ob notabilem diversitatem, quæ inter illam & scientias practicas alias intercedit. Nam in scientiis practicis aliis finis est è censu rerum naturalium, estque primum, quod in illis cognoscitur, & is cognitus est ratio cognoscendi media: in quibus proinde meritò à fine, tanquam à primo cognito, tractationis initium sumitur, & porro ad subjectum & media instituitur progressus: horum enim cognitio pendet ex cognitione illius. Theologiæ finis autem est è censu rerum supernaturalium, & quæ rationis, sibi relictæ, captum excedunt, & proinde non est primum, quod in ea cognoscitur, sed divina revelatio est id, quod primò omnium in illa cognoscitur: neque etiam is, ex divina revelatione cognitus, videtur esse ratio cognoscendi media, sed horum cognitio æquè, ac cognitio finis, ex divina revelatione accersenda venit: ut ita ratio, quæ aliàs in scientiis practicis à fine ad subjectum, & ab hoc ad media progredi suadet, in Theologia locum non invenire videatur.

II. Hoc tamen non obstante, Theologiæ non minùs, quàm scientiis practicis aliis, accommodatum esse existimamus hunc doctrinæ ordinem. Primùm enim quamvis Theologiæ finis, secundum suam rationem specificam, sit è censu rerum supernaturalium, nec aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione cognitâ, nobis innotefcat, adeoque fimpliciter primum, quod in Theologia cognofcitur, non fit, ejus tamen cognitio, licet ex divina revelatione haufta, heic etiam naturâ prior eft cognitione mediorum, itidem ex divina revelatione hauftâ; neque poffunt media in ratione mediorum, illorumque habitudo ad finem ex divina revelatione cognofci, nifi fine ex eâdem priùs cognito. Quemadmodum autem cognitio finis naturâ prior eft cognitione mediorum, licet utraque demum ex divina revelatione nobis obtingat, ita & illius confideratio horum confideratione, doćtrinæ ordine fic exigente, prior effe debet. Deinde cognitio diftinćta finis Theologiæ, qui eft Dei unius in effentia, & Trini in perfonis, intuitiva cognitio five vifio beatifica, pofterior quidem eft cognitione divinæ revelationis; fed confufa quædam illius cognitio cognitione divinæ revelationis prior eft, atque adeoque finis in Theologia etiam aliquo modo eft primum cognitum. Eft enim hominis intellećtui naturaliter, ante omnem divinam revelationem, notum, Deum effe, eumque effe bonorum remuneratorem & fcelerum vindicem; & poft hanc vitam effe aliam, in qua animæ minimùm fuperftites futuræ, & prout in hac vita benè vel malè homines fe gefferint, beatè vel miferè acturæ fint, Deo benefaćta illorum vitâ beatâ remunerante, malefacta autem miferiâ perpetuâ vindicante. Quin & naturâ infitus eft hominum mentibus quidam Numinis fupremi fenfus & beatitudinis appetitus, quo ftimulati omnes effe beati volunt, mifer effe nemo vult, ut Auguftini utar verbis ex lib. XIII. de Trin. c. III. absque quo fi effet, de Theologia addifcenda nemo facilè laboraturus, aut de revelatione divina, ex qua beatitudinis noftræ cognitio diftinćta dependet, cogitaturus effet. Tertiò etiam cognitio principiorum & mediorum, fi non diftinćta, confufa tamen, dependet ex fine, dućtu luminis naturæ faltem confusè cognito. Et quidem ubi ex parte finis cognitum eft, beatitudinem, in quocunq; tandem ejus ratio fpecifica confiftat, non effe finem, à nobis efficiendum aut acquirendum, fed à Deo confequendum (quod non folùm contenta in Scripturis revelatio, fed & ipfum naturæ lumen docet) cognofcitur oppidò, ejus causam efficientem esse Deum; impulsivam internam Dei gratiam & benevolam erga homines voluntatem. Ubi cognitum est, beatitudinem non nisi Deo propitio ejusque gratia homini obtingere, cognoscitur statim, Scripturæ & naturæ lumine duce, ut quis Deum habeat propitium, ejusque gratia beatitudinem consequatur, oportere eum à peccatis abstinere, Deumque conveniente cultu prosequi: quæ se habent ex parte mediorum ad finem, laxè dictorum. Neque id hominem ignorare patitur naturæ & Scripturæ lumen, cultum rectum Deoque convenientem esse ex ejus, velut finis objectivi cogniti, natura & attributis accersendum, atque adeò cognitionem mediorum esse bonam partem ex fine objectivo cognito petendam. Videantur, quæ suprâ in c. II. th. XXXIIX. hanc in rem disseruimus. Ubi porro cognitum est, beatitudinem non nisi Deo propitio nobis obtingere, nos autem esse peccatores, & offendere Deum quotidiè peccatis: quod utrumque ductu luminis naturæ cognosci potest; cognoscitur ulterius, confusè saltem, ad consequendam à Deo beatitudinem intervenire oportere mediatorem quendam inter Deum, peccatis offensum, hominesque peccatores, vel saltem satisfactionem quandam pro peccatis, quâ læsæ justitiæ divinæ satisfiat, Deusque, placatâ ejus irâ, hominibus reconcilietur: ut ita causæ beatitudinis nostræ meritoriæ cognitio etiam, confusa licet, ex cognitione finis & subjecti dependeat. Quamvis verò Christi, qui Dei & hominum Mediator, nostræque beatitudinis causa meritoria est, ut & fidei in Christum, causarumque fidei efficientium cognitio distincta ex fine, confusè aut distinctè cognito, haberi non possit: hæ enim salutis nostræ causæ, ut ex libera Dei voluntate & ordinatione dependent, ita aliunde, quam ex divina revelatione nobis non innotescunt; reipsa tamen Christus Mediator fidesque in Christum sunt causæ ac media consequendæ à Deo beatitudinis, &, ordine doctrinæ sic exigente, cognitionem finis ante cognitionem sui prærequirunt. Quæ sufficiunt ad hoc, ut Theologia, æquè ac aliæ scientiæ practicæ, ordine analytico rectè pertractetur. Ordo doctrinæ enim in scientiis practicis fundatur in habitudine rerum considerandarum, & prout una ad alteram finis aut medii rationem habet, ita & illarum consideratio prius aut posterius instituenda est, licet æquè sub unam communem rationem cognoscendi cadant.


### XLIIX. We therefore establish three parts of Theology, of which the first will treat…

XLIIX.

We therefore establish three parts of Theology, of which the first will treat of its end; the second of its subject; and the third of the principles and means leading to the end.

I. Some divide Theology, after the manner of Moral Philosophy, into a common and a proper part. In the former they consider what is necessary to be believed or done by all and each who are striving for blessedness, in whatever condition they may be. In the latter they treat of establishing, governing, and preserving the Church, and teach what the duties are of the individuals who are in it, both of those who teach and those who learn. They subdivide each part again into three other parts, in one of which the end is treated, in another the subject, and in the third the principles and means.

II. We, leaving this division in its own place, will persist in that which our thesis exhibits, if for no other reason, certainly for this: that it approaches more closely to the order of Theological Topics commonly received in compendiums of Theology, and does not differ from it, except that it refers the consideration of the formal end, namely eternal blessedness, to the first part, and subjoins it to the consideration of the objective end, namely God and the works of creation and providence, which is otherwise accustomed to be instituted in the last place after the doctrine concerning the consummation of the age and the final judgment.

XLIX.

The first part contains the Topics concerning God, one in essence and Triune in persons, and concerning the works of creation and providence, by which God communicates His goodness to men; and concerning the fruition of God or eternal blessedness.

I. We previously made the end of Theology twofold: objective and formal; the former of which we placed in God, as in man's infinitely perfect and supreme good; the latter we placed in the enjoyment of God. And because the formal end depends upon the objective, we must first of all treat of the objective, namely God. Now God can be considered either in Himself and by reason of His perfections; or by reason of the works by which He communicates His goodness equally to all men. In Himself He is considered first by reason of His essence and essential attributes; and then also by reason of the persons. The works, however, by which He communicates His goodness to men are the works of creation and providence.

II. The topics, therefore, pertaining to the objective end of Theology are: the first concerning God, by reason of His essence and essential attributes; the second concerning the same, viewed by reason of the persons: the third concerning the creation of this universe, and especially of man, for whose sake and for whose use all other things contained therein were created: the fourth concerning the Angels. Although indeed the Angels are immaterial substances, and therefore are not a part of this universe, their consideration is nevertheless not inconveniently referred to this part of Theology, which is concerning its objective end, namely God, not only because they are the most perfect of all the effects of God, in whom the goodness of God and His other perfections shine forth most brightly, but because through them He also abundantly communicates His goodness to man, while He sends them forth into the ministry of those who shall be heirs of salvation, Heb. 1:14. The fifth topic, finally, will be concerning the providence of God, by which He preserves, governs, and directs to their ends all the things created by Him. The consideration of which is conveniently referred to the doctrine concerning the objective end for this reason, that by it, no less than by creation itself, God communicates His goodness to man. The objective end having thus been considered, we must next treat of the formal end, namely the enjoyment of God, or the blessedness of man, the consideration of which will constitute the sixth and final topic of this part.

Latin:

XLIIX.

PArtés igitur Theologiæ tres constituimus, quarum prima de ejus fine; secunda de subjecto; & tertia de principiis & mediis, ad finem ducentibus, aget.

I. Nonnulli dividunt Theologiam, ad modum Philosophiæ Moralis, in partem communem & propriam. In priori considerant, quæ omnibus & singulis, ad beatitudinem contendentibus, quâcunque conditione sint, creditu factuve necessaria sunt. In posteriori de constituenda, regenda & conservanda Ecclesia agunt, & quæ singulorum, qui in ea sunt, cum docentium, tum discentium, munia sint, docent. Utramque partem rursum in tres alias subdividunt partes, in quarum unâ de fine, alterâ de subjecto, & tertiâ de principiis & mediis agitur.

II. Nos divisione hâc suo loco relictâ, persistemus in ea, quam thesis nostra exhibet, si non aliâ, eâ certè de causâ, quòd ad ordinem Locorum Theologicorum, vulgo in compendiis Theologiæ receptum, propius accedit, nec ab eo discrepat, nisi quod confiderationem finis formalis, beatitudinis æternæ scilicet, ad partem primam refert, & considerationi finis objectivi, Dei scilicet & operum creationis ac providentiæ, subjungit, quæ aliàs loco ultimo post doctrinam de consummatione seculi & extremo judicio institui solet.

XLIX.

PArs prima continet Locos de Deo, uno in essentia & Trino in personis, deque operibus creationis & providentiæ, quibus suam bonitatem cum hominibus Deus communicat; & de fruitione Dei sive de beatitudine æternâ.

I. Finem Theologiæ suprà faciebamus duplicem: Objectivum & formalem; quorum illum in Deo, velut hominis bono infinitè perfecto & summo; hunc in Dei fruitione constituebamus. Et quia finis formalis ab objectivo dependet, de objectivo, Deo scilicet, primò omnium agendum venit. Considerari autem potest Deus vel in se & ratione suarum perfectionum; vel ratione operum, quibus suam bonitatem cum hominibus æquè omnibus communicat. In se consideratur primò ratione essentiæ & attributorum essentialium; & deinde etiam ratione personarum. Opera verò, quibus suam bonitatem cum hominibus communicat, sunt creationis & providentiæ opera.

II. Loci ergo, ad finem Theologiæ objectivum pertinentes, sunt primus de Deo, ratione essentiæ & attributorum essentialium; secundus de eodem, ratione personarum spectato: tertius de creatione hujus universi, & cumprimis hominis, propter quem & ad cujus usum aliæ, eo contentæ, res omnes conditæ sunt: quartus de Angelis. Quanquam verò Angeli substantiæ immateriales, & proinde hujus universi pars non sunt, illorum consideratio tamen non incommodè ad hanc Theologiæ partem, quæ est de ejus fine objectivo, Deo scilicet, refertur, non tantum quòd sint effectus Dei omnium perfectissimi, in quibus Dei bonitas & perfectiones ejus cæteræ maximè relucent, sed quòd per eos etiam suam cum homine bonitatem abunde communicet, dum illos emittit in ministerium hominum, qui hæredes erunt salutis, Ebr. I. 14. Quintus denique Locus erit de providentia Dei, quâ res à se conditas universas conservat, gubernat, & in suos fines dirigit. Cujus consideratio vel ea de causâ ad doctrinam de fine objectivo commodè refertur, quòd illâ non minus, quàm ipsâ creatione, Deus bonitatem suam cum homine communicat. Considerato ita fine objectivo, deinceps de fine formali, fruitione Dei scilicet, sive de hominis beatitudine agendum erit, cujus consideratio Locum hujus partis sextum & ultimum constituet.


### I. The second part contains the topics concerning the twofold state of man, of…

I.

The second part contains the topics concerning the twofold state of man, of integrity and corruption, concerning sin both in general, as well as the fall of our first parents and original and actual sin in particular, and concerning the guilt of fault and punishment, which sin draws upon the sinner.

I. In the second part, the subject of Theology, or the end for which it exists, is treated. For just as the end for which and the end for whom, or the subject, have a great affinity between them—for the end for which is always suitable and desirable to some subject, and it only has the nature of an end insofar as it is suitable and desirable to it—so also the consideration of this doctrine rightly claims for itself a place next to the consideration of that.

II. That the subject of Theology is man the sinner, insofar as he lacks the end for whose sake Theology exists, but can become a participant in it through the principles and means which are prescribed in it, is understood from the preceding. XV. and especially from chap. II. th. X. where in the Expl. n. III. it is shown that in any practical science two things are required on the part of the subject: One, that he lacks the end for whose sake the science exists; the other, that he can become a participant in it through the principles and means which are prescribed in it. But because the lack of the perfection which is the end of Theology, namely eternal blessedness, stood otherwise on the part of man in his primitive state, or state of integrity, and stands otherwise now in the state of sin: for in the former it implied only the absence of the end, not of the powers of attaining it in God and from God; but in the latter, besides the absence of the end, it implies also the lack of the powers of attaining it in God and from God, contracted from the fall of the first man, and propagated to all by carnal generation; first of all it must be considered in what state man was originally created by God, and what the powers of the faculties of the soul, intellect and will, were for attaining blessedness. Then we must treat of the nature of sin in general, and of the fall of the first man and the original sin contracted through him in particular, and what powers man lost through the fall; and likewise the ἀδυναμίαν [inability] in those things which pertain to attaining the end of Theology, which he contracted, must be explained; and furthermore to actual sin and its various distinctions, and finally to the guilt of fault and punishment, which accompanies sin, both original and partial, and excludes man from blessedness, nay even enslaves him to perpetual misery, we must proceed, and each thing must be explained in order through certain Topics.

III. The first Topic, therefore, of the second part will be concerning the primeval state of man, or concerning the image of God in man and original righteousness, created together with man at the beginning; the second concerning the free will of man, and his powers before the fall: the third concerning sin in general; the fourth concerning the fall of the first man and the loss of original righteousness, or concerning the sin of origin: the fifth concerning the free will of man after the fall, and his innate ἀδυναμίᾳ in those things which are necessary for obtaining blessedness. The sixth concerning actual sins and their various distinctions: the seventh concerning the guilt of fault and punishment, which sins, original and actual, draw upon sinners, and concerning the misery of man, which is opposed to blessedness.

Latin:

I.

Pars secunda continet Locos de duplici hominis statu, integritatis & corruptionis, de peccato cùm in genere, tùm de lapsu primorum parentum peccatoque originali & actualibus in specie, & de reatu culpæ ac pœnæ, quem peccatori peccatum attrahit.

I. In parte secunda agitur de Theologiæ subjecto, sive fine cui. Quemadmodum enim magnam inter se affinitatem habent, finis cujus & cui sive subjectum: finis cujus enim semper alicui subjecto conveniens & expetibilis est, & id tantum habet rationem finis, in quantum ei est conveniens & expetibilis: ita & consideratio hujus doctrinæ, locum ab illius consideratione proximum jure sibi vendicat.

II. Esse autem Theologiæ subjectum hominem peccatorem, in quantum fine, cujus gratiâ Theologia est, caret, ejus verò particeps fieri potest per principia & media, quæ in illa præscribuntur, intelligitur ex superioribus. XV. & cumprimis ex cap. II. th. X. ubi in Expl. n. III. ostenditur in qualibet scientia practica requiri ex parte subjecti duo: Unum, ut careat fine, cujus gratiâ scientia est; alterum, ut ejus particeps fieri possit per principia & media, quæ in illa præscribuntur. Quia verò carentia perfectionis, quæ Theologiæ pro fine est, beatitudinis æternæ scilicet, ex parte hominis aliter se habebat in statu ejus primævo, sive integritatis, aliter nunc in statu peccati se habet: in illo enim importabat tantum absentiam finis, non virium ejus in Deo & à Deo consequendi; in hoc autem, præter absentiam finis, importat etiam carentiam virium illius in Deo & à Deo consequendi, ex lapsu primi hominis contractam, & carnali generatione ad omnes propagatam; primò omnium sic considerandum venit, quo statu homo primitus à Deo conditus fuerit, & quæ facultatum animæ, intellectus & voluntatis, vires fuerint ad beatitudinem consequendam. Deinde de natura peccati in genere, deque lapsu primi hominis & contracto per illum peccato originali in specie agendum, & quas vires homo per lapsum amiserit; quam item ἀδυναμίαν in iis, quæ ad consequendum Theologiæ finem pertinent, contraxerit, explicandum; & porro ad peccatum actuale ejusque distinctiones varias, & tandem ad reatum culpæ ac pœnæ, qui peccatum, originale pariter & partiale, comitatur, hominemque beatitudine excludit, quin & miseriā perpetuā mancipat, progrediendum, & ordine singula per certos Locos explicanda erunt.

III. Primus ergo partis secundæ Locus erit de hominis statu primævo, sive de imagine Dei in homine & justitia originali, primitus homini concreatâ; Secundus de libero arbitrio hominis, ejusque viribus ante lapsum: Tertius de peccato in genere; Quartus de lapsu primi hominis & amissione justitiæ originalis, sive de peccato originis: Quintus de libero arbitrio hominis post lapsum, éjusque ἀδυναμίᾳ connatâ in iis, quæ ad consequendam beatitudinem necessaria sunt. Sextus de peccatis actualibus illorumque variis distinctionibus: Septimus de reatu culpæ & pœnæ, quem peccatoribus peccata, originale & actualia, attrahunt, deque hominis miseriâ, beatitudini oppositâ.


### LI Finally, the third part will be occupied in explaining the Topics concerning the principles and means of obtaining the end, namely, eternal…

LI.

Finally, the third part will be occupied in explaining the Topics concerning the principles and means of obtaining the end, namely, eternal blessedness.

I. Here it must be repeated, what we also warned above in th. XIII. and XXI., namely that we do not here use the word means precisely in that strict sense in which those things are called means, to the choosing of which a known end so moves the will, that they are in turn properly called causes of obtaining the end, but in a looser sense, as that is called a means, whatever in any way exists for the sake of the end, even if it is not its cause, but a mere condition, or only a cause without which it would not be, or at least behaves as that which removes an impediment, or is connected with the end, and precedes its attainment in order. For in the third part of Theology, which is concerning the principles and means of blessedness, many things are treated which are not causes of obtaining it, but imply some other relation to it. Whence, so that the connection of the Topics pertaining here, and the relation of the things contained in them to the end of Theology, may be exhibited more clearly to the reader's view, we shall subdivide this third part, according to the diverse relation of the underlying things, into several parts or sections. II. The first section will contain the Topics which are occupied with explaining the causes and means of our blessedness, strictly speaking. Among the causes of our blessedness, however, the first is God, who out of his immense goodness, grace, and mercy did not desire the death of the sinner, and moved by that, in his eternal decree, predestined to blessedness or eternal life as many as he foresaw would finally believe in Christ. But because God is treated in the first part, in the first and second Topic, both by reason of his essence and essential perfections and by reason of his persons, here we must treat of the goodness, grace, and mercy of God, by which he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, I Tim. II. 4, which is the προηγουμένη, or internal impulsive cause of our blessedness, and is the fountain and spring of our blessedness and of all the causes and means of obtaining it. The place next to the grace of God is held by Christ the Mediator, and his merit and satisfaction for our sins, as the meritorious cause of our blessedness: the third place will be held by faith, apprehending Christ the Mediator and his merit, which is the cause of our blessedness, not by reason of itself, but by reason of the merit of Christ apprehended, and thus a less principal cause. And because God, moved by his grace and the merit of Christ and our faith in Christ, decreed from eternity to impart blessedness to all whom he foresaw would believe in Christ and would depart from this life in faith, leaning upon the merit of Christ, it is not beside the point that the decree of predestination is also numbered among the causes of our blessedness: since through it God is actually and formally constituted the cause of blessedness being imparted to us. but just as unbelief, opposed to faith in Christ, is the cause why men fall away from eternal blessedness and incur eternal damnation, so God, according to his rigid justice, decreed from eternity to exclude from the number of the blessed and to adjudge to eternal damnation whomever he foresaw would not believe in Christ but would die in unbelief; and therefore, by virtue of opposition, the doctrine concerning the decree of reprobation coheres closely with the doctrine concerning the decree of predestination. For contrary things, when placed beside one another, shine forth more clearly.

III. The topics therefore of the first Section will be, the first concerning the προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause of our blessedness, namely the goodness, grace, and mercy of God toward men fallen into sin, moved by which, He willed them to be saved: the second concerning the meritorious or principal external impulsive cause of the same, namely Christ the Mediator, and His merit and satisfaction for our sins; the third concerning the less principal cause of that, namely faith, apprehending Christ the Mediator and His merit; and the fourth concerning the decree of predestination itself, resting upon the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and foreseen faith in Christ, and the decree of reprobation opposed to it.

IV. Faith in Christ, however, is not a work of human powers, but is conferred, confirmed, and preserved by God through the Word and Sacraments: which therefore are themselves also causes of our blessedness, but remote and mediate, and instrumental, in so far as they are the organs and instruments for the kindling, confirming, and preserving of faith in us, which on our part is the proximate cause of it. Nor does faith have the status of a cause for our blessedness, except in so far as it apprehends Christ the Mediator and His merit, and by that apprehension constitutes us righteous before God, or justifies. Wherefore, subsequently, we must also treat of the causes of faith, and specifically of the Word of God as the organ for kindling it in adults (the Sacraments will be treated later), of the conversion of the sinful man by which faith is kindled, and of his justification through faith. And in explaining these, the Second Section will be occupied, the first topic of which will be concerning the Word of God as the organ for kindling faith in adults; the second concerning the production of faith itself in his heart through the Word, or concerning the conversion of the sinful man; the third concerning the justification of the man converted to God before God through faith.

V. Faith in Christ, kindled in the heart of an adult man by the power of the Word, when it has constituted the man righteous before God by apprehending the merit of Christ, and has obtained for him the remission of sins before God, is not idle, but exerts itself through works of charity toward his renewal and holiness of life. Whence, furthermore, concerning the renewal of the man justified by faith, concerning good works and their principles and the norm, a consideration is to be instituted concerning Christian virtues and the vices opposed to them: in which the third Section will be occupied, and its Topics will be, the first concerning the renewal of man, justified by faith; the second concerning good works, and their principles and causes; the third concerning the law, as the norm of good works, and its distinctions; the fourth concerning the moral law, and concerning the works and virtues prescribed in each of its tables specifically, as also concerning evil acts and vices prohibited in it.

VI. Among the instruments for kindling, confirming, and preserving faith, and the holiness of life flowing from it, the Sacraments find a place, which were some in the Church of the O.T. and are others now in the Church of the N.T. Those were Circumcision and the Paschal Lamb; these are Baptism and the Lord's Supper: to the explanation of which the fourth Section will be destined, and its first topic will be concerning the Sacraments in general, and their distinction and difference; the second concerning Circumcision; and the third concerning the Paschal Lamb, the two O.T. Sacraments; the fourth concerning Baptism; and the fifth concerning the Lord's Supper, the two N.T. Sacraments.

VII. But in order that faith may be kindled, confirmed, and preserved in the hearts of men by the Word of God and the Sacraments, as instruments instituted by God, it is necessary that they be established in use; the Word indeed through its preaching, but the Sacraments through their administration.
