Since this is a matter full of danger, and it may easily happen, whether through human ignorance or malice, that the Word of God is preached either poorly understood, or deliberately interpolated with false glosses, impurely; or, without applying due circumspection and prudence, is preached unseasonably for destruction rather than for edification, and the Sacraments are administered either not in conformity with divine institution, or not sufficiently circumspectly to the unworthy, God did not wish that the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments should be carried out by anyone at will in any corner, but He has always gathered and gathers for Himself a Church on earth, and has entrusted to it His Word and the Sacraments annexed to it, as instruments for kindling and confirming faith and procuring human salvation, with the power of designating and appointing public Teachers and Ministers, who may teach purely in public assemblies and preach the Word, and duly administer the Sacraments. Moreover, He has also committed to it the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, the power of remitting and retaining sins. Hence, furthermore, it comes to pass that we must treat of the Church and the Ecclesiastical Ministry: to which consideration the fifth Section may be destined, and its first Place will be concerning the Church, and its head, members, attributes, and marks; the second concerning the Ecclesiastical Ministry, and the calling of Ministers; the third concerning the power of the keys, granted to the Church, as the Mother of the faithful: to which may also be subjoined a fourth concerning Antichrist, who indeed sells himself as the Vicar of Christ and the visible Head of the Church, but in reality opposes himself against Christ and His Church; and a fifth concerning the persecutions which heresies and schisms, excited partly by Antichrist, partly by his precursors and the false Teachers addicted to him, have brought and do bring upon the Church. Furthermore, the members of the Church, or the faithful, according to a triple hierarchical state, can be distinguished into three orders: in the first are contained the Ministers of the Word and Sacraments; in the second, Magistrates and subjects; in the third, spouses, Parents and children, masters and servants: That is usually called the Ecclesiastical Order; this the Political, and the latter the economical. Moreover, each has its own individual duties or offices. And because the first is treated above in the second place of this section, a discussion must be instituted here concerning the two remaining, and to the five preceding Places must be subjoined: a sixth concerning the Magistrate and Subjects, and their duties or offices; a seventh concerning marriage; an eighth concerning parents and children; and a ninth concerning masters and servants.

IIX. Finally, for man, destined by the eternal decree of God to eternal life, redeemed through Christ, converted to God through the Word, baptized, inserted into the Church, and according to the measure of the state in which he has been constituted by God, pursuing the holiness of life, and thus already saved by hope, there remain to be expected Death, which is to him as a gate to the blessed life; the Resurrection from the dead, the final Judgment, the consummation or conflagration of the world, and life itself or eternal blessedness: which commonly come under the appellation of the Last Things, to be reserved for the sixth and last Section of this part; of which therefore the first There will be a Place concerning Death, as it is the way and gate to eternal life for the pious, but to eternal damnation for the impious, and concerning the worthy preparation of a Christian man for death; the second concerning the Resurrection of the dead, the third concerning the final Judgment and the conflagration of the world, the fourth concerning eternal Life, and the eternal damnation opposed to it. Although, however, life or eternal blessedness is treated in the last Place of the first part, yet those things which pertain to the perfect state of the blessed are not fully explained there, but only the essentials of blessedness. The rest, therefore, among which are also the remarkable gifts of the bodies which the blessed will enjoy, are deservedly deferred to this Place.

IX. In this series, thus delineated by a crude Minerva, it seems that the Theological Places can be arranged and explained, although when the treatment itself is reached, perhaps the order may be constituted a little differently elsewhere, and more or fewer Places may be established, as the matter may require.

Latin:

LI.

Pars tertia denique occupabitur in explicandis Locis de principiis & mediis consequendi finis, beatitudinis æternæ scilicet.

I. Hic repetendum, quod suprà etiam th. XIII. & XXI. monuimus, nempe mediis voce nos hîc nõ uti præcisè in eo stricto significatu, quo media dicuntur, ad quæ eligenda finis cognitus ita voluntatem movet, ut vicissim consequendi finis causæ propriè dictæ sint, sed in laxiori, prout medium dicitur, quicquid quoquo modo est propter finem, licet non ejus causa, sed nuda conditio, vel tantum causa sine qua non sit, vel saltem se habeat ut id quod removet impediens, vel cum fine connexum sit, & ejus adeptionem ordine præcedat. Tractantur enim in tertia Theologiæ parte, quæ est de principiis & mediis beatitudinis, multa, quæ ejus consequendæ causæ non sunt, sed aliam quandam habitudinem ad eam important. Unde ut Locorum, huc pertinentium, connexio, rerumque iis contentarum habitudo ad Theologiæ finem clariùs lectoris conspectui exhibeatur, partem hanc tertiam, pro diversa rerum substratarum habitudine, in plures partes vel sectiones subdividemus. II. Prima sectio continebit Locos, qui in explicandis causis & mediis beatitudinis nostræ, strictè dictis, occupantur. Inter causas autem beatitudinis nostræ prima est Deus, qui pro sua immensâ bonitate, gratiâ & misericordiâ noluit mortem peccatoris, eâque motus suo æterno decreto ad beatitudinem sive vitam æternam prædestinavit, quotquot finaliter in Christum credituros prævidit. Quia autem de Deo, cùm ratione essentiæ & perfectionum essentialium, tùm ratione personarum, in parte prima, Loco primo & secundo, agitur, heic agendum venit de Dei bonitate, gratiâ & misericordiâ, quâ vult omnes fieri salvos, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, I. Tim. II. 4. quæ est beatitudinis nostræ causa προηγουμένη, sive impulsiva interna, estque fons & scaturigo nostræ beatitudinis, omniumque ejus consequendæ causarum & mediorum. Locum à gratia Dei proximum sortitur Christus Mediator, ejusque meritum & satisfactio pro peccatis nostris, tanquam causa beatitudinis nostræ meritoria: tertium sortietur fides, Christum Mediatorem, ejusque meritum apprehendens, quæ beatitudinis nostræ causa est, non ratione sui, sed ratione meriti Christi apprehensi, adeoque causa minùs principalis. Et quia Deus, suâ gratiâ Christique merito, & nostrâ in Christum fide motus, ab æterno decrevit beatitudinem impertire omnibus, quos in Christum credituros, & in fide, Christi merito nixâ, ex hac vita decessuros prævidit, non præter rem decretum prædestinationis etiam in causis beatitudinis nostræ numeratur: cùm per illud Deus actu & formaliter causa beatitudinis nobis impertiendæ constituatur. quemadmodùm autem incredulitas, fidei in Christum opposita, causa est, cur beatitudine æternâ homines excidant, & æternam incurrant damnationem, ita Deus, pro sua rigida justitia, decrevit ab æterno, ex beatorum numero excludere, & damnationi æternæ adjudicare, quoscunque in Christum non credituros, sed in incredulitate morituros prævidit; & proinde, vi oppositionis, doctrina de decreto reprobationis arctè cohæret cum doctrina de decreto prædestinationis. Contraria enim, juxta se posita, magis elucescunt.

III. Loci ergo Sectionis primae erunt, primus de causa beatitudinis nostrae προηγουμένη sive impulsiva interna, bonitate scilicet, gratia & misericordia Dei erga prolapsos in peccatum homines, qua motus, illos salvos fieri voluit: secundus de causa ejusdem meritoria, sive impulsiva externa principali, Christo Mediatore scilicet, ejusque merito & satisfactione pro peccatis nostris; tertius de causa illius minus principali, nempe de fide, Christum Mediatorem ejusque meritum apprehendente; & quartus de ipso praedestinationis decreto, gratia Dei, Christique merito, & praevisa fide in Christum nixo, eique opposito decreto reprobationis.

IV. Fides in Christum autem non est humanarum virium opus, sed a Deo confertur, confirmatur & conservatur per Verbum & Sacramenta: quae proinde & ipsa beatitudinis nostrae causae sunt, sed remotae & mediatae, eaeque instrumentales, in quantum scilicet accendendae, confirmandae & conservandae in nobis fidei, quae ex parte nostri causa illius proxima est, organa & instrumenta sunt. Neque etiam fides ad beatitudinem nostram causae rationem habet, nisi in quantum Christum Mediatorem, ejusque meritum apprehendit, eoque apprehenso nos coram Deo justos constituit, sive justificat. Quamobrem deinceps etiam de causis fidei, & speciatim de Verbo Dei, ut organo ejus in adultis accendendae, (de Sacramentis agetur postea) de conversione hominis peccatoris, qua fides accenditur, deque ejusdem justificatione per fidem agendum erit. Et in his explicandis occupabitur Sectio Secunda, cujus locus primus erit de Verbo Dei, ut organo accendendae in adultis fidei; secundus de ipsa fidei in ejus corde productione per Verbum, sive de conversione hominis peccatoris; tertius de hominis ad Deum conversi justificatione coram Deo per fidem.

V. Fides in Christum, in corde hominis adulti, virtute Verbi, accensa, ubi apprehenso Christi merito hominem coram Deo justum constituit, eique remissionem peccatorum apud Deum impetravit, otiosa non est, sed exerit sese per opera charitatis ad ejus renovationem & sanctimoniam vitae. Unde porro de renovatione hominis, fide justificati, de bonis operibus illorumque principiis & norma, de virtutibus Christianis, & vitiis, illis oppositis, consideratio instituenda: in qua occupabitur Sectio tertia, eruntque ejus Loci, primus de renovatione hominis, fide justificati; secundus de bonis operibus, illorumque principiis & causis; tertius de lege, tanquam norma bonorum operum, ejusque distinctionibus; quartus de lege morali, deque operibus & virtutibus, in utraque ejus tabula præscriptis in specie, ut & de actibus malis ac vitiis, in ea prohibitis.

VI. In organis accendendæ, confirmandæ & conservandæ fidei, & hinc promanantis sanctimoniæ vitæ, locum & Sacramenta inveniunt, quæ alia olim fuêre in Ecclesia V. T. alia nunc sunt in Ecclesia N. T. Illa fuerunt Circumcisio & Agnus Paschalis; hæc Baptismus & Cœna Domini: quibus explicandis destinabitur Sectio quarta, ejusque locus primus erit de Sacramentis in genere, illorumque distinctione & differentia; secundus de Circumcisione; & tertius de Agno Paschali, duobus V. T. Sacramentis; quartus de Baptismo; & quintus de Cœna Domini, duobus N. T. Sacramentis.

VII. Ut autem Verbo Dei & Sacramentis, velut organis à Deo institutis, fides in hominum cordibus accendatur, confirmetur & conservetur, oportet ea in usu constitui; Verbum quidem per sui prædicationem, Sacramenta autem per sui administrationem. Quæ cùm periculi plena res sit, & facilè contingere possit, sive imperitiâ sive malitiâ humanâ, ut Verbum Dei vel malè intellectum, vel datâ operâ falsis glossis interpolatum, impurè; vel non adhibitâ debitâ circumspectione & prudentiâ intempestivè ad destructionem potiùs, quàm ad ædificationem prædicetur, & Sacramenta vel divinæ institutioni non conformiter, vel non satis circumspectè indignis administrentur, noluit Deus, ut à quolibet pro lubitu in quovis angulo prædicatio Verbi & Sacramentorum administratio peragatur, sed collegit colligitque sibi semper in terris Ecclesiam, eique Verbum suum & annexa illi Sacramenta, velut accendendæ & confirmandæ fidei procurandæque salutis humanæ organa, concredidit, cum potestate designandi & constituendi Doctores & Ministros publicos, qui in conventibus publicis & purè doceant ac prædicent Verbum, & ritè administrent Sacramenta. Quin & claves regni cœlorum, h. e. potestatem remittendi & retinendi peccata ei commifit. Hinc porrò etiam de Ecclesia ac Ministerio Ecclesiastico agendum venit : cui considerationi destinari potest Sectio quinta, eritque ejus Locus primus de Ecclesia, illiusque capite, membris, attributis ac notis; secundus de Ministerio Ecclesiastico, & Ministrorum vocatione; tertius de potestate clavium, Ecclesiæ, velut fidelium Matri, concessâ: quibus & subjungi possunt quartus de Antichristo, pro Christi Vicario quidem, & Ecclesiæ Capite visibili se venditante, reipsâ autem adversus Christum ejusque Ecclesiam se opponente; & quintus de persecutionibus, quas hærefes & schismata, ab Antichristo partim, partim ab ejus præcursoribus & addictis ei falsis Doctoribus excitata, Ecclesiæ intulerunt, & inferunt. Porrò Ecclesiæ membra sive fideles, pro triplici statu hierarchico, distingui possunt in tres ordines: primo continentur Ministri Verbi & Sacramentorum; secundo Magistratus & subditi; tertio conjuges, Parentes & liberi, heri & servi: Ille Ecclesiasticus Ordo specialiter; iste Politicus, & hic œconomicus vocari solet. Sunt autem singulorum sua singula munia sive officia. Et quia de primo superiùs in loco hujus sectionis secundo agitur, de duobus reliquis hîc instituenda venit tractatio, subjungendique erunt Locis præcedentibus quinque, sextus de Magistratu & Subditis, illorumque muniis sive officiis; septimus de conjugio, octavus de parentibus & liberis; & nonus de heris ac servis.

IIX. Denique homini, Dei æterno decreto ad vitam æternam destinato, per Christum redemto, per Verbum ad Deum converso, baptizato, Ecclesiæ inserto, & pro ratione status, in quem à Deo constitutus est, sanctimoniam vitæ sectanti, atque adeò jam spe salvo, expectanda restant Mors, quæ ipsi velut janua est ad vitam beatam; Resurrectio à mortuis, Judicium extremum, consummatio sive conflagratio mundi, & ipsa vita sive beatitudo æterna: quæ vulgo Novissimorum appellatione veniunt, Sectioni sextæ & ultimæ hujus partis reservanda; cujus proinde primus Locus erit de Morte, ut piis ad vitam æternam; impiis verò ad æternam damnationem via & janua est, deque hominis Christiani dignâ præparatione ad mortem; secundus de Resurrectione mortuorum, tertius de Judicio extremo & conflagratione mundi, quartus de Vita æterna, eique opposita damnatione æterna. Quanquam autem de vita sive beatitudine æterna in parte prima Loco ultimo agitur, non tamen plenè quæ ad perfectum beatorum statum pertinent, sed essentialia tantùm beatitudinis ibi explicantur. Cætera igitur, inter quæ & corporum insignes dotes sunt, quibus gaudebunt beati, meritò hunc ad Locum rejiciuntur.

IX. Hâc serie, ita rudi Minervâ delineatâ, videntur disponi & explicari posse Loci Theologici, etsi ad tractationem ipsam ubi perventum fuerit, alicubi forsan ordo paulò aliter, & Loci plures paucioresve, prout res tulerit, constitui poterunt.


## 4 Part II: On Holy Scripture, the First Principle of Revealed Theology

Just as in all other sciences, so also in Revealed Theology the formal object and the first principle of knowing, as regards the thing itself, coincide.

I. That they coincide, as regards the thing itself, is easily evident. For the formal object of any science is said to be that which is known in it primarily and of itself, and is the reason for knowing the rest which fall under its consideration. But that which is known in a science primarily and of itself, and is the reason for knowing the rest which are considered in it, is nothing other than its first principle of knowing. II. I say, however, notably: As regards the thing, they coincide. For that they differ in reason, and on account of diverse connotations are conceived by us in one way or another, we by no means deny. For the word object connotes a relation to the intellect, to which it is presented to be known, and it is called a formal object, because it is so presented to the intellect to be known, that it, being primarily known of itself, also behaves on the part of the intellect as a form or formal reason, directing it to the knowledge of other things, and determines the knowledge to which it directs it, by the mode of a form to a certain species. The word principle, however, connotes a relation to that which is principled, which, in the sciences indeed, are the conclusions which are inferred from it, and that is called the principle of knowing in any science from which, when known, the conclusion is inferred and known; but the first principle of knowing is called that from which, when it is primarily and of itself known, all conclusions which fall under the consideration of that science are ultimately inferred and known, so that in it, known of itself, the knowledge of the intellect rests, nor is it permitted for it to progress to another prior principle from which it itself might also be known. As regards the thing, however, that very thing which is presented to the intellect in some discipline as primarily to be known, and which, when known of itself, is also the reason for knowing other things which fall under its consideration, is also the first principle of knowing, and thus materially and as regards the thing they always coincide.

II.

That the formal object of Revealed Theology is the First Truth revealing, and that it includes in its concept two things: namely, the First Truth and its revelation, as two inadequate and partial formal objects of it; but which, taken together, constitute one adequate and complete formal object of the same, was stated in the previous chapter III, Thesis XXV. Which same thing holds also concerning its first principle of knowing.

I. For just as the intellect of man cannot be adequately moved to believe revealed doctrines through the First Truth alone known, as if through a formal objective reason, but it is necessary that he also have it known that they are revealed by the First Truth; so neither can theological conclusions concerning revealed things be deduced from the First Truth alone known, as if from a first principle, unless divine revelation, as the other part of the first principle of knowing, be called in as an aid, and two principles complex from this source: one from the former, the other from the latter; be formed in this manner: Whatever the primary Truth reveals is certainly and infallibly true; this, for example, that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, the primary Truth reveals. taken together, there follows finally the conclusion: Therefore, that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God is certainly and infallibly true. As therefore in other cases in a syllogism both premises, taken individually, constitute an inadequate and partial principle of knowing for the conclusion; but taken together they constitute an adequate and complete principle of knowing for the same, so in the present case the prior premise, derived precisely from the nature of the primary Truth, is an inadequate and partial principle of knowing for the conclusion; and the other, taken from the nature of divine revelation, is similarly an inadequate and partial principle of knowing for the same; but both, taken together, constitute one adequate and complete primary principle of knowing.

II. Some Scholastics indeed establish the formal object of Revealed Theology in the primary Truth alone; but they say that revelation, proceeding from it, is required for causing the assent to the conclusions only as a condition, not as a formal objective part; but wrongly, and with experience protesting. For just as this: Whatever the primary Truth reveals is certainly and infallibly true, by its own assent; so also this: That Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, the primary Truth reveals, similarly moves the intellect by its own assent into the assent of the conclusion, and just as without the assent of the former the intellect cannot be moved into the assent of the conclusion, so neither without the assent of the latter can it be moved into the assent of that. Therefore, each principle has in Revealed Theology the nature of a formal object: because each is such a thing that it is known in Theology primarily and of itself, and that which is known of itself is the reason for knowing the rest which are considered in it, which is the definition of a formal object. Neither, however, is an adequate formal object: because neither moves the intellect into the assent of the revealed thing without the assent of the other. Therefore, each, viewed separately, is an inadequate formal object. Therefore, taken together, they constitute one adequate formal object of Revealed Theology, and similarly one adequate and complete primary principle of knowing for it. Compare what we have also said on this matter in the preceding Chapter III, thesis XXV, Explanation no. IV. III. Others, although they acknowledge that the revelation of the First Truth is not a pure condition, on the part of the First Truth, required for causing the assent of theology and faith, nevertheless contend that it is not a part of the formal object, but only a tendency and application of the formal object to the material, or to the object to be believed, and that it behaves on the part of the formal object as the union of form with matter behaves on the part of the form. But just as in a composite the union of the form does not behave on the part of the form as a part of it, but as a mere tendency and application of it to the matter, so also divine revelation behaves on the part of the First Truth, not as a part of the formal object, but only as a tendency and application to the material object. Georgius de Rhodes feels this way among others, Disp. II. on Faith, qu. 1, Sect. III, §. III, fol. 546. But we deny that the revelation of the First Truth behaves on the part of the First Truth in the manner in which the union of the form behaves on the part of the form, namely as a mere tendency and application of the First Truth to the object to be believed: For the union of the form is not something distinct from the form, and just as nothing can be a part of itself, so neither can it be a part of the form. However, the revelation of the First Truth is something really distinct from the First Truth, and it enters into the formal concept of the formal object of theology in such a way that by it one responds no less aptly to the question concerning the cause and reason for assenting on account of which, than by the First Truth, nor does that, any less than this, move one through its own assent into the assent of the revealed thing. Whence, although this is applied through that in its own way to the material object, this application is nevertheless not a bare application, such as is the union of form with matter, but an application through an entity, really distinct from the applied form, namely the First Truth, and which completes the First Truth in the nature of an adequate formal object, as has been shown.

Latin:

QVemadmodum in aliis scientiis omnibus, ita & in Theologia Revelata objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum, quoad rem, coincidunt.

I. Quod, quoad rem, coincidant, facile patet. Objectum formale enim scientiæ cujusque dicitur, quod in ea primò & ex se cognoscitur, & ratio est cognoscendi cætera, quæ sub ejus considerationem cadunt. Quod autem in scientia primò & ex se cognoscitur, & ratio est cognoscendi cætera, quæ in ea considerantur, nihil est aliud, quàm ejus principium cognoscendi primum. II. Notanter autem dico: Quoad rem coincidunt. Quod enim ratione differant, & propter diversa connotata aliter atque aliter à nobis concipiantur, minimè inficiamur. Nam objecti vox connotat respectum ad intellectum, cui cognoscendum objicitur, & objectum formale dicitur, quòd ita intellectui objiciatur cognoscendum, ut ex se primò cognitum se habeat etiam ex parte intellectus ut forma sive ratio formalis, dirigens eum ad aliorum cognitionem, & cognitionem ad quam dirigit, per modum formæ ad certam speciem determinet. Principii vox autem connotat respectum ad principiatum, quod, in scientiis quidem, sunt conclusiones, quæ ex illo inferuntur, & dicitur in quavis scientia principium cognoscendi id, ex quo cognito infertur & cognoscitur conclusio; primum autem cognoscendi principium dicitur, ex quo primò & ex se cognito conclusiones omnes, quæ sub illius scientiæ considerationem cadunt, ultimò inferuntur & cognoscuntur, ita ut in eo, ex se cognito, cognitio intellectus sistat, nec ad aliud prius principium, ex quo & ipsum cognoscatur, progredi ei liceat. Quoad rem verò id ipsum, quod intellectui in disciplina aliqua primò cognoscendum objicitur, & ex se cognitum, etiam ratio est cognoscendi alia, quæ sub ejus considerationem cadunt, est etiam principium cognoscendi primum, atque adeò materialiter & quoad rem semper coincidunt.

II.

Objectum formale Theologiæ Revelatæ esse Veritatem primam revelantem, & includere in suo conceptu duo: Veritatem primam scilicet, ejusque revelationem, velut duo inadæquata & partialia objecta formalia illius; sed quæ junctim sumta ejusdem unum adæquatum & completum objectum formale constituant, dictum est in superiori cap. III. Th. XXV. Quod ipsum valet etiam de principio cognoscendi primo illius.

I. Quemadmodum enim intellectus hominis non potest adæquatè moveri ad credendas doctrinas revelatas per solam Veritatem primam cognitam, tanquam per rationem objectivam formalem, sed necesse est, ut etiam cognitum habeat, eas esse à Veritate prima revelatas; ita nec conclusiones Theologicæ de rebus revelatis ex sola veritate primâ cognitâ, velut ex principio primo deduci possunt, niti & revelatio divina, velut altera pars principii cognoscendi primi, in subsidium vocetur, & duo hinc principia complexa: unum ex illa, alterum ex hac; formentur, hunc in modum: Quicquid Veritas prima revelat, est certò & infallibiliter verum; hoc, v. g. Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum, Veritas prima revelat. Ex utraque autem, junctim sumta, sequitur demum conclusio: Ergo Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum certò & infallibiliter verum est. Sicut ergo aliàs in syllogismo utraque præmissa, sigillatim sumta, conclusionis principium cognoscendi inadæquatum & partiale; junctim verò sumtæ ejusdem principium cognoscendi adæquatum & completum constituunt, ita impræsentiarum prior præmissa, præcisè ex natura Veritatis primæ petita, conclusionis principium cognoscendi inadæquatum & partiale; & altera, ex natura revelationis divinæ desumta, ejusdem principium cognoscendi, similiter inadæquatum & partiale est; utraque verò, junctim sumta, constituit unum adæquatum & completum principium cognoscendi primum.

II. Nonnulli Scholastici quidem constituunt objectum formale Theologiæ Revelatæ in sola Veritate prima; revelationem verò, ab ea profectam, ad causandum conclusionum assensum requiri dicunt tantùm ut conditionem, non ut partem objectivam formalem; sed perperam, & reclamante experientia. Quemadmodum enim hæc: Quicquid Veritas prima revelat, est certò & infallibiliter verum, per sui assensum; ita & hæc: Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum, Veritas prima revelat, similiter per sui assensum intellectum in assensum conclusionis movet, & sicut absque assensu prioris intellectus in assensum conclusionis moveri non potest, ita nec absque assensu posterioris in illius assensum is moveri potest. Utrumque ergo principium habet in Theologia Revelata rationem objecti formalis: quia utrumque est tale quid, quod in Theologia primò & ex se cognoscitur, & quod ex se cognitum est ratio cognoscendi cætera, quæ in ea considerantur, quæ est definitio objecti formalis. Neutrum verò est objectum formale adæquatum: quia neutrum absque assensu alterius intellectum in assensum rei revelatæ movet. Ergo utrumque, seorsim spectatum, est objectum formale inadæquatum. Ergo junctim sumta unum adæquatum objectum formale Theologiæ Revelatæ, & similiter unum adæquatum & completum principium cognoscendi primum illius constituunt. Confer quæ etiam in præcedente Cap. III. th. XXV. Expl. n. IV. hanc in rem diximus. III. Alii licet agnofcant, revelationem Veritatis primæ non esse puram conditionem, ex parte Veritatis primæ, ad causandum assensum Theologiæ & fidei requisitam, contendunt tamen, eam non esse partem objecti formalis, sed tantùm tendentiam & applicationem objecti formalis ad materiale, sive ad objectum credendum, & habere se ex parte objecti formalis, ut in composito unio formæ cum materia, ex parte formæ, sese habet. Quemadmodùm autem in composito unio formæ ex parte formæ sese non habet ut pars illius, sed ut nuda tendentia & applicatio ejus ad materiam, ita & revelationem divinam habere sese ex parte primæ Veritatis, non ut partem objecti formalis, sed tantùm ut tendentiam & applicationem ad objectum materiale. Ita inter alios sentit Georgius de Rhodes Disp. II. de Fide qu. 1. Sect. III. §. III. fol. 546. Sed negamus, revelationem Veritatis primæ habere se ex parte veritatis primæ eum in modum, quo unio formæ, ex parte formæ sese habet, nempe ut nudam tendentiam & applicationem Veritatis primæ ad objectum credendum: Nam unio formæ non est aliquid distinctum à forma, & sicut nihil potest esse pars sui ipsius, ita nec ipsa potest esse pars formæ. Revelatio autem Veritatis primæ est aliquid realiter distinctum à veritate prima, & ingreditur ita conceptum formalem objecti formalis Theologiæ, ut per eam non minùs aptè respondeatur ad quæstionem de causâ & ratione assentiendi propter quam, quàm per veritatem primam, nec minùs illa, quàm hæc, per sui assensum movet in assensum rei revelatæ. Unde licet hæc per illam suo modo ad objectum materiale applicetur, non tamen applicatio hæc est applicatio nuda, qualis est unio formæ cum materia, sed applicatio per entitatem, à forma applicata, Veritate prima scilicet, realiter distinctam, & quæ Veritatem primam in ratione objecti formalis adæquati complet, uti ostensum.


### III. What the First Truth is does not require an elaborate explanation

III.

What the First Truth is does not require an elaborate explanation. For by its appellation is understood the Truth of God, not in being, nor in knowing, but in speaking or revealing, which we otherwise call the veracity of God, as has been shown above in c. III, th. XXV, where what we have taught concerning this matter may be seen.

IV.

It has been stated in the same place that the word revelation is not taken in this passage in that strict sense which the force of the word itself implies, namely for the mere manifestation of things hidden and as it were lying under a veil, but in a more general sense for the manifestation of any things whatsoever, even those which can be known by the guidance of the light of nature, brought about by God in a supernatural manner.

For although mysteries, hidden from the ages, constitute the most important part of the material object of revealed theology, and their disclosure by God is revelation strictly so called, it cannot nevertheless be denied that many things also, which can be known in their own way from the light of nature—such as the essence and attributes of God, and human actions, etc.—fall under the consideration of revealed theology and are considered under divine revelation as the objective formal and proper reason. Whence the thing itself demands that we take the word revelation here in the aforementioned more general sense for any divine and supernatural manifestation of things which fall under the consideration of theology, whether they can also be known from the light of nature or less so. Let those things be seen which we taught above in chapter III, theses XXV and XXVIII, regarding this matter.

V.

But just as the revelation of the First Truth was formerly various and manifold, and neither was revealed theology always in existence at every time with an equal degree of perfection, so the First Truth and every revelation of things to be believed and done proceeding from it can indeed be constituted as the formal object and primary principle of knowing of revealed theology, yet not every revelation at any given time, nor for theology at any given state of time, but each one is rightly constituted as the formal object and primary principle of knowing for that state of time in which it existed or exists, and for theology as it existed or exists.

I. The revelation of the First Truth can be considered either on the part of its material, namely on the part of the signs by which those things which it concerns our salvation to know are represented to the cognitive faculty; or on the side of its formal aspect, namely the sense and the things revealed. When we say that the revelation of the primary Truth was formerly various and manifold, we wish this to be understood chiefly concerning revelation viewed on the side of its material aspect. For signs, as we shall show later, and the many modes of revelations born from this, were formerly in use by God, according to that passage Heb. 1:1, πολυμερῶς κὲ πολυτρόπως, in many parts and in many ways, or, as Beza renders it, at many times and in many ways God formerly spoke to the Fathers by the Prophets.

II. On the side of the formal aspect, however, and of the things revealed, the revelation of the primary Truth, in substantial matters indeed, and those which concern the very foundation of salvation, has always been the same, and it began immediately after the fall in the protevangelium concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, revealed by God himself to our first parents. By reason of clarity, however, and more distinct knowledge, and also by reason of other parts of doctrine, circumstances, and ceremonies, divine revelation, even on the side of its formal aspect, took its increments with the progress of time. Concerning which matter we shall treat below in its proper place.

III. That not every revelation at every time constitutes the formal object and primary principle of knowing of Theology is easily evident. For in order that divine revelation may perform the function of a formal object, and move the intellect to assent to itself, and through this to assent to the things revealed, it is required both that it be given and that it be known to men. For that which does not exist, or has not become known to men, can move the intellect neither to assent to itself nor to the assent of other things. But not every revelation has existed at every time, or been known to mortals. Therefore, not every revelation has entered into the constitution of the formal object and primary principle of knowing in revealed Theology at every time.

Latin:

III.

QVid Veritas prima sit, operosâ explicatione non eget. Ejus enim appellatione intelligi Veritatem Dei, non in essendo, nec in cognoscendo sed in dicendo sive revelando, quam aliàs Dei veracitatem dicimus, ostensum est suprà c. III. th. XXV. ubi quæ hac de re docuimus, videantur.

IV.

REvelationis vocem etiam hoc loco non accipi eo stricto significatu, quem ipsa vocis vis importat, nempe pro sola rerum occultarum & sub velamine quasi latentium manifestatione, sed generaliori pro rerum quarumvis, etiam quæ luminis naturæ ductu cognosci possunt, manifestatione, à Deo modo supernaturali factâ, dictum est ibidem.

Quamvis enim mysteria, inde à seculis abscondita, potissimam partem objecti materialis Theologiæ revelatæ constituant, illarumque patefactio per Deum strictissimè sic dicta revelatio sit, negari tamen non potest, quin multa etiam, quæ ex lumine naturæ suo modo cognosci possunt: qualia sunt Dei essentia & attributa, & actiones humanæ &c. sub considerationem Theologiæ revelatæ cadant, & sub revelatione divina, tanquam ratione objectiva formali & propria, considerentur. Unde res ipsa postulat, ut revelationis vocem hîc in prædicto significatu generaliori accipiamus pro qualibet divina & supernaturali manifestatione rerum, quæ sub Theologiæ considerationem cadunt sive ex lumine naturæ etiam cognosci possint, sive minùs. Videantur, quæ supra c. III. th. XXV. & XXVIII. hanc in rem docuimus.

V.

QUemadmodùm autem Revelatio Veritatis primæ varia & multiplex olim fuit, neque omni tempore tota, vel etiam Theologia revelata semper æquali perfectionis gradu extitit, ita Veritas prima & profecta ab ea credendorum agendorumq; revelatio omnis constitui quidem potest Theologiæ Revelatæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum, non tamen quovis tempore omnis, neque Theologiæ pro quovis temporis statu, sed quælibet pro eo temporis statu, quo extitit, aut existit, & Theologiæ, prout extitit, aut existit, objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum rectè constituitur.

I. Revelatio Veritatis primæ potest considerari vel ex parte sui materialis, nempe ex parte signorum, quibus quæ nosse nostræ interest salutis, potentiæ cognoscendi repræsentantur; vel ex parte formalis sui, sensus scilicet rerumque revelatarum. Quando dicimus, revelationem Veritatis primæ fuisse olim variam & multiplicem, potissimùm id intellectum volumus de revelatione, ex parte materialis spectata. Signa enim, ut postea ostendemus, & hinc nati revelationum modi plures Deo olim in usu fuerunt, juxta illud Ebr. I, 1. πολυμερῶς κὲ πολυτρόπως multifariam, vel, ut Beza reduit, multis vicibus multisque modis Deus olim loquutus est Patribus in Prophetis.

II. Ex parte formalis autem & rerum revelatarum revelatio Veritatis primæ, in substantialibus quidem, & quæ ipsum salutis fundamentum concernunt, semper eadem fuit, cœpitque statim post lapsum in protevangelio de semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro, primis nostris parentibus à Deo ipso patefacto. Ratione clari, tatis autem & notitiæ distinctioris, itemque ratione aliarum doctrinæ partium, circumstantiarum, & ceremoniarum revelatio divina etiam ex parte sui formalis, temporis progressu, sua sumsit incrementa. Qua de re infra suo loco agetur.

III. Quòd autem non omnis revelatio omni tempore constituat Theologiæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum, facilè patet. Ut enim objecti formalis munus obeat revelatio divina, & intellectum in assensum sui, & hoc mediante in assensum rerum revelatarum moveat, requiritur, & ut detur, & ut hominibus nota sit. Quod enim non est, aut hominibus non innotuit, id nec in assensum sui, nec in aliorum assensum intellectum movere potest. Non autem omnis revelatio omni tempore extitit, aut nota fuit mortalibus. Ergo nec omnis revelatio omni tempore objecti formalis principiique cognoscendi primi constitutionem in Theologia revelata ingressa est.


### VI. There are commonly numbered, however, five species or modes of divine…

VI.

There are commonly numbered, however, five species or modes of divine revelations: namely, Discourse, Prophecy, רוח הקדש Holy Spirit (which revelation is also called illumination of the Holy Spirit, and by Paul in 2 Tim. 3:16, Θεοπνευστία, divine inspiration), אורים ותמים or Lights and Perfections, and בת קול Daughter of the voice.

VII.

OF these, the two latter modes of revelation, namely אורים and תמים Lights & Perfections, and בת קול daughter of the voice, do not pertain to this place.

I. For by neither did God reveal what was necessary for those about to attain salvation, whether to be believed or to be done (these, however, are what fall of themselves under the consideration of Theology), but by the one, when interrogated about civil causes through the high priest, clothed in the breastplate in which אורים and תמים were seen, He gave answers; by the other, if the Jews are to be believed, God began to use it in the second temple, after Prophecies had ceased and the canon of the Scriptures of the O.T. had been established, not for revealing the doctrine of faith and morals: for indeed, with the canon of Scripture already established, there was no need for a new revelation of it; but for testifying to His gracious presence, and for exciting in the hearts of the pious the hope of the Messiah long promised and soon to be sent.

II. The Jews think the latter was performed by an obscure voice, born from the repercussion of a voice fallen from heaven, and as it were its daughter, which for that reason they wish to be called בת קול daughter of the voice, concerning which, however, nothing exists in the sacred Scriptures, unless perhaps you wish to refer to this the voice heard from heaven once at the baptism of Christ, and again at his glorification on the mount, Matt. III, 17, c. XVII, 5, which whether it be rightly done or less so, let the judgment rest with others. Mention of the former mode of revelation, however, is made in Num. XXVII. 21, 1 Sam. XXVIII. 6, c. XXII. 9, although by what method the revelation was performed through אורים and תמים in the breastplate of the high priest is uncertain, concerning which almost as many opinions are circulated as there are interpreters.

VIII.

THE remaining three modes of revelation, namely discourse, Prophecy, and what is called by the Hebrews רוח הקדש, are of this place, and constitute the formal object of Theology, or certainly a certain part of it, each according to the state of that time in which it existed or exists.

IX.

DIscourse was performed by a sensible voice, from God (or an Angel, sent divinely), appearing in a conspicuous form, or through another sensible sign testifying to His presence, formed in the air beyond the order of nature. Thus under the Old Testament God appeared to the Patriarchs in the form of a man, and spoke with them with a sensible voice, Gen. 18:2, ch. 19:1 ff., ch. 22:14. To Moses He spoke from the burning bush, Exod. 3:2. To the Israelite people from a thick cloud and smoking fire, ch. 19:10 ff. With Moses He spoke otherwise familiarly, or, as Scripture says, mouth to mouth, as a friend speaks with a friend face to face and by word of mouth, Num. 12:6.

Latin:

VI.

Numerantur autem vulgò quinque revelationum divinarum sive species sive modi: Alloquium scilicet, Prophetia, רוח הקדש Spiritus sanctus (quæ revelatio etiam illuminatio Spiritus sancti, & à Paulo II. Tim. III, 16. Θεοπνευστία, divina inspiratio dicitur) אורים ותמים sive Luces & Perfectiones, & בת קול Filia vocis.

VII.

EX his duo postremi revelationum modi, אורים scilicet ותמים Luces & Perfectiones, & בת קול filia vocis, huc non spectant.

I. Neutro enim Deus, quæ salutem adepturis sive creditu sive factu necessaria erant, (hæc autem sunt, quæ per se sub Theologiæ considerationem cadunt) revelabat, sed altero ferè de causis civilibus interrogatus per Sacerdotem summum, pectorali, in quo אורים ותמים conspiciebantur, indutum responsa dabat; altero, si Judæis fides habenda, in templo secundo Deus, postquam Prophetiæ desierant, & Scripturæ V. T. canon constitutus erat, uti cœpit, non ad doctrinam fidei & morum revelandam: neque enim, canone Scripturæ jam constituto, novâ ejus revelatione opus erat; sed ad testandam suam gratiosam præsentiam, & ad spem promissi dudum & propediem mittendi Messiæ in piorum cordibus excitandam.

II. Posteriorem Judæi peractum putant voce obscurâ, ex repercussione vocis, cœlitùs delapsæ, natâ, ejusque quasi filiâ, quam propterea בת קול filiam vocis dictam volunt, de qua tamen in Scripturis sacris nihil extat, nisi forsan huc referre velis vocem semel in baptismo Christi, & iterum in ejus glorificatione in monte cœlitùs auditam, Matth. III, 17. c. XVII, 5. quod recténe fiat, an minùs? penes alios esto judicium. Prioris revelationis modi autem mentio fit Num. XXVII. 21. 1. Sam. XXVIII. 6. c. XXII. 9. quamvis quâ ratione per אורים ותמים in pectorali Sacerdotis summi peracta fuerit revelatio, incertum sit, de quo tot ferè sententiæ, quot interpretes sunt, circumferuntur.

VIII.

REliqui autem tres revelationum modi, alloquium scilicet, Prophetia, & qui Ebræis רוח הקדש dicitur, hujus loci sunt, & objectum formale Theologiæ, vel certè ejus quandam partem, quisque pro eo temporis statu, quo extitit aut existit, constituunt.

IX.

ALloquium peragebatur voce sensibili, à Deo (vel Angelo, divinitùs misso) in conspicua forma apparente, vel per aliud signum sensibile suam præsentiam testante, præter naturæ ordinem in aëre efformatâ. Ita sub V. T. Patriarchis Deus apparuit in forma hominis, & voce sensibili cum illis locutus est Gen. XIIX 2. c. XIX. 1. seqq. c. XXII. 14. Ad Mosen locutus est ex rubo ardente Exod. III, 2. Ad populum Israëlïticum ex nube densa & igne fumante, c. XIX. v. 10. seqq. Cum Mose alias locutus est familiariter, sive, ut Scriptura ait, ore ad os, ut amicus cum amico coram & oretenus loquitur, Num. XII, 6.


### X. Prophecy comprised two special modes of revelation, namely dream and vision,…

X.

Prophecy comprised two special modes of revelation, namely dream and vision, which the ancients included under the single name of Prophecy, because both were familiar to the Prophets and had a great agreement between them.

I. Both modes of revelation were performed by images of things presented by God to the Prophet's imagination, but in a dream the images of things were presented to the imagination of one sleeping or in sleep; in a vision, however, the same were presented to the imagination of one awake, but constituted in an ἐκςάσει, with the external operation of the senses ceasing.

II. A dream, therefore, was a revelation through images of the things to be revealed, or of other things which enigmatically signified that which was to be revealed, presented by God supernaturally to the imagination of the sleeper, without the concurrence of external objects and senses. A vision, however, was a revelation through the same images, but presented by God to the imagination of one awake, yet with the operation of the external senses ceasing, by which God manifested to the Prophet's intellect what He wished to be made known to him. Both God Himself included under Prophecy, the revelation familiar to the Prophets, when in Num. 12:6 He says, If there be a Prophet among you, I the Lord will appear to him in a vision, or will speak to him in a dream. Examples of revelation by dream exist in Gen. 29:12, ch. 31:10 ff., Dan. 2:1 ff. Of vision, however, in ἐκςάσει, Ezek. 1:4, ch. 37:1, Dan. 10:5 ff., Acts 10:10.

III. Where, however, a distinction must be made between a dream and a vision considered precisely in themselves, and between a Prophetic dream and vision. A bare dream and vision, especially that which occurred through images of things enigmatically signifying that which was to be revealed, did not have the nature of Prophecy and revelation by prophecy, unless another revelation might be added through illumination, by which the intellect was elevated to correctly knowing that very thing which was signified obscurely and enigmatically through the species of other things, which, if it were joined with a dream or vision, then at last they were Prophetic. Thus Dan. II. 1. and ch. V. 7. seqq. the dreams of Nebuchadnezzar, in one of which the four supreme empires of the world were enigmatically represented to him through the species of a statue of different parts, and in the other through the images of a great tree, reaching to heaven, but to be cut down, he himself and his future humiliation were enigmatically represented, were not Prophetic. For Nebuchadnezzar did not understand what was signified by the statue seen in the dream or by the tree seen: but a dream without the understanding of the things signified by the images exhibited therein was not Prophecy, not prophetic revelation, but a bare dream. But when the same statue was exhibited to Daniel, ch. II. v. 19. seqq., to be seen in a dream, and at the same time his intellect was illuminated so that he might know what was signified by the statue and its parts, then it was a Prophetic dream and a Prophetic revelation.

Latin:

X.

Prophetia duos speciales complectebatur revelationum modos, somnium scilicet & visionem, qvos uno Pophetiæ nomine veteres comprehenderunt, quòd uterque Prophetis familiaris esset, & magnam inter se convenientiam haberent.

I. Uterque revelationis modus peragebatur imaginibus Prophetæ phantasiæ à Deo objectis, sed in somnio imagines rerum objiciebantur phantasiæ dormientis sive in somno; in visione autem eædem objiciebantur phantasiæ vigilantıs, sed in ἐκςάσει constituti, cessante externâ sensuum operatione.

II. Somnium ergo erat revelatio per imagines rerum revelandarum, vel rerum aliarum, quæ id quod revelandum erat, ænigmaticè significabant, dormientis phantasiæ à Deo supernaturaliter, citra objectorum sensuumque externorum concursum, oblatas. Visio autem revelatio erat per imagines easdem, sed phantasiæ vigilantis, cessante tamen operatione sensuum externorum, à Deo objectas, quibus Prophetæ intellectui Deus, quæ ei nota fieri vellet, manifestabat. Utramque Deus ipse sub Prophetia, revelatione Prophetis familiari, comprehendit, quando Num. XII. 6. Si quis, inquit, inter vos fuerit Propheta, Ego Dominus in Visione apparebo ei, aut per somnium loquar ad illum. Exempla Revelationis per somnium extant Gen. XXIX. 12. c. XXXI 10. seq. Dan. II, 1. seqq. Visionis autem in ἐκςάσει Ezech. I 4 c. XXXVII. 1. Dan X. 5. seqq. Act. X. 10.

III. Ubi tamen distinguendum est inter somnium & visionem in se præcisè spectata, & inter somnium & visionem Propheticam. Somnium & visio nuda, præsertim quæ fiebat per imagines rerum, ænigmaticè id quod revelandum erat, significantium, non habebant rationem Prophetiæ & revelationis per prophetiam, nisi alia accederet revelatio per illuminationem, quâ ad illud ipsum, quod obscurè & ænigmaticè per species rerum aliarum significabatur, rectè cognoscendum intellectus elevabatur, quæ si cum somnio aut visione conjungebatur, tum Prophetica demum erant. Sic Dan. II. 1. & c.V.7. seqq. somnia Nebucadnezaris, quorum uno ei per species statuæ diversarum partium quatuor summa orbis imperia, altero per imagines arboris magnæ, ad cælum pertingentis, sed succidendæ, ipsemet & futura ejus humiliatio ænigmaticè repræsentabatur, Prophetica non erant. Non enim, quid per statuam in somno visam aut per arborem visam significaretur, Nebucadnezar intelligebat: somnium verò absque intelligentia rerum, per imagines, eo exhibitas, significatarum, non erat Prophetia, non revelatio prophetica, sed somnium nudum. Quando autem eadem statua Danieli c. II. v. 19. seqq. in somno conspicienda exhibebatur, & simul ejus intellectus illuminabatur, ut quid per statuam ejusque partes significaretur, cognosceret, tum somnium Propheticum, & revelatio Prophetica erat.


### XI. That which was called by the Hebrews רוח הקדש Holy Spirit, was a revelation…

XI.

That which was called by the Hebrews רוח הקדש Holy Spirit, was a revelation nobler, clearer, and more perfect than prophecy: by which, namely, the Holy Spirit manifested to holy men what He wished to be made known to them through species supernaturally infused into the intellect, or if those had pre-existed in the intellect, supernaturally excited, elevated, and applied to eliciting the knowledge of supernatural things, with the operation of the senses safe and unimpeded.

I. It is called by the Hebrews רוח הקדש Holy Spirit, by a metonymical expression, as it seems, by which the name of the cause is transferred to signify the effect, and by the effect, common to the three persons of the divinity, appropriated to the Holy Spirit, so that רוח הקדש Holy Spirit here is the same as revelation through species impressed, supernaturally infused into the intellect of man by the Holy Spirit, while the operation of the senses remains, or, if those had pre-existed, supernaturally excited and applied to eliciting the knowledge of those things which God wished to be made known to him, proceeding immediately from the Holy Spirit.

II. But because the impressed species, on the part of the intellect, behave by way of light, and are a certain kind of rays, by which things, wrapped in material phantasms, and intelligible in potentiality, are as it were illuminated, and are constituted in intelligible being in act, just as color, wrapped in darkness and visible in potentiality, is illuminated by solar rays, and is constituted in visible being in act; it follows from this that this revelation through impressed species is also called revelation through illumination, and illumination of the mind. For impressed species are a certain light, so called by metaphor, and that a mental one.

III. The Apostle Paul in 2 Timothy 3:16 calls it θεοπνευσίαν or divine inspiration, when he calls πᾶσαν γραφὴν, every or the whole Scripture, θεόπνευστον, divinely inspired, likewise by a metaphorical expression. For just as in human affairs, he who whispers secretly and into the ear of another what he wishes to make known to him is said to inspire them into him: so God, when He suggests to a man inwardly and secretly the concepts of things which He wishes to make known to him, through infused species, or through species excited and applied to elicit the concepts of things in his intellect, is said to inspire the concepts of the things to be manifested to the same man. For God does not inspire the species of things into a man by blowing into his ears, as is accustomed to be done by men, but He infuses them into the intellect immediately, or if they have pre-existed, He excites and applies them immediately to elicit in him the concepts of things: which infusion of species and elevation and application to elicit the concepts of things, as it is analogous to the inspiration by which a man whispers into the ear of another man what he wishes to reveal to him, so it is a certain inspiration so called by way of similarity. In which manner, when God suggested to all the sacred writers the concepts both of the things and of the words to be written, the whole Scripture is called by the Apostle Paul θεόπνευστος or inspired by God.

IV. The Scriptures also call the same revelation the speech of God, internal, that is, by which He spoke inwardly to the mind of holy men. Thus David in 2 Samuel 23:2 says: The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me, and His word was by my tongue, to wit, and in Hebrews 1:1 God is said to have spoken to the Fathers in the Prophets; and in Luke 1:70 through the mouth of the holy Prophets, who have been from of old. In which places a twofold speech of God is insinuated: one to the holy men, the other to the Fathers and other believers. For just as he who speaks to others through an intermediary first speaks to the intermediary, and suggests to him what he ought to speak to others, so also when God is said to have spoken through David, in the Prophets, and through the mouth of the holy Prophets, it is first signified that he spoke to David and the Prophets, by suggesting to them the concepts of things and words, which they were to bring forth to others by external speech. The former internal speech of God was, and was performed just as divine inspiration, by concepts excited through species infused or indeed pre-existing, but supernaturally awakened to others was suggested inwardly to their intellect. The latter was external and sensible, by which holy men brought forth to others by sensible voice what God suggested to them to be brought forth through internal speech or through inspired concepts, or, which amounts to the same thing, by which God, using their own tongue, brought forth to others by sensible voice what He suggested to holy men by internal speech.

V. One and therefore the same revelation, performed through species of things supernaturally infused, or pre-existing ones supernaturally awakened, is and is called both illumination, and θεοπνευστία or divine inspiration, and speech of God (internal), yet conceived in one way or another: namely, in so far as the species infused or supernaturally awakened and applied to elicit the concepts of things behave as certain rays, diffused from God, who is light, to illuminate the intellect, in so far the concepts, elicited by their aid, are and are called a certain illumination of the mind: but in so far as through the same the concepts of things are suggested inwardly to the intellect secretly, and by an action analogous to inspiration, in so far this revelation obtains the denomination of θεοπνευστία or divine inspiration: in so far, finally, as God manifests the senses of His mind to man by concepts supernaturally awakened and suggested through the same species, in so far to speak inwardly to man, and the manifestation of things which He wishes to be made known to him through those concepts, is denominated the internal speech of God.

Latin:

XI.

QVæ Ebræis dicebatur רוח הקדש Spiritus sanctus, prophetiâ nobilior, clarior & perfectior revelatio erat: quâ scilicet Spiritus sanctus per species, intellectui supernaturaliter infusas, vel si in intellectu illæ præextiterint, supernaturaliter excitatas, elevatas, & ad eliciendam cognitionem rerum supernaturalem applicatas, Viris sanctis, quæ illis nota fieri vellet, manifestabat, sensuum operatione salvâ & non impeditâ.

I. Dicitur Ebræis רוח הקדש Spiritus sanctus, locutione, ut videtur, metonymicâ, quâ nomen causæ transfertur ad significandum effectum, & effectu, tribus divinitatis personis communi, Spiritui sancto appropriato, ut רוח הקדש Spiritus sanctus hîc idem sit, quod revelatio per species impressas, à Spiritu sancto hominis intellectui, manente sensuum operatione, supernaturaliter infusas, aut, si illæ præextitissent, supernaturaliter excitatas & applicatas ad eliciendam cognitionem illorum, quæ Deus ipsi nota fieri vellet, immediatè à Spiritu sancto profecta.

II. Quia autem species impressæ, ex parte intellectus, sese habent per modum luminis, & sunt quidam quasi radii, quibus res, phantasmatibus materialibus involutæ, & potentiâ intelligibiles, quasi collustrantur, & actu in esse intelligibili constituuntur, sicut color, tenebris involutus & potentia visibilis, radiis solaribus collustratur, & actu in esse visibili constituitur; fit inde, ut revelatio haec per species impressas dicatur etiam revelatio per illuminationem, & illuminatio mentis. Sunt enim species impressae lumen quoddam, per metaphoram sic dictum, idque mentale.

III. Paulus Apostolus II. Tim. III. 16. vocat eam θεοπνευσίαν sive inspirationem divinam, quando πᾶσαν γραφὴν, omnem sive totam Scripturam θεόπνευστον divinitus inspiratam dicit, locutione itidem metaphorica. Quemadmodum enim in humanis, qui alteri secretò & in aurem insusurrat, quae ei nota facere vult, ea inspirare ipsi dicitur: ita Deus, cùm homini intùs & secretò suggerit conceptus rerum, quas ei notas facere vult, per species infusas, aut ad eliciendos in ejus intellectu conceptus rerum excitatas & applicatas, inspirare dicitur eidem rerum conceptus manifestandarum. Non enim Deus halitu in aures immisso inspirat homini species rerum, ut ab hominibus fieri solet, sed infundit eas intellectui immediatè, vel si praeextiterint, excitat & applicat eas immediatè ad eliciendos in eo conceptus rerum: quae specierum infusio & ad eliciendos rerum conceptus elevatio applicatioque, ut analoga est inspirationi, qua in aurem homo homini insusurrat, quae ei revelare vult, ita quaedam per similitudinem sic dicta inspiratio est. Quem in modum cùm Deus Scriptoribus sacris omnibus cùm rerum tum vocum scribendarum conceptus suggesserit, Paulo Apostolo Scritura tota dicitur θεόπνευστος sive à Deo inspirata.

IV. Eandem revelationem appellant Scripturae etiam locutionem Dei, internam puta, qua intùs ad animum virorum sanctorum loquutus est. Ita David II. Sam. XXIII. 2. dicit: Spiritus Domini locutus est in me, & sermo ejus per linguam meam, scil. factus est, & Ebr. I. 1. Deus dicitur locutus Patribus in Prophetis; & Luc. I. 70. per os sanctorum, qui à seculo fuerunt, Prophetarum. Quibus in locis duplex insinuatur locutio Dei: Una ad Viros sanctos, altera ad Patres & fideles alios. Sicut enim qui aliis loquitur per internuncium, primò ad internuncium loquitur, eique, quae ad alios loqui debeat, suggerit, ita & Deus cùm per Davidem, in Prophetis, & per os sanctorum Prophetarum loqvutus dicitur, primò fignificatur loquutus esse ad Davidem & Prophetas, suggerendo eis conceptus rerum & vocum, quas locutione externâ ad alios proferre debebant. Prior Dei locutio interna erat, & peragebatur perinde, ut divina inspiratio, conceptibus, per species infusas aut per præexistentes quidem, sed supernaturaliter excitatas & ad eos eliciendos applicatas, excitatis, quibus quæ ad alios loqui deberent, interiùs illorum intellectui suggerebatur. Posterior externa & sensibilis erat, quâ Viri sancti, quæ per locutionem internam sive per conceptus inspiratos Deus ipfis proferenda suggerebat, voce sensibili ad alios proferebant, sive, quod eodem redit, quâ Deus, quæ Viris sanctis locutione internâ suggerebat, ipsorum linguâ usus, voce sensibili ad alios proferebat.

V. Una igitur eademque revelatio, per species rerum supernaturaliter infusas, aut præexistentes supernaturaliter excitatas peracta, & illuminatio, & θεοπνευστία sive divina inspiratio, & locutio Dei (interna) est & dicitur, aliter tamen atque aliter concepta: nempe in quantum species infusæ aut supernaturaliter excitatæ & ad eliciendos rerum conceptus applicatæ se habent ut radii quidam, à Deo, qui lumen est, ad collustrandum intellectum diffusi, in tantum conceptus, illarum adminiculo eliciti, sunt & dicuntur illuminatio quædam mentis: in quantum verò per easdem conceptus rerum intùs intellectui secretò, & actione inspirationi analogâ, suggeruntur, in tantùm θεοπνευστίας sive divinæ inspirationis denominationem revelatio hæc sortitur: in quantum denique Deus conceptibus, per easdem species supernaturaliter excitatis & suggestis, sensa animi homini manifestat, in tantum intus ad hominem loqui, & manifestatio rerum, quas ei notas fieri vult, per illos conceptus, locutio Dei interna denominatur.


### XII. REvelations, formerly performed by the aforesaid signs and diverse modes,…

XII.

REvelations, formerly performed by the aforesaid signs and diverse modes, indeed befell from God to very few men, though conspicuous for faith and holiness of life, yet not for their own good only, but for the good of all: which therefore it was necessary to be carried over also to the knowledge of others.

XIII.

BUT they were carried over from them to the knowledge of others by voice partly by writing, with the Holy Spirit inspiring and suggesting by inspiration what was to be either spoken or committed to letters.

I. By voice and by preaching alone they were conveyed by them to others, in the beginning indeed, from the first man to the flood, and from the flood even to Moses. For no Scripture is given more ancient than Moses. But from Moses, who first began to commit to letters the revelations which had come to him divinely, until Malachi, the last of the Prophets, and the time of the Apostles, in which the Scripture of the N.T. was committed to writing, they were conveyed to others both by voice and by writings, and indeed in both ways. For the Prophets and Apostles, besides the fact that they preached in the public assemblies of the Church what was revealed to them by God, also committed to letters the revelations received from God, as the Scriptures composed by them still testify.

II. Moreover, they preached and committed to letters the revelations imparted to them divinely, not by their own judgment and effort, but by the Holy Spirit inspiring and suggesting what was to be proposed either by voice and by preaching, or committed to letters, so that lapses of memory could not be committed by them while preaching or writing, and error could not underlie their words or writings. To which Peter refers in II Epist. c. 1. 21, saying, Not by the will of man was prophecy brought at any time, but Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε, moved by the Holy Spirit (suggesting and inspiring within), the holy men of God spoke; and David, when in II Sam. XXIII. 2, he says, The Spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word by my tongue. To these agree Zacharias, the parent of the Baptist, and the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, of whom the former in Luke 1. 70 expressly testifies that God spoke by the mouth of his holy Prophets, who have been from of old; but the latter, at the beginning of the Epistle, says that God spoke of old to the Fathers in the Prophets πολυμερῶς κ πολυτρόπως, in many parts and in many ways. The same reason applies to writing, as testified by the Apostle of the Gentiles, who is above all exception, who in II Tim. III. 16 asserts that πᾶσαν γραφὴν, every or the whole Scripture, is θεόπνευστον or divinely inspired.

Latin:

XII.

REvelationes, prædictis signis modisque diversis olim peractæ, obtigerunt quidem â Deo paucis admodum, licet fide & sanctimoniâ vitæ conspicuis Viris, non tamen ipsorum tantùm, sed omnium bono: quas proinde ad aliorum etiam notitiam deferri oportuit.

XIII.

DElatæ autem sunt ab illis ad aliorum notitiam voce partim, partim scriptis, Spiritu sancto, quæ sive dicenda sive literis consignanda essent, inspirante & per inspirationem suggerente.

I. Voce & per prædicationem tantùm ab ipsis delatæ sunt ad alios, initio quidem, à primo homine ad diluvium, & à diluvio ad Mosen usque. Mose enim Scriptura nulla antiquior datur. A Mose autem, qui primus revelationes, quæ sibi divinitùs obtigerant, in literas referre cœpit, usque ad Malachiam, Prophetarum ultimum, & Apostolorum tempore, quo Scriptura N. T. consignata est, cùm voce tum Scriptis, atque adeò modo utroque ad alios delatæ sunt. Prophetæ enim & Apostoli, præterquam quòd in publicis Ecclesiæ conventibus, quæ à Deo sibi revelabantur, prædicabant, referebant etiam acceptas à Deo revelationes in literas, ut concinnatæ ab ipsis Scripturæ etiamnum testantur.

II. Prædicabant autem consignabantque literis revelationes, divinitùs sibi impertitas, non suo arbitratu & studio, sed Spiritu sancto inspirante, & quæ vel voce & per prædicationem proponenda, vel literis consignanda essent, suggerente, ne memoriæ lapsus inter prædicandum aut scribendum ab ipsis committi, & error illorum dictis aut scriptis subesse posset. Quò respicit Petrus II. Epist. c. 1. 21. Non, inquiens, voluntate hominis allata est olim Prophetia, sed Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε acti à Spiritu sancto (intùs suggerente & inspirante) locuti sunt sancti Dei homines; & David, cùm II. Sam. XXIII. 2. Spiritus Domini, ait, locutus est per me, & sermo ejus per linguam meam. Quibus accinunt Zacharias, Baptistæ parens, & Auctor Epistolæ ad Ebræos, quorum ille Luc. 1. 70. disertè testatur, Deum locutum esse per os sanctorum, qui à seculo fuerunt, Prophetarum suorum; hic verò sub initium Epistolæ dicit, Deum locutum esse olim Patribus in Prophetis πολυμερῶς κ πολυτρόπως, multis vicibus, multisque modis. Eadem ratio & scriptionis est, teste omni exceptione majore Gentium Apostolo, qui II. Tim. III. 16. πᾶσαν γραφὴν, omnem sive totam Scripturam θεόπνευστον sive divinitùs inspiratam esse asseverat.


### XIV. But it did not seem good to God to impart new revelations to the Church until…

XIV.

But it did not seem good to God to impart new revelations to the Church until the end of the world or immediately to illumine and instruct holy men, who would propagate ancient revelations to others, by voice and by writings, but after the canon of Scripture was established, new revelations ceased, but the ancient ones, with the Holy Spirit inspiring, were committed to writing, and were and are committed to learned men to be proposed and declared to others in public assemblies, who have acquired a fuller knowledge of them by their own study and labor. Moreover, while the θεοπνεύστοις (God-inspired) men were still living, men were moved to the public office of teaching who had both learned by human study and would teach the revelations promulgated by divine inspiration by voice and writings: such as in the Church of the O.T. were the Priests; but in the Church of the N.T. were the Pastors and Teachers, whom Paul mentions in 1 Cor. XII. 28. seq. Eph. IV. 11.

I. Between this twofold manner of propagating divine revelations to others, the one by inspiration, the other by knowledge acquired by human study, there intervenes much difference. For first, the propagation which was performed by the former mode was supernatural. For God, as has been said, suggested to holy men what ought to be promulgated by voice or writings, immediately by Himself, and in a manner plainly supernatural, they at least lending their tongue for preaching, and their hand and pen for writing. Wherefore God Himself is said to have spoken in them and through them; and the whole Scripture is said to be θεόπνευστος, divinely inspired, as has just been shown. But that which is performed by the latter mode is natural. For it is natural for the intellect of man to acquire for itself by study and meditation a knowledge of things divinely revealed, perceived from their preaching by hearing, or read from the Scripture in which they exist recorded, and to hand the same on to others also by voice or writing: although, in order that one may embrace them with a saving assent, and that firm and immovable, it is necessary that the intellect be illuminated and the will drawn by the grace of God, as is taught elsewhere. Which saving assent, however, is not precisely required for this, that one should propose revealed things to another by voice or writing. And from this emerges another notable difference, that the former mode of proposing is absolutely certain, to which it is entirely repugnant that falsehood should underlie it. For just as the First Truth in teaching can neither be deceived nor deceive, so neither can the holy men, who With the primary truth, or God, suggesting, inspiring, and as it were dictating within, they spoke or wrote, they could have been deceived or have deceived. For fallibility is from the intellect, which is liable to error, and which can conceive a thing otherwise than it is and propose it to others by voice or writing. But those things which were proposed by holy men by voice or writing with God inspiring, their concepts were suggested to them by God, who knows not how to be deceived or to deceive, and directing their tongue and pen immediately, so that they could not propose them by voice or writings otherwise than as the thing was. The latter, however, is not immune from the danger of falsehood. For a man, learning by his own study the revelations once made to holy men, and then teaching them to others, can err both in learning and in teaching. From which flows thirdly this distinction also, that those revelations which once befell holy men divinely do not obtain the status of formal object and first principle of knowing in Theology, except in so far as they were proposed by voice or writing with God inspiring, and were made public property. For those things which are drawn by human study, from the preaching of others or from Scripture itself, and are proposed to others, do not have certainty, except in so far as they are conformable to the revelations promulgated by θεοπνεύστοις (God-inspired) men by voice or writing, and are a derived thing and the material object of Theology, not the first principle and formal object.

Latin:

XIV.

Non autem visum est Deo ad finem usque mundi Ecclesiæ novas impertire revelationes aut immediatè illuminare & instruere Viros sanctos, qui revelationes antiqvas ad alios, voce & scriptis, propagarent, sed post constitutum Scripturæ canonem revelationes novæ defierunt, antiqvæ verò, Spiritu Sancto inspirante in literas relatæ, aliis in conventibus publicis proponendæ & declarandæ commissæ sunt committunturqve Viris doctis, qvi illarum notitiam pleniorem suo studio & labore sibi comparaverunt. Qvin & viventibus adhuc Viris θεοπνεύστοις admoti sunt publico docendi muneri Viri, qvi revelationes, ex divina inspiratione voce & scriptis promulgatas, studio humano & didicissent, & docerent: qvales in Ecclesia V. T. erant Sacerdotes; in Ecclesia N. T. autem Pastores & Doctores, qvorum Paulus 1. Cor. XII. 28. seq. Eph. IV. 11. meminit.

I. Inter duplicem hunc divinas revelationes ad alios propagandi modum, alterum per inspirationem; alterum per notitiam, studio humano acqvisitam, multum intercedit discriminis. Primùm enim quæ modo priori peragebatur propagatio, supernaturalis erat. Deus enim, uti dictum, suggerebat Viris sanctis, quæ voce aut scriptis promulgari debebant, per se immediatè, modoque planè supernaturali, ipsis saltem linguam ad prædicandum; & manum calamumque ad scribendum commodantibus. Quamobrem Deus ipse in illis & per illos loquutus esse; & Scriptura tota θεόπνευστος, divinitùs inspirata, dicitur, ut modò ostensum. Quæ autem modo posteriori peragitur, naturalis est. Naturale enim est intellectui hominis, ut studio & meditatione sibi comparet notitiam rerum, divinitùs revelatarum, ex illarum prædicatione, auditu perceptâ, vel ex Scriptura, quâ consignatæ extant, lectâ, eandemque aliis quoque voce vel scriptis tradat: licet ut assensu salutari, eoque firmo & immoto illas amplectatur, gratiâ Dei supernaturali intellectum illuminari, voluntatemque trahi oporteat, ut alibi docetur. Qui salutaris assensus tamen ad hoc, ut quis voce aut scripto res revelatas alteri proponat, præcisè non requiritur. Atque ex hoc emergit alterum notabile discrimen, quòd modus proponendi prior simpliciter certus est, cui falsum subesse prorsus repugnat. Quemadmodum enim Veritas prima in docendo nec falli nec fallere potest, ita nec Viri sancti, qui Veritate prima sive Deo intus suggerente, inspirante & quasi dictante, loquuti sunt aut scripserunt, falli aut fallere potuerunt. Fallibilitas enim est ab intellectu, errori obnoxio, & qui rem aliter, quam est, concipere & voce scriptove aliis proponere potest. Sed quæ Deo inspirante à Viris sanctis voce aut scripto proponebantur, illorum conceptus suggerebantur ipsis à Deo, falli ac fallere nescio, illorumque linguam & calamum dirigente, immediatè, ut non aliter, quàm res haberet, ea voce scriptisve proponere possent. Posterior autem à falsitatis periculo immunis non est. Homo enim, studio suo addiscens revelationes, Viris sanctis olim factas, easque deinde alios docens, errare potest cùm in discendo, tùm in docendo. Ex quo fluit tertiò hoc etiam discrimen, quòd quæ Viris sanctis olim divinitùs obtigerunt revelationes, in Theologia objecti formalis & principii cognoscendi primi rationem non obtineant, nisi in quantum Deo inspirante, voce aut scripto propositæ, & publici juris factæ sunt. Quæ enim studio humano, ex aliorum prædicatione aut ex ipsa Scriptura hauriuntur, aliisque proponuntur, certitudinem non habent, nisi in quantum conformes sunt revelationibus, à Viris θεοπνεύστοις voce aut scripto promulgatis, suntq; principiatum quid & objectum materiale Theologiæ, non principium primum & objectum formale.


### XV. Divine revelation, promulgated by voice through holy men with God inspiring,…

XV.

Divine revelation, promulgated by voice through holy men with God inspiring, can be reduced to revelation by address; and the same, as well as that which was promulgated by writing, can be reduced to revelation by illumination, and is a certain mediate illumination of the intellect.

I. It can be reduced to revelation by address: because those things which holy men, with God inspiring, once spoke to other men, God himself spoke to them, using their tongue and voice. Thus the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 1. 1., writes expressly that God once spoke to the Fathers through the Prophets, which things the Prophets, with God inspiring, spoke to them. But the speech of God, by which he suggested to holy men inwardly, and afterwards manifested through their voice to the Fathers what it concerns their and all our salvation to know, what else was it than a certain revelation by address?

II. Revelation, therefore, by address can be established as threefold. One is internal, through concepts immediately inspired in holy men, by which God manifested what He wished to be made known to them; which, as we saw above, is also called θεοπνευσία. The second is external, by which, appearing in a visible form or testifying to His presence by another sensible sign, He spoke to the Patriarchs, to Moses, and to others through a voice formed in the air, which can be called the external immediate address of God, and is that very one concerning which we treated above in thesis VIII. The third is also external, but mediate, by which, namely, He promulgated to others through the same men, by a sensible voice formed and uttered in their language and mouth, those things which He had revealed to holy men by internal address; which is a certain address of God through men and to men, and thus revelation by mediate address.

III. But that which was promulgated to others by God's inspiration, both by voice and by writing, can be reduced to revelation by illumination: because it reveals or manifests to us those things which it concerns our salvation to know, through the species of things which sensible words, signifying by institution, transmit to the intellect—elevated by the grace of God—both in preaching through hearing and in the reading of Scripture through sight; these are like rays diffused from God, the Father of lights, and His Word into the intellect, by which both the intellect and the things themselves, presented to the intellect through words, are illuminated: the latter indeed so that their truth may appear to the intellect; the former, so that the intellect may see or know the same. Wherefore the Word of God, whether proposed by voice or comprised in writing, is called a lamp and a light, Ps. CXIX. 105, Prov. VI. 23, II. Petr. I. 19, and it is attributed to it that it illuminates the eyes, namely of the mind, metaphorically so called, that is, the mind, Psal. XIX. 9; and the intellect, illuminated by the Word of God, so that it may know the future goods prepared for us, is described by metaphor through the eyes of the mind illuminated to know what is the hope to which He (God) has called, and how opulent the glory of His inheritance in the saints, etc., Ephes. I. 18.

IV. This revelation by preaching and Scripture differs from revelation by θεοπνευσία in that, although both are a certain illumination of the mind, the latter is nevertheless immediate, while the former is mediate illumination. For θεοπνευσία is a certain illumination of the intellect through species immediately infused by God, or, if they pre-existed in the intellect, immediately excited by God, and for the purpose of kindling the knowledge of revealed things, applied as a certain illumination of the mind. Revelation, however, through preaching or Scripture is a certain illumination of the intellect through species, excited in a natural way by the voice of the preacher, or acquired by human study through the reading of Scripture, and just as those who listen to preaching or devote themselves to the reading of Scripture can err in attaining the sense of the doctrine preached or the Scripture read, so this revelation placed in mediated illumination is not, on the part of him to whom it occurs, infallible in the same way as the other, which consists in immediate illumination, not because falsehood can underlie either on the part of preaching (if it is performed with God inspiring it) or on the part of the God-breathed Scripture: for that this cannot happen has been shown above at length; but because the hearers of preachers and the readers of Scripture can be deceived in attaining the doctrine preached or read.

Latin:

XV.

REvelatio divina, per Viros sanctos, Deo inspirante, voce promulgata, ad revelationem per alloquium; & eadem, ut & quæ scripto promulgata est, ad revelationem per illuminationem reduci potest, estque quædam intellectus illuminatio mediata.
