I. Ad revelationem per alloquium reduci potest: quia quæ Viri sancti, Deo inspirante, olim ad homines alios loquuti sunt, ea Deus ipse ad illos loquutus est, ipsorum linguâ & voce usus. Ita Auctor Epistolæ ad Ebræos c. 1. 1. scribit expressè, Deum olim loquutum esse Patribus per Prophetas, quæ Prophetæ, Deo inspirante, illis loquuti sunt. Locutio Dei autem, quâ viris sanctis interiùs suggessit, & illorum voce Patribus postea manifestavit, quæ nosse ipsorum & omnium nostrûm salutis interest, quid aliud fuit, quam revelatio quædam per allocutionem?

II. Revelatio igitur per allocutionem triplex constitui potest. Una interna, per conceptus Viris sanctis immediatè inspiratos, quibus Deus, quæ ipsis nota fieri vellet, manifestabat; quæ, ut suprà vidimus, etiam θεοπνευσία dicitur. Altera externa, quâ in conspicua forma apparens, vel alio sensibili signo suam præsentiam testificans, per vocem, in aëre formatam, locutus est ad Patriarchas, ad Mosen, & alios, quæ dici potest locutio Dei externa immediata, & est illa ipsa, de qua suprà th. VIII. egimus. Tertia etiam externa est, sed mediata, quâ scilicet, quæ locutione internâ Viris sanctis patefecerat, eadem aliis per eosdem voce sensibili, illorum linguâ & ore formatâ & prolatâ, promulgavit, quæ est quædam Dei locutio per homines & ad homines, atque adeò revelatio per allocutionem mediatam.

III. Ad revelationem verò per illuminationem reduci potest, quæ, Deo inspirante aliis, cùm voce tum scripto promulgata est: quia quæ nôsse nostræ interest salutis, ipsa nobis revelat sive manifestat per species rerum, quas verba sensibilia, ex instituto significantia, cùm in prædicatione per auditum, tum in Scripturæ lectione per visum ad intellectum transmittunt, Dei gratiâ elevatas, quæ sunt velut radii à Deo, Patre luminum, ejusque Verbo in intellectum diffusi, quibus & intellectus, & ipsæ res, intellectui per voces objectæ, illuminantur: hæ quidem ut illarum veritas intellectui appareat; ille, ut eandem intellectus videat sive cognoscat. Quamobrem Verbum Dei, sive voce propositum, sive scripto comprehensum, lucerna & lumen dicitur, Ps. CXIX. 105. Prov. VI. 23. II. Petr. I. 19. eique tribuitur, quòd illuminet oculos, scilicet mentis, metaphoricè sic dictos, h e. mentem, Psal. XIX. 9. & intellectus, Verbo Dei collustratus, ut parata nobis bona futura cognoscat, per metaphoram describitur per oculos mentis illuminatos ad cognoscendum, quæ sit spes, ad quam ille (Deus) vocavit, & quàm opulenta gloria hæreditatis illius in sanctis &c. Ephes. I. 18.

IV. Differt autem revelatio hæc per prædicationem & Scripturam à revelatione per θεοπνευσίαν, quòd quamvis utraq; sit illuminatio quædam mentis, hæc tamen immediata, illa mediata illuminatio est. Θεοπνευσία enim est illuminatio quædam intellectus per species, à Deo immediatè infusas, vel si in intellectu præextiterint, immediatè à Deo excitatas, & ad accendendam rerum revelatarum cognitionem, quae est quaedam mentis illuminatio, applicatas. Revelatio autem per praedicationem vel Scripturam est illuminatio quaedam intellectus per species, modo naturali voce praedicantis excitatas, vel Scripturae lectione, studio humano acquisitas, & quemadmodum in assequendo doctrinae praedicatae vel Scripturae lectae sensu errare possunt, qui praedicationi auscultant, vel Scripturae lectioni vacant, ita haec in illuminatione mediata posita revelatio ex parte ejus, cui obtingit, non perinde, ut altera, quae in illuminatione immediata consistit, infallibilis est, non quod vel ex parte praedicationis (si Deo inspirante ea peragatur) vel ex parte Scripturae theopneustos subesse possit falsitas: hoc enim fieri non posse, supra ostensum est pluribus; sed quod auditores praedicantium, Scripturaeque lectores in assequenda doctrina praedicata aut lecta falli possint.


### XVI. IF Theology is viewed in its breadth, the First Truth can indeed, with any…

XVI

IF Theology is viewed in its breadth, the First Truth can indeed, with any revelation of things that fall under its consideration proceeding from it, be constituted as its formal object and first principle of knowing, yet not for any time, nor by reason of any subject.

I. That which we said above, that it is required for the formal object and first principle of knowing in every discipline that it be the first known and the reason for knowing other things that fall under its consideration, that applies to the First Truth, taken with any of its revelations.

II. It does not, however, apply to it at any time, and by reason of any subject. For in order that divine revelation with the First Truth may perform the function of a formal object and first principle of knowing, it is necessary that it both exist and be known to men, as was said above. For it leads the intellect into the knowledge of revealed things through the knowledge of itself. But that which does not exist, or is not known to men, cannot move the intellect to the knowledge of itself, much less, by means of the knowledge of itself, lead it into the knowledge of other things. But not every divine revelation existed at any time, or was known to anyone at any time, but different revelations occurred to holy men for the most part at different times; and bethey touched upon these things in secret, which only then became known to others when they were promulgated by them and made public property. Whence those things which formerly happened in secret to holy men were, from them, the formal object and the primary principle of knowing their own theology, in which they excelled, or at least a part of it; but to others, after they were promulgated by the Holy Spirit inspiring, whether through preaching or through Scripture. And just as from the creation of the world until the flood, and from the flood until Moses, no written revelation existed, but those things which were necessary to be believed and done were made known chiefly by the address of God, or even by inspiration, so for that state of the times those revelations accomplished by the address or inspiration of God constituted the formal object and the primary principle of knowing theology, first indeed to those to whom they happened; then also to others, after they were promulgated and made public property. Among them stood out the revelation concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, which, as it is the basis and foundation of all theology, so it happened to the first-formed pair, immediately after their fall, by the address of God, Gen. III. 15, and was propagated from them by tradition to their descendants, with God also from time to time repeating it and declaring it more abundantly as to the matter. But through Moses the beginning of the sacred Scripture to be composed was made; and first the moral law, solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai, was inscribed on two stone tablets: then those five books, which hold the first place in the Code of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, and go by the name of the Pentateuch, were recorded by the same. His example was afterwards followed by the Prophets and other holy men up to Malachi, the last of the Prophets, who wrote the remaining books of the Old Testament Code. Whence from Moses until Malachi the formal object and the primary principle of knowing theology were constituted by the revelations which holy men, the Holy Spirit inspiring, promulgated equally by voice and by writings, and thus revelations handed down both by living voice and by writings. For in those times there were available to the Church θεόπνευστοι men, who proposed the revelations, received divinely, in both ways. But after Malachi until Christ, with men immediately instructed and illuminated by God failing, the formal object and the primary principle of knowing theology were constituted solely by the ancient revelations, brought into letters through Moses and the Prophets by divine inspiration, or the Scripture of Moses and the Prophets. For no new revelations were then occurring any longer to the Church. Nor indeed had anything necessary to be believed or done been revealed in earlier times which was not contained in the writings of Moses and the Prophets. At the beginning, however, of the nascent New Testament Church, God, through his Son, Heb. 1:2, and through his Apostles, immediately illuminated by him, revealed those things which were to be promulgated throughout the world concerning the Messiah already exhibited in the flesh, his office, and the other parts of Christian doctrine. Although Christ indeed left nothing of those things which he taught consigned by himself to literary monuments, his Apostles nevertheless handed down his doctrine, and the revelations which they themselves had received divinely, both by voice and by writings, with the Holy Spirit inspiring, and promulgated them throughout the world. Which at that time, together with the ancient revelations, related to letters by Moses and the Prophets at the dictation of the Holy Spirit, constituted the formal object and the primary principle of knowing of Theology.

III. Although indeed those things which were proposed by voice and those which were proposed by writings were not different, but the same revelations; for those things which were handed down by voice were also referred into letters, and conversely; yet the revelations consigned to letters were more suitable for performing the duty of a formal object and a primary principle of knowing than those proposed by voice, not because they did not proceed equally from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, or because they were not of the same certainty, but because the former could be preserved in the Church and transmitted to posterity more easily than the latter without corruptions. For the living voice, although uttered with the Holy Spirit inspiring, perishes easily in the minds of the hearers, or, interpolated with false glosses, is transmitted to posterity corruptly. But the Scripture which has once been consigned with the Holy Spirit inspiring remains, and therefore is more easily preserved undefiled and transmitted incorrupt to posterity. Whence, after the law was related to letters, God referred his people not so much to the living voice of teachers as to Scripture, as to a norm and primary principle of knowing, Deut. 17:18, 20; ch. 27:26; Gal. 3:10; Josh. 1:7, 8; ch. 23:6. And the Apostles, although they preached their doctrine with the Holy Spirit inspiring, nevertheless appealed to Scripture as to a norm and primary principle of knowing, wherever the matter demanded. Indeed, Paul openly testified, both to small and great, that he, in preaching the Gospel among the Gentiles, said nothing other than those things which the Prophets and Moses had predicted, Acts XXVI. 22, and Luke turned it to the praise of the Beroeans, because they searched the Scriptures daily, whether these things which were taught by Paul were so, ch. XVII. 11.

IV. Just as therefore the revelation of the primary Truth grew with time, so also did Theology, which relies upon it. For this extends itself as far and as widely as that, just as its formal object and primary principle of knowing extends itself; and like that, so also this, with God from time to time imparting new revelations, in the progress of time, took its increments, not indeed in those things which constitute the foundation of faith and salvation, but in others which make for their more abundant declaration and understanding, or concern rites and ceremonies, and pertain to ecclesiastical order and discipline. And because in the time of the Apostles, with the canon of the Scriptures of the N. T. established, the revelation of the primary Truth was consummated, and a signal light was kindled for the Scriptures of the O. T.; Theology at that time was also brought to its summit, for the state of the way, indeed. Which, however, I wish to be understood concerning Theology, viewed in itself and by reason of its formal object. For on the part of the subject, just as all sciences are cultivated more perfectly with time, and grow from the study and industry of men, so also Theology has been cultivated more and more with the progress of time, and has taken greater increments.

Latin:

XVI

SI in sua latitudine spectetur Theologia, potest quidem Veritas prima cum quavis revelatione rerum, quae sub ejus considerationem cadunt, ab ea profecta, objectum formale illius & principium cognoscendi primum constitui, non tamen pro quovis tempore, nec ratione cujusvis subjecti.

I. Quod supra diximus, ad objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum in unaquaque disciplina requiri, ut sit primum cognitum & ratio cognoscendi alia, quae sub ejus considerationem cadunt, id quadrat in Veritatem primam, cum quavis sua revelatione sumtam.

II. Non tamen quadrat in eam quovis tempore, & ratione cujusvis subjecti. Nam ut objecti formalis & principii primi cognoscendi munus revelatio divina cum Veritate prima obeat, necesse est, ut & extet, & nota sit hominibus, uti supra dictum. Deducit enim intellectum in cognitionem rerum revelatarum per cognitionem sui. Quae autem non extat, aut non nota est hominibus, ea non potest intellectum ad cognitionem sui movere, multo minus, mediante sui cognitione, in aliorum cognitionem deducere. Non autem quaelibet divina revelatio quovis tempore extitit, aut quaelibet quovis tempore cuivis nota fuit, sed revelationes diversae obtigerunt Viris sanctis ut plurimum diversis temporibus; & obtigerunt illis secreto, quæ aliis tum demùm innotuerunt, cùm ab illis promulgatæ & publici juris factæ sunt. Unde quæ olim secreto obtingebant Viris sanctis, ex ipsis erant objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum suæ, quâ pollebant, Theologiæ, vel certè pars ejus; aliis autem, postquam Spiritu S. inspirante, sive per prædicationem sive per Scripturam promulgatæ fuerunt. Et quemadmodùm à condito mundo usque ad diluvium; & à diluvio usque ad Mosen revelatio scripta nulla extitit, sed Dei alloquio potissimùm, vel etiam inspiratione patefactæ sunt, quæ creditu factuque necessaria erant, ita pro illo temporum statu Theologiæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum constituebant istæ Dei alloquio vel inspiratione peractæ revelationes, primùm quidem iis, quibus obtigerunt; deinde & aliis, postquam promulgatæ & publici juris factæ sunt. Inter eas eminebat revelatio de semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro, quæ ut Theologiæ totius basis & fundamentum est ita Protoplastis, statim post ipsorum lapsum, Dei alloquio obtigit, Gen. III. 15. & ab his per traditionem ad posteros ipsorum propagata est, Deo etiam subinde eam, quoad rem, repetente & uberiùs declarante. Per Mosen verò condendæ Scripturæ sacræ initium factum; & primùm lex moralis, in monte Sinai solenniter promulgata, duabus tabulis lapideis inscripta fuit: deinde quinque illi libri, qui in Codice Scripturarum V. T. primum locum obtinent, & Pentateuchi nomine veniunt, ab eodem consignati sunt. Ejus exemplum posteà sequuti sunt Prophetæ & Viri sancti alii usque ad Malachiam, Prophetarum ultimum qui cæteros Codicis V. T. libros conscripserunt. Unde à Mose usque ad Malachiam Theologiæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum constituebant revelationes, quas Viri sancti, Spiritu S. inspirante, voce pariter & scriptis promulgabant, atque adeò revelationes, & voce vivâ & scriptis traditæ. Illis enim temporibus suppetebant Ecclesiæ Viri θεόπνευστοι, qui revelationes, divinitùs acceptas, modo utroque proponerent. Post Malachiam verò usque ad Christum, deficientibus Viris, immediatè à Deo instructis & illuminatis, objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum Theologiæ constituebant solæ revelationes antiquæ, per Mosen & Prophetas ex divina inspiratione in literas relatæ, sive Scriptura Mosis & Prophetarum. Non enim novæ tùm revelationes Ecclesiae amplius obtingebant. Neque etiam anterioribus temporibus quicquam creditu aut factu necessarium revelatum fuerat, quod non in Mosis & Prophetarum Scriptis contineretur. Sub initium autem nascentis Ecclesiae Novi Testamenti Deus per Filium suum, Ebr. I. 2. & per ejus Apostolos, a se immediate illuminatos, revelabat, quae de exhibito jam in carne Messia, ejusque officio & cateris doctrinae Christianae partibus per orbem terrarum erant promulganda. Quamvis vero Christus nihil eorum, quae docuit, literarum monumentis a se consignatum reliquerit, ipsius Apostoli tamen doctrinam ejus, &, quas ipsi divinitus acceperant, revelationes simul voce & scriptis, Spiritu sancto inspirante, tradiderunt, & per orbem terrarum promulgarunt. Quae tum temporis una cum revelationibus antiquis, a Mose & Prophetis, dictante Spiritu sancto, in literas relatis, Theologiae objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum constituebant.

III. Quanquam vero quae voce, & quae scriptis proponebantur, non diversae, sed eadem revelationes erant; quae enim tradebantur voce, ea referebantur etiam in literas, & contra; literis tamen consignatae revelationes ad obeundum munus objecti formalis & principii cognoscendi primi idoneae magis erant, quam voce propositae, non quod non aeque ex immediata Spiritus sancti inspiratione procederent, vel quod ejusdem certitudinis non essent, sed quod illae facilius, quam hae sine corruptelis in Ecclesia conservari & ad posteritatem transmitti possent. Nam vox viva licet Spiritu sancto inspirante prolata in auditorum animis perit facile, aut falsis glossis interprolata transmittitur ad posteros corrupte. Quae autem Spiritu sancto inspirante semel consignata est Scriptura, manet, & propterea facilius intemerata conservatur atque incorrupta ad posteritatem transmittitur. Unde post legem in literas relatam Deus populum suum non tam ad vivam docentium vocem, quam ad Scripturam, velut ad normam & principium cognoscendi primum remisit, Deut. XVII. 18. 20. c. XXVII. 26. Gal. III. 10. Jos. I. 7. 8. c. XXIII. 6. Et Apostoli, etsi Spiritu sancto inspirante doctrinam suam praedicabant, ad Scripturam tamen velut ad normam & principium cognoscendi primum, ubicunque res postulabat, provocabant. Quin Paulus palam, tum parvo tum magno contestabatur, se praedicando Evangelium inter Gentes nihil a iud dixisse, quàm ea, quæ Prophetæ prædixerant & Moses, Act. XXVI. 22 & Lucas laudi vertebat Beroënsibus, quòd quotidiè scrutarentur Scripturas, an hæc, quæ à Paulo docebantur, ita se haberent, c. XVII. 11.

IV. Quemadmodùm ergo revelatio Veritatis primæ cum tempore crevit, ita & innixa ei Theologia. Hæc enim extendit se tam longè lateque, quàm longè lateque illa, velut ejus objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum se extendit; & ut illa, ita & hæc, Deo subinde novas revelationes impertiente, temporis progressu, sua sumsit incrementa, non quidem in iis, quæ fidei & salutis fundamentum constituunt, sed in aliis, quæ ad illorum uberiorem declarationem & intelligentiam faciunt, vel ritus ac ceremonias concernunt, & ad ordinem ac disciplinam Ecclesiasticam pertinent. Et quia tempore Apostolorum, canone Scripturarum N. T. constituto, revelatio Veritatis primæ consummata, & Scripturis V. T. lux insignis accensa fuit; Theologia tum temporis etiam ad suum fastigium, pro statu viæ quidem, perducta est. Quod tamen de Theologia, in se & ratione sui objecti formalis spectatâ, intellectum volo. Ex parte subjecti enim ut scientiæ omnes cum tempore perfectiùs excoluntur, & ex hominum studio & industria crescunt, ita & Theologia temporis progressu magis magisque exculta est, & majora incrementa sumsit.


### XVII. For the present state of the Church, however, the formal object and primary…

XVII.

For the present state of the Church, however, the formal object and primary principle of knowing of Theology constitutes the primary Truth revealing, with only the ancient revelations which were once committed to writing by Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles by divine inspiration.

I. With these alone the primary Truth constitutes the formal object and primary principle of knowing of Theology, for the present state of the Church indeed: because no other certainly and indubitably divine revelations are given. For new ones, after the canon of Scripture was established, have ceased in the Church. But the old ones, which occurred to holy men before the birth of Christ up to Malachi, and which were promulgated by Christ himself in the days of his flesh by voice, and after his ascension to heaven by his Apostles by voice and writings, in the Scriptures, by Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, recorded by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, are so fully contained, especially regarding those things which are necessary either to be believed for salvation or to be done for the holiness of life, that no others are found outside of them.

II. The Papists indeed boast that, besides these which are contained in the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, there are other divine revelations concerning things necessary to be believed and done, which the Apostles delivered to the Church by voice only, not by writings, and for that reason they call them the word of God not written, but handed down, and contend that they, together with the written revelations, must be admitted into the part of the formal object and the first principle of knowing in Theology: but wrongly. For first, they have not been able to teach up to this point that there are any revelations of dogmas concerning things necessary to be believed or done, besides these which are contained in the Canonical Scriptures of the Old and New Testament. Furthermore, if any were given, they nevertheless could not fulfill the function of the formal object and the first principle of knowing in Theology. For in order that a divine revelation may be able to fulfill the function of the formal object and the first principle of knowing in it, it is required that it depend immediately upon the primary Truth, and that it be proposed either by voice, the Holy Spirit inspiring, or that it was once committed to letters and, being comprised in them, still exists even now: for otherwise it will not obtain divine authority and certainty. For the mode of proposing divine revelations through knowledge acquired by human study is not outside the danger of error: since our labor and study, which we employ in learning, preserving, teaching, and propagating them, can be mistaken and can deceive. But θεόπνευςοι men, who propose them from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit and transmit them uncorrupted to posterity, have ceased in the Church for fifteen centuries. Nor is there any reason for the Papists to object that unwritten divine revelations are proposed and transmitted to posterity by the Church just as infallibly as by θεοπνεύςες men: since the Church is the pillar and ground of the truth, 1 Tim. III. 15, and has the promise that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, Matt. XVI. 18. For this is true of the Church, insofar as it is built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone, Eph. II. 19, which therefore is the pillar and ground of the truth by the power of the Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture, upon which it is built, and consequently in proposing and propagating those revelations which exist recorded in the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But that it is absolutely and simply infallible, and therefore the pillar and ground of the truth, even in unwritten revelations, and of which not even a trace is found in the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, the adversaries will never prove by any suitable foundation. Concerning which matter, perhaps, more will be said below in its proper place.

Latin:

XVII.

PRo hodierno autem Ecclesiæ statu constituit Theologiæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum Veritas prima revelans cum solis revelationibus antiquis, quæ à Mose, Prophetis & Apostolis olim ex divina inspiratione in literas relatæ sunt.

I. Cum his solis Veritas prima constituit Theologiæ objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum, pro hodierno Ecclesiæ statu quidem: quia aliæ certò & indubitatò divinæ revelationes nullæ dantur. Novæ enim, post constitutum Scripturæ canonem, in Ecclesia defierunt. Veteres verò, quæ ante Christum natum ad Malachiam usque Viris sanctis obtigêre, & quæ ab ipsomet Christo in diebus carnis suæ voce; & post ejus adscensionem ad cœlos ab ipsius Apostolis voce & scriptis promulgatæ sunt, in Scripturis, à Mose, Prophetis & Apostolis, Spiritu S. inspirante consignatis, ita plene continentur, praesertim quoad ea, quae sive creditu ad salutem, sive factu ad sanctimoniam vitae necessaria sunt, ut extra eas aliae nullae inveniantur.

II. Pontificii quidem jactant, praeter has, quae in Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis continentur, alias de rebus creditu factuque necessariis revelationes divinas, quas Apostoli voce tantum, non scriptis, Ecclesiae tradiderint, easque propterea verbum Dei non scriptum, sed traditum appellant, & una cum revelationibus scriptis in partem objecti formalis & principii cognoscendi primi Theologiae admittendam esse contendunt: sed perperam. Primum enim dari ullas de rebus creditu factuve necessariis revelationes dogmatum, praeter has, quae in Scripturis Canonicis Veteris & Novi Testamenti continentur, huc usque docere non potuerunt. Deinde si quae darentur, eae tamen munus objecti formalis & principii cognoscendi primi in Theologia obire non possent. Ut enim revelatio divina objecti formalis & principii cognoscendi primi munus in ea obire possit requiritur, ut immediate a Veritate prima dependeat, eaque Spiritu S. inspirante vel voce proponatur, vel olim in literas relata fuerit, & iisdem comprehensa etiamnum extet: alias enim auctoritatem & certitudinem divina non obtinebit Nam modus proponendi revelationes divinas per notitiam, studio humano acquisitam extra erroris periculum non est: cum nostra opera & studium, quod in iis cum addiscendis & conservandis, tum docendis & propagandis collocamus, falli & fallere possit. Viri θεόπνευςοι autem, qui eas ex immediata inspiratione Spiritus sancti proponant, & incorrupte ad posteritatem transmittant, inde a quindecim seculis in Ecclesia defierunt. Neque est, quod obtendant Pontificii, divinas revelationes non scriptas proponi & & transmitti ad posteritatem per Ecclesiam aeque infallibiliter, atque per Viros θεοπνεύςες: cum Ecclesia sit columna & stabilimentum veritatis, 1. Tim. III. 15. & habeat promissionem, quod portae inferorum ei non sint praevaliturae, Matth. XVI. 18. Hoc enim verum est de Ecclesia, in quantum superstructa est super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, imo angulari lapide existente Jesu Christo, Eph. II. 19. quae proinde columna est & stabilimentum veritatis vi Scripturae Propheticae & Apostolicae, cui superstructa est, atque adeo in iis proponendis & propagandis revelationibus, quæ in Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis ex immediata Spiritus sancti inspiratione consignatæ extant. Quod autem absolutè & simpliciter, etiam in revelationibus non scriptis, & quarum ne vestigium quidem in Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis invenitur, infallibilis atque adeò columna & stabilimentum veritatis sit, nunquam ullo idoneo fundamento adversarii evincent. Qua de re infrà suo loco forsan agetur pluribus.


### XVIII. Because the ancient revelations, once committed to writing by the Prophets and…

XVIII.

Because the ancient revelations, once committed to writing by the Prophets and Apostles under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, do not differ from the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, it is also not inconveniently said that the formal object and primary principle of knowing in Theology, for the present state of the Church, constitutes the First Truth together with the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, in so far as it reveals through them those things which it concerns our salvation to know.

XIX.

But just as the formal object and primary principle of knowing in any science can be considered in two ways: one materially, as the thing which is the formal object and primary principle of knowing; the other formally, in so far as it is the formal object and the reason or principle of knowing other things; so also Holy Scripture can be considered in Theology either in itself materially, as a thing or Scripture proceeding from God: or formally, as the reason or principle of knowing the rest of the things which fall under the consideration of Theology.

I. The latter consideration presupposes the former: for the thing which is the primary principle of knowing for a science cannot be rightly applied to infer its conclusions unless its nature and properties have been first exactly known: thus it claims the last place; but the former claims the first place for itself. But especially in Theology, that thing which is its formal object and primary principle of knowing, or rather constitutes a part of it, namely Holy Scripture, which, the more it is entangled in controversies and the more vehemently it is impugned by the adversaries of heavenly truth, the more diligent and accurate consideration it requires. II. Our present work, therefore, will be occupied with the consideration of Holy Scripture deferred to another place.

Latin:

XVIII.

QVia revelationes antiquæ, à Prophetis & Apostolis olim Spiritu sancto inspirante in literas relatæ, à Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis non differunt, non incommodè etiam dicitur, objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum Theologiæ, pro hodierno quidem statu Ecclesiæ, constituere Veritatem primam unà cum Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis, in quantum ea, quæ nosse nostræ interest salutis, per illas revelat.

XIX.

QVemadmodum autem objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum in quavis scientia considerari potest duobus modis: Uno materialiter, ut res, quæ est objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum; altero formaliter, in quantum est objectum formale & ratio sive principium cognoscendi alia; ita & Scriptura Sacra in Theologia considerari potest vel in se materialiter, ut res vel Scriptura, â Deo profecta: vel formaliter, ut ratio sive principium cognoscendi cætera, quæ sub Theologiæ considerationem cadunt.

I. Posterior consideratio ut priorem præsupponit: non enim res, quæ scientiæ principium cognoscendi primum est, ad inferendas ejus conclusiones rectè adhiberi potest, nisi ejus natura & affectiones priùs exactè cognitæ sint: ita postremum locum; prior verò locum primum sibi vendicat. Cumprimis verò in Theologia res illa, quæ illius objectum formale & principium cognoscendi primum est, vel potius ejus partem constituit, Scriptura sacra scilicet, quo pluribus implicatur controversiis, & ab adversariis veritatis cœlestis vehementiùs impugnatur, eò diligentiorem & accuratiorem considerationem desiderat. II. Præsens igitur nostra opera occupabitur in consideratione Scripturæ sacræ, in se materialiter spectatæ, alterâ ejusdem consideratione in alium locum rejectâ.


## 5 On the Nature and Quiddity of Holy Scripture

The appellation of Holy Scripture, although by the force of the words it can be attributed to any writing occupied with sacred matters, is nevertheless taken from the usage of speech in a stricter sense for certain books, recorded by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and indeed either for those alone, or for all those included in the same codex with them, which we commonly call the BIBLE. I. Scripture can be denominated holy (1) from its object, because it is occupied with sacred matters. (2) from its end, because it is ordained for man's faith and the holiness of life. (3) from its efficient cause, because it has the Holy Spirit as its Author. Which reasons for denomination fall in their own way also upon the writings of the ancient Fathers and recent Theologians. For these also are occupied with sacred matters, and thus they are holy on the part of the object: they are also ordained for a sacred use, namely, that they may lead their readers to the holiness of life and the salvation of the soul, and thus they are holy on the part of the end; and they have in their own way also the Holy Spirit as their Author. For they are composed with the Holy Spirit assisting and helping; nay, the things contained in them were not invented by men, but revealed by the Holy Spirit: and thus these writings can also be called holy on the part of the efficient cause. II. But from the usage of speech, Holy Scripture is taken in a more special sense for books, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and which were to be written were written, with the Holy Spirit immediately suggesting and, as it were, dictating to the pen. This is the most proper signification, derived from the efficient cause, namely the Holy Spirit, concurring through immediate inspiration to adorn it. For these books have this peculiar and proper quality above all the writings of the ancient Fathers and recent theologians. For no other books are found which were written with the Holy Spirit inspiring and immediately suggesting what was to be written, except these, which we designate properly and strictly by the name of Holy Scripture. To this, the following reason for the denomination may not inconveniently be added: that they have inherent or intimately conjoined to them the power of the Holy Spirit to illuminate, convert, and sanctify the minds of men, and thus they are also formally holy or sacred in themselves through the power of the Holy Spirit, which is always intimately conjoined to them. And this itself is peculiar and proper to them. For it does not agree with any other books or writings, unless in so far as they contain in themselves some part of the Holy Scriptures, to which it is always per se conjoined.

III. But because, with the passage of time, other books also—concerning sacred matters indeed, but composed by human effort—were added to the collection of these books, because they were judged useful and worthy to be read in the Church for the edification of faith and morals; a usage of speech prevailed such that the name of Holy Scripture is attributed even to the whole Biblical collection, and all the books contained therein are included in that scope, but by a synecdochical locution, by which the name of the more important part is transferred to signify the whole. For the other books, which the sacred collection contains besides the θεοπνεύστους, if they are viewed in themselves, deserve the name of Holy Scripture for no greater reason than other books of orthodox Fathers and theologians, which treat of sacred matters and are useful for the edification of the Church. But the reason why they are reckoned among the Holy Scriptures above others is that they were added by the ancient Church to the collection of books written by divine inspiration, and the name of the part, by accepted usage of speech, was transferred to signify the whole. We take Scripture here in the former, special, and proper signification.

IV. It is called by Christ and the Apostles sometimes without an adjunct γραφὴ, Scripture, κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν, John 2:22, 8:38, 42, and in the plural γραφαὶ, Scriptures, Matthew 21:42, 22:29, 26:54, and elsewhere throughout: sometimes with the addition of γραφαὶ ἁγίαι, holy Scriptures, Rom. I. 2, and ἱερὰ γράμματα, sacred letters, II Tim. III, 15. But the reason why it is sometimes called in the singular number γραφὴ, Scripture, and sometimes in the plural γραφαὶ, Scriptures, is that from several books, composed by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and comprised in one codex, which we call BIBLIA by way of eminence, it is both an aggregate and one, and many. One indeed by accident, in that all the books, although written in different places and times, joined into one codex, constitute one by aggregation. But many: in that the sacred books are viewed separately in themselves; which, as they were written by different authors, in different places and times, so in reality they are diverse and many Scriptures. Viewed in that way, they are rightly and conveniently called in the singular Scripture; in this, in the plural Scriptures, and sacred Scripture.

Latin:

SCripturæ sacræ appellatio, etsi vi vocum cuivis in rebus sacris occupatæ Scripturæ tribui potest, ex usu loquendi tamen accipitur in significatu strictiori pro certis quibusdam libris, Spiritu Sancto inspirante consignatis, & quidem vel pro illis solis, vel pro omnibus, in eodem cum illis codice, quem vulgò BIBLIA appellamus, comprehensis. I. Scriptura potest denominari sacra (1) ab objecto, quòd circa res sacras occupetur. (2) ex fine, quòd ad hominis fidem vitæque sanctimoniam ordinata sit. (3) ex causa efficiente, quòd Spiritum sanctum habeat Auctorem. Quæ rationes denominandi cadunt suo modo etiam in Patrum veterum & Theologorum recentium Scripta. Occupantur enim hæc quoque circa res sacras, atque sic sacra sunt ex parte objecti: Ordinantur etiam ad usum sacrum, ut scilicet ad sanctimoniam vitæ & animæ salutem lectores suos perducant, & fic sacra sunt ex parte finis; & habent suo modo etiam Auctorem Spiritum sanctum. Sunt enim Spiritu S.adsistente & adjuvante composita; quin & contentæ illis res non ab hominibus inventæ, sed à Spiritu Sancto patefactæ sunt: & sic Scripturæ hæ possunt etiam sacræ dici ex parte causæ efficientis. II. Sed ex usu loquendi Scriptura sacra accipitur in significatu specialiori pro libris, Spiritu Sancto inspirante, &, quæ scribendaeffent, immediatè fuggerente, atque in calamum quafi dictante, confcriptis. Quæ maximè propria fignificatio eft, à caufa efficiente, Spiritu fancto fcilicet, per immediatam infpirationem ad eam adornandam concurrente, petita. Hoc enim libri illi præ aliis Patrum veterum, & Theologorum recentium fcriptis omnibus peculiare & proprium habent. Nulli enim inveniuntur libri alii, qui Spiritu S. infpirante, & quæ fcribenda effent, immediatè fuggerente, confcripti effent, præter hos, quos propriè & ftrictè Scripturæ facræ appellatione indigitamus. Cui haud incommodè hæc etiam denominationis ratio addi poteft, quòd fibi infitam five intimè conjunctam habeant virtutem Spiritus fancti ad illuminandas, convertendas & fanctificandas hominum mentes, & fic etiam in fe formaliter facri five fancti fint per virtutem Spiritus fancti, fibi femper intimè conjunctam. Quod & ipfum illis peculiare & proprium eft. Neque enim aliis ullis convenit libris five Scripturis, nifi in quantum Scripturæ facræ partem aliquam, cui per fe femper conjuncta eft, in fe continent.

III. Quia autem horum librorum Codici temporis progreffu alii etiam libri, de rebus facris quidem, fed ftudio humano concinnati, adjecti funt, quòd utiles & digni judicarentur, qui ad ædificationem fidei & morum in Ecclefia legerentur; ufus loquendi obtinuit, ut Scripturæ facræ appellatio etiam toti tribuatur Codici Biblico, omnesque eo comprehenfi libri illius ambitu comprehendantur, fed locutione fynecdochicâ, quâ nomen partis potioris transfertur ad fignificandum totum. Cæteri enim libri, quos, præter θεοπνεύσης, Codex facer continet, fi in fe fpectentur, non majori ratione Scripturæ facræ nomen merentur, quàm alii orthodoxorum Patrum & Theologorum libri, qui de rebus facris agunt, & ad ædificationem Ecclefiæ utiles funt. Quòd autem illi præ aliis Scripturæ facræ accenfentur, caufa eft, quòd ab Ecclefia veteri Codici librorum, ex divina infpiratione confcriptorum, adjecti funt, & nomen partis, ex ufu loquendi recepto, ad fignificandum totum translatum eft. Nos Scripturam hîc in fignificatu priori, fpeciali & proprio, accipimus.

IV. Ea dicitur à Chrifto & Apoftolis interdum fine appofito γραφὴ, Scriptura, κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν, Joh. II. 22. c. VIII. 38. 42. & in plurali γραφαὶ, Scripturæ, Matth. XXI. 42. c. XXII. 29. c. XXVI. 54. & alibi passim: interdum cum apposito γραφαὶ ἁγίαι Scripturae sanctae Rom. I. 2. & ἱερὰ γράμματα sacrae literae, II. Tim. III, 15. Quòd autem modò singulari numero dicitur γραφὴ Scriptura, modò plurali γραφαὶ, Scripturae, causa est, quòd ex pluribus, Spiritu S. inspirante, concinnatis libris, iiśque uno codice, quem κατ' ἐξοχὴν BIBLIA appellamus, comprehensis, aggregata, & unum est, & multa. Unum quidem per accidens, in quantum omnes libri, licet diversis locis & temporibus conscripti, in codicem unum conjuncti, unum per aggregationem constituunt. Multa verò: in quantum libri sacri in se seorsim spectantur: qui ut ab auctoribus diversis, diversis locis & temporibus conscripti, ita revera Scripturae diversae & multae sunt. Illo modo spectati in singulari Scriptura; hoc in plurali Scripturae, & Scriptura sacra rectè & convenienter appellantur.


### II. But since sacred Scripture, as to the thing itself, is nothing other than…

II.

But since sacred Scripture, as to the thing itself, is nothing other than divine revelations committed to writing; and since divine revelations vary according to the diversity of the signs by which they were performed, and one revelation is by address, another by dream, another by vision, and yet another by inspiration; sacred Scripture is to be reckoned to revelation by inspiration, and in its own way also to revelation by address.

I. The diverse kinds or modes of revelations were treated at length in the preceding chapter, which may be seen there.

II. That sacred Scripture cannot be reckoned to revelation by dream or by vision is easily evident. For although some revelations, which initially occurred to holy men through dreams and visions, are contained in it, yet when they were committed to writing, they were not suggested to the sacred writers through dreams or visions, but through inspiration, as Paul teaches in II Tim. III. 15, where he calls the whole Scripture θεόπνευστον, divinely inspired, and thus signifies that even the prophetic visions and dreams themselves were committed to writing by divine inspiration. For the concepts of things and words, of which the written words are signs, were inspired into the sacred writers by the Holy Spirit: and their inspiration is a certain revelation by inspiration. The same, in so far as it consists of words, signifying by design, and those by a holy rite suggested to the Prophets and Apostles through inspiration, it can also be called revelation by address. For by words suggested to the Prophets and Apostles through inspiration, and those words uttered by the mouth of the Prophets and Apostles, God formerly addressed the Fathers under the old covenant, and the faithful from among the Jews and Gentiles under the new covenant, according to that passage Heb. 1.1, Luke 1.70. Although to address properly belongs to the voice, it is nevertheless sometimes transferred also to Scripture, and one is said to address someone who accosts him by letter and signifies what he wishes him to know. Nor without cause: for words, signifying by design, whether uttered by voice or comprised in letters, are one and the same, and therefore deservedly constitute one revelation. Yet they do not constitute any other than that which is called an address, even though its denomination is taken from the act of speaking or addressing, which is properly performed by voice.

III. But since revelation by address is twofold: one, by which God addressed men by a voice formed and uttered by Himself or in His place by an Angel; the other, by which He addressed the same by the voice of a man, or by Scripture composed by a man, while He Himself suggested the words through immediate inspiration: Holy Scripture is a certain revelation by address of the latter order. For it consists of words which God did not communicate to men by Himself or by a certain Angel by voice or writing, but which He suggested to the Prophets and Apostles through inspiration, and which He subsequently communicated to others by their mouth and pen. Let those things be seen which we said in the preceding chapter, thesis XI, explanation number IV, regarding this matter.

Latin:

II.

CÙm verò Scriptura sacra, quoad rem, nihil aliud sit, quàm divinae revelationes, in literas relatae; revelationes divinae autem pro diversitate signorum, quibus peractae sunt, varient, & alia sit revelatio per allocutionem, alia per somnium, per visionem alia, & rursum alia per inspirationem; Scriptura sacra revelationi per inspirationem; & suo modo etiam revelationi per allocutionem accensenda est.

I. De diversis revelationum generibus aut modis actum est in capite praecedente pluribus, quae ibi videantur.

II. Quod autem Scriptura sacra non possit accenseri revelationi per somnium, aut per visionem, facilè patet. Quamvis enim nonnullae revelationes, quae initio Viris sanctis per somnia & visiones obtigerunt, in ea contineantur, tamen cùm in literas referrentur, Scriptoribus sacris non suggerebantur per somnia aut visiones, sed per inspirationem, docente Paulo II. Tim. III. 15. ubi Scripturam totam θεόπνευστον, divinitùs inspiratam dicit, atque adeò ipsas etiam visiones & somnia Prophetica ex divina inspiratione in literas relata esse significat. Conceptus enim rerum & verborum, quorum signa sunt verba scripta, Scriptoribus sacris à Spiritu sancto inspirati sunt: & illorum inspiratio est revelatio quaedam per inspirationem. Eadem, in quantum constat verbis, ex instituto significantibus, iiśque à Spiritu sancto per inspirationem Prophetis & Apostolis suggestis, potest etiam dici revelatio per allocutionem. Verbis enim, Prophetis & Apostolis per inspirationem suggestis, iisque Prophetarum & Apostolorum ore prolatis, Deus olim alloqvutus est Patres sub veteri, & fideles ex Judæis & Gentibus sub novo fœdere, juxta illud Ebr. I. 1. Luc. 1. 70. Quamvis verò alloqvi propriè vocis sit, transfertur tamen quandoque etiam ad Scripturam, & dicitur quempiam alloqui, qui per literas eum compellat, & quid eum scire velit, significat. Neque præter causam: Verba enim, ex instituto significantia, voce prolata, & literis comprehensa, una eademque sunt, & proptereà meritò unam revelationem constituunt. Neque tamen aliam, quàm quæ alloquium appellatur, constituunt, utut denominatio ejus ab actu loquendi sive alloquendi, qui propriè voce peragitur, petita sit.

III. Cùm verò revelatio per allocutionem duplex sit: una, quâ Deus voce à se vel ejus loco ab Angelo formatâ & prolatâ homines allocutus est; altera, quâ eosdem voce hominis, vel Scripturâ, ab homine confectâ, allocutus est, ipso verba per immediatam inspirationem suggerente: Scriptura sacra est revelatio quædam per allocutionem posterioris ordinis. Constat enim verbis, quæ Deus non per se vel per Angelum quendam voce aut scripto cum hominibus communicavit, sed quæ Prophetis & Apostolis per inspirationem suggessit, & horum ore calamoque aliis deinceps communicavit. Videantur, quæ in cap. præced. th. XI. Expl. n. IV. hanc in rem diximus.


### III. The efficient cause therefore of Holy Scripture, and that the principal one, is…

III.

The efficient cause therefore of Holy Scripture, and that the principal one, is God, or, which amounts to the same thing, the Holy Spirit: but the causality, or formal reason, by which the Holy Spirit was constituted in the being of that cause, and provided His influence upon it, is θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration.

I. Although the names God and Holy Spirit differ, in that by the former God is denoted by reason of essence, which is common to all three persons; by the latter the third person of the divinity is denoted, yet the influence which God provides upon Scripture, namely the inspiration of the concepts, as well of the things as of the words which were to be written, is an outward work, and just like other outward works, is common to all three persons. Wherefore Scripture is rightly ascribed to God under an essential name, common to all three persons, as the efficient cause. To the Holy Spirit, however, the same is ascribed, as the efficient cause, by appropriation, or by a mode of speaking whereby that which pertains to the whole Holy Trinity is ascribed to the Holy Spirit as a work proper to Him. This is a customary mode of speech in the Holy Scriptures. Thus David says that the Spirit of the Lord spoke through him, and His word was made by his tongue, II Sam. XXIII. 2. And Paul says: God, he says, has revealed to us through His Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God, I Cor. II. 10. And again: We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we may know the things that have been given to us by Christ. Which things we also speak, not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, ibid. v. 11, 12.

II. But Paul clearly teaches, in the passage from II Tim. III. 16 [19] so often cited, where he says that all Scripture is θεόπνευστον, inspired by God, that the causality by which God provided the influence into Scripture consists in θεοπνευσίᾳ, or divine inspiration. He designates it indeed as θεόπνευστον, inspired by God, from θεοπνευσίᾳ, i.e., divine inspiration, as from the formal reason through which it depends efficiently upon God, and by which God is constituted in the being of its efficient cause.

III. Therefore, for one about to explain more distinctly what God and what the sacred writers contributed efficiently to the composing of Scripture, and what the parts and duties of the former and the latter were, first of all, one must inquire into θεοπνευσίᾳ, or divine inspiration, and explain what produced term it had and has in it. For whatever God contributed efficiently to the composing of it, He contributed entirely through θεοπνευσίαν. Now, the things that are contained in Holy Scripture, just as in any other writing whatsoever, are (1) The characters of words and letters, painted or written on paper. (2) The words themselves, of which the written characters are signs. (3) The things signified by the words, and (4) The concepts, both of the things signified by the words and of the words themselves. And Scripture contains the painted or written characters of letters and words actually and formally; but the things themselves and their concepts, as well as the words and their concepts, it contains only potentially and virtually, insofar, namely, as the written characters of words, by the pleasure or imposition of men, have the power of signifying and representing both the words and the things of which words are signs, and the concepts of both. It is therefore necessary that the θεοπνευςία or divine inspiration in the composing of Holy Scripture should have been terminated either at the external act of writing, and the very characters of the letters and words, painted and written with ink on paper, or at the words themselves, of which the written characters are signs, and at the things, of which the words are signs, according to their real being, or finally at the concepts both of things and of words, through which both things and words are objectively in the intellect. But the first cannot be said. For θεοπνευςία is a spiritual action, but the characters of words and letters painted and written with ink on paper are material. Moreover, no spiritual action can be terminated at something material: since the spiritual and the material differ as thing and thing; but an action and its terminus differ only as thing and mode of a thing, or modally. Furthermore, θεοπνευςία subjectively resides in the human intellect; but writing and written characters subjectively reside in the paper. Nor can the second be said. For words and things, signified by words, according to their real being, are outside the intellect; but θεοπνευςία, as has been said, subjectively resides in the intellect, the produced terminus of which must also reside in the intellect. For it is necessary that the action and its produced terminus have one and the same subject, since, as has been said, they differ only modally. It remains, therefore, that the θεοπνευςία or divine inspiration was terminated in the intellect of the sacred writers either at the concepts of the things which were to be recorded, or at the concepts of the words by which they were to be recorded, or at the concepts of things and words together. Whether at one or the other? and at which? or whether it was terminated at both? on this finally turns the hinge of the matter.

IV. And indeed that it was terminated at the concepts of the things which had to be committed to writing, there can hardly be any doubt. For nothing was given in the intellect of the sacred writers which could be said to have been produced in it by θεοπνευςία, except the concepts of the things and words to be written. Although indeed the concepts of things alone and without the concepts of words could have been inspired, yet on the contrary the concepts of words, which are signs of things, could not have been inspired without the concepts of things, since words, conceived in the mind, at the same time bring into the intellect the concepts of the things of which they are signs, unless perhaps someone might wish to say that the concepts of the words were inspired into their intellect, without those the power of signifying, which is absurd. For the sacred writers taught also by voice what they had received from divine revelation to be committed to writing. It is necessary, therefore, that if they received the concepts of the words to be written by inspiration, they also received the power of those words to signify, and thus at the same time the concepts of the things signified, by inspiration from God. Either, therefore, the concepts of the things alone, or the concepts of the words and things together, were inspired into their intellect. Whichever you choose, it will always remain fixed and firm that divine inspiration in the intellect of the sacred writers was terminated at the concepts of the things to be committed to writing. But if you choose neither, nothing will remain in the intellect of the sacred writers to which θεοπνευστία or divine revelation was terminated, and thus sacred Scripture will clearly not be θεόπνευστος, contrary to what Paul says, that it is entirely θεόπνευστον. Furthermore, the sacred writers themselves testify that they received the knowledge of things, whether to be handed down by voice or to be committed to writing, from God through revelation. But to us, says Paul in 1 Cor. II, 10, God has revealed through His Spirit, namely the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which He had foreordained before the ages, for our glory, etc., concerning which he had dealt in the preceding verses 6 and following. He revealed to them this wisdom hidden in a mystery in the manner then customary, not through external address, nor through dreams and visions: for God at that time used these modes of revelation either not at all, or at least very rarely; but through internal speech, or what is the same thing, through inspiration, so that the very things contained under that wisdom of God became known to their intellect. Which could not have happened, except through the concepts of those things produced by inspiration in their intellect, or through concepts inspired into their intellect. What? Since the very things signified by the words of Scripture, and their concepts, are as it were the soul of Scripture, if they had not been inspired into the intellect of the sacred writers, it would not appear how Scripture could have been called by Paul θεόπνευστος, that is, divinely inspired into their intellect.

V. But to these things perhaps someone might object, that it is indeed granted concerning mysteries and things exceeding the grasp of human reason, that their concepts were inspired into the sacred writers by God; but that in the sacred Scriptures are contained many other things which were known to the sacred writers, before they moved their hand to the pen to write, from the light of nature, or from experience. But why we should say that the concepts of these were supernaturally inspired into their intellect while writing, there is no reason: since for the recording of such things the assistance of the Holy Spirit could have sufficed for them, by which they were governed, so that they would not admit any error or lapse of memory, or anything alien to the truth and what is proper.

VI. But to this objection we oppose that Paul expressly says that πᾶσαν γραφὴν, all Scripture, is θεόπνευστον, inspired by God. For if the concepts of all the things which it contains were not inspired into the sacred writers while writing, but only of sublime things which exceed the light of nature and the grasp of human reason, while in other things they were governed by the assistance of the Holy Spirit at least in the manner already mentioned, then not the whole Scripture, but only those parts in which it contains supernatural things and those exceeding the grasp of human reason, would be θεόπνευστος or inspired by God. For θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration differs from the governance of the writer through the assistance of the Holy Spirit, so that he does not commit an error or a lapse of memory in writing. For the latter only then exerts itself when the intellect of the writer inclines toward error or something indecent while writing, by bending him otherwise, and by suggesting, through impressed species supernaturally excited, another concept conformable to the matter and not alien to what is proper, while it leaves him to his own judgment in writing the rest. But the former exerts itself in the whole act of writing, by suggesting to the intellect of the writer the concepts of all the things to be written in that order in which they are to be recorded in letters, in the same manner in which those things that ought to be written by an amanuensis are suggested by the voice of the one dictating. And this, finally, makes Scripture θεόπνευστον, not that. Furthermore, those things which are above nature and by their loftiness exceed the grasp of human reason were not written separately, nor were the others, which were known to the sacred writers from the light of nature or through experience, written separately, so that it could be conveniently said that the Holy Spirit concurred in one way for the writing of the former and in another for the latter, but both are mixed in one uninterrupted context and series, so that it must be that either both or neither were written by divine inspiration. Although it was not necessary for the concepts of the things of the latter order to be inspired into the intellect of the sacred writers in order for the things themselves to be known to them, since they were already known to them beforehand; yet it was necessary that in what order and context, according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, together with the other things exceeding the light of nature they ought to be committed to writing, and in what place each thing ought to be set, just as it is not necessary for the things themselves to be made known to an amanuensis to whom a letter about the most well-known matters is dictated for the pen, yet it is necessary that the order and context in which they ought to be written down according to the mind of the Author, and what ought to be placed first and what later, be made known to him. But enough concerning the concepts of things to be consigned to writing, which, since the Pauline saying II Tim. III. 16 declares them all to have been inspired by God without distinction, we see no reason why anyone should deny.

VII. Nor does the praised Apostle seem to signify less clearly in the same and already frequently cited passage that the concepts of the words also, by which Holy Scripture is consigned, were inspired to the sacred writers, and he signifies this likewise by the fact that he calls the whole Scripture θεόπνευστον absolutely, simply, and without any restriction. For Holy Scripture has it from the characters of the words and letters written that it is Scripture. But if the words, by whose characters it is consigned, had not been suggested to the writers through θεοπνευςίαν and their concepts inspired, Holy Scripture could not properly, absolutely, and simply, but only improperly, in a qualified sense, and at least as regards the concepts of the things signified, be called and be able to be said to be θεόπνευστος, inspired by God, just as Scripture translated into another language by human effort cannot be called properly, absolutely, and simply θεόπνευστος, because the formal words of which it consists were not suggested by the Holy Spirit through inspiration, although it may be called θεόπνευστος in a qualified sense and with a qualification, namely as regards the concepts of the things once inspired to the sacred writers, which are signified by the words of the version. To which is added that in I Cor. II. 13. Paul expressly writes that he and the other Apostles spoke or preached the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery, not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches. But the words which they used while preaching, the Holy Spirit taught them, just as the wisdom hidden in a mystery, through inspiration. For this manner of teaching the Apostles and instructing them for the undertaking of the ministry of the Word was customary for the Holy Spirit at that time. Therefore, they also committed it to writing in words not which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit taught them, by inspiring in them the concepts of those words with which they [wrote] to Scripture, not by other words, not by this other context, style and manner of speaking were they to be directed to be recorded. For it has been said more than once that the method of writing and speaking is the same, as far as the present is concerned.

VIII. But here also human curiosity has something to object: namely, that the words by which Holy Scripture is recorded are taken from common usage, and were already known to the sacred writers from their habit of speaking, so that there was no need for their concepts to be inspired into them; furthermore, that the diversity of style, which is detected in the different parts and books of Scripture, is an unmistakable indication that each writer used his own words and manner of speaking, to which he was accustomed, in composing Scripture, and not all words received from the one Holy Spirit through inspiration.

IX. But what we have just adduced from 2 Timothy 3:16 and 1 Corinthians 2:13, and have used to establish the inspiration of the concepts by which the very words to be recorded in writing were suggested, also stands against this objection. Nor does the diversity of style objected to us, or the contention that the words of Scripture were taken from common usage and were already known to the sacred writers, hinder us in any way. For as regards the former objection, although we by no means deny the diversity of style which is observed in the books and writings of the different authors, we nevertheless deny that it necessarily follows from this that the sacred writers used their own words in recording Scripture, and not words received from the Holy Spirit through their inspired concepts; but on the contrary, rather, because Paul calls Scripture, which essentially embraces the very written characters of the words, θεόπνευστον, and openly testifies that the Holy Spirit taught its authors the very words which they used in preaching and writing, as has just been shown; it must be concluded from this that the Holy Spirit, in inspiring the concepts of the words by which the very words were suggested during the writing, accommodated Himself to the genius, capacity, and accustomed manner of speaking of each writer, so that their speech and writing would not be distorted and forced for them, just as grace otherwise imitates and perfects, but does not destroy, nature. But as for the other objection, the answer is that it happens daily that those who dictate letters to an amanuensis use words taken from common usage, and whose force and meaning are known to the amanuensis. Why could the Holy Spirit not also have suggested to the sacred writers the words by which Holy Scripture is recorded, through their inspired concepts, and as it were dictate them into the pen, notwithstanding that the words were taken from usage and were already known to them beforehand. Nor is there any reason to say that their inspiration was thus not necessary, but superfluous. For although it was not necessary that the words and their power of signifying should become known to the sacred writers, since they were already known to them beforehand; yet it was necessary that it should become known to them in what order and context of words the Scripture was to be recorded, so that it might turn out to be entirely conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit: just as it is not necessary for a copyist that the very words, whose power of signifying he knows, be dictated to his pen so that the words and their meanings may become known to him in themselves, but so that it may become known to him in what order and context of words the letter is to be recorded, so that it may turn out to be entirely conformable to the mind of the Author.

X. Therefore, the whole of what God, as the principal cause, efficiently contributed to the composing of Scripture, consists in the inspiration both of the things which are contained recorded therein, and of the words by which they are recorded, and that both concepts are the term produced by the act of inspiration in the intellect of the sacred writers, from which they also differ only modally and as a thing differs from the mode of a thing.

Latin:

III.

Causa efficiens igitur Scripturæ sacræ, eaque principalis, Deus, vel, quod eodem redit, Spiritus sanctus est: causalitas autem, sive ratio formalis, quâ Spiritus sanctus in esse causæ illius constitutus est, & in illam influxum præbuit suum, est θεοπνευσία sive inspiratio divina.

I. Quanquam differunt nomina Deus & Spiritus sanctus, quòd illo Deus ratione essentiæ, quæ omnibus tribus personis communis est; hoc tertia persona divinitatis denotatur, influxus tamen, quem in Scripturam Deus præbet, inspiratio scilicet conceptuum, cùm rerum, tum verborum, quæ scribenda erant, est opus ad extra, & perinde, ut alia opera ad extra, omnibus tribus personis communis. Quamobrem rectè Scriptura Deo sub nomine essentiali, omnibus tribus personis communi, tanquam causæ efficienti adscribitur. Spiritui sancto autem adscribitur eadem, velut causæ efficienti, per appropriationem, sive modo loquendi, quo quod toti SS. Trinitati convenit, Spiritui sancto, velut opus ei proprium, adscribitur. Quæ Scripturis sacris usitata locutio est. Sic David dicit, Spiritum Domini loquutum esse per se, & sermonem ejus esse per ipsius linguam factum, II. Sam. XXIII. 2. Et Paulus: Deus, inquit, nobis revelavit per Spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei, I. Cor. II. 10. Et rursum: Nos non Spiritum mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum, qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus, quæ à Christo donata sint nobis. Quæ & loquimur, non sermonibus, quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, ibid. v. 11. 12.

II. Causalitatem autem, quâ influxum Deus in Scripturam præbuit, consistere in θεοπνευσίᾳ sive divina inspiratione, clarè docet Paulus loco ex II. Tim. III. 19. sæpiùs allegato, ubi totam Scripturam dicit esse θεόπνευστον, à Deo inspiratam. Denominat verò eam θεόπνευστον, à Deo inspiratam, à θεοπνευσίᾳ i. e. divina inspiratione, velut à ratione formali, per quam à Deo efficienter dependet, & qua Deus in esse causæ efficientis illius constituitur.

III. Explicaturo igitur distinctiùs, ad concinnandam Scripturam quid Deus; quid item Scriptores sacri efficienter contulerint, & quæ illius, quæ item horum partes & munia fuerint, primò omnium de θεοπνευσίᾳ sive divinâ inspiratione dispiciendum, & quem terminum productum in ea habuerit, habeatque, explicandum venit. Quicquid enim Deus efficienter ad eam concinnandam contulit, totum per θεοπνευσίαν contulit. Quæ autem in Scriptura sacra, perinde ut in alia quavis Scriptura, quocunque modo continentur, sunt (1) Vocum literarumque characteres, in charta picti sive scripti. (2) Voces ipsæ, quarum signa sunt characteres scripti. (3) Res, vocibus significatæ, & (4) Conceptus, cùm rerum, per voces significatarum, tùm ipsarum vocum. Et characteres quidem literarum ac vocum pictos sive scriptos continet Scriptura actu & formaliter; ipsas res verò illarumque conceptus, ut & voces atque conceptus illarum potentiâ tantùm & virtualiter, in quantum scilicet vocum characteres scripti, ex hominum placito sive impositione vim habent significandi & repræsentandi cùm voces, tùm res, quarum signa voces sunt, & utrarumque conceptus. Necesse igitur est, ut θεοπνευςία sive divina inspiratio in concinnanda Scriptura sacra terminata fuerit vel ad externum scriptionis actum, ipsosque literarum & vocum characteres, atramento in charta pictos ac scriptos, vel ad ipsas voces, quarum signa sunt characteres scripti, & ad res, quarum signa voces sunt, secundùm suum esse reale, vel denique ad conceptus cùm rerum tum vocum, per quos & res & voces objectivè in intellectu sunt. Sed primum dici non potest. Nam θεοπνευςία est actio spiritualis, vocum verò & literarum characteres atramento in charta picti ac scripti, materiales sunt. Nulla autem actio spiritualis ad materiale quid terminari potest: cùm spirituale & materiale ut res & res; actio autem & ejus terminus tantùm ut res & rei modus sive modaliter differant. Prætereà θεοπνευςία subjectivè inest hominis intellectui; scriptio verò & characteres scripti subjectivè insunt chartæ. Neque secundum dici potest. Nam voces & res, vocibus significatæ, secundum suum esse reale, sunt extra intellectum; θεοπνευςία autem intellectui, uti dictum, subjectivè inest, cujus terminum productum etiam intellectui inesse necesse est. Actionis enim & ejus termini producti oportet esse unum & idem subjectum, cùm, uti dictum, tantùm modaliter differant. Relinquitur ergò, quod terminata fuerit θεοπνευςία sive inspiratio divina in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu vel ad conceptus rerum, quæ consignandæ, vel ad conceptus vocum, quibus consignandæ erant, vel ad conceptus rerum & vocum simul. Ad alterutrosne? & ad quos? an ad utrosque terminata fuerit? in hoc demum vertitur cardo rei.

IV. Et sanè quòd ad conceptus rerum, quæ in literas referri debebant, terminata fuerit, vix dubium esse potest. Nihil enim dabatur in intellectu Scriptorum sacrorum, quod per θεοπνευςίαν in eo productum dici poterat, præter conceptus rerum & vocum scribendarum. Quamvis verò conceptus rerum soli & absque conceptibus vocum potuerint inspirari, non tamen contrà conceptus vocum, quæ sunt signa rerum, absque conceptibus rerum inspirari potuerunt, cùm voces, animo conceptæ, simul conceptus rerum, quarum signa sunt, intellectui ingerant, nisi forte quis dicere velit, conceptus vocum fuisse intellectui illorum inspiratos, absque illarum vi significandi, quod absurdum. Scriptores sacri enim docebant etiam voce, quæ ex divina revelatione literis consignanda acceperant. Necesse ergo est, ut si conceptus vocum scribendarum acceperunt per inspirationem, etiam illarum vim significandi, atque adeò simul conceptus rerum significatarum per inspirationem à Deo acceperint. Vel ergo rerum conceptus soli, vel vocum & rerum conceptus simul, illorum intellectui inspirati fuerunt. Utrum elegeris, semper manebit fixum & firmum, quod divina inspiratio in intellectu sacrorum Scriptorum terminata fuerit ad conceptus rerum literis consignandarum. Sin neutrum elegeris, nihil in intellectu sacrorum Scriptorum manebit reliquum, ad quod θεοπνευσία sive divina revelatio fuerit terminata, atque sic Scriptura sacra planè non erit θεόπνευστος, contrà quàm Paulus dicit, eam totam esse θεόπνευστον. Prætereà Scriptores sacri ipsimet testantur, se accepisse notitiam rerum sive voce tradendarum, sive scriptis consignandarum, à Deo per revelationem. Nobis autem, inquit Paulus 1. Cor. II, 10. Deus revelavit per Spiritum suum, puta sapientiam Dei in mysterio, quæ est recondita, quam præfinierat ante secula, in gloriam nostram &c. de qua præced. v. 6. seqq. egerat. Revelavit autem illis hanc in mysterio reconditam sapientiam modo tum usitato, non per alloquium externum, neque per somnia & visiones: his enim revelationum modis Deus tunc temporis vel non, vel saltem rarissimè utebatur; sed per locutionem internam, sive quod idem est, per inspirationem, ita ut ipsæ sub illa Dei sapientia contentæ res ipsorum intellectui innotescerent. Quod fieri non potuit, nisi per illarum conceptus, per inspirationem in illorum intellectu productos, sive per conceptus, illorum intellectui inspiratos. Quid? quod ipsæ res, Scripturæ verbis significatæ, illarumque conceptus velut anima sunt Scripturæ, qui si Scriptorum sacrorum intellectui inspirati non fuissent, non appareret, quomodò Scriptura θεόπνευστος, h. e. illorum intellectui divinitus inspirata dici à Paulo potuisset.

V. Sed ad hæc forte quis objiciat, de mysteriis rebusque, humanæ rationis captum excedentibus, concedi quidem, quòd illarum conceptus Scriptoribus sacris à Deo fuerint inspirati; in Scripturis sacris autem contineri alia multa, quæ Scriptoribus sacris, priusquam calamo manum ad scribendum admoverent, ex lumine naturæ, vel ex experientia nota erant. Horum verò conceptus cur illorum intellectui inter scribendum supernaturaliter inspiratos dicamus, causæ nihil esse: cùm in his talibus consignandis sufficere ipsis potuerit Spiritus S. assistentia, quâ gubernarentur, ne errorem aut memoriæ lapsum, vel quicquam à vero & decoro alieni admitterent.

VI. Verum huic objectioni opponimus, quòd Paulus disertè dicit, πᾶσαν γραφὴν totam Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον, inspiratam à Deo. Si enim non omnium, quas continet, rerum conceptus Scriptoribus sacris inter scribendum inspirati essent, sed tantum rerum sublimium, quæ naturæ lumen humanæque rationis captum excedunt, in cæteris verò Spiritus sancti adsistentiâ saltem modo jam dicto gubernati essent, tùm non Scriptura tota, sed iis saltem partibus, quibus res supernaturales & humanæ rationis captum excedentes continet, θεόπνευστος sive à Deo inspirata esset. Differunt enim θεοπνευσία sive inspiratio divina, & gubernatio Scriptoris per adsistentiam Spiritus sancti, ne in scribendo errorem vel memoriæ lapsum committat. Hæc enim tùm demum sese exerit, cùm intellectus Scriptoris in errorem vel indecens quippiam inter scribendum inclinat, flectendo eum aliter, & per species impressas, supernaturaliter excitatas, alium rei conformem, nec à decoro alienum conceptum suggerendo, cætera verò suo eum arbitratui in scribendo relinquit. Illa verò exerit se in toto scriptionis actu, suggerendo Scriptoris intellectui conceptus rerum scribendarum omnium eo ordine, quo literis consignandæ sunt, eundem in modum, quo amanuensi dictantis voce suggeruntur, quæ ab ipso scribi debent. Atque hæc demum efficit Scripturam θεόπνευστον, non illa. Prætereà quæ supra naturam sunt, & altitudine suâ humanæ rationis captum excedunt, non seorsim, nec seorsim cætera, quæ ex lumine naturæ, vel per experientiam Scriptoribus sacris nota erant, scripta sunt, ut alio modo ad illorum; alio ad horum scriptionem Spiritum S. concurrisse commodè dici possit, sed mixtim utraque in uno non interrupto contextu ac serie, ut vel utraque vel neutra ex divina inspiratione scripta esse oporteat. Quamvis verò conceptus rerum posterioris ordinis Scriptorum sacrorum intellectui inspirari, necessarium non esset, ut ipsæ res iis innotescerent: cùm jam antè ipsis notæ essent; necessarium tamen fuit, ut quo ordine & contextu, ad mentem Spiritus sancti, unà cum cæteris lumen naturæ excedentibus rebus in literas referri, & quo unumquodque loco collocari deberet innotesceret, perinde ut amanuensi epistolam de rebus notissimis dictari in calamum, necessarium non est, ut ipsæ res ipsi innotescant, necessarium tamen est, ut quo ordine & contextu, ad mentem Auctoris perscribi, quid prius, quid posteriùs locari debeat, ipsi innotescat. Sed satis de conceptibus rerum, literis consignandarum, quos sine discrimine omnes Scriptoribus sacris, vi dicti Paulini II. Tim. III. 16. à Deo inspiratos fuisse, cur quis inficias eat, causæ nihil videmus.

VII. Neque minùs clarè Apostolus laudatus in eodem jam & sæpiùs allegato loco significare videtur, conceptus vocum etiam, quibus consignata est Scriptura sacra, fuisse Scriptoribus sacris inspiratos, idque similiter per hoc significat, quod absolutè, simpliciter, & absque ulla restrictione Scripturam totam θεόπνευστον dicit. Scriptura sacra enim ex vocum & literarum characteribus scriptis habet, quòd Scriptura est. Si verò voces, quarum characteribus consignata est, Scriptoribus non fuissent suggestæ per θεοπνευςίαν & inspiratos illarum conceptus, Scriptura sacra non propriè, non absolutè & simpliciter, sed impropriè, secundum quid & quoad conceptus rerum significatarum saltem esset dicique posset θεόπνευστος, inspirata à Deo, perinde ut Scriptura, humano studio in aliam linguam translata, propriè, absolutè & simpliciter θεόπνευστος dici non potest, quòd ipsa verba formalia, quibus constat, à Spiritu sancto per inspirationem suggesta non sint, licet secundum quid & cum apposito θεόπνευστος dici queat, nempe quoad conceptus rerum, Scriptoribus sacris olim inspiratos, qui verbis versionis significantur. Quò accedit, quod in I Cor. II. 13. Paulus expressè scribit, se & Apostolos alios locutos esse sive prædicâsse sapientiam Dei, in mysterio reconditam, non sermonibus, quos humana docet sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus. Sermones verò, quibus inter prædicandum usi sunt, docuit eos Spiritus S. perinde ut sapientiam in mysterio reconditam, per inspirationem. Hic enim modus docendi Apostolos, eosque ad obeundum Verbi ministerium instruendi Spiritui S. tum temporis consuetus erat. Ergo & in literas eam retulerunt verbis, non quæ humana docet sapientia, sed quæ eosdem docuit Spiritus sanctus, inspirando ipsis conceptus illorum, quibus ad Scripturam his, non aliis, verbis, hoc non alio contextu, stylo & genere dicendi consignandam dirigerentur. Esse enim scriptionis & locutionis eandem, quoad præsens, rationem, plus simplici vice dictum est.

VIII. Sed hîc etiam habet humana curiositas, quod objiciat: nempè verba, quibus consignata est Scriptura sacra, esse ex usu desumta, & fuisse Scriptoribus sacris jam antè ex usu loquendi nota, ut illorum conceptus ipsis inspirari nihil opus fuerit: prætereà styli diversitatem, quæ in diversis Scripturæ partibus & libris deprehenditur, indicio non obscuro esse, unumquemque Scriptorem usum esse in concinnanda Scriptura suis verbis, & genere dicendi, sibi consueto, non omnes verbis, ab uno Spiritu S. per inspirationem acceptis.

IX. Verum huic etiam objectioni obstant, quæ modò ex II. Tim. III. 16. & ex I. Cor. II. 13. adduximus, & ad inspirationem conceptuum, quibus ipsa literis consignanda verba suggesta fuerint, adstruendam adhibuimus. Neque quicquam nobis obest vel objecta diversitas styli, vel quòd verba Scripturæ ex usu desumta & Scriptoribus sacris jam antè nota fuisse contenditur. Quod enim ad priorem attinet objectionem, quamvis diversitatem styli, quæ in diversorum Scriptorum libris & scriptis conspicitur, minimè diffiteamur, negamus tamen, necessariò hinc sequi, Scriptores sacros usos esse in consignanda Scriptura suis verbis, non verbis, à Spiritu sancto per inspiratos illorum conceptus acceptis, sed contrà potius, quia Paulus Scripturam, ipsos vocum characteres scriptos essentialiter complectentem, θεόπνευστον appellat, & apertè testatur, Spiritum sanctum docuisse ejus conditores ipsa verba, quibus in prædicando & scribendo usi sunt, ut modò ostensum; concludendum hinc est, Spiritum S. in inspirandis verborum conceptibus, quibus ipsa verba inter scribendum suggerebantur, accommodâsse se cujusque Scriptoris ingenio, captui & generi dicendi consueto, ne contorta & violenta ipsis esset sua oratio & Scriptura, sicut aliàs gratia imitatur & perficit, non destruit naturam.
