Quod verò alteram concernit objectionem, resp. quotidiè contingere, ut qui amanuensi in calamum dictitant Epistolas, utantur verbis, ex usu desumtis, & quorum vis ac significatio amanuensi nota est. Quidni & Spiritus sanctus potuerit Scriptoribus sacris verba, quibus Scriptura sacra consignata est, per inspiratos illorum conceptus suggerere & quasi in calamum dictitare, non obstante, quod verba ex usu desumta & jam antè ipsis nota fuerint. Neque est, quod dicatur, illorum inspirationem sic non fuisse necessariam, sed superfluam. Licet enim necessaria non fuerit, ut verba illorumque vis significandi Scriptoribus sacris innotescerent: cùm jam antè ipsis nota fuerint; necessaria tamen fuit, ut quo verborum ordine & contextu consignanda esset Scriptura, ipsis innotesceret, quò menti Spiritus sancti ea prorsus evaderet conformis: perinde ut amanvensi ipsa verba, quorum vim significandi cognitam habet, in calamum dictari necessarium non est, ut verba illorumque significationes in se ipsi innotescant, sed ut ei innotescat, quo verborum ordine & contextu Epistola, ut menti Auctoris prorsus conformis evadat, consignanda sit.

X. Totum ergo, quod ad concinnandam Scripturam Deus, velut causa principalis, efficienter contulit, consistit in inspiratione cùm rerum, quæ in eo consignatæ continentur, tùm vocum, quibus consignatæ sunt, atque conceptus utrosque esse terminum, per inspirationis actum in intellectu Scriptorum sacrorum productum, à quo etiam tantùm modaliter & ut res à rei modo, differunt.


### IV. The less principal efficient cause of Holy Scripture are the holy men who, with…

IV.

The less principal efficient cause of Holy Scripture are the holy men who, with the Holy Spirit inspiring them, set their hand to the pen and adorned Scripture in diverse places and times: namely, the Prophets under the Old, and the Apostles under the New Covenant or Testament.

I. The founders of the Scripture of the O.T. are commonly called Prophets, not because all, but because most of them were Prophets properly so called. For Prophets properly so called under the O.T. were public teachers of the Church, whose duty it was to explain the Mosaic Law and to defend it from corruptions, to rebuke the sins of the people, and to predict what good things by the grace of God were impending for the penitent, and likewise what evils by the just judgment of God were impending for the refractory and obstinate, but especially to announce and inculcate the coming of the Messiah, whom the law looked toward and foreshadowed, and his benefits to the people, for the consolation of the afflicted. In the class of writers of the O.T., however, are also contained David, Solomon, and Daniel, who did not perform the public duty of teaching in the Church, and thus were not Prophets did not hold the office. For this one was among the Princes of the Kings of Babylon and Persia; that one and the other were Kings of Israel. The name of Prophet must therefore be taken here in a looser sense for any θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed] writer of the Old Testament, or it must be said that the sacred writers of the O.T. are denominated Prophets by synecdoche from the more prominent part, because most of them were Prophets by office and strictly so called. II. The reason is the same for the writers of the New Testament, who are commonly called Apostles, not because all, but because most or almost all were Apostles, the denomination again being taken by synecdoche from the more prominent part. For in their number are also Luke, the writer of the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, and likewise Mark, the writer of his own Gospel, who nevertheless were not of the College of the Apostles. Perhaps it is also not inconveniently said that the name of Apostle is taken here in a looser sense, insofar as Apostolic Men also, or companions of the Apostles and co-workers in teaching the Gospel and planting the Church throughout the world, are included in it: in which sense Paul in Rom. XVI. 7 calls Andronicus and Junia notable among the Apostles, and in Phil. II. 25 calls Epaphroditus the Apostle of the Philippians. III. Some distinguish the writers of the N.T. into Apostles and Evangelists. But this distinction is not adequate. For if the writers of the Evangelical history are called Evangelists, Matthew and John are Evangelists; and yet they were of the college of the Apostles and thus Apostles strictly so called.

Latin:

IV.

Causa efficiens minus principalis Scripturæ sacræ sunt Viri sancti, qui Spiritu S. inspirante manum calamo admoverunt, Scripturamque locis & temporibus diversis adornârunt: Prophetæ scilicet sub Veteri, & Apostoli sub Novo Fœdere sive Testamento.

I. Conditores Scripturæ V. T. dicuntur communiter Prophetæ, non quòd omnes, sed quòd plerique propriè dicti Prophetæ fuerint. Nam propriè dicti Prophetæ sub V. T. erant publici Ecclesiæ Doctores, quorum munus erat Legem Mosaicam explicare & à corruptelis vindicare, redarguere peccata populi, & quæ Dei gratiâ bona pœnitentibus; quæ item refractariis & obstinatis mala, Dei justo judicio, imminerent, prædicere, cumprimis verò adventum Messiæ, quem lex respiciebat & adumbrabat, ejusque beneficia populo, in solatium afflictorum, denunciare & inculcare. In classe autem Scriptorum V. T. continentur etiam David, Salomon & Daniel, qui publico docendi munere in Ecclesia functi non sunt, atque adeò Prophetæ officio non fuerunt. Hic enim unus ex Proceribus Regum Babyloniæ & Persiæ; iste & ille Reges Israëlis fuerunt. Accipiendum ergo hic est Prophetæ nomen in significatu laxiori pro quovis Scriptore Veteris Testamenti θεοπνεύστῳ, vel dicendum, Scriptores sacros V. T. denominari Prophetas per synecdochen à parte potiori, quòd plerique officio & propriè dicti Prophetæ fuerint. II. Par ratio est Scriptorum Novi Testamenti, qui communiter Apostoli dicuntur non quòd omnes, sed quòd plerique sive ferè omnes Apostoli fuerint, denominatione rursum per synecdochen à parte potiori desumtâ. In illorum numero enim sunt etiam Lucas, Evangelii & Actorum Apostolicorum Scriptor, itemque Marcus, sui Scriptor Evangelii, qui tamen ex Apostolorum Collegio non fuerunt. Forsan etiam non incommodè dicitur, Apostoli nomen accipi hîc in significatu laxiori, prout Viri Apostolici quoque sive Apostolorum socii & in docendo Evangelio ac plantanda per orbem Ecclesia Coadjutores, eo comprehenduntur: quem in sensum Paulus Rom. XVI. 7. Andronicum & Juniam insignes inter Apostolos, & Phil. II. 25. Epaphroditum Philippensium Apostolum appellat. III. Quidam distinguunt Scriptores N. T. in Apostolos & Evangelistas. Sed distinctio hæc adæquata non est. Si enim Evangelistæ dicantur historiæ Evangelicæ Scriptores, Matthæus & Johannes Evangelistæ sunt; & tamen ex collegio Apostolorum atque adeò Apostoli strictè sic dicti fuerunt.


### V. But since a less principal or instrumental cause cannot act and influence an…

V.

But since a less principal or instrumental cause cannot act and influence an effect unless dependently upon the principal cause, and moved by the same, it is necessary that the Prophets and Apostles, by the very fact that they were the less principal or instrumental cause of the composing of sacred Scripture, recorded it dependently upon the Holy Spirit and moved by Him. Two things are required for an instrumental cause. One, that it influence the effect. The other, that it influence it with a power less noble than is required to produce it. The former is common to it with the principal cause; the latter, however, is proper to it, by which it is distinguished from the principal cause. For it is of the proper nature of the latter that it influences the effect with a power not less noble than is required to produce it; but it is of the proper nature of the former that it influences with a power more ignoble than is required for producing the effect. And by this very fact, that the acting power of an instrumental cause is more ignoble and insufficient for producing the effect, it is necessary that it depend in acting upon the principal cause, and be elevated by its power to produce it: just as a saw cannot cut wood unless moved by the carpenter and applied to the wood being cut; and a pen cannot write unless moved and applied by the guidance of the scribe to form letters. The same holds true of the sacred writers, whose power of acting was much more ignoble than was required for composing the sacred Scriptures, as will be evident from what is to be said presently.

VI.

They depended, however, upon Him both as to the species and as to the exercise of the act.

By the species of the act of writing we understand the act of writing, viewed in terms of the context of the words and the things signified, from which it receives its specific being. We constitute the exercise of the act of writing, however, in the writing itself as exercised, or in the act of writing itself.

VII.

As to the species of the act, they depended precisely upon θεοπνευσίά, or divine inspiration, by which the Holy Spirit suggested to them what was to be written, and dictated it to their intellect as if into a pen,

I. Above in thesis III we taught that the causality by which the Holy Spirit, as the principal cause, provided His influence upon the sacred Scriptures, consists in θεοπνευσίά or divine inspiration. Now, this is the perpetual relationship between the principal and instrumental causes, that the causality of the principal cause, by which it exerts influence into the being of the effect to be produced, is also the formal reason upon which the instrumental cause depends in acting, and by which it is elevated by the principal cause to produce the effect.

II. Moreover, for one who wishes to adorn any Scripture, three things are necessary. One, that he have the things which he wishes to comprehend in writing and to propose and explain to others conceived and known in his mind: the second, that he also have at hand the words by which he may express the concepts of his mind. The third, that he be skilled in the art of writing. Regarding the third requirement, which, in regard to Scripture viewed in its specific being, does not pertains, we shall say later. But as regards the first and second requirement, it is certain that the power of acting proper to the sacred writers was much inferior and more ignoble than was required for composing the sacred Scriptures. For first, the principal things which were to be committed to writing were supernatural, and exceeded the grasp of human reason by a very long way. For they concerned mysteries, kept silent in eternal times, Rom. XVI. 25, mysteries hidden from the ages in God, Eph. III. 9, Col. I. 26, wisdom, not of this age, nor of the princes of this age, but the wisdom of God in a mystery (lying hidden) which God had foreordained before the ages unto our glory, I. Cor. II. 7, the knowledge and concepts of which the sacred writers could not procure for themselves from themselves and their own powers. Although indeed things known from the light of nature and through experience are here and there mixed into the Scriptures, inasmuch as the Apostles had conversed with Christ in the days of his flesh, and had heard him teaching in person, and had seen with their own eyes the things which had been done by him; and the Apostolic men had also received what they wrote from the report of the Apostles, as is evident from Luke I. 2, yet this knowledge of the things to be written, acquired through the intervention of the senses and the guidance of the light of nature, was not exempt from the danger of erring, and if they had adorned their writings under the guidance of this alone, they could not be an infallible rule and norm of faith. Therefore, in order that they might compose Scriptures which were of divine authority and of certain and indubitable faith, it was necessary that the very things which were to be committed to writing should be suggested by God immediately, and in that order in which they were to be consigned to writing. Furthermore, although the sacred Scriptures were consigned in words taken from usage, and the words themselves were already known to the sacred writers from usage, yet in order that they might be of divine and altogether infallible authority, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to suggest the very words themselves immediately to them in that context in which the concepts of the things were consigned, and in that order. He suggested both the things and the words through θεοπνευσίαν, or through inspired concepts of both things and words, as was shown at greater length in the previous thesis III, and by them he elevated their intellect, beyond their natural powers, to the composing of Scripture, to which it is altogether repugnant that anything false should underlie it.

III. In order that you may understand this more correctly, it must be known that the act of writing, by which someone composes any Scripture with words signifying by design to signify the thoughts of the mind to another, is indeed an external act, efficiently produced by his hand and pen, but with the intellect, through internal concepts of both things and words, directing the hand and pen, and the concepts of things and words are as it were the form and exemplary cause, to the imitation of which the intellect directs the hand and pen in writing, and constitutes Scripture in its specific being the things and words themselves, of which those are signs, and to which external Scripture is conformed; indeed, through this, that it is conformed to them, every Scripture has its own specific being. But if the intellect has the concepts of things and words from itself, and has acquired them for itself by its own powers, then the writer is the principal cause of the Scripture, fashioned in imitation of them. For the power by which he influences it, as regards its specific being, consists entirely in the concepts of things and words, which, because he has them from himself and his own powers, not suggested to him by another, he influences it indeed by a certain power of his own, and that not less noble than is required for producing or composing it in its specific being. But when the writer does not have the concepts of things and words from himself, but from another higher principle, e.g., from a man, dictating with a living voice or prescribing with a pen, and injecting them into his intellect through hearing or sight, or from God, suggesting the same through immediate inspiration, then he is the instrumental cause of the writing and the fashioned Scripture, as far as pertains to its specific being: because the power of acting, namely the concepts of things and words by which he directs the hand and pen in writing, is not his own, but that of a certain higher principle, namely either of God inspiring, or of a man dictating or prescribing. Because therefore the whole Scripture is θεόπνευστος, as Paul says in II Tim. III. 16. and the concepts both of the things which are recorded in letters, and of the words by which they are recorded, were suggested to them by the Holy Spirit through immediate inspiration, the sacred writers were indeed merely instrumental causes in fashioning Scripture, at least as far as pertains to their specific being. They did indeed employ their intellect to direct the hand and pen in writing, but the power of acting and directing the hand and pen was not their own, but supplied to them by the Holy Spirit, and therefore the Holy Spirit and the sacred writers concurred in composing it, as regards its specific being: the former by his own supernatural power to the intellect of the sacred writers, by inspiring the concepts of things and words, and by elevating their intellect through these to direct the hand and pen; but the latter by directing the hand and pen, yet by the power of the concepts inspired in them by the Holy Spirit, so that in this way the work of both in composing Scripture was one and undivided. Of the sacred writers indeed, directing the hand and pen in writing, immediately; and of the Holy Spirit, suggesting the concepts of things and words to their intellect through inspiration, and elevating it to direct the hand and pen. And this is how the sacred writers depended on the Holy Spirit and His inspiration in composing Scripture as regards the species of the act.

Latin:

V.

Cum verò causa minùs principalis sive instrumentalis agere & in effectum influere non possit, nisi dependenter à causa principali, & ab eadem mota, Prophetæ & Apostoli eo ipso quod concinnandæ Scripturæ sacræ causa minùs principalis sive instrumentalis fuerunt, ut dependenter a Spiritu S. & ab ipso moti eam consignârint necesse est. Ad causam instrumentalem requiruntur duo. Unum, ut influat in effectum. Alterum, ut influat in eum virtute ignobiliore, quàm ad ipsum producendum requiritur. Prius ei cum causa principali commune; posterius verò eidem proprium est, quo à causa principali distinguitur. De hujus enim ratione propria est, ut influat in effectum virtute non ignobiliore, quàm ad eum producendum requitur; de ratione propria illius autem est, ut influat virtute ignobiliori, quàm ad effectum producendum requiritur. Et hoc ipso, quòd causæ instrumentalis virtus agendi ignobilior & ad producendum effectum insufficiens est, necesse est, ut in agendo à causa principali dependeat, ejusque virtute ad eum producendum elevetur: sicut serra lignum secare, nisi à fabro lignario mota & secando ligno applicata; & calamus scribere non potest, nisi ductu scribæ ad pingendas literas motus & applicatus. Idem valet de Scriptoribus sacris, quorum virtus agendi multò ignobilior erat, quàm ad concinnandas Scripturas sacras requirebatur, ut ex mox dicendis patebit.

VI.

DEpendebant autem ab eo cùm quoad speciem, tùm quoad exercitium actus.

Per speciem actus scribendi intelligimus scriptionis actum, ratione contextus verborum & rerum significatarum, à quibus suum esse specificum accipit, spectatum. Exercitium verò actus scribendi constituimus in ipsa scriptione exercita, sive in ipso actu scribendi.

VII.

QVoad speciem actus dependebant præcisè à θεοπνευσίά, sive à divina inspiratione, quâ quæ scribenda essent, Spiritus sanctus ipsis suggerebat, & intellectui illorum quasi in calamum dictitabat,

I. Suprà thesi III. docuimus, causalitatem, quâ Spiritus sanctus velut causa principalis, influxum suum in Scripturas sacras præbuit, consistere in θεοπνευσίά sive divina inspiratione. Est autem hæc perpetua inter causas, principalem & instrumentalem, habitudo, ut causalitas causæ principalis, quâ in esse effectus producendi influit, sit etiam ratio formalis, à qua causa instrumentalis in agendo dependet, & quâ à causa principali ad producendum effectum elevatur.

II. Qui autem Scripturam aliquam adornare vult, ei tria necessaria sunt. Unum, ut res, quas scripto comprehendere, aliisque proponere & explicare vult, animo conceptas & cognitas habeat: alterum ut verba quoque, quibus conceptus mentis exprimat, in promtu habeat. Tertium ut artis scribendi peritus sit. De tertio requisito, quod ad Scripturam, in suo esse specifico spectatam, non pertinet, postea dicemus. Primum vero & secundum requisitum quod attinet, certum est, virtutem agendi propriam Scriptorum sacrorum multo fuisse inferiorem & ignobiliorem, quam ad Scripturas sacras concinnandas requirebatur. Primum enim res praecipuae, quae in literas referendae erant, supernaturales erant, & humanae rationis captum longissime excedebant. Concernebant enim mysteria, temporibus aeternis tacita, Rom. XVI. 25. mysteria, a seculis abscondita in Deo, Eph. III. 9. Col. I. 26. sapientiam, non seculi hujus, neque principum seculi hujus, sed sapientiam Dei in mysterio (latentem) quam praefinierat Deus ante secula in gloriam nostram, I. Cor. II. 7. quarum notitiam & conceptus Scriptores sacri ex se & suis viribus sibi comparare non poterant. Quanquam vero Scripturis passim admixtae sunt res, ex lumine naturae, & per experientiam notae, siquidem Apostoli cum Christo in diebus carnis suae conversati fuerant, eumque coram docentem audiverant, & quae ab ipso acta fuerant, oculis suis viderant; Viri Apostolici etiam ex Apostolorum relatione, quae scripserunt, acceperant, ut ex Luc. I. 2. constat, haec tamen sensuum interventu & luminis naturae ductu acquisita rerum scribendarum notitia non erat a periculo errandi exempta, & si hujus solius ductu Scripta sua adornassent, infallibilis regula & norma fidei ea esse non possent. Ut igitur concinnarent Scripturas, quae auctoritatis divinae, certaeque & indubitatae fidei essent, necessarium erat, ut ipsae res, quae in literas referendae erant, a Deo immediate, & eo ordine, quo literis consignandae erant, suggererentur. Deinde licet Scripturae sacrae consignatae sint verbis, ex usu desumtis, & verba ipsa Scriptoribus sacris jam ex usu nota fuerint, tamen ut divinae & prorsus infallibilis essent auctoritatis, visum est Spiritui sancto, ipsa etiam verba in eo, quo conceptus rerum consignati sunt, contextu, & eo ordine ipsis immediate suggerere. Suggessit aut cum res, tum verba per θεοπνευσίαν sive per inspiratos conceptus cum rerum tum vocum, ut superiori th. III. pluribus ostensum est, iisque illorum intellectum, ultra suas naturales vires, elevavit ad condendam Scripturam, cui falsum subesse prorsus repugnet.

III. Ut rectius hoc intelligas, sciendum est, scriptionis actum, quo quis Scripturam aliquam verbis, ex instituto significantibus, ad animi sensa alteri significanda concinnat, sit quidem actus externus, ejus manu & calamo efficienter productus, sed intellectu, per conceptus internos cùm rerum tum vocum, manum & calamum dirigente, & conceptus rerum ac vocum sint velut forma & causa exemplaris, ad cujus imitationem intellectus manum & calamum in scribendo dirigit, & Scripturam in suo esse specifico constituit. Ex conceptibus enim rerum & verborum, rebusq; ac verbis, quorum illi signa sunt, & quibus Scriptura externa conformatur; quin & per hoc, quod iis conformata est, habet Scriptura quæque suum esse specificum. Quod si conceptus rerum & verborum intellectus ex se habeat, suisque viribus sibi comparaverit, tum Scripturæ, ad illorum imitationem concinnatæ, Scriptor causa principalis est. Virtus enim, quâ in illam, quoad suum esse specificum, influit, consistit tota in conceptibus rerum & verborum, quos quia ex se & suis viribus habet, non ab alio sibi suggestos, influit utique in illam virtute quâdam suâ, eaque non ignobiliori, quàm ad eam, in suo esse specifico producendam sive conficiendam, requiritur. Quando autem conceptus rerum & vocum Scriptor non ex se habet, sed ex alio altiori principio, v. g. ab homine, voce viva dictante aut calamo præscribente, eosque per auditum vel visum ejus intellectui ingerente, vel à Deo, eosdem per immediatam inspirationem suggerente, tum scriptionis Scripturæque concinnatæ is causa instrumentalis est, quod quidem ad ejus esse specificum attinet: quia virtus agendi, conceptus scilicet rerum & vocum, quibus manum & calamum in scribendo dirigit, non est ipsius propria, sed altioris cujusdam principii, nempe vel Dei inspirantis, vel hominis dictitantis aut præscribentis. Quia ergo Scriptura tota θεόπνευστος est, dicente Paulo II. Tim. III. 16. & conceptus cùm rerum, quæ literis consignatæ sunt, tùm vocum, quibus consignatæ sunt, à Spiritu sancto per immediatam inspirationem ipsis suggesti sunt, in concinnanda Scriptura Scriptores sacri utique causæ merè instrumentales fuerunt, quantum quidem ad illorum esse specificum attinet. Adhibuerunt quidem intellectum ad dirigendam manum & calamum in scribendo, sed virtus agendi dirigendique manum & calamum non fuit ipsorum propria, sed à Spiritu sancto ipsis suppeditata, & concurrerunt proinde in illa conficienda, quoad ejus esse specificum, simul Spiritus sanctus & Scriptores sacri: ille suâ, Scriptorum sacrorum intellectui supernaturali virtute, conceptus rerum & vocum infpirando, & per easdem illorum intellectum ad dirigendam manum & calamum elevando; hic verò manum & calamum dirigendo, sed virtute conceptuum, à Spiritu sancto sibi infpiratorum, ut ita utrorumque in concinnanda Scriptura una indivisa fuerit opera. Scriptorum sacrorum quidem, dirigentium manum & calamum in scribendo, immediatè; & Spiritus sancti, conceptus rerum & vocum per inspirationem illorum intellectui suggerentis, eumque ad dirigendum manum ac calamum elevantis. Et hoc est Scriptores sacros dependisse à Spiritu sancto ejusque inspiratione in concinnanda Scriptura quoad speciem actus.


### VIII. As regards the exercise of the act, however, the same men depended on the Holy…

VIII.

As regards the exercise of the act, however, the same men depended on the Holy Spirit, exciting them to write both by the very θεοπνευσίαν or immediate inspiration, by which He suggested to them the concepts of the things and words to be written, and by an external command, or a certain internal instinct, or other incentives, by which they were induced to apply the hand to the pen and to compose Scripture.

I. That as regards the exercise of the act the sacred writers also depended on the Holy Spirit, Peter expressly teaches in Epist. II. ch. 1. 21. Saying, Prophecy was not brought in old time by the will of man, but φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου ἐλάλησαν οἱ ἅγιοι θεῦ ἄνθρωποι, moved by the Holy Spirit the holy men of God spoke.

Although Peter does not speak precisely of writing, but of speaking, by which the holy men of God uttered with living voice the prophecies which had come to them divinely, and communicated them with others; yet, as has often been said, the reason for speaking and writing, as far as the present is concerned, is the same, as the Apostle cited in this very place clearly signifies. For in the immediately preceding verse the same man speaks expressly of προφητεία γραφῆς i.e. of the Prophecy of Scripture, or of Prophetic Scripture, as Erasmus interpreted it, and he gives in this 21st verse the reason why it is not of private interpretation, namely because the Prophecy of Scripture was not brought in old time by the will or judgment of man; but if the Prophetic Scripture was brought in old time by writing, and as the holy men of God then brought their prophecies into public by voice,

Φερομενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε, moved by the Holy Spirit, they both adorned the Prophecy of Scripture or Prophetic Scripture and brought it forth into public view by writing, likewise Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύ- ματος ἁγίε, moved, impelled by the Holy Spirit, and thus in writing no less than in speaking they depended upon the Holy Spirit. But when he says that prophecy was not brought forth of old by the will of man, but that they spoke moved by the Holy Spirit, and thus also reduced their prophecies to writing, he clearly signifies that they did not bring their prophecies forth into public view by their own motion and choice, but from the motion of the Holy Spirit, both by voice and by writings, and thus they girded themselves for the exercise of the act of speaking and writing.

II. Moreover, they were moved by the Holy Spirit primarily through θεοπνευσίαν (divine inspiration) itself. For when the Holy Spirit suggested to them through inspiration those things which ought to be brought forth either by voice or committed to writing, he at the same time provided his influence for the exercise of the act of both preaching and writing.

That this may become clearer, I would have you know that θεοπνευσίαν or divine inspiration can be considered in two ways: one on the part of the act; the other on the part of the product produced, or on the part of the concepts of both things and words, to which the act of inspiration in the intellect of the sacred writers was terminated. Viewed in the latter way and on the part of the product, it did not differ from the inspired concepts, and it behaved as a form and exemplary cause, according to the imitation of which the external act of writing was instituted and Holy Scripture was composed, as was shown in the preceding thesis VII, Explanation no. III. But viewed in the former way and on the part of the act of inspiring, it was an action modally distinct from the inspired concepts, by which, while the concepts of things and words were efficiently produced in the intellect of the sacred writers, at the same time their will was excited, so that it might apply itself to the act of writing and to moving the hand to the pen at his command. Furthermore, they were also sometimes excited by the Holy Spirit to write by an express command of God, as is evident from the example of Moses Deut. XXXI. 19, Isaiah ch. VIII. 1, ch. XXX. 2, Habakkuk ch. II. 2, John Apoc. I. 11, 19, ch. II. 1, 8, 12, 18, etc. Although indeed these commands were given by God to these writers in certain cases at least, nor do we read that similar ones were given to them or to others concerning the whole Scripture which they composed while the Holy Spirit was inspiring them, yet it seems certain to us that if they did not always receive express commands from God to write, they were nevertheless always excited to write by an interior divine instinct, or by divine providence suggesting the occasion and incentives, so that concerning the will of God and his assistance through θεοπνευςίαν they were all and always as certain as those who wrote when and because of an express command of God were certain.

Latin:

VIII.

QVoad exercitium actus verò dependebant iidem à Spiritu sancto, excitante eos ad scribendum cùm per ipsammet θεοπνευσίαν sive immediatam inspirationem, quâ & rerum & vocum scribendarum conceptus iis suggessit, tum per mandatum externum, vel instinctum quendam internum, aut incentiva alia, quibus ad manum calamo adhibendam & Scripturam concinnandam inducti sunt.

I. Quod quoad exercitium actus etiam Scriptores sacri à Spiritu sancto dependerint, disertè docet Petrus Epist. II. c. 1. 21. Non, inquiens, voluntate hominis allata est olim Prophetia, sed φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου ἐλάλησαν οἱ ἅγιοι θεῦ ἄνθρωποι, acti à Spiritu sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines.

Quanquam verò Petrus non præcisè de scriptione loquitur, sed de locutione, quâ voce vivâ Prophetias, quæ divinitùs sibi obtigerant, sancti Dei homines protulerunt, & cum aliis communicârunt; est tamen, ut sæpè dictum, locutionis & scriptionis, quoad præsens, par ratio, ut hoc ipso in loco laudatus Apostolus clarè significat. Nam in proximè præcedente versu loquitur idem expressè de προφητεία γραφῆς h. e. de Prophetia Scripturæ, sive de Prophetica Scriptura, ut Erasmus interpretatus est, & reddit in hoc 21. versu rationem, cur ea non sit propriæ interpretationis, quòd scilicet non voluntate sive arbitratu hominis olim allata sit Prophetia Scripturæ autem sive Scriptura Prophetica olim allata est per scriptionem, & ut voce Prophetias suas sancti Dei homines tum protulerunt in publicum,

Φερομενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε, acti a Spiritu sancto, ita & Prophetiam Scripture sive Scripturam Propheticam adornarunt & per Scriptionem protulerunt in publicum itidem Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε, acti, impulsi à Spiritu sancto, atque adeò in scribendo non minùs, quàm in loquendo pependerunt à Spiritu sancto. Quando autem dicit, Prophetiam non esse allatam olim hominis voluntate, sed actos à Spiritu sancto locutos esse, & sic etiam in literas redegisse Prophetias suas, difertè significat, eos non suô motu & arbitratu, sed ex motione Spiritus sancti protulisse Prophetias suas in publicum, cùm voce tum scriptis, atque adeò ad exercitium actus loquendi & scribendi se accinxisse.

II. Acti autem sunt à Spiritu sancto primùm quidem per ipsam θεοπνευσίαν. Quando enim Spiritus sanctus, quæ sive voce proferri sive in literas referri debebant, iis per inspirationem suggessit, simul ad exercitium actus cùm prædicationis tùm scriptionis influxum suum præbuit.

Quod ut clariùs evadat, scias velim, θεοπνευσίαν sive divinam inspirationem posse considerari duobus modis: uno ex parte actus; altero ex parte termini producti, sive ex parte conceptuum cùm rerum, tùm vocum, ad quos inspirationis actus in intellectu Scriptorum sacrorum terminatus est. Posteriori modo & ex parte termini spectata nihil differebat à conceptibus inspiratis, habebatq́; se ut forma & causa exemplaris, ad cujus imitationem externus scriptionis actus instituebatur, & Scriptura sacra concinnabatur, ut in præced. th. VII. Explic. n. III. ostensum. Priori autem modo & ex parte actus inspirandi spectata, erat actio à conceptibus inspiratis modaliter distincta, quâ dum conceptus rerum & vocum in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu efficienter producebantur, simul illorum voluntas excitabatur, ut ad scriptionis actum manuḿque calamo admovendam imperio suo applicaret. Deinde excitati etiam sunt quandoque à Spiritu sancto ad scribendum expresso Dei mandato, ut patet exemplo Mosis Deut. XXXI. 19. Esaia c. VIII. 1. c. XXX. 2. Habacuci c. II. 2. Johannis Apoc. I. 11. 19. c. II. 1. 8. 12. 18. &c. Quamvis verò mandata hæc in certis saltem casibus Scriptoribus hisce à Deo data sint, nec similia ipsis vel aliis de tota, quam Spiritu sancto inspirante concinnârunt, Scriptura data esse legamus, certum tamen nobis videtur, quôd si non mandata expressa ad scribendum à Deo omnes & semper acceperint, interiori tamen instinctu divino, aut divinâ providentiâ occasionem & incentiva suggerente, ad scribendum semper excitati fuerint, ut de Dei voluntate ejusque adsistentia per θεοπνευςίαν omnes & semper tam fuerint certi, quàm certi fuerint illi, qui & quando ex mandato Dei expresso scripserunt.


### IX. But as regards the characters of letters and syllables to be painted and formed…

IX.

But as regards the characters of letters and syllables to be painted and formed with pen and ink on paper, the sacred writers in this respect acted as the principal cause.

The reason is: because in these the writer's intellect depends upon the art of writing, which, because it is natural in substance and contributes nothing to the Scripture in constituting it in its specific being, was without doubt acquired by them through human industry and study, by the force and guidance of which they subsequently painted the figures and characters of letters on paper, without the supernatural concurrence of God, and thus were the principal causes of the painted letters: just as an amanuensis, who produces a writing, while another dictates into his pen what is to be written, is, as regards the art of writing already previously instructed in relation to the painted figures of letters, as a principal cause; but as regards the context of the words and the signified things, arranged in a certain order, he acts as an instrumental cause: for in respect of these he depends upon the intellect and voice of another; but in respect of those he acts independently, and thus by his own sufficient power.

But if perhaps some were not skilled in the art of writing, it is likely that they were instructed in it by the Holy Spirit in an extraordinary and supernatural way. For the art of writing was a requirement necessary for the office of teaching in the Church to be duly performed. And then it was indeed supernatural in the mode of production, but once bestowed, in the mode of operation it undoubtedly behaved just as an art of writing acquired by human study in others. And so much for the efficient cause of Scripture, both principal and instrumental.

X.

The matter of Scripture can be established as twofold: that from which, and that about which. The distinction of matter into matter from which and matter about which is most commonly received in the Schools. Matter from which is said that from which something is composed or is a composite. Matter about which is otherwise called by one word the object.

XI.

The matter from which the Holy Scriptures are is the very words in which it was originally recorded: Hebrew indeed the Scriptures of the O.T., Greek truly the Scriptures of the N.T.

I. There is no doubt that the words in which Holy Scripture was originally recorded are its matter from which. For they enter into its constitution. Yet they do not enter into it as its form: since they do not give the specific being of Holy Scripture, but are common to it with other writings. They enter into it, therefore, as its matter, from which it is also composed.

II. The Scripture of the O.T. is composed or put together from the words of the Hebrew idiom, because the Hebrew language was the vernacular of the Jews, among whom its writers, Moses and the Prophets, lived. Which, however, we wish to be understood concerning the matter of the O.T. Scripture, named from the more important part. For there are contained in certain of its parts, namely in Daniel, Ezra, and Jeremiah, certain pericopes and chapters recorded in the Chaldean idiom, which is very closely related to the Hebrew. And in Jeremiah indeed a single verse, 11 of chapter X, exists written in the Chaldean idiom: because it contained those very words which the Jews in the Babylonian captivity, then being familiar with the Babylonian or Chaldean idiom, were about to use, and were about to detest the idols of the Babylonians and their worship, and were about to say: אלהיא די שמיא וארקא לא עבדו יאבדו מארעא ומן־תחות שמיא אלה i.e. The gods, who did not make heaven and earth, shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens. But those things which are mentioned in Daniel from v. 4 of chapter II up to chapter VIII concern matters done in Chaldea, which, as they existed recorded in the public acts of the Chaldeans in the Chaldean idiom, so also were they related by Daniel in the same idiom into his Scripture. In the book of Ezra, those things which are had from chapter IV v. 8 up to chapter VI v. 19 and from chapter VII v. 11 up to v. 27 were written after the Babylonian captivity, and concern letters written by Chaldeans to Chaldeans, which therefore were inserted by Ezra into his history in the same idiom in which they had been written by the Chaldeans, especially since

The Jews, having returned from the Babylonian captivity, were sufficiently skilled in that language. III. The books of the New Testament were all recorded in the Greek idiom, because this language, under the far and wide diffused empire of the Greeks, had for some centuries prevailed among the Jews as well as almost all the nations in which the Church was to be planted through Apostolic preaching, and was still, in the time of the Apostles, the most common and widely accepted in use. Yet they were not written in pure Greek, but in an idiom mixed with Hebraisms or Hellenistic, both because the sacred writers, namely the Apostles, were Jews by nation, to whom the Hellenistic or Hebraism-mixed language was familiar, and because it was necessary that the Gospel of Christ be announced first of all to the Jews, for the most part dispersed among the Gentiles, who themselves used not pure Greek but the Hellenistic language, as Paul testifies in Acts 13:46 and 19:5, although very few of them were converted to Christ, on account of the blindness which had befallen them by the just judgment of God. Whence, just as churches were planted everywhere through the Gospel preached in the Hellenistic language, so also the Apostles composed their writings, by which they instructed the churches they had planted while they were absent, in the same language. IV. Concerning the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews, most of the Fathers think differently, and, led by I know not what tradition, maintain that both books were originally composed in the Hebrew idiom, though hardly any of them dared to affirm that he had seen a Hebrew copy of either or both that was indeed the original. But there is no reason for us to descend into this dispute here, since the ancient Fathers themselves acknowledge that the Greek copies which exist today are θεόπνευστα (God-breathed), and were translated by God-breathed men from the Hebrew into the Greek language, and are therefore equal in authority to the other books of the New Testament, viewed in their original Greek text.

Latin:

IX.

QVod verò ad characteres literarum & syllabarum, calamo & atramento in charta pingendos & efformandos attinet, habebant Scriptores sacri horum intuitu se per modum causæ principalis.

Ratio est: quia in his Scriptoris intellectus dependet ab arte scriptoria, quæ quia in substantia naturalis est, & ad Scripturam, in suo esse specifico constituendam, nihil confert, dubio procul industriâ & studio humano ab ipsis acquisita fuit, cujus vi & ductu deinceps literarum figuras & characteres in charta pinxerunt, citra supernaturalem Dei concursum, atque adeò literarum pictarum causæ principales fuerunt: perinde ut Amanuensis, qui Scripturam conficit, altero, quæ scribenda sunt, in calamum dictante, arte scribendi jam ante instructus in ordine ad literarum figuras pictas ut prinpalis; ad verborum contextum verò & res significatas, certo ordine dispositas, ut instrumentalis causa se habet: horum intuitu enim dependet ab alterius intellectu & voce; illarum intuitu autem independenter, atque adeò virtute propria, eáque sufficiente agit.

Quod si qui forsan artis scriptoriæ periti non fuerunt, verosimile est, eos fuisse à Spiritu S. modo extraordinario & supernaturali illâ instructos. Erat enim ars scriptoria requisitum ad munus docendi in Ecclesia ritè obeundum, necessarium. Et tùm ea in productionis modo quidem supernaturalis fuit, sed semel collata in modo operationis procul dubio perinde, ut in aliis studio humano acquisita ars scriptoria, sese habuit. Et tantum de causa efficiente Scripturæ cùm principali tùm instrumentali.

X.

MAteria Scripturæ constitui potest duplex: ex qua, & circa quam. Distinctio materiæ in materiam ex qua & materiam circa quam in Scholis usu receptissima est. Materia ex qua dicitur, ex qua aliquid componitur aut compositum est. Materia circa quam aliàs uno verbo objectum appellatur.

XI.

MAteria ex qua Scripturæ sacræ sunt ipsa verba, quibus primitus consignata est: Ebræa quidem Scripturæ V. T. Græca verò Scripturæ N. T.

I. Verba, quibus primitùs consignata est Scriptura sacra, esse illius materiam ex qua, dubium non est. Ingrediuntur enim illius constitutionem. Neque tamen eam ingrediuntur ut illius forma: cùm non dent ipsum esse specificum Scripturæ sacræ, sed eidem cum Scripturis aliis communia sint. Ingrediuntur ergo illam, ut ejus materia, ex quibus etiam composita est.

II. Composita autem sive concinnata est Scriptura V. T. ex verbis idiomatis Ebræi, quòd Judæis, inter quos vixerunt ejus Scriptores, Moses & Prophetæ, sermo Ebræus vernaculus esset. Quod tamen de materia Scripturæ V. T. à parte potiori denominatâ, intellectum volumus. Continentur enim in ejus partibus quibusdam, in Danicle scilicet, Esdra & Jeremia, pericopæ & capita quædam, idiomate Chaldaico, quod Ebræo admodùm affine est, consignatæ. Et in Jeremia quidem unicus versus 11. cap. X. idiomate Chaldaico scriptus extat: quòd contineret ipsa illa verba, quibus aliquando Judæi in captivitate Babylonica, idiomatis Babylonici sive Chaldaici tum gnari, usuri, & Babyloniorum idola illorumq; cultum detestaturi, & dicturi essent: אלהיא די שמיא וארקא לא עבדו יאבדו מארעא ומן־תחות שמיא אלה i. e. Dii, qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt, pereant è terra & sub cœlo. Quæ autem in Daniele à v. 4. capitis II. usque ad cap. VIII. commemorantur, concernunt res, in Chaldæa gestas, quæ uti in Chaldæorum actis publicis idiomate Chaldaico consignatæ extabant, ita & à Daniele eodem idiomate in suam Scripturam relatæ sunt. In Esdræ libro quæ à cap. IV. v. 8. usque ad cap. VI. v. 19. & à cap. VII. v. 11. usque ad v. 27. habentur, post captivitatem Babylonicam scripta sunt, & concernunt Epistolas, à Chaldæis ad Chaldæos scriptas, quæ proinde eodem idiomate, quo à Chaldæis scriptæ fuerant, ab Esdra Historiæ suæ insertæ sunt, præsertim cùm

Judæi, ex captivitate Babylonica reduces, linguæ illius periti satis essent. III. Scripturæ N.T. libri Græco idiomate omnes consignati sunt, quòd lingua hæc sub Græcorum longè lateque diffuso imperio, inde ab aliquot seculis inter Judæos pariter & gentes ferè omnes, in quibus Ecclesia per prædicationem Apostolicam plantanda erat, invaluisset, & adhuc Apostolorum tempore omnium vulgatissima usuque receptissima esset. Neque tamen purè Græco, sed Ebraismis permixto sive Hellenistico idiomate conscripti sunt, cùm quod Scriptores sacri, Apostoli scilicet, natione Judæi essent, quibus Hellenistica sive Ebraismis permixta lingua familiaris erat, tùm quòd Judæis, maximam partem inter Gentes dispersis, qui & ipsi non purè Græca, sed Hellenistica lingua utebantur, primo omnium Evangelium de Christo annunciari oportebat, testante Paulo Act. XIII. 46. c. XIX. 5. quamvis pauci admodum ex illis converterentur ad Christum, ob excæcationem, quæ justo Dei judicio illis obtigerat. Unde ut per Evangelium, lingua Hellenistica prædicatum, passim plantabantur Ecclesiæ, ita & Apostoli scripta sua, quibus Ecclesias à se plantatas, absentes informabant, linguâ eâdem concinnarunt. IV. De Evangelio Matthæi & Epistola ad Ebræos diversum sentiunt pleriq; Patres, &, nescio, quâ traditione ducti librum utrumque Ebraico idiomate primitùs concinnatum fuisse statuunt, quorum tamen vix quisquam alterutrius vel utriusq; exemplar Ebræum, quod quidem primigenium esset, à se visum esse affirmare ausus est. Sed ut in hanc disputationem hic descendamus, causæ nihil est: cùm ipsi Patres veteres agnoscant, quæ hodiè extant, exemplaria Græca esse θεόπνευστα, & à Viris θεοπνεύστοις ex Ebræa in Græcam linguam translata, atque adeò cæteris N. T. libris, in suo primigenio textu Græco spectatis, auctoritate paria.


### XII. AND indeed words, viewed absolutely in themselves, just as the words of any…

XII.

AND indeed words, viewed absolutely in themselves, just as the words of any other Scripture, so also the words of the Hebrew and Greek idiom viewed absolutely in themselves, are the remote matter of Holy Scripture; but when constructed in context conveniently for the usage of speech and coordinated among themselves to represent the things themselves to the reader's intellect, they are the proximate matter of the same.

XIII.

The structure of words is not everywhere and throughout the entire Scripture one and the same, but just as the sacred writers were diverse in talent, affections, and customs, and accustomed to a diverse style of speaking; so also the structure of words and the style of Scripture varies.

I. The primary author of the whole Scripture is indeed one and the same, namely the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and as it were dictation into the pen the entire sacred Scripture was founded, as we taught above from Paul in 2 Timothy 3:16, calling the whole Scripture θεόπνευστον. The secondary authors, however, who as amanuenses of the Holy Spirit composed the sacred Scriptures by his inspiration at different times and places, were many, and diverse in talent and the nature of their speech. Although in merely human writings the style is usually accustomed to be conformed to the talent, affections, and customs of the primary author, and to the style of speaking accustomed to him, and not to the talent of the amanuensis and the style of speaking accustomed to him, the matter is otherwise with the divine Scriptures. For the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of the holy Prophets and Apostles, and also wrote as it were by their hand and pen, just as in speaking, so also in writing, or rather in suggesting the concepts of both things and words, which were to be either uttered by voice or recorded by letters, and thus in governing their tongue and hand, according to his most free will, accommodated and attuned himself to the talent, affections, and accustomed style of speaking of each one, so that their speech and Scripture flowed as it were naturally and as if from the natural disposition of each one.

II. That the style of Scripture efficiently depends upon the Holy Spirit as the principal or primary author, the θεοπνευσία of sacred Scripture alone proves. For it would not be entirely θεόπνευστος, that is, divinely inspired, unless the words and the structure of words, and the style and manner of speaking also efficiently depended upon the Holy Spirit through θεοπνευσία or through immediate inspiration, as was shown above.

III. But that in inspiring the concepts of things and words and the structure and coordination of words the Holy Spirit accommodated himself to the talent and accustomed style of speaking of each writer, the matter it speaks for itself, and the diversity of style, which occurs in different parts of Scripture, clearly proves it. For we observe that the style of Scripture and the manner of speaking vary according to the nature of the sacred writers, and just as the writer was, by temperament, affections, and character, either milder and more sedate or more vehement, so also his manner of speaking is either milder and more submissive or more grave and vehement; and the more humble or high the station in which he was born, and the more he was accustomed to a humbler and less polished, or a grander and more polished manner of speaking, the more humble or high, and the more or less polished, is his discourse; and the purer and less mixed with the idioms of other languages, or the more impure, the language flourished at the time and place in which the Author lived, the purer or less pure is his discourse. Thus Isaiah, as Jerome testifies, is eloquent in his speech: being a noble man and of urban eloquence, nor having anything of rusticity mixed into his speech. Jeremiah in his speech indeed seems among the Hebrews to be more rustic than Isaiah and Hosea and certain other Prophets, but he is equal in meaning, since he prophesied by the same Spirit. Furthermore, the simplicity of his eloquence comes from the place in which he was born. For he was an Anathothite, which is even today a small village three miles distant from Jerusalem: a priest from the priests, and sanctified in his mother's womb. Ezekiel's speech is neither sufficiently eloquent nor very rustic, but is tempered as a medium between both. See the Prologues of Jerome to Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Job, who lived in a region bordering on Arabia, has in his speech idioms of the Arabic language mixed in: In Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel, Chaldaisms are mixed in here and there, and, as we saw above, some parts are found written entirely in the Chaldean idiom, because at the time in which the authors flourished, the Chaldean language was quite familiar to the people of God. Ancient Church commentators report that the Evangelist Luke was most knowledgeable in the medical art, and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Whence his speech, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, that is, in both volumes, is more polished and redolent of secular eloquence: and he uses Greek testimonies more than Hebrew ones. Matthew, however, and John, of whom the one wove his Gospel in the Hebrew language, the other in the Greek, bring forth testimony from the Hebrew, writes Jerome in his Commentary on chapter VI of Isaiah. This diversity of style has no other origin than that the Holy Spirit, in suggesting the words of Scripture, [accommodated Himself to] the temperament of each writer

and accommodated and adapted himself to the customary style of speaking. But to treat at length of the style of Scripture is not the purpose of the present undertaking. Let those be consulted who have written at length on this matter, Matthias Flacius, part II of the Clavis, in a special treatise, and Glassius, Philologia sacra, book I, treatise III, and others.

Latin:

XII.

ET quidem verba, in se absolutè spectata, ut alterius cujusque Scripturæ, ita & Ebraici ac Græci idiomatis verba in se absolutè spectata, sacræ Scripturæ remota; in contextu autem usui loquendi convenienter constructa & ad res ipsas lectoris intellectui repræsentandas inter se coordinata, ejusdem propinqua materia sunt.

XIII.

STructura verborum non ubique & per universam Scripturam una & eadem est, sed prout Scriptores sacri ingenio, affectibus, & moribus diversi, & generi dicendi diverso adsueti fuerunt; ita & structura vocum stylusque Scripturæ variat.

I. Auctor quidem primarius Scripturæ totius unus & idem est, nempe Spiritus sanctus, quo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictante condita est Scriptura sacra universa, ut superiùs ex Paulo II. Tim. III. 16. Scripturam totam θεόπνευστον dicente, docuimus. Auctores secundarii verò, qui velut Amanuenses Spiritus sancti Scripturas sacras ex ejus inspiratione, temporibus & locis diversis, concinnârunt, plures, ingenioque & indole sermonis diversi fuerunt. Quamvis verò aliàs in Scripturis merè humanis stylus ingenio, affectibus, & moribus Auctoris primarii, generique dicendi, ei consueto, conformari soleat, non ingenio Amanuensis, & generi dicendi, huic consueto fecus tamen res habet cum Scripturis divinis. Spiritus sanctus enim, qui per os sanctorum Prophetarum & Apostolorum loquutus est, atque etiam illorum manu calamoque quasi scripsit, uti in loquendo, ita & in scribendo, vel potiùs in suggerendis cùm rerum tùm vocum, quæ sive voce proferri sive literis consignari debebant, conceptibus adeóque in gubernanda illorum lingua & manu, pro sua liberrima voluntate, suo cujusque ingenio, affectibus & generi dicendi consueto se accommodavit & attemperavit, ut naturaliter quasi & velut ex sua cujusque naturali indole cùm sermo tùm Scriptura illorum flueret.

II. Quòd à Spiritu S. tanquam Auctore principali sive primario Scripturæ stylus efficienter dependeat, vel sola Scripturæ sacræ θεοπνευσία evincit. Non enim tota esset θεόπνευστος, i. e. divinitùs inspirata, nisi & verba ac verborum structura, stylusque & genus dicendi per θεοπνευσίαν sive per immediatam inspirationem efficienter à Spiritu S. dependerent, ut suprà ostensum.

III. Quod autem in inspirandis rerum & vocum conceptibus vocumque structura & coordinatione Spiritus sanctus Scriptoris cujusque ingenio & generi dicendi consueto se accommodaverit, res ipsa loquitur, & styli diversitas, quæ in diversis Scripturæ partibus occurrit, liquidò evincit. Animadvertimus enim, stylum Scripturæ genusque dicendi pro ratione Scriptorum sacrorum variare, & prout Scriptor ingenio, affectibus & moribus vel lenior & sedatior vel vehementior fuit, ita & genus dicendi illius vel lenius & submissius vel gravius & vehementius esse, & quò humiliori, vel altiori loco natus & generi dicendi humiliori minusque comto, vel grandiori comtiorique adsuetus est, eo humilior vel altior, magiśque vel minùs comtus est ejus sermo, & quò purior minusque aliarum linguarum idiotismis permixta, vel impurior lingua floruit eo tempore & loco, in quo Auctor vixit, eò purior minusve purus ejus sermo est. Ita Esaias, teste Hieronymo, in sermone suo disertus est: quippe vir nobilis & urbanæ eloquentiæ, nec habens quidquam in eloquio rustici tatis admixtum. Hieremias sermone quidem apud Hebræos Esaia & Osea & quibusdam aliis Prophetis videtur esse rusticior, sed sensibus par est, quippe qui eodem Spiritu prophetavit. Porro simplicitas eloquii de loco ei, in quo natus est, accidit. Fuit enim Anathotites, qui est usque hodiè viculus tribus ab Hierosolymis distans milliaribus: sacerdos ex sacerdotibus, & in matris utero sanctificatus. -- Ezechielis sermo nec satis disertus, nec admodùm rusticus est, sed ex utroque medio temperatus. Videantur Prologi Hieronymi in Jesaiam, Jeremiam & Ezeckielem. Jobus, qui vixit in regione, Arabiæ contermina, in sermone suo linguæ Arabicæ idiotismos admixtos habet: In Esdra, Nehemia, Jeremia, & Daniele chaldaismi passim admixti, &, ut supra vidimus, partes nonnullæ merè Chaldaico idiomate conscriptæ inveniuntur, quòd eo, quo Auctores floruerunt, tempore lingua Chaldaica populo Dei esset admodum familiaris. Evangelistam Lucam tradunt veteres Ecclesiæ tractatores Medicæ artis fuisse scientessimum, & magis Græcas literas scisse, quàm Hebræas. Unde & sermo ejus tam in Evangelio, quàm in Actibus Apostolorum, id est, in utroque volumine, comtior est, & sæcularem redolet eloquentiam: magisq́; testimoniis Græcis utitur, quàm Hebræis. Matthæus autem & Johannes, quorum alter Hebræo, alter Græco sermone Evangelia texuerunt, testimonium de Hebraico proferunt, scribit Hieronymus in Comm. in cap. VI. Esaiæ. Quæstyli diversitas aliunde originem non habet, quàm quod Spiritus sanctus in suggerendis Scripturæ verbis Scriptoris cujusque ingenio

& generi dicendi consueto se accommodavit & attemperavit. Sed de stylo Scripturæ pluribus agere præsentis instituti non est. Videantur, qui hac de re prolixè scripserunt, Matthias Flacius part. II. Clav. Tract. peculiari, & Glassius Phil. sacr. lib. I. Tr. III. & alii.


### XIV. The matter about which, or the object of holy Scripture, generally speaking,…

XIV.

The matter about which, or the object of holy Scripture, generally speaking, are all things in the commemoration of which holy Scripture is occupied; but its primary or principal object are all those things which are in themselves ordained for the salvation of man.

I. In the matter about which or the object, primary indeed and principal, holy Scripture and Theology coincide. For they have one and the same end, namely, the salvation of men; and what the one delivers as necessary to be known for the salvation of men, that the other also delivers as necessary to be known for that same end. Whence what we taught above concerning the matter about which or the object of Theology, and specifically concerning things to be believed and things to be done, find their place here also.

II. This difference, however, exists between the two, that those things which are necessary either to be believed or to be done, holy Scripture describes in a historical method, confusedly and with other things and various facts mixed in, which Theology delivers separately, digested into a certain order, by a method used and accepted in the sciences, and explains and confirms by conclusions deduced from here and there according to the rules of consequences. Whence the matter about which or the object of holy Scripture can be conveniently distinguished into those things which are in themselves ordained for the salvation of men, and concern either dogmas necessary to be believed or a life worthy of a Christian man; and the rest, which are not in themselves ordained for the salvation of men, nor are necessary to be known or done by one about to attain salvation; although they contribute somewhat to the understanding of the former, or otherwise to faith and morals: such as sacred histories, which illustrate the doctrine of faith and morals with various circumstances, and by examples of virtues and vices excite to virtue, piety, and patience, and deter from vices; various types, which mystically signify or shadow forth the doctrine of faith and morals; miracles, which confirm the same, etc. The former can be called the primary, the latter the secondary object of holy Scripture.

III. What we call the secondary object of Holy Scripture pertains in its own way also to the subject matter of Theology, and can be called its secondary object, in so far as Theology, specifically Positive, in delivering the doctrine of faith and morals, not rarely uses sacred histories, examples, types, and miracles to illustrate and confirm the same; while Exegetical Theology is occupied in the interpretation and explanation of these.

XV.

The form or formal reason of Holy Scripture, by which it is constituted in its specific being and distinguished from any other Scripture, is theopneustia or divine inspiration, in so far as it was terminated in the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles regarding the concepts both of the things which were to be consigned to writing by them, and of the words by which they had to be consigned.

I. The word 'form' in this place is not taken for the other constitutive part of a composite, such as substantial forms, which through their union with matter constitute a being per se and a substance composed of both: for Holy Scripture is an accident and a being by aggregation; but it is taken for the formal reason, or for the a priori reason, by which a thing is constituted in its specific being and distinguished from any other thing.

II. Therefore, for the form or formal reason of Holy Scripture, two things are required: One, that it be an a priori reason, or a reason that enters into the first concept of Holy Scripture. The other, that it be a reason proper to Holy Scripture, which determines it to its specific being and distinguishes it from any other Scripture. For if anything is conceived first in Holy Scripture, but is not proper to it, then it will not be the form of Holy Scripture. For it is of the nature of a form that it bestows upon a thing its specific and proper being. But that which is indeed first in Scripture, yet not proper to it, but common to it with other Scriptures, cannot determine it to its specific and proper being. But on the contrary, if anything is proper to Holy Scripture, yet does not enter into its first concept, then again it cannot be called its form or formal reason: since it is of the nature of a form or formal reason that it gives being to a thing, or that it gives to a thing its own specific being. But that which is indeed proper to Holy Scripture, yet does not enter into its primary concept, is by nature posterior to its being, or to its essence, and is a certain consequent of it, or a certain property of it, not its form.

III. But that which is primarily conceived in Holy Scripture, and which constitutes it in its specific being, namely in the being of Holy and truly divine Scripture, and distinguishes it from any other Scripture, is θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration, terminated in the intellect of the sacred writers formerly to the concepts both of the things which were to be committed to writing and of the words by which the same had to be recorded.

IV. I say, moreover: θεοπνευσία in the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles was formerly terminated to the concepts both of things and of words. For Holy Scripture was once, and indeed through the Prophets and Apostles, by God inspiring, composed and completed, and [that specific and proper being which it then received, when it was first completed by the Prophets and Apostles, by God inspiring, that is still today and remains its formal [element], in whatever codex it may be contained. For the codices of Holy Scripture which were afterwards completed by the hand and pen of scribes, [were made] according to the exemplar and imitation of that original Scripture, once composed by the Prophets and Apostles, by God inspiring; and according to the exemplar and imitation of these, others again were and are completed, so that all other codices depend upon one original exemplar, some immediately, others mediately. Whence the formal and proper reason of that original [Scripture] which once existed, the same is still today the formal and proper reason of Holy Scripture, contained in whatever Biblical codex. But Holy Scripture, originally composed by the Prophets and Apostles, by God inspiring, had its specific and proper being from θεοπνευσία or from divine inspiration, terminated in their intellect formerly to the concepts both of the things which were to be committed to writing and of the words by which they had to be recorded. Therefore, even today Holy Scripture has its specific and proper being from θεοπνευσία, terminated in the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles to the concepts both of the things which were to be committed to writing by them and of the words by which they had to be recorded.

V. In order that you may rightly understand this, it must be repeated here what we were saying a little before in th. VIII. Expl. n. II, that θεοπνευσία, as it [exists] in the Prophets

& of the Apostles' intellect, as regards the matter, was limited to the concepts of both things and words to be written, it is nothing other than the very concepts of things and words to be written, once inspired into the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles. For although the terms θεοπνευστίας and divine inspiration denote the very act of inspiring, which is a certain dependence of the term—namely, the inspired concepts—upon God, as if from an efficient cause, yet just as an action does not differ from the term produced by it except modally, and as the mode of a thing differs from the thing of which it is the mode, so divine inspiration, once limited in the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles to the concepts of both things and words to be written, did not differ from the inspired concepts except modally, and divine inspiration, taken with its connoted term, is nothing other than the inspired concepts themselves, which have their formal and specific being from inspiration as if from their modal form.

Latin:

XIV.

Materia circa quam, sive objectum Scripturæ sacræ, generatim loquendo, sunt res omnes, in quarum commemoratione Scriptura sacra occupatur; primarium verò sive principale ejus objectum sunt ea omnia, quæ per se ad hominis salutem ordinantur.

I. In materia circa quam sive objecto, primario quidem & principali, Scripturæ sacræ & Theologia coincidunt. Habent enim unum & eundem finem, hominum salutem scilicet; & quæ una, velut necessaria cognitu ad hominum salutem, tradit, ea tradit & altera, velut necessaria cognitu, ad illam. Unde quæ suprà de materia circa quam sive objecto Theologiæ, & speciatim de credendis agendisque docuimus, hic etiam locum inveniunt.

II. Hoc tamen inter utramque intercedit discriminis, quòd quæ sive creditu sive factu necessaria sunt, Scriptura sacra methodo historicâ confusè & admixtis aliis rebus & factis variis, describit, quas Theologia in certum ordinem digestas seorsim, methodo scientiis usitatâ & receptâ, tradit, & conclusionibus hinc inde juxta consequentiarum regulas deductis, explicat & confirmat. Unde Scripturæ sacræ materia circa quam sive objectum commodè distingui potest in ea, quæ per se ad hominum salutem ordinantur, & vel dogmata creditu necessaria vel vitam homine Christiano dignam concernunt; & cætera, quæ ad hominum salutem per se non ordinantur, neque adepturo salutem cognitu aut factu necessaria sunt; quamvis ad illorum intelligentiam, aut aliàs ad fidem & mores nonnihil conferant: qualia sunt historiæ sacræ, quæ doctrinam fidei & morum variis circumstantiis illustrant, exemplisque virtutum & vitiorum ad virtutem, pietatem, patientiam excitant & à vitiis absterrent; typi varii, qui doctrinam fidei & morum mysticè significant vel adumbrant; miracula, quæ eandem confirmant &c. Illa primarium; hæc secundarium Scripturæ sacræ objectum dici possunt.

III. Quæ secundarium Scripturæ sacræ objectum dicimus, pertinent suo modo etiam ad Theologiæ materiam circa quam, ejusque objectum secundarium dici possunt, in quantum scilicet Theologia, Positiva quidem, in tradenda fidei & morum doctrina non rarò historiis sacris, exemplis, typis, miraculis, ad eandem illustrandam, & confirmandam utitur; Exegetica verò in eorundem interpretatione & explicatione versatur.

XV.

FOrma sive ratio formalis Scripturæ sacræ, quâ in suo esse specifico constituitur, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distinguitur, Θεοπνευστία sive divina inspiratio est, prout quidem ea in intellectu Prophetarum & Apostolorum ad conceptus cùm rerum, quæ scripto ab iis consignari; tùm vocum, quibus consignari debuerunt, terminata fuit.

I. Formæ vox hoc loco non accipitur pro altera parte constitutiva compositi, quales sunt formæ substantiales, quæ per unionem sui cum materia unum per se, & substantiam, ex utraque compositam, constituunt: Scriptura sacra enim accidens est, & ens per aggregationem; sed pro ratione formali, sive pro ratione à priori, quâ quid in suo esse specifico constituitur, & ab alia quavis re distinguitur.

II. Ad formam ergo sive rationem formalem Scripturæ sacræ duo requiruntur: Unum, ut sit ratio à priori, sive ratio, quæ primum Scripturæ sacræ conceptum ingreditur. Alterum, ut sit ratio Scripturæ sacræ propria, quæ eam ad suum esse specificum determinet, & ab alia quavis Scriptura dirstinguat. Si quid enim primò in Scriptura sacra concipiatur, neque tamen ejus proprium sit, tùm forma Scripturæ sacræ id non erit. De ratione enim formæ est, ut rei suum esse specificum & proprium largiatur. Quod autem primum quidem in Scriptura, non tamen ejus proprium, sed ei cum aliis Scripturis commune est, id non potest eam ad suum esse specificum & proprium determinare. Contrà autem si quid Scripturæ sacræ proprium sit, non tamen ejus conceptum primum ingrediatur, tum rursum forma sive ratio formalis illius dici non potest: cùm de ratione formæ sive rationis formalis sit, ut det esse rei, sive ut rei suum esse specificum largiatur. Quod autem Scripturæ sacræ quidem propriū est, ejus tamen conceptum primum non ingreditur, id naturâ posterius est ejus esse, sive essentiâ illius, & quoddam ejus consequens, vel quædam proprietas illius, non forma.

III. Quod autem primò in Scriptura sacra concipitur, eamq́; in suo esse specifico, nempe in esse sacræ & verè divinæ Scripturæ constituit, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distinguit, θεοπνευσία sive divina inspiratio est, in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu olim ad conceptus, cùm rerum, quæ in literas referri; tùm vocum, quibus eædem consignari debuerunt, terminata.

IV. Dico autem: θεοπνευσία in Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectu olim ad conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum terminata. Scriptura sacra enim semel, & quidem per Prophetas & Apostolos, Deo inspirante, concinnata & confecta est, & [quod esse specificum ac proprium ea tum accepit, cùm per Prophetas & Apostolos, Deo inspirante, primùm confecta est, id adhuc hodiéque est manet́que ejus formale, in quocunque etiam codice contineatur. Qui enim posteà librariorum manu & calamo confecti sunt codices Scripturæ sacræ, ad exemplar & imitationem illius primigeniæ, à Prophetis & Apostolis olim, Deo inspirante, concinnatæ Scripturæ; & ad horum exemplar ac imitationem rursum alii confecti sunt & conficiuntur, ut ab uno exemplari primigenio cæteri codices omnes, alii immediatè, alii mediatè dependeant. Unde quæ illius primigeniæ ratio formalis & propria olim fuit, eadem adhuc hodieque est ratio formalis & propria Scripturæ sacræ, in quocunque codice Biblico contentæ. Scriptura sacra autem primitùs per Prophetas & Apostolos, Deo inspirante, concinnata, habuit suum esse specificum ac proprium à θεοπνευσία sive à divina inspiratione, ad conceptus cùm rerum, quæ scripto consignari, tùm verborum, quibus consignari debebant, in illorum intellectu olim terminata. Ergo adhuc hodiéq; Scriptura sacra habet suum esse specificum & proprium à θεοπνευσίᾳ, in Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectu ad conceptus cùm rerum, quæ literis ab iis consignari, tùm vocum, quibus consignari debuerunt, terminata.

V. Quod ut rectè intelligas, repetendum hîc est, quod paulò ante th. VIII. Expl. n. II. dicebamus, θεοπνευσίαν, prout in Prophetarum

& Apostolorum intellectu ad conceptus cùm rerum tum vocum scribendarum terminata fuit, quantum ad rem, nihil esse aliud, quàm ipfos rerum & vocum scribendarum conceptus, Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectui olim inspiratos. Quamvis enim θεοπνευστίας & divinæ inspirationis voces ipsum actum inspirandi denotent, qui est dependentia quædam termini, conceptuum inspiratorum scilicet, à Deo, velut à causa efficiente, tamen ut aliàs actio à termino, per eam producto, non differt, nisi modaliter, & ut modus rei à re, cujus modus est, ita divina inspiratio, in Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectu olim ad conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum scribendarum terminata, à conceptibus inspiratis non differebat, nisi modaliter, & inspiratio divina cum connotato suo termino sumta, nihil est aliud, quàm ipsi conceptus inspirati, qui ab inspiratione, velut à sua forma modali suum esse formale & specificum habent.


### XVI. But the concepts of both things and words to be written, once inspired by God…

XVI.

But the concepts of both things and words to be written, once inspired by God into the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles, have in relation to Holy Scripture the nature of both an internal and an external and exemplary form, yet in one way and respect or another.

I. The concepts of things and words, once inspired by God to the sacred writers, did not and do not import a single relation to Holy Scripture. For first, they stood on the part of the sacred writers as the reason by which God elevated their intellect to compose Holy Scripture, and directed their hand and pen in writing. Then, the same inspired concepts stood and still stand today in relation to the composed Scripture as the signified to its sign. For writings are signs of words, words are signs of concepts, and concepts are signs of things, as Aristotle teaches, περὶ ἑρμην. c. 1. Thirdly, the same stood in relation to it as an exemplar, internal to the intellect of the writers, in imitation of which the whole was composed. For just as it is necessary that he who is about to build a house or make a shoe should first have in his intellect the idea of it, as an exemplary cause, which he may imitate in building that or in making this; so he who is about to compose any Scripture, it is necessary that he have conceived in his mind the things which are to be recorded in letters, and the words by which they ought to be recorded, and their structure, and even a certain idea, which he ought to have conceived in his mind as an exemplary cause to imitate in composing Scripture. Such an idea and exemplary cause of the Holy Scripture to be composed by the Prophets and Apostles were the concepts of both things and words, inspired into their understanding by God.

II. According to the first relation, the concepts of things and words to be written, once inspired into the understanding of the Prophets and Apostles by God, stood in relation to the Holy Scripture composed by them efficiently and as a causality, by which God, as the author and principal cause of it, provided His influence upon it, as was shown at greater length above in thesis V, number III.

III. According to the second relation, the same inspired concepts stood and stand in relation to it as its form or formal reason. For just as it is common to all signs to be specified by that which they signify, so also Holy Scripture derives its formal and specific reason from the concepts of both things and words, of which the written words are signs. Whence, whatever is the formal and proper reason of the inspired concepts, of which the written words are signs, that is also the formal and proper reason of Scripture itself.

IV. But here it must again be observed that the concepts of both things and words to be written, inspired into the understanding of the sacred writers, can be considered in two ways: one in relation to the things and words which, as their expressed species, they represented to the understanding of the sacred writers. The other in relation to their efficient cause, and insofar as they were inspired by God into the understanding of the sacred writers and were supernatural. Viewed in the former way, the concepts are specified by the objects of which they are signs and expressed species. And as far as this is concerned, it makes no difference whether they are supernaturally inspired into the human understanding by God, or naturally elicited through species impressed upon it by objects through the intervention of the senses. For both are certain expressed species of either things or words, and they represent them to the understanding. But viewed in the latter way, they are specified and derive their formal reason from the act of divine inspiration, as from a modal form. For the act of inspiration, as has been said, stands in relation to the concepts produced by it, or to the inspired concepts, as the mode of a thing to the thing, and is a certain modal form of the inspired acts.

When they are considered in the former way, it is not inappropriately said that the material of Scripture is the written words; the formal is the sense itself, or, which amounts to the same thing, the concepts themselves and their objects. For the sense of the words of Scripture is nothing other than the concepts of the mind, by which those things which are composite and one in objects or things are represented to the intellect as composite and one; and those which are divided and many are represented to the same as divided and many, and furthermore the sense is the things themselves, as they are composite and one, or divided and many among themselves, signified by words and concepts. But this is the formal of sacred Scripture, not precisely as it is sacred and divine, but simply as a certain Scripture, consisting of written words, as signs signifying by institution, and of the sense and things signified. Which is a certain generic concept of sacred Scripture, which it has in common with any other Scripture, and which, when viewed in the concepts of both things and words, of which the written words are signs, precisely apart from divine inspiration, constitutes its form, is a generic rather than a specific form of it: since it does not give it the specific being from which it has that it is sacred and truly divine Scripture.

But when the concepts of both things and words, of which the written words are signs, once inspired into the intellect of the sacred writers, are considered in the latter way, namely in order to their efficient cause, and insofar as they are specified by the act of divine inspiration, as if by their modal form, and obtain their formal being, then the formal reason of sacred Scripture is rightly constituted in them, viewed precisely as it is sacred and truly divine Scripture, as its formal reason comes under consideration here. For if you run through all things which are contained or connoted in sacred Scripture, you will find nothing which is of its primary concept, and which constitutes it in the specific being of sacred and truly divine Scripture, and distinguishes it from any other Scripture, except the concepts of things and words, of which the written words are signs, once inspired into the intellect of the sacred writers by God, insofar as they are indeed specified by the act of divine inspiration, as if by their modal form, and are distinguished from any other concepts, whether of things or of words, naturally elicited by the intellect. V. We say, however, that theopneustia, taken terminatively for the concepts of things and words, or, which is the same thing, the concepts of things and words to be written, divinely inspired, viewed by reason of the aforementioned second relationship, is the internal form of Holy Scripture, not because it is intrinsic to the Scripture itself inscribed on paper, and is actually and formally contained in it: for the inspired concepts were actually and formally in the intellect of the sacred writers, and thus were entirely extrinsic to the Scripture inscribed on paper; but because it is intrinsic to the Scripture itself, which embraces both the written words and the sense, and is contained in its primary concept, as that from which it has the quality of being sacred and truly divine, in its own way, namely in the way in which the signified is said to be contained in its sign, and the sense of Scripture is said to be contained in the written words, and to penetrate to the intellect through hearing with those words uttered by voice, and through sight with the same words read, just as if it were actually and formally present in the words.

VI. According to the third relationship, theopneustia, taken terminatively for the concepts of both things and words inspired by God, is the external and exemplary form of Holy Scripture.
