For the concepts of both things and words, inspired into the intellect of the sacred writers, since they were expressed species of things and words, and represented them to the intellect of the sacred writers, were nothing other than ideas or exemplary forms, to the imitation of which both things and words, conceived by the intellect and arranged in a certain order, were also to be consigned and arranged in writing, and were also consigned and arranged by the sacred writers. These ideas were indeed exemplary forms, internal to the intellect of the sacred writers, but with respect to Holy Scripture, fashioned in their imitation, they were external forms, and they related to it as an exemplar, internal to the intellect of the sacred writers, to the exemplified, if I may so speak, or to the external exemplary effect.

VII. Through this form also, although it is external and exemplary, Holy Scripture is what it is, namely sacred and truly divine, and is rightly distinguished from any other Scripture. For all other Scriptures are fashioned in imitation of concepts of both things and words, which are elicited by human study and in a natural way by the intellect through species impressed upon it from objects by the intervention of the senses, and thus they are human, and just as the intellect of man, left to itself, can err, be deceived, and deceive, so also it is not repugnant that a falsehood should underlie the Scriptures, which were composed in imitation of concepts of that kind. For no more perfection can be present in an exemplified effect than in its cause or exemplary form. Holy Scripture, however, since it was composed in imitation of concepts, both of things and of words, which GOD Himself suggested to the intellect of the sacred writers through immediate inspiration, as an exemplary cause, is truly divine, and it is as repugnant for a falsehood to underlie it as it is repugnant for God, who is omniscient and infinitely good, to err, be deceived, or deceive in inspiring the concepts in imitation of which it was composed.

Latin:

XVI.

COnceptus verò cùm rerum tum vocum scribendarum, Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectui olim à Deo inspirati, habent ad Scripturam sacram rationem formæ cùm internæ tum externæ & exemplaris, alio tamen atque alio modo & respectu.

I. Conceptus rerum & vocum, Scriptoribus sacris olim à Deo inspirati, ad Scripturam sacram non unam importabant, importantque habitudinem. Primùm enim habebant se ex parte Scriptorum sacrorum ut ratio, quâ Deus illorum intellectum ad concinnandam Scripturam sacram elevabat, illorumque manum & calamum in scribendo dirigebat. Deinde iidem conceptus inspirati habebant, habentq; se adhuc hodieque ad Scripturam concinnatam, ut signatum ad suum signum. Scripturæ enim sunt signa vocum, voces verò conceptuum, & conceptus rerum, docente Aristotele, περὶ ἑρμην. c. 1. Tertiò iidem habebant se ad illam ut exemplar, Scriptorum intellectui internum, ad cujus imitationem tota est concinnata. Quemadmodum enim qui ædificaturus est domum vel confecturus est calceum, ejus ideam, velut causam exemplarem, quam in illa ædificanda, vel in hoc conficiendo imitetur, prius intellectu conceptam habeat oportet; ita qui Scripturam aliquam confecturus est, eum & res, quæ literis confignari,& voces,quibus confignari debent,illarumque structuram, atque adeò ideam quandam, quam velut causam exemplarem in conficienda Scriptura imitetur, animo conceptam habere oportet. Hujusmodi idea & causa exemplaris concinnandæ per Prophetas & Apostolos Scripturæ sacræ erant conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum, illorum intellectui à Deo inspirati.

II. Juxta primam habitudinem conceptus rerum & vocum scribendarum, Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectui à Deo olim inspirati,habuerunt sead confectam ab illis Scripturam sacram efficienter & ut causalitas, quâ Deus velut auctor & causa principalis illius suum in illam influxum præbuit,ut suprà th.V. n. III. pluribus ostensum est.

III. Juxta alteram habitudinem iidem conceptus inspirati habuerunt habentque se ad illam ut forma sive ratio formalis illius. Quemadmodùm enim fignis omnibus commune est, ut à suo signato specificentur, ita & Scriptura sacra à conceptibus cùm rerum tùm vocum, quorum signa sunt verba scripta, suam fortitur rationem formalem & specificam. Unde quæ est ratio formalis & propria conceptuum inspiratorum,quorum signa sunt verba scripta, ea est etiam ratio formalis & propria ipsius Scripturæ.

IV. Sed hîc rursum observandum est, quòd conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum scribendarum, sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui inspirati, considerari possint duobus modis: Uno in ordine ad res & voces, quas velut species illarum expressæ sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui repræsentabant. Altero in ordine ad sui causam efficientem, & in quantum intellectui scriptorum sacrorum à Deo inspirati & supernaturales erant. Priori modo spectati conceptus specificantur ab objectis, quorum signa & species expressæ sunt. Et quantum ad hoc nihil refert, sintne hominis intellectui à Deo supernaturaliter inspirati? an per species, interventu sensuum ei ab objectis impressas naturaliter eliciti? Utrique enim sunt species quædam expressæ sive rerum sive vocum, easque intellectui repræsentant. Posteriori autem modo spectati specificantur suamq́ rationem formalem fortiuntur ab actu divinæ inspirationis, velut à forma modali. Actus inspirationis enim, uti dictum, habet se ad conceptus per eum productos sive ad conceptus inspiratos ut modus rei ad rem, estque actuum inspiratorum forma quædam modalis.

Quando priori modo considerantur, non incommodè dicitur, materiale Scripturæ esse verba scripta; formale ipsum sensum, vel, quod eodem redit, ipsos conceptus & illorum objecta. Sensus enim verborum Scripturæ nihil est aliud, quàm conceptus mentis, quibus quæ in objectis sive rebus composita & unum sunt, intellectui ut composita & unum; & quæ divisa ac multa sunt, eidem ut divisa & multa repræsentantur, & porro sensus est ipsæ res, ut inter se compositæ & unum, vel divisæ & multæ sunt, verbis & conceptibus significatæ. Sed hoc formale est Scripturæ sacræ, non præcisè, ut sacra & divina est, sed simpliciter, ut Scriptura quædam, verbis scriptis, velut signis, ex instituto significantibus, & sensu rebusque significatis constans. Qui est genericus quidam Scripturæ sacræ conceptus, quem cum alia quavis Scriptura communem habet, & quæ in conceptibus cùm rerum tùm verborum, quorum signa sunt verba scripta, præcisâ divina inspiratione, spectatis, constituitur forma illius, generica potius quàm specifica illius forma est: cùm ei non det esse specificum, à quo habet, quod sacra & verè divina Scriptura est.

Quando autem conceptus cùm rerum tùm verborum, quorum signa sunt verba scripta, sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui olim inspirati, posteriori modo considerantur, nempe in ordine ad sui causam efficientem, & in quantum ab actu divinæ inspirationis, tanquam à sua forma modali, specificantur, & suum esse formale sortiuntur, tum rectè in illis constituitur formalis ratio Scripturæ sacræ, præcisè ut sacra & verè divina Scriptura est, spectatæ, prout hic ejus ratio formalis sub considerationem venit. Si enim omnia, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur vel connotantur, percurras, nihil invenies, quod de primo illius conceptu sit, eamque in esse specifico sacræ veréque divinæ Scripturæ constituat, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distinguat, præter conceptus rerum & verborum, quorum signa sunt verba scripta, sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui olim à Deo inspiratos, prout quidem ab actu divinæ inspirationis, velut à sua forma modali, specificantur, & ab aliis quibusvis sive rerum sive verborum conceptibus, ab intellectu naturaliter elicitis, distinguuntur. V. Dicimus autem, θεοπνευσίαν, terminativè sumtam pro conceptibus rerũ & vocum, sive, quod idem est, conceptus rerum & vocum scribendarum, divinitus inspiratos, ratione prædictæ habitudinis secundæ spectatos, formam Scripturæ sacræ internam, non quod ipsi in chartis exaratæ Scripturæ intrinseca sit, & actu ac formaliter in ea contineatur: conceptus inspirati enim actu & formaliter erant in intellectu sacrorum Scriptorum, atque adeò exaratæ in chartis Scripturæ prorsus extrinfeci; sed quod ipsi voces scriptas pariter ac sensum complectenti Scripturæ intrinseca sit, & in primo ejus conceptu, velut id, à quo habet, quod sacra ac verè divina est, suo modo contineatur, nempe eo modo, quo signatum in suo signo, & sensus Scripturæ in verbis scriptis contineri, & cum illis, voce prolatis, per auditum, & cum iisdem lectis per visum ad intellectum penetrare dicitur, non secus, ac si actu & formaliter verbis inesset.

VI. Juxta tertiam habitudinem θεοπνευσία, terminativè pro conceptibus cùm rerum tum vocum, à Deo inspiratis, accepta, est forma Scripturæ sacræ externa & exemplaris. Conceptus enim cùm rerum tùm vocum, sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui inspirati, cùm essent species expressæ rerum & vocum, easque sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui repræsentarent, nihil erant aliud, quàm ideæ sive formæ exemplares, ad quarum imitationem cùm res tum voces, intellectu conceptæ, certóque ordine dispositæ, etiam scripto consignandæ disponendæque erant, & à Scriptoribus sacris etiam consignatæ ac dispositæ sunt. Quæ ideæ erant quidem formæ exemplares, intellectui sacrorum Scriptorum internæ, sed respectu Scripturæ sacræ, ad illarum imitationem confectæ, formæ externæ erant, habebantque se ad eam ut exemplar, intellectui sacrorum Scriptorum internum, ad exemplatum, ut ita loquar, sive ad effectum exemplarem externum.

VII. Per hanc etiam, licet externam & exemplarem, formam est Scriptura sacra, quod est, nempe sacra & verè divina, & ab alia quavis Scriptura rectè distinguitur. Aliæ enim Scripturæ omnes confectæ sunt & conficiuntur ad imitationem conceptuum cùm rerum tùm verborum, qui studio humano modoque naturali ab intellectu per species, ab objectis interventu sensuum sibi impressas, eliciuntur, atque adeò humanæ sunt, & quemadmodùm intellectus hominis, sibi relictus, in concipiendis rebus & verbis errare, falli ac fallere potest, ita & Scripturis, ad imitationem id generis conceptuum confectis, falsum subesse non repugnat. Neque enim plus perfectionis inesse potest effectui exemplato, quam suae causae sive formae exemplari. Scriptura sacra autem, cum ad imitationem conceptuum, cum rerum tum verborum, quos DEUS ipse per immediatam inspirationem sacrorum Scriptorum intellectui suggessit, velut causa exemplaris, confecta sit, vere divina est, eique tam repugnat subesse falsum, quam repugnat, Deum omniscium & infinite bonum in inspirandis conceptibus, ad quorum imitationem confecta est, errare, falli aut fallere.


### XVII. We notably establish, however, that the form of Scripture, both internal and…

XVII.

We notably establish, however, that the form of Scripture, both internal and external, consists in the θεοπνευστία [divine inspiration] of both the things and the words to be written.

For through θεοπνευστία [divine inspiration], limited only to the concepts of things and not of words in the intellect of the sacred writers, Holy Scripture is not distinguished from any other Scripture. For it is not distinguished by it from Versions, which are indeed conformable to the original text. For a Version, just as it is fashioned in imitation of the original text as an external exemplary form, so if it is entirely conformable to it, its words suggest and represent to us the same concepts which the words of the original text suggest and represent to us, namely the concepts which the Holy Spirit once inspired in the sacred writers: yet a Version, even if conformable in all things to the original text, and Scripture itself viewed in its original text, are separated by as great an interval as that which separates Scripture that is αὐτόπιστος [self-authenticating] and to which faith is owed in itself, and Scripture which is not believed in itself, but only on account of another original to which it is exactly conformable; or Scripture that is normative and Scripture that is normed, Scripture to which it is repugnant that a falsehood should underlie it, and Scripture to which it is not repugnant that a falsehood should underlie it. The reason for the difference, however, consists entirely in this, that the concepts of both things and words were once inspired in the sacred writers for original Scripture; but for a Version, only the concepts of things, not of words, were inspired. Which is a notable proof that θεοπνευστία [divine inspiration], limited only to the concepts of things in the intellect of the sacred writers, is not the adequate form or formal reason by which Holy Scripture is constituted in its specific being, and is distinguished from any other Scripture, but that to this also θεοπνευσία, having been formerly terminated at the very concepts of the words in the understanding of the sacred writers, is required.

XVIII.

Some others also make a double form of Scripture; internal and external, but they declare both in a different sense and manner than we do. I. According to us, there is one form, or formal reason, through which Scripture is what it is, that is, holy and truly divine Scripture, namely θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration, accepted terminatively for the concepts of both the things which were to be consigned to writing, and the words by which they were to be consigned, being divinely inspired: which divinely inspired concepts may be called internal form in one respect, and external in another: internal indeed, insofar as they have the nature of the signified, determined by the act of inspiration, as a modal form to their specific and supernatural being, which constitute Holy Scripture in the being of holy and truly divine Scripture. But they are called external form, insofar as they behaved on the part of the intellect of the sacred writers as an exemplary form, to the imitation of which the entire exterior Scripture was arranged and fashioned, as has been declared at greater length up to this point. According to them, however, the internal and external form are two really distinct forms. II. That which they call the external form, they confess to be an accident of Scripture: for they expressly call it an accidental form, and they constitute it in the idiom, Hebrew indeed, in which the books of the Old Testament, and Greek, in which those of the New Testament were originally written, and in the propriety of speech and style, which is rather a certain material affection of Holy Scripture than a form. But if anyone wishes to call it its accidental form, we will easily allow him to abound in his own sense: thus, however, it will be permissible to number more than one accidental form of Holy Scripture, since more of its properties and affections are given. Concerning this matter we will stir up a dispute with no one. III. The form, which they call internal and essential, comes here into consideration. But they do not constitute it in θεοπνευσίᾳ or divine inspiration, as we do, but others in the authority and majesty of Scripture, from the immediate breathing of the Holy Spirit, by which it was written, and from the things, which it sets forth, deriving its origin from majesty or sublimity; others, however, place it in the θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed] sense, reasoning that, since divine inspiration acts efficiently in relation to Holy Scripture, its form cannot be constituted in it, since the efficient cause and the form are two different kinds of causes.

IV. This disagreement does not so much concern the thing itself as the use and application of the technical term, namely 'form,' to the thing, by which, therefore, students should not allow themselves to be troubled. It is granted on both sides that Holy Scripture was written by divine inspiration: it is also granted on both sides that it enjoys divine authority, and that its divine authority derives its origin from divine breath or from divine inspiration, by which it was written: finally, it is also granted on both sides that Holy Scripture contains within itself a θεόπνευστον [God-breathed] sense. But whether the intrinsic and essential form of Scripture is more correctly constituted in θεοπνευστίᾳ [God-breathedness]? Or indeed in its divine authority? Or finally in the θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed] sense? is a question which, as has been said, does not concern the thing itself, but the technical term of form, and its use and application, namely whether the term 'form' is more correctly attributed to divine inspiration, through which it was written? Or indeed to the divine authority which it possesses? Or finally to the sense which it contains, the θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed one]? In which question, as far as the thing itself is concerned, there is, as is evident, little moment, provided that the thing is agreed upon, as it is entirely agreed upon. However, because it contributes something to theological precision, and some light is added to the underlying subjects for a fuller understanding of them, if technical terms, when they are to be used or are used, are used congruously, for the sake of students we shall add a few things about the other opinions, which are somewhat different from our own.

V. We said, however, above in thesis XV, Explanation no. II, that two things are required for a form or formal reason: One, that it be an a priori reason, which enters into the primary concept of the thing. The other, that it be a reason proper to the thing whose form it is said to be, which determines it to its specific being. Whether these two requirements agree more correctly with the θεοπνευστίᾳ [God-breathedness] of Holy Scripture, taken terminatively for the concepts of things and words divinely inspired? Or indeed with the authority of Scripture? Or finally with the θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed] sense, must be examined here. Regarding θεοπνευστίᾳ [God-breathedness], however, so taken, we acted above in thesis XIV and XV at length, and that and in what manner and sense the form of Scripture is correctly constituted in it has been declared at length, to which I refer the reader. To our opinion declared there, nothing stands in the way that θεοπνευστία [God-breathedness] is also taken terminatively for the concepts of things and of the words, inspired by God, received, in its own way and in a certain respect, it also relates to Holy Scripture on the part of the efficient cause. For it relates to it efficiently, in so far as it related to the part of the sacred writers as the reason by which God governed their understanding in composing Scripture, and suggested to them both the things which were to be recorded and the words by which they ought to be recorded, and by the suggestion of these provided his influence upon the Scripture composed by them. But in so far as the concepts, both of things and of words inspired, are determined to their supernatural being by the act of inspiration, from which they differ only modally, as if by a modal form, and thus being determined by it, they relate to Holy Scripture as the signified to its sign, or even as an exemplar to whose imitation it itself was composed, in so far it relates to the same as a form, either internal or external and exemplary, as was shown at greater length above in thesis XV. Whence it is not contradictory for ϑεοπνευsτία (divine inspiration) to relate to Holy Scripture efficiently, and in a certain way and respect as the formal reason by which it is constituted in its specific being and is distinguished from any other Scripture. For since signs, of which Holy Scripture is composed, derive their formal and specific reason from the things of which they are signs; and since Holy Scripture is a sign of the concepts divinely inspired in the sacred writers, which depend upon divine inspiration at once efficiently, and are also formally constituted in their supernatural being as if by a modal form: the thing itself demands that ϑεοπνευsτία or divine inspiration should relate to Scripture both efficiently and as the causality by which God provided his influence upon it, and at the same time as the formal reason by which it is constituted in its specific being, just as it relates to the concepts themselves, whose signs it contains, on the part of the efficient cause and as the formal and specific reason of those. For whatever is the formal reason of the signified thing, that also is the formal reason of the sign, in so far as it is a sign, as has been said, and if in the former it is not contradictory to have something on the part of the efficient cause and at the same time to be the formal reason by which it is constituted in its specific being, neither will it be contradictory in this. But what is said, that the efficient cause and the form constitute two different kinds of causes, is true of the form, strictly and rigorously so called, which is the other part of the composite, and by the union of itself with matter constitutes a being per se. For this is an internal cause of the composite, entering into its constitution; but the efficient cause is an external cause, which is adequately distinguished from its effect and does not enter into its constitution. But the matter is otherwise with beings per accidens, such as Scripture is, and likewise with immanent and transient actions, and with signs, considered in the nature of signs, which do not acknowledge a form, properly so called, as a constitutive part of themselves: where the efficient cause and the form are not so adequately distinguished, but that sometimes, as regards the thing, they coincide, and one and the same effect depends efficiently from something, and at the same time depends in its formal and specific being, as has just been shown by the example of concepts divinely inspired.

VI. But as regards the authority and majesty of Holy Scripture, it is certain that it does not enter into the primary concept of Holy Scripture, but is by nature posterior to it, and flows from its nature and essence already constituted in act. For Holy Scripture, written by divine afflatus or inspiration, by the fact that it is written by divine inspiration and is a sign of the concepts both of things and of words, once inspired by God into the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles, is now actually constituted in its specific being, and from this finally flows its divine authority, as a certain property of it, and as a certain consequence of it.

VII. As regards the other opinion, which constitutes the form of Scripture in the θεοπνεύστῳ (God-breathed) sense, it seems to approach more closely to the usage of speech. For Holy Scripture is of the class of those things whose being consists in signifying. But just as it is common to all signs that they are specified by the things signified, so all Scripture seems to have its specific being from the sense of which it is a sign. Hence it is most accepted in usage that words are said to be the material, but the sense the formal, of any Scripture whatsoever. But because the same sense, expressed by the words of Scripture, can also be expressed by someone by human effort in words and comprehended in writing, whose writing, however, is not of the same nature as Holy Scripture, it seems not inconvenient that the formal reason of Holy Scripture be constituted in the θεοπνεύστῳ (God-breathed) sense, so that the sense is as it were the generic form of Scripture, which it has in common with other Scriptures; but the θεόπνευστος (God-breathed) sense is as it were its specific form. But besides the fact that thus also the specific form of Scripture finally returns to θεοπνευστίαν (divine inspiration), neither can its adequate and proper reason be constituted in the θεοπνεύστῳ (God-breathed) sense. For, as has already been shown in thesis XVI, any version of Scripture, which is indeed entirely conformable to the original text, also contains the θεοπνευστον (God-breathed) sense: for it contains the same sense which the Holy Spirit once [imparted] to the intellect of the Prophets and Apostles inspired; yet it is not of the same nature and essence as Scripture, when viewed in its original text, as is evident from the properties of each. For the latter is of divine and utterly infallible authority. The former, however, although it may not contain falsehood, since it is, as is supposed here, conformable to the original text, yet it is not repugnant for it to contain falsehood. The latter is the norm and is ἀνύπεύθυνος, the former is something normed, to which faith is not owed, except in so far as it is conformable to the original text. But for the form of Holy Scripture, it is required that it be adequate to it, and distinguish it from any other Scripture, and even from the versions of it themselves. Nothing therefore remains in which the form or formal reason of Scripture, by which it is adequately distinguished from any other Scripture, can be constituted, except the θεοπνευστίαν of the concepts, both of the things and of the written words, taken terminatively, or, which amounts to the same thing, except the concepts of the things and of the words, of which the written words are signs, once inspired by God to the Prophets and Apostles, under which also the ἐνθεόπνευστος sense is contained, as was shown above. And so much for the form or formal reason of Scripture.

Latin:

XVII.

NOtanter autem constituimus formam Scripturae tam internam, quam externam, in θεοπνευστίᾳ cum rerum tum vocum scribendarum.

Per θεοπνευστίαν enim, ad solos rerum, non vocum conceptus, in Scriptorum sacrorum intellectu terminatam, Scriptura sacra non distinguitur ab alia quavis Scriptura. Non enim distinguitur per eam a Versionibus, quae quidem textui primigenio conformes sunt. Versio enim, ut ad imitationem textus primigenii, velut formae exemplaris externae, concinnata est, ita si ei prorsus conformis sit, verba ejus nobis eosdem ingerunt & repraesentant conceptus, quos verba textus primigenii nobis ingerunt & repraesentant, nempe conceptus, quos Spiritus sanctus olim Scriptoribus sacris inspiravit: Versio tamen, etsi textui primigenio per omnia conformis, & ipsa in suo textu primigenio spectata Scriptura tanto distant intervallo, quanto distant Scriptura αὐτόπιστος, & cui per se debetur fides, & Scriptura, cui non per se creditur, sed tantum propter aliam primigeniam, cui exacte conformis est; vel Scriptura normans & Scriptura normata, Scriptura cui repugnat subesse falsum, & Scriptura, cui falsum subesse non repugnat. Ratio differentiae autem in hoc tota consistit, quod Scripturae primigeniae conceptus & rerum & vocum; Versionis autem tantum rerum, non vocum conceptus Scriptoribus sacris olim inspirati fuerunt. Quod documento insigni est, quod θεοπνευστία, ad solos conceptus rerum, in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu olim terminata, non sit forma sive ratio formalis adaequata, quâ Scripturâ sacra in suo esse specifico constituitur, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distinguitur, sed ad hanc etiam θεοπνευσία, ad ipsos conceptus vocum in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu olim terminata, requiratur.

XVIII.

NOnnulli alii faciunt etiam duplicem Scripturæ formam; internam & externam, sed alio sensu & modo, quàm nos, utramque declarant. I. Juxta nos una est forma, sive ratio formalis, per quam Scriptura est, quod est, h. e. sacra & verè divina Scriptura, nempe θεοπνευσία sive inspiratio divina, terminativè pro conceptibus cùm rerum, quæ scripto consignari, tùm vocum, quibus consignari debuerunt, divinitus inspiratis accepta: qui divinitùs inspirati conceptus alio respectu interna, alio externa forma dicatur: interna quidem, quatenus habent rationem signati, per actum inspirationis, velut formam modalem ad suum esse specificum & supernaturale determinati, qui Scripturam sacram constituunt in esse sacræ & verè divinæ Scripturæ. Externa verò forma dicuntur, in quantum ex parte intellectus Scriptorum sacrorum sese habuerunt ut forma exemplaris, ad cujus imitationem Scriptura exterior tota concinnata & confecta est, ut hactenus pluribus declaratum. Juxta illos verò forma interna & externa duæ realiter distinctæ formæ sunt. II. Quam externam dicunt formam, fatentur esse accidens Scripturæ: Vocant enim illam expressè formam accidentalem, & constituunt illam in idiomate, Ebræo quidem, quo Veteris; & Græco, quo Novi Testamenti libri primitùs conscripti sunt, inque sermonis ac styli proprietate, quæ potiùs materialis quædam Scripturæ sacræ affectio est, quàm forma. Quod si quis eam formam ejus accidentalem dicere velit, eum nos facilè patiemur suo abundare sensu: ita autem plures unâ formæ accidentales Scripturæ sacræ numerare licebit, cùm plures dentur ejus proprietates & affectiones. Qua de re nemini nos movebimus litem. III. Forma, quam internam & essentialem dicunt, venit hîc in considerationem. Eam verò non constituunt in θεοπνευσίᾳ sive divina inspiratione, ut nos, sed alii in auctoritate & majestate Scripturæ, ex immediato SpiritusS. afflatu, quo scripta est, & ex rerum, quas exponit, majestate sive sublimitate originem trahente; alii verò in sensu θεοπνεύστῳ constituunt, rati, cùm divina inspiratio in ordine ad Scripturam sacram se efficienter habeat, non posse ejus formam in ea constitui, cùm efficiens & forma sint duo diversa causarum genera.

IV. Dissensus hic non tàm concernit ipsam rem, quàm usum & applicationem termini technici, formæ scilicet, ad rem, quo proinde non est, ut turbari se patiantur discentes. Conceditur utrinque, Scripturam sacram esse ex divina inspiratione conscriptam: utrinque conceditur etiam, eam divinâ gaudere auctoritate, & divinam ejus auctoritatem trahere originem ex afflatu divino sive ex divina inspiratione, ex qua conscripta est: conceditur denique id etiam utrinque, Scripturam sacram continere in se sensum θεόπνευστον. Utrum verò forma Scripturæ intrinseca & essentialis rectiùs constituatur in θεοπνευστίᾳ? an verò in divina ejus auctoritate? an denique in sensu θεοπνεύστῳ? quæstio est, quæ, uti dictum, non ipsam rem concernit, sed terminum technicum formæ, ejusque usum & applicationem, an scilicet formæ terminus rectius tribuatur divinæ inspirationi, per quam conscripta est? an verò ejus, quâ pollet, auctoritati divinæ? an denique sensui, quem continet, θεοπνεύστῳ? quâ in quæstione, quod ad rem attinet, parum, uti patet, situm est momenti, modò de re constet, uti de ea prorsus constat. Quia autem ad ἀκρίβειαν Theologicam non nihil facit, ipsisq; rebus substratis lux aliqua ad uberiorem illarum intelligentiam accedit, si termini technici, quando adhibendi sunt, vel adhibentur, congruè adhibeantur, in discentium gratiam de cæteris & à nostra nonnihil diversis sententiis pauca adjiciemus.

V. Diximus autem suprà th. XV. Expl. n. II. ad formam sive rationem formalem requiri duo: Unum, ut sit ratio à priori, quæ primum rei conceptum ingreditur. Alterum ut sit ratio rei, cujus forma dicitur, propria, quæ eam ad suum esse specificum determinet. Quæ duo requisita conveniantne rectiùs τῇ θεοπνευστίᾳ Scripturæ sacræ, terminativè pro conceptibus rerum & vocum divinitùs inspiratis acceptæ? an verò auctoritati Scripturæ? an denique sensui θεοπνεύστῳ, dispiciendum hîc venit. De θεοπνευστίᾳ verò, sic acceptâ, actum suprà in th. XIV. & XV. prolixè, & quòd atque quo modo ac sensu Scripturæ forma in ea rectè constituatur, fusè declaratum est, quò lectorem remitto. Cui nostræ ibidem declaratæ sententiæ nihil obstat, quòd θεοπνευστία etiam terminativè pro conceptibus rerum & vocum, à Deo inspiratis, accepta, suo modo & certo respectu ad Scripturam sacram se etiam ex parte causæ efficientis habet. Habet enim se ad illam efficienter, in quantum se ex parte Scriptorum sacrorum habuit ut ratio, quâ Deus illorum intellectum in concinnanda Scriptura gubernavit, eić; cùm res, quæ consignari, tùm voces, quibus consignari debebant, suggessit, horumć; suggestione in Scripturam, ab illis concinnatam, suum influxum præbuit. In quantum verò conceptus, cùm rerum tùm vocum inspirati, ab actu inspirationis, à quo non nisi modaliter differunt, velut à forma modali determinantur ad suum esse supernaturale, & sic ab eo determinati ad Scripturam sacram se habent ut signatum ad suum signum, vel etiam ut exemplar, ad cujus imitationem ipsa concinnata est, in tantum habet se ad eandem ut forma vel interna vel externa & exemplaris, uti suprà thes. XV. pluribus ostensum. Unde non repugnat, ϑεοπνευsτίαν habere se ad Scripturam sacram efficienter, & certo modo ac respectu ut rationem formalem, quâ in suo esse specifico constituitur, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distingvitur. Cùm enim signa, quorum ex censu Scriptura sacra est, suam rationem formalem & specificam sortiantur à rebus, quarum signa sunt; Scriptura sacra verò signum sit conceptuum, Scriptoribus sacris divinitùs inspiratorum, qui à divina inspiratione simul efficienter dependent, & formaliter etiam, ut à forma modali, in esse supernaturali constituuntur: res ipsa exigit, ut ϑεοπνευsία sive inspiratio divina ad Scripturam tam se habeat efficienter & ut causalitas, quâ in illam Deus influxum suum præbuit, & simul ut ratio formalis, quâ in esse suo specifico constituitur, quàm ad ipsos conceptus, quorum signa ipsa continet, ex parte causæ efficientis, & ut istorum ratio formalis & specifica sese habet. Quæ enim est ratio formalis rei signatæ, ea etiam est ratio formalis signi, in quantum signum est, uti dictum, & si in illa non repugnat, aliquid habere se ex parte causæ efficientis, & simul esse rationem formalem, quâ in suo esse specifico ea constituitur, nec in hoc repugnabit. Quod autem dicitur, causam efficientem & formam constituere duo diversa causarum genera, verum est de forma, in rigore & strictè sic dicta, quæ est altera pars compositi, & per unionem sui cum materia ens per se constituit. Hæc enim est causa compositi interna, ejus constitutionem ingrediens; efficiens autem causa externa est, quæ ab effectu suo adæquatè distingvitur, ejusć; constitutionem non ingreditur. Secus autem res habet cum entibus per accidens, quale Scriptura est, itemque cum actionibus immanentibus & transeuntibus, cumque signis, in ratione signorum spectatis, quæ formam, propriè dictam, ut partem sui constitutivam, non agnoscunt: ubi causa efficiens & forma non ita adæquatè distinguuntur, quin quandoque, quoad rem, coincidant, & unus idemque effectus ab aliquo efficienter, & simul in suo esse formali ac specifico dependeat, ut exemplo conceptuum, divinitus inspiratorum, modò ostensum est.

VI. Quod verò ad auctoritatem & majestatem Scripturæ sacræ attinet, certum est, eam non ingredi primum Scripturæ sacræ conceptum, sed esse eo naturâ posteriorem, & fluere ex ejus jam in actu constitutæ natura & essentiâ. Nam Scriptura sacra, ex divino afflatu sive inspiratione conscripta, per hoc quod ex divina inspiratione conscripta & signum est conceptuum cùm rerû tùm verborum, Prophetarum & Apostoloru intellectui olim à Deo inspiratorum, jam actu in suo esse specifico constituta est, & ex hoc fluit demum divina ejus auctoritas, velut quædam illius proprietas, & ut quoddam consequens illius.

VII. Quod ad alteram attinet sententiam, quæ formam Scripturæ in sensu θεοπνεύστῳ constituit, videtur ea ad usum loquendi accedere propius. Est enim Scriptura sacra ex censu eorum, quorum esse in significando consistit. Quemadmodum autem signis omnibus commune est, ut à rebus signatis specificentur, ita Scriptura omnis suum esse specificum à sensu, cujus signum est, habere videtur. Hinc usu receptissimum est, ut verba materiale, sensus verò formale uniuscujusq; Scripturæ dicatur. Quia autem idem sensus, verbis Scripturæ expressus, potest etiam studio humano à quopiam verbis exprimi scriptoque comprehendi, cujus scriptum tamen ejusdem cum Scriptura sacra naturæ non est, videtur non incommodè ratio formalis Scripturæ sacræ constitui in sensu θεοπνεύστῳ, ut sensus sit velut forma Scripturæ generica, quam cum aliis etiam Scripturis habeat communem; sensus θεόπνευστος autem velut forma specifica illius. Verùm præterquam quod sic etiam forma Scripturæ specifica tandem ad θεοπνευστίαν redit, non etiam adæquata & propria ratio illius in sensu θεοπνεύστῳ constitui potest. Nam, uti jam in th. XVI. ostensum, quælibet versio Scripturæ, quæ quidem textui originali prorsus conformis est, continet etiam sensum θεόπνευστον: continet enim eundem sensum, quem Prophetarum & Apostolorum intellectui olim Spiritus Sanctus inspiravit; nec tamen ejusdem naturæ & essentiæ est cum Scriptura, in suo textu primigenio spectata, ut patet ex utriusque proprietate. Hæc enim divinæ & prorsus infallibilis est auctoritatis. Illi autem utut falsum non subsit, cùm textui originali, ut hîc supponitur, conformis sit, subesse tamen falsum non repugnat. Hæc norma & ἀνύ- πεύθυνος est, illa normatum quid, cui fides non debetur, nisi in quantum textui primigenio conformis est. Ad formam verò Scripturæ sacræ requiritur, ut ei adæquata sit, eamq; ab alia quavis Scriptura, & ab ipsis etiam versionibus illius distingvat. Nihil ergò superest, in quo Scripturæ forma sive ratio formalis, quâ adæquatè ab alia quavis Scriptura distingvatur, constitui possit, præter θεοπνευστίαν conceptuum, cùm rerum, tùm vocum scriptarum, terminativè sumtam, sive, quod eodem redit, præter conceptus rerum & vocum, quarum signa sunt verba scripta, Prophetis & Apostolis olim à Deo inspiratos, sub quibus & sensus ἐνθεόπνευστος continetur, ut suprà ostensum. Et tantum de forma sive ratione formali Scripturæ.


### XIX. Finally, the end of Holy Scripture, just like that of Theology, can be…

XIX.

Finally, the end of Holy Scripture, just like that of Theology, can be established as twofold: namely, Whose, and For Whom.

XX.

The end of which is either ultimate or intermediate.

XXI.

The ultimate is the eternal salvation of men, placed in the intuitive vision or knowledge of God, and it contains in itself God, as the infinitely perfect and highest good of man; and his intuitive or clear and perfect knowledge. They call the former its objective end; the latter its formal end.

XXII.

Its intermediate end is faith in Christ.

I. The end of Holy Scripture is the same as that of Theology. For Holy Scripture deals, just as Theology does, with the salvation of men, to be obtained through faith in Christ, according to the express words of Scripture itself: These are written, that YOU MAY BELIEVE, that Jesus is the Christ, and that by BELIEV-

that you may have life through his name, John XX. 31. Although these words do not speak of all things that are contained in Holy Scripture, but at least of the signs performed by Christ in the sight of the disciples, they can nevertheless be well applied to the whole of Holy Scripture. For all things that are contained in it tend ultimately to this, that they may lead man to faith in Christ, and through faith to eternal salvation, as the Apostle Paul teaches, who transfers what the Apostle John said about the signs of Christ indefinitely and without any restriction to the sacred letters or to Holy Scripture: The sacred letters, he says to his Timothy, can make you learned for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus, II. Tim. III. 15. By which both ends of which, intermediate and ultimate, and here both objective and formal, are comprehended. Whence what we taught above in part I. chap. III. th. VIII. & following, concerning the end of Revealed Theology, find a place here also.

II. Paul in the place already cited v. 16. enumerates several intermediate ends, namely doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction, which is in righteousness. But these (1) are not the ends of Scripture, considered simply in itself, but especially of Scripture considered in relation to the Minister of the Church, for instructing the sacred ministry: as the following v. 17. That the man of God (i.e., the minister of the Church) may be complete, equipped for every good work, suggest. (2) these ends also are consequently directed to faith in Christ. For the ministers of the Church are rendered by Holy Scripture apt and suitable for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, and for instructing their hearers in righteousness, so that by teaching, reproving, correcting, and instructing, they may lead them to faith in Christ, and to holiness of life, which perpetually accompanies it.

Latin:

XIX.

Finis denique Scripturæ sacræ, perinde ut Theologiæ, duplex constitui potest: Cujus scilicet, & Cui.

XX.

Finis cujus est vel ultimus, vel intermedius.

XXI.

Ultimus est salus hominum æterna, in visione sive cognitione Dei intuitiva posita, & continet in se Deum, velut bonum hominis infinitè perfectum & summum; & ejus cognitionem intuitivam sive claram & perfectam. Illum objectivum; hanc formalem ejus finem appellant.

XXII.

Intermedius ejus finis est fides in Christum.

I. Finis Scripturæ sacræ idem est, qui Theologiæ. Agit enim Scriptura sacra perinde, ut Theologia, de hominum salute, per fidem in Chrĩstum consequenda, juxta expressa ipsiusmet Scripturæ verba: Hæc scripta sunt, ut CREDATIS, Jesum esse Chrĩstum, & ut CRE-

habeatis per nomen ipsius, Joh. XX. 31. Quæ quamvis non de omnibus, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur, sed saltem de signis, à Christo in conspectu discipulorum editis, loquantur, benè tamen usurpari possunt de Scriptura sacra tota. Omnia enim, quæ in ea continentur, eò tandem tendunt, ut hominem ad fidem in Christum, & per fidem ad salutem æternam perducant, docente Apostolo Paulo, qui, quæ Johannes Apostolus de signis Christi dixit, indefinitè & absque ulla restrictione ad sacras literas sive ad Scripturam sacram transfert: Sacræ literæ, inquiens ad Timotheum suum, possunt te eruditum reddere ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, II. Tim. III. 15. Quibus uterque finis cujus, intermedius & ultimus, & hîc cùm objectivus, tùm formalis comprehenditur. Unde quæ supra in part. I. cap. III. th. VIII. & seqq. de fine Theologiæ Revelatæ docuimus, hîc etiam locum inveniunt.

II. Paulus loco jam citato v.16. plures recenset fines intermedios, nempe doctrinam, redargutionem, correctionem, & institutionem, quæ est in justitia. Sed hi (1) non sunt fines Scripturæ, in se simpliciter spectatæ, sed potissimùm Scripturæ, in ordine ad Ministrum Ecclesiæ, ad ministerium sacrum instruendum consideratæ: uti subsequentia v. 17. Ut integer sit Dei homo (h. e. Ecclesiæ minister) ad omne opus bonum apparatus, innuunt. (2) hi etiam fines consequenter diriguntur ad fidem in Christum. Ministri Ecclesiæ enim per Scripturam sacram redduntur apti & idonei ad docendum, ad redarguendum, ad corrigendum, & ad instituendum auditores suos in justitia, ut docendo, redarguendo, corrigendo & instituendo eos ad fidem in Christum, &, quæ eam perpetuò comitatur, sanctimoniam vitæ perducant.


### XXIII. The end for whom of Scripture, just as of Theology, is man corrupted by sin

XXIII.

The end for whom of Scripture, just as of Theology, is man corrupted by sin.

I. By the end for whom we understand the subject, for whose benefit and for whose sake are delivered whatever things are necessary to be known for the attaining of the end of which, we said above in part I. c. III. th. XV. That this is indeed man corrupted by sin, no one who has read Holy Scripture will deny. For for the sake of sinful man, and so that through faith in Christ he may be freed from sin and become a participant in eternal salvation, Holy Scripture delivers whatever it delivers by itself and principally.

II. It may also be said that the end to which Holy Scripture is directed is, in its own way, also the future Minister of the Church. For the same [Scripture] hands down for this end also those things which are necessary to be known for obtaining salvation through faith in Christ, so that it may instruct a man in those things which are necessary for performing public ministry in the Church, and for instructing others in the doctrine of faith and morals, and for leading them to salvation. To this pertains that Pauline passage: All Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction which is in righteousness: That the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work, II Tim. III. 16, 17. But just as these acts are neither the ultimate nor the adequate end of Holy Scripture, so neither is the future minister of the Church the end to which, or the adequate subject of which, it is.

XXIV.

With these things concerning the nature and causes of Holy Scripture thus declared, it can be described as the Word of God, recorded by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit through the Prophets and Apostles in the idiom of the Hebrew language in part, and in part in the Greek, instructing sinful man concerning all things necessary to be believed and done, so that, being freed from sins through faith in Christ, he may henceforth live holily and blamelessly, and finally obtain eternal life by the gift of God.

I. Holy Scripture has been defined, which, as shown above in thesis I, number III, is sometimes called simply, without addition, and κατ' εξοχην, Scripture; but sometimes with the addition, Holy Scripture. But in whichever way it is called, the matter comes to the same thing.

II. Moreover, this is a description of Holy Scripture, viewed in its original text, since to it alone does this name belong primarily, of itself, and independently. But when translated into other languages by human effort, although by usage of speech it also claims for itself the name of Holy Scripture, it does not, however, claim it in the same way primarily, of itself, and independently as it does in its original text, but secondarily, dependently, and because of its agreement with that [original], namely, that it has been fashioned in its imitation and likeness, and contains within itself the same things and doctrines as that one. But just as other analogous terms, as the rule of the Logicians holds, when placed absolutely, stand for their more famous meaning, or that which they have primarily, of themselves, and independently, and are to be defined in that, so also Holy Scripture is here deservedly accepted and described in that meaning which belongs to it primarily, of itself, and independently.

Yet the same description can also be attributed to Holy Scripture translated into other languages, just as the very name of Holy Scripture is, but secondarily and on account of its dependence upon the original Scripture and its conformity with it. For because a version of Scripture is adorned in imitation and likeness of the original Scripture, as its exemplary cause, and is conformable to it, so that it contains the very same things and doctrines as that one, and delivers them in the same manner, order, and end as that one, therefore it itself is also called the Word of God, consigned by the Holy Spirit inspiring through the Prophets and Apostles in the idiom of the Hebrew language in part, and in part in the Greek, etc. For analogous things, such as the original Scripture and Scripture translated into another language, indeed have the same name and the same common definition, yet in an unequal manner, and in such a way that both belong to one primarily and to the other secondarily. But if you add to this description of the original Scripture and the version the idiom of some other language into which it has been translated, you will then have a description of Holy Scripture viewed in the idiom of another language into which it has been translated; for example, our vernacular Scripture can be well described as being the Word of God, recorded by the Holy Spirit inspiring through the Prophets and Apostles in the idiom of the Hebrew and partly the Greek language, but translated into the German language by the work of B. Luther, etc.

III. We establish its genus as the Word of God, by a usage most accepted among theologians, although perhaps someone might doubt whether it is sufficiently convenient. For the genus, according to the rules of a good definition, ought to be common to all species, and therefore contain under itself all things which agree univocally with Holy Scripture in the reason and concept of Scripture. But the Word of God is not something common to all things which agree univocally with Holy Scripture in the reason and concept of Scripture. For many, indeed almost infinite, Scriptures are found which nevertheless are not the Word of God.

But we do not dwell on this doubt at all. For the concept in which all Scriptures in general agree with Holy Scripture is too general and remote. For if you distinguish all Scriptures into sacred and profane, then these two kinds of Scriptures will indeed agree under the common concept of Scripture; for each is a certain Scripture or verbal sign, related in letters, but each one in turn will contain under itself other multiple Scriptures, just as, for example, Holy Scripture will contain under itself that which usage calls so κατʾ ἐξοχὴν, and other Scriptures occupied in delivering and explaining sacred things, by which that general concept of Scripture does not apply immediately and proximately, but mediately and very remotely. According to the laws of a good definition, however, every thing, as far as possible, ought to be defined or described by its proximate genus, not by a more remote one. But the proximate genus of Holy Scripture, so called κατ’ ἐξοχὴν, is the WORD OF GOD, not indeed a univocal genus, but an analogous one, which applies to one of the analogates primarily and to the other secondarily, as has just been declared.

IV. It must, however, be rightly understood what is denoted by the appellation Word of God in the common definition of Holy Scripture. For by the Word of God can be understood either the Word internal to the divine intellect, or His external Word, and that either inspired into the minds of the holy Prophets and Apostles, or communicated by them from divine inspiration to other men either by voice or by writing, or finally the doctrine itself, divinely revealed and comprised in the Holy Scriptures. Taken in the first way, the Word of God consists in the concepts of the divine intellect, by which He had from eternity predetermined what is necessary to be believed and done by those who are to attain salvation: which concepts, on the part of the thing, are the divine essence itself, yet conceived by us with the connoted objects by way of acts of knowing. Taken in the second meaning, the Word of God consists in the concepts inspired by God into the minds of the Prophets and Apostles. In neither meaning, however, can the Word of God be predicated of Holy Scripture in the nominative case. For it cannot be said in the nominative case that Holy Scripture is the internal Word of God itself, or that it is the concepts of the divine mind themselves. For it is at least a sign of them. Nor is it rightly said that it is the concepts themselves divinely inspired into the minds of the Prophets and Apostles: since it is at least an external sign of these as well. In the third meaning, the Word of God is a verbal sign, signifying by institution, proceeding from God, and it abstracts from the vocal and written Word. In the fourth meaning, finally, the Word of God is the same as the object of the divine Word, both internal and external, and it is the thing or doctrine itself, which the divine concepts represented and represent to the divine intellect; and the concepts, inspired by God to the Prophets and Apostles, represented and represent to their own minds as formal signs; and the external words, signifying by institution, represented and represent as instrumental signs to the intellect of any reader. Although there are those who constitute the Word of God, taken in this fourth meaning, as the genus of Holy Scripture, and define it by the Word of God, or, which is the same thing to them, by the doctrine divinely revealed; nor is it even infrequent that the Word of God is taken for the thing itself, or the doctrine denoted by its external word, yet no one will doubt, without being beside the point, whether in the nominative case the Word of God, thus accepted, is rightly and properly predicated of Holy Scripture: since it is evident to the senses that Holy Scripture is and denotes in the nominative case a verbal sign, which can be painted and written with a pen, but it connotes the things themselves or the doctrine itself, signified by words, only in an oblique case by way of an object, which cannot be written except in words, as signs by which it is signified. Which also holds true in other signs: e.g., smoke is not in the nominative case fire, but a sign of fire, and therefore it connotes fire, as the thing signified, in an oblique case.

V. In the common and received definition of Holy Scripture, therefore, by which it is defined through the Word of God, the Word of God will most conveniently be taken in the third meaning, namely for the external Word and verbal sign. For this, just as it can be uttered by an articulate voice, so it can also be written, and once written, just as when uttered by voice, it is in the nominative case and essentially a verbal sign, drawing its origin from God as from an efficient cause, and it is indeed a sign of its sense or doctrine, which it contains, not the sense itself or the doctrine itself in the nominative case. To which is added that in the definition of Holy Scripture it is usually added that it is the Word of God, instructing us in all things necessary to be believed and done. But that which instructs us about things necessary to be believed and done is by common rule an external word, signifying by institution, and it instructs us about these things while, perceived by hearing or read, it signifies and represents them to our intellect.

VI. The specific difference of Holy Scripture is sought from its causes, all of which are contained in the delivered description, but especially from its principal efficient cause. And the principal efficient, and in its own way formal cause, is signified by the words: consigned by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But how θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration behaves on the part of the principal efficient cause, and also as the formal reason of Scripture, you may see declared in thesis XVI. Expl. n. 1. 2. The instrumental cause, however, is insinuated by the words: through the Prophets and Apostles. The material out of which it is made is denoted by the idioms, Hebrew and Greek; and the material about which it is made by things necessary to be believed and done. Finally, the final cause, and indeed the end for which it is made, is denoted by faith in Christ, holiness of life, and eternal life; of which these designate the end of which the ultimate; those and these the intermediate ones: but the end for which, or, which is the same thing, the subject, for whose benefit Holy Scripture delivers what is necessary to be believed and done, is denoted by the sinful man. But from all these causes, one and the only principal efficient cause bestows upon Holy Scripture its formal and specific being, as was shown at greater length above in thesis XV and following. For from this alone, that it was composed by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it has that it is truly divine, and a Scripture distinct from any other Scripture. But that it was composed by holy men, namely Prophets and Apostles, could also apply to other Scriptures. For those same holy men could also have composed other Scriptures at their own discretion. But if any had been composed by them at their own discretion, it would have been without doubt entirely different from their θεοπνεύςοις Scriptures: There exist also other Scriptures, recorded in the Hebrew and Greek idiom, and which instruct the sinful man concerning what is necessary to be believed and done for salvation, which nevertheless do not come into the category of Holy Scripture, strictly so called, for this one reason, that they were not written by the inspiration of God. From θεοπνευςίᾳ alone, therefore, as has been said, Holy Scripture has its formal and specific being: but the other causes are introduced into its description for the sake of greater light and clarity. And so much for this time.

Latin:

XXIII.

Finis cui Scripturæ, perinde ut Theologiæ, est homo peccato corruptus.

I. Per finem cui intelligi subjectum, cui bono & in cujus gratiam traduntur, quæcunque ad finem cujus consequendum cognitu necessaria sunt, diximus supra in part. I. c. III. th. XV. Illud verò esse hominem peccato corruptum, nemo, qui sacram Scripturam legerit, inficiabitur. In gratiam enim hominis peccatoris, & ut per fidem in Christum à peccato liberatus, salutis æternæ fiat particeps, tradit Scriptura sacra, quæcunque per se & principaliter tradit.

II. Potest etiam dici, finem cui Scripturae sacrae esse suo modo etiam futurum Ecclesiae Ministrum. Tradit enim eadem hoc etiam fine, quae ad salutem, per fidem in Christum consequendam, cognitu necessaria sunt, ut hominem instruat in iis, quae ad ministerium publicum in Ecclesia obeundum, & alios in doctrina fidei & morum instruendos, atque ad salutem perducendos necessaria sunt. Quo pertinet illud Paulinum: Tota Scriptura divinitus inspirata & utilis (est) ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quae est in justitia: Ut integer sit Dei homo, ad omne opus bonum apparatus, II. Tim. III. 16. 17. Verum quemadmodum hi actus neque ultimus neq; adaequatus Scripturae sacrae finis cujus sunt, ita nec futurus Ecclesiae minister ejusdem finis cui sive subjectum adaequatum est.

XXIV.

HIsce de Scripturae sacrae natura & causis sic declaratis, describi ea potest, quod sit Verbum Dei, Spiritu Sancto inspirante per Prophetas & Apostolos Ebraeo partim, partim Graeco sermonis idiomate consignatum, hominem peccatorem de omnibus creditu factuq; necessariis instruens, ut per fidem in Christum a peccatis liberatus, deinceps sancte & inculpate vivat, & vitam aeternam tandem Dei dono consequatur.

I. Definitum est Scriptura sacra, quae, ut supra th. I. n. III. ostenfum, interdum simpliciter, fine additamento, & κατ' εξοχην Scriptura; interdum vero cum additamento Scriptura sacra dicitur. Utro autem modo appelletur, res redit eodem.

II. Est autem haec descriptio Scripturae sacrae, in suo textu primigenio spectatae, quippe cui soli primo, per se & independenter id nominis convenit. In lingvas alias vero studio humano translata, licet ex usu loquendi etiam Scripturae sacrae nomen sibi vendicet, non tamen perinde primo, per se & independenter, ut in suo textu primigenio, sed secundario, dependenter & propter sui cum eo convenientiam id sibi vendicat, quod scilicet ad ejus imitationem & similitudinem concinnata sit, & easdem, quas illa, res & doctrinas in se contineat. Quemadmodum autem alias analoga, ut Logicorum regula habet, absolute posita, stant pro significatu famosiori, sive eo, quem primo, per se & independenter habent, inq; eo definienda sunt, ita & Scriptura sacra accipitur & describitur hic merito in eo significatu, qui ei primo, per se, & independenter convenit.

Potest tamen eadem descriptio etiam Scripturæ sacræ, in alias lingvas translatæ, perinde ut ipsum nomen Scripturæ sacræ, tribui, sed secundariò & ob suam à Scriptura primigenia dependentiam, ejusque conformitatem cum illa. Quia enim Versio Scripturæ ad Scripturæ primigeniæ, velut causæ exemplaris, imitationem & similitudinem adornata, eiq́; conformis est, ita ut easdem planè res & doctrinas, quas illa, contineat, easq́; eo modo & ordine, & fine eodem, quo illa, tradat, ideò & ipsa est & dicitur Verbum Dei, Spiritu Sancto inspirante per Prophetas & Apostolos Ebræo partim, partim Græco sermonis idiomamate consignatum &c. Analoga enim, qualia sunt Scriptura primigenia, & Scriptura in aliam lingvam translata, habent quidem idem nomen, & definitionem eandem communem, modo tamen inæquali, & ita ut uni per prius, alteri per posterius utrumq; conveniat. Quod si huic Scripturæ primigeniæ & Versioni communi descriptioni alterius cujusdam lingvæ idioma, in quod translata sit, adjicias, habebis tùm descriptionem Scripturæ sacræ in alio sermonis idiomate, in quod translata est, spectatæ, v. g. nostra vernacula Scriptura benè describi poterit, quòd sit Verbum Dei, Spiritu Sancto inspirante per Prophetas & Apostolos Ebræo partim, partim Græco sermonis idiomate consignatum, B. Lutheri operâ verò in lingvam Germanicam translatum &c.

III. Genus illius constituimus Verbum Dei, usu apud Theologos receptissimo, quamvis an satis commodè, forsan quis dubitaverit. Genus enim, juxta regulas bonæ definitionis, debet esse commune omnibus speciebus, & proinde omnia, quæ in ratione & conceptu Scripturæ cum Scriptura sacra univocè conveniunt, sub se continere. Sed Verbũ Dei non est commune quid omnibus, quæ in ratione & conceptu Scripturæ cum Scriptura sacra univocè conveniunt. Multæ enim, imò ferè infinitæ inveniuntur Scripturæ, quæ tamen Verbũ Dei non sunt.

Sed dubitationē hanc nihil moramur. Nam conceptus, in quo Scripturæ in universum omnes cum Scriptura S. conveniunt, nimis generalis & remotus est. Si enim Scripturas omnes distinguas in sacras & prophanas, tùm duo hæc Scripturarum genera sub alterna convenient quidem in communi Scripturæ conceptu; quælibet enim est Scriptura quædam sive signũ verbale, in literas relatũ, sed unumquodq; rursum sub se continebit alias multiplices Scripturas, sicut v. g. Scriptura sacra continebit sub se eam, quam κατʾ ἐξοχὴν usus sic appellat, & alias in rebus sacris tradendis & explicandis occupatas Scripturas, quibus generalis ille Scripturæ conceptus non immediatè & proximè, sed mediatè & valdè remotè convenit. Juxta leges autê bonæ definitionis unaquæq; res, quoad fieri potest, per genos proximum, non per remotius definienda vel describenda est. Proximum verò genus Scripturæ sacræ, κατ’ ἐξοχὴν sic dictæ, VERBUM DEI est, non quidem genus univocum, sed analogum, quod uni analogatorum per prius, alteri per posterius convenit, ut modò declaratum.

IV. Rectè verò intelligendum est, quid appellatione Verbi Dei in vulgari Scripturæ sacræ definitione denotetur. Potest enim per Verbum Dei intelligi vel Verbum, intellectui divino internum, vel Verbum ejus externum, idque vel inspiratum mentibus S. Prophetarum & Apostolorum, vel ab iisdem ex divina inspiratione cum aliis hominibus sive voce sive scripto communicatum, vel denique ipsa doctrina, divinitùs patefacta, & Scripturis sacris comprehensα. Primo modo acceptum Verbum Dei consistit in conceptibus intellectus divini, quibus quæ salutem adepturis creditu factuque necessaria sunt, ab æterno præfiniverat: qui conceptus ex parte rei sunt ipsa essentia divina, à nobis tamen cum connotatis objectis per modum actuum cognoscendi concepta. Altero significatu sumtum Verbum Dei consistit in conceptibus, Prophetarum & Apostolorum mentibus à Deo inspiratis. Neutro tamen significatu Verbum Dei de Scriptura sacra in casu recto prædicari potest. Non enim in casu recto dici potest, Scripturam sacram esse ipsum verbum Dei internum, vel esse ipsos conceptus mentis divinæ. Est enim saltem signum illorum. Neque rectè dicitur, eam esse ipsos Prophetarum & Apostolorum mentibus divinitus inspiratos conceptus: cùm & horum saltem externum signum sit. In tertio significatu Verbum Dei est signum verbale, ex instituto significans, à Deo profectum, & à Verbo vocali scriptoque præscindit. In significatu quarto denique Verbum Dei idem est, quod objectum Verbi divini, cùm interni, tùm externi, estque ipsa res sive doctrina, quam conceptus divini intellectui divino; & conceptus, Prophetis & Apostolis à Deo inspirati, ipsorum mentibus, ut signa formalia; & verba externa, ex instituto significantia, ut signa instrumentalia, cujusvis lectoris intellectui repræsentabant, & repræsentant. Quamvis verò sint, qui hoc quarto significatu sumtum Verbum Dei Scripturæ sacræ genus constituant, eamque definiant per Verbum Dei, sive quod ipsis idem est, per doctrinam, divinitùs revelatam; neque etiam infrequens sit, ut Verbum Dei pro ipsa re, vel doctrina, verbo ejus externo denotatâ accipiatur, non tamen præter rem quis dubitaverit, an in casu recto Verbum Dei, sic acceptum, de Scriptura sacra rectè & propriè prædicetur: cùm ad sensum pateat, Scripturam sacram esse & in casu recto denotare signum verbale, quod calamo pingi scribique potest, ipsas verò res sive doctrinam ipsam, verbis significatam, connotare eam in obliquo demum per modum objecti, quod scribi non potest, nisi in verbis, velut signis, quibus significatur. Quod & in aliis signis locum habet: v.g. fumus non est in casu recto ignis, sed signum ignis, & connotat proinde ignem, velut rem signatam, in obliquo.

V. In vulgari ergo usuque receptâ definitione Scripturæ sacræ, quâ per Verbum Dei definitur, Verbum Dei omnium commodissimè accipietur in significatu tertio, nempe pro Verbo externo & signo verbali. Hoc enim ut voce articulatâ proferri, ita & scribi potest, & scriptum æquè ac voce prolatum, in casu recto & per essentiam verbale signum est, à Deo velut à causa efficiente originem trahens, & signum quidem est sui sensus sive doctrinæ, quam continet, non sensus ipse vel ipsa doctrina in casu recto. Quò accedit, quod in definitione Scripturæ sacræ addi solet, eam esse Verbum Dei, de omnibus creditu factuque necessariis nos erudiens. Quod autem de rebus, creditu & factu necessariis, nos erudit, de lege communi verbum externum est, ex instituto significans, idque erudit nos de rebus hisce, dum auditu perceptum vel lectum intellectui nostro eas significat & repræsentat.

VI. Differentia specifica Scripturæ sacræ petitur ab ejus causis, quæ omnes in descriptione tradita continentur, cumprimis verò ab ejus causa efficiente principali. Et efficiens principalis quidem, atque suo modo formalis significatur verbis: Spiritu S. inspirante consignata. Quomodo autem θεοπνευσία sive divina inspiratio se ex parte causæ efficientis principalis, & etiam ut ratio formalis Scripturæ habeat, declaratū videas th. XVI. Expl. n. 1. 2. Instrumentalis verò insinuatur verbis: per Prophetas & Apostolos. Materia illius ex qua denotatur per idiomata, Ebræum & Græcum; & materia circa quam per necessaria creditu factuq́ue. Finalis denique causa, & quidem finis cujus denotatur per fidem in Christum, sanctimoniam vitæ, & vitam æternam; quorum hæc finem cujus ultimum; illa &ista intermedios designant: finis cui autem, sive, quod idem est, subjectum, cui bono Scriptura sacra, quæ creditu & factu necessaria sunt, tradit, denotatur per hominem peccatorem. Ex omnibus verò hisce causis una & sola efficiens principalis largitur Scripturæ sacræ suum esse formale & specificum, ut suprà th. XV. seqq. pluribus ostensum. Ex hoc solo enim, quod Spiritu sancto inspirante concinnata est, habet ea, quòd verè divina, & ab alia quavis Scriptura distincta Scriptura est. Quod autem à Viris sanctis, Prophetis scilicet & Apostolis, concinnata est, potuit etiam aliis Scripturis convenire. Potuerunt enim iidem Viri sancti etiam alias concinnare Scripturas suô arbitratu. Quod si qua ab ipsis suo arbitratu fuisset concinnata, fuisset ea citra dubium ab eorundem Scripturis θεοπνεύςοις planè diversa: Extant etiam aliæ Scripturæ, Ebræo & Græco idiomate consignatæ, & quæ hominem peccatorem de creditu factuque necessariis ad salutem instruunt, quæ tamen in partem Scripturæ sacræ, strictè sic dictæ, non veniunt, hac unâ de causa, quòd Deo inspirante conscriptæ non sunt. A sola igitur θεοπνευςίᾳ, uti dictum, habet Scriptura sacra suum esse formale & specificum: cæteræ verò causæ majoris lucis & perspicuitatis gratiâ descriptioni illius inferuntur. Et tantum hac vice.


## 6 On the Authority of Holy Scripture

The nature and quiddity of Holy Scripture having been explained, we proceed to consider its properties, among which its authority claims the first place for itself, concerning which we are about to treat in this chapter with God's blessing.

I.

Authority is attributed both to the author of some effect, and to the effect of the same, namely to his statement, or writing, law or command, but to the former primarily and in itself; to the latter secondarily and on account of their dependence upon him.

The name of authority is from the census of those things which are called by Aristotle common ἀφ' ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἓν from one or to one, or which belong to one primarily; to another secondarily. They are commonly called analogous by attribution. For authority belongs primarily and in itself to the author of any saying or writing, law or command; but to his saying or writing, law or command only on account of its dependence upon him, or because it has proceeded from an author who is in authority. Thus the testimony of a man worthy of belief has authority, and is esteemed worthy of belief, because its author is in authority and worthy of belief; and a law, enacted by a superior, has authority and is judged worthy of obedience, because its author, or he by whom it was enacted, has the authority and power of enacting laws and of obliging others to obedience to himself, so that whatever authority belongs to a saying or writing, law or command, does not belong to it primarily and of itself, as it does to its author, but dependently, secondarily, and on account of the authority of the author himself.

II.

The authority which is attributed to the author of any effect, generally speaking, is a certain ἀξία or dignity of the author, alluring and drawing the minds of others into veneration for him, or into assent to his sayings; or into obedience to be rendered to his laws or commands, resulting from his perfection, not hidden, but known.

I. Authority, as it is attributed to an author, I call the ἀξία or dignity of the author, alluring and drawing the minds of others into veneration for him, or into assent or obedience: because to be in authority, or to have authority, according to the usage of speech, is nothing else than to be held worthy of honor and veneration, etc. If the discourse is specifically about authority in speaking and testifying, to be in authority is the same as to be held worthy of assent and belief; but if about authority in commanding, it is the same as to be held worthy of obedience. Hence, abstractly, authority, as it is attributed to an author, can be nothing else than the ἀξία or dignity of the author, on account of which honor and veneration are owed to him, or assent, if the discourse is about authority in speaking; or obedience, if the discourse is precisely about authority in commanding. And just as this, which we call authority, the ἀξία or dignity, by its own nature constitutes the author to whom it belongs as worthy of honor, assent, or obedience, so it by its own nature moves, or certainly ought to move, others by whom it is known and rightly esteemed, to render honor, assent, or obedience to him, and thus authority, ascribed to an author, generally speaking, is rightly called the ἀξία or dignity of the author, alluring and drawing the minds of men into veneration for him, or into assent to his sayings, or into obedience to be rendered to his commands.

II. I say the same a̔ξían or dignity, resulting from its perfection. For every a̔ξía or dignity of a person is founded in some perfection of theirs, and is a certain consequence of it. Thus in a virtuous man the a̔ξía or dignity of honor is founded in his virtue, and results from it. Hence that trite saying was born: Honor is the companion of virtue. And the a̔ξía or dignity, which an excellent war leader possesses in his army, is founded in his prudence and military skill, joined with fortitude; and the a̔ξía or dignity of an excellent Doctor, which he possesses among the learned, is founded in his knowledge and profound erudition, joined with a̔kribéia and perspicuity in proposing and teaching; and the a̔ξía or dignity, which a Prince has in his territory and among his subjects, is founded in his power of commanding, and of obliging subjects to obedience, and results from the same. And thus the matter stands in other cases. Whence just as the perfection of an Author varies, so also his a̔ξía, dignity, and authority varies and is diverse. Every perfection, indeed, which can win authority for someone, is worthy of honor: since to an excellent war leader, and a distinguished historian, and an outstanding legislator, and an excellent Doctor, his own honor is owed. For honor and veneration is the companion of every virtue, both moral and intellectual. But truthfulness in speaking and testifying, and accuracy in teaching, are perfections to which in particular assent is owed; and the power of commanding and obliging others to obedience is a perfection, to which in particular the honor of obedience is owed. Just as therefore every a̔ξía and dignity is by its own nature such that it moves others to the honor and veneration of the Author, in whom some perfection, as its foundation, exists: so the a̔ξía or dignity specifically founded in the truthfulness of the author moves others by its own nature to apply assent to his words; and the a̔ξía or dignity founded in the author's power of commanding moves others by its own nature to show obedience to his laws or mandates.

III. I say that authority is the a̔ξía or dignity resulting from the perfection of the Author, not latent, but known. For authority formally is not the perfection of the author itself, nor his bare a̔ξía and dignity resulting from his perfection: for a notable perfection can exist in someone, and one can be most worthy of honor, faith, or obedience on account of a perfection existing in him, to whom nevertheless, if his perfection be hidden, or if there be no one who knows how to rightly estimate its excellence, no authority may be attributed to it; but it is the ἀξία or dignity of the author, resulting from his perfection, known and estimated by others, and besides the perfection of the author, it connotes the knowledge and estimation of others, just as truth, taken transcendentally, is not formally the essence of the thing itself, but its essence, as it is apt to terminate the true knowledge of itself, and connotes the knowledge which it is apt to terminate. The perfection of the Author therefore is the foundation, as it were remote, of the authority belonging to him, which being posited, his authority can be posited, but is not actually posited immediately: but the proximate foundation, which being posited, authority is actually posited, is the perfection of the author, known and estimated by others.

Latin:

EXplicatâ Scripturæ sacræ naturâ & quidditate, ad ejus affectiones considerandas progredimur, inter quas primum locum sibi vendicat auctoritas illius, de qua in hoc capite bono cum Deo acturi sumus.

I.

AUctoritas tribuitur & auctori alicujus effectus, & ejusdem effectui, dicto scilicet, vel scripto, legi aut mandato illius, sed illi primò & per se; his secundariò & propter suâ ab eo dependentiam.

Auctoritatis nomen est ex censu eorum, quæ Aristoteli dicuntur communia ἀφ' ἑνὸς, ἢ πρὸς ἓν ab uno vel ad unum, sive quæ uni conveniunt per prius; alteri per posterius. Vulgò dicuntur analoga attributionis. Convenit enim auctoritas primò & per se auctori alicujus dicti scriptíve, legis aut mandati; ejus autem dicto vel scripto, legi aut mandato tantùm propter suam ab illo dependentiam, sive proptereà quia ab auctore, qui in auctoritate est, profectum est. Sic viri fide digni testimonium habet auctoritatem, & æstimatur dignum fide, quia ejus auctor in auctoritate & fide dignus est; & lex, à superiore lata, habet auctoritatem judicaturque obsequio digna, quia ejus auctor sive is, à quo lata est, auctoritatem potestatémque ferendi leges, & alios sibi ad obsequium obligandi habet, ut ita quicquid auctoritatis convenit dicto vel scripto, legi vel mandato, non primò & per se, ut ejus auctori, sed dependenter, secundariò & propter auctoritatem ipsius auctoris, ei conveniat.

II.

QUæ Auctori alicujus effectus tribuitur auctoritas, generatim loquendo, est ἀξία sive dignitas quædam Auctoris, alliciens trahensque aliorum animos in ejus venerationem, aut in assensum ipsius dictis; vel in obsequium, illius legibus aut mandatis præbendum, resultans ex ejus perfectione non latente, sed notâ.

I. Auctoritatem, prout auctori tribuitur, dico ἀξίαν sive dignitatem auctoris, allicientem trahentémq; aliorum animos in ejus venerationem, assensumve vel obsequium: quia in auctoritate esse, vel auctoritatem habere, ex usu loquendi, nihil est aliud, quàm dignum haberi honore & veneratione, &c, si speciatim sermo sit de auctoritate in dicendo & testificando, in auctoritate esse idem est, atque dignum haberi assensu & fide; sin de auctoritate in præcipiendo, idem atque dignum haberi obsequio. Hinc abstractivè auctoritas, prout Auctori tribuitur, nihil aliud esse potest, quàm ἀξία sive dignitas auctoris, propter quam ei debetur honor & veneratio, vel assensus, si de auctoritate in dicendo; aut obsequium, si de auctoritate in præcipiendo præcisè sermo sit. Et quemadmodum hæc, quam auctoritatem dicimus, ἀξία sive dignitas suapte naturâ Auctorem, cui convenit, dignum constituit honore, assensu aut obsequio, ita alios, à quibus cognita & rectè æstimata est, suâpte naturâ movet, vel certè movere debet ad honorem, assensumve aut obsequium ei deferendum, atque adeò auctoritas, auctori adscripta, generatim loquendo, rectè dicitur ἀξία sive dignitas auctoris, alliciens trahensque hominum animos in ejus venerationem, vel in assensum illius dictis, aut in obsequium, ejus mandatis præbendum.

II. Eandem dico a̔ξían sive dignitatem, resultantem ex ejus perfectione. Omnis enim a̔ξía sive dignitas personæ fundatur in aliqua ejus perfectione, estque quoddam illius consequens. Sic in viro virtuoso a̔ξía sive dignitas honoris fundatur in ejus virtute, & resultat ex illa. Hinc natum tritum illud: Honor virtutis comes est. Et a̔ξía sive dignitas, quâ egregius Dux belli in suo exercitu pollet, fundatur in ejus prudentia & peritia militari, cum fortitudine conjuncta; & a̔ξía sive dignitas Doctoris excellentis, quâ apud eruditos pollet, fundatur in ejus scientia ac eruditione profunda, cum a̔kribéia & perspicuitate in proponendo docendoque conjuncta; & a̔ξía sive dignitas, quam Princeps in suo territorio & apud suos subditos habet, fundatur in ejus potestate præcipiendi, subditosque ad obsequium obligandi, & ex eadem resultat. Et sic in cæteris res habet. Unde prout perfectio Auctoris variat, ita & a̔ξía, dignitas & auctoritas illius variat atque diversa est. Omnis quidem perfectio, quæ auctoritatem alicui conciliare potest, digna est honore: siquidem Duci belli egregio, & historico insigni, & præstanti legislatori, & Doctori excellenti suus debetur honor. Honor enim & veneratio virtutis omnis, cùm moralis, tùm intellectualis, comes est. Sed veracitas in dicendo & testificando, & accuratio in docendo perfectiones sunt, quibus in specie debetur assensus; & potestas præcipiendi aliosque ad obsequium obligandi perfectio est, cui in specie obsequii honor debetur. Quemadmodum igitur a̔ξía & dignitas omnis suâpte naturâ talis est, ut moveat alios in honorem & venerationem Auctoris, cui perfectio aliqua, velut fundamentum illius, inest: ita a̔ξía sive dignitas speciatim, in auctoris veracitate fundata, movet suâpte naturâ alios ad assensum, ejus dictis adhibendum; & a̔ξía sive dignitas, in auctoris potestate præcipiendi fundata, movet suâpte naturâ alios ad obsequium, ejus legibus vel mandatis exhibendum.

III. Dico auctoritatem a̔ξían sive dignitatem, resultantem ex Auctoris perfectione, non latente, sed notâ.
