Auctoritas enim formaliter non est ipsa auctoris perfectio, neque nuda ejus a̔ξía & dignitas, ex ejus perfectione resultans: potest enim alicui inesse perfectio insignis, & potest quis ob perfectionem, sibi inexistentem, honore, fide, aut obsequio esse dignissimus, cui tamen, si perfectio ejus lateat, aut si nemo sit, qui ejus praestantiam recte aestimare nôrit, auctoritas nulla conveniat; sed est ἀξία sive dignitas auctoris, ex ejus perfectione, ab aliis cognita & aestimata, resultans, & praeter perfectionem auctoris, connotat aliorum cognitionem & aestimationem, perinde ut veritas, transcendentaliter sumta, formaliter non est ipsa rei essentia, sed essentia ejus, ut apta est veram sui cognitionem terminare, & connotat cognitionem, quam terminare apta est. Perfectio Auctoris igitur est fundamentum quasi remotum auctoritatis ipsi convenientis, quo posito poni potest, non autem actu statim ponitur ejus auctoritas: fundamentum autem proximum, quo posito actu ponitur auctoritas, est perfectio auctoris, ab aliis cognita & aestimata.


### III. Authority, however, belonging to the effect of an Author, namely to a statement…

III.

Authority, however, belonging to the effect of an Author, namely to a statement or writing, a law or a command, is a certain ἀξία or dignity of the statement or writing, of the law or command, alluring and drawing the minds of men into assent or obedience to it, resulting from the perfection of the author and the known dependence of that [effect] upon him.

I. Authority is not attributed to just any effects of an Author who is in authority, but only to those which are ordered to inducing others into assent or obedience, of which kind are the statements, writings, and testimonies of men who are clear and famous both for their knowledge of things and their pursuit of truth, so that there is no fear that they might deceive or be deceived in speaking or testifying; and the laws and commands of Princes, of which the former are effects worthy of assent, the latter of obedience, and are ordered of themselves to drawing others; the former indeed into assent to themselves; the latter into obedience to themselves: which ἀξία or dignity of theirs, by which they deserve either faith or obedience, is formally their authority. But to the excellent building of an excellent architect possessing notable authority; and to the notable victory of a war leader, authority is not attributed, not because they are not excellent effects, in which the notable perfections of their authors shine forth, but because these perfections do not attribute to the effects the same ἀξία or dignity which they attribute to their authors themselves. Thus the art and skill of building in an architect does not render the building worthy of the same honor as it renders its author worthy, nor does prudence and military skill, when for joined with the multitude in the leader of war, renders the victory, though notable, worthy of that honor with which it renders the leader himself worthy.

II. Authority, thus accepted, is called α̕ξία or dignity of a saying or writing, of a law or mandate, resulting from the perfection of its Author. For just as the authority of the author and of his saying or writing, law or mandate is one, as shown above, so also the foundation of both is one and the same, namely the perfection of the Author: the mode of attribution at least is different, and that which belongs to the Author because of a perfection intrinsic to himself, belongs to his sayings or writings, laws or mandates because of the same perfection, but one intrinsic to their Author; yet extrinsic to themselves. Sometimes, indeed, the intrinsic perfections of the Authors themselves also belong to their sayings or writings, laws or mandates: to sayings or writings, indeed, from the elegance of style, from the dignity and excellence of the object, from the solid reasons and foundations upon which their truth rests; to laws, indeed, from their congruence with the state and end of the republic, and their utility, etc. But those perfections either do not move one to assent or obedience, just as elegance of style does not move one to assent: since it can belong even to fabulous writings, and false things can be said and written even about a most excellent object; and to laws, most accommodated and most salutary to the state and end of the republic, obedience is not owed unless they were enacted by one who possesses the power of commanding; or they are not known, and cannot procure authority, just as a historical narrative concerning past events, which cannot become known to us from elsewhere than from the report of others, although it may be entirely conformable to the things themselves, yet that very conformity of it with the things cannot become known to us by itself; or if the conformity of a saying or writing with things appears from the evidence of the object and either from the terms themselves apprehended, or from the reasons upon which it rests, this perfection of it will procure not authority, but evidence for the writing or saying. The authority, therefore, of a saying or writing, of a law or mandate, is founded precisely upon the perfection of its author, and thus upon a perfection intrinsic to its author, but extrinsic to itself. Thus, a history of things done before our time, and which cannot become known to us from elsewhere than from the report of others, has authority, and is esteemed worthy of faith and assent, because its author had those things well known and understood, and was a good man and alien to partisan zeal, so that he, in writing history, it cannot be presumed that he either erred through ignorance, or wished to dissimulate the truth or speak falsely out of zeal, and the ἀξία or dignity which results from this known perfection of the author, on account of which assent and belief are owed to his words, that very thing is also the ἀξία or dignity of the history itself, on account of which assent and belief are owed to it.

III. The same ἀξία or dignity of a saying or writing, law or mandate, is said to result also from its dependence upon its author. For just as an author exerts his perfection, in which his authority is founded, through the production of an effect, and while he produces it in a manner suitable to his perfection, he as it were transfuses his ἀξία and dignity into it: so the ἀξία or dignity of the effect, namely of the saying or writing, law or mandate, results from both; namely from the perfection of the author, as from a foundation; and from its dependence upon him, as from the formal reason by which the ἀξία and dignity resulting from his perfection is communicated to it, applied, and as it were transfused into it. Thus the ἀξία or dignity of a history, moving others to have belief in it, results from the perfection of its author, namely from his knowledge of the things which he wrote, and his probity, as from its foundation: but the very recording of the history is the formal reason by which the author exerts his perfection, and as it were transfuses into it the ἀξία or dignity resulting from that. That both are required for the authority of an effect is easily evident. For if anyone is most knowledgeable about the things which a history contains and is a man of probity, but has not written a history, nothing of ἀξία and dignity, nothing of authority, will accrue to a history through his knowledge and probity. Conversely, however, if anyone has written a history, but is not knowledgeable about the things it contains or is not a man of probity, nothing of ἀξία and dignity, nothing of authority, will accrue to the written history from his writing. Therefore, both must concur for the authority of a saying or writing, law or mandate.

IV. Finally, the ἀξία or dignity of a saying or writing, law or mandate, is said to result from the perfection of the author and its known dependence upon him. For what we said above in Thesis II, Explanation no. III, that authority, as it is attributed to an author, is the ἀξία or dignity of the author, resulting from his perfection not being hidden, but known; the same thing also holds true regarding authority, as it pertains to an author's saying or writing, law or mandate. This at least must be added here, that for authority, taken in the latter sense, it is not sufficient that the author's perfection, from which as if from its foundation its ἀξία or dignity results, be known to others, but it is also required that the dependence of a saying or writing, law or command upon its author be known to others as well. For if you know that Livy is a good and trustworthy historian, but you do not know that the history which he wrote was written by him, no authority will accrue to the history itself from the authority of Livy in your estimation; and conversely, if you know that the history of Livy was written by him, but you do not know whether Livy is a historian established in authority or trustworthy, again no authority will accrue to the history itself from its known dependence upon him. Similarly, if you know that someone possesses the power of commanding and enacting laws, but you do not know that he has enacted these or those laws, no authority will accrue to the laws enacted by him in your estimation from the authority of the legislator; and conversely, if you know that he has enacted laws, but you do not know that he possesses the power of commanding and enacting laws, again no authority will accrue to the laws enacted in your estimation from the known dependence of the laws upon the legislator. Therefore, in order for the authority of an author to be established among others for a saying or writing, law or command, both are required, namely that both the perfection of the author and the dependence of those things upon the author be known to others.

Latin:

III.

AUctoritas verò, Auctoris effectui, dicto scilicet scriptove, legi aut mandato conveniens, est ἀξία sive dignitas quaedam dicti aut scripti, legis aut mandati, alliciens trahensque hominum animos in illius assensum aut obsequium, ex auctoris perfectione & illius ab eo dependentia cognita resultans.

I. Non quibusvis effectibus Auctoris, qui in auctoritate est, tribuitur auctoritas, sed illis tantùm, qui ordinantur ad alios in assensum aut ad obsequium inducendos, cujusmodi sunt dicta, scripta, & testimonia hominum, qui & rerum scientiâ & studio veritatis clari ac celebres sunt, ut metus non sit, ne in dicendo aut testificando fallant aut fallantur; & leges atque mandata Principum, quorum illa assensu; haec obsequio digni effectus sunt, & per se ad alios; illa quidem in sui assensum; haec in sui obsequium trahendos, ordinantur: quae illorum ἀξία sive dignitas, quâ vel fidem vel obsequium merentur, formaliter est auctoritas illorum. Sed architecti excellentis & auctoritate insigni pollentis aedificio excellenti; & Ducis belli victoriae insigni non tribuitur auctoritas, non quòd non sint effectus eximii, in quibus auctorum perfectiones insignes reluceant, sed quod perfectiones hae non eandem effectibus ἀξίαν sive dignitatem tribuant, quam tribuunt ipsis illorum auctoribus. Sic ars & peritia aedificandi in architecto non eo dignum reddit honore aedificium, quo ejus auctorem dignum reddit, nec prudentia & peritia militaris, cum fortitudine conjuncta in Duce belli eo honore dignam reddit victoriam, licet insignem, quo ipsum Ducem reddit dignum.

II. Dicitur autem auctoritas, sic accepta, a̕ξία sive dignitas dicti vel scripti, legis aut mandati resultans ex perfectione sui Auctoris. Ut enim auctoris, & ejus dicti vel scripti, legis aut mandati una est auctoritas, sicut supra ostensum, ita & fundamentum utriusque unum & idem est, perfectio scilicet Auctoris: modus attributionis saltem est diversus, & quæ Auctori convenit ob perfectionem sibi intrinsecam, ea convenit ejus dictis vel scriptis, legibus aut mandatis ob perfectionem eandem, sed intrinsecam suo Auctori; sibi verò extrinsecam. Conveniunt quandoque quidem Auctorum dictis etiam vel scriptis, legibus aut mandatis suæ perfectiones intrinsecæ: & dictis scriptisve quidem ex elegantia styli, ex dignitate & præstantia objecti, ex rationibus & fundamentis, quibus illorum veritas nititur, solidis; legibus verò, ex congruentia cum statu & fine reipublicæ, illarumque utilitate &c. Verùm perfectiones illæ vel non movent ad assensum aut obsequium, sicut elegantia styli non movet ad assensum: cùm fabulosis etiam scriptis convenire, & de objecto præstantissimo etiam falsa dici scribique possint; & legibus, reipublicæ statui ac fini accommodatissimis atque maximè salutaribus, nisi latæ sint ab eo, qui potestate præcipiendi pollet, obsequium non debetur; vel non notæ sunt, & auctoritatem conciliare non possunt, sicut narratio historica de rebus gestis, quæ aliunde nisi ex aliorum relatione nobis innotescere non possunt, licet rebus ipsis ex asse conformis sit, ipsa tamen ejus conformitas cum rebus per se nobis innotescere non potest; vel si conformitas dicti scriptive cum rebus ex evidentia objecti & vel ex ipsis terminis apprehensis, aut ex rationibus, quibus innititur, evidentibus appareat, non auctoritatem, sed evidentiam scripto dictove conciliabit hæc ejus perfectio. Auctoritas igitur dicti aut scripti, legis aut mandati, fundatur præcisè in perfectione sui auctoris, adeóque in perfectione, suo auctori intrinsecâ, sibi autem extrinsecâ. Sic historia rerum, ante nos gestarum, & quæ aliunde, quàm ex aliorum relatione nobis innotescere non possunt, habet auctoritatem, æstimaturque fide & assensu digna, quòd ejus auctor res illas probè cognitas & perspectas habuit, & vir bonus atque à partium studio alienus fuit, ut eum in scribenda historia vel per ignorantiam errâsse, vel studio veritatem dissimulare aut falsum dicere voluisse, præsumi non possit, & quæ ex hac auctoris perfectione cognita resultat ἀξία sive dignitas, propter quam ejus dictis debetur assensus & fides, ea ipsa etiam est historiæ ipsius ἀξία sive dignitas, propter quam ei debetur assensus & fides.

III. Eadem dicitur ἀξία sive dignitas dicti scriptive, legis aut mandati resultans etiam ex dependentia à suo auctore. Quemadmodum enim Auctor perfectionem suâ, in qua ejus auctoritas fundatur, per productionem effectus exerit, & dum eum suæ perfectioni convenienter producit, suam ἀξίαν ac dignitatem in illum quasi transfundit: ita ἀξία sive dignitas effectus, dicti scilicet scriptive, legis aut mandati, ex utroque resultat; ex perfectione scilicet auctoris, velut ex fundamento; & ex sua ab illo dependentia, velut ex ratione formali, quâ ejus ex sua perfectione resultans ἀξία & dignitas ei communicatur, applicatur, & in illum quasi transfunditur. Sic ἀξία sive dignitas historiæ, movens alios ad habendam sibi fidem, resultat ex perfectione sui auctoris, nempe ex scientia rerum, quas scripsit, & probitate, velut ex suo fundamento: ipsa autem historiæ consignatio est ratio formalis, quâ perfectionem suam Auctor exserit, & resultantem ex illa ἀξίαν sive dignitatem suam in illam quasi transfundit. Utrumque requiri ad auctoritatem effectus, facilè patet. Si quis enim rerum, quas historia continet, maximè gnarus & vir probus sit, historiam verò non scripserit, per ejus scientiam & probitatem historiæ nihil accedet ἀξίας & dignitatis, auctoritatis nihil. Contrà autem si quis scripserit historiam, rerum verò, quas continet, gnarus aut vir probus non sit, ex ejus scriptione etiam historiæ scriptæ nihil accedet ἀξίας & dignitatis, auctoritatis nihil. Utrumque ergò ad auctoritatem dicti aut scripti, legis aut mandati concurrat oportet.

IV. Dicitur denique ἀξία sive dignitas dicti vel scripti, legis aut mandati resultare ex perfectione Auctoris & illius ab eo dependentia cognita. Quod enim suprà Thes. II. Explicat. n. III. diximus, auctoritatem, prout auctori tribuitur, esse ἀξίαν sive dignitatem auctoris, resultantem ex ejus perfectione non latente, sed notâ; idipsum procedit etiam de auctoritate, prout convenit Auctoris dicto scriptove, legi aut mandato. Hoc saltem hîc addendum, quòd ad auctoritatem, posteriori modo acceptam, non sufficiat, quòd auctoris perfectio, ex qua velut ex fundamento suo ejus ἀξία sive dignitas resultat, aliis cognita sit, sed requiratur etiam, ut dicti vel scripti, legis aut mandati dependentia à suo auctore aliis quoque cognita sit. Si enim scias, Livium esse bonum & fide dignum historicum, nescias autem, historiam, quam scripsit, esse ab eo scriptam, ex auctoritate Livii apud te nihil accedet auctoritatis historiæ ipsius; & contra, si scias, historiam Livii esse ab eo scriptam, nescias autem, an in auctoritate constitutus sive fide dignus historicus sit Livius, historiæ ipsius ex sua ab eo dependentia cognita rursum nihil accedet auctoritatis. Similiter, si scias, aliquem pollere potestate præcipiendi legesq́; ferendi, nescias verò, eum tulisse has illasve leges, ex auctoritate legislatoris apud te nihil accedet auctoritatis latis ab eo legibus; & contra si scias, eum tulisse leges, nescias verò, eum pollere potestate præcipiendi legesque ferendi, rursum ex dependentia legum à legislatore cognita apud te nihil accedet auctoritatis legibus latis. Ut ergo dicto vel scripto, legi aut mandato auctoris sua apud alios auctoritas constet, requiritur utrumque, nempe ut & perfectio auctoris, & illorum ab auctore dependentia aliis nota sit.


### IV. The authority of Holy Scripture therefore in particular is its ἀξία or dignity,…

IV.

The authority of Holy Scripture therefore in particular is its ἀξία or dignity, alluring and drawing the minds of men into certain and indubitable assent to its sayings, and into irrefragable obedience to be rendered to its commands, resulting from the infinite perfection of its Author, namely God, and its own known dependence upon Him.

What we have taught thus far generally concerning authority, as it is attributed to the sayings or writings, laws or commands of an Author, and concerning its nature, applies also to the authority of Holy Scripture in particular. Whence, just as the authority of any other writing, so also the authority of Holy Scripture is a certain ἀξία or dignity of it, alluring and drawing the minds of men into assent to its sayings, or into obedience to be rendered to its commands, resulting from the perfection of its author and its known dependence upon Him. The specific reason for the authority, however, as in any other writing, so also in Holy Scripture, is sought from the specific reason of the perfection which is peculiar and proper to its author, and from the specific manner of dependence by which it draws its origin from its author. Therefore, in order to understand more deeply the authority of Holy Scripture in particular, two things in particular come here to be considered: namely, the perfection of the author, which he possesses in relation to the founding of Holy Scripture; and the dependence of Holy Scripture upon him.

V.

That God is the author of Holy Scripture was shown in the preceding chapter, so that there is no need to inculcate that here with more words or to go about proving it. We are speaking of the author or the principal efficient cause of Holy Scripture, which alone comes into consideration here. For just as all other writings receive their authority not from ministerial and amanuensis causes, who depend upon the mouth of another and receive from him what is to be written, but from the principal cause which composes it or dictates it to others for the pen, so too Holy Scripture has its authority not from its ministerial causes, namely the Prophets and Apostles, but from the principal cause, which is God himself. For they conducted themselves in the founding of Scripture only as amanuenses, and with God suggesting through inspiration what was to be written, they arranged it.

VI.

The perfection of God, however, in which the ἀξία or dignity of Holy Scripture is founded, is his supreme truthfulness in speaking and his power in commanding. The supreme truthfulness of God, through which he could neither be deceived nor deceive in speaking and in inspiring the sacred writers with what was to be written, rests upon his infinite knowledge, through which, just as nothing at all, so nothing of those things which Holy Scripture contains could be hidden from him; and also upon his goodness, through which it could not happen that he would inspire the sacred writers with anything otherwise than as the matter stands, and as it were dictate what was to be written. His absolute and supreme power of commanding, however, rests upon the right of creation, by which he has supreme dominion over all things he has made, and likewise over rational creatures, angels and men, and can impose laws upon them and bind them to obedience to himself under the threat of temporal and eternal punishments.

Latin:

IV.

AUctoritas Scripturæ sacræ igitur in specie est ἀξία sive dignitas illius, alliciens trahensque hominum animos in assensum certum & indubitatum, ejus dictis; & in obsequium irrefragabile, ipsius mandatis præstandum, ex Auctoris sui, Dei scilicet, perfectione infinita, suaque ab eo dependentia cognita resultans.

Quæ de auctoritate, prout Auctoris dictis, vel scriptis, legibus aut mandatis tribuitur, deque ejus natura hactenus generatim docuimus, procedunt etiam de auctoritate Scripturæ sacræ in specie. Unde ut alterius cujusvis Scripturæ, ita & Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas est quædam ejus ἀξία sive dignitas, alliciens trahensque hominum animos in assensum, ipsius dictis; vel in obsequium, ejus mandatis præbendum, ex perfectione auctorisipsius, ejusq; ab eo dependentia cognitâ resultans. Ratio specifica autem auctoritatis, ut in alia quavis Scriptura, ita & in Scriptura sacra petitur ex specifica ratione perfectionis, quæ ejus auctori peculiaris & propria est, & ex specifica ratione dependentiæ, quâ à suo auctore originem trahit. Ad auctoritatem Scripturæ sacræ in specie igitur penitiùs intelligendam, duo inprimis hîc consideranda veniunt: nempe perfectio auctoris, quam in ordine ad Scripturam sacram condendam obtinet; & Scripturæ sacræ ab illo dependentia.

V.

AUctorem Scripturæ sacræ esse Deum, in capite præcedente ostensum est, ut nihil opus sit id pluribus hîc inculcare aut probatum ire. Loquimur de auctore sive de causa efficiente Scripturæ sacræ principali, quæ sola hîc in considerationem venit. Ut enim aliæ Scripturæ omnes, non à causis ministerialibus & amanuensibus, qui ab alterius ore pendent, & quæ scribenda sunt, ex eo excipiunt, sed à causa principali, quæ eam componit aut aliis in calamum dictitat, suam accipiunt auctoritatem, ita & Scriptura sacra non à suis causis ministerialibus, Prophetis scilicet & Apostolis, sed à causa principali, quæ Deus ipse est, suam habet auctoritatem. Illi enim habuerunt se ad condendam Scripturam tantùm, ut amanuenses, & Deo per inspirationem, quæ scribenda essent, suggerente, eam concinnarunt.

VI.

PErfectio autem Dei, in qua Scripturæ sacræ ἀξία sive dignitas fundatur, est ejus summa cùm in dicendo veracitas, tùm in præcipiendo potestas. Veracitas Dei summa, per quam in dicendo, & Scriptoribus sacris, quæ scribenda essent, inspirando nec falli nec fallere potuit, nititur ejus infinitâ scientiâ, per quam ut prorfus nihil, ita nec quicquam eorum, quæ Scriptura sacra continet, eum latere potuit; tum bonitate, per quam fieri non potuit, ut quicquam aliter, quàm res habet, Scriptoribus sacris inspiraret, & scribendum quasi dictitaret. Ejusdem verò potestas præcipiendi absoluta & summa nititur jure creationis, quo ut in res, quas fecit, omnes, ita & in creaturas rationales, Angelos & homines, supremum habet dominium, iissque leges ferre & ad obsequium illos sibi obligare potest sub comminatione temporalium & æternarum pœnarum.


### VII. The dependence, however, of Holy Scripture upon God, as from its Author,…

VII.

The dependence, however, of Holy Scripture upon God, as from its Author, consists in θεοπνευσίᾳ or in divine inspiration, by which He immediately suggested to the sacred writers what was to be written, and dictated it as it were into the pen. That Holy Scripture depends upon God efficiently through θεοπνευσίαν or the immediate inspiration of those things which were to be written, we taught in the preceding chapter II, thesis III, from Paul, 2 Tim. III. 16. Where we also declared in what θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration consists. Which can be seen in the same place.

VIII.

Since, therefore, Holy Scripture depends efficiently upon God through θεοπνευσίαν or through immediate inspiration, its authority is certainly supreme, than which none greater can be given or conceived: to whose sayings, therefore, a faith entirely certain and indubitable is owed; and to whose commands an entirely irrefragable obedience is owed. I. For the authority of God and of Scripture, consigned through His inspiration, is one, as was shown above. But the authority of God, both in speaking and in commanding, is supreme. In speaking, indeed: because through His infinite knowledge He cannot be deceived in speaking, and through His infinite goodness He cannot wish to deceive. In commanding, however: because by the right of creation He is the supreme Lord of all, and possesses the absolute and supreme power of commanding, by which He can oblige all to irrefragable obedience. Therefore, such is the authority of Holy Scripture that an entirely certain and indubitable faith is owed to its sayings, and an entirely irrefragable obedience to its commands. For falsehood cannot underlie its sayings, whether on the part of its Author, God, or on the part of its dependence upon God. Not on the part of the former: because, as has been said, God through His infinite knowledge cannot be deceived in speaking, and through His infinite goodness cannot wish to deceive. Nor on the part of the latter: because θεοπνευσία or divine inspiration, by which Holy Scripture depends efficiently upon God, is a purely divine action, terminated at the concepts both of things and of words in the intellect of the sacred writers, which as in itself was infallible on account of the infinite knowledge and goodness of God, so it also excluded from the part of the writers every danger of erring or being deceived. For it left nothing to the judgment and liberty of the sacred writers, except the painting of the letters and strokes, in which, whether elegant or unadorned, there can be no falsehood, but in the very words, divinely inspired, and their meaning. Nor can anyone rightly deny obedience to His commands: because by this very fact that all depend on God through creation, and have their being, by nature all, without any exception, owe obedience to Him as their supreme Lord.

II. Therefore, the authority of Holy Scripture is rightly called ἀξία or dignity (1) alluring and drawing the minds of men into an assent that is entirely certain and indubitable to its sayings; and into an irrefragable obedience to be rendered to its commands, (2) resulting from the infinite perfection of its author, God, namely His infinite truthfulness, and His absolute and supreme power of commanding, and its own dependence upon Him. For in these consists the specific reason for the authority of Holy Scripture, by which it differs from the authority of any other writing. For there is no writing given which has been composed from the immediate inspiration of God, except this one, which we call holy κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν, the parts or books of which we shall enumerate in order later. Whence there is also no writing given, whose ἀξία or dignity is such that, precisely on account of the perfection of its author and its own dependence upon Him, an absolutely certain and clearly indubitable assent is owed to its sayings, except that one. For the authors of all other writings, although famous and profoundly learned, were nevertheless men, who in writing could suffer something human and err. And although there are supreme Princes on earth, who possess supreme power of commanding in their territories, their power, however, although it is subject to no superior human power, is nevertheless subject to divine power. Whence there is also no writing given, to whose precepts an absolute and irrefragable obedience is owed without any exception, except Holy Scripture. Because the obedience which we owe to the laws and commands of Princes is limited, and is to be understood with the exception of divine laws and commands, so that if we cannot obey both at the same time, it behooves us to put those aside and obey these alone, according to that saying of the Apostles Peter and John to the Prince of the Priests, the Elders and the Scribes: Whether it be just in the sight of God, to hear you rather than God, judge ye? Acts IV. 19.

Latin:

VII.

Dependentia verò Scripturæ sacræ à Deo, velut ab Auctore suo, consistit in θεοπνευσίᾳ sive in divina inspiratione, quâ Scriptoribus sacris, quæ scribenda essent, immediatè suggessit, & quasi in calamum dictitavit. Scripturam sacram dependere à Deo efficienter per θεοπνευσίαν sive immediatam inspirationem eorum, quæ scribenda essent, in præcedente cap. II. th. III. ex Paulo II. Tim. III. 16. docuimus. Ubi etiam in quo θεοπνευσία sive divina inspiratio consistat, declaravimus. Quæ ibidem videri possunt.

VIII.

QVia ergo Scriptura sacra per θεοπνευσίαν sive per immediatam inspirationem à Deo efficienter dependet, ejus auctoritas utique summa est, quâ major nec dari, nec cogitari potest: cujus dictis proinde fides prorsus certa & indubitata; & cujus mandatis obsequium planè irrefragabile debetur. I. Est enim una Dei & Scripturæ, ex ejus inspiratione consignatæ, auctoritas, ut suprà ostensum. Dei autem auctoritas, cùm in dicendo tùm in præcipiendo summa est. In dicendo quidem: quia per suam scientiam infinitam in dicendo non falli, & per suam infinitam bonitatem non fallere velle potest. In præcipiendo autem: quia jure creationis est supremus omnium Dominus, polletque potestate præcipiendi absolutâ & summâ, quâ ad obsequium irrefragabile omnes obligare potest. Ergo & Scripturæ sacræ ea est auctoritas, ut ejus dictis fides prorsus certa & indubitata, & ejus mandatis obsequium prorsus irrefragabile debeatur. Non enim ejus dictis falsum subesse potest, sive ex parte auctoris sui Dei, sive ex parte dependentiæ suæ à Deo. Non ex parte illius: quia, uti dictum, Deus per suam infinitam scientiam in dicendo falli non potest, & per suam infinitam bonitatem fallere velle non potest. Neque ex parte hujus: quia θεοπνευσία sive divina inspiratio, quâ Scriptura sacra à Deo efficienter dependet, est actio merè divina, ad conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum in intellectu sacrorum Scriptorum terminata, quæ ut in se infallibilis erat ob infinitam Dei scientiam & bonitatem, ita ex parte Scriptorum etiam omne errandi fallendive periculum excludehat. Neque enim quicquam Scriptorum sacrorum arbitrio & libertati relinquebat, præter picturam literarum & apicum, in qua sive eleganti, sive incomta, falsitas esse non potest, sed in ipsis verbis, divinitùs inspiratis, & illorum sensu. Neque ejus mandatis jure quis obsequium denegare potest: quia hoc ipso quod à Deo per creationem omnes dependent, suumque esse habent, naturâ ei, ut suo supremo Domino, omnes absque ulla exceptione obsequium debent.

II. Rectè igitur auctoritas Scripturæ sacræ dicitur ἀξία sive dignitas (1) alliciens trahensque hominum animos in assensum prorsus certum & indubitatum, ipsius dictis; & in obsequium irrefragabile, ejus mandatis præbendum, (2) ex auctoris sui, Dei, perfectione infinita, veracitate scilicet infinita, & potestate præcipiendi absolutâ & summâ, suaq́; ab eo dependentia resultans. In his enim consistit auctoritatis Scripturæ sacræ ratio specifica, quâ ab auctoritate alterius cujusque Scripturæ differt. Nulla enim datur Scriptura, quæ ex Dei immediata inspiratione confignata sit, præter hanc, quam κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν sacram dicimus, cujus partes sive libros postea ordine enumerabimus. Unde nulla etiam datur Scriptura, cujus ea sit ἀξία sive dignitas, ut præcisè propter perfectionem sui auctoris, suamque ab eo dependentiam ejus dictis assensus absolutè certus & planè indubitatus debeatur, præter illam. Omnium enim cæterarum Scripturarum auctores, licet celebres & profundè docti, homines tamen fuerunt, qui in scribendo humani quid pati & errare potuerunt. Et quamvis dentur Principes in terris summi, qui in suis territoriis potestate præcipiendi pollent summâ, illorum potestas tamen, licet humanæ potestati superiori nulli subsit, subest tamen potestati divinæ. Unde nulla etiam datur Scriptura, cujus præceptis absque ulla exceptione obsequium debeatur absolutum & irrefragabile, præter Scripturam sacram. Quia quod legibus & mandatis Principum debemus obsequium, limitatum est, & cum exceptione legum & mandatorum divinorum intelligendum, ut si utrisque simul parere non possimus, illa posthabere, & his solis parere nos oporteat, juxta illud Apostolorum Petri & Johannis ad Principem Sacerdotum, Seniores & Scribas: An justum sit in conspectu Dei, vobis potius obedire, quàm Deo, vos judicate? Act. IV. 19.


### IX. Hence it follows that the authority of Holy Scripture, as to the thing itself,…

IX.

Hence it follows that the authority of Holy Scripture, as to the thing itself, does not depend upon the Church, but upon God alone.

I. For the authority of Holy Scripture results from the perfection of its author, as has been said, and depends, as to the thing itself, upon this alone. But the author of it is not the Church, but God alone, inasmuch as it was composed by the sacred writers through his inspiration alone. Therefore its authority, as to the thing itself, depends upon God alone, not upon the Church.

II. I say: As to the thing itself. But whether as to us, that is, by reason of our knowledge, it depends upon the Church, or, to speak more clearly, whether and how far it becomes known to us from the testimony of the Church that Holy Scripture depends upon God efficiently, and thus by reason of its dependence upon God possesses divine authority, is another question, which will be treated later in its proper place.

X.

But just as for the authority of any author the perfection of that author and its dependence upon him is not sufficient, unless both are known, as was shown above in thesis III, explanation number IV, so in order that the divine authority of Holy Scripture may be established among men, it must be known, on the part of the divine perfections, that God is supremely truthful, and by his infinite knowledge and goodness can neither be deceived nor deceive in his assertions and sayings; and that he has absolute and supreme power of commanding and obliging men to obedience; and on the part of Holy Scripture, that it depends upon God efficiently, and was written by his inspiration.

For in the knowledge of these things is founded the entire authority of Holy Scripture.

XI.

But the knowledge of both principles is required, not as a constitutive part of the authority of Scripture, nor as its cause or foundation, nor even as a constitutive part of its foundation, but only as a condition, on the part of men, whose minds it must move, that is necessary. The foundation from which the authority of Holy Scripture results is the sole infinite knowledge and goodness of God, through which He can neither be deceived nor deceive in speaking, and His absolute and supreme power of commanding, through which He can bind all to obedience to Himself. The application of this to Holy Scripture consists in its dependence on God through θεοπνευςίαν. From both, when known by men, results this whole, that among men Scripture is esteemed to be of divine authority and worthy of assent and obedience above all things, and is apt to move them to both; and our knowledge, as it is plainly extrinsic to the perfection of God and the dependence of Scripture upon Him, so it is required on our part only as a condition for this, that its motive force may be able to penetrate our minds and draw them to assent or obedience, without which, if it were absent, it could not exert itself in them to cause either assent or obedience.

Latin:

IX.

INde fluit, quòd Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas, quoad rem, non dependeat ab Ecclesia, sed à solo Deo.

I. Resultat enim Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas ex perfectione sui auctoris, uti dictum, & dependet, quoad rem, ab hac sola. Auctor verò illius non est Ecclesia, sed solus Deus, quippe quo solo inspirante à Scriptoribus sacris concinnata est. Ergo à Deo solo dependet illius auctoritas, quoad rem, non ab Ecclesia.

II. Dico: Quoad rem. Utrum verò quoad nos, h. e. ratione notitiæ nostræ ea ab Ecclesia dependeat, sive, ut clarius dicam, utrum & quousque nobis ex testificatione Ecclesiæ innotescat, Scripturam sacram dependere à Deo efficienter, atque adeò propter suam à Deo dependentiam pollere auctoritate divina, alia quæstio est, de qua postea suo loco agetur.

X.

QVemadmodum autem ad auctoritatem Scripturæ cujuscunque Auctoris perfectio, ejusque ab illo dependentia non sufficit, nisi utraque nota sit, ut suprà th. III. Expl. n. IV. ostensum, ita ut Scripturæ sacræ sua divina auctoritas inter homines constare possit, notum esse debet, ex parte perfectionum divinarum quidem, Deum esse summè veracem, & per suam infinitam scientiam ac bonitatem in suis assertionibus & dictis nec falli nec fallere posse; & habere potestatem præcipiendi hominesque ad obsequium obligandi absolutam & summam; ex parte Scripturæ sacræ autem, eam dependere à Deo efficienter, & esse ex ejus inspiratione conscriptam.

In his enim cognitis fundatur tota Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas.

XI.

NOtitia autem principii utriusque requiritur, non ut pars auctoritatis Scripturæ constitutiva, neque ut causa vel fundamentum illius, neque etiam ut pars constitutiva fundamenti illius, sed tantùm ut conditio, ex parte hominum, quorum animos commovere debet, necessaria. Fundamentum, ex quo Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas resultat, est sola Dei infinita scientia ac bonitas, per quam in dicendo nec falli nec fallere potest, ejúsque præcipiendi potestas absoluta & summa, per quam ad obsequium sibi omnes obligare potest. Applicatio autem ejus ad Scripturam sacram consistit in dependentia ejus a Deo per θεοπνευςίαν. Ex utroque, ab hominibus cognito, resultat hoc totum, quod inter homines Scriptura divinæ auctoritatis & assensu obsequioq́; super omnia digna esse æstimatur, eosq; ad utrumque movere apta est; & cognitio nostra, uti perfectioni Dei & Scripturæ ab eo dependentiæ planè extrinseca est, ita tantùm ex parte nostri requiritur ut conditio ad hoc, ut ejus vis motiva ad animos nostros penetrare, eosque ad assensum vel obsequium trahere possit, absque qua si esset, neque ad assensum neque ad obsequium causandum in iis se exerere posset.


### XII. Moreover, as the authority of Scripture rests upon the twofold perfection of…

XII.

Moreover, as the authority of Scripture rests upon the twofold perfection of its author, namely his veracity and his power of commanding: of which the former regards the intellect of man, the latter his will: so it embraces as it were two parts within its scope: one, which is founded in the veracity of God; the other, which is founded in the same absolute and supreme power of commanding: of which the former moves and obliges the intellect to believe the sayings and narratives of Scripture; the latter, the will to obey its precepts.

XIII.

The former extends more widely than the latter, and extends itself in its own way to all things which are contained in the Holy Scriptures, even to the very precepts contained in them. For the precepts which are contained in the Holy Scriptures, besides that they prescribe what is fitting to do or not to do with the force of binding to obedience, on account of God's absolute power of commanding, are also conformable both to the divine intellect and to the things themselves which they prescribe, and have the character of truth, and thus possess authority and the power of moving the intellect to believe their conformity with the divine intellect and the things themselves, on account of the supreme truthfulness of God who commands.

XIV.

The authority of Scripture which rests upon the truthfulness of God, as is more widely evident, is also prior in the order of doctrine than the other, which is founded upon His power of commanding: for when the former is known, no difficulty can remain concerning the latter; thus it is usually considered almost alone here by theologians.

I. That the authority of Scripture which is founded upon the truthfulness of God is more extensive than that which is founded upon His power of commanding, has just been shown in the preceding thesis XIII. That the former is prior to the latter in the order of doctrine, however, is evident from the end of Holy Scripture. For its proximate and immediate end is faith, which regards its authority resulting from the supreme truthfulness of God; but holiness of life, to be conformed to the precepts of Holy Scripture, follows faith, and this regards its authority resulting from the absolute and supreme power of God to command; and the knowledge of the latter depends upon the knowledge of the former. For when it is established that Holy Scripture depends upon God, who is supremely truthful, efficiently through θεοπνευσίαν, and that He says through Scripture whatever Scripture says, it is established entirely that God Himself, whose power to command and to bind to obedience is evidently absolute and supreme, also commands through the same whatever it itself commands, and that an irrefragable obedience is as much owed to the precepts of Holy Scripture on account of the absolute and supreme power of God, who commands through it, to command, as a certain and indubitable assent is owed to its statements on account of the supreme truthfulness of the same, who speaks through it.

II. And perhaps this is the reason why theologians commonly understand by the authority of Holy Scripture simply that authority which results from the supreme truthfulness of God when known, and are occupied almost entirely with explaining this alone, while the other part of it, which is founded upon the absolute and supreme power of God to command, is passed over as being known from the knowledge of the former: whose footsteps we also shall follow, and hereafter, with God's blessing, we shall treat more fully of the authority of Scripture which is founded upon the supreme truthfulness of God and its dependence upon God.

Latin:

XII.

CÆterum Auctoritas Scripturæ ut duplici nititur perfectione sui auctoris, ejus veracitate scilicet, & potestate præcipiendi: quarum illa hominis intellectum; hæc ejusdem voluntatem respicit: ita duas quasi partes suo ambitu complectitur: Unam, quæ in Dei veracitate; alteram, quæ in ejusdem potestate præcipiendi absolutâ & summâ fundatur: quarum illa intellectum ad credendum Scripturæ dictis & narrationibus; hæc voluntatem ad obsequendum ejus præceptis movet & obligat.

XIII.

ILla hâc latiùs patet, & extendit se suo modo ad omnia, quæ in Scripturis sacris continentur, etiam ad ipsa in illis contenta præcepta. Nam præcepta, quæ in Scripturis sacris continentur, præterquam quòd quæ agere aut non agere conveniat, præscribant cum vi obligandi ad obsequium, ob Dei potestatem præcipiendi absolutam, sunt etiam conformia cùm intellectui divino, tùm rebus ipsis, quas præscribunt, habentque rationem veri, atque adeò pollent auctoritate & vi movendi intellectum ad credendam sui conformitatem cum intellectu divino rebusque ipsis, propter Dei præcipientis veracitatem summam.

XIV.

QVæ Dei veracitate nititur auctoritas Scripturæ, uti latius patet, & ordine doctrinæ prior est, quàm altera, quæ in ejus potestate præcipiendi fundatur: illâ enim cognitâ de hac nihil difficultatis superesse potest; ita à Theologis ferè sola heic considerari solet.

I. Latius patere auctoritatem Scripturæ, quæ in Dei veracitate, quàm quæ in ejus potestate præcipiendi fundatur, modò ostensum est in præced. th. XIII. Ordine doctrinæ autem esse illam hâc priorem, patet ex fine Scripturæ sacræ. Proximus enim & immediatus ejus finis est fides, quæ respicit ejus auctoritatem, ex Dei veracitate summa resultantem; fidem verò consequitur sanctimonia vitæ, præceptis Scripturæ sacræ conformandæ, quæ respicit auctoritatem illius, ex Dei potestate præcipiendi absolutâ & summâ resultantem; hujusque notitia pendet ex notitia illius. Ubi enim constat, Scripturam sacram dependere à Deo summè veraci per θεοπνευσίαν efficienter, eumque dicere per Scripturam, quæcunque Scriptura dicit, constat oppidò, Deum ipsummet, cujus potestatem præcipiendi & ad obsequium obligandi absolutam & summam esse, per se patet, præcipere etiam per eandem, quæcunque ipsa præcipit, & tam deberi præceptis Scripturæ sacræ obsequium irrefragabile propter Dei, per eam præcipientis, potestatem præcipiendi absolutam & summam, quàm ejus dictis assensus certus & indubitatus debetur propter ejusdem, per eam dicentis, veracitatem summam.

II. Atque hæc forsan causa est, cur communiter Theologi per auctoritatem Scripturæ sacræ simpliciter eam intelligant auctoritatem, quæ ex Dei summa veracitate cognitâ resultat, & ferè in hac sola explicanda occupentur, alterâ ejus parte, quæ in Dei potestate præcipiendi absoluta & summa fundatur, velut ex illius cognitione notâ, prætermissâ: quorum vestigia & nos secuturi, & deinceps de auctoritate Scripturæ, quæ in Dei veracitate summa ejusque à Deo dependentia fundatur, bono cum Deo uberiùs acturi sumus.


### XV. This authority of Holy Scripture, however, implies a twofold relation

XV.

This authority of Holy Scripture, however, implies a twofold relation: one for discerning other Scriptures and doctrines which deal with matters of faith and morals. The other for causing the assent of things to be believed in the human intellect. By reason of the former relation, it can be called canonical or normative authority, so to speak, of true and false; by reason of the latter, however, it is the motive authority and the causative of divine faith.

I. The authority of Scripture, founded in the supreme truthfulness of God and its dependence upon God through θεοπνευσίαν, is, as to the thing itself, one and the same, by which Holy Scripture is constituted both in the capacity of a canon and norm, to which all other Scriptures and doctrines concerning matters of faith and morals are to be tested and examined; and in the capacity of a formal motive for causing the assent of divine faith in the human intellect. For by this, that it is recorded by divine inspiration, it has from its author, God, who knows not how to be deceived or to deceive, that it is utterly repugnant for anything false to underlie it, and consequently whatever agrees with it is true and to be received; whatever disagrees with it is false and to be rejected: which is, that it has normative authority, or the character of a canon and norm. And by that same thing (namely, that it is recorded by divine inspiration, and has from its author, God, who knows not how to be deceived or to deceive, that nothing false can underlie it) it is fit for moving the minds of men to assent both to itself and to the doctrines contained within it: which is, that it has motive authority for assent, or the character of a formal motive. The former exerts itself when a controversy arises concerning the truth of a doctrine and the truth is to be confirmed, but falsehood is to be refuted; the latter, when through Scripture read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, either unbelievers are to be converted to the Christian faith, or the weak faith of the faithful is to be confirmed.

II. Because, however, Scripture is to be applied a little differently by way of a norm for discerning truth from falsehood; and differently by way of a formal motive for causing the assent of faith: for to this use Scripture is applied when read in any language or proposed by the voice of a teacher; but to that use it is applied in its own original text alone, by the power of its authority it exerts itself; therefore concerning the authority of Scripture by reason of both relations distinctly, and indeed concerning that same authority by reason of the prior relationship, as it functions by way of a formal motive for causing the assent of faith, we will treat first.

Latin:

XV.

HÆc verò Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas duplicem importat habitudinem: unam ad Scripturas doctrinasque alias, quæ de rebus fidei & morum agunt, dignoscendas. Alteram ad assensum credendorum, in hominis intellectu causandum. Ratione prioris habitudinis potest ea dici auctoritas Canonica sive normativa, ut ita loquar, veri & falsi; ratione posterioris verò auctoritas motiva fideique divinæ causativa.

I. Auctoritas Scripturæ, in Dei summa veracitate & ejus à Deo dependentia per θεοπνευσίαν fundata, quoad rem, una & eadem est, per quam Scriptura sacra & in ratione canonis ac normæ, ad quam exigendæ & examinandæ sunt omnes aliæ de rebus fidei & morum Scripturæ ac doctrinæ; & in ratione motivi formalis ad causandum in hominis intellectu assensum fidei divinæ constituitur. Per hoc enim, quòd ex divina inspiratione consignata est, habet ipsa ab auctore suo Deo, falli & fallere nescio, quod falsum sibi subesse prorsus repugnat, & proinde quicquid cum ea convenit, verum & recipiendum; quicquid eidem disconvenit, falsum & rejiciendum sit: quod est, eam habere auctoritatem normativam, vel rationem canonis & normæ. Et per idem illud (quod scilicet ex divina inspiratione consignata est, & ab auctore suo, Deo, falli ac fallere nescio, habet, quod falsum ei subesse non potest) eadem apta est ad movendos hominum animos ad assensum & sui, & doctrinarum in se contentarum: quod est, eam habere auctoritatem motivam ad assensum, vel rationem motivi formalis. Illa exerit se se, quando de veritate doctrinæ controversia oritur & veritas confirmanda, falsitas verò confutanda est; hæc, quando per Scripturam lectam vel docentis voce propositam vel infideles ad fidem Christianam convertendi sunt, vel fidelium infirma fides confirmanda est.

II. Quia tamen paulò aliter Scriptura adhibenda est per modum normæ ad dignoscendum verum à falso; aliter per modum motivi formalis ad causandum assensum fidei: ad hunc enim usum Scriptura in quacunque lingua lecta aut docentis voce proposita; ad illum verò in solo suo primigenio textu adhibita, vi auctoritatis suæ se se exerit; ideò de auctoritate Scripturæ ratione utriusque habitudinis distinctè, & de eâdem quidem ratione habitudinis prioris, ut per modum motivi formalis ad causandum assensum fidei sese habet, prius acturi sumus.


## 7 On the Authority of Holy Scripture in Causing the Assent of Faith

THAT the authority of Holy Scripture may move the human intellect to the assent of things to be believed, two complex principles are required. One: Whatever Scripture has been composed with God inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen, that is certainly and infallibly true. The other: Holy Scripture has been composed with God inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen.

The former is founded upon the veracity of God in itself; the latter concerns the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God through θεοπνευσίαν. As the veracity of God is supreme, so that falsehood cannot underlie His words, so it is the cause why Scripture, written with God inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen, deserves faith in itself. But the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God inspiring, and as it were dictating into the pen, is the formal reason by which the supreme veracity of God is joined with it, and it is brought about that falsehood cannot underlie it.

These things are so conspicuous and manifest from what has been said thus far, that it would be entirely superfluous to declare them at greater length.

II.

It is necessary that both be known by the intellect, if they are to move it to the assent of things to be believed. For the knowledge of one or the other alone does not suffice.

For if you do not know that God is supremely truthful, and that Scripture, which was composed with God inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen what was to be written, is infallibly true, or if you do not know that Holy Scripture was composed with God inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen what was to be written, the authority of Scripture will never move yours to believe those things which are contained in the Scriptures: or if you are ignorant of both, you will be ignorant of the entire authority of Scripture, nor will you ever, by its power at least, be moved to the assent of things to be believed. The matter stands likewise with a Scripture composed by human effort, which has some authority, e.g., with the History of Livy. The authority of the Livian History is a certain ἀξία or dignity of it, resulting from the perfection of its author, namely from his knowledge of the things to be written, and the goodness of his will, alien to the bias of parties; and from its dependence upon him, and it involves these two complex principles: Whatever history is written by an approved historian, who was neither given to the bias of parties nor unskilled in the things to be written, to it is deservedly owed belief; And the Livian history is written by a good historian, who was neither given to the bias of parties nor unskilled in the things to be written, namely by Livy: of which if you are ignorant of either one or both, the authority of the Livian history will never move you to the assent of itself and of other things which are contained in it.

Latin:

UT ad assensum credendorum Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas intellectum hominis moveat, duo requiruntur principia complexa. Unum: Quæcunque Scriptura Deo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante concinnata est, ea certò & infallibiliter vera est. Alterum: Scriptura sacra Deo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante, concinnata est.

Illud fundatur in Dei veracitate secundum se; hoc dependentiam Scripturæ sacræ à Deo per θεοπνευσίαν concernit. Veracitas Dei uti summa est, ut ejus dictis falsum subesse non possit, ita in causa est, cur Scriptura, Deo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante conscripta, per se mereatur fidem. Dependentia verò Scripturæ sacræ à Deo inspirante, & quasi in calamum dictitante est ratio formalis, quâ veracitas Dei summa cum ea conjungitur, & ut falsum ei subesse non possit, efficitur.

Hæc ex hactenus dictis ita conspicua & manifesta sunt, ut pluribus declarare prorsus supervacaneum fuerit.

II.

UTrumq; ab intellectu cognitum esse oportet, si ad assensum credendorum eum movere debeant. Sola enim alterutrius cognitio non sufficit.

Si enim nescias, Deum esse summè veracem, & Scripturam, quæ Deo inspirante, & quæ scribenda erant, quasi in calamum dictitante concinnata est, esse infallibiliter veram, vel nescias, Scripturam sacram esse Deo inspirante & quæ scribenda erant, in calamum quasi dictitante concinnatam, auctoritas Scripturæ nunquam intellectum tuum ad ea, quæ in Scripturis continentur, credenda movebit: vel si ignores utrumque, auctoritatem Scripturæ totam ignorabis, nec unquam, illius quidem vi, ad assensum credendorum moveberis. Perinde res habet cum Scriptura, humano studio concinnata, cujus aliqua est auctoritas, v. g. cum Historia Livii. Auctoritas Historiæ Livianæ est quædam ejus ἀξία sive dignitas, resultans ex perfectione sui auctoris, ex scientiâ scilicet rerum scribendarum, & bonitate voluntatis, à partium studio alienæ; & ex sua ab eo dependentia, & involvit duo hæc complexa principia: Quæcunque historia ab historico probato, & qui nec partium studio deditus, nec rerum scribendarum imperitus fuit, conscripta est, ei meritò debetur fides; Et historia Liviana est à bono historico, qui nec partium studio deditus nec rerum scribendarum imperitus fuit, nempe à Livio concinnata: quorum si alterutrum vel utrumq; ignores, auctoritas historiæ Livianæ te nunquam movebit in sui & aliorum, quæ eâ continentur, assensum.


### III. CONCERNING the knowledge of the former principle, it is easily agreed upon…

III.

CONCERNING the knowledge of the former principle, it is easily agreed upon among all.

For that God is supremely truthful, and that Scripture, composed with Him inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen, is infallibly true, is evident and known of itself from the very terms apprehended. Although whether that, thus naturally and evidently known, suffices with the other principle (that holy Scripture was composed with God inspiring) known and believed supernaturally and by divine faith, to found the assent of things to be believed, which is of divine faith? some doubt. Concerning which matter it has been treated by us elsewhere, and especially in the Tract on Conversion, Disputation IX, chapter 1, number IV and following, where he who wishes may see.

IV.

CONCERNING the knowledge of the latter principle, however, the matter is more intricate.

For that holy Scripture was composed with God inspiring is not equally evident and known to us by nature, as it is evident and known to us by nature that God is supremely truthful, and that Scripture finished from his inspiration is infallibly true. Nor also by any reason a priori can this be demonstrated. A posteriori indeed that can be shown with sufficient probability from various effects, signs, and motives, which nevertheless do not suffice for generating that knowledge of it which would indeed be divine faith.

V.

For a twofold knowledge is given, by which it becomes known to us that Holy Scripture was written by God inspiring it: namely, human faith or opinion; and divine faith. I. The word knowledge is not taken here for simple knowledge, contrasted with assent, which logicians commonly call the apprehension of simple things, but for cognition, placed in judgment and assent. II. The distinction of knowledge into knowledge of human faith, of opinion; and of divine faith is sought from the reason for assenting, and the cognition placed in assent, whose ultimate reason for assenting is human testimony, e.g., the testimony of parents, ancestors, the Church, etc., is called knowledge of human faith. Cognition joined with assent, whose ultimate reason for assenting is a probable reason generating opinion, is called opinion or opinative knowledge. Cognition placed in assent, whose ultimate reason for assenting is divine and supernatural revelation or testimony, is called knowledge of divine faith. III. Although human testimony generates nothing other than probable cognition or opinion, and human faith, as to the thing itself, is a certain opinion, yet from the usage of speaking, that which relies on human testimony is specifically called human faith; and that which relies on any other probable reason is called opinion. However, this distinction is not always observed, but the word opinion is not rarely taken also in a broader meaning, as it includes human faith under itself as well. Both kinds of cognition are contrasted with divine faith. For this is simply certain and entirely devoid of the opposite fear, on account of the certainty of divine revelation or testimony, upon which, as the ultimate reason for assenting, it relies, being entirely infallible: but it is not repugnant for falsehood to underlie neither of the former. IV. The term acquired faith is frequent among the Scholastics, in opposition to faith so-called infused. Under acquired faith, however, they include both the human faith, which we have mentioned, and opinion, which both are prepared and acquired by our own powers and our own effort. But that which we call divine faith, they call infused, thinking that it is infused into the human soul by God in an instant, in its entirety. But this hypothesis of theirs, that faith and other supernatural habits are infused into adults in an instant, not only rests on no foundation of Scripture, but is even opposed to it. For we have shown before, in a special Disputation held on faith, that faith and other supernatural habits are produced no less than natural habits, not indeed by previous natural acts acquired by our own powers; but by supernatural ones, elicited in us by divine grace through the Word of God. Whence we prefer to call it divine faith, by a term sufficiently used by Scholastic and modern Theologians alike, from the reason for assenting, which is divine, namely from divine truthfulness and revelation, rather than infused, from infusion, as if it were an instantaneous mode of production.

Latin:

III.

DE notitia principii prioris facile inter omnes convenit.

Deum enim summè veracem, & Scripturam, eo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante concinnatam, infallibiliter veram esse evidens & per se ex ipsis apprehensis terminis notum est. Quanquam sufficiatne illud, sic naturaliter & evidenter cognitum, cum altero principio (Scripturam sacram esse Deo inspirante concinnatam) supernaturaliter & fide divinâ cognito & credito, ad fundandum credendorum assensum, qui fidei divinæ sit? nonnulli dubitant. Qua de re à nobis alibi, & cumprimis in Tract. de Convers. Disp. IX. cap. 1. n. IV. seqq. fusè actum est, ubi, qui vult, videat.

IV.

DE notitia verò principii posterioris res intricatior est.

Nam Scripturam sacram Deo inspirante concinnatam esse, non æquè nobis evidens & naturâ notum est, ut Deum summè veracem, & Scripturam ex ejus inspiratione confectam, infallibiliter veram esse, evidens nobis & naturâ notum est. Neque etiam ratione aliquâ àpriori id demonstrari potest. A posteriori quidem illud satis probabiliter ostendi potest ex variis effectibus, signis & motivis, quæ tamen ad generandam ejus notitiam, quæ quidem fides divina esset, non sufficiunt.

V.

DUplex enim datur notitia, quâ Scripturam sacram Deo inspirante conscriptam esse nobis innotescit: Fides humana scilicet vel opinionis; & fidei divina. I. Notitiæ vox hic non accipitur pro notitia simplici, assensui contradistinctâ, quam Logici communiter apprehensionem simplicium dicunt, sed pro cognitione, in judicio & assensu posita. II. Petita autem est notitiæ distinctio in notitiam fidei humanæ, opinionis; & fidei divinæ, à ratione assentendi, & dicitur fidei humanæ notitia cognitio, in assensu posita, cujus ratio assentendi ultima est testificatio humana, v. g. testificatio parentum, majorum, Ecclesiæ &c. Opinionis sive opinativa notitia dicitur cognitio, cum assensu conjuncta, cujus ratio assentendi ultima est ratio probabilis, opinionem generans. Fidei divinæ notitia dicitur cognitio, in assensu posita, cujus ratio assentendi ultima est revelatio sive testificatio divina & supernaturalis. III. Quamvis verò testificatio humana non aliam, quàm probabilem cognitionem sive opinionem generet, & fides humana, quoad rem, sit opinio quædam, ex usu loquendi tamen quæ testificatione humanâ nititur, speciatim fides humana; & quæ aliâ quâcunque ratione probabili nititur, opinio appellatur. Non tamen discrimen hoc perpetuò observatur, sed opinionis vox accipitur non rarò etiam in significatu latiori, prout fidem humanam quoque sub se comprehendit. Utraque autem cognitio fidei divinæ contradistinguitur. Hæc enim simpliciter certa & formidinis oppositi planè expers est, ob certitudinem divinæ revelationis sive testificationis, quâ velut ratione assentendi ultimâ nititur, prorsus infallibilem: illarum verò neutri falsum subesse repugnat. IV. Scholasticis frequens est terminus fidei acquisitæ, in oppositione ad fidem infusam sic dictæ. Sub acquisita autem fide comprehendunt cùm humanam, quam diximus, fidem, tùm opinionem, quod utraque nostris viribus nostroque studio comparetur & acquiratur. Quam autem nos divinam vocamus fidem, illi infusam appellant, rati, eam infundi hominis animo a Deo in instanti totam. Sed haec illorum hypothesis, quod fides aliique habitus supernaturales adultis infundantur in instanti, non tantum nullo Scripturae fundamento nititur, sed ei etiam adversatur. Ostendimus enim antehac in peculiari de fide habita Disputatione, fidem aliosque habitus supernaturales produci non minus, quam habitus naturales, per praevios actus non quidem naturales, nostrisque viribus acquisitos; sed supernaturales, & gratia divina per Verbum Dei in nobis elicitos. Unde nos malumus eam, termino Scholasticis juxta ac modernis Theologis satis usitato, divinam dicere fidem, a ratione assentiendi divina, nempe a divina veracitate & revelatione, quam infusam, ab infusione, velut modo productionis instantaneo.


### VI. Because of the twofold reason for the knowledge by which the dependence of the…

VI.

Because of the twofold reason for the knowledge by which the dependence of the holy Scriptures on God inspiring us becomes known to us, namely human faith or opinion; and divine faith, a twofold question can be established: One, whence the knowledge of human or opinionative faith becomes known to us, that holy Scripture depends on God efficiently, and has been composed by his inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen: The other, whence does the knowledge of divine faith make this known to us?

VII.

Although the hinge and sum of the matter turns on the latter question, yet the former also has its significant use.

I. The hinge and sum of the matter turns on the latter question: because for Christian faith, the uncertain knowledge of human and opinionative faith regarding the dependence of holy Scripture on God inspiring is not sufficient: for otherwise the whole of Christian faith would be uncertain and joined with the fear of the opposite; but its assent is required, free from all doubt, and a truly divine faith, which is ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, & πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀὐ βλεπομένων, Hebr. XI. 1. and by which the souls of men are rendered entirely certain and secure concerning its divine origin, after the example of Abraham, the Father of all believers, who against hope believed in hope, that he would be the father of many nations according to that which is said: So shall thy seed be, and he was not weak in faith, nor did he consider his own body as good as dead, when he was about an hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb, he did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, being fully persuaded that what He had promised, He was also able to perform, Rom. IV. 18. et seqq. Whence, however, this truly divine faith may be obtained by us, by which, in likeness to the faith of Abraham, we may most firmly believe the divine origin of Holy Scripture, and not being weakened by any difficulty, or sublimity, or incredibility of the things contained therein, may we not waver through unbelief, but being strengthened in spirit, may we be most fully persuaded that it all depends upon God efficiently, and was written by God Himself inspiring and as it were dictating into the pen, which, as it is more necessary to be known, but more difficult to be explained and understood, so it requires more diligent and laborious consideration.

II. The use of the former question is also significant, first indeed in preparing the minds of infidels for the reading, hearing, and meditation of Holy Scripture. For we shall show later in its proper place that Holy Scripture itself, whether read or proposed by the voice of a teacher and perceived by hearing, with the supernatural concurrence of God, moves the minds of men to a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God, and which is of a truly divine faith, of itself immediately. I say notably, whether read or proposed by the voice of a teacher. For Holy Scripture cannot move anyone, with the concurrence of God, to an assent of itself and of the doctrine which it contains, unless it is transmitted to his mind through reading or hearing, according to that Pauline saying: Faith is from hearing, namely of the divine Word, proposed by the voice of a preacher, or from the reading of the same, related into letters by God inspiring. For we have warned more than once above that there is an equal reason for the divine Word, preached and written, and transmitted to the intellect through hearing and through reading. But because it hardly happens that infidels, falsely persuaded of the truth of their own religion which they drank in with their mother's milk, and deterred by the sublimity and incredibility of the divine mysteries which Holy Scripture hands down, should come of their own accord and with a desire to learn to its reading and meditation, the matter itself demands, and, as Augustine says in chapter XIII of On the Profit of Believing, it has been established by the majesty of Catholic discipline, that those who approach religion should have faith persuaded to them before all things, that is, that first of all they may be led to a certain human and opinative knowledge concerning the divine origin of Holy Scripture, by which, being imbued, if they do not believe it, they may at least judge it not improbable or not incredible that Holy Scripture has God as its author, and may determine in their own minds that they would not be acting imprudently if they read it and considered it more diligently. By which, although it is human faith and merely opinative knowledge, they are nevertheless prepared and led to read Holy Scripture with a mind to learn, or to hear and meditate upon the same when proposed by the voice of a teacher, so that those reading or listening to the voice of the teacher may at length, through the same, with the supernatural concurrence of God, be moved to supernatural assent and truly divine faith. Since the Manichaeans criticized this method of proceeding with the conversion of infidels, Augustine, in the already praised booklet he wrote, On the Profit of Believing, skillfully undertook to show that they were sacrilegiously and rashly attacking those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, BEFORE THEY CAN BEHOLD THAT TRUTH WHICH IS SEEN BY A PURE MIND (that is, the very truth of Christian doctrine, with the eyes of truly divine faith), are fortified by believing with human faith and are prepared by God who is about to enlighten them, as his words have it right at the beginning.

III. Furthermore, its use is also significant in confounding and refuting the most pernicious sects of recent Fanatics and Atheists, of which one altogether denies the divine authority of Holy Scripture, and even that God exists; but the other, while conceding the existence of God, admits that Holy Scripture draws its origin from God at least in those parts in which it embraces the most common notions about religion implanted in the minds of all, not indeed that it was written by divine inspiration in those parts, but that those common notions which it embraces were implanted in the minds of men by God, and thus are a certain Word of God, inscribed in them divinely, while the other parts of Christian doctrine contained in it that exceed the grasp of human reason are rejected among human inventions. By this very thing, as far as the matter pertains, they utterly deny the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God through immediate inspiration. Both kinds of men were born within the very boundaries of the Christian Church, and educated in the Christian religion, but, having been deceived by the Cartesian method of philosophizing preposterously transferred to theology, have fallen into this monstrous impiety. For when, according to the prescription of the said method, they were to free themselves from all prejudices, and to admit nothing except what was of explored truth, they began to doubt concerning the divine origin of holy Scripture and the Christian doctrine revealed through it, and even concerning the very existence of God, and the arguments showing that God exists, a posteriori and from effects, and even and to have [them], they began to weaken and evade the signs and motives of credibility, by which the divine authority of Scripture is wont to be persuaded to the Gentiles to be converted, and their minds prepared and induced to read and meditate upon the same, by means of frivolous reasons sought here and there, [and] they finally proceeded to such a point of impiety, by God's permission and Satan's instinct, that they completely defected from the Christian religion, in which they were born and educated, and some indeed invented a religion common to all peoples and nations diffused throughout the world, which embraces very few notions, and those as it were born with us, concerning God and His worship; but others indeed cast away every opinion of religion along with the knowledge of God. Neither can be convinced of their impiety and led back into the way otherwise than by arguments sought from nature, by which the existence of God is solidly demonstrated against them; and by the signs and motives of credibility, by which the divine origin of holy Scripture is persuaded to both, so that by a certain opinionative or human-faith knowledge of it generated in them, their minds may be brought back postliminiously to read and meditate upon holy Scripture with zeal and a desire to learn, in the same way in which the minds of the Gentiles to be converted were wont, from the beginning of the planted Church, to be prepared and induced to embrace the Christian religion. For they stubbornly deny the first principle of religion and the Christian faith, namely, holy Scripture. But that being denied, besides arguments sought from the light of nature and the mentioned signs and motives of credibility, nothing remains to convince them. Whence if ever a question concerning preparing minds by signs and motives of credibility to read and study holy Scripture with zeal was considered necessary, certainly it is highly necessary if only on account of these men of lost malice, especially in this last age of the aging world, in which all things rush toward the worse, and that begins to be fulfilled which Christ predicted in Luke 18:8 concerning the apostasy from the Christian faith to be feared toward the end: The Son of man, he says, when he comes, will he find faith on the earth?

Latin:

VI.

PRo duplici ratione notitiae, qua Scripturae sacrae dependentia a Deo inspirante nobis innotescit, fidei humanae scilicet vel opinionis; & fidei divinae, duplex constitui potest quaestio: Una, unde nobis innotescat notitia fidei humanae, vel opinativa, Scripturam sacram dependere a Deo efficienter, eoque inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante concinnatam esse: Altera, unde notitia fidei divinae id nobis innotescat?

VII.

QVamvis vero in quaestione posteriori cardo & summa rei vertatur, tamen prior etiam suum insignem habet usum.

I. In quaestione posteriori vertitur cardo & summa rei: quia ad fidem Christianam non sufficit incerta fidei humanae & opinativa notitia dependentiae Scripturae sacrae a Deo inspirante: alias enim fides Christiana tota incerta & cum formidine oppositi conjuncta esset; sed requiritur ejus assensus, dubitationis omnis expers, fidesque vere divina, quae sit ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, & πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀὐ βλεπομένων, Hebr. XI. 1. & qua hominum animi de divina ejus origine prorsus certi ac securi reddantur, ad exemplum Abrahami, Patris omnium credentium, qui contra spem in spem credidit, se fore Patem multarum gentium secundum id, quod dictum est: Sic erit semen tuum, & non infirmatus est fide, nec consideravit corpus suum emortuum, cum ferè centum esset annorum, & emortuum uterum Saræ, in repromissione etiam Dei non hæsitavit diffidentiâ sed confortatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo, plenissimè sciens, quod quæcunque promisit, etiam potens sit facere, Rom. IV. 18. seqq. Unde verò nobis obtingat hæc verè divina fides, quâ ad similitudinem fidei Abrahameæ divinam Scripturæ sacræ originem firmissimè credamus, & non infirmati ullâ rerum in illa contentarum difficultate, vel sublimitate, vel incredibilitate hæsitemus per diffidentiam, sed confortati animo plenissimè persuasum habeamus, eam totam dependere à Deo efficienter, & esse ipsomet Deo inspirante & quasi in calamum dictitante conscriptam, quò cognitu quidem necessarium magis, explicatu autem & intellectu difficilius est, eò diligentiori & operosiori consideratione eget.

II. Prioris verò quæstionis etiam usus insignis est, primò quidem in præparandis infidelium animis ad lectionem, auditum & meditationem Scripturæ sacræ. Inferiùs enim suo loco ostendemus, ipsammet Scripturam sacram, sive lectam, sive voce docentis propositam & auditæ perceptam, cum Dei concursu supernaturali, movere hominum animos in suæ à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem, & qui fidei verè divinæ sit, per se immediatè. Dico notanter, sive lectam sive voce docentis propositam. Scriptura sacra enim non potest quenquam cum Dei concursu in sui & doctrinæ, quam continet, assensum movere, nisi per lectionem vel auditum ad ejus animum transmissa, juxta illud Paulinum: Fides est ex auditu, Verbi divini puta, voce prædicantis propositi, vel ex lectione ejusdem, Deo inspirante in literas relati. Quod enim Verbi divini, prædicati & scripti, ejusque per auditum, & per lectionem, ad intellectum transmissi, par ratio sit, supra plus simplici vice monuimus. Quia autem vix contingit, ut infideles, de veritate suæ, quam cum lacte imbiberunt, religionis falsò persuasi, sublimitate verò & incredibilitate divinorum mysteriorum, quæ Scriptura sacra tradit, deterriti, ultrò & cum studio discendi ad ejus lectionem ac meditationem accedant, res ipsa exigit, &, ut Augustinus libr. de Utilitate credendi cap. XIII. ait, Catholicæ disciplinæ majestate institutum est, ut accedentibus ad religionem fides persuadeatur ante omnia, h. e. ut primò omnium ad quandam fidei humanæ & opinativam notitiam de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine perducantur, quâ imbuti, si eam non credant, minimùm tamen non improbabile aut non incredibile esse judicent, Scripturam sacram habere Deum auctorem, statuantque apud animum suum, se non imprudenter facturos, si eam legant & diligentiùs considerent. Quâ, licet humanâ fide & notitia merè opinativâ, præparantur tamen & inducuntur ad Scripturam sacram animo discendi legendam, vel ad eandem, voce docentis propositam, audiendam & meditandam, ut legentes aut docentis voci auscultantes per eandem cum Dei concursu supernaturali ad assensum supernaturalem fidemque verè divinam tandem permoveantur. Quem procedendi modum cum convertendis infidelibus cùm Manichæi reprehenderent, Augustinus conscripto libello jam laudato, de Utilitate credendi, scitè ostendendum sibi sumsit, quòd sacrilegè & temerè ipsi inveherentur in eos, qui catholicæ fidei authoritatem sequentes, ANTEQVAM ILLUD VERUM, QVOD PURA MENTE CONSPICITUR, (h. e. ipsam doctrinæ Christianæ veritatem, oculis fidei verè divinæ) intueri queant, credendo fide humanâ præmuniuntur & illuminaturo præparantur Deo, ut sub initium statim verba ejus habent.

III. Deinde usus ejus insignis etiam est in confundendis & confutandis recentium Fanaticorum & Atheorum perniciosissimis Sectis, quarum alia divinam Scripturæ sacræ auctoritatem, quin & Deum esse, prorsus negat; alia verò concessâ Dei existentiâ, Scripturam sacram iis saltem partibus, quibus communissimas omniumque mentibus implantatas de religione notiones complectitur, à Deo originem trahere admittit, non quidem quòd iis partibus Deo inspirante conscripta sit, sed quòd istæ communes, quas complectitur, notiones hominum mentibus à Deo insitæ, & sic Verbum quoddam Dei sint, iisdem divinitus inscriptum, cæteris in ea contentis humanæque rationis captum excedentibus doctrinæ Christianæ partibus inter humana commenta rejectis. Quo ipso, quod ad rem attinet, Scripturæ sacræ dependentiam à Deo per immediatam inspirationem penitùs inficiantur. Natum est utrumque hominum genus intra ipsa Ecclesiæ Christianæ pomœria, inque religione Christiana educatum,sed,quod Cartesiana philosophandi methodo præpostere ad Theologiam translata deceptum, & in hanc monstrosa impietatem prolapsum est.
