Cum enim ad præscriptum dictæ methodi a præjudiciis omnibus se liberaturi, nihilque, nisi quod exploratæ veritatis esset,admissuri,de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine & patefacta per eam doctrina Christiana,quin & de ipsa Dei existentia dubitare, argumenta, Deum esse, a posteriori & ex effectibus ostendentia,fusq; deque habere,signa & motiva credibilitatis,quibus divina Scripturæ auctoritas convertendis Gentibus suaderi,illorumque animi ad eandem legendam ac meditandam præparari & induci solent, hinc inde petitis frivolis rationibus labefactare & eludere cœperunt, eo tandem, Dei permissu Satanæque instinctu,processerunt impietatis, ut a religione Christiana,in qua nati & educati sunt,deficerent penitus,& alii quidem fingerent religionem,omnibus per orbem terrarum diffusis populis & gentibus communem,quæ paucissimas,easque nobiscum quasi natas de Deo ejusque cultu notiones complectatur; alii vero cum notitia Dei religionis opinionem omnem abjicerent. Neutri aliter suæ impietatis convinci & in viam reduci possunt,quam argumentis,ex natura petitis,quibus adversus illos Dei existentia demonstretur solide; & credibilitatis signis ac motivis,quibus divina Scripturæ sacræ origo utrisque suadeatur,ut ingenerata ipsis quadem ejus opinativa vel fidei humanæ notitia illorum animi eundem in modum,quo convertendorum Gentium animi inde ab initio plantatæ Ecclesiæ ad amplectendam religionem Christianam præparari&induci consueverunt,adScripturam sacram cum studio & desiderio discendi legendam &meditandam,postliminio reducantur. Negant enim primum religionis & fidei Christianæ principium,Scripturam S. scilicet,præfracte. Eo vero negato, præter argumenta,ex lumine naturæ petita,&memorata credibilitatis signa ac motiva ad illos convincendos,nihil superest. Unde si unquam quæstio de præparandis per signa & motiva credibilitatis animis ad Scripturam sacram cum studio discendi legendam consideratu necessaria fuit,certe vel propter solos hosce perditæ malitiæ homines summe necessaria est,hac ultima præsertim mundi senescentis ætate, qua omnia in pejus ruunt,& impleri incipit,quod Luc. XIIX. 8. Christus de apostasia a fide Christiana, sub finem metuenda, prædixit: Filius hominis, inquiens, cùm venerit, an reperturus est fidem in terra?


### VIII. We shall therefore consider in order both questions concerning the divine…

VIII.

We shall therefore consider in order both questions concerning the divine origin of Scripture, and the former indeed, concerning the knowledge of human and opinion-based faith, because it concerns the preparation of man for kindling in his soul the knowledge of divine faith, we shall consider first; the latter, however, concerning the knowledge of that same divine faith, whence it may be obtained by us, we shall consider later, and we shall weigh both the more deeply and diligently, the more each is of greater importance and requires a richer and more accurate treatment. Let it be therefore

Latin:

VIII.

Utramque igitur de divina Scripturae origine quaestionem ordine, & priorem quidem de notitia fidei humanae & opinativa, quia praeparationem hominis ad accendendam in ejus animo notitiam fidei divinae concernit, priùs; alteram verò de ejusdem notitia fidei divinae, unde nobis obtingat, posteriùs considerabimus, & utramque quidem eò expendemus altiùs & diligentiùs, quò majoris quaeque est momenti, & uberiorem accuratioremque tractationem desiderat. Esto igitur


## 8 On the Signs and Motives of Credibility: Internal

The knowledge of human and opinion-based faith, by which the divine origin of holy Scripture, or its dependence upon God inspiring it, becomes known to us, is born from signs and motives of credibility, as they are called.

I. By signs and motives of credibility we understand here the reasons for knowing, by which it is proved a posteriori that holy Scripture depends efficiently upon God and is truly divine, and is rendered credible to us.

II. They are called by the Scholastics signs and motives of credibility: signs indeed, because they provide not obscure indications of the divinity of Scripture and of the Christian doctrine contained in it; motives, however, because they move the intellect to assent to their divine origin. But they are called signs and motives of credibility because they do not evidently demonstrate the divine origin of holy Scripture itself or the truth of the doctrine contained in it, but at least prove that it is credible that holy Scripture and the Christian doctrine handed down in it were not invented by men, but proceeded from God himself, and are truly divine. Hence the knowledge born from them, which others call the notion of opinion and human faith, more recent Scholastics commonly call the knowledge of credibility, and the judgment of credibility, that is, the knowledge or judgment of the intellect, by which it is known and judged to be credible that the Holy Scripture and the Christian doctrine contained in it proceeded from God and is truly divine.

II.

These signs or motives are of a twofold difference. For some are taken from the intrinsic nature of Holy Scripture or its properties; others, however, are taken from outside Scripture from elsewhere. The former are called INTERNAL; the latter EXTERNAL signs and motives of credibility.

I. Both are of great weight and importance, and come here to be more fully declared and vindicated, as much on account of the modern Scholastics and Papists, as on account of the aforementioned Fanatics and Atheists of our age, of whom the former sin in excess; the latter in defect. For the former, under manifold pretense and deceit, extol their use to such a degree that they ultimately resolve the Christian faith itself into them, and especially into the testimony of the Church, which constitutes not the least part of them among them, and, as far as in them lies, having removed divine faith, they leave us a merely human and opinative faith both of the divine origin of the Scriptures and of the whole Christian doctrine contained in them. The latter, having learned rather to doubt and deny than to learn or teach and build up the truth, hold them in no place, but by various, albeit light, reasons for doubting, they first reject, impugn, and deny them as uncertain, doubtful, and not possessing explored truth, and then as false. Against the former, the genuine use of these signs and motives is to be shown below in its place; against the latter, however, the truth of the same is to be built up and vindicated.

II. But that we may proceed in order and distinctly, we shall divide the question concerning the knowledge of human faith, by which the divine origin of Scripture becomes known to us, into two Sections, in the former of which we shall treat of the internal signs of credibility; in the latter, of the external signs and motives, and of the knowledge born from both.

Latin:

FIdei humanae & opinativa notitia, quâ divina Scripturae sacrae origo, sive dependentia ejus à Deo inspirante nobis innotescit, nascitur ex signis & motivis credibilitatis, ut vocantur.

I. Per signa & motiva credibilitatis intelligimus hîc rationes cognoscendi, quibus Scripturam sacram efficienter à Deo dependere, veréque divinam esse, à posteriori probatur, nobisque credibile redditur.

II. Dicuntur autem à Scholasticis signa & motiva credibilitatis: signa quidem, quòd indicia praebeant haud obscura divinitatis Scripturae & contentae in ea doctrinae Christianae; motiva verò, quòd intellectum in assensum divinae illarum originis moveant. Credibilitatis verò signa & motiva dicuntur, quòd non ipsam divinam Scripturae sacrae originem vel contentae in ea doctrinae veritatem evidenter demonstrent, sed evincant saltem, credibile esse, Scripturam sacram & traditam in ea doctrinam Christianam non esse ab hominibus inventam, sed ab ipsomet Deo profectam, vereque divinam. Hinc natam ex illis cognitionem, quam alii opinionis & fidei humanæ notitiam appellant, Scholastici recentiores communiter cognitionem credibilitatis, & judicium credibilitatis vocant, h. e. cognitionem, sive judicium intellectus, quo cognoscitur & judicatur credibile esse, quod Scriptura sacra & contenta in illa doctrina Christiana à Deo profecta vereque divina sit.

II.

SIgna sive motiva hæc in duplici differentia sunt. Quædam enim ex intrinseca Scripturæ sacræ natura ejusve proprietatibus; alia vero extra Scripturam aliunde desumuntur. Illa INTERNA; hæc EXTERNA signa & motiva credibilitatis dicuntur.

I. Utraque magni ponderis & momenti sunt, & uberiùs declaranda atque vindicanda hîc veniunt, cùm propter Scholasticos & Pontificios modernos, tum propter prædictos nostræ ætatis Fanaticos & Atheos, quorum illi in excessu; hi in defectu peccant. Illi enim sub multiplici fuco & dolo illorum usum eò usque extollunt, ut ipsam fidem Christianam ultimò tandem in ea, & cumprimis in testificationem Ecclesiæ, quæ illorũ partem non ultimam apud ipsos constituit, resolvant, & fide divina, quantum in ipsis est, sublata, merè humanam & opinativam fidem cùm divinæ Scripturarum originis, tùm contentæ in illis totius doctrinæ Christianæ nobis relinquant. Hi dubitare potiùs & negare, quàm discere vel docere & veritatem adstruere docti, nullo ea loco habent, sed inventis variis, quamvis levibus, rationibus dubitandi primùm ut incerta, dubia, & exploratam veritatem non habentia, deinde ut falsa rejiciunt, impugnant, negant. Contra illos infra suo loco signorum & motivorum istorum usus genuinus ostendendus; contra hos verò eorundem veritas adstruenda & vindicanda est.

II. Ut autem ordine & distinctè procedamus, quæstionem de notitia fidei humanæ, quâ divina Scripturæ origo nobis innotescat, in duas dispescemus Sectiones, in quarum priori de signis credibilitatis internis; in posteriori de signis & motivis externis, deque notitia ex utrisque nata acturi sumus.


### Chapter V. First Section On the internal signs and motives of credibility I

CHAPTER V. FIRST SECTION On the internal signs and motives of credibility.

I.

Just as Holy Scripture consists of two essential parts: one material, the other formal; of which the former is constituted by the written words themselves and their structure, the latter by the sense and the things signified: so also the internal signs and motives, which make its divine origin credible to us, can be derived both from its material and from its formal part.

II.

Those which are derived from its formal part are more important. Yet, so that we do not leave those which are wont to be drawn from the material part entirely untouched, we shall bring forward here a single one, which is the SIMPLICITY OF STYLE in proposing things necessary both to be believed and to be done, joined with a GRAVITY WORTHY OF GOD ALONE.

I. That the style of Scripture is not uniform, but varied and different, according as the sacred writers were dissimilar and diverse in talent, character, and customary manner of speech, was stated above in chapter II, thesis XIII. For the Holy Spirit, in recording Scripture through His amanuenses, the Prophets and Apostles, did not use a style peculiar to Himself and different from the received custom of speaking among men, but in every part of Scripture He adapted Himself in suggesting words to the talent and customary and, as it were, connatural manner of speaking of each writer, so that their discourse and writing might not seem to them twisted and violent, as was shown ibid. Expl. n. 111. Nor, however, did He so adapt Himself to their talent, character, and customary manner of speaking, that He did not also, in proportion to the underlying subject matter, have regard for His own authority and majesty, nor, after the manner of men, demonstrate below His own condition those things which for the sake of authority simply asto propose things to be believed by bearing; or to persuade that things should be done or omitted by the enticements of words and motives sought from here and there, which it could command to be done or omitted by ordering and forbidding by virtue of its authority. These are the ways of men, who, because they can err in speaking and teaching, do not deserve assent and faith, unless insofar as the truth, according to the nature of the underlying subject matter, appears to the intellect either demonstrated a priori or a posteriori from certain and indubitable principles, or shown in some way by probable reasons or the testimonies of others, and just as the reasons for proving vary, so too the assent, leaning upon them, is accustomed to vary. Nor can they induce others to do good and avoid evil, except insofar as the things to be done or avoided are presented to their will under persuasive or dissuasive, exhorting or discouraging reasons, unless perhaps they themselves enjoy the right of superiority and are Kings or supreme Princes: who then also, mindful of their condition and superiority, are accustomed to prescribe to their subjects by authority, by ordering and forbidding, what they wish to be done or avoided by them, without persuasive or dissuasive reasons; since this style is most appropriate to their gravity and majesty. To God, however, who is both Truth itself and the supreme Lord of all, is owed both assent and faith, and obedience, in and of Himself. Assent and faith indeed, because He is Truth, and in speaking can neither be deceived nor deceive; but obedience, because He is the supreme Lord of all, and without exception has absolute and supreme power over all. And hence is born that style of Scripture, simple indeed and devoid of pretense, but tempered with such gravity that where things to be believed, or things to be done and avoided, are to be inculcated, they are proposed by simply asserting, commanding, or prohibiting, with the reason for assenting or being induced to obedience referred solely to the authority of God revealing, commanding, or prohibiting. Thus the moral Law, to whose obedience all mortals without exception are bound, was solemnly promulgated to the Israelite people from Mount Sinai, and afterwards recorded in writing by Moses in the simplest words, commanding or prohibiting, with no reason inducing to obedience premised or added, except for the sole authority of God commanding or prohibiting: I am the Lord thy God etc. Exod. XX. 2. 5. And for the Prophets, about to win faith for their sayings, nothing is more frequent than that phrase כאם יהוה

The saying of the Lord; likewise: I am the Lord; Thus says the Lord; The word of the Lord came to me, etc.

II. And in this the Holy Spirit tempered the style of Scripture, not to the genius, customs, or customary manner of speaking of the sacred writers, as if they were His amanuenses, but to His own authority and divine majesty alone. For, as has been said, it is not of man, but of God alone, to bind all mortals without exception to have faith in Him, while He brings no demonstration, or to render obedience to Him, while He commands or forbids without persuasive reasons. Kings and supreme Princes also command and forbid, as has been said, what they wish to be done and avoided, nakedly and without persuasive words, but only to subjects over whom they have power and authority: but to enjoin upon all mortals without distinction, even upon the highest Princes and Kings themselves, by so nakedly commanding and forbidding what is to be done or avoided, is not of man, but of God alone, to whom alone irrefragable obedience is owed by all men of whatever condition and status.

III. The writers of the New Testament do indeed not infrequently use testimonies of the Old Testament Scripture for the confirmation of the doctrine delivered by them, not, however, because the doctrine of faith and morals, which they delivered by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, needed proof in itself, but so that they might show it to be of the same origin and truth as the Old Testament Scripture, which was already publicly established among the Jews as having been written by the inspiration of God and as truly divine, so that the reason binding one either to faith or to obedience might thus also ultimately return to the authority of God revealing or commanding.

IV. From the property of the style of sacred Scripture, declared thus far, such an argument arises for us to establish its divine origin: That Scripture which is composed in a style worthy not of a mere man, but of divine majesty alone, it is entirely consistent with truth that not mere men, but God Himself, has it as its author, namely its primary author. But sacred Scripture is composed in a style worthy not of a mere man, but of divine majesty alone. Therefore, it is entirely consistent with truth that not mere men, but God Himself, has sacred Scripture as its author, namely its primary author. The reason for the major proposition is: because the style of Scripture argues for its author, and he whose style is worthy of divine majesty alone is of whatever status or condition he may be, that God himself has it as his author, indeed the primary one, is rightly inferred from this. The minor proposition, however, has been proven thus far from the simplicity of the style of Scripture, joined with a gravity worthy of God alone, by which things necessary to be believed are proposed through bare assertions, without demonstrations; and things necessary to be done through bare precepts, without persuasive reasons, and without the allurements of words, for authority to be believed and acted upon by all without exception: which kind of style can suit no one except God.

V. To this argument, the more recent sect of Fanatics and Atheists is accustomed to object that a firm argument for establishing its divine origin and authority cannot be drawn from the majestic style of Scripture: for such a majestic style is found even in the writings of Demosthenes, Cicero, and other famous orators. But those who object in this way do not seem to have grasped the force of our argument. For we do not establish the majestic style of Holy Scripture in elegance of speech, in the adornment and allurements of words, or in plausible reasons most suited for moving the minds of men and persuading them; such pigments and ornaments of style we readily grant are found in the writings of Demosthenes, Cicero, and other rhetoricians; but [we establish it] in the manner of proposing both things to be believed and things to be done, by authority through simple assertions without demonstrations, and through simple precepts and prohibitions without persuasive or dissuasive reasons: which kind of style we deny and utterly deny occurs in Demosthenes, or in Cicero, or in the writings of other orators. Nor indeed would any prudent person assume for himself that authority by which he would presume to oblige all mortals throughout the whole world to have faith in his words, without proofs, or to obey his commands or prohibitions, without reasons that persuade and induce obedience, but this, as has been said, belongs to God alone.

False prophets indeed, intending to procure authority and faith for their false predictions and prophecies, sometimes usurped among the people of God that phrase most customary to the Prophets, נאם יהוה, as is evident from Jer. XXIII. 31, ch. XXVIII. 2, 4, 11, ch. XXIX. 9, Deut. XVIII. 20, but deluded and persuaded by the deceits of Satan that it was God who was speaking through them, II Chron.

18. 20. et seqq. And because they were false prophets, deceived by a lying Spirit, they were severely rebuked by God through His Prophets, and their predictions were convicted of falsehood either from the underlying subject matter, because they led to strange gods, Deut. 13. 2, 5, or from the lack of fulfillment, Deut. 18. 21. et seqq., Jer. 14. 14, chap. 28. 9, who at length paid heavy penalties for their rashness by the just judgment of God, Deut. 18. 20, Jer. 28. 16. But concerning the authors of Holy Scripture, who were all men of proven faith and holiness of life; most of them also famous for miracles, nothing of the sort can be presumed without remarkable rashness, and therefore it remains entirely consistent with the truth that the Author of Scripture, written in a style so simple and grave, such as falls to no mortal, is not mere men, but God Himself, until it is shown to whom else this manner of writing can be attributed, besides God.

6. But in truth, the modern fanatics and calumniators of Holy Scripture, not content with this futile exception, proceed further, and by arguments drawn from its very style, they go about to prove that it does not have God Himself as its author: for they say it is so confused and jumbled that whatever is there is placed entirely without connection, without composition, without any order and color of words and sentences, and finally without sense and reason: a style of which sort is not worthy even of a good human writer, much less of God. It is three years since a certain wicked buffoon, who, by papers full of lies and blasphemies scattered among us and elsewhere, has openly professed his name among modern atheists, in a letter given at Rome, if the signature is to be believed, on the 6th day before the Kalends of March, having produced various passages of Scripture as examples, attempted to show this in order: That which, he says, I shall explain in a few words, since the narrowness of the paper confines me within the bounds of brevity. For indeed, who is there who would deny that Scripture is confused and jumbled, if he has examined the Proverbs of Solomon, in which it is not unusual for things of every kind to be mixed and confused like a hodgepodge even in a single chapter. It is placed without connection, e.g., Habakkuk 2. v. 1, likewise chap. 3. v. 1, where the particle 'but' connects nothing, if we wish to say what the matter is. It is also placed without any color of words, thus in Apoc. 5. and 8. chapters, all the verses without exception begin with the particle AND. It is placed without order of sentences, as in Luke 20. verse 31, eternal life

Latin:

CAPITIS V. SECTIO PRIOR De signis & motivis credibilitatis internis.

I.

Quemadmodùm Scriptura sacra duabus constat partibus essentialibus: Materiali unâ; alterâ formali; quarum illam ipsæ voces scriptæ illarumque structura; hanc sensus & res significatæ constituunt: ita & signa ac motiva interna, quæ divinam ejus originem nobis credibilem faciunt, cùm ex materiali, tùm ex formali ejus parte desumi possunt.

II.

QUæ ex parte ipsius formali desumuntur, potiora sunt, Ne tamen quæ ex parte materiali accersi solent, planè intacta relinquamus,adferemus hîc unicum,quod est STYLI SIMPLICITAS in proponendis cùm creditu tùm factu necessariis, cùm GRAVITATE, SOLO DEO DIGNA, conjuncta.

I. Scripturæ stylum non esse uniformem, sed varium & diffimilem,prout Scriptores sacri ingenio, moribus & genere sermonis consueto dissimiles & diversi fuerunt,dictum est suprà cap.II.th.XIII. Spiritus sanctus enim in consignanda per suos Amanuenses, Prophetas & Apostolos, Scriptura,non quodam sibi proprio & à recepta inter homines consuetudine loquendi diverso stylo usus est, sed in quavis Scripturæ parte in suggerendis verbis Scriptoris cujusque ingenio atque generi dicendi consueto & quasi connaturali se attemperavit,ne sua ipsis oratio & Scriptura contorta & violenta videretur, ut ibid. Expl. n. 111. ostensum. Neque tamen ita se illorum attemperavit ingenio, moribus & generi dicendi consueto, quin pro ratione materiæ substratæ etiam suæ auctoritatis & majestatis haberet rationem, nec infra suam conditionem, hominum more, rationibus demonstraret,quæ pro auctoritate simpliciter asferendo credenda proponere; vel verborum lenociniis & hinc inde petitis motivis agenda vel omittenda suaderet, quæ pro auctoritate jubendo vetandoque agenda aut omittenda imperare poterat. Hominum hæc sunt, qui quia in dicendo docendoque errare possunt, assensum & fidem non merentur, nisi in quantum veritas pro ratione materiæ substratæ vel ex principiis certis & indubitatis à priori aut à posteriori demonstrata, vel rationibus probabilibus aut aliorum testificationibus qualitercunque ostensa, intellectui apparet, & prout rationes probandi variant, ita & assensus, iisdem innixus, variare solet. Neque ad agenda bona, & fugienda mala iidem inducere alios possunt, nisi in quantum sub rationibus suadentibus aut dissuadentibus, adhortantibus aut dehortantibus illorum voluntati agenda aut fugienda exhibentur, nisi forsan ipsi superioritatis jure gaudeant, & Reges vel Principes summi sint: qui tùm etiam, suæ conditionis & superioritatis memores, pro auctoritate jubendo vetandoque suis subditis præscribere solent, quæ ab ipsis fieri aut vitari volunt, absque rationibus suasoriis aut dissuasoriis; cùm stylus hic ipsorum gravitati ac majestati maximè conveniat. Deo autem, qui & Veritas ipsa & supremus omnium Dominus est, debetur cùm assensus & fides tum obsequium per se & propter se. Assensus quidem & fides per hoc, quòd Veritas est, & in dicendo nec falli nec fallere potest; Obsequium verò per illud, quòd supremus omnium Dominus est, & absque exceptione in omnes absolutam & summam potestatem habet. Atque hinc natus est ille Scripturæ stylus, simplex quidem fucique expers, sed eâ temperatus gravitate, ut ubi credenda, aut agenda & fugienda inculcanda veniunt, simpliciter asserendo, præcipiendo aut prohibendo proponantur, ratione assentiendi aut ad obsequium inducendi in solam auctoritatem Dei revelantis, præcipientis aut prohibentis relatâ. Sic Lex moralis, ad cujus obsequium mortales sine exceptione omnes obligantur, populo Israëlitico de monte Sinai solenniter promulgata, & à Mose posteà in literas relata est verbis simplicissimis, præcipientibus aut prohibentibus, ratione ad obsequium inducente nullâ præmissâ aut subjectâ, præter solam Dei præcipientis aut prohibentis auctoritatem: Ego Dominus Deus tuus &c. Exod. XX. 2. 5. Et Prophetis, dictis suis fidem conciliaturis, nihil frequentius est, quàm illud כאם יהוה-

Dictum Domini; item: Ego Dominus; Sic dicit Dominus; Verbum Domini factum est ad me &c.

II. Atque in hoc Spiritus sanctus Scripturæ stylum attemperavit, non Scriptorum sacrorum, velut suorum Amanuensium, ingenio, moribus aut generi dicendi consueto, sed suæ soli auctoritati ac majestati divinæ. Non enim, uti dictum, hominis, sed solius Dei est obligare mortales sine exceptione omnes ad fidem sibi, sine demonstratione afferenti, habendam, vel ad obsequium sibi, absque rationibus persuasoriis præcipienti vel prohibenti exhibendum. Præcipiunt etiam prohibentque Reges & Principes summi, uti dictum, quæ fieri vitarique volunt, nudè & absque verbis persuasoriis, sed solis subditis, in quos potestatem & imperium habent: sed sine discrimine mortalibus omnibus, etiam ipsis summis Principibus ac Regibus ita nudè præcipiendo prohibendoque injungere quæ agenda aut fugienda sint, non hominis, sed solius Dei est, cui soli ab omnibus cujuscunque conditionis ac status hominibus obsequium irrefragabile debetur.

III. Scriptores N. T. utuntur quidem non rarò testimoniis Scripturæ V. T. ad confirmationem traditæ à se doctrinæ, non tamen, quòd fidei & morum doctrina, quam, Spiritu sancto inspirante, tradebant, per se probatione egeret, sed ut eam cum Scriptura V. T. quam Deo inspirante conscriptam vereque divinam esse, inter Judæos jam publicè constabat, ejusdem originis ac veritatis esse ostenderent, ut ratio sive ad fidem sive ad obsequium obligans, sic etiam in Dei revelantis aut mandantis auctoritatem ultimò rediret.

IV. Ex proprietate styli Scripturæ sacræ, hactenus declaratâ, ad adstruendam divinam ejus originem nobis tale nascitur argumentum: Quæ Scriptura concinnata est stylo, non homine nudo, sed solâ divinâ majestate digno, illam non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habere auctorem, primarium scilicet, vero prorsus consentaneum est. Atqui Scriptura sacra concinnata est stylo, non homine nudo, sed solâ divinâ majestate digno. Ergo Scripturam sacram non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habere auctorem, primarium scilicet, vero prorsus consentaneum est. Majoris propositionis ratio est: quia stylus Scripturæ arguit auctorem suum, & cujus stylus solâ majestate divinâ dignus est, nullo homine nudo, cujuscunque etiam status aut conditionis is sit, eam Deum ipsummet habere auctorem, primarium quidem, rectè hinc colligitur. Minor autem propositio hactenus probata est ex simplicitate styli Scripturæ, cum gravitate, Deo solo dignâ, conjuncta, quâ creditu necessaria per nudas assertiones, sine demonstrationibus; & necessaria factu per nudas præceptiones, sine rationibus persuasoriis, & absque verborum lenociniis pro auctoritate sine exceptione omnibus credenda & agenda proponuntur: cujusmodi stylus nemini, nisi Deo, convenire potest.

V. Ad argumentum hoc recentior Fanaticorum & Atheorum Secta excipere solet, ex stylo majestatico Scripturæ non posse argumentum firmum ad adstruendam divinam ejus originem & auctoritatem duci: inveniri enim ejusmodi stylum majestaticum etiam in Demosthene, Cicerone & aliorum celebrium Oratorum scriptis. Verùm qui ita excipiunt, non videntur vim nostri argumenti assecuti esse. Non enim stylum majestaticum Scripturæ sacræ constituimus in elegantia sermonis, verborum ornatu & lenociniis, aut in rationibus plausibilibus, ad commovendos hominum animos & persuadendum maximè accommodatis; qualia styli pigmenta & ornamenta in Demosthenis, Ciceronis & aliorum Rhetorum scriptis inveniri facilè largimur; sed in modo proponendi cùm credenda tùm agenda, pro auctoritate per simplices assertiones sine demonstrationibus, & per præceptiones ac prohibitiones simplices sine rationibus suadentibus aut dissuadentibus: cujusmodi stylum in Demosthene, vel in Cicerone, vel in aliis Oratorum scriptis occurrere, negamus & pernegamus. Neque etiam quisquam prudens eam sibi auctoritatem sumet, quá mortales omnes per orbem universum ad fidem suis dictis, sine probationibus, habendam, aut ad obsequendum suis mandatis aut interdictis, sine rationibus suadentibus & ad obsequium inducentibus, obligare præsumat, sed hoc, uti dictum, solius Dei est.

Pseudoprophetæ quidem, suis falsis prædictionibus & vaticiniis, auctoritatem & fidem conciliaturi, usurparunt quandoque in populo Dei illud Prophetis usitatissimum, נאם יהוה, ut ex Jer. XXIII. 31. c. XXVIII. 2. 4. 11. c. XXIX. 9. Deut. XIIX. 20. patet, sed Satanæ præstigiis delusi persuasique, Deum esse, qui per ipsos loqueretur, II. Paral.

XIIX. 20. seqq. & quia pseudoprophetæ erant, à Spiritu mendace decepti, à Deo per Prophetas suos graviter objurgabantur, illorumque prædictiones vel ex materia substrata, quòd ad Deos alienos ducerent, Deut. XIII. 2. 5. vel ex defectu complementi falsitatis convincebantur, Deut. XIIX. 21. seqq. Jer. XIV. 14. cap. XXVIII. 9. qui tandem temeritatis suæ, justo Dei judicio, graves dedêre pœnas, Deut. XIIX. 20. Jer. XXVIII. 16. De conditoribus Scripturæ sacræ autem, qui omnes Viri probatæ fidei, vitæque sanctimoniâ; plerique etiam miraculis clari fuêre, citra insignem temeritatem, tale nihil præsumi potest, & manet proinde adhuc vero prorsus consentaneum, Auctorem Scripturæ, stylo ita simplici & gravi, qualis in neminem mortalium cadit, conscriptæ, non esse nudos homines, sed ipsummet Deum, donec ostendatur, cui alii hæc scribendi ratio tribui possit, præter Deum.

VI. Verùm enim verò hac exceptione futili hodierni Fanatici & Scripturæ sacræ Calumniatores non contenti, procedunt longiùs, & argumentis, ex ipso ejus stylo petitis, probatum eunt, eam non habere Deum ipsummet auctorem: esse enim, inquiunt, adeò confusam, & commixtam, ut quicquid ibi est, totum sine connexione, sine compositione, absque omni verborum & sententiarum ordine & colore, & postremò absque sensu & ratione positum sit: cujusmodi stylum ne quidem bono Scriptore humano, nedum Deo dignum esse. Triennium est, cùm Scurra quidam improbus, qui sparsis apud nos & alibi locorum mendacibus & blasphemis chartis, apertè nomen suum inter hodiernos Atheos professus est, in Epistola, Romæ, si subscriptioni fides habenda, VI. Kal. Martii datâ, productis in exemplum diversis locis Scripturæ, id ordine ostendere conatus est: Id quod, inquiens, paucis edisserTABO, quippe chartæ angustia me inter brevitatis metas concludit. Enimverò quis est, qui neget, confusam & commixtam esse Scripturam, si Salomonis inspexerit Adagia, in quibus haud insolens est, in uno etiam capite omnis generis res ad instar farraginis commisceri & confundi. Posita illa est sine connexione v. c. Habacuc 2. v. 1. item cap. 3. v. 1. ubi τὸ sed nihil connectit, si, quod res est, dicere velimus. Posita etiam est absque omni verborum colore, sic Apoc. 5. & 8. cap. ad unum omnes versiculi à particula ET incipiunt. Posita est absque sententiarum ordine, ut Luc. 20. vers. 31. vita æterna


### is placed before the resurrection of the dead, which order, however, the…

is placed before the resurrection of the dead, which order, however, the Christians themselves respect. If they shall say that it is a ὕστερον πρότερον, this σοφὸν φάρμακον will fight for the Alcoran of the Turks as well. Those things at Eph. 2. vers. 1. are also placed without sense, and that whole discourse at Acts 7. vers. 1 seqq., likewise John 8. v. 25. the beginning, who also speak to you &c. Finally, those things at Exod. 20. vers. 18. are also placed without reason, the people saw the sound of the trumpets: likewise: to strip the naked of their clothes Job 20. vers. 6. Afterwards he subjoins some other things, which do not properly concern the style of Scripture, and he concludes at length: Since these things are so, Friend Reader not anointed, (i. i.e., not Christian) no man will blame me if, together with my fellow-flock (whose almost numberless count support me in Paris, Amsterdam, Leiden, in England, Hamburg, Copenhagen, as well as Stockholm and in contiguous places), I hold the entire Bible in the place of a pretty Fable, by which the Beasts, that is, the Christians, capturing their reason, and being insane with reason, are delighted.

VII. These things he says from the mind of himself and his fellow-flock, whom he boasts of: to whom he denies not only the dependence and origin of the Holy Scriptures from God, but also all truth and faith, and rejects them into the census of fables, but as wickedly and dishonestly as he does insipidly and ineptly. The principal conclusion, which he takes upon himself to prove, is this: That it should not be held against him if he holds the entire Bible in the place of a pretty Fable. He fetches the reason for proving this from the fact that the whole Scripture is so confused and mixed up that whatever is there is placed entirely without connection, without composition, without any order and color of words and sentences, and finally without sense and reason; from which this principal argument is born: That Scripture which is entirely so confused and mixed up that whatever is there is placed without connection, without composition, without any order and color of words and sentences, and finally without sense and reason, is rightly held in the place of a pretty Fable. But the Holy Scripture of the Christians is thus. Therefore. Although there would not be lacking that which could be desired in the major proposition: For the order and distinction of things in Scripture, the connection of words and sentences, the color of words, etc., pertain not precisely to the truth, but to the adornment, elegance, and perspicuity of Scripture, and some Scripture can be true, even if it is confused and mixed, etc. I shall not, however, descend to that now. In the minor proposition, however, this little man shows himself to be an overly hyperbolic slanderer of Holy Scripture. For he writes most mendaciously that the whole of Holy Scripture is confused and mixed, and whatever is there is placed without connection, without composition, without any order and color of words, and without sense and reason; which contains as many palpable lies as there are periods. In the proof of those things, the buffoon most ineptly concludes from the particular to the universal. He proves that the whole of Scripture is confused and mixed from the fact that the Proverbs of Solomon are confused and mixed, and that in even one of those chapters things of every kind are mixed together and confused like a hodgepodge: but how insipidly and how ineptly is this? For what? Are the Proverbs of Solomon the whole of Scripture? Or is whatever is in Scripture entirely mixed and confused, because in the Proverbs of Solomon, even in one chapter, various sentences are described mixedly and without a certain order? Who, unless destitute of mind, or one whose eyes of the mind Satan has completely blinded, would be so inept? He concludes that the whole of Scripture is placed without connection from the fact that Habakkuk chapter II, verse one, and chapter III, verse one, according to Luther's Version, or chapter II, verse five, according to the Hebrew text, are not connected with the preceding; he concludes that the whole is placed without any color of words from the fact that Rev. V and VIII, all the verses begin with the particle AND; he concludes that the whole is placed without order of sentences from Luke XX. 31, where eternal life is placed before the resurrection of the dead; he proves that the whole is placed without sense from the fact that Eph. II. 1, the words of Paul; and Acts VII. v. 1, seqq., the whole speech of Stephen; and John VIII. 25, the words of Christ: the beginning, who also speak to you; lack sense; finally, he proves that the whole is placed without reason from Exod. XX. 18, where the people are said to have seen the sound of trumpets, and Job XX. 6, where Job is said to have stripped the naked of their clothes: But how ineptly are all these things also inferred? For if we grant that the passages of Scripture which have been brought forward have everything as they are alleged, will the whole of Scripture therefore lack connection because two verses in the Prophet Habakkuk are not connected? Will it therefore

Will Scripture lack all color and ornament of words, because in two chapters of the Apocalypse all verses begin with the particle AND? Does it lack entirely an order of sentences, because in Luke 20:31 eternal life is placed before the resurrection of the dead? Or does it lack sense entirely, because in Eph. 2:1 the words of Paul, in Acts 7 the speech of Stephen, and in John 8:25 the words of Christ lack sense? Is it placed entirely without reason, because in Exod. 20:18 the people are said to have seen the sound of trumpets, and in Job 20:6 the holy man is said to have stripped the naked of their clothes without reason? Who does not see the nullity of all these consequences? Since they all conclude from a particular to a universal in a way more than childish.

But let us examine in order the passages cited. We admit that the Proverbs of Solomon, especially from the tenth chapter, are recorded mixedly and without a certain order: but we deny that anything is taken away from the authority of Holy Scripture on this account. For this book, especially from the tenth chapter to the end, is not occupied in explaining any determined subject matter, in which a certain method, order, and connection could be applied, but it contains maxims of every kind and brief and rounded sentences about various matters, proceeding from wisdom and leading to wisdom, recorded so concisely that individual verses complete individual, entire sentences: to require a certain method and connection in recounting these is to require order and connection in the sand. The preceding nine chapters, however, set forth like a preface, are occupied in commending the study of wisdom, and are not destitute of all order and connection. Just as, therefore, it is not a fault in a writer to recount concise sentences about various matters that do not cohere with one another without a certain order and connection: so no fault or stain, unworthy of a God-breathed writer, attaches to the book of Proverbs because various sentences about various matters that do not cohere with one another are written down mixedly without a certain method, order, and connection.

Then, in the prophecy of Habakkuk, it is not a wonder that the first verse of the second chapter is not connected with the last verse of the preceding first chapter. For connection cannot be required in all parts, chapters, or verses of Scripture or of a speech, but at least in the parts whose underlying subjects cohere. Of which parts the subjects but those which are laid underneath have no relationship with one another, no coherence; in them, not even in the human writings of the best authors, is a connection always found or considered necessary. And so it is with the matter brought forward from v. 1 of the second chapter of Habakkuk, compared to the last verse of the first chapter. In chapter I, up to the last verse, Habakkuk prophesied concerning the tyranny and cruelty of the Chaldeans, with which they were about to rage against the Jewish people, and he had solicited God with ardent prayers, that He might be willing to restrain their savagery, and to protect and preserve the pious against the same. But in the second chapter he begins to preach about the coming of the Messiah, for the consolation of the afflicted people, and he makes the beginning of this sermon in that very first verse: which, just as it did not depend on the last verse of the preceding chapter, so there was no reason for it to be connected with it. But that in the other chapter in the first verse according to the version of Luther, or in the second chapter in the fifth verse, according to the Hebrew text, there is no connection with the preceding verse, is false. The buffoon indeed says that the particle BUT connects nothing. But in the Hebrew text, which alone is the Prophet's, the particle BUT does not exist, but the particles ואף כי which can be conveniently rendered, 'nay even,' and altogether have the force of connecting, and join this verse with the preceding ones. For in the preceding verses the Prophet had prophesied concerning the coming of the promised Messiah, and had raised up the afflicted spirits with a certain and indubitable hope of him: but in the fifth verse he adds a new argument of consolation, sought from the destruction of the Babylonian kingdom, and of the King of the Babylonians, drunken, proud, and arrogant, and from the liberation that would follow from this from the most harsh servitude and tyranny of the Chaldeans, and the particles ואף כי can be conveniently rendered; 'nay even,' (just as Junius and Tremellius rendered them) so that the sense may be: 'nay even, or furthermore, the drunken, proud, and arrogant man (suppose the King of the Babylonians) who will be a terror to all, and by whose tyranny you are pressed and most grievously afflicted, will be cut off, and will become a fable and a laughingstock to all peoples, etc.'

Thirdly, that Holy Scripture is not polished with the color and paint of words, and in Apoc. ch. V and VIII all the verses begin with the particle AND, so far from detracting from its authority, rather commends it. For just as it detracted nothing from the Gospel concerning Christ crucified, which was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, 1 Cor. I. 23, that it was not by the persuasive words of human wisdom of the wise men of this age, but was preached by unlearned fishermen and those ignorant of letters, and by Paul, who indeed was instructed at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strictness of the law of the fathers, Acts XXII. 3, but was unskilled in speech, II Cor. XI. 6, in a simple and by no means painted style of discourse, and was preached to the world, with the roaring of enemies hindering nothing at all resulted in its notable commendation: so also nothing is detracted from the authority of Holy Scripture by the fact that it was recorded by the same men in a simple style, without color and paint of words, and yet was received and believed by the Churches spread throughout the whole world. For all this was done, lest the cross of Christ should be made void, I Cor. I. 17, that is, lest the Gospel concerning Christ crucified, whether preached or recorded in writing, should be obliterated by the adornment of speech and the human wisdom shining forth from it, and should be ascribed to the color and paint of words. Yet the style of Scripture is not so simple and devoid of paint and color that it does not have its elegances mixed in here and there, especially in those parts and books whose authors were accustomed to a more elegant style, just as Jerome testifies concerning the Prophet Isaiah, that he is eloquent in his speech, being a noble man and of urban eloquence, and having nothing of rusticity mixed into his discourse; concerning Ezekiel, that he is neither sufficiently eloquent nor very rustic, but moderately tempered from both; concerning Hosea, that he is concise and speaking as it were by sentences; concerning Luke, that he knew Greek letters better than Hebrew, and therefore his speech, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, that is, in both volumes, is more polished and savors of secular eloquence, etc. See his Prefaces to Isaiah, Ezekiel, upon the XII Prophets, and his Commentary on Chapter VI of Isaiah. For the Holy Spirit, as we have warned above, in suggesting the words of Scripture, conformed Himself to the genius and accustomed style of speech of each writer, and although He did not seek, He nevertheless did not entirely neglect the adornment and elegance of speech, but according to the nature of the genius and the speech accustomed to each writer, He scattered His own little flowers here and there. On which matter, among others, the most learned Flacius can be seen in part II of the Key, Tract V, on the Style of the Holy Scriptures.

Fourthly, if it were admitted that in Luke XX, 35, eternal life is placed before the resurrection of the dead by a hysteron proteron, not even so would anything be detracted from the authority of Holy Scripture. For if it is established concerning the truth of both members, as far as the order is concerned, it matters little whether one is placed before or after the other. For in popular usage and the custom of speaking, we are not precisely bound to observe the order which the things themselves have by nature. But there is no reason why we should say here that eternal life is placed before the resurrection of the dead contrary to the order natural to it. For Christ instituted in the aforementioned passage a comparison between the children of this age and those who shall be accounted worthy of the other age and the resurrection from the dead, in that the former take wives and give their daughters in marriage; but the latter neither take wives nor give in marriage. But between those who shall be accounted worthy of the other age and those who shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection from the dead—that is, to the other and blessed life—there is not given here a natural order, such that those who shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection to eternal life must necessarily be prior to those worthy of the other age: for among those who shall be accounted worthy of the other age are included all the pious whom the final day and the coming of Christ to judgment shall find alive. For just as these will neither die nor rise again from the dead, but will be changed suddenly, so they will not be posterior to the pious dead who shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection to life, but at the same moment that the latter rise at the sound of the trumpet, the former will also be changed, 1 Cor. 15:51-52, and both will be caught up together in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, 1 Thess. 4:17. Because, meanwhile, being accounted worthy of the other age extends more broadly than being accounted worthy of the resurrection to life: for all who shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection to life shall also be accounted worthy of the other age; but not conversely, for not all who shall be accounted worthy of the other age shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection, since not all die and need a resurrection; it is more convenient by the order of nature that those worthy of the other age be proposed before those who shall be accounted worthy of the resurrection of the dead. For among those things between which a reciprocal consequence is not given, that which is more general, and from which a reciprocal consequence of being does not proceed, is prior by nature, as Aristotle teaches in the Post-praedicamenta concerning the modes of the prior.

Fifthly, it is falsely asserted that the passages of Scripture Eph. 2:1, Acts 7:1, John 8:25 are placed without sense. For in Eph. 2:1 the word 'he raised' is omitted by ellipsis, which if it be repeated and supplied from verse 20 of the preceding chapter, the sense will be plain and as follows: And you also (he raised) when you were dead in sins etc. Such elliptical expressions are not unusual in the Holy Scriptures. But in Acts VII. 1, all the words of Stephen are clear and perspicuous, and have their plain meaning, as will be evident to the reader. Now, the reason why the most holy Martyr in his apology commemorates the history of the ancient Fathers so prolixly, beginning from the calling of Abraham and his being led into the land of Canaan, is that he might show that he does not believe and preach a new doctrine, but that very same doctrine concerning the Messiah promised to the Fathers, which they themselves believed and professed, and that he was therefore falsely accused of speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God. The words of Christ in John VIII. 25, however, are indeed obscure, yet they are not therefore devoid of meaning; but all interpreters, both Greek and Latin, assume as certain that they have their certain meaning, although they do not entirely agree among themselves in eliciting and explaining it, but divide into parties. To bring forward the opinions of all the Ancients, Greek and Latin Fathers, as well as of more recent Interpreters, is not the purpose of the present place and undertaking. This at least we advise, that in the Greek text, which alone is authentic, it is not written ἡ ἀρχὴ, ὅτις principium, qui etc. as the slanderer, following the Vulgate Interpreter, alleges the words, but that these are the words of Christ: τὴν ἀρχὴν, ὅ, τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν: where the accusative, τὴν ἀρχὴν, is placed adverbially for κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν, in the beginning, and by hyperbaton, most common in the Scriptures, is to be referred to the verb λαλῶ; but the particle which follows is the pronoun, ὅ, τι, which is to be read, not the conjunction ὅτι, that; the particle καὶ, moreover, seems to be redundant through a pleonasm neither unusual nor inelegant, with this meaning: I am that which I say to you from the beginning. Some take the accusative τὴν ἀρχὴν for παντελῶς, or ὅλως, altogether, so that it has the force of an asseverative particle; interpreters warn that τὴν ἀρχὴν is sometimes taken in this meaning among Greek writers: in which way there is no need for hyperbaton, and the meaning will be this: Altogether I am that which I speak, which I say to you, namely the light of the world, and he whom the Father sent, to wit, the Messiah promised to the Fathers. and now exhibited in the flesh, as he had said in the preceding v. 12, 16, 18. Which meaning is plain and perspicuous and entirely consistent with the words.

Finally, sixthly, in the passages Exod. XX. 18 and Job XXII. 6, there is nothing that is alien to right reason, provided the received custom of speaking is observed. In the former passage, the verb of sense is used, ראה, which is pertaining to sight, concerning the objects of different senses, namely concerning lightning, and smoke ascending from a mountain, pertaining to sight; and concerning thunder, and the sound of trumpets, pertaining to hearing, with the word transferred from sight, which is sharper than the others, to other external senses: in which sense when it is used, it is to be rendered not precisely by 'to see', but by 'to know', 'to perceive': In the other passage, however, the phrase: 'to strip clothes from the naked', is to be taken in a divided sense, in this way: you stripped the naked of the clothes which they had, and you are the cause why they walk about so naked or in torn clothes. Which sense Mercer and Francis Junius also render in their commentaries on this passage: the former indeed thus: 'You were stripping the clothes of the poor, thus leaving them naked'; the latter truly: 'Those who are already naked because of your injury, you will have stripped of their clothes.' But enough and more than enough concerning the internal sign or motive of credibility, sought from the material part of Scripture, namely its style. We proceed to the other internal signs or motives, which are accustomed to be drawn from its formal part.

Latin:

mortuorum resurrectioni præponitur, quem tamen ordinem ipsimet repiciunt Christiani. Si dixerint, esse ὕστερον πρότερον, etiam pro Turcarum Alcorano hoc σοφὸν φάρμακον militabit. Sine sensu posita quoq; sunt illa ad Eph. 2. vers. 1. & tota illa oratio Act. 7. vers. 1 seqq. item Joh. 8. v. 25. principium, qui & loquor vobis &c. Denique etiam sine ratione posita sunt Exod. 20. vers. 18. populus videbat sonitum tubarum: item: nudis vestes exuere Job. 20. vers. 6. Postea subjicit nonnulla alia, quæ stylum Scripturæ propriè non concernunt, & concludit tandem: Quæ cùm ita sint, Amice Lector non uncte, (i. e. non Christiane) nemo homo mihi vitio vertet, si unà cum meis Gregalibus (quorum innumerus ferè numerus mihi Lutetiæ, Amstelodami, Lugduni, in Anglia, Hamburgi, Hauniæ, nec non Holmiæ & in contiguis locis adstipulantur) universa Biblia bellæ Fabellæ loco habeam, quâ Belluæ, id est Christiani, rationem captivantes, & cum ratione insanientes, delectantur.

VII. Hæc ille ex sua & suorum, quos jactat, Gregalium mente: quibus Scripturis sacris non tantùm suam dependentiam & originem à Deo, sed & veritatem ac fidem omnem denegat, easque fabularum in censum rejicit, sed quàm nequiter & improbè, tam insulsè & ineptè. Conclusio principalis, quam sibi probandam sumit, est hæc: Vitio sibi vertendum non esse, si universa Biblia bellæ Fabellæ loco habeat. Rationem probandi accersit ex eo, quòd Scriptura tota adeò confusa sit & commixta, ut quicquid ibi est, totum sine connexione, sine compositione, absque omni verborum & sententiarum ordine & colore, postremo absque sensu & ratione positum sit; ex qua hoc nascitur principale argumentum: Quæ Scriptura tota adeò confusa & commixta est, ut quicquid ibi est, sine connexione, sine compositione, absque omni verborum & sententiarum ordine & colore, postremò absque sensu & ratione positum sit, illa jure habetur bellæ Fabellæ loco. Atqui sic sese habet Christianorum Scriptura sacra. Ergo. Quamvis verò non deesset, quod in propositione majore desiderari possit: Ordo enim & distinctio rerum in Scriptura, connexio verborum & sententiarum, color verborum &c. non præcisè ad veritatem, sed ad ornatum, elegantiam & perspicuitatem Scripturæ pertinet, & potest Scriptura aliqua esse vera, licet confusa & commixta sit &c. eò tamen nunc non descendam. In propositione minore autem homuncio hic se nimis hyperbolicum Scripturæ sacræ calumniatorem ostendit. Mendacissimè enim scribit, Scripturam sacram totam esse confusam & commixtam, & quicquid ibi est, æcum esse sine connexione, sine compositione, absque omni verborum ordine & colore, & absque sensu & ratione positum; quæ quot periodos, tot palpabilia mendacia continent. In illorum probatione Scurra ineptissimè à particulari ad universale concludit. Scripturam totam esse confusam & commixtam, probat ex eo, quod Proverbia Salomonis confusa & commixta sint, & in uno etiam illorum capite omnis generis res ad instar farraginis commisceantur, & confundantur: sed quàm infulsè & quàm ineptè hoc? Quid enim? num Proverbia Salomonis sunt Scriptura tota? an quicquid in Scriptura est, totum commixtum & confusum est, quia in Proverbiis Salomonis, in uno etiam capite, variæ sententiæ mixtim & sine certo ordine describuntur? Quis, nisi inops mentis, aut cui Satanas oculos mentis prorsus excæcavit, sic ineptiret? Scripturam totam sine connexione positam esse concludit ex eo, quòd Habacuc cap. II. versus primus; & cap. III. versus primus, juxta Versionem Lutheri, vel capitis II. versus quintus, juxta textum Ebræum, cum præcedentibus non sint connexi: totam absq; omni verborum colore positam, concludit ex eo, quòd Apoc. V. & VIII. omnes versiculi à particula ET incipiunt; totam absque sententiarum ordine positam concludit ex Luc. XX. 31. ubi vita æterna resurrectioni mortuorum præponatur; totam sine sensu positam probat ex eo, quòd Eph. II. 1. verba Pauli; & Act. VII. v. 1. seqq. Stephani oratio tota; & Joh. VIII. 25. verba Christi: principium, qui & loquor vobis; sensu careant; totam denique sine ratione positam probat ex Exod. XX. 18. ubi populus vidisse dicitur sonitum tubarum, & Job. XX. 6. ubi Jobus dicitur nudis vestes exuisse: Sed quàm ineptè etiam hæc inferuntur omnia? Si enim faciamus, quæ allata sunt loca Scripturæ, habere sic omnia, ut afferuntur, num proptereà Scriptura tota carebit connxexione, quòd duo versiculi in Propheta Habacucs non sunt connexi? num proptereà

Scriptura omni carebit verborum colore & ornatu, quòd in duobus capitibus Apocalypseos omnes versiculi à particula ET incipiunt? Num sententiarum ordine tota caret, quòd Luc. XX. 31. vita æterna præponitur resurrectioni mortuorum? An tota caret sensu, quòd Eph. II. v. 1. verba Pauli, Act. VII. oratio Stephani, & Joh. VIII. 25. verba Christi sensu carent? Num tota sine ratione posita est, quòd Exod. XX. 18. populus sonicum tubarum vidisse, & Job. XX. 6. Vir sanctus nudis vestes exuisse dicitur sine ratione? quis non videt nullitatem harum consequentiarum omnium? quippe quæ omnes à particulari ad universale plus quàm pueriliter concludunt.

Sed lustremus ordine loca adducta singula. Proverbia Salomonis, præsertim à capite decimo, mixtim & sine certo ordine confignata esse fatemur: Scripturæ sacræ auctoritati autem hinc quicquam decedere, negamus. Nam liber hic, præsertim à capite decimo ad finem usque, non occupatur in determinata aliqua materia explicanda, in qua certa methodus, ordo & connexio adhiberi possit, sed continet omnis generis gnomas brevesque ac rotundas de rebus variis sententias, à sapientia profectas, atque ad sapientiam ducentes, ita concisè confignatas, ut singuli versus singulas absolvant completas sententias: in quibus recensendis certam methodum connexionemque requirere, est in arena ordinem & nexum requirere. Præcedentia verò novem capita, præfationis instar præmissa, in sapientiæ studio commendando occupantur, nec omni ordine ac nexu destituuntur. Quemadmodùm ergo concisas de rebus variis & inter se non cohærentibus sententias sine certo ordine ac connexione recensere in Scriptore vitium non est: ita nec Proverbiorum libro quicquam accedit vitii aut maculæ, Scriptore θεοπνεύσῳ indignæ, quòd variæ de rebus variis & inter se non cohærentibus sententiæ mixtim sine certa methodo, ordine ac connexione conscriptæ sunt.

Deinde in Prophetia Habacuci versum primum capitis secundi cum versu ultimo præcedentis capitis primi connexum non esse, mirum non est. Non enim in omnibus Scripturæ aut orationis partibus, capitibus aut versiculis requiri potest connexio, sed saltem in partibus, quarum res substratæ cohærent. Quarum partium res substratæ autem inter se nullam habent cognationem, nullam cohærentiam, in iis ne in humanis quidé optimorum Auctorum scriptis semper invenitur aut necessaria ducitur connexio. Ita verò res habet cum adducto v. 1. capitis secundi Habacuci, ad versum ultimum capitis primi collato. In capite II. usque ad versum ultimum vaticinatus est Habacuc de Chaldæorum tyrannide & crudelitate, quâ in populum Judaicum sævituri essent, Deumque precibus ardentibus solicitaverat, vellet illorum sævitiam compescere, & pios contra eandem protegere & conservare. Sed in capite secundo de Messiæ adventu concionari incipit, ad solatium populi afflicti, & hujus concionis initium facit in ipso versiculo primo: qui ut à versu ultimo cap. præcedentis non dependebat, ita ut cum illo connecteretur, nihil causæ erat. In altero autem capite versu primo juxta versionem Lutheri, vel in capite secundo versu quinto, juxta textum Ebræum, nullam esse connexionem cum versu præcedente, falsum est. Dicit quidem Scurra, τό SED nihil connectit. Sed in Ebræo textu, qui solus Prophetæ est, particula SED non extat, sed particulæ ואף כי quæ commodè reddi possunt, quin etiam, & omninò connectendi vim habent, versumque hunc cum antecedentibus conjungunt. Nam in versibus antecedentibus Propheta vaticinatus fuerat de adventu promissi Messiæ, ejusque spe certâ & indubitatâ animos afflictos erexerat: in versu quinto autem superaddit novum solatii argumentum, ab excidio regni Babylonici, Regisq; Babyloniorum temulenti, superbi & arrogantis, atq; hinc secutura liberatione ex durissima servitute & tyrannide Chaldæorum petitum, & particulæ ואף כי commodè reddi possunt; quin etiam, (quemadmodùm Junius & Tremellius reddiderunt) ut sensus sit: quin etiam, vel adhuc Vir temulentus, superbus & arrogans (puta Babyloniorum Rex) qui omnibus terrori erit, & cujus tyrannide prememini & gravissimè affligemini, excindetur, & fabula ac risus fiet omnibus populis &c.

Tertiò quòd Scriptura sacra verborum colore & fuco expolita non est, & Apoc. cap. V. & VIII. omnes versiculi à particula ET incipiunt, adeò ejus auctoritati nihil detrahit, ut eam potiùs commendet. Quemadmodùm enim Evangelio de Christo crucifixo, quod Judæis scandalo, Græcis stultitia erat, 1. Cor. I. 23. nihil detrahebat, quod non à sapientibus seculi hujus persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed ab indoctis & literarum rudibus piscatoribus, & Paulo, qui quidem ad pedes Gamalielis πεπαιδευμένος κατ' ἀκρίβειαν πατρῴου νόμου, Act. XXII. 6. sed τῷ λόγῳ ἰδιώτης erat, II. Cor. XI. 6. simplici miniméque fucato sermonis genere prædicabatur, mundóque, nihil quicquam obstante hostium fremitu, persuadebatur, sed in insignem ejus commendationem cedebat: ita nec auctoritati sacræ Scripturæ per hoc aliquid decedit, quòd ab iisdem stylo simplici, absque verborum colore & fuco consignata, & tamen ab Ecclesiis, per universum terrarum orbem diffusis, recepta & credita est. Hoc totum enim factum est, ne inanis redderetur crux Christi, I. Cor. I. 17. h. e. ne Evangelio de Christo crucifixo, sive prædicato sive literis consignato, sua divina vis & efficacia sermonis ornatu & relucente ex eo sapientiâ humanâ obliteraretur, & verborum colori ac fuco adscriberetur. Neque tamen ita simplex & fuci colorisque expers est Scripturæ stylus, quin passim suas admixtas habeat elegantias, præfertim in illis partibus ac libris, quorum Auctores elegantiori stylo erant adsueti, sicut de Esaia Propheta testatur Hieronymus, quòd in sermone suo disertus sit, quippe vir nobilis & urbanæ eloquentiæ, nec habens quicquam in eloquio rusticitatis admixtum; de Ezechiele, quòd nec satis disertus, nec admodùm rusticus sit, sed ex utroque mediè tamperatus, de Hosea, quòd commaticus sit, & quasi per sententias loquens; de Luca, quòd magis Græcas literas sciverit, quàm Hebræas, & proptereà sermo ejus tam in Evangelio, quàm in Actibus Apostolorum, id est, in utroque volumine comtior sit, & secularem redoleat eloquentiam &c. Videantur ejus Præfationes in Esaiam, Ezechielem, super XII. Proph. & ejusdem Comm. in Cap. VI. Esaia. Spiritus sanctus enim, uti suprà monuimus, in suggerendis Scripturæ verbis cujusque Scriptoris ingenio & sermonis generi consueto sese conformavit, & quamvis non quæsiverit, non tamen neglexit planè sermonis ornatum & elegantiam, sed pro indole ingenii & sermonis cuique Scriptori consueti sparsim suos admiscuit flosculos. Qua de re inter alios videri potest doctissimus Flacius in part. II. Clav. Tract. V. de Stylo sacrarum literarum.

Quartò si admitteretur, quod Luc. XX, 35. vita æterna mortuorum resurrectioni per ὕστερον πρότερον præponatur, ne sic quidem Scripturæ sacræ auctoritati aliquid decederet. Si enim de membri utriusque veritate constet, quod ad ordinem attinet, parum refert, utrum præponatur vel postponatur. Non enim in populari usu & loquendi consuetudine præcisè adstringimur ad ordinem, quem ipsæ res per se habent, observandum. Sed nihil causæ est, cur hîc vitam æternam resurrectioni mortuorum contra ordinem sibi connaturalem præponi dicamus. Christus enim instituit d. l. comparationem inter filios hujus seculi, & inter eos, qui digni habebuntur seculo altero & resurrectione ex mortuis, quòd illi ducant uxores, & nuptum dent filias suas; hi verò neque ducant uxores, neque nuptum dent. Inter eos verò, qui digni habebuntur seculo altero, & inter eos, qui digni habebuntur resurrectione ex mortuis, ad alteram scilicet & beatam vitam, non datur hic naturalis ordo, ut qui digni habebuntur resurrectione ad vitam æternam, necessariò priores sint dignis seculo altero: nam inter eos, qui digni habebuntur seculo altero, comprehenduntur omnes pii, quos dies extremus Christíque adventus ad judicium deprehendet vivos. Hi enim uti nec morientur, neque ex mortuis resurgent, sed immutabuntur subitò, ita piis demortuis, qui digni habebuntur resurrectione ad vitam, posteriores non erunt, sed eodem momento, quo hi ad vocem tubæ resurgent, immutabuntur etiam illi, 1. Cor. XV. 51. 52. & utrique simul rapientur in nubibus in occursum Domini in aëra, 1. Thess. IV. 17. Quia interim dignum haberi seculo altero latiùs patet, quàm dignum haberi resurrectione ad vitam: omnes enim, qui habebuntur digni resurrectione ad vitam, habebuntur etiam digni seculo altero; non autem contrà qui habebuntur digni seculo altero, omnes habebuntur digni resurrectione, cùm non omnes moriantur & resurrectione egeant; naturæ ordine convenientius proponuntur digni seculo altero his, qui digni habebuntur resurrectione mortuorum. Inter ea enim, inter quæ non reciproca datur consequentia, naturâ prius est, quod generaliùs est, & à quo reciproca essendi consequentia non procedit, docente Aristotele in Post-præd. de modis prioris.

Quintò falsò asseritur, loca Scripturæ Eph. II. 1. Act. VII. 1. Job. VIII. 25. posita esse sine sensu. Nam Eph. II. v. 1. verbum, suscitavit, per ellipsin omissum est, quod si ex versu 20. capitis præcedentis repetatur & suppleatur, sensus planus, & hic erit: Et vos etiam (suscitavit) cùm essetis mortui in peccatis &c. cujusmodi locutiones ellipticæ Scripturis sacris inusitatæ non sunt. Act. VII. 1. verò verba Stephani omnia clara & perspicua sunt, suumque planum habent sensum, sicut legenti patebit. Quòd autem sanctissimus Martyr in sua apologia Patrum veterum historiam tam prolixè commemorat, initio à vocatione Abrahami in terram Canaan ducto, factum est, ut se non novam, sed eam ipsam doctrinam de Messia Patribus promisso, quam ipsi crediderunt & professi sunt, credere ac prædicare, atque adeò se falsò accusari, quòd loquatur verba contumeliosa in Mosen ac Deum, ostenderet. Verba Christi Joh. VIII. 25. autem obscura quidem sunt, sensu tamen propterea non destituuntur, sed interpretes omnes, cùm Græci tùm Latini, supponunt tanquam certum, quòd suum certum habeant sensum, quamvis in eo eruendo & explicando inter se non planè conveniant, sed in partes abeant. Omnium Veterum, Græcorum & Latinorum, Patrum, ut & recentiorum Interpretum sententias adferre, præsentis loci & instituti non est. Hoc saltem monemus, in Græco textu, qui solus authenticus est, non haberi ἡ ἀρχὴ, ὅτις principium, qui &c. ut calumniator, Vulgatum Interpretem sequutus, verba allegat, sed verba Christi esse hæc: τὴν ἀρχὴν, ὅ, τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν: ubi accusativus, τὴν ἀρχὴν, adverbialiter pro κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν, principio, positus, & per trajectionem, Scripturis usitatissimam, ad verbum λαλῶ referendus; quæ autem sequitur particula, pronomen est, ὅ, τι, quod legenda, non conjunctio ὅτι quod, particula καὶ autem per pleonasmum nec inusitatum nec inelegantem, redundare videtur, hoc sensu: id (scilicet sum) quod à principio dico vobis. Nonnulli accusativum τὴν ἀρχὴν accipiunt pro παντελῶς, vel ὅλως omninò, ut asseverantis particulæ vim habeat; quo significatu apud Græcos Scriptores τὴν ἀρχὴν quandoque accipi interpretes monent: quomodo trajectione non opus, sensus autem hic erit: Omninò sum id, quod loquor, quod dico vobis, nempe lux mundi, & is, quem misit Pater, puta Messias promissus Patribus. & nunc in carne exhibitus, ut præcedente, v. 12. 16. 18. dixerat. Qui sensus planus & perspicuus verbisque prorsus consentaneus est.

Sextò denique in locis Exod. XX. 18. & Jobi XXII. 6. nihil extat, quod à recta ratione alienum sit, modò consuetudo loquendi recepta observetur. In loco priori adhibetur verbum sensus, ראה ad visum pertinens, de diversorum sensuum objectis, nempe de fulguris, & de fumo, ex monte adscendente, ad visum; & de tonitru, ac sonitu tubarum, ad auditum pertinentibus, verbo a visu, qui est acutior reliquis, ad alios sensus externos translato: quâ ratione cùm usurpatur, non præcisè per videre, sed per cognoscere, percipere reddendum est: In altero loco autem phrasis: nudis vestes exuere, in sensu diviso accipienda est, hoc modo: nudis vestes, quas habuerunt, exuisti, & in causa es, cur ita nudi aut laceris vestibus incedant. Quem in sensum etiam Mercerus & Franciscus Junius in comm. suis ad h. l. verba reddunt: ille quidem sic: Pauperum vestes exuebas, ita eos nudos relinquens; hic verò: Eos, qui jam nudi sunt propter injuriam tuam, nudaveris vestibus suis. Sed plus satis de signo sive motivo credibilitatis interno, ex parte Scripturæ materiali, ejus stylo scilicet, petito. Ad cætera, interna signa sive motiva, quæ ex ejusdem parte formali desumi solent, progredimur.


### VI. Those which can be drawn from the formal part, namely from the sense and the…

VI.

Those which can be drawn from the formal part, namely from the sense and the things signified, are many and various, just as the properties of the sense and of the things signified are many and various.

We shall not consider here Scripture according to all its properties and affections, but only according to the more important properties and affections, which in any Scripture divinely granted to mortals for instruction in the true religion unto salvation: such a Scripture as we profess to be sacred; can be required from the part of the sense and the things signified, and even by natural reason itself as judge, by the consensus of all, are required.

VII.

These properties and affections can be reduced to three heads: namely TRUTH, pure from error; HOLINESS, perfect without blemish; and SUFFICIENCY for salvation, full without defect, both as to what must be believed and as to what must be done.

Just as on the part of man, about to attain eternal salvation, by the consensus of all, there is required both RIGHT FAITH in God, and a LIFE worthy of God, that is to say, instituted in conformity with divine laws and holy; thus, on the part of Scripture, in which the true religion that leads to eternal salvation is contained and described, it is required without doubt that it should perfectly hand down those things which are necessary to be known and believed concerning God and the manner of obtaining salvation with Him, and also those things necessary to be done in order to live a life holily and in conformity with the divine will. For the perfect handing down of those things which are necessary to be believed and done, there is required on its part TRUTH pure from every error. For because it was granted to the race of mortals by God, who is the first Truth itself and the source and origin of all truth, in order that He might lead men who were turned away from Him back to Himself, and instruct them for salvation, it must necessarily be true and devoid of every error. For besides the fact that nothing but what is true can proceed from God, the source of truth, Scripture also can lead no one to God unless it is true in all respects. For that which is false, or has falsehoods mixed with truths, leads away from God, it does not lead to Him, since every error and falsity, just as it departs from truth, so also departs from and leads away from God, who, as has been said, is Truth. For the perfect handing down of those things which are necessary to be done in order to live a life holily, there is required on its part holiness perfect and without blemish, that is, that all things which it hands down concerning God and His worship and the ordering of human life should be holy, and contain nothing base or foreign to what is decorous and honest. For Scripture cannot lead to God, who is wholly holy and holiness itself, if it hands down things that are indecorous, base, or sinful: since every baseness and every sin turns and separates man from God, and, unless it is remitted through intervening repentance, excludes him from salvation. For both, there is required SUFFICIENCY full and without defect. For unless it hands down without defect all things which are necessary for those to be saved to know and believe concerning God and divine matters in order to attain salvation, or to do in order to live a life holily and in conformity with the divine will, it will be able to lead no one to salvation. For by the very fact that it would not hand down all things necessary to be believed or done, it would hand down error in things necessary to be believed or done, or at the very least would leave man in ignorance of something which was necessary to be believed or done. Moreover, both error and ignorance in things necessary to be believed or done lead away from God and exclude from salvation. And in these things we think all peoples and nations agree, to whom some true religion and the salvation of souls is a care and a concern. All, I say, agree in this, that the code of Scripture, by which true and saving religion is described and contained, delivers perfectly and sufficiently, without error and without defect, both what is necessary to be known and believed for salvation, and what is necessary to be done for the holiness of life. And because it is not for man to deliver these things so perfectly, all are accustomed to boast of divine revelations, to which they attribute what their public books deliver concerning religion.

Latin:

VI.

QUæ ex parte formali, sensu scilicet & rebus significatis, desumi possunt, multa & varia sunt, prout sensus ac rerum significatarum proprietates multæ & variæ sunt.

Non considerabimus hic Scripturam secundum omnes suas proprietates & affectiones, sed tantùm secundum proprietates & affectiones potiores, quæ in aliqua Scriptura, mortalibus in religione vera ad salutem instruendis divinitus concessâ: qualem Scripturam, sacram esse profitemur; ex parte sensus rerumque significatarum requiri possunt, & vel ipsa naturali ratione judice, omnium consensu, requiruntur.

VII.

HÆ proprietates & affectiones ad tria capita reduci possunt: VERITATEM scilicet, ab errore puram; SANCTITATEM, absque nævo perfectam; & SUFFICIENTIAM ad salutem, cùm quà credenda tum quà agenda, absque defectu plenam.

Quemadmodum ex parte hominis, salutem æternam adepturi, omnium consensu, requiritur cùm RECTA in Deum FIDES, tùm VITA Deo digna, h. c. legibus divinis conformiter instituta & SANCIA; ita ex parte Scriptura, qua vera & ad salutem æternam ducens religio descripta continetur, citra dubium requiritur, ut quæ cùm de Deo deque ratione consequendæ apud ipsum salutis cognitu & creditu; tùm ad vitam sanctè ac voluntati divinæ conformiter degendam factu necessaria sunt, perfectè tradat. Ad tradendum perfectè quæ creditu factuque necessaria sunt, requiritur ex ejus parte VERITAS ab omni errore pura. Quia enim à Deo, qui ipsa prima Veritas, & veritatis omnis fons & origo est, concessa est mortalium generi, ut homines à se aversos ad se perducat, & ad salutem ipsos informet, necessariò vera errorisque omnis expers esse debet. Præterquam enim, quòd à Deo, veritatis fonte, non nisi verum provenire potest, ad Deum etiam Scriptura, nisi per omnia vera, nulla perducere potest. Nam quæ falsa est, aut veris falsa admixta habet, abducit à Deo, non perducit ad eum, siquidem error & falsitas omnis, ut à veritate, ita & à Deo, qui, uti dictum, Veritas est, recedit & abducit. Ad tradendum perfectè, quæ ad vitam sanctè degendam factu necessaria sunt, requiritur ex parte ejusdem sanctitas absque nævo perfecta, h. e. ut quæ de Deo ejusque cultu deque instituenda hominum vita tradit, sancta sint omnia, nec quicquam turpe aut à decoro & honesto alienum contineant. Non enim ad Deum, qui totus sanctus & ipsa sanctitas est, perducere potest Scriptura, quæ indecora, turpia, peccaminosa tradit: cùm omnis turpitudo, peccatum omne avertat & separet hominem à Deo, &, nisi interveniente pœnitentiâ remittatur, salute excludat. Ad utrumque requiritur SVFFICIENTIA absq; defectu plena. Nisi enim absque defectu omnia tradat, quæ salvandis sive de Deo rebusque divinis ad adipiscendam salutem cognitu & creditu; sive ad vitam sanctè divinæque voluntati conformiter degendam factu necessaria sunt, ad salutem perducere neminem poterit. Eo ipso enim, quòd non omnia sive creditu sive factu necessaria traderet, traderet errorem in creditu aut factu necessariis, vel minimùm relinqueret hominem in ignorantia alicujus, quod sive creditu sive factu necessarium esset. Abducit autem à Deo & excludit salute cùm error tùm ignorantia in creditu factuve necessariis. Atq; in his hactenus convenire arbitramur omnes populos ac gentes, quibus aliqua vera religio & animarum salus curæ cordique est. Omnes, inquam, conveniunt in eo, quòd Scripturæ codicem, quo vera & salvifica religio descripta continetur, cùm quæ ad salutem cognitu & creditu, tum quæ ad sanctimoniam vitæ factu necessaria sunt, absque errore & absque defectu perfectè & sufficienter tradat. Et quia hominis non est hæc ita perfectè tradere, divinas revelationes, quibus accepta ferant, quæ de religione tradunt sui publici codices, jactare omnes solent.


### VIII. THE TRUTH of Holy Scripture, pure from every error, can be shown I

VIII.

THE TRUTH of Holy Scripture, pure from every error, can be shown I. BY AN INDUCTION of all the dogmas which are delivered in it for the sake of our salvation, none of which can be convicted of any error. II. From the wonderful HARMONY AND AGREEMENT of the OLD TESTAMENT WITH THE NEW and of all the parts of both among themselves. III. FROM THE TRUTH OF THE PROPHECIES concerning future contingent events, PROVED by the EVENT itself and its fulfillment.

I. When we ascribe TRUTH to Holy Scripture, pure from every error, we signify that it contains nothing false. There would be no reason for us to go about proving this assertion of ours against the modern calumniators of Holy Scripture. For it would be incumbent upon those who accuse it of falsehood, or reject it into the class of fables with wicked impiety and blasphemy, to convict it of falsehood most evidently. For as long as they do not and cannot certainly and evidently convict it of any error, the presumption of Truth, pure from every error, fights for it—a truth asserted by the testimony of all pious martyrs and an infinite multitude of the faithful spread throughout the world, borne to it from the beginning of the Church, and proved by many other signs and documents of truth.
