We, however, out of an abundance of caution, will show its truth, devoid of all falsehood, partly by an induction of the parts of its doctrine, all of which either agree with right reason, or perfect the natural knowledge of it, or at least exceed it, so that they cannot be convicted of falsehood; partly indeed from their wonderful harmony and agreement among themselves; and partly, finally, from the truth of the prophecies, by the event itself

and confirmed by fulfillment. For if the plain truth of Holy Scripture, devoid of all error and falsehood, were to be called into doubt, the reason for doubting would certainly have to be established in the points already enumerated, or in some one of them: namely, either that in some dogmas concerning the salvation of the human race, for the sake of which it was entirely recorded and transmitted to posterity—whether these be many or few—it could be evidently convicted of falsehood; or that the parts of the doctrine itself are dissonant with one another, and that diverse and mutually conflicting doctrines were handed down by the different writers of the books of either or both Testaments, and it could be convicted of contradiction; or finally, that the events did not correspond to the prophecies concerning future contingencies, and that it could be convicted of falsehood from a lack of fulfillment. If nothing of such a kind can be solidly and evidently demonstrated and proven, but in these matters the undoubted truth of Holy Scripture stands firm, there will be no reason for anyone to doubt the truth of the rest. For the rest either concern histories written by authors of their own time, who lacked neither the knowledge of the things to be written nor the desire for truth, or other matters inserted as the occasion so brought it about, in which, if any difficulties occur that delay our understanding, one must not on that account doubt their truth, much less are they to be accused of falsehood on that account. For it is one thing not to understand what you read, and another for what you do not understand not to be true. For it often happens that we do not understand what we read, especially in histories and matters most remote from us, the individual circumstances of which are hidden from us, even though what we read but do not understand is most true.

II. And these three proofs of truth not only, when taken together, prove that it is entirely credible that Holy Scripture contains truth, pure from all error, but each one also, viewed individually, makes it sufficiently credible that it has God himself as its author, as will be taught below.

Latin:

VIII.

VERITAS Scripturæ sacræ ab omni errore pura ostendi potest I. PER INDUCTIONEM dogmatum omnium, quæ nostræ salutis causâ in ea traduntur, quorum nullum alicujus erroris convinci potest. II. Ex VETERIS TESTAMENTI CUM NOVO omniumque utriusque partium inter se mira HARMONIA & CONSENSIONE. III. EX VERITATE VATICINIORUM de futuris contingentibus, ipso EVENTU & complemento COMPROBATA.

I. Quando Scripturæ sacræ adscribimus VERITATEM, ab omni errore puram, significamus, eam nihil continere falsi. Quam nostram assertionem ut contra hodiernos Scripturæ sacræ calumniatores probatum iremus, causæ nihil esset. His enim, qui eam falsitatis accusant, vel nefandâ impietate & blasphemiâ in fabularum classem rejiciunt, incumberet, ut falsitatis illam evidentissimè convincerent. Quamdiu enim nullius illam erroris certò & evidenter convincunt aut convincere possunt, militat pro ipsa præsumtio Veritatis, ab omni errore puræ, omnium piorum Martyrum & infinitæ per orbem diffusæ fidelium multitudinis testimonio, inde ab initio Ecclesiæ ei perhibito, assertæ, aliisque pluribus veritatis signis ac documentis comprobatæ. Nos tamen ex abundante ejus veritatem, falsitatis omnis expertem, ostendemus partim inductione partium doctrinæ, quæ omnes, vel cum recta ratione consentiant, vel naturalem ejus cognitionem perficiant, vel saltem excedant, ut falsitatis convinci non possint; partim verò ex illarum mira inter se harmonia & consensione, partim denique ex veritate vaticiniorum, ipso eventu

& complemento comprobata. Si enim Scripturæ sacræ plana & omnis erroris atque falsitatis expers veritas in dubium vocanda esset, ratio dubitandi utique in jam enumeratis momentis, vel in aliquo illorum constituenda esset: nempe vel quòd in aliquibus dogmatibus, salutem generis humani concernentibus, quorum rectè tradendorum & ad posteritatem transmittendorum causâ tota consignata est; iisque multis aut paucis, falsitatis evidenter convinci possint; vel quòd ipsæ doctrinæ partes à se dissonent, & vel ab utriusque vel alterutrius Testamenti librorum Scriptoribus diversis diversæ & inter se pugnantes doctrinæ traditæ fuerint, & contradictionis convinci possit; vel denique quòd vaticiniis de futuris contingentibus eventus non responderit, & ex defectu complementi falsitatis ea convinci queant. Si tale nihil solidè & evidenter demonstrari & evinci possit, sed in his Scripturæ sacræ sua indubitata constet veritas, de cæterorum veritate non erit, quod quis dubitet. Cætera enim vel historias concernent, à sui temporis Auctoribus, quibus nec scientia rerum scribendarum, nec veritatis studium defuit, conscriptas, vel res alias, occasione sic ferente, infertas, in quibus si quæ difficultates, nostram intelligentiam remorantes, occurrant, non proptereà de ipsa illarum veritate dubitandum est, multò minùs falsitatis proptereà arguendæ sunt. Aliud enim est non intelligere, quod legis, aliud non verum esse, quod non intelligis. Sæpè enim contingit, ut non intelligamus, quæ legimus, præsertim in historiis & rebus à nobis remotissimis, quarum singulares circumstantiæ nos latent, ut tamen veriffima sint, quæ lecta non intelligimus.

II. Atque hæc tria veritatis documenta non tantùm junctim sumta evincunt credibile prorsus esse, quod Scriptura sacra contineat veritatem, ab omni errore puram, sed unumquodque etiam, singulatim spectatum, satis credibile facit, eam ipsummet Deum habere auctorem, ut infra docebitur.


### IX. Dogmas, recorded in Holy Scripture for the sake of human salvation, are of two…

IX.

Dogmas, recorded in Holy Scripture for the sake of human salvation, are of two kinds. Some can also be known from the light of nature; others, however, exceed the light of nature, and can become known to us from nowhere else than from God revealing them.

X.

Those things which can also be known from the light of nature concern the doctrine regarding God and His essence, attributes, providence, and worship, and regarding a life to be instituted rightly and in conformity with the divine will.

XI.

However, Holy Scripture delivers all these things, if you look at the matter itself, in a way entirely consistent with right reason; but if you look to the manner of proposing and teaching, it does so much more simply, more certainly, and more perfectly than right reason can teach them from its own principles. I. This class of men, which calls into doubt or denies the truth of Holy Scripture, and which is unwilling to admit anything beyond the light of nature and the dictates of right reason, cannot be recalled to any other norm of truth than right reason, so that they may either receive as true what is consistent with it, or, if it cannot be convicted of falsehood by it, they may not reject it as false. II. That Holy Scripture teaches the doctrine regarding God and His essence, attributes, providence, and worship, and regarding a life to be instituted rightly and in conformity with the divine will, as far as the matter is concerned, in a way entirely consistent with right reason, is evident through induction. For no part of this doctrine can be brought forward which right reason teaches consistently from the principles of nature, but that Holy Scripture also teaches it with the highest agreement. But wherever any disagreement is noticed, it is certain that reason fails in demonstrating the truth, while Holy Scripture teaches the truth and corrects the errors of reason, and this can easily be shown by invincible arguments. III. Furthermore, that Holy Scripture teaches all those things more simply, more certainly, and more perfectly than right reason, as far as the manner of teaching is concerned, the thing itself speaks. For first, Holy Scripture teaches all those things in plain and clear words through bare assertions, without demonstrations, as was shown above. Reason, however, teaches the same things from the principles of nature through demonstrations. But the method of teaching through bare assertions is much simpler than through demonstrations deduced by human reason from the principles of nature. For of that [method] all indiscriminately, the learned and the unlearned; of the latter, however, only the erudite are capable. For demonstrations, drawn from the principles of nature, are for the most part difficult, so that hardly all the erudite can grasp them. Furthermore, Holy Scripture teaches the same things, with the reason for assenting being God who reveals; but reason, when related to the same principles of nature. However, by how much more certain God is in revealing truth than the human intellect is in drawing out and demonstrating the same from the principles of nature, by so much more certain is the doctrine concerning God and His essence, attributes, and worship, and concerning a life instituted rightly and in conformity with the divine will, from divine revelation, handed down in the Holy Scriptures, than that which is sought from the principles of nature by human reason. For God, who is Truth, through His infinite knowledge as well as goodness, can neither be deceived nor deceive in revealing it. Human reason, however, in drawing out and demonstrating the same from the principles of nature, can err, and does err, deceives, or is deceived quite often, just as the Apostle of the Gentiles reports concerning the Gentiles, that, intending to investigate the right worship of God from the principles of nature, they were deceived by their own ἐξαλογισμοῖς, and when they believed themselves to be wise, they became fools, because when they had known the invisible things of God, namely His eternal power as well as His divinity from the creation of the world by the things that were made, they did not, however, glorify Him as God, but changed the glory of the immortal God through an image fashioned not only to the likeness of mortal man, but also of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things, Rom. I. 20. seqq. Thirdly, Scripture also hands down all these things more perfectly than reason from the principles of nature. For human reason, in this corrupt state of nature, is obscured to such a degree that, as Aristotle himself, the Gentile Philosopher, admits, it behaves toward those things which are by nature the most manifest of all as the eyes of bats do toward the light of day, and it often goes blind in the middle of the light of truth, especially in the doctrine concerning God and divine things, and concerning the rectitude and holiness of life. Holy Scripture, however, wherever reason fails by its own ἐξαλογισμοῖς, and wanders from the truth, supplies its defects and corrects its errors by asserting the opposite truth in plain and clear words: e.g., right reason does indeed prove the unity of God from the principles of nature through demonstrations, but they are so difficult that the simpler sort and those unlearned in letters cannot attain their force. Hence the opinion of πολυθεΐας so prevailed among the common people of the Gentiles in times past, that

It would not have been entirely permissible for the more learned philosophers to bring forth into public their own opinion regarding the unity of God, based upon certain principles of nature. Holy Scripture, however, teaches that God is one, and condemns the opinion concerning πολυθεῖα in every place, and that in words so clear and perspicuous that no one is so slow of wit, and so stupid, that he does not perceive the sense of the words at the very first hearing. See among others Deut. IV. 39, ch. VI. 3, I Cor. VIII. 4, 6. Similarly, right reason acknowledges that God is a spiritual essence, devoid of matter and of all passive power, and incorruptible, and it demonstrates this even from the principles of nature; but the simpler and illiterate do not grasp the force of those demonstrations, and therefore, contrary to the very dictate of right reason, they worship and adore various corporeal things. But Holy Scripture teaches in plain and perspicuous words that God is a spirit, and that those who worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth, and it rejects and condemns all idolatry, as among others one may read in John IV. 24, II Cor. III. 17, Deut. V. 15 ff., II Kings XVII. 35 ff. How imperfect also is the knowledge of the divine attributes, as well as of the doctrine concerning creation and providence, to which reason attains from the principles of nature, and how difficult its demonstrations are; and on the contrary, how plain, perspicuous, and perfect are those things which Holy Scripture teaches concerning the same, and by which it amends and corrects the admitted errors of reason, and thus perfects the natural knowledge of these matters, could be shown in order through individual parts, were they not already sufficiently known, and were excessive prolixity not an obstacle to us. As far as the worship of God is concerned, whether you look to one or both tables of the Decalogue, reason left to itself prescribes almost only the external acts of virtues by which it is fitting to worship God, and commands that the opposite external acts of vices be avoided, so that God may not be offended: or if it does demand and prescribe even internal acts of love, faith, hope, and other virtues, and prohibits the opposite, it prescribes only deliberate ones, but considers the indeliberate acts and motions of concupiscence to be among those things which do not hinder the salvation of man. Scripture alone, however, for true and sincere worship of God, requires an exact agreement of internal and external acts and motions with the Law of God, and that perfection of virtues which excludes even the indeliberate acts and motions of concupiscence.

Latin:

IX.

DOgmata, humanæ salutis causâ in Scriptura sacra consignata, duum generum sunt. Quædam ex lumine naturæ etiam cognosci possunt; alia verò lumen naturæ excedunt, nec aliunde, quam ex Deo revelante, nobis innotescere possunt.

X.

QVæ ex lumine naturæ etiam cognosci possunt, concernunt doctrinam de Deo & ejus essentia, attributis, providentia, ac cultu, deque vita rectè & voluntati divinæ conformiter instituenda.

XI.

HÆc autem omnia tradit Scriptura sacra, si rem ipsam spectes, rectæ rationi prorsus convenienter; si verò ad modum proponendi & docendi respicias, multò simpliciùs, certiùs & perfectiùs, quàm recta ratio ea ex suis principiis docere potest. I. Non potest hoc hominum genus, quod Scripturæ sacræ veritatem in dubium vocat vel negat, nec, præter lumen naturæ & rectæ rationis dictamen, quicquam admittere vult, ad aliam veritatis normam revocari, quàm ad rectam rationem, ut quod vel huic consentaneum est, tanquam verum recipiant, vel ex eo falsitatis convinci non potest, ut falsum non rejiciant. II. Quod autem doctrinam de Deo & ejus essentia, attributis, providentia & cultu, deque vita rectè ac voluntati divinæ conformiter instituenda Scriptura sacra, quantùm ad rem, rectæ rationi prorsus convenienter doceat, per inductionem patet. Nulla enim hujus doctrinæ pars adferri potest, quam recta ratio ex naturæ principiis convenienter doceat, neq; tamen Scriptura sacra etiam summo doceat consensu. Sicubi autem aliquis animadvertatur dissensus, ibi rationem in demonstranda veritate deficere, Scripturam sacram verò veritatem docere, & rationis errores emendare, certum est, idque facilè rationibus invictis ostendi potest. III. Quod porrò ex parte modi docendi Scriptura sacra ea omnia doceat simpliciùs, certiùs, & perfectiùs, quàm ratio recta, res ipsa loquitur. Primùm enim Scriptura sacra docet ea omnia planis & perspicuis verbis per assertiones nudas, absque demonstrationibus, ut superiùs ostensum. Ratio verò docet eadem ex naturæ principiis per demonstrationes. Multò autem simplicior est ratio docendi per assertiones nudas, quàm per demonstrationes, ab humana ratione ex principiis naturæ deductas. Illius enim promíscuè omnes, docti & indocti; hujus vero soli eruditi capaces sunt. Demonstrationes enim, ex naturæ principiis erutæ, plerumque difficiles sunt, ut eas vix eruditi omnes capiant. Deinde Scriptura sacra docet eadem, ratione assentiendi in Deum revelantem; ratio verò eâdem in principia naturæ relatâ. Quantò autem certior est Deus in revelanda veritate, quàm hominis intellectus in eâdem ex naturæ principiis eruenda ac demonstranda, tantò certior est doctrina de Deo ejusque essentia, attributis & cultu, deque vita rectè & voluntati divinæ conformiter instituenda, ex divina revelatione, in Scripturis sacris tradita, quàm quæ ex naturæ principiis ab humana ratione accersitur. Deus enim, qui Veritas est, per suam infinitam cùm scientiam tùm bonitatem in ea revelanda nec falli nec fallere potest. Ratio humana verò in eadem ex naturæ principiis eruenda ac demonstranda, & errare potest, & errat, fallit, aut fallitur sæpiùs, quemadmodùm Gentium Apostolus de Gentilibus refert, quòd, Dei cultum rectum ex naturæ principiis investigaturi, decepti sint suis ἐξαλογισμοῖς, & cùm crederent se esse sapientes, stulti facti sint, proptereà quòd cùm invisibilia Dei, æternam scilicet ejus cùm potentiam tùm divinitatem inde à condito mundo ex rebus factis cognita habuerint, eum tamen non, ut Deum, glorificaverint, sed mutaverint gloriam immortalis Dei per imaginem non solùm ad mortalis hominis similitudinem effictam, verum etiam volatilium & quadrupedum & reptilium, Rom. I. 20. seqq. Tertiò tradit etiam Scriptura hæc omnia perfectius, quàm ratio ex naturæ principiis. Ratio humana enim, pro hoc corrupto naturæ statu, usque adeò obscurata est, ut, fatente ipso Aristotele, Philosopho Gentili, ad ea etiam, quæ naturâ manifestissima omnium sunt, ut vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei se habeat, & sæpè in media veritatis luce cæcutiat, cumprimis in doctrina de Deo rebusque divinis, deque rectitudine ac sanctimonia vitæ. Scriptura sacra autem, ubicunque ratio suis ἐξαλογισμοῖς deficit, & à vero aberrat, supplet illius defectus, & corrigit ejus errores asserendo veritatem oppositam verbis planis ac perspicuis: v. g. Dei unitatem probat quidem ratio recta ex naturæ principiis per demonstrationes, sed ita difficiles, ut illarum vim simpliciores & literarum rudes assequi non possint. Hinc πολυθεΐας opinio in vulgo Gentilium ita olim invaluit, ut

Philosophis doctioribus suam certis naturæ principiis innixam sententiam de unitate Dei in publicum proferre integrum non fuerit. Scriptura sacra verò docet, Deum esse unum, damnatque opinionem de πολυθεῖα ubique locorum, idque verbis ita claris ac perspicuis, ut nemo tam tardus sit ingenio, tamque stupidus, quin primo statim auditu verborum sensum percipiat. Videantur inter alia Deut. IV. 39. c. VI. 3. I. Cor. VIII. 4. 6. Similiter Deum esse essentiam spiritualem, materiæ omnisque potentiæ passivæ expertem & incorruptibilem, ratio recta agnoscit, & demonstrat etiam ex naturæ principiis; sed simpliciores & illiterati illarum etiam demonstrationum vim non capiunt, & propterea, contra ipsum rectæ rationis dictamen, varias res corporeas colunt & adorant. Sed Scriptura sacra docet verbis planis ac perspicuis, Deum esse spiritum, & qui eum adorant, oportere illum spiritu & veritate adorare, rejicitque ac damnat omnem idololatriam, ut inter alia Joh. IV. 24. II. Cor. III, 17. Deut. V. 15. seqq. II. Reg. XVII. 35. seq. legere est. Quàm imperfecta etiam sit cognitio divinorum attributorum, itemque doctrinæ de creatione & providentia, ad quam ratio ex naturæ principiis pertingit, & quàm difficiles sint ejus demonstrationes; & contrà quàm plana, perspicua & perfecta sint, quæ de iisdem Scriptura sacra docet, & quibus admissos rationis errores emendat & corrigit, atque adeò naturalem de hisce rebus cognitionem perficit, ostendi posset ordine per partes singulas, nisi jam antè satis nota essent, & prolixitas nimia nobis obstaret. Quod ad Dei cultum attinet, sive alterutram sive utramque Decalogi tabulam respicias, ratio sibi relicta externos ferè actus virtutum, quibus Deum colere conveniat, præscribit, jubetque oppositos vitiorum actus externos, ne Deus offendatur, vitare: vel si internos etiam dilectionis, fidei, spei, cæterarumque virtutum actus exigat, & præscribat, oppositosque prohibeat, non nisi deliberatos præscribit, indeliberatos verò concupiscentiæ actus & motus in iis habet, quæ hominis saluti nihil obsint. Sola autem Scriptura ad cultum Dei verum & sincerum requirit exactam interiorum & exteriorum actuum & motuum convenientiam cum Lege Dei, & eam virtutum perfectionem, quæ etiam concupicentiæ actus & motus indeliberatos excludat.


### XII. Things which exceed the light of nature, although they cannot be demonstrated…

XII.

Things which exceed the light of nature, although they cannot be demonstrated and known from the principles of nature and reason, yet they cannot be convicted of falsehood from them either. Indeed, most are so constituted that they not only do not oppose the light of nature, but also, when they are known from divine revelation, they can be known to perfect our natural cognition and to supply its defect, with the addition of higher cognition, under the guidance of the light of nature itself.

I. Here also that monster of men, who, having rejected all supernatural revelation, or even having cast off all knowledge of God, are unwilling to admit anything other than the light of nature and the dictate of right reason, we cannot recall to any other first principle of knowing than to right reason, not that we wish these heads of Christian doctrine of a higher order, which exceed the light of nature, to be tested by right reason as if by their norm: for this would be inept and would imply a contradiction in terms; but so that it may be shown to them that they cannot be evidently convicted of falsehood from the principles of right reason, or that, when known from divine revelation, they do not overturn, but perfect, our natural cognition.

II. To illustrate the matter with examples, as far as the first beginning of man and the whole world is concerned, human reason can know and teach from its own light that neither man, nor the world, nor anything, except God, is from itself, but that all things were made by God, and that it is necessary that there be given some subject from which all material things were made, but which itself was not produced from another, but from nothing, or was created: since a progress to infinity is not given. Then, as far as the order of producing the things of which this universe consists is concerned, right reason teaches from its own light that nature begins from simpler things, and from these proceeds to composite ones, begins from more imperfect things, and from these proceeds to more perfect ones. And because among corporeal things the simplest of all are the heaven and the elements, which are the principles and foundations of this universe, it is entirely consistent with right reason that the outermost heaven, by whose circuit all other things are contained, and the elements, from which all other bodies were to be produced mixed among themselves, should have been created first of all. But since among the elements earth is the heaviest of all and dry; and since water is next to this in gravity and is fluid, the nature of the thing itself demands that earth should occupy the lowest place among them, and water the place next to it, and that these two elements should constitute a single globe, as it were, and the center of the whole world. For water, since it is fluid, cannot be contained by its own proper boundaries, but unless it is enclosed within certain spaces and contained by foreign boundaries, the entire mass of waters would diffuse itself over the surface of the earth, and would surround and cover it on all sides. Furthermore, it is necessary that the other two elements, air and fire, occupying the higher spaces by their lightness, should complete the whole machine of the world with these and the heavens, in contiguous order. But because the earth, surrounded and covered on all sides by waters, is neither fit for bringing forth plants nor for sustaining beasts or men, but is utterly sterile, and like an abyss, empty and void, the matter furthermore demanded that the waters should be reduced to their fixed places, within the boundaries of which they would be contained, leaving the earth dry in its other parts, and suitable for bringing forth and sustaining plants and living creatures of all kinds. And it was fitting, with right reason itself as judge, that all these things should be done before plants and living creatures were produced. And because most plants and living creatures can neither exist nor be preserved except in the air, and only when the sun and the other stars, by which they are cherished, exist, it was fitting that the air also should be separated and purged from the admixed watery parts, and that the heavens should be adorned with the sun and stars, again with right reason so judging. And since nature always proceeds from the more imperfect to the more perfect, and among living things brute animals are more perfect than plants, and man than brute animals; and since some living creatures are terrestrial, others aquatic, but all were made and founded for the use of man, it was fitting, according to the guidance of nature and right reason, that among living things, first of all plants, afterwards brute animals, and lastly man should be produced; and that terrestrial ones should be produced on the earth and from the earth, but aquatic ones in the water and from the water, as the predominant element. Thus, I say, and in this order, that the world and all its parts should be produced is entirely consistent with the dictate of nature itself and right reason. But whether it was actually produced by God in this way, or in another manner and order, reason, left to itself, cannot investigate from its own light. For this whole matter depends upon the most free will of God, who, by his infinite wisdom as well as power, could thus, and otherwise, or even simultaneously and in a moment, produce all things; nor can it be known by us from any other source than from God revealing it. Whence the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. XI. 3, rightly says: By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which did appear.

III. When, therefore, Moses wrote down the history of creation from its very beginnings through all parts of the world in order and distinctly, what, I ask, did he say in it that—I will not say conflicts with right reason or can be convicted of falsehood from its principles—but that is not entirely and in every respect agreeable to right reason and its principles? When he records that in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (covered with waters) and the light, which dispelled the darkness by which the entire terrestrial and aqueous globe was surrounded, Gen. I. 1, 2, 3, 4, does he not commemorate the beginning of creation as having been done by God in that manner and order which even right reason itself, from the principles of nature, recognizes and judges to be fitting for the laying of the foundations of the world? For these simple bodies are the very first foundations and principles of the world: the heaven, indeed, the outermost part of the world, encompasses and contains all its other parts; the earth, however, and the waters surrounding the earth, constituted one globe, and the center of the world, and the principles and matter of all mixed bodies to be produced: finally, the light, that is, that luminous body produced on the same day in the heaven, by its rising created the day, and by its setting the night, so that with the very first beginning of the world, time, which is the measure of all created things, might also take its start? All of which, when he says they were made in the beginning, when there was as yet nothing besides God, he signifies were produced from nothing, entirely in accordance with the dictate of right reason.

Furthermore, when he relates that God on the second day divided the upper waters from the lower, by the interposition of an aerial expanse, and condensed the upper waters, like a dense mist diffused through the air, into clouds, v. 6, and on the third day gathered the lower waters by his command and authority into the channels and basins of the earth, so that the remaining parts of the earth might appear dry, and might provide matter for producing plants and living creatures; and might offer a place and dwelling for those produced; in which also plants, herbs, shrubs, and trees of all kinds, with the power of bringing forth seed, and of propagating themselves, he brought forth, v. 9. 10. 11. 12. and on the fourth day adorned the ethereal heaven itself with stars, and brought forth two great luminaries, one to preside over the day, the other over the night, namely the sun and the moon, and the others, fixed and wandering stars, and set them for signs, and seasons, and days, and 15. 16. 17. and on the fifth day indeed brought forth living creatures, both aquatic and flying; the former from the water, the latter from the earth, as the predominant element, v. 20. 21. 22. and finally on the sixth day brought forth terrestrial animals, quadrupeds and reptiles, and at last man, a certain compendium of the world, for whose uses all other things were founded: These things, I say, when Moses commemorates them so orderly and distinctly in the history of creation, what, I ask, does his historical narrative contain that is not entirely consistent with right reason and its principles?

IV. But especially worthy of consideration are those things which Moses commemorates particularly concerning the creation of man. He commemorates, however, first indeed, that God did not create man entirely, as body and soul, material, in the way he made other living creatures, which are entirely material in themselves, consisting of elemental body and soul, drawn forth from the potentiality of matter; but that he produced the body alone from the earth, as the predominant element, but breathed in the breath of life, i.e., the soul, the principle and source of life, as a spiritual substance independent of matter, produced from nothing, and united it to the body to constitute one living suppositum, which would be material on the part of the body, but immaterial or spiritual on the part of the soul, chap. II. 7. Then he commemorates that God created man alone among all living creatures in his own image, and constituted him Lord of the earth and sea, and of all things that are in them, c. I. 27. 28. and indeed made him male and female, the former from the earth; the latter from a rib, taken from the side of the male, and with the conjugal state instituted, joined them into one flesh, both so that they might multiply themselves through carnal generation, and so that one might be a help to the other, to lighten the tedium of life. Although all these things depend on the free will of God, so that they could not be known and committed to writing by Moses from anywhere other than divine revelation, they are nevertheless so constituted that right reason can recognize from its own principles that they are either congruent with the nature of man, or contain nothing repugnant to it. For first, that the soul of man is immaterial, that is, that in its coming to be and in its being it does not depend upon matter, can be known with sufficient probability from the light of nature, and Aristotle in II de Gen. Animal. c. III does not poorly infer this from the operations of the intellect and will, which are clearly immaterial. Whence it was not fitting for the nature of man that he should be produced entirely from the elements, just as other living creatures are, but, according to the very guidance of the light of nature, it was consistent that the body should first be produced from the elements, and afterwards the soul, immaterial by its own nature, independently of matter, and thus produced from nothing, and united to the body. Next, that man alone is endowed with intellect and free will, and is in this like to God, and alone enjoys dominion over other created things, namely over the earth and all things born of the earth, over brute animals, terrestrial, flying, and aquatic, is evident to human reason; and it is entirely consistent with its principles that man was originally created in the image of his creator, and that dominion over all other created things was granted to him by the same. Nor is it repugnant to this that Holy Scripture elsewhere explains the image of God in terms of concreated wisdom and holiness. For it is fitting to a rational nature, and to its connatural state, according to the very dictate of reason, that the faculties of the soul, intellect, will, and sensitive appetite, should possess those powers by which they can rightly and in accordance with the rule of rectitude institute their connatural actions, acknowledge and worship God their creator as is fitting, and conduct their life in conformity with his will: since in this very corrupted state of nature, the education of man, by the guidance of the light of nature itself, tends entirely toward acquiring these same things, as far as possible, through instruction and habit. How, therefore, is it repugnant to the light of nature that Scripture records that the first man was created by God, who is infinitely good and perfect, from whom nothing but what is good and perfect can proceed, with the powers due to his connatural state, namely with wisdom and holiness, by which he is like his creator and bears his image, and thus was created perfect in his connatural state? Nor, finally, does it involve any contradiction that Moses in the history of creation reports that the male, as the more worthy and excellent sex, was created first, and afterwards the female, as the weaker sex, from a rib taken from the side of the man. For it is fitting that this

Latin:

XII.

QVæ lumen naturæ excedunt, ea licet ex naturæ & rationis principiis demonstrari & cognosci non possint, non tamen ex iis etiam falsitatis convinci possunt. Quin pleraque ita comparata sunt, ut non tantùm lumini naturæ non adversari, sed & ubi ex divina revelatione cognita sunt, nostram naturalem cognitionem perficere, ejusque defectum, additâ cognitione altiori, supplere, ipsius luminis naturæ ductu cognosci possit.

I. Hic etiam monstrum illud hominum, qui rejectâ omni revelatione supernaturali, vel etiam Dei notitiâ omni abjectâ, nihil admittere volunt, quàm naturæ lumen & rectæ rationis dictamen, ad aliud principium cognoscendi primum revocare non possumus, quàm ad rectam rationem, non quòd ista altioris ordinis capita doctrinæ Christianæ, quæ lumen naturæ excedunt, ad rectam rationem velut ad illorum normam exigi velimus: hoc enim ineptum esset, & contradictionem in adjecto implicaret; sed ut ex rectæ rationis principiis vel falsitatis evidenter convinci non posse, vel ex divina revelatione cognita nostram naturalem cognitionem non evertere, sed perficere ipsis ostendatur.

II. Ut exemplis rem illustremus, quod ad primum hominis & mundi universi initium attinet, ratio humana ex suo lumine cognoscere & docere potest, neque hominem, neque mundum, neque quicquam, præter Deum, esse à seipso, sed omnia esse à Deo facta, & necesse esse, ut detur aliquod subjectum, ex quo res materiales omnes factæ, ipsum verò non ex alio, sed ex nihilo productum, sive creatum sit: cùm progressus in infinitum non detur. Deinde quod ad ordinem rerum, quibus hoc universum constat, producendarum attinet, docet recta ratio ex suo lumine, naturam incipere à simplicioribus, & ab his progredi ad composita, incipere ab imperfectioribus, & ab his progredi ad perfectiora. Et quia inter res corporeas simplicissimæ omnium sunt cælum & elementa, quæ sunt principia & fundamenta hujus universi, rectæ rationi prorsus consentaneum est, omnium primò condendum fuisse cælum extremum, cujus ambitu cæteræ res omnes continentur, & elementa, ex quibus inter se mixtis cætera corpora omnia erant producenda. Inter elementa verò cùm gravissimum omnium & siccum terra; ab hac verò gravitate proximum & fluidum aqua sit, res ipsa exigit, ut inter ea locum infimum terra, & ab hac proximum aqua obtineat, & duo hæc elementa unum quasi globum & mundi totius centrum constituant. Aqua enim, cùm fluida sit, suis propriis terminis contineri non potest, sed nisi intra certa spacia conclusa terminis alienis contineatur, diffundet se in superficie terræ universa aquarum moles, eamque undique ambiet & teget. Porro cætera duo elementa, aër & ignis, per suam levitatem spacia superiora occupantia, cum his & cælo mundi machinam totam, ordine contiguo, complere necesse est. Quia autem terra, aquis undique circumdata & tecta, neque proferendis plantis, neque sustentandis brutis aut hominibus apta, sed prorsus sterilis, & instar abyssi inanis & vacua est, res præterea exigebat, ut aquæ in sua fixa reducerentur loca, quorum terminis contentæ terram cæteris sui partibus relinquerent siccam, & proferendis ac sustentandis omnium generum plantis atque animantibus idoneam. Atque hæc omnia ita fieri, priusquam producerentur plantæ & animantia, ipsa recta ratione judice, conveniens fuit. Et quia plantæ ac animantia pleraque, nec nisi in aëre, nec nisi sole ac stellis cæteris, quibus foveantur, existentibus, esse & conservari possunt, aërem etiam ab admixtis partibus aqueis separari purgarique, & cælum sole ac stellis exornari conveniebat, rursum ratione recta fic judicante. Et cùm natura semper ab imperfectioribus ad perfectiora procedat, inter viventia verò animalia bruta perfectiora sint plantis, & homo brutis animantibus; & animantium alia terrestria, alia aquatilia, omnia verò ad hominis usum facta & condita sint, conveniebat utique, juxta naturæ ac rectæ rationis ductum, ut inter viventia primò omnium plantæ, postea bruta animantia, & ultimò homo; & terrestria quidem in terra & ex terra; aquatilia verò in aqua & ex aqua, tanquam elemento prædominante, producerentur. Ita, inquam, & hoc ordine mundus ejusque partes omnes ut producerentur, ipsius naturæ & rectæ rationis dictamini prorsus consentaneum est. Utrum autem actu ipso sic à Deo productus fuerit? an modo & ordine alio? ratio sibi relicta, ex suo lumine investigare non potest. Pendet enim hoc totum ex liberrima voluntate Dei, qui pro sua infinita cùm sapientia tùm potentia sic,& aliter, vel etiam simul & in momento omnia producere potuit; nec aliunde, quàm ex Deo revelante, cognosci à nobis potest. Unde meritò Auctor Epistolæ ad Ebræos c. XI. 3. Per fidem, inquit, intelligimus perfecta fuisse secula verbo Dei, ut ex his, quæ non apparebant, ea quæ videntur, fierent.

III. Quando igitur creationis historiam Moses à suis primis initiis per omnes mundi partes ordine & distinctè conscripsit, quid quæso in ea dixit, quod, non dicam, cum recta ratione pugnet, vel ex ejus principiis falsitatis convinci possit, sed quod non rationi rectæ ejusque principiis prorsus & per omnia consentaneum sit? Quando memorat, in principio creâsse Deum cælum & terram, (aquis coopertam) & lucem, tenebras, quibus globus terrestris & aqueus totus circumfusus erat, dispellentem, Gen. I. 1. 2. 3. 4. annon creationis initium eo modo & ordine à Deo factum commemorat, quem jaciendis fundamentis mundi convenire, vel ipsa ratio recta ex naturæ principiis cognoscit & judicat? Hæc enim corpora simplicia sunt ipsa prima mundi fundamenta & principia: cælum quippe, pars mundi extrema, ambit & continet cæteras ejus partes omnes; terra verò & aquæ, terram ambientes, globum unum, & centrum mundi, corporumque mixtorum producendorum omnium principia & materiam constituebant: lux denique, h. e. corpus illud lucidum, die eodem in cælo productum, exortu suo diem; occasu verò noctem conficiebat, quò cum ipso primo mundi exordio etiam tempus, quod rerum creatarum omnium mensura est, suum sumeret initium? Quæ omnia, cùm facta dicit in principio, cùm præter Deum, nondum quicquam esset, ex nihilo producta esse significat, rectæ rationis dictamini prorsus convenienter.

Cum porro refert, Deum die altero divisisse aquas superiores ab inferioribus, interposito expanso aëreo, & condensâsse aquas superiores, instar densæ nebulæ per aërem diffusas, in nubes, v. 6. die tertiô autem congregâsse aquas inferiores jussu ac imperio suo in terræ alveos ac sinus, quò reliquæ terræ partes apparerent aridæ, & plantis ac animantibus producendis materiam; & productis locum ac domicilium præberet; in quibus etiam plantas, herbas, frutices & arbores omnium generum, cum vi proferendi semen, seque propagandi produxerit, v. 9. 10. 11. 12. & die quarto exornasse ipsum cælum æthereum stellis, & produxisse duo luminaria magna, unum, quod diei; alterum quod nocti præesset, solem scilicet & lunam, & cæteras, fixas atque erraticas, stellas, easque constituisse in signa, & tempora, & dies, & annos, & in luminaria ad illuminandum terram, v. 14. 15. 16 17. die quinto verò produxisse animantia, cùm aquatilia, tùm volatilia; illa ex aqua, hæc ex terra, velut elemento prædominante, v. 20. 21. 22. & sexto denique die produxisse animalia terrestria, quadrupeda & reptilia, & tandem hominem, mundi quoddam compendium, ad cujus usus cætera omnia condita sunt: Hæc, inquam, cùm ita ordine & distinctè commemorat Moses in historia creationis, quid, quæso, continet ejus narratio historica, quod non rectæ rationi ejusque principiis prorsus conveniens sit?

IV. Cumprimis verò consideratu digna sunt, quæ de creatione hominis Moses peculiariter commemorat. Commemorat autem, primò quidem, Deum non condidisse hominem totum, quà corpus & animam, materialem, quemadmodum cætera animantia secundum se tota materialia fecit, ex corpore elementari, & anima, ex potentia materiæ eductâ, constantia; sed corpus solum produxisse ex terra, velut elemento prædominante, spiraculum vitæ autem, h. e. animam, vitæ principium & fontem, velut substantiam spiritualem & independentem à materia, ex nihilo productam, inspirâsse & univisse corpori ad constituendum unum suppositum vivens, quod ex parte corporis materiale: ex parte animæ verò immateriale sive spirituale esset, cap. II. 7. Deinde commemorat, Deum condidisse inter omnia animantia hominem solum ad imaginem suam, & constituisse eum terræ ac maris, &, quæ in iis sunt, rerum omnium Dominum, c. I. 27. 28. & fecisse quidem eum masculum & fœminam, illum ex terra; hanc è costa, ex latere masculi desumta, & conjugali statu instituto, junxisse eos in unam carnem, cùm ut per carnalem generationem sese multiplicarent, tum ut alter alteri esset adjumento, ad levanda vitæ tædia. Quæ licet omnia ex libera Dei voluntate dependeant, ut aliunde, quàm ex revelatione divina, à Mose cognosci & in literas referri non potuerint, sunt tamen ita comparata, ut vel naturæ hominis congrua esse, vel nihil ei repugnans continere, ratio recta ex suis principiis cognoscere possit. Primùm enim animam hominis esse immaterialem, hoc est, in fieri & esse à materia non dependere, ex lumine naturæ satis probabiliter cognosci potest, idque Aristoteles II. de Gen. Animal. c. III. non malè colligit ex operationibus intellectus ac voluntatis planè immaterialibus. Unde naturæ hominis non congruebat, ut perinde, ac cætera animantia, ex elementis tota produceretur, sed, juxta ipsum luminis naturæ ductum, consentaneum erat, ut corpus prius ex elementis, posteà verô anima, suâ naturâ immaterialis, independenter à materia, atque adeò ex nihilo produceretur, & corpori uniretur. Deinde hominem solum esse intellectu ac voluntate liberâ præditum, Deoque in hoc similem, & solum gaudere dominio in res creatas alias, in terram scilicet, & omnia terrâ nascentia, in bruta animantia, terrestria, volatilia & aquatilia, evidens humanæ rationi; & ejus principiis prorsus consentaneum est, hominem primitùs conditum esse ad imaginem sui conditoris, & ab eodem dominium in res alias creatas omnes ipsi concessum. Neque ei repugnat, quòd imaginem Dei Scriptura sacra alibi locorum de concreata sapientia & sanctitate exponit. Conveniens enim est naturæ rationali, ejusque connaturali statui, juxta ipsum rationis dictamen, ut facultates animæ, intellectus, voluntas & appetitus sensitivus iis polleant viribus, quibus suas connaturales actiones ritè & regulæ rectitudinis convenienter instituere, Deum creatorem suum, ut oportet, agnoscere ac colere, vitamque suam ejus voluntati conformiter peragere possit: cùm in hoc ipso corrupto naturæ statu hominis educatio, ipsius luminis naturæ ductu, ad easdem, per informationem & assuetudinem, quoad fieri potest, acquirendas tota tendat. Quî ergo lumini naturæ repugnet, quòd hominem primum à Deo infinitè bono & perfecto, à quo non nisi bonum & perfectum provenire potest, cum viribus, suo connaturali statui debitis, cum sapientia scilicet & sanctitate, quâ suo creatori similis sit, ejusque imaginem gerat, atque adeò in suo connaturali statu perfectum conditum Scriptura commemorat? Nec denique ullam involvit repugnantiam, quòd marem, tanquam sexum digniorem & præstantiorem, priùs, & posteà fœminam, velut sexum infirmiorem, ex costa, de latere Viri desumta, conditam Moses in creationis historia refert. Convenire enim hanc


### That the man should have the prerogative, as being produced before the woman,…

That the man should have the prerogative, as being produced before the woman, on account of the greater perfection in which he excels; but that the woman should be produced from the flesh of the man, on account of their mutual inclination toward one another, and the most intimate conjunction into one flesh which ought to exist between spouses, is again clearly agreeable to the light of nature.

V. If we proceed from the primeval state of man, described by Moses in the history of creation, further to the state of corruption and sin, delineated by the same after the history of creation, it will be easily shown that nothing is contained in this either which involves any contradiction. For he who recalls to mind from the histories of any peoples and nations whatsoever that demons formerly spoke through idols and gave responses, will not consider it among the absurd or impossible that the serpent is said, Gen. 3:1 et seqq., to have spoken with the woman who was created, and to have seduced her, as the weaker sex, so that she might eat of the forbidden fruit of the tree. Nor is it foreign to right reason that Scripture records that it happened by the just judgment of God that, as a punishment for the transgression of the divine law and the sin committed, man fell from his primeval happiness, and, stripped of the wisdom and holiness created with him, began immediately to notice in himself the inordinate and shameful motions of concupiscence, to procreate children not in the image of God, which he had lost, but in his own image, which was deformed to too great a degree, and to be subjected to death and manifold calamities. For it is evident from the very light of nature that God is just and a severe avenger of crimes, and is also supremely good, and cannot be the cause of the corruption and sin that by nature exerts itself assiduously in every man, so that, according to the very dictate of right reason, it is entirely agreeable to the truth that this is the primary origin of our corruption, which Holy Scripture commemorates in the history of the fall: so far is it from being the case that it is repugnant to the dictate of right reason.

VI. If we cast the eyes of our mind to those things which concern the ultimate end of man, we find that not even regarding these is anything handed down in the Holy Scriptures which can be convicted of falsehood from the principles of nature and reason; but rather, we discover that these things also are so constituted that, where they are known from divine revelation, they do not destroy our natural knowledge concerning the ultimate end of man, but can be known to perfect it remarkably under the guidance of the light of nature itself.

Right reason can know from its own light sufficiently probably, (1) that the soul of man does not perish with the body, but remains surviving after death, and consequently that after this life there will be another, in which it will go well for the good and ill for the wicked, according as they have lived well or ill in this life. (2) That the blessedness of the soul after this life will consist in its operation concerning God, namely in the knowledge and love of God, as was shown above in part I, chapter II, thesis IX, explanation number IX. But what kind of knowledge of the soul will there be, by which it will enjoy God, abstractive? or intuitive? and whether the soul is to live forever without a body? or whether it is to be reunited to a body at some time, and to what body? the reason of man in this mortality cannot attain from its own light. But when Scripture reveals that God will at some time resurrect the bodies of the dead from the dead, and will unite them with the surviving souls, and will place the good and the wicked before the tribunal of the judge, Christ, so that retribution may be made to each according to his deeds, whether good or evil, II Cor. V. 10; that Christ the judge will condemn the impious to eternal fire, but will adjudge eternal life to the good who have departed from this life with God propitious, Matt. XXV. 32, 34, 41; and that eternal life will consist in the vision of God, or in a clear and intuitive knowledge of Him, Matt. V. 8, I Cor. XIII. 12; and that the bodies of the blessed will be glorified and rendered incorruptible and spiritual, I Cor. XV. 42, 43, 44; and thus conformed to the glorious body of Christ, Phil. III. 21. When, I say, Holy Scripture reveals these things in this way, what, I ask, is there in them that right reason from its own light could judge to be inconsistent either with the future perfection and happiness of the pious, or with the unhappiness and misery of the impious? For since God, according to the very dictate of right reason, is just and good, the avenger of crimes and the rewarder of the good, and yet does not always avenge crimes and reward good deeds in this life, according to the same dictate it is also consistent with divine justice that after this life at last that universal judgment should be held, by which to all men in general, what each has done in this life, whether good or evil, may be attributed. And because not the soul alone has done good or evil in this life, but the whole man, consisting of soul and body, it is consistent with divine justice that each one should perceive and feel the retribution, not in the soul alone, but in the body also, in proportion to his deeds, whether good or evil, and thus it is not contrary to the dictates of right reason that the bodies of the dead will be resurrected from the dead by divine power, as the Holy Scriptures so often repeat and inculcate. But with what rewards the supreme judge will one day deem the good worthy, and with what punishments he will afflict the wicked, is placed in his own most free will, which therefore can be known from nowhere else than from divine revelation. When, therefore, the Holy Scriptures reveal this mystery to us, and testify that God will avenge the crimes of the impious in their body and soul with eternal fire; but the good deeds of the pious, as to the body, with distinguished gifts of clarity, incorruptibility, spirituality, etc. but as to the soul, that he will reward them for all eternity with the light of glory, by which their intellect may be elevated to a clear or intuitive knowledge of himself, why should reason judge this revelation contrary to the light of nature or incredible, and not rather as something higher, which cannot be reached by its own natural light, and which perfects, rather than destroys, its natural knowledge, which it has concerning the ultimate end of man? But if you say that bodies numerically the same, which have been resolved into ashes, cannot be resurrected; or that the intellect of man cannot be elevated to know God clearly and intuitively, you are so far from being able to evidently prove and demonstrate with invincible reason that either or both must be held among impossibilities, that you are rather forced to confess that the limits of the infinite power of God cannot be set by the intellect of man, which is blind even to those things which are most manifest of all to nature, as the eyes of bats are to the light of day, and that it cannot be determined what can or cannot be done by it, but rather that it is credible that the future retributions of the good and the evil, which we cannot investigate according to their specific nature by the guidance of the light of nature, will be exactly as the Scriptures teach, and that God, by his omnipotence, to whom nothing is impossible, can actually do, and will certainly do, those things which they predict he will do. For why should we doubt that by divine omnipotence, by which heaven and earth and whatever is in them were produced from nothing, the dead bodies of men, turned into ashes, can also be reproduced and reunited with their still surviving souls? Why should we doubt that by divine omnipotence, by which the soul of man was produced from nothing and instructed with the natural light in which it excels, the same can be instructed with a more perfect light, and be elevated to know God himself, as he is in himself, clearly? VI. As regards the means of eternal salvation, to be obtained by the gift of God, and of avoiding eternal damnation, it is naturally known that one does not reach eternal life, nor escape eternal damnation, unless one is a worshipper of God; but that those whom He Himself deigns to favor with His grace, and to whose infirmities He succors with His aid, are the only ones who can perform the worship owed to God. Since the Holy Scriptures promise these aids of grace everywhere, they again promise nothing that could seem contrary to human reason or incredible, but rather they promise that which, according to its own dictates, is absolutely necessary for man to exhibit worship worthy of God. And because it is likewise known from the light of nature that all men are sinners; that God is just and a severe avenger of crimes, and that no one can obtain eternal life by His gift unless he is led by repentance for his sins and reconciled to God, who has been offended by sins; furthermore, on the part of the means of obtaining eternal life from God, it must first of all be known by what means a sinful man can and ought to be reconciled to God, who has been offended by sins: whether repentance, accepted in place of contrition or sorrow for sins committed, suffices for this? Or whether, besides it, satisfaction for sins committed is required? And what satisfaction is necessary and sufficient? That, indeed, can neither be investigated by the guidance of the light of nature, nor learned from anywhere else than from God Himself revealing it. For if it be posited that God can, with His justice preserved, forgive sins to sinners out of mere liberality and grace, without intervening satisfaction—which many among the ancient Fathers and modern Scholastics affirm—it is nevertheless placed in the most free will of God whether He wills to forgive the penitent his sins out of mere liberality and grace, or whether He wills to remit them only upon the intervention of satisfaction, and that performed either by the sinner himself or by another mediator and sponsor on his behalf. When the Holy Scriptures teach this, namely that for obtaining the remission of sins and reconciliation with God it was necessary to have a Mediator between God, offended by sins, and sinful men, who by His passion and death would appease the wrath of God, and that it is required on the part of the sinful man that, led by serious repentance for his sins, he should turn himself to God with faith in that Mediator and His satisfaction, and present that to Him as satisfaction performed for himself and as a λύτρον for his sins; and that this Mediator is the one and only CHRIST, the Son of God and Mary, God and man in one undivided person, again, as to the manner of reconciling sinful man with God who has been offended, they teach nothing that is repugnant to the light of nature, or that could seem incredible to natural reason, but that a Mediator between God offended by sins and sinful man is required, if reconciliation is to be made between them, is rather agreeable to the light of nature. Although, however, that this Mediator, the Son of God and man, is God and man in one undivided person, is the highest mystery of all, and reason cannot attain to it by its own thought, yet it cannot be solidly convicted of falsehood by the same. Whence it is rather to be judged credible that the revelation of this doctrine also, just like other revelations concerning things subject to the light of nature, is in every way true, proceeded from God, and is truly divine.

VII. Furthermore, what the Holy Scriptures teach concerning the justification of sinful man through faith in Christ, concerning his regeneration through Baptism and the Word, and concerning his renewal, are all such things as reason can easily attain by its own light to be possible through the grace and operation of God, nor does any evident and cogent reason appear why, in leading sinful man to eternal blessedness, it should be denied or judged incredible that God, for His immense grace and mercy, will perform and does perform these works thus, as the Scriptures teach. There remains one and only the dogma of the Trinity of persons in one undivided divine essence, which, although it far exceeds the grasp of human reason, yet if all other things which Scripture contains are, if not entirely agreeable to human reason, at least not adverse to it, nor incredible, why should we hold this one dogma, so often inculcated and handed down in the Holy Scriptures and in such clear words, among the impossible or incredible? Especially since human reason cannot deny that God cannot be comprehended or perfectly known by it in this mortality. Why, therefore, should we deny faith to the Scriptures, which so often assert that God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and yet that God is one? Since in all other things it is evident that they either speak the truth, or at least cannot be convicted of falsehood.

Latin:

Viro prærogativam, ut priùs, quàm mulier, produceretur, ob majorem, quâ pollet, perfectionem; fœminæ verò, ut ex carne viri produceretur, ob mutuam in invicem propensionem, &, quæ inter conjuges esse debet, conjunctionem arctissimam in carnem unam, naturæ lumini rursum planè consentaneum est.

V. Si à statu hominis primævo, in historia creationis à Mose descripto, longiùs ad statum corruptionis & peccati, post creationis historian ab eodé delineatum, progrediamur, in hoc etiam, quod ullam involvat repugnantiam, nihil contineri facilè ostendetur. Quod enim Gen. III. 1. seqq. serpens cum muliere condita collocutus esse, eamque, tanquam sexum infirmiorem, seduxisse fertur, ut de vetito fructu arboris comederet, in absurdis aut impossibilibus non habebit, qui ex historiis quorumvis populorum ac gentium memoriâ secum repetierit, Dæmones olim per idola locutos esse, & responsa dedisse. Neque à recta ratione alienum est, quòd memorat Scriptura, Dei justo judicio contigisse, ut in pœnam transgressionis legis divinæ & patrati peccati suâ primævâ felicitate homo excideret, & concreatâ sibi sapientiâ & sanctitate exutus, statim concupiscentiæ inordinatos ac pudendos motus in se animadvertere, liberos non ad imaginem Dei, quàm perdiderat, sed ad suam nimium quantum deformatam imaginem procreare, mortiq; ac multiplicibus calamitatibus subjici inciperet. Constat enim ex ipso lumine naturæ, Deum esse justum & scelerum vindicem severum, & esse etiam summè bonum, qui corruptionis & peccati, naturâ in homine quovis se assiduè exerentis, causa esse non possit, ut, juxta ipsum rectæ rationis dictamen, vero prorsus consentaneum sit, hanc esse corruptionis nostræ primam originem, quam Scriptura sacra in historia lapsus commemorat: tantùm abest, ut rectæ rationis dictamini id repugnet.

VI. Si ad ea, quæ hominis finem ultimum concernunt, conjiciamus oculos mentis, ne de his quidem quicquam in Scripturis sacris traditum invenimus, quod ex principiis naturæ ac rationis falsitatis convinci possit, quin contra potiùs hæc etiam sic deprehendimus comparata esse, ut ubi ex divina revelatione cognita sunt, nostram naturalem de hominis fine ultimo notitiam non destruere, sed egregiè perficere ipsius luminis naturæ ductu cognosci possit.

Cognoscere potest recta ratio ex suo lumine satis probabiliter, (1) animam hominis non interire cum corpore, sed post mortem manere superstitem, & proinde post hanc vitam futuram esse aliam, in qua bonis benè; malis malè futurum sit, prout in hac vita benè vel malè vixerint. (2) Beatitudinem animæ post hanc vitam constituram in ejus operatione circa Deum, nempe in cognitione ac amore Dei, ut supra in part. I. cap. II. th. IX. Expl. n. IX. ostensum. Qualis autem futura sit cognitio animæ, quâ Deo fruitura sit, abstractiva? an intuitiva? & utrum in perpetuum anima absque corpore victura? an verò corpori aliquando, & cui corpori redunienda sit? ex suo lumine ratio hominis in hac mortalitate assequi non potest? Quando autem Scriptura revelat, corpora demortuorum Deum aliquando ex mortuis resuscitaturum, & cum animabus superstitibus uniturum, eum bonos ac malos coram tribunali constituti à se judicis, Christi, stiturum, ut retribuatur unicuique juxta facta sua, sive bona sive mala, II. Cor. V. 10. judicem Christum dam naturum impios ad ignem æternum, bonis verò, qui Deo propitio ex hac vita decesserint, adjudicaturum vitam æternam, Matth. XXV. 32. 34. 41. & vitam æternam constituram in visione Dei, sive in clara & intuitiva ejus cognitione, Matth. V. 8. I. Cor. XIII. 12. corpora verò beatorum glorificatum & redditum iri incorruptibilia & spiritualia, I. Cor. XV. 42. 43. 44. atque adeò conformia corpori Christi glorioso, Phil. III. 21. Quando, inquam, Scriptura sacra hæc ita revelat, quid, quæso in iis est, quod vel futuræ piorum perfectioni ac felicitati; vel impiorum infelicitati ac miseriæ disconveniens ratio recta ex suo lumine judicare possit? Cùm enim Deus, juxta ipsum rectæ rationis dictamen, justus & bonus, scelerum vindex, & bonorum remunerator sit, neque tamen in hac vita semper vindicet scelera, & remuneretur benefacta, juxta ejusdem dictamen etiam consentaneum est justitiæ divinæ, ut post hanc demum vitam habeatur universale illud judicium, quo omnibus in universum hominibus, quod quisque in hac vita egit, sive bonum, sive malum tribuatur. Et quia non anima sola in hac vita, bona vel mala egit, sed totus, anima & corpore constans, homo, consentaneum est justitiæ divinæ, ut non in sola animâ, sed in corpore quoque percipiat & sentiat retributionem, quisque pro ratione suorum factorum, sive bonorum, sive malorum, & sic rectæ rationis dictamini adversum non est, quod corpora demortuorum ex mortuis divina potentia resuscitatum iri, Scripturæ sacræ toties ingeminant & inculcant. Quibus autem præmiis judex supremus bonos aliquando dignaturus, & quibus pœnis improbos afflicturus sit, in ipsius liberrima voluntate positum est, quod proinde non aliunde, quam ex divina revelatione, cognosci potest. Quando ergo Scripturæ sacræ hoc arcanum nobis revelant, testanturque, Deum vindicaturum impiorum scelera in illorum corpore & anima igni æterno; piorum vero benefacta, qua corpus, insignibus dotibus claritatis, incorruptibilitatis, spiritualitatis &c. qua animam autem lumine gloriæ, quo illorum intellectus ad claram sive intuitivam sui cognitionem elevetur, in omnem æternitatem remuneraturum, cur revelationem hanc lumini naturæ contrariam aut incredibilem judicet ratio, non vero altiorem potius, quam suo naturali lumine attingi possit, & quæ perficiat, non destruat suam notitiam naturalem, quam de fine hominis ultimo habet? Quod si dicas, corpora numero eadem, quæ in cineres resoluta sunt, resuscitari; vel intellectum hominis ad Deum clare & intuitive cognoscendum elevari non posse, tantum abest, ut ratione invicta alterutrum vel utrumque in impossibilibus habendum esse, evidenter probare & demonstrare possis, ut potius fateri cogaris, potentiæ Dei infinitæ limites ab hominis intellectu, etiam ad ea, quæ naturæ manifestissima omnium sunt, ut oculi vespertilionum ad lumen diei, cæcutiente, constitui, & quæ per eam fieri aut non fieri possint, determinari non posse, sed credibile potius esse, bonorum ac malorum futuras retributiones, quas secundum suam rationem specificam ductu naturæ luminis investigare non possumus, prorsus ita, ut Scripturæ docent, se habituras, Deumque sua omnipotentia, cui nihil est impossibile, reapse facere posse, & certo facturum esse, quæ eundem facturum illæ prædicunt. Cur enim dubitemus, divina omnipotentia, qua cœlum & terra & quæcunque in illis sunt, ex nihilo producta sunt, posse etiam hominum demortua & in cineres versa corpora reproduci & cum animabus adhuc superstitibus rursum uniri? cur dubitemus, divina omnipotentia, qua ex nihilo producta, & eo, quo pollet, naturali lumine instructa est anima hominis, posse eandem perfectiori instrui lumine, & ad ipsummet Deum, ut in se est, clare cognoscendum elevari? VI. Quod ad media salutis æternæ, Dei dono consequendæ, & damnationis æternæ evitandæ attinet, naturaliter notum est, ad vitam æternam non pertingere, neque damnationem æternam evadere, nisi cultores Dei; cultum verò, Deo debitum, præstare non posse, nisi quos ipse gratiâ suâ dignatur, & quorum infirmitatibus suâ ope succurrit. Quæ gratiæ auxilia cùm passim promittunt Scripturæ sacræ, rursum nihil promittunt, quod humanæ rationi adversum aut incredibile videri possit, sed id potius promittunt, quod, juxta ejusdem dictamen, homini ad cultum, Deo dignum, exhibendum prorsus necessarium est. Et quia homines omnes peccatores; Deum verò justum scelerumque vindicem severum esse, nec quenquam ejus dono vitam æternam consequi posse, nisi peccatorum pœnitentiâ ductum, Deoque peccatis offenso, reconciliatum, itidem ex lumine naturæ notum est; porrò ex parte mediorum consequendæ à Deo vitæ æternæ primò omnium cognitum esse oportet, quo medio homo peccator Deo, peccatis offenso, reconciliari possit, & debeat: an ad hoc sufficiat pœnitentia, pro contritione, sive dolore de peccatis admissis accepta? an, præter eam, requiratur satisfactio pro peccatis admissis? & quænam satisfactio necessaria sit & sufficiat? id verò nec ductu luminis naturæ investigari, nec aliunde, quàm ex ipso Deo revelante, addisci potest. Si enim ponatur, Deum posse, suâ justitiâ salvâ, peccata peccatoribus ex mera liberalitate & gratiâ, absque interveniente satisfactione, condonare: quod ex Patribus priscis & Scholasticis modernis multi affirmant; in Dei tamen liberrima voluntate positum est, velitne pœnitenti peccata sua ex mera liberalitate & gratiâ? an verò interveniente satisfactione demum, eâque vel à peccatore ipso, vel ab alio mediatore ac sponsore pro ipso præstitâ, remittere? Quod quando Scripturæ sacræ docent, nempe ad impetrandam peccatorum remissionem & reconciliationem cum Deo necessarium fuisse Mediatorem inter Deum, peccatis offensum, & homines peccatores, qui suâ passione ac morte iram Dei placaret, & ex parte hominis peccatoris requiri, ut pœnitentiâ peccatorum seriâ ductus, fide in Mediatorem illum ejusque satisfactionem ad Deum se convertat, eamque ipsi velut satisfactionem pro se præstitam & tanquam λύτρον pro peccatis suis sistat; huncque Mediatorem esse unum & solum CHRISTUM, Dei & Mariæ filium, Deum & hominem in una indivisa persona, rursum ea, quantum ad modum reconciliandi hominis peccatoris cum Deo offenso, nihil docent, quod lumini naturæ repugnet, aut rationi naturali incredibile videri possit, sed Mediatorem inter Deum peccatis offensum, & hominem peccatorem requiri, si reconciliatio inter eos fieri debeat, lumini naturæ potiùs consentaneum est. Quamvis verò Mediatorem hunc Dei & hominis filium, Deum & hominem esse in una indivisa persona, mysterium omnium summum sit, idque ratio suâ cogitatione adsequi non possit, non tamen falsitatis id ab eadem solidè convinci potest. Unde credibile potius judicandum est, hujus etiam doctrinæ revelationem, perinde ut alias de rebus, naturæ lumini subjectis, revelationes, undiquaque veram, à Deo profectam, veréque divinam esse.

VII. Quæ porro de justificatione hominis peccatoris per fidem in Christum, de ejus regeneratione per Baptismum & Verbum, déque ejusdem renovatione docent Scripturæ sacræ, omnia talia sunt, quæ Dei gratiâ & operatione fieri posse, ratio ex suo lumine facilè assequi potest, neque ulla apparet evidens & cogens ratio, cur in homine peccatore ad beatitudinem æternam perducendo, Deum pro sua immensâ gratiâ & misericordiâ opera hæc sic, ut Scripturæ docent, peracturum & peragere, negetur, aut incredibile judicetur. Superest unum & solum dogma Trinitatis personarum in una indivisa essentia divina, quod quamvis humanæ rationis captum longissimè excedat, tamen si cætera omnia, quæ Scriptura continet, humanæ rationi si non consentanea prorsus, non tamen adversa, nec incredibilia sint, cur hoc unum, in Scripturis sacris toties, verbisque tam perspicuis inculcatum & traditum dogma in impossibilibus aut incredibilibus habeamus? præsertim cùm humana ratio diffiteri non possit, Deum non posse in hac mortalitate à se comprehendi aut perfectè cognosci. Cur ergo Scripturæ, Deum Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum; & tamen Deum unum esse, toties asseveranti, denegemus fidem? cùm in cæteris omnibus eam vel vera dicere, vel falsitatis saltem convinci non posse, evidens sit.


### XIII. For the diversity of the parts of Christian doctrine, handed down in the Holy…

XIII.

For the diversity of the parts of Christian doctrine, handed down in the Holy Scriptures, some of which from the light of nature insofar as they can be known, and are handed down in the Holy Scriptures in a manner in every way consistent with right reason, or even more perfectly than they can be known through it in this corrupt state of nature; others fall under the light of nature according to a certain generic reason, but exceed it according to their specific reason, yet when known from divine revelation they remarkably perfect our confused knowledge which we have of them from the light of nature; finally, some simply exceed the light of nature, yet are commended to us as mysteries, revealed by God for our salvation: to establish the truth of Holy Scripture, pure from all error, various arguments can be constructed.

XIV.

That which is derived from the parts of doctrine established in the first class can be this: Whatever Scripture hands down those parts of Christian doctrine which can in some way be known from the light of nature, in a manner in every way consistent with right reason, or even more perfectly than they can be known through it for this corrupt state of nature, it hands down in the other parts of Christian doctrine also, which exceed the light of nature, and indeed simply in all other objects and things, truth, pure from all error. But Holy Scripture does hand down those parts of Christian doctrine which can in some way be known from the light of nature, in a manner in every way consistent with right reason, or even more perfectly than they can be known through it for this corrupt state of nature. Therefore Holy Scripture hands down in the other parts of Christian doctrine also, and indeed simply in all other objects and things, truth, pure from all error.

I. The minor proposition receives light from the preceding thesis XI. Expl. n. II. & III. and remains unshaken, until the contrary is evidently demonstrated, and it is solidly proven, that Holy Scripture contradicts right reason in any part of doctrine pertaining to this class.

Christian, namely concerning God, or His essence, attributes, providence, or worship, or concerning human life, to be ordered in conformity with the divine will, or to err in delivering a more perfect knowledge of anything than can be had by the guidance of the light of nature alone. None of which will the present-day contemners and calumniators of the Holy Scriptures, or anyone else, ever prove.

II. But as regards the confirmation of the major proposition, he who has thoroughly pondered with himself the innate blindness of our intellect in relation to these doctrines will not deny that from the truth of Scripture without admixture of error in the enumerated parts of Christian doctrine, one may rightly conclude to the truth of the same without admixture of error in the other parts of doctrine as well, indeed in all other objects and things. For although it is not entirely devoid of light for knowing them, that light is nevertheless so meager and weak for this corrupt state of nature that it penetrates into their truth with great difficulty, by its own power at least. Nor, however, does it ever penetrate into it so perfectly that it does not from time to time stumble, strike against obstacles, and wander from the truth; which the examples of all peoples and nations testify more than enough, whose common folk and wise men alike have at all times embraced various, and those gross and foul, errors concerning God, His attributes, providence, and worship, nor has anyone been found up to this time who, by the guidance of the light of nature alone, delivered the truth concerning them in all things without admixture of error. Moreover, to deliver those doctrines more perfectly than they can be known by the guidance of the light of nature alone in this corrupt state of nature is above the powers and condition of the human intellect. Whence if any Scripture in these parts of Christian doctrine, which can in some way be reached from the light of nature, but cannot be investigated and known perfectly and without any error by its guidance alone, delivers the truth without any error mixed in, and indeed more perfectly than can be known from the light of nature for this corrupt state of nature, it is certainly a consequence that it was not composed in these parts at least by mere human effort and the guidance of the light of nature alone, but by God, illuminating the intellect of the writer with supernatural light and suggesting what things were to be written: since an effect cannot exceed its cause in perfection, and if a greater perfection shines forth in any Scripture than could proceed from a mere man, it must be confessed entirely that it has some higher cause than mere man, namely God himself. If, however, in these parts of doctrine some Scripture has God as its author, not mere man, why not also in the other parts, which exceed the light of nature; nay, in the other objects and all things as well? Especially if the Writer himself refers his Scripture to God as Author, not only in these, but in the other parts of doctrine and all objects also, as the sacred writers constantly do, especially Paul, who testifies that the whole of sacred Scripture is θεόπνευστον, II Tim. III. 16. For besides the fact that there was a greater reason why those things which exceed the grasp of human reason, yet are of interest to our salvation to know, should be suggested to the writer supernaturally by God, rather than those which can also be known in some way from the light of nature: for in knowing the latter the intellect still has a little light remaining, but in the former none at all; nor can any reason be given why we should grant credence in part to a writer who refers his whole Scripture to God as Author, but deny it in part; why we should believe that it was composed by God's suggestion and is free from falsehood in those parts whose contained matters do not exceed the light of nature; but assert that in the other parts, whose underlying matters exceed the light of nature by their loftiness, it was composed by purely human effort and is erroneous: especially if those more sublime heads of doctrine cannot be evidently convicted of falsehood.

Latin:

XIII.

PRo diversitate partium doctrinæ Christianæ, in Scripturis sacris traditæ, quarum quædam ex lumine naturæ quodammodo cognosci possunt, & in Scripturis sacris rectae rationi per omnia convenienter, vel etiam perfectius, quam in hoc naturae statu corrupto per eam cognosci possunt, traduntur; aliae cadunt sub lumen naturae secundum rationem quandam genericam, excedunt vero illud secundum suam rationem specificam, ex divina tamen revelatione cognita nostram confusam, quam ex lumine naturae de illis habemus, cognitionem insigniter perficiunt; nonnulla denique lumen naturae simpliciter excedunt, commendantur tamen nobis ut mysteria, a Deo ad salutem nostram revelata: ad adstruendam Scripturae sacrae veritatem, ab omni errore puram, diversa extrui possunt argumenta.

XIV.

QVod a partibus doctrinae, in prima classe constitutae, desumitur, potest esse hoc: Quaecunque Scriptura eas doctrinae Christianae partes, quae ex lumine naturae quodammodo cognosci possunt, rectae rationi per omnia convenienter, vel etiam perfectius, quam pro hoc corrupto naturae statu per eam cognosci possunt, tradit, ea tradit in caeteris etiam doctrinae Christianae partibus, quae lumen naturae excedunt, imo simpliciter in caeteris objectis & rebus omnibus veritatem, ab omni errore puram. Atqui Scriptura sacra tradit eas doctrinae Christianae partes, quae ex lumine naturae quodammodo cognosci possunt, rectae rationi per omnia convenienter, vel etiam perfectius, quam pro hoc corrupto naturae statu per eam cognosci possunt. Ergo Scriptura sacra tradit in caeteris etiam doctrinae Christianae partibus, imo simpliciter in caeteris objectis & rebus omnibus veritatem, ab omni errore puram.

I. Minor propositio lucem sortitur ex praeced. th. XI. Expl. n. II. & III. & perstat inconcussa, usque dum contrarium evidenter demonstretur, evincaturque solide, Scripturam sacram contradicere rectae rationi in aliqua ad hanc classem pertinente parte doctrinae

Christianæ, de Deo scilicet, ejusve essentiâ, attributis, providentia, aut cultu, vel de vita humana, divinæ voluntati conformiter instituenda, vel errare in tradenda alicujus perfectiori cognitione, quàm ductu solius luminis naturæ haberi possit. Quorum nihil vel hodierni Scripturarum sacrarum contemptores & calumniatores, vel quisquam alius unquam evincet.

II. Ad majoris propositionis confirmationem verò quod attinet, à veritate Scripturæ absque admixto errore in enumeratis doctrinæ Christianæ partibus ad veritatem ejusdem absque admixto errore in cæteris quoque doctrinæ partibus, imò in cæteris objectis & rebus omnibus, rectè concludi, non inficiabitur, qui connatam intellectus nostri cæcitatem in ordine ad doctrinas hasce penitiùs secum expenderit. Quamvis enim is non planè nullo ad illas cognoscendas lumine polleat, illud tamen pro hoc corrupto naturæ statu ita exiguum & debile est, ut difficulter admodùm, ejus quidem vi, in illorum veritatem penetret.
