Neq; tamen unquam ita perfectè in illam penetrat, quin subinde titubet, impingat & à vero aberret; quod omnium populorum & Gentium exempla plus satis testantur, quorum & vulgus & sapientes omni tempore varios, eosque crassos & fœdos errores de Deo, ejus attributis, providentiâ & cultu amplexi sunt, nec huc usq; quisquam inventus est, qui solius luminis naturæ ductu per omnia veritatem absque admixto errore de illis traderet. Perfectiùs autem doctrinas illas tradere, quàm ductu solius luminis naturæ in hoc corrupto naturæ statu cognosci possunt, supra humani intellectus vires & conditionem est. Unde si qua Scriptura in his doctrinæ Christianæ partibus, quæ ex lumine naturæ quodammodo attingi, perfectè autem & absque omni errore illius solius ductu investigari & cognosci non possunt, veritatem absque ullo errore admixto, & perfectiùs quidem, quàm pro hoc corrupto naturæ statu ex lumine naturæ cognosci potest, tradat, consequens utique est, eam his minimùm partibus non esse studio merè humano & solius luminis naturæ ductu, sed Deo, Scriptoris intellectum lumine supernaturali collustrante, & quæ scribenda essent, suggerente, concinnatam: cùm effectus causam suam perfectione excedere non possit, & si in Scriptura aliqua major reluceat perfectio, quàm à mero homine provenire possit, fatendum omninò est, eam habere causam aliquam altiorem, quàm hominem merum, nempe ipsummet Deum. Si autem in his doctrinæ partibus Scriptura aliqua Deum auctorem habeat, non hominem merum, quidnî etiam in partibus cæteris, quæ lumen naturæ excedunt; imò in cæteris etiam objectis & rebus omnibus? præsertim si Scriptor ipse non modò in his, sed in cæteris quoque partibus doctrinæ objectisque omnibus Scripturam suam in Deum Auctorem referat, ut Scriptores sacri constanter faciunt, cumprimis Paulus, qui Scripturam sacram totam θεόπνευστον esse testatur II.Tim.III. 16. Præterquam enim quod major erat ratio, cur ea potiùs, quæ humanæ rationis captum excedunt, nosse tamen nostræ salutis interest, quàm quæ ex lumine naturæ etiam quodammodo cognosci possunt, Scriptori à Deo supernaturaliter suggererentur: in his enim cognoscendis habet intellectus pauxillum lucis adhuc reliqvum, in illis verò nihil; nulla etiam reddi potest ratio, cur Scriptori, Scripturam suam totam in Deum Auctorem referenti, fidem ex parte adhibeamus, ex parte autem denegemus; cur credamus, eam iis partibus, quarum res contentæ lumen naturæ non excedunt, Deo suggerente confignatam falsitatisque expertem esse; cæteris verò partibus, quarum res substratæ altitudine sua lumen naturæ excedunt, studio merè humano concinnatam & erroneam esse asseveremus: præsertim si sublimiora illa doctrinæ capita falsitatis evidenter convinci non possint.


### XV. FROM the parts of doctrine established in the second class, which can be known…

XV.

FROM the parts of doctrine established in the second class, which can be known confusedly and according to a certain generic reason from the light of nature, but according to their specific and proper reason exceed it, such an argument can be woven: That Scripture which delivers and explains those parts of doctrine, which can be known confusedly and according to a certain generic reason from the light of nature, but according to their specific and proper reason exceed it, so perfectly in all respects that it cannot be convicted of any error; but rather so that by their explanation our confused knowledge, which we have of them from the light of nature, does not be destroyed, but remarkably perfected, and can be known by the guidance of the light of nature itself, these do not have mere men, but God Himself as their Author, and are devoid of all error and falsehood. But Holy Scripture is thus. Therefore, Holy Scripture does not have mere men, but God Himself as its Author, and is devoid of all error and falsehood.

I. The minor proposition was proved above in thesis XII, Explanation, nos. III, IV, V, VI. & VII. where the creation of this universe and the production of our first parents, their state both of integrity and of corruption, the ultimate end of man, both objective and formal, and the means of attaining blessedness in God were treated at length, and it was shown that whatever can be known about them from the light of nature confusedly and according to a certain generic reason, but which according to their specific and proper reason exceed the light of nature, are all delivered and explained in the Holy Scriptures distinctly and according to their specific and proper reason, so that they can not only be evidently convicted of no error or contradiction, but also that our confused knowledge of them, which we have by the guidance of the light of nature, can be remarkably perfected by their explanation and the distinct knowledge born from this, as can be known from the light of nature itself.

II. This most exact harmony of both lights, namely of nature and of grace, remarkably confirms the major proposition; the former, implanted by nature in the minds of men, provides certain seeds of religion through the confused knowledge it produces in them concerning the mentioned heads of doctrine, by which they are carried toward it by nature, just as, by the testimony of Paul, they lead man as if by the hand to seek God, if perhaps by feeling after Him they might find Him, Acts 17:27. The latter, however, through the distinct knowledge of the same things which it generates in them, excites, cultivates, confirms those sown seeds of religion, and leads them to a state of religion that is full and, as far as can be had in this corruption of nature, perfect, and which suffices for salvation. Which supreme harmony of both lights, as it cannot be and be had from elsewhere than from God, the Author of both: for both lights are from God: the former indeed, as from the Author of nature through creation: the latter as from the Author of grace through supernatural revelation; so it is a remarkable proof is, that Scripture, explaining the aforementioned doctrines according to its own specific and proper nature so distinctly that it cannot be evidently convicted of falsehood in any part of itself, and perfecting our confused knowledge which we have of them from the light of nature, is in these parts in every respect true and devoid of all error. But if in these parts? why not also in all other parts is it entirely true and devoid of all error? Let those things be seen which we discussed in the preceding argument for the confirmation of the major proposition regarding this matter.

Latin:

XV.

EX partibus doctrinæ, in secunda classe constitutis, quæ scilicet confusè & secundum rationem quandam genericam ex lumine naturæ cognosci possunt, secundùm verò suam rationem specificam & propriam illud excedunt, tale necti potest argumentum: Quæ Scriptura eas doctrinæ partes, quæ confusè & secundum rationem quandam genericam ex lumine naturæ cognosci possunt, secundum suam rationem specificam verò & propriam illud excedunt, per omnia ita perfectè tradit & explicat, ut nullius convinci queat erroris; quin potiùs ut illarum explicatione nostram confusam, quam ex naturæ lumine de illis habemus, cognitionem non destrui, sed insigniter perfici, ipsius luminis naturæ ductu cognosci possit, ea non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsum habet Auctorem, estque erroris & falsitatis omnis expers. Atqui Scriptura sacra sic sese habet. Ergo Scriptura sacra non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsum habet Auctorem, estque erroris & falsitatis omnis expers.

I. Propositio minor probata est supra th. XII. Explicat. n. III, IV.V.VI. & VII. ubi de creatione hujus universi deque productione Protoplastorum nostrorum, de illorum statu cùm integritatis, tùm corruptionis, de hominis fine ultimo, cùm objectivo tùm formali, de mediis consequendæ in Deo beatitudinis fusè actum, ostensumque est, quòd quæcunque ex lumine naturæ confusè & secundum quandam rationem genericam de illis cognosci possunt, secundum suam rationem specificam & propriam verò lumen naturæ excedunt, in Scripturis sacris omnia tradantur & explicentur distinctè & secundum suam rationem specificam ac propriam, ut non solum nullius erroris aut contradictionis evidenter convinci possint, sed etiam nostram confusam, quam ductu luminis naturæ de illis habemus, cognitionem illorum explicatione & hinc natâ cognitione distinctâ insigniter perfici, ex ipso lumine naturæ cognosci possit.

II. Majorem verò propositionem egregiè confirmat hæc exactissima luminis utriusque, naturæ scilicet & gratiæ, harmonia, quorum illud, mentibus hominum naturâ implantatum, per confusam, quam de memoratis doctrinæ capitibus in illis parit, notitiam semina quædam religionis præbet, quibus naturâ in eam ferantur, perinde ut, Paulo teste, hominem manu quasi ducunt ad quærendum Deum, si fortè palpando eum inveniant, Act. XVII. 27. Hoc verò per eorundem notitiam distinctam, quam in iis generat, illa jacta religionis semina excitat, excolit, confirmat, & ad statum religionis plenum atque, quoad in hac naturæ corruptione haberi potest, perfectum, & qui ad salutem sufficiat, perducit. Quæ summa luminis utriusque harmonia ut aliunde, quàm à Deo utriusque Auctore esse & haberi non potest: nam lumen utrumque est à Deo: illud quidem, velut ab Auctore naturæ per creationem: hoc velut, ab Auctore gratiæ per supernaturalem revelationem; ita documento insigni est, Scripturam, prædictas doctrinas secundum suam rationem specificam & propriam ita distinctè explicantem, ut nulla sui parte falsitatis evidenter convinci possit, nostramque confusam, quam ex lumine naturæ de illis habemus, cognitionem perficientem, esse in hisce partibus per omnia veram & erroris omnis expertem. Si autem in his partibus? quidnî etiam in aliis partibus omnibus vera omnis que erroris expers sit? Videantur, quæ in argumento præcedente ad confirmationem propositionis majoris hanc in rem disseruimus.


### XVI. Finally, the dogmas which are established in the third class, namely those…

XVI.

Finally, the dogmas which are established in the third class, namely those which simply exceed the light of nature, yet are commended to us as mysteries revealed by God for the sake of our salvation, suggest to us such an argument for establishing the truth of Holy Scripture, pure from all error: Whatever Scripture delivers in various places as dogmas which simply exceed the light of nature, and commends them to us as mysteries hidden from human reason but revealed by God for our salvation, that is simply true and devoid of all error. But Holy Scripture delivers in various places dogmas which simply exceed the light of nature, and commends them to us as mysteries hidden from human reason but revealed by God for our salvation. Therefore, Holy Scripture is simply true and devoid of all error.

I. The minor proposition again receives light from the previously recounted chapters of Christian doctrine concerning the Trinity of divine persons in one divine essence, concerning the incarnation, the two natures and the unity of the person of Christ, concerning the redemption of the human race through the passion and death of Christ, concerning justification through faith in Christ, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning beatitude, constituted on the part of the soul in the vision or intuitive and clear knowledge of God; but on the part of the body in its glorification, etc., all of which by their sublimity far exceed the grasp of human reason, but are implicitly comprehended by the Apostle in the mystery which he commends to us, in the times kept secret in eternal times, Rom. XVI. 25. hidden from ages in God, Eph. III. 9. which was hidden from ages and from generations, Col. I. 27. and in the wisdom of God, in a mystery (hidden) which is hidden, which God foreordained before the ages unto our glory, I. Cor. II. 7. which none of the princes of this world knew, v. 8. embracing those things which eye hath not seen, and ear hath not heard, and have not ascended into the heart of man, which God hath prepared for them that love him, v. 9. The whole knowledge of which the praised Apostle attributes to divine revelation, which happened to the Prophets of old and to himself and the other Apostles: To us (the Apostles), he says, God hath revealed them by his Spirit, I. Cor. II. 10. and he says that his Gospel and his preaching concerning Jesus Christ was performed by him according to the revelation of the mystery, kept secret in eternal times, but now manifested, and by the Prophetic Scriptures according to the commandment of the eternal God, made known unto all nations for the obedience of faith, Rom. XVI. 25. 26.

II. But the major proposition is evident from the sublimity of these parts of the doctrine. For because they concern mysteries, kept secret in eternal times, and those things which eye hath not seen, and ear hath not heard, and have not ascended into the heart of man, the thing itself speaks, that they were not finally devised, fabricated, and committed to writing by human study by men, but were first made known and committed to writing by God supernaturally revealing them, which Paul also, as we have seen, testifies in express words in the places already cited. But just as nothing but truth can proceed from God who is most truthful, so Scripture, which was committed to writing by God revealing it, can be nothing but true and devoid of all falsehood, at least in those parts in which it contains doctrines so sublime, which could not have become known to men and been committed to writing by them except by God revealing them. But if it is true in these parts, written by God revealing it, and without any error mixed in, why not also in all the other parts? Since the sacred writers attribute the Scriptures committed to writing by them, not to some of their parts, but as a whole to God inspiring them. See what we said above in thesis XIV regarding this matter.

III. But here the enemies of the sacred Scriptures and of Christian doctrine, who wish to measure everything by the rule of reason and admit nothing unless it is consistent with it, might object that this argument begs the question (τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ). For it is assumed as certain that the enumerated heads of Christian doctrine are mysteries, exceeding the light of nature, which yet they conflict with the light of nature and involve a contradiction. But those things which conflict with the light of nature and involve a contradiction are false and invented by men, and have not become known through God revealing them. But that they conflict with the light of nature and imply a contradiction, they go about proving chiefly by the example of the dogma concerning the Trinity of divine persons in one divine essence. It is not long ago that Daniel Zwicker, from the sect of the Socinians, in his, as he calls it, Compelle intrare, or in his Tractatus Tractatuum, took it upon himself to demonstrate concerning the contradiction, that this dogma implies a true contradiction and therefore must be abandoned, relying on these three principles: 1) That God is some nature or essence, and that most intelligent; which it suffices to know in this place. 2) That a divine person, whatever it may be said to be, because it is intelligent, is necessarily an essence; which again suffices. 3) That one is necessarily that which is undivided in itself and its essence, and divided from any other. And because, he says further, these three must be thought and believed so necessarily, partly concerning God and the divine person, and partly concerning unity, that if this is not done, God, person, and unity are utterly removed and denied, hence the descriptions of God, person, and unity, containing those quiddities, are as true, essential, and necessary as if you were to say that man is an animal: and furthermore, whatever is opposed to them immediately and necessarily implies a true contradiction; e.g., if a person is posited without its own essence (as necessarily happens if three persons are said to be one essence in number), then it will simultaneously be and not be a person: which is contradictory. Likewise, if a singular or one-in-number essence is said to be common to three persons, then it will simultaneously be singular or one-in-number, and will not be: which again manifestly contradicts itself. These are his words.

IV. I do not indeed deny that there are no divine mysteries, nor have they become known through God revealing them, which truly conflict with the light of nature or involve a true contradiction. For the light of nature was implanted in the minds of men by God himself, the author of nature, and that which is consistent with this is as repugnant to being false as it is repugnant for falsehood to proceed from God; and on the contrary, that which truly conflicts with the light of nature and involves a contradiction, because it cannot be true, is as repugnant to being revealed by God as it is repugnant for a falsehood to be revealed by Him. Whence that principle most known to nature: Two contradictory things cannot simultaneously be true; we confess that this holds universally, as much in Theology as in Philosophy. But because in Theology, where the discourse is about things exceeding the light of nature, it is most difficult to know which things involve a contradiction or do not, and it easily happens that corrupted reason, following the guidance of its own principles, through a μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος transfers to divine matters principles which either do not hold, or only hold universally in the sphere of natural things, and thus considers as contradictory those things which are not contradictory: one must take diligent care lest a contradiction be admitted in this kind of doctrine before it has been most evidently proven, and demonstrated that the same thing is simultaneously affirmed and denied according to the same, of the same, and at the same time and respect. But if a contradiction cannot be most evidently demonstrated, then one must insist not on reason and its principles, but on the words of Scripture, nor should that which we cannot grasp from the principles of nature be rejected as impossible or false, but rather be revered as a mystery exceeding the light of nature, if Holy Scripture asserts it in clear words. Let those things be seen which we have previously taught on this matter in the Treatise on the Use of the Principles of Philosophy and Reason in Theological Controversies, Book I, Chapter IX, and Book II, Chapter XIV.

How preposterously, however, they proceed in demonstrating a conflict between the light of nature and those heads of Christian doctrine which are commended to us in Holy Scriptures as mysteries hidden from human reason, this process of Zwicker alone, which he used in the place and words alleged to prove a contradiction in the dogma of the Trinity, clearly testifies. His demonstration, if it is right to call it a demonstration, rests, as we have seen, on three principles: the first of which is: That God is some nature or essence, and that most intelligent; the second: That a divine Person, whatever it may be said to be, because it is intelligent, is necessarily an essence; the third: That one is necessarily that which in itself is its own essence, undivided, and divided from any other. Although, indeed, as regards the first, we by no means deny that God is some nature or essence, and that most intelligent, and that all theologians agree on this, we nevertheless deny that to discern and demonstrate which special predicates, attributed to God in the Holy Scriptures, truly belong to Him or are repugnant to Him, it suffices to know this, just as Zwicker contends in the same place: That, saying, is enough to know in this place. For to be some intelligent nature or essence is the most general concept of God, common to God, Angels, and men. And although Zwicker adds the little word 'supremely,' by which he seems to attribute to God an intelligence—which he has in common with Angels and men—more perfect than that of Angels and men, this nevertheless does nothing to declare the essence of God distinctly and as it is in itself. Moreover, from a generic concept of God, human reason, under the guidance of its own principles, cannot pass judgment on those things which are peculiarly attributed to Him in the Scriptures, whether they truly agree with Him or whether they are repugnant to Him. For how will you know from this, that God is an intelligent nature or essence, whether it is repugnant or not repugnant to Him that Scripture testifies in express words that He has begotten a Son, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the same? Whether it agrees or is repugnant to God that Scripture testifies that He is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? If human reason, under the guidance of its own principles, ought to pass an accurate judgment on such things as these from the nature or essence of God, it would be necessary that it should have distinct knowledge of it and of all the perfections of Him formally contained within it. Since this knowledge does not befall anyone here in the state of the journey of mortals, it must be admitted that the intellect of man cannot, with the light of nature as a guide, pass judgment on special and proper predicates of this kind, which are attributed to God in the Scriptures, as to whether they truly agree with Him or are repugnant to Him. to pass a right judgment from His essence, but if one were to stand by the light of nature alone, no judgment could be passed otherwise than by a consequence deduced from those things which agree or disagree with created intelligent natures or essences, by which it is concluded that whatever agrees or is repugnant to the finite essence of man agrees or is repugnant to the infinite essence of God: which would be a most vicious μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος.

As for the other principle of Zwicker, it must be known that the name of person, used of God, is not found in the Holy Scriptures, but only the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while it is taught in them that God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are that one eternal God. But because predicates proper to persons are attributed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, the ancient Doctors of the Latin Church employed and The Fathers used the name of person, in order to bind the enemies of this mystery more strongly, and said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, taking the word person not for essence, but for subsistence or a substantial mode of existing; the Fathers and Doctors of the Greek Church, however, used the word ὑποστάσεως in its place, and said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three ὑποστάσεις in one single or divine essence, using the word ὑποστάσεως in the same meaning in which the Latins used the name of person. Whence Zwvicker's second principle: A divine person, whatever it may be said to be, because it is intelligent, is necessarily an essence; is false for a double reason. One, because a person, as it is used by the Doctors of the Church concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and three divine persons are spoken of, is formally not an essence, but a subsistence or substantial mode of existing of the divine essence. The other, because a person, thus taken for a subsistence, is formally not intelligent, but a mode of existing of an intelligent nature or essence.

Concerning the third, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, we advise that for it to be one, it suffices that it be undivided in itself, and it is not necessarily required that it be divided from any other, as is clear from the example of the soul, which is one, and yet is not divided from any other: since it is not divided from the body, but united with it to constitute one suppositum.

With these things being so, everyone understands that Zwvicker's entire demonstration is slippery, futile, nay, null. For first, if a person is posited without its own essence, it does not immediately imply a contradiction that it is simultaneously a person and not a person. For a divine person, as has been said, is formally not the divine essence itself, but a subsistence or substantial mode of existing of the divine essence, and it suffices for the definition of a person that it be the subsistence of an intelligent essence: but that that intelligent essence be proper to this subsistence, and not also so common to another subsistence that it constitutes this person taken concretely with this subsistence, and that person taken concretely with that one, is not of the definition and primary concept of a person. In created and finite things, indeed, it is so arranged that every person has its own proper intelligent essence, of which it is the subsistence. But to argue from created and finite things to the essence and infinite subsistence of God, and from the fact that every created person has its own proper essence, to conclude that every divine person also has its own proper essence is not permitted, who is so stupid as not to understand? Nor also, whether it is fitting or repugnant to the infinite essence of God to subsist in three subsistences or substantial modes of existing, can be known from the essence of God itself: since no one at all can know it distinctly, as it is in itself, in this mortality, as has been said more often. What therefore remains, than that we confess that the dogma of the Trinity, by which three persons are said to be of one divine essence, cannot be evidently convicted of any contradiction? Similarly, that a singular or numerically one essence is common to three persons is not contradictory, nor does it follow from that that it is at once singular or numerically one, and is not, as Zuvickerus again ineptly concludes. For the singular or numerically one divine essence is not or is not said to be common to three persons through its own multiplication, or through an aptitude for being in several numerically differing things with its own multiplication, but through the identification of itself with each divine person, which is not repugnant to its singularity or numerical unity. But whether the numerically one divine essence can be so identified with the three divine subsistences that, without its own multiplication, it constitutes three really distinct persons with them, and the subsistences alone are really distinguished from one another, while the essence remains numerically one and the same? Again, such is a κενούργον [empty work], which altogether exceeds the grasp of human reason. In finite things, indeed, reason can know from its own light that this cannot be done: but we have said more than once that it is not permitted to conclude from the fact that something is repugnant to be done in finite things, that it is also repugnant to be done in the infinite essence of God. Nor does any other reason for knowing exist, from which anything can be certainly determined in either direction, except Holy Scripture, consigned by God revealing, who alone has certain knowledge of His essence and its perfections. For to look into the infinite essence of God, and to know distinctly what is fitting or repugnant to it, is, as has been said, given to no one in this mortality. Therefore, Holy Scripture must be heard here, and one must stand by it, even though the underlying matter cannot be grasped by our intellect. But enough and more than enough concerning the credibility of the truth of Scripture, pure from all error, to be shown from the condition of the doctrine which is delivered in it for the sake of our salvation, through an induction of all its parts.

Latin:

XVI.

QVæ in tertia classe denique constituuntur dogmata, nempe quæ lumen naturæ simpliciter excedunt, nobis tamen tanquam mysteria, nostræ salutis causâ à Deo patefacta, commendantur, pro adstruenda Scripturæ sacræ veritate, ab omni errore pura, nobis tale suggerunt argumentum: Quæ Scriptura passim locorum tradit dogmata, quæ lumen naturæ simpliciter excedunt, eaque ut mysteria, ab humana ratione abscondita, à Deo autem ad nostram salutem patefacta nobis commendat, ea simpliciter vera omnisque erroris expers est. Atqui Scriptura sacra tradit passim locorum dogmata, quæ lumen naturæ simpliciter excedunt, eaque tanquam mysteria, ab humana ratione abscondita, à Deo autem ad nostram salutem patefacta nobis commendat. Ergo Scriptura sacra simpliciter vera omnisque erroris expers est.

I. Minor propositio rursum lucem sortitur ex superiùs recensitis capitibus doctrinæ Christianæ de Trinitate personarum divinarum in una essentia divina, de incarnatione, duabus naturis & unitate personæ Christi, de redemtione generis humani per Christi passionem & mortem, de justificatione per fidem in Christum, de resurrectione mortuorum, de beatitudine, ex parte animæ in visione sive intuitiva & clara cognitione Dei; ex parte corporis verò in illius clarificatione constituta &c. quæ omnia sublimitate sua humanæ rationis captum longiffimè excedunt, ab Apostolo autem implicitè comprehenduntur in mysterio, quod nobis commendat, temporibus æternis tacito, Rom. XVI. 25. abscondito à seculis in Deo, Eph. III. 9. quod reconditum fuit à seculis & à generationibus, Col. I. 27. & in sapientia Dei, in mysterio (latente) quæ est abscondita, quam præfinierat Deus ante secula in gloriam nostram, I. Cor. II. 7. quam nemo principum seculi hujus cognovit, v. 8. complectente ea, quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audivit, & in cor hominis non adscenderunt, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se, v. 9. Quorum notitiam totam Apostolus laudatus divinæ revelationi, quæ Prophetis olim & sibi cæterisque Apostolis obtigerit, acceptam refert: Nobis (Apostolis) inquit, Deus revelavit per Spiritum suum, I. Cor. II. 10. & Evangelium suum ac prædicationem suam de Jesu Christo peractam à se dicit juxta revelationem mysterii, temporibus æternis taciti, manifestati verò nunc, & per Scripturas Propheticas juxta delegationem æterni Dei, in obedientiam fidei, in omnes Gentes patefacti, Rom. XVI. 25. 26.

II. Major autem propositio patet ex sublimitate harum doctrinæ partium. Quia enim mysteria concernunt, temporibus æternis tacita, & ea, quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audivit, & in cor hominis non adscenderunt, res ipsa loquitur, quòd non ab hominibus demum excogitatæ, confictæ, humanoque studio in literas relatæ sint, sed Deo supernaturaliter revelante & innotuerint primùm & literis consignatæ sint, quod & Paulus locis jam citatis, uti vidimus, expressis verbis testatur. Quemadmodùm autem à Deo summè veraci non nisi verum provenire potest, ita Scriptura, quæ Deo revelante consignata est, non nisi vera falsitatisque omnis expers esse potest, iis minimùm partibus, quibus doctrinas ita sublimes, quæ non nisi Deo revelante hominibus innotescere & in literas ab iis referri potuerunt, continet. Si autem in his partibus, Deo revelante, conscripta, & absque ullo admixto errore vera est, quidni in cæteris etiam partibus omnibus? cùm Scriptores sacri Scripturas à se consignatas, non aliquibus sui partibus, sed totas Deo inspiranti acceptas referant. Videantur, quæ supra th. XIV. hanc in rem diximus.

III. Sed hîc regerent Scripturarum sacrarum & doctrinæ Christianæ hostes, qui omnia ad regulam rationis exigere, nec quicquam, nisi quod ei consentaneum sit, admittere volunt, argumento hoc peti τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Sumi enim tanquam certum, capita doctrinæ Christianæ recensita esse mysteria, lumen naturæ excedentia, quæ tamen cum lumine naturæ pugnent, & contradictionem involvant. Quæ autem cum lumine naturæ pugnant, & contradictionem involvunt, falsa & ab hominibus conficta esse, non Deo revelante innotuisse. Quòd verò cum lumine naturæ pugnent, & contradictionem implicent, potissimùm exemplo dogmatis de Trinitate personarum divinarum in una essentia divina probatum eunt. Non ita pridem est, quòd è Socinianorum Secta Daniel Zvvickerus in suo, ut vocat, Compelle intrare, sive in Tractatu Tractatuum de contradictione demonstrandum sibi sumsit, dogma hoc veram implicare contraditionem, & propterea deserendum esse, tribus hisce innixus principiis: 1) Deum esse naturam aliquam seu essentiam, eamque summè intelligentem; quod scire hoc loco sufficiat. 2) personam divinam, quæcunque ea etiam esse dicatur, quia intelligens est, necessario esse essentiam; quod iterum sufficiat. 3) Unum necessario esse, quod in se & sua essentia indivisum est, & divisum à quovis alio. Et quia,inquit porrò, hæc tria adeò necessario partim de Deo personaque divina, partim verò de unitate, cogitari & credi debent, ut si id non fiat, Deus, persona, & unitas prorsus tollantur, & negentur, hinc descriptiones Dei, personæ & unitatis, quidditates istas continentes, tàm sunt veræ, essentiales & necessariæ, quàm si hominem animal esse dicas: & prætereà quicquid iisdem opponitur, protinùs veram contraditionem necessario implicat; V. G. si persona statuatur sine propria essentia, (prout necessario fit, si tres personæ una numero essentia esse dicantur) tùm simul erit & non erit persona: quod contradictorium est. Item si singularis seu una numero essentia communis dicatur tribus personis, tùm simul erit singularis seu una numero, & non erit: quod iterum manifestè sibi contradicit. Hæc ille.

IV. Non equidem diffiteor, mysteria divina non esse, nec Deo revelante innotuisse, quæ verè naturæ lumini repugnant, aut contradictionem veram involvunt. Lumen naturæ enim ab ipsomet Deo, Naturæ auctore, mentibus hominum implantatum est, & quod huic est consentaneum, tàm repugnat esse falsum, quàm repugnat à Deo falsum proficisci; & contrà quod cum lumine naturæ verè pugnat & contradictionem involvit, quia verum esse non potest, tam repugnat à Deo revelari, quàm repugnat falsum ab eo revelari. Unde principium illud naturæ notissimum: Duo contradictoria non posse simul esse vera; fatemur universaliter, tàm in Theologia, quàm in Philosophia, procedere. Quia autem in Theologia, ubi de rebus lumen naturæ excedentibus sermo est, quænam contradictionem involvant vel non involvant, cognitu difficillimum est, & facilè contingit, ut ratio corrupta, suorum principiorum ductum secuta, per μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος ad res divinas transferat principia, quæ vel non, vel tantùm in sphæra rerum naturalium universaliter procedunt, & sic in contradictorijs habeat, quæ contradictoria non sunt: cavendum est sedulò, ne in hoc doctrinarum genere contradictio priùs admittatur, quàm evidentissimè ea fuerit evicta, demonstratumque, idem simul affirmari & negari secundũ idem, de eodẽ, & eodem tempore ac respectu. Quod si contradictio non possit evidentissimè demonstrari, tum non rationi ejusque principiis, sed verbis Scripturæ insistendum est, nec, ut impossibile aut falsum, rejiciendum, quod ex naturæ principiis capere non possumus, sed ut mysterium, naturæ lumen excedens, suspiciendum, si Scriptura sacra verbis perspicuis id asseveret. Videantur, quæ antehac in Tr. de Usu principiorum Philos. & rationis in Controv. Theol. lib. I. c. IX. & lib. II. c. XIV. hanc in rem docuimus.

Quàm præposterè autem procedant in demonstranda pugna inter lumen naturæ & capita illa doctrinæ Christianæ, quæ in Scripturis S. nobis tanquam mysteria, ab humana ratione abscondita, commendantur, vel solus hic Zvvickeri processus, quo ad evincendam in dogmate de Trinitate contradictionem in loco & verbis allegatis usus est, liquidò testatur. Demonstratio ejus, si demonstrationem dicere fas est, tribus, ut vidimus, principiis nititur: quorum primum est: Deum esse naturam aliquam seu essentiam, eamque summè intelligentem; alterum: Personam divinam, quæcunque etiam ea esse dicatur, quia intelligens est, necessario esse essentiam; Tertium: Unum necessario esse, quod in se es sua essentia indivisum est, & divisum à quovis alio. Quamvis verò, quod ad primum attinet, minimè inficiemur, Deum esse naturam aliquam seu essentiam, eamque summè intelligentem, & in hoc omnes consentire Theologos, negamus tamen, ad dignoscendum & demonstrandum, quæ specialia prædicata, Deo in Scripturis sacris tributa, verè ipsi conveniant aut repugnent, sufficere hoc scire, sicut Zvvickerus ibidem contendit: Quod, inquiens, scire hoc loco sufficit. Nam esse naturam aliquam seu essentiam intelligentem, est conceptus Dei generalissimus, communis Deo, Angelis & hominibus. Et quamvis Zvvickerus addat voculam summé, quâ Deo intelligentiam, quam cum Angelis & hominibus communem habet, perfectiorem, quàm Angelis & hominibus, tribuere videtur, hoc tamen ad essentiam Dei, distinctè & ut in se est, declarandam nihil facit. Ex conceptu autem generico Dei ratio humana, ductu suorum principiorum, de iis, quæ ei in Scripturis peculiariter tribuuntur, an verè ipsi conveniant? an ei repugnent? judicium ferre non potest. Quomodo enim ex hoc, quòd Deus est natura seu essentia intelligens, cognosces, an ei repugnet vel non repugnet, quod Scriptura conceptis verbis testatur, eum genuisse Filium, & ab eodem procedere Spiritum sanctum? an conveniat vel repugnet Deo, quod Scriptura testatur, eum esse Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum? Si de his talibus ratio humana, suorum principiorum ductu, ex natura sive essentia Dei accuratum ferre judicium deberet, necesse esset, ut distinctè eam, omnesque in ea formaliter contentas perfectiones illius cognitas haberet. Quæ cognitio quia hîc in statu viæ mortalium nemini obtingit, fatendum est, intellectum hominis non posse, lumine naturæ duce, de hujus generis prædicatis specialibus & propriis, quæ in Scripturis Deo tribuuntur, conveniantne ei verè? an illi repugnent? ex ejus essentia judicium rectum ferre, sed si solo lumine naturæ standum esset, non posse aliter ferri judicium, quàm per consequentiam, ab iis, quæ naturis sive essentiis intelligentibus creatis conveniunt aut disconveniunt, deductam, quâ Dei essentiæ infinitæ convenire aut repugnare concludatur, quicquid hominis finitæ essentiæ convenit aut repugnat: quæ vitiosissima μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος fuerit.

Quantum ad alterum Zvvickeri principium sciendum est, personæ nomen, de Deo usurpatum, in Scripturis sacris non inveniri, sed tantùm nomina Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. dum in iis docetur, Deum esse Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, & Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum esse unum illum æternum Deum. Quia autem Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto in Scripturis tribuuntur prædicata, personarum propria, adhibuerunt veteres Ecclesiæ Latinæ Doctores & Patres personæ nomen, ad fortiùs constringendos hujus mysterii hostes, dixèruntque Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum tres personas, personæ voce non pro essentia, sed pro subsistentia sive modo existendi substantiali acceptâ; Græcæ verò Ecclesiæ Patres & Doctores ejus loco ὑποστάσεως voce usi sunt, & dixerunt, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. esse tres ὑποστάσεις in una sola sive essentia divina, ὑποστάσεως voce in significatu eodem, quo Latini personæ nomine usi sunt, adhibitâ. Unde alterum Zwvickeri principium: Persona divina, quæcunque etiam ea esse dicatur, quia intelligens est, necessariò est essentia; duplici de causa falsum est. Unâ, quòd persona, prout ab Ecclesiæ Doctoribus de Patre, Filio & Spiritu sancto adhibetur, & tres personæ divinæ dicuntur, formaliter non est essentia, sed subsistentia sive modus existendi substantialis essentiæ divinæ. Alterâ, quòd persona, sic pro subsistentiâ sumta, formaliter non est intelligens, sed modus existendi naturæ sive essentiæ intelligentis.

De tertio ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ monemus, quod ad unum sufficiat, quòd in se sit indivisum, nec necessariò requiratur, ut divisum sit a quovis alio, uti exemplo animæ patet, quæ una est, nec tamen divisa est à quovis alio: cùm non divisa sit à corpore, sed cum eo ad unum suppositum constituendum unita.

Quibus ita habentibus, nemo non intelligit, Zwvickeri totam demonstrationem esse lubricam, futilem, imò nullam. Primum enim si persona statuatur sine propria essentia, non protinùs implicatur contradictio, quòd simul sit persona, & non sit persona. Nam persona divina, uti dictum, formaliter non est ipsa essentia divina, sed subsistentia sive modus existendi substantialis essentiæ divinæ, & sufficit ad rationem personæ, quod essentiæ intelligentis subsistentia sit: ut autem essentia illa intelligens hujus subsistentiæ propria sit, non etiam alii subsistentiæ ita communis, ut cum hac subsistentia hanc concretivè sumtam; cum illa illam concretivè sumtam personam constituat, de ratione & conceptu primo personæ non est. In rebus creatis & finitis quidem sic comparatum est, ut quælibet persona suam propriam habeat essentiam intelligentem, cujus subsistentia est. Sed à rebus creatis & finitis ad Dei essentiam & subsistentiam infinitam argumentari, & ex eo, quod quælibet persona creata habet suam propriam essentiam, quamlibet etiam personam divinam suam propriam essentiam habere, cõcludere non licere, quis tam stupidus est, ut non intelligat? Neq; etiam, utrum Dei essentiæ infinitæ conveniat aut repugnet, tribus subsistere substistentris sive modis existendi substantialib9, ex ipsa Dei essentia cognosci potest: cùm eâ distinctè, ut in se est, in hac mortalitate cognoscere nemo quisquam possit, ut sæpius dictum. Quid ergò superest, quàm ut fateamur, dogma Trinitatis, quo unius essentiæ divinæ tres personæ esse dicuntur, non posse ullius contradictionis evidenter convinci? Similiter singularem seu unam numero essentiam tribus personis communem esse, contradictorium non est, neque inde sequitur, eam simul esse singularem seu unam numero, & non esse, ut rursum ineptè Zuvickerus concludit. Nam singularis sive una numero essentia divina non est aut dicitur tribus personis communis per sui multiplicationem, sive per aptitudinem essendi in pluribus numero differentibus cum sui multiplicatione, sed per identificationem sui cum qualibet persona divina, quod singularitati sive unitati numericæ illius non repugnat. Utrum verò una numero essentia divina ita cum tribus subsistentiis divinis possit identificari, ut absque sui multiplicatione tres cum illis personas realiter distinctas constituat, & subsistentiæ solæ realiter ab invicem distinguantur, essentiâ manente numero unâ & eâdem? rursum tale est κενούργον, quod humanæ rationis captum prorsus excedit. In rebus finitis quidem hoc fieri non posse, cognoscere potest ratio ex suo lumine: sed ex eo, quod in rebus finitis aliquid fieri repugnat, concludere non licere, quòd etiam in infinita Dei essentia id fieri repugnet, plus simplici vice diximus. Neque etiam ulla alia suppetit ratio cognoscendi, ex qua in alterutram partem certò aliquid determinari possit, præter Scripturam sacram, Deo revelante, qui solus certam suæ essentiæ ejusque perfectionum scientiam habet, consignatam. Nam Dei essentiam infinitam inspicere, & quid ei conveniens aut repugnans sit, distinctè cognoscere, in hac mortalitate nemini, uti dictum, datum est. Scripturæ sacræ ergo hîc audienda est, eáque standum, utut res substrata nostro intellectu capi non possit. Sed plus satis de credibilitate veritatis Scripturæ, ab omni errore puræ, ex conditione doctrinæ, quæ nostræ salutis causâ in ea traditur, per inductionem omnium ejus partium ostendenda.


### XVII. Nor does the wonderful harmony and agreement of the Old Testament with the New,…

XVII.

Nor does the wonderful harmony and agreement of the Old Testament with the New, and of all the parts of both among themselves, make the truth of Scripture, pure from all error, any less credible to us.

I. It could not have happened that so many writers, most dissimilar in talent, education, and character, and sometimes separated by the greatest intervals of place and time, who neither met nor could have met to communicate with one another, should write with such agreement concerning religion and the doctrine of salvation, and concerning the highest mysteries contained therein, that they contradicted one another in no part, but everywhere, especially in those things which concern the foundation of faith and salvation, delivered conformable teachings and conspired everywhere in one and the same opinion, unless they had written with one and the same guide and patron, the Holy Spirit. For since even in those parts of religion and divine worship which can to some extent be investigated and known from the light of nature, writers, left to their own talent, do not easily agree among themselves: if indeed in the doctrine concerning God, who can be known from the principles of nature and reason to be only one, neither the philosophers of the Gentiles agreed among themselves and with the common people, nor did the common people agree among themselves either in the past or today, but each nation invented for itself gods to worship, more or fewer, and one followed and follows its own with one kind of worship, another with another, all alike wandering from the one true God and his true worship: How could the authors of the Holy Scriptures, over fifteen hundred years (for the books of the O. and N. T. were written over a space of almost that many years), not only [teach] one God, and that no other than he who created heaven and earth, and worship due to him as the supreme God and creator of this universe, entirely in accordance with the light of nature; but also [how could they] have been able to teach and commit to writing with such agreement, as to the matter itself, the doctrine concerning three persons in one divine essence, concerning the Messiah and his incarnation, person, office, and worship, concerning the justification of the sinful man before God and his reconciliation with God through Christ, concerning the renewal of man and the true holiness of life, concerning the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and eternal life, all of which are most remote from human talent and exceed its grasp by a great distance, could have taught and committed to writing precisely the same thing as to the matter with such great agreement, if, left to themselves and their own talent, they had taught and written, and not by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit? What was said by one more briefly, was declared more fully and distinctly by another as time progressed, with God imparting a richer and more distinct knowledge: what was proposed and handed down by one obscurely and under the wrappings of types, was proposed and handed down by another in clear words, with the veil of types removed: by both, as regards the matter, it was entirely the same, from neither was it different. Divine worship could appear to have been prescribed as one thing by the writers of the Old Testament, and another, different from that, by the writers of the New Testament; but this diversity was in rites and ceremonies, not in the thing shadowed forth by them. The writers of the O.T. prescribed a worship suitable to the promised Messiah and to his being exhibited in the flesh in his own time, by which his death, by which the human race was to be redeemed, and his resurrection and all the benefits thence redounding to us were typically shadowed forth, which therefore had to consist of certain and conspicuous rites, not indeed invented by human ingenuity, but instituted by God himself: But the writers of the New Testament prescribed a worship due to the Messiah exhibited in the flesh, God and man in one undivided person, which is that same one which the rites and ceremonies described by the writers of the O.T. mystically shadowed forth, but without the shade of ceremonies and types. For those external rites and ceremonies, as shadows and images of spiritual goods to be conferred upon us through the Messiah in the flesh, had to cease after he was exhibited in the flesh and the promised benefits were actually bestowed upon us, and that very spiritual worship, comprised under those rites, was to be rendered to him without any wrapping of rites.

II. Fanatical men and sons of incredulity, especially those whose eyes of the mind Satan has blinded to such an extent in these last times that they deny that God exists, while the whole of nature and their own conscience cry out against it, do indeed boast; they boast, I say, of various contradictions with which Holy Scripture abounds, but they boast, they do not demonstrate, or if any go to prove what they boast of with examples, they bring forward as an example certain more difficult and obscure passages which at first glance may appear to conflict with one another, and they assume them to be truly conflicting, even though they have been vindicated from the stain of contradiction by interpreters perhaps a hundred times. A not obscure example of this matter was provided for us three years ago by that most wicked two-legged scoundrel, Matthias Knuzen, of Eiterstad in Holstein, whom we mentioned above in thesis II, Explanation, number VI. who here and elsewhere in various places, by means of scattered lying and blasphemous papers, by which he might utterly detract from the divine authority of Holy Scripture, which the universal Church has always asserted for it, undertook to prove that it disagrees with itself and is entirely unstable. This he did in various papers, written partly in the vernacular, partly in the Latin idiom. In the Colloquy of the Innkeeper with three guests of different religions, written in the vernacular language, he brings forward the passages Joh. XV. 27, Acts III. 15, and Joh. V. 34, likewise Acts IX. 7 and ch. XX. 9, Joh. V. 29, Isa. XXVI. 14, Ps. LXXXVIII. 12, Job XIV. 22, Luke XIV. 14, Ps. CXXXIV. 3, Luke XVII. 10, which are partly κατά το ρητον, by IS and IS NOT, opposed to one another, and partly κατά διάνοιαν and by consequence fight among themselves. But in the Epistle, given at Rome on the 6th of the Kalends of March, written in the Latin idiom, right at the beginning he says: I could, he says, prove that (namely, the canon and foundation of Christians, which they call the Bible, disagrees with itself and is entirely unstable) by six hundred examples throughout all the books of both the Old and New Testament, but there is a fear that perhaps I might create nausea for the readers by the multitude of arguments, therefore I shall bring forward only a few, so that they may be the better weighed by those who wish to read. I shall say nothing here about the measures, of which mention is made in 1 Kings VII. 26 and conversely in 2 Chronicles IV. 5, which diametrically (if I can judge anything) contradict each other in number: I shall also say nothing about the persons, e.g., if you compare Gen. XXVI. 34 with Gen. XXXVI. 2, for there Basemath, the wife of Esau, is called the daughter of Elon the Hittite, but here the daughter of Ishmael. I also pass over the fact that in different places the same things are commanded and forbidden: thus in Matt. XIX. 5, to cleave to a wife, but conversely in Mal. II. 16, it is commanded to a husband to divorce her. to divorce her, it is commanded to a husband. Concerning these and other not dissimilar things, I am not going to speak at present, but this I cannot be brought to pass over, namely that this canon of the Christians truly sounds like a Lesbian rule, as if on discordant strings, even in the Articles of faith. It is so often inculcated that the dead are to rise again, which, as we willingly grant to Christians as τῶν ἀμφῶν, so they, their own Canon granting it, must in turn grant to us that the dead are not to rise again; which is asserted partly κατά ρητὸν, partly also κατά διάνοιαν, which coincides with τῷ ῥητῷ, in the following places, Isa. XXVI. 14. Ps. LXXXVIII. 11. Ps. LXXVIII. 40. Ecclesiast. III, 19. Job XIV. 12. & others. To which he also refers on another page, that in Luke XIV. 14. the just, and in Luke XX. 35. those who shall be accounted worthy of the future age, are said to be about to rise again; but elsewhere, and indeed in Ps. CXLIII. 3, it is said that no one is just, nor is anyone worthy, but all, even if they have done everything that was commanded them, are forced to confess at last that they are unprofitable servants, Luke XVII. 10.

III. But in truth, nothing less is established by the cited passages than what that wicked detractor of Holy Scripture undertook to establish: namely, that Holy Scripture fights with itself and sounds with discordant strings, or, which amounts to the same thing, that true contradictions are contained in it, not merely apparent ones: but on the contrary, rather, while he could not find passages stronger and more suitable for establishing that, he unwittingly bore no obscure testimony to the harmony of the Scripture of the O.T. with the New, and to the most exact agreement of all parts of both with each other. For to one comparing them with each other in their context and genuine sense, and weighing them according to the laws of contradiction, it will be immediately evident that no true contradiction, no true conflict is contained therein. Where we warn above all that for a true contradiction it is not sufficient to have any affirmation and negation whatsoever, as the author most foolishly assumes: saying, Between IS and IS NOT, affirmation and negation, there is not an apparent, but a true contradiction; but it is required that the same thing be affirmed and denied of the same thing, according to the same thing, at the same time and in the same respect, which, as is most well known and is inculcated even to boys in all Logic textbooks, does not need proof. In the cited passages, however, there is not even one example given of which it is certain and indubitable that the same thing is affirmed and denied of the same thing, according to the same thing, at the same time and in the same respect, as will be evident by induction.

And indeed, to make a beginning from the passages brought forward in the Colloquy of the Innkeeper, John XV. 27 and Acts III. 15, the subject is the testimony which the Apostles, as eyewitnesses of Christ, and of his doctrine, miracles, and of his passion, death, and resurrection, were bearing and were about to bear among men for the sake of men, in order to lead them to the faith of Christ: which testimony is so far from having ever been rejected by Christ, or being recorded anywhere in the Scriptures as having been rejected, that for that purpose he rather

Latin:

XVII.

NEque minùs nobis veritatem Scripturæ, ab omni errore puram, credibilem facit Veteris Testamenti cum Novo, omniumque utriusque partium inter se mira harmonia & consensio.

I. Fieri non potuisset, ut tot ingenio, educatione ac moribus dissimilimi, locorumque ac temporum intervallis nonnunquam longissimè sejuncti Scriptores, qui ad communicandum inter se nec convenerunt, nec convenire potuerunt, de religione & salutis doctrina, deque summis in ea comprehensis mysteriis tanto scriberent consensu, ut nulla in parte alter alteri contradicerent, sed undique, in iis præsertim, quæ fundamentum fidei ac salutis concernunt, conformia traderent, & in unam ubique sententiam conspirarent, nisi uno eodemque duce & auspice Spiritu sancto scripsissent. Cùm enim ne in iis quidem religionis & cultus divini partibus, quæ ex lumine naturæ quadantenus investigari & cognosci possunt, Scriptores, suo relicti ingenio, facilè inter se consentiant: siquidem in doctrina de Deo, quem non nisi unum esse, ex naturæ & rationis principiis constare potest, nec Gentilium Philosophi inter se & cum Vulgo, nec vulgus inter se vel olim convenerunt, vel hodiè conveniunt, sed quisque populus commentus est sibi Deos, quos coleret, plures vel pauciores, alioque cultus genere hic, alio ille suos profequutus est & prosequitur, ab uno vero Deo, veroque ejus cultu pariter omnes aberrantes: Quomodò Scripturæ sacræ conditores per annos mille quingentos (tot enim ferè annorum spacio conscripti sunt V. & N. T. libri) non tantùm unum Deum, eumque non alium, quàm qui cœlum & terram creavit, cultumque eidem, ut Deo summo & conditori hujus universi debitum, lumini naturæ prorsus convenienter; sed etiam doctrinam de tribus personis in una divina essentia, de Messia, ejusque incarnatione, persona, officio, cultu, de justificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo ejusque reconciliatione cum Deo per Christum, de renovatione hominis vitæque vera sanctimonia, de resurrectione mortuorum, judicio extremo, & vita æterna, quæ omnia ab humano ingenio remotissima sunt, ejusque captum longissimè excedunt, tanto consensu idem prorsus, quoad rem, docere & in literas referre potuissent, si sibi suoq; ingenio relicti docuissent & scripsissent, non Spiritu sancto inspirante? Quod ab uno dictum est breviùs, ab alio temporis progressu, Deo uberiorem & distinctiorem notitiam impertiente, declaratum est uberius & distinctius: quod ab uno obscurè & sub typorum involucris; ab alio verbis claris, typorum velamine remoto, propositum & traditum est: ab utrisque quoad rem prorsus idem, à neutris diversum. Cultus divinus videri poterat alius à Scriptoribus V. T. alius & ab illo diversus à Scriptoribus N. T. præscriptus fuisse; sed diversitas hæc fuit in ritibus ac ceremoniis, non in re, illis adumbrata. Scriptores V.T. præscripserunt cultum, Messiæ promisso & suo tempore in carne exhibendo convenientem, quo ejus mors, quâ redimendum erat mortalium genus, ejusque resurrectio & omnia inde in nos redundantia beneficia typicè adumbrabantur, quem proinde certis & conspicuis ritibus, non quidem ab humano ingenio inventis, sed ab ipsomet Deo institutis, constare oportebat: Sed Scriptores novi Testamenti præscripserunt cultum, Messiæ in carne exhibito, Deo & homini in una indivisa persona debitum, qui idem ille est, quem ritus & ceremoniæ, à Scriptoribus V. T. descriptæ, mysticè adumbrabant, sed sine ceremoniarum & typorum umbraculo. Ritus enim & ceremoniæ illæ externæ, velut umbræ & imagines bonorum spiritualium, per Messiam in carne nobis conferendorum, cessare debuerunt, postquam in carne exhibitus & beneficia promissa reapse nobis præstita sunt, eique cultus ipse spiritualis, sub ritibus illis comprehensus, absque ullo rituum involucro deferendus erat.

II. Jactant quidem homines Fanatici & incredulitatis filii, præsertim quibus hisce ultimis temporibus Satanas oculos mentis usque adeò excæcavit, ut Deum esse, reclamante universâ rerum naturâ & suâ ipsorummet conscientiâ, negent; jactant, inquam, varias, quibus Scriptura sacra scateat, contradictiones, sed jactant, non demonstrant, vel si qui, quod jactant, exemplis probatum eant, in exemplum afferunt loca quædam difficiliora & obscuriora, quæ primo intuitu inter se pugnare videri possunt, eaque assumunt ut verè pugnantia, utut ab interpretibus vel centies à contradictionis labe vindicata fuerint. Cujus rei exemplum non obscurum præbuit nobis elapso triennio bipedum ille nequissimus Nebulo, Matthias Knuzen, Eiterstadio Holsatus, cujus suprà in th. II. Expl. n. VI. meminimus; qui hic & alibi locorum sparsis mendacibus & blasphemis chartis, quibus ut Scripturae sacrae divinam, quam ei universa semper asseruit Ecclesia, auctoritatem prorsus detraheret, probandum in se recepit, eam dissonare secum & vacillare totam. Id quod in diversis egit chartis, vernaculo partim, partim Latino idiomate consignatis. In Colloquio Cauponis cum tribus diversarum religionum hospitibus, vernacula lingua conscripto, affert loca Joh.XV.27. Act.III.15.& Joh. V.34. item Actor. IX. 7. & c. XX. 9. Joh. V. 29. Esa. XXVI.14. Psal. LXXXVIII. 12. Job. XIV. 22. Luc. XIV.14. Psal. CXXXIV. 3. Luc. XVII. 10. quae partim κατά το ρητον, per EST & NON EST, sibi invicem opponantur, partim κατά διάνοιαν & per consequentiam inter se pugnent. In Epistola verò, Romae VI. Kal. Martii Latino idiomate data, sub initium statim: Possem, inquit, id (puta Christianorum canonem & fundamentum, quod Biblia nuncupant, secum penitus dissonare & vacillare) vel sexcentis per omnes, quà veteris quà Novi Instrumenti libros statuminatum ire exemplis, sed metus est, ne fortean legentibus argumentorum multitudine nauseam creem, idcirco pauca duntaxat in medium proferam, ut ea à lecturientibus eò meliùs possint ponderari. Nihil hîc dicam de mensuris, quarum mentio fit I.Reg. VII.26. & contra II.Paral. IV. 5. quae è diametro (si quid judicare possum) sibi numero contrariantur: nihil etiam dicam de personis, v. c. si conferas Gen.XXVI. 34. cum Gen. XXXVI.2. ibi enim Basmath Esavi uxor dicitur filia Elon Hethitae, hic verò Ismaëlis. Taceo etiam, quod in diversis locis eadem praecipiantur & prohibeantur: sic Matth.XIX. 5. maritae adhaerere, è converso autem Mal.II.16. eam dimittere, marito in mandatis datur. De hisce & non dissimilibus aliis impraesentiarum nihil dicturus sum, hoc autem quin praetermittam,non possum adduci, videlicet canonem istum Christianorum verè Lesbium in Articulis quoque fidei dissonis quasi fidibus sonare. Ita saepenumero inculcatur, mortuos esse resurrecturos, quod uti Christianis τῶν ἀμφῶν lubenter largimur; sic illi eo ipso ipsorum Canone concedente, concedant nobis vicissim necesse est, mortuos non resurrecturos esse; quòd partim xτ' ρητὸν, partim etiam κτ' διάνοιαν, id quod cum τῷ ῥητῷ coincidit, asseritur in seq.locis, Esa. XXVI. 14. Psal. LXXXVIII. 11. Psal. LXXVIII. 40. Ecclesiaft. III, 19. Hiob. XIV. 12. & aliis. Quò refert etiam in alia charta, quòd Luc. XIV. 14. justi, & Luc. XX. 35. qui digni habebuntur futuro seculo, resurrecturi dicuntur; alibi verò, & quidem Psal. CXLIII. 3. dicatur, neminem esse justum, neque quenquam esse dignum, sed omnes, si vel maximè fecerint omnia, quæ ipsis mandata sunt, fateri tandem cogisse esse servos inutiles, Luc. XVII. 10.

III. Verùm enim verò locis adductis nihil minùs statuminatur, quàm quod improbus ille Scripturæ sacræ obtrectator statuminandum in se recepit: nempe Scripturam sacram pugnare secum, & dissonis sonare fidibus, sive, quod eodem redit, in ea veras dari contradictiones, non apparentes tantùm: quin contrà potiùs, dum loca ad id statuminandum firmiora magisque idonea invenire non potuit, harmoniæ Scripturæ V. T. cum Novo omniumque utriusque partium inter se consensioni exactissimæ imprudens haud obscurum perhibuit testimonium. Conferenti enim ea inter se in suo contextu & genuino sensu, & collata ad leges contradictionis expendenti, patebit oppidò, nullam contradictionem veram, pugnam veram nullam in illius contineri. Ubi ante omnia monemus, ad veram contradictionem non sufficere qualemcunque affirmationem & negationem, ut insulsissimè auctor supponit: Inter EST, inquiens, & NON EST, affirmationem & negationem, non est apparens, sed vera contradictio; sed requiri, ut idem de eodem, secundum idem, simul & eodem tempore ac respectu affirmetur & negetur, quod uti notissimum est, & pueris etiam in omnibus libellis Logicis inculcatur, ita probatione non eget. In locis adductis autem ne quidem unum datur exemplum, de quo certò & indubitatò constet, quòd idem de eodem, secundum idem, simul & eodem tempore ac respectu affirmetur & negetur, ut per inductionem patebit.

Et quidem ut à locis, in Colloquio Cauponis allatis faciamus initium, Joh. XV. 27. & Act. III. 15. agitur de testimonio, quod Apostoli, velut αὐτόπται testes de Christo, ejusque doctrina, miraculis, deque passione, morte & resurrectione ipsius hominum causâ inter homines, ut eos ad fidem Christi adducerent, perhibebant & perhibituri erant: quod testimonium tantum abest, ut unquam rejecerit, aut ullibi locorum Scripturæ rejecisse memoretur Christus, ut eum in finem po-


### chose them for the Apostleship and admitted them into His own fellowship, so…

chose them for the Apostleship and admitted them into His own fellowship, so that they might be perpetual hearers and spectators of His words and deeds, and having departed afterwards into the whole world, they might openly testify among all mortals what they had heard and seen, Acts 1:8, ch. 5:32. But in John 5:34, Christ speaks of human testimony, which He Himself, by Himself and by reason of Himself, would need to prove the divinity both of His person and of His mission from the Father, and He says in v. 34 that He does not for this purpose require or receive testimony from man, even though John bore testimony concerning Him: for this was not done because He Himself by Himself stood in need of it to assert the divinity of His person and His mission: for He has testimony greater than any exception, namely the testimony of the works which He performs, which are truly divine, and of His Father Himself; but [He mentions it] for the sake of the Jews themselves, so that, induced by the testimony of John, which they esteemed highly, they might believe in Him and be saved. The whole context demands this sense. However, these two assertions do not conflict with each other: Christ receives testimony from man, namely from the Apostles, to be borne concerning Him among men and for the sake of men, so that they may be induced by it to faith in Him, which in substance is contained in the passages John 15:27 and Acts 3:15, etc.: Christ does not receive testimony from man by Himself and by reason of Himself, as if it were necessary to Him for manifesting the divinity of both His person and His mission from the Father: since He has other greater testimonies that are abundantly sufficient for Him, namely the testimony both of His own truly divine works and of His Father: which is held in John 5:34 ff. These two propositions, I say, do not conflict with each other, since they do not affirm and deny the same thing about the same thing, according to the same thing, and in the same respect, which is nevertheless necessarily required for a true contradiction.

Nor can a contradiction be proven from the cited passages Acts 9:7 and ch. 22:9. For what Luke says in the former passage: 'But the men who were his companions on the journey stood speechless, hearing indeed the voice, but seeing no one'; it is understood either of the voice that fell from heaven and was heard by Paul, or of the voice of Paul, speaking with the Lord and responding to the voice that fell from heaven. If they are understood in the latter way, the sense will be: οἱ ᾗ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες ἀυτῷ, 'But the men who were his (Paul's) companions on the journey stood speechless, ἀκόοντες τῆς φωνῆς (ἀυτõ) hearing the voice,' namely his, Paul's, 'yet seeing no one' (with whom he was speaking). And thus every contradiction will vanish. For

Acts 22:9. Paul speaks expressly of the voice of him who was speaking with him. However, they do not conflict with one another: Paul's companions heard the voice of Paul, responding to the voice brought from heaven, which Luke (according to the later explanation) says in Acts 9:7; and Paul's companions did not hear the voice of him who was speaking with him from heaven: which Paul asserts in express words in chapter 22:9; since the same thing is not affirmed and denied of the same subject, but it is affirmed of Paul's companions that they heard the voice of Paul speaking with the Lord, and it is denied of the same that they heard the voice of the Lord speaking with Paul. But if anyone perhaps prefers to understand the words of Luke in chapter 9:7 also concerning the voice that descended from heaven, although I do not see what necessity compels this, then it can well be understood as a certain confused perception, according to a certain obscure and unarticulated sound, just as in John 12:29 the promiscuous crowd heard the voice that descended from heaven to Christ; but according to a certain unarticulated and confused sound, of which some said that thunder had been heard, others that an angel had spoken with Christ; however, the words of Paul in chapter 22:9 can be understood as a distinct perception, not only regarding the sound, but also regarding the sense: by which very thing the contradiction will again be removed. For they do not conflict with one another: Paul's companions heard the voice brought from heaven, confusedly and regarding the sound, yet without the sense, and: Paul's companions did not hear the voice brought from heaven distinctly and regarding the sense. For again, the same thing is not affirmed and denied of the same subject in the same respect, which we just said is required for a true contradiction. In short: whoever wishes to carve out a conflict or true contradiction from these two passages compared with each other, he must demonstrate with invincible arguments that Luke and Paul are speaking of one and the same voice, and that in the same sense and respect in which Paul in Acts 22:9 says that his companions did not hear the voice of him who was speaking with him, Luke in chapter 9:7 says in that very same sense and respect that they did hear the voice, namely of him who was speaking with Paul. Which is clearly impossible to demonstrate.

The matter is the same with the passages cited from 1 Kings 7:26 and 2 Chronicles 4:5, in which the magnitude and capacity of the sea cast from bronze is described, and it is said in the former that it contained two thousand baths; in the latter, that it contained three thousand baths: in which there can be neither error nor contradiction. For in both passages its magnitude and capacity are described with the highest agreement, that its diameter from one side of the brim to the other was ten cubits, and the height indeed five cubits, and the total circumference thirty cubits. Therefore, according to the description of one, that bronze vessel could not hold more or fewer baths than according to the description of the other. However, that in one place it is said to have contained two thousand baths, and in the other three thousand, it is the common opinion of interpreters that in one place its capacity is described according to the number of baths which was ordinarily brought in by the King's decree; but in the other, according to the number of baths which it held when filled completely to the brim. And not badly. For the brim of the sea, fashioned in the likeness of the brim of a cup or of lily flowers, was added not so much for daily use as for the sake of ornament, and therefore it is entirely consistent with the truth that, by common and ordinary law, that sea was accustomed to be filled not to the brim, but up to the lip, and with this view the author of the books of Kings said that it contained two thousand baths, namely for the number of baths which was brought in by ordinary and common law: which is its capacity up to the lip, the capacity of the lip not being computed. In 2 Chronicles 4:5, however, its total capacity seems to be described, from the bottom to the very top, and it is said to have been three thousand baths, so that the capacity of the lip constituted a third part of the total capacity. Nor does it seem to have happened rashly or by chance that the capacity of the aforementioned bronze sea was described in such different ways. For the books of Chronicles were written after the books of Kings, and just as many other things, omitted in these, or handed down more briefly or obscurely, are supplied in those, or are more fully described and explained, so it is truly consistent that their author wished here also to supply what could be desired in the former book of these, and with the capacity of the aforementioned sea up to the lip already described in this one, to describe its total capacity, from the bottom to the very top: which is not a contradiction, but a double description of one and the same thing: one according to its total capacity; the other according to its more important part: both true, and in every way consistent with each other; for a different consideration of the same capacity, one according to the part by which it extends from the bottom to the lip, and the other according to its whole by which it extends from the bottom to the top, removes every contradiction. For it is not contradictory that the capacity of the sea, according to one consideration, was two thousand; but according to the other, was not three thousand baths, since for a true conflict or contradiction it is required that the same thing be affirmed and denied of the same thing in the same respect. And these must remain fixed and immovable for so long, until the modern calumniators of the Scriptures shall have proven that in both places the entire capacity of the aforementioned sea is described, from the bottom to the top: which they will never prove.

Furthermore, what is objected, that Basmath, the wife of Esau, is called in Gen. 26:34 the daughter of Elon the Hittite; but in chapter 36:3 the same is called the daughter of Ishmael, is most false. For Basmath, who in Gen. 36:3 is called the daughter of Ishmael, was not that same one who in chapter 26:34 is called the daughter of Elon the Hittite, but another distinct from her. For she who is called the daughter of Elon was of two names, and by one name was called Basmath; by the other she was called Adah, as the passages of Gen. 26:34 and chapter 36:2, compared with each other, clearly show. And this one Esau had taken as a wife at the beginning, before Jacob went into exile to Mesopotamia. But the other Basmath, the sister of Nebajoth, who was also of two names, and by the other name was called Mahalath, as is evident from Gen. 28:9, was the daughter of Ishmael, whom Esau took as a wife after the departure of his brother Jacob to Mesopotamia, and Moses [mentions] in Gen. 36:4. He distinguishes [her] from the other Basmath, otherwise called Adah, because the latter bore Eliphaz to Esau; the former bore Reuel. By this very fact, every conflict, every contradiction, is again removed.

Then this also is false, which those detractors of Holy Scripture allege, that what is commanded in one place of Scripture is forbidden in another: to prove which, the passages brought forward from Matt. 19:5 and Mal. 2:16 are clearly unsuitable. For in Matt. 19, Christ deals with the rash divorces of the Jews, by which they dismissed their wives for any cause whatsoever by giving a bill of divorce, which was permitted to them in the Mosaic law, Deut. 24:1 ff., on account of their σκληροκαρδίαν [hardness of heart], and He teaches that this custom conflicts with the primeval institution of marriage, by the force of which male and female are joined into one flesh by a bond so indissoluble that it is not lawful for a husband to dismiss his wife, except for the one cause of fornication. By this very fact He teaches, indeed, that by the force of the primeval institution that rash dismissal of wives is forbidden, even though this very bad custom was tolerated among the Jews on account of their σκληροκαρδίαν, and to avoid greater evils. Nor is the contrary commanded in Mal. 2:16. For the words of the Prophet: כי שנא שלח If he hates, let him

Latin:

tius ad Apostolatum illos elegerit, & in suum consortium adsciverit, ut suorum dictorum factorumq; auditores & spectatores perpetui essent, & digressi postea in universum mundum, quæ audiverant ac viderant, inter mortales omnes palam testarentur, Act. I. 8. c. V. 32. Sed Joh. V, 34. loquitur Christus de testimonio humano, quo per se & ratione sui ipsemet egeret ad divinitatem cùm personæ tùm missionis suæ à Patre probandam, dicitque v. 34. se ad hoc non requirere, non recipere testimonium ab homine, utut Johannes testimonium de se perhibuerit: hoc enim non factum esse, quod ipse per se eo ad asserendam divinitatem personæ & missionis suæ indigeret: se enim habere testimonium omni exceptione majus, nempe testimonium operum, quæ patret, verè divinorum, & ipsiusmet Patris sui; sed propter ipsosmet Judæos, ut Johannis testimonio, quod magni æstimabant, inducti crederent in ipsum, & salvi fierent. Quem sensum totus exigit contextus. Non autem pugnant inter se duæ assertiones hæ: Christus recipit testimonium ab homine, nempe ab Apostolis de se inter homines & propter homines, ut eo ad fidem ipsius inducantur, perhibendum, quæ quoad rem continetur in locis Joh. XV. 27. & Act. III. 15. &c: Christus non recipit testimonium ab homine per se & ratione sui, quasi ad manifestandam divinitatem cùm personæ tùm missionis suæ à Patre sibi necessarium esset: cùm alia majora sibíque abundè sufficientia habeat testimonia, nempe testimonium cùm operum suorum verè divinorum, tùm Patris sui: quæ habetur Joh. V. 34. seq. Non, inquam, pugnant inter se duæ hæ propositiones, cùm non idem, secundum idem, & eodem respectu de eodem affirment & negent, quod tamen ad contradictionem veram necessariò requiritur.

Neque contradictio evinci potest ex locis Act. IX 7. & c. XXII. 9. citatis. Nam quod in loco priori Lucas dicit: Viri autem, qui erant ei comites itineris, stabant attoniti, audientes quidem vocem, neminem tamen videntes; vel intelligitur de voce, cœlitus delapsâ, & à Paulo auditâ, vel de voce Pauli, cum Domino colloquentis, & ad vocem cœlitùs delapsam respondentis. Si posteriori modo intelligantur, sensus erit: οἱ ᾗ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες ἀυτῷ, Viri autem, qui ei (Paulo) comites itineris erant, stabant attoniti, ἀκόοντες τῆς φωνῆς (ἀυτõ) audientes vocem, scilicet ejus, Pauli, neminem tamen (cum quo loqueretur) videntes. Atque sic contradictio omnis expirabit. Nam

Act. XXII. 9. loquitur Paulus expresse de voce ejus, qui secum loquebatur. Non pugnant autem inter se: comites Pauli audiebant vocem Pauli, ad vocem cœlitus delatam respondentis, quod Act. IX. 7. Lucas (juxta explicationem posteriorem) dicit; & comites Pauli vocem ejus, qui cœlitus cum eo loquebatur, non audiebant: quod cap. XXII. 9. Paulus conceptis verbis asserit: cùm non idem de eodem affirmetur & negetur, sed de comitibus Pauli affirmetur, quòd vocem Pauli, cum Domino loquentis, audiverint, & negetur de iisdém, quòd vocem Domini, cum Paulo loquentis, audiverint. Quòd si quis fortè verba Lucæ c. IX. 7. malit etiam de voce cœlitùs delapsâ accipere, quamvis quæ necessitas cogat, non videã, tùm benè id poterit intelligi de perceptione quadam confusa, secundum sonum quendam obscurum & inconditum, sicut Joh. XX. 29. promiscua plebs audiebat vocem cœlitus delapsam ad Christum; sed secundum sonum quendam inconditum & confusum, quorum alii dicebant, tonitru esse auditum; alii Angelum locutum esse cum Christo; Pauli verba autem c. XXII. 9. intelligi poterunt de perceptione distincta, non quoad sonum solùm, sed etiam quoad sensum: quo ipso rursum tolletur contradictio. Non enim pugnant inter se: Comites Pauli audiebant vocem, cœlitùs delatam, confusè & quoad sonum, absque sensu tamen, &: Comites Pauli non audiebant vocem cœlitùs delatam distinctè & quoad sensum. Rursum enim non idem secundum idem de eodem affirmatur & negatur, quod ad veram contradictionem requiri modò diximus. Breviter: qui ex hisce duobus locis, inter se collatis, pugnam sive contradictionem veram exsculpere vult, eum oportet invictis rationibus demonstrare, Lucam & Paulum loqui de una & eadem voce, & quo sensu & respectu Paulus Act. XXII. 9. dicit: Comites suos non audivisse vocem ejus, qui secum loquebatur, eo prorsus sensu & respectu dicere Lucam c. IX. 7. eos audivisse vocem, puta ejus, qui cum Paulo loquebatur. Quod demonstratu planè impossibile est.

Perinde res habet cum locis, ex 1. Reg. VII. 26. & II. Paral. IV. 5. citatis, in quibus describitur magnitudo & capacitas maris, ex ære fusi, diciturque in illo, quòd bis mille bathos; in hoc, quod ter mille bathos continuerit: in quo nec error nec contradictio esse potest. In loco utroque enim describitur ejus magnitudo & capacitas summo consensu, quòd ejus diameter ab una labri parte ad alteram decem cubitorum, altitudo verò quinque cubitorum, & circumferentia tota triginta cubitorum fuerit. Non ergò juxta unius descriptionem vas illud æneum plures aut pauciores capere potuit bathos, quám juxta descriptionem alterius. Quod autem in loco uno illud bis mille, in altero ter mille bathos continuisse dicitur, communis interpretum sententia est, in loco uno describi capacitatem ejus juxta numerum bathorum, qui ex instituto Regis ordinariè inferebatur; in altero autem juxta numerum bathorum, quem totum, ad summitatem usque impletum, capiebat. Nec malè.
