Labium enim maris, ad similitudinem labii calicis aut florum lilii confectum, non tam quotidiani usus, quàm ornatus causâ superadditum fuit, & proinde vero prorsus consentaneum est, de lege communi & ordinariè mare illud non ad summitatem, sed ad labium usque impleri consvevisse, & hoc intuitu Auctorem librorum Regum dixisse, illud continuisse bis mille bathos, pro numero scilicet bathorum : qui de lege ordinaria & communi inferebatur : quæ est capacitas ejus ad labium usque, capacitate labii non computatâ. In II. Paral. IV. 5. autem describi videtur tota ejus capacitas, à fundo ad summitatem usque, eamque ter mille bathorum fuisse dici, ut ita capacitas labii tertiam partem capacitatis totius constituerit. Neque temerè aut casu contigisse videtur, ut ita diversimodè describeretur capacitas memorati maris ænei. Nam libri Paralipomenon conscripti sunt post libros Regum, & quemadmodum alia multa, in his prætermissa, aut breviùs vel obscuriùs tradita, in illis supplentur, vel uberiùs describuntur & declarantur, ita vero consentaneum est, Auctorem illorum voluisse hîc etiã supplere, quod in horum libro priori desiderari poterat, & suppositâ capacitate prædicti maris ad labrum usque, in hoc jam descriptâ, capacitatem ejus totam, à fundo ad summitatem usque describere : quæ non est contradictio, sed unius & ejusdem rei duplex descriptio: una secundum ejus capacitatem totam; altera secundum ejusdem potiorem partem : utraque vera, sibique per omnia consentiens; Diversa enim consideratio capacitatis ejusdem, una secundùm partem, quâ à fundo ad labrum; & altera secundum se totam, quâ à fundo ad summitatem usque se porrigit, tollit omnem contradictionem. Non enim inter se pugnant, capacitatem maris, juxta unam considerationem, fuisse bis mille; juxta alteram verò, non fuisse bu, sed ter mille bathorum, cùm ad veram pugnam sive contraditionem requiratur, ut idem de eodem secundum idem affirmetur & negetur. Atque hæc tamdiu maneant oportet fixa & immota, donec moderni Scripturarum calumniatores evicerint, utroque in loco describi capacitatem prædicti maris totam, à fundo ad summitatem usque: quod nunquam evincent.

Quod porro objicitur, Basmath, Esavi uxorem, dici Gen. XXVI. 34. filiam Elonism, Hethitæ; cap. XXXVI. 3. autem eandem dici filiam Ismaëlis, falsissimum est. Nam Basmath, quæ Gen. XXXVI. 3. dicitur filia Ismaëlis, non fuit ea ipsa, quæ c. XXVI. 34. filia Elonism Hitthæi dicitur, sed alia ab ea diversa. Quæ enim Elonism filia dicitur, binominis fuit, & uno nomine Basmath; altero Ada dicta fuit, ut loca Gen. XXVI. 34. & c. XXXVI. 2. inter se collata, liquidò ostendunt. Et hanc initiò Esau duxerat uxorem, priusquam Jacob in Mesopotamiam exulatum iret. Altera verò Basmath, soror Nebajothis, quæ & ipsa binominis, & altero nomine Machalath dicta fuit, ut ex Gen. XXIIX. 9. patet, filia Ismaëlis fuit, quam Esau post abitum fratris Jacobi in Mesopotamiam in uxorem duxit, & Moses Gen. XXXVI. 4. Ab altera Basmath, aliàs Ada dictâ, distinguit, quòd hæc Eliphazum; illa Rehuelem Esavo pepererit. Quo ipso rursum omnis tollitur pugna, contradictio omnis.

Deinde falsum & hoc est, quod illi Scripturæ sacræ obtrectatores obtendunt, quod in uno Scripturæ loco præcipitur, prohiberi in altero: ad quod evincendum, quæ ex Matth. XIX 5. & Mal. II. 16. afferuntur, loca planè inidonea sunt. Nam Matth. XIX. agit Christus de temerariis Judæorum divortiis, quibus dato libello repudii uxores suas dimittebant quacunque de causa, quod in lege Mosaica Deut. XXIV. 1. seqq. ipsis ob σκληροκαρδίαν ipsorum permissum erat, docetque, consuetudinem hanc pugnare cum primæva conjugii institutione, cujus vi jungantur mas & fœmina in unam carnem vinculo ita indissolubili ut uxorem, nisi ob unam stupri causam, dimittere marito non liceat. Quo ipso docet utique, vi primævæ institutionis prohibitam esse temerariam illam uxorum dimissionem, ut tut consuetudo hæc pessima in Judæis ob illorum σκληροκαρδίαν, & ad vitanda majora mala, fuerit tolerata. Neque contrarium præcipitur Mal. II. 16. Nam verba Prophetæ: כי שנא שלח Si oderit, di-


### send her away; (to which the Author undoubtedly points his finger, thinking…

send her away; (to which the Author undoubtedly points his finger, thinking that the dismissal of hated wives, which Christ in Matthew XIX disapproves of and says conflicts with the primordial institution of marriage) can have a double meaning when commanded to them. For they can be referred either to husbands who hate their wives, just as the priests returning from the Babylonian captivity, with whom Malachi was dealing, at that time held their legitimate wives, worn out by age and cares in a long and most calamitous captivity and deformed, in hatred and contempt, and either, according to the custom accepted by the Jews, repudiated them, or, while retaining them, brought in others who were beautiful from neighboring nations, and esteemed and loved them above the former, and that not without their tears and groaning, as is clear from the context of the Prophet; or to God, who hates the custom of repudiating hated wives, although tolerated in the Jews on account of their σκληροκαρδιαν [hardness of heart], yet diametrically opposed to the primordial institution of Marriage. If the words of the Prophet are explained in the former way, then the word שלח, 'let him dismiss,' must be taken permissively, in this sense: If anyone has hated (a wife) worn out by cares and old age in long captivity, let him dismiss her, i.e., it will be permitted to dismiss her, by virtue of the custom tolerated by Moses. For that custom of repudiating hated wives, accepted among the Israelite people, had never been commanded in the divine law. The law which is held in Deut. XXIV. 1. seqq. did not command it, but presupposed it as accepted by use, and tolerated on account of the σκληροκαρδιαν [hardness of heart] of the Jews; but it forbade that anyone should, after the death of another husband, or if she had also been repudiated by him, bring back a once-repudiated woman into his house by right of return, and take her again into his bed. And according to this interpretation, the dismissal of hated wives is not commanded to the priests who returned from the Babylonian captivity to their native land, but since there were two evils: one, that they either retained hated wives in marriage, yet brought in others who were beautiful and beloved with the greatest contempt for them; which some of the aforementioned priests were doing at that time with their perpetual groans and tears; or by giving a bill of divorce, they dismissed them and restored them to their liberty, which the custom accepted among the Jews permitted; Malachi advises that they should choose what was the lesser evil, and rather dismiss the hated wives than treat them so unworthily while retained with others brought in over them. If they are explained according to the latter manner, the sense will be: Because God hates that [act of] dismissing, or that he should dismiss, namely the hated wife, as the infinitive verb [is used] in place of a noun; or [that] the finite [form] of the imperative mood is repeated by way of irony, and the reason for the dissuasion, employed in the preceding verse 15, is rendered, [as to] why those priests ought to beware of the perfidy which they had hitherto exercised against their legitimate wives, either by most unworthily placing them after foreign women introduced over them, or by dismissing the same according to the worst custom of the Jews, namely that God hates that (he should dismiss) which the Jews always had in their mouths, or that custom of dismissing wives. In which sense Franciscus Junius and Johannes Tarnovius interpret the words of Malachi, according to which they will have the force of a prohibition rather than a precept. For what God hates, that is understood to have been prohibited rather than commanded. Whichever sense is chosen, Malachi and Christ always agree most amicably, and do not conflict with one another.

IV. And from these passages produced as an example of contradictions—not apparent, but true—it is clearly evident how ineptly—or shall I say wickedly and perversely?—this most vile scoundrel conducts himself in accusing and arguing for contradictions in Holy Scripture: namely, he twists the words of Scripture, even if they are plain and easy to understand, into a foreign sense, or he appeals to passages which do not concern things necessary to be believed or done, with which Holy Scripture is occupied in itself; but [he appeals to] certain rather obscure circumstances of histories, or different names of persons unknown to us, or a certain diversity in measurements, or something similar: if a certain method of reconciling these could not be rendered by us even in the highest degree, yet Scripture should not on that account be argued to have a contradiction, but at least a difficulty or a certain obscurity in some matters, or in circumstances of things not necessary, to be ascribed to our ignorance, not to any vice or lapse of the writer: which kind of difficulties and obscurities, as every prudent and candid reader will easily understand, detract nothing from the authority and certainty of Holy Scripture.

If these little men wished to deal with the matter seriously, and to examine whether the Canon of Scripture is dissonant or consonant with itself, with the zeal and love of truth as would be fitting, not in histories of things most remote from us, which although they were clear enough to the readers of their own times and places—for to these singular circumstances, shedding light on the whole history, were known and understood; to us, however, destitute of the knowledge of them, they cannot but sometimes produce difficulty and obscurity: they ought not, I say, to cast the eyes of the mind into histories of this kind, but into the very doctrines of faith and morals necessary to be known for salvation, and whether there is one way of salvation, as regards the essentials of faith, one and the same method of obtaining salvation, by which the Holy Scriptures record that all the pious have obtained salvation since the first Adam? Or whether indeed a conflict is found in the very doctrine of faith and morals, and one method of obtaining salvation is inculcated by one writer and in one part of Scripture; another by another and in another part of it, or whether it is recorded that at one time these things, at another time others, and by that one, things different in essentials were believed and observed? For the sake of treating this doctrine sincerely and transmitting it uncorrupted to posterity, the whole Scripture was consigned to writing: as this is and was necessary to be known by all who are to obtain salvation, so it ought to have been and ought to be known at all times. In which, if the whole Scripture harmonizes with itself, there is no reason why we should doubt its consensus in other parts, not concerning matters necessary to be known for salvation, even if in certain more difficult and obscure places, on account of ignorance of places, times, and other circumstances, readers sometimes remain in doubt about them.

V. The Calumniator seems to have noticed this, who, although he has produced in a long series these passages which have nothing to do with the doctrine of faith and morals, which have already been examined and vindicated by us, in order to prove multiple contradictions in Holy Scripture, yet having noticed that they are not suitable for proving the same, he protests that he will no longer speak of these, although by the very fact that he brings them forward as an example of true contradictions, he does speak of them; he promises, however, that he will demonstrate that in the very articles of faith the Scripture sounds as if it were discordant in its seats; and he proceeded to demonstrate this by certain passages concerning the article of the resurrection of the dead. In which places, because he has placed all his strength and defense: for he does not bring forward more passages pertaining either to this or to other articles of faith; it remains to be considered whether perhaps a true contradiction underlies these.

That the dead are to rise again, which the canon of Christians frequently inculcates, he says that he willingly concedes to Christians as one of the matters in dispute; wherefore we shall not linger on proving this dogma. He demands, however, that we in turn concede to him, by that very canon of Scripture of ours asserting it, that the dead are not going to rise again. Because this is so far from being the case, that we concede it is asserted anywhere in our canon of Scriptures either ῥητῶς (expressly) or κατὰ διάνοιαν (by implication), that on the contrary we rather fearlessly assert that the perpetual and everywhere consistent opinion of Holy Scripture is that all the dead in general will rise again, some indeed to eternal life, others to judgment and eternal condemnation, according as they have lived well or ill in this age, and have departed either in faith in Christ or in unbelief, Christ, appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead, expressly teaching thus, John 5:28, it is now incumbent upon the adversaries to produce passages from that same canon of Scriptures of ours by which the contrary is asserted. They produce, however, Isaiah 26:14, Psalm 88:11. Psalm 78:39, Ecclesiastes 3:19, Job 14:12, by which, partly κτ' ῥητὸν (according to the letter), partly also κτ' διάνοιαν (according to the sense), which coincides with the letter, he says it is asserted that the dead are not going to rise again. We shall therefore run through these in order.

Isaiah 26:14, the words have it thus: מתים בל יחיו רפאים בל יקומו, i.e., the dead shall not live, the giants shall not rise: which, since they are from the count of the more difficult and obscure passages of Holy Scripture, in the explanation of which interpreters vary, cannot, and ought not to be opposed to other passages asserting the article concerning the resurrection of the dead in express words clearer even than the rays of the sun, but on the contrary, the more obscure passages ought rather to be explained according to the norm of the others, which are clear and perspicuous. For how will you oppose to clear and perspicuous words, by which it is asserted that the dead will rise again, words that are somewhat obscure and more difficult to explain, concerning the sense of which—whether it is that which you attribute to them, or another—it is not certainly and indubitably established? We do not, however, consider it worth the effort to turn aside to the diverse interpretations of this passage, but we will grant to the adversaries that the Prophet is speaking in it properly and literally about the resurrection of the dead; from the context, however, it is certain that the words, which are indefinite: מתים בל יחיו רפאים בל יקומו, the dead shall not live, the giants (tyrants) shall not rise; cannot be taken universally of all the dead, pious and impious, but ought to be taken only of tyrants and the persecutors and oppressors of the Church. For besides the fact that in the following verse 19, concerning

Latin:

mittat; (ad quæ Auctor haud dubie digitum intendit, ratus dimissionem uxorum exosarum, quam Christus Matth. XIX. improbat & cum primæva institutione conjugii pugnare dicit) iis præcipi, duplicem sensum habere possunt. Referri enim possunt vel ad maritos, qui odio habent uxores suas, sicut reduces ex captivitate Babylonica Sacerdotes, cum quibus Malachiæ res erat, tum temporis suas uxores legitimas, in diuturna & calamitosissima captivitate senio curisque confectas & deformes, odio & contemtui habebant, easque vel, juxta consuetudinem Judæis receptam, repudiabant, vel retentis alias formosas ex vicinis Gentibus superinducebant, & præ illis æstimabant atq; diligebant, idque non absque illarum lacrymis & gemitu, ut ex contextu Prophetæ patet; vel ad Deum, qui consuetudinem repudiandi uxores exosas, licet in Judæis ob illorum σκληροκαρδιαν toleratam, primævæ tamen Conjugii institutioni e diametro adversantem, odio habeat. Si priori modo verba Prophetæ explicentur, tum verbum שלח, dimittat, permissive erit accipiendum, hoc sensu: Si quis odio habuerit (uxorem) curis senioque in captivitate diuturna confectam, dimittat eam, i. e. licebit eam, vi consuetudinis, a Mose toleratæ, dimittere. Nam consuetudo illa repudiandi uxores exosas, in populo Israëlitico recepta, in lege divina nunquam præcepta fuerat. Quæ Deut. XXIV. 1. seqq. habetur Lex, non præcipiebat, sed præsupponebat illam, velut usu receptam, & ob Judæorum σκληροκαρδιαν toleratam; prohibebat vero ne quis repudiatam semel post obitum mariti alterius, vel si ab eo etiam repudiata esset, postliminio in domum suam reduceret, & rursum in thorum adscisceret. Atque juxta hanc interpretationem Sacerdotibus, ex captivitate Babylonica in terram patriam reversis, non præcipitur dimissio uxorum exosarum, sed cùm duo essent mala: unum, quòd uxores exosas vel in conjugio quidem retinebant, iis tamen alias formosas & dilectas cum ipsarum contemtu maximo superinducebant; quod tum faciebant quidam ex memoratis sacerdotibus cum perpetuis illarum gemitibus & lacrymis; vel dato libello repudii, eas dimittebant & suæ libertati restituebant, quod consvetudo inter Judæos recepta permittebat; svadet Malachias, ut quod minus esset, eligerent, & dimitterent potiùs uxores exosas, quàm retentas cum aliis superinductis tam indignè tractarent. Si modo posteriori explicentur, sensus erit: Quia odio habet Deus illud dimittere, vel illud dimittat, scilicet uxorem exosam, ut verbu infinitivum loco nominis; vel finitum imperativi modi per ironiam repetitum sit, & ratio dehortationis, in præced. v. 15. adhibitæ, reddatur, cur sibi Sacerdotes illi cavere deberent à perfidia, quam in suas uxores legitimas hactenus exercuerant, vel indignissimè illas superinductis alienigenis postponendo, vel juxta pessimam Judæorum consuetudinem easdem dimittendo, nempe quòd Deus illud (dimittat) quod semper Judæi in ore habebant, sive consuetudinem illam dimittendi uxores, odio habeat. Quô sensu Franciscus Junius & Johannes Tarnovius verba Malachiæ interpretantur, juxta quem prohibitionis potiùs, quàm præcepti vim habebunt. Quod enim Deus odio habet, id prohibuisse potiùs, quàm præcepisse intelligitur. Uter eligatur sensus, semper Malachias & Christus amicissimè consentiunt, non autem inter se pugnant.

IV. Atque ex his in exemplum contradictionum, non apparentium, sed verarum, productis locis liquidò patet, quàm, ineptè? an nequiter & perversè dicam? hic Nebulo nequissimus in accusanda & contradictionum arguenda Scriptura sacra se gerat: nempe detorquet verba Scripturæ, etsi plana & intellectu facilia, in alienum sensum, vel provocat ad loca, quæ non res creditu factuve necessarias, in quibus per se Scriptura sacra occupatur; sed historiarum circumstantias quasdam obscuriosculas, vel personarum nobis ignotarum nomina diversa, vel diversitatem quandam in mensuris, aut simile quid concernunt: quorum certa conciliandi ratio si vel maximè reddi à nobis non posset, non tamen contradictionis propterea Scriptura arguenda esset, sed difficultatis saltem aut obscuritatis cujusdam in aliquibus rebus, aut rerum circumstantiis non necessariis, nostræ ignorantiæ, non Scriptoris alicui vitio aut lapsui adscribendæ: cujusmodi difficultates & obscuritates auctoritati & certitudini Scripturæ sacræ nihil derogare, facilè quisque prudens & candidus lector intelliget.

Si seriò rem agere, & dissonetne? an consonet secum Scripturæ Canon? studio & amore veritatis, uti par esset, scrutari vellent hi homunciones, non in historias rerum à nobis remotissimarũ, quæ etsi suorum temporum & locorum lectoribus claræ satis fuerunt; his enim circumstantiæ singulares, historiæ toti lucem affundentes, cognitæ ac perspectæ fuerunt; nobis tamen, illarum notitiâ destitutis, non possunt non difficultatem quandoque & obscuritatem parere: non, inquam, in hujusmodi historias, sed in ipsas ad salutem cognitu necessarias fidei & morum doctrinas conjicere oculos mentis deberent, & sitne una, quoad substantialia fidei, via salutis, una eademq; salutis consequendæ ratio, quâ inde à primo Adamo pios omnes salutem consecutos esse Scripturæ sacræ memorant? an verò in ipsa fidei & morum doctrina inveniatur pugna, & alia consequendæ salutis ratio ab uno Scriptore & in una Scripturæ parte; alia ab alio & in alia ejus parte inculcetur, aut alio tempore hæc, alio alia, & ab illa in substantialibus diversa credita & observata esse memoretur? Hujus enim doctrinæ sincerè tractandæ, & incorruptè ad posteritatem transmittendæ causâ confignata est Scriptura tota: hæc ut omnibus salutem adepturis cognitu necessaria est & fuit, ita omni tempore notâ esse debuit debetque. In qua si consonet secum Scriptura universa, nihil causæ est, cur de ejus consensu in cæteris partibus, res ad salutem cognitu necessarias non concernentibus, dubitemus, utut in quibusdam locis difficilioribus & obscurioribus, ob locorum, temporum, aliarumque circumstantiarum ignorantiam, lectores nonnunquam dubii in illis hæreant.

V. Hoc Calumniator animadvertisse videtur, qui licet hæc ad fidei & morum doctrinam nihil attinentia loca, quæ à nobis jam excussa & vindicata sunt, ad evincendas multiplices Scripturæ sacræ contradictiones longâ serie produxerit, animadverso tamen, quòd ad easdem evincendas idonea non sint, protestatur, de his se jam non dicturum, quamvis eo ipso, quod ea in exemplum verarum contradictionum adfert, de illis dicat; pollicetur verò, se demonstraturum, in ipsis articulis fidei Scripturam dissonis quasi sedibus sonare; idque locis quibusdam, articulum de resurrectione mortuorum concernentibus, demonstratum ivit. Quibus in locis quia robur & præsidium omne positum habet: plura enim vel ad hunc vel ad alios articulos fidei spectantia loca non adfert; num hisce forsan vera subsit contradictio, considerandum superest.

Quòd mortui resurrecturi sint, inculcare canonem Christianorum sæpenumero, dicit se Christianis τῶν ἀμφῶν lubentem concedere: cui dogmati probando proinde non immorabimur. Postulat verò, ut nos vicissim sibi concedamus, eo ipso nostro canone Scripturæ asserente, mortuos non esse resurrecturos. Quod quia tantum abest, ut in nostro Scripturarum canone ullibì locorum sive ῥητῶς sive κατὰ διάνοιαν asseri concedamus, ut contrà potiùs intrepidè asseramus, Scripturæ sacræ perpetuam sibique undiquaque constantem sententiam esse, mortuos in universum omnes resurrecturos, alios quidem ad vitam æternam, alios ad judicium & condemnationem æternam, prout benè vel malè in hoc seculo vixerint, & vel in fide in Christum, vel in incredulitate decesserint, expressè sic docente Christo, constituto à Deo viventium ac mortuorum judice, Joh. V. 28. producenda jam incumbent adversariis loca ex eodem Scripturarum canone nostro, quibus contrarium asseratur. Producunt autem Esa. XXVI. v. 14. Psal. LXXXVIII. v. 11. Psal. LXXVIII. v. 39. Eccl. III. v. 19. Hiob. XIV. v. 12. quibus partim κτ' ῥητὸν, partim etiam κτ' διάνοιαν, id quod cum τῷ ῥητῷ coincidat, asseri ait, mortuos non esse resurrecturos. Ea igitur ordine percurremus.

Esa. XXVI. 14. verba habent ita: מתים בל יחיו רפאים בל יקומו, i. e. mortui non vivent, Gigantes non resurgent: quæ cùm ex censu sint difficiliorum & obscuriorum Scripturæ sacræ locorum, in quorum explicatione Interpretes variant, non possunt, neque debent aliis, articulum de resurrectione mortuorum expressis & vel ipsis radiis solaribus clarioribus verbis asserentibus locis opponi, sed contrà potius loca obscuriora, ad normam cæterorum, quæ clara & perspicua sunt, explicanda sunt. Quomodo enim verbis claris ac perspicuis, quibus mortuos resurrecturos esse asseritur, oppones verba obscuriuscula & explicatu difficiliora, de quorum sensu, sitne is, quem tu iis tribuis? an alius? non certò & indubitatò constat? Non autem operæ pretium ducimus ad diversas loci hujus interpretationes diverti, sed dabimus adversariis, Prophetam loqui in eo propriè & ad literam de resurrectione mortuorum, ex contextu tamen certum est, verba, quæ indefinita sunt: מתים בל יחיו רפאים בל יקומו mortui non vivent, Gigantes (tyranni) non resurgent; non posse accipi universaliter de omnibus mortuis, piis & impiis, sed tantùm de tyrannis & Ecclesiæ persecutoribus & oppressoribus accipi oportere. Præterquam enim, quod in seq. v. 19. de


### the pious, who are the Lord's, and have fallen asleep in the Lord, a different…

the pious, who are the Lord's, and have fallen asleep in the Lord, a different judgment is brought, and it is said in set words: יחיו מתיך your dead shall live, (O God) my corpse shall rise again: Awake and praise (the Lord) you who dwell in the dust, etc. The words immediately preceding in v. 13 also contain certain things about foreign lords or tyrants, who have lorded over the Church and oppressed it, just as Pharaoh once oppressed the Israelites with most grievous servitude, yet they were destroyed by God, as the Egyptians were once suffocated in the Red Sea and destroyed by the just judgment of God. And the words of the Prophet speak of these dead, saying: מתים בל יחיו the dead, that is, those who lorded over us and were killed by you, O Lord, shall not live. Whence, for the sake of exegesis, it is immediately subjoined: רפאים בל יקומו Giants, i.e. tyrants, who oppressed us, as the Giants once oppressed the pious, shall not rise again; and the reason is added: because you, O Lord, have destroyed them, by a just judgment, and have wiped out all memory of them. But those whom God destroys in his wrath and his severe judgment, they shall not live any longer, nor shall they rise again. This is the sense of the words, if we insist on the propriety of the letter, as we believe we must insist on it here along with most Interpreters. But because these predicates: they shall not live, they shall not rise again; can be understood either simply, that they shall live in no way at all, neither in a blessed nor a miserable kind of life, and shall not rise again at all, neither to glory nor to disgrace and damnation, in which way they ought to be understood here must be investigated from other parallel passages. But Christ says in John V. 28 in most clear words, first indeed: πάντες ALL, who are in the graves, shall hear the voice of the Son of man, and shall come forth. Therefore these tyrants and impious oppressors of the Church, destroyed by the just judgment of God, shall hear it and shall come forth, and thus shall rise again. Therefore the words of the Prophet in this place: The dead (the impious) shall not live, the tyrants (and oppressors of the Church) shall not rise again, cannot be understood absolutely and simply, that they shall live in no way at all, neither in a blessed nor a miserable kind of life, and shall not rise again at all, neither to a blessed life nor to damnation. Then he says, in equally clear words, that those who have done good shall come forth at the voice of the Son of man from the graves unto the resurrection of life (namely, blessed and everlasting), but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment or condemnation. Therefore the dead impious also and the tyrants, whom God has destroyed by a just judgment, shall come forth at the voice of the Son of man into the resurrection of judgment and condemnation. Therefore they shall live, but not well, happily, and in joy, as the blessed, but most miserably and in perpetual sorrow and torment: they shall rise again, yet not to eternal life, but to eternal damnation. Whence what is said in the words of the Prophet: they shall not live, they shall not rise again, is not to be understood simply, but in a certain manner and sense: namely, they shall not live, that is, with a happy and blessed life, which alone κατ' ἐξοχὴν and simply said is the life of the other world: but an unhappy life, and one damned to perpetual miseries and torments, is rather to be called death than life, and it is also called in the Scriptures the second death, Apoc. XX. 6. 14.

That this is the genuine sense of the words of the Prophet is evident even from this, that in v. 14 and 19 the dead impious and tyrants, and the dead pious, who are of God and have fallen asleep in the Lord, are opposed to one another, and of the latter it is expressly said that they are to live and to rise again, and to praise God; but of the former that they are not to live, not to rise again. But just as Scripture everywhere expressly testifies that the pious are to live a blessed life and to rise again to a blessed life: see John V. 29, Matt. XXV. 34. Dan. XII. 2. so it is asserted with equal certainty in the same places that the impious and tyrants are not to live a blessed life, nor to rise again to a blessed life, and the thing itself therefore speaks, that the words alleged from Isa. XXVI. 14 are not to be taken simply, that they are not to rise again at all (as those calumniators take them), but in a qualified sense, namely that the impious and tyrants, destroyed by the just judgment of God, are not to live a happy and blessed life, are not to rise again to a blessed and glorious life.

Then Ps. LXXVIII. 39, these are the words: ויזכר כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב And he remembered that they are flesh, a spirit or wind that passeth away, and cometh not again. Which clearly do not treat of the resurrection of the dead, but of the fragility of human life, which the Psalmist compares to wind, quickly passing away, and not returning to where it came from, and the sense is: that God in His wrath remembered that man is flesh, i.e., fragile, caducous, subject to various falls on account of the corruption of nature; that he quickly departs from this life, as the wind departs, and once he has departed from this life, he does not return to the same, as the wind does not return to where it came from. But concerning whether a fragile man, who like the wind quickly departs, and does not return to this fragile life, is to rise again on the last day at the voice of Christ the judge, not even a word is treated here; it is only the case that this is denied. The same reasoning applies to the passages cited from Ps. 88:11 and Job 14:12. In both, the subject is the return or resurrection of the dead to this life. And in the former passage, the most afflicted Psalmist calls upon God in his immense calamities, by which he was very nearly overwhelmed, and he asks that He hasten His help, lest, if He delay it too long, he perish, overwhelmed by the variety and magnitude of his afflictions, and he adds in v. 11: הלמתים תעשה פלא אם רפאים יקומו יודך i.e., Will you work a wonder for the dead? Will the dead rise and praise you? By which he gives the reason why he asks for help so urgently and not to be delayed any longer: namely, that if it were delayed longer, there is a danger that he might succumb to his calamities and perish; but it is not customary for God to recall the dead from death to this life by a miracle, so that they might praise Him among the living and give Him thanks for His help and deliverance. Whence he well adds: Will the dead rise and PRAISE you? That this is to be understood concerning a resurrection to this life, and concerning confession, praise, and thanksgiving in these lands in the assembly of the living, the underlying subject matter and the whole context prove. In the same manner, Job in chapter 14:12 speaks of a resurrection to this earthly life, not of the resurrection by which, toward the end of the world, all the dead are to come forth at the voice of Christ the Judge. Which, again, the whole context proves. The most afflicted Man complains of the miserable condition of man, and he shows that it is worse than the lot and condition of other, more ignoble things, among other reasons from this: that if a tree is cut down, or withers from old age, it afterwards sprouts again, and budding, is renewed to the state in which it was before; but man, if he dies, is nowhere to be found on earth anymore: he does not rise again and is not renewed to this life, he does not awaken and is not raised up, until the heavens perish. Where not only the comparison of mortal man with a tree compels us to understand the words of Job concerning his natural reviviscence or resurrection to this life: for in this the lot of the tree is shown to be better than that of man, in that the former, when cut down or withering from old age, sprouts again of itself and according to the course of nature and is renewed to the state in which it had been; but this man, once dead, does not revive of himself and according to the course of nature, he is not renewed to the state in which he had been, that is, to this life; but also the restriction added in the text: עד בלתי שמים until the heavens they will not rise, they will not awaken from sleep, which is an indication that the holy man does not deny that the dead will rise again at the end of the world, when the heavens will perish, but he denies at least that, while the heavens exist, according to the course of nature, they are to rise again into this life, just as trees that have been cut down, according to the course of nature, sprout again into that life which they had lived before.

Finally, Ecclesiastes chapter III. 19 speaks of the end and death of man according to the judgment of the senses, and by reason of external events and occurrences falling upon the senses, which men and beasts experience alike. The same changes befall both, namely old age, diseases, pains, and finally death. For the difference between men and brutes, as far as their death is concerned, cannot be detected by the senses, but if one must stand by the judgment of the senses, men will be like beasts. For as a man dies, so also does a beast: both live while the spirit is in them, but when they have breathed out their spirit, the corpse of each lies without motion, and both rot and are turned into the earth from which they were made. By this very thing, however, Ecclesiastes does not deny that there is otherwise a huge difference between man and beasts, and among other things this difference also, that beasts will never rise again, but men will indeed rise again from the dead on the last day. For in the preceding v. 16 and 17 he confesses that he saw under the sun the place of judgment and the place of justice, and having detected impiety everywhere, he said in his heart that God would judge the just and the impious in his own time (on that day of universal judgment), and at the end of Chapter XII. 14 he says openly: that God will bring every work into judgment, even the hidden one, whether it be good or evil; which, without the prior resurrection of the dead, cannot happen. And although in chapter III. v. 2 he seems to call into doubt whether the spirit of man, when it is dissolved from the body, tends upward and remains surviving, while the spirit of a beast tends downward under the earth and perishes with the body: nevertheless this also must be understood concerning the judgment of the senses, by which this difference intervening between men and beasts cannot be noticed: but below in chapter XII. v. 7 he affirms without any hesitation that the body of man, after the soul has departed from it, will return to the earth as it was before, but the spirit to God who gave it. And from these things everyone understands that even in Ecclesiastes nothing is found which contradicts the article concerning the resurrection of the dead. They have nothing more correct, which he produced in the Colloquy of the Innkeeper with three guests of different religions from Luke 14:14, chapter 20:35, and Psalm 143:3, Luke 17:10 to attack the same dogma. The sum of them comes to this: in Luke 14:14 it is said that the just, and in chapter 20:35 that those who shall be held worthy, are the only ones who will rise again. But no one is just, Psalm 143:3, and we are all unworthy and unprofitable servants, Luke 17:10. From which it follows necessarily that no one will rise again. If this (he adds) is not a true contradiction, you have not learned dialectics properly. But how childish, how inept is this argument of his? For either the major proposition is taken absolutely, and without an exclusive particle, as it is not found in the cited passages of Luke, and then the major will be this: The just and those who shall be held worthy will rise again; or it is taken exclusively, in this way: The just and those who shall be held worthy will rise again ONLY, just as the author expressly added the particle Nur/ONLY. If it is formed in the former way, and the minor premise is subsumed: But no one is just and worthy; then the minor proposition in the first figure will be negative. But that nothing follows from a negative proposition in the first figure, boys in the schools, who have barely tasted the rudiments of logic with their first lips, know well, and with little effort they will convict this insipid dialectician of absurdity with a similar argument of the same coin: Men are animals. But no brute is a man. Therefore no brute is an animal. But if he understands it exclusively, just as the particle (tantum, Nur) added by him to the words of Luke 14:14 and chapter 20:35 is an indication that he understands it, then the major proposition will be equivalent to a universal negative regarding an infinite subject, and the argument will stand thus: Whoever are not just and worthy of the resurrection of the dead, they will not rise again. But no one is just and worthy. Therefore no one will rise again: In which way indeed the form will be correct, notwithstanding that the minor proposition is negative: since the negation is contained in the subject of the major proposition, and is part of the middle term, which takes the place of the predicate in the minor: But both premises turn out to be false, nor will they be able to be proven by the passages of Scripture brought forward from Luke 14:14 and chapter 20:35. And the major indeed turns out to be false: because neither in Luke 14:14 nor anywhere else in Holy Scripture is it said exclusively that the just ONLY will rise again. Nor is it said exclusively in Luke 20:35 or elsewhere that ONLY those who shall be held worthy will rise again; but in Luke 14:14 they are pronounced blessed who show themselves beneficent toward the poor and those who cannot repay benefits received, inasmuch as the benefits bestowed upon them will be repaid in the resurrection of the just. From this it indeed follows that the just will rise again. But that the just alone will rise again, or that no one who is not just will rise again, cannot be deduced from that by any law of consequence. Indeed, in other places it is expressly said that even those who have done evil, and thus were not just and worthy, will rise again, but to judgment or condemnation, Joh. V. 29, Matt. XXV. 32, 33, 41, II. Cor. V. 10. In the other passage, however, cited from Luc. XX. 35, it is said: They who shall be accounted worthy of that world (to come) and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage. From which, I ask, by what rack will this consequence be extorted: Therefore only the worthy will rise? Who, unless he is a fool, or someone whose brain is in his heel, would conclude thus: Those who shall be accounted worthy of the future age and the resurrection from the dead will not marry nor be given in marriage. Therefore ONLY THE WORTHY will rise again from the dead?

The minor proposition, which is two-membered, fares no better. One member is: No one is just; which the Author attempts to prove with the words of the Psalmist, Ps. CXLIII. 2: No one living is just before you; the other member is: No one is worthy; or we are all unworthy and unprofitable servants, which he proves with the words of Christ in Luke XVII. 10: When you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants, etc. But in both cases the Sophist plays with equivocation and most maliciously perverts the sense of the words of Scripture. For just and worthy can be said in a double sense: one, in which those are called just and worthy who of themselves and by some righteousness, probity, works, and merits of their own are just and worthy of resurrection to life and eternal life; the other, in which those are called just and worthy who are not just and worthy of themselves and by some righteousness or merits of their own, but who, having been justified by the grace of God and the merit of Christ through faith, and having obtained the remission of sins, are such that οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, nothing that may be imputed to them for condemnation, is in them, and, striving for newness and holiness of life, they walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, as Paul speaks in Rom. VIII. 1, and, as far as can be done in this infirmity of nature, live justly and holily. In the former sense it is true that no one is given who is just and worthy, and that with David Ps. 143:3. Ps. 14:3. the whole Scripture testifies. But in the latter sense, that the just and those worthy of the resurrection to life and of eternal life itself are given, Paul expressly teaches, and with him the whole Scripture with the highest consensus. For the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ is unto all and upon all who believe; and they are justified freely by God's grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, Rom. 3:22, 24. and, those who have been justified as righteous through faith in Christ, live thereafter by faith, ch. 1:17, and are μακάριοι blessed, ch. 4:6 ff. If, however, they are blessed, they are also worthy of the resurrection to blessed life and of blessed life itself, because God, by the very fact that He justified them freely through faith in Christ, made them worthy out of grace. Thus, therefore, it is clearly evident that the minor proposition also, as regards both members, is openly false.

VI. Therefore it still remains fixed and immovable that the aforementioned calumniators of Holy Scripture, with so many places of Scripture brought forward, have not been able to demonstrate and prove even one true contradiction, but that the wonderful harmony and consensus which we asserted above of the Old Testament with the New, and of all parts of both among themselves, still stands unshaken, which again provides a distinguished testimony to the truth of Holy Scripture, pure from every error.

The argument can be this: In whatever Scripture such great harmony and consensus of doctrine delivered and believed under the O. and N. T. and of all parts of both is found, so that they do not dissent from one another in any part, nor fight among themselves, that [Scripture] does not have mere men, but God Himself as its author, namely the primary one, and is true in all things without any error mixed in. But in Holy Scripture such great harmony and consensus of doctrine delivered and believed under the O. and N. T., and of all parts of both among themselves, is found, so that they do not dissent from one another in any part, nor fight among themselves. Therefore Holy Scripture does not have mere men, but God Himself as its author, namely the primary one, and is true in all things without any error mixed in.

The minor proposition is evident through an induction of all parts of doctrine, indeed of all places of Scripture, even those which do not deal with the heads of Christian doctrine, yet [are used] by the modern calumniators of Scripture to convict the same of contradiction into the open have been brought forward, among which not even one was found that contains a true contradiction. Nor are we less certain that others containing a true contradiction can be brought forward. Indeed, the reason for the major proposition was adduced above in this very Thes. Explic. n. 1, and it was shown that it is impossible that so many writers, most dissimilar in talent, education, and character, and separated by the greatest intervals of place and time, who neither met to communicate with one another nor could have met, should write with such consensus concerning religion and the doctrine of salvation, and concerning the highest mysteries contained therein which clearly exceed the grasp of human reason, that in no part did one contradict another, but everywhere delivered things in conformity, unless they had written under the guidance and auspices of one and the same Holy Spirit, which may be seen deduced there at greater length. And so much for the second proof of the truth of Scripture, pure from all error, which is taken from the harmony and consensus of Scripture, supreme in all parts of doctrine.

Latin:

piis, qui Domini sunt, & in Domino obdormierunt, aliud fertur judicium, & conceptis verbis dicitur: יחיו מתיך vivent mortui tui, (ô Deus) sicut cadaver meum resurgent: Expergiscimini & laudate (Dominum) habitatores pulveris &c. proximè præcedentia verba v. 13. etiam continent quædam de Dominis alienis sive tyrannis, qui dominati fuerint Ecclesiæ, eamque presserint, ut Pharao olim Israëlitas gravissima servitute presserat, deleti tamen sint à Deo, ut Ægyptii olim in mari rubro suffocati & justo Dei judicio deleti sunt. Atque de hisce mortuis loquuntur verba Prophetæ, dicentis: מתים בל יחיו mortui, puta qui dominati nobis & à te, Domine, interfecti sunt, non vivent. Unde ἐξηγήσεως causâ subjungitur statim: רפאים בל יקומו Gigantes, i.e. tyranni, qui nos oppresserunt, ut Gigantes olim pios opprimebant, non resurgent; & additur ratio: quia tu Domine delevisti eos, justo judicio, & perdidisti omnem memoriam eorum. Quos autem Deus in ira sua & severo suo judicio delet, illi non vivent amplius, neque resurgent. Hic est sensus verborum, si proprietati literæ insistamus, sicut nos ei cum plerisque Interpretibus hic insistendum ducimus. Quia autem prædicata hæc: non vivent, non resurgent; possunt intelligi vel simpliciter, quòd planè non & nullo, neque beatæ, neque miseræ, vitæ genere victuri, & planè non, neque ad gloriam neque ad opprobrium & damnationem resurrecturi sint, utro modo hîc intelligi debeant, ex aliis locis parallelis investigandum est. Dicit autem Christus Joh. V. 28. clarissimis verbis, primò quidem: πάντες OMNES, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filii hominis, & prodibunt. Ergo & tyranni hi ac impii Ecclesiæ oppressores, justo Dei judicio deleti, audient eam & prodibunt, atque adeò resurgent. Ergo verba Prophetæ hoc loco: Mortui (impii) non vivent, tyranni (& Ecclesiæ oppressores) non resurgent, non possunt absolutè & simpliciter intelligi, quòd nullo planè, neque beatæ neque miseræ vitæ genere victuri, & planè non, neque ad beatam vitam, neque ad damnationem resurrecturi sint. Deinde dicit, verbis æquè claris, eos, qui bona fecerunt, prodituros ad vocem Filii hominis ex monumentis in resurrectionem vitæ (beatæ scilicet ac sempiternæ) qui verò mala egerunt, in resurrectionem judicii sive condemnationis. Ergo demortui impii etiam & tyranni, quos Deus justo judicio delevit, prodibunt ad vocem Filii hominis in resurrectionem judicii & condemnationis. Ergò vivent, non autem benè, feliciter, & in gaudio, ut beati, sed miserrimè & in perpetuo marore ac cruciatu: resurgent, non tamen ad vitam æternam, sed ad æternam damnationem. Unde quod dicitur verbis Prophetæ: non vivent, non resurgent, non simpliciter intelligendum est, sed certo modo & sensu: nempe non vivent, puta vitâ felici & beatâ, quæ sola κατ' ἐξοχὴν & simpliciter dicta alterius seculi vita est: infelix verò & ad perpetuas miserias ac cruciatus damnata vita mors potiùs, quàm vita dicenda est, & dicitur etiam in Scripturis mors secunda, Apoc. XX. 6. 14.

Hunc esse genuînum sensum verborum Prophetæ, vel inde etiam patet, quod v. 14. & 19. mortui impii ac tyranni; & mortui pii, qui Dei sunt, & in Domino obdormiverunt, inter se opponuntur, & de his expressè dicitur, quòd victuri & resurrecturi, Deumque laudaturi; de illis verò quòd non victuri, non resurrecturi sint. Quemadmodum autem pios victuros vitâ beatâ & resurrecturos ad vitam beatam ubique locorum Scriptura disertè testatur: videantur Joh. V. 29. Matth. XXV. 34. Dan. XII. 2. ita impios ac tyrannos non victuros vitâ beatâ, neque resurrecturos ad vitam beatam, æquè certò asseritur in iisdem, & loquitur proinde res ipsa, quòd verba ex Esa. XXVI. 14. allegata, non simpliciter, quòd planè non sint resurrecturi, (ut calumniatores illi accipiunt) sed secundùm quid accipienda sint, quòd scilicet impii & tyranni, justo Dei judicio deleti, non victuri sint vitâ felici & beatâ, non resurrecturi sint ad beatam & gloriosam vitam.

Deinde Psal. LXXVIII. 39. verba sunt hæc: ויזכר כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב Et recordatus est, quòd caro sint, spiritus vel ventus abiens, qui non revertitur. Quæ planè non agunt de resurrectione mortuorum, sed de fragilitate vitæ humanæ, quam Psaltes comparat vento, citò abeunti, nec eò, unde venit, revertenti, estque sensus: Deum in ira sua cogitâsse, hominem esse carnem, h. e. fragilem, caducum, ob naturæ corruptionem variis lapsibus obnoxium; eum citò decedere ex hac vita, ut ventus abit, & ubi semel decessit ex hac vita, non redire in eandem, ut ventus non eò, unde venit, revertitur. De eo autem, utrum homo fragilis, qui velut ventus citò abit, nec in fragilem hanc vitam redit, in die extremo resurrecturus sit ad vocem Christi judicis, hîc ne verbo quidem agitur; tantum abeit, ut id negetur. Eadem ratio est locorum, ex Psal. LXXXVIII. v. 11. & Job. XIV. 12. citatorum. In utroque agitur de reditu sive resurrectione mortuorum ad hanc vitam. Et in loco priori quidem invocat Psaltes afflictissimus Deum in ingentibus calamitatibus suis, quibus quin opprimeretur, parum aberat, &, ut maturet auxilium suum, petit, ne, si longiùs illud differat, afflictionum varietate & magnitudine oppressus pereat, & subjicit v. 11. הלמתים תעשה פלא אם רפאים יקומו יודך i. e. Num mortuis facies mirabile? Num mortui resurgent & confitebuntur tibi? Quibus rationem reddit, cur ita maturum nec diutius differendum auxilium petat: nempe quòd si id diutiùs differatur, periculum sit, ne in calamitatibus succumbat & pereat; Deo autem consvetum non sit, per miraculum mortuos ex morte in hanc vitam revocare, ut inter viventes ipsum laudent & pro auxilio suo & liberatione ei gratias agant. Unde bene addit: Num mortui resurgent & CONFITEBUNTUR tibi? quod ut de resurrectione ad hanc vitam, & de confessione, laudatione ac gratiarum actione in his terris in viventium cœtu accipiatur, materia substrata & totus contextus evincit. Eundem in modum Jobus cap. XIV. 12. loquitur de resurrectione ad hanc terrenam vitam, non de resurrectione, quâ sub finem mundi ad vocem Christi judicis prodituri sunt demortui omnes. Quod rursum totus contextus evincit. Conqueritur Vir afflictissimus de misera hominis conditione, eamque aliarum ignobiliorum rerum forte ac conditione deteriorem esse, inter alia ex eo ostendit, quòd si arbor præcidatur, vel senescens arescat, postea repullulascat, & germinans in eum statum, quo antea erat, renovetur, homo autem, si moriatur, nuspiam in terris amplius inveniatur: non resurgat & renovetur in hanc vitam, non expergiscatur & suscitetur, usque dum cœli pereant. Ubi non solùm comparatio hominis mortalis cum arbore cogit, ut de naturali reviviscentia sive resurrectione ejus in hanc vitam verba Jobi accipiamus: in hoc enim sors arboris melior esse ostenditur, quàm hominis, quòd illa præcisa vel præ senectute arescens ex se & juxta naturæ cursum repullulet & renovetur in eum statum, in quo fuerat; hic autem demortuus, ex se & juxta naturæ cursum, non reviviscat, non renovetur in eum statum, in quo fuerat, sive in hanc vitam; sed etiam restrictio in textu addita: עד בלתי שמים usque ad non coelos non resurgent, non expergiscentur e somno, quæ indicio est, virum sanctum non negare, mortuos sub finem mundi, quando cœli peribunt, resurrecturos esse, sed negare saltem, quòd dum cœli sunt, juxta naturæ cursum, in hanc vitam sint resurrecturi, sicut arbores præcisæ, juxta naturæ cursum, repullulant in eam vitam, quam anteà vixerant.

Ecclesiastes denique cap. III. 19. loquitur de hominis fine & obitu juxta sensuum judicium, & ratione externorum in sensus incurrentium eventuum & casuum, quos homines & jumenta eosdem experiuntur. Utrisque eædem obtingunt mutationes, senectus scilicet, morbi, dolores, & tandem mors. Discrimen enim inter homines & bruta, quod ad illorum obitum attinet, sensibus deprehendi non potest, sed si sensuum judicio standum sit, homines ut jumenta erunt. Ut enim homo moritur, ita & jumentum : ambo vivunt, dum spiritus in ipsis est, sed cùm exhalârunt spiritum, cadaver utriusque jacet absque motu, & utrumque putrescit atque in terram, ex qua factum est, convertitur. Quo ipso autem Ecclesiastes non negat, inter hominem & jumenta alioquin ingens, & inter alia hoc etiam esse discrimen, quòd jumenta nunquam resurrectura, homines verò in die extremo ex mortuis resurrecturi sint. Nam in præced. v. 16. & 17. fatetur, quòd viderit sub Sole locum judicii, & locum justitiæ, & deprehensâ ubique impietate dixerit in corde suo, Deum judicaturum suo tempore (in die illo pantocritico) justum & impium, & sub finem Cap. XII. 14. dicit apertè: Deum adducturum esse in judicium omne opus, etiam occultum, sive bonum, sive malum; quod, nisi præviâ resurrectione mortuorum, fieri non potest. Et quamvis in cap. III. v. 2. videatur in dubium vocare, an spiritus hominis, cùm dissolvitur à corpore, sursum tendat, & superstes maneat, spiritus jumenti verò deorsum subter terram, & cum corpore pereat : tamen hoc etiam de sensuum judicio intelligendum est, quo hoc inter homines & jumenta intercedens discrimen animadverti non potest: infra autē cap. XII. v. 7. affirmat absque ulla hæsitatione, corpus hominis, postquam anima ab eo discesserit, reversurum esse in terram, ut antea fuit, spiritum verò ad Deum, qui dedit illum. Atq; ex his nemo non intelligit, apud Ecclesiasten etiam nihil inveniri, quod articulo de resurrectione mortuorum repugnet. Nihil vero rectius habent, quæ in Colloquio Cauponis cum tribus diversarum Religionum hospitibus ex Luc. XIV. 14. c. XX. 35. & Psal. CXLIII. 3. Luc. XVII. 10. ad idem dogma impugnandum produxit. Illorum summa redit huc: Luc. XIV. 14. dicitur, quòd justi, & cap. XX. 3. quòd qui digni habebuntur, tantùm resurrecturi sint. Sed nemo est justus, Psal. CXLIII. 3 & omnes sumus indigni & inutiles servi, Luc. XVII. 10. Ex quibus sequitur necessariò, quòd nemo resurget. Si hæc (subjungit) vera contradictio non est, Dialecticam non probe didicistis. Sed quàm puerilis, quám inepta est hæc ejus argumentatio? Vel enim propositio major accipitur absolutè, & sine particula exclusiva, uti in locis Lucæ allegatis ea non habetur, & tunc major erit hæc: Justi & qui digni habebuntur, resurgent; vel accipitur exclusivè, hoc modo: Justi & qui digni habebuntur, TANTUM resurgent, sicut auctor particulam Nur/TANTUM, expressè addidit. Si priori modò formetur, & subsumatur: Sed nemo est justus & dignus; tum propositio minor in prima figura erit negativa. Ex propositione negativa autem in prima figura nihil sequi, pueri in Scholis, qui vix primis labris Logicæ rudimenta degustârunt, probè norunt, & facili negotio hunc insulsum Dialecticum simili ejusdem monetæ argumento: Homines sunt animalia. Sed nullum brutum est homo. Ergo nullum brutum est animal; absurditatis convincent. Sin exclusivè eam intelligat, quemadmodum illam intelligere particula (tantum, Nur) ad verba Luc. XIV. 14. cap. XX. 35. ab ipso adjecta, indicio est, tunc propositio major æquipollebit universali negativæ de subjecto infinito, habebitque argumentum ita: Quicunque non sunt justi & digni resurrectione mortuorum, illi non resurgent. Atqui nemo est justus & dignus. Ergo nemo resurget: Quo modo quidem forma rectè habebit, non obstante, quòd propositio minor negativa sit: cùm negatio in subjecto majoris propositionis contineatur, & pars sit medii termini, qui in minore prædicati locum sustinet: Sed præmissa utraque falsa evadit, nec productis in medium locis Scripturæ ex Luc. XIV. 14. & c. XX. 35. probari poterunt. Et major quidem falsa evadit: quia nec Luc. XIV. 14. nec alibi uspiam in Scriptura sacra exclusivè dicitur, quòd justi TANTUM resurrecturi sint. Neque etiam Luc. XX. 35. vel alibi exclusivè dicitur, quòd TANTUM qui digni habebuntur, resurrecturi sint; sed Luc. XIV. 14. pronunciantur beati, qui erga pauperes, & qui beneficia accepta rependere non possunt, beneficos sese exhibent, utpote quibus beneficia, in illos collata, in resurrectione justorum rependentur. Ex quo quidem sequitur, justos resurrecturos esse. Sed quòd justi soli resurrecturi sint, sive quòd nemo, qui non sit justus, resurrecturus sit,nullâ consequentiæ lege inde deduci potest. Quin alibi locorũ dicitur expressè, quòd etiam qui mala egerunt, & sic justi ac digni non fuerunt, resurrecturi sint, sed ad judicium sive condemnationem, Joh. V.29. Matt. XXV. 32. 33. 41. II. Cor. V. 10. In loco altero autem, ex Luc. XX. 35. allegato,dicitur: Qui digni habebuntur seculo illo (futuro) & resurrectione ex mortuis, neque ducunt uxores, neque nuptum dant. Ex quo quibus, quæso, fidiculis extorquebitur consequentia hæc: Ergo soli digni resurgent? Quis, nisi stolidus, aut cui cerebrum in calcaneo est, ita concludat: Qui digni habebuntur seculo futuro & resurrectione ex mortuis, non ducent uxores, neque nuptum dabunt. Ergo SOLI DIGNI resurgent ex mortuis?

Nihil etiam meliùs habet propositio minor, quæ bimembris est. Unum membrum est: Nemo est justus; quod Auctor probatum it verbis Psalmistæ, Psal. CXLIII. 3. Nemo viventium coram te justus est; alterum membrum est: Nemo dignus est; vel omnes indigni & servi inutiles sumus, quod probat verbis Christi Luc. XVII. 10. Si omnia feceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus &c. Sed utrobique ludit Sophista æquivocatione, & pervertit sensum verborum Scripturæ malitiosisimè. Nam justi & digni dici possunt duplici sensu: Uno, quo justi & digni dicuntur, qui ex se & suâ propriâ quâdam justitiâ, probitate, operibus & meritis justi & resurrectione ad vitam vitaque æternâ digni sunt? altero, quo justi & digni dicuntur, qui non ex se & suâ quâdam justitiâ, aut ex suis quibusdam meritis justi & digni sunt, sed qui ex gratia Dei & Christi merito per fidem justificati, & remissionem peccatorum consecuti sunt, ita ut οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, nihil, quod ad condemnationem ipsis imputetur, in iis sit, & novitati ac sanctimoniæ vitæ studentes, non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum ambulant, ut Paulus Rom. VIII. 1. loquitur, &, quoad in hac naturæ infirmitate fieri potest, justè & sanctè vivunt. In sensu priori verum est, quòd nullus detur justus & dignus, idque cum Davide Ps. CXLIII 3. Ps. XIV. 3. universa testatur Scriptura. Posteriori verò sensu dari justos & dignos resurrectione ad vitam & ipsâ vitâ æternâ, disertè Paulus, & cum ipso tota Scriptura summo docet consensu. Justitia Dei enim per fidem Jesu Christi est in omnes & super omnes, qui credunt; & justificantur gratis per Dei gratiam, per redemtionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Rom. III. 22. 24. &, qui justificati sunt per fidem in Christum justi, vivunt deinceps ex fide, c. I. 17. atque μακάριοι beati sunt, c. IV. 6. seqq. Si autem beati, digni etiam sunt resurrectione ad vitam beatam & ipsâ vitâ beatâ, quia Deus, eo ipso quod eos justificavit gratis per fidem in Christum, ex gratia illos dignos fecit. Ita ergo liquidò patet, minorem quoque propositionem, quà membrum utrumque, apertè falsam esse.

VI. Adhuc ergò fixum immotumque manet, memoratos Scripturæ sacræ Calumniatores, productis in medium tot Scripturæ locis, ne unam quidem contradictionem veram demonstrare & evincere potuisse, sed quam suprà asseruimus Veteris Testamenti cum Novo, & omnium utriusque partium inter se miram harmoniam & consensionem adhuc stare inconcussam, quod rursum veritatis Scripturæ sacræ, ab omni errore puræ, insigne præbet testimonium.

Argumentum potest esse hoc: In quacunque Scriptura tanta deprehenditur doctrinæ sub V. & N. T. traditæ ac creditæ omniumque utriusque partium harmonia & consensio, ut nulla in parte à se invicem dissentiant, aut inter se pugnent, ea non habet homines nudos, sed ipsummet Deum auctorem, primarium scilicet, estque per omnia absque ullo admixto errore vera. Atqui in Scriptura sacra tanta deprehenditur harmonia & consensio doctrinæ, sub V. & N. T. traditæ & creditæ, omniumque utriusque partium inter se, ut nulla in parte à se invicem dissentiant, aut inter se pugnent. Ergo Scriptura sacra non habet homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet auctorem, primarium scilicet, estque per omnia absque ullo admixto errore vera.

Minor propositio patet per inductionem partium doctrinæ omnium, imò locorum Scripturæ omnium, etiam quæ de capitibus doctrinæ Christianæ non agunt, ab hodiernis Scripturæ Calumniatoribus tamen ad eandem contradictionis convincendam in medium allata sunt, in quorum numero ne unus quidem, quo vera contradictio contineatur, inventus fuit. Neque etiam alia, quæ veram contineant contradictionem, adferri posse, certissimi sumus. Majoris verò propositionis ratio suprà in hac ipsa Thes. Explic. n. 1. adducta, ostensumque fuit, fieri non posse, ut tot ingenio, educatione ac moribus dissimilimi, locorumque ac temporum intervallis longissimè sejuncti Scriptores, qui ad communicandum inter se nec convenerunt, nec convenire potuerunt, de religione & doctrina salutis, deque summis in ea comprehensis humanæque rationis captum planè excedentibus mysteriis tanto scriberent consensu, ut nulla in parte alter alteri contradicerent, sed undique conformia traderent, nisi uno eodemque duce & auspice Spiritu sancto scripsissent, quæ ibi pluribus deducta videantur. Et tantum de altero veritatis Scripturæ, ab omni errore puræ, documento, quod ex harmonia & consensione Scripturæ summa in omnibus doctrinæ partibus desumtum est.


### XIIX. To this we subjoin a third, which is the truth of the prophecies proven by the…

XIIX.

To this we subjoin a third, which is the truth of the prophecies proven by the event and fulfillment itself.

I. Future things, especially contingent ones, and those which depend precisely upon the free will of God or of men, [are known] by no one except the one and only God, who alone possesses infinite knowledge, and has the past and future, no less than the present, always in his sight. Whence God himself proves that he alone is the true God, and that there is no other God besides him, from the fact that no one besides him can foreknow and predict future things, as is evident among other places from Isaiah 46:9. If, therefore, any Scripture predicts future contingent things, in such a way that the predictions are afterwards confirmed by the event itself at the appointed times, it is just as certain a proof that it was not composed by mere human effort, but by God suggesting and revealing it, and is therefore truly divine; as it is a certain proof that a Prophet, whose prophecies have been confirmed by event and fulfillment, was sent by God, and that God spoke through him, Jer. 28:9.

II. I say pointedly (1) especially contingent things, which depend precisely upon the free will of God or of men. For as to future things that arise from natural and necessary causes, even men and demons can sometimes foreknow and predict them from their causes; just as, for example, a mathematician can foreknow and predict a future eclipse of the sun or moon from the motion of the heavens; and can sometimes foreknow and predict famine or plague from the influence of the stars. But those things which are to happen precisely from the free will of God or of men, it is as repugnant for them to be foreknown and predicted by man or demon, as it is repugnant for a man or demon to look into and foreknow the future free thoughts and decrees of God or of men. I say (2) certainly and infallibly. For by conjectures from various circumstances, demons and even men can sometimes foreknow and predict future events which depend on free causes, just as, for example, what that personated Samuel in 1 Sam. 28:19, brought forth by the work of the Pythoness at the command of Saul, was predicting, he undoubtedly held as known through mere conjectures from various circumstances. Although, however, that prediction of that diabolical specter was then confirmed by the event, it was not nevertheless repugnant for it to fail, and predictions of that kind often fail, so that for that reason the Devil, when he gave responses about contingent future events through the idols of the Gentiles, was accustomed for the most part to play with obscure, ambiguous words conformed to be rendered in different senses, and to mock the Gentiles: lest the imposture, if the event did not correspond, should be noticed. But for contingent future events, which are to happen after several centuries from the free will of God or of men, and of which no circumstances yet exist from which anything could be presumed about them even by a light conjecture, to be predicted certainly and infallibly by man or demon in clear and perspicuous words, is simply repugnant to happen.

III. The whole of Holy Scripture is indeed full of predictions of this kind and of events exactly corresponding to them: to bring them all forward in order would be too prolix. We shall bring forward one or two from the later ones, whose fulfillments are more manifest. It was predicted to the first-formed pair immediately after their fall by God himself, as Moses reports in Gen. 3:15, that the Messiah would be sent into the world by the most free will of God, and that he would be the seed of the woman. Afterwards it was predicted that he would be the seed of Abraham, Gen. 12:3, ch. 18:18, ch. 22:18, arising from the posterity of Isaac, Gen. 26:4, and of Jacob, ch. 28:14, and that he would come forth from the tribe of Judah, Gen. 49:10, and from the stock of Jesse, and from his roots, Isa. XI. 1. that he would be the son and sprout of David, chap. IX. 6, 7. Jer. XXIII. 5. chap. XXXIII. 15. from the descendants of David, chap. IX. 6, 7. and from a Virgin, Isa. VII. v. 14. and in Bethlehem Ephrathah, a city of Judah, Mic. V. 1. to be born: all of which were most exactly fulfilled, according to all circumstances. For Christ is the seed of the woman, conceived of the Virgin Mary, without male seed, the Holy Spirit overshadowing her, Luke I. 27. ff. chap. II. 27, 35. he was born in Bethlehem, in the city of David, chap. II. 4, 7. He is the Son of David and Abraham, Matt. I. v. 1. He was born when the Scepter had been taken away from Judah and devolved to the Romans, Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, taxing the whole world subject to him, and in it also Judea, Luke II. 1. ff. What things were predicted throughout the entire Scripture of the O.T. concerning the Prophetic office of Christ, and the duty of teaching, which he was to perform in the days of his flesh, and concerning his forerunner, John the Baptist, concerning his Mediatorial office, and concerning his sacrifice, to be offered for us on the altar of the cross, concerning his intercession, passion, and death; concerning his exaltation, and his kingdom both of grace, to be propagated through the Apostles throughout the whole world, and of power and glory, by which, exalted to the right hand of the Father, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he most powerfully governs all things, both those which are on earth and those which are in heaven, have again been most exactly fulfilled according to all circumstances. Which, by comparing the passages of the Scriptures of the O.T. containing the predictions themselves with the passages of the Scriptures of the N.T. which exhibit their fulfillments in clear and plain words, could be shown clearly and more brightly than the midday sun itself, were they not already known among all. Similarly, what things were predicted concerning bodily matters, good and evil, e.g., concerning the servitude of the Israelites in Egypt, and their wonderful liberation from hard servitude, Gen. XV. 13, 14. concerning the Babylonian captivity of the Jewish people, and the first destruction of Jerusalem, and its liberation and the return of the people to their native land, and the restoration of Jerusalem, Isa. XXXIX. 6. ff. Jer. XVI. 13. ff. chap. XX. 4. ff. concerning the supreme Empires of the world, and their vicissitudes, Dan. II. 38. ff. chap. VII. 4. ff. chap. VIII. 3. ff. concerning the blinding and rejection of the Jewish people, Isa. VI. 9. ff. chap. XXIX. 10. ff. Rom. XI. 25. and concerning the second destruction of the City of Jerusalem, never to be restored, Dan. IX. 26. Matt. XXIV. 2. Luke XIX. 43. ff. chap. XXI. 24. and concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the Church, Gen. XII. 3. chap. XXII. 18. chap. XXVI. 4. chap. XXVIII. 14. Hos.

Hof. II. 23. Mich. IV. 1. et seqq. and concerning countless other things, which no one could have known beforehand, no one could have predicted, except God and the holy men of God to whom God revealed them: of whose fulfillments, however, the entire Scripture of the N.T. in part, and experience in part, testifies more than sufficiently. The prophecies which have not yet obtained their fulfillment pertain to the last times, which will be fulfilled toward the end as certainly as the others concerning the Messiah, his office, his benefits, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, and other things were fulfilled and confirmed by the event itself. III. Hence such an argument arises for us again: Those Scriptures which contain prophecies concerning future contingencies, which depend precisely either upon the most free will of God or upon the free will of men, and consequently could not have been foreknown or predicted by any mortal unless God revealed them, to which, however, the event responded most exactly and according to all circumstances, those were composed not by mere human study, but by God revealing and suggesting through revelation what ought to be written, and thus are true without any admixture of error. And the sacred Scriptures are so constituted. Therefore. The major proposition obtains light from those things which we discussed above in Expl. n. I. and II., so that it does not need further proof. The minor proposition, however, has been proven thus far by the various prophecies brought forward in the preceding n. III.: e.g., the mission of the Messiah into the flesh was a future contingency, depending solely upon the most free will of God. For God could have, if He had willed, not sent the Messiah, but left the entire human race eternally in the destruction into which it had fallen by its own fault through sin: He could have raised him up and sent him into the flesh from a lineage other than that of Abraham, from a mother other than the Virgin Mary, at a time other than that of Augustus Caesar, in a place other than Bethlehem of Judah, if He had willed: but that he would come into the flesh under these circumstances and in this way was predicted more than a thousand, indeed several thousand years earlier, with the event responding most exactly to the predictions according to all circumstances; all that can be attributed to nothing but God and His revelation, with which He deigned to favor the sacred writers above other mortals. Similarly, that the Jews would fall away from God, would maliciously despise, obstinately reject, close the eyes of their minds to his saving doctrine, blind themselves, and harden their hearts, and would perish by their own fault, were future contingent events, about to proceed from their own most free will, most stubbornly despising the grace of God out of mere malice, and as it were trampling it underfoot: which again no one could certainly foreknow, and so predict that the event would respond most exactly, except God, and those to whom God might reveal it: God could also have spurned the blinded, impious, and idolatrous Gentiles, and left them in their blindness and impiety, if He had willed. But that He was about to call them into the place of the rejected Jews, to convert them to Christ, and to lead them to eternal salvation; and that at the time, and no other, in which He actually did it, no one could foreknow and predict, except God, and he to whom God might reveal it: and so also the matter stands with prophecies concerning other future contingencies: which, when compared with their fulfillment for the truth of Holy Scripture, pure from all error and falsehood, provides an invincible argument. But enough and more than enough concerning the truth of Holy Scripture, pure from all error, which was the first criterion of the divinity of Scripture. We proceed to the second, which we established above in thesis VII in its holiness, perfect without blemish.

Latin:

XIIX.

EI subjungimus tertium, quod est Vaticiniorum ipso eventu & complemento comprobata veritas.

I. Futura, contingentia præsertim, & quæ præcisè ex Dei aut hominum voluntate libera dependent, præter unum & solum Deum, qui solus infinitâ pollet scientiâ, & præterita pariter ac futura, non minùs, quàm præsentia, semper in conspectu habet. Unde Deus ipse se solum verum Deum, &, præter se, Deum alium non esse, ex eo probat, quod præter se nemo futura prænôsse ac prædicere possit, ut inter alia ex Jesa. XLVI. 9. patet. Quod si qua Scriptura igitur futura contingentia prædicat, ita ut prædictiones posteà statutis temporibus ipso eventu comprobatæ sint, tam certo id documento est, eam non esse studio merè humano, sed, Deo suggerente ac revelante, concinnatam, atque adeò verè divinam; quàm certo documento est, Prophetam, cujus vaticinia eventu & complemento comprobata sunt, à Deo missum, & Deum per eum loquutum esse, Jer. XXVIII. 9.

II. Notanter dico (1) contingentia præsertim, quæ præcisè ex Dei aut hominum libera voluntate dependent. Nam quæ ex naturalibus & necessariis causis proveniunt futura, homines etiam & Dæmones quandoque ex suis causis præscire & prædicere possunt; sicut v. g. Eclipsin solis aut Lunæ futuram Mathematicus ex motu cœli; & famem aut pestem ex influxu astrorum quandoque præscire & prædicere potest. Sed quæ præcisè ex Dei aut hominum voluntate libera eventura sunt, tam repugnat ab homine aut Dæmone præsciri & prædici, quàm repugnat, hominem aut Dæmonem Dei vel hominum futuras cogitationes & decreta libera introspicere, ac præscire. Dico (2) certò & infallibiliter. Nam per conjecturas ex circumstantiis variis possunt nonnunquam Dæmones & homines etiam futura, quæ à causis liberis dependent, prænosse & prædicere, sicut v. g. quæ I. Sam. XXIX. 19. personatus ille Samuel, Saulis jussu operâ Pythonissæ productus, prædicebat, dubio procul per meras conjecturas ex variis circumstantiis cognita habebat. Quamvis verò illa spectri istius Diabolici prædictio eventu tum comprobata fuerit, non tamen repugnabat eam fallere, & fallunt id generis prædictiones sæpè, ut proptereà Diabolus, quando per idola Gentilium de futuris contingentibus responsa dedit, plerumque obscuris, ambiguis & ad diversos sensus reddendos conformatis verbis ludere, Gentibusque illudere consvevit: ne impostura, si eventus non responderet, animadverteretur. Sed futura contingentia, quæ post aliquot secula ex Dei aut hominum voluntate libera eventura, & quorum nondum ullæ extant circumstantiæ, ex quibus vel levi conjecturâ quicquam de iis præsumi possit, verbis claris & perspicuis certò & infallibiliter ab homine aut Dæmone prædici, fieri simpliciter repugnat.

III. Hujus generis verò vaticiniorum eventuumque, exactè illis respondentium, plena est universa Scriptura sacra: quæ omnia ordine adferre nimis foret prolixum. Unum atque alterum ex posterioribus, quorum complementa extantiora sunt, adferemus. Messiam Dei liberrimâ voluntate in mundum mittendum, eumque semen Mulieris futurum prædictum est Protoplastis statim post illorum lapsum ab ipsomet Deo, referente Mose Gen. III. 15. Postea prædictum est, eum futurum esse Abrahami semen, Gen. XII. 3. c. XIIX. 18. c. XXII. 18. oriundum ex posteritate Isaac, Gen. XXVI. 4. & Jacobi c. XXIX. 14. ex tribu Juda, Gen. XLIX. 10. egressurum ac stirpe Isaï, & de radicibus ejus, Jesa. XI. 1. fore filium & germen Davidis, cap. IX. 6. 7. Jerem. XXIII. 5. cap. XXXIII. 15. ex Davidis posteris, c. IX. 6. 7. & ex Virgine, Jesa. VII. v. 14. & in Bethlehem Ephratha, civitate Juda, Mich. V. 1. nascendum: quæ omnia exactissimè, secundum omnes circumstantias, impleta sunt. Est enim Christus semen mulieris, ex Virgine Maria, absque virili semine, Spiritu sancto eam obumbrante, conceptus, Luc. I. 27. seqq. cap. II. 27. 35. est natus Bethlehemi, in civitate David, cap. II. 4. 7. Est Filius Davidis & Abrahami, Matth. I. v. 1. Est natus, cum Sceptrum de Juda ablatum & ad Romanos devolutum esset, Augusto, Romanorum Imperatore totum orbem, sibi subjectum, & in eo etiam Judæam censente, Luc. II. 1. seqq. Quæ de officio Christi Prophetico, & munere docendi, quo in diebus carnis suæ functurus erat, desque ipsius præcursore, Johanne Baptista, de officio ejus Mediatorio, desque ipsius sacrificio, in ara crucis pro nobis immolando, de ejus intercessione, passione ac morte; de ipsius exaltatione, regnoque tùm gratiæ, per Apostolos per universum terrarum orbem propagando, tùm potentiæ ac gloriæ, quo ad dextram Patris exaltatus unà cum Patre ac Spiritu S. omnia, cùm quæ in terris tùm quæ in cœlis sunt, potentissimè gubernat, per universam Scripturam V. T. prædicta sunt, rursum exactissimè secundùm omnes circumstantias completa sunt. Quod collatis locis Scripturarum V. T. ipsas prædictiones continentibus, cum locis Scripturarum N. T. quæ illorum complementa claris & perspicuis verbis exhibent, liquidò & ipso sole meridiano clariùs oftendi posset, nisi jam antè inter omnes nota essent. Similiter quæ de rebus corporalibus, bona & mala, prædicta sunt, v. g. de Israëliturum servitute in Ægypto, desque illorum mirabili liberatione ex dura servitute, Gen. XV. 13. 14. de populi Judaici captivitate Babylonica, & primo Hierosolymæ excidio, desque ejus liberatione & reductione populi in terram patriam, & Solymorum restauratione, Jes. XXXIX. 6. seqq. Jer. XVI. 13 seqq. c. XX. 4 seqq. de summis mundi Imperiis, illorumque vicissitudinibus, Dan. II. 38. seqq. c. VII. 4. seqq. c. VIII. 3. seqq. de excæcatione & rejectione populi Judaici Jes. VI. 9. seq. c. XXIX. 10. seqq. Rom. XI. 25. desque altero excidio Urbis Solymorum, nunquam restaurandæ, Dan. IX. 26. Matth. XXIV. 2. Luc. XIX. 43. seq. c. XXI. 24. & de vocatione Gentium ad Ecclesiam, Gen. XII. 3. c. XXII. 18. c. XXVI. 4. c. XXVIII. 14. Hos.

Hof. II. 23. Mich. IV. 1. feqq. & de aliis rebus innumeris, quas prænosse nemo, prædicere nemo potuit, præter Deum, & sanctos Dei viros, quibus ea Deus revelavit: de quorum complementis tamen partim Scriptura N. T. universa, partim experientia satis superque testatur. Quæ suum complementum nondum fortita sunt vaticinia, ad ultima tempora pertinent, quæ sub finem complebuntur tam certò, quàm certò cætera de Messia, ejus officio, beneficiis, de vocatione Gentium & alia completa & ipso eventu comprobata sunt. III. Hinc nobis rursum tale nascitur argumentum: Quæ Scripturæ continent vaticinia de futuris contingentibus, quæ præcisè vel ex Dei voluntate liberrima, vel ex libera hominum voluntate dependent, & proinde à nemine mortalium præsciri prædicique potuerunt, nisi Deo revelante, quibus tamen exactissimè & secundum omnes circumstantias respondit eventus, illæ non studio merè humano, sed Deo revelante, & per revelationem, quæ scribenda essent, suggerente, concinnatæ, adeoque absque omni admixto errore veræ sunt. Atque sic comparatæ sunt Scripturæ sacræ. Ergo. Major propositio ex iis, quæ superiùs Expl. n. I. & II. disseruimus, sortitur lucem, ut ulteriori probatione non egeat. Minor autem propositio hactenus probata est productis in præced. n. III. in medium variis vaticiniis: v. g.
