Missio Messiæ in carnem erat futurum contingens, ex Dei solius liberrima voluntate dependens. Potuisset enim Deus, si voluisset, non mittere Messiam, sed genus humanum universum in exitio, in quod suâ culpâ per peccatum inciderat, æternùm relinquere: potuisset eum ex alia, quàm Abrahami posteritate, ex alia matre, quàm Maria Virgine, alio tempore, quàm Augusti Cæsaris, alio loco, quàm Bethlemi Judæ suscitare & in carnem mittere, si voluisset: quod autem sub hisce circumstantiis & hoc modo eum in carnem venturum, plus mille, imò aliquot mille annis priùs prædictum est, eventu prædictionibus secundum omnes circumstantias exactissimè respondente, id totum non nisi Deo ejusque revelationi, quâ Scriptores sacros præ aliis mortalibus dignatus est, acceptum referri potest. Similiter Judæos à Deo defecturos, Messiam, illorum Patribus promissum, malitiosè contemturos, obstinatè rejecturos, oculos mentis ad ejus salutiferam doctrinam occlusuros, sese excæcaturos, animumque obduraturos, & suâ culpâ perituros esse, futura contingentia erant, à liberrima ipsorum voluntate, gratiam Dei ex mera malitia pertinacissimè contemnente, & pedibus quasi conculcante, proventura: quæ rursum certò prænosse, & ita ut exactissimè responderet eventus, prædicere nemo potuit, præter Deum, & eos, quibus Deus id revelaret: poterat etiam Deus Gentes excæcatas, impias & idololatras aspernari, & in sua cæcitate & impietate relinquere, si voluisset. Quod autem eas in locum rejectorum Judæorum vocaturus, ad Christum conversurus, & ad salutem æternam perducturus erat; idque eo, quo reapse fecit, tempore, non alio, prænosse & prædicere nemo potuit, præter Deum, & cui id Deus revelaret: & sic etiam cum vaticiniis de futuris contingentibus cæteris res habet: quæ cum suo complemento collata pro Scripturæ sacræ veritate, ab omni errore & falsitate pura, invictum præbet argumentum. Sed plus satis de veritate Scripturæ sacræ, ab omni errore pura, quæ erat primum divinitatis Scripturæ κριτήριον. Ad alterum, quod suprà th. VII. in ejus sanctitate, absque nævo perfecta, constituebamus, progredimur.


### XIX. The holiness of Scripture, perfect without any blemish, just as its truth, pure…

XIX.

The holiness of Scripture, perfect without any blemish, just as its truth, pure from all error, can be shown by induction.

I. Holy Scripture is called sacred or holy for more than one reason. For it is called sacred or holy (1) by reason of its object, because it is occupied with sacred or holy things, (2) by reason of its end, because it directs man to a sacred or holy end, namely the salvation of the soul, (3) by reason of its efficient cause, because it has the Holy Spirit as its immediate author, and was written by His inspiration, and always has His power of working intimately joined to it, as was shown above in Chapter II, thesis I, Explanation n. I & II. But here we consider the holiness of Scripture in relation to the eternal law of God, implanted in the minds of men, and repeated and promulgated by God on Mount Sinai, with the whole Israelite people watching and listening, in a sonorous voice, Exod. XX, which is the rule and norm of all rectitude and holiness, and we call it holy because it itself in its entirety, and the whole doctrine contained in it, is conformable to the eternal and immutable law of God, and has nothing mixed in, which is base, or alien to what is right and becoming. For we consider here in this place, as was said above in thesis VI, Holy Scripture by reason of its properties, which is required in it in relation to man's ultimate end. But whatever holiness is required in any Scripture in relation to this end, without doubt consists in conformity with the eternal law of God. For in order that any Scripture may be able to order and lead man to God, who is holiness, and to the attainment, by His gift, of eternal life, as to an ultimate end, even by the judgment of right reason itself, it is required that whatever it delivers concerning God and concerning the means of attaining eternal life by His gift, all should be holy, that is, conformable to the eternal law of God, and contain nothing dishonest or unbecoming.

II. The eternal and immutable law of God, however, to which, as to a norm, all holiness of doctrine must be tested, comprises two parts or tables: one, which orders and directs man to the most holy God and His holy worship; the other, which orders and directs the same man to living his life justly and holily toward himself and his neighbor. In both parts Holy Scripture is, that is, is entirely conformable to the eternal law of God. For it teaches nothing concerning God and His worship, and concerning the life of man to be lived justly and holily, which either departs from or in any part falls short of either the first or the second table of the law.

III. The first table of the divine law contains precepts concerning the right acknowledgment of God, and concerning the worship convenient and due to Him, to the norm of which if you test whatever Holy Scripture delivers concerning the acknowledgment and worship of God, you will discover immediately that all things are holy, and that nothing inconsistent with the divine law is found in them. They are, however, as we saw in the previous thesis VIII and following, in a twofold difference, which Holy Scripture teaches concerning the right acknowledgment of God, and concerning the worship convenient and due to Him. For some things can also be known to a certain extent by the guidance of the light of nature; of this kind are those which it delivers concerning the acknowledgment of God by reason of His essence and essential attributes, and likewise by reason of His providence, works, and divine benefits, and concerning faith, trust, and hope toward God, concerning the love of God above all things, concerning the fear of God, concerning His invocation in necessities, concerning thanksgiving for benefits received, concerning the praising and celebration of God on account of benefits exhibited. But others exceed the light of nature, nor can they become known to us from anywhere else than from divine

revelation: of this kind are those things which it teaches concerning the knowledge of God by reason of the persons, personal properties, and works and benefits, either proper or appropriated to each person, and concerning the worship convenient and due to the three persons, and to Christ himself as man, on account of the personal union of the two natures, divine and human, of which he consists, and the communication of idioms resulting therefrom. That the former part of the doctrine concerning the right knowledge of God and the worship convenient and due to him is entirely conformable to the holy sacred Scripture, that is, to the eternal law of God, and contains nothing of these things which disagrees with the first table of the law, or departs from it, the thing itself speaks. For whatever right reason teaches concerning the chapters of the first order already enumerated, pertaining to the knowledge and worship of God, in conformity with the principles of nature and reason, and thus with the eternal law of God, all those things sacred Scripture also teaches in entire agreement with the same. This will remain fixed and firm for so long as not even a single particle of the enumerated doctrines is brought forward, concerning which Scripture might teach otherwise and in disagreement with the eternal law of God. Nay, rather, sacred Scripture teaches all these things far more perfectly and more conveniently to the eternal law of God than reason can from its own light, and thus prescribes and demands from the part of the man to be saved a much greater holiness than reason can prescribe and demand from its own light. For reason, in this corrupt state of nature, subsists in whatever deliberate acts of virtues, pertaining to the first table of the law, there may be, but it does not exclude or prohibit the indeliberate acts and sudden motions of concupiscence, doubts, diffidence, timidity, hatred, and others conflicting with the first table of the law: nay, even in prescribing the very external acts of divine worship, it very often errs from that eternal law of God impressed upon the minds of men, and sometimes prescribes worship entirely unworthy of God, as we saw above in thesis XI, Explanation no. III, from Paul, and as experience abundantly testifies. Sacred Scripture, however, does not persist in these acts, but prescribes and demands an all-encompassing conformity of acts of this kind with the eternal law of God, and a perfect holiness, which excludes all, even the inordinate acts and motions of concupiscence, doubts, diffidence, hatred, etc., and thus directs man to a worship of God that is in every way perfect on the part of the first table, and in every way holy, according to that: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, Deut. VI. 5. Matt. XXII. 37. Luc. X. 27.

Nor is the matter less clear concerning the acknowledgment and worship appropriate and due to God as triune in persons and to Christ as man. For when once it has been established from divine revelation that God is triune in persons, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that the Son of God assumed human nature into the unity of his person, and was made man, and by virtue of the communication of idioms, which occurred in the unity of his person, whatever belongs to him as God belongs also to him as man: and likewise that the Son of God redeemed us in the assumed human nature from sins, death, the Devil, and hell, and is the mediator of God and men, through whom we may have grace and remission of sins before God; that the Holy Spirit regenerates and renews us through the Word and Sacraments, and that our creation and preservation, etc., are appropriated to God the Father. then it can no longer be denied that whatever the Holy Scripture hands down concerning the acknowledgment and worship of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is entirely consistent with the eternal law of God and is therefore holy. For, according to the eternal law of God, God is to be acknowledged as he has revealed himself to the mortal race, whether in nature or through supernatural revelations. Nor is any other worship prescribed in Scripture to be rendered to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and to Christ as man, than that which is prescribed to be rendered to God as one in essence, consistently with the eternal law of God in the same, and by right reason, by virtue of the eternal law of God implanted in itself. For just as the Deity of the three divine persons is one, so also the worship of the same must be one and the same, so that if it is holy, i.e. conforms to the first table of the law, the worship due to God as one in essence, which is prescribed in the Holy Scriptures, it must also be that the worship which is prescribed in them to be rendered to God as triune in persons is holy.

At least this difference intervenes between the worship which is prescribed according to the first table of the law by right reason, and that which is prescribed according to the same through Holy Scripture, that the latter renders the faithful worshiper of God certain and secure about obtaining grace and remission of sins before God: For it includes trust in Christ the Mediator, through whom sinners have been reconciled to God, who was offended by their sins, and have παῤῥησίαν, and access with confidence in one Spirit to the Father,

Eph. II. 18. & III. 12. & through whom they are led by faith into this grace, in which they stand reconciled to God and boast in the hope of the glory of God, Rom. V. 2. Moreover, as many as are the promises of God, through Christ they are also, and through him, Amen, to the glory of God, II. Cor. I. 20. & whatever they shall ask the Father in his name, he will give to them, John XVI. 23. However, the worship which reason can prescribe or does prescribe from the principles of nature, can make no one certain and secure about obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God. For just as reason, left to itself, is ignorant of Christ and his merit and satisfaction for the sins of the human race, so it also has nothing which it can oppose to divine wrath in the agonies of conscience on account of sins and the doubts arising thence concerning the grace of God, and it cannot make an anxious conscience certain and secure concerning being heard and obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God. Concerning which matter more will be said in the following thesis XXI according to the nature of the undertaking.

IV. The second table of the law contains the precepts concerning the life of man to be lived justly and holily toward himself and his neighbor, to the standard of which if you also examine whatever the Holy Scripture teaches concerning the holiness of life, you will again discover that all things are holy, and that nothing inconsistent with the law implanted in the minds of men is contained in them; indeed, you will discover that through all the precepts Scripture demands a far greater and more perfect holiness than human reason can demand by the power of the law implanted in itself: e.g., that the law: You shall love your neighbor as yourself, (which contains the sum of the whole second table) includes even an enemy under the term neighbor, and demands of us that we love even him; that the law concerning not killing forbids also anger, hatred, words, and gestures by which we signify even slightly an adverse spirit toward a neighbor, and all private vengeance; that the law concerning not committing adultery forbids also the interior lust for another's wife, even the very look at her joined with the movement of inordinate lust, and condemns it as the crime of adultery, and that the law concerning not coveting in general commands that all inordinate movements of lust, by whatever name they come, even those which arise suddenly and anticipate the judgment of reason and the consent of the will, be absent, reason by the power of the law implanted in it by nature cannot know and teach, yet Holy Scripture teaches it, and in it especially Christ; Our only Master, whom God commended to us to be heard by a voice fallen from heaven, in words by no means obscure Matt. V. 44. Luke VI. 27. 28. 35. Exod. XXIII. 4. 5. Prov. XXV. 21. Rom. XII. 14. I. Cor. IV. 12. 13. I. Pet. III. 9. Matt. V. 21. seqq. I. John III. 15. Matt. V. 28. c. XV. 19. seq. Rom. VII. 7. &c. In short: Holy Scripture requires on the part of the man to be saved the most exact conformity of all the faculties of the soul, and of all acts and motions, both interior and exterior, with the law, and thus a holiness of life, absolute and perfect in all numbers and ways, such as no other religion, no other code of Scripture, in which the religion of any nation or people is contained and described, prescribes or demands.

V. Hence I argue thus: Whatever Scripture prescribes a religion so perfectly and in all its parts holy, that human reason by its own light cannot reach to its holiness at that degree of perfection, that Scripture does not have mere men, but God himself as its Author. But Holy Scripture prescribes a religion so perfectly and in all its parts holy, that human reason by its own light cannot reach to its holiness at that degree of perfection. Therefore Holy Scripture does not have mere men, but God himself as its author. The minor proposition has been proven thus far by the induction of all parts of the Christian religion, compared to both tables of the law. The major, however, is evident. For the holiness of that Scripture is higher and more perfect than can be taught and prescribed by human reason from the principles of nature, it is necessary that it draws its origin from a higher principle. But that higher principle cannot be anything other than God, from whose inspiration the sacred writers composed Holy Scripture. And so much also for the second internal criterion of the divinity of Scripture, namely, the holiness of Scripture, perfect without blemish. We proceed to the third, which we established above in thesis VII regarding sufficiency.

Latin:

XIX.

SAnctitas Scripturæ, absque ullo nævo perfecta, perinde ut ejus veritas, ab omni errore pura, per inductionem ostendi potest.

I. Scriptura sacra dicitur aliàs sacra sive sancta non una de causa. Dicitur enim sacra sive sancta (1) ratione objecti, quòd circa res sacras sive sanctas occupetur, (2) ratione finis, quòd ad finem sacrum sive sanctum, animæ salutem scilicet, hominem ordinet, (3) ratione causæ efficientis, quòd auctorem immediatum habeat Spiritum sanctum, eoque inspirante confignata sit, ejusque virtutem operandi semper intimè sibi conjunctam habeat, ut supra Cap. II. th. I. Expl. n. I. & II. ostensum est. Hic verò sanctitatem Scripturæ consideramus in ordine ad legem Dei æternam, hominum mentibus implantatam, & in monte Sinai à Deo, spectante & audiente toto populo Israëlítico, sonorâ voce repetitam & promulgatam, Exod. XX. quæ rectitudinis & sanctitatis omnis regula ac norma est, eamque dicimus sanctam, quòd & ipsa tota, & contenta in ea doctrina universa, legi Dei æternæ ac immutabili conformis sit, nec quicquam habeat admixtum, quod turpe, aut a recto & decoro alienum sit. Consideramus enim hic loci, ut supra th. VI. dictum, Scripturam sacram ratione suarum proprietatum, quæ in ordine ad hominis finem ultimum in illa requiritur. Quæ autem in ordine ad hunc finem in Scriptura aliqua requiritur sanctitas, citra dubium consistit in conformitate cum lege Dei æterna. Ut enim ad Deum, qui sanctitas est, & ad consequendam, ejus dono, vitam æternam, velut ad finem ultimum, Scriptura aliqua hominem ordinare & perducere possit, vel ipsa recta ratione judice, requiritur, ut quæcunque de Deo deque mediis consequendæ ejus dono vitæ æternæ tradit, sancta, h.e. legi Dei æternæ conformia sint omnia, neque quicquam inhonesti aut indecori contineant.

II. Lex Dei æterna & immutabilis autem, ad quam, velut ad normam, exigenda est doctrinæ sanctitas omnis, duas complectitur partes sive tabulas: unam, quæ hominem ad Deum sanctissimum ejusque cultum sanctum; alteram, quæ eundem ad vitam erga se & proximum juste ac sancte degendam, ordinat & dirigit. Ex utraque parte Scriptura sancta, h.e. legi Dei æternæ prorsus conformis est. Neque enim ea quicquam docet de Deo ejusque cultu, deque vita hominis, juste ac sancte degenda, quod sive a prima sive a secunda legis tabula recedat aut ulla ex parte deficiat.

III. Prima divinæ legis tabula continet præcepta de agnitione Dei recta, deque cultu, ipsi conveniente ac debito, ad quorum normam si exigas, quæcunque Scriptura sacra de agnitione cultuque Dei tradit, deprehendes oppido, sancta esse omnia, neque quicquam legi divinæ disconveniens in iis inveniri. Sunt autem, ut superiori th. IIX. & seq. vidimus, in duplici differentia, quæ de agnitione Dei recta, deque cultu ipsi conveniente ac debito Scriptura sacra docet. Quædam enim ductu luminis naturæ etiam quadantenus cognosci possunt; cujusmodi sunt, quæ de agnitione Dei ratione essentiæ & attributorum essentialium, itemque ratione providentiæ, operum ac beneficiorum divinorum, & de fide, fiducia ac spe erga Deum, de dilectione Dei super omnia, de timore Dei, de ejus invocatione in necessitatibus, de gratiarum actione pro acceptis beneficiis, de laudatione ac celebratione Dei propter beneficia exhibita tradit. Alia vero lumen naturæ excedunt, nec aliunde, quam ex divina re-

velatione nobis innotescere possunt: cujusmodi sunt, quæ de agnitione Dei ratione personarum, proprietatum personalium, operumque & beneficiorum, cuique personæ sive propriorum sive appropriatorum, deqve cultu, tribus personis, ipsique Christo homini ob duarum, quibus constat, naturarum, divinæ & humanæ, unionem personalem & inde resultantem communicationem idiomatum, conveniente ac debito eadem docet. Quâ priorem doctrinæ partem de agnitione Dei recta, cultuque, ipsi conveniente ac debito, Scripturam sacram sanctam, h. e. legi Dei æternæ prorsus conformem esse, nec quicquam horum continere, quod primæ legis tabulæ disconveniat, aut ab ea recedat, res ipsa loquitur. Quæcunque enim recta ratio de recensitis jam prioris ordinis capitibus, ad agnitionem & cultum Dei pertinentibus, naturæ & rationis principiis, atq; adeò legi Dei æternæ conformiter docet, ea omnia docet etiam Scriptura sacra eidem prorsus convenienter. Quod tantisper fixum & firmum manebit, dum vel unica doctrinarum enumeratarum particula, de qua aliter & legi Dei æternæ disconvenienter Scriptura doceat, afferatur. Quin imò Scriptura sacra docet hæc omnia longè perfectiùs legique Dei æternæ convenientiùs, quàm ratio ex suo lumine, atque adeò multò majorem præscribit & ex parte hominis salvandi exigit sanctitatem, quàm ratio ex suo lumine præscribere & exigere potest. Ratio enim, pro hoc corrupto naturæ statu, subsistit in qualibuscunque externis ac internis virtutum, ad primam legis tabulam pertinentium, actibus deliberatis, indeliberatos verò concupiscentiæ, dubitationum, diffidentiæ, timiditatis, odii aliosque cum prima legis tabula pugnantes actus & motus subitaneos non excludit, non prohibet: imò in ipsis externis cultus divini actibus præscribendis aberrat ea à lege Dei æterna, hominum mentibus impressa, sæpissimè, præscribitque nonnunquam cultum Deo prorsus indignum, uti suprà th. XI. Expl. n. III. ex Paulo vidimus, & experientia abundè testatur. Scriptura sacra verò in hisce actibus non persistit, sed præscribit & exigit id generis actuum omnimodam convenientiam cum lege Dei æterna, sanctitatemque perfectam, quæ omnes, etiam inordinatos concupiscentiæ, dubitationum, diffidentiæ, odii &c. actus ac motus excludat, atque adeò dirigit hominem ad cultum Dei, ex parte tabulæ primæ undiquaque perfectum, undiquaque sanctum, juxta illud: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota mente tua, Deut. VI. 5. Matt. XXII. 37. Luc. X. 27.

Neque minus res clara est de agnitione ac cultu, Deo ut trino in personis & Christo homini conveniente ac debito. Ubi enim semel ex revelatione divina constiterit, Deum esse in personis trinum, Patrem scilicet, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, & Filium Dei assumsisse naturam humanam in unitatem personæ suæ, hominemque factum esse, & vi communicationis idiomatum, in unitate personæ ipsius factæ, convenire ipsi homini, quicquid ei, ut Deo, convenit: itemque Filium Dei redemisse nos in assumta humana natura a peccatis, morte, Diabolo, & inferno, esse mediatorem Dei ac hominum, per quem habeamus apud Deum gratiam ac remissionem peccatorum; Spiritum sanctum regenerare & renovare nos per Verbum & Sacramenta, Deo Patri verò appropriari nostram creationem & conservationem &c. tum negari ampliùs non potest, legi Dei æternæ prorsus convenientia atque adeò sancta esse, quæcunque Scriptura sacra de agnitione & cultu Patris, Filii, ac Spiritus sancti tradit. Nam, juxta legem Dei æternam, Deus agnoscendus est, ut ipse sive in natura sive per supernaturales revelationes se mortalium generi patefecit. Neque alius cultus præscribitur in Scriptura Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto, Christoque homini deferendus, quam qui Deo in essentia uni, legi Dei æternæ convenienter in eadem, & a ratione recta, vi legis Dei æternæ sibi implantatæ, deferendus præscribitur. Quemadmodum enim una trium divinarum personarum Deitas est, ita & cultus earundem unus atque idem esse debet, ut si sanctus, h.e. primæ legis tabulæ conformis sit cultus, Deo ut uni in essentia debitus, qui in Scripturis sacris præscribitur, etiam sanctum esse oporteat cultum, qui in iisdem Deo, ut in personis trino, deferendus præscribitur.

Illud saltem intercedit discriminis inter cultum, qui juxta primam legis tabulam a ratione recta; & qui juxta eandem per Scripturam sacram præscribitur, quòd hic cultorem Dei fidelem de impetranda apud Deum gratia ac remissione peccatorum certum & securum reddit: Includit enim fiduciam in Christum Mediatorem, per quem peccatores Deo, peccatis offenso, reconciliati sunt, & παῤῥησίαν, atque aditum cum fiducia habent in uno Spiritu ad Patrem,

Eph. II. 18. & III. 12. & per quem fide perducuntur in gratiam hanc, in qua Deo reconciliati stant & gloriantur sub spe gloriæ Dei, Rom. V. 2. Quin quotquot sunt promissiones Dei, per Christum sunt etiam, & per ipsum, Amen, Deo ad gloriam, II. Cor. I. 20. & quæcunque petierint Patrem in nomine ejus, dabit ipsis, Ioh. XVI. 23. Cultus autem, quem ratio ex naturæ principiis præscribere potest aut præscribit, neminem de impetranda apud Deum gratia & remissione peccatorum certum & securum reddere potest. Quemadmodùm enim ratio, sibi relicta, Christum ejusque meritum & satisfactionem pro peccatis generis humani ignorat, ita nec habet, quæ in conscientiæ angoribus ob peccata & hinc exorientibus dubitationibus de gratia Dei iræ divinæ opponat, & de exauditione ac impetranda apud Deum gratia ac remissione peccatorum conscientiam anxiam certam & securam reddere possit. Qua de re in seq. th. XXI. plura pro ratione instituti dicentur.

IV. Secunda legis tabula continet præcepta de vita hominis, erga se & proximum justè ac sanctè degenda, ad quorum normam si etiam exigas, quæcunque Scriptura sacra de sanctimonia vitæ docet, rursum omnia sancta esse, nec quicquam disconveniens legi, mentibus hominum implantatæ, in iis contineri; imò per præcepta omnia Scripturam longè majorem & perfectiorem exigere sanctitatem, quàm ratio humana vi legis sibi implantatæ exigere possit, oppidò deprehendes: v. g. quòd lex: Diliges proximum tuum, sicut te ipsum, (quæ continet summam totius tabulæ secundæ) contineat sub proximo etiam inimicum, & ut hunc etiam diligamus, à nobis exigat; quòd lex de non occidendo etiam iram, odium, verba & gestus, quibus vel leviter animum adversum erga proximum significamus, omnemque vindictam privatam interdicat; quòd lex de non mœchando etiam interiorem concupiscentiam uxoris alterius, etiam ipsum aspectum illius cum inordinatæ concupiscentiæ motu conjunctum prohibeat, & adulterii criminis damnet, & quòd lex de non concupiscendo generatim omnes inordinatos concupiscentiæ motus, quocunque nomine veniant, etiam eos, qui subitò oriuntur, & rationis judicium ac voluntatis consensum antevertunt, abesse jubeat, ratio vi legis, naturâ sibi implantatæ, cognoscere ac docere non potest, docet tamen Scriptura sacra, & in ea in primis Christus; Magister noster unicus, quem Deus voce cælitùs delapsâ nobis audiendam commendavit, verbis minimè obscuris Matth. V. 44. Luc. VI. 27. 28. 35. Exod. XXIII. 4. 5. Prov. XXV. 21. Rom. XII. 14. I. Cor. IV. 12. 13. I. Petr. III. 9. Matth. V. 21. seqq. I. Joh. III. 15. Matth. V. 28. c. XV. 19. seq. Rom. VII. 7. &c. Breviter: Scriptura sacra requirit ex parte hominis salvandi exactissimam omnium animæ facultatum, omniumque actuum ac motuum, cùm interiorum, tùm exteriorum, conformitatem cum lege, atque adeò sanctimoniam vitæ, omnibus numeris ac modis absolutam & perfectam, qualem alia religio nulla, nullus Scripturæ codex alius, quo alicujus gentis aut populi religio descripta contineatur, præscribit aut exigit.

V. Hinc ita argumentor: Quæcunque Scriptura præscribit religionem ita perfectè & per omnes sui partes sanctam, ut ad ejus sanctitatem eo perfectionis gradu humana ratio ex suo lumine pertingere non possit, ea non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habet Auctorem. Atqui Scriptura sacra præscribit religionem ita perfectè & per omnes sui partes sanctam, ut ad ejus sanctitatem eo perfectionis gradu humana ratio ex suo lumine pertingere non possit. Ergo Scriptura sacra non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habet auctorem. Minor propositio hactenus per inductionem omnium Christianæ religionis partium, ad utramque legis tabulam collatarum, probata est. Major autem evidens est. Cujus Scripturæ sanctitas enim altior & perfectior est, quàm ut à ratione humana ex naturæ principiis doceri ac præscribi possit, eam ab altiori principio originem trahere necesse est. Illud verò altius principium aliud esse non potest, quàm Deus, ex cujus inspiratione Scriptores sacri Scripturam sacram concinnarunt. Et tantum etiam de secundo divinitatis Scripturæ κριτηρίῳ interno, nempe de Sanctitate Scripturæ, absque nævo perfecta. Ad tertium procedimus, quod suprà th. VII. in sufficientia constituebamus.


### XX. Finally, the full sufficiency for salvation, both as to what must be believed…

XX.

Finally, the full sufficiency for salvation, both as to what must be believed and as to what must be done, is evident from the fact that nothing can be shown which could be desired in it, whether from one side or from both.

Among all things which are necessary for this state of corrupted nature for the sake of obtaining salvation by the gift of God, the reconciliation of the sinful man with God, who is offended by sins, claims the first place for itself. For all men sin daily, and they offend God by their sins, and move him to anger. But from God, when he is offended and angered by sins, the sinner does not obtain salvation, unless after he has been reconciled to him, his anger having been appeased. For salvation is a gift of a propitious God, and it is the highest of all things that can befall the human race. Whence no religion, no Scripture can suffice for salvation, unless it, among other things, hands down and prescribes a certain and indubitable method of reconciling the sinful man with God and of obtaining the remission of sins from him. But no religion, except the one and only Christian, and no Scripture, except the one and only sacred one, hands down and prescribes that.

II. The modern Naturalists, as they are called, who reduce the sum of the whole Catholic and salvific religion to five articles known by nature, constitute it in repentance, taking the word repentance for contrition, and in faith in God, or in trust, fixed upon God's goodness and mercy, by which he remits sins to the penitent freely, and without the intervention of satisfaction. But neither suffices for that. Not repentance or bare contrition: because this on the part of the sinner imports nothing, except sorrow or grief and anxiety of mind, arising from the recognition, displeasure, and detestation of sins, through which it comes about that he does not wish to hold the committed sins as ratified, nor to persevere in them, but morally retracts them, and, if it were possible, would wish to render them undone: but it exhibits no satisfaction for the offense and injury brought upon God by sins, which is required by common law for the remission of sins. Nor faith or trust in God's goodness and mercy. For whether God can, with his justice preserved, and also wills to pardon their sins to penitent sinners out of mere goodness and mercy, comes into question, and although not a few ancient Fathers and most Scholastic Doctors affirm that he can do so (which we now leave to its own place), yet that he wills to do so, no article known by nature, no reason drawn from common providence can teach or assert for certain. For this whole matter is placed in the most free will of God. But what God in those things which are in his most free will, whether He actually wills it or not, besides God Himself, no one can know. Moreover, God has nowhere revealed in nature, nowhere promised through nature, that He wills to remit the sins of sinners, who acknowledge and pray against their sins, out of His mere liberality, without an intervening satisfaction. Whence confidence of obtaining grace and remission of sins before God from His goodness alone, without the intervention of satisfaction, by the guidance of the light of nature alone, can be held by no mortal, since he is destitute of a divine promise, which alone can provide a foundation for confidence fixed in the goodness of God; or if it be conceived and cherished in the mind by anyone, without a divine promise, it will be a rash and fallacious presumption, not a true confidence resting upon its own certain foundation. Concerning this matter, let those things be seen which I previously discussed at length in a special Disputation on the insufficiency of the light of nature for salvation, opposed to the Naturalists of today, when I treated of the insufficiency of repentance or contrition to expiate sins, and of the vanity of confidence in obtaining grace and remission of sins before God from His goodness alone, without an intervening satisfaction, which was reprinted nine years ago and added to the end of my Dissertation on the eternal decree of election. Therefore, the method of expiating sins through repentance and faith in God alone without an intervening satisfaction, handed down by Edward Herbert and other Naturalists, since it rests upon no certain foundation, is slippery, and furthermore, the religion built by them upon five articles known by nature is entirely vain and insufficient for salvation.

III. Nor is there any other religion under the sun, or any Scripture, which hands down a full, certain, and indubitable method of expiating sins, besides the Christian religion and the Holy Scripture in which it is contained. In this alone has God revealed that He is unwilling to receive anyone into grace and to make them safe, except through JESUS CHRIST, appointed by Him as the sole Mediator of God and men, who gave Himself as ἀντίλυτρον or the price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. II. 5, 6. Him, with Holy Scripture alone attesting, He proposed from the beginning to the human race, first indeed in the promises, the first of which occurred in the protevangelium Gen. III. 15 to the first-formed, as soon as they had fallen into sin; then in the sacrifices, typically foreshadowing His future satisfaction for the sins of the human race, whose rites some of the Gentiles themselves, spread far and wide throughout the world, imitated through a certain κακοζηλίαν, and finally exhibited in the flesh in reality, and announced to the whole world through Apostolic preaching, that he might be ἱλαστήριον, a propitiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate Rom. III. 25. that he might be ἱλασμὸς, a propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world, 1. Joh. II. 2. that through his death we might be reconciled to him, when we were enemies, and by his blood we might be saved from wrath, Rom. V. 9. 10. that everyone who believes in him might not perish, but have eternal life. Joh. III. 16. Whence all the Prophets bear witness to Christ alone, that everyone who believes in him shall receive remission of sins, Act. X. 43. and the Apostle Peter openly testifies that there is salvation in no other, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved, Act. IV. 12. More testimonies and proofs regarding this matter occur everywhere in the Holy Scriptures. But all other books of scriptures, in which the religions of other nations and peoples are described, just as they are ignorant of or deny Christ as the Mediator of God and men, and the redeemer of the human race, and neither provide nor can provide any other method of reconciling sinful man with God that is based on its own certain foundations, so they all fail in this regard, nor can any of them suffice for man to obtain salvation. Whence they are all insufficient for salvation: but Holy Scripture alone, as far as it pertains to the doctrine of the reconciliation of sinful man with God, is perfect, full, and sufficient for salvation. But that Holy Scripture perfectly delivers everything in the other parts of doctrine as well, concerning both what must be believed and what must be done, so that nothing more can be desired in them, while all other religions and all other books of scriptures fail in many ways and are imperfect and insufficient, has been shown above in thesis X. and following by a lengthy induction, where they may be seen.

IV. With these things being so, we argue again in this manner: Whatever Scripture delivers all things necessary for a man about to obtain salvation to believe and to do, so sufficiently that nothing of them can be desired, it has not mere men, but God himself as its author. Yet Holy Scripture delivers all things necessary to be believed and done by a man about to attain salvation, so sufficiently that nothing of them can be desired. Therefore Holy Scripture has not mere men, but God himself as its author. The major proposition is evident: because no mortal can know, teach, or commit to writing all things necessary to be believed and done by a man about to attain salvation, unless God assists, suggests, and reveals. For in them are contained many abstruse things which exceed the grasp of human reason: such as mysteries, hidden from the ages, and especially the mystery of the incarnation and, what is related to this, the mystery of the Trinity, and likewise the free decrees of God concerning our salvation, to be restored through Christ and restored at the appointed time, and concerning our regeneration, justification and renovation, and others enumerated above, which can become known to no one except through God, and by his revealing them, as has been shown. As regards the minor proposition, it is established from what has been said thus far, and it has been shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently by the induction of all things which are necessary to be believed and done by those about to attain salvation, or which can be required as necessary to be believed or done, both those which in some way fall under the light of nature and those which exceed it, that they are delivered in Holy Scripture so perfectly and sufficiently that nothing can be desired in them.

And let these things suffice, according to the nature of our undertaking, concerning the internal criteria of Scripture, which can make its divine origin credible to anyone, even to a pagan man.

Latin:

XX.

SUfficientia denique ad salutem plena, cùm quà credenda, tùm quà agenda, vel inde patet, quòd nihil ostendi potest, quod sive ex alterutra sive ex utraque parte in ea desiderari possit.

Inter omnia, quæ pro hoc naturæ corruptæ statu ad consequendam Dei dono salutem necessaria sunt, primas sibi vendicat reconciliatio hominis peccatoris cum Deo, peccatis offenso. Peccant enim homines omnes quotidiè, offenduntque Deum peccatis, & commovent eum ad iram. A Deo autem, peccatis offenso iratoque peccator non consequitur salutem, nisi postquam ei, placatâ ipsius irâ, reconciliatus est. Salus enim est donum Dei propitii, idque omnium, quæ mortalium generi obtingere possunt, summum. Unde religio ad salutem nulla, Scriptura nulla sufficere potest, nisi quæ inter alia rationem reconciliandi hominis peccatoris cum Deo impetrandæque apud ipsum remissionis peccatorum certam & indubitatam tradit & præscribit. Eam verò religio nulla, præter unam & solam Christianam, Scriptura nulla, præter unam & solam sacram, tradit & præscribit.

II. Hodierni Naturalistæ, ut vocantur, qui summam totius Catholicæ & salvificæ religionis ad quinque naturâ notos articulos reducunt, constituunt eam in pœnitentia, voce pœnitentiæ pro contritione acceptâ, & in fide in Deum, sive in fiducia, defixa in Dei bonitate ac misericordia, quâ pœnitenti peccata gratis, & absque interventu satisfactionis remittat. Sed neutra ad illam sufficit. Non pœnitentia sive contritio nuda: quia hæc ex parte peccatoris nihil importat, præter dolorem sive mœrorem & anxietatem animi, ex agnitione, displicentia & detestatione peccatorum oborta, per quam sit, ut non rata habere peccata commissa, non perseverare in illis velit, sed moraliter ea retractet, &, si fieri posset, reddere vellet infecta: satisfactionem autem pro offensa & injuria, Deõ peccatis illata, quæ de lege communi ad remissionem peccatorum requiritur, nullam exhibet. Neque fides sive fiducia in Dei bonitate & misericordia. Utrum enim Deus possit, justitiâ suâ salvâ, & velit etiam peccatoribus pœnitentibus peccata sua ex mera bonitate & misericordia condonare, in quæstionem venit, & quamvis id eum posse, Patres veteres non pauci, & Doctores Scholastici plerique affirment (quod suo loco nunc relinquimus) eum tamen id facere velle, nullus naturâ notus articulus, ratio ex communi providentia desumta nulla docere, aut pro certo asseverare potest. Hoc enim totum in Dei liberrima voluntate positum est. Quid autem Deus in iis, quæ in liberrima ipsius voluntate posita sunt, actu velit aut non velit, præter ipsummet Deum, nemo nôsse potest. Nuspiam autem Deus in natura revelavit, promisit nuspiam per naturam, se velle peccatoribus, peccata sua agnoscentibus & deprecantibus, peccata remittere ex mera sua liberalitate, sine interveniente satisfactione. Unde fiducia impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum ex sola ipsius bonitate, absque interventu satisfactionis, ductu solius luminis naturæ, haberi à mortalium nemine potest, cùm destituatur divina promissione, quæ sola defixæ in Dei bonitate fiduciæ fundamentum præbere potest; vel si à quopiam concipiatur & foveatur animo, absque divina promissione, temeraria & fallax præsumtio, non vera & suo certo fundamento innixa fiducia erit. Qua de re videantur, quæ antehac in peculiari Disputatione de insufficientia luminis naturæ ad salutem, hodiernis Naturalistis oppositâ, cùm de insufficientia pœnitentiæ sive contritionis ad expianda peccata, cùm de vanitate fiduciæ de impetranda apud Deum gratia ac remissione peccatorum ex sola ejus bonitate, absque interveniente satisfactione, fusè egi, quæ ante annos novem recusa & Dissertationi meæ de æterno electionis decreto sub calcem adjecta est. Ratio ergo expiandi peccata per solam pœnitentiam & fidem in Deum absque interveniente satisfactione, ab Edoardo Herbert aliisque Naturalistis tradita, cùm nullo certo nitatur fundamento, lubrica, & porro religio, quinque naturâ notis articulis ab ipsis superstructa, tota vana & ad salutem insufficiens est.

III. Neque alia ulla sub sole religio datur, Scriptura ulla, quæ rationem expiandi peccata plenam, eamque certam & indubitatam, tradat, præter religionem Christianam, & quâ ea descripta continetur, Scripturam sacram. In hac sola Deus revelavit, se nolle quemquam recipere in gratiam, & salvum facere, nisi per JESUM CHRISTUM, constitutum à se Mediatorem Dei & hominum unicum, qui semetipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον sive redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Tim. II. 5. 6. Hunc, solâ attestante Scripturâ sacrâ, proposuit inde ab initio generi humano, primùm quidem in promissionibus, quarum prima in protevangelio Gen. III. 15. protoplastis, simul ac in peccatum prolapsi fuerant, obtigit; deinde in sacrificiis, futuram ejus satisfactionem pro peccatis generis humani typicè adumbrantibus, quorum ritus nonnullos ipsi Gentiles, per orbem terrarum longe lateque diffusi, per κακοζηλίαν quandam imitati sunt, & denique in carne reapse exhibitum, & per prædicationem Apostolicam orbi terrarum toti annunciatum, ut esset ἱλαστήριον, placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad demonstrandam justitiam suam per remissionem peccatorum, quæ præcesserunt, Deo illa tolerante, Rom. III. 25. ut esset ἱλασμὸς propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris tantum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis, 1. Joh. II. 2. ut per ejus mortem reconciliaremur ipsi, cùm inimici essemus, & sanguis illius justificati servaremur ab ira, Rom. V. 9. 10. ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Joh. III. 16. Unde uni & soli Christo Prophetæ omnes perhibent testimonium, quòd remissionem peccatorum accepturus sit, quisquis credit in eum, Act. X. 43. & Petrus Apostolus testatur aperte, non esse in alio quoquam salutem, neque aliud nomen esse sub cælo datum, in quo nos oporteat salvos fieri, Act. IV. 12. Plura hanc in rem testimonia ac documenta ubique locorum in Scripturis sacris occurrunt. Cæteri autem Scripturarum Codices omnes, quibus aliæ gentium ac populorum religiones descriptæ continentur, quemadmodum Christum Mediatorem Dei & hominum, ac redemtorem generis humani ignorant vel negant, nec aliam suis certis fundamentis innixam rationem reconciliandi hominis peccatoris cum Deo tradunt aut tradere possunt, ita hoc in passu deficiunt omnes, nec illarum ulla homini ad adipiscendam salutem sufficere potest. Unde ad salutem insufficientes omnes sunt: sola autem Scriptura sacra, quod ad doctrinam de reconciliatione hominis peccatoris cum Deo attinet, perfecta, plena & ad salutem sufficiens est. Quod autem in cæteris etiam doctrinæ partibus, cùm quæ credenda, tùm quæ agenda concernunt, Scriptura sacra omnia perfectè tradat, ut nihil amplius in iis desiderari possit, cæteræ autem religiones omnes, Scripturarum Codices cæteri omnes multis modis deficiant, & imperfectæ ac insufficientes sint, ostensum est suprà thes. X. & seqq. per inductionem prolixè, ubi videantur.

IV. Quibus ita habentibus, rursum argumentamur hunc in modum: Quæcunque Scriptura omnia homini salutem adepturo creditu factuque necessaria, ita sufficienter tradit, ut eorum nihil desiderari possit, illa non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habet auctorem. Atqui Scriptura sacra tradit omnia, homini salutem adepturo creditu factuque necessaria, ita sufficienter, ut nihil eorum desiderari possit. Ergo Scriptura sacra non homines nudos, sed Deum ipsummet habet auctorem. Major propositio patet: quia omnia, homini salutem adepturo creditu factuque necessaria, nemo mortalium ex se nosse, docere, aut literis consignare potest, nisi Deo adjuvante, suggerente, & revelante. In iis enim multa continentur abstrufa, quæ humanæ rationis captum excedunt: qualia sunt mysteria, inde à seculis abscondita, & cumprimis mysterium incarnationis &, quod huic affine est, mysterium Trinitatis, itemque decreta Dei libera de nostra salute, per Christum reparanda & statuto tempore reparata, deque nostra regeneratione, justificatione & renovatione, aliisque suprà enumeratis, quæ nemini innotescere possunt, nisi per Deum, ipsoque revelante, ut ostensum. Minorem propositionem quod attinet, constat ex hactenus dictis, ostensumque est satis superque per inductionem omnium, quæ salutem adepturis creditu factuque necessaria sunt, aut ut necessaria creditu factuve requiri possunt, cùm quæ sub lumen naturæ quodammodò cadunt, tùm quæ illud excedunt, quòd in Scriptura sacra tradantur ita perfectè & sufficienter, ut nihil in illis desiderari possit.

Atque hæc de κριτηρίοις Scripturæ internis, quæ divinam ejus originem cuivis, etiam homini pagano, credibilem facere possunt, pro ratione instituti nostri sufficiant.


## 9 On the Signs and Motives of Credibility: External

I.

Among the external signs and motives of credibility, from which the divine origin of Holy Scripture becomes known to us in its own way, we assign the first place to its ANTIQUITY. I. That those things are called external signs and motives of credibility which are derived not from the intrinsic nature of Holy Scripture, but from elsewhere outside of it, has been stated above in Sect. I, th. II. Among these, however, we deservedly assign the first place, and the one closest to the internal signs and motives, to ANTIQUITY. For this coheres most closely with the internal signs and motives and with the very intrinsic nature of Holy Scripture, so that in a certain way it can also be referred to the internal signs and motives. For the antiquity of any thing (created, of which we are speaking here) is nothing other than its long-lasting duration or permanence in its being, drawing its beginning from long times past. However, the duration of a thing does not differ from the thing enduring, or the permanence of a thing in its being from the thing remaining, except in reason. Nevertheless, antiquity connotes time, by which the measured long-lasting duration finally obtains the character of antiquity. Because this is extrinsic to the thing enduring and remaining in its being, antiquity is also rightly numbered among its extrinsic affections, and consequently the antiquity of Holy Scripture among its external signs and motives.

II. The antiquity of Holy Scripture can be considered either on the part of its formal aspect, namely on the part of the doctrine both of faith and of morals; or on the part of its material aspect, namely on the part of the written words. Although, indeed, on the part of its material aspect, Holy Scripture, especially as it pertains to Mosaic history, is more ancient than the books of all the Gentiles, here however we consider its antiquity primarily by reason of its formal aspect, namely the doctrine contained in it, in view of which the more ancient it is, the greater it is in authority.

III. Holy Scripture, viewed on the part of its formal aspect, began with the very beginning of the world. For the doctrine concerning the right acknowledgment and worship of God, and concerning life to be lived justly and holily, which is the sum and nucleus of the entire Scripture, began when the human race itself began. For the eternal law of GOD, which is the rule of divine worship and of life to be lived justly and holily, was impressed upon the minds of the first parents by God in their very creation, and was propagated by them to their descendants partly through generation, partly through tradition. For both the first humans and all their descendants begat, and still beget today, children with the eternal law of God implanted in their minds, as a rule, according to the prescription of which they were to acknowledge and worship God their Creator, and their life ought to establish in conformity with His will, although in a degree far inferior to that which was impressed by God upon the Protoplast in the first creation, so that the knowledge of the eternal law of God which is born with descendants, when compared to the knowledge implanted in the same Protoplast in the first creation, may be seen as certain remnants and ruins of it. But those things which could not be known from the eternal law of God implanted in minds, yet are necessary to be known for the worship of God and for living a holy life, and thus for attaining salvation: such as the mystery of the Trinity, of the incarnation, of our redemption through Christ, the state and distinct nature of our future blessedness, etc., were without doubt revealed to the Protoplasts, partly before the fall, and partly after their fall by God, who conversed with them more familiarly, and were propagated by them through tradition to their descendants. For just as man was originally created for blessedness, placed in the intuitive knowledge of the Triune God, so that in the state of perfection in which he was created he had knowledge of his ultimate end, both objective and formal, it seems consistent with the truth that God revealed to him immediately after his creation and in that very primeval state of his perfection both things, namely that He is three in persons; and that we shall know Him in the future state of blessedness, as He is one in essence and three in persons, clearly and intuitively, since the former is intrinsically contained in man's objective end; and the latter constitutes his formal end. But those things which are furthermore necessary to be known in the state of sin, the first of them, and the basis and foundation of all the rest, is the doctrine concerning the Messiah or Christ, the only Mediator between God and men, which God revealed to the Protoplasts as soon as they had fallen in the protevangelium concerning the Seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, and concerning the bruising of His heel by the serpent, Gen. 3:15. Because this implicitly contains the sum of the doctrine concerning Christ, and concerning the method of expiating sins through His sacrifice, to be immolated for us on the altar of the cross, there is no doubt that it was subsequently declared to them more abundantly by God, and propagated to posterity partly through more frequent revelations, and partly through the tradition of parents and Teachers, and was preserved in the same. What? That even the rite of sacrificing, by which the future expiatory sacrifice of the Messiah is foreshadowed, was prescribed to the Protoplasts by God Himself and by them to was propagated to posterity. A not obscure proof of this matter are the sacrifices offered to God by Cain and Abel, the first sons of Adam, whose rite it is not credible that they received from elsewhere than from their parents, who were divinely instructed concerning it, whatever the Papists may allege concerning the rite of sacrifices instituted by the law of nature: which is opposed, among other things, by the fact that the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. XI. 4, says: By faith Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice to God than Cain, etc. For faith concerning an offered sacrifice, which would be pleasing and acceptable to God, could not have been conceived by Abel, unless there was a prior knowledge of the rite of sacrificing itself instituted by God, and of the divine promise concerning its benevolent acceptance, imparted to the Protoplasts.

But whatever knowledge of sublime mysteries was either implanted by nature in the minds of men as the eternal law of God, or was imparted to the Protoplasts through supernatural revelation before or after their fall, that was afterwards propagated by them through tradition to their posterity up to the flood, first privately by parents, or those who were in the place of parents; and afterwards, when public worship of God began to be established, by the holy Patriarchs, who were peculiarly instructed and illuminated by God for this purpose, and who performed the duty of teaching in public assemblies. That this happened in the time of Enosh, in the third century from the creation of the world, Moses, instructed by the Holy Spirit concerning this matter and by His inspiration, records in Gen. IV. 26. How after the flood this very doctrine concerning the Messiah was propagated by the Patriarchs and Prophets up to Christ, exhibited in the flesh, partly by voice, partly by writings, illustrated by various sacrifices and types, and more fully declared as God from time to time imparted clearer revelations; and how it was fulfilled by Christ, exhibited in the flesh, according to all its parts and circumstances, and thus from the first Adam was always one and the same doctrine, preserved and propagated without any variation of itself in substantial matters, has been shown in the preceding Sect. I. th. XVII. Expl n. 1. and th. XIX. Expl. n. III. Which indeed clearly proves that Holy Scripture, viewed from its formal side, is the most ancient of all. For no mortal is more ancient than the Protoplasts, with whom it took its origin partly through notions implanted in their minds by God at their very creation, and partly through divine revelations, and from whom, by the peculiar providence of God, it has been preserved and propagated to us, unchanged, along with the human race itself; No religion, no worship offered or to be offered to God, no rule of human life is more ancient.

IV. Corruptions of doctrine, both of faith and of morals, and false worships did indeed flourish from the very first times, and from the fratricide of Cain down to the flood, especially in the posterity of Cain; and after the flood in the descendants of Japheth and Ham and in the countless nations and peoples that descended from them down to these times: but prior and more ancient than all these is the religion and worship, and the manner of living one's life, which the first-formed humans received from God himself, and which the pious posterity of Seth preserved undefiled down to Noah; and afterwards the pious posterity of Shem preserved it down to Christ, exhibited in the flesh, and Moses was the first of all to begin to commit it to writing. For from this, first handed down by Adam to his sons, and publicly preached by the patriarchs descending from Seth, the impious Cainites fell away, and following the lead of their own corrupted reason, they eventually devised a peculiar and new religion and worship: and the peoples who descended from the two sons of Noah, Japheth and Ham, fell away in the progress of time from that same religion, which had been received from Noah, the herald of righteousness, and preserved in the pious posterity of Shem, and they instituted their own peculiar assemblies, and fashioned for themselves another kind of doctrine and worship, different from that one, and indeed varied and manifold.

Furthermore, no false religion and doctrine has always endured without its own variation, but all have been changed and are changed quite often, so that as many as there are peoples and nations, so many different religions are found among them; yet none, which began either before the flood in the posterity of Cain, or after the flood in the posterity of Japheth or Ham, has persisted without its own variation. But that first one alone, which began immediately with the first-formed humans, and drew its origin from the eternal law of God, partly implanted in their minds, and partly from supernatural revelations which came to them divinely, persisted unvaried in the posterity of Seth down to the flood; and after the flood in the pious posterity of Shem, the second-born son of Noah, down to the birth of Christ, and it will persist without any mutation of itself as long as heaven and earth, and the Church militant on earth, shall persist. It remains, therefore, fixed and immovable that Holy Scripture, by reason of the doctrine concerning things necessary to be believed and done which it contains, is the first of all, the most ancient of all, and that nothing more ancient than it can be given or conceived. But just as everything that is first and everything that is most ancient is most true: so also it is necessary that Holy Scripture, since, by reason of the doctrine necessary for belief and action, it is the first of all and the most ancient of all, and has drawn its origin from God himself along with the human race itself, is most true, nay, divine.

V. The argument in form can be this: Whatever Scripture, by reason of the doctrine necessary for belief and action which it contains, is the first and most ancient of all, that is the most true of all and truly divine. But Holy Scripture, by reason of the doctrine necessary for belief and action which it contains, is the first and most ancient of all. Therefore, Holy Scripture is the most true of all and truly divine. The major proposition is evident. For in every matter, truth is prior to falsehood and lying, and than that which nothing is prior, nothing is more ancient, than that nothing is or can be more true. For truth is founded in the thing itself, nay, it is the thing itself, as it is apt to terminate a true knowledge of itself, to which whatever knowledge is conformable, that also is true. On the other hand, however, falsehood is when a thing, apt to terminate a true knowledge of itself, is conceived otherwise than it is: but to conceive a thing otherwise than it is, is something posterior to the thing itself, which is apt to terminate a true knowledge of itself, and thus falsehood is always posterior, but truth is prior. But if a thing, apt to terminate a true knowledge of itself, exceeds the light of nature, and cannot become known to the mortal race unless God reveals it, then truth is to be estimated from its congruence with the divine intellect, and defined by the conformity of knowledge with the divine intellect, and because God cannot reveal the things which it is in our interest to know for our salvation otherwise than conformably to his own intellect: for he cannot, through his infinite knowledge and goodness, be deceived or deceive in revealing; whatever is revealed by him must be true, and thus also truth is prior to falsehood. For falsehood here is when a thing is known disconformably to the divine intellect, or, which comes to the same thing, otherwise than it was revealed by God. But it is prior that things necessary for belief and action be revealed by God, and thus conformable to the divine intellect and true, than that they be known otherwise than they were revealed by God, or disconformably to the divine intellect. It is therefore universally true that everything first and most ancient is most true. But the minor proposition has already been proved in the preceding n. III. and IV. of the explanation of this thesis,

Latin:

I.

INter signa & motiva credibilitatis externa, ex quibus divina Scripturæ sacræ origo suo modo nobis innotescit, locum primum tribuimus ejus ANTIQUITATI. I. Externa credibilitatis signa & motiva appellari, quæ non ex intrinseca Scripturæ sacræ natura, sed extra eam aliunde desumuntur, dictum est suprà Sect. I. th. II. Inter illa autem meritò primum & à signis ac motivis internis proximum locum tribuimus ANTIQUITATI. Hæc enim cum signis & motivis internis & cum ipsa intrinseca Scripturæ sacræ natura arctissimè cohæret, ut certo modo etiam ad signa & motiva interna referri possit. Nam antiquitas cujusque rei (creatæ, de qua hîc sermo est) nihil aliud est, quàm ejus diuturna, & inde à longis temporibus initium trahens duratio sive permanentia in suo esse. Duratio rei autem à re durante, sive permanentia rei in suo esse à re permanente non differt, nisi ratione. Connotat tamen antiquitas tempus, quo mensurata duratio diuturna demùm antiquitatis rationem sortitur. Quod quia rei duranti & in suo esse permanenti extrinsecum est, antiquitas etiam in extrinsecis ejus affectionibus, & consequenter Scripturæ sacræ antiquitas in externis ejus signis & motivis rectè numeratur.

II. Potest autem Scripturæ sacræ antiquitas considerari vel ex parte sui formalis, ex parte doctrinæ scilicet cùm fidei tum morum; vel ex parte sui materialis, nempe ex parte vocum scriptarum. Quamvis verò, ex parte sui materialis, Scriptura sacra, præsertim quod ad historiam Mosaïcam attinet, omnium Gentilium libris sit antiquior, hic tamen consideramus ejus antiquitatem potissimùm ratione sui formalis, doctrinæ scilicet, in ea contentæ, cujus intuitu quo antiquior, eo auctoritate major est.

III. Cœpit autem Scriptura sacra, ex parte formalis sui spectata, cum ipso mundi exordio. Nam doctrina de recta agnitione & cultu Dei, deque vita, justè & sanctè degenda, quæ Scripturæ universæ summa & nucleus est, cœpit, cùm ipsum genus humanum cœpit. Nam lex DEI æterna, quæ divini cultus vitæque justè & sanctè degendæ regula est, Protoplastorum mentibus in ipsa illorum creatione à Deo impressa, & ab iisdem partim per generationem, partim per traditionem ad illorum posteros propagata fuit. Generârunt enim & primi homines, & illorum posteri omnes, generantque adhuc hodieque liberos cum implantata illorum mentibus lege Dei æternâ, velut regulâ, ad cujus præscriptum Deum Conditorem suum agnoscere & colere, vitamque ejus voluntati conformiter instituere deberent, quamvis gradu multò inferiori, quàm in prima creatione Protoplastis à Deo impressa fuit, ut quæ posteris connascitur notitia legis Dei æternæ, ad ejusdem Protoplastis in prima creatione implantatam notitiam collata, velut quædam illius reliquiæ & rudera videri possint. Quæ autem ex implantata mentibus lege Dei æterna cognosci non poterant, cognitu tamen ad Dei cultum vitamque sanctè degendam, atque adeò ad salutem adipiscendam necessaria sunt: cujusmodi sunt mysterium Trinitatis, incarnationis, redemtionis nostræ per Christum, futuræ beatitudinis nostræ status & ratio distincta &c. dubio procul Protoplastis ante lapsum partim, partim post illorum lapsum à Deo, familiariùs cum illis conversante, supernaturaliter revelata, & ab his per traditionem ad posteros suos propagata sunt. Quemadmodùm enim homo ad beatitudinem, in Dei Trinunius cognitione intuitiva positam, primitùs conditus fuit, ita ut in eo, quo conditus fuit, perfectionis statu finem suum ultimum, cùm objectivum, tùm formalem, cognitum haberet, vero consentaneum videtur, Deum revelâsse ei statim post ejus creationem & in ipso primævo perfectionis suæ statu utrumque, nempe se esse in personis trinum; & nos cognituros esse eum in futuro beatitudinis statu, ut in se unus in essentia & trinus in personis est, clarè & intuitivè, cùm illud in hominis fine objectivo intrinsecè contineatur; hoc ipsum ejus finem formalem constituat. Quæ autem in statu peccati præterea necessaria sunt cognitu, illorum primum, & cæterorum omnium basis & fundamentum est doctrina de Messia sive Christo, Mediatore Dei & hominum unico, quam Protoplastis Deus, simul ac lapsi fuerant, revelavit in protevangelio de Semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro, deque conterendo per serpentem calcaneo illius, Gen. III. 15. Quod quia summam doctrinæ de Christo, deque ratione expiandi peccata per ejus sacrificium, in ara crucis pro nobis immolandum, implicitè continet, dubium non est, quin à Deo subinde ipsis uberius declaratum, & per revelationes crebriores partim, partim per raditionem parentum & Doctorum ad posteritatem propagatum, & in eadem conservatum fuerit. Quid? quod etiam sacrificandi ritus, quo futurum Messiæ sacrificium expiatorium adumbratur, Protoplastis ab ipsomet Deo præscriptus & ab his ad posteros propagatus fuit. Cui rei documento haud obscuro sunt sacrificia, à Caino & Abele, primis Adami filiis, Deo oblata, quorum ritum aliunde, quàm à parentibus, divinitùs de eo edoctis, eos accepisse, credibile non est, quicquid etiam Pontificii de sacrificiorum ritu, per legem naturæ instituto, obtendant: quibus inter alia repugnat, quòd Auctor Epist. ad Ebr. c. XI. 4. Per fidem, ait, uberiorem hostiam Abel obtulit Deo, quàm Cain &c. Neque enim fides ad Deum de oblato sacrificio, quod Deo gratum & acceptum futurum esset, concipi ab Abele potuit, nisi præviâ notitiâ instituti à Deo ipsius ritus sacrificandi, divina̧que promissionis de ejusdem acceptatione benevola, Protoplastis impertitæ.

Quæ autem sive mentibus hominum naturâ implantata legis Dei æternæ; sive per revelationem supernaturalem Protoplastis ante vel post illorum lapsum impertita fuit mysteriorum sublimium cognitio, ea ab iisdem posteà per traditionem ad posteros ad diluvium usque propagata est, primùm parentibus, vel qui parentum loco erant, privatim; & posteà, ubi cultus Dei publicus instaurari cœpit, sanctis Patriarchis, à Deo peculiariter ad hoc instructis & illuminatis, in conventibus publicis docendi munere fungentibus. Quod Enoschi tempore, seculo à condito mundo tertio contigisse, Moses, à Spiritu S. hac de re edoctus, ipsoque inspirante memorat Gen. IV. 26. Quomodo post diluvium hæc ipsa de Messia doctrina à Patriarchis & Prophetis usque ad Christum, in carne exhibitum, voce partim, partim scriptis propagata, sacrificiis & typis variis illustrata & uberius, Deo subinde clariores revelationes impertiente, declarata; à Christo autem, in carne exhibito, secundum omnes sui partes & circumstantias impleta, atque adeò inde à primo Adamo semper una & eadem doctrina, absque ulla sui, in substantialibus, variatione conservata & propagata fuerit, ostensum est in præced. Sect. I. th. XVII. Expl n. 1. & th. XIX. Expl. n. III. Quod profectò liquidò evincit, Scripturam sacram, ex parte sui formalis spectatam, esse omnium antiquissimam. Protoplastis enim, quibuscum partim per notitias, in ipsa creatione illorum mentibus à Deo insitas, partim per divinas revelationes suam sumsit originem, & à quibus cum ipso genere humano ad nos usque, Dei peculiari providentiâ, invariata conservata propagatáque est, mortalium nemo antiquior; nulla religio, cultus Deo delatus aut deferendus nullus, regula vitæ humanæ nulla antiquior est.

IV. Viguerunt quidem corruptelæ doctrinæ, cùm fidei tum morum, cultusque falsi ipsis primis statim temporibus, & inde à Caini parricidio ad diluvium usque, in Caini posteritate cumprimis; & post diluvium in Japheti & Chami posteris &, quæ ab illis descenderunt, Gentibus ac populis innumeris ad hæc usque tempora: sed his omnibus prior & antiquior est religio & cultus, vitæque degendæ ratio, quam ab ipso Deo acceperant Protoplasti, & Sethi pia posteritas ad Noachum usque; & posteà pia Semi posteritas usque ad Christum, in carne exhibitum intemeratam conservavit, & primus omnium Moses in literas referre cœpit. Ab hac enim, primùm per Adamum filiis suis traditâ, & per descendentes è Setho Patriarchas publicè prædicatâ, defecerunt Cainitæ impii, ductumque suæ rationis corruptæ seqvuti, peculiarem & novam religionem cultumque demùm commenti sunt: & qui ex duobus filiis Noæ, Japheto & Chamo, descenderunt populi, defecerunt temporis progressu ab eadem, à Noacho, præcone justitiæ, accepta, & in pia Semi posteritate conservatâ, & suos peculiares cœtus instituerunt, aliudque, ab illo diversum, idque varium & multiplex doctrinæ cultusque genus sibi confinxerunt.

Prætereà nulla religio & doctrina falsa duravit semper absque sui variatione, sed omnes mutatæ sunt mutanturque sæpiùs, ut quot populi ac Gentes, tot diversæ in illis religiones inveniantur nulla verò, quæ vel ante diluvium in Caini; vel post diluvium in Japheti aut Chami posteris cœperit, absque sui variatione perseveravit. Sola autem prima illa, quæ cum Protoplastis statim cœpit, & ex lege Dei æterna, ipsorum mentibus implantatâ partim, partim ex supernaturalibus, quæ iisdem divinitùs obtigerunt, revelationibus originem traxit, in Sethi posteris usque ad diluvium; & post diluvium in Semi, Noachi filii secundogeniti, pia posteritate usque ad natum Christum invariata perstitit, persistetque absque ulla sui mutatione, quamdiu cœlum & terra, & militans in terris Ecclesia persistet. Fixum ergo immotumque manet, Scripturam sacram, ratione doctrinæ de rebus, creditu factuque necessariis, quam continet, esse omnium primam, omnium antiquissimam, eáque antiquiorem nec dari nec cogitari posse. Quemadmodum autem primum quodque, & antiquissimum quodq; verissimum est: ita & Scripturam sacram, cùm, ratione doctrinæ creditu factúque necessariæ, prima omnium, omnium antiquissima sit, & ab ipsomet Deo cum ipso genere humano suam originem traxerit, verissimam, imò divinam esse necesse est.

V. Argumentum in forma potest esse hoc: Quæ Scriptura ratione doctrinæ, creditu factuque necessariæ, quam continet, omnium prima & antiquissima est, ea omnium verissima, vereq; divina est. Atqui Scriptura sacra ratione doctrinæ, creditu factuque necessariæ, quam continet, omnium prima & antiquissima est. Ergo Scriptura sacra omnium verissima vereque divina est. Major propositio evidens est. Veritas enim omni in re prior est falsitate & mendacio, & quo nihil prius, nihil antiquius est, eo verius nihil est aut esse potest. Fundatur enim veritas in ipsa re, imò est ipsa res, ut apta est veram sui cognitionem terminare, cui quæcunque cognitio conformis est, ea & vera est. Contra autem falsitas est, cùm res, veram sui cognitionem terminare apta, aliter, quàm est, concipitur: concipere autem rem aliter, quàm est, posterius quid est ipsâ re, veram sui cognitionem terminare aptâ, & sic falsitas semper posterior, veritas autem prior est. Quod si res, veram sui cognitionem terminare apta, lumen naturæ excedat, nec nisi Deo revelante mortalium generi innotescere possit, tum æstimanda est veritas ex congruentia cum intellectu divino, & definienda per conformitatem cognitionis cum intellectu divino, & quia res, quas nosse nostræ interest salutis, Deus non aliter, quàm suo intellectui conformiter, revelare potest: non enim per suam infinitam scientiam & bonitatem in revelando falli aut fallere potest; verum sit oportet, quicquid ab eo revelatur, atque sic etiam veritas prior est falsitate. Nam falsitas hic est, cùm res divino intellectui difformiter, seu, quod eodem redit, aliter, quàm à Deo revelata est, cognoscitur. Prius autem est, res creditu factuve necessarias esse à Deo revelatas, adeoque intellectui divino conformes & veras quàm eas aliter, quàm à Deo revelatæ sunt, vel intellectui divino difformiter cognosci. Est ergo universaliter verum, quòd primum & antiquissimum quodque verissimum sit. Minor autem propositio in præced. n. III. & IV. explicationis hujus theseos jam probata est,


### II. The place next to antiquity is deservedly claimed by the ἀξιοπισία…

II.

The place next to antiquity is deservedly claimed by the ἀξιοπισία (trustworthiness) of the sacred writers, through which faith and assent are rightly owed to them.

I. Sacred Scripture is written historically, and it also comprises a great part of histories, yet with doctrines of faith and morals interspersed. However, in any good historian and teacher, in order to win faith for his sayings or writings, two things are primarily required: one, a certain knowledge of the things to be narrated or explained and handed down; the other, a zeal for truth, sincere and without any bias of parties or affections. Both are found and are prominent in all the sacred writers.

II. As regards knowledge, the things which are recorded in writing in the sacred Scriptures are of two different kinds. For some things could not have become known to mortals from any other source than divine revelation. Others, however, are subject to the light of nature or even to the senses, and concern either principles known by nature, or conclusions deduced from them, or things done by men or among men. But of whatever kind or order the things contained in the sacred Scriptures may be, it will easily be evident to one considering them that the sacred writers did not lack knowledge of them, to the extent that it could suffice for recording them in writing.

III. The things which Moses, first of all, records concerning the works of creation, produced in the space of six days at the beginning of Genesis, are of the first class. For although it may be known in a certain way by the guidance of the light of nature what the connatural order of things to be produced is, what it was fitting to be produced first, what later, etc., yet that all things were produced successively, not simultaneously; that they were produced in the space of six, not more or fewer days; that they were produced by the Word of God, and by saying that they should be made; that on this day these things, and no more, were produced, and on that day those things, and no others; and many more particulars of that kind are matters of fact, and depend upon the free will of God: indeed, they were done before man, who could testify concerning their production, was in the nature of things: which, therefore, could not have become known to men unless God revealed them. Whether, therefore, you say that Moses himself, or only Adam, or both, though at different times and places, received knowledge of them through immediate revelation from God, yet you will have no reason why you should deny that Moses, writing those things, was instructed with sufficient, certain, and indubitable knowledge of them, especially since he described everything so exactly according to various particular circumstances, and followed every minute detail as accurately as if he himself had been present at the work of creation and had seen everything with his own eyes. If you say the first or the third, the matter will be in shallow water. For there is no knowledge given that is more certain than that which God, who is Truth itself and the source of all truth, suggests to any writer through immediate revelation, and suggested to Moses as he wrote. But if the second? Not even then will there be any reason why you should call his credibility into doubt on account of a lack of knowledge of the things to be written. For thus it must be said, that the knowledge of them was derived from Adam and his descendants down to Moses through tradition. Although that span of time from the foundation of the world down to Moses is sufficiently long, and encompasses in its circuit two thousand four hundred years and more, the history of creation, for that state of men, could well have been preserved undefiled through tradition throughout that whole span of time and propagated to Moses (1) on account of the very great importance of the matter. For just as it is a matter of the greatest importance, and contributes much to illustrating and celebrating the glory of God, to know more distinctly the origin of man and the whole world, so there is no doubt that the Protoplasts, once they had received the knowledge of this history from God through revelation, assiduously recalled it among themselves, and inculcated it to their sons, and these in turn, especially those who were of the pious lineage of Seth, to the sons born to them, and so on indefinitely down to Moses, just as was done with the Protevangelium, announced by God himself immediately after the fall of the Protoplasts, the memory of which was propagated down to Moses by tradition alone. (2) On account of the liveliness and fixed memory of men, for the state of those times. As the nature of men at that time was very lively and robust, so that it sometimes extended the limit of life to the eighth and ninth century and beyond, so also their memory was much more vivid and firm than it is now, so that it was not difficult to propagate things worthy of memory to late posterity through tradition. Indeed, the parent of Moses, Amram, saw and heard both his grandfather Levi and his great-grandfather Jacob, and what they had received from their ancestors through tradition, from them could know. The Patriarch Jacob saw and heard Abraham, and he could learn from him what he had received as handed down from his ancestors. Terah, the father of Abraham, saw and heard Noah, and Lamech, the father of Noah, saw Adam himself, with whom he lived for fifty-six years, so that the propagation of tradition was easy from Adam down to Lamech, from Lamech through Noah to Terah, from Terah through Abraham to Jacob, and through him to Amram the father of Moses, and to Moses himself. The same must be thought concerning the fall of our first parents, and concerning the protoevangelium, revealed by God himself to the first-formed, but described by Moses in Chapter III. of Genesis, and likewise concerning the double genealogy, one derived from Cain, the other from Seth, the former of which he described in chapter IV, the latter in chapter V of Genesis, and concerning other matters, done before and after the flood down to the times of his own fathers, which he noted in the chapters immediately following: if you deny that he received the knowledge of all these things from God through immediate revelation, you will nevertheless not be able to deny that it had been derived to him through tradition, as much indeed as was certain and necessary for weaving the history of them, and could suffice. But the remaining things, which were consigned to writing by Moses, concern matters done by himself, or certainly in the doing of which he was present, so that nothing of them could have been hidden from him. Finally, the remaining books of the O.T., both Historical, and Prophetic and Hagiographic, as they are accustomed to be distinguished and called, concern either deeds done, consigned to writing by the authors of their own time, or doctrines of faith and morals, handed down by the sacred writers themselves, or future events, predicted by the same, of which it would be foolish for anyone to go about denying, against manifest experience, that the sacred writers had been sufficiently instructed.

IV. The things which the writers of the N.T. consigned to literary monuments are likewise either historical or dogmatic. But can it be said that the knowledge of neither, as much indeed as was necessary and could suffice for them to be conveniently committed to writing, was lacking to them?
