Not of historical matters: because they did not weave ancient histories, but histories of their own times concerning matters in the doing of which they were either present themselves, or at the very least received from those who had been present: just as two Evangelists, Matthew and John, were from the number of the twelve Apostles, who as inseparable companions of Christ, during the whole time of his Ministry, were spectators of all his works, and hearers of his words,

And, which is most important, and concerns the basis and foundation of the whole Christian religion, they had seen with their own eyes the Lord affixed to the cross, breathing out his soul, buried, and three days later brought back from the sepulchre and alive again, and finally, after forty days had elapsed from the resurrection, during which he had spent time on earth, and during which he had shown himself to be seen by them and others subsequently, ascending to heaven with the eleven Apostles and other faithful. Although indeed Mark and Luke, the Evangelists, were not from the college of the Apostles, they were nevertheless disciples and companions of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, and it is the constant opinion of the ancients that Luke received his Gospel from Paul, who was taught immediately by Christ himself in the third heaven; but Mark from Peter, an eyewitness of all things, although concerning most of the things which they wrote, it was more than sufficiently established even from the report of others and public fame. For Christ had both taught the people in the temple and outside the temple in a great frequency of listeners publicly, and similarly had performed his miracles publicly, with the people watching: he had suffered, died, and been buried in Jerusalem, at the approaching feast of the Passover, when the entire Jewish people had been gathered from all parts and corners of the world. Brought back from the sepulchre, he had been seen not only by the Apostles more than once, but also by other faithful, and indeed by five hundred and more brethren at once, I Cor. XV. 5 seqq. He had ascended to the heavens, with all the Apostles and certain other faithful present and watching, Luc. XXIV. 50. seq. Act. I. 12. so that nothing of these things could be hidden from Mark and Luke. Whence Luke c. I. 1. skillfully calls his Evangelical narrative διήγησιν περὶ τῶν πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων, a narrative of the things which among us (the faithful) have been fully certified, or made certain. For τὸ πληροφορεῖσθαι, when it is referred to a person, means to be made certain by someone; but when accommodated to the things themselves, it signifies things so proven by certain testimonies that it cannot deservedly be doubted concerning them, as Beza notes at this place. He adds besides: Καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται γενόμενοι τοῦ λόγου, as they delivered to us, who from the beginning were themselves eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, to signify that he did not receive what he wrote from uncertain rumor, but from the Apostles, eyewitnesses, and those who were themselves present at the events, and who lent their service to the Lord.

The Acts of the Apostles, however, concern things performed after the ascension of Christ to the heavens by the Apostles themselves, partly at Jerusalem, partly in other parts of the world, whither by Christ’s command they had departed to preach the Gospel and plant churches throughout the world, in which Luke, their writer and companion of the Apostle Paul, as an αὐτόπτης, was himself present for a good part. But by the consensus of all historian, and as proof that knowledge of the things to be written was not lacking to him, if he himself was present at the deeds which he describes, and saw with his own eyes what he writes. Nor is there any reason why anyone should doubt whether they were imbued with sufficient knowledge of the doctrine which they publicly taught among Jews and Gentiles, and committed to writing. For although the writers of the New Testament, except for Paul, were all unlearned, fishermen, and ignorant of letters and arts, so that if they had been left to their own natural ability to undertake the duty of teaching and to compose the Scriptures which they produced, it is certain that they would have been fit for nothing less than these very duties: yet because they actually performed that task excellently, for which by their own ignorance and lack of training they were not fit of themselves—namely, they derived, clearly explained, and solidly confirmed the doctrines of faith and morals from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which, apart from Paul, none of them had learned, and this both by voice and by writings, so that nothing can rightly be found wanting in them—the thing itself speaks, that they were not destitute of the knowledge required for both teaching those things and committing them to writing. For the effect testifies to its cause, and where the effect is certain, its cause can no longer be doubted. But because no unlearned person, according to the course of nature, suddenly becomes learned, and the writers of the New Testament were indeed ignorant of letters and arts, and even of the Holy Scripture, and suddenly, without their own study and labor, became teachers of the whole Church, it is rightly inferred from this that they were instructed for this duty by the Holy Spirit in a supernatural manner, and received their knowledge of doctrine, both of faith and of morals, from His immediate inspiration: which, as it is superior and more certain than any other knowledge, so it procures for the writer greater authority and credibility than any other knowledge of things to be written. And so much for the former requirement of ἀξιοπιστία in a good writer, namely, certain knowledge of the things to be committed to writing.

Latin:

II.

LOcum ab antiquitate proximum meritò sibi vendicat Scriptorum sacrorum ἀξιοπισία, per quam jure ipsis fides & assensus debetur.

I. Scriptura sacra historicè conscripta est, & complectitur etiam magnam partem historias, doctrinis tamen fidei & morum sparsim admixtis. In quolibet autem bono historico & doctore, ut dictis scriptisve suis fidem conciliet, duo cumprimis requiruntur: unum, notitia rerum narrandarum vel explicandarum & tradendarum certa; alterum, studium veritatis, absque ullo partium & affectuum studio sincerum. Utrumque in omnibus sacris Scriptoribus invenitur & eminet.

II. Notitiam quod attinet, in duplici differentia sunt, quæ literis consignata in Scripturis sacris continentur. Quædam enim non aliunde, quàm ex divina revelatione, mortalibus innotescere potuerunt. Alia verò lumini naturæ, vel etiam sensibus subjecta sunt, & concernunt vel naturâ nota principia, vel conclusiones, ex illis deductas, vel res ab hominibus aut inter homines gestas. Cujuscunque verò generis aut ordinis sint res, in Scripturis sacris contentæ, consideranti tamen patebit facilè, illarum notitiam, quanta ad eas literis consignandas sufficere poterat, Scriptoribus sacris non defuisse.

III. Quæ primus omnium Moses de operibus creationis, sex dierum spacio productis sub initium Geneseos commemorat, ex prima classe sunt. Quamvis enim luminis naturæ ductu cognosci quodammodò possit, qui rerum producendarum ordo connaturalis sit, quæ priùs, quæ posteriùs produci conveniret &c. tamen successivè, non simul, producta esse omnia; sex, non plurium aut pauciorum dierum spacio esse producta: Verbo Dei, & dicendo, ut fierent, esse producta, hoc die hæc, non plura, illo illa, non alia esse producta, & ejus generis particularia plura res facti sunt, & à Dei voluntate libera dependent: quin facta sunt, priusquam homo, qui de illorum productione testari posset, in rerum natura esset: quæ proinde non, nisi Deo revelante, hominibus innotescere potuerunt. Sive ergo Mosen ipsum; sive Adamum tantùm, sive utrumque, diversis tamen temporibus & locis, illorum notitiam per immediatam revelationem à Deo accepisse dicas, causæ tamen nihil habebis, cur Mosen, ea scribentem, notitiâ illorum sufficiente, eâque certâ & indubitatâ instructum fuisse neges, præsertim cùm ita exactè secundum circumstantias particulares varias omnia descripserit, & minutias quasque ita accuratè perseqvutus sit, ac si creationis operi ipse intersuisset, suisque oculis omnia vidisset. Si primum aut tertium dixeris, res in vado erit. Nulla enim datur notitia certior eâ, quam Deus, qui ipsa Veritas & omnis veritatis fons est, per immediatam revelationem alicui Scriptori suggerit, & Mosi scribenti suggessit. Sin secundum? ne sic quidem quicquam erit causæ, cur fidem ejus ob defectum notitiæ rerum scribendarum in dubium voces. Ita enim dicendum erit, notitiam illorum derivatam esse ab Adamo ejusque posteris ad Mosen usque per traditionem. Quamvis verò tractus ille temporis à condito mundo usque ad Mosen satis longus sit, annosque bis mille quadringentos, & quod excurrit, suo ambitu complectatur, historia creationis tamen, pro illo hominum statu, benè potuit toto illo temporis tractu per traditionem intemerata conservari & ad Mosen propagari (1) ob rei momentum maximum. Quemadmodùm enim res maximi momenti est, & ad illustrandam celebrandamque Dei gloriam plurimùm facit hominis & mundi universi originem distinctiùs nosse, ita dubium non est, quin memoriam hujus historiæ Protoplasti, ubi semel illius notitiam per revelationem à Deo acceperunt, assiduò secum recoluerint, & filiis suis, & hi vicissim, præsertim qui ex pia Sethi prosapia erant, genitis à se filiis, & sic deinceps indefinenter ad Mosen usque inculcaverint, perinde ut cum Protevangelio, post lapsum statim Protoplastis per ipsummet Deum denunciato, factum, ejusque memoria usque ad Mosen solâ traditione propagata est. (2) Ob hominum, pro illorum temporum statu, vivacitatem & memoriam fixam. Ut natura hominum tum temporis admodùm vivax & robusta erat, ut ad octavum nonumque seculum, & ultrà, terminum vitæ quandoque porrigeret, ita & illorum memoria multò vividior & firmior erat, quàm nunc est, ut difficile non esset, res memoratu dignas per traditionem ad seram posteritatem propagare. Sanè parens Mosis, Amram, vidit & audivit cùm avum suum Levi, tùm proavum suum, Jacobum, & quæ hi à majoribus suis per traditionem acceperant, ex illis cognoscere potuit. Jacobus Patriarcha vidit & audivit Abrahamum, & quæ hic à majoribus suis tradita acceperat, ex illo cognoscere poterat. Thare, pater Abrahami, vidit & audivit Noachum, & Lamech, pater Noachi ipsum Adamum, cum quo annos quinquaginta sex vixit, ut facilis fuerit traditionis propagatio ab Adamo usque ad Lamechum, à Lamecho per Noachum ad Thare, à Thare per Abrahamum ad Jacobum, & per hunc ad Amram patrem Mosis, ipsumque Mosen. Idem sentiendum est de lapsu primorum parentum, deque protevangelio, ab ipsomet Deo Protoplastis revelato, à Mose autem Cap. III. Genes. descripto, itemque; de genealogia duplici, altera à Caino, à Setho altera deducta, quarum illam in cap. IV. hanc in cap. V. Genesis descripsit, & de rebus cæteris, ante & post diluvium usque ad suorum patrum tempora gestis, quas in capitibus proximè sequentibus annotavit: quorum omnium notitiam si à Deo per immediatam revelationem eum accepisse neges, negare tamen non poteris, per traditionem ad ipsum derivatam fuisse, quanta quidem ad texendam illorum historiam certam & necessaria erat, & sufficere poterat. Reliqua autem, quæ per Mosen literis consignata sunt, concernunt res ab ipsomet gestas, vel certè quibus gerendis ipse interfuit, ut illorum nihil eum latere potuerit. Cæteri V. T. libri denique, cùm Historici, tùm Prophetici & Hagiographi, ut distingui & appellari solent, concernunt vel res gestas, à sui temporis auctoribus consignatas, vel doctrinas fidei & morum, ab ipsismet sacris Scriptoribus traditas, vel res futuras, ab iisdem prædictas, quarum notitia sufficiente Scriptores sacros instructos fuisse fatuus esset, qui contra experientiam manifestam negatum iret.

IV. Quæ Scriptores N. T. literarum monumentis consignarunt, similiter vel historica, vel dogmatica sunt. Neutrorum verò notitiam, quanta quidem ad hoc, ut convenienter in literas referrentur, necessaria erat & sufficere poterat, ipsis defuisse dici potest? Non rerum historicarum: quia non texuerunt antiquas, sed suorum temporum historias de rebus, quibus gerendis vel ipsi interfuerunt, vel ab iis minimùm, qui interfuerant, acceperunt: sicut Evangelistæ duo, Matthæus & Johannes ex numero duodecim Apostolorum erant, qui velut comites individui Christi, toto tempore Ministerii ipsius, omnium ejus operum spectatores, dictorumque; auditores fuerunt,

&, quod potissimum est, ac totius religionis Christianæ basin atque fundamentum concernit, Dominum cruci affixum, animamque exhalantem, sepultum, & triduo pòst ex sepulchro reducem ac redivivum, & denique elapsis à resurrectione diebus quadraginta, quibus in terris egerat, iisque & aliis subinde se conspiciendum exhibuerat, ad cœlum adscendentem cum novem co-Apostolis & fidelibus aliis oculis suis viderant. Quamvis verò Marcus & Lucas, Evangelistæ, ex Apostolorum collegio non fuerint, Apostolorum tamen, Petri & Pauli, discipuli & comites fuerunt, estque constans veterum sententia, Lucam accepisse Evangelium suum à Paulo, per ipsummet Christum in tertio cœlo immediatè edocto; Marcum verò à Petro, teste omnium αὐτόπτῃ, quanquam de plerisque quæ scripserunt, etiam ex aliorum relatione & fama publica satis superque constabat. Christus enim & docuerat populum in templo & extra templum in magna auditorum frequentia publicè, & similiter miracula sua publicè, spectante populo, ediderat: passus, mortuus & sepultus fuerat Hierosolymis, instante festo Paschatos, cùm populus Judaicus universus ex omnibus orbis partibus & angulis congregatus esset. Redux ex sepulchro non solùm ab Apostolis plus simplici vice, sed & ab aliis fidelibus, quin & à quingentis & pluribus fratribus simul visus fuerat, I. Cor. XV. 5 seqq. adscenderat ad cœlos, præsentibus & spectantibus omnibus Apostolis, & quibusdam fidelibus aliis, Luc. XXIV. 50. seq. Act. I. 12. ut Marcum & Lucam horum nihil latere posset. Unde Lucas c. I. 1. suam narrationem Evangelicam scitè vocat διήγησιν περὶ τῶν πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων, narrationem rerum, quæ inter nos (fideles) prorsus certificate, vel certioratæ sunt. Nam τὸ πληροφορεῖσθαι, cùm ad personam refertur, certiorem ab aliquo fieri; ad res autem ipsas accommodatum, res significat, ita certis testimoniis comprobatas, ut de iis ambigi meritò non possit, annotante Beza ad h. l. Addit prætereà: Καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται γενόμενοι τοῦ λόγου, sicut tradiderunt nobis, qui ab initio ipsi viderunt, & administri fuerunt sermonis, ad significandum, se non ex incerto rumore accepisse, quæ scripsit, sed ab Apostolis, testibus oculatis, & qui rebus gerendis ipsi interfuerunt, Dominoque operam suam commodârunt.

Acta Apostolica autem concernunt res, post Christi adscensionem ad cœlos ab ipsismet Apostolis, Hierosolymis partim, partim in aliis orbis partibus, quò Christi jussu ad prædicandum Evangelium & plantandas per orbem Ecclcsias digressi fuerant, gestas, quibus Lucas, illarum Scriptor, & Apostoli Pauli comes, velut αὐτόπτης, bonam partem ipse interfuit. Omnium verò consensu pro nota boni & fide digni historici, documentóque, quòd rerum scribendarum notitia ei non defuerit, habetur, si rebus gestis, quas describit, ipse interfuerit, & suis oculis, quæ scribit, viderit. Neque causa est, cur de doctrina, quam inter Judæos ac Gentes publicè docuerunt, literísq; consignârunt, fuerintne ejus notitiâ sufficiente imbuti? quis dubitet. Quamvis enim Scriptores N. T. excepto Paulo, omnes idiotæ, piscatores & literarum artiuḿque rudes fuerint, ut si suo relicti ingenio munus docendi obire, Scripturasque, à se confectas, conficere debuissent, certum sit, ad nihil minùs, quàm ad hæc ipsa munia eos aptos futuros: tamen quia reapse id egregiè præstiterunt, ad quod præstandum per suam inscitiam & ruditatem ex se apti non erant, nempe doctrinas fidei & morum ex Scripturis V. T. quas, præter Paulum, illorum nemo didicerat, ita dilucidè deduxerunt, perspicuè declarârunt, & solidè confirmârunt, id́que voce & scriptis, ut quod jure in illis desiderari possit, non occurrat; res ipsa loquitur, quòd notitiâ, ad ea & docenda & literis consignanda requisitâ, destituti non fuerint. Effectus enim testatur de sua causa, & ubi de effectu constat, de ejus causa ampliùs dubitari non potest. Quia autem nemo rudis, juxta naturæ cursum quidem, repentè fit doctus, Scriptores N. T. verò literarum & artium, imò & Scripturæ sacræ rudes fuerant, & subitò, sine studio & labore suo, universæ Ecclesiæ Doctores evaserunt, rectè hinc colligitur, eos fuisse à Spiritu S. modo supernaturali ad munus hoc instructos, & ex ejus immediata inspiratione accepisse suam doctrinæ, cùm fidei tùm morum, notitiam: quæ ut aliâ notitiâ quâvis superior certioŕque est, ita Scriptori majorem, quàm alia ulla rerum scribendarum scientia, auctoritatem fidemque conciliat. Et tantum de priori ἀξιοπιστίας in bono Scriptore requisito, notitiâ scilicet rerum, literis consignandarum, certâ.


### V. The second is a sincere pursuit of truth, without any bias of parties and…

V. The second is a sincere pursuit of truth, without any bias of parties and affections: in which the sacred writers certainly snatch the palm from all other writers and historians. For besides the fact that all were conspicuous and famous for the holiness of their life, of which a not insignificant part is the love and pursuit of truth; and most were also conspicuous and famous for the prodigies and miracles brought forth by them for the confirmation of their doctrine, nor can anything be brought forward by which they could be moved to a zeal for emotions and parties, and to represent things otherwise than they are in truth and factions, and to be induced to record things otherwise than they were in truth. Not by fear of danger. For although heavenly truth always has had and still has its most bitter enemies, namely the world and the devil, the sacred writers were so far from allowing themselves to be deterred from its pure and uncorrupted profession by the fear of persecutions, that they rather intrepidly faced prisons, torments, any tortures whatsoever, and even the most ignominious death itself, rather than recede from it by even a hair's breadth, and sacred histories testify that most of the Prophets and Apostles were punished with death on account of their intrepid and constant confession of the truth, and obtained the crown of martyrdom. Nor by any hope of gain or private advantage. For what they recorded in writing either concerned the doctrines of faith and morals, or deeds pertaining to others or to themselves. Moreover, the doctrines of faith and morals were equally necessary for all to believe or to do; and on the contrary, falsehood, if deliberately mixed in while writing, would have harmed their own salvation no less, or rather more, than that of others. What is more? The doctrine of faith and morals handed down by them was, as has been said, exposed to perpetual persecutions, so that its confession threatened its confessors with the most adverse and dire things rather than promising any gain or temporal advantage. Nor indeed could things done by others, and in no way pertaining to themselves, create for them any hope of gain or temporal advantage, or move them to write anything otherwise than it was in the truth of the matter. For no trace of this, not even a slight one, can be shown in all their writings. But as for the things that pertained to them, and concerning which there could be a suspicion that perhaps out of a zeal for factions, or to hunt for praise and the fame of their name, or to avoid envy, ignominy, or some stain of disgrace, they either suppressed things that should have been said or wrote otherwise than the truth of the matter required, it is so far from the case that we should suspect them of having yielded to any such emotions or having suffered any human failing, that it must rather be admitted that they preferred the truth everywhere and always far above their own honor and the fame of their name, whenever their own affairs, as occasion so permitted, they touched upon in their writings. In which matter, to be shown from their writings, that theologian of great name and most deserving of the Church of Christ, Dr. Aegidius Hunnius, was more industrious than others in his booklet on the Majesty of Scripture, Κριτηρ. X. Tom. 1. Op. Col. 15. seq., whose words, although somewhat numerous, are nevertheless worthy to be read here. In weaving the Biblical history, he says, we see a custom observed that is far different from that which all profane writers are otherwise accustomed to hold. For where is there any one among the writers of pagan antiquity who does not hunt for his own praise and glory in writing? Wherefore if at any time they are occupied with commemorating their own domestic affairs, they know how to recount to a nicety those things which they judge will be for their own praise and commendation among others, having assigned all the circumstances of their deeds, sometimes inventing something by which they trust their praises can be amplified in the minds of the readers. Furthermore, those things which are thought to be about to sprinkle some stain of disgrace or to obscure the fame of their name, how, good God!, do they pass over them with dry foot and suspended step: with what profound silence do they cover and dissimulate them, or if, the history so demanding, their writing cannot sail past those rocks: what hiding places do they look for, in which they may hide their sins and wicked deeds? What colors, what paints do they seek out, by which they may excuse, palliate, paint, and feign their less praiseworthy actions, so that no stain of ignominy may adhere to them. So much so that the thing itself cries out almost with an emitted voice that they do not thirst for and seek the praise of God entirely, but primarily their own praise and the fame of their name. But the Biblical writers do none of these things: who, when the reason of history demands that they touch upon some part of their own life, because of a most constant love of truth, do not even spare their own reputation among men, but where anything has been committed beyond duty, where religious piety toward God has been violated, where that most holy governess of human actions, honesty, has been injured: they do not hesitate to confess ingenuously in their writings before God and men for their own confusion, but for the praise and proclamation of God alone. Which is an undoubted indication that they have no other goal set before them in writing than the celebration of the one God, and the most simple truth of the history which they are weaving, to which they are so devoted with all their efforts, so deeply given, that they would rather break the affection of nature than diminish or detract even a little from the truth of the narrative. Thus the Prophet Moses neither suppressed his own hesitation or lack of faith at the waters of contradiction, nor kept silent about his sister's impious murmuring, nor concealed the horrible lapse and idol-mania of his brother Aaron, nor did he wish to be silent about the wicked deeds of the Patriarch Levi, from whom he himself drew his origin: he did not think that the robbery with which he attacked the Shechemites, nor the perjury with which he nefariously violated the faith given to them, nor the parricide with which he planned to remove his most innocent brother Joseph, nor the cruelty noted in the paternal testament, nor his savage and bloodthirsty weapons should be buried in silence, when God and the truth of history wished this manifold impiety of Levi, the great-grandfather of Moses, to be recorded in writing and made known to all posterity. Thus, that David in the inscription of Psalm 51 declares and publishes his own crime by a humble confession; that Jonah [records] his own unpraiseworthy disobedience toward the calling of God; that [he records] the immoderate sickness and impatience of his own mind; that [he records] his impious desire for the destruction of the Ninevites, however much they were repenting; that he himself described other sins of his with his own hands and letters; that likewise Matthew records in the public letters of his Gospel how lost and profligate a tax collector he had been, how immersed in the deep filth of avarice, before he left that seat of frauds, rapine, and all injustice and iniquity, the toll-booth, at the command of Christ calling him; that for a similar reason Peter not only suffers his most foul lapse of the denial of Christ to be betrayed to the memory of all men with a calm mind, but he himself even dictates that sad history of a most sad lapse to the Evangelist Mark as if to a pen, so that its memory may exist for the posterity of all ages; that finally the Apostle Paul himself confesses that he had been a devastator of the Churches, violent against Christians, and a blasphemer against Jesus Christ: Who, in examples of this kind, would not almost touch with his own hands that the sole and unique study of divine truth was proposed to these writers of the Old and New Testament? and therefore in the histories which they produced, there is nothing anywhere of fraud, nothing of imposture, nothing which does not in every respect savor of a consistent and solid truth; for those servants of God had sworn so sacredly to it, that they would rather reveal their own sins, even at the loss and expense of their own glory (of which men are otherwise by their own nature desirous and greedy), than by concealing them in any way to contaminate or obscure the truth of the histories.

VI. With these things being so, there arises for us again such an argument: Those writers who are conspicuous and shine with the marks and illustrious signs of αξιοπιστιας mentioned thus far, their writings, which they commend to us as divine, are not to be rashly rejected as merely human and inventions of human ingenuity. But all the sacred writers enjoy and shine with the marks and illustrious signs of αξιοπιστιας mentioned thus far. Therefore, the writings of the sacred writers are not to be rashly rejected as merely human and inventions of human ingenuity. Both premises receive light from what has been said thus far, and radiate with their own light.

Latin:

V. Alterum est studium veritatis, absq; ullo partium & affectuum studio, sincerum: in quo sanè Scriptores sacri aliis Scriptoribus & historicis omnibus palmam præripiunt. Præterquam enim, quod omnes sanctimoniâ vitæ, cujus pars non postrema amor & studium veritatis est; & plerique etiam prodigiis & miraculis, ad doctrinæ suæ confirmationem à se editis, conspicui & clari erant, nihil etiam afferri potest, quo ad affectuum & partium studium permoveri, & ad res aliter, quàm in veritate haberent, consignandas induci se passos esse, prudenter quis suspicari possit. Non metu periculi. Quamvis enim veritas cœlestis semper suos habuerit habeatque hostes insensissimos, mundum scilicet & diabolum, Scriptores sacri tamen ab ejus professione pura & incorruptâ adeò non passi sunt se persecutionum metu deterreri, ut intrepidè potiùs carceres, tormenta, cruciatusque quosvis & ipsam ignominiosissimam mortem obirent, quàm vel latum ungem ab ea recederent, & testantur historiæ sacræ, quòd Prophetæ & Apostoli plerique ob intrepidam & constantem veritatis confessionem morte multati, martyriique coronam consecuti sint. Neque spes aliqua lucri aut commodi privati. Quæ enim literis consignabant, vel concernebant doctrinas fidei & morum, vel res gestas, ad alios, vel ad se pertinentes. Doctrinæ autem fidei & morum æquè omnibus creditu factuve necessariæ erant; & contrà falsitas, datâ operâ inter scribendum admixta, non minùs suæ, imò magis suæ, quàm aliorum nocuisset saluti. Quid? quod tradita ab illis fidei & morum doctrina perpetuis, uti dictum, persecutionibus exposita erat, ut confessio ejus confessoribus suis adversa & dirissima quæque potiùs comminaretur, quàm quicquam lucri aut commodi temporalis polliceretur. Neque verò res, ab aliis gestæ, & ad se nihil pertinentes, aliquam spem lucri aut commodi temporalis ipsis facere, aut ad quicquam aliter, quàm in rei veritate haberet, scribendum eos permovere potuerunt. Nullum enim hujus rei vel leve vestigium, in omnibus illorum scriptis ostendi potest. Quæ autem ad ipsos pertinebant res, & de quibus suspicio esse poterat, ne fortè partium studio vel ad aucupandam laudem & nominis famam, vel ad declinandam invidiam, ignominiam, aut turpitudinis maculam quandam vel dicenda subticuerint, vel aliter, quàm rei veritas ferret, scripserint, tantum abest, ut in his talibus quicquam affectibus dedisse, aut humani quid passos esse suspicemur, ut fatendum potiùs sit, eos prætulisse ubique & semper veritatem suo honori & nominis famæ longissimè, quandocunque res suas, occasione sic ferente, in scriptis suis attigerunt. Qua in re, ex illorum scriptis ostendenda, præ aliis operosus fuit ille magni nominis & de Ecclesia Christi meritissimus Theologus, D. Ægidius Hunnius in libello de Majestate Scripturæ, Κριτηρ. X. Tom. 1. Op. Col. 15. seq. cujus verba, quamvis pluscula, digna tamen sunt, quæ hîce legantur. In historia Biblica, inquit ille, texenda videmus observatum morem longè diversissimum ab eo, quem omnes profani Scriptores aliàs tenere solent. Ubi enim quisquam est ex Ethnicæ vetustatis Scriptoribus, qui non suam in scribendo venetur laudem atque gloriam? Quamobrem si quando circa res domesticas suas commemorandas occupati sunt, quæ sibi laudi & commendationi apud alios futura judicant, norunt ad ungvem percensere, assignatis factorum omnibus circumstantiis, interdum admentientes quippiam, quo laudes suas amplificari apud animos legentium posse confidant. Quæ porro aliquam turpitudinis maculam aspersura, aut famam nominis obscuratura putantur, quàm ibi, Deum immortalem! sicco pede suspensoque gradu transeunt: quàm profundo silentio ea tegunt atque dissimulant, aut si, historia sic efflagitante, præternavigare illorum scriptio scopulos istos haud potest: quas respectant latebras, in quibus peccata flagitiaq́ sua abdant? quos colores, quos fucos conquirunt, quibus actiones suas minùs laudatas excusent, pallient, pingant, ac fingant, ne qua ignominiæ labes sibi adhærescat. Adeò res ipsa tantùm non emissâ voce clamat, eos non Dei in solidum, sed cumprimis suam laudem nominisque famam sitire & quærere. At Biblici Scriptores nihil horum: qui ubi historiæ ratio postulat, ut vitæ suæ partem aliquam attingant, præ constantissimo veritatis amore, ne propriæ quidem apud homines existimationi parcunt, sed ubi quid præter officium est admissum, ubi violata religiosa in Deum pietas, ubi læsa sanctissima illa humanarum actionum gubernatrix honestas: non dubitant in sui confusionem, in DEI verò solius laudem & prædicationem scriptis suis coram Deo & hominibus ingenuè confiteri. Quod non dubium est indicium, non ullum alium in scribendo scopum eos sibi habere præfixum, quàm unius Dei celebrationem, & historiæ, quam texunt, veritatem simplicissimam, cui totis studiis sic addicti, sic penitißimè dediti, ut malint affectum naturæ frangere, quàm de veritate narrationis vel tantillum diminuere, atque detrahere. Sic Propheta Moses neque suam ad contradictionis aquas hæsitationem aut dißidentiam suppressit, nec sororis murmur impium reticuit, nec fratris Aaronis horribilem prolapsum & idolomaniam dissimulavit, nec Patriarchæ Levi, ex quo ipse suam originem trahebat, scelerata facta silere voluit: non latrocinium, quo is in Sichemitas est grassatus, non perjurium, quo datam illis fidem nefariè violavit, non parricidium, quo innocentissimum fratrem Josephum tollere cogitavit, non immanitatem, Testamento patrio notatam, non sæva & truculenta ejus arma silentio sepelienda duxit, quando Deus historiæque veritas hanc multiplicem impietatem Levi, proavi Mosis, in literas relatam universæ posteritati voluit innotescere. Sic quòd David inscriptione Psalmi LI. suum scelus ingenua confessione edictat & propalat ipse; quod Jonas illaudatam suam inobedientiam erga vocationem Dei; quod immoderatum animi sui morbum & impatientiam; quod desiderium impium exitii Ninevitarum, quantumvis resipiscentium; quod alia peccata sua suis ipse descriptu manibus atque literis; quòd item Matthæus in publicas literas Evangelii sui refert, quàm fuerit perditus & profligatus publicanus, quàm profundis avaritiæ sordibus immersus, priusquam ad Christi vocantis jussum illam fraudum, rapinarum, omnisque injustitiæ iniquitatisq; sedem, telonium, relinqueret; quod consimili ratione Petrus lapsum suum fœdissimum abnegationis Christi, non solum æquo animo patitur omnium hominum memoriæ prodi, sed ipsemet insuper Evangelistæ Marco tristem illam tristissimi lapsus historiam quasi ad calamum dictat, ut ejus memoria ad omnium seculorum posteritatem extet; quòd denique Paulus Apostolus se vastatorem Ecclesiarum, violentum in Christianos & blasphemum in Jesum Christum fuisse fatetur ipse: Quis in istiusmodi exemplis non ipsis propè manibus contrectet, solum atque unicum divinæ veritatis studium hisce veteris novique Testamenti Scriptoribus propositum fuisse? & proinde historiis, quas prodiderunt, nihil uspiam subesse fraudis, nihil imposturae, nihil quod non undiquaque sibi constantem ac solidam veritatem sapiat; quippe in quam ita sancte juraverant illi Dei servi, ut vel sua gloria (cujus alias suopte ingenio cupidi avidique sunt homines) jactura, dispendioque fama peccata sua mallent prodere, quam tegendo illa veritatem historiarum ullo pacto vel contaminare vel obscurare.

VI. Quibus ita habentibus nobis rursum tale nascitur argumentum: Qui Scriptores commemoratis hactenus αξιοπιστιας notis & signis illustribus conspicui sunt & fulgent, illorum Scripta, quae velut divina nobis commendant, non sunt temere ut mere humana, & humani ingenii commenta rejicienda. Atqui Scriptores sacri omnes gaudent fulgentque commemoratis hactenus αξιοπιστιας notis & signis illustribus. Ergo Scriptorum sacrorum Scripta non sunt temere ut mere humana, & humani ingenii commenta rejicienda. Utraque praemissa ex hactenus dictis lucem sortitur, suaque luce radiat.


### III. We assign the third place among the external motives and signs of credibility…

III.

We assign the third place among the external motives and signs of credibility to miracles, by which the sacred writers showed and confirmed both their mission from God and the divinity of their doctrine.

I. This criterion and sign sought from miracles leads us closer to recognizing the divine origin of Holy Scripture. For a miracle, according to Thomas, part I, q. CX, a. IV, is said to occur when something is done beyond the order of nature. Since, however, something can be said to be done beyond the order of nature in two ways: one, that it is done beyond the order of some particular nature; the other, that it is done beyond the order of the whole of created nature, it is not sufficient for the definition of a miracle, properly so called, if something is done beyond the order of some particular nature, but it is required that it be done beyond the order of the whole of created nature. Whence Thomas well adds in the same place: But it is not sufficient for the definition of a miracle if something is done beyond the order of some particular nature. Because thus, when someone throws a stone upward, he would be performing a miracle, since this is beyond the order of the nature of a stone. From this, therefore, something is said to be a miracle, because it is done beyond the order of the whole created nature. But because God alone can act beyond the order of the whole created nature: since whatever an Angel or any other creature does by its own power, it is done according to the order of some created nature; the praised Doctor rightly concludes from this that God alone can perform miracles. Where, however, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ I add: that for the definition of a miracle, properly so called, it is not sufficient that something be done beyond the order of the whole created nature. For there are given effects of sanctifying grace, such as the regeneration of man, renewal, etc., which, just as they cannot be produced by any created nature by its own power, so they are rightly said to be produced and done by God beyond the order of the whole created nature, yet they are not called miracles: since they contain in themselves nothing unusual, and which might draw a man into admiration of them. For a miracle, therefore, besides the fact that it is done beyond the order of the whole created nature, it is also required that it be of the number of those things which happen rarely. This requirement Thomas perhaps implicitly included when he defined a miracle, properly so called, by the fact that it is done beyond the order of the whole created nature. For because God in His actions has bound Himself to the order of nature by His most free will, it certainly happens rarely that He does something beyond the order of the whole created nature, and thus a rare action, or a rare work, must be that which is done beyond the order of the whole created nature. Which, as it is most true regarding the class of effects that are in substance natural (to which Thomas undoubtedly looked), so it is false regarding the class of effects of sanctifying grace. For all the works of sanctifying grace are done, as has been said, beyond the order of the whole created nature, yet not rarely, but daily, and not in an unusual way, but in a customary one, according to the customary order of the means of grace divinely instituted. Whence miracles, properly speaking, are rare and unusual effects, produced by God beyond the order of the whole created nature. For which reason also Scripture ascribes to God alone that He can perform and does perform miracles. Ps. 72:18, Ps. 77:14-15, Ps. 136:4, Exod. 15:11.

Miracles, therefore, because they are effects produced beyond the order of the whole created nature, and cannot be produced except by divine power, are rightly held as signs, from which it is evident that those who perform them perform them by divine power, and that they are sent by God, and that the doctrine which they deliver in His name

& just as they commend the divine to mortals by voice or writings, it may become known to us that they have truly received it from God. For God does not assist false prophets and malicious seducers of souls by working through them in a manner entirely unusual and beyond the order of the whole created nature, and by performing miracles to deceive the minds of men and to persuade them that He has sent those to teach whom He has not in fact sent. For this is diametrically opposed to His infinite truthfulness and goodness. For this reason, God also, when sending Moses out of the ordinary course, both to the Israelite people and to Pharaoh, King of the Egyptians, would first instruct him with miracles by which he might prove his divine mission to both, and gain credence for his words which he was to speak to them in the name of God, before He sent him, Exod. IV. 3. 6. 30. c. VII. 9. seqq. & the disciples of John the Baptist, who had come to Christ to ask whether He was the Messiah promised to the Fathers and expected until now, Christ sent back simply to the miracles performed by Him, as to witnesses of His divine mission, greater than any exception: 'Go and tell John,' He said, 'the things which you hear and see: The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the glad tidings of the Gospel preached to them,' Matth. XI. 5. Luc. VII. 22.

It is certain, however, concerning the Scripture of both Testaments, that its authors became renowned by performing many remarkable and stupendous miracles, and thus the doctrine also, committed to writing by them, and its divine origin, were confirmed by manifold stupendous miracles, among which the miracles of MOSES, CHRIST, and the APOSTLES stand out, a long catalog of which we could weave here, were they not already most well-known to all.

Just as, therefore, miracles performed in confirmation of the doctrine contained in the Holy Scriptures have always provided an effective argument for demonstrating its divine origin and that of the whole Scripture against infidels: so also to modern fanatics, who with nefarious daring deny the divine origin of Holy Scripture and the doctrine contained in it, this argument, drawn from the same source, is rightly opposed: That doctrine and Scripture which has been confirmed by God through many stupendous and truly divine miracles does not have mere men, but God Himself, as its author. But the doctrine and Holy Scripture [have been confirmed] by many stupendous and confirmed by truly divine miracles. Therefore, doctrine and Holy Scripture have not mere men, but God himself as their author. The major proposition is evident from the very nature of miracles, just declared. For because miracles are effects produced beyond the order of all created nature, and thus by the infinite power of God alone; and since God cannot, through his infinite truthfulness and goodness, produce such effects to deceive the minds of men and to persuade them that a Scripture or the doctrine contained in it proceeded from him, which did not proceed from him; what else follows from this, than that the doctrine and Scripture, which is confirmed by such manifold, stupendous, and truly divine miracles, has proceeded from God and is truly divine? The minor proposition, however, can be proven through an induction of the miracles of Moses, the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, which, as they are most well-known, are placed beyond all risk of doubt.

II. To this argument, more recent thinkers, emerging from the Cartesian School, Fanatics, and Atheists, raise various objections. The author of the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus on the Freedom of philosophizing, a writing of monstrous impiety and absurdity, will go on to deny the major proposition. For in Chapter VI, which is about miracles, he is much and laboriously engaged in attacking the received opinion, already declared by us, concerning the nature of miracles—that they are effects produced beyond the order of all created nature—and he contends most pertinaciously to the contrary that miracles are works of nature itself, but which surpass the grasp of human reason, or are believed to surpass it: for the name of a miracle cannot be understood except relatively to the opinions of men, and signifies nothing other than a work whose natural cause we cannot explain by the example of another customary thing, or at least he himself cannot, who writes or narrates the miracle. His reason is that nothing can happen against nature. This he went on to prove from the fact that the intellect of God is not distinguished from his will, and we affirm the same when we say that God wills something as when we say that God understands that same thing; wherefore, by the same necessity by which it follows from the divine nature and perfection that God understands a thing as it is, it follows from the same that God wills it as it is. Since, however, nothing is necessarily true except by the divine decree alone, hence, he says, it most clearly follows that the universal laws of nature are mere decrees of God, which follow from the necessity and perfection of the divine nature. If, therefore, anything were to happen in nature which was repugnant to its universal laws, that would necessarily also be repugnant to the decree, and to the intellect, and to the divine nature; or if anyone were to maintain that God acts against the laws of nature, he would at the same time be compelled to maintain that God acts against his own nature, than which nothing is more absurd. His words exist on page 68 and following. But if you say that miracles are not indeed done against nature, but are done beyond or above nature, he replies on page 72 that he recognizes no difference here between a work against nature and a work above nature (that is, as some say, a work which indeed is not repugnant to nature, yet cannot be produced or effected by it itself); for since a miracle is not done outside of nature, but within nature itself, even though it is posited as above nature, it is nevertheless necessary that it interrupt the order of nature, which we otherwise conceive as fixed and immutable by the decrees of God. If, therefore, anything were to happen in nature which did not follow from its own laws, that would necessarily be repugnant to the order which God established in nature eternally through the universal laws of nature, and thus it would be against nature and its laws, and consequently its credibility would make us doubt everything and would lead to atheism. With these things thus deduced, he concludes on page 73 that a miracle, whether against or above nature, is a mere absurdity; and therefore that by a miracle in the sacred scriptures nothing else can be understood than a work of nature which surpasses human comprehension or is believed to surpass it. From which he further infers that we cannot know God and his existence and providence through miracles. If this is true, then the divine origin of the doctrine handed down by the sacred writers and consigned to letters will not be able to be known from them, and the major proposition of our argument will fall of its own accord.

Latin:

III.

TErtium locum inter motiva & signa credibilitatis externa tribuimus miraculis, quibus Scriptores sacri & suam a Deo missionem, & doctrinae suae divinitatem ostenderunt & confirmarunt.

I. Hoc a miraculis petitum κριτηριον & signum deducit nos propius ad divinam Scripturae sacrae originem agnoscendam. Nam miracula, juxta Thomam part. I. q. CX. a. IV. dicitur, cum aliquid fit praeter ordinem naturae. Cum autem duobus modis aliquid dici possit praeter ordinem naturae fieri: uno, quod fiat praeter ordinem alicujus particularis naturae; altero, quod praeter ordinem totius naturae creatae fiat, ad rationem miraculi, proprie dicti, non sufficit, si aliquid fiat praeter ordinem naturae alicujus particularis, sed requiritur, ut fiat praeter ordinem totius naturae creatae. Unde ibidem bene addit Thomas: Sed non sufficit ad rationem miraculi, si aliquid fiat praeter ordinem naturae alicujus particularis. Quia sic, cum aliquis projicit lapidem sursum, miraculum faceret, cum hoc sit praeter ordinem naturæ lapidis. Ex hoc ergo aliquid dicitur esse miraculum, quod fit præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ. Quia autem solus Deus præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ facere potest: cùm quicquid Angelus vel quæcunque alia creatura propriâ virtute facit, secundum ordinem alicujus naturæ creatæ fiat; rectè colligit hinc Doctor laudatus, Deum solum facere posse miracula. Ubi tamen ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ addo: ad rationem miraculi, propriè dicti, non sufficere, quod aliquid fiat præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ. Dantur enim effectus gratiæ sanctificantis, quales sunt hominis regeneratio, renovatio &c. qui uti à nulla natura creata virtute propriâ produci possunt, ita rectè præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ à Deo produci & fieri dicuntur, miracula tamen non appellantur: cùm nihil insoliti, & quòd hominem in sui admirationem trahat, in se contineant. Ad miraculum ergo, præterquam quod propter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ fit, requiritur etiam, ut ex eorum numero sit, quæ rarò fiunt. Quod requisitum Thomas forsan implicitè complexus est, quando miraculum propriè dictum per hoc definivit, quòd fiat præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ. Quia enim Deus in actionibus suis ad naturæ ordinem liberrimâ voluntate se alligavit, rarò certè contingit, ut præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ aliquid faciat, atque adeò raram actionem, vel opus rarum esse oportet, quod præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ fit. Quod uti de genere effectuum, in substantiâ naturalium, (quò dubio procul Thomas respexit,) verissimum; ita de genere effectuum gratiæ sanctificantis falsum est. Nam gratiæ sanctificantis opera omnia fiunt, uti dictum, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, non tamen rarò, sed quotidiè, neque modo insolito, sed consveto, juxta consvetum ordinem mediorum gratiæ, divinitùs institutum, fiunt. Unde miracula, propriè loquendo, sunt effectus rari & insoliti, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, à Deo producti. Quamobrem etiam Scriptura Deo soli adscribit, quod miracula facere possit & faciat Psal. LXXII. 18. Psal. LXXVII. 14. 15. Psal. CXXXVI. 4. Exod. XV. 11.

Miracula ergo, quia effectus sunt, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ producti, nec nisi divinâ virtute produci possunt, rectè habentur in signis, ex quibus, qui ea patrant, divinâ virtute illa patrare, atque à Deo missos esse, & doctrinam, quam ejus nomine tradunt,

& velut divinam mortalibus voce aut scriptis commendant, verè à Deo accepisse, nobis innotescat. Deus enim non adsistit PseudoProphetis & malitiosis animarum seductoribus, præter ordinem naturæ creatæ universæ modo prorsus insolito per eos operando, miraculaque patrando, ad fallendos hominum animos, iísque persvadendum, se misisse illos ad docendum, quos tamen non miserit. Hoc enim ejus veracitati & bonitati infinitæ è diametro repugnat. Quamobrem etiam Deus Mosen, extra ordinem, cùm ad populum Israëliticum, tùm ad Pharaonem, Ægyptiorum Regem, mittendum, miraculis priùs instruebat, quibus utrisque suam divinam missionem probaret, verbísque suis, quæ Dei nomine ad illos locuturus esset, fidem conciliaret, quàm eum mitteret, Exod. IV. 3. 6. 30. c. VII. 9. seqq. & Johannis Baptistæ discipulos, qui ad Christum venerant quæsitum, num Patribus promissus, & huc usque expectatus Messias ipse esset, remittebat Christus simpliciter ad edita à se miracula, velut ad testes suæ missionis divinæ, omni exceptione majores: Renunciate, inquiens, Johanni ea, quæ auditis & videtis: Cæci visum recipiunt, & claudi ambulant, leprosi mundantur, & surdi audiunt, mortui excitantur, & pauperes lætum accipiunt Evangelii nuncium, Matth. XI. 5. Luc. VII. 22.

Constat autem de Scriptura utriusque Testamenti, quòd ejus conditores editis pluribus insignibus & stupendis miraculis inclaruerint, atque sic doctrina etiam, ab illis in literas relata, ejusque divina origo multiplicibus stupendis miraculis confirmata fuerit, inter quæ eminent MOSIS, CHRISTI, & APOSTOLORUM miracula, quorum longum catalogum hîc texere possemus, nisi jam antè omnibus notissima essent.

Quemadmodum ergo miracula, in confirmationem doctrinæ, Scripturis sacris comprehensæ, edita, illius & Scripturæ totius divinæ origini contra infideles ostendendæ, semper efficax præbuerunt argumentum: ita & hodiernis Fanaticis, divinam Scripturæ sacræ & contentæ in ea doctrinæ originem ausu nefario negantibus, rectè hoc, ex eodem fonte haustum, opponitur argumentum: Quæ doctrina & Scriptura pluribus stupendis & verè divinis miraculis à Deo confirmata est, ea non homines nudos, sed ipsummet Deum auctorem habet. Atqui doctrina & Scriptura sacra pluribus stupendis & verè divinis miraculis confirmata est. Ergo doctrina & Scriptura sacra non homines nudos, sed ipsummet Deum habet auctorem. Major propositio ex ipsa, modò declarata, natura miraculorum evidens est. Quia enim miracula sunt effectus, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, atque sic solius Dei virtute infinitâ producti; hujusmodi effectus autem Deus per suam infinitam veracitatem & bonitatem producere non potest ad fallendos hominum animos, & ad persuadendum illis, quòd à se profecta sit Scriptura aut contenta in ea dòctrina, quæ ab eo profecta non sit; quid aliud hinc sequitur, quàm à Deo profectam & verè divinam esse doctrinam & Scripturam, quæ tam multiplicibus, stupendis, & verè divinis miraculis confirmata est? Minor autem propositio probari potest per inductionem miraculorum Mosis, Prophetarum, Christi, & Apostolorum, quæ, uti notissima, ita extra omnem dubitationis aleam posita sunt.

II. Ad argumentum hoc recentiores, ex Schola Cartesiana prodeuntes, Fanatici & Athei varia excipiunt. Auctor Tractatus Theologico-Politici de Libertate philosophandi, Scripti monstrosæ impietatis & absurditatis, propositionem majorem negatum ibit. Est enim in Capite VI. quod de miraculis est, multus & operosus in impugnanda recepta & à nobis jam declarata sententia de natura miraculorum, quòd sint effectus, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ producti, & contrà contendit pertinacissimè, miracula esse ipsius naturæ opera, sed quæ humanæ rationis captum superent, aut superare credantur: miraculi nomen enim non posse, nisi respectivè ad hominum opiniones intelligi, & nihil aliud significare, quàm opus, cujus causam naturalem exemplo alterius rei solitæ explicare non possimus, vel saltem ipse non possit, qui miraculum scribit aut narrat. Ratio ejus est, quòd nihil fieri possit contra naturam. Id quod probatum ivit ex eo, quòd Dei intellectus ab ejus voluntate non distinguatur, & idem nos affirmemus, cùm dicimus, Deum aliquid velle, ac cum dicimus, Deum id ipsum intelligere; quare eâdem necessitate, quâ ex naturâ & perfectione divina sequitur, Deum rem aliquam, ut est, intelligere, ex eadem sequatur, Deum eandem, ut est, velle. Cùm autem nihil, nisi ex solo divino decreto necessariò verum sit, hinc, ait, clarissimè sequi, leges naturæ universales mera esse decreta Dei, quæ ex necessitate & perfectione naturæ divinæ sequuntur. Si quid igitur in natura contingeret, quod ejus universalibus legibus repugnaret, id decreto, & intellectui, & naturæ divinæ necessario etiam repugnaret; aut si quis statueret, Deum aliquid contra leges naturæ agere, is simul etiam cogeretur statuere, Deum contra suam naturam agere, quo nihil absurdius. Verba ejus extant pag. 68. seq. Quod si dicas, miracula non quidem fieri contra naturam, fieri tamen præter vel supra naturam, regeret pag. 72. se hîc nullam agnoscere differentiam inter opus contra naturam, & opus supra naturam (hoc est, ut quidam ajunt, opus, quod quidem naturæ non repugnat, attamen ab ipsa non potest produci aut effici) nam cum miraculum non extra naturam, sed in ipsa natura fiat, quamvis supra naturam statuatur, tamen necesse esse, ut naturæ ordinem interrumpat, quem aliàs fixum atque immutabilem ex Dei decretis concipiamus. Si quid ergo in natura fieret, quod ex ipsius legibus non sequeretur, id necessariò ordini, quem Deus in æternum per leges naturæ universales in natura statuit, repugnaret, adeoque id contra naturam ejusque leges esset, & consequenter ejus fides nos de omnibus dubitare faceret, & ad Atheismum duceret. Quibus ita deductis concludit p. 73. miraculum sive contra sive supra naturam, merum absurdum esse; & proptereà per miraculum in sacris literis nihil aliud posse intelligi, quàm opus naturæ, quod captum humanum superet aut superare credatur. Ex quo porrò infert, nos per miracula Deum ejusque existentiam & providentiam cognoscere non posse. Quod si verum est, etiam doctrinæ, à Scriptoribus sacris traditæ & literis consignatæ divina origo ex illis cognosci non poterit, cadetque argumenti nostri propositio major ultrò.


### But in truth, all these are futile and absurd inventions, which the Psalmist…

But in truth, all these are futile and absurd inventions, which the Psalmist casts down and overturns as if with a single blow, in Psalms 72:18 and 136:4, when he says in express words: The Lord God, the God of Israel, the Lord of lords, does נפלאות לבדו MIRACLES ALONE. If God alone does miracles, nature (the created one, of which this discourse is) does not do them. For God, as the first and supreme cause, and nature, or the natural order and complex of secondary causes, are here distinguished from one another. Therefore, miracles are not works of nature: for otherwise nature would do them, not God alone. Therefore, they are works either against or beyond they are done beyond nature: since they are done by divine power alone, with nature, that is, secondary causes, not concurring and cooperating by their own power.

Nor does anything stand in the way of God being able to perform, and performing, miracles alone, beyond the order of nature. For since He alone produced all secondary causes and indeed the entire universe out of nothing, and arranged them in this very order which they have among themselves, what can prevent Him, even now, when they exist, from being able to work alone and without their effective concurrence, and to produce some unusual effects beyond the customary order of nature or secondary causes? Or is it perhaps a lesser thing or of lesser power for the entire universe to be produced by God alone out of nothing, than for some particular effect, and an unusual one at that, to be produced by Him alone beyond the order of nature, and without its effective concurrence, such that you would affirm the former falls under the infinite power of God, but deny that the latter falls under the same?

The arguments of the Author, by which he attempted to persuade us that nothing can be done against or beyond or above nature, are either weak or fabricated without foundation. And first, indeed, that everything which God wills involves eternal necessity is an absurd fiction. God did indeed will from eternity whatever He wills, since His will is immutable: but He did not necessarily will, nor does He will, all things which He willed from eternity, and now wills in time, much less do all things involve eternal necessity. For God willed from eternity, and still wills, many contingent things, and things which, viewed absolutely in themselves, could have been and could not have been, and He willed them freely, so that He could have not willed the same. Next, it is true that the intellect of God and His will, on the part of God, do not differ really: for the essence of God is most simple, into which no real distinction falls. They differ, therefore, only by reason, on account of different extrinsic connotations. Yet we do not therefore affirm the same thing when we say that God wills something as when we say that God understands that same thing. For God understands all possible things, even the sins

of men, and yet he does not will either all possible things, or the sins of men. These phrases therefore differ: that God wills something, and that the same God understands it, not indeed on the part of God willing and understanding, but on the part of the connoted objects, which formally include [these things] in their concepts, and are the reason why it can be rightly affirmed that God understands something, which cannot be said to be willed by him. Nor can it be deduced by any law of consequence from the fact that the intellect and will of God, on the part of God, do not really differ, that by the same necessity by which it follows from the divine nature and perfection that God understands a thing as it is, it follows from the same that God wills the same thing as it is. For many things, which fall under the divine intellect on account of its infinite perfection, and cannot but be understood by it, import a certain disconvenience with the divine will, which therefore God, by the nature and infinite perfection of his will, by no necessity wills, nay, clearly cannot will: just as he neither wills, nor can will, sins. Thirdly, it is a most absurd fiction which says that nothing is necessarily true except by the sole divine decree. Certainly, that Peter denied Christ, that Judas despaired, etc., is necessarily true: for otherwise the opposite could be true, that Peter did not deny Christ, and that Judas did not despair. Neither, however, is true by divine decree. For God did not decree that either should happen: otherwise God would be the cause of sin in himself and directly. Fourthly, it is said ambiguously that the universal laws of nature are the decrees of God, which follow from the necessity and perfection of the divine nature. For either by the universal laws of nature are understood the most universal principles of nature and the most common notions concerning the knowledge and worship of God, and concerning the right and blameless institution of human life, or the very order of things and natural causes which they observe in acting and producing their effects. But in neither sense is the assertion true. Not in the former: because those most universal principles of nature do not depend on divine decrees, nor are they decrees of God, properly speaking, but have both truth and the power of obliging eternally from their own intrinsic nature without any divine decree, as will be shown elsewhere in its place. Nor in the latter: for it is most absurd that the very order of things and natural causes are the decrees of God, which follow from the necessity and perfection of the divine nature. For the universal laws, which secondary causes in producing their natural effects continually observe, are improperly called laws, and are outside of God in the secondary causes themselves, each one acting according to its own nature and native power of operating, which it received from God, as the first cause, acting: But the decrees of God are formally acts of the divine will, intrinsic to God. Hence, fifthly, it is most false that if anything should happen in nature (taken for the order and complex of natural or secondary causes) which would be repugnant to its universal laws, that is, to the universal order which secondary causes observe in producing their effects, that it would necessarily also be repugnant to the decree, and to the intellect, and to the divine nature: all of which rests upon that fiction that the universal laws of nature, which secondary causes observe in producing their effects, are mere divine decrees, which follow from the necessity and perfection of the divine nature. Which falling, that other thing which is built upon it must also necessarily fall. In the works of nature and common providence, God has indeed bound Himself by His most free will to the universal laws of nature, that is, to the order of nature which secondary causes observe in producing their effects, and He concurs with secondary causes according to the requirement of the nature and power of operating of each; yet He has not decreed that He will never and in no case act without secondary causes and their effective concurrence, or in a manner unusual in nature, and therefore if He does anything which in its mode of production is repugnant to the universal laws of nature, He will do nothing that is repugnant to any decree of His, or to His intellect and divine nature. Nor do they conflict with one another, that nature observes an eternal, fixed, and immutable order in producing its effects, which the Author repeats quite often; and yet that God sometimes produces certain particular effects beyond the order of nature. For these effects produced beyond the order of nature are not effects of nature, taken as secondary causes, but of another higher order of cause, namely of God Himself, as the first and supreme cause of all, whom—while secondary causes retain their fixed and immutable order in producing their effects—who will deny that He can operate beyond and above the order of secondary causes? For if He alone could produce all secondary causes, and indeed the whole of nature, out of nothing, why should He not be able even now, while nature and secondary causes exist, to produce some particular effects alone and without their effective concurrence, or in a manner unaccustomed and unusual for secondary causes?

But the first falsehood, upon which all the mentioned commentaries of the Author are built, is Atheism, which, although he otherwise strives to dissimulate and hide under the wrapping of various ambiguous expressions, he here nevertheless in chapter VI on miracles reveals not obscurely. For by the name of God, which he bandies about everywhere, he understands nothing other than Nature, or, which is the same thing, the order and complex of natural things and causes, which, since it always keeps its own fixed and immutable order in its operations, and is (in his opinion) the cause of all effects, is commonly conceived by way of an intelligent Mind, governing all things by its providence, the Prince and Lord of this universe, just, merciful, etc. and he thinks that these concepts, which the common people form about God, arise from the false imagination that they do not correctly know the causes of things, nor understand that nature or the order and complex of natural causes itself is the cause of all effects, and thus God. And to this pertains the fact that in chapter VI on miracles, page 69, he denies that the power and virtue of nature is limited, and that its laws are adapted only to certain things, not to all, and he adds: Since the virtue and power of nature IS THE VERY VIRTUE AND POWER OF GOD, and the laws and rules of nature are THE VERY DECREES OF GOD, it must be entirely believed that THE POWER OF NATURE IS INFINITE, and its laws so broad that they extend to all things which are conceived even by the divine intellect itself. But on page 71 he says that the operations of nature FOLLOW FROM THE VERY ESSENCE OF GOD; and on page 75 the decrees and commands of God, and consequently providence, are in reality nothing EXCEPT THE ORDER OF NATURE, that is, when Scripture says that this or that was done by God or by the will of God, it in reality understands nothing other than that that very thing was done according to the laws and order of nature, etc. And again on page 69 he says that nothing happens against nature, but that it itself keeps an eternal, fixed, and immutable order, which can be easily shown from this, that the power of nature is the very divine power and virtue; but divine power is the very essence of God, etc. But if the power and virtue of nature is not limited, if it is the very virtue and power of God, if it is infinite, if the operations of nature follow from the very essence of God, if the

Latin:

Verùm enim verò hæc omnia futilia & absurda commenta sunt, quæ uno quasi ictu dejicit & evertit Psaltes, Psalmis LXXII. 18. & CXXXVI 4 quando conceptis verbis dicit: Dominum Deum, Deum Israelis, Dominum Dominorum, facere, נפלאות לבדו MIRACULA SOLUM. Si Deus solus facit miracula, natura (creata, de qua hîc sermo est) ea non facit. Deus enim veluti causa omnium prima & suprema & natura, sive causarum secundarum naturalis ordo & complexus hîc sibi invicem contradistinguuntur. Non ergo miracula sunt opera naturæ: aliàs enim natura faceret ea, non Deus solus. Ergo sunt opera vel contra, vel præter naturam: Sed contra naturam ea fieri, nos ipsi inficiamur. Ergo præter naturam fiunt: cùm solâ divinâ virtute fiant, naturâ, h. e. causis secundis ex sua propria virtute non concurrentibus & cooperantibus.

Neque quicquam obstat, quò minus Deus, præter naturæ ordinem, facere possit faciatque miracula solus. Quia enim solus causas secundas omnes atque adeò naturam universam ex nihilo produxit, easque hoc ipso, quem inter se habent, ordine disposuit, quid prohibere potest, quo minùs etiam nunc, ubi illæ existunt, solus & absque illarum effectivo concursu operari, & præter naturæ sive secundarum causarum consvetum ordinem effectus aliquos insolitos producere possit? An forsan minus quid aut virtutis minoris est naturam universam produci à Deo solo ex nihilo, quàm effectum aliquem particularem, eumque insolitum, produci ab eo solo præter naturæ ordinem, & absque effectivo ejus concursu, ut illud sub infinitam Dei potentiam cadere affirmes; hoc sub eandem cadere neges?

Rationes Auctoris, quibus nihil contra vel præter aut supra naturam fieri posse nobis persuasum ivit, vel infirmæ, vel sine fundamento confictæ sunt. Et primùm quidem omne, quod Deus vult, æternam necessitatem involvere, absurdum commentum est. Voluit quidem Deus ab æterno, quæcunque vult, cùm ejus voluntas sit immutabilis: non autem necessariò voluit aut vult omnia, quæ voluit ab æterno, & nunc in tempore vult, multò minùs omnia æternam necessitatem involvunt. Voluit enim Deus ab æterno, & etiamnum vult multa contingentia, & quæ, in se absolutè spectata, potuerunt esse & non esse, eaque voluit liberè, ut eadem potuisset non velle. Deinde intellectum Dei & voluntatem ejus, ex parte Dei, non differre realiter, verum est: Dei essentia enim est simplicissima, in quam nulla cadit realis distinctio. Differunt ergo sola ratione, ob diversa connotata extrinseca. Non tamen idem proptereà affirmamus, cùm dicimus, Deum aliquid velle, ac cùm dicimus, Deum id ipsum intelligere. Deus enim intelligit omnia possibilia, etiam hominum pec-

cata, nec tamen vel omnia possibilia, vel hominum peccata vult. Differunt ergo phrases hæ : Deum velle aliquid, & eundem intelligere illud, non quidem ex parte Dei volentis & intelligentis, sed ex parte objectorum connotatorum, quæ formaliter in suis conceptibus includunt, & in causa sunt, cur rectè Deum aliquid intelligere affirmari possit, quod eum velle dici nequeat. Neque etiam ex hoc, quod intellectus & voluntas Dei, ex parte Dei, realiter non differunt, ullâ consequentiæ lege deduci potest, eâdem necessitate, quâ ex natura & perfectione divina sequitur, Deum rem aliquam, ut est, intelligere; sequi ex eadem, Deum eandem, ut est, velle. Nam multæ res, quæ sub intellectum divinum, ob ejus perfectionem infinitam, cadunt, & ab eo non possunt non intelligi, important disconvenientiam quandam cum voluntate divina, quas proptereà Deus per voluntatis suæ naturam & perfectionem infinitam nullâ necessitate, imò planè non vult, nec velle potest: sicut peccata nec vult, nec velle potest. Tertiò absurdissimum commentum est, quòd dicit, nihil, nisi ex solo divino decreto, necessariò verum esse. Sanè Petrum abnegâsse Christum, Judam desperâsse &c. necessariò verum est : aliàs enim verum esse posset oppositum, Petrum non abnegâsse Christum, & Judam non desperâsse. Neutrum tamen, ex divino decreto, verum est. Neutrum enim Deus, ut fieret, decrevit: aliàs enim Deus per se & directè peccati causa esset. Quartò leges naturæ universales esse decreta Dei, quæ ex necessitate & perfectione naturæ divinæ sequuntur, ambiguè dicitur. Vel enim per leges naturæ universales intelliguntur universalissima naturæ principia notionesque communissimæ de Dei agnitione & cultu, deque hominis vita, rectè & inculpatè instituenda, vel ipse rerum & causarum naturalium ordo, quem in agendo & producendis suis effectibus servant. Neutro autem sensu assertio vera est. Non priori : quia illa universalissima naturæ principia non dependent à decretis divinis, neque sunt decreta Dei, propriè loquendo, sed ex sua intrinseca natura absque ullo decreto divino, æternam habent & veritatem & vim obligandi, ut alibi suo loco ostendetur. Neque posteriori: Nam ipsum rerum & causarum naturalium ordinem Dei decreta esse, quæ ex necessitate & perfectione naturæ divinæ sequuntur, absurdissimum est. Leges universales enim, quas causæ secundæ in producendis suis effectibus naturalibus perpetuò servant, impropriè leges dicuntur, suntque extra Deum in ipfis caufis secundis, unaquaque pro sua natura & nativa virtute operandi, quam à Deo, velut causa prima, accepit, agente: Decreta Dei autem formaliter actus voluntatis divinæ sunt, Deo intrinseci. Hinc quintò falsissimum est, quòd si quid in natura (pro ordine & complexu causarum naturalium sive secundarum acceptâ) contingeret, quod ejus legibus universalibus, h.e. ordini universali, quem causæ secundæ in producendis suis effectibus servant, repugnaret, id decreto, & intellectui, & naturæ divinæ necessario etiam repugnaret: quod totum nititur commento illo, quòd leges naturæ universales, quas in producendis suis effectibus causæ secundæ servant, sint mera decreta divina, quæ ex necessitate & perfectione naturæ divinæ sequantur. Quo cadente, alterum illud, quod ei superstructur, etiam cadere necesse est. In operibus naturæ & communis providentiæ alligavit se quidem Deus liberrimâ voluntate ad leges naturæ universales, h. e. ad ordinem naturæ, quem causæ secundæ in producendis suis effectibus servant, & concurrit cum causis secundis pro exigentia cujusq; naturæ & virtutis operandi, non tamen decrevit, se nunquam & nullo casu absq; causis secundis illarumque effectivo concursu, aut modo in natura insolito acturum, & proptereà si quid faciat, quod in productionis modo universalib, legibus naturæ repugnet, nihil aget, quod ulli suo decreto, aut suo intellectui & naturæ divinæ repugnet. Neq; etiam pugnant inter se, naturam servare in producendis suis effectibus æternum, fixum & immutabilem ordinem, quod sæpiùs Auctor ingeminat; & tamen Deum producere quandoq; effectus aliquos particulares, præter naturæ ordinem. Nam hi præter ordinem naturæ producti effectus non sunt naturæ, pro causis secundis acceptæ, effectus, sed alterius altioris ordinis causæ, nempe ipsius Dei, velut causæ omnium primæ & supremæ, quam præter & supra ordinem causarum secundarum operari posse, causis secundis in producendis suis effectibus suum fixum & immutabilem ordinem retinentibus, quis negabit? Si enim causas secundas omnes, atque adeò naturam universam, solus ex nihilo potuit producere, quidni possit etiam nunc, naturâ & causis secundis existentibus, aliquos particulares effectus solus & absque effectivo illarum concursu, vel modo causis secundis inconsueto & insolito, producere?

Sed πρῶτον ψεῦδος, cui commemorata Autoris commenta omnia superstructa sunt, Atheismus est, quem ut ut aliàs sub variarum locutionum ambiguarum involucro dissimulare & occultare studet, hic tamen cap. VI. de miraculis haud obscurè prodit. Nomine Dei enim, quòd ubique jactat, nihil intelligit aliud, quàm Naturam, sive, quod idem est, rerum & causarum naturalium ordinem & complexum, qui cùm in operationibus suis semper suum fixum & immutabilem ordinem servet, & effectuum omnium (ex ejus opinione) causa sit, vulgo concipiatur per Modum Mentis intelligentis, providentiâ suâ omnia gubernantis, Principis ac Domini hujus universi, justi, misericordis &c. & hos conceptus, quos de Deo vulgus format, provenire putat ex falsa imaginatione, quòd rerum causas non rectè cognoscant, nec intelligant, naturam sive causarum naturalium ordinem & complexum ipsum esse effectuum omnium causam, atque adeò Deum. Atque huc pertinet, quòd cap. VI. de miraculis pag. 69. naturæ potentiam & virtutem limitatam, ejusque leges ad certa tantùm, non ad omnia aptas esse, negat, & subjicit: Cùm virtus & potentia naturæ SIT IPSA DEI VIRTUS ET POTENTIA, leges autem & regulæ naturæ IPSA DEI DECRETA, omninò credendum est, POTENTIAM NATURÆ INFINITAM esse, ejusque leges adeò latas, ut ad omnia, quæ & ab ipso divino intellectu concipiuntur, se extendant. Pag. 71. verò ait, operationes naturæ ex IPSA DEI ESSENTIA CONSEQUI; & pag. 75. Dei decreta & mandata, & consequenter providentiam nihil esse revera, PRÆTER NATURÆ ORDINEM, hoc est, quando Scriptura dicit, hoc vel illud à Deo vel Dei voluntate factum, nihil aliud revera intelligere, quàm quòd id ipsum secundum leges & ordinem naturæ fuerit factum &c. Et rursum pag. 69. ait, nihil fieri contra naturam, sed ipsam æternum, fixum & immutabilem ordinem servare, posse ex hoc facilè ostendi, quòd potentia naturæ sit ipsa divina potentia & virtus; divina autem potentia sit ipsissima Dei essentia &c. Si autem naturæ potentia & virtus limitata non est, si est ipsa Dei virtus & potentia, si infinita est, si operationes naturæ ex ipsa Dei essentia consequuntur, si Dei


### decrees and commands of God are in reality nothing but the order of nature, and…

decrees and commands of God are in reality nothing but the order of nature, and when Scripture says that this or that was done by God or by the will of God, it understands nothing else in reality than that that very thing was done according to the laws and order of nature, etc. What remains but that we say that God is not the author and founder of nature, but that nature itself and the order and complex of natural causes is to be understood by the name of God. To which also tends the fact that in chapter IV, page 48 and following, he laboriously inquires whether we can conceive by natural light of God as a legislator or prince, prescribing laws to men? And among other things, page 50, he attributes to Moses that, through error, he imagined God as a ruler, legislator, king; as just, merciful, etc. he imagined for himself, and page 51 he finally concludes: that God is described as a legislator or prince and called just, merciful, etc., only from a defect of thought (perhaps it should be read 'cognition'), and that God in reality acts and directs all things from the sole necessity of his own nature and perfection, and that his decrees and volitions are finally eternal truths, and always involve necessity, etc. But that he ascribes decrees and volitions to God is a mere coloring and play of words. For by the decrees and volitions of God he understands nothing else than truths founded in the very causes and natural things, which, in so far as they are founded in the natural things themselves, are called ideas which God, that is, that complex of natural things and causes, has and understands; but when the same are considered as they are contained or founded in the divine nature, that is, in the complex of natural things and causes, from the sole necessity of nature, and not from the necessity of his essence and properties, then they are called the volitions and decrees of God, as he himself explains his mind on page 48 and following, and illustrates with the example of a triangle. But in truth these inventions are so inept, so insipid, that to have recited them is to have refuted them. For that God is an intelligent mind, just, merciful, etc. is of most free will and infinite power, is superior to all natural things and causes and their entire complex, is the prince and lord of this universe, and the supreme legislator, both Holy Scripture and the whole of nature cry out, and his own conscience convinces everyone within. Which could be shown at present by more, if this were the place and purpose.

Page 75. The author indeed attempted to demonstrate with examples from Scripture that the decrees and commands of God and providence itself are nothing other than the order of nature. But the examples brought forward, if they prove anything at all, prove only this one thing: that God sometimes uses the ministry of secondary causes in executing his decrees and in the works of his providence, for example, when he was about to send Saul to Samuel, I Sam. IX. 15, 16, he used the occasion of the lost donkeys of his father, which, when Saul had gone out to seek them, God by his providence brought about that by the counsel of his servant he should approach Samuel; and that which is said in Psalm CV. 24, that God changed the mind of the Egyptians so that they would hate Israel, that this was done according to the order of nature, with their excessive fecundity providing the occasion for the Egyptians to hate them, by which they had been multiplied beyond measure and had become a source of fear to the Egyptians, and had struck them with the fear that perhaps in time of war they might take up arms against them and join their own strength with the forces and powers of their enemies, Exod. I. 10, which no one denies. But that natural causes, by whose ministry God sometimes uses in executing his decrees, are the very decrees of God, and that the order of natural causes is GOD himself, no one who has a sound mind, and whose eyes of the mind Satan has not completely blinded, will conclude or understand from that. But to dwell on these things is not, as has been said, the purpose of the present work.

We return to our argument, drawn from the nature of miracles.
