The author did not stop at the comments brought forward and hitherto refuted by us concerning the nature of miracles, but on page 73, having progressed further, he also attempted to prove by the authority of Scripture that God cannot be known from miracles. But if God cannot be known from them, then neither can the divine mission of a certain Prophet or Apostle, or the immediate dependence of his doctrine upon God, be known from them. To prove this, however, he brought forward the passage from Deut. XIII. 1, et seqq., where Moses commanded the Israelites that they should condemn to death a Prophet, even if he performs miracles. The author cites and translates the words of Moses in the aforementioned place thus: And (even if) a sign and a wonder should happen, which he foretold to you, etc., do not (however) assent to the words of that Prophet, etc., because the Lord your God is testing you, etc. That Prophet (therefore) shall be condemned to death, etc. From which, he says, it clearly follows that miracles can be performed even by false prophets, and that men, unless they are properly fortified by a true knowledge of God and custom, could just as easily embrace false gods as the true one. So he says.

But in this place also the Author has nowhere to plant his foot, nor anything to serve for plastering over his commentary. Throughout this whole chapter Moses instructs the Israelites to be solicitous in guarding themselves against false prophets and any seducers whatsoever, who lead them away from the religion and worship once received from God to a foreign and unknown worship, and not to spare them, even if they were brothers, sons, or daughters, wives or friends, and whether they were few in number, or many, or entire cities; and he warned them specifically about false prophets, not to believe them, even if they should promise to convince them of their words by signs and wonders, and should exhibit them in very deed and action, because God, by permitting those signs and wonders to be done, is testing them to explore their constancy in religion and the true worship of Himself. From which, if anything, this can be concluded: that certain signs and wonders can, by God's permission, be done even by false prophets, and that men, unless they tenaciously adhere to the Word of God already delivered to them, can be deceived by them and led into idolatry: which is most true. From that, however, it cannot be deduced by any law of consequence that false prophets can also perform miracles, properly and strictly so called. For נפלאות miracles, properly so called, אותות signs, and מופתים wonders differ. For signs and wonders extend more widely than נפלאות miracles, properly so called. For all miracles are also signs and wonders, since all are unusual and rare effects; but not conversely are all signs and wonders miracles, since it is of the nature of a miracle, properly so called and true, that it be an effect produced beyond the order of the whole created nature: but not all signs and wonders are produced in this way. Whence, just as Moses here attributes to false prophets that they can perform signs and wonders, so David in Psalm 72:18 and Psalm 136:4 expressly testifies that God alone performs נפלאות miracles.

Therefore, that false prophets can perform נפלאות miracles, as Moses does not say in the cited passage, nor could the Author prove it from any other suitable passage of Scripture, so it is deservedly rejected by us as his own invention.

Furthermore, the signs and wonders which Moses in the said place implies can be done by false prophets are of two kinds. For they consist either in preStygian and Diabolical delusions, or in effects that are indeed real, but produced by Diabolical power, yet through natural causes, in a manner unusual in nature. Signs and portents of the former order, magicians and enchanters, of whose number false prophets are also wont to be, can produce and do produce by the help of demons, by deluding the senses of men through some change made either in the object, or in the medium, or in the sensory organ. In the object indeed, either by its rapid agitation, or by its different situation, or by its sudden concealment, or by a certain disposition of it toward the eye of the observer, or by the formation of some body out of air, which may have the appearance of a true object, etc. In the medium, however, by the infection of the air with some quality, by which the species carried through the medium are so modified that they represent the object otherwise than it is in truth, etc. In the sensory organ, finally, by moving the spirits and humors, and by ordering and disposing in a certain way the images and species of things which are preserved in the imagination, so that through them those things appear to be or to happen in the imagination which neither are nor happen. By the latter mode, however, the same persons produce signs and portents by the speed of local motion, by which, through the virtue and power of demons, they either so suddenly substitute one effect of nature for another that the fraud cannot be noticed by human senses, or they move secondary causes and excite winds, storms, earthquakes, etc., or they apply natural agents to patients, in a manner unusual in nature, to produce suddenly effects which otherwise they could not produce except successively and by long-continued action, and by previous alteration continued for a certain time. Both of which, if it were of this place and purpose, could be shown here at length by examples from Holy Scripture and profane histories.

But to these perhaps our Anonymous author, or other Fanatics and Atheists like him, will object that the miracles of Moses, Christ, and the Apostles were also produced, if not by the power of demons (which they will scarcely concede to exist), yet by other natural causes, however occult they may be to us. Truly, the wicked labor of the Author aims at this end, by which he has gone about to demonstrate laboriously that miracles are nothing else than works of nature, the natural causes of which we cannot explain by the example of other familiar things, or at least he cannot, who writes or narrates them, and that on page 75 and following he has striven to explain the miracles mentioned in the Scriptures through natural causes, on page 77 finally concluding: that all things which are truly narrated in Scripture to have happened, happened necessarily according to the laws of nature, as do all things, and if anything is found which can be apodictically demonstrated to be repugnant to the laws of nature, or could not have followed from them, it is to be clearly believed that it was added to the sacred writings by sacrilegious men.

Latin:

decreta & mandata revera nihil sunt præter naturæ ordinem, & quando Scriptura dicit, hoc vel illud à Deo vel Dei voluntate factum, nihil aliud revera intelligit, quàm quòd id ipsum secundum leges & ordinem naturæ fuerit factum &c. quid superest, quàm ut dicamus, non esse Deum, naturæ auctorem & conditorem, sed ipsam naturam causarumque naturalium ordinem & complexum nomine Dei intelligendum esse. Quò collineat etiam, quòd in cap. IV. pag. 48. & seqq. operosè disquirit, num lumine naturali concipere possimus Deum veluti legislatorem aut principem, leges hominibus præscribentem? & inter alia pag. 50. Mosi tribuit, quòd, per errorem, Deum, ut Rectorem, legislatorem, Regem; ut justum, misericordem &c. sibi imaginatus sit, & pag. 51. tandem concludit : Deum non nisi ex solo defectu cogitationis (cognitionis forsan legendum est) tanquam legislatorem aut Principem describi, & justum, misericordem &c. vocari, Deumque revera ex solius suæ naturæ & perfectionis necessitate agere, & omnia dirigere, & ejus denique decreta & volitiones æternas esse veritates, semperque necessitatem involvere &c. Quod verò Deo decreta & volitiones adscribit, merus verborum fucus & lusus est. Per decreta enim & volitiones Dei nihil intelligit aliud, quàm veritates, in ipsis causis & rebus naturalibus fundatas, quæ in quantum in ipsis rebus naturalibus fundantur, ideæ, quas Deus, h. e. complexus ille rerum & causarum naturalium habeat, & intelligat, ipsi dicuntur; sed cùm eædem considerantur, ut in natura divina, h. e. in complexu rerum & causarum naturalium, ex sola necessitate naturæ, & non ex necessitate essentiæ & proprietatum suarum, continentur, sive fundantur, tùm dicuntur eidem volitiones & decreta Dei, uti p. 48. seq. ipse mentem suam explicat, & exemplo trianguli illustrat. Verùm enim verò commenta hæc ita inepta, ita insulsa sunt, ut ea recitâsse refutâsse sit. Deum enim esse Mentem intelligentem, justam, misericordem &c. esse liberrimæ voluntatis, & potentiæ infinitæ, esse rebus & causis naturalibus omnibus totoque illarum complexu superiorem, Principem & Dominum hujus universi, legislatoremque supremum, cùm Scriptura sacra, tùm natura universa clamat, & intùs sua quemque conscientia convincit. Quod impræsentiarum ostendi posset pluribus, si hujus loci & instituti id esset.

Pag. 75. Auctor exemplis Scripturæ qvidem demonstratum ivit, Dei decreta & mandata ipsamq; providentiam nihil aliud esse, quàm naturæ ordinem. Sed exempla allata, si qvicqvam, hoc unum evincunt, Deum uti qvandoq; in exeqvendis suis decretis, & in operibus providentiæ suæ causarum secundarum ministerio, v. g. cùm missurus esset Saulum ad Samuelem, I. Sam. IX. 15. 16. usum esse occafione amissarum afinarum patris ejus, qvas cum qvæsitum abiifset Saul, suâ providentiâ Deus effecerit, ut de confilio famuli sui Samuelem adiret; & qvod Psal. CV. 24. dicitur, Deum mutâsse Ægyptiorum animum, ut odio haberent Israëlem, factum id esse secundum naturæ ordinem, occafionem Ægyptiis ad illorum odium præbente nimiâ illorum fœcunditate, qvâ supra modum multiplicati Ægyptiis formidini facti fuerant, & metum incusserant, ne fortè tempore belli contra ipsos caperent arma, viresqve suas cum ipsorum hostium copiis & viribus conjungerent, Exod. I. 10. id qvod nemo negat. Qvod autem causæ naturales, qvarum ministerio Deus in exeqvendis suis decretis qvandoq; utitur, sint ipsa Dei decreta, & causarum naturalium ordo DEUS ipse, nemo, cui sanum est synciput, & cui Satanas oculos mentis non prorsus excæcavit, inde colliget aut intelliget. Sed hisce immorari, præsentis, uti dictum, instituti non est.

Ad nostrum argumentum, ex natura miraculorum petitum, revertimur. Auctor in allatis & hactenus à nobis confutatis commentis de miraculorû natura non substitit, sed pag. 73. longius progressus etiã auctoritate Scripturæ probatum ivit, ex miraculis Deum cognosci non posse. Qvod si Deus ex illis cognosci non potest, neq; divina Prophetæ aut Apostoli cujusdam missio, vel doctrinæ ejusdem dependentia immediata à Deo, ex illis cognosci poterit. Ad hoc autem evincendum in medium produxit locum ex Deut. XIII. 1. seqq. ubi Moses Israëlitis præcepit, ut Prophetam, quamvis faciat miracula, mortis tamen damnent. Verba Mofis citat & transfert Auctor d. l. ita: Et (qvamvis) contigerit signum & portentum, quod tibi prædixit &c. noli (tamen) assentire verbis ejus Prophetæ &c. quia Dominus vester Deus vos tentat &c. Propheta (igitur) ille mortis damnetur &c. Ex quibus, inqvit, clarè sequitur, miracula à falsis etiam prophetis posse fieri, & homines, nisi Dei verâ cognitione & more probè sint muniti, æquè facilè ex miraculis falsos Deos, ac verum, posse amplecti. Hæc ille.

Verùm in hoc etiam loco Auctor non habet, ubi pedem figat, aut quod incrustando suo commento inserviat. Per totum hoc caput præcepit Moses Israëlitis, ut solicitè sibi caverent à pseudo-Prophetis & Seductoribus quibusvis, à religione & cultu, semel à Deo accepto, ad alienum & ignotum cultum abducentibus, nec iis parcerent, etiamsi fratres, filii, aut filiæ, uxores vel amici, iiq́; numero pauci, vel multi, aut integræ civitates essent, & de pseudo-Prophetis speciatim eos præmonuit, ne iis crederent, si vel maximè signis & portentis se verbis suis fidem facturos polliceremtur, eaq́; ipsâ re & opere exhiberent, propterea quòd Deus, permittendo signa & portenta illa fieri, tentet illos ad explorandam illorum in religione & vero sui cultu constantiam. Ex quo si quicquam, hoc concludi potest, signa & portenta quædam posse, Deo permittente, etiam à falsis Prophetis fieri, & homines, nisi Verbo Dei jam sibi tradito, tenaciter inhæreant, posse illis decipi & ad idololatriam induci : quod verissimum est. Inde autem nullâ consequentiæ lege deduci potest, quod pseudo-Prophetæ etiam miracula, propriè & strictè sic dicta, facere possint. Differunt enim נפלאות miracula, propriè dicta, אותות signa, & מופתים portenta. Signa enim & portenta patent latiùs, quàm נפלאות miracula, propriè dicta. Nam omnia miracula sunt etiam signa & portenta; cùm omnia sint effectus insoliti & rari; sed non contrà omnia signa & portenta sunt miracula, cùm de ratione miraculi, propriè dicti & veri, sit ut sit effectus, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ productus : sic autem non producuntur omnia signa & portenta. Unde quemadmodùm hîc pseudoprophetis tribuit Moses, quòd facere possint signa & portenta, ita David Psal. LXXII. 18. & Psal. CXXXVI. 4. testatur disertè, Deum solum facere נפלאות miracula.

Pseudoprophetas igitur facere posse נפלאות miracula, uti Moses loco citato non dicit, nec ex alio Scripturæ loco idoneo Auctor probare potuit, ita meritò à nobis ut commentum ipsius rejicitur.

Signa porro & portenta, quæ à Prophetis falsis fieri posse, Moses d. l. innuit, duplicis generis sunt. Vel enim consistunt in prestigiis & delusionibus Diabolicis, vel in effectibus realibus quidem, sed virtute Diabolicâ, per causas naturales tamen, modo in natura inusitato productis. Prioris ordinis signa & portenta Magi & incantatores, quorum è censu & falsi Prophetæ esse solent, Dæmonum ope, edere possunt, eduntq́; deludendo sensus hominum mutatione aliquâ vel in objecto, vel in medio, vel in organo sensorio factâ. In objecto quidem, vel celeri ejus agitatione, vel diversâ illius situatione, vel subitâ occultatione, aut certâ quâdam dispositione illius ad oculum videntis, vel efformatione corporis cujusdam ex aëre, quod veri objecti speciem habeat &c. In medio verò, infectione aëris qualitate aliqua, quâ species per medium delatæ ita modificentur, ut objectum aliter, quàm in rei veritate est, repræsentent &c. In organo sensorio denique commovendo spiritus & humores, & rerum imagines ac species, quæ in phantasiâ conservantur, certa ratione ordinando & disponendo, ut per illas phantasiæ esse aut fieri appareant, quæ neque sunt, neque fiunt. Posteriori autem modo iidem edunt signa & portenta celeritate motus localis, quo, Dæmonum virtute & potentiâ, vel unum naturæ effectum pro altero ita subitò substituunt, ut humanis sensibus fraus adverti non possit, vel causas secundas commovent, ventosq́;, procellas, terræ motus &c. excitant, vel naturalia agentia patientibus, modo in natura inusitato, applicant ad producendos subitò effectus, quos aliàs non, nisi successivè & actione diuturnâ, & præviâ alteratione, ad certum tempus continuatâ, producere possunt. Quod utrumque, si hujus loci & instituti esset, exemplis ex Scriptura sacra & historiis profanis hîc prolixè ostendi posset.

Sed ad hæc forsan excipient noster Anonymus, vel alii ejus similes Fanatici & Athei, Mosis, Christi & Apostolorum miracula etiam fuisse, si non virtute Dæmonum (quos dari vix concedent) tamen per alias naturales, quamvis nobis occultas, causas edita. Sanè huc collineat tandem Auctoris improbus labor, quo operosè demonstratum ivit, miracula nihil esse aliud, quàm opera naturæ, quorum causas naturales exemplo aliarum rerum solitarum explicare non possumus, vel saltem ille non potest, qui ea scribit aut narrat, & quòd pag. 75. seqq. miracula, in Scripturis commemorata, per causas naturales explicare annixus est, pag. 77. tandem concludens: Omnia, quæ in Scriptura verè narrantur contigisse, ea secundum leges naturæ, ut omnia, necessariò contigisse, & si quid reperiatur, quod apodicticè demonstrari potest, legibus naturæ repugnare, aut ex iis consequi non potuisse, planè credendum, id à sacrilegis hominibus sacris literis adjectum fuisse.


### Thus these scoundrels invent, affirm, and deny anything more quickly, and…

Thus these scoundrels invent, affirm, and deny anything more quickly, and invert and pervert everything, even the words of Scripture, clearer than the rays of the sun, rather than yield to the truth, and confess what the whole of nature and everyone's own conscience dictates, and what the whole human race has believed since the foundation of the world, namely that there is a God, who both made and governs all things by His providence, and can also work above the whole created nature, and does work where and when it seems good to Him. But let us approach the matter more closely.

That Moses was a sorcerer, and performed signs and wonders by diabolical illusions or by the power of demons through natural causes in one way or the other, from the aforementioned, who will say, I will not say demonstrate, but at least prudently suspect? Since Moses himself, in the name and authority of God, most severely forbade all sorceries and diabolical illusions under penalty of death, and ordered that not only all sorcerers and illusionists, but also those who consult them or use their help, be punished with the death penalty, Lev. XIX. v. 31. c. XX. 6. 27. Deut. XVIII. 10. 11. Furthermore, the Magi and sorcerers of Egypt indeed emulated Moses, and the signs and wonders which he performed before Pharaoh and his servants, they also dared to perform, but with unhappy success. For although they performed certain works similar to the Mosaic signs and wonders, they were so far from having performed miracles of the same kind, or having been able to perform them, that their signs and prodigies could not contend with the Mosaic signs and prodigies: just as their staves, thrown down in imitation of the staff of Moses, although they appeared to be turned into serpents, Exod. VII. 11. were nevertheless consumed by the staff of Moses, which had been turned into a serpent, v. 12. The Magi appeared to turn water into blood, ibid. v. 22. to produce frogs, c. VIII. 7. yet they were not able either to restore the water, which had been turned into blood by the staff of Moses, to its original state, or to remove the frogs, which had been produced by Moses and Aaron to afflict the Egyptians, and to avert this plague from the Egyptians as they were able, which Moses and Aaron were able to do by their prayers to God, v. 13, 14. They even emulated Moses and Aaron in producing lice from the dust of the earth, but by no magical arts, by no diabolical power were they able to produce them, so that at length they were compelled to acknowledge and confess before Pharaoh that a greater and higher power underlay the miracles of Moses, and that it was by the finger of God, that is, produced by divine power, ch. VIII. 18, 19. Nor were they able to emulate the production of insects of various kinds, by a huge flood of which all Egypt, with the sole exception of the land of Goshen, was overwhelmed, or any of the subsequent signs brought forth by Moses; nay, struck with boils, as were all the Egyptians, they could not even stand any longer in the sight of Moses, as may be read in chapter IX. 11. All of which are a manifest proof that the signs and wonders brought forth by Moses and Aaron in the sight of Pharaoh and the Egyptian magicians were true miracles, that is to say, effects produced beyond the order of all created nature; but that the signs of the Egyptian magicians and enchanters were either mere illusions, or certain effects similar to the Mosaic miracles, yet produced by diabolical power through natural causes, in some one of the ways mentioned above. What? That many other miracles, and those superior to the powers of all nature, and joined with an effect so solid, were brought forth by Moses, that no one would say they were produced by the powers of nature or were illusions, unless his mind were fascinated and his brain enchanted by diabolical illusions. For what enchantment could bring it about that the sea should be cut in the middle, that the waters should rise on high, and provide a dry and unobstructed passage for the Israelites? What magical art was able to achieve that a rock struck by a staff should immediately pour forth a huge supply of water? What sorceress could in any way bring it about that by bread given daily from the clouds for forty years, so many thousands of men should be fed in a desert place, without any other human food? What superstition could be strong enough to accomplish such a work that the earth, opening itself with a huge chasm, should swallow up the impious and wicked band of a proud faction? That fire coming forth should devour and consume the camp of the seditious with a fatal and memorable punishment? What diabolical power, finally, was so strong that the garments and shoes of the Hebrews, by no rains, no showers, no winter snows, by no labors, journeys, and travels, up to the fortieth year, would either be broken or worn away by age? Anyone understands that these prodigies are altogether ἀδύνατα for all creatures to imitate, and thus the outcome has taught us that by these powerful deeds and miracles the doctrine of Moses has been confirmed for all ages. Which the holy Prophets then explained more fully, and illustrated with their clearest prophecies; who themselves were partly distinguished by miracles, and partly, by their prophecies and their manifest outcome, obtained the most certain testimony of truth, that the prophecy brought by them was not human, but that holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. These are the words of the most learned Hunnius, in the place cited above, in Argument XIII, taken from the miracles of Moses, Col. 22 seq.

To the same effect, he discourses elegantly concerning the miracles of Christ in Argument XIV, by which he went to assert the authority of the Scripture of the New Testament from the perpetual tradition of the hands. Where, Col. 31, among other things: Come, he says, let us unfold the Evangelical annals, and let us draw forth some examples from here. In the fifth chapter of John, Christ commands a man, almost consumed by a long-standing disease, to arise and carry home the pallet on which he had lain for thirty-eight years. He arises, sound immediately at the voice of Christ, and in his whole body firm and whole. Where, at the nod of the Savior, the disease is suddenly rooted out, which had previously settled most deeply in all his limbs, and, having grown old over the space of so many years, had almost passed into the nature of the man. In turn, there succeeds a far different state of the whole body, and a clearly new vigor, so that he who before could scarcely move himself from the spot, now, with his limbs consolidated and his strength gathered in a wonderful manner, leaps to his feet, takes up his bed himself, and goes home, while all who were present looked on with the greatest admiration. Thus, in the ninth chapter of Matthew, before a frequent assembly of the Jews, he cures a man so weakened by a notable paralysis, so exhausted and lost in his strength, that it seemed utterly desperate that the integrity of his health could be recovered. He commands him likewise to arise, to take up his bed, to go home. At which voice the paralytic, by a memorable prodigy, suddenly acquires such new strength that in the sight of the people, who were in a most frequent and had flocked in a run to the Lord Jesus, he might cast his bed upon his shoulders without the help of others, and go away to his home; not immediately vanishing from the eyes of men, but surviving for a long time still, so that he might announce the glory of Christ and proclaim among mortals the benefit received from Him. What trickery can be imagined here, even now, or could have been imagined then by the Pharisees, those most deplorable enemies of the words and deeds of Christ? Who, at the voice by which He announced the forgiveness of sins to the paralytic, did indeed grunt, murmur, snarl, resist, and blaspheme: but the miracle itself they neither dared nor were able to deny because of its evidence, nor to censure because of the manifest power and sense of divine majesty. Thus in the Gospel of John, chapter nine, Christ opens the eyes of a man blind from his earliest infancy, and illuminates him with the light of vision, and that miracle soon becomes famous in all the borders of Judea. And what fraud can underlie this sign? That man was born blind from his mother's womb; he had struggled with this evil of blindness for forty continuous years. That man knew this as evidently as anyone knows his own fingers, inasmuch as he could not but be conscious of his own misery; and he even professes this very thing with an ingenuous confession before the Senate of the Chief Priests and Pharisees, not without great danger to himself. His parents knew and openly testified to this very thing, and all knew it, as many as had known him from a boy. And (that I may reduce the principal deeds of the Savior into a summary) by what trickery, pray, could it be brought about that He recalled to this human and familiar life, to be spent for a very long time still among mortals, the daughter of Jairus, a leader of the Jewish Synagogue, for whom funeral rites were being prepared, the son of the widow, already to be buried, and Lazarus, already dwelling in the tomb, whom all the actions they performed and the works they did demonstrated most solidly and irrefragably that they were truly living? What superstition could cause the Lord Jesus to heal lepers, who had been recognized and judged as such by public censure, with a single word? That with five loaves and two fish He fed more than five thousand men in a desert place, and from the remainder were taken up twelve baskets or hampers of fragments? that at the wedding celebrated in Cana he turned water into wine? that at his command the waves of the raging sea and the winds suddenly grew calm? that at his passion and death the sun, contrary to the law of nature at the time of the full moon, was darkened; the veil of the temple was torn; the rocks were broken and split apart; the globe of the earth, swelling with unusual tremors, shook far and wide; the graves cast out the bodies of the dead, and he himself, truly dead on the cross, truly buried in the garden, rose again on the third day from the monument secured by the precaution of a seal, and his glorious resurrection became known to the Pharisees and the Chief Priests through the account of the guards; and thus the fame of his signs no longer contained itself within the borders of Judea and Galilee, nor did it merely extend and spread itself to neighboring regions; but it also reached even to the most remote nations through celebrated and constant preaching, so that there was no shore anywhere so deserted that the name of Christ did not travel through it with incredible speed. Just as that visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, accomplished by the power of the reigning Christ on the day of Pentecost, was such a notable miracle that no creature anywhere could have performed it, or even now could imitate it; namely, that men hitherto illiterate suddenly conceived in their minds an exact understanding of the Prophetic Scriptures, and in a moment attained knowledge of all the languages that are under heaven. This prodigy could in no way be hidden among the Jewish people; since it was not designated in some corner, not performed in an obscure village, not seen by the eyes of a few, but in a most crowded city, before a most celebrated crown of many thousands, who had flocked to Jerusalem from all the nations of the world to celebrate the solemnity of the feast, as is read in the Acts. And the thing itself demonstrated the certainty of the miracle to the eyes, ears, and minds of all peoples. For unless the Apostles had been enlightened from heaven with this gift of tongues, but had held only their vernacular; how could it have happened that in the course of a very short time the Gospel became known to all peoples of all languages and idioms in the entire Empire

Latin:

Ita Nebulones hi fingunt, affirmant, negant citiùs quidvis, invertuntǫ; & pervertunt potiùs omnia, etiam verba Scripturæ, vel solis radiis clariora, quàm veritati ut cedant, & quod natura universa & sua cuique conscientia dictitat, indeǫ; à condito mundo genus humanum totum credidit, fateantur, nempe esse Deum, qui & fecerit & gubernet suâ providentiâ omnia, & supra naturam creatam totam quoque operari possit, opereturǫ; ubi & quando ipsi visum sit. Sed ad rem propiùs accedamus.

Mosen fuisse incantatorem, & præstigiis Diabolicis aut virtute Dæmonum per causas naturales alterutro, ex prædictis, vel utroque modo edidisse signa & portenta, unde, non dicam demonstrabit, sed prudenter quis saltem suspicabitur? cùm incantationes & præstigias Diabolicas quasque Moses ipse, Dei nomine & auctoritate, severissimè sub mortis pœna interdixerit, & non tantum incantatores ac præstigiatores omnes, sed & qui illos consulunt, aut illorum ope utuntur, capitis supplicio afficere jusserit, Lev. XIX. v. 31. c. XX. 6. 27. Deut. XIIX. 10. 11. Prætereà Magi & incantatores Ægyptiaci æmulati quidem sunt Mosen, & quæ hic coram Pharaone ejusǫ; servis edidit signa & portenta, etiam ipsi ausi sunt edere, sed successu infelici. Quamvis enim quædam signis & portentis Mosaicis similia ediderint opera, tantum tamen abest, ut specie eadē miracula ediderint, aut edere potuerint, ut illorum signa & prodigia cum signis & prodigiis Mosaicis contendere non potuerint: sicut illorum baculi ad imitationem baculi Mosis projecti, etsi visi sunt in serpentes versi, Exod. VII. 11. à baculo Mosis tamen, in serpentem converso, absumti sunt, v. 12. Visi sunt Magi aquam convertere in sanguinem, ib. v. 22. producere ranas, c. VIII. 7. non tamen vel aquam, Mosis baculo in sanguinem versam, ad suum pristinum statum reducere, vel ranas, per Mosen & Aaronem ad Ægyptios affligendos productas, amovere, & plagam hanc ab Ægyptiis avertere potuerunt, quod precibus suis ad Deum Moses & Aaron poterant, v. 13. 14. Æmulati etiam sunt Mosen & Aaronem in producendis pediculis ex pulvere terræ, sed nullis artibus magicis, nullâ virtute Diabolicâ eos producere potuerunt, ut tandem agnoscere & coram Pharaone fateri cogerentur, Mosis miraculis majorem & altiorem subesse virtutem, eaq; Dei digito, h. e. divina edi virtute, c. VIII. 18. 19. Neque etiam in producendis insectis variorum generum, quorum ingenti colluvie universa Ægyptus, sola terrâ Gosen exceptâ, obruebatur, aut subsequentium à Mose editorum signorum ullum æmulari; quin ulceribus, ut Ægyptii omnes, percussi, ne quidem consistere ampliùs in Mosis conspectu poterant, ut cap. IX. 11. legere est. Quæ omnia documento manifesto sunt, signa & portenta, in Pharaonis & Magorum Ægyptiacorum conspectu à Mose & Aarone edita, vera fuisse miracula, effectus scilicet, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ productos; Magorum verò & Incantatorum Ægyptiacorum signa vel meras fuisse præstigias, vel effectus aliquos, miraculis Mosaicis similes, virtute Diabolicâ tamen per causas naturales, aliquo ex supra commemoratis modo, productos. Quid? quod alia miracula plura, eaq; viribus naturæ universæ superiora, & cum effectu ita solido conjuncta, per Mosen edita sunt, ut ea vel naturæ viribus producta, vel præstigias fuisse, nemo dixerit, nisi præstigiis Diabolicis fascinatus sit animus ejus, cerebrumque excantatum. Quæ enim incantatio præstare potuit, ut mare secaretur medium, aquæ in altum surgerent, & Israëlitis siccum & expeditum præberent transitum? Quæ Magica ars consequi valuit, ut lapis baculo percussus ingentem copiam aquarum confestim profunderet? Quæ præstigiatrix qui verat ullo pacto efficere, ut pane è nubibus dato indies ad annos quadraginta, tot millia hominum deserto loco, sine ullo alio cibo humano, pasceretur? Quæ superstitio ad tantum conficiendum opus valere potuit, ut terra ingenti hiatu sese aperiens, impiam ac sceleratam manum superbæ factionis absorberet? ut ignis egrediens castra seditiosorum fatali memorabiliq; supplicio devoraret & absumeret? Quæ denique potentia Diabolica tantum valebat, ut vestes & calcei Hebræorum nullis pluviis, nullis imbribus, nullis hybernis nivibus, nullis laboribus, profectionibus & itineribus nullis, in quadragesimum usque annum vel vetustate rumperentur, vel attererentur? Haec prodigia ut cunctis creaturis imitatu prorsus ἀδύνατα esse quivis intelligit, sic eventus nos edocuit, potentibus hisce factis atque signis in omnia secula confirmatam esse Mosis doctrinam. Quam deindè fusius explicarunt, & clarissimis vaticiniis suis illustrarunt sancti Prophetae; qui & ipsi partim miraculis insignes fuerunt, partim verò, vaticiniis suis eorumque manifesto eventu, certissima veritatis testimonium adepti sunt, quod non humanitùs ipsorum allata Prophetia, sed Spiritu S. impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Verba sunt Doctissimi Hunnii, loco suprà citato, Argumento XIII. à miraculis Mosis petito, Col. 22 seq.

Eundem in sensum de miraculis Christi idem eleganter disserit Argum. XIV. quo autoritatem Scripturae N. T. assertum ivit à perpetua manuum traditione. Ubi Col. 31 inter alia: Agite, inquit, explicemus annales Evangelicos, & exempla hinc quaedam depromamus. Johannis V. capite jubet Christus hominem, diuturno morbo penè confectum, surgere, & grabbatum, in quo triginta octo annos decubuerat, perferre domum. Surgit ille, ad vocem Christi sanus confestim, totoque corpore firmus & integer. Ubi ad Salvatoris nutum subitò radicitus exterminatur morbus, qui altissimè priùs omnibus membris insederat, & tot annorum spacio inveteratus, propè in naturam hominis abierat. Succedit vicissim totius corporis habitus longè alius, ac vigor planè novus, ut qui priùs se vix loco movere quiverat, nunc, consolidatis membris collectisque miranda ratione viribus in pedes exiliat, lectum suum tollat ipse, domumque vadat, cunctis, qui aderant, summa cum admiratione inspectantibus. Sic Matthaei nono coram frequenti Judaeorum concione curat hominem, insigni paralysi sic debilitatum, sic viribus exhaustum ac deperditum, ut de recuperanda valetudinis integritate penitissimè videretur desperatum. Eum jubet itidem surgere, lectum tollere, domum vadere. Ad quam vocem paralyticus memorabili prodigio sic novum repentè acquirit robur, ut in conspectu populi, qui frequentissimo accursu ad Dominum Jesum confluxerat, lectum suum citra aliorum opem in humeros conjiciat, & domum suam abeat; non protinus ex hominum oculis evanescens, sed multo adhuc temporis superstes, ut gloriam Christi annunciare acceptumque ab illo beneficium inter mortales prædicare posset. Quid hîc præstigiarum fingi saltem vel nunc potest, vel tum poterat à Pharisæis, deploratissimis dictorum & factorum Christi hostibus? qui ad vocem, quâ peccatorum veniam nunciabat paralytico, grunniebant quidem, murmurabant, ringebantur, ressectabant sese, blasphemabant: miraculum verò ipsum neque negare ob evidentiam, neque reprehendere ob manifestam divinæ majestatis vim atque sensum vel audebant vel poterant. Sic in Evangelio Johannis capite nono Christus hominis ab ultima infantia cæci oculos aperit, & visionis lumine collustrat, idque miraculum mox in cunctis Judææ finibus inclarescit. Quid & huic signo potest subesse fraudis? cæcus fuit ille ex matris utero productus; cum hoc cæcitatis malo conflictatus jam quadraginta continuos annos. Quod tam evidenter noverat homo ille, quam quisque suos novit digitos, upote qui non poterat non esse miseriæ suæ sibi conscius; atque hoc ipsum profitetur etiam ingenua confessione coram Senatu Pontificum & Pharisæorum, non sine grandi suo periculo. Sciebant & palam testabantur ipsum hoc parentes ejus, sciebant omnes, quotquot illum à puero noverant. Et (ut præcipuas res gestas Salvatoris in compendium redigam) quibus tandem præstigiis fieri poterat, ut Jairi, primarii Synagogæ Judaicæ, filiam, cui exequiæ parabantur, ut viduæ filium, jam sepeliendum, ut Lazarum in sepulcro jam agentem, ad vitam revocaret humanam istam ac familiarem, inter mortales longissimo adhuc tempore exigendam, quos verè vivere, actiones omnes, quas præstabant, & opera, quæ faciebant, irrefragabilia quàm solidissimè commonstrabant: Quæ superstitio poterat efficere, ut Dominus Jesus leprosos, qui publicâ censurâ tales agniti judicatique fuerant, unico sanaret verbo? ut quinque panibus & duobus piscibus plus quàm quinque hominum millia deserto loco pasceret, & de residuo tollerentur duodecim fragmentorum sportæ sive calathi? ut in nuptiis Canæ celebratis aquam in vinum converteret? ut ad ipsius imperium sævientis maris fluctus atque venti subitò consilescerent? ut ad passionem & mortem illius Sol præter naturæ legem plenilunii tempore obtenebraretur; discinderetur velum templi; rumperentur ac dissilirent petræ; orbis terrarum inusitatis motibus intumescens longè latéque tremeret; sepulcra defunctorum corpora ejicerent, ipseque verè in cruce mortuus, verè in horto sepultus, die tertia è monumento, sigilli cautione communito resurgeret, ejusque gloriosa resurrectio custodum narratione Pharisæis Sacerdotumque Principibus innotesceret; atque adeò fama signorum ejus non jam intra Judææ & Galilææ terminos se contineret, nec in finitimas duntaxat regiones se proferret ac diffunderet; sed etiam ad gentes longissimè remotas celebri constantique prædicatione pervaderet, ita ut nulla usquam esset ora tam deserta, quam non Christi nomen incredibili celeritate pervagaretur. Quemadmodùm etiam visibilis illa Spiritus sancti effusio super Apostolos, virtute regnantis Christi perfecta in die Pentecostes, tam fuit insigne miraculum, ut id nulla uspiam perficere potuerit, vel etiamnum imitari possit creatura; nimirum quòd homines illiterati hactenus, Scripturarum Propheticarum exactam intelligentiam animis conceperunt subitò, cunctarumque linguarum, quæ sub cælo sunt, notitiam momento sunt consecuti. Quod prodigium in populo Judaico occultum esse nullo modo potuit; cùm non in angulo aliquo designatum, non obscuro pago gestum, non paucorum oculis conspectum sit, sed in frequentissima urbe, coram celeberrima corona plurimorum millium, qui Jerosolymam è cunctis nationibus orbis ad festi solennitatem frequentandam confluxerant, ut in Actis legitur. Et certitudinem miraculi ad omnium populorum oculos, aures atque animos demonstravit res ipsa. Nisi enim hoc linguarum dono cælitùs illustrati fuissent Apostoli, sed solam tenuissent vernaculam; quî fieri poterat, ut brevissimi temporis decursu Evangelium omnibus omnium linguarum & idiomatum populis innotesceret in universis Imperii


### Romans to the provinces, and to foreign kingdoms and islands

Romans to the provinces, and to foreign kingdoms and islands? just as indeed the Apostle Paul in those times of his, almost around the first rising of the Evangelical light, writes that the doctrine concerning Christ was preached among every creature under heaven, and diffused far and wide into this most vast orb of all lands and nations. Who is there who does not understand, who does not notice, that this could not have been done except by the aid of very many, and indeed of all, languages? He [writes] this most correctly concerning the miracles of Christ from the weighed circumstances of them. For the circumstances brought forward from the Evangelical history are so evident that they evidently prove that all things were produced without any Diabolical tricks, without any force and power of either Diabolical or natural causes, and that therefore all were true miracles. The same judgment applies to the miracles of the Apostles, performed by the power of Christ among the Jews and Gentiles throughout the world, which, according to the promise of Christ in John XIV. 12, were for the most part not inferior to the miracles of Christ, but equal, especially in the circumstances which provide by no means doubtful evidence for distinguishing true miracles from fictitious ones. Concerning these, our Hunnius writes thus in the same place, Col. 33: The Acts of the Apostles testify how great prodigies Christ, sitting at the right hand of power, performed also through the hands of the Apostles, as Scripture speaks. Which could not have been fabricated by the author of the book, Luke the Evangelist, because in their recitation places, regions, and cities are designated; persons are expressed, in whom they were performed. The enemies of the Christian name, Jews and Gentiles alike, would have accused this narrative of notorious vanity and would have clearly convicted it, if it had been composed from fables rather than from things so done. Indeed, the Gentiles and Jews were so far from daring to do this, that Ethnic writers, on account of these very miracles by which the Church had been ennobled, called the Christian religion a malevolent superstition. By which reproach they do not so much declare the inveterate hatred with which they burn and seethe against the Confessors of the Gospel, as they bear witness, even against their will, to the miracles with which the blessed Apostles illustrated the Church. Under which pretext also Paul, writing to the Corinthians, had boasted of the signs of his Apostleship, performed by him in their midst, with all patience and signs and wonders, and mighty works, if the Corinthians had known that no sign was performed by Paul in their city? And with what face would Paul in his epistles everywhere, and likewise Luke in the public writing of the Acts of the Apostles, have dared to make any mention of the miraculous gift of tongues, with which those who received the sacred rite of Baptism from the Apostles were suddenly enriched: if that most illustrious sign had nowhere been seen or observed by anyone in the world? We see, therefore, how excellently both the miracles of Christ and of the Apostles are fortified on every side against every suspicion of either deceit or uncertainty, and how effectively they seal for us the truth of the Apostolic doctrine. These things, again, the praised Hunnius [writes] skillfully and learnedly concerning the miracles of the Apostles also. For the circumstances which are also detected in these things evidently prove that they were no less than the miracles of Christ, joined with a solid and supernatural effect, and thus without deceit, without illusions, and yet not by any natural [power] of secondary causes; but were performed entirely by the truly divine power of Christ; e.g., the lame man, whom Peter and John, about to ascend into the temple, had healed in Acts 3:6-7, had suffered from this defect of the feet from his mother's womb, so that unless he was carried, he could not move himself from place to place. Which escaped no one among the citizens of Jerusalem. For he was forty years old, and had sat daily in the public way at the gate of the temple, which is called Beautiful, so that for the sake of sustaining his life he might ask for alms from those entering and leaving, so that it was known to all that he had been truly lame, and yet not with a slight defect curable by natural causes; but that he had been lame from a defect of the feet born with him and contracted in his mother's womb. Nor was health restored to him in a corner or some hidden place, but in a public square, which they frequented in crowds, who were entering and leaving the temple. Nor did he who had been healed withdraw himself from the sight of men on the spot, but having entered the temple with Peter and John, he was walking and leaping and praising God, before all the people, and being recognized, that he was the very one who, born lame, had sat daily for so many years at the gate of the temple for the sake of asking for alms, he seized everyone in admiration of the stupendous sign. Moreover, the Apostles, Peter and John, having been dragged to the Jerusalem Sanhedrin for judgment, intrepidly he had accompanied, and had presented himself to be seen by the high priest, the elders of the people, and the scribes, c. V. 10. Moreover, the manner of the restoration of health proves that this sign was performed by Peter and John neither by the powers of nature nor by diabolical power. For by command and word, without any natural causes or means being employed, his soles and ankles were consolidated in a moment, in such a way that, having been raised up by his hand being grasped, he immediately leaped up and stood, and having entered the temple, by walking and leaping for joy, he demonstrated the strength of his feet by the very act, as received by the word and command of the Apostles. Where was the fraud? What illusions? What natural or diabolical powers could have been feigned or even attributed to such a miracle, which could be accepted under any appearance of probability? Whence not even the most hostile enemies of the Christian name, who, stirred up by this very miracle, had thrown Peter and John into prison and afterwards dragged them into judgment, and were striving in every way for their death, found anything which they could allege against the truth of the miracle under any color or pretext; but, convinced by the evidence of the circumstances, with their opinions compared among themselves, they finally confessed ingenuously that there was no fraud, no illusion underlying it: saying, What shall we do to these men? For that a conspicuous sign has been performed by them is manifest to all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it, Acts IV. 16. The matter stands the same with the other miracles performed by the Apostles.

However much these things are clearer than the midday sun, our Anonymous author nevertheless is persuaded that he can most clearly show the contrary from the circumstances which are noted by the sacred writers in the description of the miracles of Moses and the Prophets, as well as of Christ and the Apostles, namely, that the miracles were performed through natural causes, and that nothing is done against or beyond the order of nature. The circumstances of the miracles, he says on page 76, clearly show that they themselves require natural causes. Namely, that the Egyptians might be infested with boils, it was necessary that Moses should scatter ashes into the air; (see Exod. ch. 9, verse 10.) the locusts also, by the natural command of God, namely from an east wind blowing for a whole day and night, sought the region of the Egyptians, and by a very strong west wind left the same (see Exod. ch. 10, verses 14, 19.) by the same command of God also the sea opened a way for the Jews (see Exod. ch. 14, v. 21.) namely by an east wind which blew most strongly throughout the night. Then, in order for Elisha to awaken the boy who was believed to be dead, he had to lie upon the boy several times, until he first grew warm, and finally opened his eyes (see 2 Kings ch. 4, v. 34, 35); thus also in the Gospel of John, ch. 9, certain circumstances are narrated which C Scriptures, all of which sufficiently show that miracles require something other than the absolute command of God, as they say. Wherefore it must be believed that, although the circumstances of miracles and their natural causes are not always, nor all, narrated, miracles nevertheless did not occur without them. Which is also evident from Exodus ch. 9, verse 27, where it is only narrated that the sea swelled up again at the mere nod of Moses, and no mention of wind is made. And yet in the Canticle (ch. 15, verse 10) it is said that this happened because God blew with His wind (that is, a very strong wind); wherefore this circumstance is omitted in the history, and the miracle seems greater for that reason.

But these things prove nothing less than what it was incumbent upon the Author to prove, namely that all miracles were produced through natural causes and by the power of nature, and that nothing can be done beyond or above nature. For first, the mentioned circumstances occur in at least some miracles, not in all. For in others, a far different mode of production is narrated, and some things are even said to have been produced by word alone and bare command: just as Lazarus, after the fourth day from his death, was raised from death by the voice of Christ, 'Lazarus, come forth,' without any natural cause being applied, and came forth from the tomb, John 11:43. And just as in chapter 9:6 ff. of the same Evangelist it is narrated concerning the man born blind that, with clay smeared on his eyes and washed off in the waters of the pool of Siloam; so in Mark 10:52 it is reported that to Bartimaeus the blind man, by the voice: 'Go, your faith has made you whole'; and in Luke 18:42, that to another blind man in the same manner by saying: Ἀνάβλεψον, 'receive your sight, your faith has made you whole,' his sight was restored. Then the circumstances adduced, if anything, at least prove this, that God in performing miracles sometimes employed certain natural things. But that He employed them out of the necessity of nature, as the Author wishes, and as their natural causes, and by their natural power efficiently produced them, (which is the only thing that comes into question here) not even the Author dares to assert, but he says at least that the circumstances of the miracles clearly show that they (the miracles) themselves require natural causes. But that they require them as their efficient causes, by whose natural power they were made and brought forth, and not at least as signs or mere instruments, employed by the free will of God, so that even without them they could have been produced by divine power alone, neither do the mentioned circumstances clearly show, nor does the Author teach by any reasoning by what law of consequence they show this, which nevertheless he ought to have taught above all else. Indeed, they rather clearly show and solidly prove the contrary. For what natural power could reside in one or another handful of ashes, scattered upward into the air by Moses and Aaron, to infest the bodies of men and beasts, and to produce ulcers and pustules in them? What natural power could reside in an east wind, blowing for a whole day and night, to produce locusts in an unheard-of multitude, so that they covered all of Egypt? We do not deny that an east wind is hot, and can contribute something by its heat to the equivocal generation of locusts and other insects from putrid matter. But that by its blowing alone locusts could be naturally generated in such a multitude that they covered all of Egypt in one day and night, this is what we deny, and what the sacred history tacitly denies by the very fact that it records their arrival, predicted one day before at the command of Moses, to have happened in such a multitude, beyond the customary order of nature. What natural power could reside in an east wind, blowing most strongly for an entire night, to divide the Red Sea, and to hold back the waters on either side, so that they would not flow away, but would stand on both sides like a wall, and open a path for the Israelites to cross on dry foot? Winds, blowing strongly, do indeed have the power of agitating seas, exciting their waves, and drying the earth: but they could not by any natural power effect the dividing of the Red Sea, the holding back of the waters on the right and left, so that, enclosed by no foreign boundaries, they stood motionless on both sides like a wall, and provided a safe passage for the whole Israelite people.

Latin:

Romani provinciis, exterisque regnis & insulis? sicut quidem Apostolus Paulus suis illis temporibus, ferè circa primum Evangelicæ lucis exortum, doctrinam de Christo apud universam creaturam sub cælo prædicatam, & in hunc vastissimum cunctarum terrarum atque gentium orbem longè lateque diffusam esse scribit. Quod non nisi plurimarum adeoque omnium linguarum præsidio fieri potuisse, quis est, qui non intelligat? non animadvertat? Hæc ille de miraculis Christi ex perpensis illorum circumstantiis rectissimè. Sunt enim adductæ ex historia Evangelica circumstantiæ ita evidentes, ut absque ullis præstigiis Diabolicis, absque ulla vel Diabolica vel causarum naturalium vi & potentia producta omnia, atque adeò miracula vera omnia fuisse, evidenter evincant. Idem judicium est de miraculis Apostolorum, virtute Christi Judæos inter & Gentes passim in orbe terrarum editis, quæ, juxta promissionem Christi Joh. XIV. 12. pleraque Christi miraculis haud inferiora, sed æqualia fuerunt, præsertim in circumstantiis, quæ miraculis veris à fictis discernendis documenta minimè dubia præbent. De his ibidem noster Hunnius Col. 33. ita scribit: Per Apostolorum quoque manus, ut Scriptura loquitur, quanta prodigia Christus in dextra virtutis sedens ediderit, Acta testantur Apostolica. Quæ ab Auctore libri, Luca Evangelista, confingi proptereà non valebant, quòd in illorum recitatione designantur loca, regiones & urbes; exprimuntur personæ, in quibus ea sunt edita. Quam narrationem notoriæ vanitatis accusâssent, & perspicuè convicissent hostes Christiani nominis, Judæi simul & Gentiles, si ex fabulis ea potiùs, quam rebus ita gestis fuisset conflata. Id verò adeò non sunt ausi vel gentiles vel Judæi, ut Scriptores Ethnici ob hæc ipsa miracula, quibus nobilitata erat Ecclesia, Christianam religionem appellarint superstitionem maleficam. Quo convitio non tam declarant odium inveteratum, quo adversum Confessores Evangelii flagrant & æstuant, quàm vel inviti testimonium dicunt de miraculis, quibus Ecclesiam illustrarunt beati Apostoli. Quo etiam prætextu Paulus ad Corinthios scribens jactâsset signa Apostolatus sui, à se in ipsorum medio peracta, cum omni patientia & fignis & prodigiis, & potentibus factis, si Corinthii nullum à Paulo signum in sua urbe editum scivissent? Et quâ fronte Paulus in suis passim Epistolis, Lucas item publico scripto Actorum Apostolicorum, ullam ausi fuissent mentionem facere mirandi linguarum doni, quo subitò fuerunt locupletati, qui Baptifmatis sacrum ab Apostolis percipiebant: si præclarissimum illud signum nusquam cuiquam in orbe visum conspectumque fuisset? Videmus ergo, quàm egregiè & Christi & Apostolorum miracula adversus omnem vel doli vel incertitudinis suspicionem undiquaque munita sint, & quàm efficaciter nobis doctrinæ Apostolicæ veritatem obsignent. Hæc rursum laudatus Hunnius de Apostolorum quoq; miraculis scitè & eruditè. Nam quæ in his etiam deprehenduntur circumstantiæ, evincunt evidenter, quòd non minus, quàm Christi miracula, cum effectu solido, eoque supernaturali conjuncta, atque adeò absq; dolo, absque præstigiis, nec tamen ullâ naturali causarum secundarum; sed in solidum Christi verè divinâ virtute peracta fuerint; v. g. Claudus, quem Act. III. 6. 7. Petrus & Johannes, in templum adscensuri, sanaverant, ab utero matris hoc pedum vitio laboraverat, ut nisi bajulatus, de loco in locum se conferre non posset. Quod neminem civium Hierosolymitanorum latebat. Erat enim annorum quadraginta, & quotidiè in via publica ad portam templi, quæ speciosa dicitur, consederat, ut sustentandæ vitæ causâ eleemosynam ab ingredientibus & egredientibus peteret, ut eum verè claudum fuisse, neque tamen levi & per causas naturales curabili; sed ex connato & in utero matris contracto pedum vitio claudicâfse, omnibus notum esset. Neque etiam in angulo aut loco quodam occulto sanitas ei restituta fuit, sed in platea publica, quam catervatim frequentabant, qui templum ingrediebantur & egrediebantur. Neque è vestigio hominum conspectui se subduxit, qui sanatus fuerat, sed cum Petro & Johanne templum ingressus, ambulabat & saliens laudabat Deum, coram toto populo, & agnitus, quòd is ipse esset, qui claudus natus tot annis petendæ eleemosynæ causâ quotidiè ad portam templi consederat, omnes in signi stupendi admirationem rapiebat. Quin & Apostolos, Petrum & Johannem, ad Synedrium Hierosolymitanum in judicium protractos, intrepidè comitatus fuerat, & Sacerdoti summo, Senioribus populi, Scribisq; se conspiciendum exhibuerat, c. V. 10. Modus præterea restituendæ sanitatis evincit, nec naturæ viribus, nec virtute Diabolica signum hoc a Petro & Johanne patratum esse. Jussu enim, verboq;, absque ullis adhibitis naturalibus causis aut mediis, momento consolidatæ sunt plantæ ejus & tali, ut apprehensa ipsius manu erectus statim exiliens steterit, templumq; ingressus, ambulandoque & præ gaudio saliendo acceptum, Apostolorum verbo & jussu, robur pedum ipso opere ostenderit. Ubi quæ fraus? quæ præstigiæ? quæ naturales aut Diabolicæ vires, quibus tantum miraculum ulla probabilitatis specie acceptum referri posset, vel fingi potuerunt? Unde ne hostes quidem nominis Christiani infensissimi, qui hoc ipso miraculo excitati Petrum & Johannem in carcerem conjecerant, & postea in judicium protraxerant, omnibusq; modis in illorum necem incumbebant, quod adversus miraculi veritatem ullo colore aut prætextu obtenderent, invenerunt, sed circumstantiarum evidentia convicti, sententiis inter se collatis, nihil fraudis, nihil præstigiarum ei subesse, ingenue tandem fassi sunt: Quid, inquientes, faciemus hominibus istis? Nam conspicuum signum editum esse per eos, omnibus habitantibus Hierosolymis manifestum est, nec possumus inficiari, Act. IV. 16. Perinde cum cæteris per Apostolos editis miraculis res habet.

Hæc utut vel sole meridiano clariora sunt, noster tamen Anonymus persuasum sibi habet, se posse ex circumstantiis, quæ in descriptione miraculorum cùm Mosis & Prophetarum, tum Christi & Apostolorum à Scriptoribus sacris annotatæ sunt, contrarium clarissimè ostendere, nempè miracula per causas naturales facta esse, nihilque fieri contra vel præter naturæ ordinem. Circumstantiæ miraculorum, inquit pag. 76. clarè ostendunt, ipsa causas naturales requirere. Nempe ut Ægyptii scabie infestarentur, opus fuit, ut Moses favillam in aërem sursum spargeret; (vide Exod. cap. 9. vers. 10.) locustæ etiam ex mandato Dei naturali, nempe ex vento orientali, integro die & nocte flante, Ægyptiorum regionem petiverunt, & vento occidentali fortissimo eandem reliquerunt (vide Exod. c. 10. vers. 14. 19.) eodem etiam Dei jussu mare viam Judæis aperuit (vide Exod. c. 14. v. 21.) nempe Euro, qui fortissimè integrâ nocte flavit. Deinde ut Elisa puerum, qui mortuus credebatur, excitaret, aliquoties puero incumbere debuit, donec prius incaluerit, & tandem oculos aperuerit (vide Reg. lib. 2. c. 4. v. 34. 35.) sic etiam in Evangelio Johannis cap. 9. quædam narrantur circumstantiæ, quibus Christus usus est ad sanandum cæcum, & sic alia multa in Scripturis reperiuntur, quæ omnia satis ostendunt, miracula aliud, quàm absolutum Dei, ut ajunt, mandatum requirere. Quare credendum, quamvis circumstantiæ miraculorum, eorumque naturales causæ non semper, neque omnes enarrentur, miracula tamen non sine iisdem contigisse. Quod etiam constat ex Exodi cap. IX. vers. 27. ubi tantum narratur, quòd solo nutu Mosis mare iterum intumuit, nec ulla venti mentio fit. Et tamen in Cantico (cap. 15. vers. 10.) dicitur, id contigisse ex eo, quod Deus vento suo (id est, vento fortissimo) flaverit; quare hæc circumstantia in historia omittitur, & miraculum ea de causa majus videtur.

Verùm hæc nihil minus evincunt, quàm quod Auctori probandum incumbebat, nempe miracula omnia producta esse per causas naturales & naturæ virtute, nec quicquam præter vel supra naturam fieri posse. Primùm enim commemoratæ circumstantiæ in aliquibus saltem occurrunt miraculis, non in omnibus. In aliis enim longè alius narratur productionis modus, dicunturq; quædam etiam verbo tantum & nudo imperio producta: sicut Lazarus post quartum demum ab ejus obitu diem voce Christi, Lazare veni foras; sine ulla causa naturali adhibita, ex morte suscitatus, è sepulchro prodiit, Joh. XI. 43. & quemadmodùm cap. IX. 6. seqq. ejusdem Evangelistæ de cæco nato narratur, quòd luto, oculis ejus illito, & aquis piscinæ Siloæ abluto; ita Marci X. 52. refertur, quòd Bartimæo cæco voce: Abi, fides tua te salvum fecit; & Luc. XIIX. 42. quòd alii cæco eundem in modum dicendo: Ἀνάβλεψον, visum recipito, fides tua te salvum fecit, visus restitutus sit. Deinde circumstantiæ adductæ, si quicquam, hoc saltem evincunt, Deum in edendis miraculis adhibuisse quandoque aliquas res naturales. Quod autem eas ex necessitate naturæ, ut Auctor vult, & ut illorum causas naturales adhibuerit, & illarum virtute naturali ea efficienter produxerit, (quod unum hic in quæstionem venit) ne Auctor quidem afferere audet, sed dicit saltem, circumstantias miraculorum clarè ostendere, ipsa (miracula) causas naturales requirere. Quod auté eas requirant ut causas sui efficientes, quarum naturali vi facta & edita sint, non saltem ut signa vel instrumenta nuda, Dei liberâ voluntate adhibita, ut etiam absque illis solâ divinâ virtute produci potuerint, neque clarè ostendunt commemoratæ circumstantiæ, neque etiam Auctor, quâ consequentiæ lege id ostendant, ullâ ratione docet, quod tamen ante omnia docere debebat. Quin contrarium potiùs illæ clarè ostendunt & solidè evincunt. Quæ enim uni alterive pugno favillæ, à Mose & Aarone sursum in aërem sparsæ, naturalis vis inesse poterat infestandi hominum & brutorum corpora, & ulcera ac pustulas in illis producendi? Quæ vento orientali, die & nocte totâ flanti, naturalis vis inesse poterat ad producendas locustas multitudine inauditâ, ut totam Ægyptum operirent? Ventum orientalem esse calidum, & posse calore suo aliquid conferre ad locustarum aliorumq́; insectorum generationem æquivocam ex materia putrida, non inficiamur. Sed solo ejus flatu locustas tantâ multitudine, ut totam operirent Ægyptum, unâ die & nocte naturaliter generari potuisse, hoc est, quod negamus, quodque historia sacra eo ipso tacitè negat, quo illarum immissionem, uno ante die prædictam, ad Mosis imperium tantâ multitudine, præter usitatum naturæ ordinem, factam commemorat. Quæ naturalis vis inesse poterat Euro, integrâ nocte fortissimè flanti, ad dividendum mare rubrum, & aquas ex parte utraque cohibendas, ne diffluerent, sed ut utrinque instar muri consisterent, & Israëlitus ad transeundum sicco pede viam aperirent? Habent quidem venti, fortiter flantes, vim commovendi maria, illorum fluctus excitandi, terramq́; exiccandi: sed dividendi mare rubrum, cohibendi aquas à dextra & sinistra, ut nullis terminis alienis clausæ, utrinque instar muri immotæ consisterent, & populo Israëlitico toti tutum præberent transitum, nullâ vi naturali efficere potuerunt.


### What natural power could reside in the heat of the Prophet Elisha, lying upon…

What natural power could reside in the heat of the Prophet Elisha, lying upon the dead boy once and again until he grew warm, to resuscitate him from death to this temporal life? For heat, coming extrinsically to a dead body, cannot restore life as life consists essentially in the union of the soul with a body naturally fitted for vital actions, and therefore the soul is defined by Aristotle, II de Anim. t. IV, as being the act of an organic body having life in potentiality. However, when through death the soul is separated from the body, and the vital power in the whole body is destroyed, then neither by external heat, nor by any other natural agent, can the lost vital power be restored, or the separated soul be reunited with the body, but both are a gift and work of divine omnipotence. Nor is there any reason for someone to object that the boy was not dead, but had suffered a syncope, and still had life in him in the first act, just as the Author says he was believed to be dead, implying that he was not truly dead. For Scripture says expressly that he was dead, II Kings IV. 20, and likewise v. 32, and c. VIII. 5. What natural power, finally, could reside in clay, or in the waters of the pool of Siloam, to restore sight to one born blind, when Christ smeared clay, mixed with spittle, on the eyes of the blind man, and the blind man, at the command of Christ, washing his eyes in the waters of Siloam, recovered his sight? Since in all these natural things, employed to perform miracles, no natural power by which they were produced can be shown, what remains but that we say they were not employed out of the necessity of nature, and as natural causes of those things being performed, but by the most free will of God, both for other reasons known to Himself, and especially so that they might be sensible signs, which, perceived by the senses, would testify in the eyes of the Israelites and Egyptians to His singular presence and operation, which He was exerting through these very servants of His, Moses and Aaron, beyond the order of nature, and would remove from the Egyptians, who were especially demented by superstitious and Magicians' frauds and incantations, the opinion that these things happened by chance or were performed by Magical arts. To this also pertains the fact that at Pharaoh's request Moses never removed the plagues that had been sent, unless a time was first set by Pharaoh himself when they should be removed, so that even from this the Egyptians might understand that it was by the free will of God alone that they were both sent and removed or taken away.

But indeed we said above that such things or natural causes were not always and in all miracles performed employed, but that many miracles were also read of in the Scriptures as performed by word and bare command, or in response to the faith or prayers of men. Which the aforementioned Author acknowledges and objects to himself: But, he says, page 77, perhaps someone will insist that we, through to find many things in the Scriptures which seem in no way able to be explained by natural causes, such as that the sins of men and their prayers can be the cause of rain and the fertility of the earth, or that faith could heal the blind, and other things of this sort which are narrated in the Bible. He thinks, however, that he has already responded to these points when he showed that Scripture does not teach things through their proximate causes, but only narrates things in that order and with those phrases by which it can most move men, and especially the common people, to devotion, and for this reason speaks of God and of things very improperly, because, of course, it strives not to convince the reason, but to affect and occupy the fantasy and imagination of men. For if Scripture, he says further, were to narrate the devastation of some empire, as political historians are accustomed to do, that would move the common people not at all, but on the contrary it would move them greatly if it depicts everything poetically and refers it to God, which it is accustomed to do. When, therefore, Scripture narrates that the earth is sterile on account of the sins of men, or that the blind were healed by faith, those things ought not to move us any more than when it narrates that God, on account of the sins of men, becomes angry, is saddened, repents of a good promised and done, or that God, from the fact that He sees a sign, remembers a promise, and many other things which are either said poetically or related according to the opinion and prejudices of the writer. Wherefore we conclude here absolutely that all things which are truly narrated in Scripture to have happened, happened necessarily according to the laws of nature, as do all things, and if anything is found which can be demonstratively proven to be repugnant to the laws of nature, or could not have followed from them, it is to be clearly believed that it was added to the Sacred writings by sacrilegious men: for whatever is against nature is against reason, and what is against reason is absurd, and therefore also to be refuted.

But the Author falsely persuades himself that he has responded to the objection brought forward. For what he says, and opines to have been shown by himself, that Scripture does not teach things through their proximate causes, is true not simply, but in a certain sense: namely, if the sense is that it is not the function of Scripture to teach things through demonstrations deduced from their proximate causes, so that the ultimate reason for assenting to the causes of the conclusions refer to the proximate causes; we do not object. For this is the method customary in the philosophical sciences, since they do not move to assent except through first principles, which are immediate, prior by nature and better known, and which contain the proximate cause of the conclusion, as happens in demonstration a priori; or certainly through principles that are indeed certain and necessary, but at least better known to us, as happens in demonstration a posteriori, and concluding from effect to cause. However, it is appropriate for Holy Scripture in itself to recount things as they were revealed to the sacred writers by God, and to propose them to mortals to be believed on account of the authority of God who reveals them. But in the sense in which the Author understands it, the assertion is most false. The sense, however, which he intends is this: that Scripture, in recounting divine things and actions, does not assign their proximate and true causes, but narrates them according to the opinion, imagination, and persuasion of men, especially the common people, even if false, absurd, and contradictory, and consequently suppresses the causes of things, or if it does assign any, it does not assign the true ones, but only those from the opinion of the common people, so that it may affect their fantasy and imagination, occupy them, and move the common people to devotion. This sense is hinted at by the words immediately following: that it narrates things only in that order and with those phrases by which it can most move men, and especially the common people, to devotion; and the Author inculcates this in express words throughout the whole Treatise in almost all chapters and pages. As this assertion utterly overturns the truth and certainty of Holy Scripture, so at the very first hearing it is absurd, impious toward God, blasphemous, and injurious in the highest degree to the goodness and truthfulness of God, and is the source and fountainhead of all Fanatical opinions and of the Atheism that is growing stronger every day: so far is it from containing a true and solid response to the previous objection, that very many miracles can in no way be explained by natural causes.

This indeed is true, that when it is a matter of God, His attributes, decrees, and other immanent acts of both intellect and will, Holy Scripture accommodates itself to our capacity, and just as we know these things, not as they are in themselves and on the part of God, but through concepts taken from men and human affairs, because of the imperfection of our intellect; so in the same manner Scripture describes those things with words and phrases taken from men and human affairs, and proposes them to us to be known, which therefore concerning

Those applied to God must be freed from material conditions and imperfections, which they import in humans, so that with these removed, only the formal element, which consists in perfection simply without any admixture of imperfection, may be conceived to exist in God. But there is no question about this at present, but about divine miracles, the cause of which Scripture assigns to sins, or prayers, or the faith of men, or the bare command of Christ, e.g., when Scripture narrates that on account of the sins and idolatry of the Israelite people, the heaven was closed for three years and six months at the prayers of Elijah so that it would not rain, and that when the Baalite priests were killed and the wrath of God appeased, at his same prayers the heaven was opened so that it would rain again and the earth would bring forth its fruits, 1 Kings 17:1, 18:1, 41, James 5:17-18; that likewise Christ restored sight to the blind at their faith, Mark 10:52. Luke 19:42; that he raised Lazarus from the dead, John 11:43 ff., Jairus's daughter from the dead, Mark 5:41, the widow's son from the dead, Luke 7:14, by a word from death, etc. Of these, I say, and similar miracles the question here is, whether they can be explained by natural causes, i.e., whether it can be shown that they were not produced beyond the order of nature, but through natural causes, and thus are works of nature? Nor indeed is the question about any kind of causes, but only about the efficient cause. For that Christ, moved by his mercy as a προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause, and by the misery, faith, and prayers of men as προκαταρκτικαῖς or external impulsive causes, e.g., restored sight to the blind; and God, moved by his justice as a προηγουμένη or internal impulsive cause, and, e.g., by the iniquity of the Egyptians against his people, and the latter's most harsh servitude and prayers, as προκαταρκτικαῖς or external impulsive causes, sent so many plagues upon the Egyptians to bend their stubborn minds so that they would release the Israelites; this was nothing preternatural. For God, from the perfection of his nature, is both just and merciful, and likewise Christ; and it is connatural to both that they be moved by the impiety and crimes of men to take vengeance, and by the misery, faith, and prayers of the pious to mercy and their liberation from their calamities. The whole question therefore, as has been said, is about the efficient cause, namely, whether the mentioned and other similar miraculous effects, produced either on account of the sins of men or for the faith and prayers of the pious, were produced by God or by Christ beyond the order

Latin:

Quæ naturalis vis inesse poterat calori Elisæ Prophetæ, puero demortuo semelatq; iterum, donec incalesceret, incumbentis, ad resuscitandum eum ex morte in hanc temporalem vitam? Non enim calor, extrinsecùs adveniens corpori demortuo, vitam restituere potest. Nam vita consistit essentialiter in unione animæ cum corpore ad actiones vitales apto nato, & proptereà anima ab Aristotele II. de Anim. t. IV. definitur, quòd sit actus corporis organici, potentiâ vitam habentis. Quando autem per mortem anima à corpore separata, & potentia vitalis in corpore toto destructa est, tùm nec per calorem externum, nec per ullum aliud agens naturale vel potentia vitalis deperdita restaurari, vel anima separata cum corpore rursum uniri potest, sed utrumque divinæ omnipotentiæ munus & opus est. Neque est, quod quis obtendat, puerum non fuisse mortuum, sed syncopen passum, vitam adhuc in actu primo in se habuisse, sicut Auctor dicit, eum creditum fuisse mortuum, subinnuens, verè mortuum non fuisse. Nam Scriptura dicit expressè, eum fuisse mortuum, II. Reg. IV. 20. itemq; v. 32. & c. VIII. 5. Quæ deniq; naturalis vis inesse poterat luto, aut aquis piscinæ Siloæ, ad restituendum cæco nato visum, quando oculis cæci Christus lutum, sputo mixtum, illevit, & cæcus, jussu Christi, aquis Siloæ oculos abluens, visum recuperavit? Cùm in his omnibus rebus naturalibus, ad patranda miracula adhibitis, nulla naturalis vis, quâ producta sint, ostendi possit, quid superest, quàm ut dicamus, eas non esse adhibitas ex necessitate naturæ, & ut illorum patrandorum causas naturales, sed Dei liberrimâ voluntate, cùm aliis, sibi notis, de causis, tùm imprimis, ut essent sensibilia signa, quæ sensibus percepta, de ejus singulari præsentia & operatione, quam per hos ipsos servos suos, Mosen & Aaronem, præter naturæ ordinem, exerebat, in Israëlitarum & Ægyptiorum oculis testarentur, & superstitiosis præcipuè Magorumq; fraudibus & incantationibus dementatis Ægyptiis opinionem, ea casu evenire, aut artibus Magicis patrari, eximerent. Quò pertinet etiam, quòd Pharaonis rogatu Moses nunquam plagas immissas removit, nisi constituto prius per ipsummet Pharaonem tempore, quando removeri deberent, ut vel hinc etiam intelligerent Ægyptii, solius Dei liberâ voluntate eas & immitti & remitti sive auferri.

At verò diximus suprà, non perpetuò & in omnibus miraculis patrandis hujusmodi sive res sive causas naturales fuisse adhibitas, sed patrata etiam in Scripturis legi miracula multa, verbo & imperio nudo, vel ad fidem aut preces hominum. Quod d. l. Auctor agnoscit & sibi ipsi objicit: At, inquiens, pag. 77. forsan instabit aliquis, nos per plura in Scripturis reperire, quæ nullo modo per causas naturales videntur posse explicari, ut quòd peccata hominum, eorumque precationes possunt esse pluviæ terræque fertilitatis causa, aut quod fides cæcos sanare potuit, & alia adhunc modum, quæ in Bibliis narrantur. Putat autem, se ad hæc jam respondisse, quando ostenderit, Scripturam res non docere per proximas suas causas; sed tantùm res eo ordine, iisque phrasibus narrare, quibus maximè homines, & præcipuè plebem ad devotionem movere potest, & hac de causa de Deo & de rebus admodùm impropriè loqui, quia nimirum non rationem convincere, sed hominum phantasiam & imaginationem afficere, & occupare studeat. Si enim Scriptura, ait porrò, vastationem alicujus imperii, ut historici politici solent, narraret, id plebem nihil commoveret, at contra maximè, si omnia poëtice depingat, & ad Deum referat, quod facere solet. Cum itaque Scriptura narrat, terram propter hominum peccata sterilem esse, aut quòd cæci ex fide sanabantur, ea nos non magis movere debent, quàm cùm narrat, Deum propter hominum peccata irasci, contristari, pœnitere boni promissi & facti, aut quòd Deus ex eo, quod signum videt, promissi recordetur, & alia plurima, quæ vel poëtice dicta sunt, vel secundum Scriptoris opinionem & præjudicia relata. Quare hic absolutè concludimus, omnia quæ in Scriptura verè narrantur contigisse, ea secundum leges naturæ, ut omnia, necessariò contigisse, & si quid reperiatur, quod apodicticè demonstrari potest, legibus naturæ repugnare, aut ex iis consequi non potuisse, planè credendum id à sacrilegis hominibus Sacris literis adjectum fuisse: quicquid enim contra naturam est, id contra rationem est, & quod contra rationem, id absurdum est, ac proinde etiam refutandum.

Verùm Auctor falso sibi persuasum habet, se ad objectionem allatam respondisse. Quod enim dicit, & à se ostensum esse opinatur, Scripturam res non docere per proximas suas causas; non simpliciter, sed certo sensu verum est: nempe si sensus sit, Scripturæ munus non esse, per demonstrationes, ex suis causis proximis deductas, res docere, ita ut rationem assentiendi ultimam in causas conclusionum proximas referat; non repugnamus. Hæc enim scientiis Philosophicis consueta methodus est, quippe quæ ad assensum non movent, nisi per principia prima, immediata, naturâ priora & notiora, & quæ continent causam conclusionis proximam, ut fit in demonstratione à priori; vel certè per principia, certa quidem & necessaria, sed nobis saltem notiora, ut fit in demonstratione à posterio i,& ex effectu ad causam concludente. Scripturæ sacræ autem per se convenit res, prout Scriptoribus sacris à Deo revelatæ sunt, commemorare, easq; propter auctoritatem Dei revelantis mortalibus credendas proponere. Eo autem sensu, quo Auctor intelligit, assertio falsissima est. Sensus autem, quem intendit, hic est: Scripturam in commemorandis rebus & actionibus divinis non assignare illarum causas proximas & veras, sed narrare eas ex hominum, vulgi præsertim, opinione, imaginatione & persuasione, licet falsâ, absurdâ, contradictoriâ, & subticere proinde rerum causas, vel si quas assignet, non assignare veras, sed tantum ex opinione vulgi, ut ejus phantasiam & imaginationem afficiat, occupet & ad devotionem plebem moveat. Quem sensum & verba proximè subsequentia: quòd tantum res eo ordine iisq; phrasibus, narret, quibus maximè homines, & præcipuè plebem ad devotionem movere potest; innuunt, & Auctor per Tractatum totum in omnibus ferè capitibus & paginis verbis expressis inculcat.
