Quæ assertio ut Scripturæ sacræ veritatem & certitudinem funditus evertit, ita primo statim auditu absurda, impia in Deum, blasphema, & in Dei bonitatem ac veracitatem summam injuriosa, omniumq; Fanaticarum opinionum & totius indies invalescentis Atheismi fons & scaturigo est: tantum abeft, ut ad objectionem superiorem, quòd miracula perplura nullo modo per causas naturales explicari possint; veram & solidam responsionem contineant.

Hoc quidem verum est, quòd cùm de Deo, ejus attributis, decretis, aliisq; cùm intellectus tùm voluntatis actibus immanentibus agitur, Scriptura sacra ad nostrum captum se accommodet, & quemadmodum nos ea, non ut in se & ex parte Dei sunt, sed per conceptus, ab hominibus rebusque humanis desumtos, cognoscimus, propter imperfectionem nostri intellectus; ita eundem in modum Scriptura verbis & phrasibus, ab hominibus rebusq; humanis desumtis ea describat, nobisq; cognoscenda proponat, quæ proinde de

Deo adhibitæ à materialibus conditionibus & imperfectionibus, quas in hominibus important, liberandæ sunt, ut iis remotis solum formale, quod in perfectione simpliciter absque ulla admixta imperfectione consistit, Deo inesse concipiatur. Sed de hoc nulla impræsentiarum quæstio est, sed de divinis miraculis, quorum causam Scriptura peccata, vel preces, vel fidem hominum vel nudum Christi imperium assignat, v. g. quando Scriptura narrat, quòd propter peccata & idololatriam populi Israëlitici cœlum, ne plueret, ad Eliæ preces tribus annis & sex mensibus clausum, & quòd occisis Sacerdotibus Baaliticis, irâque Dei placatâ, ad ejusdem preces cœlum, ut rursum plueret, & terra fructus suos proferret, apertum fuerit 1. Reg. XVII. 1. c. XVIII. 1. 41. Jacob. V. 17. 18. quòd item cæcis ad illorum fidem Christus verbo visum restituerit, Marc. X. 52. Luc. XIX. 42. quòd Lazarum mortuum Joh. XI. 43. seq. Jairi filiam mortuam, Marc. V. 41. Viduæ filium mortuum Luc. VII. 14. verbo ex morte resuscitaverit &c. De his, inquam, & similibus miraculis quæstio hîc est, an per causas naturales explicari possint, h. e. an ostendi possit, quòd non præter ordinem naturæ, sed per causas naturales producta, atque adeò naturæ opera sint? Neque verò de quovis causarum genere quæstio est, sed tantùm de causa efficiente. Quòd enim Christus suâ misericordiâ, velut causâ προηγουμένη sive impulsivá internâ, & hominum miseriâ, fide ac precibus, velut causis προκαταρκτικαῖς sive impulsivis externis motus v. g. cæcis visum restituit; & Deus suâ justitiâ, velut causâ προηγουμένῃ sive impulsivá internâ, & v. g. Ægyptiorum iniquitate in suum populum, hujusque durissimâ servitute ac precibus, velut causis προκαταρκτικαῖς sive impulsivis externis commotus, tot plagas immisit Ægyptiis ad flectendos illorum contumaces animos, ut dimitterent Israëlitas; non erat præternaturale quid. Deus enim ex perfectione naturæ suæ & justus est & misericors, & similiter Christus; & utrique connaturale est, ut hominum impietate & sceleribus ad sumendam vindictam; piorum miseriâ verò, fide & precibus ad misericordiam, & illorum liberationem ex suis calamitatibus commoveatur. Quæstio tota igitur, uti dictum, est de causa efficiente, an scilicet commemorati & alii similes effectus miraculosi, vel propter hominum peccata, vel ad piorum fidem & preces producti, à Deo vel à Christo præter ordi-


### of the whole of created nature

of the whole of created nature; or whether, in truth, they were efficiently produced through natural and secondary causes, so that just like other natural effects, which God as the primary cause produces efficiently along with secondary causes, they may be called works of nature?

The Author, therefore, when he descends to the affirmative side, either knows some of those natural causes by whose natural powers Christ, for example, restored sight to the blind, strengthened the feet and ankles of the lame and made them walk, raised the dead, etc., or he knows none. If he knows some, why does he not indicate them, and explain to us what their natural powers were for producing these effects? If he knows none, why does he so rashly deny that they were produced beyond the order of the whole of created nature, and so boldly affirm that they are works of nature?

But the Author, in the aforementioned place, objects: I. That Scripture does not always narrate the circumstances of miracles, nor all their natural causes, yet miracles did not occur without them, which is evident from Exodus 14:27, where it is only narrated that the sea swelled again at the mere nod of Moses, and no mention of wind is made; and yet in the Canticle, chapter 15:10, it is said that this happened because God blew with His wind (that is, a very strong wind), wherefore this circumstance is omitted, and the miracle appears greater for that reason. II. Although he himself cannot indicate the natural causes of the aforementioned miracles, since Holy Scripture has not indicated them, he is nevertheless certain that their natural causes exist, since nothing can happen beyond or against nature, or without natural causes. Which he opines has been shown and proven by him.

But in truth, as regards the first exception, that Holy Scripture does not always narrate all the circumstances of miracles, we readily grant this, and it is not poorly gathered, among other things, from the cited chapter 14:27 of Exodus: where no mention is made of the wind blowing most strongly as the waters of the Red Sea returned to their original force and place, of which, however, Moses made express mention in his Canticle in the following chapter 15:10. But at present the question is not about the circumstances of miracles, whether all are narrated everywhere in Scripture, but about their causes, whether they are from God alone beyond the order of nature, or whether they were produced efficiently by nature and through natural causes, and were works of nature? Where, in order to assert the latter part of the question, it should not be said that Scripture does not always recount all the natural causes of miracles, but it had to be proven that natural causes for them are given. As regards the wind, by the blowing of which the waters of the Red Sea were both divided and returned to their original place, the Author has not yet proven that it was the natural cause of the waters being either divided or returned to their place. From the Mosaic history, certainly, neither of these can be proven, but rather the opposite of both. The historical description of this miracle is not contained in Exodus ch. XV, where the magnitude of the miracle is celebrated at least by a Canticle composed and sung in praise of God; but in ch. XIV, where in v. 16 et seqq. the very causes of the miracle are recounted. And indeed in v. 16 these words of God to Moses are read: And you (Moses) lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea, וּבְקָעֵהוּ and cleave (cut into two parts) it, and let the children of Israel enter into the midst of the sea on dry land, or dry ground. Which contain two things. One, the division of the sea into parts, which is, if I may so speak, the very substance of the miracle; the other, the drying up of the bed of the sea, so that the Israelites could cross on dry foot, which is a certain circumstance or a certain consequence of it. The division of the sea, and thus the miracle itself, God does not ascribe to the wind, but to Moses, lifting his rod with his hand extended over the sea: You, Moses, lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea, and cleave or divide it. To the wind, however, only the drying up of the sea bed seems to be ascribed, of which mention is finally made in the following v. 21 in the description of the execution, in these words: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord caused the sea to go back, by an east wind all the night (blowing) and made the sea into dry ground. Where again the division of the sea is ascribed to Moses, stretching his rod over the sea, and to God, causing the waters to go back at the rod of Moses extended; but to the wind, blowing all night, that it dried up the bed of the sea, which is described for that reason, that it was an east wind, by nature hot and dry, and that a violent one, which the more violently it blows, the more strongly it exerts its power of drying. Similarly, when the waters were to be brought back to their original place to submerge the Egyptians, God said to Moses in ch. XIV. 26: Stretch out your hand over the sea, and the waters shall return upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen; and likewise in the description of the execution it is said, v. 27: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned &c. Where also the return of the waters to their former place is ascribed to Moses, lifting his rod over the sea, and to God, bringing back the waters upon that which was lifted over it, as if to a cause. But the wind, of which it is said in the Song of Moses v. 10, that, it blowing, the sea covered the Egyptians, seems to have been employed not so much to bring back the waters, as to terrify the Egyptians, and to delay them, lest they might escape the danger by haste, and to cast them down into the sea, of which it is said in chap. XIV. v. 24, that God overthrew the wheels of the chariots of the Egyptians, and cast down their horsemen, that he led them into heaviness, i.e., caused them to walk heavily &c. although there are not wanting those who in the Song of Moses c. XV. 10. of Exodus by the little word רוח wish to be understood not wind, but the impulse of God, by which the waters were cast down, which stood motionless like walls on each side. Rivet, Comm. on Exod. c. XV. 10, does not poorly on this matter. Whether, he says, wind is taken for the command of God, by which it was brought about that the waters fell from the embankments on which they stood, as if frozen, taking spirit for impulse or incitement; or the spirit or breath of God is taken for a stormy wind excited, by which the return of the waters was made faster and more savage, it will be the same; and both are true. For that this was done by divine impulse, when before the waters had stood still by the power of God, is clear in itself: Then it is likely that God, with lightnings, thunder, and storms, also excited a strong wind, so that the waves might overwhelm the Egyptians &c. Whatever the case may be, this is certain, that the blowing wind was not the natural cause either of the divided waters of the Red Sea, so that they stood motionless like walls on the right and left of the passing Israelites, or of the same being returned to their place to drown the Egyptians, but that both were done by the rod and hand of Moses, stretched out over the sea, by the absolute power of God, beyond the order of all created nature, the Scripture asserting this in express words. I return to where I digressed.

Furthermore, what the Author contends in the second exception, that it has been shown and proven by him that nothing happens or can happen beyond nature, is begging the question. For so far is he from having proven this, that rather, while he labored in proving it, he has done nothing but deal in trifles and sold to the unwary reader mere trifles, which we have discussed at length above. Although indeed Holy Scripture does not teach the aforementioned matter in the manner of its proximate causes through demonstrations deduced from them, nevertheless, just as it commemorates miracles in a historical style, as it does other things, so it is accustomed not to pass over their proximate causes and principal circumstances entirely, but to note them in the same style, e.g., when in John 9:6 ff. Scripture describes the miracle of Christ, by which He restored sight to the man born blind, it then notes the efficient cause, both principal and instrumental, and both of them proximate. For after the occasion has been mentioned, that Christ, passing by, saw the man blind from his mother's womb, and the question concerning the cause of why he was born blind, raised by the disciples on this occasion, and Christ's response subjected to it; the Apostle proceeds to the description of the miracle itself, and first of all describes the efficient causes: the principal one, indeed, Christ, who spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle (mixed with earth), and smeared the clay on the eyes of the blind man; the instrumental ones, however, the clay smeared on the eyes, and the waters of the pool of Siloam, with which the blind man washed his eyes at Christ's command. Scripture thus commemorates these proximate causes of that miracle in a historical style. But by what power did Christ restore sight to the blind man through these means? Was it by some natural art of healing? Or by His own divine power? Likewise, what did the clay and what did the water of the pool of Siloam contribute to this effect? whether some natural force belonged to either or both for repairing sight to the man born blind? Holy Scripture does not teach this, but leaves it to Theology to investigate and declare. Theology, however, having pondered the matter more deeply, and having considered that in the visual organ of the man born blind there is no natural power to receive sight—for this was lacking in the mother's womb itself, when the body was being formed, through an error or defect of nature, and cannot be repaired except by the Author of nature, God—infers from this that sight was not restored to the blind man by Christ through the clay and the waters of Siloam as connatural means by medical art and natural power: for there was not in either or both means any natural force by which, when applied to the eyes of the blind man through medical art, the power to receive sight could be repaired and sight restored. It concludes, therefore, that in the clay and the water of Siloam there was only an obediential power to restore sight to the man born blind, which was brought about by no natural agent, but by the absolute power of God alone and of Christ the God-man, beyond the order of the whole created nature, with that elevating it to produce this effect, could be transferred into act. And these are the proximate causes of this miracle, which Scripture did not pass over in silence, but expressed: nor did it note any others, not because it is not its place to record historically the proximate causes of things, but because there were no others. Thus when Mark ch. X. 46. seqq. & Luke ch. XIIX. 35. & seq. describe the miracle of Christ, performed in two other blind men at their own prayers and faith, they report, after noting the circumstances of place and time, Mark indeed v. 52. that sight was restored to the blind Bartimaeus who was asking by the VOICE OF CHRIST: GO, your faith has made you whole; Luke however v. 42. that it was restored to the other blind man who was asking by the VOICE of the same, saying: Ἀνάβλεψον, which Erasmus rendered: RECEIVE SIGHT; your faith has made you whole. Which again contain all the proximate causes of both miracles: namely CHRIST and his VOICE and the PRAYERS and FAITH of both blind men. But what the relation and force of each was for restoring sight to both, Scripture again does not explain, but leaves it to be explained by Theology. This, however, having weighed the matter more deeply, teaches that the PRAYERS and FAITH of both blind men did not stand in relation to Christ as physically efficient causes, but as external motive or impulsive causes, in consideration of which Christ took pity on them, and allowed himself to be moved to restore sight to them. The proximate efficient causes therefore were CHRIST, and his VOICE: the former principal, the latter instrumental. But because in the voice of Christ there was no natural power to restore sight to the blind, it remains that we say it was an instrumental obediential cause, which could not be brought into act by any power of created nature, but only by the divine power of Christ, exerting itself through it beyond the order of the whole created nature. And these are the proximate causes of these miracles also, which Scripture by no means passed over in silence, but expressed in sufficiently clear words. But it did not note other causes, not because it was not its place to describe miracles through their proximate causes, but because there were no other causes of them. Let the same judgment be held concerning other miracles of this kind and order.

But as for what the Author feigns, that these were not the true causes of the miracles, but fictitious ones, and falsely assigned from the opinion of the common people to exaggerate the miracles in his eyes and ears, is that greater impiety? or should one argue for greater stupidity in him? I truly do not know. For to say that Holy Scripture, in its narration of the miracles adduced, has not assigned the true causes, but those which were falsely held to be their causes out of the opinion of the common people and their erroneous imagination, in order to exaggerate the magnitude of the miracles and to move the common people to devotion, is to accuse Scripture and its author, God, of lying and deceit: which is impious. To reject the causes assigned in Holy Scripture in such clear words as fictitious and false, while being able to indicate no other true ones to which the miracles owed their origin, is stupid. And so much also for miracles, the third external sign of credibility.

Latin:

nem totius naturæ creatæ; an verò per causas naturales & secundas efficienter producti sint, ut perinde ac alii naturales effectus, quos Deus velut causa prima cum causis secundis efficienter producit, naturæ opera dici possint?

Auctor igitur, quando in affirmativam partem descendit, vel novit aliquas illorum causas naturales, quarum naturalibus viribus Christus v. g. cæcis visum restituerit, claudorum plantas ac talos consolidaverit & ambulare fecerit, mortuos resus citaverit &c. aut nullas novit. Si aliquas novit, quare eas non indicat, & quænam illarum vires naturales ad producendos hosce effectus fuerint, nobis exponit? Si nullas novit, quare præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ productos ita temerè negat, & naturæ opera esse, tam audacter affirmat?

Sed Auctor d. l. excipit, I. circumstantias miraculorum, eorumque causas naturales Scripturam non semper, neque omnes enarrare, miracula tamen non sine iisdem contigisse, quod constet ex Exod. XIV. vers. 27. ubi tantùm narretur, quod ex solo nutu Mosis mare iterum intumuerit, nec ulla venti mentio fiat; & tamen in Cantico cap. XV. v. 10. dicatur, id contigisse ex eo, quod Deus vento suo (id est, vento fortissimo) flaverit, quare hanc circumstantiam omitti, & miraculum ea de causa majus videri. II. Quamvis prædictorum miraculorũ causas naturales indicare ipse non possit: cùm Scriptura sacra eas non indicaverit; se tamen certum esse, quòd illorum causæ naturales dentur: cùm nihil præter aut contra naturam, vel absque causis naturalibus fieri possit. Quod à se ostensum & evictum esse opinatur.

Verum enim verò, quod ad primam attinet exceptionem, Scripturam sacram non semper omnes miraculorum circumstantias enarrare, facilè largimur, idque inter alia non malè colligitur ex allegato cap. XIV. v. 27. Exodi: ubi venti, aquis maris rubri ad suum pristinum vigorem & locum redeuntibus, fortissimè flantis nulla fit mentio, cujus tamen sequente c. XV. v. 10. Moses in Cantico suo expressam mentionem fecit. Sed impræsentiarum quæstio non est de circumstantiis miraculorum, an ubiq; omnes in Scriptura enarrentur, sed de illorum causis, an à Deo solo præter naturæ ordinem, an verò à natura & per causas naturales efficienter producta, & naturæ opera fuerint? Ubi posteriorem quæstionis partem asserturo, non dicendum; Scripturam non enarrare semper omnes miraculorum causas naturales, sed dari illorum causas naturales probandum erat. Ventum quod attinet, quo flante aquæ maris rubri & divisæ & in locum pristinum reversæ sunt, Auctor nondum evicit, eum vel divisarum, vel in locum suum reversarum aquarum causam naturalem fuisse. Ex historia Mosaica certè hujus neutrum, sed utriusq; potiùs oppositum probari potest. Historica verò hujus miraculi descriptio non continetur Exodi c. XV. ubi saltem Cantico in laudem Dei composito & decantato miraculi magnitudo celebratur; sed c. XIV. ubi v. 16. seqq. ipsæ causæ miraculi enarrantur. Et quidem v. 16. leguntur hæc verba Dei ad Mosen: Et tu (Moses) eleva virgam tuam, & extende manum tuam super mare, וּבְקָעֵהוּ & finde, (seca in duas partes) illud, & ingrediantur filii Israël in medium maris per aridam, sive siccum. Quæ duo continent. Unum, divisionem maris in partes, quæ ipsa, ut ita loquar, substantia miraculi est; alterum exiccationem alvei maris, ut sicco pede Israëlitæ transire possent, quæ ejus quædam circumstantia vel consequens quoddam est. Divisionem maris, atque adeò miraculum ipsum Deus non adscribit vento, sed Mosi, virgam suam manu extensâ super mare elevanti: Tu, Moses, eleva virgam tuam, & extende manum tuam super mare, & finde sive divide illud. Vento autem sola alvei maris exiccatio adscribenda videtur, cujus seq. v. 21, demum in descriptione executionis mentio injicitur, his verbis: Et extendit Moses manum suam super mare, & abire fecit Dominus mare, vento orientali tota nocte (flante) & posuit mare in siccum. Ubi rursus divisio maris Mosi, virgam suam super mare extendenti, & Deo, ad virgam Mosis extensam aquas abire facienti, adscribitur; vento autem, totâ nocte flanti, quòd alveum maris exiccaverit, qui proptereà describitur, quòd ventus orientalis fuerit, naturâ calidus & siccus, isq; vehemens, qui quò vehementiùs flat, eò fortiùs suam vim exiccandi exerit. Similiter cùm aquæ ad submergendos Ægyptios in suum locum pristinum reducendæ essent, dixit Deus ad Mosen c. XIV. 26. Extende manum tuam super mare, & revertentur aquæ super Ægyptios, super currus illorum, & super equites illorum; itemque in descriptione executionis dicitur v. 27. Et extendit Moses manum suam super mare, & reversum est mare &c. Ubi etiam reversio aquarum in locum pristinum Mosi, virgam suam super mare elevanti, & Deo, ad virgam super illud elevatam aquas reducenti velut causæ adscribitur. Ventus autem, de quo in Cantico Mosis v. 10. dicitur, quòd, eo flante, mare Ægyptios operuerit, non tam ad reducandas aquas, quàm ad terrendos Ægyptios, & ad eos remorandos, ne festinatione periculum evadere possent, & ad eosdē in mari dejiciendos adhibitus fuisse videtur, de quo cap. XIV. v. 24. dicitur, quòd subverterit Deus rotas curruum Ægyptiorum, & dejecerit equites illorum, quòd duxerit eos in gravitatem, h. e. effecerit, ut graviter incederent &c. quanquam non desunt, qui in Cantico Mosis c. XV. 10. Exodi per voculam רוח non ventum, sed impetum Dei, quo dejectæ sint aquæ, quæ ex utraq; parte instar murorum immotæ consistebant, intellectum velint. Non malè hanc in rem Rivetus Comm. in Exod. c. XV. 10. Sive, inquit, ventus accipiatur pro jussu Dei, quo factum est, ut deciderent ex aggeribus, quibus subsistebant, velut congelatæ aquæ, sumpto spiritu pro impetu, sive incitatione; sive spiritus aut flatus Dei accipiatur pro excitato procelloso vento, quo recursus aquarum celerior & sævior factus est, perinde erit; & utrumque verum est. Id enim factum fuisse impulsione divinâ, quum anteà Dei potentiâ substitissent aquæ, per se liquet: Deinde verisimile est, Deum cum fulminibus, tonitru & procellis ventum quoque validū excitasse, ut fluctus obruerent Ægyptios &c. Quicquid tandem sit, hoc certum est, ventum flantem non fuisse caufam naturalem vel divisarum aquarum maris rubri; ut à dextra & sinistra transeuntium Israë̈litarum instar murorum immotæ consisterent, vel earundem, ad submergendos Ægyptios, in suum locum reducendarum, sed utrumq; ad virgam & manum Mosis, super mare extensam, Dei potentiâ absolutâ, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ per actum fuisse, disertis verbis id asserente Scripturâ. Eò unde digressus sum, revertor.

Quod porrò in exceptione altera contendit Auctor, à se ostensum & evictum esse, quòd nihil præter naturam fiat aut fieri possit, eo petit τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Tantum enim abest, ut hoc evicerit, ut potius, dum in eo evincendo desudavit, meras egerit lectoriq; incauto vendiderit nugas, quas supra prolixe excussimus. Quamvis vero Scripturae sacrae no fit res praedictum in modum per suas causas proximas docere per demonstrationes, ex illis deductas, tamen quemadmodum ipsa stylo historico, ut res caeteras, sic & miracula commemorat, ita illorum causas proximas & circumstantias praecipuas non plane praeterire, sed stylo eodem annotare consuevit, v. g. quando Joh. IX. 6. seq. Scriptura miraculum Christi, quo caeco nato restituit visum, describit, tum annotat causam efficientem tam principalem quam instrumentale, & utramq; proximam. Post commemoratam enim occasionem, quod Christus praeteriens hominem inde ab utero matris caecum viderit, & quaestionem de causa, cur caecus is natus esset, a discipulis hac occasione motam, Christique responsionem subjectam; pergit Apostolus ad ipsius miraculi descriptionem, & primo omnium describit causas efficientes, principalem quidem, Christum, qui expuerit in terram, fecerit lutum ex sputo (cum terra mixto) illeveritq; lutum oculis caeci; instrumentales vero lutum, oculis illitum, & aquas piscine Siloe, quibus Christi jussu caecus oculos abluit. Hasce istius miraculi causas proximas commemorat Scriptura sic stylo historico. Qua autem virtute Christus per haec media visum caeco restituerit, an quadam arte medendi naturali? an sua potentia divina? quid item lutum, quid aqua piscinae Siloe ad effectum hunc contulerint? an alterutri vel utrique vis quaedam naturalis convenerit ad reparandum caeco nato visum? Scriptura sacra non docet, sed Theologiae investigandum & declarandum relinquit. Haec vero, re penitius perpensa, consideratoq;, quod organo visorio in caeco nato nulla infit naturalis potentia ad recipiendum visum: haec enim in ipso utero materno, cum corpus formaretur, per errorem sive defectum naturae defuit, neq;, nisi per naturae Auctorem, Deum, reparari potest; infert hinc, visum non fuisse arte medica & virtute naturali per lutum & aquas Siloe, tanquam media connaturalia, caeco a Christo restitutum: neque enim in alterutro vel utroq; medio ullam fuisse vim naturalem, qua per artem Medicam oculis caeci applicata potentia ad recipiendum visum reparari visusq; restitui potuerit. Concludit ergo, in luto & aqua Siloe tantum fuisse potentiam obedientialem ad restituendum caeco nato visum, quae a nullo agente naturali, sed solius Dei Christiq; θεανθρώπου potentia absoluta, praeter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, ea ad producendum hunc effectum elevante, in actum transferri potuit. Atque hæ sunt causæ hujus miraculi proximæ, quas non subticuit, sed expressit Scriptura : neque alias ullas annotavit, non quòd ejus non sit, causas rerum proximas historicè commemorare, sed quòd aliæ nullæ fuerint. Sic cùm Marcus c. X. 46. seqq. & Lucas c. XIIX. 35. & seq. Christi miraculum, in aliis duobus cæcis ad ipsorum preces & fidem editum, describunt, referunt, post annotatas loci ac temporis circumstantias, Marcus quidem v. 52. quòd Bartimæo cæco petenti visus restitutus sit VOCE CHRISTI: ABI, fides tua te salvum fecit; LUCAS verò v. 42. quòd cæco alteri petenti ab eodem restitutus sit VOCE ejusdem, dicentis: Ἀνάβλεψον, quod reddidit Erasmus: VISUM RECIPITO; fides tua te salvum fecit. Quæ rursum causas miraculi utriusque proximas omnes continent : CHRISTUM scilicet ejusq́; VOCEM & cæci utriusque PRECES ac FIDEM. Quæ autem cujusque habitudo & vis fuerit ad reparandum utrique visum, Scriptura rursum non explicat, sed Theologiæ explicandum relinquit. Hæc verò, re penitiùs perpensâ, docet, quòd PRECES & FIDES cæci utriusque ad impetrandum à Christo visum se non habuerint ex parte Christi, ut causæ efficientes physice, sed ut causæ motivæ sive impulsivæ externæ, quarum intuitu Christus illorum misertus, & ad visum ipsis restituendum se moveri passus sit. Causæ efficientes igitur proximæ fuerunt CHRISTUS, ejusq́; VOX: ille principalis; hæc instrumentalis. Quia autem in voce Christi nulla erat vis naturalis, ad restituendum cæcis visum, superest, ut dicamus, eam fuisse causam instrumentalem obedientialem, quæ à nulla vi naturæ creatæ, sed solâ Christi divinâ potentiâ, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ per illam sese exerente, in actum traduci potuerit. Atq; hæ sunt horum etiam miraculorum causæ proximæ, quas Scriptura minimè subticuit, sed verbis satis perspicuis expressit. Alias verò ipsa non annotavit, non quòd ejus non fuerit miracula per suas causas proximas describere, sed quòd illorum aliæ causæ non fuerint. Idem esto judicium de cæteris hujus generis & ordinis miraculis.

Quod autem Auctor fingit, hæc non fuisse veras miraculorum causas, sed fictas, & ex opinione vulgi, ad exaggeranda in ejus oculis & auribus miracula falsò assignatas, id majoremne impietatem? an stoliditatem majorem in eo arguat? equidem nescio. Dicere enim, Scriptura sacra in narratione adductorum miraculorum non veras assignasse causas, sed quæ falso ex opinione vulgi & erronea ejus imaginatione pro illorum causis habitæ sint, ad exaggerandam miraculorum magnitudinem, & plebem ad devotionem movendam, est Scripturam ejusq; auctorem Deum mendacii doliq; in simulare: quod impium est. Rejicere causas, in Scriptura sacra verbis ita perspicuis assignatas, tanquam fictas & falsas; alias veras autem, quibus natales suos miracula debuerint: nullas indicare posse, stolidum est. Et tantum etiam de miraculis, signo credibilitatis externo tertio.


### IV. We assign the fourth place to the Church, diffused throughout the whole world,…

IV.

We assign the fourth place to the Church, diffused throughout the whole world, by the concordant and consenting testimony from everywhere, ever since the times of the Apostles.

I. The Church diffused throughout the whole world has received the Holy Scriptures with wonderful consensus as divine and recorded by divine inspiration, the authority of which is the greater because it contains within its scope the very flower of the human race and whatever men learned and cultivated in disciplines and morals are or have been under heaven, among whom those first believers deserve the primary place, who received the autographs of the Scriptures from the hands of their authors, so that they could not be ignorant of which books were composed, and by which writers, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it credible that such an innumerable multitude of believers dispersed throughout the whole world conspired, or could have conspired, in any lie, so as to testify with such consensus that the sacred books were written under God's inspiration, if each writer had composed the ones he produced by his own judgment and human effort.

II. But here also those who have come forth from the school of Descartes, the Fanatics, have their reasons for doubting, by which they go about undermining the consenting testimony given by the Church concerning the authority of Scripture; among whom not the least is Edward, Baron Herbert of Cherbury, who as an Anonymous author, with whom we had to deal in defending the immediately preceding motive, held up a torch for impugning the divine authority of Holy Scripture and for encrusting various commentaries tending toward that end, in a double Appendix added at the end of his Treatise on the Causes of Errors, was industrious in this matter. In the former Appendix, immediately at the beginning: Clearly, he says, it is evident that, according to the variety of the age and region, there exist at present, and formerly existed, Faiths or Religions, none of which the Lawgivers have not asserted to be, as it were, handed down from heaven; so that a traveler finds this one in Europe, that one in Africa and Asia, and yet another in the Indies themselves; for my part, I would scarcely prefer arguments derived from one's native soil anywhere. For Asia boasts of its own excellent Philosophers, Apostles, and Doctors; Africa of its most acute minds and supreme Theologians; India of its Gymnosophists, Brahmins, Baxiamos, and Bongos; and finally, Europe of its own Princes and Leaders. So much so that the Prelates have contended that the true worship of God, a visible Hierarchy, austerity of life, and the compendium to eternal Blessedness exist among them alone. In the second Appendix, among other doubtful questions, he proposes this one in the fourth place: Whether those things which, by the Authority of the Holy Books (as they are called) received in any age or region, were accustomed to be added to these (the five articles known by nature mentioned in the preceding question II), are not in their origin suspect, involved, and controversial, and indeed rejected in their entirety by those groups to whom other Faiths were pleasing, as being supported by no necessary Demonstration? And he adds: For although it is an undoubted Axiom that the supreme God is most truthful, and can neither deceive nor be deceived, yet by what means will different Legislators or Priests in different parts of the world mutually prove 1. That the supreme God spoke with His own mouth, or (according to some) by the mouth of an Angel or some inferior Deity. 2. Or that that discourse was preserved in their memory, and subsequently faithfully recited to others. 3. Or that true copies of that discourse were consigned to posterity, so that nothing was added, taken away, or changed for subsequent ages through the fault or carelessness of the scribes. 4. That that particular discourse, made to a particular Legislator or Priest, not only pertains to all other Legislators or Priests, but also binds the Laity themselves everywhere in such a way that they can be impelled thereby to accept new and hitherto unknown Laws, or new dogmas of faith; especially where they would be forced for that reason to fail or depart from the principles of Right reason, etc.

What has been brought forward from the previous Appendix comes down to this at last: Since there are many different Faiths or Religions described in different sacred Codices, and any group bears witness to the divinity of its own Codex, in which its own faith and religion is contained, there can be no greater authority for the testimony of one group than for that of the others. To this point the Author's words tend: Indeed, I would scarcely prefer arguments derived from one's native soil (that is, from the authority and testimony of any Nation concerning its own sacred Codex) anywhere. Those things which we have produced from the second Appendix aim at the same mark. For when, at the beginning, he asks whether those things which are usually added to these by the authority of the Holy Codices (as they are called), received in any age or region, are not in their origin suspect, involved, and controversial, etc. He holds Holy Scripture in an equal place and condition with the Codices of all other Nations and Sects, in which the religion and faith of each is recorded: for there is no greater reason why those things which are added to the five aforementioned articles—1. That there is some supreme Deity. 2. That that Deity ought to be worshipped. 3. That virtue and piety, together with faith in God and intimate love for Him, are the principal part of divine worship. 4. That one must repent of sins. 5. That a reward or punishment is given after this life—in one [Codex] should be received as true, rather than those which are usually added to them in another, but that all things are equally suspect, involved, and controversial in their origin; nor are those things which are added to them in one codex supported by any more necessary demonstration than those which are read as superadded to them in other codices. But the things which he further subjoins in the second Appendix touch more closely upon the testimony of the Church and call its certainty into doubt, with the reason for doubting being sought from the fact that Priests, or the Church, of which the Priests are the principal part, cannot testify either that God spoke with His own mouth to the holy men to whom we attribute the reception of Holy Scripture, or that the holy men kept that speech in their memory and subsequently recited it faithfully to others, or that they consigned true copies of that speech to posterity, so that nothing was superadded, taken away, or changed by the fault or carelessness of the scribes in following centuries, or finally that that particular speech, made to a particular Lawgiver or Priest, not only necessarily pertains to all other Lawgivers or Priests, but also so binds the Laity themselves everywhere that they are thereby impelled to accept new and, before that time, unknown Laws or new dogmas so that they may, &c. These reasons for doubting rest upon those four conditions of revelation, formerly made to Priests (Prophets & Apostles), under which at last a Layman may be able to place faith in his Priest, preaching it (or in the Church testifying concerning the same), inculcated by the Author in his Opusculum de Veritate almost towards the end of page 290, the first of which is, that the Priest or Church must prove that the Revelation happened to the Priest (Prophet or Apostle formerly), and place that beyond all doubt. The second, that he must prove that that Revelation proceeded from the Supreme God, either speaking with His own mouth (as was said formerly), or using the ministry of a good Angel. The third, that he must prove that the Revelation, or oracle, or that Word was faithfully recited and rendered by the Priest (Prophet or Apostle), or where there was need, written or inscribed, and transmitted to posterity from the autograph of the Priest (Prophet or Apostle), so that if anything had been added, diminished, or changed over frequent centuries, all that might be corrected, restored, and amended by the authority of that Autograph. Fourthly, finally, that he must prove that that Revelation so intimately concerns posterity that it necessarily passes into an article of faith, then especially for this reason, that almost all things of this kind depend upon the faith of a single witness. He concludes at last: Let the Priest (Church) indeed prove these things, before the Layman commits himself entirely to his Revelation, which he preaches (or to the Scripture, which he testifies to be divine).

But these objections do not have in reserve what they seemed to promise the Author at the outset, or what they perhaps can seem or do seem to promise other Fanatics. To show this a little more fully, first of all we think it must be noted that the Author in both Appendices assumes as certain that holy Scripture is the particular Code of a certain group or Church, circumscribed by a certain part of the world, and that the testimony concerning its divine origin, which we here reckon among the motives or signs of credibility, is the testimony of a certain particular Church, enclosed within the borders of Europe, or Asia, or Africa, which is most false, and conflicts with notorious truth. For the histories of all times testify that the Church, which bears witness concerning the divine origin of holy Scripture, is not contained in any one part of the world, namely Europe, Asia, or Africa, but is diffused throughout the whole world, and embraces within its scope not only peoples, the most cultivated in letters and morals throughout all the regions of the world, but also among the barbarian peoples themselves, the Parthians, Ethiopians, Indians, and Iberians, etc., having once had its assemblies diffused far and wide, as may be read in Socrates, book I, chapters XIX and XX, Theodoret, book I, chapter XX and following, and Rufinus, book I, chapters IX and X. Moreover, there is no other book under the sun, held as sacred, to which any assembly diffused throughout the whole world, by whatever name it may go, has ever borne constant and unanimous testimony of immediate dependence upon God; but if any peoples have certain books which they attribute to God, just as the Turks have their Alcoran, they will certainly be obscure, barbarian, uncultivated, superstitious peoples, circumscribed by certain parts of the globe, whose testimony no one can equate with the testimony of the Church of Christ, diffused throughout the whole world, without notable ignorance or wickedness.

Latin:

IV.

LOcum quartum tribuimus Ecclesiæ, per universum terrarum orbem diffusæ, jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus concordi & consentienti undique testimonio.

I. Universa per orbem terrarum diffusa Ecclesia miro consensu recepit Scripturas sacras, tanquam divinas, & ex divina inspiratione consignatas, cujus eò major est auctoritas, quòd ipsum florem generis humani & quicquid eruditorum disciplinisq; ac moribus excultorum hominum sub cœlo est, aut fuit, suo ambitu continet, inter quos inprimis locum merentur primi illi fidelium, qui Scripturarum autographa ex suorum Auctorum manibus acceperunt, ut qui libri, & a quibus Scriptoribus, Spiritu Sancto inspirante, concinnati sint, ignorare non possent. Neque credibile est, tam innumeram per totum orbem dispersam fidelium multitudinem in aliquod mendacium conspirasse, aut conspirare potuisse, ut tanto consensu testarentur, Deo inspirante conscriptos esse libros sacros, si suo quisque Scriptor arbitratu studioq; humano, quos confecit, confecisset.

II. Sed hîc etiam habent, qui ex Cartesii Schola prodierunt, Fanatici suas rationes dubitandi, quibus Ecclesiæ de auctoritate Scripturæ perhibitum consentiens testimonium labefactatum eunt, quos inter non ultimus est Eduardus, Baro Herbert de Cherbury, qui Anonymus, quocum nobis in proximè præcedente motivo vindicando res fuit, ad impugnandam Scripturæ sacræ divinam auctoritatem, & varia eò tendentia commenta ejus incrustanda facem prætulit, in Appendice duplici, Tractatui de Causis errorum sub calcem adjectâ, hac in re operosus fuit. In Appendice priori sub initium statim: Planè, inquit, liquet, multas pro seculi & Regionis varietate, in præsens extare, & olim extitisse Fides sive Religiones, quarum nullam utique non tanquam cælitus quodammodo traditam asseveraverint Nomothetæ; adeò ut hanc in Europa, illam in Africa & Asia, aliam demum in ipsis Indiis comperiat Viator; equidem à Natali solo deducta argumenta vix ullibi prætulerim. Asia enim Philosophos egregios, Apostolos & Doctores, Africa ingenia acutissima, & Theologos summos, India Gymnosophistas, Brachmannos, Baxiamos & Bongos: Europa tandem suos sibi Proceres Primoresque venditat. Adeo ut verum Dei cultum, Hierarchiam conspicuam, vitæ austeritatem, & compendium ad Beatitudinem æternam penes se solos extare contenderint Antistites. In Appendice altera inter alias quæstiones dubias quarto loco hanc proponit: Annon ea, quæ ex Authoritate SS. Codicum (ut vocantur) quovis seculo vel regione receptorum hisce (in præced. q. II. commemoratis quinque naturâ notis articulis) addi solebant, sint sua in origine suspecta, involuta, & controversa, quin & à cœtibus illis, quibus aliæ placuêre Fides, toto genere rejecta, uti quæ nullâ Demonstratione necessaria fulciantur? & subjicit: Tametsi enim indubium sit Axioma, Deum summum veracissimum esse, quinneq; fallere neq; falli posse, quâ tamen mutuò probabunt diversi in diversis mundi partibus sive Legislatores, sive Sacerdotes 1. Deum summum proprio ore, vel (juxta aliquos) Angeli aut inferioris alicujus Numinis ore locutum fuisse. 2. Vel sermonem illum in memoria eorum servatum, aliosque subinde fideliter recitatum fuisse. 3. Vel exemplaria vera sermonis illius posteris consignata fuisse, adeò ut nihil ex Amanuensium vitio vel incuria sequentibus seculis superadditum, demptum, vel immutatum esset. 4. Sermonem illum particularem, particulari Legislatori vel Sacerdoti factum, non tantum ad omnes alios Legislatores vel Sacerdotes spectare, sed & ipsos Laicos ita ubique obstringere, ut ad novas & ante id temporis incognitas Leges, vel nova fidei dogmata acceptanda inde impelli possint; præsertim ubi à Rectæ rationis principiis deficere vel decedere eam ob causam cogerentur &c.

Quæ ex Appendice priori adducta sunt, huc tandem redeunt: Cùm plures diversæ diversisq́; Codicibus sacris descriptæ Fides sive Religiones dentur, & quilibet cœtus de divinitate sui Codicis, in quo sua continetur fides & religio, testimonium perhibeat, non majorem unius, quàm cæterorum cœtuum testimonii auctoritatem esse posse. Quò tendunt verba Auctoris: Equidem à natali solo (h. e. à Nationis alicujus auctoritate & testificatione de suo Codice sacro) deducta argumenta vix ullibiprætulerim. Eodem collineant, quæ ex Appendice altera produximus. Quando enim sub initium quærit, Annon ea, quæ ex authoritate SS. Codicum (ut vocantur) quovis sæculo vel regione receptorum, hisce addi solent, sint sua in origine suspecta, involuta & controversa &c. Scripturam sacram pari loco & conditione habet cum cæteris omnium Gentium & Sectarum Codicibus, quibus sua cujusq́; religio & fides consignata extat: non enim majorem esse rationem, cur ut vera recipiantur, quæ quinque prædictis articulis, 1. Esse supremum aliquod Numen. 2. Numen illud coli debere. 3. Virtutem & pietatem unà cum fide in Deum amoreq́; ejus intimo conjunctam, esse præcipuam partem cultus divini. 4. Resipiscendum esse à peccatis. 5. Præmium vel pœnam post hanc vitã dari; in uno, quàm quæ in altero illis addi solent, sed æquè omnia esse in sua origine suspecta, involuta, controversa; neque magis quæ in uno codice illis adduntur, necessariâ demonstratione fulciri, quàm quæ eis in codicibus aliis superaddita leguntur. Quæ autem in Appendice altera porro subjicit, testimonium Ecclesiæ propius attingunt, ejusque certitudinem in dubium vocant, ratione dubitandi inde petitâ, quòd Sacerdotes, vel Ecclesia, cujus præcipua pars Sacerdotes sunt, testari non possint, vel Deum ore proprio ad Viros sanctos, quibus acceptam referimus Scripturam sacram, loquutos esse, vel Viros sanctos sermonem illum in memoria servâsse, aliisq́; subinde fideliter recitâsse, vel exemplaria vera sermonis illius posteris consignâsse, ut nihil ex Amanuensium vitio vel incuriâ sequentibus seculis superadditum, demptum vel immutatum esset, vel denique sermonem illum particularem, particulari Legislatori vel Sacerdoti factum, non tantùm ad omnes alios Legislatores vel Sacerdotes necessariò spectare, sed & ipsos Laicos ita ubiq́; obstringere, ut ad novas & ante id temporis incognitas Leges vel nova dogmata acceptanda inde impelli possint &c. Quæ rationes dubitandi nituntur quatuor illis conditionibus revelationis, Sacerdotibus, (Prophetis & Apostolis) olim factæ, sub quibus demum Sacerdoti suo, eam prædicanti (vel Ecclesiæ de eadem testificanti) Laicus fidem adhibere possit, in Opusculo de Veritate ab Auctore ferè sub finem pag. 290. inculcatis, quarum prima est, ut probet Sacerdos vel Ecclesia, Revelationem Sacerdoti (Prophetæ vel Apostolo olim) obtigisse, idque extra omne dubium ponat. Altera, ut probet, Revelationem illam à Deo Summo sive proprio ore, (uti olim dictum) loquenti, sive Angeli boni ministerio utenti profectam fuisse. Tertia, ut probet, Revelationem, sive oraculum sive Verbum illud fideliter recitatum redditumque à Sacerdote (Propheta vel Apostolo) fuisse, aut ubi opus esset, scriptum vel exaratum, & ad posteros ex Sacerdotis (Prophetæ vel Apostoli) autographo transmissum, adeò ut si aliquid frequentibus seculis auctum, imminutum, immutatum esset, id omne ex Autographi illius authoritate corrigi, restitui, emendari possit. Quartò denique, ut probet, Revelationem illam ad posteros ita intimè spectare, ut in articulum fidei necessario transeat, tùm ob id præsertim, quòd ex testis singularis fide hujusmodi omnia ferè pendeant. Concludit tandem: Hæc quidem Sacerdos (Ecclesia) probet, priusquam Laicus sese totum ejus Revelationi, quam prædicat (vel Scripturæ, quam divinam esse testificatur) credat.

Verùm objectiones hæ in recessu non habent, quod à fronte Auctori polliceri visæ sunt, aut Fanaticis aliis forsan polliceri videri possunt aut videntur. Quod paulò uberiùs ostensuri, primò omnium monendum ducimus, Auctorem in Appendice utraque sumere tanquam certum, Scripturam sacram esse Codicem particularem Cœtus sive Ecclesiæ cujusdam particularis, certa quadam orbis parte circumscriptæ, & testimonium de divina ejus origine, quod motivis sive signis credibilitatis externis hîc accensemus, esse cujusdam particularis Ecclesiæ, intra Europæ, vel Asiæ, vel Africæ terminos conclusæ, testimonium, quod falsissimum est, & cum notoria veritate pugnat. Testantur enim omnium temporum historiæ, Ecclesiam, quæ de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine testimonium perhibet, non contineri unâ aliquâ orbis parte, Europâ scilicet, Asiâ, vel Africâ, sed esse per totum terrarum orbem diffusam, & complecti suo ambitu non solum populos, literis ac moribus cultissimos quosque per omnes mundi plagas, sed etiam inter ipsos barbaros populos, Parthos, Æthiopes, Indos & Iberos &c. suos longe lateq; diffusos cœtus olim habuisse, ut apud Socratem lib. I. cap. XIX. XX. Theodorectum lib. I. c. XX. seq. & Ruf. l. I. c. IX. X. legere est. Nullus autem sub sole datur Codex alius, sacer habitus, cui aliquis per totum terrarum orbem diffusus cœtus, quocunq; nomine is veniat, unquam immediatæ a Deo dependentiæ constans & consentiens testimonium perhibuerit, sed si qui populi quosdam habeant Codices, quos Deo acceptos referant, sicut Turcæ suum Alcoranum habent; obscuri sane, barbari, inculti, superstitiosi, certisq; orbis partibus circumscripti populi erunt, quorum testimonium testimonio Ecclesiæ Christi, per totum terrarum orbem diffusæ, citra insignem sive imperitiam, sive nequitiam, æquiparare nemo potest.


### Furthermore, that which the Author contends in the second objection, that the…

Furthermore, that which the Author contends in the second objection, that the five articles noted by nature, which he has listed, are added to the book of Holy Scripture, and are rejected in their entirety by those assemblies to whom other faiths have pleased, is indeed true, but it detracts nothing at all from the authority of the Catholic Church and its unanimous testimony concerning the divine origin of Holy Scripture. For just as other faiths, different from the Christian faith and religion which Holy Scripture contains, are not faiths but infidelities, falsehoods, and fabrications, so those assemblies of infidels, Jews, Turks, and Pagans who are addicted to them are blinded synagogues of Satan, utterly inept at judging the truth of Christian doctrine and faith, whose dissent, therefore, in the question concerning the divine origin and authority of the sacred book is not to be heeded or estimated as being of any moment or weight. Furthermore, it is also true that they rely on no demonstration, properly so called. For because they are above nature, revealed supernaturally by God, they cannot be demonstrated from the principles of nature, but are simply to be believed on account of the truthfulness of God who reveals them. But what the Author adds, that they themselves are suspect in their origin, is most false. For although they cannot be demonstrated a priori, and exceed the grasp of human reason by their loftiness, they cannot, however, be suspect in their origin to a prudent man, whose mind is not preoccupied with preconceived false opinions or fascinated by the deceptions of Satan, provided they are read with a love of truth and a desire for learning in the book of Holy Scripture. For besides the fact that all things are consistent with right reason and the five mentioned articles, or at least do not conflict with them or other principles of nature and reason: all things are also so arranged that, once known from the Holy Scriptures, they remarkably perfect our natural knowledge of God and His worship and of living life rightly, even in the judgment of natural reason itself, as was shown at length above in Section 1, thesis XII. But if you look to their origin, which the Holy Scriptures record, you will discover entirely that, in their substantial parts, they drew their origin immediately from God Himself at the very beginning of the world with the first-formed humans, as we taught at greater length in the previous thesis I of this Section, where we treated the antiquity of Holy Scripture, viewed in terms of its formal aspect. To this are added the other signs of credibility, partly internal, from the truth and holiness of Scripture and its sufficiency for salvation; partly external, from the trustworthiness of the sacred writers, miracles, and other sources, the former of which we brought forward in the preceding section, and one or another of the latter in this very Section: which, when deeply pondered by good readers who love the truth, place all those things beyond any risk of suspicion or doubt. Nor are they obscure to readers who love equity and truth. For whatever Scripture, beyond the five mentioned articles known by nature, hands down from divine revelation, if it is necessary to be believed for salvation or to be done for the holiness of life, it hands down all those things, if not in every place, yet in some places in words sufficiently clear and perspicuous, so that they can be easily understood, provided the reader's mind is free from prejudices and false preconceived opinions, as is shown elsewhere. But that certain things come into controversy among Christians is accidental, and arises from the malice, blindness, and obstinacy of men, which can in no way prejudice the divine origin of the sacred Book, especially since controversies are agitated at least concerning the sense of some passages of Scripture or some particular dogmas, yet the very passages concerning whose sense there is controversy, or in which the controversial dogmas are founded, are truly contained in the sacred Book and have God as their author, as Christians spread throughout the world and all true believers acknowledge and confess with one voice. Thus far, therefore, nothing has been brought forward by Edward Herbert that could render the testimony of the Church suspect, but rather the contrary, because the whole Book of Holy Scripture, and all the doctrines contained in it, as many as are simply necessary to be believed for salvation or to be done for the holiness of life, the faithful dispersed throughout the whole world receive with unanimous consent, it must be concluded that Holy Scripture is not suspect in its origin, nor involved, or among true Christians and the faithful in these least parts, which have happened that in a doctrine suspect, involved, and controversial, all true believers from the birth of Christ (to say nothing now of the faithful under the Old Testament) to these present times should have agreed among themselves, and with the highest consent and one voice have borne constant testimony concerning the divinity of the Code in which it is founded. But that in other things not altogether necessary some things somewhat obscure, difficult to understand, and controversial are found in it, or even that other necessary things are called into controversy by infidels and heretics, from this it is not simply permitted to infer that Scripture is in its origin involved and controversial. For either a fallacy is committed from a statement in a certain respect to a statement simply, or that which happens to Holy Scripture by accident and from the malice of infidels and heretics is attributed to it itself, as if it belonged to it in itself.

The reasons for doubting, drawn from the four conditions of Revelation reviewed above, by which the Author labored to render suspect and doubtful the testimony of the Church consenting everywhere concerning the divine origin of Scripture and the doctrine contained in it, are not of great weight. And first, indeed, the Church, as we accept it here, can certainly prove that Revelations once happened to the Prophets and Apostles. By the name of it, however, we do not understand a certain particular Church of a certain time or place, but the universal multitude of the faithful, which from the birth of Christ to these present times has existed diffused throughout the whole world. Nor do we entirely exclude from it the faithful who lived under the Old Testament up to Christ, since to their testimony borne concerning the Scriptures of the Old Testament, the Church of the New Testament testifying concerning the same must finally come. This Church, however, certainly had and has well known and perceived that Revelations happened to the holy Men who recorded the Scriptures of both Testaments. For the Israelite Church which existed in the time of Moses had it most clearly perceived that God appeared to Moses immediately at the beginning of his calling, Exod. III. 2, and afterwards very often, that He stayed with him on Mount Sinai for forty days and nights, Exod. XXIV. 18, c. XXXIV. 27, and spoke with him familiarly, as a friend speaks with a friend, Num. XII. 8. that he promulgated the precepts of the Decalogue from Mount Sinai with a resounding voice, while Moses remained on the mountain with him, and that this was watched and heard by the whole people, Exod. XX. 1. seqq. that Moses received the law from God himself, inscribed by the finger of God on two stone tablets, Exod. XXIV. 12. c. XXXI. 18. That the same man, out of righteous indignation on account of the people's defection and idolatry, cast the two tablets of the law to the ground and shattered them, Exod. XXXII. 19. and that he made, by God's command, two others, and inscribed upon them the same precepts of the moral law, Exod. XXXIV. 1. 4. 27.

Nor was it less known and understood by the Israelite Church, what revelations had occurred to each Prophet in the progress of time up to Malachi, the last of the Prophets. For the Prophets did not come forth in public to teach the people unless sent by God, and those sent did not hide either their calling or the revelations they had received from God for the people, but they announced the former to the people; they preached the latter publicly in their assemblies; they repeated more often that the Word of the Lord had come to them, that the Lord had appeared to them, had revealed to them what they announced to the people in his name, through dreams, through visions, etc., as can be read throughout their prophecies. To which also pertains that passage Num. XII. 8. If there shall be a Prophet among you, I the Lord will show myself to him in a vision, I will speak with him in a dream; and the fact that David also, although not by office a Prophet, yet by the Prophetic Spirit and divine revelations in no way inferior to the Prophets, professes in set words that the Holy Spirit has spoken through him, and his word has been made through his tongue, II. Sam. XXIII. 2.

But just as no one can be more certain of a divine revelation than he to whom it happens, and who perceives its infallible sense within himself, so no one can testify more certainly that a revelation has occurred to someone from God than he himself to whom it happened, namely the Prophets and holy men, to whom and through whom God has spoken to his people. Which testimony of theirs was held and esteemed in the Church of the O.T. to be of such certainty that Zechariah, the parent of John the Baptist, in his Canticle Luc. I. 70. and Peter the Apostle in the sermon delivered to the Israelite people Act. III. 18. professed in set words that God had spoken and foretold BY THE MOUTH OF ALL THE PROPHETS WHO HAVE BEEN FROM OF OLD, the benefits of salvation which accrued to the human race through the work of redemption exhibited in the flesh and accomplished by the Messiah, and this was acknowledged as the primary principle of faith, no less in the Jewish Church of that time than afterwards in the Church of the New Testament, and was placed beyond all hazard of doubt among all the faithful.

Let the same judgment apply to the Apostles and holy men in the Church of the New Testament. For those who had conversed with Christ during the whole time of his ministry, besides the fact that they had received divine revelations from the mouth of Christ, and had seen with their own eyes what Christ had done and suffered in the carrying out of the work of redemption, were also, by the Holy Spirit sent upon them in the visible form of tongues of fire, instructed by a stupendous miracle in a moment with the knowledge of all languages and of heavenly doctrine, so that they spoke of the mighty works of God in various languages which they had never learned, while the whole people looked on, listened, and marveled, Acts II. 3. seqq. Paul, however, although he was not with Christ in the days of his flesh, yet being taught immediately by him in the third heaven, openly testifies that he received by divine revelation whatever he taught by voice or writing among the Jews and Gentiles, II. Cor. XII. 2. seqq. I. Cor. II. 10. seqq. Gal. I. 1. 12. Which could not have been unknown to the Church of that time. But just as the Jewish Church could certainly testify, and did testify, concerning the revelations divinely made to Moses and the Prophets, while they were living and teaching by voice and writing; and the primitive Christian Church concerning the revelations which divinely befell the Apostles, so in the course of time the testimony of both was propagated from hand to hand by uninterrupted tradition to the Churches of succeeding times, so that these also could testify of them, although with a lower degree of certainty. For the testimony of the Churches which existed and exist in later times is founded upon the testimony of the primitive Church of both Testaments, and derives its authority and certainty from it. And let this suffice for the present to have replied to Herbert's first reason for doubting: which, although they do not rest upon demonstration, or have physical or metaphysical evidence, are nevertheless morally evident and certain, so that they cannot be called into doubt without significant rashness.

Latin:

Deinde quod contendit Auctor in objectione altera, quæ recensitis a se quinque naturâ notis articulis in Codice Scripturæ sacræ adduntur, esse a cœtibus illis, quibus aliæ placuêre fides, toto genere rejecta, verum quidem est, sed auctoritati Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ejusq; consentienti testimonio, de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine nihil quicquam derogat. Quemadmodum enim aliæ & a fide ac religione Christiana, quam Scriptura sacra continet, diversæ Fides, non fides, sed infidelitates, falsitates, commenta sunt, ita qui illis addicti sunt infidelium, Judæorum, Turcarum, Paganorum cœtus, excæcatæ Satanæ Synagogæ sunt, ad judicandum de doctrinæ & fidei Christianæ veritate prorsus ineptæ, quorum dissensus proinde in quæstione de divina Codicis sacri origine & auctoritate attendendus aut ullius momenti vel ponderis æstimandus non est. Deinde verum & hoc est, quod ea nullâ nitantur demonstratione, propriè sic dictâ. Quia enim supra naturam sunt, a Deo supernaturaliter revelata, ex naturæ principiis demonstrari non possunt, sed simpliciter propter veracitatem Dei revelantis credenda sunt. Quod autem addit Auctor, ea ipsa esse sua in origine suspecta, falsissimum est. Quamvis enim a priori demonstrari non possint, captumq; humanæ rationis suâ altitudine excedant, non tamen homini prudenti, & cujus animus præconceptis falsis opinionibus præoccupatus aut Satanæ præstigiis fascinatus non est, sua in origine suspecta esse possunt, modò cum amore veritatis & studio discendi in codice Scripturæ sacræ legantur. Præterquam enim quòd rectæ rationi & memoratis quinque articulis consentanea omnia sunt, vel certè cum iis aliisve naturæ & rationis principiis non pugnant: omnia etiam ita comparata sunt, ut ex Scripturis sacris cognita nostram naturalem de Deo ejusque cultu vitaq; rectè degenda cognitionem, vel ipsâ naturali ratione judice, insigniter perficiant, ut suprâ Sect. 1. th. XII. prolixè ostensum. Quod si ad illorum Originem, quam Scripturæ sacræ memorant, respicias, deprehendes oppidò, quòd, in suis substantialibus, sub ipsum mundi exordium cum Protoplastis statim ab ipsomet Deo originem suam traxerint, ut superiori th. I. hujus Sectionis, ubi de antiquitate Scripturæ sacræ, ex parte sui formalis spectatæ, actum, pluribus docuimus. Quò accedunt & cætera credibilitatis signa, interna partim, à veritate & sanctitate Scripturæ, ejusq; sufficientia ad salutem; partim externa, à Scriptorum sacrorum ἀξιοπισίᾳ, miraculis & aliunde petita, quorum illa in præcedente; horum verò unum atque alterum in hac ipsa Sectione adduximus: quæ penitiùs perpensa apud bonos & veritatis amantes lectores ea omnia extra omnem suspicionis aut dubitationis aleam constituunt. Neq; involuta sunt æquis veriq; amantibus lectoribus. Quæcunq; enimScriptura, præter memoratos quinque naturâ notos articulos, ex divina revelatione tradit, si ad salutem creditu, vel ad vitæ sanctimoniam factu necessaria sint, ea omnia, si nõ ubiq; locorũ, in aliquibus tamen locis tradit verbis satis claris & perspicuis, ut intelligi facilè possint, modò à præjudiciis & præconceptis opinionibus falsis lectoris animus liber sit, ut alibi ostenditur. Quòd autem quædam inter Christianos in controversiam veniunt, per accidens est, & ex hominum malitia, cæcitate & obstinatione provenit, quod divinæ Codicis sacri origini nihil præjudicare potest, præsertim cùm saltem de sensu aliquorum locorum Scripturæ aut particularibus aliquibus dogmatibus controversiæ agitentur, ipsa autem loca, de quorum sensu controvertitur, vel in quibus dogmata controversa fundantur, in Codice sacro verè contineri, & Deum auctorem habere, diffusi per orbem Christiani & verè fideles omnes agnoscant, & uno ore fateantur. Hactenus ergo ab Edoardo Herbert allatum nihil est, quod testimonium Ecclesiæ suspectum reddere possit, sed contra potiùs quia Scripturæ sacræ Codicem totum, & contentas in illo doctrinas omnes, quotquot sive ad salutē creditu, sive ad sanctimoniam vitæ factu simpliciter necessariæ sunt, fideles toto terrarum orbe dispersi unanimi recipiunt consensu, concludendum est, Scripturam sacram suâ in origine non esse suspectam, nec involutam, aut inter veros Christianos & fideles in his minimùm partibus, quæ cuivis creditu factuve necessariæ sunt, controversam. Neq; enim fieri potuit, ut in doctrina suspecta, involuta, controversa omnes verè fideles inde à nato Christo, (ut de fidelibus sub V. T. nunc nihil dicam) ad hæc usque tempora inter se convenerint, & de divinitate Codicis, in quo fundatur, summo consensu unoque ore constans perhibuerint testimonium. Quod autem in cæteris non prorsus necessariis quædam obscuriuscula, intellectu difficilia & controversa in eo reperiuntur, vel etiam alia necessaria ab infidelibus & hæreticis in controversiam vocantur, ex eo non simpliciter inferre licet, Scripturam esse sua in origine involutam & controversam. Vel enim committitur fallacia à dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter, vel quod per accidens & ex infidelium & hæreticorum malitia Scripturæ sacræ supervenit, tribuitur ipsi, ac si ei per se conveniret.

Rationes dubitandi, ex quatuor Revelationis conditionibus, suprà recensitis, depromtæ, quibus Ecclesiæ undiquaque consentientis testimonium de divina Scripturæ & contentæ in ea doctrinæ origine Auctor suspectum & dubium reddere laboravit, magni ponderis non sunt. Et primùm quidem Revelationes Prophetis & Apostolis olim obtigisse, probare utique potest Ecclesia, prout hîc eam accipimus. Ejus appellatione verò non intelligimus particularem quandam certi temporis aut loci Ecclesiam, sed universam fidelium multitudinem, quæ inde à nato Christo ad hæc usq; tempora per totum terrarum orbem diffusa extitit. Neq; ab ea prorsus excludimus fideles, qui sub V. T. ad Christum usq; vixerunt, quippe ad quorum de Scripturis V. T. perhibitum testimoniũ Ecclesiæ N. T. de iisdē testificanti, tandē deveniendũ est. Hæc verò Ecclesia habuit utiq; habetq; probè cognitum & perspectũ, Revelationes obtigisse Viris sanctis, qui Scripturas utriusq; Testamenti consignarunt. Quæ enim Mosis tempore extitit Ecclesia Israëlitica, perspectissimum habuit, Deum apparuisse Mosi statim sub initium suæ vocationis, Exod. III. 2. & postea sæpissimè, commoratum esse cum eo in monte Sinai quadraginta dies & noctes, Exod. XXIV. 18. c. XXXIV. 27. locutum esse cum eo familiariter, ut amicus cum amico loquitur, Num. XII. 8. promulgâsse Decalogi præcepta de monte Sinai sonorâ voce, Mose in monte cum ipso manente, idque spectante & audiente toto populo, Exod. XXII. 1. seqq. Mosen ab ipso Deo accepisse legem, Dei digito duabus tabulis lapideis inscriptam, Exod. XXIV. 12. c. XXXI. 18. Eundem tabulâ utrâq; legis, ex justa indignatione, ob populi defectionem & idololatriam, in terram projectâ & confractâ, Exod. XXXII. 19. confecisse, Dei jussu, duas alias, iisque eadem inscripsisse legis moralis præcepta, Exod. XXXIV. 1. 4. 27.

Neque minùs cognitum & perspectum habebat Ecclesia Israë- litica, quæ temporis progressu cuiq; Prophetæ usq; ad Malachiam, Prophetarum ultimum, revelationes obtigissent. Non enim Prophetæ in publicum prodibant ad docendum populum, nisi missi à Deo, & missi non occultabant vel vocationem suam, vel acceptas à Deo revelationes suas ad populum, sed illam denunciabant populo; has prædicabant in ejus conventibus publicè; ingeminabant sæpiùs, Verbum Domini ad se factum esse, Dominum apparuisse sibi, revelásse sibi, quæ populo, ejus nomine, denunciabant, per somnia, per visines &c. ut passim in illorum Prophetiis legere est. Quò pertinet etiam illud Num. XII. 8. Si quis fuerit Propheta Vobis, Ego Dominus in visione me ostendam ei, in somnio loquar cum eo; & quòd David quoq;, etsi non officio Propheta, Spiritu Prophetico tamen & revelationibus divinis Prophetis minimè inferior, conceptis verbis profitetur, Spiritum Sanctum locutum esse per se, & sermonem ejus per suam linguam factum esse, II. Sam. XXIII. 2.

Quemadmodùm autem de divina revelatione nemo certior esse potest, quàm is, cui obtingit, & qui ejus sensum minimè fallacem in semetipso animadvertit, ita nec quisquam certiùs testari potest, revelationem obtigisse alicui à Deo, quàm is ipse, cui obtigit, Prophetæ scilicet & Viri sancti, ad quos & per quos Deus ad populum suum loqvutus est. Quod illorum testimonium etiam in Ecclesia V. T. tantæ certitudinis habitum & æstimatum est, ut Zacharias, Johannis Baptistæ parens, in Cantico suo Luc. I. 70. & Petrus Apostolus in habita ad populum Israëliticum concione Act. III. 18. conceptis verbis profiterentur, Deum locutum esse & prænunciâsse PER OS OMNIUM, QUI à SECULO FUERUNT, PROPHETARUM, quæ per Messiam in carne exhibitum & peractum ab eo redemtionis opus generi humano obtigerunt beneficia salutis, idq; tùm temporis in Ecclesia Judaica non minùs, quàm postea in Ecclesia N. T. pro primo fidei principio agnitum & apud fideles omnes extra omnem dubitationis aleam positum fuit.

Idem esto judicium de Apostolis & Viris sanctis in Ecclesia N. T. Qui enim cum Christo toto tempore ministerii ipsius conversati fuerant, præterquàm quòd revelationes divinas ex Christi ore acceperant, & quæ in opere redemtionis peragendo Christus fecerat & perpessus fuerat, suis oculis viderant, à Spiritu S. etiam super se in visibili specie linguarum ignearum misso, stupendo miraculo in momento omnium linguarum, doctrinæq; cælestis notitia insigni instructi sunt, ut magnalia Dei variis linguis, quas nunquam didicerant, spectante, audiente & admirante toto populo, eloquerentur, Act. II. 3. seqq. Paulus verò, licet cum Christo in diebus carnis ejus non fuerit, ab ipso tamen in tertio cælo immediatè edoctus, per revelationem divinam se accepisse palàm testatur, quæcunque voce aut scriptis inter Judæos & Gentes docuit, II. Cor. XII. 2. seqq. I. Cor. II. 10. seqq. Gal. I. 1. 12. Quæ illius temporis Ecclesiæ ignota esse non poterant. Sicut autem de revelationibus, Mosi & Prophetis divinitùs factis, Ecclesia Judaica, quæ illis viventibus & voce ac scriptis docentibus; & de revelationibus, quæ Apostolis divinitùs obtigerunt, Christiana primitiva Ecclesia certò testari potuit, & testata est, ita procedente tempore testimonium utriusque per traditionem non interruptam ad sequentium temporum Ecclesias de manu ad manum propagatum est, ut hæ etiam de illis testari possent, quamvis gradu certitudinis inferiori. Quæ enim posterioribus temporibus extiterunt & existunt Ecclesiæ, illarum testimonium fundatur in testimonio primitivæ utriusque Testamenti Ecclesiæ, & ab eo auctoritatem & certitudinem habet. Atque hæc ad primam Herberti rationem dubitandi respondisse impræsentiarum sufficiat: quæ quamvis non demonstratione nitantur, vel physicam aut metaphysicam evidentiam habeant, moraliter tamen evidentia & certa sunt, ut citra insignem temeritatem in dubium vocari non possint.


### As regards his second reason, why he demands that for the certainty of the…

As regards his second reason, why he demands that for the certainty of the testimony of the Church, the revelations which were made to holy men divinely have come, whether it proceeded from God the highest, either speaking with HIS OWN MOUTH or USING THE MINISTRY OF AN ANGEL, does not appear. For God revealing did not always and everywhere use revelation by address, speaking to holy men by His own mouth or that of an Angel (to speak thus with the Author), but with Moses he but to the Prophets by vision or dreams, God Himself attesting, Num. XII. 8. To David and other holy ones He used revelation by θεοπνευςίαν or immediate inspiration. And that by this third mode of revelation God suggested to all the sacred Writers what things were to be written, the Apostle of the Gentiles is a witness greater than any exception, who in II. Tim. III. 16. expressly writes that πᾶσαν γραφὴν all (sacred) Scripture is θεόπνευςον, inspired by God. But that the highest God spoke to Moses partly with His own mouth, and partly used the ministry of a speaking Angel, could not be obscure or doubtful to the Israelite Church which existed in his time, as has just been shown, and is evident even from this, that in Num. XII. 8. God Himself said to Aaron and Miriam, with the whole Israelite people listening, that He speaks with Moses mouth to mouth. Moreover, the voice by which the moral law was promulgated from Mount Sinai by God, Stephen the protomartyr in Acts VII. 38. and Paul the Apostle in Gal. III. 19. expressly ascribe to an Angel speaking, and to the ministry of Angels.

Thirdly, that the revelation, or oracle, or that word received from God, was faithfully recited and rendered by the Prophets and Apostles, or where there was need, written or inscribed; and transmitted to posterity from their autographs (which the Author's third reason for doubting demands to be proved) needs no proof. For what God spoke to Moses by a sensible voice; to the Prophets by visions or dreams, and to the Apostles by θεοπνευςίαν, those things He subsequently spoke in them, and through them also to others, with the holy men lending Him their own mouth and tongue, according to that of Zechariah in Luke I. 70: As He (God) spoke by the mouth of His holy Prophets, who have been from of old; and of Peter in Acts III. 18: God had foretold by the mouth of all His Prophets. To which David also sings in harmony, testifying in II. Sam. XXIII. 2. that the Spirit of the Lord spoke through him, and His word was made through his tongue; and the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews c. I. v. 1. saying, that God at many times and in many ways spoke in time past by the prophets, and likewise the Apostle Peter, saying, ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φε- ρόμενοι that holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. But that the Apostle Paul testifies concerning Holy Scripture, that it was composed by the inspiration of God, has just been shown from II Tim. III. 16. But as for those revelations which were announced to others by holy men, with God himself speaking through them, and with the same God inspiring what was to be written, and which were committed to writing, no one can doubt that they were faithfully conveyed to others by voice, pen, and writings, unless he wishes to doubt the supreme truthfulness of God.

Nor is there any reason for anyone to say that it is not indeed the truthfulness of God that is doubted, but the truthfulness of the witnesses brought forward, Zechariah, Peter, David, Paul, saying that God spoke through the mouth of the Prophets and through their tongue, and that He, through inspiration, suggested to the sacred writers what they wrote, etc. For in order for someone, without the mark of rashness, circumspectly and prudently, to call into doubt the testimony of anyone, it is not enough to have brought forward reasons for doubting of whatever kind, sought from a lack of physical or metaphysical evidence, or of evident demonstration, as our Herbert, along with other fanatics, has persuaded himself, but it is necessary that he bring forward evidence of some falsehood, or signs and proofs of deceit and seduction, which might underlie the testimony. Otherwise, nothing certain will exist in human affairs. To say nothing of other signs of truth, sought partly from the intrinsic nature of Holy Scripture itself, partly from the ἀξιοπισίᾳ of the sacred writers, from miracles, and from elsewhere, which procure for them both authority and undoubted credibility. Having considered all these things thoroughly, to hold their testimony as suspect or doubtful, because it is not evident to us that God spoke to them or through them, is not the act of a sane man, but of one who is insane with reason.

But with how much care the autographs of Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles were guarded in the Church, sacred histories speak. The stone tablets, on which the moral law was inscribed, were, by the command of God himself, placed into the ark of the covenant, and were sacredly guarded in it, Deut. X. 5. with which they were brought into the sanctuary of the temple, built by the same, in the time of King Solomon, and were preserved in it, I Kings VIII. 9. II Chron. V. 10. At the side of the ark of the covenant, or rather, as authors maintain, in a chest placed at its right side, was deposited the autograph of the Pentateuch, written out by the hand of Moses, Deut. XXXI. 24. which without a doubt when the ark of the covenant was afterwards brought into the Solomonic temple, and was kept there: Where also in the time of Josiah, King of Judah, after it had been lost either through the negligence of the priests, or had been hidden for some time by their care and solicitude, lest it should be abolished by the cruelty of Manasseh and other kings who degenerated from the piety of their ancestors, it was found by Hilkiah, the high priest, II Kings XXII. 8. II Chronicles XXXIV. 14. For it is entirely consistent with the truth that this was the very autograph of Moses. For it is said expressly in II Chronicles XXXIV. 14. ספר תורת ביד משה the book of the law by the hand of Moses, and there is no compelling reason to prevent us from understanding this as the book of the law written by the hand of Moses or through Moses, especially since Moses himself had handed over his autograph to the Levites to be placed at the side of the ark of the covenant, and had ordered it to be preserved there for the perpetual memory of the Israelites, Deut. XXXI. 26. In the same place were also deposited and preserved the autographs of the other prophets and of other θεοπνεύστων (God-inspired) men; just as Samuel is said to have deposited his book, in which he had recorded all the rights of the kings, לפני יהוה before the Lord, that is, in a chest at the side of the ark of the covenant, where the Lord was accustomed to appear and testify to His presence, I Sam.
