X. 25. so that there is no doubt that the autographs of Moses and the prophets were preserved and kept in the Church of the Old Testament with the greatest care and zeal until the destruction of the first temple. But that after the first temple was destroyed by the Chaldeans, and likewise during the Babylonian captivity, and after it, copies of the Scripture, conformable to their autographs and uncorrupted, survived, is clear from the fact that when the Jews returned from captivity, God, through Malachi, the last of the prophets, towards the end of his prophecy, by which the final hand was placed upon the Code of Scripture, chap. IV. v. 4, commended with the greatest zeal the perpetual memory of the Mosaic law or Pentateuch, and the strict observance of the moral, ceremonial, and forensic laws contained in it, which He would not have done unless copies of the Pentateuch and the prophetic books, conformable to their autographs and uncorrupted, had still survived in the Church. Nor is it to be believed that Ezra, ch. VIII. 2, produced any other code of the divine law for the sight of the people, and read and explained it to the people, than one which was conformable to the autograph and uncorrupted. But with what care Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue, among whom were also the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, subsequently reviewed the books of the Old Testament Scripture, and with what solicitude and diligence they collected, arranged, and digested into one body codices from various places, and with what dexterity they amended and restored to their pristine integrity those things which had been corrupted by the injury of time under harsh and long-lasting captivity, is better known than that it should be commemorated at length here from ancient history by them in this matter is to be esteemed the greater, because Ezra and the already mentioned Prophets, men truly θεόπνευστοι, constituted a part of that Synagogue. To which is added also the testimony of Christ and the Apostles, greater than any exception, which they bore to the integrity of the Scripture of the O.T., as often as they alleged it as an undoubted rule of the doctrine of faith and morals, proved and confirmed from it the doctrines proposed by themselves, and commended it to the Churches and all the faithful to be read, meditated upon, and searched. I pass over now the care and diligence of the Tiberian Masoretes, which they applied around the five-hundredth year from the birth of Christ in adorning critical notes: whose industry and labor all aimed at preserving the codices of the Scripture of the O.T. pure and undefiled from errors. Indeed, the critical notes of them and others, with כתיב and קרי, are even now seen added in the margins of Hebrew Bibles.

Nor with less care and diligence did the Churches, planted throughout the world by the preaching of the Apostles, preserve and guard the autographs of the Scripture of the N.T. Almost all the Epistles of Paul were written and transmitted to certain Churches planted by himself, or certainly to the Bishops of certain Churches, whose autographs were held in neglect by the Churches and their Bishops, but rather were preserved and guarded with the greatest zeal as an invaluable treasure—who would say this, or believe one who said it? Tertullian, who lived toward the end of the second century, testifies openly that in his own time the authentic letters of the Apostles were held in the Churches over which the Apostles once presided and were read at stated times: Come now, he says, you who wish to exercise your curiosity better in the business of salvation, run through the APOSTOLIC CHURCHES, in which the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their places, in which their AUTHENTIC LETTERS are recited, sounding the voice, representing the

Latin:

Ad alteram ejusdem rationem quod attinet, cur ad certitudinem testimonii Ecclesiæ probari postulet, Revelationes, quæ Viris sanctis divinitùs obtigêre, à Deo summo sive PROPRIO ORE loquenti, sive ANGELI MINISTERIO UTENTI profectam fuisse, non apparet. Non enim Deus revelans semper & ubique usus est revelatione per allocutionem, suo vel Angeli ore (ut cum Auctore ita loquar) ad Viros sanctos loquendo, sed cum Mose loquutus est ore ad os, ut amicus cum amico loquitur; ad Prophetas verò per visionem aut somnia, attestante ipfomet Deo, Num. XII. 8. Ad Davidem & alios sanctos revelatione per θεοπνευςίαν sive immediatam inspirationem usus est. Atq; hoc tertio revelationis modo Deum Scriptoribus sacris omnibus, quæ scribenda essent, suggessisse, testis exceptione omni major est Gentium Apostolus, qui in II. Tim. III. 16. expressè scribit, πᾶσαν γραφὴν totam Scripturam (sacram) esse θεόπνευςον, à Deo inspiratam. Quòd autem ad Mosen Deus summus partim ore proprio loqvutus, partim Angeli loquentis ministerio usus sit, Israëliticæ Ecclesiæ, quæ ejus tempore extitit, obscurum aut dubium esse non potuit, ut modò ostensum, & vel inde etiam patet, quod Num. XII. 8. Deus ipse ad Aaronem & Miriam, audiente toto populo Israëlitico, dixit, se ore ad os loqui cum Mose. Vocem autem, quâ de monte Sinai lex moralis à Deo promulgata est, Stephanus protomartyr Act. VII. 38. & Paulus Apostolus Gal. III. 19. expressè Angelo loquenti, & Angelorum ministerio adscribunt.

Tertiò revelationem, sive oraculum, sive verbum illud, à Deo acceptum, fideliter recitatum redditumq;, esse à Prophetis & Apostolis, aut ubi opus esset, scriptum vel exaratum; & ad posteros ex illorum autographis transmissum (quod tertia Auctoris ratio dubitandi probandum postulat) probatione non eget. Quæ enim Deus ad Mosen voce sensibili; ad Prophetas per visiones aut somnia, & ad Apostolos per θεοπνευςίαν loqvutus est, ea deinceps in illis, & per illos etiam loqvutus est ad alios, Viris sanctis ipsi os suum & linguam suam commodantibus, juxta illud Zachariæ Luc. I. 70. Sicut loquutus est (Deus) per os sanctorum, qui à seculo fuerunt, Prophetarum suorum; & Petri Act. III. 18. Deus prænunciaverat per os omnium Prophetarum suorum. Quibus accinunt & David, testificans II. Sam. XXIII. 2. Spiritum Domini loqvutum esse per se, & sermonem ejus esse per suam linguam factum; & Auctor Epistolæ ad Ebræos c. I. v. 1. dicens, Deum multis vicibus, multisq modis olim loquutum esse per Prophetas, itemq́; Petrus Apostolus, ajens, ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενοι à Spiritu Sancto actos loquutos esse sanctos Dei homines. De Scriptura sacra autem Paulum Apostolum testari, quòd Deo inspirante tota concinnata sit, modò ex II. Tim. III. 16. ostensum est. Quæ revelationes autem à Viris sanctis, Deo ipso per eos loquente, aliis denunciatæ, & eodem, quæ scribenda essent, inspirante, in literas relatæ sunt, eas fideliter voce calamoq́; & scriptis ad alios delatas esse; dubitare nemo potest, nisi qui de summa Dei veracitate dubitare velit.

Neque est, quod quis dicat, non quidem dubitari de veracitate Dei, sed de veracitate adductorum testium, Zachariæ, Petri, Davidis, Pauli, dicentium, Deum per os Prophetarum & per illorum linguam locutum esse, eumq́; per inspirationem Scriptoribus sacris, quæ scripserunt, ipsis suggessisse &c. Nam ut quis absque temeritatis nota, circumspectè, & prudenter testimonium alicujus in dubium vocet, non sufficit qualescunq; ex defectu evidentiæ Physicæ vel Metaphysicæ, aut demonstrationis evidentis petitas rationes dubitandi adduxisse, ut Herbertus noster cum Fanaticis aliis sibi persuasum habet, sed necesse est, ut evidentia alicujus falsitatis, aut doli, & seductionis, quæ testimonio subsit, indicia & documenta afferat. Aliàs nihil quicquam certi in rebus humanis dabitur. Ut taceam alia veritatis signa, partim ex ipsa Scripturæ sacræ natura intrinseca, partim à Scriptorum sacrorum ἀξιοπισίᾳ, miraculis & aliunde petita, quæ iisdem & auctoritatem & fidem indubitatam conciliant. Quibus omnibus fusque deq; habitis, illorum testimonium suspectum aut dubium habere, quòd nobis non evidens sit, Deum ad illos, vel per illos loquutum esse, non sani, sed cum ratione insanientis hominis est.

Quantâ curâ verò Autographa Mosis, Prophetarum, Apostolorumq́;, in Ecclesia custodita fuerint, historiæ sacræ loquuntur. Tabulæ lapideæ, quibus lex moralis inscripta erat, ipsius Dei jussu, in arcam fœderis repositæ, inq́; ea sanctè custoditæ sunt, Deut. X. 5. cum qua tempore Salomonis Regis sacrario templi, ab eodem extructi, illatæ & in eo asservatæ sunt I. Reg. VIII. 9. II. Paral. V. 10. In latere arcæ fœderis, vel potiùs, ut Auctores volunt, in capsula ad latus dextrum ejus collocata, repositum fuit autographum Pentateuchi, Mosis manu exaratum, Deut. XXXI. 24. quod dubio procul cum arca fœderis postea templo Salomoneo illatum, ibiq; custoditum est: Ubi etiam Josiæ Regis Judæ tempore, postquam vel ex negligentia Sacerdotum amissum, vel illorum cura & solicitudine, ne Manassis aliorumq; ab avita pietate degenerantium Regum crudelitate aboleretur, aliquandiu occultatum fuerat, per Hilkiam, Sacerdotem summum repertum est, II. Reg. XXII. 8. II. Paral. XXXIV. 14. Id enim fuisse ipsum autographum Mosis, vero prorsus consentaneum est. Dicitur enim expresse II. Par. XXXIV. 14. ספר תורת ביד משה liber legis per manum Mose, quod cur non de libro legis, Mosis manu vel per Mosen exarato intelligamus, nulla impedit cogens ratio, præfertim cum ipsum autographum suum Moses Levitis in latere arcæ fœderis reponendum tradidisset, & ad perpetuam Israë̈litarum memoriam ibi asservare jussisset, Deut. XXXI. 26. Ibidem reposita & asservata etiam sunt cætera Prophetarum & aliorum Virorum θεοπνεύστων autographa; sicut Samuel suum librum, quo omnia Regum jura consignaverat, לפני יהוה coram Domino, puta in capsula ad latus arcæ fœderis, ubi Dominus apparere & suam præsentiam testari solebat, deposuisse fertur I. Sam. X. 15. ut ita dubium non sit, autographa Mosis & Prophetarum in Ecclesia V. T. summa cura & studio usque ad eversionem templi primi fuisse asservata & custodita. Quod autem post eversum per Chaldæos templum primum, itemq; in captivitate Babylonica, & post eam, exempla Scripturæ, suis autographis conformia & incorrupta superfuerint, vel inde liquet, quod ex captivitate reversis Judæis Deus per Malachiam, Prophetarum ultimum, sub finem Prophetiæ suæ, qua Codici Scripturæ ultima manus imposita fuit, cap. IV. v. 4. legis Mosaicæ sive Pentateuchi perpetuam memoriam, & contentarum in eo moralium, ceremonialium & forensium legum strictam observantiam summo studio commendavit, non id facturus, nisi apographa Pentateuchi librorumq; Propheticorum suis autographis conformia & incorrupta in Ecclesia adhuc superfuissent. Neq; credendum, Esdram c. VIII. 2. alium produxisse Codicem legis divinæ in conspectum populi, populoq; prælegisse & explicasse, quam qui Autographo conformis & incorruptus esset. Qua vero cura postea Esdras & Viri Synagogæ magnæ, quos inter & Prophetæ Haggæus, Zacharias atq; Malachias erant, libros Scripturæ V. T. recensuerint, quâ solicitudine & diligentiâ ex locis variis codices collegerint, ordinaverint, & in unum corpus digesserint, quâ dexteritate, quæ temporum injuriâ sub dura & diuturna captivitate vitiata fuerant, emendaverint & integritati pristinæ restituerint, notius est, quàm quòd hîc ex historia veteri prolixè commemorari debeat. Quorum hac in readhibita cura & opera eò majoris est æstimanda, quòd Esdras & jam memorati Prophetæ, viri sanè θεόπνευστοι, Synagogæ illius partem constituerunt. Quò accedit etiam Christi & Apostolorum testimonium omni exceptione majus, quod integritati Scripturæ V. T. perhibuerunt, quotiescunque eam velut regulam doctrinæ fidei & morum indubitatam allegârunt, propositas à se doctrinas ex illa probarunt & confirmarunt, & Ecclesiis cunctisq; fidelibus illam legendam, meditandam, ac scrutandam commendârunt. Taceo nunc curam & diligentiam Masoretharum Tiberiensium, quam circa annum à nato Christo quingentesimum in adornandis notis criticis adhibuerunt: quorum industria & labor omnis ad Codices Scripturæ V. T. à mendis puros & intemeratos conservandos collineabat. Illorum verò aliorumq; notæ Criticæ, cum כתיב & קרי etiamnum in Bibliorum Ebraicorum marginibus adjectæ cernunnuntur.

Neque minori curâ & diligentiâ Ecclesiæ, Apostolorum prædicatione per orbem terrarum plantatæ, autographa Scripturæ N.T. asservârunt & custodiverunt. Epistolæ Pauli ferè omnes ad certas ab ipsomet plantatas Ecclesias, vel certè ad Ecclesiarum quarundam Episcopos perscriptæ & transmissæ sunt, quarum autographa ab Ecclesiis illarumq; Episcopis neglectim habita, non autem velut inæstimabilem thesaurum summo studio asservata & custodita fuisse, quis dixerit, aut dicenti crediderit? Tertullianus, qui sub finem seculi secundi vixit, testatur apertè, suo adhuc tempore Apostolorum literas authenticas in Ecclesiis, quibus Apostoli olim præsederunt, habitas & statis temporibus recitatas fuisse: Age, inquiens, qui voles curiositatem tuam meliùs exercere in negocio salutis, percurre ECCLESIAS APOSTOLICAS, apud quas ipsæ adhuc cathedræ Apostolorum suis locis præsidentur, apud quas AUTHENTICÆ LITERÆ eorum recitantur, sonantes vocem, repræsentantes


### face. Is Achaia nearest to you

face. Is Achaia nearest to you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi. If you can head into Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you are adjacent to Italy, you have Rome, etc. The words exist in the book On Prescriptions against Heretics, by which he hints not obscurely that the autograph copies of Paul's Epistles indeed at Corinth; to the Philippians at Philippi; to the Ephesians at Ephesus; to the Romans at Rome. The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle records that the Gospel of John, written by his own hand, still existed in the Ephesian Church in the time of the Emperor Honorius, towards the end of the fourth century. Nor is there any doubt that the autograph copies of the other writers of the New Testament, as precious κειμήλια, were preserved in the Churches for many centuries. Furthermore, there exist monuments and writings of the Fathers, both of the most ancient, who were able to consult the very autographs of the Apostles, and of the following centuries, in which most of the places and words of the New Testament Scripture are found cited here and there, agreeing exactly with our codices, which is an unmistakable proof that our modern codices are clearly the same as the autographs and copies which they used constantly, both immediately after the times of the Apostles and in the following centuries. But these things are ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, to treat of which by design is for another place.

That the author fourthly and finally demands to be proved, that a Revelation, once made to a Prophet or Apostle, so intimately concerns posterity that it necessarily passes into an article of faith, presents no difficulty. For the way to salvation is one for all; and what is necessary to be believed by one for salvation, whether that revelation has come divinely to one individual Prophet or Apostle, or to many, that is necessary to be believed by all to whom that revelation has been promulgated and made known, and is an article of faith, just as the revelations which came to the Prophets under the Old Testament, and to the Apostles under the New, were promulgated and made public property by them to the Israelite Church, and by the latter to the Churches recently planted throughout the world, by voice and by writings.

The authority of the Church, therefore, concerning the divine origin of Holy Scripture, with nothing at all standing in the way of the reasons brought forward by the Author for doubting, remains firm, through which assent is owed to it. Which the Author finally cannot deny. For after in his treatise On Truth, page 296, he had referred universal tradition, universal history, and finally that whole body of things which is handed down from long ago concerning events, whether truly, falsely, piously, or impiously performed, to the class of those things which, with respect to us, are probable, not true, inasmuch as they depend upon the authority of the narrator some remarks concerning probable things and their difference from true things; he objected to himself on page 298: But, he says, do you thus pull down and weaken the credibility of histories, as if we seemed to have done too little, who have handed down the history of the Creation, the Redemption of the world, etc.? And he replied in the same place that the credibility of sacred history is by no means destroyed or detracted from by these things, to which, along with the greatest part of mankind, he gives assent so most willingly that he would entirely believe that God had done these and greater things, if they were proclaimed; but that he distinguishes knowledge and certain science from faith by hearing in such a way that he notes in every religion what can be known and what can be believed; and he concludes: Let that book, therefore, stand supreme among books, that of Holy Scripture, of which, although there have been various authors, whom this later age has composed in a wonderful connection among themselves, yet what in the whole context is not θεόπνευστον, what cannot be piously believed as a holy work and one that has proceeded from God? That book, therefore (setting others aside), we receive with the highest veneration, nor do we obtain comfort or firmer protection elsewhere. And following, page 299. Why should anyone alone doubt, when the authority of any history, whether sacred or profane, is fortified, supported, and defended by many most famous provinces, ages, and writers?

But those things which we brought forward above from both Appendices, annexed to the Treatise on the causes of errors, do not seem to agree with these, namely that in the later Appendix, immediately at the beginning, he contends that the orthodox religion is to be begun and established rather from the principles of divine universal providence than from those theses of faith which, derived from certain particular revelations in some part of the world (as if done long ago), suppose that the secret counsels of God have been thus revealed to posterity or for all time; and that afterwards in the annexed question IV, he treats all the Codices in which the diverse religions of nations and peoples are recorded, received in any age or region, on an equal footing with the volume of Holy Scripture; and likewise because in Question V he equally censures all particular assemblies that have sworn to the words of some sacred volume, because many sects and schisms have arisen among them while various interpretations of the meaning of the volume are brought forward; tacitly implying that one should not swear to the words of any sacred volume, but simply insist upon those five articles, often inculcated by himself, in which he wishes the entire Catholic religion to be comprised. To which is added that in the sixth question he says: That it may be granted among many, who have existed or exist, Sacred Volumes, that some one (the rest being set aside) can be undoubtedly received, and all controversies can be removed, yet it must be inquired whether the new dogmas which are forged from thence are indiscriminately published by the Prelates for the good of the human race, etc. By which indeed, as if he had a hypothesis not granted, that among many, who have existed or exist, some one sacred volume (the rest being set aside) can be undoubtedly received, etc.

With these things standing, how can that supreme volume of Holy Scripture stand among the books or sacred volumes? How can he receive it with the highest veneration while the others are set aside? It does not easily appear.

Nor does the Author extricate himself by the distinction between knowledge and faith, that knowledge is more certain than faith; nay, that knowledge alone is certain, but faith is not certain, but only a probable cognition, under which falsehood can lie, and very often does lie. For although this may be conceded concerning human faith, concerning divine faith, however, which the Author will scarcely acknowledge to exist, it is most false. For faith, leaning upon divine revelation, which we call divine, is as certain as any knowledge is or can be, on account of the infinite knowledge and goodness of God who reveals, through which He can neither be deceived in revealing, nor deceive. Nor does the distinction between knowledge and faith find a place within the very bounds of Scripture in that sense, as if Scripture itself delivers some things scientifically and through demonstrations; but others through divine revelation and to be accepted by faith. For just as the whole of Scripture is θεόπνευστος or divinely inspired, so also it is to be embraced entirely by faith, on account of divine inspiration or revelation. Although indeed some things are also found in it which can be known from the light of nature, and of which knowledge can be had can, yet their demonstrations do not pertain to Holy Scripture, but to Philosophy. For the formal object of Holy Scripture does not consist in the scientific and evident principles of nature, but in obscure divine revelation. The author, however, within the very limits of Scripture, distinguishes between science and faith, so that he contends that only those things are to be received as certain, and such as cannot contain falsehood, which can be known from the light and principles of nature: of which kind are those five, by him more often inculcated, most common and among all peoples received articles, That God exists, that He is to be worshipped, etc., in which he wishes the center and sum of all Scripture and the Catholic religion to be constituted; and those things which for the fuller declaration of these are handed down in Holy Scripture, or can be inferred from them by way of conclusions. All other things, which are handed down as revealed, whether in the Code of Holy Scripture, or in other Codes held as sacred, he wishes to be held not as true, but as probable, or possible, or those which in their origin are suspect, involved, controversial, or finally as false, and that nothing be received as true, unless it squares entirely with the principles of nature and reason. For he says that what is believed by faith does not consist in any proper judgment of the faculties, but is resolved into the knowledge of the author from whom the credibility of the history flowed, and that what is true in the narrator is only probable in the receiver: for there is no norm of another's truth, but what seems to sound true in the author can in reality be false, etc. Concerning which matter he discourses at greater length in Op. de Ver. page 297 et seq.

These things notwithstanding, it must finally be admitted that the Author, when in the cited Opusculum de Veritate page 298 he says: Let that one, Holy Scripture, stand as the HIGHEST among books; and likewise after a few words interposed: We receive that book (Holy Scripture) with the highest veneration, nor do we find comfort or firmer protection anywhere else; grants to the Code of Holy Scripture a certain prerogative over other Codes held as sacred, for a double reason, as it seems: One, because the aforementioned five articles most known by nature are more frequently inculcated and more fully declared in it than in any other Code. The other, because it is more replete with deeds done and miracles conspicuous for their antiquity and confirmed by the testimony of the Church. The Author insinuates both in the words immediately following in the same place, when he is about to render a reason for his assertion that he receives this book (of Scripture) with the highest veneration, and that he finds no comfort or firmer support anywhere else: For while, he says, knowledge is restored by common notions, with which it abounds, as faith is by miracles, the whole inner man is awakened, and is composed for the future state of life (which is explicitly enunciated): namely, he professes that he receives the Code of Holy Scripture with the highest veneration, not precisely because of the infallible truth and certainty of divine revelation, through which it might depend immediately from God: for this he does not acknowledge; but because of the common notions with which it abounds, and in so far as knowledge is restored by them, and the whole inner man is awakened, and is composed for the future state of life. As these common notions are evident and have been and are confirmed by the consensus of all nations and peoples who are and have been under the sun, so the code of Holy Scripture, in which it is more replete with them than other books held as sacred, is to be received with the greater veneration, according to him, both because of their evidence and indubitable certainty, and because of the consenting testimony of all peoples and nations. And this is his prior reason why he thinks the Code of Holy Scripture should be regarded with the highest veneration, others being set aside: which, although in its own way it also returns to human testimony, yet for our present purpose it does little or nothing. For the Author does not simply derogate certainty from all human testimony, but only from testimony concerning past things, the knowledge of which cannot be obtained from the faculties of the soul well-formed, as he speaks, but depends on the knowledge and faith of another. Whence we do not appeal so much to this cause of the prerogative which he assigns to the Code of Scripture, as to the other, which he establishes in the testimony of the Church concerning past things. He insinuates this in the same place, when he says that knowledge is restored by notions; and FAITH by miracles and sacred things performed, expressly establishing the reason for assenting to the narratives concerning miracles performed of old and concerning past things also in the testimony of the Church or with that of those in whose Code they are contained. And in this also the Author prefers the Code of Holy Scripture to the codices of other assemblies, and thus compelled by the force of truth he finally acknowledges that faith must be given to the testimony of the universal Church concerning the divinity of Holy Scripture, and indeed with greater right than to the testimony of other assemblies, which falsely claim the divinity of their own codices, as they call them, and thus even against his will he descends to our side. Thus in the former Appendix, page 9 and following. Where therefore, he says, among the various Churches or assemblies which have claimed the Word of God for themselves alone, you, O Traveler, have taken into your hands their sacred codex (by whatever name it may be distinguished), it must be seen what is judged to be consistent with RIGHT REASON, that is, with a sound conformation of the faculties, and what is further judged to be consistent with FAITH CONCERNING PAST EVENTS, so that he may decide about each separately. And thus our European (Traveler) will find the Holy Scriptures, handed down to the Jews and thence to the Gentiles, more conspicuous than the rest both in ANTIQUITY and in excellent AUTHORITY. For which reason, in all things WHICH ARE DECLARED TO HAVE BEEN DONE OF OLD, he can apply CONSUMMATE FAITH (BY THE AUTHORITY OF THE CHURCH), etc. By which, just as he refers the certainty of doctrine, necessary to be believed, to its agreement with right reason, so he refers the certainty of historical faith concerning past events not obscurely to the testimony of the Church, and he confesses that it cannot be despised or rejected without rashness. To which also pertains what he says, after a few words are interposed, in the same place: Certainly, he says, things very wonderful are handed down in Holy Scripture more than in all other histories, but they are things which do not blunt the intellect, but exercise or sharpen it. But let the Church see to these things. For those things which (if she were silent) I would not have known, I would never have believed WITHOUT HER TESTIMONY. Indeed, in his Work on Truth, cited page 299, he says that he accepts miracles everywhere not only as possible to be done, but as actually done (especially when they have been performed for some good end); and he adds: For why should anyone alone doubt, when the authority of any history, whether sacred or profane, is supported, surrounded, and fortified by many most famous provinces, centuries, and writers? But to pursue these things more extensively is not the purpose of the present undertaking.

I proceed to the other signs and motives of credibility, not however to list all, but only the more important ones, and those at least intending to commemorate by theses rather than to explain by a full treatment, and to defend against doubts offered on both sides. For because the pages already seem to have exceeded their limit by their own bulk, it is not permitted for me to be more prolix now.

Latin:

faciem. Proxima est tibi Achaja? habes Corinthum. Si non longè es à Macedonia, habes Philippos. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiæ adjaces, habes Romam &c. Verba extant in libr. de Præscriptionibus adversus hæreticos, quibus haud obscurè innuit, Pauli authographa Epistolarum, ad Corin:thios quidem Corinthi; ad Philippenses Philippis; ad Ephesios Ephesi; ad Romanos Romæ tùm temporis extitisse, & custodita fuisse. Evangelium Johannis, ipsâ ejus manu scriptum, adhuc Honorii Imperatoris tempore, sub finem seculi quarti, in Ecclesia Ephesina extitisse, Auctor Chronici Alexandrini memorat. Neque dubium est, quin cæterorum etiam Scriptorum N. T. autographa, velut pretiosa κειμήλια, multis seculis in Ecclesiis conservata fuerint. Extant prætereà monumenta & Scripta Patrum cùm Antiquissimorum, qui ipsa Apostolorum autographa consulere potuerunt; tùm sequentium seculorum, in quibus pleraq; Scripturæ N. T. loca & verba, cum codicibus nostris ad amussim congruentia, sparsim allegata inveniuntur, quod non obscuro documento est, Codices hodiernos eosdem planè esse cum autographis & apographis, quibus illi cùm post Apostolorum tempora proxime, tum sequentibus seculis constanter usi sunt. Sed hæc ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, de quibus ex instituto agere alterius loci est.

Quòd quartò denique auctor probari postulat, Revelationem, Prophetæ aut Apostolo olim factam, ad posteros ita intimè spectare, ut in articulum fidei necessario transeat; difficultatem non habet. Nam via ad salutem omnibus una est; & quod uni ad salutem creditu necessarium est, sive uni singulari Prophetæ vel Apostolo, sive pluribus ejus revelatio divinitùs obtigerit, id omnibus, quibus ejus revelatio promulgata & nota est, creditu necessarium, & articulus fidei est, sicut quæ sub Testamento Veteri Prophetis; & sub Novo Apostolis obtigêre revelationes, ab illis Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ; ab his recens per orbem terrarum plantatis Ecclesiis voce & scriptis promulgatæ & publici juris factæ sunt.

Testimonio Ecclesiæ igitur de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine, nihil quicquam obstantibus Auctoris rationibus dubitandi allatis, sua constat auctoritas, per quam assensus ei debetur. Quod Auctor tandem diffiteri non potest. Postquam enim in Opusculo de Veritate pag. 296. Universam traditionem, Historiam universam, universum illud demum, quod demandatur olim de rebus, sive verè, sive falsè, sive piè, sive impiè gestis, in illorum retulerat classem, quæ respectu nostri verisimilia, non vera sint, quippe quæ à narrantis authoritate pendeant, & de verisimilibus illorumq; à Veris differentia nonnulla subjecerat, objecit pag. 298. sibi ipsi: Sed, inquiens, itáne historiarum fidem convellis, infirmas, quasi parum fecisse videamur, qui historiam Creationis, Redemtionis mundi &c. tradiderunt? & respondit ibidem, nequaquam hisce concidere vel detrahi historiæ sacræ fidem, cui cum maxima hominum parte adsensum ita lubentissimè præbeat, ut & ista & majora fecisse Deum, si prædicarentur, omninò crederet; sed cognitionem & certam scientiam à fide per auditionem se ita distinguere, ut quid sciri, quid credi possit, in omni religione advertat; & concludit : Stet igitur inter libros Summus, ille Scripturæ sacræ, cujus ut varii fuerint Auctores, quos miro nexu inter se composuit seculum istud posterius, quid tamen non θεόπνευστον toto contextu, quid non tanquam sanctum, & à Deo profectum opus, piè credi possit? Istum igitur librum (cæteris sepositis) summa veneratione accipimus, neque allibi solamen comparamus vel præsidium firmius. Et seq. pag. 299. Quorsum solus dubitaret quispiam, cùm pluribus celeberrimis Provinciis, sæculis, Scriptoribus Authoritas Historiæ alicujus sive sacræ sive prophanæ vallata, stipata, munita sit?

Verùm cum his non convenire videntur, quæ supra ex Appendice utraque, Tractatui de causis errorum annexa, adduximus, nempe quòd in Appendice posteriori sub initium statim contendit, religionem orthodoxam inceptandam stabilendamque potiùs esse ex divinæ Universalis providentiæ principiis, quàm ex iis fidei thesibus, quæ à revelationibus quibusdam particularibus in aliqua orbis parte (ceu olim factis) deductæ, arcana Dei consilia ita posteris vel in omne ævum patefacta esse supponunt;& quòd postea in subnexa quæstione IV. omnes Codices, quibus diversæ Gentium & populorum religiones consignatæ sunt, quovis seculo vel regione receptos, cum Scripturæ sacræ Codice pari loco habet; itemque quòd Quæst. V. æquè omnes cœtus particulares, qui in Codicis alicujus sacri verba jurârunt, perstringit, quòd complures Sectæ & Schismata inter illos suborta sint, dum aliæ & aliæ interpretationes sensus Codicis adducuntur; tacitè subinnuens, in nullius Codicis sacri verba jurandum, sed simpliciter quinque illis, sæpè ab ipso inculcatis articulis, quibus religionem Catholicam totam comprehensam vult, insistendum esse. Quò accedit, quòd in sexta quæstione dicit: Ut detur inter multos, qui extitêre vel extant, Sacros Codices, unum aliquem (reliquis sepositis) indubiè recipi, controversiasque omnes tolli posse, inquiri tamen debere, num nova, quæ exinde procuduntur, dogmata humani generis bono ab Antistitibus promifcuè evulgentur &c. Quibus sanè, velut hypothesin non concessam habet, quòd inter multos, qui extitêre vel extant, sacros Codices unus aliquis (reliquis sepositis) indubiè recipi possit &c.

Quibus stantibus quomodo inter libros sive Codices sacros Summus stare possit ille Scripturæ sacræ Codex? quomodo eum cæteris sepositis summâ veneratione accipere possit? non facilè apparet.

Neque Auctor se expedit distinctione inter scientiam & fidem, quòd scientia certior sit fide; imò scientia sola certa, fides verò non certa, sed verisimilis tantùm cognitio sit, cui falsum subesse possit, & sæpissimè subsit. Quamvis enim hoc concedi possit de fide humana, de fide divina tamen, quam dari Auctor vix agnoscet, falsissimum est. Fides enim, divinæ revelationi innixa, quam divinam dicimus, tam certa est, quàm certa ulla scientia est aut esse potest, ob infinitam Dei revelantis scientiam & bonitatem, per quam nec falli in revelando, nec fallere potest. Neque etiam distinctio inter scientiam & fidem intra ipsos Scripturæ cancellos locum eo invenit sensu, quasi ipsa Scriptura quædam scientificè & per demonstrationes; alia verò per divinam revelationem & fide acceptanda tradat. Quemadmodum enim Scriptura tota θεόπνευστος sive divinitùs inspirata est, ita & tota fide amplectenda est, propter divinam inspirationem sive revelationem. Quamvis verò nonnulla etiam in ea reperiantur, quæ ex lumine naturæ cognosci possunt, & quorum scientia haberi potest, illorum demonstrationes tamen ad Scripturam sacram non pertinent, sed ad Philosophiam. Objectum formale enim Scripturæ sacræ non consistit in naturæ principiis scientificis & evidentibus, sed in obscura revelatione divina. Auctor verò intra ipsos Scripturæ limites distinguit inter scientiam & fidem, ut velut certa, & quibus falsum subesse non possit, ea solùm recipienda contendat, quæ ex lumine & principiis naturæ cognosci possunt: cujusmodi sunt quinque illi, ab ipso sæpiùs inculcati, communissimi & inter omnes populos recepti articuli, Esse Deum, eum esse colendum &c. in quibus centrum & summam totius Scripturæ & religionis Catholicæ constitutam vult; & quæ ad horum uberiorem declarationem in Scriptura sacra traduntur, aut per modum conclusionum ex illis inferri possunt. Cætera omnia, quæ sive in Scripturæ sacræ Codice, sive in aliis pro sacris habitis Codicibus, velut revelata, traduntur, non in veris, sed verisimilibus, vel possibilibus, vel iis, quæ sua in origine suspecta, involuta, controversa sunt, vel denique in falsis haberi, nec quicquam ut verum recipi vult, nisi quod ad naturæ & rationis principia ex asse quadret. Quod enim fide creditur, nullo proprio Facultatum judicio constare, sed resolvi in cognitionem authoris, à quo historiæ fides manavit, & quod in narrante verum, in accipiente esse solummodò verisimile ait: alienæ enim veritatis nullam esse normam, sed quod verum in authore sonare videtur, re ipsa falsum esse posse &c. Qua de re in Op. de Ver. pag. 297. seq. pluribus disserit.

Hisce tamen non obstantibus, fatendum tandem est, Auctorem, quando in allegato Opusculo de Veritate pag. 298. dicit: Stet inter libros SUMMUS, ille Scriptura sacra; itemque post pauca interjecta: Istum librum (Scripturæ sacræ) summa veneratione accipimus, neque ullibì solamen comparamus vel præsidium firmius; concedere Codici Scripturæ sacræ prærogativam quandam præ aliis Codicibus, pro sacris habitis, duplici, ut videtur, de causa: Unâ, quòd memorati quinque naturâ notissimi articuli in illo frequentiùs inculcentur & uberius declarentur, quàm in alio ullo Codice. Alterâ, quòd rebus gestis & miraculis antiquitate conspicuis Ecclesiæque testimonio comprobatis refertior sit. Utramque Auctor verbis, ibidem immediatè subjectis, insinuat, quando assertionis suæ, quòd istum (Scripturæ) librum summâ veneratione accipiat, neque ullibi solamen comparet vel præsidium firmius; rationem redditurus: Dum enim, ait, Notitiis communibus, quibus scatet, instauratur scientia, uti miraculis fides, totus internus homo exuscitetur, & in futurum (qui disertè enunciatur) vitæ statum componitur: nempe Codicem Scripturæ sacræ summâ veneratione se accipere profitetur, non præcisè propter infallibilem veritatem & certitudinem revelationis divinæ, per quam immediatè à Deo dependeat: hanc enim non agnoscit; sed propter notitias communes, quibus scateat, & in quantum illis scientia instauretur, totusque homo internus exuscitetur, & in futurum vitæ statum componatur. Quæ notiones communes uti evidentes & omnium, qui sub sole sunt & fuerunt, Gentium & populorum consensu comprobatæ sunt & comprebantur, ita Scripturæ sacræ codex, quo illis refertior est, quàm codices sacri habiti alii, eò majori veneratione, juxta eum, recipiendus est, cum propter illarum evidentiam & indubitatam certitudinem, tum ob omnium populorum & gentium consentiens testimonium. Atque hæc prior ejus ratio est, cur Scripturæ sacræ Codicem cæteris sepositis, summâ veneratione suspiciendum putet: quæ licet suo modo etiam in testimonium humanum redeat, ad præsens tamen institutum nostrum parum aut nihil facit. Non enim Auctor simpliciter omni testimonio humano certitudinem derogat, sed tantum testimonio de rebus præteritis, quarum cognitio non ex facultatibus animæ benè conformatis, ut ille loquitur, comparari potest, sed ab alterius scientia & fide pendet. Unde non tam ad hanc prærogativæ, quam Codici Scripturæ assignat, causam provocamus, quàm ad alteram, quam in testimonio Ecclesiæ de rebus præteritis constituit. Hanc insinuat ibidem, quando Notitiis scientiam; miraculis rebusque sacris gestis FIDEM instaurari ait, rationem assentiendi narrationibus de miraculis olim patratis deque rebus præteritis expressè etiam in testimonio Ecclesiæ vel cum illorum, in quorum Codice continentur, constituens. Atque in hoc etiam præfert Auctor Codicem Scripturæ sacræ aliorum Cœtuum Codicibus, atque sic veritatis vi coactus agnoscit tandem, testimonio universæ Ecclesiæ de Scripturæ sacræ divinitate adhibendam esse fidem, & majori quidem jure, quàm testimonio aliorum Cœtuum, quod de suorum, quos dicunt, Codicum divinitate falsò perhibent, atq; adeò vel invitus in nostras partes descendit. Ita in Appendice priori pag. 9. seq. Ubi igitur, ait, inter diversas, quæ sibi solis Dei vendicaverint Verbum Ecclesias sive Cœtus, Codicem illorum sacrum (quocunque nomine insigniatur) in manus sumpseris Viator, videndum, quid RATIONI RECTÆ, probæ scilicet Facultatum conformationi, quid FIDEI porro CIRCA PRÆTERITA existimetur congruum, ut de utraque seorsim statuat. Atque ita Europæus noster (Viator) præ cæteris conspicuas tum ANTIQVITATE tum AUTHORITATE eximiâ S. S. Judæis, & inde Gentibus traditas inveniet. Quibus idcircò in omnibus, QVÆ OLIM GESTA prædicantur (EX ECCLESIÆ AUTHORITATE) FIDEM CONSUMMATAM adhibere potest &c. Quibus ut certitudinem doctrinæ, creditu necessariæ, in ejus convenientiam cum recta ratione; ita fidei historicæ certitudinem de rebus præteritis haud obscurè in Ecclesiæ testimonium refert, idq; citra temeritatem contemni aut rejici non posse fatetur. Quò pertinet etiam, quod, post pauca interjecta, ibidem: Certè, inquit, mira admœdùm in S. S. plusquàm in reliquis omnibus Historiis traduntur, sed quæ non retundunt intellectum, sed exercent vel acuunt. Sed de his viderit Ecclesia. Quæ enim (illâ tacente) haud rescivissem, CITRA ILLIUS TESTIMONIUM haud credidissem unquam. Quin in Opus. de Verit. citatâ pag. 299. dicit, miracula se non solùm ceu factu possibilia, sed ceu reverà facta (maximè verò cum in bonum aliquem finem edita fuerint) ubique accipere; & subjungit: Quorsum enim solus dubitaret quispiam, cùm pluribus celeberrimis, Provinciis, sæculis, Scriptoribus Authoritas Historiæ alicujus sive sacræ sive prophanæ, vallata, stipata, munita sit? Sed hæc fusiùs persequi præsentis instituti non est.

Ad cætera credibilitatis signa & motiva progredior, non tamen omnia, sed tantùm potiora subjuncturus, eaq; succinctis saltem thesibus commemoraturus potiùs, quàm justâ tractatione explicaturus, & à dubiis ultrò citroque; oblatis vindicaturus. Quia enim jam dum chartæ mole suâ modum excessisse videntur, nunc prolixiori mihi esse non licet.


### V. We therefore assign the fifth place to the more than human constancy of…

V.

We therefore assign the fifth place to the more than human constancy of innumerable Martyrs of every sex and age, by which they intrepidly asserted the truth of the divine Word amidst the most grievous tortures, and sealed with their own blood the testimony which they bore to it.

I. To the sign of the divinity of Scripture, sought from the testimony of the Church, this one taken from the constancy of the Martyrs is not inconveniently subjoined. For martyrdom, whether you look at the force of the word or the usage of speech, is a certain testimony. For the words Μάρτυς and Μαρτύριον are Greek in origin, and the former signifies a witness, the latter testimony. But from the usage of speech, both words are sometimes taken generally for any witness and testimony in any cause whatsoever, just as II. Cor. XIII, 1. it is said: In the mouth of δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν of two witnesses or three shall every word stand, i.e., by the testimony of two or three witnesses in any cause whatsoever faith shall be had; but sometimes it is said specially and κατ' ἐξοχήν that a Martyr is a witness who testifies specifically concerning the divine origin and truth of Christian doctrine and sacred Scripture, so that by shed blood and his very death he confirms and as it were seals his testimony; and martyrdom is testimony concerning the divinity of Christian doctrine and sacred Scripture, which someone confirms and seals by the passions, tortures, and very death brought upon him by the hand of persecutors. And in this latter and special signification are the words Martyr and martyrdom taken at present. Although, however, this sign or argument taken from the constancy of the Martyrs and the one immediately preceding, which was taken from the testimony of the Church, agree in this, that both are taken from testimony, they differ nevertheless from one another, (1.) by reason of the witnesses. For the former is founded on the testimony of the universal Church, which has existed spread throughout the world from the times of the Apostles. But this latter relies upon the testimony of a certain part of the Church, namely of those faithful and holy ones who, amid raging persecutions, shed their own blood for heavenly truth. (2.) By reason of the testimony. For that former testimony is verbal, which they bore by voice and writings in professing, teaching, and defending heavenly truth against heresies. But this latter is real rather than by a verbal profession of it, but especially by the endurance of sufferings and tortures and by death itself, so much so that martyrdom, by usage of speech, is often taken for the very tortures and death which someone undergoes for the heavenly truth in a time of persecution. Whence (3.) that one is and has been perpetual. For the Church, at appointed times, always has its public assemblies in which it may teach the Word of God and testify concerning its truth and divine origin, unless perhaps in some places it is sometimes hindered by the cruelty and tyranny of persecutors: which will be accidental. But this one exerts itself only in the Church in a time of persecution. However, just as the persecutions of the Church are not perpetual, but are accustomed to be stirred up by Satan and the world, God permitting, at certain intervals of time and in certain places, so neither are martyrdoms always and everywhere given in the Church.

II. The power of testifying of both relies upon the divine virtue inherent in the Word of God, written and preached, or, which amounts to the same thing, upon the supernatural assistance and concurrence of God, by which, with His divine virtue joined in the first act and in an inseparable bond to the Word of God both written and preached, He illuminates the mind of man, strikes, bends, draws, and determines the will to command the intellect to the assent of faith, and thus testifies inwardly in the heart of man concerning the divinity and infallible truth of His Word, both preached and written. And this divine power or virtue of testifying shines forth equally in both testimonies, that of the Church and that of the martyrs. For from it the whole Church has that it offers undoubted assent to the Word of God, written and preached, and believes that this is the Word of God and that it proceeded from His immediate revelation, and it professes this very thing also in public assemblies by the voice and preaching of those who teach, and, outside of them, also in public writings, and teaches others. From the same also the holy martyrs had, in a time of persecution, that they bore testimony to the Word of God, written and preached, and to the whole Christian doctrine in the sight of the persecutors, as often as they professed themselves to be Christians. For he who then in the sight of the persecutors had called himself a Christian, had said everything. But because this special profession of the holy Martyrs is surrounded and as it were walled in on all sides by the most immediate dangers to those professing, by passions and most exquisite tortures, and by the most ignominious death itself, for the enduring of which human strengths are equal, therefore in this profession or testimony of the Martyrs that divine power with the Word of God already believed, and the Holy Spirit, dwelling through faith in their hearts, also in another peculiar way on the part of the professing or testifying Martyrs both formerly exerted itself and even now exerts itself, namely by strengthening and exciting their faith to the confession of the truth with great παῤῥησίᾳ, with nothing at all standing in the way of the most immediate dangers and tortures, by raising them up with effective comforts, and by strengthening and confirming their minds against the infirmities of the flesh, and sustaining them, lest in enduring the most immense tortures and most bitter death they succumb and fail. Although indeed in the testimony of the holy Martyrs that power, intimately joined to the Word of God, exerts itself and makes itself conspicuous in both ways, because however it has the former in common with the testimony of the Church, not so much that one, as this other mode of operation, by which it exerts itself for the enduring of any tortures whatsoever and death itself for the sake of heavenly truth, is attended to in it; and from this especially the argument drawn from the constancy of the martyrs has its force, strength, and efficacy. And we indeed, who enlightened by the power of the Word, have acknowledged its divinity, and with divine faith have embraced it, with the Thessalonians 1. Thess. 11. 13. Acts XVII. not as the word of men, but (as it is truly) as the Word of God, with divine faith, we are certain by divine faith of its invincible strength. For our knowledge, which we have concerning the power of the divine Word in both ways of testifying to its divine origin, rests upon divine revelation, John XIV. 16. 26. c. XVI. 1. 1. Tim. III. 15. Matt. XVI. 18. c. X. 19. 20. Mark XII. 11. Luke XIX. 11. 12. c. XXI. 14. II. Cor. I. 3. 4. Rom. VIII. 38. 39. But in relation to infidels, who have not yet experienced the divine power of the Word in themselves, nor believe its promises, the argument, drawn both from the testimony of the Church and from the constancy of the martyrs, begets opinion, and the force of its concluding consists in this, that it cannot be that a multitude of believers diffused through the whole world in a false doctrine everywhere should agree, and from the time of the Apostles have constantly agreed; the reason for this conclusion, however, is that the pains and tortures, which martyrs of all sexes and ages in an innumerable multitude sustained, they could not have endured that very bitter and most ignominious death, unless God by His grace through His Word, had raised them up in their afflictions with effective consolation, had strengthened and confirmed them against the infirmities of the flesh, and had sustained them so that they would not succumb; but God, who is truth, would stand by no one, either to establish and propagate errors, or to sustain afflictions, tortures, and death itself for the sake of false and erroneous doctrines.

III. That the force of the argument may become more manifest, certain circumstances must be observed here. And first indeed it must be observed, that its force of concluding is not constituted in any kind of tolerance of tortures and death; but in their voluntary tolerance for the sake of the confession of divine truth alone. For wicked men are also accustomed to endure tortures and death itself, but unwillingly and because of crimes committed, for which they pay just penalties, from which also, if they could escape the hands of the lictors and executioners, they would most gladly withdraw themselves. The martyrs, however, conspicuous to all by the praise of innocence and holiness, did not undergo torments and tortures because of any crime committed: for they were not accused and sought for punishments under any other name than that they were Christians and confessors of the Christian religion, which they all could have escaped, if they had been willing to fall away from their confession and deny Christ. But that they preferred to undergo the most exquisite torments and tortures and any most bitter and ignominious death, rather than to recede even a fingernail's breadth from the truth of the Christian religion and its confession, that indeed is an argument that, being divinely persuaded of the invincible truth of the Christian religion and doctrine, and excited by the Holy Spirit to its intrepid confession, they were raised up and confirmed in the midst of pains and tortures. Next, it must be observed that we do not constitute the force of the argument in the tortures and death which one or another perhaps, or some few, and those of the more worthy sex and more confirmed age, who are accustomed to be more present-minded in dangers and fearful things; but which the faithful of both sexes and all ages in crowds they endured with the greatest patience. For they sometimes even endure tortures and death for their heresies; just as Nicephorus, book IV of his History, chapter XXIII, reports from Apollinaris, that heretics have sometimes even boasted of their falsely called martyrs; but that happens rarely, by a few, in one or another corner of the world, from the power and deceptions of Satan, by which he has fascinated their minds and hardened them in heresy. But true martyrs, as often and wherever persecutions have been stirred up in the world, by God's permission, in an innumerable multitude, and among them men and women, boys and girls, adolescents and tender virgins, as well as decrepit old men, have indiscriminately undergone any tortures whatsoever and the most bitter death for the confession of heavenly truth with an intrepid spirit, so much so that in the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, most dire tyrants and persecutors, at Nicomedia, among twenty thousand and more Christians of all sexes, ages, and stations, who had gathered in the temple to celebrate the Lord's Nativity, not even one could be found who, fearing death, would go out of the temple at the herald's voice, as one who wished to live, and burn incense on the nearby altar of Jupiter, otherwise, if he had not done this, he was to be burned together with the house itself; who would have preferred his life to death and would have gone out of the temple, but the voice of all was one: We are all Christians, we believe that Christ is the one and only God and King, and we are all readily prepared to sacrifice to Him and to His Father and to the Holy Spirit, and to offer ourselves all together, as may be read in Nicephorus, book VIII of his History, chapter VI. But that such a multitude of Christians of both sexes and any age should meet death for heavenly truth, this is what we profess to be above human strength and constancy, and to be attributed to the special grace and help of God. Thirdly, the force of the argument, drawn from the constancy of the martyrs, is increased by the greatest alacrity and cheerfulness of spirit, with which not only those Christians who were recognized and sought out, but sometimes those who were unknown and who could have remained hidden, flocked together and voluntarily professed themselves to be Christians. Thus Eusebius concerning the Diocletian persecution in the Thebaid, book VIII of his History, chapter IX. We ourselves, he says, saw many together in one day, some suffering decapitation, others the punishment of fire, so that the executioner blunted his sword, and failed from labor, and the exhausted slayers succeeded one another, when also we saw the most illustrious ALACRITY AND TRULY DIVINE virtue and promptness of spirit of those who had believed in Christ of God. For as soon as the sentence had been passed in the preceding case, others from elsewhere would leap forward, confessing themselves to be Christians, and having no care for any of the bitter and various kinds of torments, but with an unbroken spirit, trusting in the piety toward the God of all, they received the final sentence of death with joy, laughter, and cheerfulness, so that they sang psalms and directed hymns and thanksgivings to the God of all even to the final exhalation of their breath. And Nicephorus, in the cited book VII, chapter VIII, writes concerning the same persecution: It was possible to observe in our people ALACRITY AND A VIVID ARDOR OF FAITH IN CHRIST: for when the sentence of condemnation had scarcely been pronounced by the judge against the former ones, others flowing in from elsewhere would profess themselves to be Christians, exulting before the very tribunal, and not regarding the bitterness of the torments, they most willingly received the supreme sentence with great joy of soul: to such an extent that with thanksgiving they would sing hymns and praises to God very decently even to the end. Similar things are read everywhere among the Ecclesiastical Historians. But that people of both sexes and of any age should undergo any tortures and the most bitter death for the sake of the confession of truth with such alacrity and joy of soul is, again, not a matter of human strength, but of divine power and assistance, and it provides an unmistakable proof of it. Fourthly, finally, the kinds of torments and tortures to which the martyrs were subjected were so various, so exquisite, and so cruel that they were far above human strength and human constancy, and had the holy martyrs not been raised up, strengthened, and confirmed by divine power, hardly anyone could have subjected himself to them and exhibited his constancy in them by the very act. Concerning the Egyptian Christians, not to go far afield, and their persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, Eusebius reports in the aforementioned book, chapter VIII, that innumerable men, together with women and children, because of the doctrine of our Savior, despising this temporary life, underwent VARIOUS kinds of death, of whom some, after scrapings and tortures and most grievous beatings and a thousand others, various and horrible to hear of, were delivered to the fire, others were immersed in the sea, others offered their heads to be truncated by lictors, others again were suspended on a cross, part after the manner of criminals, part even worse, fixed to trunks with heads hanging down and kept alive for a time on gallows, until they were killed by hunger. The same author commemorates more kinds of torments and tortures in the preceding and following chapter, and they occur noted here and there in other places in him and other historians, so that there is no need to waste time in recounting them.

Latin:

V.

QVintum ergo locum tribuimus innumerabilium cujusvis sexus & ætatis Martyrum constantiæ plus quàm humanæ, quâ gravissimos inter cruciatus Verbi divini veritatem intrepidè asseruerunt, &, quod ei perhibuerunt, testimonium suo sanguine obsignarunt.

I. Signo divinitatis Scripturæ, à testimonio Ecclesiæ petito, non incommodè subjungitur hoc à constantia Martyrum desumtum. Martyrium enim, sive vim vocis sive usum loquendi spectes, testimonium quoddam est. Nam Μάρτυς & Μαρτύριον voces origine Græcæ sunt, & illa testem, hæc testimonium significat. Ex usu loquendi verò vox utraque accipitur interdum generaliter pro quolibet teste & testimonio in quacunque causa, sicut II. Cor. XIII, 1. dicitur: In ore δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν duorum testium aut trium consistet omne verbum, h. e. duorum aut trium testium testimonio in quacunque causa fides habebitur; interdum verò specialiter & κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur Martyr testis, qui de divina doctrinæ Christianæ Scripturæque; sacræ origine & veritate in specie testificatur, ita ut effuso sanguine & ipsâ morte suâ testimonium suum confirmet, & quasi obsignet; martyrium verò testimonium de doctrinæ Christianæ & Scripturæ sacræ divinitate, quod quis illatis persecutorum manu passionibus, cruciatibus & ipsa morte confirmat & obsignat. Atque in hoc posteriori ac speciali significatu Martyris & Martyrii voces impræsentiarum accipiuntur. Quamvis verò hoc, à constantia Martyrum petitum signum sive argumentum & proxime præcedens, quod à testimonio Ecclesiæ desumebatur, in hoc conveniant, quod utrumque à testimonio desumtum sit, differunt tamen ab invicem, (1.) ratione testium. Prius enim fundatur in testimonio universæ Ecclesiæ, quæ inde ab Apostolorum temporibus per orbem terrarum diffusa extitit. Hoc alterum verò certæ cujusdam partis Ecclesiæ, illorum scilicet fidelium & sanctorum, qui sævientibus persecutionibus pro veritate cœlesti sanguinem suum profuderunt, testimonio nititur. (2.) ratione testimonii. Illud enim verbale est, quod veritati cœlesti profitendo, docendo, & adversus hæreses eam tuendo voce & scriptis perhibuerunt. Hoc autem reale magis, quàm verbale est, quippe quod veritati cœlesti non solùm verbali ejus professione, sed maximè tolerantiâ passionum & cruciatuum ipsaque morte perhibetur, adeò ut martyrium, ex usu loquendi, sæpe pro ipsis cruciatibus & morte, quam quis pro veritate cœlesti, persecutionis tempore, obit, accipiatur. Unde (3.) illud perpetuum est & fuit. Ecclesia enim, statis temporibus, semper suos habet conventus publicos, in quibus Verbum Dei doceat, deq; ejus veritate & divina origine testificetur, nisi alicubi locorum forsan sævitiâ & tyrannide persecutorum quandoque impediatur: quod per accidens erit. Hoc verò tempore persecutionis tantùm in Ecclesia se exerit. Quemadmodùm autem persecutiones Ecclesiæ non perpetuæ sunt, sed certis temporum intervallis certisque locis, Deo permittente, à Satana & mundo excitari solent, ita nec martyria semper & ubique locorum in Ecclesia dantur.

II. Utriusque vis testificandi nititur virtute divina, Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato, insitâ, sive, quod eodem redit, Dei supernaturali adsistentiâ & concursu, quo suâ divinâ virtute, Verbo Dei cum scripto tùm prædicato in actu primo semper & nexu individuo conjunctâ, mentem hominis illuminat, voluntatem pulsat, flectit, trahit, & ad assensum fidei intellectui imperandum determinat, atque adeò de divinitate ac infallibili veritate Verbi sui, & prædicati & scripti, intùs in hominis corde testificatur. Atque hæc divina testificandi vis sive virtus æquè in testimonio utroq;, Ecclesiæ & martyrum, relucet. Ab ea enim habet Ecclesia universa, quòd Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato, indubitatum præbet assensum, idq; Dei Verbum, & ab ejus immediata revelatione profectum esse credit, & hoc ipsum etiam in conventibus publicis docentium voce & prædicatione, &, extra eos, etiam publicis scriptis profitetur, aliosq; docet. Ab eadem etiam habuerunt sancti Martyres persecutionis tempore, quòd Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato, doctrinæq; Christianæ toti in persecutorum conspectu perhibuerunt testimonium, quotiescunq; se Christianos esse profitebantur. Qui enim tum in conspectu persecutorum se Christianum dixerat, omnia dixerat. Sed quia hæc specialis sanctorum Martyrum professio præsentissimis profitentium periculis, passionibus & cruciatibus exquisitissimis, & ipsa morte ignominiosissima, quibus perferendis humanæ vires pares non sunt, undique circumdata & quasi circumvallata est, ideò in hac Martyrum professione sive testificatione virtus illa divina cum Verbo Dei jam credito, & Spiritus sanctus, per fidem in illorum cordibus habitans, etiam alio peculiari modo ex parte profitentium sive testificantium Martyrum se & olim exeruit, & etiamnum exerit, nempe confortando & excitando illorum fidem ad confessionem veritatis cum magna παῤῥησίᾳ, nihil quicquam obstantibus periculis & cruciatibus præsentissimis, erigendo solatiis efficacibus, roborandoq; & confirmando illorum animos adversus carnis infirmitates, eosq; sustentando, ne in perferendis cruciatibus immanissimis & morte acerbissima succumbant & deficiant. Quamvis verò in sanctorum Martyrum testimonio vis illa, Verbo Dei intimè conjuncta, modo utroque sese exerat, seq; conspicuam faciat, quia tamen priorem cum Ecclesiæ testimonio communem habet, non tam ille, quàm hic alter operationis modus, quo ad quosvis cruciatus ipsamque mortem, propter veritatem cœlestem perferendam sese exerit, in eo attenditur; & ab hoc potissimùm habet argumentum à constantia martyrum petitum, suam vim, robur & efficaciam. Et nos quidem, qui virtute Verbi collustrati, ejus divinitatem agnovimus, fideq; divinâ illud, cum Thessalonicensibus 1. Thess. 11. 13. Act. XVII. non ut verbum hominum, sed (sicut est verè) ut Verbum Dei, fide divinâ amplexi sumus, de ejus invicto robore fide divinâ certi sumus. Nostra enim, quam de Verbi divini vi modo utroque de divina sui origine testificandi habemus, cognitio divinâ nititur revelatione, Joh. XIV. 16. 26. c. XVI. 1. 1.Tim. 111. 15. Matth. XVI. 18. c. X. 19. 20. Marc. XII. 11. Luc. XIX. 11. 12. c. XXI. 14. II. Cor. I. 3. 4. Rom. VIII. 38. 39. Sed in ordine ad infideles, qui divinam Verbi vim nondum in se experti sunt, neque ejus promissionibus credunt, argumentum, cùm à testimonio Ecclesiæ, tum à constantia martyrum petitum, opinionem gignit, & consistit illius vis concludendi in hoc, quòd fieri non possit, ut diffusa per totum orbem multitudo fidelium in doctrina falsa ubique locorum consentiant, & inde ab Apostolorum tempore constanter consenserint; hujus verò concludendi ratio est, quòd dolores & cruciatus, quos martyres omnium sexuum & ætatum innumerabili multitudine sustinuerunt, ipsamque acerbissimam & ignominiosissimam mortem perferre non potuissent, nisi Deus suâ gratiâ iis in mediis afflictionibus suis supernaturaliter adstitisset, per Verbum suum eorum mentes illuminâsset, in afflictionibus suis solatio efficaci erexisset, adversus infirmitates carnis roborâsset, confirmâsset, & ne succumberent, sustentâsset; Deus autem, qui veritas est, nemini adsistat, vel ad incrustandos & propagandos errores, vel ad afflictiones, cruciatus, ipsamq; mortem propter falsas & erroneas doctrinas sustinendam.

III. Ut vis argumenti manifestior evadat, quædam circumstantiæ hîc observandæ veniunt. Et primùm quidem observandum est, quòd ejus vis concludendi non constituatur in qualicunque tolerantia cruciatuum & mortis; sed in illorum tolerantia voluntaria propter solam divinæ veritatis confessionem. Nam homines scelerati etiam perferre solent cruciatus & ipsam mortem, sed inviti & propter perpetrata scelera, quorum justas pœnas luunt, quibus etiam, si lictorum & carnificum manus evadere possent, lubentissimè se subducerent. Martyres verò, innocentiæ & sanctitatis laude omnes conspicui, non subiêre tormenta & cruciatus propter ullum patratum scelus: non enim alio nomine, quàm quòd Christiani religionisque Christianæ Confessores essent, accusati & ad supplicia requisiti sunt, quæ etiã evadere omnes potuissent, si à confessione sua deficere, Christumq; abnegare voluissent. Quòd verò tormenta & cruciatus exquisitissimos quosque & quamvis acerbissimam & ignominiosissimam mortem obire, quàm à veritate religionis Christianæ ejusque confessione vel latum unguem recedere maluerunt, id verò argugumento est, quòd de invicta veritate religionis & doctrinæ Christianæ divinitùs persuasi, & ad ejusdem intrepidam confessionem à Spiritu Sancto excitati, atque in mediis doloribus & cruciatibus erecti & confirmati fuerint. Deinde observandum, quòd vim argumenti non constituamus in cruciatibus & morte, quos unus alterve forsan, vel aliqui pauci, iiq; sexus dignioris & ætatis confirmatioris, qui in periculis rebusq; formidolosis animo magis præsenti esse solent; sed quos utriusq; sexus; omniumq; ætatum fideles catervatim summâ patientiâ sustinuerunt. Nam hæreticos etiam perferunt interdum cruciatus & mortem propter suas hæreses; sicut Nicephorus lib. IV. Hist. c. XXIII. ex Apollinari refert, hæreticos etiam quandoq; gloriatos esse de suis falso dictis Martyribus; sed id contingit rarò, â paucis, in uno alterove orbis angulo, ex Satanæ vi & præstigiis, quibus eorum animos fascinavit, & in hæresi obfirmavit. Martyres veri autem, quotiescunque & ubicunq; locorum persecutiones, Dei permissu, in orbe terrarum excitatæ sunt, innumerabili multitudine, & inter eos viri & mulieres, pueri & puellæ, adolescentes & virgines teneræ, ut & senes decrepiti, promiscuè cruciatus quosvis & quamvis acerbissimam mortem pro confessione veritatis cœlestis intrepido obière animo, adeò ut in persecutione sub Diocletiano & Maximiano, tyrannis & persecutoribus dirissimis, Nicomediæ inter vicies mille & plures omnium sexuum, ætatum & statuum Christianos, qui intemplo ad celebrandum Natalem Domini convenerant, ne unus quidem inveniretur, qui mortem extimescens ad præconis vocem, ut qui vivere vellet, ex templo exiret, & in proxima arâ Jovis thura adoleret, alioqui nisi hoc fecisset, unà cum domo ipsa conflagraturus; vitam suam morti prætulisset, & templo egressus efset, sed omnium unâ vox fuit : Omnes Christiani sumus, unum eumque solum Deum & Regem credimus esse Christum, & ipsi Patrique ejus & Spiritui Sancto sacrificare, atque nos omnes unà offerre facilè parati sumus, ut apud Nicephorum lib. VIII. Hist. c. VI. legere est. Tantâ verò multitudine Christianos ex utroque sexu, & ætate quavis pro veritate cœlesti obire mortem, hoc est, quod supra vires & constantiam humanam esse, Deią; speciali gratiæ & auxilio acceptum ferendum profitemur. Tertiò vim argumenti, â constantia Martyrum petiti, auget summa alacritas animią, hilaritas, quâ non tantùm agniti & requisiti Christiani, sed nonnunquam ignoti, & qui latêre poterant, confluxerunt, & Christianos se esse ultrò professi sunt. Ita Eusebius de persecutione Diocletiana in Thebaïde lib. VIII. Hist. c. IX. Vidimus, inquit, & ipsi complures uno die cumulatim, alios capitis truncationem, alios ignis supplicium perpeti, ita ut lictor gladium suum hebetaret, laborandoque deficeret, ac delassati occisores sibi invicem succederent, quando etiam præclarissimam ALACRITATEM AC VERE DIVINAM virtutem animique promtitudinem eorum, qui in Christum Dei crediderant vidimus. Etenim mox atque in præcedente lata esset sententia, assiliebant aliunde alii, seque ipsos Christianos esse confitentes, nec ullam acerborum ac variorum tormentorum generum curam habentes, sed animo infracto pietate erga Deum omnium confisi cum gaudio, risuque ac hilaritate extremam mortis sententiam suscipiebant, ita ut psallerent, hymnosque & gratiarum actiones omnium Deo ad ultimam usque spiritus exhalationem destinarent. Et Nicephorus citato lib. VII. c. VIII. de eadem scribit persecutione: Animadvertere erat in hominibus nostris ALACRITATEM & FIDEI IN CHRISTUM ARDOREM VIVIDUM: quum enim vix contra priores sententia condemnationis à judice prolata esset, alii aliunde confluentes, Christianos se esse profitebantur, pro tribunali ipso exultantes, neque tormentorum acerbitatem respicientes, cum magna animorum lætitia libentissimè supremam excipiebant sententiam: usque adeò, ut cum gratiarum actione ad finem usque perquam decenter hymnos laudesque Deo canerent. His gemina leguntur passim apud Historicos Ecclesiasticos. Tantâ verò animi alacritate & lætitiâ utriusque sexus, & cujusvis ætatis homines quosvis cruciatus & accerbissimam quamque mortem obire, propter confessionem veritatis, rursum non humanarum virium, sed divinæ virtutis & adsistentiæ res est, ejusque non obscurum documentum præbet. Quartò denique tormentorum & cruciatuum genera, quibus subjecti fuerunt martyres, tam varia, tam exquisita, tamque crudelia fuerunt, ut longè supra humanas vires, humanamque constantiam essent, & nisi divinâ virtute erecti, roborati & confirmati fuissent sancti Martyres, vix quisquam se illis subjicere fuamq; in iis constantiam ipso facto exhibere potuisset. De Ægyptiis Christianis, ne longè abeam, illorumque persecutione sub Diocletiano & Maximiano refert Eusebius d. l. c. VIII. quod innumeri Viri una cum mulieribus ac pueris, propter Servatoris nostri doctrinam, temporariam hanc vitam contemnentes VARIA mortis genera subierint, quorum alii post rasuras & torturas gravissimasq; verbera & mille alios varios audituq; horrendos cruciatus igni traditi, alii pelago immersi fuerint, alii lictoribus capita sua truncanda porrexerint, rursum alii cruce suspensi sint, pars ad morem facinorosorum, pars pejus etiam capite demisso truncis affixi ac vivi tantisper in patibulis servati fuerint, dum fame enecarentur. Plura tormentorum & cruciatuum genera commemorat idem in præcedente & subsequente capite, & alibi locorum apud ipsum & alios Historicos passim annotata occurrunt, ut in iis recensendis tempus terere nihil opus sit.


### VI. The place next to the constancy of the Martyrs is claimed, not irrelevantly, by…

VI.

The place next to the constancy of the Martyrs is claimed, not irrelevantly, by the happy and sudden propagation of Christian doctrine throughout the whole world.

These two signs or motives flow from one source, namely from the divine power and efficacy of Scripture and the sacred doctrine contained in it. For from Christian doctrine, fixed in their hearts, and its truly divine power and efficacy, the holy martyrs have had, as has been shown, and still have, that in the time of persecution they underwent and undergo for the confession of the same every kind of torment, every kind of torture, every kind of most ignominious and bitter death with incredible and more than human constancy: and from the same, preached by the voice of the Apostles, and its power and efficacy, it comes about that in the time of the planting of the Church of Christ it was propagated so suddenly that immediately at the beginning in Jerusalem at one sermon of Peter three thousand souls were converted to Christ, Acts II. 41, and at another the number of believers grew to five thousand, c. IV. 4: Afterwards the assembly of the Church, becoming larger day by day, was propagated so quickly to other parts of the earth that the Apostle Paul testified in his time that the Apostolic preaching had already gone out into all the earth, and unto the ends of the world, Rom. X. 18. Wherever, however, we turn the eyes of our mind, we find nothing to which such speed of propagated religion and Christian doctrine can be ascribed, except its divine power and the assistance of God, helped by which it was effective in the hearts of men, and testified within the hearts of men to its divine origin and truth, and in a supernatural way drew minds into a certain and indubitable assent to itself. Miracles, as certain effects of divine power, indeed had the force of testifying outwardly to the divinity of Holy Scripture and the doctrine contained in it; but inwardly they have no force to illuminate the minds of men and to convert them to Christ. But all the other things that concurred were so arranged that, without that virtue and divine efficacy inherent in the Word, they would have hindered its propagation rather than promoted it. For on the part of those to be converted, the inveterate error of the Jews concerning the earthly kingdom of the Messiah and the Levitical worship that was never to cease stood in the way of its rapid propagation among other things; on the part of the pagans, their stubborn error in religion, or rather superstition and idolatry, which they had received from their ancestors and had, as it were, imbibed with their mother's milk; furthermore, on the part of the doctrine to be propagated, the sublimity of the mysteries, especially the mystery of redemption through Christ, and its height, which far exceeded the grasp of human reason, stood in the way, by which it came about that Christ crucified, who is the basis and foundation of the whole Christian religion, was preached by the Apostles as a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, as the Apostle of the Gentiles himself testifies, 1. Cor. 1. 23. c. 11. 14. On the part of those propagating it, it could have been an obstacle that they were instructed neither by eloquence nor by human wisdom, nor by other aids necessary for teaching and persuading. For they were all unlettered, fishermen, and unlearned men, with the exception of Paul, who had indeed been accurately instructed in the law of his fathers at the feet of Gamaliel, Acts XXII. 6, yet he could not deny that he was unlearned in speech, II. Cor. XI. 6. It could also have been an obstacle on their part that they were not aided by the public favor of princes and magnates, nor by the counsel of the wise of this world; but rather, hindered everywhere by the opposing force and cruelty of persecutors and tyrants, they performed the duty of teaching. But that, notwithstanding all these things, the Christian religion and doctrine was propagated with such speed throughout the whole world amidst the harshest persecutions, that is indeed an evident proof that it is truly the Word of God and is endowed with a singular and truly divine power for winning the souls of men to itself, otherwise it would by no means have proceeded so far.

Latin:

VI.

Locum à constantia Martyrum proximum haud præter rem sibi vendicat felix & subita doctrinæ Christianæ per totum terrarum orbem propagatio.

Duo hæc signa sive motiva ex uno promanant fonte, nempè ex Scripturæ & contentæ in ea doctrinæ sacræ divina virtute & efficacia. A doctrina Christiana enim, cordibus suis infixâ, ejusq; vi & efficacia verè divina habuerunt, uti ostensum, habentq; sancti martyres, quòd persecutionis tempore pro ejusdem confessione nulla non tormenta, nullos non cruciatus, nullum non ignominiosissimæ & acerbissimæ mortis genus incredibili & plusquàm humanâ constantiâ subierunt & subeunt: & ab eâdem, Apostolorum voce prædicatâ, ejusq; virtute & efficaciâ provenit, quod tempore plantandæ Ecclesiæ Christi tàm subitò propagata est, ut sub initium statim Hierosolymis ad unam Petri concionem animæ ter mille ad Christum converterentur, Act. II. 41. ad alteram verò credentium numerus ad quinquies mille excresceret, c. IV. 4: Postea Ecclesiæ cœtus indies auctior redditus ita celeriter ad alias terræ partes propagatus est, ut suo tempore Paulus Apostolus testaretur, prædicationem Apostolicam jam tum exiisse in omnem terram, & in fines orbis terrarum, Rom. X. 18. Quocunq; autem circumferimus oculos mentis, nihil invenimus, cui tanta propagatæ religionis & doctrinæ Christianæ celeritas possit adscribi, præter divinam ejus virtutem Deiq́; adsistentiam, quâ adjuta in hominum cordibus efficax, deq́; divina sui origine & veritate intus in hominum cordibus testificata est, & modo supernaturali mentes in sui assensum certum & indubitatum traxit. Miracula, velut effectus quidam divinæ potentiæ, habebant quidem vim exterius testificandi de divinitate Scripturæ sacræ doctrinæq; in ea contentæ; interiùs verò hominum mentes illuminandi, ipsasq; ad Christum convertendi vim nullam habent. Cætera verò quæ concurrebant, omnia ita comparata erant, ut absque illa Verbo insita virtute & efficacia divina fuisset, propagationem ejus impedivissent potiùs, quàm promovissent. Nam ex parte convertendorum, Judæorum quidem, obstabat ejus celeri propagationi inter alia inveteratus illorum error de regno Messiæ terreno, deq́ue cultu Levitico nunquam cessaturo: paganorum verò ex parte eorundem pertinax error in religione vel potiùs superstitione & idolatria, quam à Majoribus acceptam, cum lacte quasi imbiberant; ex parte doctrinæ propagandæ porrò obstabat mysteriorum, præsertim mysterii redemptionis per Christum, sublimitas & humanæ rationis captum longissimè excedens altitudo, per quam fiebat, ut Christus crucifixus, qui totius Christianæ religionis basis & fundamentum est, ab Apostolis prædicaretur Judæis scandalum; Græcis stultitia, attestante ipso Gentium Apostolo, 1. Cor. 1. 23. c. 11. 14. ex parte propagantium obstare poterat, quòd nec ab eloquentia, nec à sapientia humana, aliisve ad docendum & persuadendum necessariis adminiculis instructi erant. Omnes enim illiterati, piscatores, idiotæ erant, uno excepto Paulo, qui ad pedes Gamalielis quidem in lege patria accuratè institutus fuerat, Act. XXII. 6. nec tamen diffiteri poterat, τῷ λόγῳ sive sermone se idiotam esse, II. Cor. XI. 6. Obstare etiam poterat ex eorundem parte, quòd non Principum & Magnatum favore publico, non prudentum hujus mundi consilio adjuti; quin potius persecutorum & tyrannorum obnitente vi & sævitia apertâ ubique impediti docendi munus obibant. Quód autem his omnibus nihil quicquam obstantibus, religio & doctrina Christiana inter dirissimas persecutiones tanta celeritate per universum terrarum orbem propagata est, id verò documento evidenti est, eam verè Dei Verbum & vi ad devinciendos sibi hominum animos singulari ac verè divinâ instructam esse, tam longè alioqui haudquaquam processuram.
