### VII. Seventhly, among the external signs of credibility, there is also deservedly…

VII.

Seventhly, among the external signs of credibility, there is also deservedly counted the unshaken preservation of Christian doctrine and religion amidst so many tyrannies and persecutions.

I. All republics, all empires, even the most flourishing and powerful, have been exposed to various vicissitudes and have had their determined periods, upon the completion of which they have finally perished, either subdued and destroyed by the force and arms of external enemies, or dissolved and overturned by internal dissensions and seditions. The most powerful kingdom of the Assyrians, the Medes destroyed; the Medes, the Persians; the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans finally destroyed the kingdom of these. Nor was this, although the most robust of all, stable, but in the western part it was so diminished, worn down, and broken in the progress of time by the Goths, Vandals, Huns, Lombards, and Turks, that scarcely any ruins of it remain among the Germans: but in the eastern part, it was gradually weakened and devastated by the incursions of other barbarian peoples, and finally utterly overturned and destroyed by the Turks. But the Christian doctrine and religion and its confessors, or which amounts to the same thing, the Christian Church, just as it is diffused throughout the whole world, so from its very cradle it has experienced enemies, not the Assyrians alone, not the Medes or Persians alone, not the Greeks or Romans alone, but the whole world, and with the world the Devil and all his angels or evil spirits. For the whole host of philosophers and orators, and whatever anywhere possessed any praise of learning or (worldly) wisdom, with one zeal, with one impetus, exerted all the force and faculty of their genius against the doctrine of the Gospel, and turned all their weapons thither, as if to a fixed target, eagerly and profusely, so that it, punished with eternal exile, might be cut off from human affairs. But those who were all-powerful on earth simultaneously deployed all the resources of their wealth and strength with incredible effort, by which they might tear up from the very root the Church recently planted by the Word of God. Hence ten notable and most long-lasting persecutions are numbered, which for three hundred continuous years wonderfully exercised the Christians, stirred up by the highest and most powerful monarchs, the Roman Emperors. And to comprehend it in a number, the power of the whole world had conspired for the destruction of the Church: the very gates of hell and the armies of the devils, as if having joined standards and united forces, they fought against it in a hostile column. But all their effort was dissipated into smoke and vanished, and under these very storms and waves of persecutions the Church grew miraculously, not weakened or diminished by the blood of the holy Martyrs, but rather planted and irrigated, as Ecclesiastical Writers and Fathers attest, who stood as faithful witnesses of these notable events. This great movement of persecutions having been scarcely settled in any part, when now pious and moderate Caesars began to preside at the helm of the Roman Empire, the Devil, envying the Church those halcyon days, soon brought forth other machines, and produced other infernal furies from the pit of the abyss, by whose work he might disturb the tranquility of Christian affairs anew, and move everything from its lowest foundations. He brought heretics into the battle line, through whom he threatened, with no lighter effort, the downfall of religion indeed, and for the Christian Churches, perpetual destruction and devastation. And nevertheless, against all those most savage storms, the ship of the Church stood unshaken, relying on the protection of its supreme pilot, Christ: even when pressed, like a palm tree, it raised itself on high against the weight, and from its enemies it repeatedly carried off most glorious victories, since it was built upon the rock of salvation in such a way that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it, just as the Lord solemnly promised, when he promised everywhere that he would be a wall of fire and a most firm bulwark to it. Wherefore from these things also it is more than manifest that, if this assembly, which embraces the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, relied solely on human and not on God's help; it could not have lasted even a month, let alone so many centuries, in these furies of Satan, in this extreme effort of his instruments, in such varied vicissitudes of kingdoms, in the most sad ruins of empires, in such unexpected changes of human affairs, and finally in such great confusions of opinions, heresies, and most diverse religions. These are the words of the most learned Theologian, Dr. Aegidius Hunnius, in his Tractate on the Majesty of Scripture, argument 16, column 35, following.

II. This sign or motive flows from a twofold source: one of the virtue and power implanted in Christian doctrine and religion, truly divine; the other of divine providence. For just as everything, by which it is generated, by that same thing it is also preserved, so by that power by which the Christian doctrine and religion moves and draws the minds of men into its own supernatural assent, and that simply certain and indubitable, by that same power it also retains them in its certain and indubitable assent, and against the carnal διαλογισμοὺς of corrupted reason, and the doubts suggested by Satan, and the cruelty of persecutors, it fortifies, corroborates, confirms, and preserves them, so that they would rather die a hundred times than fail from the faith and heavenly truth acknowledged, or recede by a hair's breadth. Nor does Christ, the Head of the Church, ever forget his promises, but is present with her by his grace all days even to the consummation of the age, Matt. last, v. last; he cooperates inwardly with his Word, fixed in the hearts of the faithful, and excites, increases, and confirms faith in them; outwardly, however, he powerfully protects them against the insults and rages of enemies, and sets limits to their cruelty, beyond which they cannot proceed, etc.

Latin:

VII.

Septimò in signis credibilitatis externis etiam meritò numeratur doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ inter tot tyrannides & persecutiones inconcussa conservatio.

I. Omnes Respublicæ, imperia omnia, etiam florentissima & potentissima, variis vicissitudinibus exposita fuerunt, suasque determinatas periodos habuerunt, quibus expletis vel hostium externorum vi & armis subacta & destructa, vel dissidiis intestinis ac seditionibus dissoluta & eversa tandem perierunt. Regnum Assyriorum potentissimum Medi; Medorum Persæ: Persarum Græci, & horum regnum Romani tandem destruxerunt. Neq; hoc, etsi omnium robustissimum, stabile fuit, sed ex parte occidentali per Gothos, Vandalos, Hunnos, Longobardos, Turcas ita temporis progressu diminutum, protritum & fractum est, ut ejus vix rudera quædam penes Germanos supersint: ex parte orientali verò aliorum barbarorum populorum incursionibus paulatim labefactatum, vastatum & à Turcis tandem funditus eversum ac deletum est. Doctrina & religio Christiana verò ejusque Confessores, sive quod eodem redit, Ecclesia Christiana, ut per universum terrarum orbem diffusa est, ita inde ab incunabulis suis hostes experta est non Assyrios solos, non solos Medos aut Persas, non Græcos aut Romanos solos, sed universum mundum, & cum mundo Diabolum omnesq; ejus Angelos sive spiritus malos. Universum enim agmen Philosophorum & Oratorum, & quicquid uspiam eruditionis aut sapientiæ (mundanæ) laude aliquâ pollebat, uno studio, uno impetu, contra Evangelii doctrinam ingenii sui vim & facultatem explicabat omnem, atque huc velut ad præfixum scopum tela universa sua certatim & effusè convertebat, ut illa sempiterno exilio multata è rebus humanis excinderetur. Qui verò præpotentes erant in terris, suarum opum viriumq; copias simul omnes incredibili molimine expediebant, quo Ecclesiam Verbo Dei recens plantatam ab ima radice revellerent. Hinc decem numerantur insignes maximeque diuturnæ persecutiones, quæ trecentis annis continuis Christianos mirificè exercuerunt, concitatæ à summis & potentissimis Monarchis, Romanis Imperatoribus. Et ut numero comprehendam, in excidium Ecclesiæ conspiraverat totius orbis potentia: ipsæ portæ inferorum & Diabolorum exercitus, quasi collatis signis junctisque copiis, adversus eam infesto agmine præliabantur. Sed in fumum dissipatus evanuit omnis eorum conatus, & sub his ipsis tempestatibus ac fluctibus persecutionum mirabiliter crevit Ecclesia, sanctorum Martyrum sanguine non debilitata aut imminuta, sed potiùs plantata & irrigata, sicut Scriptores Ecclesiastici atque Patres, contestantur, qui insignium istarum rerum astitere fides testes. Hoc ingenti motu persecutionum vix aliqua parte sedato, cum jam Imperii Romani gubernaculis pii & moderati Cæsares præsidere inciperent, Diabolus, invidens Ecclesiæ ista halcyonia, mox alias protulit machinas, alias infernales furias ex abyssi puteo produxit, quarum operâ tranquillitatem rerum Christianarum de novo disturbaret, omniaque ex imis sedibus commoveret. Hæreticos in aciem produxit, per quos haudquaquam leviore conatu, religioni quidem occasum; Ecclesiis Christianis verò perpetuum excidium vastitatemque minabatur. Atq; nihilo minùs contra omnes illas tempestates sævissimas inconcussa perstitit Ecclesiæ navis, summi gubernatoris Christi freta præsidio: pressa etiam nonnunquam palmæ instar, in altum se contra pondus erexit, deque suis hostibus gloriosissimas subinde reportavit victorias, quippe supra petram salutis sic ædificata, ut portæ inferorum adversus eam prævalere nequeant, quemadmodum Dominus sanctè pollicitus est, quando se illi murum igneum firmissimumque propugnaculum fore passim promisit. Quamobrem ex his quoque dictis plus quàm manifestum est, si humano duntaxat & non Dei niteretur auxilio cœtus iste, qui scripta Prophetica & Apostolica complectitur; eum in his furoribus Satanæ, in hoc extremo conatu organorum ipsius in tam variis vicissitudinibus regnorum, in tristissimis imperiorum ruinis, in tam inopinatis humanarum rerum commutationibus, in tantis denique opinionum, hæresium, diversissimarum religionum confusionibus, ne mensem quidem, nedum tot secula constare potuisse. Verba sunt Doctissimi Theologi D. Ægidii Hunxii in Tract. de Majest. Script. arg. XVI. col. 35. seq.

II. Fluit hoc signum sive motivum ex duplici fonte: uno virtutis, doctrinæ & religioni Christianæ insitæ, verè divinæ; altero divinæ providentiæ. Quemadmodùm enim unumquodque, per quod generatur, per illud etiam conservatur, ita quâ virtute doctrina & religio Christiana hominum mentes in sui assensum supernaturalem, eumque simpliciter certum & indubitatum, movet & trahit, illâ easdem etiam in sui assensu certo & indubitato detinet, adversus rationis corruptæ διαλογισμοὺς carnales, suggestasque à Satana dubitationes, & persecutorum sævitiam munit, corroborat, confirmat & conservat, ut vel centies mori, quàm à fide & veritate cælesti agnitâ deficere, vel latum unguem recedere malint. Neque Christus, Ecclesiæ Caput, unquam suarum obliviscitur promissionum, sed adest ipsi gratiâ suâ omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi Matth. ult. v. ult. cooperatur intus Verbo suo, fidelium cordibus infixo, fidemque in iis excitat, auget & confirmat; exteritus verò tuetur eos adversus hostium insultus & fremitus potenter, ponitque illorum sævitiæ limites, ultra quos progredi non possunt &c.


### VIII. To the motives of credibility are also usually added other arguments not to be…

VIII.

To the motives of credibility are also usually added other arguments not to be despised: one from the universal testimony of almost all peoples, which they have borne to the Church of both the Old and New Testament, and to its doctrine and the things done in it; another from the natural hatred both of vicious and depraved human nature and of Satan against the Word of God, contained in the Prophetic and Apostolic Writings; and a third taken from the punishments of the persecutors, heretics, and contemners of it.

That is a notable proof that the things which the Holy Scriptures teach or commemorate concerning the divinity of the Christian doctrine and religion and the things done in the Church are not fabricated, but were known even in the most ancient times to peoples and nations very far removed; the latter shows the source from which all persecutions of the Christian doctrine and religion spring, which would by no means be struggling with so many adversities if it had been brought forth by corrupted reason and with Satan as its author, and to the conthe desires of the flesh and the allurements of the world to be followed; but it was not entirely composed by God, the source of all Truth and Holiness, for the truth of faith, the holiness of life, and the salvation of men. This, finally, provides no obscure indication of divine providence in preserving and protecting Christian doctrine, and in avenging the evils inflicted upon its confessors. The aforementioned Hunnius has pursued these motives more extensively in the said work, in arguments XVIII, XX, and XXI, or the last one, to which I refer the reader. From a long digression, we must finally return to the path.

IX.

The knowledge of the immediate dependence of the Holy Scriptures upon God, drawn from the mentioned internal as well as external signs and motives, most recent Scholastics call evident knowledge of credibility, and likewise an evident judgment of credibility.

I. They call it evident, on account of the evidence of the signs and motives from which it is born, following Thomas in II. II. q. 1. a. IV. to the second point, where he says that those things which are subject to faith are seen under the common reason of credible by him who believes; and he adds: For he would not believe, unless he saw that these things were to be believed, either on account of the evidence of signs or on account of something of this kind. By which Thomas asserts two things: One, that the doctrines of faith, considered under the reason of credible, are seen, that is, evidently known by him who believes, not indeed in themselves and their specific reason, but in the common reason of credible, that is, that the believer has it evidently known that they are credible. The other, that this evident knowledge of credibility is obtained by the believer from the evidence of the signs or motives of credibility, which we have for the most part enumerated thus far.

II. But they call it evident in opposition to opinative or probable knowledge. For they think that knowledge drawn from the signs and motives of credibility is more certain than probable and opinative knowledge: for the latter is joined with a fear of the opposite, or at least does not exclude a prudent fear of the opposite; but the former is of such certainty that it excludes the fear of the opposite. Where, however, they distinguish between knowledge that is physically and morally evident. They call physically evident that knowledge which is based on physical principles, by which the intellect is so determined to assent that it cannot withhold it; as if someone were to hear God speaking aloud with a sensible voice, it would be physically evident to him that God is speaking. They call morally evident that which, based on moral principles and the rules of prudence, moves the intellect to assent, not indeed excluding every doubt simply, but which is nevertheless so certain that, without prejudice to the rules of prudence, the intellect cannot dissent; as if a serious man and a lover of truth should assert something from which he could hope for no advantage or profit, they say it is morally evident that he is telling the truth, and that no one, without prejudice to the rules of prudence, can dissent, especially if he has confirmed the assertion with an oath. They therefore commonly establish that, for the evidence of credibility concerning the divine origin of Holy Scripture, moral evidence can suffice.

III. But those Scholastics look for a knot in a bulrush. For what they call a morally evident judgment is, as regards the thing itself, nothing other than opinion or human faith. For it is not clearly known through it that Holy Scripture was composed by the inspiration of God, neither a priori through any cause: since that is the first and immediate principle of Theology and the Christian faith, which therefore cannot be demonstrated a priori and through any cause of its own: nor can it be known from the terms apprehended: since it is non-evident and obscure; nor finally can it be evidently demonstrated a posteriori and from effects: since there are given no evident effects of the inspiration that was once granted to holy men. They derive the judgment of credibility entirely either from human testimony; and in so far as our knowledge relies on this as a motive, it is human faith; or from miracles performed in its confirmation, or other signs and motives sought either from the condition of the doctrine or from elsewhere: and in so far as it relies on these, it is opinion. Although, however, we do not deny that signs and motives of credibility, when duly proposed and well perceived, can in a well-disposed and capable subject generate knowledge which excludes the fear of the opposite, yet by this it will not cease to be knowledge of opinion or human faith. For it is not of the nature of opinion that it be actually conjoined with the fear of the opposite, but it is sufficient if through it the object is not apprehended so evidently, or so distinctly and clearly, that it simply excludes every reason for fearing the opposite, as Vazquez in p. 1. Thom. Disp. V. c. 11., Mendoza Disp. X. de Anim. Sect. V. §. 48., and others teach from the Scholastics themselves. That such knowledge is a judgment of credibility, which they call morally evident, they admit by the very fact that they acknowledge it does not absolutely and simply exclude every doubt, and in this they distinguish it from a physically evident judgment. But the reason why they are so solicitous in distinguishing the physical and moral evidence of the judgment of credibility from its probability, and why they so strongly inculcate and contend that it must not be probable, but morally evident, is that they resolve divine faith into those signs and motives of credibility, and the judgment of credibility born from them, as if into the ultimate reason for assenting. For they see that if that judgment were only probable, and did not exclude the fear of the opposite, the entire certainty of the Christian faith would perish. This matter will be treated later. IV. In the meantime, so that it may be more correctly understood what the certainty of the knowledge drawn from the signs and motives of credibility brought forward and declared thus far is, it must be known that those signs can be considered either in relation to faithful men, who already have the divine origin of Holy Scripture known by divine faith, or in relation to infidels, to whom it has not yet become known, and who must be induced to read and meditate upon Holy Scripture, so that they may be moved to embrace its divine origin by divine faith from that reading and meditation. If they are viewed in the former way, it seems it cannot be denied that some of them can generate an assent which is of divine faith. For some rely on divine revelation, as for example that the Church is ruled by the Holy Spirit, so that it may never entirely err and fail in the substantials of the faith and the Christian religion; that God also assists the martyrs in the act of confession, and through His Word fixed in their hearts and rooted by faith, raises, consoles, corroborates, and confirms them in the midst of torments, lest they be oppressed by their cruelty and bitterness and succumb and fail; that the Christian doctrine and religion, by its own divine power in which it excels, moves and draws the souls of men into its own supernatural assent; and that by the same powerful protection of God, the faith and its confessors are preserved in the midst of persecutions against all the assaults of the world, the flesh, and Satan, so that there may always be and remain a Church on earth;

Likewise, miracles are effects and pledges of divine omnipotence, etc., revealed in the Holy Scriptures and are a matter of faith. But if assertions of this kind, resting upon divine revelation, are applied under the aspect of divine revelation to establish the divine origin of Holy Scripture, they will certainly yield conclusions that are of faith. Indeed, certain signs and motives are so constituted that, when they are properly weighed by a mind willing to learn, through attentive consideration and meditation upon them, they can move the human intellect to a supernatural assent to them: such are, for example, the truth of Scripture and of Christian doctrine, pure from all error; its harmony and exact agreement in all its parts, the truth of the prophecies, confirmed by the event itself, etc. which, as they do not really differ from Holy Scripture itself and the doctrine contained in it—for the truth of Scripture does not really differ from true Scripture, and the agreement of Christian doctrine or Holy Scripture in all its parts, as regards the thing itself, is nothing other than the parts of Scripture or doctrine agreeing among themselves—so, while they are constituted in act through the reading and meditation of Scripture itself or through the hearing and explanation of the doctrine comprehended in it, and are applied to the human intellect to manifest the divine origin of Holy Scripture, they can at the same time exert themselves, and do exert themselves, by their own divine power in which they excel, to kindle supernatural assent and divine faith, unless perhaps an obstacle is placed internally by man to the grace of the Holy Spirit, and its operation is checked. Whence, although for the truly faithful the enumerated signs and motives of credibility are not necessary in themselves, since they already have and believe the divine origin of Holy Scripture known by divine faith, yet in the struggle of flesh and spirit, and in the heat of temptation, when faith begins to languish and its sense to fail, these also have their significant use for exciting, raising up, fortifying, and confirming faith against the infirmity of the flesh and the doubts and Diabolical temptations arising from it. But the question at present is not about this use of them, but about the other, which they have in converting infidels, to whom the divine origin of Holy Scripture and sacred doctrine has not yet become known.

V. In order to convert these, therefore, the signs and motives of credibility do not behave otherwise than as motives, generating human faith or an opinion about the divine origin of Holy Scripture and sacred doctrine. For the Church, testifying to the divine origin of Scripture and sacred doctrine, cannot be considered by an infidel man otherwise than as a multitude of men, embracing one doctrine of faith and religion, diffused throughout the world; nor can the force of the testimony, borne by the same to Scripture and the Christian religion, be established in any other way than that it is not credible that such a multitude of men, diffused throughout the world, should have conspired and should conspire for so many centuries in one false religion, and with such consensus should have sold the Code of Scripture, in which it is recorded, as Scripture composed by divine inspiration, if it had been invented by men and composed by merely human effort. For infidels are ignorant of, or certainly do not believe, the divine promises made to the universal Church, that (in the substantials of faith) it will never entirely err or fall away from the true faith and religion. The matter stands likewise with signs and other motives, which can be applied to converting infidel men in no other way than that declared above, as motives generating opinion. Which, viewed individually, although perhaps one may possess greater force than another for moving the minds of men, yet taken together, since they conspire from all sides toward the divine origin of sacred Scripture and the Christian religion, and proclaim as if with one mouth that it was not invented by men but revealed by God himself to the human race, they generate certain knowledge, superior to all other human faith or opinion. Although for this, that an infidel man may be induced to read and meditate upon sacred Scripture, not to be utterly spurned, but with a mind and desire to learn, even knowledge based on fewer signs and motives concerning the divinity of Scripture and the Christian religion may suffice, provided it is probable, even if it does not entirely exclude the fear of the opposite. For these signs and motives are not applied to generate in the man being converted divine faith itself, but at least to excite in him a prudent judgment that Scripture is not to be spurned, but to be read and meditated upon. But sacred Scripture itself afterwards kindles divine faith, when it is read or proposed for meditation to the man being converted by the voice of a teacher, by its own divine power which it possesses, immediately through itself. And so much for the first question, whence the knowledge of human and opinative faith becomes known to us, that sacred Scripture, by reason of its formal aspect, that is, by reason of the sense, doctrines, and things contained in it, is efficiently from God, or was written by divine inspiration

Latin:

VIII.

Motivis credibilitatis quoque accenseri solent argumenta alia non contemnenda: Unum ab universali omnium ferè populorum testimonio, quod Ecclesiæ cum Veteris tum Novi Testamenti, ejusque doctrinæ & rebus, in ea gestis, perhibuerunt; alterum à naturali odio cum vitiosæ & depravatæ naturæ humanæ, tùm & Satanæ contra Verbum Dei, in Propheticis & Apostolicis Scriptis comprehensum; & tertium à pœnis persecutorum, hæreticorum & contemptorum illius desumtum.

Illud insigni documento est, quæ de divinitate doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ dequ; rebus in Ecclesia gestis Scripturæ sacræ docent aut commemorant, conficta non esse, sed innotuisse etiam, temporibus antiquissimis, populis & gentibus longissimè dissitis; istud fontem ostendit, ex quo omnes scaturiunt persecutiones doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ, cum tot adversitatibus minimè conflictaturæ, si ratione corrupta Satanæque Autore prolata, & ad concupiscentias carnis, mundiq; illecebras sectandas comparata; non autem à Deo, Veritatis & Sanctitatis omnis fonte, ad fidei veritatem, vitæ sanctimoniam, hominumq; salutem tota composita esset. Hoc denique providentiæ divinæ in conservanda & protegenda doctrina Christiana, vindicandisq; malis, ejus confessoribus inflictis, indicium non obscurum præbet. Motiva hæc fusius proseqvutus est laudatus Hunnius d. l. Argumentis XVIII. XX. & XXI. sive ultimo: quò lectorem remitto. Ex diverticulo longo nobis tandem in viam redeundum est.

IX.

Notitiam immediatæ Scripturarum sacrarum dependentiæ à Deo, ex commemoratis cùm internis tum externis signis & motivis haustam, Scholastici recentiores plerique cognitionem credibilitatis evidentem, itemque judicium credibilitatis evidens appellant.

I. Vocant illam evidentem, ob evidentiam signorum & motivorum, ex quibus nascitur, seqvuti Thomam in II. II. q. 1. a. IV. ad secundum, ubi ea, quæ subsunt fidei, sub communi ratione credibilis visa esse dicit ab eo, qui credit; & addit: Non enim crederet, nisi videret, ea esse credenda, vel propter evidentiam signorum vel propter aliquid hujusmodi. Quibus duo asserit Thomas: Unum, doctrinas fidei, sub ratione credibilis consideratas, esse visas, h. e. evidenter cognitas ab eo, qui credit, non quidem in se & sua ratione specifica, sed in communi ratione credibilis, h. e. credentem ea, quæ sunt fidei, habere evidenter cognitum, quòd sint credibilia. Alterum, hanc evidentem credibilitatis cognitionem obtingere credenti ex evidentia signorum sive motivorum credibilitatis, quæ maximam partem hactenus enumeravimus.

II. Evidentem verò eam dicunt in oppositione ad cognitionem opinativam sive probabilem. Putant enim, cognitionem, ex signis & motivis credibilitatis haustam, certiorem esse cognitione probabili & opinativâ: hanc enim conjunctam esse cum formidine oppositi, vel certè non excludere prudentem formidinem oppositi: illam verò tantæ esse certitudinis, ut formidinem oppositi excludat. Ubi tamen distingvunt inter cognitionem, physicè, & moraliter evidentem. Physice evidentem dicunt cognitionem, principiis physicis innixam, quibus intellectus ita determinatur ad assensum, ut distentire non possit; ut si quis Deum voce sensibili coram loqui audiret, ei physice evidens esset, Deum loqui. Moraliter evidentem vocant, quæ principiis moralibus & prudentiæ regulis innixa intellectum ad assensum movet, non quidem simpliciter omnem dubitationem excludentem, qui ita tamen certus sit, ut, salvis prudentiæ regulis, intellectus dissentire non possit, ut si vir gravis & veritatis amans aliquid asseveret, è quo nihil commodi aut lucri sperare possit, moraliter evidens esse dicunt, eum dicere verum, nec posse quempiam, salvis prudentiæ regulis, dissentire, præsertim si jurejurando assertionem confirmaverit. Statuunt ergo communiter, ad evidentiam credibilitatis de divina Scripturæ sacræ origine, sufficere posse evidentiam moralem.

III. Verùm Scholastici illi nodum in scirpo quærunt. Quod enim moraliter evidens judicium vocant, quoad rem, nihil aliud est, quàm opinio, aut fides humana. Non enim per illud clarè cognoscitur; Scripturam sacram esse Deo inspirante concinnatam, neque à priori per aliquam causam: cùm id primum & immediatum Theologiæ & fidei Christianæ principium sit, quod proinde à priori & per aliquam sui causam demonstrari non potest: neque etiam ex terminis apprehensis cognosci potest: cum inevidens & obscurum sit; nec denique à posteriori & ex effectibus evidenter demonstrari potest: cùm inspirationis, olim Viris sanctis factæ, effectus evidentes nulli dentur. Accersunt autem judicium credibilitatis totum, vel ex testificatione humana; & in quantum hâc, velut motivo, nititur cognitio nostra, fides humana est; vel ex miraculis, in ejus confirmationem editis, aliisvè, sivè à conditione doctrinæ sive aliunde petitis signis & motivis: & in quantum his nititur, opinio est. Quanquam verò non inficiamur, signa & motiva credibilitatis, ubi ritè proposita & benè percepta sunt, in subjecto benè disposito & capaci posse generare cognitionem, quæ formidinem oppositi excludat, per hoc tamen ea non definet opinionis aut fidei humanæ cognitio esse. Non enim de ratione opinionis est, ut actu cum formidine oppositi conjuncta sit, sed sufficit, si per eam non ita evidenter, sive ita distinctè & clarè objectum apprehendatur, ut simpliciter omnem rationem formidandi oppositum excludat, ut ex ipsis Scholasticis docent Vazquez in p. 1. Thom. Disp. V. c. 11. Mendoza Disp. X. de Anim. Sect. V. §. 48. & alii. Cujusmodi cognitionem esse judicium credibilitatis, quod moraliter evidens dicunt, eo ipso fatentur, quod id non absolutè & simpliciter omnem dubitationẽ excludere agnoscunt, & in hoc à judicio physice evidente distinguunt. Quod autem in distinguenda evidentia judicii credibilitatis physica & morali ab ejusdem probabilitate ita soliciti sunt, idque non probabile, sed moraliter evidens esse oportere, tantoperè inculcant & contendunt, causa est, quod fidem divinam in signa illa & motiva credibilitatis, & hinc natum judicium credibilitatis, velut in rationem assentiendi ultimam resolvunt. Vident enim, si judicium illud probabile saltem esset, & formidinem oppositi non excluderet, fidei Christianæ certitudinem totam perituram esse. Qua de re agetur postea. IV. Ut interim quæ cognitionis, ex adductis & hactenus declaratis signis & motivis credibilitatis haustæ, certitudo sit, rectiùs constet, sciendum, signa illa considerari posse vel in ordine ad homines fideles, & qui divinam Scripturæ sacræ originem jam fide divinâ cognitam habent, vel in ordine ad infideles, quibus ea nondum innotuit, & qui ad Scripturam sacram legendam ac meditandam, ut ad divinam ejus originem ex illius lectione ac meditatione fide divina amplectendam permoveantur, induci debent. Si priori modo spectentur, negari non posse videtur quædã illorũ gignere posse assensum, qui sit fidei divinæ. Quædam enim divinâ nituntur revelatione, sicut v. g. Ecclesiam regi à Spiritu Sancto, ut in substantialibus fidei & religionis Christianæ nunquam tota erret & deficiat; Martyribus etiam Deum in Confessionis actu adsistere, & per Verbum suum in illorum cordibus defixum fideq́; radicatum, erigere, consolari, corroborare & confirmare eosdem in mediis cruciatibus, ne illorum immanitate & acerbitate oppressi succumbant & deficiant; doctrinam & religionem Christianam suâ divinâ, quâ pollet, virtute movere & trahere hominum animos in sui assensum supernaturalem; & eâdem Deiq́; potenti protectione conservari fidem ejusq́; Confessores in mediis persecutionibus adversus omnes mundi, carnis Satanæque insultus, ut semper sit maneatq́; in terris Ecclesia;

itemq; miracula este divinæ omnipotentiæ effectus & pignora &c. in Scripturis sacris revelatum & de fide est. Quod si hujusmodi affertiones, divinæ revelationi innixæ, sub ratione revelationis divinæ adhibeantur ad adstruendam divinam Scripturæ sacræ originem, inferent utique conclusiones, quæ de fide sint. Quædam verò signa & motiva ita comparata sunt, ut ubi animo discendi probè expenduntur, per attentam sui considerationem ac meditationem intellectum hominis in sui assensum supernaturalem permovere possint: cujusmodi sunt v. g. veritas Scripturæ doctrinæq; Christianæ ab omni errore pura; ejus harmonia & exacta consensio in omnibus suis partibus,veritas vaticiniorum,ipso eventu comprobata &c. quæ ut ab ipsa Scriptura sacra & contenta in illa doctrina realiter non differunt: Nam veritas Scripturæ à Scriptura vera realiter non differt;& consensio doctrinæ Christianæ aut Scripturæ sacræ in omnibus suis partibus, quoad rem, nihil aliud est, quàm partes Scripturæ aut doctrinæ inter se consentientes; ita dum per lectionem & meditationem Scripturæ ipsius vel per prædicationem & explicationem doctrinæ, in eo comprehensæ, auditu perceptam, in actu constituuntur, hominisq; intellectui ad divinam Scripturæ sacræ originem manifestandam applicantur,simul sese exerere possunt,exeruntq; sese suâ divinâ,qua pollent,virtute ad sui assensum supernaturalê fidemq; divinam accendendam, nisi ab homine forsan gratiæ Spiritus Sancti interius ponatur obex, ejusq; operatio sufflaminetur. Unde licet verè fidelibus signis & motivis credibilitatis enumeratis per se opus non sit; cùm divinam Scripturæ sacræ originem jam fide divinâ cognitam habeant & credant, in lucta tamen carnis & spiritus, & in tentationis æstu, cum fides languescere, ejusq; sensus deficere incipit, in his etiam suum insignem habent usum, ad fidem adversus infirmitatem carnis & hinc emergentes dubitationes tentationesq; Diabolicas excitandam, erigendam, muniendam & confirmandam. Verùm de hoc illorum usu impræsentiarum quæstio non est, sed de altero, quem habent in convertendis infidelibus, quibus divina Scripturæ & doctrinæ sacræ origo nondum innotuit.

V. In ordine ad hos igitur convertendos signa & motiva credibilitatis se aliter non habent, quàm ut motiva, fidem humanam aut opinionem de divina Scripturæ doctrinæq; sacræ origine generantia. Ecclesia enim, de divina Scripturæ doctrinæq; sacræ origine testiticans, ab homine infideli non aliter considerari potest, quàm ut multitudo hominum, unam fidei doctrinam religionemq; amplectentium, per orbem terrarum diffusa, neq; vis testimonii, Scripturæ & religioni Christianæ ab eadem perhibiti, in alio constitui potest, quàm quòd credibile non sit, tantam per orbem terrarum diffusam multitudinem hominum per tot secula in unam falsam religionem conspirâsse & conspirare, tantoq; consensu Scripturæ Codicem, in quo consignata est, pro Scriptura, ex divina inspiratione concinnata venditâsse, si ab hominibus adinventa, studioq; merè humano concinnata esset. Promissiones divinas enim, Ecclesiæ universali factas, quòd (in substantialibus fidei) nunquam tota erratura aut à fide & religione vera defectura sit, ignorant, vel certè non credunt infideles. Perinde res habet cum signis & motivis cæteris, quæ convertendis hominibus infidelibus non alio, quàm superiùs declarato modo, ut motiva, opinionem generantia, applicari possunt. Quæ singulatim spectata, licet forsan unum altero majori polleat vi hominum animos commovendi, junctim tamen sumta, cum undique in divinam Scripturæ sacræ religionisque Christianæ originem conspirent, eamque non ab hominibus inventam, sed ab ipfomet Deo mortalium generi patefactam esse, uno quasi ore clament, generant cognitionem certam, omniq; aliâ sive humana fide sive opinione superiorem. Quamvis ad hoc, ut ad Scripturam sacram, non prorsus aspernandam, sed animo ac studio discendi legendam & meditandã homo infidelis inducatur, etiã paucioribus signis & motivis innixa notitia de Scripturæ & religionis Christianæ divinitate sufficere possit, modò probabilis sit, licet formidinem oppositi non prorsus excludat. Signa enim & motiva hæc non adhibentur ad generandam in homine convertendo ipsam fidem divinam, sed saltem ad judicium prudens de non aspernanda, sed legenda & meditanda Scriptura in eo excitandum. Fidem divinam verò accendit postea ipsa Scriptura sacra, cùm legitur aut docentis voce homini convertendo meditanda proponitur, suâ divinâ, quâ pollet, virtute perse immediatè. Et tantum de quæstione prima, unde nobis notitia fidei humanæ & opinativâ innotescat, Scripturam sacram ratione formalis sui, h. e. ratione sensus, doctrinarum & rerum, in ea contentarum, esse efficienter à Deo, sive esse ex divina inspiratione conscriptã


## 10 On the Authority of Holy Scripture in Causing Divine Faith

Concerning the knowledge of divine faith, by which the divine origin of Holy Scripture becomes known to us, the Scholastics vary greatly.

I. Scotus in III Sent. Dist. XXIII. q. unica §. De primo certum est, maintains that Christian doctrine is revealed by God, and was committed to writing by divine revelation, and cannot become known to us except by acquired faith, from the testimony of the Church. The question which he took upon himself to examine is this: Whether it is necessary to posit infused faith concerning credible things revealed to us? And after having adduced four arguments for the negative side; and for the affirmative side having cited a single passage, Heb. 11:6, he promises that he will speak; first, concerning what is certain, namely, that there is an acquired faith of things to be believed; then, concerning what is not so manifest, namely, whether an infused faith is given, and if it is given, how it inclines the intellect to the acts of believing. Concerning the first, he says, it is certain that there is in us an acquired faith of revealed credible things, which is evident through Augustine in his Epistle against the foundation of the Manichaeans, who says that he would not believe the Gospel unless he believed the Catholic Church. It is evident, therefore, through him, that the books of the sacred Canon are not to be believed, except because one must first believe the Church approving and authorizing these books, and the things contained in them, etc. Regarding the second point, however, whether infused faith is given, and how it moves the intellect to assent to things to be believed? he says it is uncertain. His most powerful reason for doubting is that it cannot be certain to us that sacred doctrine was revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation, except through the testimony of the Church and acquired faith; and if infused faith were given, one of two things would have to be admitted: that it inclines the intellect to assent to things to be believed either because of the testimony of the Church, believed by acquired faith, or because of the truthfulness of God himself who reveals, believed by infused faith. If the former? the assent of infused faith would depend on the assent of acquired faith, as if from a principle, which is absurd. If the latter? a progress to infinity would have to be admitted. For if you say that you believe by infused faith, e.g. that God is triune and one, because God revealed that he is triune and one; the question returns, why do you believe (by infused faith) that God revealed that he is triune and one? But if you say that you believe that God revealed that he is triune and one, because God revealed that he revealed that, it can again be asked why you believe (by infused faith) that God revealed that he revealed that he is triune and one, and thus a progress to infinity will be given. Finally, however, he devised a twofold way in which infused faith can be said to move the intellect to a supernatural assent to things to be believed, both indeed, in his opinion, probable, but neither certain. One, that it be said that infused faith inclines the intellect to assent to things to be believed by means of acquired faith, namely because of divine revelation, believed by acquired faith, which rests upon the testimony of the Church. The other, that it be said that it inclines the intellect to a supernatural assent to those things, not because of divine revelation previously believed, but by itself immediately. He proposed the former way of speaking in d. 1. §. Secundò de fide infusâ &c. The latter in the following §. Aliter potest poni &c. Gabriel Biel followed him closely in II. Sent. Dist. XXIII. q. II. a. 1. from whom the other Nominalists do not seem to differ.

II. The Thomists, however, commonly establish that in order for Christian doctrine to be believed by divine faith, it is absolutely required that it be believed by the same faith that it is revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine inspiration, and that this is believed by divine faith not because of another revelation, but by itself immediately. But how it can be that it is believed by divine faith by itself immediately, they divide into parties in declaring this. All have recourse to signs and motives of credibility, and especially to the testimony of the Church, and some indeed contend that, in order to believe by divine faith that Christian doctrine was revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation, it is required first of all that this be known from the testimony of the Church or other signs and motives of credibility, and be believed by human faith; then that divine faith be directed toward the same revealed doctrine, and believe that it was revealed by God, in itself immediately; but that the testimony of the Church and other signs of credibility relate to this assent of divine faith, not as a formal object and reason for assenting, but only as a condition without which it would not be. For unless it is known from the testimony of the Church or other signs of credibility that Christian doctrine was revealed by God, the intellect cannot believe this by divine faith in itself immediately. Others, however, contend that the signs of credibility, proposed to the intellect, cause in it a morally evident judgment; by which it is known that it is credible that the doctrines proposed for belief were revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation, so that it cannot be prudently doubted; and that by this evident judgment of credibility the will is moved to command the intellect to assent; and that the intellect subsequently elicits the assent of divine faith at the command of the will, and believes that very thing in itself immediately. Gregorius de Valentia, Tom. III, Disp. 1, q. 1, Punct. 1, joins both inventions, and in the resolution of divine faith imagines a double process. One, in which inquiry is made concerning the cause of faith itself according to its nature; the other, in which inquiry is made concerning the cause for which a man has been induced to wish to believe. In the former process, he bids one who asks for another reason why he believes, e.g., that God is triune and one, to answer: because God has revealed it. To one who asks further whence he knows that God has revealed it, he bids him answer that he does not indeed know it clearly: yet he believes it by the same (divine) faith infallibly, and that indeed not because of another revelation, but indeed because of the infallible proposition of the Church, as because of a condition required for believing it. In the latter process, however, one who is asked concerning the cause and formal reason why he has been induced to wish to believe, [is referred] to the signs and motives of credibility, by which he himself has been induced and anyone a prudent person can be induced to accept such a faith, or to be willing to believe. See his Summa resolutionis fidei d. 1. at the end of point 1. In the former process, Valentia agrees with those Scholastics who establish a double assent, by which it is believed that the doctrines of faith were revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation: one of human faith, [based] on the testimony of the Church or other signs of credibility; the other of divine faith, leaning upon the revelation itself, of which the former stands to the latter not as a cause, but only as a condition. In the latter process, however, he agrees with the other modern Scholastics, who say that signs and motives of credibility are required for a morally evident judgment of credibility, by which the will is moved to command the intellect to give assent to divine revelation, as a prerequisite for this, so that the intellect may be able to elicit the assent of divine faith, by which it is believed per se and immediately that the doctrines of faith were revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation.

III. The source and origin of such diverse commentaries concerning the object or formal motive of faith is that they regard Holy Scripture and the doctrine contained in it, as far as the motive force for its assent is concerned, as no different from any other scripture or doctrine, which, namely, move the intellect to their assent either by the force of the object, if it is evident, or by the force of some effects or signs, or by human testimony, if it is not evident; nor do they acknowledge in it any force of a higher order, which is supernatural and truly divine. But because they see that it is absurd at the very first hearing to say that the doctrine and Christian religion, revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation, is not believed by the intellect per se and immediately, but only mediately and on account of the testimony of the Church or other signs and motives of credibility, and that divine faith, by which we are truly believers and Christians, is entirely destroyed; they have entered upon so many diverse paths by which this difficulty might be removed, and the manner shown by which the intellect might be moved to believe that Christian doctrine is revealed by God and recorded in writing from divine revelation, on account of the authority and testimony of the Church or other signs of credibility, so that nevertheless the ultimate reason for assenting might not return ultimately to the authority of the Church and other signs of credibility, but to divine revelation itself. But those paths and diverse manners are mere deceptions and illusions, by which the simpler-minded are imposed upon and their eyes are darkened, so that they may not easily see that divine faith is being utterly destroyed by the Sophists. This I have shown at length heretofore in Tract. de Convers. Disp. VI. c. 1. n. VII. seq. & n. XV. & seqq., and more lengthily in Tract. de Eccles. part. I. Disp. IX. Indeed, among the more recent Scholastics, Cardinal de Lugo, in Disp. I. de Virt. Fidei Sect. VI., has already laboriously attacked the aforementioned inventions, and in Sect. VII. he finally frankly admitted what others have striven to hide under a manifold disguise and coloring of words, namely, that the faith which all sell as divine is ultimately resolved into the proposition of the Church through signs and motives of credibility, as if into the object or formal motive of faith, if not total, at least partial. Yet, lest he be forced to admit that faith would thus be merely human, by another and new invented escape, he feigns that the proposition and testimony of the Church, and likewise miracles and other signs, are some speech of God, or a certain voice of God by which He speaks to us, albeit mediately, which therefore, joined with the revelation formerly made to the Prophets and Apostles, constitute one adequate formal motive of faith, and a certain speech of God, known to us of itself immediately, though obscurely. But this invention also is a mere disguise, by which, under a highly improper and abusive use of speech, he foists upon us the testimony of the Church and other signs of credibility as revelation or the speech of God, from which, however, they differ in many ways. Whence by this invention, no less than by the preceding ones, divine faith is utterly destroyed, and a merely human faith is left to us. Which has been demonstrated by us at length in the cited Disp. IX. part. I. de Ecclesia n. XLIII. & seqq. where he who wishes may see.

IV. These things, although Scholastic, are not to be passed over here in silence, but are to be duly weighed for the sake of learners, first indeed because of the frauds of the modern Sophists in the Papacy, for whom nothing is more frequent than to teach in words that divine faith ought to be resolved ultimately into the sole veracity of God revealing and His revelation, as into the formal object and proper reason for assenting; and that the revelation formerly made to the Prophets and Apostles, and recorded in letters by them under God's inspiration, or, which is the same thing, Holy Scripture, is to be believed through and for itself: yet in reality they resolve faith into the authority of the Church and other motives of credibility, as into the formal object and ultimate reason for assenting, and that under manifold and with the pigments of fictitious arguments they act with every effort, so that they may lead the minds of men away from the Holy Scriptures and the divine revelation contained in them, which alone with God the revealer constitutes the formal object of divine faith, and having led them away, may lead them to the authority of the Church, and especially of the Roman Pontiff, whom they understand by the name of the Church, and to other signs and motives of credibility, as if to the ultimate reason for assenting, and furthermore under this fallacious motive may speciously foist upon and persuade the incautious of any fictitious doctrines whatsoever, even those of demons. These things are not so Scholastic that they contain themselves within the idle speculations of the Schools, but they go forth outside to seduce the miserable souls of the simpler and unlearned. For as many Impostors as have hitherto appeared in public have appeared equipped with these very arts and frauds, and with these, God permitting, not without success, having been translated into practice and use, they have wickedly deceived not a few, Illustrious, Noble and ignoble, learned and unlearned, and men of any sex and rank, and have induced them to apostasy and defection from the truth once acknowledged. Therefore, these things must be diligently inculcated to those learning, so that they may learn both to guard themselves more rightly against them, and to go to meet those seducers with greater success, and to fortify the souls committed to their care against all the deceits of unrighteousness, as they are called by Paul. Then those Impostors go to attack the orthodox opinion concerning the ultimate reason for assenting to divine faith, yet in such a way that, having attacked and entangled it with various calumnies, they render it suspect to the unlearned, and afterwards fight with their own inventions, as if they were our own opinion, and thus fight with masks rather than with us. But just as contraries placed next to each other shine forth more clearly, so the truth concerning divine faith and its analysis, or concerning Holy Scripture, moving the minds of men by itself immediately to its own assent, will be more rightly understood if, once the calumnies of the Sophists, placed like dense mists before the eyes of the incautious, have been dispersed and their various fictions solidly refuted, the true opinion, as it is taught by us, is more deeply sought and declared from its own principles, and placed as it were in the very midday sun. Which, with God's blessing, we shall do by means of several assertions in order. Let there be therefore

Latin:

De notitia fidei divinae, qua divina Scripturae sacrae origo nobis innotescat, valde variant Scholastici.

I. Scotus in III. Sent. Dist. XXIII. q. unica §. De primo certum est, statuit, doctrinam Christianam esse a Deo revelatam, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam, non posse nobis innotescere, nisi fide acquisita, ex testificatione Ecclesiae. Quaestio, quam excutiendam sibi sumsit, est haec: Utrum de credibilibus nobis revelatis necesse sit ponere fidem infusam? & post adducta quatuor argumenta pro parte negativa; pro affirmativa autem unico loco Ebr. XI. 6. allalato, dicturum se; promittit, primo quod certum est, dari scilicet fidem credendorum acquisitam; deinde quod non ita manifestum est, an scilicet detur fides infusa, & si detur; quomodo ad actus credendi intellectum inclinet. De primo, inquit, certum est, quod in nobis est fides revelatorum credibilium acquisita, quod patet per Augustinum in Epistola contra fundamentum Manichaei, qui dicit, quod non crederet Evangelio, nisi crederet Ecclesiae Catholicae. Patet igitur per eum, quod libris Canonis sacri non est credendum, nisi quia primo credendum est Ecclesiae approbanti & auctorizanti libros istos, & contenta in eis &c. De secundo autem, utrum fides infusa detur, & quomodò intellectum in credendorum assensum moveat? incertum esse ait. Ejus ratio dubitandi potissima est, quod doctrinam sacram revelatam à Deo, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam esse, constare nobis non possit, nisi per testificationem Ecclesiæ, fideque acquisitâ; & si daretur fides infusa, alterutrum admittendum foret, quòd intellectum vel propter testificationem Ecclesiæ, fide acquisitâ creditam, vel propter ipsam Dei revelantis veracitatem, fide infusâ creditam, intellectum in credendorum assensum inclinet. Si illud? dependeret assensus fidei infusæ ab assensu fidei acquisitæ, velut à principio, quod absurdum. Sin hoc?-admittendus esset progressus in infinitum. Si enim dicas, te credere fide infusâ, v. g. Deum esse trinum & unum, quia Deus revelavit, se esse trinum & unum; redit quæstio, cur credas (fide infusâ) Deum revelâsse, se esse trinum & unum. Quod si dicas, te credere, Deum revelâsse, se esse trinum & unum, quia Deus revelavit, se id revelâsse, rursum quæri poterit, cur credas (fide infusâ) Deum revelâsse, se revelâsse, se esse trinum & unum, & sic progressus dabitur in infinitum. Tandem tamen duplicem commentus est modum, quo fides infusa intellectum in credendorum assensum supernaturalem movere dici possit, utrumque quidem, ex ejus opinione, probabilem, neutrum verò certum. Unum, ut dicatur, fidem infusam inclinare intellectum in credendorum assensum mediante fide acquisitâ, propter divinam revelationem scilicet, fide acquisitâ, testificationi Ecclesiæ innixâ,creditam. Alterum ut dicatur, eam inclinare intellectum in assensum illorum supernaturalem, non propter divinam revelationem, prius creditam, sed per se immediatè. Priorem dicendi modum proposuit d. 1. §. Secundò de fide infusâ &c. Posteriorem seq. §. Aliter potest poni &c. Eum κατὰ πόδα seqvutus est Gabriel Biel II. Sent. Dist. XXIII. q. II. a. 1. à quibus nec cæteri Nominales abludeve videntur.

II. Thomistæ verò communiter statuunt, ut fide divinâ credatur doctrina Christiana, omninò requiri, ut fide eâdem credatur, eam esse à Deo revelatam, & ex divina inspiratione in literas relatam, atque hoc credi fide divinâ non propter aliam revelationem, sed per se immediatè. Quomodò autem fieri possit, ut fide divina per se immediate id credatur, in eo declarando in partes abeunt. Omnes recurrunt ad signa & motiva credibilitatis, & cumprimis ad testificationem Ecclesiæ, contenduntq; nonnulli quidem, ad credendum fide divina, doctrinam Christianam esse a Deo revelatam, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam, requiri primo omnium, ut ex testificatione Ecclesiæ aliisve credibilitatis signis & motivis id cognoscatur, fideq; humana credatur; deinde ferri fidem divinam in eandem doctrinam revelatam, & credere, eam esse a Deo revelatam, per se immediate; testificationem Ecclesiæ vero & signa credibilitatis alia habere se ad hunc fidei divinæ assensum, non ut objectum formale & rationem assentiendi, sed tantum ut conditionem sine qua non. Nisi enim ex testificatione Ecclesiæ aliisve signis credibilitatis cognitum sit, doctrinam Christianam esse a Deo revelatam, intellectum non posse id fide divina per se immediate credere. Alii vero contendunt, signa credibilitatis, intellectui proposita, causare in eo judicium moraliter evidens; quo cognoscatur credibile esse, doctrinas, ad credendum propositas, esse a Deo revelatas, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatas, ut prudenter de eo dubitari non possit; hoc autem credibilitatis judicio evidente moveri voluntatem ad imperandum intellectui assensum; & intellectum elicere postea ad imperium voluntatis assensum fidei divinæ, & credere illud ipsum per se immediate. Gregorius de Valentia Tom. III. Disp. 1. q. 1. Punct. 1. conjungit commentum utrumque, & in resolutione fidei divinæ duplicem fingit processum. Unum, quo de causa ipsius fidei secundum se; alterum, quo de causa, propter quam homo animum induxerit velle credere, inquiritur. In processu priori quærenti ex altero, cur credat, v. g. Deum esse trinum & unum, respondere jubet, quia Deus revelavit. Quærenti porro, unde cognoscat, Deum id revelasse, respondere jubet, se quidem non nosse id clarè: credere tamen eâdem (divinâ) fide infallibiliter, & id quidem non ob aliam revelationem, bene tamen ob infallibilem propositionem Ecclesiæ, tanquam ob conditionem ad id credendum requisitam. In processu posteriori autem, interrogatum de causa & ratione formali, cur animum induxerit velle credere, ad signa & motiva credibilitatis, quibus ipse inductus sit & quivis prudens induci possit ad acceptandam ejusmodi fidem, sive ad volendum credere, devenire jubet. Videatur ejus Summa resolutionis fidei d. 1. sub finem puncti 1. In processu priori consentit Valentia cum illis Scholasticis, qui duplicem statuunt assensum, quo doctrinas fidei à Deo revelatas, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatas esse creditur: unum fidei humanæ, testificationi Ecclesiæ aliisve credibilitatis signis; alterum fidei divinæ, revelationi ipsi innixum, quorum ille ad hunc non ut causa, sed tantùm ut conditio sese habeat. In processu posteriori verò consentit cum cæteris modernis Scholasticis, qui signa & motiva credibilitatis requiri dicunt ad judicium credibilitatis moraliter evidens, quo voluntas moveatur ad imperandum intellectui assensum divinæ revelationis, ad hoc prærequisitum, ut assensum divinæ fidei, quo doctrinas fidei à Deo revelatas, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatas esse per se immediatè credatur, intellectus elicere possit.

III. Fons & origo tam diversorum de objecto sive motivo formali fidei commentorum est, quòd Scripturam sacram & contentam in ea doctrinam,quod ad vim motiva in ejus assensum attinet, non alio habent loco, quàm quo aliam quamvis Scripturam doctrinamve habent, quæ scilicet vel vi objecti, si illud evidens sit, vel vi aliquorum effectuum aut signorum, aut testimonio humano, si id inevidens sit, intellectum in sui assensum movent; nec ullam altioris ordinis vim, quæ supernaturalis & verè divina sit, in ea agnoscunt. Quia autem vident, primo statim auditu absurdum esse dicere, doctrinam & religionem Christianam, à Deo revelatam, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam esse,non credi ab intellectu per se immediatè, sed mediatè tantùm & propter testificationem Ecclesiæ aliave credibilitatis signa & motiva, fidemq́; divinam, quâ verè fideles & Christiani sumus; totam tolli; tot diversas ingressi sunt vias, quibus difficultas hæc tolli, modusq́; ostendi possit, quo intellectus moveatur ad credendum, doctrinam Christianam esse à Deo revelatam, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam, propter auctoritatem & testificationem Ecclesiæ vel signa credibilitatis alia, ut tamen ratio afsentiendi ultima non in auctoritatem Ecclesiæ & credibilitatis signa alia,sed in ipsam divinã revelationẽ ultimò redeat.Sed viæ illæ modiq́; diversi meri fuci præstigiæq́; sunt, quibus simplicioribus imponitur, illorumq; oculi obfuscentur, ne fidem divinam a Sophistis prorsus tolli, facile videant. Quod antehac in Tract. de Convers. Disp. VI. c. 1. n. VII. seq. & n. XV. & seqq. prolixe, prolixius autem in Tract. de Eccles. part. I. Disp. IX. ostendi. Quin ex recentioribus Scholasticis etiam Cardinalis de Lugo Disp. I. de Virt. Fidei Sect. VI. memorata jam commenta operose impugnavit, & quod alii sub multiplici verborum fuco ac colore occultare studuerunt, in Sect. VII. tandem ingenue fassus est, nempe fidem, quam pro divina omnes venditant, resolvi ultimo in propositionem Ecclesiæ per signa & motiva credibilitatis, tanquam in objectu sive motivum formale fidei, si non totale partiale tamen. Ne tamen admittere cogatur, fidem sic fore mere humanam, alio eoque novo invento effugio, fingit, propositionem & testificationem Ecclesiæ, miracula item & signa cætera esse aliquam locutionem Dei, aut quandam vocem Dei, qua ad nos loquatur, quamvis mediatam, quæ proinde cum revelatione, Prophetis & Apostolis olim facta, conjuncta, constituant unum adæquatum formale motivum fidei, & quandam locutionem Dei, nobis per se immediate, obscure tamen, notam. Sed hoc etiam inventum merus fucus est, quo sub locutione admodum impropria & abusiva testificationem Ecclesiæ & signa credibilitatis alia pro revelatione sive locutione Dei nobis obtrudit, a quo tamen multis modis differunt. Unde commento hoc non minus, quam præcedentibus, fides divina prorsus tollitur, & fides mere humana nobis relinquitur. Quod a nobis fuse demonstratum est in citata Disp. IX. part. I. de Ecclesia n. XLIII. & seqq. ubi, qui vult, videat.

IV. Hæc, etsi Scholastica, non tamen silentio hic prætereunda, sed in discentium gratiam probe expendenda sunt, primo quidem ob fraudes modernorum Sophistarum in Papatu, quibus nihil frequentius est, quam ut verbis doceant, fidem divinam ultimo resolvi debere in solam Dei revelantis veracitatem ejusque revelationem, tanquam in objectum formale & rationem assentiendi propriam; & revelationi, Prophetis olim & Apostolis factæ, & ab iisdem Deo inspirante in literas relatæ, sive, quod idem est, Scripturæ sacræ credi per & propter se: re ipsa tamen fidem in auctoritatem Ecclesiæ & motiva credibilitatis alia, tanquam in objectum formale & rationem assentiendi ultimam resolvunt, idq; sub multiplicibus verborum rationumque commentitiarum pigmentis omni agunt conatu, ut à Scripturis sacris & contentâ in illis revelatione divinâ, quæ sola cum Deo revelante fidei divinæ objectum formale constituit, hominum mentes abducant, abductasq; ad auctoritatem Ecclesiæ, & cumprimis Pontificis Romani, quem Ecclesiæ nomine intelligunt, cæteraq; credibilitatis signa & motiva, velut ad rationem assentiendi ultimam, deducant, & porro sub hoc fallaci motivo quasvis commentitias ipsasq; dæmoniorum doctrinas incautis speciosè obtrudant & persuadeant. Non hæc ita Scholastica sunt, ut intra otiosas Scholarum speculationes se contineant, sed egrediuntur foras ad seducendas simpliciorum & imperitorum miseras animas. Quotquot enim hactenus in publicum prodierunt Impostores, his ipsis artibus & fraudibus instructi prodierunt, iisq;, Deo permittente, non absque successu, ad praxin & usum translatis, non paucis, Illustribus, Nobilibus & ignobilibus, doctis indoctis, & cujusvis sexus, & fortis hominibus nequiter imposuerunt, eosq; ad apostasiam & defectionem à veritate agnita induxerunt. Inculcanda igitur sedulò sunt discentibus, ut & sibi ab illis rectiùs cavere, & seductoribus illis majori cum successu obviam ire, & commissas suæ curæ animas adversus omnes injustitiæ fraudes, ut à Paulo vocantur, præmunire discant. Deinde sententiam orthodoxam de fidei divinæ ratione assentiendi ultima Impostores illi impugnatum eunt, ita tamen ut variis calumniis impetitam, involutamq; imperitis suspectam reddant, & posteà cum suis figmentis, ac si ipsa nostra sententia essent, atque adeò cum larvis potiùs, quàm nobiscum pugnent. Quemadmodum autem aliàs contraria juxta se posita, magis elucescunt, ita ad declarandam veritatem de fide divina, ejusque analysi, sive de Scriptura sacra, mentes hominum per se immediatè in sui assensum movente, rectiùs intelligetur, si Sophistarum calumniis, instar densarum nebularum incautorum oculis objectis, discussis eorundemque commentis variis solidè confutatis, sententia vera, ut à nobis docetur, altiùs ex suis principiis accersita & declarata, in ipso quasi solis meridie constituatur. Quod, bono cum Deo, per aliquot assertiones ordine facturi sumus. Esto ergo


### II. First assertion: For the assent of divine faith to things to be…

II.

First assertion: For the assent of divine faith to things to be believed it is altogether required that divine revelation itself be believed also by divine faith, or, which amounts to the same thing, that it be believed by divine faith that the doctrines contained in the Holy Scriptures were revealed by God and committed to writing from divine revelation.

I. This assertion is opposed to the two preceding comments of Scotus: To the one, indeed: That for divine faith it is not required that the divine revelation of things to be believed be known and believed by divine faith, but that when the revealed doctrine is proposed to the intellect and apprehended by it, divine faith inclines it to assent to them of itself immediately. To the other, however: That for divine faith it suffices if divine revelation, or, which amounts to the same thing, that the doctrine contained in the Holy Scriptures was revealed by God and committed to writing from divine revelation, be believed by acquired or human faith.

II. For the sake of greater clarity, I advise here that the word revelation denotes at times, customarily, the act of revealing, terminated in the intellect of holy men in the concepts of things to be believed, from which it differs just as other actions differ from their terms, modally, or as the mode of a thing differs from the thing, e.g., as heating differs from the heat produced by it. Sometimes, however, the same word is taken also for the term of revelation, namely, for the very concepts of things to be believed, once inspired in the sacred writers. For the concepts of things to be believed, once inspired in the sacred writers, since they were express images of the things to be believed and formally represented them to their intellect, were a certain formal revelation of them; but the act of revelation, by which the concepts of things were efficiently produced in their intellect, was a certain effective revelation of the same. In the present assertion, when we say that divine revelation must be believed by divine faith, we take revelation for the act of revelation, and the sense of the assertion is that for the assent of divine faith to things to be believed, it is required that it also be believed by divine faith that the concepts of the things to be believed, which are a certain formal revelation of them, were once supernaturally inspired by God in the holy men by whom they were first conveyed by voice and afterwards by writings to others and propagated even to us, or that they were efficiently produced in their intellect by God through the act of revelation or inspiration. The same also holds true of Holy Scripture, which we showed at length in chapter II, theses III and XI, was composed by the sacred writers with God revealing and inspiring the concepts of both the things and the words to be written. This itself is also sometimes called divine revelation, with the word revelation taken as a term for the product of the act of revealing. For the words of Scripture, as they are signs of concepts, having been produced formerly in the intellect of the sacred writers through the act of revelation, are thus transmitted to our intellect by reading or hearing, and manifest the same to us, generating in us concepts similar to the concepts formerly inspired in the intellect of the sacred writers, by which both the concepts themselves, formerly inspired in the sacred writers, and the things signified by them, are formally represented. Whence it is also commonly said of the Holy Scriptures that, in order to believe them with divine faith, it is required that their revelation be believed with the same faith, or that it be believed that they were written with God revealing, with the word revelation taken likewise for the act of revealing.

III. Scotus, therefore, dissenting from us, judges that for the assent of divine faith it is either not necessary that the revelation itself also be believed, that is, that it be believed that the concepts of the things to be believed, which the sacred writers formerly had and according to whose guidance they composed Holy Scripture, came to them from God through a supernatural act of revelation or inspiration; or, if this also is necessary to be believed, that it is not necessary that it be believed with divine faith, but that it suffices if it be believed with human faith. But neither of his opinions can be admitted.

IV. And indeed, the former is contradicted by what we showed above in chapter IV, thesis II, that for the authority of Holy Scripture, so that it may move the human intellect to assent to it, two complex principles are required: one, that its Author, God, is supremely truthful, and that Scripture, composed with God revealing or inspiring, is certainly and infallibly true; the other, that Holy Scripture was composed with God revealing or inspiring, and that both must be known, so that if you are ignorant of either, the authority of Holy Scripture cannot fulfill the role of the formal motive of faith and move the intellect to assent to itself and to the things to be believed. Thus, if you have knowledge that God in testifying and revealing is truthful, so that He can neither be deceived nor deceive, but you do not know, or do not believe, that He testifies or reveals in the Scriptures, e.g., that He is one in essence and three in persons, the authority of God cannot move you to assent to the mystery of the Trinity: since no authority, as has been said, moves the intellect to assent to a statement, dogma, or writing of any author, unless it is known that it proceeded from that author. Nor is there any reason for you to object that divine faith has this peculiarity, that it inclines the intellect to assent to revealed doctrines of itself and immediately, after they have been proposed to it and apprehended by it. For this is a fiction, repugnant to the very nature of faith. For faith acts on the part of the knowing faculty, and by way of an effective principle of assent, not on the part of the object, and by way of its formal motive. However, just as the intellect cannot of itself and immediately assent to an object which does not appear to it to be true of itself and immediately; so neither can faith incline the intellect to assent to revealed doctrines of itself and immediately, which do not appear to the intellect to be true of themselves and immediately, but only through divine revelation. Divine faith, therefore, is by its own nature such that it inclines the intellect to the supernatural assent of revealed doctrines, through divine revelation known and believed. But the latter comment of Scotus is absurd at the very first hearing. For if divine revelation is not believed except by acquired and human faith, the assent of divine faith and its certainty will ultimately be resolved into the assent of acquired and human faith, and thus the ultimate reason for assenting to divine faith will not be the authority of God testifying or revealing; but the testimony of the Church and other signs and motives of credibility. Once this is admitted, divine faith will perish entirely, and no other than human faith will be left to us. For faith has its specific being from its ultimate reason for assenting, and it is divine, whose ultimate reason for assenting is divine authority, or, which amounts to the same thing, God revealing and His revelation; but it is human, whose ultimate reason for assenting is human authority, or man testifying and his testimony. Now, if I ask you why you believe by divine faith that God is three and one, and you answer that you believe this because God has revealed in the Holy Scriptures that He is three and one; I ask again, why do you believe that God has revealed in the Scriptures that He is three and one? But if you now answer that you believe this because the Church testifies to it, and it is rendered credible through signs and other motives of credibility, you now stop ultimately at the testimony of the Church and other motives of credibility, and these are your reason for assenting. The testimony of the Church, however, produces human faith; and the other signs of credibility [produce] opinion. Therefore, your faith, by which you believe that God has revealed in the Holy Scriptures that He is triune and one, is merely human, not divine. For although you may say that you believe that God is triune and one because God has revealed it, nevertheless, the divine revelation for you has all its motive force for assent from human testimony and other signs of credibility, and in so far as it depends on these motives, it can generate no other than human faith. Divine faith, therefore, according to this opinion, is not given at all. Because this, according to its own authors, is absurd, it is necessary that the opinion itself is also absurd. IV. It remains, therefore, to be said that for the assent of divine faith to revealed doctrines, it is required that their revelation also be believed by divine faith, which is our first assertion.

Latin:

II.

Assertio prima: Ad assensum fidei divinæ credendorum omninò requiritur, ut ipsa divina revelatio etiam fide divinâ credatur, sive, quod eodem redit, ut fide divina credatur, doctrinas, in Scripturis sacris comprehensas, esse à Deo revelatas, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatas.

I. Assertio hæc opponitur duobus superioribus Scoti commentis: Uni quidem: Ad fidem divinam non requiri, ut divina credendorum revelatio fide divinâ cognita & credita sit, sed ubi doctrina revelata intellectui proposita, & ab eodem apprehensa sunt, fidem divinam inclinare eum in illarum assensum per se immediatè. Alteri verò; Ad fidem divinam sufficere, si revelatio divina, sive quod eodem redit, doctrinam, in Scripturis sacris comprehensam, à Deo revelatam, & ex divina revelatione in literas relatam esse, fide acquisitâ sive humanâ credatur.

II. Majoris perspicuitatis causâ hic moneo, revelationis vocem denotare aliàs usitatè actum revelandi, in intellectu Virorum sanctorum ad conceptus rerum credendarum terminatum, à quibus perinde, ut actiones aliæ à suis terminis, modaliter, sive ut modus rei à re, v. g. ut calefactio à calore, per eam producto, differt. Nonnunquam verò accipi eandem etiam pro termino revelationis, nempe pro ipsis rerum credendarum conceptibus, Scriptoribus sacris olim inspiratis. Conceptus enim credendorum, Scriptoribus sacris olim inspirati, cùm essent imagines expressæ rerum credendarum, easque illorum intellectui formaliter repræsentarent, erant quædam illorum revelatio formalis; revelationis actus verò, quo conceptus rerum in illorum intellectu efficienter producebantur, erat eorundem quædam revelatio effectiva. In assertione præsenti, cùm revelationem divinam fide divina credi oportere dicimus, revelationem accipimus pro revelationis actu, estque sensus assertionis, ad assensum fidei divinæ credendorum requiri, ut etiam fide divina credatur, conceptus rerum credendarum, qui sunt quædam formalis illarum revelatio, fuisse olim Viris sanctis, à quibus primùm voce, & posteà scriptis ad alios delati & ad nos usque propagati sunt, supernaturaliter à Deo inspiratos, sive eos fuisse in illorum intellectu per revelationis sive inspirationis actum efficienter à Deo productos. Idem valet etiam de Scriptura sacra, quam, Deo revelante & conceptus cùm rerum tùm vocum scribendarum inspirante, à Scriptoribus sacris concinnatam esse, suprà cap. II. th. III. & XI. prolixè ostendimus. Quæ & ipsa quandoque revelatio divina appellatur, revelationis voce pro termino, per actum revelandi producto, acceptâ. Verba Scripturæ enim, ut sunt signa conceptuum, per revelationis actum in intellectu Scriptorum sacrorum, olim productorum, ita lectione audituve ad nostrum transmissa intellectum, eosdem nobis etiam manifestant, generantœ; in nobis conceptus, similes conceptibus, Scriptorum sacrorum intellectui olim inspiratis, quibus & ipsi sacris Scriptoribus olim inspirati conceptus, & res illis significatæ, formaliter repræsentantur. Unde de Scripturis sacris etiam dici solet, ad credendum illis fide divinâ requiri, ut fide eâdem credatur illarum revelatio, sive ut credatur, eas Deo revelante conscriptas esse, revelationis voce, itidem pro actu revelandi acceptâ.

III. Scotus ergo, à nobis dissentiens, censet, ad assensum fidei divinæ vel non esse necessarium, ut ipsa etiam revelatio credatur, h. e. ut credatur, conceptus rerum credendarum, quos Scriptores sacri olim habuerunt, & ad cujus ductum Scripturam sacram concinnârunt, obtigisse ipsis à Deo per revelationis sive inspirationes actum supernaturalem; vel si hoc etiam creditu necessarium sit, non tamen necessarium esse, ut fide divinâ credatur, sed sufficere, si credatur fide humanâ. Sed neutra ejus opinio admitti potest.

IV. Et priori quidem repugnat, quod suprà cap. IV. th. II. ostendimus, ad auctoritatem Scripturæ sacræ, ut intellectum hominis in sui assensum movere possit, duo requiri principia complexa: Unum, ejus Auctorem, Deum, esse summè veracem, & Scripturam, Deo revelante sive inspirante concinnatam, esse certò & infallibiliter veram; alterum, Scripturam sacram esse Deo revelante sive inspirante concinnatam, & utrumque oportere esse cognitum, ut si alterutrum ignores, auctoritas Scripturæ sacræ rationem motivi formalis fidei obire, & intellectum ad sui & credendorum assensum movere non possit. Sic si cognitum habeas, Deum in testificando & revelando esse veracem, ut nec falli nec fallere possit, nescias verò, vel non credas, eum in Scripturis testificari sive revelare, v. g. se esse unum in essentia & trinum in personis, auctoritas Dei non potest te in assensum mysterii Trinitatis movere: cùm nulla auctoritas, uti dictum, intellectum in assensum dicti, dogmatis aut scripti alicujus Auctoris moveat, nisi ab auctore id profectum esse cognitum sit. Neque est, quod obtendas, fidem divinam habere hoc peculiare, ut intellectum in assensum doctrinarum revelatarum, postquam ei propositæ & ab eodem apprehensæ sunt, per se immediatè inclinet. Hoc enim figmentum est, ipsi fidei naturæ repugnans.
