Fides enim habet se ex parte potentiæ cognoscentis, & per modum principii effectivi assensus, non ex parte objecti, & per modum motivi formalis illius. Quemadmodum autem intellectus non potest per se immediatè assentiri objecto, quod ei non per se immediatè verum esse apparet; ita nec fides potest inclinare intellectum in doctrinarum revelatarum assensum per se immediatè, quæ intellectui non per se immediatè, sed tantùm mediante divinâ revelatione veræ esse apparent. Fides divina ergo suâpte naturâ talis est, ut inclinet intellectum in supernaturalem doctrinarum revelatarum assensum, mediante divina revelatione cognitâ & creditâ. Posterius verò Scoti commentum primo statim auditu absurdum est. Si enim divina revelatio non creditur, nisi fide acquisitâ & humanâ, assensus fidei divinæ ejusq́; certitudo ultimò resolvetur in assensum fidei acquisitæ & humanæ, atque adeò fidei divinæ ratio assentiendi ultima non erit auctoritas Dei testificantis sive revelantis; sed testificatio Ecclesiæ & signa ac motiva credibilitatis alia. Quo semel admisso fides divina peribit tota, nec alia, quàm humana, nobis relinquetur. Fides enim à sua ratione assentiendi ultima habet suum esse specificum, & divina est, cujus ratio assentiendi ultima est divina auctoritas, sive, quod eodem redit, Deus revelans ejusq́; revelatio; humana verò, cujus ratio assentiendi ultima est, auctoritas humana, sive homo testificans ejusq́; testificatio. Jam verò si quæram ex te, cur credas fide divinâ, Deum esse trinum & unum, & tu respondeas, te credere hoc, quia Deus in Scripturis sacris revelavit; quæro ego rursum, cur credas, Deum revelâsse in Scripturis, se esse trinum & unum? Quod si jam respondeas, te credere hoc, quia Ecclesia id testificatur, & per signa ac motiva credibilitatis alia credibile redditur, jam in testificatione Ecclesiæ & motivis credibilitatis aliis sistis ultimò, & hæc sunt tuæ ratio assentiendi ultima. Testificatio Ecclesiæ autem gignit fidem humanam; & signa credibilitatis cætera opinionem. Ergo tua fides, quâ credis, Deum revelâsse in Scripturis sacris, se esse trinum & unum, est merè humana, non divina. Licet enim dicas, te credere, Deum esse trinum & unum, quia Deus revelavit, revelatio divina tamen apud te omnem vim motivam ad assensum habet à testificatione humana & signis credibilitatis aliis, & in quantum ab his motivis dependet, non aliam, quàm humanam fidem generare potest. Fides divina igitur, juxta hanc opinionem, nulla datur. Quod quia, juxta ipsosmet ejus auctores, absurdum est, absurdam etiam opinionem ipsam esse necesse est. IV. Dicendum ergo relinquitur, ad assensum fidei divinæ doctrinarum revelatarum requiri, ut illarum revelatio etiam fide divina credatur, quæ est nostra prima assertio.


### III. Our second assertion is

III.

Our second assertion is: Divine revelation, contained in Holy Scripture, or, which is the same thing, Holy Scripture moves the intellect of man to the supernatural assent of itself and of its dependence upon God, of itself and immediately.

In this assertion, the Scholastics, who indeed maintain against Scotus and the Nominalists that for the assent of divine faith it is required that divine revelation and its dependence upon God be believed by divine faith, seem, at first glance, to agree with us. For they say in open words that it is believed by divine faith, not because of another revelation, nor because of any reason for assenting different from it, but of itself and immediately. However, it could not be believed of itself and immediately unless it possessed a certain power of moving the intellect to its own assent of itself and immediately. But we have just said that they deceive the reader, and acknowledge nothing less than such a certain motive force in Holy Scripture, but whatever it is that can move the intellect to the assent of the revelation contained in the Scriptures as depending upon God, they refer it entirely to the proposition of the Church and to other signs and motives of credibility, as has just been shown. Now we shall declare our assertion, and we shall confirm it with the foundations of the Scriptures.

II. But in it the word 'revelation' is contained twice; once explicitly on the part of the subject, and again implicitly on the part of the predicate, though in one sense and then another. For on the part of the subject it is taken for the term of revelation, namely for the concepts produced long ago in the intellect of holy men by the act of revelation or inspiration, which, as has been said, are a certain formal however, viewed in itself precisely as its term, just as it is nowhere given, so neither can it of itself immediately move the human intellect to assent to it. Therefore, the concepts, efficiently produced in the intellect of holy men long ago by the act of revelation by God, and which are still produced in us today by the words of Scripture, whether transmitted to our intellect by the voice of teachers or the reading of the Scriptures, move it to its supernatural assent. These, however, as they can be viewed either by reason of their dependence on God through the act of revelation, or by reason of their conformity with the things which they represent and of which they are signs, so it can be understood in two ways what is said in the assertion, that divine revelation, taken terminatively for the concepts produced by the act of revelation, moves the intellect to its supernatural assent of itself immediately. In one way, that it of itself immediately moves the intellect to the supernatural assent of its dependence on God through the act of revelation. In another, that it of itself immediately moves the intellect to the supernatural assent of its conformity with the object, or of its truth. Our assertion is taken here in the former way, and that divine revelation moves the intellect to its supernatural assent, as regards the thing, is the same as that the concepts, produced by the act of revelation in the intellect of the sacred writers, and which are still produced in us today by the words of Scripture, move the intellect to the supernatural assent of their revelation, that is, of their dependence on God through the act of revealing: so that the word revelation, on the part of the predicate, must be taken entirely for the act of revealing, not for its term.

III. What we say here about revelation, taken terminatively for the concepts produced by the act of revelation, holds also for sacred Scripture, which is a certain divine revelation, taken terminatively, comprised in letters, and just as the concepts, produced long ago in the intellect of holy men by the act of revelation, moved their intellect to the supernatural assent of their dependence from God revealing by Himself immediately, so also the Holy Scriptures, since they were composed according to the guidance of those concepts which had been produced in their intellect by the act of revelation, instill into our intellect those very concepts which were once inspired in the sacred writers, which consequently, being excited in us by the words of Scripture, just as they did for them, move the intellect into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing by Himself immediately. And because divine revelation, taken as the term of revelation, does not exist today except in the Holy Scriptures, in which it is contained as a thing signified in its signs, and it differs in nothing from the Scriptures themselves, composed by God inspiring; and since the whole question now is about this, the sum of our assertion finally returns to Holy Scripture, which will therefore be proposed more clearly in less ambiguous words in this manner: Holy Scripture moves the intellect of man into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing by Himself immediately.

IV. The Holy Scriptures frequently call divine revelation, taken terminatively, the Word of God, since through it, or through the concepts produced in the intellect of holy men by the act of revealing, God once spoke to holy men and manifested what was to be believed; and the words, as signs of the inspired concepts, whether uttered by voice or comprised in writing, are the external Word of God, by which He still speaks to us even now. Whence the matter will return to the same thing, whether it is said that the Word of God, or divine revelation, or Holy Scripture moves the intellect of man into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing by Himself immediately, except that divine revelation and the Word of God extend more broadly than Holy Scripture. For divine revelation and the Word of God can be and for a long time was in the Church without Scripture, although today it is not given and preserved except in Holy Scripture.

V. Paul, however, delivers our assertion not obscurely in Romans 10:17, when he says that faith comes from hearing. That this statement of his must be accepted concerning divine faith has been shown by me previously against Scotus and the Nominalists who follow him in a special Disputation on Faith. By the phrase, however: Faith is from hearing; the Apostle denotes nothing else than that faith is from the Word of God preached and perceived by hearing, as the immediately following words: and hearing by the Word of God; and those which precede in verse 14: But how shall they hear without a preacher; sufficiently clearly indicate. But that faith is from the hearing of the Word, that is, from the Word of God, proposed by the voice of the preacher and perceived by hearing, according to the usage of speech, is nothing else than that the ultimate reason for assenting to divine faith is the Word of God, proposed by the voice of the preacher and perceived by hearing, in which the assent finally rests, as is evident by the induction of other locutions not dissimilar to this, e.g., when I say, human faith is from the testimony of a truthful and trustworthy man, no one understands it otherwise than that the ultimate reason for assenting, in which the assent of human faith rests, is the authority and testimony of a truthful and trustworthy man: and when the Philosopher in I. Post. Anal. c. II. says, that knowledge is from the first, immediate, better known, and prior [principles] and causes of the conclusion, by the consensus of all this signifies that the ultimate reason for assenting to knowledge is the first, immediate, better known, and prior principles, and those which contain the cause, on account of which the predicate of the conclusion is inherent in the subject. And if I say, that the faith of the Jews, saying to Christ, what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you, John VI. 30, was from the miracles of Christ that were seen, the sense is certainly that the ultimate reason for assenting, by which they were moved to believe Christ, and in which their assent finally rested, was the miracles of Christ. In the same manner when Paul says concerning divine faith, faith is from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God, the sense is, that the Word of God, proposed by the voice of the preacher and perceived by hearing, is the ultimate reason for assenting to divine faith, and that it moves the intellect by itself immediately into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing, and by means of this its assent into the assent of revealed things, and specifically into the assent of the doctrine concerning Christ. For acts and habits of assenting derive their specific reason, denomination, and distinction from the ultimate reason for assenting, not from the intermediate. To which also pertains that which in the place already alleged v. 8. the Apostle expressly calls the preached Word of God the Word of faith, not only because it is a Word to be believed by faith, but primarily, because it is a Word to be believed by itself and for its own sake, and which by itself immediately moves the intellect into the assent of divine faith.

VI. Incidentally I advise here, what I have also advised elsewhere more than once, that under hearing is also comprehended the reading of the divine Word, which is brought about by means of sight. For just as through the hearing (of the Word) very many have believed, so through the reading (of it) many have believed. For to this end were the Gospels written, that (by their reading or preaching faith might be kindled, and) they might believe. These things are written, says John in chapter 20 of his Gospel, that you may believe, and believing may have life, writes Estius learnedly in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. X. 17.

Latin:

III.

Altera nostra assertio est: Revelatio divina, in Scriptura sacra comprehensa, sive, quod idem est, Scriptura sacra movet hominis intellectum in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem per se immediatè.

In assertione hac Scholastici, qui quidem contra Scotum & Nominales statuunt, ad assensum fidei divinæ requiri, ut revelatio divina ejúsque à Deo dependentiæ fide divina credatur, videntur, primo intuitu, nobiscum consentire. Dicunt enim apertis verbis, eam credi fide divinâ, non propter revelationem aliam, neq; propter ullam, ab ea diversam, rationem assentiendi, sed per se immediatè. Non posset autem per se immediatè credi, nisi vi quadam intellectum in sui assensum per se immediatè movendi polleret. Sed modò diximus, eos fucum facere lectori, nec quicquam minùs, quàm talem quandam vim motivam in Scriptura sacra agnoscere, sed quicquid est, quod intellectum in assensum dependentis à Deo revelationis, in Scripturis contentæ, movere possit, totum in propositionem Ecclesiæ & signa ac motiva credibilitatis alia referunt, ut modò ostensum. Jam nostram declarabimus assertionem, eamq; Scripturarum fundamentis confirmabimus.

II. In ea verò revelationis vox bis continetur; semel ex parte subjecti explicitè, & iterum ex parte prædicati implicitè, alio tamen atque alio significatu. Ex parte subjecti enim accipitur ea pro termino revelationis, nempe pro conceptibus, in intellectu virorum sanctorum per revelationis sive inspirationis actum olim productis, qui, uti dictum, formalis quædam credendorum revelatio sunt. Revelationis actus autem, in se præciso suo termino spectatus, uti nuspiam datur, ita nec in sui assensum intellectum hominis per se immediatè movere potest. Conceptus ergo, per revelationis actum olim in intellectu Virorum sanctorum efficienter à Deo producti, & qui verbis Scripturæ, sive docentium voce sive Scripturarum lectione ad nostrum intellectum transmissis, adhuc hodieque in nobis efficienter producuntur, movent eum in sui assensum supernaturalem. Hi verò, uti spectari possunt vel ratione suæ dependentiæ à Deo per revelationis actum, vel ratione suæ conformitatis cum rebus, quas repræsentant, & quarum signa sunt, ita duobus modis intelligi potest, quod dicitur in assertione, revelationem divinam, terminativè pro conceptibus, per revelationis actum productis, acceptam movere intellectum in sui assensum supernaturalem per se immediatè. Uno modo, quòd per se immediatè moveat intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ dependentiæ à Deo per revelationis actum. Altero, quòd per se immediatè moveat intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ conformitatis cum objecto, sive suæ veritatis. Assertio nostra accipitur hic priori modo, & revelationem divinam movere intellectum in sui assensum supernaturalem, quoad rem, idem est, atque conceptus, per revelationis actum in sacrorum Scriptorum intellectu productos, & qui verbis Scripturæ adhuc hodieque in nobis producuntur, movere intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ revelationis, h. e. suæ dependentiæ à Deo per actum revelandi: ut ita revelationis vox, ex parte prædicati, omnino accipienda sit pro actu revelandi, non pro ejus termino.

III. Quod hîc dicimus de revelatione, terminativè pro conceptibus, per revelationis actum productis, acceptâ, valet etiam de Scriptura sacra, quæ est quædam divina revelatio, terminativè sumta, literis comprehensa, & quemadmodum conceptus, in intellectu Virorum sanctorum olim per revelationis actum producti, movebant illorum intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ dependentiæ à Deo revelante per se immediatè, ita & Scripturæ sacræ, cùm ad ductum illorum conceptuum, qui per revelationis actum in illorum intellectu producti erant, concinnatæ sint, intellectui nostro illos ipsos conceptus, qui Scriptoribus sacris olim inspirati fuerunt, ingerunt, qui proinde, verbis Scripturæ in nobis excitati, perinde ut illi intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo revelante dependentiæ per se immediatè movent. Et quia revelatio divina, pro termino revelationis accepta, hodiè non superest, nisi in Scripturis sacris, in quibus velut res signata in suis signis continetur, eaque à Scripturis ipsis, Deo inspirante concinnatis, nihil differt; & de hac omnis nunc quæstio est, assertionis nostræ summa redit tandem ad Scripturã sacram, quæ proinde verbis minùs ambiguis proponetur clariùs hunc in modum: Scriptura sacra movet hominis intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo revelante dependentiæ per se immediatè.

IV. Revelationem divinam, terminativè sumtam, Scripturæ sacræ frequenter vocant Verbum Dei, cùm per eam, sive per conceptus, actu revelandi in intellectu Virorum sanctorum productos, Deus olim locutus sit Viris sanctis, & quæ credenda erant, manifestaverit; & verba, velut signa conceptuum inspiratorum, sive voce prolata, sive scripto comprehensa, sint Verbum Dei externum, quo etiamnum ad nos loquitur. Unde eodem res redibit, sive dicatur, Verbum Dei, sive dicatur, divinam revelationem, sive dicatur, Scripturam sacram movere intellectum hominis in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo revelante dependentiæ per se immediatè, nisi quòd revelatio divina, Verbumq́, Dei latiùs patent, quàm Scriptura sacra. Nam revelatio divina & Verbum Dei potest esse & longo tempore fuit in Ecclesia absque Scriptura, licet hodiè non, nisi in Scriptura sacra, detur & conservetur.

V. Assertionem nostram verò haud obscurè tradit Paulus Rom. X. 17. cùm fidem ex auditu esse ait. Quod ejus dictum de fide divina accipiendum esse, antehac contra Scotum, &, qui eum sequuntur, Nominales, in Disputatione peculiari de Fide à me ostensum est. Phrasi autem: Fides est ex auditu; Apostolus nihil denotat aliud, quàm fidem esse ex Verbo Dei prædicato, audituq́, percepto, ut proximè sequentia: auditus autem per Verbum Dei; & quæ v. 14. præcedunt: Quomodo autem audient absq; prædicante; satis perspicuè indicant. Fidem verò esse ex auditu Verbi, h. e. ex Verbo Dei, prædicantis voce proposito audituq́; percepto, ex usu loquendi, nihil est aliud, quàm rationem assentiendi fidei divinæ ultimam esse Verbum Dei, prædicantis voce propositum audituq́; perceptum, in quo ultimò sistit assensus, ut patet inductione aliarum huic non absimilium locutionum, v. g. cum dico, fides humana est ex testificatione hominis veracis & fide digni, nemo aliter intelligit, quàm rationem assentiendi ultimam, in qua sistit assensus fidei humanæ, esse auctoritatem & testificationem hominis veracis & fide digni: & cum Philosophus I. Post. Anal. c. II. dicit, scientiam esse ex primis, immediatis, notioribus & prioribus & causis conclusionis, omnium consensu hoc significat, rationem assentiendi ultimam scientiæ esse principia prima, immediata, notiora & priora, & quæ contineant causam, propter quam prædicatum conclusionis subjecto insit. Et si dicam, fidem Judæorum, dicentium Christo, quod facis signum, ut videamus & credamus tibi, Joh. VI. 30. fuisse ex visis miraculis Christi, sensus utique est, rationem assentiendi ultimam, quâ ad credendum Christo movebantur, & in qua illorum assensus ultimò sistebat, fuisse miracula Christi. Eundem in modum cùm de fide divina dicit Paulus, fides est ex auditu, auditus autem per Verbum Dei, sensus est, Verbum Dei, prædicantis voce propositum, audituq́; perceptum, esse fidei divinæ rationem assentiendi ultimam, idque movere intellectum per se immediatè in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo revelante dependentiæ, & mediante hoc sui assensu in assensum rerum revelatarum, & speciatim in assensum doctrinæ de Christo. Actus enim & habitus assentiendi sortiuntur suam specificam rationem, denominationem & distinctionem à ratione assentiendi ultima, non ab intermedia. Quò pertinet etiam, quod loco jam allegato v. 8. Apostolus Verbum Dei prædicatum expiessè vocat Verbum fidei, non solùm quòd sit Verbum, fide credendum, sed inprimis, quòd sit Verbum, per se & propter se credendum, & quod per se immediatè intellectum in assensum fidei divinæ movet.

VI. Obiter hîc moneo, quod etiam alibi plus simplici vice monui, sub auditu comprehendi etiam lectionem Verbi divini, quæ fit mediante visu. Sicut enim per auditum (Verbi) plurimi, ita per lectionem (ejus) multi crediderunt. Nam ad hoc scripta sunt Evangelia, ut (eorum lectione vel prædicatione accendatur fides, &) credant. Hæc scripta sunt, ait Johannes Evangelii sui cap. 20. ut credatis, & credentes vitam habeatis, scitè scribit Estius in Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. c. X. 17.


### IV. Third assertion: Holy Scripture, read or proposed and explained by the voice of…

IV.

Third assertion: Holy Scripture, read or proposed and explained by the voice of a teacher, and perceived by hearing, moves the human intellect to a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing, indeed immediately of itself, but with the supernatural concurrence of God.

I. This assertion is directly opposed to the aforementioned inventions of the Scholastics and Sophists in the Papacy, who, although they teach in words that Holy Scripture does indeed move the intellect to a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God immediately of itself, nevertheless contend that this cannot happen unless either its dependence upon God has been known by the intellect through discourse, deduced from signs and motives of credibility; or the will has been induced and moved by the same to wish to believe and to command the intellect to assent. By this very thing they utterly deny the power of Holy Scripture, by which it moves the intellect to a supernatural assent of itself and its dependence upon God immediately of itself. And indeed those who contend that divine revelation, or, which amounts to the same thing, Holy Scripture, moves the intellect to an assent of its dependence upon God immediately of itself, but only then, when it has been known through discourse, deduced from signs and motives of credibility, must assert one of two things: either that the dependence of Scripture upon God is represented to the intellect immediately of itself through discourse deduced from signs of credibility, so that from the terms apprehended the identity of the predicate with the subject immediately appears to it; or that it is represented only by way of a conclusion, deduced from premises, so that the intellect is determined to its assent by the premises. The former cannot be said. For the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God, after the discourse deduced from the signs of credibility, remains as non-evident and obscure to the intellect in itself as it was non-evident and obscure to it in itself before the discourse, nor can the identity of the predicate with the subject be known immediately by itself from the apprehended terms after it any more than before it. Nor is there any reason to object that divine faith is by its own nature such that it moves the intellect into a supernatural assent of revelation, after it has been known from the signs and motives of credibility, immediately by itself, and that it has that previous assent only as a condition without which it cannot be, but by no means as its cause. I say, there is no reason why they should so except or object. For it is repugnant to the account of all habits of the mind, both natural and supernatural, which is that they incline the intellect to assent according to the requirement of their object: immediately by itself indeed, if the identity of the predicate with the subject appears to the intellect immediately from the apprehended terms in the object, or certainly if it possesses by some supernatural power the ability to move the intellect to its own assent immediately by itself: but mediately, if the identity of the predicate with the subject in the object cannot be known by the intellect except from a reason of knowing, sought from the very nature of the object or from elsewhere. Since therefore the Scholastics, with whom we are now dealing, deny that the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God can be known immediately by the intellect from the apprehended terms, or that it can be so clearly proposed to the intellect through a discourse deduced from the signs of credibility that its truth appears to the intellect immediately from the apprehended terms, it must be admitted by them at any rate that it is not the nature of divine faith that, after the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God is known through a discourse deduced from the signs and motives of credibility, it inclines the intellect to its supernatural assent immediately by itself, but on the contrary one of two things must be admitted: either that the intellect is clearly not inclined to its supernatural assent immediately by itself, but only through a discourse deduced from the signs of credibility, and thus that divine faith is nothing, but is feigned; or that there is given some supernatural power of divine revelation or Holy Scripture, by which it moves the intellect immediately by itself into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God, although it be non-evident and obscure, which our third assertion maintains, but the aforementioned Sophists deny. Whence nothing remains to be said, except that they refer the assent of divine revelation, or, which is the same thing, of Holy Scripture and its dependence upon God, to signs and motives of credibility, not as a condition without which it is not, but as the ultimate reason for assenting. And the thing itself speaks to this. For to one asking them why they believe that God is triune and one, they can respond in no other way than that they believe this on account of divine revelation, or because God has revealed it in the Scriptures. Furthermore, to one asking whence they know, or why they believe, that God has revealed this in the Scriptures, Gregorius de Val. d. l. bids them respond that they indeed do not know that clearly, yet they believe it with the same faith infallibly, and that indeed not on account of another revelation, but indeed on account of the infallible proposition of the Church, as if on account of a condition required for believing that. Now if you reduce the response given to both questions into syllogistic form, the matter will be plain. From the response to the former question, which is the principal one, this principal syllogism will arise: Whatever God reveals in Scripture is to be believed certainly and infallibly. But God reveals in Scripture that He is triune and one. Therefore, that God is triune and one is to be believed certainly and infallibly. The major premise, since it is evident, does not need proof. The minor premise, however, which is not evident and needs proof, now comes into question, namely whence they know, or why they believe, that God has revealed in the Scriptures that He is triune and one, and the response given to it will produce this prosyllogism: Whatever the Church proposes as to be believed infallibly, that is to be believed without doubt. But the Church proposes as to be believed infallibly that God has said or revealed in Scripture that He is triune and one. Therefore, that God has said or revealed in Scripture that He is triune and one is to be believed without doubt. Where, just as in the principal argument divine revelation is the proximate reason for assenting, so in the other prosyllogism brought forward for the confirmation of the minor proposition, the infallible proposition of the Church, without doubt, is the remote and ultimate reason for assenting, not a mere condition without which it is not. Or if they wish to contend more stubbornly that it is a mere condition, not a cause or reason for assenting, let them show what, then, is the true reason and cause for assenting? None, they can bring forward none, unless they admit with us a certain supernatural power of divine revelation, by which of itself it immediately moves the intellect to its supernatural assent, which they acknowledge and establish, which however they refuse to do up to this point. For the things which they have invented regarding this matter are mere illusions and trifles, as has just been shown.

But those who contend that the will, after it has been moved to wish to believe through a process of reasoning deduced from signs and motives of credibility, moves and determines the intellect by its own command so that it may assent to divine revelation immediately in itself, fall into the same difficulty. This is acknowledged among the more recent Scholastics themselves by Cardinal de Lugo, Diss. I. de Virt. Fidei divinæ Sect. III. 32, and he shows well that it cannot happen that the will, induced by motives and signs of credibility, moves the intellect so that it may assent to divine revelation immediately in itself, and yet not know it in itself immediately in itself, just as it cannot happen that the will loves medicine for its own sake, and yet its goodness, lovable in itself and for its own sake, does not appear in it. Either, therefore, the signs and motives of credibility, inducing the will to command the intellect to elicit an assent to divine revelation in itself and immediately, also represent to the intellect divine revelation and its dependence on God in itself, and by way of a first principle, or they represent it by the force of reasoning alone and by way of a conclusion. The former cannot be said, as has just been shown. But if the latter is said, that which is imagined will fall, namely that the will, induced by signs and motives of credibility, can command the intellect, and by that very act command it to assent to divine revelation and its dependence on God immediately in itself, or to assent to it as a first principle, known immediately in itself, and it must be confessed to the contrary that it cannot command the intellect to assent to divine revelation otherwise than as to a conclusion, known from signs of credibility, and thus mediately and through reasoning.

II. These Scholastic inventions and trifles being therefore dismissed, we return to our third assertion. Although the Scholastics here commonly use the term revelation, yet because we are now dealing precisely with Holy Scripture, which, as to the thing itself, is divine revelation, taken terminatively, committed to writing by God inspiring it, or written divine revelation, for the sake of greater clarity we have formed our assertion concerning Holy Scripture. When, however, we say that Holy Scripture, read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, explained and perceived by hearing, moves the intellect of man into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God with the supernatural concurrence of God, we signify that the assent of divine faith, by which the divine origin of Holy Scripture is believed, depends both upon Scripture itself and upon God, concurring with it, as upon a formal motive, and thus upon both together and jointly, but from neither separately and apart.

III. That it is from God, the Holy Scriptures teach clearly. For first, the Apostle of the Gentiles, 1 Thess. 2:13, gives thanks to God that the Thessalonians received the λόγον ἀκοῆς, the word of hearing, i.e., the Word of God preached and perceived by hearing, not as the word of men, but as it is truly, as the Word of God. Where to receive the Word, preached by men, not as the word of men, but as the Word of God, is to receive it in such a way that you are convinced in your mind that it is not the mere word of man, but the word which God Himself speaks, with him who preaches lending his tongue and voice, which is the same as believing that God Himself is saying or testifying to that which is proposed to be believed through the preaching. But that the Thessalonians received it in that way, Paul ascribes entirely to God, who testifies to it in their hearts, and persuades them to believe that it proceeded from Him and is His word, as is gathered partly from the thanksgiving which he directs to God on this account: We give thanks, he says, to God without ceasing, because when you received the word of God which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but (as it is truly) as the Word of God; partly from the words immediately following: Who also works in you who believe, i.e., He moves your hearts interiorly, and effectively persuades them so that you believe the word which you heard from us to be the Word of God. Divine faith, therefore, by which it is believed that the preached Word of God is the Word of God, and depends upon Him revealing it, is from God, and the preached Word of God moved the intellect of the Thessalonians into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God with the supernatural concurrence of God. By what power, however, the Word of God, preached by the Apostles, moved the Thessalonians to believe that it is not the mere word of man

Latin:

IV.

Affertio tertia: Scriptura sacra, lecta vel voce docentis proposita & explicata, audituq; percepta, movet hominis intellectum ad assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo revelante dependentiæ per se immediatè quidem, sed cum Dei concursu supernaturali.

I. Assertio hæc directè opponitur commemoratis superius commentis Scholasticorum & Sophistarum in Papatu, qui licet verbis doceant, Scripturam sacram movere quidem intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ per se immediatè, contendunt tamen, hoc fieri non posse, nisi postquam vel ejus dependentia à Deo per discursum, ex signis & motivis credibilitatis deductum, ab intellectu cognita; vel voluntas per eundem ad volendum credere, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum inducta & permota est. Quo ipso Scripturæ sacræ vim, quâ intellectum in sui suæque à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem per se immediatè moveat, prorsus denegant. Et quidem qui contendunt, divinam revelationem, sive, quod eodem redit, Scripturam sacram movere intellectum in assensum suæ à Deo dependentiæ per se immediatè, sed tùm demùm, cùm ea per discursum, ex signis & motivis credibilitatis deductum, cognita est, necesse habent alterutrum asserere, vel per discursum, ex signis credibilitatis deductum repræsentari intellectui dependentiam Scripturæ à Deo per se immediatè, ita ut ex terminis apprehensis statim identitas prædicati cum subjecto ei appareat: aut repræsentari eò tantum per modum conclusionis, ex præmissis deductæ, ut ad ejus assensum intellectus per præmissas determinetur. Prius dici non potest. Nam dependentia Scripturæ sacræ à Deo, post discursum, ex signis credibilitatis deductum, tam manet in se intellectui inevidens & obscura, quàm inevidens & obscura ei in se fuit ante discursum, nec magis post eum potest identitas prædicati cum subjecto ex apprehensis terminis per se immediatè cognosci, quàm ante eum. Neque est, quod obtendatur, fidem divinam suâpse naturâ talem esse, ut intellectum in assensum revelationis supernaturalem, postquam ex signis & motivis credibilitatis cognita est, moveat per se immediatè, & illum assensum prævium habere se tantùm ut conditionem sine qua non, minimè verò ut causam ejus. Non, inquam, est, quod ita excipiant aut obtendant. Repugnat enim commento omnium, cùm naturalium tùm supernaturalium habituum mentis ratio, quæ est, ut inclinent intellectum in assensum pro exigentia sui objecti: per se immediatè quidem, si in objecto identitas prædicati cum subjecto statim ex apprehensis terminis, atq; adeò per se immediatè intellectui appareat, vel certè si vi quâdam supernaturali id polleat movendi intellectum in sui assensum per se immediatè: mediatè autem, si in objecto identitas prædicati cum subjecto non nisi ex ratione cognoscendi, ex ipsa objecti natura, vel aliunde petitâ, ab intellectu cognosci possit. Quia ergo Scholastici, quibuscum nobis nunc res est, negant, dependentiam Scripturæ sacræ à Deo ex apprehensis terminis statim ab intellectu cognosci, vel per discursum, ex signis credibilitatis deductum, ita clarè intellectui proponi posse, ut ex apprehensis terminis statim ejus veritas intellectui appareat, fatendum ipsis utiq; est, fidei divinæ eam rationem non esse, ut postquam per discursum, ex signis & motivis credibilitatis deductum, dependentia Scripturæ sacræ à Deo cognita est, intellectum in illius assensum supernaturalem per se immediatè inclinet, sed contra admittendum alterutrum, vel intellectum planè non inclinari in supernaturalem illius assensum per se immediatè, sed tantùm per discursum ex signis credibilitatis deductum, atque adeò fidem divinam nullam esse, sed fingi; vel dari aliquam divinæ revelationis sive Scripturæ sacræ vim supernaturalem, quâ per se immediatè intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ, licet inevidentis & obscuræ, moveat, quod nostra affertio tertia vult, memorati Sophistæ autem negant. Unde nihil superest dicendum, quàm illos referre assensum divinæ revelationis, vel, quod idem est, Scripturæ sacræ ejusque dependentiæ à Deo in signa & motiva credibilitatis, non velut in conditionem sine qua non, sed velut in rationem assentiendi ultimam. Quod & res ipsa loquitur. Quærenti enim ex illis, cur credant, Deum esse trinum & unum, non aliter respondere possunt, quàm se credere hoc propter divinam revelationem, sive quia Deus in Scripturis revelavit. Quærenti porro, unde cognoscant, vel cur credant, Deum in Scripturis hoc revelâsse, respondere jubet Gregorius de Val. d. l. se quidem non nôsse illud clarè, credere tamen eâdem fide infallibiliter, & id quidem non ob aliam revelationem, benè tamen ob infallibilem propositionem Ecclesiæ, tanquam ob conditionem, ad id credendum requisitam. Jam si ad utramque quæstionem reddita responsio in formam syllogisticam reducas, res erit plana. Ex responsione ad priorem, quæ principalis est, quæstionem hic proveniet syllogismus principalis: Quicquid Deus in Scriptura revelat, est certò & infallibiliter credendum. Atqui se esse trinum & unum, Deus in Scriptura revelat. Ergo Deum esse trinum & unum certò & infallibiliter credendum est. Major cum evidens sit, non eget probatione. Minor verò, quæ inevidens est & probatione eget, venit jam in quæstionem, unde scilicet cognoscant, aut cur credant, Deum revelâsse in Scripturis, se esse trinum & unum, & responsio ad eam reddita hunc pariet prosyllogismum : Quicquid Ecclesia infallibiliter credendum proponit, illud est indubitatò credendum. Atqui Deum dixisse sive revelâsse in Scriptura, se esse trinum & unum Ecclesia infallibiliter credendum proponit. Ergo Deum dixisse sive revelâsse in Scriptura, se esse trinum & unum, indubitatò credendum est. Ubi quemadmodum in argumento principali divina revelatio est ratio assentiendi proxima, ita in altero ad confirmationem propositionis minoris allato prosyllogismo propositio Ecclesiæ infallibilis, citra dubium, est ratio assentientiendi remota & ultima, non nuda Conditio sine qua non. Vel si pertinaciùs contendere velint, eam esse nudam conditionem, non causam sive rationem assentiendi, ostendant, quæ tandem sit ratio & causa assentiendi vera? Nullam, nullam afferre possunt, nisi nobiscum vim quandam divinæ revelationis supernaturalem, quâ per se immediatè intellectum in sui assensum supernaturalem moveat, agnoscant & statuant, quod tamen huc usque recusant. Nam quæ hanc in rem commenti sunt, meras præstigias & nugas esse, modò ostensum est.

Qui verò contendunt, voluntatem, postquam per discursum, ex signis & motivis credibilitatis deductum, mota est ad volendum credere, movere & suo imperio determinare intellectum, ut assentietur divinæ revelationi per se immediatè, eandem incurrunt difficultatem. Quod agnoscit inter ipsos Scholasticos recentiores Cardinalis de Lugo Diss. I. de Virt. Fidei divinæ Sect. III. 32. ostenditq; benè, fieri non posse, ut voluntas, per motiva & signa credibilitatis inducta, moveat intellectum, ut assentietur divinæ revelationi per se immediatè, nec tamen eam in se ipsa per se immediatè cognoscat, perinde ut fieri non potest, ut medicinam voluntas amet propter seipsam, nec tamen in illa appareat bonitas per se & propter se amabilis. Aut ergo signa & motiva credibilitatis, voluntatem ad imperandum intellectui divinæ revelationis assensum, per se & immediatè eliciendum inducentia, repræsentant etiam intellectui revelationem divinam ejusq; dependentiam à Deo in se ipsa, & per modum principii primi, aut repræsentant eam vi solius discursus & per modum conclusionis. Priùs dici non potest, uti modò ostensum. Sin posterius dicatur, cadet, quod fingitur, voluntatem, signis & motivis credibilitatis inductam, posse intellectui imperare, & actu ipso imperare ei, ut divinæ revelationi ejusque à Deo dependentiæ assentietur per se immediatè, sive ut ei assentietur ut principio primo, per se immediatè cognito, & fatendum contra est, eam non posse intellectui aliter assensum divinæ revelationis imperare, quàm ut conclusioni, ex signis credibilitatis, atque adeò mediatè & per discursum cognitæ.

II. Hisce ergo commentis & nugis Scholasticis missis ad nostram assertionem tertiam revertimur. Quamvis verò Scholastici hîc communiter revelationis termino utantur, quia tamen nos præcisè de Scriptura sacra nunc agimus, quæ, quoad rem, est revelatio divina, terminativè sumta, Deo inspirante in literas relata, sive revelatio divina scripta, assertionem nostram, majoris perspicuitatis causâ, de Scriptura sacra formavimus. Quando autem dicimus, Scripturam sacram, lectam aut voce docentis propositam, explicatam & auditu perceptam, movere hominis intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ cum concursu Dei supernaturali, significamus, assensum fidei divinæ, quâ divina Scripturæ sacræ origo creditur, dependere & ab ipsa Scriptura, & à Deo, cum ea concurrente, velut à motivo formali, atque adeò ab utroque simul & junctim, à neutro autem seorsim & separatim.

III. Quòd à Deo sit, luculenter docent Scripturæ sacræ. Primùm enim Gentium Apostolus 1. Thess. II. 13. agit Deo gratias, quòd Thessalonicenses λόγον ἀκοῆς sermonem auditum, i. e. Verbum Dei prædicatum, audituque perceptum, acceperint, non ut sermonem hominum, sed sicut est verè, ut Dei sermonem. Ubi Verbum, ab hominibus prædicatum, excipere non ut sermonem hominum, sed ut sermonem Dei, est ita illud excipere, ut apud animum tuum persuasus sis, quòd non sit nudus hominis sermo, sed sermo, quem Deus ipse loquatur, illo qui prædicat, linguam & vocem commodante, quod idem est, atque credere, Deum ipsum dicere seu testificari id, quod per prædicationem credendum proponitur. Quod autem Thessalonicenses illud ita exceperunt, adscribit Paulus in solidum Deo, in ipsorum cordibus illud testificanti, iisque ut à se profectum suumque verbum esse crederent, persuadenti, ut colligitur partim ex gratiarum actione, quam hoc nomine ad Deum dirigit: Gratias, inquiens, agimus Deo indesinenter, quòd acceptum de Deo sermonem, quem audistis ex nobis, exceperitis, non ut sermonem hominum, sed (sicut verè est) ut Dei sermonem; partim ex verbis, immediatè sequentibus: Qui etiam in vobis, qui creditis, operatur, h. e. interiùs corda vestra movet, iisque efficaciter persuadet, ut sermonem, quem ex nobis audistis, Dei sermonem esse credatis. Fides divina igitur, quâ creditur, Verbum Dei prædicatum esse Dei Verbum, & dependere ab eo revelante, est à Deo, & Verbum Dei prædicatum movit Thessalonicensium intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ cum concursu Dei supernaturali. Quâ autem virtute Verbum Dei, ab Apostolis prædicatum, Thessalonicenses movit ad credendum, quòd non sit nudus hominis ver-


### but the Word of God, or the Word, which God himself spoke in the Apostles and…

but the Word of God, or the Word, which God himself spoke in the Apostles and through them, that sacred Scripture still moves even now, when it is read or perceived by hearing as proposed by the voice of a preacher, the hearts of men, so that they may believe that it has proceeded from God, and that what it says, God says or testifies. The reason is: because the Word of God, preached by the Apostles from divine inspiration; and Scripture, composed from divine inspiration, do not differ, except accidentally, in that the former consists of words uttered by mouth; the latter of words consigned to writing. However, in relation to the intellect of the believing man, the objective formal reason of both is one, the motive force of the intellect toward assent is one and the same.

Then the same Apostle, Eph. 1:17 seqq., establishes the motive force, by which God concurs with His Word to cause the assent of divine faith, in its very divine δυνάμει or power. For thus among other things: God, he says, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, through the knowledge of Him, the eyes of your mind being enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which He has called you, etc., and what is the excellent greatness of His power toward us, who believe according to the efficacy of the might of His strength. Where what else is τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως Ἰησῦ, & τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, the excellent greatness of the power of God, and the might of His strength, according to the efficacy of which the Ephesians believed, than His divine power, joined with His very Word, which exerted itself effectively in their hearts with the Word and through it to kindle faith in them. To which is added, that this very power, which God exerts in us believers to cause the assent of faith, is also said to have been exerted in Christ, when He raised Him from the dead, etc. But the power by which God raised Christ from the dead is His very own divine power.

Thirdly, I Cor. 2:5, the aforementioned Apostle refers again the assent of divine faith, which the converted Corinthians offered to the Word of God preached by Paul, to the power of God. My speech, he says, and my preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: that your faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. Where are opposed to one another the persuasive words of human wisdom, and the demonstration of the Spirit and of power; likewise also the wisdom of men and the power of God, as two formal motives, by the one of which the pseudo-Apostles were attempting to lead the Corinthians into their errors, and by the other the Apostle had led them to the faith of Christ: the former relied upon persuasive arguments, drawn from human wisdom and encrusted with the paint of words; the latter relied upon the Word of God, proposed through a simple style of speech, without the paint of words, by means of preaching, but joined with the power of the Holy Spirit, or the power of God, so that ultimately the faith of the former might be resolved into human wisdom; but the faith of the latter into the power of God, not indeed viewed in itself separately, but exerting itself with the Word and through it: That there is, as regards the present, the same reason for Holy Scripture, whether read or proposed by the voice of a teacher and perceived by hearing, as there was for the Word of God, preached by the Apostles and perceived by hearing, has just been said.

Fourthly: the aforementioned Apostle calls the Gospel of Christ, or the Gospel concerning Christ, more than once the power of God. I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek, he says in Rom. 1. 16. That speech concerning the cross is to them indeed that perish foolishness, but to them which are saved, that is, to us, it is THE POWER OF GOD, 1 Cor. 1. 18. We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness. But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, THE POWER OF GOD and the wisdom of God, ibid. v. 23, 24. In which places the Gospel of Christ, the speech concerning the cross, and the preaching of Christ crucified, as regards the thing itself, are nothing else than the doctrine concerning Christ, divinely revealed, and proposed by the Apostles through preaching for belief. It is called, however, the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, without doubt, because through it God is powerful and efficacious in the souls of men, and moves them through it, so that they may believe, and believers may attain salvation. For otherwise, if it were and were called the power of God in itself precisely, apart from the concurrence of the divine power, it would be and would be called the power of God because either the words, inspired by God, by which He speaks to us, and in which He is powerful and efficacious, by their own nature and through their native power of signifying, could move and do move the intellect to believe, or because the things signified by them are by their own nature powerful and efficacious, so that the intellect, when they are proposed to it through words and apprehended, by itself they can move and do move to their supernatural assent. Third, that from which the doctrine revealed concerning Christ could precisely, without the concurrence of God and of divine power, have the force of moving the intellect to a supernatural assent to itself, and could be called the power of God unto salvation to the believer, cannot even be imagined. But no one would say the first. For the words of which the doctrine revealed concerning Christ consists are taken from the usage of speech, and have obtained their force of signifying from that, which, viewed in and of itself, can move the intellect no further than to the simple apprehension of the things signified, which has been shown by us at greater length elsewhere. Nor are the things signified by the words, by their own nature, such that they can, of themselves, move the intellect to a supernatural assent to them, once they have been proposed to it by words and apprehended by the same, which was the second member of our disjunctive. For these are non-evident, and exceed the grasp of human reason to such a degree that, when left to itself, they seem absurd and foolish, 1 Cor. 1. 23, ch. 2. 14. It remains, therefore, that the Gospel concerning Christ is and is called the power of God unto salvation to the believer, because it always has the power of God joined to it, and with it and through it God exerts His divine power in the hearts of believers, and moves them to the supernatural assent of faith.

Fifth, in 1 Thess. 1. 5, the praised Apostle says: Our Gospel was toward you ὀυκ ἐν λόγῳ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν δυνάμει καὶ πνέυματι ἁγίῳ, i.e., not by word only, but also by power and the Holy Spirit. By these words he shows a twofold relation of the Gospel preached by him to the conversion and faith of the Thessalonians: one of λόγος, of word; the other of δυνάμεως καὶ πνέυματος ἁγίου, of power and the Holy Spirit, concurring together with the λόγος or word of the Gospel, and he ascribes to both jointly, and to neither separately, the fact that the Thessalonians had received his word, that is, the Gospel preached by him. By this very thing he confirms our third assertion above in almost as many words.

We are indeed not unaware that some understand by δύναμιν in this passage miracles, as if they were works of δύναμις, that is, of virtue or divine power; and by πνέυμα ἅγιον, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as were the gifts of tongues, of prophecy, of healings, etc. But they depart from the propriety of the words, with no necessity compelling them. For the Apostle distinguishes here on the one hand, indeed, λόγον, the word, from the other truly δύναμιν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, power and the Holy Spirit, as two things conjoined in the very Gospel preached by him, and exerting themselves together through his preaching for the conversion and faith of the Thessalonians, and it signifies that they were converted and brought to faith, not by the bare and sole λόγῳ or word of the Gospel, but by that τῷ λόγῳ or word, and by the δυνάμει or power of the Holy Spirit conjoined with it, taken together and exerting themselves simultaneously. And the whole context demands this sense. For in that whole passage, the subject is the effects proper to the Gospel. And indeed in the preceding. v. 3. the Apostle commends the faith, hope, and charity of the Thessalonians, and in v. 4 he recalls to their memory their ἐκλογὴν or election, by which, namely, they had been called forth and selected by God from the rest of the multitude of unbelieving men, and he teaches in this v. 5 that this was done through the Gospel preached among them by him, which was not placed ἐν λόγῳ μόνον, in word only, or in bare words, but with the words it comprised a certain higher δύναμιν, namely the δύναμιν or divine power of the Holy Spirit, and it is to this, exerting itself together with the word of the Gospel, that it must be attributed that they were converted and became imitators of the Apostles and of Christ, and received their word with much affliction and with the joy of the Holy Spirit, as he teaches in the same place v. 6. All of which are proper effects of the Holy Spirit and his power, conjoined with the λόγῳ or word of the Gospel, and can by no means be ascribed to miracles or to the power of performing miracles. Nor do we read anything in the Acts of the Apostles about any miracle performed, or about δυνάμεσι or the power of performing miracles, which exerted itself with the preaching of the Gospel among the Thessalonians for their conversion and faith, so that Paul could be seen to point his finger there, but Luke, who in Acts XVII. 2, 3, 4 described their conversion, and in v. 11, 12 that of the neighboring Beroeans, mentions in both places only the preached Gospel, and precisely ascribes the conversion of both to this. But we do not wish to be more prolix in a manifest matter, and to bring forward more passages of Scripture which exist here and there.

Nor does that need further proof here, that the assent of divine faith also depends on Holy Scripture. For in all the passages adduced, the word of the Gospel, or the preached Word of God, the Gospel of Christ, the word of the cross, etc., are conjoined with God, and the power of God, and both together; to neither separately and apart do they ascribe the assent of supernatural faith, as will be evident to one considering it. To this also may be referred the passage cited above from Rom. XI. 17, where Paul writes in express terms that faith is from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God, which, as to the matter, is the same as faith being from the preached Word, and perceived by hearing. To the same point pertains that which is said of the faithful, that they believe through the word of the Apostles, i.e., through the Word of God preached by the Apostles, John XVII. 20, etc.

Latin:

bum, sed Verbum Dei, sive Verbum, quod Deus ipse in Apostolis & per eos loqueretur, illa movet etiamnum Scriptura sacra, cum legitur vel prædicantis voce proposita auditu percipitur, corda hominum, ut eam a Deo profectam esse, & quæ illa dicit, Deum dicere sive testificari credant. Ratio est: quia Verbum Dei, ab Apostolis ex divina inspiratione prædicatum; & Scriptura, ex divina inspiratione concinuata, non differunt, nisi accidentaliter, in quantum illud verbis, ore prolatis; hæc verbis, scripto consignatis, constant. In ordine autem ad intellectum hominis credentis una utriusq; est ratio objectiva formalis, vis motiva intellectus ad assensum una & eadem.

Deinde idem Apostolus Eph. I. 17. seqq. constituit vim motivam, qua cum Verbo suo Deus ad assensum fidei divinæ causandum concurrit, in ipsa ejus divina δυνάμει sive potentia. Ita enim inter alia: Deus, inquit, Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Pater gloriæ, det vobis Spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis, per agnitionem sui, illuminatos oculos mentis vestræ, ut sciatis, quæ sit spes, ad quam ille vocavit &c. & quæ sit excellens magnitudo potentiæ illius in nos, qui credimus secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ejus. Ubi quid aliud est τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως Ἰησῦ, & τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, excellens magnitudo potentiæ Dei, & robur fortitudinis ejus, secundum cujus efficaciam Ephesii crediderunt, quam divina ejus potentia, cum ipso ejus Verbo conjuncta, quæ in illorum cordibus cum Verbo & per illud efficaciter se ad fidem in illis accendendam exeruit. Quò accedit, quòd hanc ipsam potentiam, quam in nobis credentibus Deus ad causandum fidei assensum exerit, etiam exeruisse dicitur in Christo, cum suscitaret eum ex mortuis &c. Sed potentia, qua Deus ex mortuis Christum suscitavit, est ipsa ejus divina potentia.

Tertiò I. Cor. II. 5. refert Apostolus laudatus rursum assensum fidei divinæ, quem conversi Corinthii Verbo Dei, per Paulum prædicato, præbuerunt, in potentiam Dei. Sermo meus, ait, & prædicatio mea non erat in persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed in ostensione Spiritus & potentiæ: ut fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei. Ubi inter se opponuntur persuasoria humanæ sapientiæ verba, & ostensio spiritus & potentiæ; itemque sapientia hominum & potentia Dei, tanquam duo motiva formalia, quorum altero pseudoApostoli Corinthios in errores suos perducere conabantur, altero Apostolus illos ad fidem Christi perduxerat : illi rationibus persuasoriis, ex sapientia humana depromtis, verborumq́; fuco incrustatis; hic Verbo Dei, simplici sermonis genere, absq; verborum fuco, per prædicationem proposito, sed cum virtute Spiritus sancti, sive potentia Dei conjuncto nitebatur, ut ultimò illorum fides in sapientiam humana; horum verò fides in potentiam Dei, non quide in se seorsim spectatam, sed cum Verbo & per illud sese exerentein resolveretur: Esse autem, quoad præsens, eande ratione Scripturæ sacræ, sive lectæ, sive voce docentis propositæ audituq́; perceptæ, quæ fuit Verbi Dei, ab Apostolis prædicati audituq; percepti, modò dictũ est.

Quartò: vocat Apostolus laudatus Evangelium Christi, sive Evangelium de Christo plus simplici vice potentiam Dei. Non pudet me Evangelii Christi : potentia siquidem est Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Judæo primùm, tùm etiam Græco, inquit Rom. 1. 16. Sermo ille de cruce iis quidem qui pereunt, stultitia est, iis autem qui servantur, id est, nobis POTENTIA DEI est, 1. Cor. 1. 16. Nos prædicamus Christum crucifixum Judæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis verò stultitiam. Ipsis autem vocatis tùm Judæis, tùm Græcis, DEI POTENTIAM & Dei sapientiam, ibid. v. 23. 24. Quibus in locis Evangelium Christi, sermo de cruce, & prædicatio Christi crucifixi, quoad rem, nihil aliud sunt, quàm doctrina de Christo, divinitus revelata, & per prædicationem ab Apostolis ad credendum proposita. Dicitur autem Dei potentia ad salutem omni credenti, dubio procul, quòd per eam Deus potens & efficax sit in hominum animis, eosque per eam moveat, ut credant, & credentes salutem consequantur. Aliàs enim si in se præcisè, citra Dei potentiæq; divinæ concursum potentia Dei esset ac diceretur, esset & diceretur Dei potentia, quòd vel voces, à Deo inspiratæ, quibus ad nos loquitur, & in nobis potens & efficax est, suâpte naturâ, & per suam nativam vim significandi intellectum ad credendum movere possint & moveant, vel quòd res iis significatæ suâ naturâ potentes & efficaces sint, ut intellectum, ubi per voces ei propositæ & apprehensæ sunt, per se ad sui assensum supernaturalem movere possint & moveant. Tertium, à quo doctrina de Christo revelata, præcisè citra Dei potentiæq; divinæ concursum habeat vim movendi intellectum ad assensum sui supernaturallem, & credenti potentia Dei ad salutem dici queat, ne fingi quidem potest. Primùm autem nemo dixerit. Voces enim, quibus doctrina de Christo revelata constat, ex usu loquendi defumtæ sunt, & ex eo suam significandi vim obtinuerunt, quæ, per se & in se spectata, non longiùs, quàm ad apprehensionem simplicem rerum significatarum intellectum movere possunt, quod alibi pluribus à nobis ostensum est. Neque etiam res, vocibus significatæ, suâpte naturâ tales sunt, ut intellectum, ubi ei per voces propositæ & ab eodem apprehensæ sunt, per se ad sui assensum supernaturalem movere possint, quod alterum nostræ disjunctivæ membrum erat. Hæ enim sunt inevidentes, exceduntq; humanæ rationis captum usque adeò, ut ei, sibi relictæ, absurdæ & stultæ videantur, 1. Cor. 1. 23. c. II. 14. Relinquitur ergo, quòd Evangelium de Christo sit & dicatur potentia Dei ad salutem credenti, quòd Dei potentiam semper sibi conjunctam habeat, & cum illo atq; per illud Deus suam divinam potentiã in credentium cordibus exerat, eaq; ad assensum fidei supernaturalem moveat.

Quintò 1. Thess. 1. 5. ait laudatus Apostolus : Evangelium nostrum fuit erga vos ὀυκ ἐν λόγῳ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν δυνάμει καὶ πνέυματι ἁγίῳ i. e. non per sermonem solum, sed etiam per virtutem & Spiritum sanctum. Quibus duplicem Evangelii, à se prædicati, habitudinem ad Thessalonicensium conversionem & fidem ostendit : Unam λόγου sermonis; alteram δυνάμεως καὶ πνέυματος ἁγίου, virtutis & Spiritus sancti, simul cum λόγῳ sive sermone Evangelii concurrentis, & utrique junctim; neutri separatim adscribit, quòd sermonem suum, h. e. Evangelium à se prædicatum Thessalonicenses receperant. Quo ipso nostram superiorem afsertionem tertiam ferè totidem verbis confirmat.

Non quidem nescui sumus, per δύναμιν intelligere nonnullos hoc loco miracula, tanquam opera δυνάμεως h. e. virtutis sive potentiæ divinæ; per πνέυμα ἅγιον verò dona Spiritus sancti, cujusmodi erant dona linguarum, prophetiæ, curationum &c. sed illi discedunt à proprietate verborum, nullâ urgente necessitate. Apostolus enim distinguit hîc ex una parte quidem λόγον sermonem, ex altera verè δύναμιν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, virtutem & Spiritum Sanctum, tanquam duo, in ipso à se prædicato Evangelio conjuncta, & per ejus prædicationem ad Thessalonicensium conversionem & fidem se simul exerentiæ, & significat, eos conversos & ad fidem perductos esse, non nudo & solo λόγῳ sive sermone Evangelii, sed τῷ λόγῳ sive sermone illo, & δυνάμει sive potentia Spiritus sancti, cum eo conjunctâ, junctim sumtis & simul se exerentibus. Atque hunc sensum totus exigit contextus. In eo toto enim agitur de effectibus, Evangelii propriis. & quidem in præced. v. 3. commendat Apostolus Thessalonicensium fidem, spem & charitatem, iisq; v. 4. in memoriam revocat suam ἐκλογὴν sive electionem, quâ scilicet è reliqua hominum infidelium multitudine à Deo evocati & selecti fuerint, idq; hoc v. 5. factum docet per Evangelium, inter ipsos à se prædicatum, quod non ἐν λόγῳ μόνον, in sermone solùm, sive in nudis verbis positum fuerit, sed cum verbis altiorem quandam δύναμιν, nempe Spiritus sancti δύναμιν sive virtutem divinam complexum sit, & huic cum sermone Evangelii simul se exerenti acceptum ferendum esse, quod conversi & Apostolorum Christiq; imitatores facti, sermonem ipsorum cum afflictione multa & cum gaudio Spiritus sancti receperint, ibidem v. 6. docet. Quæ omnia spiritus sancti ejusque potentiæ, cum λόγῳ sive sermone Evangelii conjunctæ, effectus proprii sunt, miraculis verò, aut virtuti efficiendi miracula adscribi nequaquam possunt. Neque etiam in Actis Apostolicis quicquam legimus de ullo edito miraculo, vel de δυνάμεσι sive virtute miracula edendi, quæ cum prædicatione Evangelii apud Thessalonicenses ad eorum conversionem & fidem se exeruerit, ut Paulus eò digitum hic intendere videri possit, sed Lucas, qui Act. XVII. 2. 3. 4. illorum; & v. 11. 12. vicinorum Berrœensium conversionem descripsit, utrobiq; solius meminit Evangelii prædicati, & huic utrorumque conversionem præcisè adscribit. Sed nolumus in re manifesta esse prolixiores, & plura, quæ passim extant, Scripturæ loca adferre.

Neque illud ulteriori probatione hîc eget, quòd à Scriptura sacra etiam assensus fidei divinæ dependeat. In locis enim adductis omnibus conjunguntur sermo Evangelii, sive Verbum Dei prædicatum, Evangelium Christi, sermo crucis &c. cum Deo, potentiaq; Dei, & utrique simul junctim; neutri seorsim & separatim assensum fidei supernaturalem adscribunt, ut consideranti patebit. Quo etiam referri potest locus, supra ex Rom. XI. 17. citatus, ubi Paulus conceptis verbis scribit, fidem esse ex auditu, auditum autem per Verbum Dei, quod, quoad rem, idem est, atque fidem esse ex Verbo prædicato, audituq́; percepto. Eodem pertinet, quod fideles credere dicuntur per sermonem Apostolorum, h. e. per Verbum Dei; ab Apostolis prædicatum, Joh. XVII. 20. &c.


### V. Fourth assertion: The supernatural concurrence of God with His revelation, or…

V.

Fourth assertion: The supernatural concurrence of God with His revelation, or with Holy Scripture, which comprises divine revelation, pertains to the very formal objective reason of divine faith, and is included in it.

I. This assertion is opposed to modern Scholastics, who, although compelled by the force of truth they cannot finally deny that for Holy Scripture, or, as they love to speak, for divine revelation (contained in Holy Scripture) to move the human intellect to assent to itself and its dependence on God, it is required that God concur with it by His divine power and simultaneously influence the assent of faith, nevertheless contend that the concurrence of God with it does not pertain to the formal objective reason of faith: for they claim this consists in divine revelation alone, viewed precisely in itself; but that the concurrence of God and His divine power relates only to the side of the faculties, the intellect and the will, by way of an efficient cause, and as the effective reason for the assent of faith. Thus Gregorius de Valentia, Tom. III. Theol. Schol. Disp. I. q. I. p. I.; Adamus Tannerus in II. II. Thomæ Disp. I. q. I. dub. III. assert. VII. and Suarez Disp. III. de Fide Sect. III., whose words we have previously produced in Tract. de Conv. Disp. VI. cap. IV., where they may be seen.

Their most powerful reason is that the formal objective reason is the reason for knowing, which, being first known, leads the intellect through the knowledge of itself into the knowledge of other things, and thus, through the act of knowledge by which the identity of the predicate with the subject is represented to it, determines it by way of an exemplary form. This, they argue, does not happen through God's concurrence with His revelation, but through divine revelation alone, conceived and known by the intellect. But the concurrence of God with His revelation relates to the assent of faith as its efficient cause, not as its formal objective reason. III. But notwithstanding these things at all, our constant opinion is that the supernatural concurrence of God, or, which amounts to the same thing, that divine δύναμις, always conjoined in the first act with revelation or with Holy Scripture, through which God concurs to move the minds of men with His revelation, pertains to the very objective formal reason of divine faith, and is included in the formal motive power of divine revelation or Holy Scripture itself.

And first, indeed, that divine revelation stands in relation to the assent of divine faith by way of an object, the thing itself speaks, nor is it denied by anyone, so far as I know. For it is established by words, signifying by design, which in relation to our cognition and assent perform the role of objects, and what credible objects cannot do by themselves—namely, that through the intervention of the senses they might penetrate by certain images of themselves to the imagination, and further to the intellect, and move it to the knowledge and assent of themselves—the words of revelation perform in their place, which, whether read in the Scriptures through sight, or perceived from the mouth of a preacher through hearing, penetrate to the imagination, and further to the intellect, and objectively move it to the knowledge and assent of themselves and of the revealed things of which they are signs. Therefore, also, the supernatural concurrence of God through His divine δύναμις with divine revelation, just as much as divine revelation itself, stands objectively in relation to the assent of divine faith. For that divine δύναμις, through which Holy Scripture and the divine revelation contained in it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, is always conjoined with it for this purpose, and the supernatural concurrence of God with it is entirely prepared for this, that divine revelation may be completed in the formal objective reason of divine faith, and may be constituted sufficient in the first act for moving the intellect to the supernatural assent of itself and of the things to be believed.

Then those very authors with whom we are concerned here confess with us with one voice that the formal objective reason of faith consists in divine revelation, and that it is not believed by divine faith on account of another divine revelation, nor on account of any other formal motive, but through itself immediately. Either, therefore, divine revelation by itself alone, without the supernatural concurrence of God, is the complete motive reason of the intellect for the supernatural assent of itself and of the things to be believed, or without it, it is not its complete motive reason for itself and the things to be believed supernatural assent. If the latter is said, I have what I want: namely, that the supernatural concurrence of God pertains to the formal objective reason of divine faith, and completes divine revelation in its formal objective reason. For nothing else by which it might be completed can even be imagined, unless you wish to recur to the signs and motives of credibility mentioned above, concerning which we have already acted, and that they are not suitable for grounding the assent of divine faith has been shown more than enough, which the Scholastics, against whom we are arguing here, also readily acknowledge. Nor can the former be said. For divine revelation, which divinely inspired Scriptures contain, viewed in itself apart from the supernatural concurrence of God, imports nothing in its concept beyond the words, once committed to writing by divine inspiration, and the things signified. If these, by themselves alone, apart from the supernatural concurrence of God, are the complete formal objective reason of faith, they either move the intellect to a supernatural assent of itself by the force of the words of which it consists, or by the force of the things which the words signify. But neither can be said. Not the former: because the words of Scripture, as such, and apart from any supernatural concurrence of God, cannot move the intellect further than to a simple apprehension of the things they signify. For when some evident proposition moves the intellect to assent to it beyond that, then it is not precisely by the force of the words, but by the force and evidence of the things signified, which, known by the force of the words through simple apprehension, determine it of themselves immediately to assent to them. Nor the latter: because if the things themselves, signified by the words of revelation, ought to move the intellect to assent, it is necessary that they either move and determine it to assent by some evidence and clarity of their own, or draw the will into consent by some convenience and goodness of their own, and move it to command assent from the intellect. But neither of these can be said either. Not the former: because the things to be believed, even when they are represented to the intellect by the words of revelation and apprehended by it, are and remain non-evident and obscure, so much so that they seem to be foolishness to it, I Cor. II. 14. Nor the latter: because although the things to be believed possess their own remarkable goodness, yet since the will is by nature dead in relation to them, it cannot be enticed by the mere knowledge of their goodness and moved to acts that are spiritually good, such as the act of commanding assent from the intellect, any more than A dead person cannot be affected by the goodness of natural things and be drawn into the desire for them. Therefore, divine revelation, by itself alone and without the supernatural concurrence of God, is not the complete formal objective reason for faith. Therefore, the supernatural concurrence of God with divine revelation pertains to the complete formal objective reason of divine faith, and is included in it.

IV. As regards the reason brought to the contrary by Valentia, Tanner, and Suarez, we do not deny that it is required for the formal objective reason that, being known by itself immediately, it should move the intellect into the knowledge and assent of other things; however, we deny that this does not apply to divine revelation, taken with the supernatural concurrence of God and viewed in its complete objective reason. In order that you may understand this more correctly, it must be known that the adequate and complete object or formal motive of divine faith is God revealing and His revelation, and when it is commonly said that divine revelation is the formal objective reason of divine faith, it is to be understood with the connoted God revealing, as the author and efficient cause of the revelation. Whence, in order that divine revelation may actually perform the function of the object or formal motive of divine faith, two complex principles are required: by one, God revealing [is connected] with the infallible truth of the revealed thing, which He imparts to it through the act of revelation; by the other, He is connected with the revealed things through the act of revelation, as was also shown above in chapter IV, thesis 11. The former concerns the supreme veracity of God revealing in itself; the latter, His union with Holy Scripture through the act of revelation. The former can be proposed thus: Whatever Scripture is composed with God revealing or inspiring, that is certainly and infallibly true. The latter in this manner: Holy Scripture is composed with God revealing or inspiring. The same things are also accustomed to be enunciated in other words thus: Whatever God, who is supremely truthful, says or reveals, is certainly and infallibly true; Whatever is contained in Holy Scripture, God, who is supremely truthful, says or reveals. Both are contained in the formal objective reason of divine faith, and that which is known first and by itself is the reason for knowing other things. And the former indeed is evident, the truth of which appears to the intellect immediately from the perceived terms themselves. And concerning this, it is true without doubt that, objectively understood in its may move the cognition immediately by itself, and, being known from itself, may determine the same by way of an exemplary form to the cognition and assent of others.

But in order that the same may be evident concerning the latter, it must be known that what is said, that God speaks or reveals what is contained in Holy Scripture, can be understood in two ways: In one way, that He says that in actus signatus, directly and expressly, just as when in Exodus 20:1 God says through Moses: And God spoke all these words; and He adds: I am the Lord thy God, etc. In actus signatus He says that He is saying those words; in another way, that He says that in actus exercitus, indirectly and through the reflection of the very act of speaking or revealing, by which He says the very things contained in Holy Scripture, by the very words of Scripture which He once suggested to the sacred writers and dictated as it were into their pen. For this, reflected upon God Himself speaking, says in actus exercitus that He is saying that which He says in the Scriptures by the words once inspired by Him to the sacred writers: e.g., when in John 1:14 He says by the words suggested to John the Evangelist and dictated as it were into his pen: The Word was made flesh, while He says this in actus signatus by these words, at the same time in actus exercitus, and through the reflection of this very act of speaking, He says that He is saying that the Word was made flesh. And when God pronounced the very words of the Decalogue from Mount Sinai with a sonorous voice, with the whole people listening, by pronouncing them with a sonorous voice He was saying those ten commandments in actus signatus; but in actus exercitus, and through the reflection of the very act by which He was pronouncing them, He was also saying that He was saying them.

Latin:

V.

QVarta assertio: Concursus Dei supernaturalis cum sua revelatione, sive cum Scriptura sacra, divinam revelationem comprehendente, pertinet ad ipsam rationem objectivam formalem fidei divinæ, & in ea includitur.

I. Assertio hæc opponitur modernis Scholasticis, qui quamvis vi veritatis convicti diffiteri tandem non possint, ad Scripturam sacram, sive, ut illi loqui amant, ad divinam revelationem (in Scriptura sacra contentam) ut intellectum hominis in sui suæq́; à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem moveat, requiri, ut Deus sua divinâ potentiâ cum ea concurrat, & simul in assensum fidei influat, contendunt tamen, concursum Dei cum ea non pertinere ad rationem objectivam formalem fidei: hanc enim consistere in sola revelatione divina, in se præcise spectata; concursum Dei verò potentiæq́; divinæ habere se tantùm ex parte potentiarum, intellectus & voluntatis, per modum causæ efficientis, & ut rationem effectivam assensus fidei. Ita Gregorius de Valentia Tom. III.Theol. Schol. Disp. I. q. I. p. I. Adamus Tannerus in II. II. Thomæ Disp. I. q. I. dub. III. assert. VII. & Suarez Disp. III. de Fide Sect. III. quorum verba antehâc in Tract. de Conv. Disp. VI. cap. IV. produximus, ubi videri possunt.

Ratio illorum potissima est, quòd ratio objectiva formalis sit ratio cognoscendi, quæ primò cognita, intellectum per sui cognitionem in cognitionem aliorum deducat, atq; fic per cognitionis actum, quo identitas prædicati cum subjecto ei repræsentatur, per modum formæ exemplaris determinet. Id quod non fiat per Dei concursum cum revelatione sua, sed per solam divinam revelationem, intellectu conceptam & cognitam. Concursum Dei autem cum sua revelatione habere se ad assensum fidei, ut ejus causam efficientem, non ut rationem objectivam formalem. III. Verùm his nihil quicquam obstantibus nostra constans est sententia, quòd concursus Dei supernaturalis, vel, quod eodem redit, divina illa δύναμις, cum revelatione sive cum Scriptura sacra in actu primo semper conjuncta, per quam Deus ad movendos hominum animos cum sua revelatione concurrit, ad ipsam rationem objectivam formalem fidei divinæ pertineat, & in ipsa divinæ revelationis sive Scripturæ sacræ vi motiva formali includatur.

Et primùm quidem revelationem divinam habere se in ordine ad assensum fidei divinæ per modum objecti, res ipsa loquitur, nec à quoquam, quod sciam, negatur. Constat enim verbis, ex instituto significantibus, quæ in ordine ad nostram cognitionem & assensum vicem objectorum obeunt, & quod objecta credibilia per se non possunt, ut scilicet interventu sensuum per sui quasdam imagines ad phantasiam, & porro ad intellectum penetrent, eumque ad sui notitiam & assensum moveant, id illorum loco præstant verba revelationis, quæ sive in Scripturis lecta per visum, sive ex prædicantis ore percepta per auditum ad phantasiam, & porro ad intellectum penetrant, eumq; ad sui & rerum revelatarum, quarum signa sunt, notitiam & assensum objectivè movent.
