Ergo & concursus Dei supernaturalis per suam divinam δύναμιν cum divina revelatione, æquè ac ipsa revelatio divina, ad assensum fidei divinæ objectivè sese habet. Est enim divina illa δύναμις, per quam Scriptura sacra, & contenta in ea revelatio divina potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti, ad hoc semper cum ea conjuncta, & Dei concursus supernaturalis cum illa totus ad hoc comparatus est, ut revelatio divina in ratione objectiva formali fidei divinæ compleatur, & ad movendum intellectum in sui & credendorum assensum supernaturalem in actu primo sufficiens constituatur.

Deinde illi ipsi Auctores, quibuscum nobis hîc res est, fatentur nobiscum uno ore, rationem objectivam formalem fidei consistere in revelatione divina, eamque non credi fide divinâ propter aliam revelationem divinam, neque propter ullum motivum formale aliud, sed per se immediatè. Aut ergo revelatio divina per se sola citra supernaturalem Dei concursum est completa ratio motiva intellectus in sui & credendorum assensum supernaturalem, aut absque eo non est completa ratio motiva ejus in sui credendorumq; assensum supernaturalem. Si posterius dicatur, habeo quod volo: nempe Dei concursum supernaturalem pertinere ad rationem objectivam formalem fidei divinæ, & complere revelationem divinam in ratione objectiva formali. Neque enim aliud quid, quo compleatur, vel fingi potest, nisi ad signa & motiva credibilitatis, superiùs commemorata, recurrere velis, de quibus supra actum, & quòd ad fundandum assensum fidei divinæ idonea non sint, satis superque ostensum est, quod & ultrò agnoscunt Scholastici, contra quos hîc disputamus. Neque priùs dici potest. Nam revelatio divina, quam Scripturæ divinitus inspiratæ continent, in se præciso Dei concursu supernaturali spectata, nihil importat in suo conceptu, præter verba, ex divina inspiratione olim in literas relata, & res significatas. Quæ si per se sola, citra Dei concursum supernaturalem ratio objectiva formalis fidei completa est, aut movet intellectum in supernaturalem sui assensum vi verborum quibus constat, aut vi rerum, quas verba significant. Sed neutrum dici potest. Non prius: quia verba Scripturæ, ut talia, & præciso omni concursu Dei supernaturali, non possunt intellectum ulterius, quàm ad simplicem rerum, quas significant, apprehensionem movere. Quando enim propositio aliqua evidens intellectum ad sui assensum prætereà movet, tùm sit illud non præcisè vi verborum, sed vi & evidentiâ rerum significatarum, quæ ex vi verborum notitiâ apprehensionis simplicis cognitæ eum per se immediatè ad sui assensum determinant. Neque posterius: quia si res ipsæ, verbis revelationis significatæ, intellectum ad assensum movere debeant, necesse est, ut vel suâ quâdam evidentiâ & claritate eum ad assensum sui moveant & determinent, vel suâ quadam convenientiâ & bonitate voluntatem in consensum trahant, eamƁ; ad imperandum intellectui assensum moveant. Sed horum etiam neutrum dici potest. Non prius: quia res credendæ tùm etiam, cùm verbis revelationis intellectui repræsentatæ & ab ipso apprehensæ sunt, inevidentes & obscuræ sunt & manent, adeò ut ei stultitia esse videantur, I. Cor. II. 14. Neque posterius: quia quamvis res credendæ suâ insigni polleant bonitate, tamen cum in ordine ad illas voluntas naturâ emortua sit, sola bonitate illarum cognitâ allici & ad actus spiritualiter bonos, qualis est actus assensum intellectui imperandi, moveri tam non potest, quàm mortuus bonitate rerum naturalium affici & in illarum appetitionem trahi non poteft. Ergo revelatio divina, per se sola & citra supernaturalem Dei concursum non est ratio objectiva formalis fidei completa. Ergo concursus Dei supernaturalis cum divina revelatione pertinet ad rationem objectivam formalem completam fidei divinæ, inque ea includitur.

IV. Quod ad rationem, à Valentia, Tannero & Suarez io in contrarium allatam attinet, non diffitemur nos, ad rationem objectivam formalem requiri, ut per se immediatè cognita intellectum in cognitionem assensumq; aliorum moveat, negamus autem, quòd revelationi divinæ, cum concursu Dei supernaturali sumtæ, & in sua ratione objectiva completa spectatæ, hoc non conveniat. Quod ut rectius intelligas, sciendum, objectum sive motivum formale fidei divinæ adæquatum & completum esse Deum revelantem ejusq; revelationem, & cùm vulgò dicitur, divinam revelationem esse fidei divinæ rationem objectivam formalem, intelligendum id est cum connotato Deo revelante, velut revelationis auctore & causa efficiente. Unde ut objecti sive motivi formalis fidei divinæ munus divina revelatio actu obeat, duo requiruntur complexa principia, quorum uno Deus revelans cum infallibili veritate rei revelatæ, quam per revelationis actum ei impertit; altero cum rebus revelatis per revelationis actum connectatur, ut supra etiam cap. IV. th. 11. ostensum. Prius concernit Dei revelantis summam veracitatem secundum se; posterius ejusdem unionem cum Scriptura sacra per revelationis actum. Illud potest sic proponi: Quæcunque Scriptura Deo revelante sive inspirante concinnata est, ea certò & infallibiliter vera est. Posterius hunc in modum: Scriptura sacra Deo revelante sive inspirante concinnata est. Eadem solent etiam verbis aliis sic enunciari: Quicquid Deus summè verax dicit sive revelat, certò & infallibiliter verum est; Quicquid in Scriptura sacra continetur, Deus summè verax dicit sive revelat. Utrumq; continetur in ratione objectiva formali fidei divinæ, & primò ac per se cognitum est ratio cognoscendi alia. Et prius quidem evidens est, cujus veritas statim ex ipsis perceptis terminis intellectui apparet. Et de hoc citra dubium verum est, quod, objectivè intellectum in sui cognitionem per se immediate moveat, &, ex se cognitum, eundem per modum formæ exemplaris ad aliorum cognitionem & assensum determinet.

Ut autem de posteriori idem pateat, sciendum, dupliciter intelligi posse, quod dicitur, Deum dicere, sive revelare, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur: Uno modo, quod illud dicat in actu signato, directè & expressè, sicut cum Exod. XX. 1. Deus per Mosen dicit: Et Deus locutus est omnia hæc verba; Et subjicit: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus &c. in actu signato dicit, se dicere verba illa; altero quod illud dicat in actu exercito, indirectè & per reflexionem ipsius actus dicendi sive revelandi, quo ipsas res in Scriptura sacra contentas, ipsismet verbis Scripturæ, quæ Scriptoribus sacris olim suggesit, & quasi in calamum dictitavit, dicit. Hoc enim, in ipsum Deum dicentem reflexo, in actu exercito dicit, se dicere id, quod verbis, Scriptoribus sacris à se olim inspiratis, in Scripturis dicit: v. g. quando Joh. I. 14. verbis, Johannis Evangelistæ suggestis & quasi in calamum dictatis dicit: Verbum caro factum est, dum hoc in actu signato verbis hisce dicit, simul in actu exercito, & per reflexionem hujus ipsius actus dicendi dicit se dicere, Verbum carnem factum esse. Et cum ipsa verba Decalogi Deus de monte Sinai sonorâ voce, audiente toto populo, pronunciaret, pronunciando ea sonorâ voce in actu signato dicebat decem illa præcepta; in actu exercito autem, & per reflexionem ipsius actus, quo ea pronunciabat, dicebat etiam, se dicere ea.


### For the truth of the latter principle, therefore

For the truth of the latter principle, therefore: God says or reveals what is contained in Holy Scripture; it is not necessary that God in actus signatus, directly and expressly, says that He is saying or revealing those things which are contained in Holy Scripture, but it suffices that He says these very things, which are contained in Holy Scripture, in actus signatus by the words once suggested by Him to the sacred writers and dictated as it were into their pen. For by this His act of speaking, by which He says them in actus signatus, reflected upon Himself speaking, He at the same time says in actus exercitus that He is saying those things which are contained in Holy Scripture. The matter will become clearer by an example taken from human affairs: When you hear a man, worthy of belief, recounting some deed that has been done, which pertains to nothing concerning himself, and from which he neither hopes for any advantage nor fears any danger can, these two complex principles immediately present themselves to your intellect: That a man worthy of belief says that a thing, sufficiently explored by him, but pertaining in no way to himself, and from which he can hope for no advantage or fear any harm, was done, it is to be believed that it was done just as he reports; and he says that this or that in this or that matter, sufficiently explored by him and pertaining in no way to himself, etc., was done thus. Where, for the truth of the latter principle, it is not required that he who recounts the deed should say in the signate act that he is saying or recounting it, but while you hear him recounting or saying the deed in the signate act, from his act of speaking, perceived by hearing, you understand that he is recounting or saying it. For the act of speaking, by which he recounts or says the deed in the signate act, reflected back upon the speaker, at the same time says in the exercised act that he is saying that. For you understand just as easily from the recounting of a deed that he is recounting or saying it, as you would easily understand it if he were to say in the signate act and expressly, I say or recount this, and were to subjoin the recounting of that thing afterwards.

The matter is the same with the internal act of speaking, by which God formerly spoke to the Prophets and Apostles through immediate inspiration, and suggested to them the concepts of the things and words to be written, and by which even now He speaks to us through the words formerly suggested to the sacred writers and committed to letters, and excites in us the same concepts through His words existing in the sacred Scriptures, whether read or proposed by the voice of a preacher. When God spoke inwardly to the mind of the writers through the act of inspiration, and signified to them through the concepts of things and words what and in what words they ought to write, then through the inspired concepts in the signate act, He directly and expressly said or dictated to them both the things and the words to be written; but by the same act, reflected back upon Himself as the inspirer, He at the same time indirectly and in the exercised act said that He was saying or dictating to them those things and words to be written. For the act of inspiration, and its terminus, namely the inspired concepts, as has been shown above in chapter II, thesis VIII, explanation no. II, and thesis XV, explanation no. V, and more often elsewhere, do not differ really, as thing and thing, but only modally, as thing and mode of a thing, and the inspired concepts, as in the signate act and directly they were the things and words to be written, of which they were signs, so in the exercised act, indirectly and through the reflection of itself upon God inspiring, also represented God to the intellect as their efficient cause, so that the sacred writers might understand from this that God inspired these things into them, and dictated them as if into a pen, which things ought to be written in which words. And when God still concurs supernaturally with His words contained in Holy Scripture, and through them read, or proposed by the voice of a preacher and perceived by hearing, speaks to us, and persuades us of the things which are signified by them, so that we believe them with divine faith, induced by no other cause or other motivating reason than that God Himself, who is the primary Truth, knowing neither how to be deceived nor to deceive, says or reveals those things to us through His very words contained in the Holy Scriptures, by this very act of speaking, by which God concurs with the words of Scripture, and with them and through them speaks to us of the things signified as if in an act signified, and supernaturally persuades our intellect of their truth, in God Himself, thus speaking to us, reflected at the same time in an exercised act, He says that He says those things which are contained in Holy Scripture. How, however, God concurs with His words contained in Holy Scripture, and with them and through them speaks to us in a supernatural manner, and moves us into a supernatural assent to the things signified by them, and furthermore by this very act of speaking, reflected in itself as if speaking or saying, in an exercised act says that He says those things which are contained in Holy Scripture, will soon be explained in the following assertions.

And from these things, thus declared, it is clearly evident what we had undertaken to show: namely, that this principle, 'God says what is contained in Holy Scripture,' which we said includes Holy Scripture in its objective reason and formal motivating power of divine faith, performs the function of the formal object of divine faith just as much as this other principle: 'Whatever God says in the Holy Scriptures is certainly and infallibly true'; that it moves our intellect into the knowledge and assent of other things through itself immediately, and just as this one, so that one also, being known first of itself, moves our intellect into the knowledge and assent of other things, by means of the knowledge and assent of itself.

…V. But perhaps someone will object to these things: (1) That the reflexive act of speaking does not relate to the assent of our faith by way of a formal object: since it does not differ in substance from the act of speaking by which He says that which is contained in Scripture. The act of speaking, however, by which He says that which is contained in Holy Scripture, is the material object of our faith: thus, for example, the act of speaking, by which God in John 1:14 said that the Word was made flesh, is in reality nothing other than this proposition: The Word was made flesh, recorded in letters through John, with God inspiring. But this proposition is the very material object of our faith, which terminates the act of believing, not the formal object, by which our intellect is moved into the act of believing. Therefore, the reflexive act of speaking, by which He indirectly and in the act exercised says that He is saying, for example, that the Word was made flesh, is the material object of the act of believing, not the formal.

(II.) The formal object must be known primarily of itself, and be the reason for knowing other things. But the reflexive act of speaking, by which God in the act exercised and indirectly says that He is saying, for example, that the Word was made flesh, is not known primarily of itself, but only after the act of speaking by which He says, for example, that the Word was made flesh. For it is prior that the act of speaking, by which a thing is said, be known, than that it be reflected back upon the speaker through another act of knowing. But that which in the order of our cognition is by nature posterior to the act of speaking, by which the thing itself is said, cannot be the formal object and reason for knowing it.

(III.) The formal object does not relate to assent efficiently, but only objectively, by terminating it, as has been said. But the act of speaking, with which God says, for example, that the Word was made flesh, as well as the reflexive one, by which in the act exercised He says that He is saying it, does not relate to assent merely objectively, that is, only by terminating it, but joined with the supernatural concurrence of God, it also relates to the same efficiently. Whence the authority of Scripture is wrongly confused here with its efficacy. Only the authority of Holy Scripture is the formal object or motive of divine faith; its efficacy, however, is the effective principle or efficient cause of the same.

VI. These objections, even if at first glance they might perhaps seem to some to be of any value, yet in the background they do not have what they promise at the front, and there are ready answers to all of them.

And to the first indeed we respond by denying that the act of speaking, by which God says that which is contained in Holy Scripture, for example, that the Word was made flesh, becomes the material object of our faith. For the act of speaking, by which God says something, for example, that the Word was made flesh, is one thing; His very saying itself, for example, that the Word was made was made. The dictum of God, to which His act of speaking is terminated, is the material object of our faith; but the act of speaking, terminated to that dictum, is the formal object of the same. For if I should ask of you why you believe this dictum: The Word was made flesh; are you not compelled to answer, because God said it? When, however, you answer thus, do you not distinguish between this dictum of God: The Word was made flesh; and between the act of speaking by which God said this, and assign to the former the status of the material object of our faith, but to the latter the status of the formal object? Whence it is false that the act of speaking, by which God, for example, says that the Word was made flesh, is nothing other than this proposition: The Word was made flesh. For this proposition is the terminus of the very act of speaking by which He said it; but the act of speaking consists in its dependence upon God, as upon the speaker: for example, the act of speaking by which God was saying this proposition to John the Evangelist, and was as it were dictating it to be written by the pen, consisted in the act of inspiration by which He suggested it to his intellect to be written through inspired concepts. Although, however, the act of speaking and the dictum itself, to which it is terminated, do not differ as thing and thing, they are not nevertheless entirely the same, but as any action and its terminus differ, so also the act of speaking and its terminus differ as thing and mode of a thing. Which suffices for this, that the act of speaking, by which God says something, may stand in relation to His very dictum as the formal objective reason; and in our assent of faith that dictum, as the material object, which terminates the act of faith; but the act of speaking, as the formal object, which moves the intellect into the act of believing. But just as the act of speaking, by which God says, for example, that the Word was made flesh, is the reason for believing that the Word was made flesh, so the same act reflected upon God speaking, by which He indirectly and in the act exercised says that He is saying that, is the reason for believing that God is saying, for example, that the Word was made flesh.

To the other objection we respond, that in the assent of faith, by which we believe what is contained in Scripture on account of divine revelation, or because God says or reveals them, a double discourse is virtually included: One, which stands as the principal argument; the other, which stands as a prosyllogism. The prior discourse is this: Whatever God says or reveals in Scripture inspired by Him is certainly and infallibly true. But, for example, the Word that it was made flesh is said or revealed in Scripture inspired by Himself. Therefore, that the Word was made flesh is certainly and infallibly true. And this is the principal syllogism, whose middle term of concluding and formal objective reason is the very act of speaking, by which God once said to John the Evangelist through an internal act of inspiration concurring supernaturally with the words consigned to letters by John from divine inspiration, He says the same thing to us internally to our mind through those very words, and reveals it to us. But the latter discourse is necessary when a doubt arises concerning its minor premise, namely, whence you know and believe that God says this which is contained in Scripture, e.g., The Word was made flesh. Where you cannot answer that you believe it on account of another divine revelation, but it must be said that you believe it through the very act of speaking by which God says it internally to your mind through the words of Scripture, which were committed to letters by divine inspiration, and persuades you. For by that act, reflected upon God Himself speaking, He says indirectly and in the act exercised that He says this to your mind through the words of Scripture. And in this second discourse, the reflected act of speaking is the reason for knowing the speaker, just as the signified act of speaking is the reason for knowing the thing said. Although, however, the signified and exercised acts of speaking are simultaneous in time and are known simultaneously, yet as it is prior by nature for it to depend upon the speaker, and for the knowledge of the speaker to insinuate itself into our intellect, than to represent the things said to us, so the knowledge of the same act of speaking, as depending upon God and thus reflected upon God speaking, is by nature prior to the knowledge of it as representing the things signified to us: and thus as viewed in the signified act. But just as elsewhere the minor proposition of the principal syllogism is the reason for assenting to the conclusion, and this acts as the material object, that as the formal object; but in the prosyllogism, the reason for assenting to the minor proposition of the principal syllogism acts as the formal object, while the minor proposition of the same, which now becomes the conclusion, acts as the material object; so at present in the principal argument, the signified act of speaking, by which God says this or that, acts as the reason for knowing the thing said and as its formal object; but in the prosyllogism, the reflected act of speaking, by which God in the exercised act says that He is speaking, acts as the formal object and reason for knowing in relation to the signified act by which He says this or that; but the latter acts as the material object and as the thing known. To the third objection we respond, that the formal object does not relate to its own assent efficiently, but only objectively, by terminating it, is not universally true, but proceeds only concerning an evident formal object, which, from the apprehended terms known to the intellect, represents the identity of the predicate with the subject per se immediately, and determines it to the assent of itself through that, known in the apprehended terms. However, when the formal object is non-evident, so that the identity of the predicate with the subject cannot be perceived and known in the apprehended terms, as is the case with the formal object of divine faith; then it is not repugnant for the formal object to relate to its own assent in its own way also efficiently, provided that what it contributes efficiently to it, it contributes in place of the object, as will be shown more fully a little later in assertion VI.

Nor is there any reason to say that the authority of Scripture and its efficacy are thus confused. For it is one thing for one to be confused with the other; it is another for one to be joined with the other in an objective formal reason. The authority of Scripture, as shown above in chapter III, thesis IV, is the ἀξία or dignity of Scripture, alluring and drawing the minds of men into a certain and indubitable assent to be held to its sayings, resulting from the infinite perfection of God and its own known dependence upon Him: which, when it is known, moves the intellect to the assent of other things objectively, not efficiently. But for it to be said to be known by us, two things are necessary to be known: one, that God is supremely truthful in speaking, and can neither be deceived nor deceive; the other, that He is the Author or efficient cause of Holy Scripture, or which is the same thing, that Scripture depends upon Him efficiently, and was written by holy men with Him inspiring it, as in the said place, thesis III, Explanation, number 1. and thesis X. shown. Just as, however, the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God through inspiration is not evident to us, but non-evident and obscure; and cannot become known to us except by God testifying in us through Scripture itself, so the matter itself demands that, for the dependence of Scripture to be known by the assent of divine faith, God, concurring with the inspired Scripture, also concurs actively or efficiently to the assent of divine faith: which concurrence, although it could otherwise also be referred to the efficacy of Scripture, here, however, because it supplies the place of the object, and contributes that very thing which otherwise the object by the force of its objective reason formal [reason] ought to contribute, as will be shown later, cannot and ought not to be excluded from the objective formal reason of divine faith. Whence the authority and efficacy of Scripture are not confused, when the supernatural concurrence of God with Scripture is required for knowing its dependence upon God; but the authority of Scripture, notwithstanding this, is and remains the ἀξία or dignity of Scripture, resulting from God's supreme truthfulness in speaking and its own dependence upon God being known; but efficacy is and remains a certain active force, productive of supernatural acts and effects; and the former is related to its acts as known objectively; the latter as unknown effectively, although for knowing the dependence of Scripture upon God through immediate inspiration, which is prerequisite to the authority of Scripture, its efficacy must also concur. All of which will become more manifest from what is to be said shortly.

Latin:

Ad veritatem ergo principii posterioris: Quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur, Deus dicit sive revelat; necessarium non est, ut Deus in actu signato, directè, & expressè dicat, se dicere sive revelare ea, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur, sed sufficit, quòd hæc ipsa, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur, verbis, Scriptoribus sacris à se olim suggestis & quasi in calamum dictitatis, in actu signato dicat. Hoc enim suo actu dicendi, quo ea in actu signato dicit, in se dicentem reflexo, simul in actu exercito dicit, se dicere ea, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur. Exemplo, à rebus humanis petito, res evadet manifestior: Cùm audis Virum, fide dignum, commemorare rem aliquam gestam, ad se nihil pertinentem, & ex qua neque aliquid commodi sperare aut quicquam periculi metuere potest, ingerunt sese tuo intellectui statim duo hæc complexa principia: Quod Vir fide dignus in re sibi satis exploratâ, ad se autem nihil pertinente, & è qua neque aliquid commodi sperare, aut quicquam damni metuere potest, gestum esse dicit, id ita, ut ille refert, gestum esse credendum est; & hoc vel illud in hac illave re sibi satis explorata, & ad se nihil pertinente &c. sic gestum esse dicit. Ubi ad veritatem principii posterioris non requiritur, ut qui rem gestam commemorat, in actu signato dicat, se dicere sive commemorare illam, sed dum eum rem gestam in actu signato commemorare sive dicere audis, ex ejus actu dicendi, auditu percepto, intelligis, eum commemorare sive dicere illam. Actus enim dicendi, quo rem gestam in actu signato commemorat sive dicit, in dicentem reflexus, simul in actu exercito dicit, eum dicere illud. Tàm enim facilè ex commemoratione rei gestæ intelligis, eum commemorare sive dicere illam, quàm facilè id intelligeres, si in actu signato & expressè diceret, ego dico sive commemoro hoc, & commemorationem ejus rei posteà subjiceret.

Perinde res habet cum actu dicendi interno, quo Deus olim per immediatam inspirationem locutus est ad Prophetas & Apostolos, iisque conceptus rerum & vocum scribendarum suggessit, & quo etiamnum verbis, Scriptoribus sacris olim suggestis & in literas relatis ad nos loquitur, & eosdem conceptus per sua in Scripturis sacris extantia verba, sive lecta sive prædicantis voce proposita, in nobis excitat. Quando Deus per inspirationis actum interius ad Scriptorum animum loquebatur, iisq́; per conceptus rerum & vocum, quæ & quibus verbis scribere deberent, significabat, tum per conceptus inspiratos in actu signato, directè, & expressè dicebat sive dictitabat illis & res & verba scribenda; eodem autem, in se inspirantem reflexo, simul indirectè, & in actu exercito dicebat, se dicere sive dictitare illis eas res & verba scribenda. Actus enim inspirationis, & ejus terminus, conceptus inspirati scilicet, uti supra in cap. II. th. VIII. Expl. n. II. & th. XV. Expl. n. V. & alibi sæpiùs ostensum, non differunt realiter, ut res & res, sed tantùm modaliter, ut res & rei modus, & conceptus inspirati, ut in actu signato & directè res & verba scribenda, quorum signa erant, ita in actu exercito, indirectè & per reflexionnm sui in Deum inspirantem etiam Deum, tanquam causam sui efficientem, intellectui repraesentabant, ut Deum eos sibi inspirare, & quasi in calamum dictare, quae res, quibus verbis scribi deberent, Scriptores sacri hinc intelligerent. Et quando Deus cum suis in Scriptura sacra contenis verbis etiamnum supernaturaliter concurrit, & per ea lecta, vel praedicantis voce proposita atque auditu percepta, ad nos loquitur, & quae per illa significantur, nobis persuadet, ut fide divina ea credamus, non alia de causa, aut alia ratione motiva inducti, quam quod Deus ipse, qui Veritas prima est, falli & fallere nescia, per ipsa sua in Scripturis sacris contenta verba nobis illa dicat sive revelet, hoc ipso actu dicendi, quo cum verbis Scripturae Deus concurrit, & cum illis ac per illa res significatas velut in actu signato ad nos loquitur, illarumque veritatem nostro intellectui supernaturaliter persuadet, in ipsum Deum, sic ad nos loquentem, reflexo simul in actu exercito dicit, se dicere ea, quae in Scriptura sacra continentur. Quomodo autem Deus cum suis in Scriptura sacra contentis verbis concurrat, & cum illis ac per illa ad nos modo supernaturali loquatur, nosque in supernaturalem rerum, illis significatarum, assensum moveat, & porro hoc ipso locutionis actu, in se velut loquentem sive dicentem reflexo, in actu exercito dicat se dicere ea, quae in Scriptura sacra continentur, mox in subsequentibus assertionibus explicabitur.

Atque ex his, sic declaratis, liquido patet, quod nobis ostendendum sumseramus: nempe principium hoc, Deus dicit, quae in Scriptura sacra continentur; quod Scripturam sacram in sua ratione objectiva & vi motiva formali fidei divinae includere diximus, obire munus objecti formalis fidei divinae aeque, ac hoc alterum principium: Quicquid Deus in Scripturis sacris dicit, certo & infallibiliter verum est; per se immediate, & quemadmodum hoc, ita & illud ex se primo cognitum movere intellectum nostrum in aliorum cognitionem & assensum, mediante sui cognitione & assensu.

V. Sed ad haec forsan quis excipiet (1) Actum dicendi reflexum non habere se ad assensum fidei nostrae per modum objecti formalis: cum ab actu dicendi, quo id quod in Scriptura continetur, dicit, quoad rem non differat. Actus dicendi autem, quo id dicit, quod in Scriptura sacra continetur, est objectum materiale nostræ fidei: sic v.g. actus dicendi, quo Deus Joh. 1. 14. dixit, Verbum carnem factum esse, quoad rem nihil est aliud, quàm hæc propositio: Verbum caro factum est, per Johannem, Deo inspirante, in literas relata. Sed hæc propositio est ipsum objectum materiale fidei nostræ, quod actum credendi terminat, non formale, quo in actum credendi intellectus noster movetur. Ergo actus dicendi reflexus, quo indirectè & in actu exercito dicit se dicere, v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse, objectum materiale actus credendi est, non formale.

(II.) Objectum formale debet esse ex se primò cognitum, & ratio cognoscendi alia. Sed actus dicendi reflexus, quo Deus in actu exercito & indirectè dicit se dicere, v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse, non cognoscitur ex se primò, sed demum post actum dicendi, quo dicit, v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse. Prius enim est, actum dicendi, quo res dicitur, cognosci, quàm eum per alium actum cognoscendi in dicentem reflecti. Quod autem in ordine ad nostram cognitionem naturâ posterius est actu dicendi, quo ipsa res dicitur, id non potest esse objectum formale & ratio cognoscendi illius.

(III.) Objectum formale non habet se ad assensum sui efficienter, sed tantùm objectivè, terminando eum, uti dictum. Sed actus dicendi, cùm quo Deus dicit v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse, tùm reflexus, quo in actu exercito dicit se id dicere, non habet se ad assensum sui merè objectivè, tantùm scilicet eum terminando, sed cum Dei supernaturali concursu conjunctus habet se ad eundem etiam efficienter. Unde malè hîc confunditur auctoritas Scripturæ cum ejus efficacia. Sola Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas est fidei divinæ objectum sive motivum formale; efficacia verò ejus est ejusdem principium effectivum, sive causa efficiens.

VI. Objectiones hæ etsi primo intuitu cuipiam quantivis pretii esse videri forsan possunt, in recessu tamen non habent, quod à fronte pollicentur, suntque quæ ad omnes respondeantur, in promptu.

Et ad primam quidem respondemus, negando, quod actus dicendi, quo Deus id, quod in Scriptura sacra continetur, v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse, dicit, fit objectum materiale fidei nostræ. Aliud enim est actus dicendi, quo Deus aliquid dicit, v. g. Verbum carnem esse factum; aliud ipsum ejus dictum, v.g. Verbum caro factum est. Dictum Dei, ad quod ejus actus dicendi terminatur, est objectum materiale fidei nostræ; actus dicendi verò, ad illud dictum terminatus, est ejusdem objectum formale. Si enim quæram ex te, cur credas hoc dictum: Verbum caro factum est; annon respondere cogeris, quia Deus dixit? Quando autem ita respondes, annon distinguis inter dictum hoc Dei: Verbum caro factum est; & inter actum dicendi, quo Deus hoc dixit, & illi rationem objecti materialis fidei nostræ; huic verò rationem objecti formalis, ipse assignas? Unde falsum est, quod actus dicendi, quo Deus, v. g. Verbum carnem factum esse dicit; nihil aliud sit, quàm propositio hæc: Verbum caro factum est. Nam propositio hæc est terminus ipsius actus dicendi, quo eam dixit; actus dicendi autem consistit in dependentia ejus à Deo, tanquam à dicente: v. g. actus dicendi, quo Deus Johanni Evangelistæ propositionem hanc dicebat, & scribendam in calamum quasi dictitabat, consistebat in actu inspirationis, quo illam scribendam per conceptus inspiratos ejus intellectui suggerebat. Quamvis verò actus dicendi, & dictum ipsum, ad quod terminatur, non differant ut res & res, non tamen prorsus idem sunt, sed ut aliàs actio quævis & ejus terminus, ita & actus dicendi ejúsque terminus differunt ut res & rei modus. Quod sufficit ad hoc, ut actus dicendi, quo Deus aliquid dicit, ad ipsum ejus dictum ut ratio objectiva formalis; & in nostro assensu fidei dictum illud, ut objectum materiale, quod actum fidei terminat; actus dicendi verò, ut objectum formale, quod intellectum in actum credendi movet, sese habeat. Quemadmodum autem actus dicendi, quo Deus dicit, v. g. Verbum carnem factum esse, est ratio credendi, Verbum esse carnem factum, ita idem in Deum dicentem reflexus, quo indirectè & in actu exercito dicit, se dicere illud, est ratio credendi Deum dicere, v. g. Verbum carnem factum esse.

Ad objectionem alteram respondemus, in assensu fidei, quo credimus, quæ in Scriptura continentur, propter divinam revelationem, sive quia Deus ea dicit sive revelat, virtualiter duplicem includi discursum: Unum, qui per modum argumenti principalis; alterum qui per modum prosyllogismi se habeat. Prior discursus est hic: Quicquid Deus in Scriptura à se inspirata dicit, sive revelat, certò & infallibiliter verum est. Atqui v. g. Verbum carnem factum esse in Scriptura à se inspirata dicit sive revelat. Ergo Verbum carnem factum esse certò & infallibiliter verum est. Et hic est syllogismus principalis, cujus medium concludendi & ratio objectiva formalis est ipse actus dicendi, quo Deus olim Johanni Evangelistæ per internum inspirationis actum dixit, Verbum carnem factum esse, & quo cum verbis, à Johanne ex divina inspiratione literis consignatis, supernaturaliter concurrens per ea ipsa nobis idem interius ad animum nostrum dicit, nobisŇ revelat. Posteriori verò discursu tum opus est, cum de illius minore oritur dubitatio, unde scilicet scias & credas, Deum dicere hoc, quod in Scriptura continetur, v.g. Verbum carnem factum esse. Ubi respondere non potes, te credere illud propter aliam divinam revelationem, sed dicendum, te credere illud per ipsum actum dicendi, quo per verba Scripturæ, ex divina inspiratione in literas relata, Deus id interius ad animum tuum dicit, tibique persuadet. Eo enim, in ipsum Deum dicentem reflexo, dicit indirectè & in actu exercito, se dicere hoc per verba Scripturæ ad animum tuum. Et in hoc altero discursu actus dicendi reflexus est ratio cognoscendi dicentem, perinde ut actus dicendi signatus est ratio cognoscendi rem dictam. Quamvis verò tempore simul sint actus dicendi signatus, & exercitus, & simul cognoscantur, tamen ut naturâ prius est eum dependere à dicente, dicentisŇ notitiâ intellectui nostro insinuare; quàm res dictas nobis repræsentare, ita ejusdem actus dicendi, ut dependentis à Deo, atq; adeò in Deum dicentem reflexi cognitio naturâ prior est cognitione ejus, ut res significatas nobis repræsentantis: atque adeò in actu signato spectati. Sicut autem aliàs propositio minor syllogismi principalis est ratio assentiendi conclusioni, & hæc ut objectum materiale, illa ut objectum formale; in prosyllogismo autem ratio assentiendi minori propositioni syllogismi principalis, ut objectum formale; propositio autem minor ejusdem, quæ nunc conclusio sit, ut objectum materiale sese habet, ita impræsentiarum in argumento principali actus dicendi signatus, quo Deus hoc vel illud dicit, habet se ut ratio cognoscendi rem dictam, & ut objectum formale illius; in prosyllogismo autem actus dicendi reflexus, quo Deus in actu exercito dicit se dicere, ad actum signatum, quo hoc vel illud dicit, ut objectum formale & ratio cognoscendi; hic verò ut objectum materiale & ut res cognita se habet. Ad objectionem tertiam respondemus, objectum formale non habere se ad sui assensum efficienter, sed objective tantum, terminando eum, universaliter verum non est, sed procedit tantum de objecto formali evidente, quod ex apprehensis terminis cognitum intellectui identitatem prædicati cum subjecto per se immediate repræsentat, eumq; per illam, in apprehensis terminis cognitam, ad assensum sui determinat. Quando autem objectum formale inevidens est, ut identitas prædicati cum subjecto in terminis apprehensis perspici & cognosci non possit, ut cum objecto formali fidei divinæ res habet; tum non repugnat, objectum formale habere se ad sui assensum suo modo etiam efficienter, modo quod efficienter ad eum confert, loco objecti conferat, ut paulo post in assertione VI. pluribus ostendetur.

Neque est, quod dicatur, Auctoritatem Scripturæ & ejusdem efficaciam sic confundi. Aliud enim est alteram cum altera confundi; aliud alteram cum altera in ratione objectiva formali conjungi. Auctoritas Scripturæ, uti supra cap. III. th. IV. ostensum, est a̓ξia sive dignitas Scripturæ, alliciens trahensq; hominum animos in assensum certum & indubitatum, ejus dictis habendum, ex Dei perfectione infinita, suaq; ab eo dependentia cognita resultans: quæ ubi cognita est, movet utiq; intellectum in assensum aliorum objective, non efficienter. Ut autem a nobis cognita dicatur, duo cognitu necessaria sunt: Unum, Deum esse in dicendo summe veracem, & nec falli nec fallere posse; alterum, eum esse Scripturæ sacræ Auctorem sive causam efficientem, vel quod idem est, Scripturam dependere ab eo efficienter, & esse a Viris sanctis ipso inspirante conscriptam, ut d. l. th. III. Expl. n. 1. & th. X. ostensum. Quemadmodum autem dependentia Scripturæ sacræ a Deo per inspirationem nobis evidens non est, sed inevidens & obscura; nec nisi Deo per ipsammet Scripturam in nobis testificante nobis notitia fidei divinæ innotescere potest, ita res ipsa exigit, ut ad dependentiam Scripturæ, assensu fidei divinæ cognoscendam, Deus cum Scriptura inspirata concurrens, etiam active sive efficienter ad assensum fidei divinæ concurrat: qui concursus quamvis alias etiam ad efficaciam Scripturæ referri possit, hic tamen quia objecti vicem supplet, & id ipsum confert, quod alias objectum vi suæ rationis objectivæ formalis conferre debebat, ut postea ostendetur, à ratione objectiva formali fidei divinæ excludi nec potest, nec debet. Unde auctoritas & efficacia Scripturæ non confunduntur, quando Dei concursus supernaturalis cum Scriptura ad cognoscendam ejus à Deo dependentiam requiritur; sed auctoritas Scripturæ, hoc non obstante, est & manet ἀξία sive dignitas Scripturæ, ex Dei summa in dicendo veracitate & sua à Deo dependentia cognita resultans; efficacia verò est & manet vis quædam activa, actuum & effectuum supernaturalium productiva; & illa cognita objectivè; hæc incognita efficaciter ad actus suos se habet, licet ad cognoscendam Scripturæ dependentiam à Deo per immediatam inspirationem, ad auctoritatem Scripturæ prærequifitam, ejus efficaciam etiam concurrere oporteat. Quæ omnia ex mox dicendis manifestiora evadent.


### VI. Fifth assertion: Holy Scripture, with the supernatural concurrence of God,…

VI.

Fifth assertion: Holy Scripture, with the supernatural concurrence of God, moves the intellect into a supernatural assent to its dependence upon God by way of a non-evident motive, with the will drawn into consent, and supernaturally moved and induced to command the intellect to assent.

I. This assertion concerns the manner in which Holy Scripture moves the intellect into a supernatural assent to itself and to its dependence upon God. For just as the habits of the intellect are of a twofold difference, and some are evident, others non-evident, so according to the diversity of the habits, the objective formal reason also, by which the intellect is moved into its assent, is twofold, and one is evident, the other non-evident: indeed, habits have it from the objective formal reason, whether evident or non-evident, that they are and are called evident or non-evident. An evident objective formal reason is that by which the identity of the predicate with the subject is clearly represented through the apprehended terms, and by the same, perceived in the apprehended terms, the intellect is determined to assent, so that it cannot dissent. Non-evident is that by which the identity of the predicate with the subject is not indeed clearly represented through the apprehended terms themselves, yet, though it is known obscurely, the will is affected, enticed, and drawn into consent, so that by its command it may determine the intellect to assent. II. By this fifth assertion, therefore, it is declared that the objective formal reason of Holy Scripture, by which it moves the intellect to assent to itself and to its own dependence upon God, is non-evident, and that it entices and draws the will into consent, though known obscurely, so that by its command it may determine the intellect to its own assent. This will be more clearly evident from the subsequent sixth assertion.

VII.

Sixth assertion: Therefore, to cause the assent of divine faith, Scripture exerts itself with the supernatural concurrence of God, both in the intellect of man and in his will.

This assertion flows from the one immediately preceding. For because Holy Scripture, with the supernatural concurrence of God, moves the intellect by way of a non-evident motive into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God, with the will drawn into consent, it is certainly necessary that it exert its own motive force on both parts, namely, on the part of the intellect and on the part of the will. What, however, its functions are on the part of the intellect, and likewise what they are on the part of the will, must now be weighed and declared distinctly and in order.

VIII.

Seventh assertion: On the part of the intellect, Holy Scripture exerts itself with the supernatural concurrence of God by illuminating it through the species of things, of which the words of Scripture are signs, both those impressed and those expressed.

I. This, and the eighth assertion which will follow it, concern the sum and hinge of the matter, which therefore must be weighed more deeply by us, and must be explained and declared more diligently in order. And as regards this one, which is of the present place, it must be known above all that Holy Scripture, since it is the external Word of God, consigned to letters, cannot actually exert its motive force to cause assent to itself and to the things to be believed, unless it is transmitted within to the intellect and, as it were, fixed in it. It is transmitted, however, to the intellect and fixed in it, just as any other Word and any other writing, in a connatural way, by the intervention of the senses—of hearing, indeed, when it is preached, taught, and explained by a living voice: in which regard The Apostle says in Rom. 10:17 that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God, namely, the preached word; but by the intervention of sight, when it is read in the Biblical Codex or other writings. For then the sensible words, whether transmitted to the imagination by voice through hearing or by writing through sight, produce first of all in it their likenesses or images, which are called phantasms; and these, elevated by the agent intellect, produce in the possible intellect what are called intelligible species, which, because they are produced in the possible intellect by phantasms elevated by the agent intellect and are as it were impressed upon it, are called impressed species, in distinction to the acts of knowing themselves, elicited in the intellect by their aid, which, because they are certain expressed images of them, are called expressed species. Furthermore, the words of Scripture, by the very fact that they are signs of things, signifying by convention, besides the fact that they introduce themselves into the mind through the intervention of the senses by their own species impressed upon the intellect, also lead the intellect into the knowledge of other things, namely, those of which they are signs. For this reason, Augustine in Book II of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 1, defines a sign in general as a thing which, beyond the species it introduces to the senses, makes something else come into knowledge from itself. And in the book On the Principles of Dialectic, chapter 5, that it represents itself to the sense, and, besides itself, something else to the mind.

II. Although sacred Scripture and the δύναμις of God, His power and virtue, concurring together to illuminate the intellect of man, are always joined in the first act, even outside of use, and, as will be shown below in chapter 8, flow together into the illumination of our intellect: nevertheless, just as grace otherwise does not destroy but perfects nature, so grace or the δύναμις and efficacious virtue of God, joined to the Word of sacred Scripture, does not destroy its native power and character, which it shares with any other word, but leaves to it its parts and functions, yet supplies with its supernatural concurrence what is lacking to it when viewed in its merely native power and character, and elevates it to supernatural acts and effects, to the causing of which it cannot attain by itself alone, or by its own sole native power and character which it shares with any other word. Whence it must further be examined here what is natural to the words of Scripture, and common to them with the words of any other writing; what is supernatural to the same, and peculiar and proper to them above the words of any other writing, so that it may become more manifest, and be more rightly explained and understood, what Holy Scripture contributes to the illumination of the intellect by the native force of its words, and what likewise by the force of the divine virtue or power always conjoined with it. Which, when duly explained and more deeply understood in the doctrine concerning Conversion, will have its signal use for accurately distinguishing the external and pedagogical acts of conversion, and the internal and spiritual acts of the same.

Moreover, it is natural for the words of holy Scripture, as read in the Biblical Codex through sight, or proposed by the voice of a teacher through hearing, to penetrate to the intellect, and to move it objectively both to the cognition of themselves and of the things of which they are signs, which Logicians call the apprehension of simples, and distinguish from judgment, or cognition placed in assent. For the words of Scripture are by their own nature sensible signs, and indeed when written fall under sight, but when uttered by voice fall under hearing. Moreover, it is natural for every sensible object, and thus also for every external and sensible Word, to transmit a certain species of itself through the external senses to the phantasy, and furthermore, through the phantasm as a certain image of itself, with the concurrence of the agent intellect, to imprint upon the passive or possible intellect a certain species of itself, which they call intelligible, and by it to move and determine it to the cognition or simple apprehension of itself. Now the words of Scripture are signs signifying by institution, i.e., signs instituted to signify something else, so that when known they move the intellect into the cognition of other things, to signify which they were instituted, and they have all the power of signifying in which they are potent from the pleasure and will of the institutor, and from the usage of speaking. These, I say, are common and as it were natural to holy Scripture with any other Scripture whatsoever, and are included in the double definition of a sign brought forward above from Augustine; the one: that a sign is a THING, besides the species which it brings into the senses, making something else come into cognition from itself; the other, that a sign is that which represents itself to the sense, and besides itself something to the mind.

But how words, besides the species which they bring into the senses, also make other things come into cognition, and represent them to the mind, seems to have some difficulty, and to stand in need of explanation. For since the signified things, which, besides themselves, words make to come into cognition, cannot be conceived and known by the intellect, unless through species impressed by them, hence the difficulty arises, from where do the species of the signified things come to the intellect? Is it from words, as their signs? Or are they indeed impressed upon it by the signified things themselves? Which difficulty, although it may be common to the words of Holy Scripture with any other words signifying by convention: for it is common to all that, besides the knowledge of themselves, they also convey to the intellect the knowledge of the things of which they are signs; here, however, for the sake of explaining and understanding more deeply the supernatural concurrence of God with Holy Scripture, it must be examined here.

Certainly, it cannot be said that the species of things are impressed upon the intellect by the words themselves, as signs of things. For words, signifying by convention, whether uttered by voice and perceived by hearing, or written down in letters and read, can indeed transmit their own images or species to the intellect through the intervention of the senses, but not those of the signified things. For between them and the signified things there is no similarity, no correspondence, through which it could happen that, when perceived by the senses, they transmit to the intellect and impress upon it at once the species of themselves and of the signified things, but the whole reason of the sign which they possess depends upon the will of the one imposing it and the usage of speaking, and is extrinsic to them.

It must be said, therefore, that the species of the signified things, through which the intellect is made sufficient in the first act for knowing the things themselves and is constituted in the manner of a complete principle, are transmitted to the intellect through the intervention of the senses from the things themselves, and, having been impressed upon it by things already known beforehand, pre-exist in the one who reads the words or hears them proposed by the voice of a teacher: the words of Scripture, however, transmitted to the intellect, by their own power of signifying, which they have from the will of the one imposing it and the usage of speaking, move the intellect objectively to coordinate the species of things, already impressed upon it and pre-existing, in conformity with the things, and to elicit the knowledge of things through the same, in that order in which the external words are ordered and constructed, coordinated and disposed in conformity with the words. This is evident from the very nature of external speech, viewed both on the part of the speaker and on the part of the listener. For on the part of the speaker, speech is the manifestation of things conceived in his intellect through words signifying the same by convention, and it presupposes on the part of the speaker the species of things already known by the intellect and to be signified

Latin:

VI.

QVinta assertio: Scriptura sacra cum Dei concursu supernaturali movet intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ per modum motivi inevidentis, voluntate in consensum tractâ, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum supernaturaliter motâ & inductâ.

I. Assertio hæc concernit modum, quo Scriptura sacra intellectum in supernaturalem sui suæque à Deo dependentiæ assensum movet. Quemadmodùm enim habitus intellectus in duplici differentia, & alii evidentes, alii inevidentes sunt, ita pro diversitate habituum ratio objectiva formalis etiam, quâ intellectus in ejus assensum movetur, duplex, & alia evidens, alia inevidens est: imò habitus à ratione objectiva formali, evidente vel inevidente, habent, quòd evidentes vel inevidentes sunt & dicuntur. Evidens ratio objectiva formalis est, quâ identitas prædicati cum subjecto per terminos apprehensos clarè repræsentatur, & per eandem, in terminis apprehensis perspectam, intellectus ad assensum determinatur, ut dissentire non possit. Invidens est, quâ identitas prædicati cum sub jecto, non quidem per ipsos terminos apprehensos, clarè repræsentatur, cognitâ tamen, licet obscurè, voluntas afficitur, allicitur, & in consensum trahitur, ut imperio suo intellectum ad assensum determinet. II. Hac ergo quinta assertione declaratur, Scripturae sacrae rationem objectivam formalem, qua intellectum in sui suaeque a Deo dependentiae assensum movet, esse inevidentem, & obscure cognitam allicere & in consensum trahere voluntatem, ut imperio suo intellectum ad sui assensum determinet. Id quod ex subsequente assertione sexta clarius patescet.

VII.

Sexta assertio: Ad causandum igitur assensum fidei divinae exerit se Scriptura cum Dei concursu supernaturali cum in hominis intellectu, tum in ejus voluntate.

Assertio haec fluit ex proxime praecedente. Quia enim Scriptura sacra cum Dei concursu supernaturali intellectum per modum motivi inevidentis in supernaturalem assensum suae a Deo dependentiae movet, voluntate in consensum tracta, necesse utique est, ut ex parte utraque suam ipsa vim motivam exerat, ex parte intellectus scilicet, & ex parte voluntatis. Quae autem ex parte intellectus, quae item ex parte voluntatis munia ejus sint, nunc expendendum, & ordine distincteque declarandum venit.

VIII.

Septima assertio: Ex parte intellectus exerit se Scriptura sacra cum Dei concursu supernaturali, illuminando eum per species rerum, quarum signa Scripturae verba sunt, cum impressas tum expressas.

I. Haec, & quae eum sequetur, octava assertio nostra concernunt summam & cardinem rei, quae proinde altius nobis expendendae, & ordine diligentius enodandae declarandaeque veniunt. Et hanc, quae praesentis loci est, quod attinet, sciendum est ante omnia, Scripturam sacram, cum Verbum Dei externum sit, literis consignatum, non posse suam vim motivam ad causandum sui rerumque credendarum assensum actu exerere, nisi intus ad ejus intellectum transmissa, eique quasi infixa sit. Transmittitur autem ad intellectum & infigitur ei, perinde ut aliud quodvis Verbum, & alia quaevis Scriptura, modo connaturali, interventu sensuum, auditus quidem, quando voce viva praedicatur, docetur & explicatur: quo intuitu Apostolus dicit Rom. X. 17. Fidem esse ex auditu, auditum verò per Verbum Dei, scilicet prædicatum; visu verò interventu, quando in Codice Biblico vel scriptis aliis legitur. Tunc enim verba sensibilia, sive voce per auditum, sive scripto per visum ad phantasiam transmissa, producunt primò omnium in illa sui simulacra sive species, quæ phantasmata dicuntur; & hæc ab intellectu agente elevata producunt in intellectu possibili species, ut vocantur, intelligibiles, quæ quòd per phantasmata, ab intellectu agente elevata, in intellectu possibili productæ, eiq; quasi impressæ sint, species impressæ dicuntur, ad differentiam ipsorum actuum cognoscendi, illarum adminiculo in intellectu elicitorum, qui quòd quædam illorum imagines expressæ sint, species expressæ appellantur. Deinde verba Scripturæ hoc ipso, quod signa sunt rerum, ex instituto significantia, præterquam quod semetipsa, sensuum interventu, animo ingerunt per sui species, intellectui impressas, deducunt intellectum etiam in cognitionem rerum aliarum, illarum scilicet, quarum signa sunt. Quamobrem Augustinus lib. II. de Doctr. Christ. c. 1. signum in genere definit, quod sit res, præter speciem, quam ingerit sensibus, aliquid aliud ex se faciens in cognitionem venire. Et lib. de principiis Dialecticæ cap. V. quòd se ipsum sensui, &, præter se, aliquid animo repræsentet.

II. Quamvis verò Scriptura sacra & Dei δύναμις, potentia & virtus, ad illuminandum hominis intellectum simul concurrens, in actu primo semper, etiam extra usum, sint conjunctæ, &, ut inferiùs in cap. VIII. ostendetur, in illuminationem nostri intellectus simul influant: tamen quemadmodùm aliàs gratia non tollit, sed perficit naturam, ita gratia sive δύναμις & virtus Dei efficax, Verbo Scripturæ sacræ conjuncta, non tollit nativam eiq; cum quovis alio verbo communem vim & indolem, sed relinquit ei suas partes & munia, supplet autem suo supernaturali concursu, quæ ei in sua merè nativa vi & indole spectato, desunt, elevatq; illud ad actus & effectus supernaturales, ad quos causandos per se solum, sive suâ solâ nativâ sibiq; cum alio quovis verbo communi vi & indole pertingere non potest. Unde porro hic expendendum venit, quid naturale verbis Scripturæ, iisq; cum alterius cujusvis Scripturæ verbis commune; quid iisdem supernaturale, & præ alterius cujusvis Scripturæ verbis peculiare & proprium sit, ut quid Scriptura sacra vi verborum nativâ; quid item vi virtutis sive potentiæ divinæ, sibi semper conjunctæ, ad intellectus illuminationem conserat, manifestiùs fiat, rectiúsq; explicetur & intelligatur. Quæ ritè explicata & penitiùs intellecta in doctrina de Conversione ad conversionis actus externos & pædagogicos, & ejusdem actus internos & spirituales accuratè discernendos suum usum insignem habebit.

Naturale autem est verbis Scripturæ sacræ, ut in Codice Biblico lecta per visum; vel docentis voce proposita per auditum ad intellectum penetrent, eumq; cùm ad sui tum ad rerum, quarum signa sunt, cognitionem, quam apprehensionem simplicium Logici appellant, & judicio, sive in assensu positæ cognitioni contradistingvunt, objectivè moveant. Sunt enim verba Scripturæ suâpte naturâ signa sensibilia, & scripta quidem sub visum, voce autem prolata sub auditum cadunt. Naturale autem est omni objecto sensibili, atq; sic etiam omni Verbo externo & sensibili, ut per sensus externos sui quandam speciem ad phantasiam transmittat & porrò per phantasma velut sui quoddam simulacrum cum concursu intellectus agentis intellectui passivo sive possibili sui quandam speciem, quam intelligibilem appellant, imprimat, eâque illum ad sui cognitionem sive apprehensionem simplicem moveat, & determinet. Sunt autem Scripturæ verba signa, ex instituto significantia, h. e. signa, ad aliud significandum instituta, ut cognita intellectum in cognitionem rerum aliarum, ad quas significandas instituta sunt, moveant, habentq; omnem, quâ pollent, vim significandi ex placito & voluntate instituentis, usuq́; loquendi. Hæc, inquam, Scripturæ sacræ cum alia quavis Scriptura communia & quasi naturalia sunt, includunturq; in superiori ex Augustino allata duplici definitione signi; unâ: signum esse REM, præter speciem, quam ingerit sensibus, aliquid aliud ex se facientem in cognitionem venire; alterâ, signum esse, quod se ipsum sensui, & præter se aliquid animo repræsentat.

Quomodò autem verba, præter speciem, quam ingerunt sensibus, etiam res alias faciant in cognitionem venire, animoque repræsentent, nonnihil difficultatis habere, & explicatione egere videtur. Cùm enim res significatæ, quas, præter se, verba in cognitionem venire faciunt, ab intellectu concipi cognosciq; non possint, nisi per sui species impressas, oritur hinc difficultas, unde rerum significatarum species impressæ intellectui obveniant? an à verbis, velut illarum signis? an verò ab ipsis rebus significatis ei imprimantur? Quæ difficultas licet verbis Scripturæ sacræ cum aliis quibusvis ex instituto significantibus verbis communis sit: omnibus enim commune est, ut, præter sui cognitionem, etiam rerum, quarum signa sunt, cognitionem intellectui ingerant; hîc tamen ad Dei concursum supernaturalem cum Scriptura sacra dextrè explicandum & penitiùs intelligendum, hîc excutienda venit.

Sanè ab ipsis verbis, velut signis rerum, species rerum intellectui imprimi, dici non potest. Verba enim, ex instituto significantia, sive voce prolata audituq; percepta, sive literis consignata & lecta, sui quidem imagines sive species sensuum interventu à se ad intellectum transmittere possunt, non tamen rerum significatarum. Inter ea enim & res significatas nulla est similitudo, nulla convenientia, per quam fieri possit, ut sensibus percepta simul sui & rerum significatarum species ad intellectum transmittant, eiq; imprimant, sed tota, quam habent, ratio signi dependet à voluntate imponentis, usuq; loquendi, estq; iis extrinseca.

Dicendum ergò, species rerum significatarum, per quas intellectus ad ipsas res cognoscendas in actu primo sufficiens inq; ratione principii completi constituitur, transmitti ad intellectum sensuum interventu ab ipsis rebus, & à rebus, jam antè cognitis, ipsi impressas, præexistere in eo, qui verba legit vel docentis voce proponi audit: verba Scripturæ autem, ad intellectum transmissa, suâ vi significandi, quam ex voluntate imponentis usuque loquendi habent, movere intellectum objectivè ad rerum species, ei jam ante impressas & præexistentes, rebus conformiter coordinandas, & ad rerum cognitionem per easdem, eâ serie, quâ verba externa ordinata & constructa sunt, coordinatas & dispositas, verbis conformem eliciendam. Id quod patet ex ipsa locutionis externæ natura, cùm ex parte loquentis, tùm ex parte audientis spectata. Ex parte loquentis enim locutio est manifestatio rerum, ejus intellectu conceptarum, per verba, easdem ex instituto significantia, & præsupponit ex parte loquentis, species rerum, intellectu jam cognitarum, aliisq; significan-


### to others: for they could not be conceived or known without the pre-existing…

to others: for they could not be conceived or known without the pre-existing species of those things. But on the part of the hearer, speech looks entirely to this end, that it may lead him, by means of words signifying by convention, as if by known signs, into the knowledge of the things signified, and it presupposes on his part that the force and meaning of the words are already known to him: for otherwise, if he is ignorant of the force and meaning of the words, he will not understand the speech, according to that saying of Paul: If I come to you speaking in tongues (unknown to you), what shall I profit you? I Cor. XIV. 6. Unless you give by the tongue a significant speech (the force of which the hearers have known), how will it be understood what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. v. 9. If I do not know the force of the voice, I shall be to him who speaks a barbarian, and he who speaks, a barbarian to me, ibid. v. 11. Therefore speech also presupposes, on the part of the hearer, the species of things, into the knowledge of which it ought to lead him, pre-existing in his intellect. For to know the meanings of words is to know of which things the words are signs. But to know of which things the words are signs is to know the words, and the things which they signify, to be signified by them. But that the things which words signify are signified by them cannot be known without the impressed species of the things signified by the words. Therefore speech, on the part of the hearer, presupposes the impressed species of the things signified, just as it does the knowledge of the words. It does not, therefore, finally imprint those upon his intellect. The same must be thought concerning Holy Scripture, which is a certain external speech of God, consigned to letters, by which, through the words of which it consists, signifying by convention, it leads us into the knowledge of the things signified. And hence it is that the very highest mysteries of our faith, which are altogether unknown to human reason, e.g., the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, Holy Scripture describes with words taken from usage, and explains to us and exhibits for knowledge through concepts taken from sensible things, the species of which have already been impressed upon the intellect by objects.

But it remains to be examined how far the knowledge of the things signified extends, into which the words of Holy Scripture, like those of any other, lead the intellect by their native force of signifying. But it does not extend further than to the first operation of the mind, which logicians call the apprehension of simples. For words, known by the intellect, by virtue of their power of signifying received from the will of the one imposing them, have no more force than to move the intellect to excite the pre-existing impressed species of things, and, according to the rationale of their context, to coordinate them in a manner convenient to the things. The impressed species, however, which, having been excited and coordinated according to the guidance of the words, concur with the intellect by way of a principle and partial cause to elicit the cognition of things, cannot move it to any further degree of cognition than that which is of simple apprehension. For any impressed species whatsoever, as it is the species only of itself and not of another object, so it can determine the intellect only to the cognition or simple apprehension of its own object. But when the species of things, from the intellect moved by words arranged and constructed in a certain order, are coordinated according to the guidance of the words and determine it to the cognition of the whole discourse, then this cognition, in so far as it depends precisely upon the impressed species coordinated with one another in a manner convenient to the things, is a cognition of the first operation, situated in the apprehension of simples, and does not reach to assent, which pertains to the second operation of the mind. But if indeed the concepts of things, elicited through impressed species coordinated to the guidance of the words, represent to the intellect the identity of the predicate with the subject of itself immediately, as is wont to happen in evident principles, then the intellect is moved to judgment and is determined to assent, which pertains to the second operation of the mind, not precisely through the words, nor precisely through the impressed species coordinated to the guidance of the words, but through the things themselves, clearly represented as one among themselves in the concepts elicited through the impressed species, so that the intellect, as it were, sees the identity of the predicate with the subject in those very concepts of them that have been elicited. But if the concepts of things, elicited by the intellect through impressed species coordinated to the guidance of the words, represent things as agreeing and the same in a third thing, then again the things, known as agreeing and the same in a third thing, move the intellect to assent by means of that third thing, in which they agree, being known. But if the concepts elicited through species coordinated to the guidance of the words represent to the intellect things as divided and disagreeing, then again the intellect is moved to judgment, and that situated in dissent, through the things represented as disagreeing and divided, and so in the rest.

In spiritual objects, however, and matters of faith, neither the words of Scripture by their power of signifying, which they have from imposition, nor the things signified can move the intellect to the assent of things to be believed. Not the words of Scripture: because these, as has just been shown, have in common with the other words of any other Scripture that they move the intellect by their native power of signifying to excite the pre-existing species of things impressed and to coordinate them conformably to their context, by which it is determined to know them by simple apprehension, and is constituted in the nature of a complete principle of knowing; nor can they besides contribute anything of themselves: Nor can the things signified, known by simple apprehension through expressed species conveniently coordinated with words, move the human intellect to their assent through the identity of the subject with the predicate, either of themselves immediately or represented clearly by means of some third thing. Not of themselves immediately: because they are non-evident. Nor by means of some third thing: because if, apart from the supernatural concurrence of God, the intellect, from its own natural light alone, ought to compare the relations of spiritual things known by simple apprehension with one another, and judge whether they are the same among themselves either immediately or by means of some third thing, it is so far from ever being able to reach the perception of their identity and the attainment of their truth, and to provide assent, that it is rather carried into all things contrary, and judges those things which are of the Spirit of God to be foolishness by a most perverse judgment, 1 Cor. II. 14. It remains therefore fixed and immovable that the knowledge into which the words of Scripture move the intellect by their native power and character is not, and cannot be, other than the notion of simple apprehension. This indeed happens not rarely, that the impious, born and educated in the Church, who have imbibed the heads of Christian doctrine as if with their mother's milk, sometimes embrace and believe them with some sort of assent, led by the authority of parents, teachers, and the Church. But this faith is not from spiritual objects known by simple apprehension, but from extrinsic motives, namely the authority of parents, teachers, the Church, etc., as the reason for assenting, and as much as it is, it is entirely natural, which theologians otherwise call literal and historical faith, and they readily admit that it can fall to an unregenerate man. But there is no question at present concerning this assent of faith. From which things thus declared, it flows as a ready consequence.

(1.) That the knowledge of simple apprehension of the things signified by the words of Scripture is natural, and falls even to unregenerate men, Gentiles and pagans, who indeed are knowledgeable of the language in which Holy Scripture is recorded, and have the signifying force of the words and the grammatical construction known. For it depends upon causes merely natural, namely upon the native force of words, by which, as in any other speech, whether by voice uttered or written, so in Holy Scripture read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, they penetrate to the intellect in a connatural way through the intervention of the senses; but being known in their force of signifying, which they have from imposition, they move the intellect by their force of signifying again in a connatural way to excite and rightly coordinate the pre-existing species of the things of which they are signs. Which species, by the very fact that they pre-exist in the intellect before the words of Scripture are perceived, are natural. But with the impressed species, excited and coordinated in the intellect by the force of the words of signifying, it is natural that they should concur with the intellect, as a partial principle of knowing, for the simple apprehension of things, or for eliciting the knowledge of the simple apprehension of them.

(2.) That illumination, required on the part of the intellect for the assent of divine faith, does not consist in it, as Pelagius once taught, and as the Socinians, who still follow Pelagius in this κρησφύγετα, even now contend. We do not indeed deny that the Word of God, written and preached, can in a looser sense, even through its native force of signifying, which words have from imposition and usage of speaking, be called a light; and the knowledge of simple apprehension, which is introduced into the mind through that read or perceived by hearing, be called a certain illumination, if indeed light be called πᾶν τὸ φανερώμενον, everything that manifests something; and illumination be the manifestation of every thing, according to that of Paul, Eph. V. 13, πᾶν τὸ φανερώμενον φῶς ἐστι, everything that manifests is light. For the Word of God, written and preached, through its genuine force of signifying, is φανερώμενον, manifestative, if I may so speak, of the things of which the words are signs, and thus a certain light, and the knowledge, even if it be only of simple apprehension, to which it moves the intellect of the reader or hearer through words signifying by institution, is a certain manifestation of them, and thus a certain illumination of the knowing intellect. But when in the Holy Scriptures the Word of God is called light, and it is attributed to it that it minds

Latin:

darum: non enim absque illarum speciebus præexistentibus concipi cognosciq; potuerunt. Ex parte audientis verò locutio huc tota spectat, ut eum per verba, ex instituto significantia, velut signa nota, in cognitionem rerum significatarum deducat, & præsupponit ex ejus parte, vim & significationem verborum esse ei jam ante cognitam: aliàs enim si vim & significationem verborum ignoret, locutionem non intelliget, juxta illud Pauli: Si veniam ad vos linguis (vobis ignotis) loquens, quid vobis prodero? I. Cor. XIV. 6. Per linguam nisi significantem sermonem (cujus vis significandi auditores cognitam habeant) dederitis, quomodo intelligetur, quid dicitur? eritis enim in aërem loquentes. v. 9. Si nesciero vim vocis, ero ei, qui loquitur, barbarus, & qui loquitur, apud me barbarus, ibid. v. 11. Ergo locutio præsupponit etiam, ex parte audientis, species rerum, in quarum notitiam eum deducere debet, in ejus intellectu præexistentes. Nam nôsse vocum significationes est nôsse, quarum rerum signa sint voces. Nôsse autem, quarum rerum signa sint voces, est nosse voces, & res, quas significant, iis significari. Res autem, quas voces significant, iis significari, cognosci non potest, absq; rerum, vocibus significatarum, speciebus impressis. Ergo locutio ex parte audientis ut notitiam vocum, ita & rerum significatarum species impressas præsupponit. Non ergo illas ejus intellectui demum imprimit. Idem sentiendum est de Scriptura sacra, quæ est quædam Dei locutio externa, literis consignata, quâ per verba, quibus constat, ex instituto significantia, nos in rerum significatarum cognitionem deducit. Atque hinc est, quod ipsa summa fidei nostræ mysteria, quæ humanæ rationi prorsus ignota sunt, v. g. Trinitatis, incarnationis mysteria, Scriptura sacra vocibus, ex usu desumtis, describit, & per conceptus, à rebus sensibilibus, quarum species intellectui ab objectis jam impressæ sunt, desumtos nobis explicat & cognoscenda exhibet.

Quousque autem se extendat cognitio rerum significatarum, in quam ut alterius cujusq;, ita & sacræ Scripturæ verba ex sua nativa vi significandi intellectum deducunt, dispiciendum superest. Non autem ea longiùs se porrigit, quàm ad primam mentis operationem, quam Logici apprehensionem simplicium appellant. Verba enim, ab intellectu cognita, per suam ab imponentis voluntate acceptam vim significandi non plus valent, quàm ut ad præexistentes rerum species impressas excitandas, &, pro ratione ipsorum contextus, rebus convenienter coordinandas intellectum moveant. Species impressæ autem, quæ ad ductum verborum excitatæ & coordinatæ, cum intellectu per modum principii & causæ partialis ad eliciendam rerum cognitionem concurrunt, non possunt eum ad ulteriorem quendam cognitionis gradum movere, quàm qui apprehensionis simplicis est. Quælibet enim species impressa, ut sui tantùm, non alterius objecti species est, ita non nisi ad sui objecti cognitionem sive apprehensionem simplicem intellectum determinare potest. Quando autem species rerum ab intellectu, verbis certo ordine dispositis & constructis moto, ad verborum ductum coordinatæ, eum ad cognitionem orationis totius determinant, tum adhuc cognitio hæc, in quantum à speciebus impressis, inter se rebus convenienter coordinatis præcisè dependet, primæ operationis cognitio est, in apprehensione simplicium posita, & ad assensum, qui ad secundam mentis operationem pertinet, non pertingit. Quod si verò rerum conceptus, per species impressas ad verborum ductum coordinatas, eliciti repræsentent intellectui identitatem prædicati cum subjecto per se immediatè, ut in principiis evidentibus fieri solet, tum movetur intellectus ad judicium, & determinatur ad assensum, qui ad secundam mentis operationem pertinet, non præcisè per verba, nec præcisè per species impressas, ad verborum ductum coordinatas, sed per ipsas res, in conceptibus, per species impressas elicitis ut unas inter se, clarè repræsentatas, ut identitatem prædicati cum subjecto intellectus in ipsis illarum conceptibus elicitis quasi videat. Si autem conceptus rerum, per species impressas ad verborum ductum coordinatas, ab intellectu eliciti, repræsentent res, ut convenientes & easdem in uno tertio, tum rursum res, ut in uno tertio convenientes & eædem cognitæ, movent intellectum ad assensum mediante illo tertio, in quo conveniunt, cognito. Si conceptus verò per species, ad verborum ductum coordinatas, eliciti repræsentent intellectui res, ut divisas & disconvenientes, tum rursum intellectus movetur ad judicium, idque in dissensu positum, per res, ut disconvenientes & divisas repræsentatas, & sic in cæteris.

In objectis spiritualibus verò & rebus fidei nec verba Scripturæ per suam vim significandi, quam ex impositione habent, neq; res significatæ intellectum ad assensum credendorum movere possunt. Non verba Scripturæ: quia hæc, ut modò ostensum, cum aliis cujusque alterius Scripturæ verbis commune habent, ut suâ nativâ vi significandi intellectum moveant ad præexistentes rerum species impressas excitandas & suo contextui conformiter coordinandas, quibus ad easdem, apprehensione simplici cognoscendas, determinetur, & in ratione principii cognoscendi completi constituatur; nec prætereà quicquam per se conferre possint: Neque res significatæ per species expressas, verbis convenienter coordinatas, apprehensione simplici cognitæ, possunt intellectum hominis per identitatem subjecti cum prædicato vel per se immediatè, vel mediante aliquo tertio clarè repræsentatam, ad sui assensum movere.
