Non per se immediatè: quia inevidentes sunt. Neque mediante aliquo tertio: quia si citra supernaturalem Dei concursum habitudinem rerum spiritualium, apprehensione simplici cognitarum, intellectus ex suo solo lumine naturali ad se invicem conferre, & eædémne inter se vel immediatè vel mediante aliquo tertio fiat? judicare debeat, tantum abest, ut ad percipiendam illarum identitatem veritatemq; assequendam unquam pertingere, & assensum præbere possit, ut potiùs in contraria omnia feratur, & ea, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, perversissimo judicio stultitiam judicet, 1. Cor. II. 14. Fixum ergo immotumque manet, cognitionem, in quam verba Scripturæ suâ nativâ vi & indole intellectum movent, non esse, nec posse esse aliam, quam notitiam simplicis apprehensionis. Hoc quidem contingit non rarò, ut impii, in Ecclesia nati & educati, qui doctrinæ Christianæ capita cum lacte quasi imbiberunt, qualicunq; assensu ea quandoque amplectantur & credant, auctoritate parentum, præceptorũ, Ecclesiæ ducti. Sed fides hæc non est ab objectis spiritualibus, apprehensione simplici cognitis, sed à motivis extrinsecis, auctoritate parentum scilicet, præceptorum, Ecclesiæ &c. velut ratione assentiendi, & quanta est, tota naturalis est, quam aliàs Theologi literalem & historicam fidem appellant, & in hominem non renatum cadere ultrò fatentur. Verum de hoc fidei assensu impræsentiarum nulla quæstio est. Ex quibus ita declaratis pronâ fluit consequentiâ.

(1.) Notitiam apprehensionis simplicis rerum, verbis Scripturæ fignificatarum, esfe naturalem, & cadere etiam in homines non renatos, Gentiles & paganos, qui quidem linguæ, quâ Scriptura sacra confignata est, gnari sunt, & vocum vim fignificandi constructionemq́; Grammaticam cognitam habent. Dependet enim ex causis merè naturalibus, nempe ex vi vocum nativa, quâ intellectum, ut in alia quavis oratione, voce prolatâ aut scriptâ, ita in Scriptura sacra lecta aut docentis voce propositâ, modo connaturali, sensuum interventu penetrant ad intellectum; cognita autem in sua vi fignificandi, quam ex impositione habent, movent intellectum suâ vi fignificandi rursum modo connaturali ad rerum, quarum signa sunt, species præexistentes excitandas & ritè coordinandas. Quæ species hoc ipso, quod ante verba Scripturæ percepta in intellectu præexistunt, naturales sunt. Speciebus impressis autem, verborum vi fignificandi in intellectu excitatis & coordinatis, naturale est, ut cum intellectu, velut principium cognoscendi partiale, concurrant ad simplicem rerum apprehenfionem, sive ad notitiam apprehenfionis simplicis illarum eliciendam.

(2.) In ea non consistere illuminationem, ex parte intellectus ad assensum fidei divinæ requisitam, ut olim Pelagius docuit, & etiamnum Sociniani, qui Pelagium in hoc κρησφύγετα sequuntur, contendunt. Non quidem inficiamur, Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, posse in fignificatu laxiori, etiam per suam nativam vim significandi, quam verba ex impositione & usu loquendi habent, lumen; & notitiam apprehenfionis simplicis, quæ per illud lectum vel auditu perceptum, animo ingeritur, illuminationem quandam dici, si scilicet lumen dicatur πᾶν τὸ φανερώμενον, omne, quod aliquid manifestat; illuminatio verò omnis rei manifestatio, juxta illud Pauli Eph. V. 13. πᾶν τὸ φανερώμενον φῶς ἐστι, omne quod manifestat, lumen est. Verbum Dei enim, scriptum & prædicatum, per suam genuinam vim fignificandi, est φανερώμενον, manifestativum, ut ita loquar, rerum, quarum signa sunt verba, atque adeò lumen quoddam, & cognitio, licet tantum apprehenfionis simplicis fit, ad quam illud lectoris vel auditoris intellectum per verba, ex instituto fignificantia movet, est quædam illarum manifestatio, atque adeò quædam intellectus cognoscentis illuminatio. Verùm quando in Scripturis sacris Verbum Dei lumen dicitur, eique tribuitur, quòd mentes


### illuminates men, e.g., that it is a lamp to our feet, and a light to our paths,…

illuminates men, e.g., that it is a lamp to our feet, and a light to our paths, Ps. 119:105; that it is a lamp appearing in a dark place, and as the day star shining in our hearts, 2 Pet. 1:19, etc.; then especially the finger is pointed to its supernatural and truly divine illuminating power, which it has from the supernatural concurrence of God and His illuminating virtue, always conjoined to it in the first act; and the knowledge of things to be believed which it imparts supernaturally to the intellect through this, they call finally the illumination of Holy Scripture absolutely. For this, as it is the only saving [illumination], so it is entirely spiritual and from God, just as the Apostle also prays for it for his Ephesians from God alone: I do not cease, he says, giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation through the knowledge of Him, the EYES OF YOUR MIND BEING ILLUMINATED, that you may know what is the hope to which He has called you, and how opulent the glory of His inheritance in the saints, Eph. 1:16 ff. But the knowledge of simple apprehension which is brought into the intellect through the Word of God, read or preached, precisely from the native power of the words to signify, is natural, as has been shown, and can stand together with the thick darkness of the mind, which even denies, impugns, or judges as foolish those things which are of the Spirit of God, even when thus known: such men, on account of the thick darkness of the intellect, are more rightly called σκότος darkness, Eph. 5:8, ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ darkened in their mind, ch. 4:18, than they are called Φῶς light or illuminated in the eyes of the mind on account of any apprehension of things to be believed, without assent, inasmuch as they know neither what the hope is to which God has called them, nor how opulent the glory of His inheritance is in the saints, nor anything rightly about spiritual things.

III. Therefore, that we may approach the matter more closely, and explain in order, distinctly, and as clearly as possible, by what reason the Word of God, written and preached, when it is read or heard being taught, supernaturally illuminates the intellect with the power and concurrence of God, first of all it must be weighed here, from which part of the divine Word, written or preached, transmitted to the mind of the hearer or reader through reading or preaching, the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit concurs in his intellect, and exerts itself to illuminate him?

For it is evident from what has been said thus far that the Word of God, written and preached, when it has been transmitted to the intellect through reading or hearing and is as it were fixed within it, brings with it on the part of the intellect two kinds of impressed species: one of external words signifying by convention, whether written or proposed by voice; the other of the things signified. The former represent to the intellect the words themselves and their power of signifying, which they have from imposition and the usage of speaking. The latter, conveniently arranged and coordinated in the context of words in a man's intellect, represent to the same the things signified, or, which is the same thing, the sense and doctrines signified by the words duly constructed in their context. It must therefore be examined: is that illuminating power joined in a man's intellect to the impressed species of words? Or of things? Or finally of both? And if to one or the other, to which? And to which of the two? Or does God use both as instruments to illuminate him?

Moreover, it is the constant opinion of the Doctors of our Church that the illuminating power of God is not precisely joined with the words, whether written or uttered by voice, but with the sense. In explaining this matter, our predecessors in this Academy, above others, devoted excellent effort at the time of the Rathmannian controversy in their judgments and censures, both written and published, which now exist in the newest Appendix to the Consilia of Dedekind, fol. 171 et seqq. Among many other things, they write on fol. 240. 1. When we ascribe to Holy Scripture, that is, to the revealed written Word of God, an inward power of illumination and quickening, it is by no means the intention that we attribute a natural, or even a magical and sorcerous power to the signifying letters and external words; rather, we teach from God's Word concerning God's Word thus: that it has pleased God the Lord to save through the foolishness of preaching those who believe in it, 1 Cor. 1:21; that is, God has, by a voluntary ordinance, assigned to the inward sense and understanding, in which the formal aspect of Holy Scripture consists, an inward power of illumination, for the sake of which the Word is rightly considered a powerful and effective Word. And fol. 267: We by no means attribute to the words/ syllables and letters/ as they are written on the paper, a secret/ hidden/ natural or magical/ or even supernatural power, but rather to the inner form of the Holy Scripture, that is/ from the inner sense/ counsel/ and opinion of God, in the external words and save men, &c. If therefore in the external Word of God, written & preached, outside the understanding of man, the enlightening power of the Holy Spirit is joined not to the external words, but to the sense and doctrine signified by the external words, it follows naturally that also interiorly in the human intellect it is joined not to the species of the external words, but to the species of the sense and the things signified impressed upon it. For there is no greater reason why it should be necessary for it to be joined in the human intellect to the impressed species of words rather than outside it to the external words themselves. For just as it is the function of external words, signifying by institution, that when read or perceived by hearing they imprint upon the intellect both their own species and the species of the things signified, by which it is determined to the knowledge of the things themselves, and excite and coordinate them in the same, as was shown above; so also it is the function of the species impressed upon the intellect by external words, whether read or perceived by hearing, to represent to it both the external words, whose species they are, and their power of signifying: and just as external words, as the cited theologians admit, perform both of these by themselves without the supernatural grace or enlightening power of the Holy Spirit; the former indeed by this, that they are sensible words, and consigned to paper by characters of letters they penetrate to the intellect through sight; but when uttered by voice they penetrate through hearing, and just like any other sensible objects, through the intervention of their phantasms, elevated by the agent intellect, they naturally imprint their intelligible species upon it; the latter indeed by their native power of signifying, which they have from imposition and the use of speech, not from any enlightening power communicated to them supernaturally; so also the impressed species of words represent to the intellect by themselves, without the supernatural concurrence of the Holy Spirit and his enlightening power, both the external words and their power of signifying: the former indeed by this very fact, that their impressed species are; this, however, through that, because they are species of words signifying by institution. For from this alone, that they are species of words signifying by institution, they have that they represent those things to the intellect not merely by reason of letters and syllables, but with their power of signifying, not from any illuminating virtue communicated to them.

It remains, therefore, that we say that the illuminating virtue of the Holy Spirit, on the part of the intellect, is joined by divine ordination to the impressed species of the senses or of the things signified themselves, not to the impressed species of the words, and that it exerts itself for its illumination not through these, but through those. Which our predecessors and teachers in this Academy elegantly taught in their above-praised Judgment on the Rathmann Controversy, loc. cit., fol. 193, whose words are these: The Word, as God's seed, falls first into the ears, and thereafter from the ears into the heart, and if it is to remain therein, so that it may bring forth fruit, God the Holy Spirit must give the growth, and He also wills to give it, provided one does not otherwise resist Him, and place a bolt as it were before it, or give more place and room to the world and fleshly lusts, as also to Satan himself, than to the Holy Spirit. By which they excellently declare what pertains to the Word of God, written and preached as a spiritual seed, precisely by reason of the words; and what likewise pertains to it by reason of the sense and the things signified in order to our illumination. And by reason of the words, according to them, it pertains to it first that it is preached into the ears, but written, it insinuates itself into the eyes; then that it falls from the ears or eyes into the heart. That happens through the external species of words, which the spoken voice transmits to the ears of the hearers, but the written [word] to the eyes of the readers. This happens through the intelligible species of the same, impressed upon the intellect. For the external species of words penetrate through the external senses to the imagination, and by the power of their own nature impress certain images, which are called phantasms, and the phantasms furthermore, elevated by the agent intellect, penetrate to the passive intellect, and impress upon it their own spiritual species, which are commonly called intelligible. These, however, impressed upon the intellect, besides the fact that they represent to the intellect the words themselves, of which they are the species, excite in the same, through the power of signifying of the words, which they simultaneously represent, the species of the things signified themselves, and dispose and they order them to the things signified and to the sense, to be represented conveniently to the order and construction of the words, as was shown at greater length a little before. And all these things are natural and common to the Word of God with any other word whatsoever, as was demonstrated in the same place, and this the praised Theologians inculcate everywhere in their Censures. But with regard to the sense and the things signified, it agrees, according to them, with the Word of God, as with a spiritual seed, which remains in the field of the heart, so that it may take root and bring forth fruit. It remains in it, indeed, through the species of the things signified that have been impressed, since they are permanent qualities, but it takes root and brings forth fruit through the salutary meditation of the things signified, which is carried out through the same species of things signified that have indeed been impressed upon it, yet not by them alone, but with the supernatural concurrence of God through His illuminating power, joined to them by an inseparable bond, by which God elevates them to the eliciting of spiritual and salutary acts of knowing in the intellect, for the eliciting of which in it, being entirely blind and darkened toward spiritual things, they alone of themselves do not suffice. And this is what the praised Theologians mean when they say: It (the Word of God) must remain therein (in the heart) so that it may bring forth fruit; thus God the Holy Spirit must give the growth.

Latin:

hominum illuminet, v. g. quòd sit lucerna pedibus nostris, & lumen semitis nostris, Psal. CXIX. 105. quòd sit lucerna, apparens in loco caliginoso, & velut phosphorus, lucens in cordibus nostris, II. Petr. I. 19. &c. tùm inprimis digitus intenditur ad ejus supernaturalem vereque divinam vim illuminatricem, quam ex Dei concursu supernaturali ejusq; virtute illuminatrice, sibi in actu primo semper conjunctâ, habet; & quam credendorum cognitionem per hanc intellectui supernaturaliter impertit, eam dicunt demum Scripturæ sacræ absolutè illuminationem. Hæc enim uti sola salutaris, ita tota spiritualis & à Deo est, quemadmodum etiam eam Apostolus Ephesiis suis à Deo solo precatur: Non desino, inquiens, gratias agere pro vobis, mentionem vestri faciens in precibus meis, ut Deus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Pater gloriæ, vobis det Spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis per agnitionem sui, ILLUMINATOS OCULOS MENTIS vestræ, ut sciatis, quæ sit spes, ad quam ille vocavit, & quam opulenta gloria hæreditatis illius in sanctis, Eph. I. 16. seqq. Quæ autem intellectui per Verbum Dei, lectum aut prædicatum, præcisè ex nativa vocum vi significandi ingeritur cognitio apprehensionis simplicis, naturalis est, uti ostensum, & cum spissis tenebris mentis, etiam ea, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, sic cognita, negantis, impugnantis, vel stultitiam judicantis, simul stare potest: cujusmodi homines, ob spissas tenebras intellectus, rectius σκότος tenebræ, Eph. V. 8. ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ obtenebrati mente, c. IV. 18. quàm propter qualemcunque credendorum apprehensionem, sine assensu, Φῶς lux, aut mentis oculis illuminati dicuntur, utpote qui nec quænam spes, sit, ad quam eos Deus vocavit, neque quàm opulenta sit gloria hæreditatis illius in sanctis, nec quicquam de rebus spiritualibus rectè sciunt.

III. Ut ergo ad rem accedamus propiùs, & quâ ratione Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, cùm legitur vel doceri auditur, cum Dei virtute & concursu intellectum supernaturaliter illuminet, ordine, distinctè, &, quoad fieri potest, clarè explicemus, primò omnium expendendum hîc venit, utra ex parte Verbi divini, scripti aut prædicati, per lectionem aut prædicationem ad auditoris vel lectoris animum transmissi, Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, in ejus intellectu concurrat, & ad eum illuminandum sese exerat?

Constat enim ex hactenus dictis, Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, cùm per lectionem vel auditum ad intellectum transmissum, eíque quasi infixum est, importare ex parte intellectus species impressas duplices: unas externorum ex instituto significantium verborum, sive scriptorum, sive voce propositorum; alteras rerum significarum: illæ repræsentant intellectui ipsa verba, illorúmque vim significandi, quam ex impositione usuque loquendi habent. Hæ verborum contextui in hominis intellectu convenienter dispositæ & coordinatæ, repræsentant eidem res significatas, sive quod idem est, sensum & doctrinas, verbis in suo contextu ritè constructis, significatas. Dispiciendum ergo, verborumne? an rerum? an denique utrorumq; speciebus impressis virtus illa illuminatrix in hominis intellectu conjuncta sit, & alterutrisne? & utris? an utrisq; Deus velut instrumentis ad eum illuminandum utatur?

Est autem constans Doctorum Ecclesiæ nostræ sententia, virtutem Dei illuminatricem non esse præcisè cum verbis, sive scriptis, sive voce prolatis, conjunctam, sed cum sensu. Qua in re explicanda præ cæteris egregiam navarunt operam nostri in hac Academia Antecessores tempore controversiæ Rathmannianæ in suis judiciis & Censuris, tùm conscriptis & editis, quæ nunc extant in Consil. Dedek. Appendice novissima, fol. 171. seqq. Inter alia multa scribunt fol. 240. 1. Wenn wir der H. Schrifft/ das ist/ dem geoffenbahrten geschriebenen Wort Gottes eine innerliche Erleuchtungsund lebendigmachungs-Krafft zuschreiben/ so hat es gar nicht die Meinung/ als wann wir eine natürliche/ oder auch Magische und zäuberische Krafft denen bedeutenden Buchstaben und eusserlichen Wörtern zulegten/ sondern wir lehren aus Gottes Wort von Gottes Wort also/ daß es Gott dem Herrn wolgefallen/ durch die thörichte Predigt selig zu machen/ die so daran gläuben/ 1. Cor. I. v. 21. das ist/ Gott hab aus freywilliger Ordnung dem innerlichen Sinn und Verstand/ darinnen das formale der H. Schrifft bestehet/ eine innerliche Erleuchtungs-Krafft zugeordnet/ umb welcher willen das Wort für ein kräfftiges und würckliches Wort billich wird geachtet. Et fol. 267. Wir legen keines weges den Wörtern/ Syllaben und Buchstaben/ wie sie auf dem Papier geschrieben/ eine heimliche/ verborgene/ natürliche oder Magische/ oder auch übernattürliche Krafft zu/ sondern von der innerlichen Form der heiligen Schrifft/ das ist/ vom innerlichen Sinn/ Rath/ und Meinung Gottes/ in den eusserlichen Worten verfasset/ sagen wir/ daß Gott der HErr denselben die Krafft des heiligen Geistes die Menschen zu erleuchten/ zu bekehren/ und selig zu machen/ aus freywilliger Gnade zugeordnet habe/ &c. Si ergo in Verbo Dei externo, scripto & prædicato, extra intellectum hominis Spiritus S. virtus illuminatrix non verbis externis, sed sensui, doctrinæque, verbis externis significatæ, conjuncta est, sequitur ultrò, quòd etiam interiùs in hominis intellectu ea non verborum externorum; sed sensus & rerum significatarum speciebus impressis sit conjuncta. Non enim major ratio est, cur eam in hominis intellectu verborum speciebus impressis potiùs, quàm extra illum verbis externis ipsis, conjunctam esse oporteat. Quemadmodum enim verborum externorum, ex instituto significantium, munus est, ut lecta vel auditu percepta intellectui cùm sui species imprimant, tum rerum significatarum species, quibus ad ipsarummet cognitionem determinetur, in eodem excitent & coordinent, ut supra ostensum; ita & specierum, à verbis externis, sive lectis sive auditu perceptis, intellectui impressarum munus est, cùm ut verba externa, quorum species sunt, tum ut illorum vim significandi eidem repræsentent: & quemadmodùm verba externa, fatentibus laudatis Theologis, utrumq; per se citra supernaturalem Spiritus Sancti gratiam sive virtutem illuminatricem præstant; illud quidem per hoc, quod verba sensibilia sunt, & literarum characteribus in charta consignata per visum; voce autem prolata per auditum ad intellectum penetrant, & perinde ut alia quævis objecta sensibilia, interventu suorum phantasmatum, ab intellectu agente elevatorum, sui species intelligibiles ei naturaliter imprimunt; hoc verò per suam nativam vim significandi, quam ex impositione & usu loquendi, non ab ulla virtute illuminatrice, sibi supernaturaliter communicatâ, habent; ita & species verborum impressæ repræsentant intellectui per se citra supernaturalem Spiritus sancti ejusque virtutis illuminatricis concursum & verba externa, & illorum vim significandi: illa quidem per hoc ipsum, quod illorum species impressæ sunt; hanc verò per illud, quòd verborum ex instituto significantium species sunt. Ex hoc solo enim, quod verborum, ex instituto significantium species sunt, habent, quòd intellectui ea non nudè ratione literarum & syllabarum, sed cum sua vi significandi repræsentant, non ab aliqua virtute illuminatrice sibi communicatâ.

Relinquitur ergo, ut Spiritus sancti virtutem illuminatricem, ex parte intellectus, ipsis sensus sive rerum significatarum speciebus impressis, non impressis speciebus verborum, ex divina ordinatione conjunctam esse, eamque non per has; sed per illas ad ejus illuminationem se exerere dicamus. Quod eleganter nostri in hac Academia Antecessores & Præceptores docuerunt in supra laudato Judicio suo de Controv. Rathmann. d. l. fol. 193. quorum hæc sunt verba: Das Wort/ als Gottes Same/ fället erstlich in die Ohren/ und darnach aus den Ohren in das Hertz/ und soll es darinnen bleiben/ daß es Frucht bringe / so muß Gott der heilige Geist das Gedeyen geben/ und wils auch geben/ wo man anders ihme nicht widerstrebet/ und einen Riegel gleichsam fürschiebet / oder der Welt und fleischlichen Lüsten / wie auch dem Satan selbst mehr Platz und Raum giebet/ als dem heiligen Geist. Quibus quid Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato velut semini spirituali, præcisè ratione verborum; quid item ratione sensus & rerum significatarum in ordine ad nostram illuminationem conveniat, egregiè declarant. Et ratione verborum quidem juxta ipsos, convenit ei primò, quod prædicatum in aures; scriptum verò in oculos se insinuat; deinde quòd ex auribus oculisve in cor decidit. illud fit per verborum species externas, quas voce prolata ad auditorum aures; scripta verò ad lectorum oculos transmittunt. Hoc per eorundem species intelligibiles, intellectui impressas, fit. Species verborum externæ enim penetrant per sensus externos ad phantasiam, imprimuntque vi sui quasdam imagines, quæ phantasmata dicuntur, & phantasmata porro, ab intellectu agente elevata, penetrant ad intellectum passivum, imprimuntque ei species sui spirituales, quæ vulgo intelligibiles appellantur. Hæ verò, intellectui impressæ, præterquam quod ipsa verba, quorum species sunt, intellectui repræsentant, excitant in eodem per verborum vim significandi, quam simul repræsentant, species ipsarum rerum significatarum, disponuntq́; & ordinant eas ad res significatas sensúmque, verborum ordini & constructioni convenienter repræsentandum, ut paulò ante pluribus ostensum est. Atq; hæc omnia naturalia & Verbo Dei cumalio quovis verbo communia esse ibidem demonstratum est, idq́; laudati Theologi in ipsorum Censuris nullibi non inculcant. Ratione sensus verò & rerum significatarum convenit, juxta eosdem, Verbo Dei, velut semini spirituali, quòd in agro cordis manet, ut radices agat, & fructus proferat. Manet autem in eo quidem per species rerum significatarum impressas, quippe quæ qualitates permanentes sunt, sed radices agit, & fructus profert per salutarem rerum significatarum meditationem, quæ per easdem rerum significatarum species impressas quidem in eo peragitur, non tamen solas, sed cum Dei concursu supernaturali per suam virtutem illuminatricem, iisdem nexu individuo conjunctam, quâ Deus eas elevat ad actus cognoscendi spirituales salutaresque in intellectu eliciendos, ad quos in eo, ad spiritualia prorsus cæco & obtenebrato, eliciendos per se solæ non sufficiunt. Atque hoc laudati Theologi volunt, cum dicunt: Soll es (das Wort Gottes) darinnen (im Hertzen) bleiben / daß es Frucht bringe / so muß Gott der heilige Geist das Gedeyen geben.


### To the same effect they write ibid

To the same effect they write ibid. fol. 212. So that the Holy Scripture could instruct us concerning God's essence and will, concerning Christ's person and office, and similar necessary matters, see, thus God the Lord has revealed the sense and the meaning, the doctrine of such matters in the external words, and in a hidden way has connected them through His Divine order with the external Scripture. For if such Divine sense and meaning were not contained and connected in the Holy Scripture with the external words, then we could not be instructed unto salvation out of and through the Scripture, but we would have to expect the understanding, sense, and meaning from God's immediate working, and by no means seek it in the Holy Scripture. And thus far they attribute to these external words of Holy Scripture that its sense, namely the doctrine concerning the essence and will of God, and concerning the person and office of Christ and other parts of Christian doctrine, through its native power of signifying in itself may contain, and manifest to us in the manner declared above. They add, however, immediately: Furthermore, so that we might be enlightened, converted to God, made believing and blessed by means of such revealed written Word, God the Lord has, in His voluntary order, given to such sense, meaning, and understanding a divine power of life and enlightenment, so that the Holy Spirit, through such a powerful Word, and the Word in the power of the Holy Spirit, could accomplish this spiritual effect in us. By this very thing they teach openly that God has communicated an illuminating power to the sense according to His most free ordination. But because the sense of Scripture is present in our intellect partly through species of things signified by external words impressed, and partly expressed: through the former indeed in first act; through the latter in second act: it is consequently certain that the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit in our intellect is conjoined to the species of things signified by the words of Scripture, partly impressed and partly expressed, not to the impressed or expressed species of the words. Which the thing itself also declares: for words are for the sake of the sense, and when they have led the intellect into the knowledge or simple apprehension of that sense by their native power of signifying, they have finished their duty, and can vary according to the variety of languages in which Scripture has been recorded or into which it has been translated, while the sense remains one and the same among all. To which sense also Aristotle περὶ ἑρμην. c. 1, concerning any writing or spoken word: As, he says, not all use the same letters, so neither do they use the same words. But indeed the senses (concepts) of the mind, of which words are primarily the signs, and the things, of which the senses (concepts) are the likenesses or expressed species, are the same among all. But to lead the intellect into a deeper and saving knowledge of the sense and of the things signified is the work of the impressed species, not those by which external words and their power of signifying are represented to the intellect; but those by which the things themselves signified are represented to the intellect; and of the Holy Spirit, concurring at the same time through His illuminating power, which is always conjoined with them in the intellect of the hypocrite and the impious in first act, and [leading] them beyond their native power to spiritual acts of knowing in the intellect of the one eliciting and elevating, is the duty: which, however, they exercise in it simultaneously and jointly, not divided.

III. Thus, therefore, I think it is established what the illuminating power of the divine Word, written and preached, is; and how it is joined to the same, once fixed in the hearts of men: namely, to repeat in a word, the illuminating power of the divine Word is the very power of the Holy Spirit, by which He illuminates the darkened minds of men through it: but it is joined in the human intellect to the sense of that [Word], that is, to the species of things impressed, representing the sense and the signified things to the intellect, in the first act indeed always, even in those who place an obstacle to its salutary operation, and are never illuminated in the second act. Now, furthermore, by what reason it exerts itself in the second act for the illumination of the human intellect, must be examined. But it is certain that it exerts itself in it together with the species of things impressed, representing the very sense of the divine Word and the signified things, through acts of knowing elicited in the intellect, not through the immediate infusion of any supernatural qualities or powers, as the Papists contend, that the habit of faith is infused by God immediately, although some more recent ones among our own seem to establish that I know not what passive spiritual powers, ordered not for acting but for receiving, which precede all supernatural acts of knowing, are thus infused, as if they were the meritorious cause of the faith to be infused for a previous act of believing. This is proved from the very nature of the illuminating power communicated to the Word of God, written and preached, which, although, as to the thing itself, it is the very infinite power and potency of the Holy Spirit to act, and in itself, absolutely considered, without doubt could infuse into the intellect spiritual powers of knowing and believing, or a certain habitual light without any previous act of knowing, and thereby illuminate it, yet because by the most free will of God it is so bound to His Word that it never and nowhere exerts itself in the human intellect in the second act for its illumination without it, except with the Word, fixed in the intellect through the impressed species of the signified things, and through it, so that there may be one undivided operation of both, which depends upon the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power indeed, as from the principal agent, but from the impressed species, as from the instrumental agent, it is rightly gathered from this the Holy Spirit exerts His illuminating power in the human intellect for its illumination, in a manner congruent with impressed species. And from this, as a mode of operating better known to us, we must finally judge concerning the mode of operating of that illuminating power, by which it exerts itself for the illumination of the human intellect. However, the impressed species of things are, in themselves and by their nature, ordered toward acts of knowing. For they are partial principles of eliciting actual cognition, which constitute the intellect in the manner of a complete principle of knowing, and at that moment, when they are excited in the intellect by the words of Scripture, read or perceived by hearing, and are conveniently coordinated with the signified things, they determine the intellect to the actual cognition of the signified things, which is and is called the apprehension of simples, and they concur with it immediately, to elicit that by the act itself, efficiently, as whoever reads or hears taught the Word of God, written, or preached, or even any other word, experience in themselves. For this, as shown above, is common to the written and preached Word of God, with any other word, handed down by writing or voice. But what is commonly said, that impressed species represent to the intellect the things of which they are species (in which manner we also are accustomed to speak with common usage), is not to be understood of formal representation: for it belongs only to expressed species to represent things formally to the intellect; but of effective representation, if I may so speak, so that the things of which they are species are said to represent to the intellect, because they determine it to the acts of knowing, which are the species of those things expressed, and by efficiently concurring with it to elicit those, they cause the signified things to be formally represented to it. Whence impressed species on the part of the intellect can represent nothing, and not even the things of which they are species, to the intellect in act, except by means of the acts of knowing, which are of simple apprehension, which they efficiently produce with the intellect and in it. The matter stands similarly with impressed species, remaining in the intellect after the first acts of knowing, which are still in themselves and by their nature ordered toward eliciting acts of knowing, nor can they exert themselves toward any effects, whether natural in themselves, or supernatural with the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, except through acts of knowing, or through themselves, or elicited with the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit. These, I think, admit of no doubt.

In which acts of knowing, however, the illumination of the intellect consists, and by what reason, or in what order the impressed species, with the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit conjoined to them, exert themselves for the eliciting of those acts in and with the intellect, although it is more difficult to state and explain, I nevertheless consider it certain that here, as elsewhere, grace imitates and perfects nature, and just as nature in our natural cognition proceeds gradually from more imperfect acts of knowing to more perfect ones; so also the Holy Spirit, with His illuminating power and His Word, fixed in the intellect through the impressed species of things, in the supernatural illumination of our intellect, which, as has been said, consists entirely in acts of knowing, makes a beginning from more imperfect acts of knowing, and subsequently proceeds to more perfect ones, so that the illumination of the human intellect through the Word of God may have its beginnings, and by common law and ordinarily indeed slight ones, which afterwards, through the same Word of God read, heard, or meditated upon, makes greater progress and receives greater increases.

The first beginning is commonly constituted in an inspired holy thought. Which, however, is not to be understood of a holy thought immediately inspired by the Holy Spirit, but one which is excited in man's intellect by Him through His Word, whether read or perceived by hearing, suddenly, no differently than if it were immediately inspired by Him. But a holy thought immediately inspired and one which is excited by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, read or preached, differ in that the former is produced by the Holy Spirit in man's intellect through impressed species, immediately excited and coordinated in it by Him; but the latter is produced by the same in man's intellect through impressed species, excited and coordinated in it by the words of the divine Word, which signify by design, read or perceived by hearing, which the Holy Spirit uses as instruments for the holy thought by which the beginning of illumination is made. For the Holy Spirit, as was said above, has bound His illuminating power, by His most free will, to His Word, as to the ordinary medium of illumination, and by common law He does not exert it in man's intellect through concepts, as if illumin-

Latin:

Eundem in sensum scribunt ibid. fol. 212. Damit die heilige Schrifft uns könte von Gottes Wesen und Willen / von Christi Person und Ambt/ und dergleichen nothwendigen Stücken unterrichten/ siehe so hat Gott der HErr den Sinn und die Meinung/ die Lehre von solchen Stücken in den eusserlichen Worten offenbahret/und verborgener weise durch seine Göttliche Ordnung mit der eusserlichen Schrifft verbunden. Denn wenn solcher Göttlicher Sinn und Meinung nicht wäre in der heiligen Schrifft mit den eusserlichen Wörtern verfasset und verbunden / so könten wir aus und durch die Schrifft nicht unterwiesen werden zur Seeligkeit / sondern wir müsten den Verstand / Sinn und Meinung aus Gottes unmittelbarer Wirckung erwarten/ und keines weges in der heiligen Schrifft suchen. Atque his hactenus tribuunt verbis externis Scripturæ sacræ, quòd ejus sensum, doctrinam scilicet de essentia & voluntate Dei, deque Christi persona, officio aliisque doctrinæ Christianæ partibus per suam nativam vim significandi in se contineant, nobisque modo fupra declarato manifestent. Subjungunt autem statim: Ferner damit wir vermittels solches geoffenbahrten geschriebenen Worts möchten erleuchtet / zu Gott bekehret / gläubig und selig gemacht werden / so hat Gott der HErr in freywilliger Ordnung / solchem Sinn / Meinung und Verstand eine Göttliche Lebensund Erleuchtungs-Krafft gegeben / daß also der heilige Geist durch solch kräfftiges Wort / und das Wort in Krafft des heiligen Geistes / diese geistliche Wirckung in uns vollbringen könte. Quo ipso docent apertè, Vim illuminatricem communicasse Deum pro suâ liberrimâ ordinatione sensui. Quia autem Sensus Scripturæ nostro intellectui per rerum, verbis externis significatarum, species impressas partim, partim expressas inest: per illas quidem in actu primo; per has in actu secundo: consequens utique est, virtutem Spiritus Sancti illuminatricem in intellectu nostro conjunctam esse speciebus rerum, verbis Scripturæ significatarum, impressis partim, partim expressis, non verborum impressis aut expressis speciebus. Quod etiam res ipsa loquitur: Verba enim sunt propter sensum, in cujus notitiam sive apprehensionem simplicem ubi per suam nativam vim significandi intellectum deduxerunt, suo defuncta sunt officio, possuntque variare pro varietate linguarum, quibus consignata, aut in quas translata est Scriptura, sensu manente apud omnes uno & eodem. Quem in sensum etiam Aristoteles περὶ ἑρμην. c. 1. de quovis scripto aut voce prolato verbo: Ut, inquit, non iisdem literis, sic nec vocibus quidem omnes iisdem utuntur. At verò & sensa (conceptus) animi, quorum primùm verba notæ sunt, & res, quarum sensa (conceptus) simulacra sive species expressæ, sunt apud omnes eadem sunt. Intellectum verò in penitiorem eamque salutarem sensus rerumque significatarum cognitionem deducere, specierum impressarum est, non quibus verba externa, illorumque vis significandi; sed quibus ipsæ res significatæ intellectui repræsentantur; & Spiritus Sancti, per suam vim illuminatricem, quæ cum illis etiam in intellectu hypocritæ & impii in actu primo semper conjuncta est, simul concurrentis, easque ultra suam vim nativam ad spirituales cognoscendi actus in intellectu eliciendos elevantis, munus est: quod tamen simul & junctim, non divisum in eo exercent.

III. Ita ergo constare puto, quænam Verbi divini, scripti & prædicati, vis illuminatrix; & quomodo eidem, cordibus hominum infixo, ipsa conjuncta sit: nempe, ut verbo repetam, Verbi divini virtus illuminatrix est ipsa Spiritus Sancti virtus, quâ hominum mentes obtenebratas per illud illuminat: conjuncta autem est in hominis intellectu sensui illius, h. e. speciebus rerum impressis, sensum & res significatas intellectui repræsentantibus, in actu primo quidem semper, etiam in iis, qui ejus operationi salutari obicem ponunt, & actu secundo nunquam illuminantur. Jam porro, quâ ratione ea actu secundo ad intellectus humani illuminationem se exerat, expendendum venit. Certum autem est, eam exerere se in eo cum speciebus rerum impressis, ipsum Verbi divini sensum & res significatas repræsentantibus, per actus cognoscendi, in intellectu elicitos, non per immediatam infusionem ullarum qualitatum aut virium supernaturalium, ut Pontificii contendunt, habitum fidei infundi a Deo immediato, licet ad prævium actum credendi supernaturalem, velut causam infundendæ fidei meritoriam, & recentiores quidam ex nostris nescio quas vires spirituales passivas, non ad operandum, sed ad recipiendum ordinatas, quæ omnes actus cognoscendi supernaturales præcedant, sic infundi statuere videntur. Id quod probatur ex ipsa natura virtutis illuminatricis, Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato communicatæ, quæ licet, quoad rem, ipsa Spiritus Sancti infinita virtus ac potentia operandi sit, & in se, absolutè spectata, citra dubium vires cognoscendi credendique spirituales, vel lumen quoddam habituale absque ullo prævio actu cognoscendi intellectui infundere, eâq; illum illuminare possit, tamen quia Dei liberrimâ voluntate ad Verbum ipsius ita alligata est, ut nunquam & nusquam absq; eo in hominis intellectu actu secundo ad ejus illuminationem sese exerat, nisi cum Verbo, intellectui per impressas rerum significatarum species infixo, & per illud, ita ut utriusq; una indivisa operatio sit, quæ à Spiritu Sancto ejusque virtute illuminatrice quidem, velut ab agente principali, à speciebus impressis verò, tanquam ab agente instrumentali dependeat, rectè hinc colligitur, Spiritum Sanctum exerere suam virtutem illuminatricem in hominis intellectu ad ejus illuminationem, modo speciebus impressis congruo. Atque ex hoc, velut modo operandi, nobis notiori, judicandum demum est de modo operandi virtutis illius illuminatricis, quo ad illuminationem intellectus humani sese exerit. Species rerum impressæ autem, per se & naturâ suâ ordinantur ad actus cognoscendi. Sunt enim principia eliciendæ actualis cognitionis partialia, quæ intellectum in ratione principii cognoscendi completi constituunt, & eo momento, quo verbis Scripturæ, lectis vel auditu perceptis, in intellectu excitantur, rebusque significatis convenienter coordinantur, deteterminant intellectum ad actualem rerum significatarum cognitionem, quæ est & dicitur simplicium apprehensio, concurruntq; cum eo statim, ad illam ipso actu eliciendam, efficienter, ut in semetipsis experiuntur, quicunque Verbum Dei, scriptum, vel prædicatum, vel etiam aliud quodvis Verbum legunt vel doceri audiunt. Hoc enim, uti suprà ostensum, Verbo Dei scripto & prædicato, cum alio quovis verbo, scripto aut voce tradito, commune est. Quod autem vulgo dicitur, species impressas repræsentare intellectui res, quarum species sunt, (quem in modum & nos cum usu communi loqui solemus) non intelligendum est de repræsentatione formali: solarum enim specierum expressarum est res formaliter intellectui repræsentare; sed de repræsentatione effectiva, ut sic loquar, ut res, quarum species sunt, intellectui repræsentare dicantur, quòd eum ad actus cognoscendi, qui illarum species expressæ sunt, determinent, & cum eo ad illos eliciendos efficienter concurrentes faciant res significatas ipsi formaliter repræsentari. Unde species impressæ ex parte intellectus nihil, & ne res quidem, quarum species sunt, intellectui actu repræsentare possunt, nisi mediantibus actibus cognoscendi, qui sunt apprehensionis simplicis, quos cum intellectu & in eo efficienter producunt. Perinde res habet cum speciebus impressis, post primos cognoscendi actus in intellectu manentibus, quæ adhuc per se & naturâ suâ ad actus cognoscendi eliciendos ordinantur, neque ad ullos effectus, vel naturales per se, vel supernaturales cum Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminatrice se exerere possunt, nisi per actus cognoscendi, sive per se, sive cum Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminatrice elicitos. Hæc, puto, dubium non habere.

In quibus actibus cognoscendi autem illuminatio intellectus consistat, & quâ ratione, quove ordine species impressæ cum Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminatrice, sibi conjunctâ, ad eos in & cum intellectu eliciendos, se exerant, etsi dictu explicatuque difficilius est, existimo tamen certum & hoc esse, quòd ut aliàs ita & hîc gratia imitetur & perficiat naturam, & quemadmodum natura in nostra cognitione naturali gradatim ab actibus cognoscendi imperfectioribus ad perfectiores procedit; ita & Spiritus Sanctus sua virtute illuminatrice cum Verbo suo, intellectui per species rerum impresfas infixo, in supernaturali intellectus nostri illuminatione, quæ, uti dictum, tota in actibus cognoscendi consistit, ab actibus cognoscendi imperfectioribus faciat initium, & deinceps ad perfectiores progrediatur, ut ita illuminatio intellectus humani per Verbum Dei sua habeat initia, & de lege communi quidem ac ordinariè tenuia, quæ posteà per idem Dei Verbum lectum, vel auditum meditatumǫ; majores faciat progressus, & majora capiat incrementa.

Primùm initium constituitur communiter in inspirata cogitatione sancta. Quod tamen intelligendum non est de cogitatione sancta, immediatè à Spiritu Sancto inspiratâ, sed quæ per Verbum ejus, sive lectum sive auditu perceptum, ab ipso in hominis intellectu excitatur subitò, non secus ac si immediatè ab ipso inspiraretur. Differunt autem cogitatio sancta, immediatè inspirata, & quæ per Verbum Dei, lectum aut prædicatum, à Spiritu S. excitatur, quòd illa à Spiritu S. in hominis intellectu producitur per species impressas, ab ipsomet immediatè in illo excitatas, & coordinatas; hæc verò producitur ab eodem in hominis intellectu per species impresfas, à verbis Verbi divini, ex instituto significantibus, lectis vel auditu perceptis, in eodem excitatas & coordinatas, quibus velut instrumentis Spiritus Sanctus ad cogitationem sanctam, quâ illuminationis initium fiat, utitur. Spiritus Sanctus enim, ut suprà dictum, alligavit suam virtutem illuminatricem, liberrimâ voluntate, ad Verbum suum, velut ad medium illuminationis ordinarium, eamque de lege communi non exerit in hominis intellectu per conceptus, velut illumi-


### acts of illumination, suggested or inspired immediately without the concurrence…

acts of illumination, suggested or inspired immediately without the concurrence of the Word, as the Enthusiasts dream.

Nor is it to be thought that the holy thought, by which the beginning of illumination is made, is one and the same in all, but according as the intellect of this person falls into this part of doctrine and its meditation, and that person into that, so the Holy Spirit is accustomed to excite a pious and holy thought in this one concerning this part, in that one concerning another, and again in another concerning yet another part of doctrine, through the very species of things impressed and coordinated, perceived from the divine Word read or heard. Nor can the moment of time in which the Holy Spirit makes the beginning of illumination by a holy thought, excited through the Word read or preached, be established as one and the same in all, but just as the Spirit blows where He wills, as Christ says in John 3:8, so the Holy Spirit works according to His most free will by His illuminating power through His Word, read or preached, and makes the beginning of illumination by an excited holy thought, wherever and whenever He wills: although as to why this happens sooner in some, later in others, and in many never at all, men themselves are for the most part the cause. And those indeed in whom the illumination of the mind is not even begun are themselves the sole cause that they remain in darkness, inasmuch as they either utterly despise the Word of God through obstinate resistance and do not deign even to hear or read or meditate upon it, or through the cares of this world or the pleasures of the flesh they place an obstacle to the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined to His Word, and hinder His gracious operation: but in those in whom the beginning of illumination occurs sooner or later through an excited holy thought, they themselves are for the most part the cause of this, in that they begin to turn their mind and to read, hear, and meditate upon the Word of God with a desire to learn and with attention, either sooner or later.

Therefore, as regards the holy thought—as the authors like to speak—that is inspired, hold this concerning it: When those things which are of the Spirit of God are proposed to the intellect of an unregenerate man to be known through the Word of God, written or preached, and the intellect fixes its thoughts upon that which is known by simple apprehension by the force of the words, in order that, by applying judgment, it may investigate whether they are true or false, then it is as inept at discerning the truth of them as a man blind by nature is inept at discerning colors, and immediately there arise for him reasons

for doubting and dissenting, diametrically opposed to the Word of God, now impressed upon his heart through the species of things, by which he is moved to deny what it affirms, or to affirm what it denies, or to reject as foolish, absurd, etc., what it commends to us as the wisdom of God: but he can never, of himself and through himself, approve of these things with assent or spiritual judgment, even if they are known by simple apprehension, according to that Pauline saying: The natural man οὐ δέχεται, does not grasp, does not perceive, does not receive with assent the things that are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, καὶ οὐ δύναται γνῶναι, AND HE CANNOT KNOW, because they are judged πνευματικῶς, spiritually. When, therefore, the natural or unregenerate man is thus occupied in the meditation of spiritual objects, known to some extent by simple apprehension, with his darkened intellect, and treats them with such a perverse judgment, it happens sometimes suddenly, that the Holy Spirit, through the species of those things, impressed upon him by the power of external words, excites a certain thought, congruent with the underlying matters, and inclining toward their assent: e.g., when Peter in his first Pentecostal sermon to the Jews, who had persecuted and crucified Christ, taking the occasion from the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which they were wondering at, explained the Prophetic predictions concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit to be dispensed in the Church of Christ in the time of the Messiah, and subsequently asserted the resurrection of Christ, who had been killed by the Jews, from the dead, and confirmed it with the predictions of the Scriptures, Luke says that those hearers were PRICKED in their heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the Apostles: What shall we do, men and brethren? This PRICKING of the heart without doubt implied, on the part of the intellect, a thought or some holy thoughts concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit, especially the gift of tongues, then exercising itself in the Apostles in a miraculous way, by which they concluded that it was bestowed upon them by God, and that the prediction of Joel was truly fulfilled, the Holy Spirit elevating the species of things, impressed upon the intellect by the words of Scripture, to elicit this thought and eliciting it through them in him and with him. Nor is there any doubt that similar holy thoughts were excited in the same persons through the Word, perceived by external hearing, concerning Christ and his death and resurrection, by which the intellect was inclined to a saving recognition of Christ and of their own wickedness perpetrated in his crucifixion. On the part of the will, however, that PRICKING of the heart undoubtedly brought with it the pangs of conscience, on account of crimes committed against Christ, joined with a certain inclination of the will toward Christ and a pious affection for believing, excited by the power of the same divine Word and the Holy Spirit concurring with it. For the illumination of the intellect through the Word is always joined with pious motions of the will, as will be shown in the following assertion.

To the same point pertains what Paul reports in Acts 16:14 concerning Lydia, a seller of purple in the city of the Thyatirans, that when she heard him teaching near the river, the Lord opened her heart while she was listening, so that she might attend to the things that were being said by him. Where the heart opened to attend to the preached Word is undoubtedly opposed to a heart inwardly closed and as it were bolted, so that the voice of the preacher, perceived by hearing, could not penetrate and move the mind to an attentive meditation of the things that were being proposed. And just as the word 'heart,' in the style of the Scriptures, denotes the intellect and the will, or the soul by reason of both faculties, so in this place a closed heart denotes a soul bolted by the bars of blindness and ignorance on the part of the intellect, and by the bars of innate malice on the part of the will; and to open the heart is to remove the bolts and bars by which it is prohibited from attention to the preached Word and its meditation. These are removed, however, on the part of the intellect, by acts of illumination by which the innate darkness of the mind is dispelled, the first of which in the aforementioned Lydia was an excited holy thought concerning those parts of Christian doctrine which were proposed to her and the other listeners by Paul in the sermon he gave, by which the intellect, through the Word of God perceived by hearing, was inclined toward a judgment consistent with the doctrine delivered, with the Holy Spirit concurring by His illuminating power, and elevating the impressed species of spiritual things beyond their native force to form such a spiritual judgment, although not without hesitation and struggle of the intellect, which is by nature blind to objects of that kind; on the part of the will, however, a certain holy desire, excited by the power of the same Word and the Holy Spirit, by which the intellect was stimulated to greater attention and to making richer progress in the salutary knowledge of spiritual things: which acts of spiritual knowledge were afterwards excited by others and still others, through the Word by the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power elevating the impressed species, until a full assent of faith was obtained. Between the first holy thought and subsequent other supernatural acts of knowing, the Scholastics establish this distinction: that the former are indeliberate, the latter deliberate; yet they ascribe neither, in their supernatural being, to the Word of God, written or preached, but to the Holy Spirit, who concurs immediately on the part of the intellect by way of an efficient cause. For they admit no divine power in the Word of God, written or preached. We, however, who acknowledge no supernatural acts of knowing by which the intellect of man is illuminated to embrace spiritual things with saving assent, except those which the Holy Spirit, by His illuminating power communicated to His Word, supernaturally excites and produces in him with and through it, do not admit this distinction in any other sense than that in which the first holy thought is called indeliberate, not because it is inspired into the human intellect immediately by the Holy Spirit without the hearing of the Word, but because it is excited in the same, naturally blind in spiritual matters, by the Holy Spirit through the Word read or perceived by hearing, without any previous deliberation; but the subsequent spiritual acts of knowing are called deliberate because they are elicited in the intellect of man, already to some extent illuminated by some holy knowledge and, by the force of that holy thought excited within him, already in some way inclining toward spiritual things, by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, in such a way that it was in the power of the will to turn thoughts away from spiritual objects, to suppress the inspired first holy thought, or to suffocate it under the thorns of the cares of this world or of carnal pleasures, and to prevent others from being excited in the ordinary way through the Word heard or read; then we admit it. But to pursue this at greater length, and likewise to explain by what reason the first holy thought receives increases through subsequent supernatural acts of knowing, excited by the power of the Holy Spirit and the divine Word, is not the task of this place, but pertains to the place concerning Conversion, to which we refer them.

The first holy thought and other subsequent acts of knowing, concerning those things which are of the Spirit of God, excited by the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power through the species of things impressed, by which the intellect is inclined to the assent of those things already known by simple apprehension, are altogether all supernatural acts of illumination, and have the nature of either a certain thinner spark, or of light less perfect, according as the acts of knowing are either more imperfect at the beginning, or with time, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the Word that illuminates, they take on increases and turn out more perfect.

And indeed the acts of illumination are: both because they open the eyes of the mind, having dispersed its innate darkness, so that they may begin to see the truth of heavenly doctrine in act or to know it with assent, to see or to know which with assent they are by nature closed and utterly blind, and because they instruct the intellect, terminated toward a mental Word proportionate to itself, that is, a spiritual one, with spiritual light to see or to know the same with assent, of which it is otherwise by nature entirely destitute. For just as the acts of knowing, by which the intellect is inclined to the assent of spiritual things, are a certain actual light of the intellect, diffused into the intellect from the Holy Spirit and his illuminating power, as from the fountain of all spiritual light, through the impressed species of things, by the aid of which they have been excited, so the mental word of each act of knowing, to which it is terminated, as a spiritual quality produced by the same, is a certain spiritual light, by which the intellect is rendered able and fit to see heavenly truth, that is, to know it with assent.

But the acts of illumination are supernatural, because the intellect, by nature blind to objects of this kind, when it comes to knowing and approving with its own assent the truth of them, even if they are known by simple apprehension from external words, cannot rise so far by the power of impressed species, that it is rather carried into dissent on account of its innate blindness, and judges it to be foolishness, as was shown above from the Pauline saying 1 Cor. 2. 14. Whence, since it is inclined through impressed species to the assent of objects of this kind, known by simple apprehension, it is necessary that this be done beyond its natural inclination and above its natural powers, and thus be supernatural, and therefore it is to be ascribed entirely to the Holy Spirit and his illuminating power, as to a substantial light and the fountain of all spiritual light, elevating the impressed species to elicit these acts beyond and above the natural powers of the intellect.

III. I have said, however, that the Holy Spirit exerts his illuminating power, always joined to the Word of God, written and preached, in the first act, also through the EXPRESS species of things. That you may rightly understand this, it must be known that any act of knowing, whether natural or supernatural, produces in the intellect a certain mental word, which is a spiritual quality, formally representing the object to the intellect: which is therefore called the EXPRESS species of the object. This indeed can be either natural or supernatural to the intellect, according as the act of knowing is natural or supernatural. For the act of knowing, and its produced term, as they differ only modally, so as regards natural and supernatural being they are of the same nature among themselves, so that if the act of knowing is natural in substance, the mental word produced by it must also be natural in substance; and if it is supernatural, the mental word produced by it must also be supernatural in substance. From which it follows that also any act of knowing concerning spiritual things, supernaturally excited by the species of them impressed by the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power, by which the intellect is inclined toward their assent, efficiently produces a mental word, and that a supernatural one, in it, by which the object is formally represented to the intellect as if by an expressed species or image. That thing, however, by this very fact, that it is an expressed species or image of the object, and formally represents it to the intellect, is a certain light of the mind; and because it is produced in the intellect by the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit and His Word through a supernatural act of knowing, it is a light supernatural in substance, diffused into the intellect from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning, as James speaks in Epist. ch. 1:17, as the source of all spiritual light of which we are made partakers in this mortality: and finally because it inheres in the intellect by way of a permanent quality: for the Word of the mind is not a transitory act, but a quality, terminating the act of knowing; it is an habitual light. It is not, however, idle, but, besides the fact that it formally represents the known object to the intellect, it sometimes also shines before it for the knowing of other spiritual objects, just as one part of Christian doctrine known and believed is often to the intellect a reason for knowing and believing another: e.g., the doctrine concerning the merit and satisfaction of Christ known and believed, through the Word of the mind, produced by supernatural acts of knowing and believing, to the intellect it holds up a torch, as it were, for knowing and believing the doctrine concerning the justification of a sinful man before God. Just as, therefore, both IMPRESSED & EXPRESSED SPECIES of things to be believed are, on the part of the human intellect, the WORD OF GOD, fixed in it through His external Word, written or preached: for both are signs of the same revealed things, of which the external and sensible words of the divine Word are signs by the institution of signification: and the expressed ones are indeed formal signs, while the impressed ones are instrumental signs of them: the former represent their objects to the intellect formally; the latter only effectively, as has been said: so the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit is always joined to both in the intellect of man in the first act, and consequently the Holy Spirit uses both these and those in illuminating the intellect of man. By the former, indeed, in exciting supernatural acts of knowing, which incline immediately to the assent of spiritual objects: by the latter, however, in exciting supernatural acts of knowing concerning other things, the knowledge and assent of which depend upon the prior knowledge of other things. Which happens especially in the comparison of different passages of Scripture; and of different chapters of Christian doctrine, one of which, known and understood through its expressed species, with the concurrence of the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power, moves and leads into the knowledge of another, likewise supernatural, as is evident from the example of the doctrine concerning Christ's merit and satisfaction for our sins already brought forward, since it is known to our intellect as the reason for knowing, by which reason and for which cause God remits their sins to sinners in justification, etc. and it shines before it, as it were, through expressed species for attaining a deeper knowledge of it. But here it can be objected that the acts of knowing, excited by the power of the Word and the illuminating Holy Spirit, do not represent spiritual objects to the intellect clearly and evidently in themselves, nor do they contain in themselves any reason for assenting, by which they could incline it to the assent of them. How, therefore, can the intellect be inclined by them to the assent of known things? For the intellect cannot, unless perhaps violently, be drawn or determined into the assent of things whose truth it knows neither in themselves immediately nor in any known reason for assenting. But we respond to this objection by conceding that through supernatural acts of knowing of this kind, excited by the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit and His Word, spiritual objects are not represented to the intellect clearly and evidently in themselves, but remain non-evident and obscure even to the illuminated intellect, since even the faithful, whose intellect is illuminated, see now through a glass and in a riddle, and know in part, 1 Cor. 13:12, so that their faith is called by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 11:1, ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, the substance of things hoped for, and ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, the evidence of things not seen. And from this it rightly follows that the aforementioned supernatural acts of knowing do not move the intellect to the assent of spiritual objects through a clear representation of them. But that they contain in themselves absolutely no reason or power to incline it, without violence, to the assent of spiritual objects, we deny and utterly deny. For whatever things are proposed to be believed in the Word of God, written or preached, all those things are proposed in it as spoken or revealed by God, and these supernatural acts of knowing, excited in the human intellect by the Holy Spirit and the illuminating power of His Word, just as they depend efficiently on the Holy Spirit, so in the same they argue by themselves and by their nature God, who is supremely truthful, to whom assent is due by Himself, as their author, just as effects otherwise argue their cause, and consequently incline the intellect by the power of their dependence on God to their own supernatural assent, just as the living voice of a trustworthy man, by which he recounts to another some non-evident thing that is difficult to believe, moves his intellect to the assent of the event by the power of its dependence on the trustworthy man, although the intellect sees its truth neither in itself immediately, nor in any reason for assenting distinct from the voice of the one recounting and its dependence on him. Concerning this matter, it was treated above in Assertion IV, Explanation no. IV, and in the subsequent thesis XI, perhaps more will be said as the occasion arises.

Latin:

nationis actus, absque concursu Verbi immediatè suggestos sive inspiratos, ut Enthusiastæ somniant.

Neque existimandum est, cogitationem sanctam, quâ illuminationis initium fiat, in omnibus unam & eandem esse, sed prout intellectus hujus in hanc; illius in illam doctrinæ partem ejusque meditationem incidit, ita Spiritus Sanctus in hoc de hac, in illo de alia, & rursum in alio de alia doctrinæ parte piam sanctamque cogitationem excitare solet per ipsas à Verbo divino lecto audituve percepto excitatas coordinatasque rerum species impressas. Neque temporis momentum, quo Spiritus Sanctus cogitatione sanctâ, per Verbum lectum aut prædicatum excitatâ, illuminationis initium facit, in omnibus unum & idem constitui potest, sed sicut Spiritus, ubi vult, spirat, dicente Christo Joh. III. 8. ita Spiritus Sanctus pro sua liberrima voluntate operatur suâ illuminatrice virtute per Verbum suum, lectu vel prædicatum, facitq; excitatâ cogitatione sanctâ, illuminationis initium, ubicunq; & quandocunq; vult: quamvis cur id in aliquibus citiùs, in aliis tardius, in multis nunquam fiat, maximam partem ipsimet homines in causa sint. Et illi quidem, in quibus ne inchoatur quidem illuminatio mentis, soli in causa sunt, quòd in tenebris manent, utpote qui vel per obstinatam resistentiam Verbum Dei prorsus aspernantur, & ne audire vel legere quidé meditarive dignantur, vel per curas hujus seculi aut voluptates carnis Spiritus Sancti virtuti illuminatrici, Verbo ipsius conjunctæ, obicem ponunt, ejusq; gratiosam operationem impediunt: in quibus autem citiùs, vel tardiùs per excitatam cogitationem sanctam illuminationis initium fit, illi plerumque per hoc in causa sunt, quòd vel citiùs, vel tardiùs animum advertere, & cum studio discendi cumq; attentione Verbum Dei legere, audire, & meditari incipiunt.

Quod ergò ad inspiratam, uti Auctores loqui amant, cogitationem sanctam attinet, de ea ita habeas: Quando intellectui hominis non renati ea, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, Verbo Dei, scripto vel prædicato cognoscenda proponuntur, & in illa, vi verborum apprehensione simplici cognita, intellectus suas defigit cogitationes, ut adhibito judicio, vera? an falsa sint? investiget, tùm ad veritatem illorum dignoscendam tam ineptus est, quàm ineptus est naturâ cæcus ad dignoscendos colores, statimque ei oboriuntur ra-

tiones dubitandi & dissentlendi, Verbo Dei, jam ejus cordi per rerum species impressas infixo, è diametro repugnantes, quibus movetur ad negandum, quæ illud affirmat, vel ad affirmandum, quæ illud negat, vel ut stolida, absurda &c. rejicienda, quæ illud, velut Dei sapientiam, nobis commendat: assensu autem sive judicio spirituali ea, licet apprehensione simplici cognita, quomodocunq; comprobare, ex se & per se nunquã potest, juxta illud Paulinum: Animalis homo ὐ δέχεται, non capit, non percipit, non recipit cum assensu, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt: sunt enim ei stultitia, καὶ ὐ δύναται γνῶναι, NEC POTEST COGNOSCERE, quòd πνευματικῶς spiritualiter dijudicantur. Quando igitur homo animalis sive non renatus sic in meditatione objectorum spiritualium, apprehensione simplici quadantenus cognitorum, suo obtenebrato intellectu versatur, & judicio ita perverso ea tractat, contingit quandoq; subitò, ut Spiritus Sanctus per illorum species, vi externorum verborum ipsi impressas, cogitationem quandam, rebus substratis congruam, inq; illorum assensum inclinantē, excitet: v. g. cum Petrus in sua prima concione Pentecostali Judæis, qui Christum persecuti fuerant & crucifixerant, occasione à miraculosa effusione Spiritus Sancti, quam mirabantur, sumtâ, vaticinia Prophetica de donis Spiritus Sancti, Messiæ tempore in Ecclesia Christi dispensandis, exponeret, & deinceps Christi, à Judæis interemti, resurrectionem à mortuis assereret, eamque Scripturarum vaticiniis confirmaret, dicit Lucas, quòd auditores illi COMPUNCTI fuerint corde, & dixerint ad Petrum & cæteros Apostolos: Quid faciemus, Viri fratres? Hæc COMPUNCTIO cordis citra dubium importabat, ex parte intellectus, cogitationem vel aliquas cogitationes sanctas, de donis Spiritus Sancti, præsertim linguarum dono, in Apostolis modo miraculoso se tùm exerente, quâ à Deo id ipsis collatum, & Joëlis vaticinium verè impletum esse statuebant, Spiritu Sancto species rerum, verbis Scripturæ intellectui impressas, ad hanc cogitationem eliciendam, elevante eamque per illas in eo & cum eo eliciente. Neque dubium est, quin similes cogitationes sanctæ in iisdem per Verbum, externo auditu perceptum, de Christo, ejusque morte & resurrectione excitatæ fuerint, quibus intellectus ad salutarem Christi suæque in ejus crucifixione patratæ nequitiæ agnitionem inclinaretur. Ex parte voluntatis autem COMPUNCTIO illa cordis haud dubiè importabat conscientiæ morfus, ob patrata in Christum scelera, cum voluntatis quadam inclinatione in Christum & pia credendi affectione conjunctos, ejusdem Verbi divini & Spiritus Sancti cum eo concurrentis virtute excitata. Illuminatio intellectus enim per Verbum semper cum voluntatis piis motibus conjuncta est, ut in assertione sequente ostendetur.

Eodem pertinet, quod Ast. XVI. 14. Paulus refert de Lydia, purpurarum venditrice in Civitate Thyatirorum, quòd cùm se, prope flumen, docentem audiret, Dominus ei inter audiendum cor aperuerit, ut attenderet his, quæ à se dicerentur. Ubi cor apertum ad attendendum Verbo prædicato opponitur haud dubiè cordi interiùs clauso & quasi obserato, ne prædicantis vox, auditu percepta, penetrare, & ad eorum, quæ proponebantur, attentam meditationem animum commovere posset. Et quemadmodum cordis vox, Scripturarum stylo, intellectum & voluntatem, vel animam ratione utriusque facultatis denotat, ita hoc loco cor claufum denotat animam, ex parte intellectus cæcitatis & ignorantiæ feris; ex parte voluntatis autem connatæ malitiæ repagulis obseratam; & cor aperire est seras & repagula, quibus ab attentione ad verbum prædicatum ejusque meditatione prohibetur, removere. Removentur autem, ex parte intellectus, per illuminationis actus, quibus connatæ tenebræ mentis dispelluntur, quorum primus in laudata Lydia fuit excitata cogitatio sancta de iis doctrinæ Christianæ partibus, quæ à Paulo in concione habita ipsi & cæteris auditoribus propositæ fuerunt, quâ intellectus per Verbum Dei, auditu perceptum, inclinabatur in judicium, doctrinæ traditæ conveniens, Spiritu Sancto suâ virtute illuminatrice concurrente, & species rerum spiritualium impressas ultra suam nativam vim ad ejusmodi spirituale judicium formandum elevante, quamvis non absque dubitatione & lucta intellectus, naturâ ad id generis objecta cæci; ex parte voluntatis autem sanctum quoddam desiderium, ejusdem verbi & Spiritus Sancti virtute excitatum, quibus intellectus ad majorem attentionem, & uberiores in salutari rerum spiritualium cognitione progressus faciendos stimulabatur: quos cognitionis spiritualis actus posteà alii atq; alii, per Verbum à Spiritu Sancto ejusq; virtute illuminatrice, species impressas elevante, excitati sunt, usque dum assensus fidei plenus obtineretur. Inter primam cogitationem sanctam & subsequentes alios actus cognoscendi supernaturales Scholastici id statuunt discriminis, quòd illa indeliberata; hi deliberati sint; qui tamen neutros, in suo esse supernaturali, Verbo Dei, scripto aut prædicato, sed Spiritui Sancto, ex parte intellectus immediatè per modum causæ efficientis concurrenti, utrosque adscribunt. Virtutem divinam enim in Verbo Dei, scripto aut prædicato, nullam admittunt. Nos verò, qui nullos agnoscimus actus cognoscendi supernaturales, quibus intellectus hominis ad spiritualia salutari assensu amplectenda illuminetur, nisi quos Spiritus Sanctus suâ virtute illuminatrice, Verbo suo communicatâ, cum eo & per illud supernatuliter in eo excitat & producit, distinctionem hanc non alio admittimus sensu, quàm quo prima cogitatio sancta indeliberata dicitur, non quòd absque auditu Verbi hominis intellectui immediatè à Spiritu S. inspiretur, sed quòd in eodem, in spiritualibus naturâ cæco, per Verbum lectum vel auditu perceptum, à Spiritu Sancto absque ulla præviâ deliberatione excitetur; sequentes verò actus cognoscendi spirituales deliberati dicuntur, quòd in hominis intellectu, jam aliqua cognitione sancta quadantenus collustrato, & vi illius in se excitatæ cogitationis sanctæ jam aliquo modo in spiritualia propendente, à Spiritu S. per Verbum Dei eliciti sint, ita ut in voluntatis potestate esset cogitationes ab objectis spiritualibus avertere, inspiratam primam cogitationem sanctam supprimere, aut sub spinis curarum hujus seculi, voluptatumve carnalium suffocare, & ne modo ordinario per Verbum auditum vel lectum alii excitari possent, impedire; tùm eam admittimus. Sed hæc pluribus prosequi; itemque quâ ratione prima cogitatio sancta per subsequentes actus cognoscendi supernaturales, virtute Spiritus Sancti & Verbi divini excitatos, incrementa capiat, explicare hujus loci non est, sed ad locum de Conversione pertinet, quò ea remittimus.

Prima cogitatio sancta & subsequentis actus cognoscendi alii, circa ea quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, à Spiritu Sancto ejusque virtute illuminatrice per species rerum impressas excitati, quibus intellectus in assensum illorum, jam apprehensione simplici cognitorum, inclinatur, in universum omnes sunt actus illuminationis supernaturales, habentǫ; rationem vel scintillulæ cujusdam tenuioris, vel luminùs perfectiores, prout actus cognoscendi vel sub initium imperfectiores sunt, vel cum tempore, Spiritus S. & Verbi virtute illuminatrice, incrementa capiunt & perfectiores evadunt.

Et quidem illuminationis actus sunt: cùm quia oculos mentis, connatis ejus tenebris discussis, aperiunt, ut veritatem doctrinæ cœlestis actu videre sive cum assensu cognoscere incipiant, ad quam videndam sive cum assensu cognoscendam naturâ clausi & prorsus cæci sunt, tum quia ad Verbum mentale, sibi proportionatum, h. e. spirituale terminati intellectum lumine spirituali ad eandem videndam, sive cum assensu cognoscendam instruunt, quo aliàs naturâ in totum destituitur. Quemadmodum enim actus cognoscendi, quibus intellectus in assensum rerum spiritualium inclinatur, actuale quoddam intellectus lumen sunt, à Spiritu Sancto ejusque virtute illuminatrice, velut à fonte omnis luminis spiritualis, per species rerum impressas, quarum adminiculo excitati sunt, in intellectum diffusum, ita cujusque actus cognoscendi verbum mentale, ad quod terminatur, velut qualitas spiritualis, eodem producta, est lumen quoddam spirituale, quo intellectus ad veritatem cœlestem videndam, h. e. cum assensu cognoscendam, habilis & idoneus redditur.

Supernaturales verò actus illuminationis sunt, quia intellectus, ad hujus generis objecta naturâ cæcus, cùm ad veritatem illorum, licet ex verbis externis apprehensione simplici cognita sint, vi specierum impressarum cognoscendam & suo assensu comprobandam usq; adeò adsurgere non potest, ut potiùs pro sua connata cæcitate in dissensum feratur, eamque stultitiam judicet, ut supra ex dicto Paulino 1. Cor. 11. 14. ostensum. Unde cùm per species impressas in hujus generis objectorum, apprehensione simplici cognitorum, assensum inclinatur, præter naturalem ejus inclinationem, & supra naturales ejus vires id fieri, atque adeò supernaturale esse necesse est, & proinde Spiritui Sancto ejusque virtuti illuminatrici, velut lumini substantiali, & fonti omnis lucis spiritualis, species impressas ad hos actus ultra & supra naturales intellectus vires eliciendos elevanti, in solidum adscribendum est.

III. Dixi autem, Spiritum Sanctum exerere suam virtutem illuminatricem, Verbo Dei, scripto & prædicato, in actu primo semper conjunctam, etiam per species rerum EXPRESSAS. Quod ut recte intelligas, sciendum, quemlibet actum cognoscendi, cum naturalem, tum supernaturalem, producere in intellectu verbum quoddam mentale, quod est qualitas spiritualis, objectum intellectui formaliter repræsentans: quod propterea species objecti EXPRESSA appellatur.
