Id vero potest intellectui vel naturale vel supernaturarale esse, prout actus cognoscendi naturalis aut supernaturalis est. Actus cognoscendi enim, & ejus terminus productus, ut modaliter tantum differunt, ita quoad esse naturale & supernaturale inter se ejusdem sunt rationis, ut si actus cognoscendi in substantia naturalis sit, etiam verbum mentale, eo productum, in substantia naturale; & si is supernaturalis sit, etiam verbum mentale, eo productum, in substantia supernaturali esse oporteat. Ex quo sequitur, quod etiam quilibet actus cognoscendi circa spiritualia, per species illorum impressas a Spiritu Sancto ejusque virtute illuminatrice supernaturaliter excitatus, quo intellectus in illorum assensum inclinatur, verbum mentale, idque supernaturale in eo efficienter producat, quo velut specie sive imagine expressa objectum intellectui formaliter repræsentetur. Illud vero hoc ipso, quod objecti species sive imago expressa est, idque intellectui formaliter repræsentat, mentis quoddam lumen est; & quia Spiritus Sancti ejusque Verbi illuminatrice virtute per actum cognoscendi supernaturalem in intellectu productum est, lumen in substantia supernaturale est, a Patre luminum, apud quem non est transmutatio aut conversionis obumbratio, ut Jacobus Epist. c. 1. 17. loquitur, velut omnis luminis spiritualis, cujus in hac mortalitate reddimur participes, fonte in intellectum diffusum: & denique quia intellectui per modum qualitatis permanentis inest: Verbum mentis enim non actus transitorius, sed qualitas est, actum cognoscendi terminans; lumen habituale est. Otiosum tamen non est, sed, præterquam quod objectum cognitum intellectui formaliter repræsentat, prælucet ei quandoque etiam ad alia objecta spiritualia cognoscenda, perinde ut una doctrinæ Christianæ pars cognita & credita intellectui sæpe est ratio cognoscendi & credendi aliam: v. g. doctrina de Christi merito & satisfactione cognita & credita, per Verbum mentis, actibus cognoscendi & credendi supernaturalibus productum, intellectui facem quasi præfert ad cognoscendam credendamq́; doctrinam de justificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo. Quemadmodùm ergo utræque, IMPRESSÆ & EXPRESSÆ credendorum SPECIES ex parte intellectus humani VERBUM DEI sunt, per ejus Verbum externum, scriptum aut prædicatum, ei infixum: utræque enim earundem rerum revelatarum signa sunt, quarum Verbi divini externi externa & sensibilia ex instituto significantia verba signa sunt: & expressæ quidem formalia; impressæ verò instrumentalia illarum signa sunt: illæ repræsentant intellectui objecta sua formaliter; hæ effectivè tantum, uti dictum: ita Spiritus Sancti illuminatrix virtus utrisque in hominis intellectu in actu primo semper conjuncta est, & utitur proinde Spiritus Sanctus in illuminando hominis intellectu cùm his, tùm illis. Illis quidem in excitandis cognoscendi actibus supernaturalibus, immediatè in assensum objectorum spiritualium inclinantibus: his verò in excitandis actibus cognoscendi supernaturalibus de rebus aliis, quarum cognitio & assensus ex prævia rerum aliarum cognitione pendet. Quod potissimùm contingit in collatione diversorum locorum Scripturæ; diversorumque doctrinæ Christianæ capitum, quorum unum cognitum intellectum per sui speciem expressam, cum concursu Spiritus Sancti ejusque virtutis illuminatricis, movet & deducit in cognitionem alterius, itidem supernaturalem, ut patet exemplo doctrinæ de Christi merito & satisfactione pro peccatis nostris jam allato, quippe quæ cognita intellectui nostro est ratio cognoscendi, quâ ratione & qua de causa Deus in justificatione peccatoribus peccata sua remittat &c. eíque per species expressas ad penitiorem illius cognitionem consequendam quasi prælucet. Sed hîc objici potest, quòd actus cognoscendi, virtute Verbi & Spiritus Sancti illuminatrice excitati, objecta spiritualia intellectui non in se clarè & evidenter repræsentant, nec etiam rationem aliquam assentiendi, per quam eum in illorum assensum inclinare possint, in se continent. Quomodo ergo intellectus per eos in rerum cognitarum assensum inclinari potest? Intellectus enim non potest, nisi forsan violenter, trahi aut determinari in assensum rerum, quarum veritatem nec in se immediatè nec in aliqua ratione assentiendi cognita cognoscit. Sed ad objectionem hanc respondemus, concedendo, quod per hujus generis actus cognoscendi supernaturales, Spiritus Sancti ejusque Verbi virtute illuminatrice excitatos, objecta spiritualia intellectui non repræsententur in se clarè & evidenter, sed ei, etiam illuminato, inevidentia & obscura maneant, siquidem fideles etiam & quorum intellectus illuminatus est, cernunt nunc per speculum & in ænigmate, cognoscuntq; ex parte I. Cor. XIII. 12. ita ut illorum fides Auctori Epistolæ ad Hebræos c. XI. 1. dicatur ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων substantia rerum sperandarum, & ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, argumentum eorum, quæ non videntur. Atque hinc rectè sequitur; quod prædicti actus cognoscendi supernaturales intellectum non moveant in assensum objectorum spiritualium per claram illorum repræsentationem. Quod autem planè nullam in se rationem aut vim inclinandi eum, citra violentiam, in assensum objectorum spiritualium in se contineant, negamus & pernegamus. Quæcunque enim in Verbo Dei, scripto aut prædicato, credenda proponuntur, ea omnia proponuntur in eo ut dicta sive revelata à Deo, & ipsi supernaturales actus cognoscendi, à Spiritu S. ejusque Verbi virtute illuminatrice in hominis intellectu excitati, ut à Spiritu S. efficienter dependent, ita in eodem arguunt per se & naturâ sua Deum, summè veracem, cui per se debeatur assensus, sui auctorem, ut alias effectus suam arguunt causam, & inclinant proinde intellectum vi suæ à Deo dependentiæ in sui assensum supernaturalem, perinde ut viri fide digni vox viva, quâ rem aliquam inevidentem & creditu difficilem alteri commemorat, vi suæ dependentiæ à viro fide digno ejus intellectum in assensum rei gestæ movet, licet ejus veritatem intellectus nec in se immediatè, nec in aliqua ratione assentiendi, à voce commemorantis ejusque ab eo dependentia diversâ, videat. Qua de re supra in Assert. IV. Expl. n. IV. actum, & in subseq. thes. XI. pro re nata forsan plura dicuntur.


### IX. Eighth Assertion: On the part of the will, Holy Scripture or the Word of God,…

IX.

Eighth Assertion: On the part of the will, Holy Scripture or the Word of God, written or preached, exerts itself with the supernatural concurrence of God through the expressed species of spiritual objects, by alluring and drawing it into consent, so that by its command it may determine the intellect to the assent of spiritual objects.

I. Above in Assertion V, we showed that Holy Scripture, with the supernatural concurrence of God, moves the intellect to its own assent by way of a non-evident motive, with the will drawn into consent, and supernaturally moved and induced to command the intellect to assent. For although supernatural acts of knowing, excited by the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit and of the Word itself, incline the intellect by its own nature and by the force of its dependence on God to its own assent, as was said toward the end of the preceding assertion and also shown above, yet just as their spiritual objects are non-evident to us, and therefore on the part of the intellect we are by nature blind to them, and various doubts and perverse judgments born from these are wont to arise: so for their actual assent, and that a supernatural one, it is altogether necessary that the will also be drawn into consent, and by its command the intellect, notwithstanding any doubts emerging here and there, be determined to assent.

II. I say, however, first, that Holy Scripture, or the Word of God, written or preached, exerts itself on the part of the will, WITH THE SUPERNATURAL CONCURRENCE OF GOD, to signify that the Word of God does not allure and draw the will into consent by a mere manifestation and representation of spiritual objects under some aspect of suitability and good, but that it is necessary that on the part of the objects the supernatural power of the Holy Spirit, joined to the Word of God, also concur to allure and draw it. For the will follows the condition of the intellect, and just as this in relation to spiritual objects is utterly darkened and σκότος, darkness, Eph. IV. 18, c. V. 8, so that it cannot attain their truth, even if proposed to it in the clearest words, without the supernatural illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, I Cor. II. 14, so it is likewise dead to the same, and by its innate πώρωσιν is utterly alienated from them, Eph. II. 1, Col. II. 13, Eph. IV. 18, so that by their goodness alone, even if known by the intellect and exhibited to it, without the supernatural concurrence of the Holy Spirit, it cannot be allured and, to command the intellect to assent, in cannot be drawn into consent: but rather πᾶν τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, everything that the carnal man savors, wills, thinks, or desires, is enmity against God, and so diametrically opposed to those things which are of the Spirit of God, that neither the intellect in knowing them, nor the will in desiring the same, is subjected to the law of God, or can in any part be subjected, Rom. VIII. 7.

Hence the Apostle expressly ascribes that motion of the will, by which it is enticed and drawn into consent to spiritual things, to God and His power, joined with His Word: saying, The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ divinely POWERFUL for the demolition of strongholds, by which we demolish counsels, and every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God, and we lead captive every thought to the obedience of Christ, II. Cor. X. 4. 5. To which he compares the Word of God, by the preaching of which the kingdom of Satan was being attacked and the kingdom of Christ was being planted, to military weapons, and calls it the weapons of our (spiritual) warfare, not carnal, but δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ powerful to God, among other things for capturing πᾶν νόημα, every thought under the obedience of Christ. Moreover, he calls the Word of God weapons δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ powerful to God, i.e., divinely, as Beza rendered it, or from God, as others render it, on account of the δύναμιν or power of God, which was shown at length above in Assert. III. Expl. n. IV. to be always joined to it in the first act. But by πᾶν νόημα he understands every thought raising itself against the knowledge of God, as the immediately preceding words have it, i.e., every thought, whether affirming, or denying, or by consequence inferring something that fights against the true acknowledgment of God, or against the doctrine of Christ revealed in His Word: which are captured under the obedience of Christ, not only when they are argued against, refuted, and attacked by the Word of God, so that the intellect, with the Word shining before it, sees their vanity; but especially also when the will is affected, enticed, and drawn into consent by the Word of God and its power or virtue, so that by its own command it may turn the intellect away from such vain and perverse thoughts, and determine it to the assent of the doctrine revealed by God. Which determination to assent, proceeding from the command of the will divinely excited, is truly its captivity, so called by metaphor.

This motion of the will, on the part of the intellect, joined with some supernatural acts of knowing, Christ calls, by a similar metaphor, ἕλκυσιν, a drawing, and ascribes it entirely to GOD his Father: No one, he says, comes to me, unless my Father ἑλκύσῃ, HAS DRAWN him. Where coming to Christ is believing in him, as is evident from the preceding v. 35, in which these two phrases are used indiscriminately. But just as the medium for kindling faith in the heart of man is the Word of God, read or preached and perceived by hearing, according to that of the Apostle: Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God, Rom. X. 17, so God does not draw a man, that he may come to Christ, i.e., that he may believe in him, immediately, but through his Word, whether read, or preached and perceived by hearing. For he does not draw one who is ignorant by leading, or one who is contradicting and resisting by violence, so that he may believe what he is entirely ignorant of, or denies and rejects as folly, but he draws him in a manner connatural to our intellect, so that, with the salutary knowledge of spiritual goods kindled through the Word, he makes one who was ignorant knowing, and one who was contradicting consenting. Nor does he draw one who is unwilling and reluctant by force, but in such a way that, by exciting a pious desire and a pious affection toward God revealing and the spiritual goods revealed by him, he induces the assent of things to be believed by a sweet inclination to command the intellect, already illuminated by some spiritual light, and thus makes one who was unwilling willing. The divine ἕλκυσις or DRAWING of man, that he may come to Christ, therefore embraces both, namely, the salutary knowledge of Christ and his benefits and the other heads of Christian doctrine on the part of the intellect, and a pious desire and pious affection for believing on the part of the will, excited by the representation of spiritual goods through the Word with the supernatural concurrence of God, and it consists formally in the supernatural inclination of the will toward God revealing and the goods revealed, with the knowledge of spiritual things, drawn from the Word of God, shining before on the part of the intellect.

III. Next I say, the Word of God, written or preached, exerts itself on the part of the will with the supernatural concurrence of God through EXPRESSED SPECIES of spiritual objects. For because that divine δύναμις, power or virtue of acting, exerting itself in the Word of God and through it in the hearts of men to kindle faith, [is] to the SENSE The divine Word, whether written or preached, is not joined or united to words, which are the marks or signs of meaning, as was shown above at greater length; it is certainly necessary that it be joined either to the impressed species of the things signified by the words, or to the expressed species of the same in the human intellect, and that it exert itself in the will through one or the other or through both. For besides these, nothing is given in the human intellect by which the meaning of the divine Word can be said to be present in it. Although indeed, as was shown in the preceding Assertion, it is joined to both kinds of species, and on the part of the intellect it exerts itself through both for its illumination: yet on the part of the will, so that, having been enticed and drawn into consent, it may command and does command the intellect to assent to things to be believed, the same exerts itself only through the expressed species of the objects. For the function of impressed species is nothing other than to move the intellect, in place of the objects, toward the simple apprehension of them, and to concur efficiently with it for the eliciting of the concepts of the same; but they can contribute nothing of themselves toward the eliciting of the acts of the will. For the acts of the will depend upon the will and the objects represented to it by the intellect: but it is the function of the expressed species to represent and exhibit objects to the will, since they alone are the formal signs of objects, and they represent them formally; not the impressed species, which are only instrumental signs of them, and do not represent them except effectively through their concepts or expressed species, which they produce efficiently with the intellect. But just as, on the part of objects, their truth and goodness do not really differ, so one and the same expressed species represent one and the same objects simultaneously to the intellect as true, and to the will as suitable and good. If, therefore, for the sake of enticing and drawing the will into consent, so that it may determine the intellect to assent by its command, the supernatural concurrence of God is required, just as it is certain that it is required, and has already been shown: it is necessary that it be joined with the EXPRESSED SPECIES of the objects, and that it exert itself through these.

Although indeed concerning the cognition of the intellect, by which its objects are represented to the will, or which comes to the same thing, concerning the expressed species of objects, whether they concur efficiently on the part of the will for the eliciting of its acts? or through the mere representation of objects, without an effective influx? among the Scholastics, especially the ancients, there is no slight disagreement, concerning which among others Vazquez may be consulted in 1. II. Disp. XXXVI. c. 11. & seqq. The more recent ones, however, both Scholastics and modern Philosophers and Theologians, commonly embrace the latter part of the question, to whose opinion we also subscribe elsewhere. Nor does it seem that any other conclusion should be reached concerning cognition or the expressed species of spiritual objects: which, even if they pertain most of all to the second operation of the mind, and are in substance supernatural, yet by the very fact that they are species or expressed images of objects, they seem by themselves alone to be able to perform no other function, on the part of the will, than to exhibit and represent spiritual objects to it as suitable and good. But because they are the WORD OF GOD, and formally represent its sense to the intellect, they have within them, joined to themselves interiorly in the intellect of man, that divine δύναμιν or power by which the Holy Spirit concurs toward the supernatural effects of His Word, and it must be said entirely that they concur with the spiritual objects, which they represent and exhibit to the will, for enticing and drawing the will also efficiently, not indeed precisely through their power of representing objects, nor precisely through the actual representation of them: for these, on the part of the will, which is dead to spiritual things, are by no means sufficient to arouse it from the death of sin; but through that δύναμιν or power of God joined to them, through which the Word of God is and is called by the Apostle the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 18. 24. or, as Eph. I. 19. the praised Apostle speaks, through the exceeding greatness of the power of God to us-ward who believe, according to the working of the strength of his might, which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead. Through this, just as God raised Christ from the dead by a real and physical influx, so He arouses the will of man, which is utterly dead to spiritual things, from spiritual death, and entices and draws it similarly in a real manner and by physical influx through spiritual acts and motions, yet with the concurrence of the Word and according to its requirement, aroused within it.

Latin:

IX.

Octava Assertio: Ex parte voluntatis exerit sese Scriptura sacra vel Verbum Dei, scriptum aut prædicatum, cum Dei concursu supernaturali per objectorum spiritualium species expressas, alliciendo, trahendoque eam in consensum, ut imperio suo intellectum ad assensum objectorum spiritualium determinet.

I. Suprà in Assert. V. ostendimus, Scripturam sacram cum Dei concursu supernaturali movere intellectum in sui assensum per modum motivi inevidentis, voluntate in consensum tractâ, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum supernaturaliter motâ & inductâ. Quamvis enim actus cognoscendi supernaturales, à Spiritus Sancti & ipsius Verbi virtute illuminatrice excitati, intellectum suâpte naturâ & vi suæ dependentiæ à Deo in sui assensum inclinent, ut sub finem assertionis præcedentis dictum, & superiùs etiam ostensum est, tamen quemadmodum illorum objecta spiritualia nobis inevidentia sunt, & proptereà ex parte intellectus ad ea naturâ cæci, variæ dubitationes & hinc nata judicia perversa oboriri solent: ita ad actualem illorum assensum, eumque supernaturalem, omninò necessarium est, tut voluntas quoque trahatur in consensum, ejusque imperio intellectus, nihil quicquam obstantibus hinc inde emergentibus dubitationibus, ad assensum determinetur.

II. Dico autem primò, Scripturam sacram, vel Verbum Dei, scriptum aut prædicatum, exercere se ex parte voluntatis, CUM DEI CONCURSU SUPERNATURALI, ad significandum, Verbum Dei non allicere, & in consensum trahere voluntatem nuda objectorum spiritualium manifestatione & repræsentatione sub aliquâ ratione convenientiæ & boni, sed necessarium esse, ut ex parte objectorum etiam Spiritus Sancti virtus supernaturalis, Verbo Dei conjuncta, ad eam alliciendam trahendamque concurrat. Voluntas enim sequitur conditionem intellectus, & quemadmodum hic in ordine ad objecta spiritualia prorsus obtenebratus & σκότος, tenebræ est, Eph. IV. 18. c. V. 8. ut eorum veritatem, licet verbis clarissimis sibi propositam, citra supernaturalem Spiritus S. virtutem illuminatricem, assequi non possit, I. Cor. II. 14. ita illa pariter ad eadem emortua, & per suam connatam πώρωσιν ab illis prorsus abalienata est, Eph. II. 1. Col. II. 13. Eph. IV. 18. ut solâ illorum bonitate, licet ab intellectu cognitâ, eique exhibitâ, citra Spiritus Sancti supernaturalem concursum, allici, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum, in consensum trahi non possit : quin potius πᾶν τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, omne quod sapit, vult, cogitat aut desiderat homo carnalis, inimicitia est adversus Deum, atque adeò iis, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, è diametro adversum, ut nec intellectus in iis cognoscendis; nec voluntas in iisdem appetendis, legi Dei subjiciatur, aut ulla ex parte subjici possit, Rom. VIII. 7.

Hinc motionem illam voluntatis, quâ allicitur & in rerum spiritualium consensum trahitur, Apostolus expressè Deo ejusque potentiæ, Verbo ipsius conjunctæ, adscribit: Arma, inquiens, militia nostræ non carnalia sunt, sed δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ divinitùs POTENTIA ad demolitionem munitionum, quibus consilia demolimur, & omnem celsitudinem, quæ extollitur adversus cognitionem Dei, & captivam ducimus ad obediendum Christo, II. Cor. X. 4. 5. Quibus Verbum Dei, cujus prædicatione regnum Satanæ impugnatum; Christi regnum verò plantatum ibant, comparat armis militaribus, & vocat illud arma militiæ nostræ (spiritualis) non carnalia, sed δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ potentia Deo, inter alia ad captivandum πᾶν νόημα, omnem cogitationem sub obedientiam Christi. Dicit autem Verbum Dei arma δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ potentia Deo, i. e. divinitùs, ut Beza reddidit, vel ex Deo, ut alii reddunt, propter Dei δύναμιν sive potentiam, quam ei in actu primo semper conjunctam esse, suprà Assert. III. Expl. n. IV. prolixè ostensum est. Per πᾶν νόημα verò intelligit omnem cogitationem, extollentem se adversus cognitionem Dei, ut proximè præcedentia verba habent, h. e. omnem cogitationem, sive affirmantem, sive negantem, sive per consequentiam inferentem aliquid, quod cum vera Dei agnitione, aut cum doctrina Christi, in Verbo ejus patefacta, pugnat: quæ captivantur sub obedientiam Christi, non tantùm, cùm per Verbum Dei arguuntur, confutantur, impugnantur, ut intellectus prælucente Verbo, illarum vanitatem videat; Sed inprimis etiam, cùm Verbo Dei ejusque potentiâ sive virtute voluntas afficitur, allicitur, & in consensum trahitur, ut imperio suo ab id generis vanis & perversis cogitationibus intellectum avertat, eumque ad assensum revelatæ â Deo doctrinæ determinet. Quæ à voluntatis, divinitùs excitatæ, imperio profecta determinatio ad assensum verè est ejus per metaphoram sic dicta captivatio.

Hanc voluntatis motionem, ex parte intellectus, cum aliquibus actibus cognoscendi supernaturalibus conjunctam, vocat Christus, per similem metaphoram, ἕλκυσιν tractionem, eamque in solidum DEO Patri suo adscribit: Nemo, inquiens, venit ad me, nisi Pater meus ἑλκύσῃ TRAXERIT eum. Ubi venire ad Christum est credere in eum, uti ex præced. v. 35. patet, in quo duæ hæ phrases promiscuè adhibentur. Quemadmodùm autem medium accendendæ in hominis corde fidei Verbum Dei, lectum vel prædicatum audituq́; perceptum, est, juxta illud Apostoli: Fides est ex auditu, auditus autem per Verbum Dei, Rom. X. 17. ita Deus non trahit hominem, ut veniat ad Christum, h. e. in eum credat, immediatè, sed per Verbum suum, sive lectum, sive prædicatum audituque perceptum. Non enim ductu vel cæco ignorantem, vel violento contradicentem & repugnantem trahit, ut quod prorsus ignorat, aut negat & velut stultitiam rejicit, credat, sed trahit eum modo intellectui nostro connaturali, ut accensâ per Verbum bonorum spiritualium salutari notitiâ ex ignorante scientem, & ex contradicente consentientem faciat. Neque etiam invitum & nolentem per vim trahit, sed ita ut ejus voluntatem, excitato pio desiderio, piaque affectione erga Deum revelantem & revelata ab ipso bona spiritualia, suavi inclinatione ad imperandum intellectui, jam aliqua luce spiritualia collustrato, credendorum assensum inducat, & sic ex nolente volentem faciat. Divina igitur ἕλκυσις sive TRACTIO hominis, ut veniat ad Christum, utrumque complectitur, salutarem scilicet notitiam Christi, ejusq́; beneficiorum & cæterorum doctrinæ Christianæ capitum ex parte intellectus, & desiderium pium, piamq́; credendi affectionem ex parte voluntatis, bonorum spiritualium repræsentatione per Verbum cum Dei concursu supernaturali excitatam, consistitque formaliter in supernaturali voluntatis inclinatione in Deum revelantem & bona revelata, prælucente ex parte intellectus notitiâ rerum spiritualium, ex Verbo Dei haustâ.

III. Deinde dico, Verbum Dei, scriptum aut prædicatum, exerere se ex parte voluntatis cum concursu Dei supernaturali per objectorum spiritualium SPECIES EXPRESSAS. Quia enim divina illa δύναμις, potentia sive virtus agendi, in Verbo Dei & per illud in hominum cordibus ad accendendam fidem sese exerens, SENSUI Verbi divini, cùm scripti tùm prædicati, non verbis, quæ sensus notæ sive signa sunt, conjuncta sive unita est, uti superiùs pluribus ostensum, necesse utiq; est, ut vel speciebus impressis rerum, verbis significarum, vel earundem expressis speciebus in hominis intellectu conjuncta sit, & per alterutras vel per utrasque in ejus voluntate sese exerat. Præter has enim nihil datur in hominis intellectu, per quod sensus Verbi divini ei inesse dicatur. Quamvis verò, ut in præcedente Assertione ostensum, speciebus utrisq; conjuncta sit, & ex parte intellectus etiam per utrasque ad ejus illuminationem sese exerat: ex parte voluntatis tamen, ut allecta & in consensum tracta assensum credendorum intellectui imperare possit & imperet, exerit eadem sese per solas objectorum species expressas. Specierum impressarum enim non aliud est munus, quàm ut, objectorum loco, intellectum ad illorum apprehensionem simplicem moveant, & ad eorundem conceptus eliciendos efficienter cum illo concurrant; ad eliciendos actus voluntatis autem per se nihil conferre possunt. Nam voluntatis actus dependent à voluntate & objectis, per intellectum ei repræsentatis: Objecta autem voluntati repræsentare & exhibere specierum expressarum est, quippe quæ solæ objectorum signa formalia sunt, eaque formaliter repræsentant; non specierum impressarum, quæ tantùm instrumentalia illorum signa sunt, eaq; non repræsentant, nisi effectivè per illorum conceptus sive species expressas, quas cum intellectu efficienter producunt. Quemadmodum autem, ex parte objectorum, veritas & bonitas illorum realiter non differunt, ita unæ & eædem species expressæ repræsentant una & eadem objecta simul intellectui ut vera, & voluntati ut convenientia & bona. Si ergo ad alliciendam & in consensum trahendam voluntatem, ut imperio suo intellectum ad assensum determinet, Dei concursus supernaturalis requiritur, sicut eum requiri certum, & jam ostensum est: necesse est; ut cum objectorum SPECIEBUS EXPRESSIS conjunctus sit, & per has sese exerat.

Quamvis verò de cognitione intellectus, quâ voluntati objecta sua repræsentantur, sive quod eodem redit, de objectorum speciebus expressis, concurrantne ex parte voluntatis ad eliciendos ejus actus efficienter? an per solam objectorum repræsentationem, absque effectivo influxu? inter Scholasticos, veteres cumprimis, non levis disfenfio sit, de qua inter alios videri potest Vazquez in 1. II. Disp. XXXVI. c. 11. & seqq. recentiores tamen, cùm Scholastici, tùm moderni Philosophi ac Theologi communiter posteriorem quæstionis partem amplectuntur, quorum sententiæ & nos aliàs subscribimus. Neq; aliter statuendum videtur de cognitione sive speciebus expressis objectorum spiritualium : quæ si vel maximè ad secundam mentis operationem pertineant, & in substantiâ supernaturales sint, tamen hoc ipso quod objectorum species sive imagines expressæ sunt, per se solæ non alio, ex parte voluntatis, munere fungi posse videntur, quàm ut objecta spiritualia ei ut convenientia & bona, exhibeant & repræsentent. Quia autem VERBUM DEI sunt, ejusq; sensum intellectui formaliter repræsentant, divinam utique δύναμιν sive virtutem illam, quâ ad supernaturales Verbi sui effectus Spiritus S. concurrit, interiùs in hominis intellectu sibi conjunctam habent, & dicendum omninò est, eas concurrere cum objectis spiritualibus, quæ voluntati repræsentant & exhibent, ad alliciendam, trahendamq; voluntatem etiam efficienter, non præcisè quidem per suam vim repræsentandi objecta, nec per actualem illorum repræsentationem præcisè: hæc enim ex parte voluntatis, ad spiritualia emortuæ, ad eam ex morte peccati excitandam nequaquam sufficiunt; sed per illam sibi conjunctam δύναμιν sive potentiam Dei, per quam Verbum Dei Apostolo est & dicitur potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 18. 24. vel, ut Eph. I. 19. Apostolus laudatus loquitur, per excellentem magnitudinem potentiæ Dei in nos, qui credimus secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ejus, quam exercuit in Christo, cùm suscitaret eum ex mortuis. Per hanc, ut Christum ex mortuis Deus suscitavit reali & physico influxu, ita voluntatem hominis, ad spiritualia prorsus emortuam, suscitat ex morte spirituali, allicitque & trahit eam similiter realiter & influxu physico per actus & motus spirituales, cum concursu Verbi tamen & pro ejus exigentia in ea excitatos.


### X. Assertion nine: On both sides Holy Scripture, or the Word of God, written or…

X.

Assertion nine: On both sides Holy Scripture, or the Word of God, written or preached, exerts itself, together with the supernatural concurrence of God, both by illuminating the intellect and by enticing and drawing the will.

I. By nature, it is indeed prior for the intellect to be illuminated by the Word of God than for the will to be moved, enticed, and drawn by it. For the will cannot be enticed and drawn unless by an object previously known and represented to itself through cognition, which pertains to the illumination of the intellect; yet in time they are simultaneous. For the expressed species of objects, to which the acts of knowing, produced in the intellect by the Word of God and its illuminating power, are terminated, represent the known objects simultaneously to the intellect under the aspect of the true, and to the will under the aspect of the good, as has been said; and just as the illuminating power of the divine Word concurs efficiently on the part of the intellect with the impressed species of things toward the acts of knowing, by which, as if by expressed species, the things themselves are formally represented to the intellect; so also on the part of the will it is not idle, but exerts itself through the same expressed species with the objects represented to it, by knocking, enticing, and drawing it through supernatural acts and motions, as soon as the expressed species, produced in the intellect, represent spiritual objects to it.

II. And hence it is that the converted, when they feel on the part of the intellect, by the force of the illuminating power joined to the Word of God, some saving knowledge of spiritual things being excited in them, and some spiritual light shining upon them, they simultaneously notice also on the part of the will holy impulses and motions in themselves. For example, in the case of the eunuch of the Queen of the Ethiopians, the treasurer of Candace, from the passage of Isaiah 53:7-8, which he was reading, being more fully explained to him by Philip from other places of Scripture, there shone upon him simultaneously on the part of the intellect so much light and saving knowledge, and on the part of the will there arose such affection and readiness, that with a willing mind he both professed his faith in Christ and asked for baptism to be administered to him: 'See, water,' he said to Philip, 'what prevents me from being baptized?' But when Philip said, 'If you believe with all your heart, you may,' he replied, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God,' and he was baptized, Acts 8:36-37. To Lydia, a seller of purple, through the Word preached by Paul, both a holy thought and a pious desire (for it was shown above that both are comprehended by the opening of her heart) were inspired by God, so that, led by a desire for learning, she attended to those things which were said by Paul, and being converted, she received baptism, ch. 16:14 ff. And the hearers of Peter's sermon in Acts 2, from hearing him, were illuminated simultaneously on the part of the intellect, and were pricked in heart from the part of the will, so that with the truth of the doctrine concerning Christ acknowledged, and repentance for the crimes committed against Christ, they were led to say to the Apostles: What shall we do, men and brethren? v. 37. Many examples from sacred and profane histories could be brought forward, if there were need. We shall bring forward one example of the Christian Gerson, a converted Jew, which is quite illustrative for this matter. He was converted to the Christian faith at the end of the last century, and in the history of his conversion, certain details of which Mr. Dr. Georgius Calixtus left to us, translated into the Latin language in his Treatise on the Authority of Scripture, page 56 and following, he thus commemorates the occasion and manner of his conversion: A certain poor Christian woman, my neighbor, was pledging a copy of the German New Testament, translated by Luther: to whom I lent eight shillings, so that I might earn interest in my own way, and meanwhile peruse the book, not indeed because I doubted the truth of the Jewish religion, or believed any article of the Christian faith to be correct, but so that I might know what that error was, so greatly effective, which seduced so many myriads of souls and cast them headlong into destruction. Therefore, in the presence of my two kinsmen, Lazarus and Simeon, I read it through entirely, not without blasphemies. Meanwhile, however, my heart was struck, and when I had noticed that the Evangelists and Apostles and Christ himself so often appeal to the Old Testament, and repeatedly cite passages from it one after another, I was enticed to read it again, secretly indeed, with no one aware, not even my wife, and to compare the cited passages with the text of the Old Testament itself. When I did this, such a great light shone upon me that on that account I owe eternal thanks to God. Thus he! By which he signifies two things pertaining to this. One, that the Scripture of the New Testament exerted its divine power first in his will through its impulse and motion, rather than in the intellect through some beginning of saving knowledge concerning objects known by simple apprehension. Meanwhile, he says, for instance, when he was reading through the copy of the New Testament without the desire to learn, with the intellect knowing the things signified by the words either by simple apprehension alone, without assent, or by a rash presumption concerning the truth of the Jewish religion; but condemning the Christian religion as false by a precipitate and perverse judgment, not without blasphemies, he felt his heart struck. The second: having observed the passages of the Old Testament Scripture more frequently cited by the Evangelists, the Apostles, and Christ himself, he was enticed or induced to repeat the reading of the New Testament Scripture: which induction without doubt implied, on the part of the intellect indeed, a holy thought concerning the truth of the New Testament Scripture excited by the power of the Word, and on the part of the will, a pious desire to read and meditate upon it more diligently, of which the former was the beginning of illumination, and the latter of pious affection toward the New Testament Scripture, and both afterwards, as greater light shone upon the intellect during reading day by day, and as the pious affection of believing grew in the will along with the light of the intellect, took on greater increases, so that he finally embraced the truth of Christian doctrine with undoubted assent, and publicly professed it, even with danger to his life.

Latin:

X.

Affertio nona: Ex parte utraque exerit sese Scriptura sacra, vel Verbum Dei, scriptum aut prædicatum, cum Dei concursu supernaturali simul, cum illuminando intellectum, tùm alliciendo trahendoque voluntatem.

I. Naturâ quidem prius est intellectum illuminari per Verbum Dei, quàm voluntatem per illud moveri, allici & trahi. Voluntas enim allici trahiq́; non potest, nisi ab objecto prius cognito sibiq́; per cognitionem, quæ ad illuminationem intellectūs pertinet, repræsentato; tempore tamen simul sunt. Nam objectorum species expressæ, ad quas actus cognoscendi, per Verbum Dei ejusq́; virtutem illuminatricem in intellectu producti, terminantur, repræsentant objecta cognita simul intellectui sub ratione veri; & voluntati sub ratione boni, uti dictum, & quemadmodùm Verbi divini virtus illuminatrix ex parte intellectūs cum rerum speciebus impressis ad actus cognoscendi, quibus velut speciebus expressis ipsæ res intellectui formaliter repræsentantur, efficienter concurrit; ita nec ex parte voluntatis ea otiosa est, sed exerit se per easdem species expressas cum objectis, ei repræsentatis, pulsando, alliciendo trahendoq́; illam per actus & motus supernaturales, simul ac species expressæ, in intellectu productæ, objecta spiritualia ei repræsentant.

II. Atq; hinc est, quòd conversi, cùm ex parte intellectus vi virtutis illuminatricis, Verbo Dei conjunctæ, aliquam salutarem rerum spiritualium notitiam in se excitari, & aliquid lucis spiritualis sibi affulgere sentiunt, simul etiam ex parte voluntatis pulsus & motus sanctos in se animadvertunt. v. g. Eunucho Reginæ Æthiopum, Præfecto Candacis, ex loco Jes. LIII. 7. 8. quem legebat, à Philippo ex aliis Scripturæ locis sibi uberiùs declarato, simul ex parte intellectus tantum affulgebat lucis notitiæq; salutaris, & ex parte voluntatis tanta oboriebatur affectio & promtitudo, ut prona voluntate & suam fidem in Christum profiteretur, & baptismum sibi administrari peteret: Ecce aqua, inquiens ad Philippum, quid vetat, quo minus baptizer? Dicenti autem Philippo: Si credis ex toto corde, licet; respondebat: Credo, Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum, & baptizatus est, Act. VIII. 36. 37. Lydiæ, purpurarum venditrici per Verbum, à Paulo prædicatum, simul & cogitatio sancta & pium desiderium (utrumq; enim apertione cordis ejus comprehendi suprà ostensum est) à Deo inspiratum est, ut desiderio discendi ducta attenderet his, quæ dicebantur à Paulo, & conversa baptismum susciperet, c. XVI. 14. seq. Et auditores concionis Petrinæ Act. II. ex ejus auditu illuminabantur simul ex parte intellectus, & compungebantur ex parte voluntatis, ut agnitâ veritate doctrinæ de Christo, & pœnitentiâ scelerum, in Christum commissorum, ducti dicerent ad Apostolos: Quid faciemus, Viri fratres? v. 37. Exempla plura ex historiis sacris & profanis possent adferri, si opus esset. Unum Christiani Gersonis, Judæi conversi, hanc in rem admodum illustre, exemplum adferemus. Conversus is est ad fidem Christianam seculo superiori exeunte, & in historia conversionis suæ, cujus particulas quasdam Dn. D. Georgius Calixtus in Tr. de Auctoritate Scripturæ pag. 56. seq. in Latinam linguam translatas, nobis reliquit, quibus occasionem & modum conversionis suæ ita commemorat: Paupercula quædam Christiana fœmina, vicina mea, tradebat pignori codicem Novi Testamenti Germanici, à Luthero conversi: cui ego mutuos dabam octo solidos, ut usuram meo more lucrarer, & librum interim evolverem, non quidem, quòd de veritate Judaicæ religionis dubitarem, aut ullum Christianæ fidei articulum rectum crederem, sed ut cognoscerem, quisnam ille tantopere efficax error, qui tot animarum myriades seduceret, & in exitium præcipites daret. Præsentibus igitur duobus meis affinibus Lazaro & Simeone, totum perlegi non sine blasphemiis. Interim verò cor meum percellebatur, & cum animadvertissem, Evangelistas & Apostolos & Christum ipsum toties ad Vetus Testamentum provocare, & subindè loca ex eo alia post alia adducere, illectus fui, ut dennò legerem, clanculum quidem, nemine conscio, ne quidem uxore mea, & ut loca adducta cum ipso Veteris Testamenti textu contenderem. Quod ubi feci, tanta lux mihi illuxit, ut eo nomine æternas Deo debeam gratias. Hæc ille! quibus duo, huc spectantia, significat. Unum, Scripturam N. T. exeruisse suam divinam virtutem priùs in sua voluntate per ejus pulsum motumœ, quàm in intellectu per initium quoddam salutaris notitiæ de objectis, apprehensione simplici cognitis Interim, ait, puta cum Codicem N. T. absque studio discendi perlegeret, intellectu res, verbis significatas, vel solâ apprehensione simplici, absque assensu, cognoscente, vel ex temeraria præsumtione de religionis Judaicæ veritate; Christianæ verò falsitate, præcipitato perverso judicio, non absque blasphemiis, falsitatis damnante, PERCULSUM esse cor suum. Alterum: animadversis locis Scripturæ V. T. ab Evangelistis, Apostolis & ipsomet Christo crebriùs allegatis, se ILLECTUM sive inductum esse ad iterandam Scripturæ N. T. lectionem: quæ inductio citra dubium importabat, ex parte intellectûs quidem, excitatam virtute Verbi cogitationem sanctam de veritate Scripturæ N. T. ex parte voluntatis verò desiderium pium diligentiùs eam legendi & meditandi, quarum illa illuminationis; hoc piæ erga Scripturam N. T. affectionis initium fuit, & utraq; posteà, affulgente intellectui inter legendum indies luce majori, & crescente cum lumine intellectus piâ affectione credendi in voluntate, majora sumsit incrementa, ut veritatem doctrinæ Christianæ cum assensu indubitato tandem amplecteretur, & publicè, etiam cum vitæ periculo, profiteretur.


### XI. FROM these things declared and extensively deduced concerning the motive power…

XI.

FROM these things declared and extensively deduced concerning the motive power of the Holy Scripture or the Word of God, written or preached, upon the intellect toward the assent of its dependence upon God, everyone understands, first of all, that it is true, as we said above in Assertion IV, that the supernatural Concurrence of God with His Word, perceived by reading or hearing, pertains to the very formal objective reason of divine faith.

I. For although it acts efficiently to produce the very supernatural acts of the intellect and will, by which the former is illuminated, the latter is drawn into consent, and is moved to command the intellect to assent, nevertheless all this which it contributes efficiently, it contributes in the place of objects, and thereby it performs what objects that are of the natural order can and do contribute by their mere objective influence to elicit natural acts of the intellect and will: namely, those objects which are of the natural order, when they are either evident, so that in terms apprehended the identity of the predicate with the subject immediately appears to the intellect, or they rely upon evident reasons for assenting, can move the intellect to their assent by objective influence alone, either by themselves immediately, or by means of some third thing previously known. But the things that are of the Spirit of God are so profound, so recondite and abstruse, that when known by simple apprehension, they neither by themselves immediately, nor by means of by some third thing, previously known, they can move [the intellect] to assent to themselves. Whence also our intellect is entirely blind to objects of this kind, nor does it have even so much as a glimmer of light: e.g., when Holy Scripture teaches in the clearest words that God is the Father, is the Son, is the Holy Spirit, and that these three are one God, the intellect, by means of the impressed species of these objects, excited and coordinated within it by the force of the words of Scripture, indeed recognizes with simple apprehension easily that God and the Father are composed and identified with one another, and similarly God and the Son, and likewise God and the Holy Spirit are composed and identified with one another; and again that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are signified as being the same as God. Although, however, in all these propositions the predicate is inherently and immediately present in the subject, yet the underlying things are so abstruse and so hidden to our intellect that it can never attain to the fact that the predicate belongs to the subject, either inherently and immediately, or by means of some third thing previously known. When, therefore, the Holy Spirit, with His illuminating power, concurs with the impressed and expressed species of the objects, which take their place, and elevates them beyond their native power, both for supernatural acts of knowing on the part of the intellect, by which it is inclined to assent to them, and for pious acts and holy motions on the part of the will, by which it is drawn to consent, does He not do all this—although efficiently—in the stead and place of the objects, and perform that very thing which the objects, represented to the intellect and will through their expressed species, ought to have performed on the part of both faculties, and would in fact have performed by their own objective influence alone, if they were evident to us? That the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined in the intellect to the impressed and expressed species of the objects, performs in their stead the task of moving the faculties of the soul to their supernatural assent and consent, certainly pertains to the formal objective reason of divine faith.

II. Nor is there any reason for anyone to object here, as the Papists object, that the supernatural concurrence of God is required for eliciting the aforementioned supernatural acts and motions, not on the part of the object and formal motive, to complete its formal objective reason, but only on the part of the faculties of the soul, the intellect and the will, in order to instruct them with spiritual powers to elicit those acts. No, I say, there is no reason for anyone to object thus. For first, what are those powers of believing, by which the faculties, intellect and will, aided, elicit the first supernatural acts and motions of holy thought and pious desire? They are either the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit itself, joined to the impressed species of spiritual things, or spiritual qualities, efficiently produced by the Holy Spirit in the intellect. If the former? I have what I want: namely, that the supernatural concurrence of God behaves itself on the part of the object: since the impressed species of things behave themselves on the part of the object, and perform its role in the intellect. Nor does it hinder that the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined with the impressed species, also efficiently concurs toward the acts of holy thought and pious desire. For the impressed species also, which without doubt perform the role of objects, concur with the intellect toward acts of simple apprehension efficiently, and yet at the same time objectively: objectively indeed, in so far as they determine the intellect to produce the cognition of this, not another object, and whose produced terminus is the expressed image of this, not another thing; efficiently indeed, in so far as they constitute the intellect in the capacity of a complete effective principle of its acts, and concur with it efficiently to produce them. Thus at present, in order for the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined to the impressed species of objects, to be said to behave itself on the part of the objects, it suffices that with the impressed species of these it moves the intellect to the supernatural assent of these, not others, notwithstanding that it also efficiently concurs toward the production of the acts of assenting. But if the latter is said, then one or the other must be admitted, that the Holy Spirit confers those powers of believing by His own concurrence, either through His Word, read or perceived by hearing, and dependently upon it; or without His Word and independently of it? If through the Word, and dependently upon it? then the powers of believing, which are conferred by the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined to the impressed species of things, will not precede the first supernatural acts and motions: since the Word of God does not offer its influx into the spiritual powers, to be conferred upon one or both faculties, otherwise than through supernatural acts, elicited by the power of the Holy Spirit with the impressed species, which, as they are terminated toward a spiritual quality inclining the faculties of the soul toward other similar acts and motions, so through their own limits, they finally bring together the first beginnings of spiritual powers, which then, through other spiritual acts and motions, excited by the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, joined with the impressed and expressed species of objects, take their increases through their produced limits. But if you say that the spiritual powers independently of His Word, and without its concurrence, then you tear the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit away from His Word, and you constitute the Word of God as a dead letter: since you ascribe the powers of believing, and also the subsequent acts of believing, not to the Word itself, as a cause, but to the Holy Spirit separately, without the concurrence of the Word. Which savors of Schwenckfeldianism and Enthusiasm.

III. One thing, before I depart from here, I advise: that I have used here examples of merely spiritual objects, which altogether exceed the grasp of human reason, because in these the concurrence of the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power with the Word of God is more illustriously conspicuous. Besides these, however, there are found in the Holy Scriptures many other things which are of the natural order, and whose truth can also be known by the guidance of the light of nature, which we nevertheless by no means wish to be excluded from the census of things to be believed. For although the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit is not simply necessary for the assent to these, yet so that the assent to them might be more certain, and might also more easily find a place in the minds of the simpler sort, it pleased God to dictate these also, as it were, to the pen for the sacred writers to record through supernatural inspiration, in which, therefore, God, no less than in merely spiritual objects, joined His illuminating power to His Word, by which they exist recorded, so that, joined with their impressed species in the human intellect, it might work assent in the same manner as that of merely spiritual objects.

Latin:

XI.

EX hisce de Scripturæ sacræ vel Verbi Dei, scripti aut prædicati, vi motiva intellectus in assensum suæ à Deo dependentiæ declaratis, & fusè deductis, nemo non intelligit, primùm quidem verum esse, quòd suprà Assert. IV. diximus, Concursum Dei supernaturalem cum suo Verbo, lecto vel auditu percepto, pertinere ad ipsam rationem objectivam formalem fidei divinæ.

I. Quamvis enim ad producendos ipsos intellectus & voluntatis actus supernaturales, quibus ille illuminatur; hæc in consensum trahitur, & ad imperandum intellectui assensum movetur, efficienter se habeat, tamen totum hoc, quod efficienter confert, objectorum loco confert, eoq; id præstat quod objecta, quæ naturalis ordinis sunt, ad intellectus & voluntatis actus naturales eliciendos suo solo objectivo influxu conferre possunt & conferunt: nempe quæ naturalis ordinis sunt objecta, cùm vel evidentia sint, ut in terminis ap- -prehensis statim identitas prædicati cum subjecto intellectui appareat, vel rationibus assentiendi evidentibus nitantur, possunt intellectum solo objectivo influxu, vel per se immediatè, vel mediante aliquo tertio, prius cognito, in sui assensum movere. Sed quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, ita profunda, ita recondita & abstrusa sunt, ut simplici apprehensione cognita, intellectum nec per se immediatè, nec mediante aliquo tertio, prius cognito, in assensum sui movere possint. Unde & intellectus noster ad hujus generis objecta prorsus cæcus est, nec vel tantum lucis habet: v. g. cum Scriptura sacra verbis clarissimis docet, Deum esse Patrem, esse Filium, esse Spiritum Sanctum, & hosce tres esse unum Deum, intellectus per species impressas horum objectorum, vi verborum Scripturæ in eo excitatas & coordinatas, cognoscit quidem apprehensione simplici facilè, Deum & Patrem componi & identificari inter se, & similiter Deum & Filium, itemq; Deum & Spiritum S. componi & identificari inter se; & rursum Patrem, Filiū & Spiritum Sanctum fignificari ut eosdem cum Deo. Quamvis verò in omnibus hisce propositionibus prædicatum subjecto per se immediatè insit, tamen res substratæ intellectui nostro ita sunt abstrusæ, ita absconditæ, ut prædicatum subjecto vel per se immediatè, vel mediante aliquo tertio, prius cognito, convenire, nunquam assequi possit. Quando ergo Spiritus Sanctus sua virtute illuminatrice cum objectorum speciebus impressis & expressis, quæ illorum vices gerunt, concurrit, illasque ultra suam nativam vim elevat cùm ad supernaturales cognoscendi actus ex parte intellectus, quibus in illorum assensum inclinetur; tum ad pios actus & motus sanctos ex parte voluntatis, quibus in consensum trahatur, eliciendos, annon hoc totum, licet efficienter, objectorum vice & loco tamen facit, & id ipsum præstat, quod objecta, per sui species expressas intellectui & voluntati repræsentata, ex parte facultatis utriusque præstare debebant, & reapse suo solo influxu objectivo præstitura essent, si nobis evidentia essent? Quod autem Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, objectorum speciebus, impressis & expressis, in intellectu conjuncta, ad movendas facultates animæ in illorum assensum & consensum supernaturalem in solidum illorum loco præstat, id pertinet utique ad rationem objectivam formalem fidei divinæ.

II. Neque est, quod quis hîc excipiat, sicut Pontificii excipiunt, concursum Dei supernaturalem requiri ad eliciendos prædictos actus & motus supernaturales, non ex parte objecti & motivi formalis, ad complendam ejus rationem objectivam formalem, sed tantùm ex parte facultatum animæ, intellectus & voluntatis, ut viribus spiritualibus eas ad illos eliciendos instruat. Non, inquam, est, ut quis sic excipiat. Primùm enim quænam sunt illæ vires credendi, quibus adjutæ facultates, intellectus & voluntas, primos actus & motus supernaturales cogitationis sanctæ & pii desiderii eliciunt? Aut sunt ipsa Spiritus Sancti illuminatrix virtus, rerum spiritualium speciebus impressis conjuncta, aut qualitates spirituales, à Spiritu S. in intellectu efficienter productæ. Si prius? habeo, quod volo: nempe concursum Dei supernaturalem habere se ex parte objecti: cum species rerum impressæ ex parte objecti sese habeant, & ejus vice in intellectu fungantur. Neque impedit, quod Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, cum speciebus impressis conjuncta, ad actus sanctæ cogitationis & pii desiderii etiam efficienter concurrit. Nam species impressæ etiam, quæ citra dubium objectorum vicem gerunt, concurrunt cum intellectu ad actus apprehensionis simplicis efficienter, & tamen simul objectivè: objectivè quidem, in quantum intellectum determinant ad producendam cognitionem hujus, non alterius objecti, & cujus terminus productus sit hujus, non alterius rei imago expressa; efficienter verò, quatenus intellectum in ratione principii, actuum suorum effectivi completi constituunt, & cum eo ad illos producendos efficienter concurrunt. Ita impræsentiarum ad hoc, ut Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, objectorum speciebus impressis conjuncta, ex parte objectorum se habere dicatur, sufficit, quod cum horum speciebus impressis intellectum ad horum, non aliorum assensum supernaturalem movet, non obstante, quod ad productionem actuum assentiendi etiam efficienter concurrat. Sin posterius dicatur, tum alterutrum admittendum erit, quòd Spiritus Sanctus suo concursu supernaturali vires illas credendi conferat vel per Verbum suum, lectum, vel auditu perceptum, & dependenter ab illo; vel absq; Verbo suo & independenter ab illo? Si per Verbum, & dependenter ab illo? tùm vires credendi, quæ à Spiritus S. virtute illuminatrice, rerum speciebus impressis conjuncta, conferuntur, non præcedent primos actus & motus supernaturales: cùm Verbum Dei in hominis intellectu & voluntate non aliter suum præbeat influxum in vires spirituales, alterutri vel utrique facultati conferendas, quàm per actus supernaturales, Spiritus Sancti virtute cum speciebus impressis elicitos, qui ut ad qualitatem spiritualem, in alios similes actus & motus facultates animæ inclinantem, terminantur, ita per suos terminos productes conferunt demum prima virium spiritualium initia, quæ deinde per alios actus & motus spirituales, Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminatrice, cum objectorum speciebus impressis & expressis conjunctâ, excitatos illorumƉ; terminos productos incrementa capiunt. Sin dicas, vires illas spirituales conferri à Spiritu S. independenter à Verbo suo, & absque ejus concursu, tùm Spiritus Sancti virtutem illuminatricem à Verbo ejus divelles, & Verbum Dei literam mortuam constitues: cùm vires credendi, & subsequentes etiam actus credendi non ipsi Verbo, ut causæ, sed Spiritui Sancto seorsim, absque Verbi concursu, adscribas. Quod Schvvenckfeldianismum & Enthusiasmum sapit.

III. Unum, priusquam hinc abeam, moneo, me hîc usum esse exemplis objectorum merè spiritualium, quæ humanæ rationis captum prorsus excedunt, quòd in his concursus Spiritus S. ejusƉ; Virtutis illuminatricis cum Verbo Dei illustrior magisƉ; conspicuus sit. Præter hæc autem reperiuntur in Scripturis sacris alia multa, quæ naturalis ordinis sunt, & quorum veritas etiam ductu luminis naturæ cognosci potest, quæ ex credendorum censu tamen minimè exclusa volumus. Quamvis enim ad horum assensum Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix non simpliciter necessaria sit, tamen ut certior esset illorũ assensus, & faciliùs etiam in simpliciorum animis inveniret locum, placuit Deo hæc etiam Scriptoribus sacris per supernaturalem inspirationem consignanda in calamum quasi dictitare, in quibus proinde Deus non minùs, quàm in objectis merè spiritualibus, suam virtutem illuminatricem Verbo suo, quo consignata extant, conjunxit, ut illorum speciebus impressis in hominis intellectu conjuncta eundem in modum, quo objectorum merè spiritualium, asensum operetur.


### XII. Then it is also evident from what has been said thus far that it is true, which…

XII.

Then it is also evident from what has been said thus far that it is true, which we taught above in the same Assertion IV, Explanation no. IV, p. 484, that the Word of God, written and preached, moves the intellect into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God through the same acts and motions by which it moves it, with the supernatural concurrence of God, into the assent of the very things to be believed, but reflected.

I. For the Word of God, written and preached; and the Word of God, fixed in the intellect by the impressed species of objects, is one and the same Word of God, nor do they differ, except that the one is written or preached in external words, as if by sensible signs, outside the intellect; the latter is contained in the intellect by impressed species, as if by spiritual signs. Whence whatever God contributes through his illuminating power, joined with the impressed species of objects, inwardly on the part of the intellect for its illumination; and with the expressed species of the same on the part of the will for drawing it into consent, and thus for causing the supernatural assent of things to be believed, all that he contributes through his Word, by acts and spiritual motions really depending upon him and his Word. Just as every effect argues for its cause, and moves the intellect into the dependency of itself upon its cause, so the supernatural acts of knowing of the intellect and the supernatural acts and motions of the will move the intellect all the more into the cognition of their dependency upon God, because they inhere subjectively in the faculties of the soul themselves, the intellect and the will, nor are they produced in them by God without a certain sense of themselves. How certainly, therefore, do we know, e.g., from the narration of a man worthy of faith, when we hear him speaking to us and commemorating to us a thing worthy of memory, that he is speaking to us and commemorating to us that thing worthy of memory, just as certainly do we know from the supernatural acts and motions, which the Holy Spirit by his illuminating power supernaturally excites in our intellect through the impressed species of objects, and in our will through the expressed species of the same, that they depend upon God, and thus that it is God who excites them through his Word in our intellect and will, and moves us into the supernatural assent of objects.

II. But to these perhaps someone might object, that there is a disparate reason for the narration of some deed, performed by the voice of a man worthy of faith, and the acts of knowing and holy motions, supernaturally excited in our intellect and will by the Holy Spirit through the Word fixed in the intellect: that the former is done by a sensible voice, and who it is that commemorates the deed is known by the senses; but these latter are spiritual, and although they are known by the intellect by itself in the being of vital and immanent acts, and thus by reason of their dependency upon the intellect and the will, as vital powers, yet not known by themselves by reason of their supernatural dependence on God: e.g., those who are born and educated in the Church, some of them believe with a truly divine faith, others with a human faith only: and both know that they believe from the acts of believing reflected upon themselves, and thus know the dependence of their acts of believing upon the intellect, as upon a vital power: but that the others believe by acts of human faith, and others by acts of divine faith, and that their supernatural dependence on God and His Word cannot be known from the acts of believing themselves reflected upon by them.

To resolve this doubt, for the sake of greater clarity, we think it must be answered distinctly. And first, indeed, as regards infidels who are converted to the Christian faith from Judaism, Paganism, etc., it is certain that supernatural acts of illumination on the part of the intellect, and likewise supernatural acts and motions on the part of the will, are not excited in them by the Holy Spirit and His illuminating power, joined to His Word, without a sense of themselves and their supernatural dependence on God, even as regards their supernatural being, but are excited in such a way that the intellect, from those reflected acts, knows as certainly that it is being illuminated supernaturally, and that the will is being prompted, enticed, and drawn likewise supernaturally by God Himself, as certainly as anyone knows from the audible voice of a speaker, whom he hears mentioning something, that he is speaking and mentioning that thing. For the intellect, which was utterly darkened and blind to those things which are of the Spirit of God, when now, with a certain light shining upon it from the Word of God, perceived by reading or hearing, it is inclined through certain supernatural acts of knowing excited within itself to the assent of those things for which it sees no reason for assenting, indeed which it held to be false, absurd, and foolish; it cannot but feel that it is beginning to be illuminated and to struggle out of darkness by a power of the Word higher than merely objective, namely, a truly divine power: and similarly the will, which was utterly dead to the same objects and as inept for eliciting any good acts and motions in itself concerning them as a dead man is inept for eliciting any vital acts and motions in himself; when now it is prompted, enticed, and drawn by the power of the same Word, so that it begins to incline toward the same, it cannot but feel within itself a power of prompting, enticing, and drawing higher than that which could depend upon objects alone, apprehended by the intellect, namely, a truly divine power. But these very supernatural acts of the intellect and will, as they depend supernaturally upon God as the principal cause, are thus directed not only toward their objects, but, being reflected upward toward God, from whom they depend in their becoming and being, they are carried along and draw the hearts of men upward with them as if to God, so that the intellect may recognize, even from this, that they depend upon God as their author. Thus, in the examples cited above, the Eunuch of the Queen of the Ethiopians, when he perceived so much light from the Scripture explained to him by Philip that he recognized Christ to be the true Messiah, certainly knew from the supernatural acts of saving knowledge excited within him, by which his intellect was illuminated, and likewise from the impulse, motion, and drawing of his will, which he observed in himself, that he was being illuminated, impelled, moved, and drawn by God through the Word preached to him supernaturally; and he was so certain of this that he professed without hesitation that he believed Jesus Christ to be the Son of God, Acts 8:36. And Peter's hearers in Acts 2 certainly observed in themselves the supernatural light shining upon them from his sermon on the part of the intellect, and supernatural acts and motions on the part of the will, excited within them by the same, when, pricked in their hearts, they asked the Apostles what they must do and received the baptism of Christ. And the two disciples who had heard the Scripture explained to them by Christ on the road to Emmaus had perceived so much light from his explanation on the part of their intellect, and such effective and sensible motions on the part of their will, that they openly confessed both that the Scripture had been opened to them and that their heart had burned, Luke 24:32. In the same manner, the aforementioned Christian Gerson confessed that he had felt within himself the impulse of the Holy Spirit, by which his heart was struck during his first reading of the Scripture of the New Testament, and such great light shining upon him from the repeated reading of it, that on that account he owed eternal thanks to God.

Next, as regards the faithful born and raised in the Church, it must be admitted that they obtain faith immediately in early infancy, when the sense of supernatural acts and motions, due to the lack of the use of reason, cannot have a place as it does in adults. Nor do they obtain it through the Word of God, read or preached, of which they are not yet capable; but they obtain it through baptism, which is not the subject here. Afterward, however, with the arrival of the use of reason, they imbibe the necessary heads of Christian doctrine as if with milk, and they grow in saving knowledge, likewise through supernatural acts of illumination in their intellect, and holy motions in their will, excited by the power of the Word, although not as sensible as in adult infidels when they are first converted; of the sense of which, however, they are not entirely destitute. For just as Scripture, divinely inspired, is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness, as Paul teaches in II. Tim. III. 16, so it exerts itself by its own illuminating power even in those who, having been gifted with faith through baptism in early infancy and instructed in some knowledge of Christian doctrine at the beginning of their age, by teaching and by illuminating their intellect through doctrine, so that they may grow in the saving knowledge of Christ, by reproving erroneous and false doctrines so that they may beware of them; by correcting those who sin, by arguing their sins, by terrifying their hearts through the threats of the law, by bringing back those turning away from the right path and soliciting them to the amendment of life; by training them for righteousness and the manner of life to be lived in conformity with the divine will, by showing [the way], by inducing them to holiness of life through divine promises, by consoling the afflicted and those anxious from the sense of their sins, and by raising them up through evangelical promises, etc. all of which the Word of God performs, read or preached, not without supernatural acts and motions of illumination, confidence, hope, etc., excited from time to time by its power, the sense of which truly faithful people certainly have within themselves, and from these reflected acts they know that God is dealing with them and is supernaturally exciting them within themselves through His Word, so that he who believes in the Son of God has the testimony (of God) in himself, I John IV. 10, and our spirit, being already certain from the reflected acts of faith, confidence, hope, etc., of their supernatural dependence upon God, together with the Holy Spirit, who excites these same supernatural acts and motions in us through His Word and testifies through them in us, testifies that we are children of God, Rom. VIII. 15. That this cannot happen without a certain sense of spiritual acts and motions and their supernatural dependence upon God, even in those who are born and educated in the Church, is evident. But to pursue these things more fully is not the purpose of the present undertaking. For we are not dealing here with the power of the Word in relation to any spiritual acts and motions in the regenerate, but with its power of causing divine faith, now to be kindled for the first time, and specifically with its power by which it moves the intellect of man into assent to its supernatural dependence upon God, or, which is the same thing, concerning the power by which it moves the mind of man to believe that God says what the Holy Scripture says and proposes to us to be believed.

Latin:

XII.

Deinde constat etiam ex hactenus dictis verum esse, quod suprà eâdem Assert. IV. Explicat. n. IV. p. 484. docebamus, Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, movere intellectum in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ per eosdem actus & motus, quibus eum cum Dei concursu supernaturali in ipsarum rerum credendarum assensum movet, sed reflexos.

I. Verbum Dei enim, scriptum & prædicatum; & Verbum Dei, intellectui per species objectorum impressas infixum, unum & idem Dei Verbum est, neque differunt, nisi quod scriptum aut prædicatum verbis externis, velut signis sensibilibus, extra intellectum; hoc speciebus impressis, velut signis spiritualibus in intellectu continetur. Unde quicquid Deus per suam virtutem illuminatricem, cum objectorum speciebus impressis conjunctam, interiùs ex parte intellectus ad ejus illuminationem; & cum eorundem speciebus expressis ex parte voluntatis ad eam in consensum trahendam, atque adeò ad causandum credendorum assensum supernaturalem confert, id omne confert per Verbum suum, actibus & motibus spiritualibus ab ipso & ejus Verbo realiter dependentibus. Quemadmodum autem omnis effectus arguit suam causam, & intellectum in sui dependentiam à causa sua movet, ita intellectus actus cognoscendi supernaturales & voluntatis actus motusq́; supernaturales eò magis movent intellectum in cognitionem suæ à Deo dependentiæ, quòd ipsis facultatibus animæ, intellectui & voluntati, subjectivè insunt, nec absq; sui sensu quodam à Deo in iis producuntur. Quàm certò igitur cognoscimus, v. g. ex narratione Viri fide digni, quando eum ad nos loqui, & rem memoratu dignam nobis commemorare audimus, eum loqui ad nos, & commemorare nobis illam memoratu dignam rem, tam certò cognoscimus ex actibus & motibus supernaturalibus, quos Spiritus Sanctus suâ virtute illuminatrice per objectorum species impressas in nostro intellectu, & per eorundem species expressas in voluntate nostra supernaturaliter excitat, eos dependere à Deo, atque adeò Deum esse, qui eos per Verbum suum in nostro intellectu & voluntate excitat, nosq́; in objectorum assensum supernaturalem movet.

II. Sed ad hæc forsan quis excipiat, esse disparem rationem narrationis alicujus rei gestæ, voce Viri fide digni peractæ, & actuum cognoscendi motuumq́; sanctorum, à Spiritu S. per Verbum, intellectui infixum, in nostro intellectu & voluntate supernaturaliter excitatorum: illam fieri voce sensibili, & quisnam sit, qui rem gestam commemoret, cognosci sensibus; hos verò esse spirituales, & quamvis ab intellectu per se cognoscantur in esse actuum vitalium & immanentium, atq; sic ratione suæ dependentiæ ab intellectu & voluntate, tanquam potentiis vitalibus, non tamen cognofci per fe ratione suæ dependentiæ supernaturalis à Deo: v. g. qui in Ecclefia nati & educati funt, eorum alios credere fide verè divinâ, alios fide humanâ tantùm: & utrosq; cognofcere se credere ex actibus credendi in fe reflexis, atq; cognofcere fic dependentiam fuorum actuum credendi ab intellectu, tanquam à potentia vitali: alteros autem credere actibus fidei humanæ, alteros actibus fidei divinæ, & cum illorum supernaturali dependentia à Deo ejusq; Verbo, ex ipfis actibus credendi reflexis ab illis cognofci non posse.

Ad dubitationem hanc excutiendam, majoris lucis causâ, distinctè refpondendum ducimus. Et primùm quidem quod attinet ad infideles, qui ex Judaismo, Paganismo &c. ad fidem Christianam convertuntur, certum est, illuminationis actus supernaturales ex parte intellectus, itemque actus & motus supernaturales ex parte voluntatis non excitari in ipsis à Spiritu S. ejusque virtute illuminatrice, Verbo suo conjuncta, absq; fensu sui suæque supernaturalis dependentiæ à Deo, etiam quoad esse supernaturale, sed excitari ita, ut intellectus ex illis reflexis tâm certò cognoscat, se illuminari supernaturaliter, & voluntatem pulsari, allici & trahi itidem supernaturaliter ab ipfomet Deo, quàm certò quis ex voce sensibili loquentis, quem aliquid commemorare audit, eum loqui & commemorare illud cognoscit. Nam intellectus, qui ad ea, quæ Spiritus Dei funt, prorsus obtenebratus & cæcus erat, cùm jam affulgente fibi ex Verbo Dei, lecto vel auditu percepto, luce quâdam per excitatos in se actus quosdam cognoscendi supernaturales inclinatur in assensum eorum, quorum rationem assentiendi nullam videt, imò quæ pro falsis, absurdis, stolidis habebat; non potest non sentire, se incipere illuminari & è tenebris eluctari virtute Verbi altiori, quàm merè objectivâ, nempe virtute verè divinâ: & similiter voluntas, quæ ad eadem objecta prorsus emortua & ad ullos circa ea actus motusq; bonos in se eliciendos tam inepta erat, quàm ineptus homo mortuus est ad ullos actus motusq; vitales in se eliciendos; cùm jam virtute ejusdem Verbi pulsatur, allicitur, trahiturq;, ut in eadem propendere incipiat, non potest non in se sentire virtutem pulfandi, alliciendi, trahendique altiorem, quàm quæ à solis objectis, intellectu apprehensis, dependere possit, nempe virtutem verè divinam. Quin ipsi supernaturales intellectus & voluntatis actus, ut a Deo, tanquam a causa principali, supernaturaliter dependent, ita non solum directe in objecta sua; sed reflexi etiam sursum in Deum, a quo in fieri & esse dependent, feruntur, hominumq; corda secum sursum quasi ad Deum trahunt, ut a Deo, velut auctore, eos dependere intellectus vel hinc cognoscat. Sic in exemplis supra allatis, Eunuchus Reginæ Æthiopum, cum ex Scriptura, per Philippum sibi explicata, tantum perciperet luminis, ut Christum verum Messiam esse agnosceret, cognoscebat utique ex excitatis in se notitiæ salutaris actibus supernaturalibus, quibus intellectus ejus illuminabatur, itemq; ex pulsu, motu, tractuq; voluntatis suæ, quem in se animadvertebat, se illuminari, pulsari, moveri & trahi a Deo per Verbum sibi prædicatum supernaturaliter, deque hoc ita certus erat, ut sine hæsitatione profiteretur, se credere, Filium Dei esse Jesum Christum, Act. VIII. 36. Et Petri Auditores Act. II. animadvertebant in se utique affulgentem sibi ex ejus concione lucem supernaturalem ex parte intellectus, & supernaturales actus ac motus ex parte voluntatis, per eandem in se excitatos, quando compuncti cordibus, quid sibi agendum esset, ex Apostolis quærebant, & Christi baptismu suscipiebant. Et discipuli duo, qui in itinere Emauntico Scripturam a Christo sibi explicari audiverant, ex ejus explicatione tantum perceperant luminis ex parte intellectus sui, & motus tam efficaces ac sensibiles ex parte voluntatis suæ, ut & Scripturam sibi apertam esse, & cor suum arsisse, palam faterentur, Luc. XXIV. 32. Eundem in modum supra memoratus Christianus Gerson fatebatur se sensisse in se pulsum Spiritus Sancti, quo in lectione prima Scripturæ N. T. cor ejus percellebatur, & lucem tantam, ex iterata illius lectione sibi affulgentem, ut eo nomine æternas gratias Deo deberet.

Deinde quod ad fideles, in Ecclesia natos & educatos, attinet, fatendum est, eos consequi fidem in prima statim infantia, ubi sensus actuum & motuum supernaturalium, usu rationis deficiente, non æque, ut in adultis, locum habere potest. Neque per Verbum Dei, lectum vel prædicatum, cujus nondum capaces sunt; sed per baptismum, de quo hic non agitur, eam consequuntur. Postea autem, accedente usu rationis, imbibunt necessaria capita doctrinæ Christianæ cum lacte quasi, & crescunt in salutari agnitione, similiter per supernaturales illuminationis actus, in ipsorum intellectu, sanctósq; motus in voluntate illorum, virtute Verbi excitatos, licet non ita sensibiles, ut in adultis infidelibus, cùm primùm convertuntur; quorum sensu tamen non prorsus destituuntur. Quemadmodùm enim Scriptura, divinitùs inspirata, utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in justitiâ, docente Paulo II. Tim. III. 16. ita eadem exerit se suâ virtute illuminatrice in illis etiam, qui in prima infantia fide per baptismum donati, & ineunte ætate etiam aliqua doctrinæ Christianæ notitiâ instructi sunt, docendo, & per doctrinam illuminando illorum intellectum, ut in salutari agnitione Christi crescant, redeargendo doctrinas erroneas & falsas, ut ab illis sibi caveant; corripiendo peccantes, illorum peccata arguendo, per comminationes legis corda illorum terrendo, deflectentes à recto tramite reducendo, & ad emendationem vitæ solicitando; instituendo eos ad justitiam, & rationem vitæ, voluntati divinæ conformiter degendæ, monstrando, promissionibus divinis ad sanctimoniam vitæ inducendo, afflictos & ex sensu peccatorum anxios consolando & promissionibus Evangelicis erigendo &c. quæ omnia peragit Verbum Dei, lectum aut prædicatum, non absque supernaturalibus illuminationis, fiduciæ, spei &c. actibus & motibus supernaturalibus, ejus virtute subinde excitatis, quorum sensum verè fideles utiq; in se habent, & ex quibus reflexis Deum secum agere, eosq; in se per Verbum suum supernaturaliter excitare cognoscunt, ut ita qui credit in Filium Dei, testimonium (Dei) habeat in seipso, I. Joh.
