IV. 10. & spiritus noster, ex actibus fidei, Fiduciæ, spei &c. reflexis de illorum supernaturali à Deo dependentia jam certus, unà cum Spiritu Sancto, eosdé supernaturales actus & motus in nobis per Verbum suum excitante, & per illos in nobis testificante testetur, nos esse filios Dei, Rom. VIII. 15. Quæ absq; sensu quodam actuum & motuum spiritualium, illorumque supernaturalis dependentiæ à Deo, etiam in iis, qui in Ecclesia nati & educati sunt, fidelibus fieri non posse evidens est. Sed hæc fusiùs prosequi, præsentis instituti non est. Non enim hic agimus de virtute Verbi in ordine ad quosvis actus & motus spirituales in renatis, sed de ejus virtute causativa fidei divinæ, jam primùm accendendæ, & speciatim de ejus virtute, quâ movet hominis intelle&tum in assensum suæ supernaturalis dependentiæ à Deo, sive, quod idem est, de virtute, quâ movet hominis animum ad credendum, Deum dicere, quæ Scriptura sacra dicit, & credenda nobis proponit.


### XIII. Thirdly, it is also evident from the motive force of Holy Scripture regarding…

XIII.

Thirdly, it is also evident from the motive force of Holy Scripture regarding the assent of the intellect to itself and its own dependence upon God, which we have hitherto delivered and declared, that it is falsely imputed to our Churches by the Papists that they ultimately resolve the assent of divine faith into the private sense and spirit of each believer.

For our Churches, and their Doctors, do not ascribe the assent of divine faith to any acts or motions excited in us separately outside of or without the Word of God, which the Enthusiasts do; but they all attribute it to the constant Word of God, which signifies by established words, and to its illuminating power, jointly and not dividedly. Moreover, just as the signifying words, of which the written and preached Word of God consists, do not contain our private sense, but the very sense of God Himself, and present it to us to be known and embraced with undoubted assent, so also the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, communicated and joined to the sense of those words, does not move our intellect through interior acts and motions of illumination and attraction toward the assent of any other sense than that which the words contain and present to us to be known and believed. This, however, as has been said, is not our private sense or spirit, nor that of any believer, but the sense of God alone, revealed long ago by Him to the Prophets and Apostles, and proposed through the Scriptures, consigned by divine inspiration, to every believer and to the universal Church to be known and believed.

XIV.

This doctrine, although obscure and difficult to explain, is nevertheless necessary to be known and most useful. It is agreed among all that the Word of God, written and preached, cannot exert its motive force for assent to itself and its supernatural dependence on God in the human mind, unless it is read or preached, and transmitted through the senses to the intellect. Furthermore, it is also certain that neither the words themselves, written or spoken aloud, by themselves; nor even the things signified by themselves, enter our intellect, but both do so through their species, partly impressed, partly expressed. Thirdly, it is the constant opinion of our theologians that the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, on the part of our intellect, is joined to the sense of the divine Word, not to the words. All of which require explanation; but they cannot be accurately explained unless the physical doctrine concerning sensitive and intellective cognition is called to aid, and the terms of sensible and intelligible species, of external and internal species, of impressed and expressed species, etc., are employed. For the words of the divine Word do not exist in our intellect, as has been said, except through their impressed and expressed species; nor does the sense exist in it, except through the impressed and expressed species of the things signified; and that the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit is joined to the sense of Scripture or the Word of God, written or preached, on the part of the intellect, as regards the thing itself, is nothing other than that it is joined to the impressed and expressed species of the objects or things signified, which are fixed in the intellect. For besides these, on the part of the intellect, there is nothing given by which the sense of Scripture can be said to be contained and to exist within it. Therefore, intending to declare more distinctly what the words of Scripture contribute through their power of signifying; what likewise the sense of the words contributes, with the power of the Holy Spirit joined to it, on the part of our intellect, for its illumination; and what they contribute on the part of the will for knocking at it, moving it, and drawing it into consent, he cannot avoid calling to aid the aforementioned terms from the physical doctrine concerning the soul, and pointing out the things underlying them with the words he is accustomed to use, unless perhaps he wishes to invent new and unaccepted terms, which the current haters and contemners of the liberal arts and sciences are accustomed to do, but with no fruit. For this reason, in the preceding assertions, especially the seventh and eighth, the mentioned physical terms occur frequently, since no others accepted by usage are given, which perhaps will cause some obscurity in this matter for those who are ignorant of them, which, however, I think is sufficiently clear to those who understand their force and meaning. Although succinct descriptions and explanations of terms are added almost everywhere, so that even from this their genuine meanings can be easily known even by those who otherwise have not been accustomed to them. Nor is there any reason for our detractors to reproach us with these, as if they were Philosophical or Scholastic, on account of certain things mixed in concerning our natural reason of knowing. For when we are engaged in explaining the knowledge of revealed things from the Word of God, written or preached, which agrees with our natural reason of knowing in certain respects, and indeed, in that part which concerns simple apprehension, includes it in itself; but in other respects differs much from it, especially as regards assent, it sometimes cannot be otherwise than that, for the benefit of learners, for the sake of greater clarity, something from Physical doctrine should be brought in concerning our natural reason of knowing, the underlying subject matter so requiring, especially where it must be more distinctly taught and explained what the Word of God, written and preached, contributes naturally by the force of its words; and likewise what it contributes by the force of its sense, together with the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, to the supernatural illumination of our intellect. But as for the Scholastic Doctors, they are so far from having led the way for us in this matter that they rather stubbornly deny the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, communicated to the Word of God and concurring on its part to the illumination of our intellect. In which matter, however, to be handed down more fully from its genuine principles, this whole work of ours is occupied.

II. This doctrine is nevertheless necessary to be known and useful for a more accurate and solid knowledge of Theology for many reasons. For first, you cannot penetrate and solidly refute the deceits and frauds of the Sophists in the Papacy, which they commit in delivering the object or formal motive of divine faith, nor accurately explain its true nature, unless you have a proper knowledge and understanding of the nature and motive power of Holy Scripture, in what it consists, and in what manner, and by what acts it moves the intellect and will by itself immediately to assent to itself and its dependence upon God. Furthermore, nothing is more frequently on everyone's lips than that the faith of true believers is one thing, and the faith of hypocrites mixed into the assemblies of believers is another; and that the faith of the former rests on divine revelation; that of the latter on human testimony. But indeed, even hypocrites, who have been so informed from their tender years that Holy Scripture was written by divine revelation or inspiration, believe in their own way that God has revealed what is contained in Scripture, and when asked why they believe, for example, that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, they respond with an unfeigned heart that they believe this because God has revealed it; but that God has revealed this, because the holy Scripture says so. Therefore, you cannot solidly explain to students how the faith of these and those differs, unless you have known and perceived that the faith of the truly faithful rests ultimately in divine revelation or in the revealed Word of God, so that through this they believe that God has revealed what is contained in Scripture, because the Word of God itself, by its illuminating power, by illuminating the intellect and moving the will and drawing it into consent, moves them to believe this immediately by itself, without the concurrence of any other reason for assenting; but the faith of hypocrites and the wicked does not rest ultimately in divine revelation, but in human testimony. For although to one asking why they believe, for example, that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, they respond that they believe this on account of divine revelation, or because God has revealed it, yet if you ask further why they believe that God has revealed or said what Scripture says, they cannot respond that they believe this on account of Scripture itself, by its own divine power immediately by itself, by illuminating the intellect, and moving the will and drawing it into consent, testifying this in itself: for the Word of God, written or preached, effects none of these things in hypocrites and the wicked, who place an obstacle to its illuminating power; but their ultimate reason for believing is that they were so informed from their tender years, and have imbibed this doctrine as it were with their mother's milk, that holy Scripture was written from divine revelation, and that God says through it whatever it says. Thirdly, concerning revealed Theology, there is one mind and opinion among us all, that its formal object and the ultimate reason for assenting is divine revelation, or the Word of God, committed to writing from divine revelation. But because it is evident from experience that there are not rarely even among hypocrites and the impious those who possess as exact, or even more exact, knowledge of all things that are taught in Theology, than can be or is given even in the most pious theologian: hence arises the question, whether the habit of Theology can be given even in hypocrites and the impious, and whether it is sometimes given? Which question, just as it fixes a cross for students, so for the past fifty years and more at Magdeburg between the Rector of the Gymnasium and certain Ministers of the Church was debated with the greatest contention of minds. But the solid foundation for deciding it is again provided by this one doctrine concerning the proper motive force of Holy Scripture for the assent to itself and its own dependence upon God. For because revealed Theology, as all admit, has as its object or formal motive divine revelation, comprised in the Holy Scriptures, or which is the same thing, Holy Scripture, composed by the inspiration of God, and since its proper motive force moves in no other way than that hitherto declared, namely by illuminating the intellect and by alluring and drawing the will into assent to itself and its own dependence upon God, it is necessary that the habit of Theology should refer all its conclusions to this, and that their assent should ultimately rest in this motive force of Holy Scripture, and not proceed to any further reason for assenting. But the habit of declaring, confirming, and defending those things which have been revealed for the sake of our salvation, which is also found in hypocrites and the impious, does not have as its ultimate reason for assenting divine revelation, or Scripture composed by divine inspiration. For its assent does not rest ultimately in divine revelation, illuminating the intellect and striking and moving the will, and thus drawing the intellect by itself immediately into a supernatural assent to itself and its own dependence upon God. For hypocrites and the wicked, because they place an obstacle to the illuminating power of the divine Word, experience nothing of this kind in themselves, but when asked why they believe that the things contained in Holy Scripture are revealed by God and true, if they examine themselves and summon to their aid everything they can from every side, they will nevertheless not find anything to which they ultimately ascribe this assent of theirs, except human testimony, because they have been informed thus from their tender years by parents, by teachers, and by the Church. But just as the habits of the mind are specified by the ultimate reason for assenting, and divine revelation, illuminating the intellect by itself and moving the will and drawing it into consent, and thus causing a supernatural assent to itself and its own dependence upon God; and the testimony of parents, teachers, and the Church concerning Holy Scripture and its dependence upon God, are two different reasons for assenting: so also [are] the habit of Theology, of which the one [is] in divine revelation and its supernatural motive force, as just declared; but the other [is] in the testimony of parents, teachers, and the Church concerning Holy Scripture and its dependence on God stands ultimately, it is necessary that the habits of Theology be diverse. Let those things be seen which we taught above in part 1, chapter III, theses XLII and XLIV regarding this matter: where you will also find more fully declared what difference exists between both habits of Theology, and in what they likewise agree.

III. I think these things are clear, perspicuous, and easy to understand, so that they may be understood by learners once they have been rightly taught concerning the motive power of Holy Scripture, or the divine Word, written and preached, to assent to itself and its own dependence on God: for whose sake, therefore, it seemed good to explain the whole matter more fully. But if in so difficult and arduous a business I have not everywhere hit the nail on the head, as the saying goes, I hope the candid and fair reader will either forgive my slip or kindly point out better things. I will not only bear with a fair mind one who warns me and points out better things, but I will also gladly follow them.

Latin:

XIII.

TErtiò constat etiam ex Scripturæ sacræ vi motiva intellectus in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem, à nobis hactenus tradita & declarata, Ecclesiis nostris affingi à Pontificiis per calumniam, quòd assensum fidei divinæ in cujusq; credentis sensum & spiritum privatum ultimò resolvant.

Non enim Ecclesiæ nostræ, non Doctores ejus adscribunt assensum fidei divinæ ullis sive actibus sive motibus, extra Verbum Dei, aut absque eo seorsim in nobis excitatis, quod Enthusiastæ faciunt; sed ipsi verbis ex instituto significantibus constanti Verbo Dei, ejusq; virtuti illuminatrici junctim, non divisim, eum omnes acceptum referunt. Quemadmodùm autem verba significantia, quibus Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, constat, non nostrum privatum sensum, sed ipsummet Dei sensum in se continent, nobisq; cognoscendum & assensu indubitato amplectendum exhibent, ita & Spiritus S. virtus illuminatrix, illorum sensui communicata & conjuncta, per interiores illuminationis, tractionisq; actus & motus intellectum nostrum non movet in alius sensus assensum, quàm ejus, quem verba continent, nobisq; cognoscendum credendumq; exhibent. Hic autem, uti dictum, non est noster aut ullius credentis privatus sensus aut spiritus, sed solius Dei sensus, Prophetis & Apostolis olim ab ipso revelatus, & per Scripturas, ex divina inspiratione consignatas, cuiq; credenti & Ecclesiæ universæ ad cognoscendum credendumq; propositus.

XIV.

DOctrina hæc, etsi obscura & difficilis explicatu, necessaria tamen cognitu & maximè utilis est. inter omnes, Verbum Dei, fcriptum & prædicatum, non poffe fuam vim motivam ad affenfum fui fuæq́; à Deo dependentiæ fupernaturalem in hominis animo exerere, nifi lectum prædicatumve, per fenfus ad intellectum transmiffum. Deinde conftat etiam, non ipfa verba, fcripta aut voce prolata, per fe; neque etiam res fignificatas per fe noftrum ingredi intellectum, fed utraque per fui fpecies, impreffas partim, partim expreffas. Tertiò conftans eft Theologorum noftrorum fententia, Spiritus S. virtutem illuminatricem, ex parte intellectus noftri, conjunctam effe fenfui Verbi divini, non verbis. Quæ omnia egent explicatione; explicari autem accuratè non poffunt, nifi in fubfidium vocatâ doctrinâ phyficâ de cognitione fenfitivâ & intellectivâ, & adhibitis terminis fpeciei fenfibilis & intelligibilis, fpeciei externæ & internæ, fpeciei impreffæ & expreffæ &c. Verba enim Verbi divini intellectui noftro, uti dictum, non infunt, nifi per fui fpecies impreffas & expreffas; neque fenfus ei ineft, nifi per rerum fignificararum fpecies impreffas & expreffas; & fenfui Scripturæ aut Verbi Dei, fcripti aut prædicati, ex parte intellectus conjunctam effe Spiritus Sancti virtutem illuminatricem, quoad rem, nihil eft aliud, quàm eam esfe conjunctam objectorum five rerum fignificararum fpeciebus impreffis & expreffis, intellectui infixis. Præter has enim, ex parte intellectus, nihil datur, quo fenfus Scripturæ contineri, eique inesfe dicatur. Declaraturus igitur diftinctiùs, quid verba Scripturæ per fuam vim fignificandi; quid item verborum fenfus cum Spiritus Sancti virtute fibi conjuncta, ex parte intellectus noftri, ad ejus illuminationem; quid ex parte voluntatis ad eam pulfandam, movendam & in confenfum trahendam conferant, fubterfugere non poteft, quin prædictos terminos ex doctrina Phyfıca de anima in fubfidium vocet, & res fubftratas iis, quibus ufus confvevit, verbis indigitet, nifi forfan novos & ufu non receptos terminos fingere velit, quod hodierni bonarum artium & fcientiarum Ofores & Contemtores facere folent, fed nullo cum fructu. Quamobrem in fuperioribus asfertionibus, præfertim feptima & octava, memorati termini phyfici crebriùs adhibiti occurrunt, cùm alii ufu recepti non dentur, quod iis forfan, qui illorum ignari funt, hac in re nonnullam pariet obfcuritatem, quæ tamen, illorum vim & fignificationem intelligentibus fatis, puto, perfpicua eft. Quanquam ferè nullibi non succinctæ terminorum descriptiones & explicationes sint adjectæ, ut vel hinc genuinæ illorum significationes etiam ab iis, qui aliàs illis adsveti non fuerunt, cognosci facilè possint. Neq; est, quod nostri obtrectatores hæc, tanquam Philosophica aut Scholastica, nobis exprobrent, ob quædam de nostra naturali ratione cognoscendi admixta. Ubi enim in explicanda rerum revelatarum cognitione ex Verbo Dei, scripto aut prædicato, versamur, quæ cum nostra naturali ratione cognoscendi in quibusdam convenit, imò eâ parte, quâ apprehensionem simplicem concernit, in se illam includit; in quibusdam verò ab ea multum differt, cumprimis quod ad assensum attinet, fieri quandoq; aliter non potest, quàm ut, discentium bono, majoris perspicuitatis causâ de nostra naturali ratione cognoscendi, materiâ substratâ sic exigente, ex doctrina Physica aliquid adferatur, præsertim ubi, quid Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, ex vi vocum naturaliter; quid item ex vi sensus cum Spiritus S. virtute illuminatrice ad supernaturalem intellectus nostri illuminationē conferat, distinctiùs docendū & explicandum est. Quod verò ad Doctores Scholasticos attinet, tantum abest, ut in hac materia nobis præiverint, ut potiùs Spiritus S. virtutem illuminatricem, Verbo Dei communicatam, & ex parte ejus ad illuminationem intellectus nostri concurrentem præfractè negent. Qua in re tamen, uberiùs ex suis genuinis principiis tradenda, hæc nostra opera tota occupatur.

II. Necessaria tamen est cognitu & utilis doctrina hæc ad accuratiorem & solidiorem Theologiæ cognitionem multis de causis. Primùm enim Sophistarum in Papatu præstigias & fraudes, quas in tradendo objecto sive motivo formali fidei divinæ committunt, penetrare & solidè confutare; veram autem ejus naturam accuratè explicare non potes, nisi de natura & vi motiva Scripturæ sacræ, in quo consistat, & quâ ratione, quibusq; actibus intellectum & voluntatē in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum per se immediatè moveat, probè cognitum & perspectum habeas. Deindè nihil frequentiùs in omnium ore est, quàm aliam esse verè fidelium, aliam hypocritarum, fidelium cœtibus admixtorum fidem; & illorum fidem niti revelatione divinâ; horum humano testimonio. At verò hypocritæ etiam, qui inde à teneris ita informati sunt, quòd Scriptura sacra ex divina revelatione sive inspiratione conscripta sit, credunt suo modo, Deum revelâsse, quæ in Scriptura continentur, & interrogati, cur credant, v. g. Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum; respondent ex animo non ficto, se credere hoc, quia Deus revelavit; Deum verò hoc revelâsse, quia Scriptura sacra dicit. Quid ergo differat horum & illorum fides, discentibus solidè explicare non potes, nisi cognitum & perspectum habeas, verè fidelium fidem sistere in divina revelatione sive in Verbo Dei revelato ultimò, ita ut per hoc credant, Deum revelâsse, quæ in Scriptura continentur, quòd ipsum Verbum Dei suâ illuminatrice virtute intellectum illuminando, voluntatemq; movendo & in consensum trahendo, per se immediatè, citra ullius alterius rationis assentiendi concursum, ad hoc credendum eos moveat; hypocritarum verò & malorum fidem non sistere in divina revelatione ultimò, sed in humano testimonio. Quamvis enim quærenti, cur credant, v. g. Christum esse Filium Dei ungenitum, respondeant, se credere hoc propter divinam revelationem, sive quia Deus revelavit, tamen si ulteriùs quæras, cur credant, Deum revelâsse aut dicere, quæ Scriptura dicit, respondere non possunt, se hoc credere propter ipsam Scripturam, suâ divinâ virtute per se immediatè, intellectum illuminando, voluntatemq; movendo & in consensum trahendo, hoc in se testificantem: horum enim nihil Verbum Dei, scriptum aut prædicatum, in hypocritis & malis, ejus virtuti illuminatrici obicem ponentibus, efficit; sed ultima illorum ratio credendi est, quòd à teneris sic informati sint, & cum lacte quasi doctrinam hanc imbiberint, quòd Scriptura sacra ex divina revelatione conscripta sit, & Deus per eam dicat, quæcunq; illa dicit. Tertiò de Theologia revelata apud nos una omnium mens & sententia est, ejus objectum formale & rationem assentiendi ultimam esse revelationem divinam, sive Verbum Dei, ex divina revelatione in literas relatum. Quia verò experientiâ constat, dari etiam inter hypocritas & impios non rarò, qui tàm exactâ, vel etiam exactiori omnium, quæ in Theologia traduntur, polleant scientiâ, quàm exactâ etiam in pientissimo quoque Theologo dari potest aut datur: emergit hinc quæstio, an Theologiæ habitus etiam in hypocritis & impiis dari possit, & quandoq; detur? Quæ quæstio ut crucem figit discentibus, ita elapsis quinquaginta, & quod excurrit, annis Magdeburgi inter Rectorem Gymnasii & quosdam Ecclesiæ Ministros summa animorum contentione disceptata fuit. Ejus verò decidendæ fundamentum solidum rursum hæc una præbet doctrina de Scripturæ sacræ propria vi motiva intellectus in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum. Quia enim Theologia revelata, omnibus fatentibus, divinam revelationé, Scripturis sacris comprehenfam, sive quod idem est, Scripturam sacram, Deo inspirante confignatam, pro objecto sive motivo formali habet, hujus verò vis motiva propria non alio, quàm hactenùs declarato, modo, illuminando scilicet intellectum, alliciendoq; & trahendo voluntatē in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum movet, necesse est, ut Theologiæ habitus suas conclusiones huc omnes referat, illarumq; assensus in hac Scripturæ sacræ vi motiva ultimò sistat, nec ad ullam ulteriorem assentiendi rationem procedat. Qui autem in hypocritis & impiis etiam datur habitus declarandi, confirmandi & defendendi ea, quæ nostræ salutis causâ revelata sunt, is pro ratione assentiendi ultima non habet revelationem divinam, sive Scripturam, ex divinâ inspiratione confignatam. Non enim ejus assensus sistit ultimò in divina revelatione, intellectum illuminante, voluntatemque pulsante, movente, atq; adeò intellectum per se immediatè in sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem trahente. Nam hypocritæ & mali, quia Verbi divini virtuti illuminatrici obicem ponunt, tale nihil in se experiuntur, sed interrogati, cur credant à Deo revelata & vera esse, quæ in Scriptura sacra continentur, si semetipsos excutiant, & undique omnia, quæ possunt, in subsidium vocent, non tamen invenient, cui hunc suum assensum ultimò adscribant, præter testimonium humanum, quòd inde à teneris sic à parentibus, à præceptoribus, ab Ecclesia informati sint. Quemadmodum autem habitus mentis à ratione assentiendi ultima specificantur, revelatio divina autem, per se intellectum illuminans voluntatemq; movens, & in consensum trahens, atq; adeò sui suæq; à Deo dependentiæ assensum supernaturalem causans; & parentum, præceptorum, Ecclesiæ testimonium de Scriptura sacra ejusq; dependentiâ à Deo, duæ diversæ rationes assentiendi sunt: ita & habitum Theologiæ, quorum alter in divina revelatione ejusq; vi motiva supernaturali, modò declaratâ; alter verò in parentum, præceptorum, Ecclesiæ testimonio de Scriptura sacra ejusq; dependentia à Deo sistit ultimò, habitus Theologiæ diversos esse necesse est. Videantur, quæ supra part. 1. c. III. th. XLII. & XLIV. hanc in rem docuimus: ubi etiam, quid inter habitum Theologiæ utrumq; intercedat discriminis, in quo item conveniant, uberius declaratum invenies.

III. Hæc puto clara, perspicua & intellectu facilia esse, ut à discentibus, ubi de Scripturæ sacræ sive Verbi divini, scripti & prædicati, vi motiva intellectus in assensum sui suæq; dependentiæ à Deo rectè fuerint edocti: in quorum gratiam proptereà rem totam uberius explicare visum fuit. Quod si in tam difficili & arduo negotio non ubique rem acu, quod dicitur, tetigi, spero candidum & æqvum lectorem mihi vel condonaturum lapsum, vel rectiora amicè monstraturum. Monentem & rectiora monstrantem non solùm æquo feram animo, sed etiam lubens sequar.


## 11 On the Authority of Holy Scripture as the Norm of Doctrine

I.

There is one authority, as regards the thing itself, of Holy Scripture, by which it both moves the intellect to the assent of divine faith by way of an object or formal motive, and is the canon, rule, and norm of the doctrine of faith and morals.

For through this Holy Scripture has the power that it moves the intellect to a supernatural assent to itself and to things to be believed, because it has proceeded from God, who knows not how to be deceived or to deceive, and has been recorded by His inspiration: and through this same thing it also has the power that it is the canon, rule, and norm of the doctrine of faith and morals. Let those things be seen which we said above in chapter III, thesis XI regarding this matter.

II.

Whatever, therefore, [is said] concerning the authority of Scripture, in order to to cause the assent of faith considered by way of a formal object, we have taught thus far, all those things proceed also concerning that, considered in relation to the doctrine of faith and morals by way of a canon, norm, and rule.

I. But what we have taught concerning the authority of Holy Scripture, considered in relation to causing the assent of divine faith by way of a formal object, comes down almost to these heads: (1) Because the authority of Scripture results from the supreme truthfulness of God, through which He can neither be deceived nor deceive in speaking or revealing; and from its dependence on God inspiring, it is necessary that both, namely the truthfulness of God and the dependence of Holy Scripture on God revealing or inspiring, be known, if it is to perform the function of a formal object on the part of our intellect and move it to the assent of divine faith. And since there is no difficulty or controversy concerning the former, namely the supreme truthfulness of God in speaking: for it is agreed among all that God is supremely truthful, and can neither be deceived nor deceive in speaking or revealing; concerning the latter, from where does the dependence of Holy Scripture on God become known to us? is the whole difficulty and controversy. (2) That the dependence of Holy Scripture on God can be known by us either by knowledge of human and opinionative faith, from various, as they call them, signs and motives of credibility; or by knowledge of divine and entirely certain faith, by the Holy Spirit with His illuminating power, communicated to Holy Scripture, and always joined to it in the first act, through it illuminating the intellect, and enticing the will, and drawing it into consent. (3) That Holy Scripture, by its divine authority in which it excels, may be able to perform the function of a formal object in us to cause the assent of divine faith, it is required that its dependence on God become known to us by knowledge of divine faith, and that it itself, by its own illuminating power, communicated to it by and joined with the Holy Spirit, begets that in us.

II. But all these things proceed also concerning the authority of Holy Scripture, considered in relation to the doctrine of faith and morals by way of a canon, norm, and rule. For that Holy Scripture is the norm of the doctrine of faith and morals, as regards the matter, is nothing other than that it is the norm and rule, according to which judgment must be passed concerning the truth and falsehood of doctrine pertaining to faith and morals, and it is therefore necessary that the truth of the doctrine of faith and morals, revealed by God in the Holy Scriptures, be known before other doctrines pertaining to faith and morals can be tested by its of judgment whether they agree with it or differ from it. This, however, especially in those things which are of the Spirit of God, cannot be known unless the Holy Scripture, by the illuminating power communicated to it by the Holy Spirit, illuminates the human intellect and draws the will into consent, and thus testifies of its own dependence upon God immediately in the heart of man, according to that saying of Paul: The natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned, I Cor. II. 14.

Latin:

I.

Vna, quoad rem, auctoritas est Scripturæ sacræ, quâ & per modum objecti sive motivi formalis intellectum ad assensum fidei divinæ movet, & doctrinæ fidei ac morum canon, regula & norma est.

Per hoc enim habet Scriptura sacra, quod intellectum in sui & credendorum assensum supernaturalem movet, quòd à Deo, falli & fallere nescio, profecta, & ex ejus inspiratione consignata est: & per hoc ipsum etiam habet eadem, quòd doctrinæ fidei & morum canon, regula & norma est. Videantur, quæ suprà c. III. th. XI. hanc in rem diximus.

II.

Quæcunq; igitur de auctoritate Scripturæ, in ordine ad causandum assensum fidei per modum objecti formalis spectata, hactenus docuimus, ea omnia procedunt etiam de illa, in ordine ad doctrinam fidei & morum per modum canonis, normae & regulae considerata.

I. Quae autem de auctoritate Scripturae sacrae, in ordine ad causandum fidei divinae assensum per modum objecti formalis spectata, docuimus, fere ad haec redeunt capita: (1) Quia auctoritas Scripturae ex Dei summa veracitate, per quam in dicendo sive revelando nec falli nec fallere potest; & ex ejus dependentia a Deo inspirante, resultat, oportere utrumq;, veracitatem Dei scilicet, & Scripturae sacrae dependentiam a Deo revelante sive inspirante, esse cognitum, si objecti formalis munus ex parte nostri intellectus obire, eumq; in assensum fidei divinae movere debeat. Et cum de priori, Dei summa in dicendo veracitate scilicet, nihil difficultatis aut controversiae sit: Deum enim esse summe veracem, & in dicendo sive revelando nec falli nec fallere posse, inter omnes convenit; de posteriori, unde Scripturae sacrae dependentia a Deo nobis innotescat? difficultatem & controversiam omnem esse. (2) Posse autem Scripturae sacrae dependentiam a Deo cognosci a nobis vel notitia fidei humanae & opinativa, ex variis, uti vocant, signis & motivis credibilitatis; vel notitia fidei divinae & prorsus certa, Spiritu Sancto sua illuminatrice virtute, Scripturae sacrae communicata, eiq; in actu primo semper conjuncta, per illam intellectum illuminante, voluntatemque alliciente, & in consensum trahente. (3) Ut Scriptura sacra sua divina, qua pollet, auctoritate ad causandum assensum fidei divinae objecti formalis munus in nobis obire possit, requiri, ut ejus dependentia a Deo notitia fidei divinae nobis innotescat, eamque ipsa sua virtute illuminatrice, a Spiritu S. sibi communicata & conjuncta, in nobis pariat.

II. Haec vero omnia procedunt etiam de auctoritate Scripturae sacrae, in ordine ad doctrinam fidei & morum per modum canonis, normae & regulae spectata. Nam Scripturam sacram esse normam doctrinae fidei & morum, quoad rem, nihil aliud est, quam eam esse normam & regulam, juxta quam cognitam de doctrinæ, ad fidem & mores pertinentis, veritate & falsitate ferendum sit judicium, & oportet proinde veritatem doctrinæ fidei & morum, in Scripturis sacris à Deo revelatam, priùs cognitam esse, quàm aliæ ad fidem & mores pertinentes doctrinæ ad ejus amussim exigi, & congruantne cum illa? an ab ea discrepent? adhibito judicio dignosci possit. Hoc autem, in iis præsertim, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, cognosci non potest, nisi Scripturâ S. suâ à Spiritu S. sibi communicatâ virtute illuminatrice intellectum hominis illuminante, voluntatemq; in consensum trahente, atque sic de sua dependentia à Deo per se immediatè in hominis corde testificante, juxta illud Pauli: Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; stultitia siquidem illi sunt, nec potest cognoscere, quòd spiritualiter dijudicantur, I. Cor. II. 14.


### III. Whence by the same reasons and foundations by which we teach against the…

III.

Whence by the same reasons and foundations by which we teach against the Papists that the authority of Holy Scripture, viewed in relation to causing the assent of divine faith, does not become known to us from the testimony of the Church alone; by these we also teach against the same that the Canonical, or, if I may so speak, the Normative authority of Holy Scripture for the doctrine of faith and morals does not become known to us from the testimony of the Church alone.

IV.

This at least is the difference between its authority, considered in that way and in this, that in the former consideration for causing the assent of divine faith, Holy Scripture is sufficient in any language, whether it was originally written in it, or was later translated into it in imitation of the original text; but in the latter consideration, it cannot be safely used to norm the doctrine of faith and morals, except in its original text.

I. The reason for the diversity is that the motive power of Holy Scripture for the intellect into the assent of divine faith consists in the SENSE. The power of For grace, in that it works in us the assent of divine faith by illuminating the intellect and by moving the will and drawing it into consent, is communicated or joined to the SENSE of Scripture, not to the WORDS, which is certain and placed beyond controversy in our Churches. And because the sense of Scripture is one and the same and remains so, in whatever words of Scripture it may be enunciated, whether the original or another into which it has been translated, therefore also the power to illuminate the minds of men and to cause in them the assent of divine faith, being joined to the sense, is one and the same without any variation of itself, and exerts itself in the hearts of men just as effectively through any Version of Scripture whatsoever as through the original Scripture, provided the version be perspicuous and congruent with the original text.

But the power of norming the doctrines of faith and morals resides not only in the sense, but also in the words which contain the sense and lead us into the knowledge of it. For to the norm of the doctrine of faith and morals, there is required also on the part of the words absolute certainty and infallibility, which excludes every danger of error. But absolute infallibility and certainty, on the part of the words, is not given except from the immediate dependence of the words upon God inspiring: which, however, has no place except in the original text of holy Scripture. For the words which Versions of Scripture, fashioned by human study, contain, although they may be congruent with the authentic text and may conveniently express the sense and mind of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless do not have infallibility: since they have proceeded from men, who could suffer something human and err in translating Scripture: so that all Versions of this kind depend upon the original text, to the imitation of which, as an exemplary cause, they were fashioned, in the matter of certainty and truth, and are not to be received except in so far as they agree with the authentic and original text. Hence

II. To cause the assent of divine faith, it is sufficient if the sense of Scripture, as far as is necessary to be known for salvation, be known and perceived from the words: but that all the minutiae of the words and all the things which are contained in the sense be scrupulously examined is by no means necessary. But for norming the doctrine of faith and morals, a more exact consideration of the words and the underlying things is required, and there are sometimes, especially in more difficult matters and controversies, words and the significations of words, and even the syllables, letters, and all the points of words, and likewise The context and grammatical construction of words, the antecedents, the consequents, the underlying subject matter, the scope of the speaker, and parallel passages must be accurately weighed, so that we may penetrate into a certain and indubitable knowledge both of the sense and of the underlying matters: into which, however, we cannot penetrate except through the original text of Holy Scripture, inasmuch as it is in its words alone, immediately inspired by God, that we can ultimately rest, not in the words of any version composed by human study, since these, as having been applied by men who could err to the imitation of the original text through human and fallible study, must always, wherever a doubt occurs, be examined and weighed according to the standard of the words of the original text. From which it follows that

III. To cause the assent of divine faith, it suffices by the knowledge of divine faith to know that Holy Scripture depends upon God as the inspirer, as regards its formal element or sense, just as in our churches the faithful who use the German version of Blessed Luther know well that the words in which it is recorded were not suggested to Luther by God through immediate inspiration and, as it were, dictated to his pen. Yet the version of Luther itself, when read by them or proposed by the voice of a teacher and perceived by hearing, is no less valid and efficacious for causing the assent of faith than Scripture read or preached in its original text, and it suffices therefore to cause the assent of divine faith, because it testifies of its own dependence upon God, as regards the formal element, namely the sense, by its own divine power conjoined to itself on the part of the sense, in their souls in the manner declared above, and generates in them a supernatural assent. But for the purpose of the Canon and as a standard of the doctrine of faith and morals, it is necessary to know besides that Holy Scripture, to which we flee as to a standard in controversies that have arisen, depends also on the part of its material element, namely on the part of the words, upon God through immediate inspiration.

Latin:

III.

Unde quibus rationibus & fundamentis contra Pontificios docemus, auctoritatem sacræ Scripturæ, in ordine ad causandum fidei divinæ assensum spectatam, non innotescere nobis ex solo Ecclesiæ testimonio; iis docemus etiam contra eosdem, Scripturæ sacræ auctoritatem Canonicam, sive, ut ita loquar, Normativam doctrinæ fidei & morum non innotescere nobis ex solo Ecclesiæ testimonio.

IV.

Hoc saltem intercedit discriminis inter ejus auctoritatem, illo & hoc modo consideratam, quòd in consideratione priori ad causandum assensum fidei divinæ sufficit Scriptura sacra in qualibet lingua, sive primitus eâ conscripta, sive postea ad textus primigenii imitationem in illam translata sit; in posteriori verò consideratione ad normandam doctrinam fidei & morum tutò adhiberi non potest, nisi in suo textu primigenio.

I. Ratio diversitatis est, quòd Scripturæ sacræ vis motiva intellectus in assensum fidei divinæ consistit in SENSU. Virtus divina enim, quâ illuminando intellectum, voluntatemq; movendo & in consensum trahendo assensum fidei divinæ in nobis operatur, SENSUI Scripturæ, non VERBIS communicata sive conjuncta est, quod in Ecclesiis nostris certum & extra controversiam positum est. Et quia sensus Scripturæ unus & idem est & manet, cujuscunq; sive primigeniæ, sive alterius, in quam translata est, Scripturæ verbis enuncietur, ideò & virtus ad illuminandos hominum animos, causandumq; in iis fidei divinæ assensum, sensui conjuncta, absque ulla sui variatione una & eadem est, & æquè efficaciter ad hunc effectum per Versionem Scripturæ quamcunq;, ac per Scripturam primigeniam, sese in hominum cordibus exerit, modò versio perspicua, & textui primigenio congrua sit.

Vis verò normandi doctrinas fidei & morum non soli inest sensui, sed & verbis, quæ sensum continent, & in ejus cognitionem nos deducunt. Ad normam enim doctrinæ fidei & morum requiritur etiam ex parte verborum certitudo & infallibilitas absoluta, quæ omne erroris periculum excludat. Infallibilitas verò & certitudo absoluta, ex parte verborum, non datur, nisi ex immediata verborum dependentia â Deo inspirante: quæ verò non locum habet, nisi in primigenio Scripturæ sacræ textu. Quæ enim verba Versiones Scripturæ, humano studio concinnatæ, continent, licet textui authentico congrua sint, & sensum ac mentem Spiritus Sancti convenienter exprimant, infallibilitatem tamen non habent: cùm ab hominibus, qui humani quid pati, & in transferenda Scriptura errare potuerunt, profecta sint: ut ita hujus generis Versiones omnes â textu primigenio, ad cujus, velut causæ exemplaris, imitationem concinnatæ sunt, in ratione certitudinis & veritatis dependeant, nec recipiendæ sint, nisi quatenus cum textu authentico & primigenio conveniunt. Hinc

II. Ad causandum assensum fidei divinæ sufficit, si sensus Scripturæ, quantum ad salutem cognitu necessarium est, ex verbis cognitus & perceptus sit: ut autem omnes vocum, omnesq; rerum, quæ in sensu continentur, minutiæ scrupulosè excutiantur, necessariû minimè est. Sed ad normandam doctrinam fidei & morum exactior verborum & rerũ substratarũ consideratio exigitur, suntq; quandoq;, præsertim in rebus & controversiis difficilioribus, voces vocumq; significationes, quin & vocum syllabæ, literæ, & apices omnes, itemq; vocum contextus & constructio Grammatica, antecedentia, consequentia, materia substrata, scopus dicentis & loca parallela accuratè expendenda, ut in certam & indubitatam cùm sensus tùm rerum substratarum cognitionem penetremus: in quam verò penetrare non possumus, nisi per primigenium Scripturæ sacræ textum, utpote in cujus solius à Deo immediatè inspiratis verbis ultimò sistere possumus, non in verbis ullius studio humano concinnatæ Versionis, quippe quæ, ut ab hominibus, qui labi potuerunt, ad imitationem textus primigenii humano & labili studio adhibita, ita ubicunque dubitatio occurrit, semper ad normam verborum textus primigenii exanimanda & expendenda sunt. Ex quo fluit, quòd

III. Ad causandum assensum fidei divinæ sufficiat notitiâ fidei divinæ nosse Scripturam sacram dependere à Deo inspirante, quoad suum formale sive sensum, sicut in nostris Ecclesiis fideles, qui B. Lutheri Versione Germanicâ utuntur, probè norunt, verba, quibus consignata est, non fuisse Luthero per immediatam inspirationem à Deo suggesta, & in calamum quasi dictitata. Ipsa tamen Lutheri Versio, ab iis lecta aut docentis voce proposita, & auditu percepta, ad causandum assensum fidei non minùs valida & efficax est, quàm in suo textu primigenio lecta vel prædicata Scriptura, & sufficit proinde ad causandum assensum fidei divinæ, quod de sui dependentia à Deo, quoad formale, sensum scilicet, suâ divinâ virtute, ex parte sensus sibi conjunctâ, in illorum animis modo supra declarato testificetur, suiƣ; assensum supernaturalem in illis generet. Ad rationem Canonis verò & normam doctrinæ fidei & morum nosse prætereà oportet, Scripturam sacram, ad quam velut ad normam in exortis controversiis confugimus, dependere etiam ex parte materiali sui, ex parte verborum scilicet, à Deo per immediatam inspirationem.


### V. But from whence may it become known to us in what idiom Holy Scripture was…

V.

But from whence may it become known to us in what idiom Holy Scripture was originally recorded, and which is the original text of each book? It remains to be examined.

I. This question, however, must be accurately distinguished from another question, which is a matter of controversy for us with the Papists, namely, from whence the divine dependence of Holy Scripture upon God becomes known to us? For this concerns Scrithe whole of Holy Scripture, viewed in terms of its formal and material aspects together. But what comes here to be examined concerning the original text of Holy Scripture, from whence it may become known to us, concerns only the material of Scripture, namely the words and the idiom of the words in which it was originally recorded. To that, the Doctors of our Church and all of them, so far as I know, respond with one voice that the divine authority of Holy Scripture does not become known to us from the testimony of the Church alone, but also from other criteria and signs, partly internal and partly external, and especially from the internal testimony of Holy Scripture, by which it testifies of its dependence upon God immediately in the hearts of men by itself; whose opinion we have hitherto declared at length, having produced in order the more important signs and criteria, both internal and external, and we have shown that from these the divine authority of Holy Scripture becomes known to us only by an opinative knowledge of human faith; but that it becomes known by a knowledge of divine faith from the internal testimony of Scripture alone through its illuminating power, by which it illuminates the intellect of man, and strikes, entices, and draws the will into consent, and thus moves the minds of men by itself immediately into a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God. The question, however, concerning the material of Scripture, namely the words and the context of the words in which each book of Scripture was originally recorded by its Author, which now comes to be considered, is HISTORICAL, and comes down to this: from whence may it become known to us in what idiom or language each book of Scripture was originally recorded by its Author and delivered to the Church which flourished at that time?

VI.

This, however, cannot be known by us more certainly than from the testimony of the primitive Church.

This question is one of fact, concerning a sensible thing, namely the written Word, and its sensible tradition, by which it reached the Church either through the hands of the sacred writers themselves who were present, or through the messengers of those who were absent under their sensible subscription. In resolving this, it is not permitted to have recourse to the internal illuminating power of Holy Scripture, by which it might testify of the original text of each sacred book supernaturally in the hearts of men by itself. For this divine power of testifying is joined to the sense of Scripture, not to its words, which, when read in their original text, do not testify any more of the divinity of their idiom than when read in the vernacular Version of Blessed Luther they testify of the divinity of our vernacular idiom in which it is recorded, but it testifies in both cases concerning the divinity of the sense and doctrine, proposed in words either original or of another interpreter. Nor can other criteria and signs, whether internal or external, of a certain and determined, e.g., Hebrew or Greek idiom, in which each book of Scripture was recorded by its author, provide certain and indubitable proof. We did indeed enumerate above in Chapter V, Section 1, among the internal criteria or signs, the simplicity of style, joined with a gravity worthy of God, in the first place, which although it pertains in its own way to the material of Scripture, namely the words and their context, and confusedly argues that God is also the author of the material of Scripture, in whatever determined idiom that may consist, yet a certain and determined Hebrew or Greek idiom of speech, in which each book of Scripture was originally recorded, cannot certainly be inferred from this. For this affection and property of style is common to the Scriptures of both Testaments, whose books, however, were originally recorded some in the Hebrew, others in the Greek idiom; and interpreters can also express the same in their versions: e.g., what God proposes in the Scriptures of the O. and N. T. to be believed or done by simply asserting and commanding, that is read in the Version of B. Luther to be proposed in the same manner without the paint and allurements of words, asserting those things by authority without demonstrations; commanding these things without persuasive reasons. If anywhere also from the proper names employed, and their interpretations, or from elsewhere, some indications of a certain and determined idiom, in which any book was originally written, should occur, they will certainly occur more rarely, and in small particles of Holy Scripture, and will by no means produce knowledge of divine faith, but only probable and opinative knowledge.

But the other criteria and internal signs, from which the divine authority of Holy Scripture becomes known to us in some way, are taken from the formal aspect of Scripture, namely the sense and the things signified, and they return to three heads, namely truth, pure from error, holiness, perfect without blemish, and its sufficiency for salvation, full without defect; but these, just as the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit communicated to Holy Scripture, testify concerning the divinity of the sense and doctrine revealed in it, not concerning the divinity of the words and the idiom in which it is recorded. For the truth of the doctrine remains without admixed error, and its holiness without blemish, and its sufficiency for salvation without defect, are distinguished proofs of the divinity of Scripture, in whatever idiom it may be contained, whether the original or another into which it has been translated. But those things which, when viewed in the sacred Scripture in its original text and in any version conformable to the original text, equally agree, cannot be the κριτήρια and signs of any certain and determined idiom in which sacred Scripture was originally recorded.

Among external signs we have numbered the antiquity of sacred Scripture, the ἀξιοπιστίαν of the sacred writers, the miracles performed by Moses, Christ, and the Apostles, the consensus of the Church, the testimony of the martyrs, the happy and sudden propagation of Christian doctrine throughout the world, and its unshaken preservation amidst so many tyrannies and persecutions, etc. All of which, with the exception of the testimony of the Church alone, bear witness to the divinity of the sense and doctrine alone, not to the determined idiom of any language in which each book of Scripture was originally recorded. And the antiquity of Scripture indeed, which we named in the first place, besides the fact that in its concept it implies no determined kind of language and idiom in which it was originally written, is also estimated in the question concerning the divinity of sacred Scripture chiefly from its formal aspect, namely its sense and doctrine, by the consideration of which alone it is more ancient than every other religion and every other doctrine concerning the salvation of men, inasmuch as it took its beginning with the Protoplasts themselves, partly through their creation, partly through divine revelation, as was shown above in chapter V, section II. And Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, writers who were indeed ἀξιόπιστοι, attribute the Scriptures composed by them to God, yet neither he nor they mention anywhere that they recorded them originally, by God's inspiration, in the Hebrew or the Greek idiom. Similarly, miracles were performed in confirmation of the doctrine handed down by Moses, Christ, and the Apostles; which also was propagated so suddenly and happily throughout the world, not under one determined idiom, but in various languages. Furthermore, the question for the persecutors of the Church was not about this or that idiom of Scripture, but about the Christian doctrine itself, which the faithful of Christ embraced, but which they were unwilling to tolerate; and that the pious martyrs, fearing no tortures and no kind of most ignominious death, intrepidly confessed this before their persecutors, and with their confession sealed it with their own blood, the sacred histories record. Nothing therefore remains, from which anything can be determined with certainty concerning the original text, in which each book of Scripture was consigned by its Author, except the testimony of the PRIMITIVE CHURCH.

II. By the name of the PRIMITIVE CHURCH, however, we understand the Church which flourished in those times when the writers of the books of both Testaments lived in the flesh: namely, the Jewish, which from Moses down to Malachi, the last of the Prophets; and the Christian, which, newly planted by the Apostles throughout the world, and while they, or some of them, were still alive, served under the banner of Christ. For during that tract of time the books of the Old, and during this the books of the New Testament were all written, and were delivered by their Authors to the Jewish Church and the Christian Church respectively; and both, relying on the testimony of the senses, could know and testify with equal certainty which books, written in what idiom of language and speech, they had received from the hands of their Authors. This, I think, no one will deny. But whether this testimony of both Churches can be possessed by us today, perhaps someone might doubt.

To remove this scruple, therefore, it must be known that this testimony was propagated by the first Churches through tradition from hand to hand to posterity, first indeed with the very autographs of the sacred books, preserved with the greatest care and zeal and transmitted to posterity, so that in what idiom of speech each book was originally consigned, the Churches of later centuries could be certain not only from the tradition of the former, but also from the ocular inspection of the autographs themselves. Thus under the Old Testament, the Church which existed in the time of Moses saw with its own eyes that the two Tables brought down by Moses from Mount Sinai, on which the precepts of the Decalogue were inscribed, were written in the Hebrew idiom; and this very autograph of Moses was afterwards, by God's command, deposited in the Ark of the Covenant as a peculiar and invaluable κειμήλιον of the Church; and in the progress of time, with the ark, it was brought into the Sanctuary of the temple built by King Solomon, and kept there, Deut. X. 5. I Kings VIII. 9. II Chron. V. 10. Afterwards, the ocular inspection of the Church again taught that the Pentateuch was written by Moses in the Hebrew idiom. And the very copy written by the hand of Moses was preserved at the side of the same ark, where, by Moses' command, it was deposited, Deut. XXXI. 25. In the same manner, the Church, which from their hands

Latin:

V.

Unde autem nobis innotescat, quo idiomate Scriptura sacra primitùs consignata, & quinam cujusque libri textus primigenius sit? dispiciendum superest.

I. Est autem quæstio hæc accuratè distingvenda ab altera, nobis cum Pontificiis controversa quæstione, unde scilicet divina Scripturæ sacræ dependentia à Deo nobis innotescat? Hæc enim concernit Scripturam sacram totam, ex parte sui formalis & materialis simul spectatam. Quæ autem hic de Scripturæ sacræ textu primigenio, unde nobis innotescat? excutienda venit, solum materiale Scripturæ, verba scilicet & verborum idioma, quo primitus consignata est, concernit. Ad illam Ecclesiæ nostræ ejusq́; Doctores uno ore, quod sciã, omnes respondent, divinam Scripturæ sacræ auctoritatem non innotescere nobis ex solo Ecclesiæ testimonio, sed etiam ex aliis, internis partim, partim externis κριτηρίοις & signis, cumprimis verò ex interna Scripturæ sacræ testificatione, quâ de sua dependentia à Deo per se immediatè in hominum cordibus testatur; quorum sententiam nos hactenus fusè declaravimus, signis & κριτηρίοις potioribus, cùm internis, tùm externis, ordine productis, oftendimusq́;, ex illis innotescere nobis divinam Scripturæ sacræ auctoritatem tantum humanæ fidei opinativâ notitiâ; notitiâ fidei divinæ verò innotescere eam ex sola Scripturæ interna testificatione per suam virtutem illuminatricem, quâ intellectum hominis illuminat, voluntatemq́; pulsat, allicit & in consensum trahit, atque adeò per se immediatè hominum mentes in assensum supernaturalem suæ à Deo dependentiæ movet. Quæstio autem de materiali Scripturæ, verbis scilicet & verborum contextu, quo quisq; Scripturæ liber primitùs à suo Auctore consignatus est, quæ nunc consideranda venit, HISTORICA est, & huc redit: unde nobis innotescat, quo idiomate vel linguâ quisque Scripturæ liber ab Auctore suo primitus consignatus, & Ecclesiæ, quæ illo tempore floruit, traditus sit?

VI.

Hoc verò certiùs à nobis cognosci non potest, quàm ex testimonio Ecclesiæ primitivæ.

Quæstio hæc facti est, de re sensibili, Verbo scilicet scripto, ejusque sensibili traditione, quâ vel per præsentium Scriptorum sacrorum manus, vel absentium nuncios sub illorum subscriptione sensibili ad Ecclesiam pervenit. In qua enodanda ad internam Scripturæ sacræ virtutem illuminatricem, quâ de cujusque libri sacri textu primigenio per se ipsam supernaturaliter in hominum cordibus testificetur, confugere non licet. Hæc enim divina testificandi vis Scripturæ conjuncta est sensui, non verbis ejus, quæ in suo textu primigenio lecta non magis de divinitate idiomatis sui, quàm in vernacula B. Lutheri Versione lecta de divinitate nostri vernaculi idiomatis, quo consignata est, testificatur, sed ea testificatur utrobiq; de divinitate sensus doctrinæq;, verbis sive primigeniis sive alterius Interpretis propositæ. Neque etiam alia sive interna sive externa κριτήρια & signa certi & determinati v. g. Ebræi vel Græci idiomatis, quo quisq; Scripturæ liber ab Auctore suo consignatus sit, certum & indubitatum documentum præbere possunt. Numeravimus quidem suprà Cap. V. Sect. 1. inter κριτήρια sive signa interna simplicitatem styli, cum gravitate, Deo dignâ conjunctam, primo loco, quæ licet suo modo ad materiale Scriptuæ, verba scilicet eorumq; contextum pertineat, & confusè Deum etiam materialis Scripturæ, in quocunque determinato idiomate illud consistat, Auctorem arguat, non tamen certum & determinatum, Ebræum vel Græcum sermonis idioma, quo primitus quisq; Scripturæ liber consignatus sit, hinc certò colligi potest. Nam hæc styli affectio & proprietas Scripturis utriusque Testamenti communis est, quarum tamen libri alii Ebræo, alii Græco idiomate primitùs consignati sunt; & possunt eandem interpretes etiam in Versionibus suis exprimere: v. g. quæ in Scripturis V. & N. T. Deus credenda aut agenda simpliciter asserendo & jubendo proponit, ea in Versione B. Lutheri eundem in modum absque verborum fuco & lenociniis, pro auctoritate, illa sine demonstrationibus asserendo; hæc sine rationibus persuasoriis jubendo proponere legitur. Sicubi etiam ex adhibitis nominibus propriis, illorumq; interpretationibus, vel aliunde certi & determinati idiomatis, quo primitus liber aliquis conscriptus sit, indicia aliqua occurrant, ea certè occurrent rariùs, & in exiguis Scripturæ sacræ particulis, nec nisi notitiam probabilem & opinativam, minimè verò fidei divinæ notitiam gignent.

Cætera verò κριτήρια & signa interna, ex quibus divina Scripturæ sacræ auctoritas nobis aliquo modo innotescit, ex formali Scripturæ, sensu scilicet & rebus significatis desumta sunt, & ad tria redeunt capita, veritatem scilicet, ab errore puram, sanctitatem absq; nævo perfectam, & ejus sufficientiam ad salutem absq; defectu plenam; sed hæc perinde, ut Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, Scripturæ sacræ communicata, de divinitate sensus & doctrinæ in ea revelatæ testantur, non de divinitate verborum & idiomatis, quibus ea consignata est. Manent enim veritas doctrinæ sine admixto errore, ejusq; sanctitas fine nævo, & sufficientia illius ad salutem sine defectu documenta divinitatis Scripturæ insignia, quocunque ea, sive primigenio sive alio, in quod translata est, idiomate contineatur. Quæ autem Scripturæ sacræ in suo primigenio textu, & in quacunq; textui primigenio conformi Versione spectatæ, æquè conveniunt, ea non possunt certi & determinati cujusdam idiomatis, quo primitus Scriptura sacra confignata sit, κριτήρια & signa esse.

In externis signis numeravimus Scripturæ sacræ antiquitatem, Scriptorum sacrorum ἀξιοπιστίαν, miracula, à Mose, Christo & Apostolis patrata, Ecclesiæ consensum, testimonium Martyrum, felicem & subitam doctrinæ Christianæ propagationem per orbem terrarum, ejusdemq; inter tot tyrannides & persecutiones inconcussam conservationem &c. Quæ omnia, uno Ecclesiæ testimonio excepto, de solius sensus & doctrinæ divinitate, non de determinato cujusdam linguæ & sermonis idiomate, quo primitus quisq; Scripturæ liber confignatus sit, testimonium perhibent. Et Antiquitas Scripturæ quidem, quam primo nominavimus loco, præterquam quod in suo conceptu nullum determinatum linguæ & idiomatis genus, quo primitis conscripta sit, importat, æstimatur etiam in quæstione de divinitate Scripturæ sacræ potissimùm ex suo formali, sensu scilicet & doctrina, cujus solius intuitu aliâ religione omni, omniq; alia doctrinâ de hominum salute antiquior est, quippe quæ cum ipsis Protoplastis, partim per illorum creationem, partim per divinam revelatione suum sumfit initium, ut suprà c. V. Sect. II. ostensum. Et Moses, Prophetæ & Apostoli, Scriptores utiq; ἀξιόπιστοι, Scripturas à se concinnatas Deo quidem acceptas ferunt, non tamen vel ille aut isti, quòd Ebræo; vel hi quòd Græco idiomate eas, Deo inspirante, primitus consignarint, ullibi locorum memorant. Similiter miracula in confirmationem doctrinæ, à Mose, Christo & Apostolis traditæ, patrata sunt; quæ etiam non sub uno determinato idiomate, sed in lingvis variis tam subitò & feliciter per orbem terrarum propagata est. Prætereà persecutoribus Ecclesiæ non de hoc aut illo Scripturæ idiomate, sed de ipsa doctrina Christiana, quam Christi fideles amplectebantur, illi autem tolerare nolebant, quæstio erat; & hanc pios Martyres, nullos cruciatus, nullum ignominiosissimæ mortis genus veritos, coram suis persecutoribus intrepidè confessos esse, & confessione suam sanguine suo obsignâsse, historiæ sacræ memorant. Nihil ergo superest, ex quo de textu primigenio, quo quisq; Scripturæ liber à suo Auctore consignatus est, certò quid determinari possit, præter ECCLESIÆ PRIMITIVÆ testimonium.

II. ECCLESIÆ PRIMITIVÆ appellatione autem intelligimus Ecclesiam, quæ iis floruit temporibus, quibus Scriptores librorum utriusq; Fœderis in carne vixerunt: Judaicam scilicet, quæ à Mose usque ad Malachiam, Prophetarum ultimum; & Christianam, quæ recens ab Apostolis per orbem terrarum plantata iisq;, vel aliquibus illorum adhuc vivis sub Christi vexillo militavit. Illo enim temporis tractu Veteris; hoc Novi Fœderis libri omnes conscripti, & illi Ecclesiæ Judaicæ; hi Christianæ Ecclesiæ à suis Auctoribus traditi sunt, & potuit utraq;, sensuum testimonio nixa, pari certitudine nôsse & testari, quos libros, quo linguæ & sermonis idiomate scriptos ex suorum Auctorum manibus accepisset. Id quod nemo, puto, negaverit. Utrum verò hoc Ecclesiæ utriusque testimonium à nobis hodiè haberi possit, forsan quis dubitaverit.

Ad eximendum ergo hunc scrupulum, sciendum, testimonium hoc ab Ecclesiis primis per traditionem de manu ad manum ad posteritatem propagatum esse, primò quidem cum ipsis librorum sacrorum autographis, summâ curâ & studio asservatis & ad posteros transmissis, ut quo sermonis idiomate quisque liber primitus consignatus fuerit, posteriorum seculorum Ecclesiæ non tantum ex anterioris traditione, sed etiã ex oculari ipsorummet autographorum inspectione constare posset. Sic sub Veteri Fœdere, quæ Mosis tempore fuit Ecclesia, duas à Mose de monte Sinai delatas Tabulas, quibus Decalogi præcepta inscripta erant, Ebraico idiomate scriptas esse, ipsis oculis suis vidit, & hoc ipsum Mosis autographum postea, Dei jussu, velut peculiare & inæstimabile Ecclesiæ κειμήλιον, in arca Fœderis repositum; & temporis progressu cum arca Sacrario templi, à Salomone Rege extructi, illatum, ibiq; custoditum est, Deut. X. 5. I.Reg.VIII.9. II.Paral.V.10. Postea Pentateuchum Ebraico idiomate à Mose scriptum esse, Ecclesiam rursum ocularis inspectio docuit. Ipsum verò Mosis manu exaratum exemplar in latere ejusdem arcæ, ubi, Mosis jussu, repositum fuit, asservatum est, Deut. XXXI. 25. Eundem in modum Prophetarum aliorumq; Virorum sanctorum autographa Ebraico idiomate scripta fuisse, Ecclesia, quæ ex illorum manibus


### received the autographs of the Prophets and other holy men written in the…

received the autographs of the Prophets and other holy men written in the Hebrew idiom, certainly recognized them by the benefit of the senses, and guarded them with equal care and zeal, and propagated them to posterity, so that the autographs of the Holy Scriptures were available to the Church of the Old Testament for long centuries, and whenever there was need, they could be produced into view. Then the same testimony of the primitive Church concerning the original text of Holy Scripture was also propagated to posterity along with the copies of the autographs. For because the Church guarded the autographs themselves, like a precious treasure, with the greatest care, copies of them were adorned by scribes in imitation and likeness of the autographs with the greatest care and diligence that could be achieved, both for the public use of the Church and for the use of individual believers. And just as these were in all respects conformable to the autographs in words, and in the letters, syllables, and points of the words, so the more numerous they were, agreeing with one another from every side, existing at all times in the Church, and propagated to posterity, the more certain witnesses of the original text, and beyond all exception, they were for the Churches of all times. And this twofold way of propagating the testimony concerning the original text of each book is and was common to both [the Old and New Testament] primitive Churches. For there is no doubt that the recently planted Apostolic Churches preserved the autographs of the books of the New Testament received from the Apostles and Apostolic men with care and zeal no less than the Church of the Old Testament preserved the autographs of its books, and transmitted them to their posterity by the tradition of hands. Although indeed the Christian Church, from its very infancy, was exposed to the most dire persecutions, and took its beginnings and growth with the shed blood of pious martyrs, so that in so many most grievous persecutions, in which both teachers and hearers were dragged off in crowds to martyrdom, it could easily happen that the autographs of the Apostolic writings perished along with the holy confessors of Apostolic doctrine themselves: nevertheless Tertullian, who flourished at the end of the second century, testifies in his booklet De Praescriptione that the authentic letters of the Apostles still survived in the Apostolic Churches in his time. Come, he says, you who wish to exercise your curiosity better in the business of salvation, run through the APOSTOLIC CHURCHES, in which the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their places, in which their AUTHENTIC LETTERS are recited, sounding the voice, representing the face. Is Achaia near to you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi. If you can reach Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you are adjacent to Italy, you have Rome, etc. Where the Author undoubtedly understands by AUTHENTIC LETTERS of the Apostles their very autographs, which different Churches had received from them themselves. For copies existed everywhere in all the Churches, so that for their sake there was no need to travel through the Churches to which the Epistles had been written. Moreover, in the primitive Church, copies of the sacred Scriptures existed in such greater abundance, and they testified to the original text of each book all the more certainly, the further it was spread throughout the world, and the more particular Churches, which were most extensive in their scope, it comprised than the Jewish one. For the Churches spread throughout the world communicated with one another, and transmitted to each other copies of the sacred books which they had received from the sacred writers, entirely conformed to the autographs, most faithfully, so that in a short time, and while the sacred writers themselves were still living, even Churches most widely separated from one another obtained genuine and undefiled copies of all the Apostolic writings. Which subsequently bore clear testimony to posterity at all times concerning the original text of each book. Concerning the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews, whether they were originally written in the Greek or the Hebrew idiom? It was once doubted. To explain whence this arose is not the purpose of this place. For the present it suffices that the primitive Church acknowledged with the highest consensus that these very books, if not originally written in the Greek idiom, were nevertheless translated into the Greek language by divine inspiration, and always held them in the Greek text in the Code of the authentic N.T. Scripture, following the example of the Hebrew, which, although undoubtedly original, was scarcely seen by any ancient Church.

To the testimony of the Jewish Church concerning the original text of the O.T. Scripture, two things further are added, by which the method of preserving it and propagating it to late posterity was aided and increased. One is the subsequent notable testimony of Ezra and the Great Sanhedrin. For when in the total destruction of Jerusalem and the conflagration of Solomon's temple not a few autographs and copies of the sacred books had perished, and the examples that remained during the time of the harshest servitude for a long time had been held in neglect, Ezra, Scribe and interpreter of the law, a man distinguished by talent and learning, undoubtedly stirred by the singular instinct and providence of God, immediately after the return of the people from their long and harsh servitude to their native land and the restored City of Jerusalem, reviewed all the books of Scripture with the greatest care and labor, collected those that were dispersed, arranged those that were disordered, and gathered them into one codex, distinct in a certain number, comprising twenty-two books, and distributed into three great parts, the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, having taken into the fellowship of his labor and effort the men of the Great Synagogue, among whom were the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, all of them θεόπνευστοι (God-breathed) men. And these, by joined studies and counsels, established the codex of the authentic Old Testament Scriptures by public authority, so that no one could have any doubt concerning the number and the original text of the books. Which codex was subsequently held in the Church as authentic, and all copies were adorned according to its exemplar, and in an uninterrupted order, even until Christ exhibited in the flesh, they were propagated as if from hand to hand and preserved undefiled. The other is the infallible testimony of Christ and the Apostles. For this very Hebrew Scripture, comprised in the codex well-ordered by Ezra and distributed into the LAW, PROPHETS, and HAGIOGRAPHA, the copies of which were then worn by the hands of all, Christ and the Apostles, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, approved by their very use, and commended to the Churches as genuine and inspired by God, as among other places can be read in Luke 16:29, 24:44, Acts 26:22, and 28:23. Hence, having obtained new authority, the Scripture of the Old Testament was received in the Apostolic or universal Christian Church with the highest consensus, and has been propagated to us in its undefiled copies by uninterrupted tradition.

Although indeed the copies of the books alone, which at all times existed in innumerable multitude in the Churches and were transmitted by continued tradition to posterity and even to us, might suffice for propagating the testimony of the primitive Apostolic Church concerning the original text of the Scripture of both Covenants; nevertheless, there exist express testimonies of the most ancient Fathers concerning the Canon of Scripture, both of the Old and New Testament, by which it is taught which sacred books, under what original text, from the times of the Apostles, to the Churches were in use: which even now survive among the most ancient writers of undoubted credibility. Among them, by his own merit, stands out St. Melito, Bishop of Sardis in Asia, a man of great name among his own, who lived in the middle of the second century, and, having been asked by Onesimus to compile for him certain excerpts from the Law and the Prophets which pertained to the Savior and to our entire faith, and likewise to record how many in number and in what order the books of the Old Testament were written, for the sake of greater certainty he traveled to the East, where those things were both preached and done, and having traveled through the churches and accurately explored the canon of the books of the Old Testament, he records in his Epistle to the aforementioned Onesimus that he found no others, nor more, nor in a different order than they are held in the Hebrew Code established by Ezra. A fragment of the Epistle, in which the canon of the books, explored by him in the Oriental churches, is recounted, exists in Eusebius, Book IV of Church History, chapter XXVI. In the same number and order in which Melito did, Origen, who flourished in the third century, reviewed the books of the Old Testament in his exposition of the first Psalm; but he reviewed the books of the New Testament in the same number and order in which they are still in the canon among us today, partly in Book I of his Exposition on Matthew, and partly also in Book V of his Exposition on John. Regarding the Epistle to the Hebrews, however, he revealed his own judgment specifically in the Homilies which he wrote on this Epistle, as can be seen in Eusebius, Book VI, chapter XXV. Although Origen indeed had his flaws, and not light ones at that, he was nevertheless able to investigate and teach the number and order of the sacred books of both Testaments all the more correctly because he was more skilled in the Hebrew language, closer to the age of the Apostles, and had devoted almost all his study to interpreting the Scriptures. Nor is the testimony of Eusebius regarding the canon of the New Testament to be esteemed any less. For although he is nearly two hundred years younger than Melito and a hundred and something years younger than Origen, there still existed in his age monuments of the most ancient Fathers, some of whom had seen certain Apostles in the flesh; some had seen some of their hearers and disciples and had conversed with them; while others were otherwise very close to the time of the Apostles, which he handled with tireless study by night and by day, and from their testimonies he wove together a catalog of the books of the New Testament, in the exact same order and number in which it still exists in the Christian Church today. And indeed, after he had dealt with each of the sacred writers in order and at length, and had accurately taught which books each had written and in what language, having brought forward from all sides the most ancient Fathers He finally subjoined to the testimonies in Book III, Chapter XXV, the Canon of the New Testament Scripture received in the universal Church from the time of the Apostles, in this order and number: 'Moreover,' he says, 'it seems opportune in this place to review summarily the books of the New Testament, of which we have already spoken. First, therefore, the sacred quadriga of the Gospels must be placed; which the Acts of the Apostles then follow. Next are to be numbered the Epistles of Paul. Then that former one of John, and likewise the Epistle of Peter, is to be accepted. Finally, if it shall seem so, the revelation of John is to be added: concerning which we shall explain in its own place what the ancients thought. And these indeed have been received by the common consent of all.' So he: where he does not indeed specifically express the Quadriga of the Holy Gospels; which, however, he had enumerated in order and distinctly in the immediately preceding chapter, having assigned the first place to the Gospel of Matthew; the second to Mark; the third to Luke; and the fourth to John. Nor does he distinctly review the Epistles of Paul, thinking that to be unnecessary, since it was agreed among all which and how many they were: nevertheless, in the previous Chapter III of this book, he had said that they were fourteen in number, and all προδήλυς καὶ σαφεῖς, that is, manifest and explored, and he had warned concerning the one which is to the Hebrews that it was doubted by some whether it had been written originally in Hebrew or in Greek; concerning which matter he treated more prolixly afterwards in this same Book III, Chapter XXXVIII, and Book VI, Chapters XI and XIII. Furthermore, concerning the Apocalypse of John, Eusebius notably adds in the place cited above: 'If it shall seem so,' and, 'concerning which we shall explain in its own place what the ancients thought.' For its authority had been doubted by some. Concerning which matter he discourses at length afterwards in Book VIII, Chapter XXIII, from Dionysius of Alexandria, who lived in the middle of the third century, and transcribed his words, by which he had gone to assert its divine authority. Moreover, Eusebius subjoins: Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐν ὁμολογυμένοις, i.e., AND THESE INDEED (the enumerated writings) HAVE BEEN RECEIVED BY THE COMMON CONSENT OF ALL, as the Valesian Version renders the Greek words.
