Next to these he adds other parts of the N.T. Canon, inferior to the former in this, that concerning these there had been doubt by some Churches formerly about their divine origin; whereas concerning those, there had never been doubt by any Churches, which he reviews in the same order and number in which they are still held among us, in these words: 'But of those which are called into doubt, yet are seen to be commemorated by many, there is'

The Epistle which is called of JAMES, and that of JUDE, and the SECOND of PETER, likewise the SECOND and THIRD of JOHN, whether they were composed by the Evangelist himself in truth, or by another of the same name. These books of Scripture are called today by some, in distinction from the others which have never been called into doubt, ἀδευτεροκανονικοὶ or of the second canonical order. But to pursue this at greater length is not the purpose of the present undertaking. Let us return from the digression to the path.

III. From this testimony, drawn from the very beginning of both the Church, namely of the Old and New Testament, and derived to us through uninterrupted tradition, we deem it necessary to learn in what language and idiom of speech each book of Scripture was originally written, and we assert fearlessly that a more certain witness of this matter cannot be given. If any Church existing in later centuries and more remote from the primitive one should presume to pass a different judgment on this question, and one diverse from the testimony of the primitive Church, and to receive into the Canon some books not acknowledged and received by it, or to exterminate from the same those once received by the primitive one: the former of which the Pontifical Church has dared to do up to this point; then its judgment shall not be heard.

Latin:

illa accepit, sensuum beneficio certò cognovit, eaq; pari curâ & studio custodita ad posteros propagavit, ut ita Ecclesiæ V. T. longis seculis Sanctorum Scriptorum autographa in promptu fuerint, & quandocunque opus esset, in conspectum produci potuerint. Deinde idem Ecclesiæ primitivæ testimonium de primigenio Scripturæ sacræ textu propagatum etiam est ad posteros cum Autographorum Apographis. Quia enim autographa ipsa Ecclesiæ, velut pretiosum thesaurum, summâ curâ custodiebant, Apographa illorum à librariis ad imitationem & similitudinem Autographorum summâ, quâ fieri potuit, curâ & diligentiâ adornata sunt, cùm ad publicum Ecclesiæ, tùm ad singulorum fidelium usum. Quæ ut autographis per omnia in verbis, verborumq; literis, syllabis & punctis conformia erant, ita quò plura numero, undiquaq; sibi consentientia, omni tempore in Ecclesia existebant, & ad posteritatem propagabantur, eò certiores textus primigenii omniq; exceptione majores testes omnium temporum Ecclesiis erant. Atque hæc duplex testimonii de cujusq; libri textu primigenio propagandi via Ecclesiæ primitivæ utriq; communis est & fuit. Neque enim dubium est, quin plantatæ recens Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ accepta ab Apostolis Virisq; Apostolicis autographa librorum N. T. curâ & studio haud minori, quàm V. T. Ecclesia suorum librorum autographa, asservaverit, & manuum traditione ad posteros suos transmiserit. Quamvis verò Ecclesia Christiana, inde à primis incunabulis, dirissimis persecutionibus exposita fuerit, & cum effuso piorum Martyrum sanguine sua & initia & incrementa sumserit, ut in tot persecutionibus gravissimis, quibus & Doctores & auditores catervatim ad martyria abripiebantur, facilè contingere posset, ut Scriptorum Apostolicorum autographa cum ipsis sanctis doctrinæ Apostolicæ Confessoribus perirent: Tertullianus tamen, qui exeunte seculo secundo floruit, in libello suo de Præscript. testatur, adhuc suo tempore Apostolorum authenticas literas in Ecclesiis Apostolicis superfuisse. Age, inquit, qui voles curiositatem tuam meliùs exercere in negotio salutis, percurre ECCLESIAS APOSTOLICAS, apud quas ipsæ adhuc cathedræ Apostolorum suis locis præsidentur, apud quas AUTHENTICÆ LITERÆ eorum recitantur, sonantes vocem, repræsentantes faciem. Proxima est tibi Achaja? habes Corinthum. Si non longè es à Macedonia, habes Philippos. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiæ adjaceris, habes Romam &c. Ubi haud dubie Auctor per AUTHENTICAS Apostolorum LITERAS ipsa illorum autographa, quæ diversa Ecclesiæ diversæ ab ipsis acceperant, intelligit. Apoprapha enim ubique locorum in omnibus extabant Ecclesiis, ut illorum causâ Ecclesias, ad quas Epistolæ perscriptæ erant, percurrere nihil opus esset. Extabant autem in primitiva Ecclesia Apostolica Scripturarum sacrarum apographa tanto majori copiâ, & testabantur de textu libri cujusq; primævo eò certiùs, quò longiùs diffusa per orbe, pluresq; Ecclesias particulares, quàm Judaica, easq; amplissimas suo ambitu comprehendebat. Communicabant enim diffusæ per orbem Ecclesiæ inter se, & transmittebant sibi invicem suorum, quæ à sacris Scriptoribus acceperant, librorum sacrorum apographa, autographis prorsus conformia, fidelissimè, ut brevi tempore & ipsis adhuc viventibus Scriptoribus sacris etiam longissimè ab invicem dissitæ Ecclesiæ omnium Scriptorum Apostolicorum genuina & intemerata Apographa consequerentur. Quæ deinceps de cujusq; libri textu primigenio luculentu apud posteritatem testimonium omni tempore perhibuerunt. De Evangelio Matthæi & Epistola ad Ebræos, sintne Græco? an Ebræo idiomate primitùs conscripta? dubitatum olim fuit. Quod unde provenerit, explicare hujus loci non est. Ad præsens sufficit, quod hos ipsos libros, si non primitùs Græco idiomate scriptos, ex divina inspiratione tamen in Græcum sermonem translatos esse, summo consensu Ecclesia primitiva agnovit, eosq; in textu Græco semper in Codice authenticæ N. T. Scripturæ habuit, exemplo Ebræo, quod indubitatò quidem primigenium esset, vix ab ulla Ecclesia veteri conspecto.

Ad Ecclesiæ Judaicæ testimonium de Scripturæ V. T. textu primigenio duo insuper accedunt, quibus ejus conservandi, & ad seram posteritatem propagandi ratio adjuta & aucta est. Unum est Esræ & Synedrii Magni subsequens insigne testimonium. Cùm enim in πανολεθρίᾳ Hierosolymitana & conflagratione templi Salomonéi autographa & apographa librorum sacrorum non pauca periissent, & quæ superant exempla tempore durissimæ servitutis diu neglectim habita fuissent, Esra, Scriba & interpres legis, Vir ingenio & doctrina insignis, haud dubiè singulari Dei instinctu & providentia excitatus, statim post reditum populi ex diuturna & dura servitute in terram patriam & Solymorum Urbem restauratam, libros Scripturae omnes summa cura & labore recensuit, dispersos collegit, indigestos ordinavit certoq; numero distinctos in unum codicem, duos & viginti libros complectentem, & in tres magnas partes, Legem, Prophetas & hagiographa distributum, congessit, adscitis in societatem laboris & operae Viris Synagogae magnae, quos inter Prophetae Haggæus, Zacharias & Malachias, θεόπνευστοι Viri omnes, erant. Atq; hi V. T. Scripturarum authenticarum Codicem junctis studiis & consiliis auctoritate publica constituerunt, ut de numero & textu primigenio librorum nemini dubium esse posset. Qui codex postmodum in Ecclesia, velut authenticus habitus, & ad ejus exemplar Apographa omnia adornata, & ordine non interrupto usque ad Christum, in carne exhibitum, de manu ad manum quasi propagata & intemerata conservata sunt. Alterum est Christi & Apostolorum infallibile testimonium. Hanc ipsam enim Scripturam Ebraicam, in Esrae bene ordinato & in LEGEM, PROPHETAS & HAGIOGRAPHAM distributo Codice comprehensam, cujus apographa tum omnium terebantur manibus, Christus & Apostoli, a Spiritu S. collustrati, ipso usu comprobarunt, Ecclesiis ut genuinam & a Deo inspiratam commendarunt, ut inter alia Luc. XVI. 29. c. XXIV. 44. Act. XXVI. 22. c. XXVIII. 23. legere est. Hinc novam nacta auctoritatem Scriptura V. T. in Ecclesia Apostolica sive Christiana universa summo consensu recepta, & in suis Apographis intemeratis ad nos usque, traditione non interrupta, propagata est.

Quamvis vero ad propagandam Ecclesiae primitivae Apostolicae testimonium de Scripturae utriusq; Foederis textu primigenio vel sola librorum apographa, quae omnibus temporibus innumerabili multitudine in Ecclesiis extiterunt, & traditione continuata ad posteros, & ad nos usq; transmissa sunt, sufficere possint; extant tamen Patrum antiquissimorum de Canone Scripturae, cum Veteris tum Novi Testamenti, expressa testimonia, quibus quinam libri sacri, sub quo primigenio textu, inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, Ecclesiis in usu fuerint, docetur: quæ etiamnum apud antiquissimos indubitatæ fidei Scriptores supersunt. Inter eos merito suo eminet S. MELITO, Sardium in Asia, magni apud suos nominis Episcopus, qui medio seculo secundo vixit, & ab Onesimo rogatus, ut excerpta quædam ex Lege & Prophetis, quæ ad Servatorem & ad universam fidem nostram pertinerent, sibi componeret, itemq; libros V. T. quot numero, & quo sint ordine conscripti, consignaret, majoris certitudinis causâ in Orientem, ubi ista & prædicata & gesta sint, profectum, & peragratis Ecclesiis, librorumq; V. T. canone accuratè explorato, non alios, nec plures, nec alio ordine, quàm in constituto ab Esra Codice Ebræo habentur, se invenisse in Epistola ad laudatum Onesimum, memorat. Fragmentum Epistolæ, quo Canon librorum, in Ecclesiis Orientalibus ab ipso exploratus, recensetur, extat apud Eusebium lib. IV. Hist. Eccles. c. XXVI. Eodem numero & ordine, quo Melito, libros V. T. recensuit Origenes, qui tertio floruit seculo, in expositione Psalmi primi; libros N. T. autem eo numero & ordine, quo adhuc hodieq; apud nos in canone sunt, partim in lib. I. Expos. in Matth. partim etiam lib. V. Expos. in Johan. recensuit. De Epistola ad Ebræos autem peculiariter suum aperuit judiciu in Homil. quas in hanc Epistolã scripsit, ut videre est apud Euseb. lib. VI. c. XXV. Quanquam verò Origenes suos habuit nævos, eosq; non leves, numerũ tamen & ordinẽ librorũ sacrorũ utriusq; Fœderis eò rectius investigare & docere potuit, quod linguæ Ebraicæ peritior, Apostolorumq; ætati vicinior erat, & ad interpretandas Scripturas omne ferè studium contulerat. Neq; minoris æstimandum est Eusebii testimonium de Canone N.T. Quamvis enim Melitone ducentis ferè; & Origene centũ & quod excurrit, annis junior sit, extabant tamen ejus ætate adhuc monumenta Patrum antiquissimorum, quorum alii Apostolos quosdam; nonnulli aliquos illorum auditores & discipulos in carne viderant, & cum illis conversati fuerant; cæteri verò Apostolorum tempori aliàs admodùm vicini fuerant, quæ indefesso studio nocturnâ diurnaq; manu versavit atq; ex illorum testimoniis librorum N.T. catalogum contexuit, eodem prorsus ordine & numero, quo etiamnum in Ecclesia Christiana extat. Et quidem postquam de singulis Scriptoribus sacris ordine & prolixè egerat, & quos libros, quâ linguâ quisque scripsifset, accuratè docuerat, productis undiq; Patrum vetustissimorumtestimoniis subjecit tandem lib. III. c. XXV. Canonem Scripturæ N. T. inde ab Apostolorum tempore in Ecclesia universa receptum, hoc ordine & numero : Cæterum, inquit, opportunum videtur hoc loco novi Testamenti libros, de quibus jam diximus, summatim recensere. Primò igitur collocanda est sacra Evangeliorum quadriga; quam deinde consequuntur Actus Apostolorum. Post numerandæ sunt Pauli Epistolæ. Inde prior illa Johannis, ac similiter Petri Epistola suscipienda est. Postremò adjungenda, si ita videbitur, Johannis revelatio: de qua quid veteres senserint, suo loco exponemus. Et hæc quidem communi omnium consensu recepta sunt. Ità ille: ubi Quadrigam Sanctorum Evangeliorum quidem non speciatim exprimit; quam tamen in proximè præcedente capite ordine & distinctè enumeraverat, primo loco Matthæi; secundo Marci; tertio Lucæ, & quarto Johannis Evangelio assignato. Neq; Pauli Epistolas distinctè recenset, ratus, id necessariũ non esse, cùm quæ & quot essent, inter omnes constaret: superiori tamen capite III. hujus libri eas numero quatuordecim esse, omnesŕ; προδήλυς καὶ σαφεῖς antè manifestas & exploratas esse dixerat, & de unica, quæ ad Ebræos est, monuerat dubitari à quibusdam, Ebraicè? an Græcè primitùs conscripta fuerit? qua de re posteà hoc ipso lib. III. c. XXXVIII. lib. VI. c. XI. & c. XIII. prolixius egit. De Apocalypsi Johannis porrò notanter addit Eusebius loco suprà citato: Si ita videbitur; &, de qua quid veteres senserint, suo loco exponam. De ejus autoritate enim ab aliquibus fuerat dubitatum. Qua de re posteà lib. VIII. c. XXIII. ex Dionysio Alexandrino, qui medio seculo tertio vixit, prolixè disserit, ejusŕ; verba, quibus illius auctoritatem divinam adsertum iverat, transcripsit. Subjungit autem Eusebius porrò: Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐν ὁμολογυμένοις, i. e. Et HÆC QUIDEM (enumerata scripta) COMMUNI OMNIUM CONSENSU RECEPTA SUNT, ut Valesiana Versio verba Græca reddit. His deinceps alias superaddit Canonis N. T. partes, prioribus in hoc inferiores, quòd de his ab aliquibus Ecclesiis de divina illarum origine olim; de illis à nullis Ecclesiis unquam dubitatum fuerit, quas eodem ordine & numero, quo adhuc apud nos habentur, recenset his verbis: Ex iis verò, quæ in dubium revocantur, à multis tamen commemorari videmus, est

Epistola, quæ dicitur JACOBI, & quæ JUDÆ, & SECUNDA PETRI, JOHANNIS item ALTERA ET TERTIA, sive illæ ab ipso revera Evangelista, sive ab altero ejusdem nominis compositæ sint. Hi Scripturæ libri dicuntur hodiè à quibusdam, ad differentiam cæterorum, qui nunquam in dubium vocati sunt, ἀδευτεροκανονικοὶ sive secundi ordinis canonici. Sed hæc pluribus prosequi, præsentis instituti non est. Ex diverticulo in viam redeamus.

III. Ex hoc, ab ipso Ecclesiæ utriusque, Veteris scilicet & Novi Testamenti, primordio deducto, & per traditionem non interruptam ad nos derivato testimonio, quâ linguâ sermonisq́; idiomate quisque Scripturæ liber primitùs conscriptus sit, discendum ducimus, eoque certiorem hujus rei testem dari non posse, intrepidè asserimus. Si qua fequioribus seculis existens & à primitiva remotior Ecclesia de hac quæstione aliud, & à testimonio Ecclesiæ primitivæ diversum judicium ferre, & aliquos ab illa non agnitos & receptos libros in Canonem recipere, aut à primitiva olim receptos ex eodem exterminare præsumserit: quorum prius huc usque Ecclesia Pontifica ausa est; tum judicium ejus audiendum non erit.


### VII. Although, however, it is known to us with certainty from the testimony of the…

VII.

Although, however, it is known to us with certainty from the testimony of the primitive Church alone in what language and idiom of speech each book of Holy Scripture was originally written, yet if Holy Scripture is to perform the office of canon and norm among us, it must be believed with divine faith that it was written under that idiom in which it was originally composed, namely Hebrew for the Old Testament, and Greek for the New Covenant, by divine inspiration.

I. The distinction which we inculcated above in thesis IV between the authority of Holy Scripture in order to cause assent to the doctrine of faith, and the same in order to regulate the doctrine of faith and morals, namely that for the former it suffices to know that Holy Scripture depends on God through inspiration as to its formal element, that is to say, the sense and doctrines, but for the latter it is furthermore necessary to know that it depends also on God as to its material element, that is to say, the words and idiom of speech, this also finds a place here, and the reason for the diversity is rendered in the same place, that the causative power of Holy Scripture is communicated by God to the SENSE of the assent of divine faith, and the assent of divine faith is ultimately resolved in its dependence upon God as regards its formal aspect; but the normative power of the doctrine of faith and morals at once resides in the material and formal, that is, in the WORDS and SENSE, and the truth of the doctrine regulated is ultimately resolved into both. But just as we showed at length in the previous chapter VI against the Scholastics, that for the authority of Holy Scripture, so that it may move our intellect into a supernatural assent to the doctrine of faith, it is required that it be believed by divine faith that it depends upon God as regards its formal aspect, namely the sense and the doctrines contained in it; so now it remains to be examined whether, for the authority of the same, viewed by way of Canon and norm, it ought to be believed by divine faith that it depends also upon God as regards its material aspect, namely the Hebrew idiom of speech on the part of the Old, and the Greek idiom of speech on the part of the books of the New Testament?

II. It seems to militate for the negative, that we have hitherto shown at length that the language and idiom of speech in which each book of Scripture, of the Old and New Testament, was originally written by its author, does not become known to us certainly and indubitably, except from the testimony of the primitive Church. But the testimony of the primitive Church begets human faith, not divine. This notwithstanding, we do not fear to assert that for the authority of Scripture, thus also viewed by way of norm, it is required altogether that its dependence upon God as regards its material aspect also be believed by divine faith. Our reason is: because otherwise we could not simply be certain by divine faith concerning the truth of Christian doctrine, which rests entirely upon the authority of Holy Scripture as a norm, and is to be held and received as divine only insofar as it agrees with its original text as a norm, especially when controversies arise concerning one or another part of it. For although Christian doctrine itself, insofar as it is necessary for everyone to believe for salvation, testifies of itself immediately concerning its dependence upon God in the hearts of men, as was shown in the previous chapter VI against the Papists, nevertheless that internal testimony of it, so that it may be distinguished from the impulses and raptures of Enthusiasts and other Fanatics, is bound to Holy Scripture itself, and therefore is to be held as divine testimony, because the doctrine contained in Holy Scripture itself and its words is that which testifies of itself in the hearts of men. But when any part of the doctrine is called into controversy, then this is sought above all, whether that controversial doctrine is conformable to Holy Scripture, and is in faith, we cannot avoid recurring to the original text of Scripture, as to an infallible norm, which unless we are also most certain by divine faith that it depends immediately upon God, it does not appear how our faith can ultimately rest in the divine authority of Holy Scripture.

III. But there is a difficulty concerning the manner by which it becomes known to us by divine faith that the original text of Holy Scripture, just as its sense, depends immediately upon God. I think it is certain that it does not become known to us in the same way that its formal element, namely the sense, becomes known to us by divine faith to depend immediately upon God. For as regards the formal element, that Holy Scripture depends immediately upon God, it becomes known to us through the divine power itself, communicated to it by God on the part of its formal element, or sense, by which, through acts of illumination which it excites in us on the part of the intellect, and through spiritual motions, impulses, and drawings which it excites in us on the part of the will, and through the reflections of these concerning the divinity of the sense or doctrine which it contains, it testifies in our hearts, as was shown at length in the preceding chapter VII, Assertions IV, VII, and VIII. But this divine power of testifying, because it has not been so communicated by God to Holy Scripture, when viewed on the part of its material element, even in its original text, according to the received opinion of our Church, the thing itself speaks, that even when viewed in its original text, it cannot testify in the hearts of men concerning the dependence of its material element upon God as equally immediately as it does concerning the dependence of its formal element upon Him.

IV. There is, however, another mode of divine testimony by which the dependence of Holy Scripture, when viewed in its original text, upon God as regards its material element can become known to us by divine faith, and does become known: namely, MEDIATE and BY CONSEQUENCE. For although God has not distinctly and determinately revealed in Holy Scripture in what idiom of speech each book of Scripture was recorded from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, yet He has revealed confusedly and generally in it that all and singular of its books are in some, and that indeed, in the idiom in which they were originally written, having been written by divine inspiration, when He revealed through His Apostle Paul in 2 Tim. 3:16 that all Scripture is Θεόπνευστον, i.e., inspired by God. For just as Holy Scripture could not be written except in some idiom of language and speech—for only the characters of words, letters, and syllables can be written by themselves as signs of things and concepts, not the things and concepts themselves—so too a θεόπνευστος or divinely inspired Scripture cannot be given without some idiom of language and speech in which it is written. Whence, for Holy Scripture to be θεόπνευστος is for it to have been inspired by God in some idiom for the purpose of writing, and as it were dictated into the pen. But it cannot have been inspired by God for the purpose of writing, and dictated by inspiration into the pen, in any other idiom of words and language than that in which it was originally recorded. From which this major proposition follows by inevitable consequence: In whatever idiom the θεόπνευστος Scripture was originally recorded, in that same idiom it was also inspired by God for the purpose of writing and recorded by divine inspiration. But if I subsume: And yet the θεόπνευστος Scripture of the O.T. was originally recorded in the Hebrew idiom, and the θεόπνευστος Scripture of the N.T. in the Greek idiom; this conclusion will follow: Therefore, the θεόπνευστος Scripture of the O.T. was inspired by God for the purpose of writing and recorded by divine inspiration in the Hebrew idiom, and the θεόπνευστος Scripture of the N.T. in the Greek idiom: which is a matter of divine faith, on account of the major proposition, most solidly founded in the aforementioned Pauline statement 2 Tim. 3:16, which is a proposition of divine faith.

Nor is it an objection that the minor proposition does not rest upon divine revelation, but only upon the testimony of the primitive Church. For from one revealed premise and another (metaphysically or morally) evident one, a conclusion follows that is revealed and to be believed by divine faith, as can be shown by this one example: Any believer can believe, and does believe by divine faith, that he has been reborn of God through baptism, adopted as a son of God, and has obtained the right to enter into the heavenly inheritance. But this faith of his does not rest upon immediate divine revelation, but only upon mediate, and by consequence, by the force of this discourse: Whoever is baptized, he is reborn of God through baptism, adopted as a Son of God, and has obtained the right to enter into the heavenly inheritance. But this person, that believer, has been baptized. Therefore, he has been reborn through baptism, adopted as a Son of God and has obtained the right of entering upon the heavenly inheritance. The conclusion is without doubt of divine faith, and if any believer should thus conclude concerning himself individually, the conclusion, believed by divine faith, will pertain to the πληροφοριαν of his own faith. The minor proposition, however, is not revealed, but rests upon human testimony, if he was baptized in tender infancy; or upon the testimony of the senses, if he who subsumes concerning himself was baptized at an adult age. See what we have discussed at length regarding this matter in Tr. de Usu principiorum Ratio. in Theol. lib. II. c. XIII. & seqq.

V. In the Ratisbon Colloquy, D. Jacob Heilbrunner and D. Aegidius Hunnius declared their mind regarding this difficulty, which had been raised and objected to them by the Jesuits D. Jacob Gretser and D. Adam Tanner, in this manner: That the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of men concerning the dependence of Holy Scripture upon God as to its formal part, namely the sense and the doctrines, through Scripture itself; and the testimony of the primitive Church concerning its dependence upon God as to its material part, namely the words, together generate the assent of divine faith concerning the dependence of the whole of Holy Scripture upon God, both as to the formal and as to the material, and thus as to both. For when in the controversy concerning the judge of controversies of faith the Jesuits, Gretser and Tanner, intending to prove that the sole Holy Scripture is not the judge of controversies of faith, urged among other things that it must necessarily be believed by the faithful that certain books are sacred and Canonical. But that this is not contained expressly in Scripture, nor evidently deduced from it; D. Heilbrunner responded, as it is in the Acts of the Colloquy, Sess. XI, page 243 of the edition, by applying a distinction between articles of faith necessary for salvation; which he said he constantly affirmed were all contained in Holy Scripture; and historical faith, which respects the testimony of the primitive Church, which existed in the time of the Apostles and Evangelists: which testifies that these books were written by the Apostles and Evangelists, but adds nothing, nor constitutes anything new concerning religion and worship, just as it is said at Romans 3, the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews. From that, however, it does not follow that the Jews can add anything new to the written word, or constitute any article of faith. By which he refers the question concerning the books of Scripture, which ones, and in what idiom were written by the Apostles & Evangelists, expressly among historical questions, to be determined through the testimony of the primitive Church, which existed in the time of the Apostles & Evangelists. Heilbrunner and Hunnius had inculcated the same thing in Session X, page 220 et seq. However, Tanner insisting, and repeating that through the testimony of the primitive Church of the Apostles we know that this or that book is Canonical; Heilbrunner replied that there are also other and far more evident κριτήρια (criteria), which indicate manifestly that this Scripture proceeded from the Holy Spirit. To which he also adds other internal κριτήρια (criteria) to the testimony of the primitive Church, which prove that this Scripture proceeded from the Holy Spirit. Tanner urging further that he should say whether we ought to believe with equal certainty and by the same catholic faith that this or that book is Canonical, as we believe that Christ is incarnate? Heilbrunner replied on p. 244 that both are to be believed with certainty, but that the reason for the faith is not the same. What he had said, that the reason for the faith is not the same, Hunnius, assisting him, deduced and declared more fully in the same place: It must be distinguished, he says, between the faith by which we believe the volume of the Holy Bibles to be canonical, and the faith which believes the incarnation of Christ. The Catholic faith is indeed the same, but it has different objects. Wishing to explain this: I say, he continues, that that catholic faith, which is not distracted from itself, has different objects: One is historical tradition, which tradition is attributed in its own way not only to the primitive Church, but also to the rejected Synagogue of the Jews. For just as we have received from the primitive Church testifying concerning the writings of the Apostles that these or those writings are of Paul, Peter, John, etc. Thus to the Jewish Synagogue were entrusted the oracles of God, λόγια τῦ Θεῦ (oracles of God), the Testaments, Rom. 3 & 9. Therefore, just as the Jewish Synagogue, rejected by God, does not add any new dogma to the books of the Old Testament by its testimony: so the primitive Church by its testimony does not add any new and peculiar article, or establish a dogma by its testimony. For the UNDISTRACTED CATHOLIC faith, besides this object of HISTORICAL TRADITION, also has another object, namely the CONTENTS IN THE BOOKS. Therefore, as was said yesterday, just as any messenger, delivering letters

the Prince to the subject, and testifying, that they were received from the hand of the Prince, this man by his testimony in real matters, which the Prince wished to write to the subject, adds nothing: and the subject, having inspected the internal κριτηρίοις, the subscription of the hand, and likewise the contents of the letters, now judges from the internal κριτηρίοις that the letters are authentic, so that he no longer has need of the testimony of the messenger: So also when the primitive Church hands down the Apostolic Scriptures to subsequent Churches, and they, having inspected the originals, now receive them with full faith, and now unfold the book itself open or the open scripture, and thus because of internal κριτήρια, and at the same time because of the sealing of the divine Spirit Rom. 8. believe that they proceeded from the Apostles, then the primitive Church, among those in whose minds the majesty and authority of the sacred letters is now established, has performed its duty, so that there is no further need among Christians to dispute whether this or that book is of this or that Apostle, whether it is Canonical or not Canonical. To the same effect see p. 246. Hunnius, to Tanner, asking again from Heilbrunner whether that tradition or testimony of the Church is to be believed as an article of faith; replies that it is to be believed with EQUAL FAITH, THAT THESE OR THOSE BOOKS ARE CANONICAL, AND THAT NOT ONLY BECAUSE OF THE TESTIMONY OF THE CHURCH, but also BECAUSE OF INTERNAL κριτήρια. And page 247. It is to be observed, he says, that the testimony of the Church is not solitary, nor does it alone induce us to believe in the books which are contained in the volume of the Bible: but that, having unfolded them, because of the majesty of God speaking in them, and the traces of heavenly truth expressed therein, we recognize from internal κριτηρίοις that that Scripture is clearly Sacrosanct and Canonical. Therefore, that the Epistle of Paul to the Romans is Paul's, we have from the testimony of the primitive Church: but that it is sacrosanct, Canonical, and a rule of faith, that we do not have and derive from the testimony of the Church, but from internal κριτηρίοις. The sum of what has been said returns to this; that from the testimony of the primitive Church it is known that these or those books, in this original idiom in which they exist, were written by the Sacred Writers, and that this is believed by historical faith; but that the doctrines contained in them proceeded from God and are truly divine is known from the internal κριτηρίοις of Scripture, especially indeed from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, by which He testifies in the hearts of men through the Scriptures themselves concerning their immediate dependence upon God, or concerning their divinity. From these things, however, believed partly by historical faith, partly by divine faith, there arises one undivided Catholic faith, by which it is believed that these books are Canonical, and those are not Canonical. And so much also concerning the authority of Holy Scripture viewed as a Canon and norm, and its dependence upon God regarding its material, namely the words by which it was originally recorded, God inspiring it, whence may it become known to us? What more could be brought forward concerning the number of Canonical books, and concerning their distinction from the Apocrypha; and likewise concerning the judge of Controversies, we shall bring forward and declare below in their proper places. Now we proceed to the EFFICACY OF SCRIPTURE, its affection, next in order from its authority.

Latin:

VII.

QUamvis verò quo linguæ & sermonis idiomate quisque Scripturæ sacræ liber primitùs conscriptus sit, ex solo Ecclesiæ primitivæ testimonio nobis certò innotescat, tamen si canonis & normæ munusScriptura sacra apud nos obire debeat, omninò fide divinâ credendum est, eam sub illo idiomate, quo primitùs conscripta est, Ebræo scilicet Veteris; & Græco Novi Fœderis Scripturam, ex divinâ inspiratione conscriptam esse.

I. Quod suprà th. IV. inculcavimus discrimen inter auctoritatem Scripturæ sacræ in ordine ad causandum assensum doctrinæ fidei, & inter eandem in ordine ad normandam fidei & morum doctrinam, quòd scilicet ad illam sufficiat nôsse, Scripturam sacram dependere à Deo per inspirationem quoad formale suum, sensum scilicet& doctrinas, ad hanc verò cognitu prætereà necessarium sit, eam dependere etiam à Deo quoad materiale suum, verba scilicet, & sermonis idioma, id hic etiam locum invenit, estq; diversitatis ratio ibidem reddita, quòd Scripturæ sacræ virtus causativa assensus fidei divinæ SENSUI à Deo communicata sit,& fidei divinæ assensus in ejus dependentiam à Deo quoad formale suum ultimò resolvatur; virtus normativa verò doctrinæ fidei & morũ simul penes materiale & formale, h. e. penes VERBA & SENSUM sit, & veritas doctrinæ normatæ in utrumque ultimò resolvatur. Quemadmodùm autem in superiori cap. VI. contra Scholasticos fusè ostendimus, ad auctoritatem Scripturæ sacræ, ut in supernaturalem doctrinæ fidei assensum intellectum nostrum moveat, requiri,ut eam quoad formale suum, sensum scilicet & doctrinas, in ea contentas,à Deo dependere,fide divinâ credatur; ita nunc dispiciendum superest, annon ad auctoritatem ejusdem, per modum Canonis & normæ spectatæ, fide divinâ creditum esse oporteat, eam dependere etiam à Deo quoad materiale suum, Ebraicum scilicet, ex parte Veteris; & Græcum sermonis idioma ex parte Novi Fœderis librorum?

II. Pro negativa militare videtur, quòd hactenus fusè ostendimus, quo linguæ & sermonis idiomate quisque Scripturæ, Veteris & Novi Fœderis, liber primitùs ab auctore suo conscriptus sit, non innotescere nobis certò & indubitatò, nisi ex Ecclesiæ primitivæ testimonio. Testimonium Ecclesiæ primitivæ verò fidem humanam gignit, non divinam. Hoc tamen non obstante nos haud veremur asserere, ad auctoritatem Scripturæ, sic etiam per modum normæ spectatæ, requiri omninò, ut ejus dependentia à Deo quoad suum materiale quoque fide divinâ credatur. Ratio nostra est: quia aliàs de veritate doctrinæ Christianæ, quæ in solidum Scripturæ sacræ auctoritate, velut normâ nititur, & eatenus pro divina habenda & recipienda est, quatenus cum ejus textu primigenio, velut normâ, convenit, non possemus simpliciter fide divinâ esse certi, præsertim cum de una alteráve ejus parte controversiæ oriuntur. Quamvis enim doctrina christiana ipsa, in quantum quidem cuivis ad salutem creditu necessaria est, per se immediatè de sui dependentia à Deo in hominum cordibus testificetur, ut in superiori cap. VI. contra Pontificios ostensum, tamen interna illa ejus testificatio, ut ab Enthusiastarum & aliorum Fanaticorum motibus & raptibus distingvatur, ad ipsam Scripturam sacram alligata est, & propterea pro testificatione divina habenda, quòd ipsius Scripturæ Sacræ ejusque verbis contenta doctrina est, quæ in cordibus hominum de se testificatur. Quando autem doctrinæ aliqua pars in controversiam vocatur, tum hoc inprimis quæritur, an doctrina illa controversa Scripturæ sacræ conformis sit, & in ejus formali sive sensu verè contineatur? Quo in casu fidem nostram firmaturi subterfugere non possumus, quin ad textum Scripturæ primigenium, velut ad normam infallibilem, recurramus, quem nisi etiam immediatè à Deo dependere fide divinâ certi simis, non apparet, quomodò fides nostra in divina Scripturæ sacræ auctoritate ultimò sistere possit.

III. De modo autem, quo Scripturæ sacræ textum primigenium æquè, ac ejus sensum, immediatè à Deo dependere, fide divinâ nobis innotescat, difficultas est. Quod non eo modo id nobis innotescat, quo ejus formale, sensum scilicet, à Deo immediatè dependere fide divinâ nobis innotescit, puto certum esse. Nam quoad formale dependere Scripturam sacram immediatè à Deo, innotescit nobis per ipsam virtutem divinam, ex parte formalis sui, sive sensus ei à Deo communicatam, quâ per actus illuminationis, quos ex parte intellectus; & per motus, pulsus & tractus spirituales, quos ex parte voluntatis in nobis excitat, eosq́; reflexos de divinitate sensus sive doctrinæ, quam continet, in cordibus nostris testificatur, ut in præced. cap. VII. Assert. IV. VII. & VIII. prolixè ostensum. Hæc autem divina testificandi virtus, quia Scripturæ sacræ, ex parte materialis sui, etiam in suo textu primigenio spectatæ, juxta receptam Ecclesiæ nostræ sententiam, sic à Deo communicata non est, res ipsa loquitur, quod etiam in suo textu primigenio spectata de depentia sui materialis à Deo non æquè immediatè, ut de dependentia sui formalis ab illo, in cordibus hominum testificari possit.

IV. Datur tamen alius divinæ testificationis modus, quo Scripturæ sacræ, in suo textu primigenio spectatæ, dependentia à Deo quoad materiale suum fide divinâ nobis innotescere possit, & innotescat: MEDIATUS scilicet & PER CONSEQVENTIAM. Quanquam enim, quo sermonis idiomate quisque Scripturæ liber ex immediata Spiritus S. inspiratione consignatus sit, in Scriptura sacra Deus distinctè & determinatè non revelavit, confusè tamen & generatim revelavit in ea, omnes & singulos ejus libros esse aliquo, & eo quidem, quo primitus scripti sunt, idiomate ex divina inspiratione conscriptos, quando per Apostolum suum Paulum II. Tim. III. 16. revelavit, Scripturam totam esse Θεόπνευστον, i. e. à Deo inspiratam. Sicut enim Scriptura sacra scribi non potuit, nisi sub aliquo linguæ & sermonis idiomate: nam soli verborum characteres, literæ & syllabæ, velut signa rerum & conceptuum per se scribi possunt, non ipsæ res & conceptus; ita nec θεόπνευστος sive divinitus inspirata dari potest Scriptura absque aliquo linguæ & sermonis idiomate, quo scripta sit. Unde Scripturam sacram θεόπνευστον esse, est eam esse à Deo sub aliquo idiomate ad scribendum inspiratam, & quasi in calamum dictitatam. Non autem sub alio, quàm quo primitus consignata est, verborum & linguæ idiomate à Deo ad ascribendum inspirata, & per inspirationem in calamum dictitata esse potest. Ex quo consequentiâ inevitabili hæc fluit major propositio: Quo idiomate Scriptura θεόπνευστος primitus consignata est, eo etiam à Deo ad scribendum inspirata & ex divina inspiratione consignata est. Quod si subsumam: Atqui Scriptura θεόπνευστος V. T. Ebræo; & Scriptura θεόπνευστος N. T. Græco idiomate primitiùs consignata est; sequetur conclusio hæc: Ergo Scriptura θεόπνευστος V. T. Ebræo; & Scriptura θεόπνευστος N. T. Græco idiomate à Deo adscribendum inspirata & ex divina inspiratione consignata est: quæ fidei divinæ est, ob propositionem majorem, in superiori dicto Paulino II. Tim. III. 16. solidissimè fundatam, quæ fidei divinæ propositio est.

Neque obstat, quod propositio minor non etiam divinâ revelatione, sed tantùm testificatione Ecclesiæ primitivæ nititur. Nam ex una præmissa revelata, & altera (Metaphysicè aut moraliter) evidente, sequitur conclusio revelata, & fide divinâ credenda, ut vel hoc uno exemplo ostendi potest: Quilibet fidelis fide divinâ credere potest creditq́;, se per baptismum à Deo renatum, in filium Dei adoptatum & jus adeundæ hæreditatis cælestis consecutum esse. Sed hæc ejus fides non nititur immediatâ revelatione divinâ, sed mediatâ tantùm, & per consequentiam, vi hujus discursus: Quicunq; baptizatus est, is per baptismum à Deo renatus, in Filium Dei adoptatus & jus adeundæ hæreditatis cælestis consecutus est. Atqui hic, ille fidelis baptizatus est. Ergo per baptismum renatus, in Filium Dei adoptatus & jus adeundæ hæreditatis cælestis consecutus est. Conclusio citra dubium est fidei divinæ, & si quis fidelis de se in individuo sic concludat, conclusio, fide divinâ credita, pertinebit ad πληροφοριαν fidei ipsius. Minor tamen propositio revelata non est, sed nititur testificatione humanâ, si in tenerâ infantiâ; vel sensuum testimonio, si in ætate adultâ baptizatus sit, qui de se subsumit. Videantur, quæ in Tr. de Usu principiorum Ratio. in Theol. lib. II. c. XIII. & seqq. fuse hanc in rem disseruimus.

V. Paulò aliter in Colloquio Ratisbonensi D. Jacobus Heilbrunnerus & D. Ægidius Hunnius de hac difficultate, à Jesuitis D. Jacobo Gretsero & D. Adamo Tannero sibi motâ & objectâ, mentem suam declararunt, hunc in modum: Testificationem internam Spiritus Sancti in hominum cordibus de sacræ Scripturæ dependentia à Deo ex parte sui formalis, sensus scilicet & doctrinarum, per ipsammet Scripturam; & testificationem Ecclesiæ primitivæ de ejusdem à Deo dependentia ex parte sui materialis, verborum scilicet, junctim generare assensum fidei divinæ de totius Scripturæ sacræ à Deo dependentia, cùm quoad formale, tùm quoad materiale, atq; adeo quoad utrùmque. Cùm enim in controversia de judice controversiarum fidei Jesuitæ, Gretserus & Tannerus, probaturi, judicem controversiarum fidei non esse solam Scripturam sacram, inter alia urgerent, quòd necessario credendum sit fidelibus, aliquos libros esse sacros & Canonicos. Sed hoc non contineri expressè in Scriptura, nec inde evidenter deduci; respondit D. Heilbrunnerus, ut est in Actis Colloquii Sess. XI. pag. m. 243. adhibitâ distinctione inter articulos fidei ad salutem necessarios; quos omnes in sacra Scriptura contineri se constanter affirmare ajebat; & inter historicam fidem, quæ respicit testificationem primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quæ fuit tempore Apostolorum & Evangelistarum: quæ testatur, hos libros ab Apostolis & Evangelistis esse scriptos, nihil autem addit, aut aliquid novi constituit circa religionem & cultum, sicut ad Rom. 3. dicitur, Judæis concredita sunt oracula Dei. Inde tamen non sequitur, quòd Judæi possint aliquid novi addere ad verbum scriptum, aut aliquem fidei articulum constituere. Quibus quæstionem de libris Scripturæ, quinam, & sub quo idiomate ab Apostolis & Evangelistis scripti sint, expresse inter quaestiones historicas, per testificationem Ecclesiae primitivae, quae fuit tempore Apostolorum & Evangelistarum, determinandas refert. Gemina inculcaverant Heilbrunnerus & Hunnius Sess. X. pag. 220. seq. Instante autem Tannero, & repetente, quòd per testificationem primitivae Ecclesiae Apostolorum sciamus, quòd iste vel iste liber sit Canonicus; respondit Heilbrunnerus, alia etiam esse interna & longè evidentiora κριτήρια, quae indicent manifestè, hanc Scripturam à Spiritu S. profectam esse. Quibus testificationi Ecclesiae primitivae etiam alia adjungit κριτήρια interna, quae evincant, hanc Scripturam esse profectam à Spiritu Sancto. Urgente Tannero ulterius, ut diceret, utrum æquè certò ac eâdem fide catholicâ debeamus credere, quòd hic vel ille liber sit Canonicus, quâ credimus, quòd Christus sit incarnatus? respondit Heilbrunnerus p. 244. utrumque esse certò credendum, sed non esse parem rationem fidei. Quod dixerat, non esse parem rationem fidei, id Hunnius, ei subveniens, ibidem uberius deduxit & declaravit: Distinguendum, inquiens, est inter fidem, quâ credimus sacrorum Bibliorum Codicem esse canonicum, & inter fidem, quae credit incarnationem Christi. Eadem quidem est fides Catholica, habet autem diversa objecta. Quod explicaturus: Dico, ait porrò, fidem illam catholicam, quae à semetipsa non distrahitur, diversa habere objecta: Unum est traditio historica, quae traditio non tantum Ecclesiae primitivae, sed etiam reprobatae Judaeorum Synagogae suo modo attribuitur. Sicut enim ab Ecclesia primitiva testificante de scriptis Apostolorum accepimus haec vel illa scripta esse Pauli, Petri, Johannis &c. Sic Synagogae Judaicae concredita erant oracula Dei, λόγια τῦ Θεῦ, Testamenta, Rom. 3. & 9. Sicut ergo Judaica Synagoga, reprobata à Deo, suâ testificatione non adjicit dogma novum ullum libris Veteris Testamenti: sic Ecclesia primitiva suâ testificatione non adjicit aliquem articulum novum & peculiarem, aut suâ testificatione dogma constituit. Fides enim CATHOLICA INDISTRACTA, praeter hoc objectum HISTORICAE TRADITIONIS habet quoque objectum aliud, nimirum CONTENTA IN LIBRIS. Proinde, sicut heri dictum, quemadmodum nuncius quispiam, reddens literas

Principis subdito, & testificans, ex manu Principis illas esse acceptas, hic sua testificatione in realibus, quæ Princeps scribere voluit ad subditum, nihil adjicit: & subditus inspectis internis κριτηρίοις, subsignatione manus, similiter & contentis in literis, jam ex internis κριτηρίοις judicat, literas esse authenticas, ut testimonio nuncii porro opus non habeat: Sic quoque quando Ecclesia primitiva tradit Scripturas Apostolicas subsequentibus Ecclesiis, & illæ, inspectis originalibus, jam plena fide eas accipiunt, & jam evolvunt ipsum librum apertum sive scripturam apertam, & sic propter interna κριτήρια, atque simul propter obsignationem divini Spiritus Rom. 8. credunt ab Apostolis eas esse profectas, tùm Ecclesia primitiva apud hos, in quorum animis jam sancita est sacrarum literarum majestas & autoritas, suo functa est officio, ut porro non opus sit inter Christianos disceptare, num hic vel ille liber sit hujus vel illius Apostoli, sit Canonicus vel non Canonicus. Eundem in sensum seq. p. 246. Hunnius, Tannero, quærenti iterum ex Heilbrunnere, anne illa traditio sive testificatio Ecclesiæ credenda sit tanquam articulus fidei; respondet, quòd PARI quidem FIDE credendum sit, HOS VEL ILLOS LIBROS ESSE CANONICOS, IDQUE NON MODO PROPTER TESTIFICATIONEM ECCLESIÆ, sed & PROPTER INTERNA κριτήρια. Et pag. 247. Observandum est, inquit, quòd Ecclesiæ testificatio solitaria non sit, nec illa sola nos inducit ad credere libris, qui continentur in Bibliorum volumine: sed evolutos, propter majestatem loquentis in illis Dei, & vestigia cœlestis veritatis, ibidem expressa, ex κριτηρίοις internis agnoscere, quòd Scriptura illa plane sit Sacrosancta & Canonica. Itaque quòd Epistola Pauli ad Romanos sit Pauli, habemus ex Ecclesiæ primitivæ testimonio: quod autem sit sacrosancta, Canonica & fidei regula, id non ex testificatione Ecclesiæ, sed ex internis κριτηρίοις habemus & desumimus. Summa dictorum redit huc; ex testificatione Ecclesiæ primitivæ cognosci, hos, illos libros, sub hoc, quo extant, primigenio idiomate, esse à Sacris Scriptoribus conscriptos, idq́; credi fide historica; doctrinas autem, in illis contentas, esse à Deo profectas & verè divinas, cognosci ex κριτηρίοις Scripturæ internis, cumprimis verò ex testificatione Spiritus Sancti, quâ per ipsasmet Scripturas de illarum immediata à Deo dependentia, sive de divinitate illarum in hominum cordibus testificatur. Ex hisce autem, historica partim; partim divina fide creditis, nasci unam indistractam fidem Catholicam, quâ credatur, hos libros esse Canonicos, illos non esse Canonicos. Et tantum etiam de auctoritate Scripturæ sacræ per modum Canonis & normæ spectatæ, ejusq́; dependentia à Deo quoad materiale suum, verba scilicet, quibus primitùs, Deo inspirante, consignata est, unde nobis innotescat? Quæ plura de numero librorum Canonicorum, deq́; illorum ab Apocryphis distinctione; itemq́; de judice Controversiarum adferri poterant, infra suis locis adferemus & declarabimus. Nunc pergimus ad EFFICACIAM SCRIPTURÆ, affectionem ejus, ab illius auctoritate proximam.


## 12 On the Efficacy of Holy Scripture

Although the efficacy of Holy Scripture has been treated here and there in the previous chapter as the occasion required: for the AUTHORITY and EFFICACY of Scripture are most closely connected in actual practice and use, so that they cannot be torn apart from one another; yet because they are two distinct affections of it, for the sake of those who are beginning, I shall now treat of this separately, yet briefly and succinctly.

I.

That Holy Scripture is efficacious for producing supernatural effects of grace in the hearts of men appears from Scripture itself in many places.

For Scripture is to us, who attain salvation, the power of God, 1 Cor. 1. 18, 24. It is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1. 16. It does not consist in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of power, that our faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God, 1 Cor. 2. 4, 5. It is sent into the hearts of men through preaching or reading as λόγος ἔμφυτος, the engrafted Word, which is able to save our souls, James 1. 21.

The word of truth, by which God begat us, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures, ibid. v. 18, can instruct us unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, II Tim. III. 15. It is the living and active Word of God, and sharper than any two-edged sword, Heb. IV. 12, by which the eyes of the Gentiles are opened, that they may turn from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, Acts XXVI. 18. Although these passages speak in large part of the Word of God preached by the Apostles, they nevertheless rightly apply also to Holy Scripture, which is nothing other than the Word of God committed to writing, and they differ in no other way than as speech comprehended in writing and speech uttered by voice, as we have frequently noted above.

II.

The efficacy of Holy Scripture is, however, a certain supernatural δύναμις, or force and active power, conferred upon it by God for converting, regenerating, and renewing the minds of men.

I. The term efficacy is taken, according to usage, in two ways: one, for the second act, namely for the actual operation itself, which is otherwise called by the Greeks, and in the Scripture of the New Testament also by the Apostle Paul, ἐνέργεια, Eph. I. 19, c. III. 7. The other, for the first act, namely for the δυνάμει ἐνεργητικῇ itself, or the power of operating. In which sense Paul also, in the places already cited, distinguishes between the δύναμιν τοῦ Θεοῦ and the ἐνέργειαν τῆς δυνάμεως ἀυτοῦ, as between the first act and the second act. Although the Latin term for efficacy seems to denote the second act rather than the first, here, however, when we speak of the efficacy of Scripture, we take the term efficacy for the first act, namely for the δυνάμει ἐνεργητικῇ itself, or the effective power of the spiritual effects of grace.

II. That it is not, however, a δύναμις or force of acting that is natural to Holy Scripture, strictly speaking, but supernatural, is evident from its effects. For whatever δύναμις, force, and efficacy is natural to any writing, that belongs to it either by virtue of the words or by virtue of the things signified, of which the former affect, allure, and draw the minds of men into their assent and consent through the elegance and ornamentation of the words, and the latter through their evidence and goodness, or by reason of both together, and it is

the motive force of both is entirely objective, which on the part of both the intellect and the will presupposes active powers for the acts of knowing, assenting, willing, and likewise desiring, to which they move, to be elicited within themselves. But the spiritual effects which are ascribed to Holy Scripture, e.g., the illumination of the intellect in those things which are of the Spirit of God, the conversion of man, by nature turned away from God and dead to every good, to God, the regeneration by which he who was born of flesh as flesh becomes spirit, and the renewal by which one, having mortified the old man, becomes new, etc., are in substance supernatural, for the producing of which within themselves, when Holy Scripture moves objectively by the force of its words and the force of the things signified, the intellect and will of man have no power at all, but the intellect in those things which are of the Spirit of God is by nature blind, so that it neither perceives nor can know them, 1. Cor. II. 14. is ἐsκοτιsμένος, darkened, Eph. IV. 18. and sκότος, darkness, V. 8. but the will is by nature dead to every spiritual good, Eph. II. 1. Col. II. 5. alienated from the life of God, Eph. IV. 18. and the φρόνημα of both, or the whole of that which the mind thinks, savors, and the will wills and desires, is enmity against God, i.e., utterly and in all respects hostile to God, Rom. VIII. 7. for the producing of which supernatural effects, therefore, a certain higher δύναμις and force is necessarily required than that which can otherwise belong to the force of the words or things of Scripture, namely a certain ἐνεργητικὴ or effective force, which, because it far exceeds the natural motive force of Holy Scripture, which it has either by the force of its words or the force of the things signified, is altogether supernatural to it.

But if any theologians have called the efficacy of Holy Scripture a certain natural δύναμις, force, or power, it is not to be understood in the sense as if it constituted the nature of Holy Scripture itself, or flowed from its nature of itself, but they called it natural because, by God's ordination, it is so intimately and inseparably connected with the nature of Holy Scripture, just as the natural motive force which any writing has by the force of its words and the things signified is connected to it: otherwise, however, they have by no means denied that it is supernatural, insofar as that is called supernatural which exceeds the natural powers of a thing, and has been granted to it by the free will and ordination of God for the producing of certain supernatural effects. Whatever this is, our predecessors here in Jena, D. Johannes Major, D. Johannes Gerhard, and D. Johannes Himmelius, among those in holy rest, have elegantly explained in their judgment concerning the Rathmannian Controversy, in Dedekind, in the final Appendix to Question VI. § 3. fol. 263, whose words are these: It is undisputed among the orthodox Church teachers that the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is ascribed to the Word of God not ex physica necessitate, in a natural way, as if such a natural power were in the Word, like the burning power in fire, the nourishing power in bread, the power to make healthy in medicine. For God's Word does not work in a natural way, as fire naturally burns, bread naturally nourishes, medicine naturally makes healthy; otherwise it could not work illumination, conversion, and salvation, which are not a natural, but a Divine work. Indeed, some have used the word 'naturally' in this (Rathmannian) dispute, and said: The Word of God has its inward power, which one may well call the natural life-power of the Word, but they have clearly explained that they opposed the little word 'naturally' not to the ὑπερφυσικῷ, but to the παραφυτικῷ of Rathmann, not to the supernatural, but to the accidental, auxiliary addition and accession which Rathmann teaches, and accordingly they have by no means intended to indicate by this modum aliquem naturalis inhæsionis, as if this power belonged to the Word naturaliter, in a natural way, but solely and alone this: that the power of illumination is internal to the Word, and is not first added and joined to it from the outside in use by the Holy Spirit, but belongs (as it were) to the nature and entire perfection of the Word, etc.

Latin:

Qvamvis de efficacia Scripturæ sacræ in capite superiori pro re nata passim actum sit: cohærent enim AUCTORITAS & EFFICACIA Scripturæ, in ipsa praxi & usu, arctissimè, ut ab invicem divelli non possint; quia tamen duæ distinctæ ejus affectiones sunt, in nascentium gratiam de hac seorsim nunc agam, breviter tamen & succinctè.

I.

Efficacem esse Scripturam sacram ad supernaturales gratiæ effectus in hominum cordibus producendos, ex Scriptura ipsa passim locorum apparet.

Est enim Scriptura nobis, qui salutem consequimur, potentia Dei, 1. Cor. 1. 18. 24. Est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. 1. 16. Non consistit in persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed in demonstratione spiritus & potentiæ, ut fides nostra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei. 1. Cor. II. 4. 5. immissa per prædicationem vel lectionem in corda hominum est λόγος ἔμφυτος Verbum insitum, quod potest servare animas nostras, Jac. I. 21.

Verbum veritatis, quo nos Deus progenuit, ut essemus primitiæ quædam suarum creaturarum, ib. v. 18. potest nos instruere ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, I. Tim. III. 15. Est vivum & efficax Verbum Dei, & penetrantius quovis gladio ancipiti, Ebr. IV. 12. quo aperiuntur oculi gentium, ut convertantur à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanæ ad Deum, Act. XXVI. 18. Quæ quamvis magnam partem de Verbo Dei, ab Apostolis prædicato, loquantur, rectè tamen procedunt etiam de Scriptura sacra, quæ nihil aliud est, quam Verbum Dei, literis consignatum, neque aliter differunt, quàm ut oratio, scripto comprehensa, & voce prolata, ut supra sæpiùs monuimus.

II.

ESt autem Scripturæ sacræ efficacia ejus supernaturalis quædam δύναμις sive vis & potentia activa, ad hominum mentes convertendas, regerandas & renovandas ipsi à Deo collata.

I. Efficaciæ vox accipitur, ex usu loquendi, duobus modis: uno, pro actu secundo, nempe pro ipsa actuali operatione, quæ aliàs Græcis; & in Scriptura N. T. etiam Paulo Apostolo ἐνέργεια dicitur, Eph. I. 19. c. III. 7. Altero pro actu primo, pro ipsâ scilicet δυνάμει ἐνεργητικῇ sive potentia operandi. Quem in sensum & Paulus locis jam citatis distingvit inter δύναμιν τοῦ Θεοῦ, & inter ἐνέργειαν τῆς δυνάμεως ἀυτοῦ, velut inter actum primum & actum secundum. Quamvis verò Latinis efficaciæ vox actum secundum potiùs, quàm actum primum denotare videatur, hîc tamen, quando de efficacia Scripturæ agimus, efficaciæ vocem accipimus pro actu primo, nempe pro ipsa δυνάμει ἐνεργητικῇ sive potentia effectrice spiritualium gratiæ effectuum.

II. Eam verò non esse δύναμιν sive vim agendi, Scripturæ sacræ naturalem, propriè quidem loquendo, sed supernaturalem, patet ex ejus effectibus. Nam quæ δύναμις, vis & efficacia Scripturæ alicui naturalis est, ea convenit illi vel vi vocum, vel virerum significatarum, quarum illæ per sui elegantiam & ornatum; hæ per sui evidentiam & bonitatem hominum mentes afficiunt, alliciunt, & in sui assensum consensumq́; trahunt, vel ratione utrorumq; simul, estq́;

utrorumq; vis motiva tota merè objectiva, quæ ex parte cùm intellečus tùm voluntatis vires activas, ad actus cognoscendi, assentiendiq;, volendi, item & desiderandi, ad quos movent, in se eliciendos præsupponunt. Effectus spirituales verò, qui Scripturæ sacræ adscribuntur, v. g. illuminatio intellectus in iis, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, conversio hominis, à Deo naturâ aversi, & ad omne bonum emortui, ad Deum, regeneratio, quâ qui de carne caro natus erat, fiat spiritus, & renovatio, quâ quis, mortificato homine veteri, fiat novus &c. in substantia supernaturales sunt, ad quos cùm Scriptura sacra, cùm vi vocum tùm vi rerum significatarum objectivè movente, in se producendos hominis intellectus & voluntas nihil quicquam habent virium, sed intellectus in iis, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, naturâ cæcus est, utea nec percipiat, nec cognoscere possit, 1. Cor. II. 14. est ἐsκοτιsμένος, obtenebratus, Eph. IV. 18. & sκότος tenebræ, V. 8. voluntas verò est ad omne bonum spirituale naturâ emortua, Eph. II. 1. Col. II. 5. abalienata à vitâ Dei, Eph. IV. 18. & utriusq; φρόνημα, sive totum id, quod mens cogitat, sapit, & voluntas vult, desiderat, est inimicitia adversus Deum, h. e. Deo prorsus & per omnia inimicum, Rom. VIII. 7. ad quos supernaturales effectus producendos proindè necessariò altior quædam δύναμις & vis, quám quæ alias vi vocum aut rerum Scripturæ alicui convenire potest, nempe vis quædam ἐνεργητικὴ sive effectiva requiritur, quæ quia Scripturæ sacræ vim motivam naturalem, quam sive vi vocum sive vi rerum significatarum habet, longissimè excedit, omninò ei supernaturalis est.

Quod si qui Theologi efficaciam Scripturæ sacræ naturalem quandam ejus δύναμιν vim aut potentiam dixerunt, non eo id sensu intelligendum est, ac si Scripturæ sacræ naturam ipsa constituat, vel ex ejus natura per se fluat, sed naturalem dixerunt, quòd cum natura Scripturæ sacræ, ex Dei ordinatione, tàm intimè & indivulsé, ac Scripturæ cuivis sua naturalis vis motiva, quam vi suarum vocum & rerũ significatarum habet, connexa est: aliàs autem eam supernaturalem esse, prout supernaturale dicitur, quod naturales rei vires excedit, & ex Dei libera voluntate ac ordinatione ad producendos effectus quosdã supernaturales ei concessum est, minimè inficiati sunt. Hoc quicquid est, eleganter explicarunt nostri in hac Salana Antecessores, D. Johannes Major, D. Johannes Gerhardus & D. Johannes Himmelius, τῶν ἐν ἁγίοις, in suo judicio de Controv. Rathmanniana, ap. Dedek. in Appendice ultima Quæst. VI. § 3. fol. 263. quorum hæc sunt verba: Es ist bey den Rechtgläubigen Kirchenlehrern unstreitig / daß die Krafft der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seligmachung dem Wort Gottes zugeschrieben werde nicht ex physica necessitate, natürlicher weise / als ob eine solche natürliche Krafft im Wort wäre / wie die Brennungs-Krafft im Feuer / die Nahrungs-Krafft im Brod / die Krafft gesund zu machen in der Artzeney. Denn Gottes Wort wircket nicht natürlicher Weise / wie das Feuer natürlich brennet / das Brod natürlich nehret / die Artzeney natürlich gesund machet / sonsten würde es die Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seligmachung / welche nicht ein natürliches / sondern Göttliches Werck / nicht können wircken. Es haben zwar etliche das Wort natürlich in diesem (Rathmannischen) Streit gebraucht / und gesagt: Das Wort Gottes habe seine inwendige Krafft / welche man wohl die natürliche Lebens-Krafft des Worts nennen könne / aber sie haben sich deutlich erklärt / daß sie das Wörtlein natürlich entgegen gesetzt / nicht dem ὑπερφυσικῷ, sondern dem παραφυτικῷ Rathmanniano, nicht dem übernatürlichen / sondern der zufälligen beyständlichen Anund Zufügung / welche Rathmannus lehret / und demnach haben sie keines weges hiermit andeuten wollen modum aliquem naturalis inhæsionis, als wenn dem Worte naturaliter, natürlicher weise diese Krafft zustünde / sondern einig und allein dieses / daß die Krafft der Erleuchtung sey dem Worte innerlich / und werde demselben nicht erst im Gebrauch von aussen durch den heiligen Geist beyund zugefügt / sondern gehöre (gleichsam) zur Natur und gantzen Vollkommenheit des Worts &c.


### III. The efficacy of Holy Scripture, therefore, is not to be sought in the…

III.

The efficacy of Holy Scripture, therefore, is not to be sought in the cultivation and splendor of speech, nor in the gravity of the sentences or the weight of the reasons and arguments which rhetoricians otherwise use to persuade and move the minds of the hearers.

For besides the fact that these things, viewed precisely in themselves, only move the intellect and will of man objectively, as has been said,

Paul also testifies in express terms that his speech and his preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, and that he speaks those things which are of the Spirit of God, not in words which human wisdom teaches, 1 Cor. 2:4, 13.

IV.

Nor is it to be sought in any created and finite power of acting. For to illuminate men whose minds are darkened, to convert to God those who are by nature turned away from God, to raise the dead in sins from spiritual death, to regenerate those born of the flesh so that they may become spirit, etc., are by the consent of all effects of God's infinite power, nor can they be produced by any created and finite power any more than men can be produced from nothing by a created and finite power. See among others B. Chemnitius, Part 1, Loc. cap. 1, on Creation.

V.

It must therefore be sought and established in the infinite power of God, which God, according to His wisdom and will, has communicated to it for these supernatural effects.

I. That it must be established in the infinite power of God, the Apostle of the Gentiles teaches expressly in Eph. 1:17 ff., when he prays to the God of our Lord Jesus Christ for his Ephesians for the Spirit of wisdom and revelation for the knowledge of Him, that the eyes of their minds might be enlightened, so that they may know what is the hope to which He has called them, and how opulent the glory of His inheritance in the saints, and what is the excellent greatness of His power toward us who believe, according to the efficacy of the might of His strength, which He exercised in Christ when He raised Him from the dead, etc. By which, without doubt, he speaks of the spiritual effects of the divine Word, namely the illumination of the intellect and saving faith, and he prays that these be conferred upon the Ephesians by God, as by the efficient cause, not indeed separately and independently of His Word, but through His Word as the instrument for producing the same, which is therefore called the Word of faith in Rom. 10:8, the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, etc., as we just showed from Rom. 1:16 and other Pauline passages. But the force or active virtue, which exerts itself through the Word of God for the purpose of illuminating the intellect of man, and for kindling faith, the praised Apostle establishes in the proper and essential POWER OF GOD, which is his very omnipotence. For he prays for his Ephesians that, their eyes of the mind being enlightened, they may know among other things also, what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of the strength of his might, i.e., what is the excellent magnitude of his power toward us, who believe according to the efficacy of the strength of his might. Where both the exceeding greatness of the power of God, and the strength of his might, are descriptions of divine omnipotence, and denote the divine power, exerting itself abundantly, excellently, and strongly for the kindling of faith in us through the Word of God. And that he speaks of the power of God, exerting itself so excellently for the kindling of faith in us through his Word, he hints by the added determination: in us, who believe according to the efficacy of the strength of his might. For the little word κατὰ in this place is a mark of cause, and to believe according to the efficacy of the strength of his might denotes the same thing as to believe through the efficacy of the strength of his might. But to believe through the efficacy of the strength of God, what else is it than to believe through the power of God, exerting itself most efficaciously in his Word and through it in us. Which very thing, that the Apostle might express more clearly, and exclude every doubt, he adds in v. 20: Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, etc. signifying that one and the same is the power by which God kindles faith in men, dead in sin, and recalls them from spiritual death into life; and by which he raised Christ from corporal death into life. Hence perhaps was born that most trite saying of the Ancients: That it is of no less power to convert a sinful man than to raise the dead. But the power which God exercised in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, is his very omnipotence. Therefore also the power by which he illuminates the darkened minds of men through his Word, and kindles faith, is the very Divine omnipotence. To the same sense the Apostle in Eph. III. 7 says that the gift of grace, according to which he was made a minister of the Gospel, was given to him κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, according to or through the efficacy of his power. And Col. II, 12, the faith, by which we are buried together with Christ through baptism they rise again from the death of sin into spiritual life, he calls it πίστιν τῆς ἐνεργείας τῦ Θεῦ, τῦ ἐγείραντος αὐτὸν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, the faith of the operation of God, who raised him (Christ) from the dead: not indeed of the operation of God alone without the Word, but of the operation exerting itself through his Word. Whatever, however, God works, whether in conferring gifts upon ministers, necessary for undertaking the ministry of the Gospel, or in sanctifying gifts, such as is the faith of the operation of God, or in other things, all that he works through his power, which in respect of the thing itself is his very essence.

II. Although indeed it is one and the same divine power by which God raised Christ from the dead, and by which he illuminates men dead in sins, kindles faith in them, and raises them from the death of sin, the manner of operation is nevertheless different. For God raised Christ from the dead by that power immediately; but he raises us from spiritual death by the same power mediately, namely by means of his Word, whether read in Scripture, or preached, and perceived by hearing. It is, however, a perpetual custom with God that, whenever he exerts his infinite power through intermediate causes to produce certain effects, whether natural or supernatural, he exerts it according to the reason and requirement of the intermediate causes: as for example of God, as the first cause, the concurrence with secondary causes is nothing else than the concurrence of God through his infinite power with secondary causes, acting through their own created and finite power of acting; with which, however, he does not exert it in every way, but according to their requirement, and in a manner congruent to their power of acting, so that if secondary causes fail in operating, on account of some defect of natural powers, the infinite power of God does not even produce the effect by itself alone and without the concurrence of secondary causes, although he could produce it by himself alone, if God wished to produce it absolutely and without the influx of secondary causes through it. The matter stands likewise with the infinite power of God, communicated to his Word, written or preached, which God does not exert upon men, dead in sins, to be raised from the death of sin in the very same way in which he exerted it to raise Christ from bodily death. For he raised Christ from the dead by it absolutely and without the intervention of any intermediate cause. But us sinners he raises from the death of sin through his Word, written or preached, to which it is joined, and according to its nature and requirement. But the reason for the divine Word, written and preached, is such that if it ought to exert itself to rouse a man dead in sins from the death of sin, it must be read or heard and considered with a zeal for learning: because this is an external and pedagogical work, man, even if spiritually dead, can do and omit it by his own carnal powers: and furthermore if he omits it, and does not deign to read, or hear and meditate upon the Word of God, then neither the Word of God, written or preached, nor the power of God which is joined to it, exerts itself to rouse him from the death of sin; or even if through the thorns of the pleasures and cares of this age he places an obstacle internally to its operation, he can prevent himself from being roused from the death of sin through the Word, even when read or perceived by hearing, and its divine δύναμιν, and cause himself to remain in death. Whence the Reformed wrongly infer from the fact that we are converted by the same divine power by which Christ was raised from death, that we are converted by God irresistibly.

III. That that δύναμις or divine power has been communicated to Holy Scripture by God, the thing itself speaks. For that the Word of God (under which Scripture is also contained) is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1:16, that it enlightens the eyes of the mind, Eph. 1:18, Ps. 19:11, 2 Pet. 1:19, that it is living, effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, Heb. 4:12, that it opens the eyes of the Gentiles, that they may turn from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, Acts 26:18, it certainly has that from the divine virtue and power in which it excels. But Holy Scripture cannot have this independently of itself: for thus God alone has it. Therefore it has it dependently from God, and communicated to it by the same. In which sense the Witeberg theologians well write in the Censura super controvers. Rathmannia in Dedekennus fol. 168, col. 2, write: Then furthermore to be known, that this power does not naturally reside in the letters and words themselves; but we hold that such power is a supernatural one, and indeed originally only the power of the Holy Spirit, who communicates such to the Word, and makes the same (actu secundo) alive when it is read, preached, and considered, so that it becomes a Word of Life, John 6.

v. 68. a word of salvation / Acts 11. v. 14. a fragrance of life to life / 2. Cor. 2. v. 16. To which the Jena theologians sing in response ibid. fol. 242. col. 2. in these words: The power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is and remains originally and essentially God's own; but because it has pleased God to illuminate, convert, and save us through the revealed Word, we must also honor God in this His holy order, and recognize His holy Word as a powerful means of illumination, conversion, and salvation. The power which is ascribed to God's Word proceeds solely and alone from the fact that it is God's Word; therefore, God's honor is not diminished thereby when divine power is ascribed to the revealed Word. Thus there is also no other power of illumination and salvation in the Word than that which is recognized in God, but God the LORD, to whom this power originally belongs, manifests the same in the Word and through the Word, etc.

Latin:

III.

Efficacia Scripturæ sacræ igitur quærenda non est in orationis cultu & splendore, nec in sententiarum gravitate aut rationum & argumentorum pondere, quibus aliàs Rhetores ad persuadendum & commovendos auditorum animos utuntur.

Præterquam enim quòd hæc, in se præcisè spectata, hominis intellectum & voluntatem, uti dictum, objectivè tantùm movent,

Paulus etiam testatur conceptis verbis, sermonem suum & prædicationom suam non fuisse in persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, & se loqui ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, non sermonibus, quos docet humana sapientia, 1. Cor. II. 4. 13.

IV.

Neque quærenda est in ulla vi agendi creata & finita. Nam homines, mente obtenebratos, illuminare, à Deo naturâ aversos ad Deum convertere, mortuos in peccatis ex morte spirituali suscitare, natos ex carne regenerare, ut fiant spiritus &c. omniũ consensu Dei infinitæ potentiæ effectus sunt, nec magis vi quâdam creatâ & finitâ produci possunt, quàm homines ex nihilo creatâ & finitâ vi produci possunt. Videatur inter alios B. Chemnitius part. I. Loc. cap. I. de Creatione.

V.

Quærenda ergo & constituenda est in Dei potentia infinita, quam Deus ad hosce supernaturales effectus pro sua sapientia & voluntate ei communicavit.

I. Quòd in Dei potentia infinita constituenda sit, docet disertè Gentium Apostolus Eph. I. 17. seqq. quando Ephesiis suis precatur à Deo Domini nostri Jesu Christi Spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis ad agnitionem sui, illuminatos oculos mentis ipsorum, ut sciant, quæ sit spes, ad quam ille vocavit, & quàm opulenta gloria hæreditatis illorum in sanctis, & quæ sit excellens magnitudo potentiæ illius in nos, qui credimus secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ejus, quam exercuit in Christo, cùm suscitaret eum ex mortuis &c. Quibus citra dubium loquitur de effectibus spiritualibus Verbi divini, illuminatione intellectus scilicet & fide salvifica, eosq́; precatur Ephesiis à Deo, tanquam à causa efficiente, non quidem seorsim & indepenter à Verbo ejus, sed per verbum ipsius, velut organon eorundẽ producendorum, conferendos, quod proptereà dicitur Verbum fidei Rom. X. 8. potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti &c. ut modò ex Rom. I. 16. & aliis locis Paulinis ostendimus. Vim verò sive virtutem activam, quæ per Verbum Dei ad illuminandum hominis intellectum, & ad fidem accendendam se exerit, constituit Apostolus laudatus in POTENTIA DEI propria & essentiali, quæ est ipsa ejus omnipotentia. Precatur enim Ephesiis suis illuminatos oculis mentis inter alia etiam, ut cognoscant τί τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, i. e. quæ sit excellens magnitudo potentiæ ipsius in nos, credentes secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ipsius. Ubi & ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως Θεοῦ, & τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, sunt descriptiones omnipotentiæ divinæ, & denotant potentiam divinam, ad accendendam in nobis fidem per Verbum Dei ubertim, excellenter, & fortiter se exerentem. Et quòd loquatur de potentia Dei, ad fidem per Verbum suum in nobis accendendam ita excellenter se exerente, innuit προσδιορισμῷ adjecto: in nobis, qui credimus secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ipsius. Nam vocula κατὰ hoc loco causæ nota est, & credere secundum efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ipsius idem denotat, atque credere per efficaciam roboris fortitudinis ipsius. Credere autem per efficaciam roboris fortitudinis Dei, quid aliud est, quàm credere per potentiam Dei, in ipsius Verbo & per illud se in nobis efficacissimè exerentem. Quod ipsum ut clariùs exprimeret, & dubium omne excluderet Apostolus, subjicit v. 20. Quam exercuit in Christo, cùm suscitaret eum ex mortuis &c. significans, unam & eandem esse potentiam, quâ Deus accendit fidem in hominibus, in peccato mortuis, eosque ex morte spirituali in vitam revocat; & quâ Christum ex morte corporali suscitavit in vitam. Hinc forsan natum illud Veterum dictum tritifsimum: Non minoris virtutis esse hominem peccatorem convertere, quàm mortuum suscitare. Sed potentia, quam Deus exercuit in Christo, cùm eum suscitaret ex mortuis, est ipsa ejus omnipotentia. Ergo & potentia, quâ per Verbum suum illuminat obtenebratas hominum mentes, fidemque accendit, est ipsa omnipotentia Divina. Eundem in sensum Apostolus Eph. III. 7. donum gratiæ, secundum quod Evangelii minister factus est, sibi datum esse dicit κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, secundum sive per efficaciam potentiæ ipsius. Et Col. II, 12. fidem, quâ consepulti cum Christo per baptismum ex morte peccati resurgunt in vitam spiritualem, vocat πίστιν τῆς ἐνεργείας τῦ Θεῦ, τῦ ἐγείραντος αὐτὸν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, fidem operationis Dei, qui excitavit eum (Christum) ex mortuis: non quidem operationis Dei solius absque Verbo, sed operationis, per Verbum ejus se exerenti. Quæcunq; autem Deus operatur, sive in conferendis donis ministrantibus, ad obeundum ministerium Evangelii necessariis, sive in donis sanctificantibus, quale est fides operationis Dei, sive in rebus aliis, id omne operatur per suam potentiam, quæ ex parte rei ipsa ejus essentia est.

II. Quamvis verò una & eadem potentia divina sit, quâ Deus Christum ex mortuis suscitavit, & quâ homines in peccatis mortuos illuminat, fidem in iis accendit, & ex morte peccati eos suscitat, modus operationis tamen diversus est. Nam Christum excitavit Deus per illam ex mortuis immediatè; nos autem excitat per eandem ex morte spirituali mediatè, mediante scilicet Verbo suo, sive lecto in Scriptura, sive prædicato, & auditu percepto. Est autem Deo in more perpetuo positum, ut quandocunq; potentiam suam infinitam per causas intermedias ad effectus quosdam, sive naturales, sive supernaturales, producendos exerit, pro ratione & exigentia causarum mediarum eam exerat: sicut v. g.
