Dei, velut causæ primæ, concursus cum causis secundis nihil est aliud, quàm concursus Dei per suam potentiam infinitam cum causis secundis, per suam vim agendi creatam & finitam agentibus; cum quibus tamen non omni modo eam exerit, sed pro illarum exigentia, & modo illarum virtuti agendi congruo, ut deficientibus causis secundis in operando, ob aliquem naturalium virium defectum, Dei potentia infinita etiam effectum non per se sola & absq; causarum secundarum concursu producat, quamvis eum per se sola producere posset, si Deus absolutè & absq; causarum secundarum influxu eum per illam producere vellet. Perindè res habet cum Dei infinita potentia, Verbo suo, scripto aut prædicato, communicata, quam Deus ad homines, in peccatis mortuos, ex morte peccati suscitandos non eodem planè modo exerit, quo eam ad Christum ex morte corporali suscitandum exeruit. Nam Christum suscitavit per eam ex mortuis absolutè & absque ullius causæ mediæ interventu. Nos peccatores autem suscitat ex morte peccati per Verbum suum, scriptum vel prædicatum, cui conjuncta est, & pro ejus ratione & exigentia. Verbi divini autem, scripti & prædicati, ea est ratio, ut si ad hominem in peccatis mortuum ex morte peccati excitandum se exerere debeat, cum studio discendi legatur vel audiatur & consideretur: quod quia externum & pædagogicum opus est, homo, etsi spiritualiter mortuus, ex suis carnalibus viribus facere & omittere potest: & porro si id omittat, atq; Verbum Dei legere, vel audire & meditari non dignetur, tùm nec Verbum Dei, scriptum vel prædicatum, nec, quæ ei conjuncta est, potentia Dei ad eum ex morte peccati excitandum se exerit; vel etiam si per spinas voluptatum & curarum hujus seculi interius operationi ejus obicem ponat, impedire potest, quò minùs per Verbum, etiam lectum vel auditu perceptum, ejusq; divinam δύναμιν ex morte peccati excitetur, & facere, ut maneat in morte. Unde malè Reformati ex eo, quòd eâdem potentiâ divinâ, quâ Christus ex morte suscitatus est, convertimur, inferunt, nos converti à Deo irresistibiliter.

III. Quòd illa δύναμις sive potentia divina Scripturæ sacræ à Deo communicata sit, res ipsa loquitur. Quod enim Verbum Dei (sub quo & Scriptura continetur) est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. quòd illuminat oculos mentis, Eph. I. 18. Psal. XIX. 11. II. Petr. I. 19. quòd vivum, efficax & penetrantius est, quovis gladio ancipiti, Ebr. IV. 12. quòd aperit oculos Gentium, ut convertantur à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanæ ad Deum, Act. XXVI. 18. id habet utiq; illud à divina, quâ pollet, virtute & potentia. Hanc autem non potest Scriptura sacra à se independenter habere: sic enim solus Deus eam habet. Ergo habet eam dependenter à Deo, & ab eodem sibi communicatam. Quem in sensum benè Theolog. Witebergenses in Censura super controvers. Rathmannia apud Dedekennum fol. 168. col. 2. scribunt: Da dann ferner zu wissen / daß diese Krafft nicht eben in den Buchstaben und Worten natürlicher weise stecke; sondern wir halte dafür/daß solche Krafft sey eine übernatürliche/und zwar ursprünglich allein des heilige Geistes Krafft/welcher solche dem Wort mittheilet/ und dasselbe/wann es gelesen/geprediget/betrachtet wird/also (actu secundo) lebendig machet/ daß es wird ein Wort des Lebens/ Joh. 6.

v. 68. ein Wort des Heils / Act. 11. v. 14. ein Geruch des Lebens zum Leben / 2. Cor. 2. v. 16. Quibus accinunt Theologi Jenenses ibid. fol. 242. col. 2. his verbis: Die Krafft der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seeligmachung ist und bleibt ursprünglich und wesentlich Gottes eigen / aber weil es Gott gefallen / durch das geoffenbahrte Wort uns zu erleuchten / zu bekehren und selig zu machen / so müssen wir auch Gott in solcher seiner heiligen Ordnung ehren / und sein heiliges Wort für ein kräfftiges Mittel der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seeligmachung erkennen. Die Krafft / welche Gottes Wort zugeschrieben wird / rühret einig und allein daher / dieweil es Gottes Wort ist / darumb wird dadurch Gottes Ehre nicht vergeringert / wann dem geoffenbahrten Wort Göttliche Krafft wird zugeschrieben. So ist auch keine andere Erleuchtungsund Seeligmachungs-Krafft im Wort / als welche in Gott wird erkennet / sondern Gott der HERR / dessen diese Krafft ursprünglich eigen ist / erweiset dieselbe im Wort und durchs Wort &c.


### VI. Moreover, this divine power has been communicated to Holy Scripture, not as…

VI.

Moreover, this divine power has been communicated to Holy Scripture, not as heat is communicated from fire by heating, for example, to water, so that it resides in it formally and subjectively; nor by way of πα- ρέκβασιν and external assistance, so that Scripture, viewed in itself, is devoid of it, and the letter is ineffective and dead, but in use, through the active power of the Holy Spirit approaching from the outside, it finally begins to be a living and effective organ of illumination, conversion, and regeneration: but by its intimate and inseparable union with it.

I. This divine power has not been communicated to Holy Scripture in such a way that it resides in it formally and subjectively; because this divine power, in terms of the thing itself, is the very essence of God, and thus God Himself: that this should be communicated to any created thing in such a way that it resides in it formally and subjectively is clearly repugnant. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say that the Word of God, considered formally, cannot be ascribed to the class of creatures, since it is a divine concept, the mind of God, the counsel of God, which, in terms of the thing itself, are God Himself. For although the concept of God, the mind and counsel of God, on the part of God, that it is his very essence, we may easily grant, yet we deny that the Word of God, concerning whose efficacy we are here treating, is formally the very concept of God, the very mind and counsel of God, and on the part of the thing, God himself. For it is a sign at least by institution signifying, by which God manifests to us his concepts, his mind, his counsel, which on the part of the thing is God himself, e.g., the concepts inspired in holy men, by which as signs he revealed his concepts to them, and the words, signifying by institution, by which, whether uttered by voice or configured in writing, holy men in turn signified to others the concepts divinely inspired in them, and consequently also the very concepts of God, were a created thing, and were as distant from God himself as a creature is distant from its creator: in which, therefore, the divine force and power, which on the part of the thing is the very uncreated essence of God, cannot formally and subjectively inhere.

II. Nor is it communicated to it in use only through mere παρέστασιν and external assistance, so that, viewed in itself and outside of use, it is destitute of the power of illuminating and converting the minds of men, and is ineffective and a dead letter: For the places of Scripture, alleged above and repeated several times, contradict this, which prove that Scripture is always effective in itself, and possesses the power of illuminating and converting the minds of men, whether it is viewed in use or in itself outside of use.

This is to be observed against Hermann Rathmann, formerly Pastor of St. Mary's Church in Danzig, who, in the sharp controversy stirred up fifty years ago and more concerning the efficacy of Holy Scripture, is said to have taught and held that Holy Scripture, viewed in itself and outside of use, possesses no divine power by which it can be effective for illuminating and converting the minds of men; but that when it is placed in use, that power supervenes upon it extrinsically from the Holy Spirit, elevating it to produce those effects, in the manner in which, to an axe placed in use, the power of cutting wood supervenes from the woodworker, moving it and applying and elevating it to cut wood. To this end looked the distinctions inculcated by him between Holy Scripture, committed to paper; and between the living Word of God, constituted by God in its operation; and between the twofold office of Scripture: one, by which it teaches objectively, by showing, by demonstrating, what is true, what is false, what is faith, hope, love etc. pleasing to God. The other, by which it effectively confers, by which it reveals and shows, as God, Christ, and eternal life, but exalted, and brought into living operation by the Holy Spirit &c. He attributed to the Holy Scriptures, committed to paper, or contained in the Biblical codex, no other power than an objective one, common to it with any other writing, by which, namely, written words, as signs of concepts and things, acting as objects, signify the things themselves to the intellect, and move and determine it to elicit their concepts within itself. And in this regard he compared it to a signpost, or a statue of Mercury, which, just as the latter, although devoid of life and dead, nevertheless objectively shows where one must go, so the former, although destitute of vivifying power to illuminate man's intellect and convert his will, and as it were dead, nevertheless objectively shows which way is true, which is deceptive &c. But by the living Word of God itself, which he distinguished from the Scripture committed to paper, he seems to have understood the internal concepts of things themselves, elicited by the power of words, whether perceived by reading Scripture or by hearing, and he seems to have thought that to this Word of God, established within the intellect, there finally supervenes a divine power from the Holy Spirit, not indeed always, nor in every man who has read Scripture or heard it taught, but where and when it has seemed good to God; and by that supervening power that internal Word is elevated, and established in its operation by the Holy Spirit in the manner in which an axe, by the supervening active power of the carpenter, is elevated and established in its operation for cutting wood. And in this regard he compared Holy Scripture to an axe, which does not have the power of cutting wood in itself and outside of use, but in use receives it externally from the carpenter. For more on this matter, let him who wishes see the Censures of the praised Wittenberg and Jena theologians on the writings of Rathmann, in the aforementioned place, fol. 163 et seqq.

III. It remains therefore to be said that that divine power or potency of illuminating and converting the souls of men has been communicated to Holy Scripture through an intimate and inseparable union of itself with it, so that it is and remains formally the power or potency proper to the Holy Spirit; but it is attributed to Holy Scripture that it is intimately joined or united to it, and that it [the power] exerts itself in it and through it, whether read or perceived by hearing, no less effectively to illuminate and convert the souls of men

and to produce in them other supernatural effects of grace, than if it were formally and subjectively inherent in it. Thus the Wittenberg theologians in their Censure in Dedek. loc. cit. fol. 167. col. 1, when Rathmann attributed to them that they maintained that the force and power of God was included or annexed to the external words of the preacher, declared that they were not speaking of a physical inclusion, but of a hyperphysical conjunction of the Word and divine power. Their words are these: He (Rathmann) blames us at the end of the demonstration, as if we taught that the power and might of God were enclosed in the external words of the preacher, whereas we speak of no physical inclusion, but only OF THE HYPERPHYSICAL CONJUNCTION OF THE WORD AND DIVINE POWER. In the same sense the Jena theologians in their judgment describe the manner in which the power of illuminating, converting, and saving is inherent in Holy Scripture, throughout by its UNION or CONJUNCTION with Scripture, or the Word of God, comprised in Scripture: e.g., fol. 246. col. 2. Luther understands by the Gospel not only the external sound and noise of the preached Gospel, or also only the externally signifying letters of the written Gospel, but at the same time also the internal Word, namely the sense and understanding, as also the divine power, which by divine ordinance is connected with the same. And after a few words interposed: According to Luther's opinion, the power of salvation is predicated and expressed by the Word of the Gospel, because the power of salvation is united with the preaching of the Gospel in such a way that the Gospel truly has an internal power of quickening and salvation in and with itself. And fol. 264. 1. When some orthodox teachers have written: The power of illumination is necessarily in the Word, they do not look to the absolute power of God, but the ordinary; their opinion is that by virtue of a voluntary ordinance made by God himself, the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is always and indissolubly united with the Word, so that ordinarily, in the regular way, no one can be illuminated, converted, and saved, unless it happens through the Word of God, etc., fol. 265, col. 2. Because by virtue of Divine order, this power is united with the Word in such a way that therefore the Apostle himself describes the Word as being a power of God that saves those who believe in it, Rom. 1:16, as if one could not unreasonably say in such a sense &c. fol. 266. col. 1. the power of illumination is internal to the Word, and by virtue of Divine order is connected with the Word in such a way that it belongs to the internal perfection of the Word &c. ibidem: Meanwhile, the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is not, strictly speaking, enclosed in the Word, but is united with it in a wonderful and inscrutable way through God's order; in the same way as the body of Christ is not enclosed in the blessed bread, and Christ's blood is not enclosed in the blessed wine, but is united through Christ's order in a wonderful, inscrutable way. In all of which places the Jena theologians describe the manner in which the Holy Spirit communicates the power of illuminating and converting the minds of men to His Word, through the union and conjunction of that [power] with the Word, or through His free binding to the Word.

Latin:

VI.

COmmunicata autem est vis hæc divina Scripturæ sacræ, non ut calor ab igne per calefactionem communicatur, v. g. aquæ, ut ei formaliter, & subjectivè insit; nec per παρέκβασιν & adsistentiam externam, ut in se spectata Scriptura ejus expers, litera inefficax & mortua sit, in usu verò per vim activam Spiritus Sancti, forinsecus accedentem, demum vivum & efficax organon illuminationis, conversionis & regenerationis esse incipiat: sed per sui unionem cum illa intimam & individuam.

I. Non communicata est Scripturæ sacræ vis hæc divina ita ut ei formaliter & subjectivè insit; quia vis hæc divina, ex parte rei, est ipsa Dei essentia, atque adeò Deus ipse: quam alicui rei creatæ ita communicari, ut ei formaliter & subjectivè insit, planè repugnat. Neq; est, quod quis dicat, Verbum Dei, formaliter consideratum, non posse creaturarum classi adscribi, cùm sit conceptus divinus, mens Dei, consilium Dei, quæ, quoad rem, sint ipse Deus. Quamvis enim conceptum Dei, mentem & consilium Dei, ex parte Dei, ipsam ejus essentiam esse, facilè largiamur, negamus tamen, Verbum Dei, de cujus efficacia hîc agitur, formaliter esse ipsum Dei conceptum, ipsam Dei mente & consilium, & ex parte rei Deum ipsum. Est enim signum saltem ex instituto significans, quo Deus suos conceptus, mentem suam, suum consilium, quod ex parte rei Deus ipse est, nobis manifestat, v. g. conceptus, Viris sanctis inspirati, quibus velut signis conceptus suos illis revelabat, & verba, ex instituto significantia, quibus sive voce prolatis sive scripto configuratis Viri sancti rursum conceptus, sibi divinitùs inspiratos, & consequenter etiam ipsos conceptus Dei aliis significabant, erant creatum quid, & tantum distabant ab ipso Deo, quantum creatura à creatore suo distat: quibus proinde divina vis & potentia, quæ ex parte rei ipsa Dei increata essentia est, formaliter & subjectivè inesse non potest.

II. Neque communicatur ei in usu demum per nudam παρέστασιν & externam adsistentiam, ita ut in se & extra usum spectata vi illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos destituta, inefficax & litera mortua sit: Repugnant enim loca Scripturæ, superiùs allegata, & aliquoties repetita, quæ Scripturam in se semper efficacem esse, & vi illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos pollere, evincunt, sive ea in usu, sive in se extra usum spectetur.

Observandum hoc est contra Hermannum Rathmannum, Ecclesiæ Dantiscænæ ad D. Mariæ quondam Pastorem, qui excitatâ ante annos quinquaginta, & quod excurrit, controversiâ acri de Scripturæ sacræ efficacia docuisse & sensisse fertur, Scripturam sacram, in se & extra usum spectatam, nullâ pollere vi divinâ, quâ ad illuminandos convertendosq; hominum animos efficax esse possit; in usu autem constitutæ supervenire illam forinsecus à Spiritu Sancto, eam ad effectus illos producendos elevante, eum in modum, quo securi, in usu constitutæ, supervenit vis scindendi ligna à fabro lignario, eam movente, & ad secanda ligna applicante ac elevante. Quò spectabant inculcatæ ab ipso distinctiones inter Scripturam sacram, chartæ traditam; & inter Verbum Dei vivum, in sua operatione à Deo constitutum; & inter duplex Scripturæ officium: unum, quo objectivè doceat, ostendendo, demonstrando, quæ vera, quæ falsa, quæ fides, spes, charitas &c. Deo grata. Alterum, quo effective conferat, qua indicando & oftendendo repandit, ut Deum, Christum, & vitam æternam, sed exaltata, inque vivam operationem a Spiritu Sancto deducta &c. Scripturæ sacræ, chartæ traditæ, sive in codice Biblico contentæ non aliam tribuebat vim, quam objectivam, cum alia quavis Scriptura ipsi communem, qua scilicet voces scriptæ, velut signa conceptuum & rerum, objectorum vicem obeuntes, ipsas res intellectui significant, eumq; ad illarum conceptus, in se eliciendos, movent & determinant. Atq; hoc intuitu eam comparabat Indici, seu statuæ Mercuriali, quod sicut hæc, licet vitæ expers & mortua, objective tamen ostendit, quo eundum sit, ita illa, licet vi vivifica ad illuminandum hominis intellectum convertendamq; ejus voluntatem destituta & quasi mortua, objective tamen ostendat, quæ via vera, quæ fallax &c. Per ipsum vero Verbum Dei vivum, quod Scripturæ, chartæ traditæ, contradistingvebat, intellexisse videtur ipsos internos rerum conceptus, vi vocum sive lectione Scripturæ, sive auditu perceptarum, elicitos, & sensisse videtur, quod huic intus in intellectu constituto Verbo Dei demum superveniat vis divina a Spiritu Sancto, non quidem semper, nec in omni homine, qui Scripturam legerit vel doceri audiverit, sed ubi & quando Deo visum est; & ea vi superveniente elevari Verbum illud internum, constituiq; in sua operatione a Spiritu Sancto eum in modum, quo securis superveniente vi activa fabri lignarii elevatur & in sua operatione constituitur ad secandum lignum. Atque hoc intuitu Scripturam sacram comparabat securi, quæ vim scindendi ligna in se & extra usum non habet, in usu autem eam forinsecus a fabro lignario accipiat. Plura hanc in rem, qui vult, videat in Censuris laudatorum Theologorum Witebergensium & Jenensium super Rathmanni scriptis d. l. fol. 163. seqq.

III. Dicendum ergo superest, quod divina illa vis sive potentia illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos Scripturæ sacræ communicata sit per unionem sui cum illa intimam ac indivulsam, ita ut formaliter quidem sit & maneat vis sive potentia Spiritus Sancti propria; Scripturæ sacræ autem tribuatur, quod ei intime conjuncta sive unita sit, seq; in ea ac per eam, sive lectam, sive auditu perceptam, ad illuminandos & convertendos hominum ani-

mos aliosq́; supernaturales gratiæ effectus in iis producendos non minùs efficaciter sese exerat, ac si formaliter & subjectivè ei inesset. Ita Theologi Witebergenses in Censura suâ apud Dedek. d. l. fol. 167. col. 1. cùm ipsis Rathmannus tribueret, quòd statuerent, vim & potentiam Dei verbis externis prædicantis inclusam vel annexam esse declararunt se, quòd non loquuti sint de physica inclusione, sed de hyperphysica Verbi & divinæ potentiæ conjunctione. Verba illorum sunt hæc: Er (Rathmann) gibt uns Schuld am Ende der Demonstration, als lehreten wir/ daß den eusserlichen Worten des Predigers die Krafft und Macht Gottes sey eingeschlossen/ da wir doch von keiner physica inclusione, sondern allein DE HYPERPHYSICA VERBI ET DIVINÆ POTENTIÆ CONJUNCTIONE reden. Eundem in sensum Theologi Jenenses in suo judicio describunt modum, quo vis illuminandi, convertendi & salvandi Scripturæ sacræ inest, passim per ejus UNIONEM vel CONJUNCTIONEM cum Scriptura, sive Verbo Dei, in Scriptura comprehenso: v. g. fol. 246. col. 2. Lutherus verstehet durch das Evangelium nicht nur den eusserlichen Schall und Schall des gepredigten Evangelii/ oder auch allein die eusserlichen bedeutende Buchstaben des geschriebenen Evangelii/ sondern zugleich auch das innerliche Wort/ nemlich den Sinn und Verstand/ wie auch die Göttliche Krafft/ so aus Göttlicher Ordnung mit demselben verbunden. Et post pauca interjecta: Lutheri Meinung nach wird die Krafft der Seeligmachung vom Wort des Evangelii prædiciret/ und ausgesprochen/ weil die Krafft der Seeligmachung mit der Predigt des Evangelii solcher gestalt vereiniget/ daß das Evangelium warhafftig eine innerliche Lebendigmachungsund Seeligmachungs-Krafft in und bey sich habe. Et fol. 264. 1. Wenn etliche rechtgläubige Lehrer geschrieben: Die Krafft der Erleuchtung sey im Wort nothwendig/ so sehen sie nicht auf die absolutam Dei potentiam, sed ordinariam, ihre Meinung ist/ daß vermöge freywilliger von Gott selbst gemachten Ordnung die Krafft der Erleuchtung/ Bekehrung und Seeligmachung immerdar und unauflößlich mit dem Wort vereinbahret/ also daß ordinarie, ordentlicher weise niemand möge erleuchtet/ bekehret/ und seelig gemachet werden/ es geschehe denn durchs Wort Gottes &c. fol. 265. col. 2. Weil vermöge Göttlicher Ordnung / diese Krafft mit dem Wort solcher gestalt vereinbahret / daß dannenhero der Apostel selber das Wort also beschreibet / daß es sey eine Krafft Gottes / die da seelig mache / so daran gläuben / Rom. 1. v. 16. als könte man in solchem Verstande nicht unbillich sagen &c. fol. 266. col. 1. die Erleuchtungs-Krafft ist dem Wort innerlich / und vermöge Göttlicher Ordnung solcher gestalt mit dem Wort verbunden / daß sie zur innerlichen Vollkommenheit des Worts gehöret &c. ibidem: Unterdessen ist die Krafft der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seeligmachung in dem Wort / eigentlich zu reden / nicht eingeschlossen / sondern durch Gottes Ordnung wunderbahrer unerforschlicher weise mit demselben vereiniget; gleicher weise / wie der Leib Christi in dem gesegneten Brod / und Christi Blut in dem gesegneten Wein nicht eingeschlossen / sondern durch Christi Ordnung wunderbahrer / unerforschlicher weise vereiniget. Quibus in locis omnibus Theologi Jenenses modum, quo vim illuminandi & convertendi hominum animos Spiritus Sanctus Verbo suo communicat, per unionem & conjunctionem illius cum Verbo, aut per liberam ejus alligationem ad Verbum describunt.


### VII. Moreover, this δύναμις or power of illuminating and converting the minds of men…

VII.

Moreover, this δύναμις or power of illuminating and converting the minds of men is always present in Holy Scripture in the first act, even outside of use; but it exerts itself in the second act only in use, namely when it is read, or when it is proposed by the voice of a teacher and perceived by hearing, unless an obstacle is placed in its operation internally by man.

I. By the first act we understand the very divine force and power of illuminating and converting the minds of men: but by the second act, its actual influx into the illumination and conversion of man. The former, by divine ordination, is always present in Holy Scripture, whether it is contained in the Biblical codex, outside of use; or whether it is read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, and perceived by hearing, and established in its legitimate use; but it is not present in it in the second act, or rather, it does not exert itself through it in the second act for the illumination and conversion of man to be performed, unless when Scripture is established in use through reading or preaching. And when Holy Scripture is established in use, that divine power always exerts itself in second act, unless its operation is hindered on the part of men by the security of the flesh, or the thorns of the pleasures or cares of this world, and the seed of the divine Word, received in the field of the heart, is suffocated, as Christ teaches at length in the parable of the seed and the fourfold part of the field, Matt. 13:19 ff. The Wittenberg theologians declare this beautifully in their Censura, loc. cit., fol. 166, col. 1. Their words are these: As concerns the cooperation of the Holy Spirit and the power of Holy Scripture, it can be considered either as to the first act, that it can work and that the Holy Spirit wills to work through it; or as to the second act, that it works effectively and the Holy Spirit is actually busy through it. The first act and the will of the Holy Spirit to work are always found with Holy Scripture and the Word of God when it is read or heard, and should never be considered without it; for just as an axe always physically has the power of cutting, and medicine the power of healing, even if the axe does not cut in second act, nor the medicine heal; so the read and preached Word of God has hyperphysically and through the order of the Holy Spirit in itself the power of enlightening and converting, even if it does not always and in all hearers enlighten and convert in second act. But the second act and the effective working are not always found with Scripture and the Word, for example, when Jews, hypocrites, or sinners read it; but not as if the Holy Spirit did not want to work through such read Word, or that it did not have the power to work; rather, this happens only per accidens, because of the unbelief and disobedience of men.

II. Here Rathmann dissents, and grants no power of enlightening and converting the souls of men to Holy Scripture contained in the Biblical Codex, but only to the Word of God, as an instrument of the Holy Spirit to the internal intellect of man, enlightening and converting the souls of men through it. He considers the Holy Scripture itself contained in the Biblical Codex as a dead letter. His reason is: because that which leads and converts to God, sanctifies, purifies, saves, ought to enter the soul and be received into it. But Holy Scripture, as it is comprised in letters, does not enter the soul, but remains in its tablets, etc. Its words, in the Censura of the Wittenberg Theologians, d. l. fol. 168, are as follows: What leads us to God, converts, sanctifies, purifies, saves, that must come into the soul and be received. But now Holy Scripture, insofar as it is composed and recorded in the letter, does not come into the soul, but remains in its tablets; but the illumination and the Spirit occur in the soul. Therefore Scripture, insofar as it is composed in the letter, does not grasp the soul and the human being and change them unto conversion, sanctification, salvation. But this argument of Rathmann is clearly slippery, and it proves nothing less than that Holy Scripture, contained in the Biblical Codex, is a dead letter and does not have the divine power of illuminating, etc., even in its first act. For what is said, that what leads to God, converts, sanctifies, etc., ought to enter the soul, can be understood in a double sense. First, that it ought to enter the soul according to its real being. Second, that it ought to enter it according to its intentional being, and through a certain species of itself. Understood in the former sense, the assertion is most false. For it is not required for intelligible objects, such as Holy Scripture comprised in letters also is, in order that they may move the human intellect and will to elicit acts concerning them, that they enter the soul according to their real being, but it suffices that they enter it according to their intelligible species and thus according to their intentional being. But if the assertion is understood in the latter sense, it is most false what Rathmann says, that Holy Scripture, comprised in letters, does not enter the soul. For when Holy Scripture, comprised in letters in the Biblical Codex, is read, the individual words transmit their species through sight to the imagination, and the phantasms of the words impressed upon the imagination, elevated by the agent intellect, further produce in the possible intellect their intelligible species, and thus Holy Scripture, comprised in letters, in whatever part it is read, enters the intellect through its intelligible species, and thus intentionally. But if, from the fact that Holy Scripture, comprised in letters, remains in its tablets, if Rathmann wishes to gather that it does not enter the intellect intentionally and through its own species, he will be most inept, and it will be just as if he were to say that horses, oxen, when they are seen in their stables, and stones, when they are seen on the ground, and are known by the intellect, do not enter the intellect intentionally and through their own species, because those remain in their stables, these on the ground. For from that, if anything, at least this follows, that Holy Scripture does not enter the intellect according to its real being, which it has in written tablets, which is most true, and cannot come into question among men who are indeed of sound mind.

III. But, someone might say, if the divine force and power of illuminating and converting the souls of men is always present in Holy Scripture in the first act through its inseparable union or conjunction with it, even outside of all use, one or the other must be admitted, that it is joined or united either with the words written on paper, or with their sense. But neither can be said. Not the former: because the theologians themselves, who attribute this force to Holy Scripture, consider it among the absurdities that a supernatural and truly divine force of illuminating and converting is present in the words, whether through union with itself, or in another way, and they fear to assert that. Nor the latter: because the sense is not present in Holy Scripture, except by means of the words, as its signs, and thus the sense is not present in Scripture in act through a real and actual coexistence of itself with the words, but in power, and through the force of the words of signifying, and then at last it begins to be in act and to coexist with the words, when the words, whether through reading or through preaching transmitted to the intellect, represent it to the intellect in act. Therefore that divine force and power of illuminating is not present in Holy Scripture, viewed in the Biblical Codex outside of all use, nor can it be present to it through a real union of itself.

IV. To this objection it can be answered that that divine force is said to be joined to Holy Scripture, contained in paper, in the first act, not because it is precisely joined with the words, or precisely joined with the sense of the words, and united by an inseparable bond, but because it has been so established by the free will and ordinance of God, that wherever the Word of God, whether written, or uttered by voice, or fixed in the intellect through internal species and concepts, is held, there the Holy Spirit, with His own force and power of illuminating and of producing other supernatural effects through it, both outside the intellect and within it, is present alongside the same, and by this power renders it efficacious and potent in first act to produce those same effects, so that in second act it also exerts this power together with the Holy Spirit, from whom it has it, whenever it attains to producing those effects in their supernatural being. That this may be more correctly declared and understood, it must be known that the Word of God, in so far as it is considered as the instrument of our illumination and conversion, can be viewed either in its sensible signs, namely words, uttered by a sensible voice, or comprised in writing, or in the intelligible species of the things signified, excited and coordinated in the intellect by sensible words, as also in the concepts of the mind, or rather in the Word of the mind, produced in the intellect through acts of illumination.

In whatever way the Word of God is viewed, the power of illuminating and converting the minds of men is always in it in first act, though in a diverse manner. In the Word of God, through the species of the things signified and the concepts already fixed in the intellect, that [power] is present in first act most especially through its union, primarily indeed with the IMPRESSED SPECIES of the things signified themselves. For in these is contained, on the part of the intellect, the Word of God in first act. The reason is: because the illumination of the mind consists in supernatural acts of knowing, and that which, on the part of the Word of God fixed in the intellect, is the instrumental cause of the supernatural acts of knowing to be produced in the intellect, must also have joined or united with it that divine power of illuminating, as the principal virtue of acting and producing them. For it is necessary that the virtue of the principal cause be joined and united with the instrumental cause, if the effect is to be produced by both jointly. But for the supernatural acts of knowing to be efficiently produced in the intellect, the impressed species of revealed things behave, on the part of the Word, by way of an instrumental cause. For these, as they take the place of revealed objects in the intellect, so they determine the intellect in place of the objects in supernatural illumination just as in any other natural cognition, for acts of simple apprehension to be elicited in conformity with the things, and they concur in both cases with it to elicit them efficiently. Therefore, it is necessary that with the impressed species that divine power of which we are speaking be joined, as the virtue of the principal cause of illumination. Indeed, joined with these, that power exerts itself for the acts of illumination to be produced directly in the intellect, having first excited a holy thought concerning those things which are of the Spirit of God; and then subsequently others, by the same, having kindled supernatural acts of knowledge and faith, as was shown at greater length above in Chapter VI, Assertion VII; and the species of revealed things, impressed upon the intellect, together with that divine power of illuminating the minds of men conjoined to itself, are that LIGHT of the Word, concerning which the Psalmist says in Psalm CXIX. 105: Thy word is a LIGHT unto my feet, and a lamp unto my paths; and Solomon in Proverbs VI. 23: The commandment is a lamp, and the law is LIGHT; and Peter in II Epistle I. 19: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which while you attend as to a lamp appearing in a dark place, you do well, etc. are, into which the spiritual LIGHT of the mind in the first act; but exerting themselves with it toward acts of supernatural knowing, to be elicited in the intellect, are the spiritual LIGHT of the mind in the second act, and the acts of supernatural knowing themselves, elicited through them, are the actual illumination itself, of which the sacred Scriptures speak throughout.

Then in the Word of God, through the species impressed and the concepts of revealed things fixed in the intellect, there resides also that divine illuminating power through the union of itself with the WORD OF THE MIND, through acts of knowledge produced in the intellect. By the word of the mind, however, I understand here the term of supernatural knowledge or intellection, which is a certain quality and species or image of the thing known, expressed, efficiently produced in the intellect by the act of knowledge; which, although it is a certain effect of that divine power conjoined to the Word of God, and posterior to it, indeed a certain habitual light of the intellect, kindled by the efficacy of the Word, nevertheless in order to elicit other supernatural acts of knowledge it behaves sometimes as a reason for knowing, and conjoined with that illuminating power of the Holy Spirit, it holds a torch, as it were, before the intellect for the knowledge of other things; but reflected into itself, it testifies also concerning itself, and its dependence upon God in the hearts of men, and is said therefore, he who believes, to have the testimony of God in himself, I John V. 10, as we taught at greater length above in Chapter VI, Assertion IV, Explanation no. III, and Assertion VII, Explanation no. IV.

In the Word of God, however, in its sensible signs, namely external words, that which can be uttered by a sensible voice, or inscribed with ink, has within it a divine power of illuminating and converting the minds of men in the first act, not only in use, when it is transmitted to the intellect through hearing by the sensible voice of the teacher, or through sight by the reading of the Biblical Code, but also outside of use, when there is no one who reads it in the Biblical Code, or proposes it to another by voice, and thus transfers it to use. Although our blessed predecessors, in their Judgment on the Rathmann controversy, loc. cit., fol. 268, col. 1, reckon the question concerning the efficacy of Scripture in the first act, outside of all use, among questions that have arisen alongside, and which are not of faith, they nevertheless proceed to support the affirmative part of it there with several arguments. However, it is said by them that the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit is in the Word of God outside of use, not because it is really conjoined and united to the very tips of the words, written on paper, just as species are impressed upon the intellect; nor because it really resides precisely in the sense of the words, outside of the intellect, but because it is so ordained and constituted by the free will of God, that the Word of God, consisting of words and sense, wherever it exists, is always an effective organ of conversion, and the Holy Spirit is present to it with His own power and potentiality of illuminating and converting, and wills to exert Himself effectively through it also for the illumination and conversion of men, whenever it penetrates to the soul, whether by preaching through hearing, or by reading through sight, and is applied to illuminating and converting it. In this manner they explain this matter in their Censure, loc. cit., fol. 199, col. 2, when, from certain observations handed down by themselves concerning the operation of Scripture, they infer among other things, that the Scripture or the written Word of God, even before our reading and contemplation, as a means chosen and powerful by God, has the power and light for conversion; that is, it is useful and capable (the like of which cannot be said of any other profane book) and dedicated, written, and left and presented to the world by God for this purpose, that we should hereby be instructed in the way of salvation, and it does not receive such power and might only from our reading, or during our reading, no otherwise than if it were to be considered a dead letter beforehand, and would only then be acquired, and animated with the power of conversion, equipped and attired/ when it is taken in hand by us &c. Where they expressly explain that Scripture, even before our reading and meditation, has power and light to accomplish our conversion, through the fact that it is useful and suitable, and ordained by God for this purpose, written, and left and proposed to the world,

But that it is not really conjoined and united to the letters and points of words written on paper, the same authors admit freely in various places. We by no means attribute to the words, syllables, and letters, as they are written on paper, a secret, hidden, natural or magical, or even supernatural power; they write in the same place, fol. 267, col. 1. Compare fol. 200, col. 1, 270, col. 2, fol. 240, col. 1.

But they say more than once that it is conjoined to the sense, as the form of Scripture. The Divine order, they write on fol. 273, 2, consists not only in the fact that the heard, read, and contemplated Word should work faith in the hearts of those who hear, read, and contemplate it, but also in the fact that with the sense, understanding, and meaning, in which the inner form of the Word consists, the Divine power to work faith should always be united, whether it be in the mind of the Apostles, or be preached by them, or written in a book, or be in the mind of those who read it. And fol. 267, 1. Concerning the inner form of Holy Scripture, that is, concerning the inner sense, counsel, and meaning of God, contained in the external words, we say that the Lord God has, out of free grace, assigned to it the power of the Holy Spirit to enlighten, convert, and save men. Conf. fol. 240, 1.

But these things which they say concerning the divine power conjoined to the sense can be understood either of the sense of the words of Scripture outside the intellect, or of the same sense once it has been apprehended by the intellect. Viewed in either way, the divine power of illuminating and converting the minds of men is said to be inherent in it, but in different ways. Viewed in the intellect, it is inherent through its actual conjunction or union with the species of the signified things, which are impressed and expressed. For in these is contained the sense of the divine Word, written and preached, in the human intellect, as has been said.

But viewed outside of the intellect, it is said to be present, because God by His most free will has so ordained that the Holy Spirit, even outside of the intellect, is always and everywhere present with His divine force and power of illuminating and converting the souls of men, and together with it, when read or proposed by the voice of a teacher, penetrates at the same time to the soul of man, and there, united with the species of the things signified, partly impressed and partly expressed, exerts itself through them for conversion.

Latin:

VII.

Inest autem Scripturæ sacræ hæc δύναμις sive vis illuminandi & convertendi hominum animos actu primo semper, etiam extra usum; exerit autem sese actu secundo in usu demùm, quando scilicet legitur, vel voce docentis proposita auditu percipitur, nisi ejus operationi interiùs ab homine obex ponatur.

I. Per actum primum intelligimus ipsam vim & potentiam divinam hominum animos illuminandi & convertendi: per actum secundum verò ejus actualem influxum in hominis illuminationem & conversionem. Illa, ex divinâ ordinatione, semper inest Scripturæ sacræ, sive in codice Biblico contenta, extra usum; sive lecta aut docentis voce proposita, audituq́; percepta in suo legitimo usu constituta sit; sed actu secundo non inest ei, vel potiùs actu secundo non exerit se per eam ad illuminationem & conversionem hominis peragendam, nisi quando Scriptura per lectionem vel prædicationem in usu constituitur. Et quando in usu constituitur Scriptura sacra, exerit se vis illa divina semper actu secundo, nisi ex parte hominum securitate carnis, spinisve voluptatum aut curarum hujus seculi ejus operatio impediatur, & semen Verbi divini, in agro cordis receptum, suffocetur, uti in parabola de semine & quadruplici parte agri pluribus docet Christus Matth. XIII. v. 19. seqq. Pulchrè hæc declarant Witebergenses Theologi in Censura sua d. l. fol. 166. col. 1. Verba illorum sunt hæc: Was anlanget die cooperationem Spiritus Sancti, und die Krafft der H. Schrifft / so kan dieselbe betrachtet werden / vel quoad actum primum, daß sie wircken kan/und daß der H. Geist dadurch wircken wil: vel quoad actum secundum, daß sie thätlich wircket / und der heilige Geist dadurch in der That geschäfftig ist. Der actus primus und der Wille des H. Geistes zu wircken / findet sich allezeit bey der H. Schrifft/ und dem Wort Gottes/ wann es gelesen oder gehöret wird/ soll auch ohne dieselbe niemals betrachtet werden; Dann wie eine Axt allezeit physicè hat potentiam secandi, und die Artzney potentiam curandi, ob schon die Axt actu secundo nicht hauet / noch die Artzney heilet; also hat das gelesene und gepredigte Wort Gottes hyperphysicè und durch des H. Geistes Ordnung an sich potentiam illuminandi & convertendi, ob es schon actu secundo nicht allezeit/ und alle Zuhörer erleuchtet und bekehret. Der actus secundus aber / und die thätliche Wirckung finden sich nicht allezeit bey der Schrifft und dem Wort / zum Exempel / wenn dasselbe lesen Jüden/ Heuchler / Sünder; nicht aber als wann der H. Geist nicht wircken wolte durch solches gelesene Wort / oder dasselbe nicht hätte die Krafft zu wircken; sondern es geschicht dieses allein per accidens, wegen des Unglaubens und Ungehorsams der Menschen.

II. Hîc dissentit Rathmannus, & Scripturæ sacræ, in Codice Biblico contentæ, nullam concedit vim illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos, sed soli Verbo Dei, hominis intellectui interno, velut instrumento Spiritus Sancti, hominum animos per illud illuminantis & convertentis. Ipsam verò in Codice Biblico contentam Scripturam sacram pro litera mortua habet. Ratio ejus est: quia quod ad Deum ducit & convertit, sanctificat, purificat, salvat, animam ingredi, & in ea recipi debet. Sed Scriptura sacra, prout literis comprehensa est, non ingreditur animam, sed manet in suis tabulis &c. Verba ejus, in Theologorum Witebergensium Censura d. l. fol. 168. habent ita: Was uns zu Gott führet/ bekehret/ heiliget/ reiniget/ beseliget/ das muß in die Seele kommen und aufgenommen werden. Nun aber kömt die H. Schrifft/ so ferne sie im Buchstaben verfasset und verzeichnet ist/ nicht in die Seele/ sondern bleibet in ihren Taffeln/ aber die Erleuchtung und der Geist ereignet sich in der Seelen. Darumb die Schrifft/ so fern sie im Buchstaben verfasset ist/ die Seele und den Menschen nicht fasset und wandelt zur Bekehrung/ Heiligung/ Beseeligung. Verùm hæc Rathmanni ratio planè lubrica est, nec quicquam minùs, quàm Scripturam sacram, in Codice Biblico contentam, literam mortuam esse, & vim divinam illuminandi &c. ne actu primo quidem habere, evincit. Quod enim dicitur, quod ad Deum ducit, convertit, sanctificat &c. animam ingredi oportere, duplici sensu intelligi potest. Uro, quòd ingredi oporteat animam secundum suum esse reale. Altero, quòd eam ingredi oporteat secundum suum esse intentionale, & per sui quandam speciem. Priori sensu intellecta assertio falsissima est. Non enim ad objecta intelligibilia, quale etiam Scriptura sacra, literis comprehensa, est, ut hominis intellectum & voluntatem ad actus circa se eliciendos movere possint, requiritur, ut secundum suum esse reale animam ingrediantur, sed sufficit, quod secundum sui species intelligibiles atq; adeò secundum suum esse intentionale eam ingrediantur. Posteriori autem sensu si intelligatur assertio, falsissimum est, quod dicit Rathmannus, Scripturam sacram, literis comprehensam, non ingredi animam. Quando enim Scriptura sacra, literis in Codice Biblico comprehensa, legitur, voces singulæ transmittunt sui species per visum ad phantasiam, & phantasiæ impressa vocum phantasmata, ab intellectu agente elevata, producunt porro in intellectu possibili illarum species intelligibiles, atq; adeò Scriptura sacra, literis comprehensa, quacunq; parte legitur, ingreditur intellectum per sui species intelligibiles, atque sic intentionaliter. Quod si verò ex eo, quòd Scriptura sacra, literis comprehensa, in suis tabulis manet, Rathmannus colligere velit, eam non ingredi intellectum intentionaliter & per sui species, ineptissimus erit, & perinde erit, ac si dicat, equos, boves, cum in suis stabulis, & lapides, cùm in terra conspiciuntur, & ab intellectu cognoscuntur, non ingredi intellectum intentionaliter, & per sui species, quòd illi in suis stabulis, hi in terra maneant. Inde enim, si quicquam, hoc saltem sequitur, Scripturam sacram non ingredi intellectum secundum suum esse reale, quod in tabulis scriptis habent, quod verissimum est, nec in quæstionem venire potest apud homines, qui quidem sanæ mentis sunt.

III. At, dicat quis, si divina vis & potentia illuminandi & convertendi hominum animos actu primo semper inest Scripturæ sacræ per sui unionem sive conjunctionem cum illa indivulsam, etiam extra omnem usum, alterutrum admittendum erit, quòd vel cum verbis scriptis in charta, vel cum illorum sensu conjuncta sive unita sit. Sed neutrum dici potest. Non prius: quia vim illuminandi & convertendi supernaturalem vereq́; divinam inesse verbis, sive per unionem sui, sive modo alio, ipsimet Theologi, qui Scripturæ sacræ vim hanc tribuunt, in absurdis habent, idq́; asserere verentur. Neq; posterius: quia sensus non inest Scripturæ sacræ, nisi mediantibus verbis, velut suis signis, atq; adeò sensus non inest Scripturæ actu per realem & actualem sui coexistentiam cum verbis, sed potestate, & per verborum vim significandi, & tùm demum actu esse & verbis coëxistere incipit, cum verba, sive per lectionem sive per prædicationem ad intellectum transmissa, intellectui eum actu repræsentant. Ergo divina illa vis & potentia illuminandi non inest Scripturæ sacræ, in Codice Biblico extra omnem usum spectatæ, nec ei per realem sui unionem inesse potest.

IV. Ad objectionem hanc responderi potest, vim illam divinam dici Scripturæ sacræ, in chartæ comprehênsæ, actu primo conjunctam, non quòd præcisè cum verbis, vel præcisè cum sensu verborum conjuncta, & nexu individuo unita sit, sed quòd ex Dei liberâ voluntate & ordinatione ita constitutum sit, ut ubicunq; Verbum Dei, sive scriptum, sive voce prolatum, sive per species & conceptus internos intellectui infixum habetur, ibi Spiritus Sanctus suâ vi & potentiâ illuminandi aliosq́; effectus supernaturales per illud producendi cùm extra intellectum, tùm in illo, cum eodem præitò fit, eâq; illud ad eosdem producendos actu primo potens & efficax reddat, ita ut actu secundo etiam vim hanc cum Spiritu Sancto, à quo eam habet, exerat, quandocunq; ad effectus illos, in suo esse supernaturali producendos, pertingit. Quòd ut rectiùs declaretur, & intelligatur, sciendum est, Verbum Dei, in quantum consideratur ut organon nostræ illuminationis & conversionis, spectari posse vel in suis sensibilibus signis, verbis scilicet, voce sensibili prolatis, vel scripto comprehensis, vel in speciebus intelligibilibus rerum significatarum, per verba sensibilia in intellectu excitatis & coordinatis, ut & in conceptibus mentis, vel potiùs in Verbo mentis, per illuminationis actus in intellectu producto.

Quocunq; modo Verbum Dei spectetur, vis illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos actu primo ei semper inest, modo tamen diverso. Verbo Dei, per species rerű significatarũ & conceptus, intellectui jam infixo, inest ea actu primo maximè per unionem sui, primò quidem cum ipsis rerum significatarum SPECIEBUS IMPRESSIS. His enim continetur, ex parte intellectus, Verbum Dei in actu primo. Ratio est: quia illuminatio mentis consistit in actibus cognoscendi supernaturalibus, & quod, ex parte Verbi Dei, intellectui infixi, est causa instrumentalis producendorum in intellectu actuum cognoscendi supernaturalium, cum eo etiam conjunctam sive unitam esse oportet vim illam illuminandi divinam, velut virtutem agendi eosq; producendi principalem. Oportet enim virtutem causæ principalis cum causa instrumentali conjungi & uniri, si ab utraq; junctim effectus produci debeat. Sed ad actus cognoscendi supernaturales, in intellectu efficienter producendos, habent se, ex parte Verbi, maximè species rerum revelatarum impressæ, per modum causæ instrumentalis. Hæ enim, ut objectorum revelatorum vicem gerunt in intellectu, ita determinant intellectum objectorum loco in supernaturali illuminatione æquè, ac in alia quavis naturali cognitione, ad actus apprehensionis simplicis, rebus conformiter eliciendos, & concurrunt utrobiq; cum eo ad illos eliciendos efficienter. Ergo cum speciebus impressis vim illam, qua de agimus, divinam, velut virtutem causæ principalis illuminationis, conjungi necesse est. Quin cum his conjuncta vis illa exerit sese ad actus illuminationis in intellectu producendos directè, excitatâ primùm cogitatione sanetâ de iis, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt; & deinde subinde aliis, per easdem, accensis cognitionis & fidei actibus supernaturalibus, ut suprà Cap. VI. Assert. VII. pluribus ostensum; & species rerum revelatarum, intellectui impressæ, cum vi illa divina illuminandi hominum animos sibi conjunctâ, sunt LUMEN illud Verbi, de quo Psal. CXIX. 105. dicit Psaltes: Verbum tuum LUMEN est pedibus meis, & lucerna in semitis meis; & Salomo Prov. VI. 23. Lucerna mandatum, & lex LUX est; & Petrus II. Ep. I. 19. Habemus firmiorem sermonem Propheticum, cui dum attenditis ceu lucernæ apparenti in obscuro loco, benefacitis &c. sunt, in quam LUMEN mentis spirituale in actu primo; sed exerentes sese cum illa ad actus cognoscendi supernaturales, in intellectu eliciendos, sunt LUMEN mentis spirituale in actu secundo, & ipsi actus cognoscendi supernaturales, per illas eliciti, sunt ipsa actualis illuminatio, de qua passim loquuntur Scripturæ sacræ.

Deinde Verbo Dei, per species impressas & conceptus rerum revelatarum intellectui infixo, inest etiam vis illa divina illuminatrix per unionem sui cum VERBO MENTIS, per cognitionis actus supernaturales in intellectu producto. Per verbum mentis autem intelligo hîc terminum cognitionis sive intellectionis supernaturalis, qui est qualitas quædam & species sive imago rei cognitæ expressa, per cognitionis actum in intellectu efficienter producta; quæ licet sit effectus quidam illius virtutis divinæ, Verbo Dei conjunctæ, eâq; posterior, imò lumen quoddam habituale intellectus, efficaciâ Verbi accensum, tamen in ordine ad eliciendos alios supernaturales actus cognoscendi habet se quandoq; ut ratio cognoscendi, & cum illa Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminatrice conjunctum facem quasi intellectui præfert ad aliorum cognitionem; in se autem reflexum, testificatur etiam de semetipso, suáque dependentia à Deo in hominum cordibus, & dicitur proptereà qui credit, habere testimonium Dei in seipso, I. Joh. V. 10. ut suprà in Cap. VI. Assert. IV. Explic. n. III. & Assert. VII. Expl. n. IV. pluribus docuimus.

Verbo Dei autem, in suis sensibilibus signis, verbis externis scilicet, quæ sensibili voce proferri, vel atramento exarari possunt, spectato inest divina vis illuminandi convertendiq; hominũ animos actu primo, non solum in usu, quando ex ore docentis voce sensibili per auditum, vel lectione Codicis Biblici per visum ad intellectum transmittitur, sed etiam extra usum, quando nemo est, qui in Codice Biblico id legat, vel alteri voce proponat, & sic ad usum transferat. Quanquam quæstionem de efficacia Scripturæ in actu primo, extra omnem usum, beati Antecessores nostri in suo Judicio de controv. Rathmann. d. l. fol. 268. col. 1. quæstionibus juxtà enatis, & quæ de fide non sunt, accensent, adfirmativam tamen ejus partem ibidem argumentis pluribus adstructum eunt. Dicitur autem ipsis Spiritus S. virtus illuminatrix Verbo Dei extra usum inesse, non quòd ipsis verborum apicibus, in charta scriptis, perinde ut speciebus impressis in intellectu, realiter conjuncta & unita sit; neq; quòd præcisè sensui verborum, extra intellectum, realiter insit, sed quòd Dei liberâ voluntate ita ordinatum & constitutum fit, ut Verbum Dei, verbis & sensu constans, ubicunq; extet, semper organon conversionis efficax sit, eiq; Spiritus Sanctus suâ vi & potentiâ illuminandi & convertendi adsit, & per illud etiam ad hominum illuminationem & conversionem efficaciter se exerere velit, quandocunq; sive prædicatione per auditum, sive lectione per visum ad animum penetrat, & ad eum illuminandum ac convertendum applicatur. Hunc in modum rem hanc explicant in sua Censura d. l. fol. 199. col. 2. quando ex quibusdam, à se traditis, observationibus de operatione Scripturæ inter alia inferunt, daß die Schrifft oder das Schrifftliche Wort Gottes auch vor unserm Lesen und Betrachten / als ein von Gott auserkohrnes und kräfftiges Mittel die Macht und Licht zur Bekehrung habe / das ist / sie sey dienlich und tüchtig (dergleichen von keinem andern ProphanBuch kan gesagt werden) und von Gott hierzu gewidmet / geschrieben / und der Welt hinterlassen und vorgestellet / daß wir hierdurch sollen unterrichtet werden den Weg der Seeligkeit / und bekomme solche Krafft und Macht nicht erst aus unserm / oder unter unserm Lesen / anders nicht / als wann sie zuvor wäre für einen todten Buchstaben zu halten / und würde erst aquiret / und mit der Krafft der Bekehrung animiret / ausgeruͤstet und angethan/ wenn sie von uns unter die Hand genom= men &c. Ubi Scripturam, etiam ante nostram lectionem & meditationem, vim & lucem habere ad nostram conversionem peragendam, expressé explicant per hoc, quòd utilis & idonea sit, & à Deo ad hoc ordinata, scripta, & mundo relicta ac proposita, ut per eam erudiamur ad vitam æternam, &c.

Quòd autem non verborum literis & apicibus, in charta scriptis, realiter conjuncta & unita sit, fatentur iidem passim locorum ultrò. Wir legen keines weges den Woͤrtern/ syllaben und Buch= staben / wie sie auf dem Papier geschrieben / eine heimliche / ver= borgene / natuͤrliche oder Magische/ oder auch uͤbernatuͤrliche Krafft zu / scribunt d. l. fol. 267. col. 1. Confer fol. 200. col. 1. 270. col. 2. fol. 240. col. 1.

Sensui vèrò, tanquam formæ Scripturæ, eam conjunctam dicunt plus simplici vice. Die Goͤttliche Ordnung/ scribunt fol. 273. 2. bestehet nicht allein in dem / daß das gehoͤrte/ gelesene und betrach= tete Wort den Glauben in den Hertzen derer / so es hoͤren/ lesen und betrachten / wircken soll / sondern auch in dem/ das bey dem Sinn / Verstand und Meinung / darin die innerliche Form des Worts bestehet/ die Goͤttliche Krafft den Glauben zu wircken allzeit vereiniget seyn solle / es sey im Gemuͤthe der Apostel / oder werde von ihnen geprediget/ oder in ein Buch geschrieben/ oder sey im Ge= muͤth derer die es lesen. Et fol. 267. 1. Von der innerlichen Form der H. Schrifft / das ist / vom innerlichen Sinn / Rath und Mei= nung Gottes/ in den eusserlichen Worten verfasset / sagen wir/ daß Gott der Herr demselben die Krafft des heiligen Geistes die Men= schen zu erleuchten / zu bekehren und seelig zu machen / aus freywillis ger Gnade zugeordnet habe. Conf. fol. 240. 1.

Verùm hæc, quæ de vi divina, sensui conjuncta, dicunt, intelligi possunt vel de sensu verborum Scripturæ extra intellectum; vel de eodem, intellectu jam apprehenso. Utroq; modo spectato inesse dicitur vis divina illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos, sed aliter atq; aliter. In intellectu spectato inest ea per sui actualem conjunctionem sive unionem cum speciebus rerum significatarum impressis & expressis. His enim continetur sensus Verbi divini, scripti & prædicati, in hominis intellectu, uti dictum.

Extra intellectum autem spectato inesse eadem dicitur, quòd Deus suâ liberrimâ voluntate ita ordinaverit, ut Scripturæ sacræ, etiam extra intellectum, Spiritus Sanctus sua divinâ vi & potentiâ illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos semper & ubique adsit, & cum eâdem, lectâ vel docentis voce propositâ, simul ad hominis animum penetret, ibiq; cum speciebus rerum significatarum impressis partim, partim expressis unita ad conversionē sese per illas exerat.


### VIII. Although, however, this divine δύναμις or force of illuminating and converting…

VIII.

Although, however, this divine δύναμις or force of illuminating and converting the souls of men, and the Word of God, both in use and outside of use, are always most closely joined together, so that they can neither be torn apart from one another nor should be, they can nevertheless be considered distinctly: the former, indeed, as a δύναμις or power essential and proper to God; the latter as the Word προφορικὸν, uttered by the voice or consigned to writing by God's inspiration, and thus really distinct from God: the former has been communicated to the latter by the most free will of God for producing its supernatural effects of illumination, conversion, etc.: the latter, by that which has been communicated to it, works in the minds of men, and through it produces them.

1. That they are always most closely joined both in use and outside of use, and can neither be torn apart from one another nor should be, is evident from what has been said thus far. For the Word of God, to repeat in a word, always is and remains the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 18. 24. living and effectual, and sharper than any two-edged sword, Heb. IV. 12. a light to illuminate the eyes of our darkened mind, etc. Eph. I. 18. etc., whether one reads it, or hears it taught and considers it, or no one reads, hears, and meditates upon it. For these things are extrinsic to the Word of God, and add nothing to nor take anything away from its efficacy, viewed in its first act. But without that divine δύναμις of illuminating and converting, the Word of God could not be the power of God unto salvation, not a light to illuminate our darkened minds, not living and effectual, etc. but in relation to man, who is by nature blind and dead to those things which are of the Spirit of God, the letter would be ineffectual and dead. II. That this statement can be considered distinctly, the thing itself speaks. For they are in reality and without the operation of the mind thus distinct. For that δυναμις of the divine Word is in reality the δυναμις or essential and proper power of God; but it has been communicated to the Word of God by the free will of God in reality and without the operation of our mind. But those things which are distinguished in reality and with no one thinking of them, they can also be considered distinctly, according to that trite saying: As a thing is in being, so it is in being known.

III. Whence also theologians everywhere consider them as distinct, yet always inseparably connected among themselves: e.g., the Wittenberg theologians in their Censure on the Rathmann controversy, fol. 167. 1., distinguish between the Word of God and the divine power of moving the hearts of men, and say they are joined together hyperphysically. And (Rathmann), they say, blames us at the end of the demonstration, as if we taught that the power and might of God were enclosed or attached to the external words of the preacher, whereas we speak of no physical inclusion, but only of the HYPERPHYSICAL CONJUNCTION of the Word and the divine power of moving. And fol. 168. 2. Then furthermore it is to be known that this power does not reside in the letters and words themselves; but we hold that such power is a supernatural one, and indeed originally only the power of the Holy Spirit, which communicates such to the Word, and makes it, when it is read, preached, or contemplated, so alive that it becomes a word of life, John 6:68, a word of salvation, Acts 11:18, a fragrance of life unto life, 2 Cor. 2:16, and they add: This is the clear confession of all upright teachers concerning the power of the Divine Word, by which we also separate ourselves from the Chiliasts, Anabaptists, Calvinists, and other such enthusiasts. But those things which are joined together hyperphysically or supernaturally, so that one of them is the property of God alone and the other is supernatural, these, although they are always most closely joined and should never be torn apart, are nevertheless rightly considered as distinct and different in the manner declared. And the Jena theologians, after they had said in the aforementioned place, fol. 263, that it is beyond controversy in the orthodox churches that the power of illuminating, converting, and saving is not ascribed to the Word of God by physical necessity, and in a natural way, as if a natural power of this kind were inherent in the Word, just as the power of burning is in fire, etc. They add on the following folio that some indeed in this controversy have used the word natural, not, however, in that meaning by which natural is opposed to τῷ ὑπερφυσικῷ, to the supernatural, but to the Rathmannian ἀδιστικτῷ, and that it was not their intention that the Word has such power in a natural way; but rather they taught that it has it in a supernatural way. Then the same authors teach in the said place that the power of illuminating, converting, and saving is inherent in the Word not from any absolute necessity, but from the free will of God, according to that passage in I Cor. 1:21: It pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. Thirdly, they teach that that power is in the Word, not independently and originally, but dependently, so that it has been communicated to it by the Holy Spirit, and through this communication of it the Word has been made an effective medium of illumination, conversion, and salvation. But those things which are joined together hyperphysically or supernaturally, and of which one is inherent in the other in a supernatural way, not from absolute necessity, but from the free will of God, not independently and originally, but dependently upon God, so that it has been communicated to it by God, although they are most closely joined together and never to be torn apart, it is nevertheless necessary that they can be distinguished and distinctly considered from one another.

Latin:

VIII.

Qvamvis verò hæc divina δύναμις sive vis illuminandi convertendiq; hominum animos; & Verbum Dei, cùm in usu, tùm extra usum, inter se semper conjunctissima sint, ut ab invicem divelli nec possint, nec debeant, distinctè tamen considerari possunt: illa quidem, ut δύναμις sive potentia Deo essentialis & propria; hoc ut Verbum προφορικὸν, Deo inspirante vel voce prolatum, vel scripto consignatum, atq; adeò à Deo realiter distinctum: illa huic ad producendos suos supernaturales effectus illuminationis, conversionis &c. Dei voluntate liberrimâ communicata est: hoc eadem sibi communicatâ in mentibus hominum operatur, & per illam eos producit.

1. Quòd cùm in usu tùm extra usum semper conjunctissima sint, nec divelli ab invicem possint aut debeant, patet ex hactenus dictis. Verbum Dei enim, ut verbo repetam, semper est & manet potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. I. Cor. I. 18. 24. vivum & efficax, & penetrantius quovis gladio ancipiti, Ebr. IV. 12. lumen ad illuminandum oculos obtenebratæ mentis nostræ &c. Eph. I. 18. &c. sive quis illud legat, vel doceri audiat & consideret, sive nemo illud legat, audiat & meditetur. Hæc enim sunt Verbo Dei extrinseca, & ejus efficaciæ, in actu primo spectatæ, nihil superaddunt aut detrahunt. Sed sine illa divina δύναμις illuminandi & convertendi Verbum Dei non posset potentia Dei esse ad salutem, non lumen ad mentes nostras obtenebratas illuminandas, non vivum & efficax &c. sed in ordine ad hominem, ad ea quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, naturâ cæcuum, & emortuum, litera inefficax & mortua esset. II. Quod tamen dictum in modum distinctè considerari possint, res ipsa loquitur. Sunt enim reapse & citra mentis operationem sic distincta. Nam δυναμις illa divina Verbi divini reapse δυναμις sive potentia Dei essentialis & propria; Verbo Dei autem liberâ Dei voluntate reapse & citra mentis nostræ operationem communicata est. Quæ autem reapse & nemine cogitante distingvuntur, ea possunt etiam distinctè considerari, juxta illud tritum: Ut res sehabet inesse, ita & in cognosci.

III. Unde etiam Theologi ea passim ut distincta, inter se tamen indivulsè semper connexa, considerant: v. g. Theologi Witebergenses in Censura sua super Controv. Rathmann. fol. 167. 1. distingvunt inter Verbum Dei, & inter divinam potentiam movendi hominum corda, & dicunt, ea conjungi inter se hyperphysicè. Er (Rathman) inquiunt, gibt uns Schuld am Ende der Demonstration, als lehreten wir/daß den eusserlichen Worten des Predigers die Krafft und Macht Gottes sey eingeschlossen oder angehefftet/ da wir doch von keiner physica inclusione, sondern allein de HYPERPHYSICA Verbi & divinæ potentiæ movendi CONJUNCTIONE reden. Et fol. 168. 2. Da dann ferner zu wissen/ daß diese Krafft nicht eben in den Buchstaben und Wörtern stecke; sondern wir halten dafür/ daß solche Krafft sey eine übernatürliche/ und zwar ursprünglich allein des H. Geistes Krafft/ welcher solche dem Worte mittheilet/ und dasselbe/ wenn es gelesen/ geprediget/ betrachtet wird/ also lebendig machet/das es wird ein Wort des Lebens/ Joh. 6. v. 68. ein Wort des Heils/ Act. 11. v. 18. ein Geruch des Lebens zum Leben/ 2. Cor. 6. v. 16. & addunt: Dieses ist aller rechtschaffenen Lehrer deutliche Confession von der Krafft des Göttlichen Worts/ dadurch wir uns auch von den Chiliasten/ Wiedertäuffern/Calvinisten und andern dergleichen Schwärmern absondern. Quæ autem hyperphysicè sive supernaturaliter inter se conjunguntur, ita ut unum illorum sit solius Dei proprium, & alteri supernaturale, ea, licet semper conjunctissima, nec unquam divellenda sint, rectè tamen ut distincta & modo declarato differentia considerantur. Et Theologi Jenenses, postquam d. l. fol. 263. dixerant, in Ecclesiis orthodoxis extra controversiam esse, quòd vis illuminandi, convertendi & salvandi non adscribatur Verbo Dei ex necessitate physica, & naturali modo, quasi hujusmodi naturalis vis inesset verbo, sicut visurendi in igne &c. subjungunt fol. seq. quosdam quidem in hac controversia usos esse voce naturalis, non tamen eo significatu, quo naturale opponitur τῷ ὑπερφυσικῷ, supernaturali, sed τῷ ἀδιστικτῷ Rathmanniano, illorumq́; mentem non fuisse, quòd Verbum naturali modo ejusmodi vim habeat; sed docuisse potiùs, quod eam modo supernaturali habeat. Deinde docent iidem d. l. vim illuminandi, convertendi, & salvandi inesse Verbo non ex absoluta quadam necessitate, sed ex libera Dei voluntate, juxta illud I. Cor. I. 21. Placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes. Tertiò docent, vim illam esse in Verbo, non independenter & originaliter, sed dependenter, ita ut à Spiritu S. ei communicata sit, & per hanc ejus communicationem Verbum illuminationis, conversionis & salvationis medium efficax factum sit. Quæ autem hyperphysicè sive supernaturaliter inter se conjuncta sunt, & quorum unum alteri inest modo supernaturali, non ex necessitate absoluta, sed ex Dei voluntate libera, non independenter & originaliter, sed dependenter à Deo, ita ut ei à Deo communicatum sit, ea licet inter se conjunctissima nec unquam divellenda sint, ab invicem tamen distingui & distinctè considerari posse necesse est.


### IX. AND because the δύναμις or power of GOD, and of the WORD himself, to illuminate…

IX.

AND because the δύναμις or power of GOD, and of the WORD himself, to illuminate and convert is one and the same, but one which belongs to the former primarily, independently, and by essence, while to the latter it belongs dependently and by communication, therefore also the effects of illumination, conversion, and other similar supernatural grace are efficiently produced by the same power from both together and jointly in one undivided influx, yet in a different manner: namely, from GOD as from the principal cause, but from his WORD as from a less principal or instrumental cause.

II. This assertion flows from the preceding. For the fact that there is one and the same δύναμις or power of illuminating and converting the souls of men, which belongs both to GOD and to his WORD, yet in an unequal way: to the former primarily, independently, and by essence; to the latter dependently & by communication, it has been shown and declared above in theses V. & VI. so that it does not need further declaration or confirmation. When, however, two agents concur simultaneously and jointly toward one and the same effect in number by one and the same power in number, but which does not belong to both equally, but to one of itself and independently, and to the other, however, dependently and by communication, then the mode of operating always follows the mode of inbeing, so that to whom the power of operating belongs primarily, of itself and independently, to him the effect is attributed as to the principal cause; and to whom the same belongs dependently from another superior agent and by communication, to him the effect is attributed as to a less principal or instrumental cause. For the principal and instrumental cause are estimated, defined, and distinguished from the power of acting, proper and connatural to each, and a cause is called principal when its own proper power of acting is proportionate to the effect being produced, and, if not nobler, is yet not less noble than is required to produce it; but a less principal or instrumental cause is called such if its own proper and connatural power of acting is disproportionate to the effect being produced and less noble than is required to produce it, and therefore it is necessary that it be aided or elevated by the power of another superior agent, joined or communicated to it, and by its influx for the producing of the effect. And hence have arisen the definitions of causes, principal and instrumental, most received by usage: of the former, that it is a cause which influences an effect by a power (its own proper one) not less noble than is required to produce it; of the latter, however, that it is a cause which influences an effect by a power (its own proper one) less noble than is required to produce it.

Since, therefore, the power of illuminating and converting the minds of men, joined to the Word of God, is the very essential and proper δύναμις or power and virtue of God, so proportionate to the aforesaid supernatural effects of grace that it is not only not less noble, but even nobler than is required to produce them, and consequently abundantly suffices to produce these as well as other nobler effects, no one will deny that God is their principal efficient cause. On the other hand, however, because the connatural and proper power of the Word of God (i.e., the power of acting, which of itself and from itself, either by the force of the words or by the force of the things of the things signified, or finally by the force of both) is more ignoble than is required for producing the effects of illumination, conversion, and other similar effects of grace, and it cannot produce them unless aided and elevated by the power of God to illuminate and convert, communicated to it; the thing itself speaks that the Word of God is not the efficient cause of those things in the same way that God is, but in a certain inferior way, and one which is proper to instrumental causes. For the natural power of the divine Word to act and move, which it has of itself either by reason of the words or by reason of the things signified, is merely OBJECTIVE, which can move neither the intellect to elicit acts of cognition, nor the will to elicit acts of volition, desire, etc., unless it is in those things for the knowing of which the former has some light, and for the seeking of which the latter has some strength. But in those things which are of the Spirit of God, the intellect is by nature blind and utterly darkened, nay, it is darkness; and the will is by nature dead and utterly turned away from God, so that the former has no light, nor the latter any strength, as was shown above. Therefore, in order that it may be able to illuminate the intellect of man which is by nature blind, and to rouse the will which is by nature dead and turned away from God from spiritual death and convert it to God, a certain power of acting is necessarily required that is higher than that natural and proper power of the Word, and that merely objective power of moving, namely a certain ἐνεργητικὴ and effective power, proportioned to the producing of the aforementioned effects of illumination, conversion, and similar supernatural effects, by which it may be aided and elevated in producing the same. This, however, as has been said, is not, nor can it be, any other than the very δύναμις or power and virtue of God to illuminate, convert, etc. The Word of God is therefore the efficient cause of these effects of grace, not by its own proper power alone, but elevated and aided by the divine power, which is essential and proper to God, communicated to it. And in this way the sacred writers also speak of these effects, and attribute them to God as the principal cause, but to His Word as the instrumental cause, and one dependent on God for the power of acting: e.g., It pleased GOD BY THE FOOLISHNESS OF PREACHING to save them that believe, says Paul, I Cor. 1:21. I pray not for them (the Apostles) only, but for them also who SHALL BELIEVE (you, Father, working their faith) THROUGH THEIR WORD in me, says Christ, John XVII. 20. To which also these following things pertain: Faith is (from God) from hearing, but hearing through the Word of God, Rom. X. 17. He who supplies the Spirit to you, and works mighty works in you, is it from the works of the law, or FROM THE HEARING OF FAITH (i.e., from the preaching of the doctrine of faith, perceived by hearing?) Gal. III. 5. He (God, the Father of lights) brought us forth by the WORD of truth, James I. 18. Born again not of mortal seed, but immortal, THROUGH THE WORD of the living and abiding God forever, I Pet. I. 23. In all of which places our salvation, faith, and regeneration are ascribed to God as the principal cause; but to the Word of God as the intermediate and instrumental cause.

III. In the same manner our Symbolic books also speak concerning this matter, and expressly call the Word of God an INSTRUMENT of the supernatural effects of grace: Through the Word and Sacraments, as through INSTRUMENTS, the Holy Spirit is given, who works faith (through them) in those who hear the Gospel, where and when it has seemed good to God, says Aug. Confess. Art. V. And the Authors of the Formula of Concord, in the place on Free Will, page 671. Through this, they say, MEDIUM or INSTRUMENT, namely the preaching and hearing of the WORD, GOD works, softens our hearts, and draws man: so that from the sermons of the law he may both recognize his sins and the wrath of God, and feel true terrors and contrition in his heart. And through the announcement and meditation of the Gospel concerning the free and most merciful remission of sins in Christ, a spark of faith is kindled in his heart, which embraces the remission of sins for Christ's sake, and consoles itself with the promise of the Gospel: and in this way the Holy Spirit, WHO WORKS ALL THESE THINGS (namely through the Word), is sent into the heart. By which they ascribe the aforementioned supernatural effects of grace in express words to God, as the principal cause, by His own proper power; but to the Word of God, as a medium or instrument, or as an intermediate and instrumental cause, producing the same things with God, but by power communicated to it by God.
