These subsequent words of theirs aim at the same point: But although both, both the planting and watering of the preacher, and the hearer's running and willing, would be altogether in vain, nor would conversion follow, unless the power and operation of the Holy Spirit were to approach: who through the Word preached and heard illuminates and converts hearts, so that men may be able to believe and assent to the Word: nevertheless, neither the preacher nor the hearer ought to doubt concerning this grace and operation of the Holy Spirit, etc. By which they distinguish not at all obscurely between the proper power of the Word preached and heard, which it has by the force of the words and the things signified, and the power of illuminating and converting, which is proper and essential to the Holy Spirit, and communicated to His Word by His free will, and they expressly teach that the former is too ignoble to produce these effects of grace, and that they would never be produced by it, unless the divine power of the Holy Spirit, as their principal cause, were joined with it, and at the same time concurred with it in one undivided influx to produce the same. Our often-praised predecessors also declared this matter excellently in their judgment on the Rathmann controversy, in the same place, fol. 266. Where among other things they write: There is no other illumination and conversion and salvation which proceeds from the Holy Spirit, and another illumination, conversion and salvation which proceeds from the Word, but the illumination, conversion and salvation of the Word is the illumination, conversion and salvation of the Holy Spirit, which the Holy Spirit works through the Word in the hearts of men. The Holy Spirit works indeed as the principal cause, the Word as the instrumental cause, nevertheless it is only one effect. And after one or two lines inserted: It is indeed the effect of the Holy Spirit and of the Scripture not one and the same effect: For the Holy Spirit works as the principal cause, the Holy Scripture works as the instrumental cause, but yet so it is and remains one effect. For the Holy Spirit and the Holy Scripture work conjunctly as subordinate causes, as principal and instrumental causes, united by divine order. Illumination is therefore attributed equally to the Word and to the Holy Spirit, but not in an equal manner. And fol. 267. Just as there is one effect, which proceeds from the Holy Spirit and from the Word, so also there is one power

Latin:

IX.

ET quia DEI, & VERBI ipsius, una eademque δύναμις sive vis illuminandi convertendiq; est, sed quæ illi primò, independenter & per essentiam; huic autem dependenter & per communicationem convenit, ideò & illuminationis, conversionis aliiq; similes supernaturales gratiæ effectus per eandem ab utroq; simul & junctim uno indiviso influxu efficienter producuntur, modo tamen diverso: à DEO nempe, ut à causa principali; ab ejus VERBO autem, ut à causa minùs principali sive instrumentali.

II. Assertio hæc fluit ex præcedentibus. Quòd enim una eademq́; sit δύναμις sive vis illuminandi convertendiq́; hominum animos, quæ & DEO & ejus VERBO, modo tamen inæquali, conveniat: illi primò, independenter & per essentiam; huic dependenter & per communicationem, oftensum declaratumq́; est supra th. V. & VI. ut ulteriori sive declaratione sive confirmatione non egeat. Quando autem duo agentia per unam & eandem numero potentiam quidem, sed quæ non utriq; æqualiter, sed uni per se & independenter: alteri verò dependenter & per communicationem convenit, ad unum numero effectum simul & junctim concurrunt, tum semper modus operandi sequitur modum inessendi, ut cui potentia operandi primò, per se & independenter convenit, ei effectus ut causæ principali; & cui eadem dependenter ab alio superiori agente & per communicationem convenit, ei ut causæ minus principali sive instrumentali effectus tribuatur. Nam causa principalis & instrumentalis æstimantur, definiuntur & distingvuntur ex virtute agendi, cuiq; propria & connaturali, & dicitur causa principalis, cùm ejus virtus agendi propria producendo effectui proportionata, &, si non nobilior, nec tamen ignobilior est, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur; minus principalis verò sive instrumentalis causa dicitur, si ejus virtus agendi propria & connaturalis producendo effectui improportionata & ignobilior sit, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, & proptereà necesse sit, ut virtute alterius superioris agentis, sibi conjunctâ, vel communicatâ ejusq́; influxu ad effectum producendum adjuvetur sive elevetur. Atq; hinc natæ sunt definitiones causarum, principalis & instrumentalis, usu receptissimæ: illius quidem, quòd sit causa, quæ influit in effectum virtute (suâ propriâ) non ignobiliori, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur; hujus verò, quòd sit causa, quæ influit in effectum virtute (suâ propriâ) ignobiliori, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur.

Quia ergo virtus illuminandi & convertendi hominum mentes, Verbo Dei conjuncta, ipsa Dei essentialis & propria δύναμις sive potentia & virtus est, prædictis supernaturalibus gratiæ effectibus ita proportionata, ut non solùm non ignobilior, sed & nobilior sit, quàm ad eos producendos requiritur, & proinde ad hos pariter & alios nobiliores effectus producendos abunde sufficiat, nemo inficiabitur, Deum esse illorum causam efficientem principalem. Contra autem quia VERBI Dei virtus connaturalis & propria, (h. e. virtus agendi, quam per se & ex se vel vi verborum, vel vi rerum significatarum, vel deniq; vi utrorumq; habet) ignobilior est, quàm ad illuminationis, conversionis aliosq; similes gratiæ effectus producendos requiritur, eosq; producere non potest, nisi Dei virtute illuminandi & convertendi, sibi communicatâ, adjuta & elevata, res ipsa loquitur, quòd non eodem modo Verbum Dei, quo Deus, illorum causa efficiens sit, sed modo quodam inferiori, & qui causarum instrumentalium proprius est. Naturalis enim Verbi divini vis agendi movendiq; , quam ex se vel ratione verborum, vel ratione rerum significatarum habet, merè OBJECTIVA est, quæ nec intellectum ad cognitionis, nec voluntatem ad volitionis, desiderii &c. actus eliciendos movere potest, nisi in iis, ad quæ cognoscenda ille aliquid lucis; & ad quæ expetenda hæc aliquid virium habet. In iis autem, quæ Spiritus Dei sunt, intellectus naturâ cæcus & prorsus obtenebratus, imò tenebræ est; & voluntas naturâ emortua & à Deo prorsus aversa est, ut nec ille quicquam lucis; neque hæc quicquam virium habeat, ut suprà ostensum. Ut ergo hominis intellectum naturâ cæcum illuminare, & voluntatem naturâ emortuam & à Deo aversam ex morte spirituali excitare & ad Deum convertere possit, necessariò altior quædam agendi virtus, quàm illa Verbi naturalis & propria, eaq; merè objectiva movendi virtus est, requiritur, nempe virtus quædam ἐνεργητικὴ & effectiva, producendis memoratis illuminationis, conversionis & similibus supernaturalibus effectibus proportionata, quâ in iisdem producendis adjuvetur & elevetur. Hæc verò, uti dictum, non alia est, aut esse potest, quàm ipsa Dei δύναμις sive potentia & virtus illuminandi, convertendi &c. Est ergo Verbum Dei horum gratiæ effectuum causa efficiens, non suâ solâ virtute propriâ, sed virtute divinâ, Deo essentiali & propriâ, sibi communicatâ elevatum & adjutum. Atq; hunc in modum loqvuntur etiam Scriptores sacri de hisce effectibus, tribuuntq; eos Deo ut principali; ejus Verbo autem ut instrumentali & in virtute agendi à Deo dependenti causæ: v. g. Placuit DEO PER STULTITIAM PRÆDICATIONIS SALVOS facere credentes, ait Paulus I. Cor. I, 21. Non rogo pro iis (Apostolis) tantùm, sed & pro iis, qui CREDITURI sunt (te, Pater, fidem illorum operante) PER SERMONEM eorum in me, inquit Christus, Joh. XVII. 20. Quò pertinent & hæc sequentia: Fides est (à Deo) ex auditu, auditus autem per Verbum Dei, Rom. X. 17. Qui subministrat vobis Spiritum, & operatur virtutes in vobis, utrum ex operibus legis, an EX AUDITU FIDEI (h. e. ex prædicatione doctrinæ fidei, auditu percepta?) Gal. III. 5. Is (Deus, pater luminum) progenuit nos SERMONE veritatis, Jac. I. 18. Renati non ex semine mortali, sed immortali, PER SERMONEM viventis Dei & manentis in æternum, I. Pet. I. 23. Quibus in locis omnibus salus, fides, regeneratio nostra Deo ut causæ principali; Verbo Dei autem ut causæ intermediæ & instrumentali adscribitur.

III. Eundem in modum loqvuntur etiam hac de re nostri libri Symbolici, vocantq́; Verbum Dei expresse INSTRUMENTUM supernaturalium gratiæ effectuum: Per Verbum & Sacramenta, tanquam per INSTRUMENTA donatur Spiritus Sanctus, qui fidem (per illa) efficit in iis, qui audiunt Evangelium, ubi & quando visum est Deo, ait August. Confess. Art. V. Et Auctores Form. Concord. loco de Lib. Arb. pag. 671. Per hoc, inquiunt, MEDIUM seu INSTRUMENTUM, prædicationem nimirum & auditionem VERBI, DEUS operatur, emollit corda nostra, trahitque hominem: ut ex concionibus legis & peccata sua & iram Dei agnoscat, & veros terrores atque contritionem in corde suo sentiat. Et per annunciationem ac meditationem Evangelii de gratuita & clementissima peccatorum remissione in Christo, scintillula fidei in corde ipsius accenditur, quæ remissionem peccatorum propter Christum amplectitur, & sese promissione Evangelii consolatur: & hoc modo Spiritus Sanctus, QVI HÆC OMNIA (puta per Verbum) OPERATUR in cor immittitur. Quibus prædictos supernaturales gratiæ effectus conceptis verbis Deo, ut causæ principali, suâ propriâ virtute; Verbo Dei autem, ut medio vel instrumento, sive ut causæ intermediæ & instrumentali, eosdem cum Deo, sed virtute à Deo sibi communicatâ, producenti adscribunt. Eodem collineant hæc subsequentia illorum verba: Etsi autem utrumque, tum concionatoris plantare & rigare, tum auditoris currere & velle, frustra omninò essent, neque conversio sequeretur, nisi Spiritus Sancti virtus & operatio accederet: qui per Verbum prædicatum & auditum corda illuminat & convertit, ut homines Verbo credere & assentiri possint: tamen neque concionator neque auditor de hac Spiritus Sancti gratia, & operatione dubitare debent &c. Quibus haud obscurè distingvunt inter virtutem Verbi prædicati & auditi propriam, quam vi verborum & rerum significatarum habet, & inter virtutem illuminandi convertendique, Spiritui Sancto propriam & essentialem, Verboq; ipsius libera ejus voluntate communicatam, & expressè docent, illam esse ignobiliorem, quàm ad hos gratiæ effectus producendos requiritur, eosq; per illam nunquam productum iri, nisi Spiritus Sancti, velut illorum causæ principalis, divina virtus cum ea conjuncta esset, & simul uno indiviso influxu ad eosdem producendos cum illa concurreret. Egregiè etiam rem hanc declararunt nostri Antecessores sæpius laudati in suo judicio de Controv. Rathmann. d. l. fol. 266. Ubi inter alia scribunt: Es ist keine andere Erleuchtung und Bekehrung und Seligmachung/ welche vom heiligen Geist herrühret/ und eine andere Erleuchtung/ Bekehrung und Seligmachung/ welche von dem Wort herrühret/ sondern die Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seligmachung des Worts ist die Erleuchtung/ Bekehrung und Seligmachung des heiligen Geistes/ welche der Heilige Geist durchs Wort in den Herzen der Menschen wircket. Der heilige Geist wircket zwar als die Haupt=Ursache/ das Wort als die Mittel=Ursache/ gleichwohl aber ists nur eine Wirckung. Et post unam atq; alteram lineam interjectam: Es ist zwar des H. Geistes und der Schrifft wirckung nicht einerley Wirckung: Denn der heilige Geist wircket als die Haupt=Ursach/ die H. Schrifft wircket als die Mittel=Ursach/ aber doch so ists und bleibets eine Wirckung. Denn der heilige Geist und die heilige Schrifft wircken conjunctim tanquam causæ subordinatæ, als Hauptund Mittel = Ursachen / durch Göttliche Ordnung vereiniget. Æquè igitur Verbo tribuitur illuminatio ac Spiritui Sancto, sed non æqualiter. Et fol. 267. Wie auch eine Wirckung ist/ welche vom heiligen Geist/ und vom Wort herrühret/ also ist auch eine Krafft


### of illumination, conversion, and salvation in the Holy Spirit and in the Word,…

of illumination, conversion, and salvation in the Holy Spirit and in the Word, because the Holy Spirit cannot and should not be separated from the Word, nor the Word from the Holy Spirit; the only difference is this, that the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation belongs originally to the Holy Spirit as the primary cause, but to the Word by way of communication as the instrumental cause / ordained by Divine order as the powerful means of illumination / conversion and salvation.

IV. Furthermore, regarding the terms instrument and instrumental cause, whether they are attributed sufficiently appropriately to Holy Scripture in relation to man's illumination, conversion, and similar effects of grace, some theologians have doubted, especially at the time of the Rathmannian controversy, thinking that it is more correctly, or at least more safely, called a medium or intermediate cause of such supernatural effects, rather than an instrument and instrumental cause. And it seems to militate in favor of this opinion that an instrument and instrumental cause, as shown above, are estimated by the power of acting, and an instrument is defined by this, that its power of acting is less noble than is required to produce the effect, and therefore it cannot perform the function of a cause and produce the effect in act, unless it is elevated by the power of another principal cause to produce it. Which does not seem to apply to Holy Scripture. For it has in itself, even outside of use, a power of acting not less noble than is required to illuminate the intellect of man and to convert his will: for it has in itself, as we have hitherto proven, the very power of God to illuminate and convert, which certainly is not less noble than is required to illuminate and convert the souls of men. But that which has in itself a power not less noble than is required to produce an effect is not an instrument, but a principal agent; and if it actually influences the effect with a power not less noble than is required to produce it, it will be its principal cause in second act, not instrumental.

On the other hand, it is opposed to this opinion that Holy Scripture attributes the illumination and conversion of man to GOD alone, as the principal cause, but to His Word only as an instrument and instrumental cause; and very illustrious on this matter is the Pauline passage, 1 Cor. 3:6–7: Who is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers through whom you believed, and as the Lord gave to each? I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but he who gives the increase, God. By which the Apostle calls himself and his fellow-worker, Apollo, ministers, THROUGH WHOM the Corinthians had believed, inasmuch as they, by their ministry through the preaching of the Word of God, which he calls planting and watering by a metaphor taken from gardeners, had cast the seed of the divine Word into the hearts of men: Paul indeed, who had first preached the Gospel at Corinth, and by his preaching had planted the garden of the Church, had performed the office of him who plants a garden; Apollo however, who coming after had confirmed and increased the faith kindled by his preaching, had performed the office of him who waters. Yet he attributes to neither that he had flowed into the effect by a power of the Word not less noble than was required for kindling, confirming, and increasing faith in the hearts of the Corinthians, but he attributes the power of kindling and confirming faith and its influx entirely to GOD, as the principal cause, when he adds: But GOD GAVE THE INCREASE. For by this very thing he signifies that the fact that his planting and Apollo's watering, performed through the preaching of the divine Word, was effective, and that faith in the hearts of men had its beginnings and increases by kindling, confirming, and augmenting, was all brought about by GOD, concurring with His power of illuminating and converting, and at the same time flowing through the Word preached by them. To which sense also the Formula of Concord skillfully [speaks], in the words a little before alleged from the Loc. de Lib. Arbitr. page 671: Although, he says, both the planting and watering of the Preacher, and the running and willing of the hearer, would be altogether in vain, UNLESS THE POWER AND OPERATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT WERE ADDED: who illuminates and converts hearts through the Word preached and heard, so that men can believe and assent to the word, etc. But that which flows into an effect with a power less noble than is required to produce it, [is] not without the concurrence of the principal cause & can produce it by a nobler influx, that is certainly not its principal but its instrumental cause.

V. To discuss this difficulty, therefore, and to remove every scruple, one must properly weigh what is to be understood in the common definitions of PRINCIPAL & INSTRUMENTAL causes by a VIRTUE LESS NOBLE, & not LESS NOBLE, than is required to produce an effect: namely, the virtue which some agent has in any way is not to be understood: for every instrumental cause, by the very fact that it is elevated by the virtue of the principal cause to produce an effect, has, at least in use, the virtue of the principal cause, and thus a virtue not less noble than is required to produce the effect, joined to itself, and thus it has it in some way; but these causes are estimated each FROM THE VIRTUE CONNATURAL AND PROPER TO ITSELF, which they have of themselves and through themselves. For whatever virtue some cause has imparted or communicated to it by another principal agent, that is not so much its own virtue as that of the other superior agent, and the influx which it provides into the effect by the power of that [virtue] is not so much its own influx as that of the other principal agent, to whom this imparted virtue properly belongs. This holds universally for every principal and instrumental cause, both of natural and of supernatural effects. Whatever cause has a power of acting that is connatural and proper to the producing of an effect, and is not inferior or less noble than is required to produce it, that is the principal cause of the produced effect; and conversely, whatever cause has a power of acting that is connatural and proper to the producing of an effect, and is disproportionate and inferior or less noble than is required to produce it, that is the instrumental cause of the produced effect, even if a virtue of some other principal agent, not less noble than is required to produce the same effect, also resides in it in some way, namely dependently upon the principal cause and by communication. For this influx of a not less noble virtue is not, however, that of the one to whom this virtue belongs dependently and by communication, but that of the cause to whom the same belongs of itself and independently: e.g., the influx which the illuminating virtue of the Holy Spirit, communicated to the Word, imparts with the Word and through it into the illumination of the human intellect, is not so much an influx of the WORD, to which it belongs dependently from the Holy Spirit and through communication, as of the Holy Spirit, to whom it belongs of itself and independently.

That you may understand these things more correctly, I would have you know that instruments are of two kinds. For some always have the principal cause conjoined to them, even outside of use, by supposition and by power: of which kind are the members of the human body, which are instruments of the soul, and have the soul as the principal cause of their effects always conjoined to them by supposition, so to speak, and by power, even outside of use. Others, however, are not conjoined with the principal cause except in use, of which kind are a hammer, an axe, a writing pen, and other things of that sort. Instruments of the latter order, as they are not conjoined to the principal cause outside of use, so neither do they have its power of acting in themselves, but receive it from it only in use, when they are applied and elevated to produce an effect: just as, for example, a writing pen does not have in itself the power of painting letters and writing, but receives it only extrinsically from the hand and guidance of the scribe, according to the instruction of the art of writing, and an axe does not have in itself the power of moving itself and splitting wood, but receives it extrinsically from the woodworker, who elevates it and impresses upon it the force of splitting wood by his own motion, etc. Instruments of the former order, however, as they always have the principal cause conjoined to them by supposition and by power, so they also always have its power of acting in themselves, nor do they receive it only from the principal cause when they are applied to use: since they already have it in themselves beforehand; they are nevertheless elevated in the very use to produce an effect, not by a new added power of acting, which they did not have before, but by an actual influx, which the principal cause provides with them and through them by means of the power already communicated to it beforehand: for example, the hand, which is called by Aristotle ὄργανον ὀργάνων, the instrument of instruments, as it always has the soul conjoined to it by supposition and by power, so it has its motive power in itself even outside of use, nor does it receive it only in use: in use, however, it is elevated by the soul to produce an effect, not by any motive power added to it, since it already has its motive power in itself beforehand; but by an actual influx, which through the same motive power already communicated to it beforehand, the soul puts forth into effect with it and through it. And to the class of these instruments belongs Holy Scripture, which, just as it always has the Holy Spirit conjoined to it by supposition and power, even outside of use, so it also has in itself the power of the Holy Spirit, as the principal cause, to illuminate and convert, even outside of use. But because it does not have this from itself and through itself, as natural and proper to it, but dependently from the Holy Spirit, to whom alone it is connatural and proper, and communicated to it by His free will, therefore it is and remains the cause of illumination, conversion, etc. instrumental, for this one reason, that its native, or connatural and proper power, which it has independently from itself, is too ignoble for what is required to illuminate and convert the souls of men; but the power which it has communicated to it by the Holy Spirit is not its own, but the Holy Spirit's connatural and proper power, and by it, not so much it itself, as the Holy Spirit with it and through it, flows into the illumination and conversion of man. Which the Pauline passage, from 1 Cor. 3:6-7, just cited, clearly proves. The Apostle was not unaware that the Word of God has the power of illuminating and converting the souls of men in itself, yet dependently upon the Holy Spirit, and communicated to it by His free will. For he had said in the same Epistle, preceding chapter 1:18, 24, that the word of the cross and the preaching of Christ crucified is to those who obtain salvation, THE POWER OF GOD, and chapter 2:4-5. the Word of God, preached by him, to be in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that the faith of the Corinthians might not be in the wisdom of men, but IN THE POWER OF GOD, etc. And yet he says that the increase of his preaching is not from it (the preaching) but FROM GOD, to such an extent that neither he who plants through the preaching of the Word, nor he who waters through the same, is anything in order to the supernatural effects produced, but GOD, who as the principal cause concurs with the preaching, and by His actual influx gives the INCREASE. But these things would not be rightly said by Paul if, by the fact that the preached Word of God always has the illuminating power of the Holy Spirit in itself and communicated to it, it (the Word of God) were the principal cause of the faith produced in the Corinthians; but on the contrary, it should have been said that he indeed, as a minister of God, had planted through the pre-

Latin:

der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seligmachung im H. Geist und im Wort / weil der H. Geist vom Wort / und das Wort vom H. Geist nicht kan noch soll getrennet werden/ nur allein ist diß der Unterscheid / daß dem heiligen Geist die Krafft der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seligmachung zustehet ursprünglich / als der Haupt-Ursache / dem Wort aber Mittheilungs-weise / als der Mittel-Ursache / aus Göttlicher Ordnung zum kräfftigen Mittel der Erleuchtung/ Bekehrung und Seligmachung verordnet.

IV. Cæterùm de terminis instrumenti & causæ instrumentalis, an Scripturæ sacræ in ordine ad hominis illuminationem, conversionem & similes gratiæ effectus satis convenienter tribuantur, dubitârunt nonnulli Theologi, præsertim tempore controversiæ Rathmannianæ, rati, eam rectiùs, vel certè tutiùs dici medium vel causam intermediam hujusmodi effectuum supernaturalium, quàm instrumentum & causam instrumentalem. Et videtur pro hac sententia militare, quòd instrumentum & causa instrumentalis, ut suprà ostensum, æstimantur ex virtute agendi, & instrumentum per hoc definitur, quòd ejus virtus agendi ignobilior sit, quàm ad effectū producendū requiritur, & proptereà etiam actu causæ munere fungi & effectum producere non possit, nisi ab alterius principalis causæ virtute ad eum producendum elevetur. Id quod Scripturæ sacræ non convenire videtur. Hæc enim habet in se, etiam extra usum, virtutem agendi non ignobiliorem, quàm ad illuminandum hominis intellectum ejusque voluntatem convertendam requiritur: habet enim in se, ut hactenus probatum dedimus, ipsam Dei virtutem illuminandi & convertendi, quæ certè ignobilior non est, quàm ad illuminandos convertendosq; hominum animos requiritur. Quod autem in se habet virtutem non ignobiliorem, quàm ad producendum effectum requiritur, non instrumentum, sed agens principale est; & si actu in effectum virtute non ignobiliori, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, influat, erit id ejusdem causa principalis in actu secundo, non instrumentalis.

Contra autem adversatur huic opinioni, quòd Scriptura sacra hominis illuminationem & conversionem DEO soli, ut causæ principali; VERBO ipsius autem tantùm ut instrumento & causæ instrumentali adscribit, estŃ; hanc in rem valdè illustris locus Paulinus I. Cor. III. v. 6. 7. Quis est Paulus, quis autem Apollo, nisi ministri, per quos credidistis, & ut cuique Dominus dedit? Ego plantavi, Apollos rigavit, sed Deus dedit incrementum. Itaque neque qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed qui dat incrementum, Deus. Quibus Apostolus se & coadjutorem suum, Apollo, ministros dicit, PER QVOS Corinthii credidissent, quippe qui ministerio suo per prædicationem Verbi Dei, quam per metaphoram, ab hortulanis desumtam, plantationem & rigationem appellat, semen Verbi divini in corda hominum immiserant: Paulus quidem, qui primus Evangelium Corinthi prædicaverat, & prædicatione sua Ecclesiæ hortum plantaverat, ejus qui plantat hortum; Apollo verò, qui superveniens prædicatione sua fidem accensam confirmaverat, auxerat, ejus qui rigat, officio functus fuerat. Neutri tamen tribuit, quòd per prædicationem Verbi virtute non ignobiliori, quàm ad fidem in Corinthiorum cordibus accendendam, confirmandam & augendam requirebatur, influxerit, sed virtutem accendendæ & confirmandæ fidei proportionatam ejusŃ; influxum in solidum tribuit DEO, velut causæ principali, cùm addit: Sed DEUS DEDIT INCREMENTUM. Hoc ipso enim significat, quòd suâ plantatio & ipsius Apollo rigatio, per prædicationem Verbi divini peracta, efficax fuit, & accendendo, confirmando augendoŃ; fidem in cordibus hominum sua habuit initia & incrementa, id totum DEUM, sua virtute illuminandi convertendiŃ; concurrentem, & simul per Verbum ab ipsis prædicatum influentem, effecisse. Quem in sensum etiam scitè F. Concord. verbis, paulò antè ex Loc. de Lib. Arbitr. pag. 671. allegatis: Etsi autem, inquit, utrumque, tùm Concionatoris plantare & rigare, tùm auditoris currere & velle, frustra omninò essent, NISI SPIRITUS SANCTI VIRTUS ET OPERATIO ACCEDERET: qui per Verbum prædicatum & auditum corda illuminat & convertit, ut homines verbo credere & assentiri possint &c. Quod autem virtute ignobiliori influit in effectum, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, nec absŃ; principalis causæ concursu & influxu nobiliori eum producere potest, id utiq; non principalis sed instrumentalis ejus causa est.

V. Ad discutiendam ergo hanc difficultatem, omnemq́; eximendum scrupulum, probè expendendum est, quid in vulgaribus causarum, PRINCIPALIS & INSTRUMENTALIS, definitionibus per VIRTUTEM IGNOBILIOREM, & non IGNOBILIOREM, quàm ad producendum effectum requiritur, intelligendum veniat: nempe non intelligenda est virtus, quam agens aliquod quocunq; modo habet: nam omnis causa instrumentalis eo ipso quod virtute causæ principalis ad producendum effectum elevatur, habet, minimum in usu, virtutem causæ principalis, atq; adeò virtutem non ignobiliorem, quàm ad effectum producendum requiritur, sibi conjunctam, atq; sic habet eam aliquo modo; sed causæ hæ æstimantur quæq; EX VIRTUTE SIBI CONNATURALI ET PROPRIA, quàm ex se & per se habent. Quam enim causa aliqua ab alio principali agente sibi impertitam sive communicatam habet, ea non tam ipsius, quàm alterius superioris agentis virtus est, & influxus, quem vi illius in effectum præbet, non tam ejus, quàm alterius principalis agentis, cujus hæc impertita virtus propria est, influxus est. Quod universaliter de omni causa principali & instrumentali, cùm naturalium, tùm supernaturalium effectuum, procedit. Cujuscunq; causæ virtus agendi connaturalis & propria effectui producendo proportionata, nec inferior sive ignobilior est, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, ea est effectus producti causa principalis; & contrà cujuscunq; causæ virtus agendi connaturalis & propria effectui producendo improportionata & inferior sive ignobilior est, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, ea effectus producti causa instrumentalis est, utut alterius principalis cujusdam agentis virtus non ignobilior, quàm ad effectum eundem producendum requiritur, etiam aliquo modo, nempe dependenter à causa principali & per communicationem ei insit. Nam hic virtutis non ignobilioris influxus non tamen ejus, cui virtus hæc dependenter & per communicationem; quàm illius est causæ, cui eadem per se & independenter inest: v. g. influxus, quem Spiritus Sancti virtus illuminatrix, Verbo communicata, cum Verbo & per illud in illuminationem intellectus humani impertit, non tam VERBI, cui ea dependenter à Spiritu S. & per communicationem inest, quàm Spiritus S. cui per se & independenter inest, influxus est.

Ut rectiùs hæc intelligas, scias velim, instrumenta esse in duplici differentia. Quædam enim causam principalem, etiam extra usum, sibi semper conjunctam habent supposito & virtute: cujusmodi instrumenta sunt membra corporis humani, quæ animæ instrumenta sunt, & animam tanquam causam suorum effectuum principalem sibi semper supposito, ut ita loquar, & virtute conjunctam habent, etiam extra usum. Alia verò cum causa principali conjuncta non sunt, nisi in usu, cujusmodi sunt malleus, securis, calamus scriptorius & id genus alia. Posterioris ordinis instrumenta, ut extra usum causæ principali conjuncta non sunt, ita nec ejus virtutem agendi in se habent, sed accipiunt eam ab illa demùm in usu, cùm ad producendum effectum adhibentur & elevantur: sicut v. g. calamus scriptorius virtutem pingendi literas & scribendi in se non habet, sed eam demùm extrinsecus à Scribæ manu & ductu, ad præscriptum artis scriptoriæ instituto, accipit, & securis in se non habet virtutem movendi se, & scindendi lignum, sed accipit eam extrinsecus à fabro lignario, eam elevante, & vim scindendi lignum suo motu ei imprimente &c. Prioris ordinis instrumenta verò ut causam principalem semper supposito & virtute sibi conjunctam habent, ita & ejus virtutem agendi semper in se habent, nec eam accipiunt demum à causa principali, cùm ad usum adhibentur: cùm eam jam antè in se habeant; elevantur tamen in ipso usu ad producendum effectum, non per novam additam virtutem agendi, quam ante non habuerint, sed per actualem influxum, quem causa principalis per virtutem jam antè ei communicatam, cum illis & per illa præbet: v. g. manus, quæ Aristoteli dicitur ὄργανον ὀργάνων, instrumentum instrumentorum, ut animam semper supposito & virtutute sibi conjunctam habet, ita ejus virtutem motricem etiam extra usum in se habet, nec eam in usu demum accipit: in usu tamen elevatur ab anima ad producendum effectum, non per aliquam virtutem motricem ipsi additam, cùm ejus virtutem motricem jam antè in se habeat; sed per actualem influxum, quem per eandem jam ante ei communicatam virtutem motricem anima cum ea & per illam in effectum præbet. Atq; ad horum inftrumentorum classem pertinet Scriptura sacra, quæ ut semper, etiam extra usum, Spiritum Sanctum supposito & virtute sibi conjunctum habet, ita habet etiam ejus, tanquam causæ principalis, virtutem illuminandi & convertendi semper, etiam extra usum in se. Quia autem eam non ex se & per se, ut sibi naturalem & propriam, sed dependenter à Spiritu S. cui soli connaturalis & propria est, ejusq; liberâ voluntate sibi communicatam habet, ideò ipsa est & manet causa illuminationis, conversionis &c. instrumentalis, hac una de causa, quòd ejus nativa, sive connaturalis & propria virtus, quam ex se independenter habet, ignobilior est, quàm ad illuminandos & convertendos hominum animos requiritur; quam autem à Spiritu Sancto sibi communicatam habet, ea non ipsius, sed Spiritus Sancti connaturalis & propria virtus est, eâq; non tam ipsa, quàm Spiritus Sanctus cum illa, & per illam in hominis illuminationem & conversionem influit. Quod locus Paulinus, ex 1. Cor. III. 6. 7. modò adductus, liquidò evincit. Non nesciebat Apostolus, Verbum Dei habere virtutem illuminandi & convertendi hominum animos in se, dependenter tamen à Spiritu Sancto, & ejus liberâ voluntate sibi communicatam. Dixerat enim in eadem Epistola præced. c. I. 18. 24. Sermonem crucis & prædicationem Christi crucifixi esse iis qui salutem consequuntur, DEI POTENTIAM, & c. II. 4. 5. Verbum Dei, à se prædicatum, esse in ostensione Spiritus ac potentiæ, ut fides Corinthiorum non esset in sapientia hominum, sed IN POTENTIA DEI &c. & tamen dicit, incrementũ suæ prædicationis non esse ab illa (prædicatione) sed A DEO, usq; adeò, ut nec qui per Verbi prædicationem plantat, nec qui per eandem rigat, sit aliquid in ordine ad effectus supernaturales productos, sed DEUS, qui velut causa principalis cum prædicatione concurrit, suoq; actuali influxu INCREMENTUM dat. Non autem hæc rectè à Paulo dicerentur, si per hoc, quod Verbum Dei prædicatum Spiritus Sancti virtutem illuminatricem semper in se sibiq; communicatam habet, ipsum (Verbum Dei) fidei in Corinthiis productæ causa principalis esset, sed contrà dicendum fuisset, se quidem, tanquam Dei ministrum, plantâsse per præ-


### preaching of the Word, and Apollos watered, but that the INCREASE came from the…

preaching of the Word, and Apollos watered, but that the INCREASE came from the very Word preached, and therefore neither he who plants, nor he who waters, is anything, but the Word, from which the INCREASE is. But that he ascribes the production of faith and the conversion of the Corinthians to the preached Word, not as the principal cause, but only as an agent with a virtue more ignoble than is required for producing these effects; and to GOD, AS THE PRINCIPAL AGENT, from whom the increase of the preaching was, is not because the power of God to enlighten and convert was not in the Word preached by him, but because it was not in it by itself and independently, as a virtue connatural and proper to it, but dependently on God and by communication, through which therefore GOD himself, as the principal cause, with the Word and through it, as through an instrument; not the WORD by itself and without God, as the principal agent, kindled faith in the hearts of the Corinthians, and carried out their conversion.

VI. Whence Holy Scripture quite congruously calls the Word of God the instrument and instrumental cause of our illumination and conversion; but GOD the principal cause of the same: since the definition of an instrumental cause fits the former, and the definition of a principal cause fits the latter exactly and precisely, and Paul also in the place already cited, and elsewhere throughout Holy Scripture speaks in this manner concerning God and his Word, written and preached; concerning the former as the principal cause; concerning the latter as the instrumental cause of the aforementioned effects, and our symbolic books and the common usage of speaking, received in the Church at all times, have approved and do approve this same manner of speaking.

From this, however, it by no means follows, nor is it inferred except most ineptly, that the Word of God does not have the power of enlightening and converting always, even outside of use, in itself, provided, however, in the manner declared, namely dependently on God and by communication. For just as there are instruments which always have the principal cause supposed and joined to them in virtue; and by the very fact that they have it supposed and joined to them in virtue, they also always have its power of acting in themselves: so it is not repugnant to be something an instrument properly so called, and yet to have the virtue of the principal cause always, even before and outside of all use in itself. And because the Word of God, both written and preached, is of the census of these, therefore also the Word of God well it can be an instrument and instrumental cause of God in order to the aforementioned supernatural effects to be produced or already produced, so that it nevertheless always has within itself, even outside of use, the power of God to illuminate and convert the souls of men: indeed, by this very fact, that it has God always joined to itself in subject and power, it cannot but always have within itself, even outside of use, the same power to illuminate and convert. It suffices therefore on the part of the divine Word for the definition of an instrument, that it has the power to illuminate and convert not independently from itself, but dependently upon God, and communicated to it by the same, so that God, as the principal cause, may flow into the effect to be produced through it; but His Word, by its own connatural and proper power, while producing a less noble effect, flows in, and both agents jointly produce the effect by one undivided influx.

VII. But as regards the term of medium and intermediate cause, if anyone prefers to use this appellation rather than that of instrument or instrumental cause, his freedom of speech is deservedly left to him, although the term of medium also extends widely and admits of its various acceptations. For a medium is sometimes called generally whatever is interposed between a cause and an effect, even if it has no power of operating, just as, for example, air is called the medium of vision and illumination, which nevertheless contributes nothing efficiently to vision or to illumination. Sometimes, however, that is called a medium which is so interposed between the principal agent and its effect that it also flows into the effect with the principal cause, yet with a less noble power than is required to produce it, and then medium and instrument, likewise intermediate cause and instrumental cause, coincide. Again, those are also called media which are so interposed between the principal agent and its effect that they flow into the effect efficiently with it, and indeed with a power not less noble than is required to produce it, yet in another genus or order of causes; just as, for example, medicine is a medium for restoring health, and it flows into the restoration of health according to the prescription of the Physician, and indeed by its own power, and that not less noble than is required to restore it, but otherwise than the Physician. For the Physician flows into the restoring of health to the sick person by prescribing the medicine, by driving out the disease with a suitable one, and by applying it to the sick person, and he performs this by the power of his art medical; but medicine, applied to the sick, drives away disease and restores health physically, by producing its own proper effect and that by a virtue not less noble. And if anyone should call Scripture a MEDIUM of illumination and conversion, he will indeed avoid the danger of Rathmannian error: for media of this kind have their power of acting always, even outside of all use, in themselves. But he will just as easily avoid it who calls it an INSTRUMENT, always subordinate to the principal cause, namely the Holy Spirit, and joined with it in power. For these instruments also have the power of their principal cause always, even outside of all use, in themselves, as has been shown hitherto. The latter expression, however, seems more convenient than the former for a twofold reason. One, indeed, that the nature of an instrument, always joined with the principal cause, suits Holy Scripture more correctly than the nature of a medium, such as medicine is. For the nature of an INSTRUMENT ALWAYS JOINED WITH THE PRINCIPAL CAUSE consists in this, that it always has in itself the power of its principal cause, even outside of use, yet dependently upon the principal cause, and communicated to it by the same, just as, for example, the motive force which is always present in the hand as the instrument of the soul, is not present in it independently of itself, but dependently upon the soul: which fits Holy Scripture most exactly, since the power of illuminating and converting is no less present in it, just as the motive power of the soul is in the hand, always present, but dependently upon the Holy Spirit and communicated to it by the same. The nature of a MEDIUM, however, such as medicine is, consists in this, that it always has in itself a power of acting, different from the power of acting of the principal cause, and connatural to itself, by which, when applied for working, it could produce the effect by itself alone without the physical influx of the principal cause, just as the power of driving away disease and restoring health which is in medicine is different from the power which is in the Physician as the principal cause, and is in it by itself, and independently of the Physician, by which, when applied to the sick, it can by itself and without the physical influx of the Physician drive away disease and restore health. Which clearly does not fit Holy Scripture. The other, that the inequality of the manner in which the power of illuminating is in Holy Scripture, and likewise in the Holy Spirit; in the former indeed dependently upon the Holy Spirit and through communication; in the latter, however, by itself and independently, is involved in the very appellation of an instrument, always conjoined with the Holy Spirit as with the principal cause, which inequality, however, is not involved in the appellation of a medium (when Holy Scripture is called the medium of illumination): since, as is evident from the example of a medicine, something can be a medium which has its power of acting independently from itself, and that power different from the power of the principal cause, and whoever has called Holy Scripture the medium of illumination and conversion, if he must afterwards declare what that power of Scripture to illuminate and convert is, and how it resides in it, he will not be able to escape in the end from coming down to the distinction between both, which has been inculcated thus far, and saying that God and His Word do indeed concur to produce these effects through one and the same power of illuminating and converting, but in a different way: God indeed as the principal cause; but the Word, to which the same indeed belongs, but dependently upon God and through communication, concurs through the same as an instrumental cause, and therefore the Word of God, written and preached, is not in the exact same way a medium or intermediate cause of illumination and conversion as a medicine is a medium and intermediate cause of restoring health. This our predecessors of blessed memory well observed and weighed, who in the often-praised judgment on the Controversy of Rathmann, in the said place, folio 267, dealt by design with the terms of instrument and instrumental cause, and likewise of medium and intermediate cause; and having pondered the matter more deeply, they arrived at the opinion that neither, when rightly understood, has any inconvenience, and since both have been received in the use of the Church, both can be retained. Their words are as follows: Finally, and for the fourteenth point, some are of the opinion that it is more convenient that Holy Scripture be called a medium or intermediate cause of illumination, conversion, and salvation, rather than an instrument or tool of these internal spiritual effects. And indeed it is the case that Holy Scripture is not merely an instrumentum passivum, such a tool as an axe or the like, which must first be lifted up for that purpose, and the hewing power must be impressed upon it and communicated from the outside when it is to hew, but it is an instrumentum cooperativum, a cooperating instrument, As the living hand and seeing eye in man is a cooperating instrument, which has received its inner power of life and action from the soul, in such wise that the Word is therefore called a living and powerful word, Heb. 4:12; yet it has nevertheless always been customary in the Church of God that one has called God’s Word not only a means or instrumental cause, but also an instrument or tool of illumination, conversion, and salvation; wherefore, as in the Augsburg Confession, Art. 5, the word instrument is used in the Latin exemplar, the word means has been set in its place in the German exemplar: Ut hanc fidem consequamur, institutum est ministerium docendi Evangelium & porrigendi Sacramenta. Nam per Verbum & Sacramenta, tanquam per instrumenta donatur Spiritus Sanctus. Through the Gospel and the Sacraments, as through means, God gives the Holy Spirit. Selneccerus part. 3. Exam. p. 215. There is only one efficient (principal) cause of conversion, which works and is efficacious through the Word, as through an instrument and medium. If one wishes to say that Holy Scripture is a means of conversion, one must understand it as a medium not only by reason of presence, but also of efficacy, of an acting medium or instrumental cause. If one wishes to say that Holy Scripture is the instrument of conversion, through which the Holy Spirit works the same in us, one must understand it not de instrumento passivo, of a lifeless and powerless one, but as an activo instrumento, of a living and powerful instrument.

Latin:

dicationem Verbi, & Apollo rigâsse, sed INCREMENTUM tulisse ex ipso VERBO prædicato, & proinde non eum qui plantat, nec eum qui rigat, esse aliquid, sed VERBUM, ex quo INCREMENTUM est. Quod autem productionem fidei & conversionem Corinthiorum VERBO prædicato, non ut causæ principali, sed tantùm ut agenti virtute ignobiliori, quàm ad producendos hosce effectus requiritur; DEO autem, UT AGENTI PRINCIPALI, à quo prædicationis incrementum fuerit, adscribit, causa non est, quòd in Verbo ab ipso prædicato Dei virtus illuminandi & convertendi non fuerit, sed quòd non per se & independenter, ut virtus ei connaturalis & propria, in eo fuerit, sed dependenter à Deo & per communicationem, per quam proinde DEUS ipse, ut causa principalis, cum Verbo & per illud, tanquam per instrumentum; non VERBUM à se & absq; Deo, ut principale agens, fidem in Corinthiorum cordibus accenderit, & illorum conversionem pergerit.

VI. Unde satis congruè Scriptura Sacra & Verbum Dei instrumentum & causa instrumentalis nostræ illuminationis & conversionis; DEUS autem ejusdem causa principalis dicitur: cùm illi definitio causæ instrumentalis; huic verò principalis causæ definitio exafse & ad amussim conveniat, & Paulus etiam loco jam citato, & alibi passim Scriptura sacra hunc in modum de Deo ejusque Verbo, scripto & prædicato; de illo ut de causa principali; de hoc ut de causa instrumentali prædictorum effectuum loquatur, & eundem modum loquendi etiam nostri libri symbolici & communis usus loquendi, in Ecclesia omni tempore receptus, comprobaverit & comprobet.

Ex hoc autem minimè sequitur, nec nisi ineptissimè infertur, Verbum Dei non habere virtutem illuminandi & convertendi semper, etiam extra usum, in se, modo tamen declarato, dependenter scilicet à Deo & per communicationem. Quemadmodùm enim dantur instrumenta, quæ causam principalem semper supposito & virtute sibi conjunctam habent; & eo ipso, quod illam supposito & virtute sibi conjunctam habent, etiam illius virtutem agendi semper in se habent: ita non repugnat, esse aliquid instrumentum propriè dictum, & tamen habere virtutem causæ principalis semper, etiam ante & extra omnem usum in se. Et quia horum ex censu Verbum Dei, cùm scriptum, tùm prædicatum, est, ideò & Verbum Dei benè potest esse instrumentum & causa instrumentalis Dei in ordine ad prædictos supernaturales effectus producendos aut productos, ut tamen Dei virtutem illuminandi convertendíq; hominum animos semper, etiam extra usum, in se habeat: imò hoc ipso, quòd Deum supposito & virtute sibi semper conjunctum habet, non potest non ejusdem virtutem illuminandi & convertendi semper, etiam extra usum, in se habere. Sufficit ergo ex parte Verbi divini ad rationem instrumenti, quòd virtutem illuminandi & convertendi non à se in-dependenter, sed dependenter à Deo, & ab eodem sibi communicatam habet, ita ut in effectum producendum per illam Deus, tanquam causa principalis; Verbum ejus autem suâ connaturali & propriâ virtute, producendo effectu ignobiliori, in fluat, & utrumque agens junctim uno indiviso influxu effectum producat.

VII. Quod autem ad terminum medii & causæ intermediæ attinet, si quis malit hoc, quàm instrumenti aut causæ instrumentalis, appellatione uti, ei meritò sua relinquitur loquendi libertas, quanquam & medii terminus latè patet, & suas diversas acceptiones admittit. Dicitur enim interdum medium generaliter, quicquid inter causam & effectum interponitur, licet virtutem operandi nullam habeat, sicut v. g. visionis & illuminationis medium aër dicitur, qui tamen nec ad visionem nec ad illuminationem quicquam efficienter confert. Interdum verò medium dicitur, quod ita inter agens principale & ejus effectum interponitur, ut & ipsum cum causa principali in effectum in fluat, virtute tamen ignobiliori, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, & tum medium & instrumentum, causa item intermedia & causa instrumentalis coincidunt. Rursum dicuntur etiam media, quæ ita inter agens principale & ejus effectum interponuntur, ut cum eo efficienter in effectum influant, & quidem virtute non ignobiliori, quàm ad eum producendum requiritur, in alio tamen genere vel ordine causarum; sicut v. g. medicamentum est medium reparandæ sanitatis, idq; in fluit ad præscriptum Medici in reparandam sanitatem, & quidem virtute propriâ, eâq; non ignobiliori, quam ad eam reparandam requiritur, sed aliter, quàm Medicus. Medicus enim influit in reparandam ægro sanitatem præscribendo medicamentum, pellendo morbo idoneum, & ægroto illud applicando, idq; præstat vi artis Medicæ; sed medicamentum, ægroto applicatum, pellit morbum, & reparat sanitatem physicè, suâ propriâ eaq́; producendo effectu non ignobiliori virtute. Et si sic Scripturam illuminationis & conversionis MEDIUM quis dixerit, is periculum erroris Rathmanniani quidem vitabit: hujusmodi media enim habent suam virtutem agendi semper, etiam extra omnem usum, in se. Sed id æquè facilè vitabit, qui eandem INSTRUMENTUM, causæ principali, Spritui Sancto scilicet, semper supposito & virtute conjunctum dixerit. Nam hæc etiam instrumenta habent virtutem suæ causæ principalis semper, etiam extra omnem usum, in se, ut hactenus ostensum. Posterior autem locutio duplici de causa videtur priori convenientior esse. Unâ quidem, quòd ratio instrumenti, cum causa principali semper conjuncti, Scripturæ sacræ rectiùs, quàm ratio, medii, quale medicamentum est, convenit. Nam ratio INSTRUMENTI CUM CAUSA principali semper conjuncti, consistit in hoc, quòd virtutem suæ causæ principalis, etiam extra usum, semper in se habet, dependenter tamen à causa principali, & ab eodem sibi communicatam, sicut v. g. vis motrix, quæ manui velut instrumento animæ semper inest, non inest ei à se independenter, sed dependenter ab anima: quod exactissimè in Scripturam sacram quadrat, quippe cui virtus illuminandi & convertendi non minùs, quàm manui animæ motrix virtus, semper inest, sed dependenter à Spiritu Sancto & ab eodem illi communicata. Ratio MEDII autem, quale medicamentum est, consistit in hoc, quod virtutem agendi, à virtute agendi causæ principalis diversam, eamq́; sibi connaturalem in se semper habet, quâ ad operandum applicatum, citra physicum causæ principalis influxum per se solum producere effectum possit, sicut quæ medicamento inest virtus pellendi morbum & reparandi sanitatem à virtute, quæ Medico velut causæ principali inest, diversa est, eiq́; per se, & independenter à Medico inest, quâ ægroto applicatum per se & citra physicum Medici influxum morbum pellere & sanitatem reparare potest. Quod in Scripturam sacram planè non quadrat. Alterâ, quòd inæqualitas modi, quo virtus illuminandi Scripturæ sacræ; quo item Spiritui Sancto inest, illi quidem dependenter à Spiritu Sancto & per communicationem; huic verò per se & independenter, in ipsa appellatione instrumenti, cum Spiritu Sancto, velut causa principali semper conjuncti, involvitur, quæ inæqualitas tamen in appellatione medii (cùm Scriptura sacra illuminationis medium dicitur) non involvitur: cùm, uti exemplo medicamenti patet, aliquid medium esse possit, quod suam virtutem agendi à se independenter, eamq́; à virtute causæ principalis diversam habet, & qui Scripturam sacram illuminationis & conversionis medium dixerit, is si postea declarare debeat, quænam illa Scripturæ vis illuminandi & convertendi sit, & quomodo ei insit, subterfugere tandem non poterit, quin ad inculcatum hactenus discrimen inter utrumq; agesis deveniat, dicatq́;, Deum & Verbum ipsius concurrere quidem ad producendos hosce effectus per unam & eandem virtutem illuminandi & convertendi, sed modo diverso: Deum quidem ut causam principalem; Verbum verò, cui eadem quidem convenit, sed dependenter à Deo & per communicationem, concurrere per eandem, ut causam instrumentalem, & esse proinde Verbum Dei, scriptum & prædicatum, non eo prorsus modo medium aut causam intermediam illuminationis & conversionis, quo medicamentum reparandæ sanitatis medium & causa intermedia est. Quod probè observârunt & ponderârunt nostri Antecessores beatæ memoriæ, qui in laudatossæpè judicio de Contr. Rathm. d. l. fol. 267. de terminis instrumenti & instrumentalis causæ, itemq́; medii & causæ intermediæ ex instituto egerunt; & re altiùs perpensa in eam descenderunt sententiam, neutros, rectè intellectos, habere aliquid incommodi, & cùm utriq; in Ecclesiæ usu recepti sint, posse utrosq; retineri. Verba illorum habent ita: Endlich und vors vierzehende sind etliche der Meinung/ es sey bequemer / daß die heilige Schrifft ein Mittel / oder Mittel-Ursache der Erleuchtung/ Bekehrung und Seeligmachung/als ein instrument oder Werckzeug derselben innerlichen geistlichen Wirckungen genennet werde. Und zwar ist es an deme/daß die heilige Schrifft nicht bloß dahin ist ein instrumentum passivum, ein solch Werckzeug/wie eine Axt/oder dergleichen/welche erst muß darzu erhoben / und die Hauwings-Krafft ihr imprimirt, und von aussen mitgetheilet werden/ wenn sie hauen soll / sondern es ist ein instrumentum cooperativum, ein mitwirckendes instrument, wie die lebendige Hand / und sehendes Auge am Menschen ein mitwirckendes instrument ist / welches seine innerliche Lebensund WirckungsKrafft von der Seelen mitgetheilet hat / inmassen dannenhero das Wort ein lebendiges und kräfftiges Wort genennet wird / Ebr. 4. v. 12. Aber doch ist es in der Kirchen GOttes bißhero allzeit bräuchlich gewesen / daß man GOttes Wort nicht allein ein Mittel oder MittelUrsach / sondern auch ein instrument oder Werckzeuge der Erleuchtung / Bekehrung und Seeligmachung genennet hat. Darumb als in der Augspurgischen Confession art. 5. das Wort instrument im lateinischen exemplar gebrauchet / ist an desselben Stelle im teutschen exemplar das Wort Mittel gesetzt worden. Ut hanc fidem consequamur, institutum est ministerium docendi Evangelium & porrigendi Sacramenta. Nam per Verbum & Sacramenta, tanquam per instrumenta donatur Spiritus Sanctus. Durchs Evangelium und Sacramenta, als durch Mittel / gibt GOtt den heiligen Geist. Selneccerus part. 3. Exam. p. 215. Una tantùm est causa efficiens (principalis) conversionis, quæ per Verbum, tanquam per instrumentum & medium operatur & efficax est. Wil man sagen / die H. Schrifft sey ein Mittel der Bekehrung / muß mans verstehen de medio non solùm ratione præsentiæ, sed etiam efficaciæ, von einem wirckenden Mittel oder Mittel-Ursache. Wil man sagen / die H. Schrifft sey das Werckzeug der Bekehrung / dadurch der heilige Geist dieselbe bey uns wircket / muß mans verstehen nicht de instrumento passivo, von einem lebund krafftlosen / sondern activo instrumento, von einem lebendigen und kräfftigen Werckzeuge.


### X. Because it is of the nature of an instrumental cause that its native and proper…

X.

Because it is of the nature of an instrumental cause that its native and proper power, by which it influences the effect, should be disproportionate to the effect and less noble than that it could be produced by it alone, and therefore it is necessary that the principal cause should concur at the same time with its more noble power, and by its influx assist and elevate that one to produce the effect; to Holy Scripture, by the very fact that it is the instrumental cause of our illumination and conversion, it is necessary that this same thing also belongs.

This assertion also flows from the immediately preceding points, by which it was shown that the nature of an instrument and an instrumental cause in relation to man's illumination and conversion properly belongs to Holy Scripture, notwithstanding the fact that it always has within itself the power of the Holy Spirit to illuminate and convert, yet dependently upon the Holy Spirit and communicated to it by Him. If, however, it is the instrument and instrumental cause of these effects, it is certainly necessary that its connatural and proper power of acting, by which it influences them along with the power of the Holy Spirit communicated to it, be disproportionate and less noble than is required to produce them, and that it be RAISED by the HOLY SPIRIT to produce the same through its power communicated to it by Him. For in this, as has been said, consists the nature and quiddity of an instrument and an instrumental cause, properly so called, so that whoever, along with Scripture, with our Symbolic books, and with the most accepted usage of speaking in the Church, has called Holy Scripture the instrumental cause of our illumination, conversion, and salvation, and yet has denied that it is raised by the Holy Spirit, as the principal cause of the same, to produce these effects beyond its native power of acting, incurs an open contradiction.

XI.

The instrumental cause is indeed raised by the principal cause beyond its native power of acting through an actual influx, which it provides into the effect with it and through it by its own nobler power, and by which it assists its own native and proper power, which is less noble than the effect being produced, to produce the same.

To raise an instrumental cause beyond its native power, as to the thing itself, is nothing other than to influence the effect simultaneously with it and through it by a nobler power proportionate to the effect being produced, and to assist its power with its own less noble influx, so that the elevation of the instrumental cause only then takes place when it is established in the use and being of a cause, and is actually employed to produce the effect. Whence neither its ELEVATION can be constituted in anything other than the actual INFLUX, which the principal cause, by its own nobler power, provides simultaneously with it into the effect through it, and by which it assists the less noble power of the same for producing the effect.

Latin:

X.

Qvia de ratione causæ instrumentalis est, ut ejus nativa & propria virtus, quâ in effectum influit, effectui improportionata & ignobilior sit, quam ut per eam solam produci possit, & proptereà causam principalem suâ nobiliori virtute simul concurrere, ejusque influxu illam ad producendum effectum adjuvare & elevare oportet; Scripturæ sacræ eo ipso, quòd illuminationis & conversionis nostræ causa instrumentalis est, id ipsum etiam conveniat necesse est.

Fluit hæc etiam assertio ex proximè præcedentibus, quibus ostensum est, Scripturæ sacræ convenire rationem instrumenti & causæ instrumentalis in ordine ad hominis illuminationem & conversionem propriè, non obstante, quòd ipsam Spiritus S. virtutem illuminandi & convertendi semper in se, dependenter tamen à Spiritu S. & ab eo sibi communicatam, habeat. Si autem horum effectuum ea instrumentum & causa instrumentalis est, necesse utiq; est, ut ejus connaturalis & propria virtus agendi, quâ cum Spiritus Sancti virtute sibi communicatâ in eosdem influit, iis improportionata & ignobilior sit, quàm ad eos producendos requiritur, & ut ad eosdem producendos A SPIRITU S. per suam eidem communicatam virtutem ELEVETUR. In hoc enim, uti dictum, consistit ratio & quidditas instrumenti & causæ instrumentalis, propriè sic dictæ, ut qui cum Scriptura, cum nostris libris Symbolicis, & cum usu loquendi in Ecclesia receptissimo Scripturam sacram nostræ illuminationis, conversionis & salvationis causam instrumentalem dixerit, & tamen eam ad producendos hosce effectus ultra suam nativam vim agendi à Spiritu S. velut causâ eorundem principali elevari negaverit, apertam contradictionem incurrat.

XI.

Elevatur verò causa instrumentalis à causa principali ultra suam nativam virtutem agendi per actualem influxum, quem suâ nobiliori virtute cum ea & per eam in effectum præbet, & quo ejusdem nativam & propriam, producendo effectu ignobiliorem, virtutem ad eundem producendum adjuvat.

Elevare causam instrumentalem ultra suam nativam virtutem, quoad rem, nihil aliud est, quàm nobiliori & producendo effectui proportionata virtute cum ea, & per eam simul in effectum influere, ejusq; virtutem ignobiliore suo influxu adjuvare, ut ita elevatio causæ instrumentalis tum demum locum habeat, cùm in usu & esse causæ constituta est, & ad effectum producendum actu adhibetur. Unde nec ejus ELEVATIO in alio constitui potest, quàm in actuali INFLUXU, quem suâ nobiliori virtute causa principalis simul cum illa per illam in effectum præbet, & quo ejusdem virtutem ignobiliorem ad producendum effectum adjuvat.


### XII. But just as instrumental causes vary, and do not bear one and the same relation…

XII.

But just as instrumental causes vary, and do not bear one and the same relation to their principal causes: for some are not joined to their principal causes except in use; others, however, have their principal causes joined to them always, even outside of use, in supposition and in power: so also their elevation varies.

XIII.

Instrumental causes of the former order are elevated by their principal causes to produce their effects EXTRINSICALLY, by the external power of those causes coming upon them from the outside. Instrumental causes of the latter order, however, are elevated by their principal causes to produce their effects INTRINSICALLY, by the power of those causes communicated to them and internal to them.

I. That instruments are of a twofold difference, and that some have their principal causes joined to them always, even outside of all use, in supposition and in power; but others are not joined to their principal causes except in use; and outside of use are separated from them in supposition and in power, has been stated and shown above in thesis IX. Expl. n. V. Which diversity of instruments the Jena theologians also observed and inculcated in Dedek. d. l. fol. 224, where among other things: An axe, they say, is an instrument, NOT JOINED, but SEPARATED; not living, but inanimate; nor does it act by an inherent power, but by one impressed extrinsically, whence it is called, especially from the hypothesis of Rathmann, a passive instrument, although it acts in its own way in use. On the contrary, however, the hand in an animate body is a JOINED instrument, living, acting by an inherent and intrinsic force, whence it is called an active and cooperative instrument. Compare ibid. fol. 272. l. §. Vors neundte. & fol. 269. 2. §. Endtlich und vors neundte &c. II. From this diverse relationship of instruments to their principal causes flows a notable diversity in the mode of ELEVATION. For those things which are not joined to their principal causes except in use, just as they are separated from them outside of use both in subject and in power, and do not have their principal power in themselves, so they cannot be elevated by them, except by their power external to them and coming upon them from the outside: just as, for example, a writing pen cannot be elevated by a Scribe to write, except EXTERNALLY, by his guidance for painting letters according to the art of writing coming upon it from the outside. But those things which always have their principal causes, even outside of use, joined to them in subject and in power, those are elevated by their principal causes INTERNALLY, by their principal power indeed, but communicated to them and inseparably joined: just as, for example, the hand is elevated by the soul, whose instrument it is, to produce its connatural effects, internally, by its motive power inseparably communicated to it and always existing within it. And since Holy Scripture is also of the census of these instruments, and it, as was shown above, has the Holy Spirit as the principal cause of its effects, always joined to it, both in subject and in its power of illuminating and converting, even outside of use, the thing itself speaks, that when established in use it is not elevated by the Holy Spirit EXTERNALLY, like an axe, a saw, a pen, etc. when established in use are elevated: but INTERNALLY, by the Holy Spirit's power of illuminating and converting communicated to it, and existing within it through communication.

Someone might ask: What need is there for Holy Scripture to be elevated by the Holy Spirit to illuminate and convert the souls of men, if it always has within itself His power of illuminating and converting, communicated to it? For to what good does it have it, unless it operates through it, without the concurrence of another superior agent, and illuminates and converts men? But to this objection the answer was shown above in thesis IX, and it was shown that for something to act by itself and without the concurrence of another principal agent, it is not sufficient that it have the power of the principal agent in itself in any way, but it is required that it have it in itself by itself independently and as a power connatural and proper to itself. Holy Scripture, however, does not have the Holy Spirit's power of illuminating and converting in itself by itself and independently, but from Him to itself communicated, as has been said more often. And because this power of the Holy Spirit to illuminate and convert, as regards the thing itself, is His very essence, therefore Holy Scripture always has the Holy Spirit Himself conjoined with His power, so that whenever it is established in use and exerts its power of illuminating and converting in the hearts of men, the Holy Spirit, with that same power communicated to it, concurs with it as the principal cause, and provides His own influx together with it and through it into the effect, and thus one and the same effect depends upon the one undivided influx of both, but in an unequal manner: and indeed from the influx of the Holy Spirit as the principal cause; but from the influx of Scripture as the instrumental cause, and one dependent upon the Holy Spirit in acting. Scripture attributes to the Word of God the power and virtue of illuminating, converting, and regenerating men in many places, but not in such a way that it is an essential and constitutive part of the Word that it produces those effects WITHOUT THE OPERATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, as the Wittenberg theologians wisely write in Dedekennus, loc. cit., fol. 269. 2. §. Was Rostius &c. And again: How could the WORD produce any effects WITHOUT THE OPERATION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT? Likewise: The power and potency itself is not so innate and essential to the Word that it resides in the Word even WITHOUT THE HOLY SPIRIT, AND OPERATES THROUGH IT. In the same place, that the Holy Spirit indeed flows in together in act into the illumination and conversion of man with Scripture, by His power of illuminating and converting communicated to it, and assists it with the influx of His own nobler power to produce these effects, which are nobler than its own native and proper power, what is this other than to ELEVATE it to produce these effects?

And this was the source and origin of the error of Rathmann and Movius, that they reckoned Holy Scripture among those instruments which are not joined to their principal causes except in use. Once this was admitted, it certainly had to be admitted further that Holy Scripture in itself and outside of use has no power of illuminating and converting, but is a dead letter, and like an axe lying under a bench, which in itself has no motive force; but in use is elevated extrinsically, by the external power of the Holy Spirit coming upon it. Concerning which matter our blessed predecessors thus state in the often-cited judgment concerning this controversy, d. l. fol. 226. l. §. 16: In the eleventh place, they say, Rathman teaches that the revealed written Word of God does not have within itself an inner power of illumination and conversion, but that the same is only added to it from without by the Holy Spirit in its use, and they allege to this effect from Rathman's book, 'Constant Doctrine of the Fathers,' page 105, these words of his: 'But that you pretend that the Word brings itself into the heart, that it is no kind or sword that is raised by the power of the Spirit, but that the power is already inside, that the Holy Spirit can never be separated from the Word, to this I give you as an answer that you hereby publicly contradict the Scripture,' etc. More is adduced in the same place from his other writings, where it can be read. They report similar things about the same man and Movius, fol. 268. 2. §. 3. As far as this side-question is concerned, Rathman repeats often in his writings that God's Word, outside of its use, has no inner power of illumination, conversion, and salvation in and with itself, etc., and after his words are alleged, they add: 'Similar things writes Movius in his Confession, cap. 7, p. 32, cap. 8, p. 38: God's Word does not have the life-power with it outside of its use,' etc. And ibid. §. 4: 'Yes, Movius has no hesitation in his defense, cap. 1, p. 1, to write thus: That God's Word does not have the life-power with it outside of the right use, all orthodox theologians teach, for my part.' And fol. 272, they write: 'For the ninth, the Word of God is not an instrumentum passivum, a passive and receiving tool, which is only raised to power and effect in its use, like an axe is raised by one who wants to hew with it, and the hewing-power is added and joined to it from without, as Rathman and Movius always aim at, but it is a living and powerful Word, and therefore an instrumentum activum & cooperativum, a powerful co-working tool, like the hand or eye of a living person; therefore it also has its inner life- and light-power with it before its use, which is not first added and joined to it from without in its use.' And this is the very reason why one should not deny that the Word also has its inner power in and with itself outside of its use, namely, so that one does not, with Rathman and Movius, make the Word of God into a passive instrument; just as Movius, when he said: That the Word of God has no internal power outside of use, finally arrives at the point where he writes in his defense H. III. f. 1. it is by no means absurd, when one says: That the grace-light of the Holy Spirit or the enlightening power comes to the Word from the outside.

Now Caspar Movius was, as I note here in passing, a Minister of the Church of Kaunas in Lithuania, who in most things blew the same horn as Rathmann, and, as his words, cited by the praised Theologians, teach, he denied with him that Holy Scripture has, outside of use, the power of the Holy Spirit to enlighten and convert communicated in and to itself, through which the Word always becomes living and efficacious: and on the contrary he asserted with him that the power of the Holy Spirit to enlighten and convert is joined with Holy Scripture only in use, and is raised by it to enlighten and convert the souls of men EXTRINSICALLY, just as the axe of a carpenter is raised by the external motive power in use to cut wood, and that outside of use Holy Scripture is as separated from and devoid of the power of the Holy Spirit to enlighten and convert, as an axe is separated from and devoid of the motive power of the carpenter outside of use. Whatever more could be brought forward here and discussed for the benefit of students concerning the errors of Rathmann, Movius, and likewise Schvvenckfeld and other Fanatics regarding the doctrine of the efficacy of Holy Scripture, we relegate to the Commonplace on the Word of Law and Gospel, as the organic or instrumental cause of kindling faith and effecting conversion. And so much for this time.

Latin:

XII.

PRout autem causæ instrumentales variant, nec unam & eandem ad suas causas principales habitudinem important: Quædam enim suis causis principalibus non conjunguntur, nisi in usu; alia verò habent suas causas principales sibi semper, etiam extra usum, supposito & virtute conjunctas: ita & illarum elevatio variat.

XIII.

PRioris ordinis causæ instrumentales elevantur à suis causis principalibus ad producendos suos effectus EXTRINSECUS, virtute illarum externâ ipsis extrinsecus superveniente. Posterioris verò ordinis causæ instrumentales elevantur à suis causis principalibus ad producendos suos effectus INTRINSECUS, virtute illarum ipsis communicatâ, eisque internâ.

I. Instrumenta esse in duplici differentiâ, & quædam habere suas principales causas sibi semper, etiam extra omnem usum, supposito & virtute conjunctas; alia verò suis causis principalibus non conjungi, nisi in usu; extra usum verò esse ab illis supposito & virtute separatas, dictum ostenfumŅ; est supra in thes. IX. Expl. n. V. Quam instrumentorum diversitatem observarent & inculcarunt etiam Theologi Jenenses apud Dedek. d. l. fol. 224. ubi inter alia: Securis, inquiunt, est instrumentum, NON CONJUNCTUM, sed SEPARATUM; non vivum, sed inanime; nec agit virtute insitâ, sed extrinsecus impressâ, unde vocatur, ex hypothesi præsertim Rathmanni, instrumentum passivum, quamvis suo modo in usu agat. Contra verò manus in corpore animato est instrumentum CONJUNCTUM, vivum, insitâ & intrinsecâ vi agens, unde vocatur instrumentum activum & cooperativum. Confer ibid. fol. 272. l. §. Vors neundte. & fol. 269. 2. §. Endtlich und vors neundte &c. II. Ex hac instrumentorum diversa habitudine ad suas causas principales notabilis fluit diversitas in modo ELEVATIONIS. Nam quæ suis principalibus causis non conjunguntur, nisi in usu, ea ut extra usum ab illis supposito & virtute separata sunt, illarumq́; virtutem principalem non in se habent, ita ab illis elevari non possunt, nisi illarum virtute sibi externa, & extrinsecùs superveniente: sicut v. g. calamus scriptorius ad scribendum à Scriba elevari non potest, nisi EXTRINSECUS, ejus ductu ad pingendas literas juxta artem scriptoriam extrinsecùs ei superveniente. Quæ autem suas causas principales semper, etiam extra usum, supposito & virtute sibi conjunctas habent, illa elevantur à suis causis principalibus INTRINSECUS, illarum virtute principali quidem, sed sibi communicatâ, & inseparabiliter conjunctâ: sicut v. g. manus ad suos effectus connaturaliter producendos elevatur ab anima, cujus instrumentum est, intrinsecus, virtute ejus motrice ipsi inseparabiliter communicatâ, eiq; semper inexistente. Et cum horum instrumentorum ex censu etiam Scriptura sacra sit, eaq́;, ut suprà ostensum, Spiritum S. velut causam suorum effectuum principalem, sibi semper, cùm supposito, tum suâ virtute illuminandi & convertendi, etiam extra usum, conjunctum habeat, res ipsa loquitur, quòd in usu constituta à Spiritu S. non elevetur EXTRINSECUS, ut securis, serra, calamus &c. in usu constituta elevantur: sed INTRINSECUS, Spiritus Sancti virtute illuminandi & convertendi sibi communicatâ, & per communicationem sibi inexistente.

Inquiat quis: Quid opus est Scripturam sacram à Spiritu Sancto ad illuminandos & convertendos hominum animos elevari, si ipsam ejus virtutem illuminandi & convertendi, sibi communicatam, semper in se habet? Cui bono enim eam habet, nisi ut per illam, sine alterius superioris agentis concursu, operetur, hominesq́; illuminet & convertat? Sed ad objectionem hanc responsum supra thes. IX. ostensumq́; est, ut aliquid per se & citra alterius agentis principalis concursum agat, non sufficere, quod virtutem principalis agentis quocunq; modo in se habeat, sed requiri, ut eam per se independenter & ut virtutem sibi connaturalem ac propriam in se habeat. Scriptura sacra autem non habet Spiritus Sancti virtutem illuminandi & convertendi per se & independenter in se, sed ab eadem sibi communicatam, ut saepius dictum. Et quia haec Spiritus S. virtus illuminandi & convertendi, quoad rem est ipsa ejus essentia, ideo & ipsum Spiritum Sanctum Scriptura sacra cum ejus virtute semper sibi conjunctum habet, ut quandocunq; in usu constituta suam virtutem illuminandi & convertendi in hominum cordibus exerit, Spiritus S. eâdem, ei communicatâ, virtute velut causa principalis cum illa concurrat, suumq; influxum simul cum illa & per illam in effectum praebeata, atq; sic unus idemq; effectus ab uno utriusq; indiviso influxu dependeat, sed modo inaequali: & ab influxu Spiritus S. quidem velut causae principalis; ab influxu Scripturae verò, ut causae instrumentalis, & à Spiritu S. in agendo dependentis. Verbo Dei potentiam & virtutem illuminandi, convertendi & regenerandi homines multis in locis tribuit Scriptura, sed non ita, quòd ea sit pars essentialis & constitutiva Verbi, quòd illos effectus producat CITRA SPIRITUS SANCTI OPERATIONEM, scitè scribunt Theologi Witebergenses apud Dedekennum d. l. fol. 269. 2. §. Was Rostius &c. Et rursum: Quomodo SINE SPIRITUS S. OPERATIONE effectus ullos producat VERBUM? Item: Ipsa virtus & potentia non est ita Verbo congenita & essentialis, ut etiam ABSQUE SPIRITU SANCTO VERBO INSIT, AC PER ILLUD OPERETUR.
